0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
Acts is not primarily a history of the early church — it is the history of the risen Christ continuing his work through the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke begins with a deliberate hinge: the “first book” (his Gospel) recorded all that Jesus “began to do and teach.” The operative word is began. What follows in Acts is what Jesus continued — not in the flesh now, but in the power of the Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses.

Luke wrote for Theophilus, likely a Roman official being catechised in the faith. But the scope of the narrative exceeds any single reader. Luke traces the gospel’s movement along the spine of the Roman Empire — Jerusalem to Rome, Jewish synagogue to Gentile household, from a frightened upper room to Caesar’s capital. This is not accident; it is Providence. The same God who told Abraham “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” is the God who compels a tentmaker from Tarsus to stand in the Areopagus and announce that the Unknown God has a name.

The Holy Spirit is the true protagonist of Acts. He falls at Pentecost like a sovereign flame. He speaks through Philip on a desert road. He stops Paul from entering Asia. He binds Paul to go to Jerusalem though chains await. He is not a vague presence but a Person with a will — the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the risen Son at the command of the Father, to accomplish the Father’s eternal purpose: a people for his name drawn from every tongue and tribe and nation.

Reformed readers will find in Acts not an argument for the faith but something far more bracing: the sovereignty of God in mission. The gates of hell do not hold. Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment opens courts to preach. Shipwreck lands an apostle on the right island. Nothing is accidental; everything is appointed. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” The final words are without hindrance. The empire could chain the man but not the Word.

Who wrote Acts, and when? The same author as Luke’s Gospel: both are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts begins by referring back to the first book (1:1). In several passages the story shifts to “we” (16:10–17; 20:5–28:16), so the writer travelled with Paul, and the early church agreed that he was Luke, the beloved physician (Col 4:14; cf. Philem 24; 2 Tim 4:11). Some date Acts in the 80s. The more likely date is the early 60s: the book ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome after two years (28:30), and says nothing of his death, Nero’s persecution or the fall of Jerusalem, events Luke could hardly have left out had they already happened.

Should churches copy everything in Acts? Acts is history, the record of what God did as the church was founded. What it describes is not automatically a command. A pattern binds us when the rest of the New Testament teaches it, or when Luke shows it as God’s settled way: preaching Christ, baptizing believers, appointing elders, devotion to the apostles’ teaching and prayer. But the casting of lots (1:26), the sharing of all property (4:32), and the signs that marked the apostles (2:43; 5:12) belonged to that unrepeatable time.

Read Acts with your eyes open to the God who is always working — in the upper room, in the council chambers, in the storm, in the jail at midnight. He is the same God today.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
Acts is the second volume of Luke’s work, written for the same Theophilus as his Gospel. The Gospel told what Jesus “began” to do and teach; Acts tells what the risen Jesus goes on doing by his Spirit through his church, as the gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Rome in about thirty years. Chapter 1 is the hinge between the two volumes. For forty days the risen Jesus shows himself alive and teaches about the kingdom. He tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised baptism with the Holy Spirit. When they ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers that the timing is the Father’s business; their business is to receive power and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth, a sentence that maps out the whole book. Then he is taken up into heaven, and angels promise he will return in the same way.

The second half of the chapter shows the church waiting: about a hundred and twenty believers, including Jesus’ mother and his once-sceptical brothers, praying together in an upper room. Peter explains from the Psalms that Judas’s betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture and that his place must be filled, so that the Twelve, symbolising the renewed Israel, are complete before the Spirit comes. Two men who had been with Jesus from the beginning and witnessed the resurrection are nominated, the church prays, lots are cast, and Matthias is added to the apostles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke reminds Theophilus that his first book covered all that Jesus began to do and teach until he was taken up, after giving instructions through the Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. After his suffering Jesus gave them many convincing proofs that he was alive, appearing over forty days and speaking about God’s kingdom. While eating with them he told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the Father’s promised gift: John baptised with water, but in a few days they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit. When they asked whether he was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel, he said it was not for them to know the times the Father has set, but they would receive power when the Spirit came on them, and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he was taken up before their eyes and a cloud hid him. As they stared into the sky, two men in white told them that this same Jesus would come back in the same way they had seen him go.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but the exaltation of Jesus. He who died and rose now reigns at the right hand of the Father (Psalm 110:1), exercising all authority in heaven and on earth. The church does not act in the absence of its king; it acts under the authority of its enthroned king. The cloud that received him is the glory-cloud of the Old Testament, and Daniel had already described the scene from the other side: one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, to receive a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13-14). The Reformed churches have insisted that the ascension is essential to the gospel and not an epilogue to it: without it Christ does not send the Spirit (John 16:7), does not intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and does not carry our nature into the presence of God, where it now permanently is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Eleven men were given a promise with no date, a mission far beyond their means, and an order to stay put until God moved. They obeyed the hardest part first, which was the waiting.

Now: The church lives in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that brings him back. The temptations at either end are unchanged: to stand looking into heaven, absorbed in timetables the Father reserved to himself, or to rush at the work in a strength that was never promised. The command is the same as it was on the hillside — receive, and then witness.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.

Meaning first. Acts is the second volume of Luke’s two-part work. The Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what he continued to do and teach, from heaven, by the Holy Spirit, through his apostles. It covers about thirty years, from the ascension (around AD 30) to Paul under house arrest in Rome (around AD 62). It is the story of how the gospel went from Jerusalem to Rome, from a handful of Jewish disciples to churches across the empire, and how God kept his promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring. Its hero is not Peter or Paul but the risen Lord, working by his Spirit.

In the first book, O Theophilus. “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus (Luke 1:1–4). His name means friend of God. Ancient books were usually dedicated to a patron, who paid for the copying, and Luke puts the same name at the head of both volumes. In the Gospel he calls him most excellent Theophilus (Luke 1:3), and that is not a courtesy Luke scatters about: the only other men in his writing who receive it are the Roman governors Felix and Festus (23:26; 26:25). So Theophilus was in all likelihood a real man of rank, perhaps a Roman official, with the means to underwrite a work this long and the standing to be addressed like a magistrate. Here, at the head of the second volume, the honorific has quietly gone. He is simply Theophilus. That proves nothing on its own, but it reads like a friendship that has moved indoors. And the man writing is Luke the doctor, Paul’s travelling companion (Colossians 4:14), who will slip into the story himself in chapter 16 with a quiet change from “they” to “we”.

All that Jesus began to do and teach. Then comes the sentence that gives the whole book its shape. Began. A man summarising a completed biography does not reach for that verb. He reaches for it because he does not think the story finished at the tomb, or at the cloud. Volume one was the beginning of the works and words of Jesus; volume two is their continuation, and it is still Jesus doing them. Read on and Luke will say it in so many words. It is the Lord who adds to the church day by day (2:47). It is Jesus who pours out the Spirit (2:33). It is Jesus who asks why do you persecute me, when the people actually being hunted are Christians in Damascus (9:4–5). It is the Spirit of Jesus who closes the road into Bithynia (16:7), and the Lord who opens Lydia’s heart while Paul is talking by a river (16:14). The apostles are the instruments. The agent has not changed.

A book with no last page. Notice, too, how this book ends, or rather how it does not. Paul is in a rented house in Rome, preaching to whoever comes up the stairs, and Luke simply stops. No verdict, no execution, no farewell, not even a closing benediction. Of the many theories offered for the abruptness, the simplest is that a book about what Jesus continues to do has no natural last page, because the work has not stopped. If you want to know what the risen Christ is occupied with this morning, the title of this book is the answer.

Until the day when he was taken up. The ascension is the hinge between the two books. Luke’s Gospel ends with it (Luke 24:50–51) and Acts begins with it, so that the same event is told twice, once as the close of the earthly ministry and once as the launch of the heavenly one. What looks like an ending from the ground is, from the throne, a beginning.

After he had given commands through the Holy Spirit. One clause here is easy to read straight past. The risen Son, standing in a resurrection body, with all authority in heaven and on earth already granted him, still speaks and acts by the Spirit. His whole ministry had been carried out in that power: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, he read in Nazareth (Luke 4:18). Whatever else that means, it means the Spirit who is about to fall at Pentecost is not a replacement brought in to cover an absence. He is the same Spirit by whom Jesus was conceived, at whose descent he was anointed at the Jordan, in whose power he drove out demons, and by whom he now issues his last orders. The church is not handed a substitute for Christ. It is given the Spirit of Christ, and therefore Christ.

To the apostles whom he had chosen. They did not apply. He chose them, after a night of prayer on a mountain (Luke 6:12–13), and their authority in the rest of this book is never their own. Everything they will say with such boldness rests on the fact that they were picked and sent.

Did Luke contradict himself about the ascension? Luke’s Gospel appears to run from the empty tomb to the ascension in one unbroken stretch, so that a reader closes Luke 24 with the impression that Jesus went up on Easter evening, while Acts 1 says forty days. But it is the same man writing, with his own first volume at his elbow, quoting its opening line in his second sentence. He is not correcting himself; he is filling in. Luke 24 names events in order without dating them, which is what compressed endings do in every language: the close of a scroll contracts and the opening of the sequel expands. If the two accounts genuinely cancelled each other, the author would have to have forgotten his own ending within a paragraph of citing it.

So how is Jesus still working today? He works chiefly where he promised to: through the gospel preached and believed, through his Spirit giving new birth, through the Scriptures read and obeyed, through prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and through ordinary believers caring for one another. That sounds less dramatic than Acts, but it is the same Lord doing the same work. When a hardened man is converted, when a believer endures grief without letting go of God, when a small church keeps preaching Christ for decades, Jesus is acting from heaven. He does not need you to detect a sensation before you may believe he is at work. His promise is enough: I am with you always (Matthew 28:20).

In a sentence. Luke told Theophilus that his first book covered all Jesus began to do and teach until the day he was taken up, after giving instructions through the Spirit to his chosen apostles.

On a Tuesday. Read the news of the day, or the state of your own church, and ask the question this verse forces: who is the main actor here? If the answer in your head is always some human being, a government, a pastor, yourself, then the word began has not yet reached you. The book you are about to read is about what the risen Christ does. That changes how you pray for a struggling congregation, how you speak of a friend who seems far from God, and how you think about the things you were too weak to do this week. You are not the hero of the story you are in.

For worship. The hands that touched a leper in Galilee were not folded in retirement when the cloud received them. The same Jesus who stood over a paralysed man let down through a roof and said, your sins are forgiven (Luke 5:20), says it still from the throne, every time a sinner believes, and each of those pardons is as truly his own deed as the healing in that crowded house. He began, and he has not stopped. He began, and he will finish, and the last page of his work will be written on the morning he comes back in person to sign it.
verseByVerse.note: “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus. “Began” implies that Acts records what Jesus continued to do through his Spirit and his church.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me;

He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs. Luke chooses a technical word for the evidence. Many proofs renders tekmēria, a term the ancient world used in the law courts and in medicine for the kind of evidence that settles a matter: not a hint pointing somewhere, but a demonstration closing a case. It occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. The man who opened volume one by telling his patron he had investigated everything carefully (Luke 1:3) reaches here for the strongest word available to him, and then says what it consisted of: not one apparition in a dim room, but appearances spread across forty days, to individuals and to crowds, on roads and beside a lake and behind locked doors, with conversation, and with food. Jesus let them touch him and showed them his wounds (Luke 24:39; John 20:27), and Paul could list more than five hundred witnesses, most of them still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:5–8).

Ghosts do not get hungry. That last detail carries more weight than it looks. The margin of most Bibles notes that staying with them in verse 4 may equally be rendered eating with them. Either way the point holds, because Luke has already shown us the risen Jesus asking whether there is anything in the house and eating a piece of broiled fish while they watched (Luke 24:41–43). Visions do not chew. Whatever happened on the third day happened to a body, and the men who are about to be flogged for saying so had eaten breakfast with the evidence.

Appearing to them during forty days. Forty is a number Scripture uses for seasons of preparation before a new stage: Moses forty days on the mountain before the law was given (Exodus 24:18), Elijah forty days on the road to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), Jesus forty days in the wilderness before his ministry began (Luke 4:2). Now forty days of the risen Lord, before the church is sent.

And speaking about the kingdom of God. Then an arresting silence. Forty days of teaching about the kingdom of God, and Luke reproduces not one sentence of it. No transcript, no outline, no lost book. But he does not need to reproduce it, because the rest of the volume is the exposition. Everything the apostles preach from Pentecost onward, that the crucified Nazarene is Lord and Christ, that the promises made to the fathers have landed in him, that the door stands open to Gentiles who were never inside it, is not something they pieced together afterwards in committee. It is what he told them in those six weeks. The theme of his ministry has not changed: God’s reign, which had come in Jesus. Acts ends with Paul in Rome still proclaiming the kingdom of God (28:31). Acts is the transcript, in the only form that finally proves anything: men living on it, and dying on it.

Evidence and surrender. It is worth adding, before anyone builds too much on the word proofs, that evidence and surrender are not the same thing. In this very book men will hear the apostolic testimony, find nothing in it they can refute, and stroll away amused (17:32). Others will hear it and tremble and still do nothing but postpone (24:25). Good evidence removes an excuse; it does not manufacture a will. So the honest thing to say to a friend who insists he would believe if only the case were stronger is that the case is already stronger than he thinks, and that the obstacle has probably never been in the case at all.

He ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father. And then the order, which is the strangest element in the paragraph. A man with a message that is going to remake the world tells eleven of them to go nowhere. Not to plan, not to organise, not to begin: to wait. That is the command that costs a willing person more than any other, because it looks exactly like doing nothing, and it spends the one asset a new movement has, which is momentum. But the promise had to arrive before the mission did. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, promised through the prophets (Joel 2:28) and by Jesus himself (Luke 24:49; John 14:16–17). They must not begin their mission in their own strength.

Why Jerusalem. And notice where he made them wait. The city where they had failed, where they had run for the dark, where Peter had sworn in a courtyard that he had never met the man. To send them out from there in their own strength would have been cruelty wearing the clothes of a commission. He kept them still until what they needed was inside them, and then he sent them out from the very place of their shame, so that the first sermon of the church would be preached within sight of the spot where its preacher had collapsed.

If the resurrection is so well proved, why do I still have doubts? Because doubt is not only a matter of evidence. Fear, grief, tiredness, temperament and the pressure of a world that assumes the dead stay dead all press on a believer’s mind. Even some who saw the risen Jesus doubted at first (Matthew 28:17; Luke 24:41), and he did not throw them out; he showed them his hands and ate in front of them. So when doubt comes, do not pretend it is not there, and do not treat it as proof that you have no faith. Go back to the evidence the Spirit has preserved for you, the Gospels and 1 Corinthians 15, and pray with the father in Mark 9:24: I believe; help my unbelief. Faith that has looked at its doubts honestly and is still holding on is not weak faith.

Does this mean I should wait for a feeling before I serve God? No. The waiting in this verse was unique. The Spirit had not yet been poured out, and the apostles were told to stay put until a once-for-all event in history arrived. That event has happened. Every believer now has the Spirit (Romans 8:9), and nobody needs to wait for an experience before obeying a clear command, such as loving a neighbour, confessing sin or telling a friend about Christ. What does carry over is the posture: dependence before activity. Pray before you plan. Ask God for help before you start the thing you think you can manage on your own, because the work of God is never done in human strength.

In a sentence. After his suffering Jesus showed himself alive to them with many convincing proofs, appearing over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God, and told them to stay in Jerusalem and wait for the Father’s promise, which they had heard from him.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection is not wishful thinking; it is backed by many proofs, and you are allowed to lean your whole weight on it. So the next time a friend tells you that people in the ancient world believed anything, you can tell them about a careful doctor who used a lawyer’s word and named his witnesses. And the next time you are about to begin something for God in a rush of energy, notice the order of this verse: promise first, then mission. Stop and pray first. The church that waited ten days in an upper room got more done in the following ten years than any committee since.

For worship. The Lord of glory spent his first six weeks of resurrection life eating fish with fishermen, letting doubters touch his scars, and teaching slow men about his kingdom. He did not hurry them. He did not send them out broken. He held them in the city of their failure until the Father’s promise came down on them, and he will be no less patient with you. The one who conquered death has hands you could touch and a table he still invites people to.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls other periods of preparation in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.

For John baptized with water. John the Baptist had drawn this contrast himself, standing in the Jordan with the water running off his hands: I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, and he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). John’s baptism was outward, a sign of repentance. Now the mightier one stands on the far side of an empty tomb and says the promise is days away. Water was the picture; the Spirit is the thing pictured. Water goes over a man. The Spirit goes into him.

But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. The word baptizō means to immerse, to plunge, to drench. They are about to be plunged into the life of God himself, overwhelmed by the Spirit as a man is overwhelmed by water.

Not many days from now. It turns out to mean ten, and they did not know that. They knew only that it was near. This is very often the shape of Christian waiting: a promise that is certain, a nearness that is real, and a date that is withheld. They could only stay where they had been put and keep asking. Ten days is long enough for a man to wonder whether he misheard.

The one who holds the Spirit. Notice who does the baptising. John, the greatest prophet born of women, could pour a river over a man; he could not pour God into him, and he said he was not worthy to untie the sandals of the one who could (Luke 3:16). Only God gives God. In the Old Testament it is always the LORD who promises his own Spirit: I will pour out my Spirit (Joel 2:28); I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:27). Here the risen Jesus speaks of that outpouring as his own appointment, and within ten days Peter will say outright that he has received the Spirit from the Father and poured him out (2:33). The promise of Spirit baptism is a claim of deity made in the passive voice.

Why the phrase is contested. The phrase baptized with the Holy Spirit has become one of the most contested in the New Testament, and a reader deserves to know why. A large and sincere part of the church teaches that this is a second work of grace, distinct from and later than conversion: that a man is born again when he trusts Christ and then, perhaps years afterwards, is baptised in the Spirit and enters power, usually with speaking in tongues as the sign to mark it. The case is built almost entirely from this book, and it is not built out of nothing: in Acts the Spirit does sometimes come visibly and later, and Luke plainly regards those moments as significant.

The four doors. The difficulty is that Acts is narrative, and narrative tells you what happened, not always what must happen. When the letters take up the phrase directly, they define it the other way: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). All, not the advanced; and the effect is membership, not promotion. And the four occasions in Acts where the Spirit comes with visible drama are not four random Christians. They are the four boundary-crossings of the mission: Jews at Pentecost (chapter 2), Samaritans (chapter 8), Gentiles in a Roman officer’s house (chapter 10), and men still living inside John’s baptism who had not heard the story finished (chapter 19). Each is a first. Each has apostles present as witnesses. Luke is not laying down a pattern for private experience; he is recording how the door was opened, one hinge at a time, and how heaven certified it in public so that nobody could later say the wrong people had been let in.

Where Christians differ: Spirit baptism. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching holds that Spirit baptism is a second blessing after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and that every believer should seek it. Verdict: Pentecost was a unique, unrepeatable event in the history of salvation: the Spirit poured out on the church once for all, as the cross and resurrection happened once for all. For believers since, Spirit baptism happens at conversion: all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). We are to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), but there is no second-class Christian waiting for a second baptism. Brothers and sisters who hold the other view love Christ and often shame the rest of us by their prayerfulness and zeal, and the difference should be argued from Scripture with warmth, not contempt.

Two guards. Two guards belong on that. The first is for the believer who has never had an experience he could point to and has begun to suspect he is a second-class Christian. If the Spirit is what makes a man belong to Christ at all (Romans 8:9), then a person who trusts Christ, hates his sin, and loves the brethren has the Spirit, whatever his emotional weather has been. There is no unbaptised remainder in the body of Christ. The second guard runs the other way, against the temptation to answer all this with a shrug. This same book will describe men already filled at Pentecost being filled again in a shaken room (4:31), which means fresh and powerful visitations of God are a thoroughly biblical category and not an embarrassment. To want more of God is right. The label may be wrong; the hunger is not.

Then what does being filled with the Spirit mean? Being baptised with the Spirit is the once-for-all beginning: God joins you to Christ and comes to live in you. Being filled is the ongoing condition of a believer whose life is increasingly yielded to the Spirit’s control, and it can grow and be renewed. Paul’s command is in the present tense, keep on being filled (Ephesians 5:18), and he describes what it looks like: singing to the Lord, giving thanks always, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:19–21). So in practice you seek the Spirit’s fullness by staying close to Scripture, confessing sin quickly, praying, and obeying what you already know. And you may ask: the heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

In a sentence. John baptised with water, but in a few days they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ and have spent years half-believing you missed the real thing, put that fear down. You were plunged into the Spirit when you were joined to Christ, and the evidence is not a single moment but a direction: you trust him, you want to be holy, you love his people. Then do what the Spirit-filled church in Acts did: pray, ask for boldness, open your mouth. Fresh fullness is given along that road, not in a waiting room.

For worship. John could get a man wet and send him home to try harder. What is promised here is God himself, taking up residence in people who a few weeks earlier had scattered like birds. It is a staggering thing that the Holy One should choose such lodgings, and stranger still that he should call it a promise rather than a condescension. The Son who was anointed with the Spirit at the Jordan now pours that same Spirit on the people he died for, so that what rested on him rests on them.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority.

Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? This is the last question the apostles ever put to Jesus on earth, and it is about politics. After three years of teaching, a crucifixion, a resurrection and six weeks of instruction on the kingdom of God, what they want to know is whether the occupation is about to end. Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence, driving out the Romans and re-establishing David’s kingdom; the two on the Emmaus road had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel (Luke 24:21). And notice what they were living in: a foreign garrison in the temple city, a governor who had already executed their master to keep the peace, taxes flowing to a Caesar who took divine titles. Their Scriptures had promised a son of David on a real throne. They were not inventing the expectation. They were asking when the book would come true.

He does not call the question foolish. And Jesus does not tell them the hope is wrong. He has just spent forty days on the kingdom, and he corrects two things only: the timing, and their assumed right to know it.

It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. Two words for time are paired. Times (chronous) are durations, the length of the stretch; seasons (kairous) are the right moments, the appointed occasions. Both are fixed, and both are fixed by the Father by his own authority, a matter kept inside his own jurisdiction. Not unknowable in principle. Not theirs. Jesus had said the same of the day of his return: concerning that day or that hour, no one knows (Mark 13:32). Date-setting for the end is forbidden ground.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and Israel. Dispensationalists read this to mean that a political kingdom will be restored to national Israel in a future millennium, and that Jesus only postponed it. Verdict: Jesus redirects their question from a political kingdom to a worldwide mission: his next sentence begins with but (v. 8). The kingdom is restored to Israel as the Messiah reigns from heaven (2:30–36) and gathers a renewed Israel of Jewish and Gentile believers (15:16–17; Galatians 6:16). The Old Testament promises are fulfilled in Christ and his church, and will be completed in the new creation. This is the amillennial view. Paul still hopes for a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26), and that hope remains. It does not follow that God is finished with the Jewish people, and the New Testament will not let that conclusion stand (Romans 11:1). A reader can hold the mission of verse 8 with both hands and still expect God to keep every promise he ever made, without needing a chart to show him how.

A throne higher than the one they asked for. The question deserves one more look, because the answer to it arrived within a fortnight and was larger than the question. They wanted a son of David on David’s throne. At Pentecost Peter will tell this same city that God swore to David to seat one of his descendants on his throne, and that he has done it: Jesus, raised from the dead and exalted to God’s right hand, is the one David called Lord (2:30–36). The kingdom was not postponed on the Mount of Olives. It was about to be proclaimed from a throne higher than Jerusalem’s, with a King who could no longer be killed, over subjects gathered from every nation. They asked whether the King would take back the land. He was about to take the world.

What does amillennial mean? The word comes from Revelation 20, where Christ reigns for a thousand years. Amillennialists understand that thousand years not as a future golden age on earth after Christ returns, but as the present reign of Christ from heaven, between his first and second comings, while the gospel goes to the nations and the saints who have died reign with him. On this view there is one return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, the world is judged and the new creation begins. The kingdom is already here, because the King is on his throne; and it is not yet complete, because his enemies are still being made his footstool (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25). Premillennial brothers, many of them faithful and learned, see a further earthly reign after his return; the difference is real, but it is not a difference about whether Jesus is coming.

The cost of the calendar. What is not negotiable is the practical edge of the rebuke, and it has cut every generation since. There has never been a decade without someone announcing the date. Farms have been sold and careers abandoned, and the morning after has always come, with the faithful poorer and the watching world confirmed in its suspicion. When a teacher tells you he has worked out what the Father reserved to his own authority, you have all the information you need about him, and you need not examine his arithmetic.

A secret, not an evasion. Notice what Jesus did not say. He did not say there is no date. He said the date is not yours. Somewhere in the counsel of God there is a day already fixed, as fixed as any day in the diary, on which every wrong currently running unchecked will be stopped where it stands. That is not a vagueness offered to keep people quiet; it is a certainty withheld to keep them free. A man who knew the date would spend his life either presuming on the time remaining or paralysed by its shortness. Not knowing, he is left to do the only sane thing, which is to be found faithful whenever it comes. The Father is not being coy with his children. He is keeping his own counsel, which is one of the things it means to be God.

Is it wrong to think about the end times at all? No. The New Testament talks about the last things constantly, and always for the same reasons: to give hope to the suffering, to warn the careless, and to keep believers awake and faithful (1 Thessalonians 4:18; 2 Peter 3:11–14). What Jesus forbids is not interest in his return but the attempt to fix its date and to read the calendar out of the newspapers. So study what Scripture plainly teaches: Christ will come personally and visibly, the dead will be raised, all will be judged, and God will make all things new. Hold the details loosely where good Christians differ. And if a book or a preacher leaves you more fascinated by charts than eager to love Christ and your neighbour, put it down.

In a sentence. When they asked if he would now restore the kingdom to Israel, Jesus said it was not for them to know the times and seasons that the Father had set by his own authority.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you spend your anxiety on. Many Christians carry a low hum of worry about the future: the state of the nation, the next election, whether the end is near. Jesus does not say those things are unreal; he says the timing belongs to the Father. Hand it back to him. Don’t waste your energy on calculating the end. Spend it on the mission he gives in the very next breath, and on the person in front of you today.

For worship. The Son himself lived by the Father’s calendar. In John’s Gospel his hour has not yet come, again and again (John 7:30), and then, on the night of the supper, it has (John 13:1); he walked into it without flinching, because the hour of his death was a season the Father had fixed. The same hand that appointed the day of the cross and the morning of the empty tomb holds the day that is still to come. Empires that thought themselves eternal have risen and fallen inside that calendar, and not one of its dates has slipped. The Father kept every appointment he made with his Son, and he will keep the last one.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.

But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. He answers a question about the calendar with a sentence about a map. They asked when; he tells them where, and how far. And the first word out of his mouth is not an instruction but a gift: you will receive power. Not summon it, not work up to it: receive it. The word is dynamis: ability, strength, the capacity to do what you could not otherwise do. It is not political power, and it is not given for private experience. It is given for witness.

What the power turned out to be. It is worth being exact about this, because the word invites daydreams. Within three chapters these men are in custody. Within seven, one of their number is dead under a pile of stones. The power promised here did not make them untouchable; it made them unstoppable, which is a different and better thing. What Luke actually records after Pentecost is boldness where there had been hiding, clarity where there had been confusion, and joy in places where joy has no business being: a flogging that ends in rejoicing (5:41), a midnight hymn from a prison floor (16:25). A Christian waiting for power to feel like invincibility may miss it when it comes as the ability to speak where speaking costs him something.

And you will be my witnesses. And what they are made is not preachers, not apologists, not strategists, but witnesses. A witness tells what he has seen and heard: we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard (4:20). The word is martyres, and English took it over as martyr, not because the word means dying, but because of what kept happening to the people it described. Luke himself watches the shift begin: by the time Paul is telling his story he speaks of Stephen as your witness, and every reader knows what happened to Stephen (22:20). But keep the courtroom sense first, because it is the one that sets a nervous believer free. A witness is not the barrister. He is not asked to win the case, construct the argument, or hold his own against a hostile expert. He is asked one thing: say what you saw. He may be cross-examined by people cleverer than he is, and it does not touch his qualification, because he was there and they were not. Anyone who has been dealt with by Jesus Christ has standing in that witness box, and nobody can take his testimony away from him.

Is this command to every believer, or a promise to the apostles? In the first place it was spoken to the apostles, who would be witnesses of the resurrection in a unique sense, as eyewitnesses (v. 22). But Acts goes on to show ordinary believers telling the good news wherever they went (8:1–4), and Peter tells every Christian to be ready to give a reason for his hope (1 Peter 3:15). The apostles’ eyewitness testimony is now written down; the witness to it belongs to all.

In Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. Then the geography, and it doubles as the table of contents. Jerusalem fills chapters 1 to 7; Judea and Samaria, chapters 8 to 12; the end of the earth, chapters 13 to 28, ending in Rome, the centre of the known world. Notice where Samaria sits. Not last, where it could be indefinitely deferred, but second: the people a Judean would cross a river to avoid, placed in the middle of the itinerary so that no one could reach the ends of the earth while stepping over the neighbours he despised. And the end of the earth is a quotation waiting to be identified. It comes from Isaiah’s servant, appointed as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6), which Paul will one day pick up and apply to his own mission (13:47).

The Servant’s light in his witnesses’ hands. That quotation tells us whose mission this is. In Isaiah the light for the nations is the Servant of the LORD, and Luke has already told us who the Servant is: old Simeon took the infant Jesus in his arms in the temple and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). So the end of the earth is not a target the church has set itself. It is the Servant’s own commission, the reach God promised to his Son, and Jesus hands it to his witnesses because the light they carry is himself. That is why Paul can apply the Servant’s words to his own preaching without arrogance. The Servant is still shining, through the mouths of those he sends.

What it does not mean. This verse is preached wrongly more often than almost any other. It is regularly turned into a method, reach your Jerusalem first, then your Judea, then the world, as though local outreach must be completed before anyone may go abroad. That is not what the sentence is. It is Luke’s map of one historical expansion, not a sequence of permissions, and the book itself refuses the reading: the gospel reaches Samaria because a persecution scattered people who had no strategy at all (8:1–4), and Antioch is evangelised by men whose names nobody bothered to record (11:20). God has never waited for a city to be finished before starting on another one.

Does power mean I should expect miracles? The Spirit’s power is promised to every believer, but its main form in this verse is witness: courage, clarity and endurance in speaking of Christ. The signs and wonders in Acts cluster around the apostles and those closely linked to them, and the New Testament calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), given to confirm the message when it was first delivered (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation laid and the Scriptures complete, we hold that those revelatory and sign gifts have ceased, though many fine Christians disagree. But God has not stopped acting. He answers prayer, he heals when he pleases, and he does the greatest miracle of all every time a dead heart is made alive. Expect that power, and pray for it.

So what do I actually do? Start with the people already in your life, and with what Christ has actually done for you. You do not need a speech. You need to be honest when someone asks why you go to church, why you are not afraid of dying, or how you got through the year you got through. Pray by name for a few people who do not know Christ, and ask God for one opportunity this week. When it comes, say one true thing about Jesus, and leave the results with him. A witness has done his job when he has told the truth.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came on them, and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

On a Tuesday. Where is your Jerusalem? Not a strategy, a place: the kitchen, the office, the street, the group chat. Start there. And ask honestly whether there is a Samaria in your life, a person or a kind of person you would quietly prefer the gospel to skip. The map Jesus drew went straight through the people his disciples least wanted to meet, and he has not redrawn it for you.

For worship. He spoke of the end of the earth to eleven provincials with no money and no standing, on a hill outside a city that had crucified him, and he spoke of it as already settled. That is the confidence of a King who has bought what he is about to claim. The nations were his inheritance before a single witness set out (Psalm 2:8), and the Spirit he promised has carried his name into languages Luke never heard of and as far as the reader of this page. Every stammered sentence about Jesus spoken to a friend since then has been one more province of his inheritance being brought in.
verseByVerse.note: This verse outlines the book: Jerusalem (chs 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and the end of the earth (13–28).

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,

As they were looking on, he was lifted up. Luke’s care as a reporter shows in five words: as they were looking on. This is not something they inferred the next morning from an empty hillside. They watched it happen. And what they watched was not a fading, not a dissolving, not a body becoming gradually transparent. He was lifted, and then a cloud came between, and the hillside was one man emptier than it had been a minute before. The ascension was a real, bodily event, and it marks his exaltation to the right hand of the Father, where he reigns over all things (2:33; Ephesians 1:20–22) and intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

And a cloud took him out of their sight. The cloud is the detail everything turns on, and it is not weather. All through Israel’s Scriptures the cloud is where God is pleased to be visible without being looked at. It goes ahead of the people through the wilderness as a pillar (Exodus 13:21); it wraps Sinai in thunder (Exodus 19:16); it fills the tabernacle so thickly that Moses cannot get in (Exodus 40:34–35); it comes down on the temple so that the priests have to stop the service and stand there (1 Kings 8:10–11); it overshadows the mountain of transfiguration while the Father speaks (Luke 9:34–35). When a cloud takes a man out of sight in this literature, he has not gone behind a weather front. He has gone inside the glory. The cloud is not a means of transport, but a sign that he has entered the presence of God.

The underside of a coronation. Which means the scene has to be read from both ends to be read at all. From the hillside it is a departure, and it looks like loss. From the other side of the cloud it is an arrival, and Daniel had described it centuries before: one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before the Ancient of Days, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). Notice the direction of travel in Daniel. He is not coming down to earth in that vision; he is coming up to the throne. The disciples are watching the underside of a coronation. And the psalm the apostles will quote more than any other text in their Scriptures is about what happens when he gets there: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool (Psalm 110:1). Peter will preach it within a fortnight (2:34–35).

Two men stood by them in white robes. Angels, as at the tomb, where two men in dazzling apparel met the women (Luke 24:4). Heaven sent the same kind of messengers to explain the empty grave and the empty sky.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that heaven is a place somewhere above the sky, as if Jesus flew upward through space. Someone will ask, reasonably, whether heaven is really up. It is not, in the sense of being a distance measurable in miles above Jerusalem; a man who kept rising would run out of air long before he ran out of sky. But the question mistakes a sign for a map. He went up because a body must leave visibly if witnesses are to testify that it left, and because upward is what exaltation looks like to creatures who walk about on the ground. The ascension is the visible sign of his passing into God’s presence, into a dimension beyond ours. The direction was for their eyes. The destination was the throne.

He took his body with him. There is something else here that is rarely said and ought to be. Jesus did not shed his body at the cloud. He took it with him. There is at this moment, in the presence of God, a human being, with hands, with a voice, with a memory of Nazareth and of nails, and he is not visiting. The nature he assumed in the womb of a Galilean girl he has never laid down and never will. Here the Reformed churches have insisted on care: a real body is somewhere, and being somewhere means not being everywhere, so when Christ promises to be with his people always he is with them by his Spirit and in his deity, not by his flesh being spread thin across the world. Lutheran Christians have taken a different line on that last point and have not been foolish to do so; the disagreement is old and serious and is not about whether Christ is truly present with his church. But the pastoral weight of it belongs to everyone. Our nature is not a costume he wore for thirty years and more. It has been carried into the immediate presence of God and seated there.

Why did Jesus have to leave? Wouldn’t it be better if he were still here? Jesus himself said no: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you (John 16:7). While he walked in Galilee, he could be in only one village at a time. Now, by his Spirit, he is present with every believer in every place at once. And his going was not retirement but enthronement: from the Father’s right hand he rules history for the good of his church, sends the Spirit, and prays for his people. You are not worse off than the disciples who could see him. In one way you are better placed, because the Spirit they had to wait ten days for has been given to you.

What is Jesus doing now? He is reigning, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), working all things toward the day his enemies are put under his feet. He is interceding: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), so that at this moment a man who knows your name is praying for you in the presence of God. He is preparing a place for his people (John 14:2–3). He is building his church through the gospel. And he is waiting, with perfect patience, for the day the Father has fixed, when he will come back.

In a sentence. After saying this, Jesus was taken up while they watched, and a cloud hid him from their sight, and as they stared into the sky, two men in white stood beside them.

On a Tuesday. When you pray, remember who is on the other end. Not a distant force, but a man in our nature at the Father’s right hand, who knows tiredness, hunger and grief from the inside and has carried that knowledge into glory. Bring him the small things as well as the large. He has never forgotten what it was like down here.

For worship. Stand back from it and the wonder is not that they gazed. It is that heaven received him. The one by whom all things were made had been spat at by soldiers who were too bored to look him in the face, and had let them; and now the glory that Moses was not permitted to see closes over him like a door opening. He did not ascend to become glorious. He ascended because he always was, and because the work he came to finish was finished. Every knee in that hidden place bent as he came in, and the marks in his hands went in with him and are there still. Our Saviour reigns in glory, in our human nature, at the Father’s right hand.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence.

parallels.desc: two men in dazzling apparel

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”

Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? Angels have a way of asking questions that are really instructions. The men are not doing anything wrong; they are doing something finished. He has gone. The sky has nothing further to show them, and the next thing God has for them is at the bottom of the hill. And they are addressed as men of Galilee, which is not a compliment in Jerusalem. It is the label that will be thrown at Peter beside a fire and at the whole company at Pentecost (2:7). Provincials with an accent. Heaven uses the word without a flicker of apology, and then tells these particular provincials that the next act of world history runs through them.

This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven. This Jesus: the same Jesus, personally. Not some other figure, not a successor, not a spirit of Jesus distinct from the man. The one they had walked the roads with is the one who will return.

Will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven. The promise itself turns on those words, in the same way, and they are the anchor of Christian hope. Whatever the ascension was, the return will match it. He left personally, and a person will come back: not an influence, not a movement, not an era of improved conditions. He left bodily, and a body will return: the same body, the same man, the same face. He left visibly, in front of witnesses, and the return will be public: the world will not be informed of it, it will see it, every eye (Revelation 1:7). And he left in a cloud, which is where Daniel had said the Son of Man belonged, and where Jesus said he would be seen coming with power and great glory (Matthew 24:30).

What the phrase rules out. That phrase quietly rules out a good deal. It rules out the teaching that Christ already returned invisibly, whether in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or at some private date since. Something did happen in AD 70, and Jesus had said it would; but the angels are not describing a change in the spiritual climate. They are standing beside men whose eyes still hurt from watching, and they say: like that. It equally rules out the reduction of the second coming to a figure of speech for death, or for progress, or for the gradual improvement of the human race. The Christian expectation is not that things will get better. It is that a particular man will arrive.

Where Christians differ: a secret rapture? Some teach that Christ will return secretly to remove believers before a tribulation, then visibly later. Verdict: the angels promise one return, in the same way he went: visible and bodily. The New Testament knows one second coming, at which believers are gathered, the dead raised, and the world judged (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). No secret rapture.

But doesn’t 1 Thessalonians 4 speak of being caught up? It does, and it is anything but secret: a cry of command, the voice of an archangel, the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). It is hard to imagine a noisier passage in the Bible. Paul says believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, and the word for meet was used of citizens going out of a city to greet an arriving king and escort him back in. The picture is not of the church being taken away while the world carries on, but of his people going out to welcome him as he comes. The same chapter flows straight into the day of the Lord (5:1–3). One coming, seen by all, with his people gathered to him.

The religion of the raised binoculars. And the angel’s question rules out, by the plain force of the rebuke, the religion of the raised binoculars. There has always been a kind of believer whose whole interest in the future is diagrams: who can tell you the sequence of the last seven years but has not spoken to his neighbour in nine of them. The first men ever tempted to that were interrupted mid-stare by angels, and the interruption is in the Bible. The correct response to he is coming back has never been to stand still and calculate. It is to be found doing something he asked for when he arrives.

A docket that has been kept. But the promise deserves better than to be used only as a corrective, because it is not primarily a rebuke; it is the sentence a great many Christians have died holding. Measure it against what is actually wrong with the world. Somewhere today a woman is being told the results were not what anyone hoped. Someone who was harmed as a child has watched the man who did it live comfortably into old age and die unaccused. Injustices are not merely unpunished; whole categories of them are now unrecoverable, the witnesses dead, the record lost. To all of it this sentence says: there is a date, and on that date the one who was in the room the whole time will come back in the open, and nothing will be left buried. That is not a poetic way of saying things will feel better eventually. It is a man on a cloud, and a docket that has been kept.

How do I live ready without being anxious? Readiness in the New Testament is not nervous watching of the sky; it is faithful work and trust in Christ. The servants in Jesus’ parables are ready because they are doing what their master told them, not because they have guessed the hour (Luke 12:42–43). If you belong to Christ, his coming is not a threat hanging over you but the arrival of your Saviour, and there is no condemnation waiting for you (Romans 8:1). So keep short accounts with God, love the people around you, do your ordinary work well, and say each night, as the church has said from the beginning, come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).

In a sentence. The angels asked the men of Galilee why they stood looking into heaven, for this same Jesus would come back in the same way they had seen him go.

On a Tuesday. Don’t stand gazing at the sky. He is coming back. Get on with his work. And when the news is unbearable, or a wrong in your own life has gone unanswered for years, say this verse to yourself out loud: this Jesus will come in the same way. They walked down the hill. There is no record of any of them looking back up, and the next thing Luke tells us is that they went to pray.

For worship. The Lord who went up from Olivet will come again in glory, not as a rumour or a mood but as himself, with the same scarred hands that blessed his disciples as he left. Every tear will be answered by a face, every hidden wrong by the one who saw it, every grave by the voice that raised Lazarus. The church has waited two thousand years and has not been disappointed yet, because the one who promised has never broken his word. He went in a cloud, attended by angels, with no one but eleven men to watch; he will come in the same cloud, and the whole world will watch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, about a kilometre away, and went to the upstairs room where they were staying: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James. They all devoted themselves to prayer together, with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among about a hundred and twenty believers. He said that the Scripture the Holy Spirit spoke through David had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus, though he had been one of them and shared in their ministry. Judas had bought a field with the money from his wickedness, and there he fell headlong, burst open and died; everyone in Jerusalem heard of it, and the field became known as Akeldama, Field of Blood. The Psalms say his place should be deserted and someone else should take his office. So one of the men who had been with them throughout Jesus’ ministry, from John’s baptism to the ascension, must become a witness with them to the resurrection. They proposed Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. They prayed that the Lord, who knows every heart, would show which one he had chosen, then cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was added to the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Apostolic College and Its Significance

The reconstitution of the Twelve before Pentecost is deliberate. The Twelve answer to the twelve tribes and represent the reconstituted people of God (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30); an incomplete Twelve would be a broken sign at the moment the sign was about to be needed. The qualifications Peter states (v. 22) mark the apostolic circle as a closed and historically anchored group — the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. The New Testament does use apostle more widely of sent ones and church messengers, but no one alive can meet the terms stated here, which is why the church has no further foundational word to wait for. Judas, meanwhile, stands as the sober warning at the door of the book: he was numbered among them, sent out with them, and trusted with the money, and nearness to Jesus did not save him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A hundred and twenty people with no money, no standing and no strategy prayed together for ten days, settled a painful question from Scripture rather than by argument, and appointed a man who is never mentioned again.

Now: The church's preparation for anything God intends to do has not changed shape: gathered, praying, working from the text, willing to be led, and made up very largely of people whose names will appear nowhere. Barsabbas, qualified and passed over in front of everyone, was, so far as we know, still among them when the Spirit fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.

They returned to Jerusalem. They walk back. That is the first thing, and it is an act of obedience with a cost, because Jerusalem was the last place on earth a follower of the executed Nazarene had any business being. It was the city with the arrest warrants, the city with the council that had already shown what it would do, the city where every one of them could be identified by half a dozen people in the temple courts. Jesus had told them to stay there (v. 4), and so they went back into it. Luke’s Gospel adds that they went back with great joy (Luke 24:52).

From the mount called Olivet. The Mount of Olives rises east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley; Luke 24:50 places the ascension near Bethany, on its eastern slope. It is a hill with a history. Zechariah had foretold the day when the LORD’s feet would stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), and it was from there that Jesus had wept over the city and ridden down into it on a donkey. The King left the world from the same hill on which the prophets placed his coming.

A Sabbath day’s journey away. Luke measures the walk in a way that tells you something about his sources. A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the rabbis permitted on the day of rest, about two thousand cubits, roughly a kilometre or two-thirds of a mile. They derived it from texts such as Exodus 16:29 and Joshua 3:4. It is the only appearance of the phrase in the New Testament. Luke’s Greek-speaking patron did not need the rule; Luke keeps it because it is how the people who were there described the distance. Small untranslated habits like that are what a report looks like when it comes from inside.

The eleven by name. Then the roll-call, and it deserves more attention than it usually gets. Luke could have written the eleven and moved on. He writes out every name, matching the list in his Gospel (Luke 6:14–16), minus Judas Iscariot. A movement staking everything on the claim that certain men saw a dead man alive has to be able to say who they were, and Luke names them, in a city where any one of them could be found and questioned within the hour. Notice also the order, which is not the order in the Gospel. Andrew has moved down and John has moved up to stand beside Peter at the head of the list, because those two are about to work as a pair through the opening chapters of this book, at the temple gate, before the council, and on the road into Samaria. Luke is arranging the names for the story he is about to tell.

Judas the son of James. Two of the names need a word. Judas the son of James is not Iscariot, and Luke says so by naming the father; he is probably the apostle who appears as Thaddaeus in the other lists, and the awkwardness of the double naming is itself a mark of honesty. A church inventing its own records does not saddle itself with a second Judas.

Simon the Zealot and Matthew. Simon bore a name that points to zeal for the law, and possibly to the movement that believed the answer to Rome was a knife. Sitting in the same small room is Matthew, who had made his living collecting Rome’s money from his own people. In any village in Galilee those two men were natural enemies of the sharpest kind: the collaborator and the man sworn to cut collaborators’ throats. They are now praying together, and will shortly be arrested together. Nothing in politics does that. Jesus had called each of them himself, Matthew from the tax booth with two words, follow me (Luke 5:27, where Luke calls him Levi), and Simon from wherever zealots were found, and had kept them at one table for three years. What held them was not a compromise between their causes but a Lord who had died for them both, and who had shown each of them that the thing he was trying to save the nation from was smaller than the thing he himself had been saved from.

They went up to the upper room, where they were staying. The upper room was a rented or borrowed space up the outside stairs of a Jerusalem house. Christian tradition has long linked it with the room where the Passover was eaten, and others have suggested the house of Mary the mother of John Mark, where the church later met to pray (12:12). Either may be right, though Luke does not press the point. What matters is the scale. The risen Lord of heaven and earth has been enthroned at the right hand of God, and his entire visible operation on earth is a borrowed room upstairs with about a hundred and twenty people in it, most of whom have no money and one of whom is still living down the worst night of his life. Everything in this book grows from that room.

What if my church contains people whose politics I find hard to bear? Then you are in the church Jesus built. He deliberately chose a tax collector and a zealot and put them in the same company, not by asking them to stop caring about the world but by giving them a Lord who mattered more than their causes. You may still hold your convictions, and some political questions are moral questions on which Scripture speaks. But the person across the aisle who votes differently is, if he trusts Christ, your brother for eternity, and the election will be forgotten long before he is. Pray with him. Eat with him. Let the gospel be louder in your conversation than the news, and you will find, as Matthew and Simon did, that you have more in common than you had in conflict.

In a sentence. They returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, a short walk away, and went up to the upper room where the eleven apostles were staying.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your church you would least naturally choose to spend an evening with. Then remember the upper room, with a tax collector and a zealot at the same prayer meeting. Ask God for a chance this week to do one ordinary kindness for that person. And if you are discouraged by how small and unimpressive your church is, remember that the whole visible church of Jesus Christ once fitted up a flight of stairs.

For worship. The Lord of glory went up from Olivet and left behind him no palace, no treasury and no army, only a staircase and a list of names. He did not count his kingdom in acres. He counted it in people, each one called by him, and he has never forgotten one of them: the fisherman, the tax collector, the zealot, the second Judas whom the lists struggle to name. Every church that has met since in a borrowed hall or a front room has met under the same reign. From a hundred and twenty people up a flight of stairs he has gathered a multitude no one can number, and he still knows each by name.
verseByVerse.note: A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the traditions allowed on the Sabbath, a little over half a mile. The list of eleven matches the Gospels’ lists; Judas the son of James is probably Thaddaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,

All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer. Luke gives the waiting church one adverb and it becomes a signature: homothymadon, with one accord, of one mind and one impulse together. He will use it again and again in the early chapters, in the temple courts (2:46), in a prayer meeting after an arrest (4:24), in Solomon’s Portico (5:12), until it is almost the church’s second name. And the prayer is not occasional. The verb (proskarterountes) is continuous: they were devoting themselves to it, persisting, holding fast, the way a man keeps at something he cannot do without. They had been given a promise with no date attached and the only work available to them was asking. The church was born in persistent, united prayer, and waiting for the Spirit was not passive.

Together with the women. Look at who is in the room. The women are there, and Luke is the writer who always says so. These are probably the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee, supported him from their own means and witnessed the cross and the empty tomb (Luke 8:2–3; 23:49; 24:10). In a world where a woman’s word carried little weight in a court, women had been the last at the cross, the first at the tomb, and are now in the founding prayer meeting of the Christian church. Nobody constructing a respectable origin story in the first century would have arranged it that way.

And Mary the mother of Jesus. Mary is there too, and this is the last time she is named in the New Testament. It is worth pausing on where Scripture chooses to leave her, because a great deal has been built on her since. She is not on a platform. She is not being asked for anything. She is on her knees in a crowded room with a hundred and nineteen other people, waiting for the Holy Spirit like everyone else. She is honoured, blessed among women, and the church should not be so nervous of the abuse that it forgets the text; but she is honoured as one of the redeemed, not as a channel of redemption. Her son had said as much when a woman in a crowd blessed the womb that bore him and he answered, blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27–28). Here she is doing exactly that, and the New Testament closes the door on her with her hands together and her face down, which is the most honourable place she could possibly be left.

Should Christians pray to Mary? No. Scripture never shows a believer praying to Mary or to any departed saint, and it gives a reason why we need not: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Mary herself called God her Saviour (Luke 1:47), which means she needed saving like the rest of us. The right way to honour her is the way the Bible does: to call her blessed, to imitate her faith and humility, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38), and to do what she told the servants at Cana, do whatever he tells you (John 2:5). She points away from herself to her Son, and so should we.

And his brothers. But the phrase that should stop a reader is the last one. These are the men who a few years earlier had come to collect him because his family had decided he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). These are the brothers of whom John flatly records that not even they believed in him (John 7:5). They had grown up in the same small house, eaten at the same table, watched him work in the same trade, and concluded he was deluded. And now they are in the prayer meeting. One of them, James, will be leading the Jerusalem church within a few years, presiding over the council that decides the Gentile question (15:13).
