He will write a letter, and it will open by calling his own elder brother Lord and himself his servant. Another, Jude, will do the same. Whatever else happened in the forty days, this happened: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). Paul mentions it in a single clause and does not elaborate, and it is one of the most eloquent clauses in the Bible.

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus (Matthew 13:55–56; Luke 2:7, where Jesus is her firstborn son; Matthew 1:25). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, read them as cousins or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage; but Scripture never suggests either. Once unbelieving (John 7:5), they are now among the praying disciples.

For the one praying for an unbelieving relative. Anyone praying for a relative who will not believe should not be handed a formula here, and should be handed this. It took years. Mary lived a long time in a house where her other sons thought her firstborn was mad, and there is no indication she was given any assurance in the meantime. What she was given, eventually, was a room with all of them in it. The case is never closed while a man is alive, and the people who know you best and have the most reason to dismiss you are not out of reach; the risen Christ went looking for one of them personally. That is not a promise that every son and every brother will come. It is a plain fact that the hardest cases in the New Testament include the ones who had shared a childhood with him, and they came.

In those days Peter stood up among the brothers. And then Peter stands up. Luke slips the crowd size in as an aside, the company of persons was in all about a hundred and twenty, and it is a strikingly modest number to set against the promise of the end of the earth. Ten times twelve, perhaps a quiet hint of a renewed Israel. It is also, some have noted, the number later Jewish tradition required before a town could constitute its own council; whether or not Luke intends the echo, the point is that the entire visible harvest of the ministry of Jesus of Nazareth could sit down together in one upstairs room. Within a chapter it will be three thousand more.

Why pray, if God has already promised? Because the promise is the reason to pray, not a reason to stop. The disciples knew the Spirit was coming; Jesus had said so. And they spent the ten days asking for exactly that. Daniel did the same when he read in Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years: he did not sit back, he turned to God in prayer (Daniel 9:2–3). God has chosen to bring about his purposes through the prayers of his people, so that when the answer comes they know it came from him. Pray most confidently for what God has promised: the spread of the gospel, the holiness of his church, the coming of his kingdom.

In a sentence. They all prayed together constantly, with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers, and one day Peter stood up among the believers, about 120 of them, and said...

On a Tuesday. Great movements of God begin in prayer meetings, and most prayer meetings are small, unglamorous and easy to skip. Go to yours. If your church has none, find two or three others and start one. And keep praying for the brother, the son, the parent who still thinks your faith is foolish. The Lord who appeared to James has not lost his way to unbelieving families.

For worship. Luke once told us that the boy Jesus went down to Nazareth and was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). Now the order of that house has been turned the right way up. The mother is a disciple on her knees, the brothers are servants waiting on his word, and the son who once did as he was told in a carpenter’s home is the Lord of heaven about to pour out what he promised. He bore with his own family’s unbelief for years and did not let them go. The grace that reached into that household does not stop at the door of ours.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ brothers, who had not believed during his ministry, are now among the believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.

Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled. Consider who is speaking. The last time Peter opened his mouth in Jerusalem about Jesus of Nazareth, he was standing at a charcoal fire in a courtyard swearing he had never met the man, and then he went out and wept. Now he is on his feet in front of a hundred and twenty people, opening the Scriptures, handling the hardest subject the young church has, the treachery of one of their own, and doing it with composure. Nobody voted him into that. Something was restored on a beach in Galilee, and this is what restoration looks like a few weeks later: not a man excused, but a man working. Had to (edei) is the language of divine necessity, the same word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 24:26). Even the betrayal had been foretold. God was not surprised.

Which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David. His first move is to reach for a text. Notice the double authorship stated without any awkwardness: the Spirit spoke, and he spoke by the mouth of David. Not instead of David’s mouth, and not merely through it as a hollow pipe: David’s vocabulary, David’s grief, David’s own experience of a friend at his table who turned on him, and the Holy Spirit speaking in all of it. This is a clear statement of inspiration. Scripture has a divine author and a human author (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), and that is how these men understood the book they were reading. It is why Peter can treat a thousand-year-old lament as an instruction for a decision this week.

Concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. Peter states the facts plainly. A guide: the man who knew the garden because he had prayed in it with Jesus led the soldiers there with torches.

If God planned it, was Judas to blame? Had to be raises the question plainly: if Scripture had to be fulfilled, was Judas ever free to do otherwise, and is God then the author of the worst act in human history? Luke does not dodge this, and he will state both halves of the answer twice more, more starkly than anyone would dare to invent. At Pentecost Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath says you crucified and killed him (2:23). In a prayer meeting a few weeks later the church says that Herod and Pilate and the nations gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (4:27–28). The Bible never treats these as two positions to be chosen between. It puts them in one sentence.

God did not put the greed there. What Scripture never says is that God implanted the sin. Judas was not overpowered. He was a thief with his hand in the common purse long before he went to the priests (John 12:6), and what he did in the end was exactly what he had been doing in small amounts for years, which is to convert Jesus into money. He was not a man forced into a role; he was a man who found a buyer. God did not implant the appetite, and he did not compel the transaction. He wove a free and filthy act into a purpose that the man committing it knew nothing about. That is not tyranny. It is something more frightening and more reassuring: there is no evil so deliberate that it can get outside the plan of God, and no evil so useful to that plan that the man doing it is thereby excused. The Westminster Confession says it with care: God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet so that he is not the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creature (Westminster 3.1).

Mercy held out to the last. And no one may say he was never given a chance. He had three years of it. His feet were washed by the man he had already agreed to sell, in the same room, on the same night. He was warned repeatedly, and warned in a way that let him withdraw without public exposure: the others at that table had no idea who was meant, which means Jesus had shielded him even while confronting him. He was called friend in the garden with the kiss still wet on the face. Mercy was held out to Judas until the last hour, and he walked past it every time. Whatever mystery sits behind the word predestined, it does not sit between Judas and a door he wanted to go through.

For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry. Peter’s last words here are the ones that ought to be carried out of the room. Judas was not an outsider who got in. He was on the list. He was sent out to preach with the rest and, as far as the Gospels ever indicate, things happened when he did. He was trusted with the money. And when Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, not one of the eleven looked at Judas; every man there suspected himself first. Three years of the closest proximity any human being has ever had to Jesus Christ, and it did not save him. He was a real apostle outwardly, and yet he was never truly Christ’s (John 6:70; 17:12). Office and outward service are not proof of salvation: on that day many will say, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and he will say, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Proximity is not possession.

Judas is not your mirror. That sentence has frightened tender consciences for centuries, so one thing must be added to it. Judas is not a mirror for the believer who is afraid he loves Christ too little. Judas was never afraid of that for a moment. He did not want Christ and fear he was failing him; he wanted what Christ could be turned into, and when the exchange rate disappointed him he cashed out. A man who is anxious because he longs to love Jesus more than he does has already given the evidence that Judas never gave in three years of standing closer than anyone.

How do I examine myself without falling into despair? Scripture tells us to examine ourselves (2 Corinthians 13:5), but it never tells us to look only at ourselves. Ask simple questions. Am I trusting Christ, not my record, for my acceptance with God? Do I hate my sin and want to be rid of it, even when I fail? Do I love God’s word and God’s people, however weakly? Those are the marks of the Spirit’s work. Then look away from yourself to Christ, because assurance grows by looking at him, not by staring at your own pulse. If you find no faith at all, the answer is not to despair but to come to him now: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Peter said Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke through David about Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus, though he had been one of them and shared their ministry.

On a Tuesday. Having a share in ministry is not the same as belonging to Christ. If you teach, lead, serve or sing, ask yourself not how useful you are but whether you love him. And if there is a small, secret dishonesty you have been practising for years, as Judas practised with the purse, deal with it today. The great betrayals are usually the small ones grown up.

For worship. Jesus knew the Scripture about his betrayer long before Peter quoted it, and he walked toward its fulfilment with open eyes. He sat at table with the man David’s psalms had described and did not turn him out, and he went out into the night to the garden where he knew the torches would come. No treachery took him by surprise, and none could stop him saving his people. The worst thing one friend ever did to him became the road by which he made friends of his enemies, and the Saviour who was betrayed by a friend is the friend who will never betray you.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)

Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness. These two verses are Luke talking, not Peter. The giveaway is the clause in their own language. Peter’s hearers spoke that language every day. Luke has stepped out of the speech to tell his Greek-reading patron what the field was called and why. The whole thing is a footnote, and English Bibles are right to put it in brackets.

Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood. It is also the kind of footnote that quietly does a great deal of work. A story invented at a distance does not stop to give the local name of a piece of ground, preserve it untranslated in the original Aramaic, and then explain it. Akeldama was a real place with a real name that people in that city were still using when Luke wrote, and any reader in Jerusalem could have gone and looked at it. Legends do not usually leave a forwarding address. It was called Field of Blood because it was bought with blood money, and because of the bloody death that took place there. Tradition places it in the Hinnom valley south of Jerusalem, the valley whose name became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for hell.

Who bought the field? Two apparent collisions with Matthew’s account have to be faced, and they come apart more easily than their reputation suggests. The first is the purchase. Matthew says the chief priests took the returned silver and bought the field, because it was blood money and could not go into the treasury (Matthew 27:3–8); Luke says Judas acquired it with the reward of his wickedness. But that is ordinary legal speech about a dead man’s money. The silver was legally his; the priests would not touch it for sacred use and could not simply return it to a corpse, so it was spent on his account, and the ground went down under his name. Luke is telling you whose money paid for it, which is precisely why the city attached his crime to the deed and called the place what it called it.

And falling headlong he burst open. The second is the death itself. Matthew says he hanged himself; Luke says he fell headlong and burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. Read as two claims about the same instant they are irreconcilable, and read as two moments in one afternoon they are not. A body left hanging does not stay hanging indefinitely, and the ravine country south of Jerusalem is rock. The rope gives, or the branch does, or the corpse comes down of its own weight in the heat, and what is found at the bottom is what Luke describes, with a doctor’s plainness. Matthew tells you what Judas did. Luke tells you what was found, and why the field got the name it kept. Neither writer is contradicting the other; they are standing at different ends of the same terrible day.

The whole return on the transaction. Luke does not moralise over the corpse, but he does not tidy it either. Matthew’s thirty pieces of silver was a real sum and it bought a real thing: a field nobody wanted, with his name on it for ever, and a body in the middle of it. That is the whole return on the transaction. Sin always pays its wages (Romans 6:23), and the wages are never what was promised.

The blood the field was named for. But ask whose blood gave the field its name. Matthew records that Judas came back to the priests saying he had betrayed innocent blood, and that they counted the silver as the price of blood (Matthew 27:4–6). The blood in Akeldama is first of all the blood of Jesus, priced, sold and paid for in coins. And here is the wonder Luke’s own book will spell out. The blood that could buy a traitor only a field of shame is the blood with which God obtained the church (20:28). The one innocent man in the whole transaction was led outside the city walls and paid in full the wages Judas earned, for everyone who will come to him. The field of blood is a grave; the blood of Christ is a purchase.

What it does not mean. One thing must be guarded here, because this passage is read by people carrying something heavy. Judas is not in Scripture as a case study in suicide, and he must not be used as one. What is said about him is said about a man who sold the Son of God for money and never once repented of the wanting, only of the outcome. The manner of his death is reported; it is not what he is condemned for. A reader who has buried someone who took their own life, a son, a wife, a friend who was in agony and could not see a morning, is not looking at that person’s portrait in these verses, and anyone who hands it to them as one has misread the passage badly. Despair and treachery are not the same sin, and the God who reads hearts has never confused them.

Can a Christian who takes his own life be saved? Suicide is a grave sin, the taking of a life God gave, and no one should ever think of it as a way out. But Scripture nowhere calls it the unforgivable sin, and salvation does not depend on the state of a person’s mind in his last moment. It depends on Christ, who saves to the uttermost those who come to God through him, and from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28). A true believer overwhelmed by illness or despair is still covered by the blood that covered all his sins. If you are grieving such a loss, bring your grief and your questions to God and to your pastor. If you are thinking of ending your life yourself, please tell someone today, a pastor, a doctor, a friend, and let them help you carry what you cannot carry alone.

In a sentence. Judas bought a field with his wicked reward, and falling headlong burst open, and all Jerusalem heard, so the field was called Akeldama, Field of Blood.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are tempted to trade Christ for. Not thirty pieces of silver, probably, but a promotion, a relationship, a reputation, a comfortable silence when you should speak. Every one of those trades ends in a field of blood: it never delivers what it promised. And if you are carrying the grief of a loved one’s suicide, do not let anyone use this passage against them. Take your sorrow to the God who reads hearts.

For worship. Judas acquired one field, and nobody would ever live in it. Christ has acquired an inheritance that cannot perish, spoil or fade, kept in heaven for his people (1 Peter 1:4), and he does not hold it alone: he makes those he bought heirs of God and fellow heirs with himself (Romans 8:17). The traitor’s estate was a plot of ground and a nickname. The Saviour’s estate is a new heavens and a new earth, every acre of it inhabited, and every inhabitant someone who once deserved Akeldama and has been given a home.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field; the two accounts are often harmonised as a hanging followed by a fall. Akeldama is Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’

For it is written in the Book of Psalms. Peter’s warrant for what he is about to propose is two lines of Hebrew poetry, and it is worth watching how he uses them, because it shows how the first Christians read their Bible. Psalm 69 is David hunted and hated, drowning in trouble, with the scorn of those who reproach God falling on him. It is among the psalms most often applied to Jesus in the New Testament: zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17), they hated me without a cause (John 15:25), the reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (Romans 15:3). Psalm 109 is David betrayed by a man he had loved, who repaid friendship with accusation. Neither psalm names Judas; both are the cry of the Lord’s anointed under treachery. And that is exactly why Peter reaches for them. If David’s sufferings were the shadow, then the greater Son of David betrayed by a table companion is the substance, and if the righteous sufferer is Christ, his chief enemy is the man who sold him.

May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it. He alters one thing, and he does it in the open. The psalm has their camp and their tents, plural, a whole party of enemies (Psalm 69:25); Peter makes it singular, his camp. He is not misquoting. He is doing what the psalm itself invites, narrowing a corporate judgement down onto the representative case, the way a general verdict lands on the man who actually stood in the dock. The word for camp (epaulis) means a homestead, a dwelling place, and the ESV here translates the Greek of Acts. The field of blood is the camp, and no one would ever live there.

Let another take his office. The second citation, Psalm 109:8, is the operative one. The word behind office (episkopē) means oversight, the position of responsibility, and it is the word that would later give the church its term for an overseer, or bishop. Peter reads it as a mandate, not a comment. The seat is not abolished by the man who disgraced it; it is vacated, and it is to be filled.

The office outlived the man. That is the point the whole chapter has been building toward, and it is worth saying plainly because it steadies people who have watched a leader fall. Treachery at the top did not destroy the apostolate. Churches have been broken by the discovery that someone trusted was a fraud, and the temptation afterwards is always the same: to conclude that the whole thing was a fraud, or that the position itself was the problem and should quietly be left empty. Peter’s answer is to open the Scriptures and appoint a successor. The work is bigger than the worst man who ever did it.

How Peter reads the Psalms. He reads David’s psalms as speaking ultimately of Christ, David’s greater son, and of his enemies. This is how Jesus taught them to read, in that very upper-room season: everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). The psalms of the righteous king find their fullest meaning in the true King.

Does this mean every psalm is about Jesus? Not as though every line were a coded prediction. Read each psalm first as what it is: a real prayer of a real believer, often David, in a real situation. Then ask how it fits into the larger story. Some psalms speak directly of the coming King (Psalms 2 and 110). Many are the prayers of the anointed king, and Christ is the King who prays them most truly. Others are the prayers of God’s people, and we pray them in Christ, with him as our representative. Some lines, such as David’s confessions of sin in Psalm 51, Jesus could not pray of himself, though he bore those sins for us. Following the apostles, you will find the Psalms lead you to Christ again and again.

The prayers that ask God to ruin somebody. But there is a genuine difficulty here. These are the imprecatory psalms. May his camp become desolate. And anyone who turns up Psalm 109 to check the reference will find that the line immediately after the one Peter quotes asks that the man’s children be fatherless and his wife a widow. How is a Christian, who has been told to pray for those who persecute him, supposed to hold a book that contains prayers like that?

Three things that make it bearable. First, an imprecation is the opposite of vengeance, not an instance of it. A man who prays that God will judge his enemy is a man who has just handed the matter to a court and taken his own hands off it. Paul makes the same move: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19). The alternative to the imprecatory psalm is not gentleness; it is the knife. Second, the enemies in view are not personal irritants but the settled adversaries of God’s anointed and God’s purpose, which is why Peter can apply the psalm to a man who sold the Son of God, and why it would be nonsense applied to a neighbour who is difficult about the boundary hedge. And third, these prayers are ultimately in the mouth of Christ himself, the righteous sufferer the psalms were describing all along, and he is the one who has the right to ask for judgement and the one who on a cross asked for the opposite.

A caution and a permission. So there is a real caution here, and there is also a real permission. The caution is that no Christian may use these psalms as ammunition for a grudge; the moment a man prays desolation on someone who has merely wounded his pride, he has stopped praying and started cursing. The permission is for the other reader, the one who has been genuinely and terribly wronged, who has discovered that he wants justice with an intensity that frightens him, and who has concluded that wanting it makes him a bad Christian. It does not. Scripture has given him words for that, and the words are prayers, which means the right destination for the fiercest thing in him was never the offender, and never the polite suppression of it either, but God.

In a sentence. Peter quoted the Psalms: let his dwelling be desolate with no one living there, and let another take his office.

On a Tuesday. Read the Psalms with Christ in view. They speak of him. This week, take one psalm a day, read it first as David’s prayer and then ask how it is fulfilled in Jesus. And if there is someone who has done you real harm, do not carry the anger in silence or spill it on the people around you. Tell God, in the words he has given, and leave the judgement with him.

For worship. The Holy Spirit wrote the story of Christ into David’s tears a thousand years before Bethlehem, so that the betrayal of the Son of God was already in the hymnbook of Israel when it happened. Nothing done to our Lord was outside the plan of the God who spoke through the prophets. And one office in this story will never fall vacant. Judas left his post, and another had to take it; but the Righteous Sufferer of the Psalms holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever (Hebrews 7:24). No one will ever have to stand up in a room and propose his successor.

may another take his office

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.

One of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us. Peter now states the job description, and it is the narrowest in the New Testament. Two things are required, and no more. The man must have been with them throughout the ministry of Jesus, beginning from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up; and he must be able to testify to the resurrection as something he saw. That is the whole specification. Nothing about gifting, eloquence, education, or promise. The apostolic office is not a set of abilities. It is a position in history.

The ones who stayed. Something quietly wonderful is buried in the first requirement. Peter assumes there is more than one such man available, and he is right: two are produced within the minute. Which means that for three years there had been people following Jesus from the Jordan to Olivet, through the crowds and the opposition and the night of the arrest, whose names appear nowhere in any Gospel. They were there when the five thousand were fed and there when almost everyone walked away (John 6:66). They had no title and no mention. And the qualification for the highest office the church would ever have turned out to be precisely the thing they had been doing unnoticed the entire time, which was staying.

One of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection. The second requirement fixes what an apostle is for. He is a witness to the resurrection: that is the office in one phrase. Not a manager, not a visionary, not the holder of a private revelation. A man under oath about an event. Paul argues his own apostleship the same way: have I not seen Jesus our Lord? (1 Corinthians 9:1). Everything the church has ever had to say begins with a factual claim about something that happened outside a wall in Jerusalem on a particular Sunday, and the Twelve exist to say that they were there when it was verified.

Are there apostles today? Many churches say so, and some ordain men to the title. The answer has to be given in two parts, because the New Testament itself uses the word in two ways. In the wider sense an apostle is simply a sent one, and Scripture applies it freely: Barnabas is called one (14:14), Epaphroditus is his church’s messenger, its apostolos, to Paul (Philippians 2:25), and there are men described as messengers of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). If a modern believer means by the word a pioneering missionary who opens new ground, he is using it in a way the New Testament allows, and the ministry he is describing is badly needed.

A foundation is laid once. But the office Peter is filling in this room is not that, and it is closed by the very terms he has just read out. Nobody alive has accompanied Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension. Nobody alive saw the risen Christ in the way this qualification demands. Paul is the one apparent exception, and he is careful to present himself as exactly that, an appearance granted out of sequence, last of all, as to one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8), and to say last. The Twelve, with Paul beside them, are the foundation of the household of God (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. A builder who keeps returning to lay more foundation has stopped building.

Where Christians differ: apostolic succession. Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican teaching hold that bishops today are successors of the apostles, with their authority passed down. Verdict: by these qualifications, no one after the first generation could be an apostle in this sense. Paul was the exception, as one who saw the risen Lord, as to one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Their authority continues today not in successors but in their writings, the New Testament. When James was killed (12:2), no replacement was chosen.

A test any believer can apply. That gives an ordinary Christian a workable test. The question is not what a man calls himself; it is what he claims his title entitles him to. If a leader means that he plants churches and takes responsibility for regions, no harm is done and the church is the better for him. If he means that his word carries the weight the apostles’ words carried, that he may add to Scripture, or bind a conscience where Scripture has not, or require obedience that is not accountable to the text, then he is claiming something Peter’s own criteria exclude him from, and the humblest believer in the room has the right to say so with a Bible open at this page.

So do pastors and elders have any authority today? Yes, but it is a derived and limited authority, not an apostolic one. Elders are given by Christ to shepherd and oversee his flock (20:28; 1 Peter 5:1–3), and believers are told to obey their leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17). But their authority is the authority of the word they teach. They may not invent doctrine, bind consciences beyond Scripture, or lord it over the flock. Christians differ on the best form of church government, with elders, bishops or congregations holding different roles, and each tradition makes its case from Scripture. All agree that every leader is under the word, accountable for how he handles it, and answerable to the Chief Shepherd.

The comfort of a closed door. And there is a comfort in the closed door that is easy to miss. Look at how Peter measures the office: from the baptism of John to the day the Lord Jesus was taken up. The apostles are defined entirely by his life. Their office closed because his work had closed: he died once for sins, was raised never to die again (Romans 6:9), and ascended once to the right hand of God. There is nothing more to see, and so no more need of eyewitnesses. That is why the church is not waiting on any further foundational word. Nobody is going to arrive with a revelation that changes the terms, because nobody is going to arrive with a further work of Christ to report.

In a sentence. Peter said that one of the men who had been with them all the time Jesus was among them, from John’s baptism to the ascension, must become with them a witness to his resurrection.

On a Tuesday. When you open the New Testament, you are hearing the apostles. Treat it that way. Before you read a Christian book, a social media post or a confident new teaching, ask whether it agrees with what the eyewitnesses wrote. And if you have been following Christ quietly for years with no title and no notice, take heart from the unnamed men who stayed from the Jordan to Olivet. Staying is what Jesus looks for.

For worship. For three years the Lord Jesus went in and out among a few working men, on roads and in boats and at ordinary tables, and they would spend the rest of their lives telling the world what they had seen him do. The builders rejected him and put him to death outside the city; God raised him and made him the cornerstone (4:11), and every word his witnesses wrote is laid against that stone. The Son of God was willing to be watched, handled and remembered by fishermen, so that people who would never see him could still know exactly who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.

And they put forward two. The church does its part, choosing qualified candidates, and one of the two is about to become the most quietly instructive figure in the chapter. Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, carries three names: Joseph his Hebrew name, Barsabbas his family name (son of the Sabbath, or son of Sabba), and Justus, a Latin one. That is the ordinary signature of a Jew who moved easily in the wider world of the empire; many Jews had Latin or Greek names too. Both men clear the bar Peter has just set, and it is a high one: both had been with Jesus from the Jordan to Olivet, through everything, for three years. Of Matthias nothing more is known from Scripture, and later traditions about where he preached are unreliable.

Then one of them is not chosen. This is what a modern reader most needs from the passage, and it is almost never preached. Barsabbas did not fail to qualify. He was not passed over for a defect, or a sin, or a lack. He was found fit, publicly, on the record, by the eleven, and then he lost, in front of a hundred and twenty people. The lot fell, the room saw it fall, and he had to walk home through Jerusalem knowing that the man beside him was now one of the Twelve and he was not.

The taste of being passed over. Anyone who has been passed over knows the particular taste of that, and it is not the same as failure. Failure at least gives you something to work on. This is the other thing: being genuinely good enough, being told so, and watching it go elsewhere. The elder’s role that went to the other man. The post you had trained for and he had not. The ministry you would plainly have done well, handed to someone whose only advantage was that God chose him. It is a specific grief and it is a lonely one, because there is nobody to blame and therefore nothing to do with it.

No cheap comfort. Scripture will not hand out a cheap comfort here, and it is important not to invent one. The text does not say God had something better in mind for Barsabbas. It does not say he was spared a burden, or that his real calling lay elsewhere, or that everything worked out. It says he was not chosen, and then it never mentions him again. Sometimes faithfulness has to be carried on without an explanation, and pretending otherwise only adds a lie to a disappointment.

He stayed. But watch what the silence afterwards does and does not contain. There is no schism and no faction of the aggrieved. Barsabbas, so far as Luke tells us, is simply among the believers at Pentecost: one of the hundred and twenty on whom the Spirit falls a few days later is a man who has very recently had the biggest door in the world shut in his face. Whatever it cost him, and Luke does not tell us, he stayed.

What the lot could not take. And notice what qualified him in the first place. Not a gift or a title, but three years with Jesus: the Jordan, the hillsides, the boat, the upper room, the risen Lord seen with his own eyes. The lot decided an office. It could not touch that. Jesus had once told disciples returning elated from a mission not to rejoice that the spirits were subject to them, but that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). A man can lose the vote and keep the only thing that was ever worth having, because what he has is not a position but a person. Barsabbas walked home without the apostleship. He did not walk home without Christ.

The people named once. And it is worth remembering that Matthias is never mentioned again either. Both men disappear into the same silence, one of them an apostle and one of them not, and both of them spent the rest of their lives serving a Lord who had seen the whole business and kept the accounts himself. The people whose names occur once in the Bible and then never again are not the margin of the story. They are most of the church, in every generation, and the reason the story reached us at all.

Is it wrong to want a position of service, or to put myself forward? No. Paul says that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1), and both these men allowed their names to go forward. Wanting to serve Christ in a particular way is not pride, provided the desire is held open-handed. Test it: would you be glad to see someone else chosen, and keep serving gladly in the background? Are you willing for the church to say no? Let others weigh your gifts and character, pray, and accept the outcome as from the Lord. The aim is not the title but the glory of Christ, and he can be glorified as much by the one who was not chosen as by the one who was.

In a sentence. They nominated two men, Joseph called Barsabbas, also named Justus, and Matthias.

On a Tuesday. Joseph Barsabbas was faithful and passed over, and he is remembered here. If you have been passed over, for a role, a job, a recognition you were fit for, do not let the disappointment turn into a grievance. Stay. Keep serving. And if you were the one chosen, be kind to the one who was not, and remember that the choice was God’s, not a verdict on your worth.

For worship. Our Lord knows the taste of this from the inside. A few weeks earlier, in the same city, a crowd had been offered a choice between two men, and it asked for Barabbas and shouted that Jesus should be crucified (Luke 23:18–21). He was despised and rejected by men, and he bore it without bitterness, all the way to the cross. So there is no believer who has watched the honour go elsewhere whom he cannot understand, and none whom he will ever pass over. The one man the world refused to choose is the one who chose us, and his choosing never falls on anyone by accident.

parallels.desc: Judas called Barsabbas

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.”

And they prayed. They pray before they draw, and the prayer is short. There is no eloquence in it and no preamble. They tell God what they cannot do, ask him to do it, and stop.

You, Lord, who know the hearts of all. The word they use for him is unusual enough to be worth stopping on. Kardiognōstēs, heart-knower, is a title that appears twice in the whole New Testament, here and at 15:8, the first in the company’s prayer and the second on Peter’s lips, and both times the church is trying to decide who truly belongs. Here it is two candidates who look identical from the outside. There it will be a house full of Gentiles nobody expected God to accept. In each case the church has run out of evidence it can see, and reaches for the one who reads what no one else can. Knowing the heart is a divine attribute: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). It is a name for God born out of the church’s own helplessness, and both times it settles the matter.

Praying to Jesus. Notice also who is being addressed. They say Lord, and the immediate antecedent in this passage is the one who chose the original apostles (v. 2): Jesus, who knew what was in man (John 2:24–25). So within a few weeks of the ascension, before a single council, creed or doctrinal controversy, a room full of Jewish monotheists is praying to a man they had eaten breakfast with, addressing him by a title that in their Scriptures belongs to God, and attributing to him the knowledge of every human heart. The first recorded prayer of the church is addressed to the risen Jesus. Nobody argues for it. Nobody defends it. They simply do it, in the most instinctive act a religious person ever performs. The deity of Christ was not voted in at a later council; it was already the posture of the church before the church had a vocabulary for it.

He knows the hearts of all. And there is a searching mercy in what they ask him to do. He knows the hearts of all. That means, for one thing, that he was not taken in by either candidate’s best behaviour in a difficult fortnight, and it means he is not taken in by anyone’s now. The estimate of you that your church holds is assembled from what you have let it see. His is not. That cuts in the direction most people fear first: he has read the thing you would resign over if it were known. It also cuts the other way, and this is the side worth resting on. He has read the part of you that nobody has ever believed: the repentance that was real even though nothing changed for months, the love for him that survives in someone whose life makes it look implausible, the reason you did the thing that everyone misread. There is one person in the universe who has never once misunderstood you, and he is the one who went to a cross knowing all of it in advance.

Show which one of these two you have chosen. Not help us choose, but show us whom you have already chosen. Apostles are chosen by Christ. And the shape of their praying is worth copying. They did not ask God to reveal his choice and then sit back; they did the work first. They established the qualifications from Scripture, applied them honestly, narrowed the field to two men who genuinely met them, and only then said: show us. Guidance in the Bible almost always arrives on the far side of homework. God is not usually in the business of doing for people the part they could have done with a clear head and an open Bible.

To take the place in this ministry and apostleship. The word is topos, place: literally, to take the place in this ministry. It is a word Luke is about to use again with a darker meaning.

From which Judas turned aside to go to his own place. The last clause is the darkest in the chapter and the church handles it in a single phrase. Judas left his place among the apostles to go to his own place. They do not enlarge on it, do not speculate about it, and do not soften it. The phrase says only that he arrived somewhere that fitted him, a destination matched to a direction he had been travelling for years. He went where he belonged. The restraint is a lesson in itself. Where Scripture draws a line and stops, it is safest to stop there too, and it is telling that the men who had most cause to be bitter about Judas said less about his end than almost any preacher since.

Does his own place mean Judas is lost? That is the most natural reading, and the rest of Scripture supports it. Jesus said of his betrayer that it would have been better for that man if he had not been born (Mark 14:21), and called him the son of destruction (John 17:12). Those words could not be said of anyone who would finally be saved. Scripture teaches that those who die without Christ face conscious, eternal punishment, and Judas, who stood closest to the light and turned from it, is its most solemn example. But notice the church’s restraint, and copy it. We are not told to speculate about the eternal state of people we have known; we are told to warn the living and to flee to Christ ourselves.

In a sentence. They prayed to the Lord who knows every heart to show which of the two he had chosen for the apostolic ministry that Judas abandoned to go to his own place.

On a Tuesday. The Lord knows every heart, including yours. Pray to him with honesty: you cannot impress him and you need not perform. Tell him what you cannot do. And before you ask him to show you his will in a decision, do the homework: what does Scripture say, what do wise people say, what do the facts say? Then pray, and trust him with the outcome.

For worship. Every man goes in the end to a place. Judas went to the one his own heart had been travelling toward for years. The people of Christ go to a place their hearts never earned, prepared for them by the Lord who read those hearts through and through and still said, I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2). He knows what is in us better than we do, and the knowledge has not driven him away. The heart-knower is the host, and the room he has made ready is in his Father’s house.

parallels.desc: God, who knows the heart

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

And they cast lots for them. Luke does not say how the lot was cast; perhaps two marked stones were shaken until one fell out. That is how the twelfth apostle of Jesus Christ was appointed, and a modern reader is right to find it startling. But it was not superstition and it was not a coin toss dressed up in prayer. Casting lots was a means God had himself appointed in Israel. The land was divided by it (Joshua 18:6), the goat for the Day of Atonement was chosen by it (Leviticus 16:8), the priests’ duties were arranged by it, and the high priest carried the Urim and Thummim for seeking the LORD’s decision. The proverb that governs the practice says exactly what the eleven were counting on: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33). They were not gambling. They were using the last instrument of the old order on the last morning it existed.

And the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles. And then the lot disappears from the New Testament entirely. It is never used again after this chapter, because ten days later God moved in. Matthias is numbered with the eleven; the Twelve stand complete, matching the twelve tribes they were always meant to answer to (Luke 22:30); and the church, a renewed Israel gathered round its Messiah, is ready for what is about to happen to it.

The King keeps his number. Behind the lot stands a promise of Jesus. At the last supper he told the Twelve that they would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke 22:30), and before the night was out one of them had gone to sell him. Judas’s treachery tore a hole in the King’s own promise. It is the risen Lord, the one the church has just addressed as knower of hearts, who fills it, by choosing Matthias. The number Jesus set at the beginning stands whole on the morning of Pentecost. He keeps his promises down to the arithmetic.

Did they get it wrong? A good many teachers have said the eleven acted in the flesh, using lots before the Spirit had come, jumping ahead of God, and that the real twelfth apostle was Paul, whom the Lord would choose himself a few chapters later. It is usually pressed by noting that Matthias is never mentioned again.

The evidence does not support it. Luke records the episode without a breath of disapproval, and he is not a man who hides the church’s failures: he will tell us about Ananias lying to the Spirit, about the Greek-speaking widows being neglected, about Paul and Barnabas quarrelling so sharply that they parted company. Here there is no such note. On the contrary, when the Spirit falls in the next chapter Peter stands up with the eleven (2:14), which makes twelve, and Luke says nothing to suggest the number is wrong. Nor were they improvising: Peter is following a text, and the text says let another take his office (Psalm 109:8). They prayed before they drew, and they used the means God himself had appointed for exactly this purpose (Proverbs 16:33).

Why not Paul. The silence about Matthias afterwards proves nothing either, because Acts is silent about nearly all of them. Ten of the Twelve are never heard from again in this book as actors in the story; only Peter and John, with a brief mention of James’s death, get a narrative. By that test the whole apostolate was a mistake. And Paul cannot have been the man in view here, because he fails the stated qualification in the plainest way: the replacement had to have accompanied Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension, and Paul had done nothing of the kind. He is not the twelfth apostle to Israel; he is the apostle to the Gentiles, which is a different thing and no smaller. The Twelve had to be twelve because they answer to the twelve tribes, and the gap had to be closed before Pentecost.

Where Christians differ: should we cast lots today? Some say the apostles were wrong to do this, and should have waited for Paul. Others use lots or similar methods for guidance today. Verdict: Luke records no disapproval, and the choice was valid. But after Pentecost, the church never cast lots again. With the Spirit given and the Scriptures complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel and the judgment of the church (15:28; Romans 12:2). We don’t need dice.

So how does God guide you today, if not by lots? Not by dice, omens, opening the Bible at random or putting out a fleece, but by the settled means he has since given in fuller measure: his completed word, a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Psalm 119:105), the indwelling Spirit, prayer, sanctified wisdom, and the counsel of godly friends. The lot belonged to the brief gap before Pentecost and before the New Testament was written; we stand on the far side of both, and are the richer for it.

How do I make a big decision, then, practically? First, settle what Scripture commands or forbids; God will never lead you against his word. Second, if more than one path is right, pray, and ask God for wisdom, which he promises to give generously (James 1:5). Third, gather the facts honestly and think, because a renewed mind is meant to be used (Romans 12:2). Fourth, ask mature Christians who know you, and listen especially if they all say the same thing. Fifth, weigh your gifts, your responsibilities to family and church, and the opportunities actually in front of you. Then decide, and do not torment yourself afterwards about whether you missed a hidden signal. Within the bounds of his word, God is glad for his children to choose, and he rules over the outcome either way.

In a sentence. They cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was added to the eleven apostles.

On a Tuesday. God’s guidance is not a lottery for you. Seek it in his word, in prayer, and with wise counsel. If there is a decision in front of you this week, write down what Scripture says about it, who you could ask, and what you would choose if you trusted God to be good to you either way. Then choose, and get on with serving him.

For worship. Jesus said in his prayer on the night he was betrayed that he had guarded those the Father gave him, and none of them was lost except the son of destruction (John 17:12). On this morning even that gap is closed. And the promise reaches past the Twelve to every one of his people: this is the will of the one who sent him, that he should lose nothing of all that the Father has given him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). When the last day comes and his people stand complete, not one place at his table will be empty, and none will have been filled by chance.
verseByVerse.note: Casting lots left the choice to God; it is not mentioned again after the Spirit is given.

parallels.desc: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is the most neglected event in the Christian calendar — and one of the most theologically freighted. It is not simply that Jesus left; it is that he was enthroned. Psalm 110:1 — “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” — is the most-quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament. The early church was obsessed with it because it explained everything: Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand, over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is not waiting to begin his kingdom; his kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church. Every prayer prayed in his name, every sermon preached, every soul converted is an act of the reigning Christ extending his dominion.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples in Jerusalem, staring at the sky, confused about timing and kingdom, learning that faithfulness in the interval between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness. They had no map, no strategy document, no budget — only a promise and an upper room.

Now: We live in the same interval — between the first coming and the second, between the already and the not-yet. The temptation is still to stand looking into heaven, obsessing over the date of the return, while the mission sits unfinished at our feet. The command is unchanged: wait in prayer, go in the Spirit, witness to the ends of the earth. He is coming. In the meantime, there is work.

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. <sup>2</sup>And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. <sup>3</sup>And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. <sup>4</sup>And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. <sup>5</sup>Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. <sup>6</sup>And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. <sup>7</sup>And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? <sup>8</sup>And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? <sup>9</sup>Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, <sup>10</sup>Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, <sup>11</sup>both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians—we hear them telling in our <sup>15</sup>For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. <sup>16</sup>But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: <sup>17</sup>‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream <sup>21</sup>And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’ <sup>22</sup>“Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. <sup>24</sup>God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. <sup>25</sup>For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; <sup>26</sup>therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. <sup>34</sup>For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he <sup>47</sup>praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Pentecost (Greek for “fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Israel thanked God for the wheat harvest by offering the first loaves of the new crop (Leviticus 23:15–21). By New Testament times some Jews also linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai, which Exodus places in the third month after the exodus. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims from across the Jewish world. On that day, ten days after the ascension, the Spirit came as Jesus promised: a sound like a rushing wind, flames resting on each believer, and the disciples speaking in the languages of the pilgrims, so that people from Parthia to Rome heard God’s mighty works in their own native tongues. At Babel, God confused human languages to scatter proud rebels; now he speaks in every language to gather a people for himself.

Some mocked, saying the disciples were drunk. Peter stood and preached the first Christian sermon. This, he said, is what Joel promised for the last days: the Spirit poured out on all kinds of people, and salvation for everyone who calls on the Lord’s name. Then he proclaimed Jesus: attested by miracles, handed over by God’s plan and killed by them through lawless men, but raised by God, as David foresaw in Psalm 16. Exalted to God’s right hand, Jesus has poured out the Spirit, and God has made him both Lord and Christ. Cut to the heart, the crowd asked what to do. Repent and be baptised in Jesus’ name, Peter said, and you will receive forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. About three thousand did. The chapter ends with a portrait of the new community: devoted to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, sharing generously, meeting in the temple and in homes, praising God, and growing daily as the Lord added to their number.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the day of Pentecost the believers were all together in one place. Suddenly a sound like a violent wind came from heaven and filled the house where they were sitting. They saw what looked like tongues of fire that separated and settled on each of them, and all of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them. Devout Jews from every nation were staying in Jerusalem, and when they heard the sound a crowd gathered, bewildered, because each one heard the believers speaking in his own language. Amazed, they asked how these Galileans could be speaking in their native languages: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, visitors from Rome, Jews and converts to Judaism, Cretans and Arabs. All heard God’s wonderful works declared in their own tongues. Amazed and perplexed, they asked what it meant, while others mocked and said the believers had drunk too much wine.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Age He Opens

The Old Testament had promised a day when God would put his Spirit not on a handful of officeholders but on his whole people — Joel 2, Ezekiel 36–37 and Jeremiah 31 all say it, and Moses had wished for it out loud some fourteen centuries earlier (Numbers 11:29). Pentecost is that day arriving. This governs how the event should be read. The Spirit's coming is not a private enrichment handed to a hundred and twenty people who happened to pray hard enough; it is a public, datable, once-for-all act in the history of salvation, standing alongside the birth, the cross and the empty tomb. Christ was born once, died once, rose once, and poured out his Spirit once. What is repeated afterwards is not the outpouring but the filling — and Luke will use that second word again of Peter and the company (4:8, 4:31), and later of Paul (13:9), which is a mercy, because it means what happened to them is not sealed inside one morning in the first century.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, residents of Mesopotamia — the first four names on Luke's list are exile addresses. Assyria deported the northern tribes and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), and seven centuries later the descendants of the deported are standing in a Jerusalem street hearing the mighty works of God in the language of the country their forefathers were carried off to. Now: The same thing happens every time the Bible is put into a language that has never had it. The God who gave the church its first sermon in fifteen languages at once has never shown the slightest interest in making anyone learn a holy one first.

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.

Meaning first. Acts 2 is the birthday of the church as the Spirit-filled people of the new covenant. The risen and exalted Christ pours out the Holy Spirit, as promised. The disciples speak in languages they never learned, Peter preaches the first Christian sermon, three thousand believe and are baptised, and a new community is formed. Pentecost is a once-for-all event in the history of salvation, like the cross and the resurrection: the Spirit comes to dwell in God’s people for ever.

When the day of Pentecost arrived. Luke dates the morning with care. Pentecost means fiftieth: it was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). Fifty days had been counted off since the sabbath of Passover week, exactly as Leviticus prescribes, by every observant household in the empire; and on the morning the count reached its end, the thing the counting had been counting toward walked into the room. That calendar had been pregnant for fifteen centuries. Jews from across the world were in Jerusalem for it.

The feast of firstfruits. Consider what the feast was for. At Passover a farmer brought the first sheaf of barley and waved it before the LORD. Fifty days later, at Weeks, he brought two loaves of ordinary bread baked from the new wheat, and, alone among Israel’s offerings, baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17). The whole feast was firstfruits: a handful brought in early as the guarantee that the fields were coming. Before the day is out, three thousand people will be brought in as the firstfruits of a harvest that is still coming. Later Jewish tradition also linked the feast with the giving of the law at Sinai, and if that link was already known, the fit is exact: on the day Israel remembered the law written on stone, the Spirit came to write it on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3).

Counted from an empty tomb. And notice where the counting began. The fifty days ran from the waving of that first sheaf in Passover week (Leviticus 23:10–16), and that year Passover week was the week of the cross and the empty tomb. Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the harvest feast that falls fifty days later is the day his harvest begins to come in. John had already said that the Spirit could not be given until Jesus was glorified (John 7:39), and Peter will say before nine o’clock is long past that it is the exalted Jesus who has poured him out (2:33). Pentecost is counted from Easter, because it is the risen Lord’s gift.

They were all together in one place. Probably the hundred and twenty (1:15), perhaps in the upper room, perhaps somewhere in the temple courts, where a crowd could gather quickly. Luke does not say, and the point is not the building but the company: all of them, together, where obedience had put them.

Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind. Then the sound. Luke, who is careful with words, does not write that a wind came. He writes that there came a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and he marks the comparison as a comparison. Nothing was blowing; what filled the house was the noise of a gale without the gale. In both Hebrew (ruach) and Greek (pneuma) the same word can mean wind, breath and spirit, and Jesus had compared the Spirit to the wind that blows where it wishes (John 3:8). The word Luke chooses here, pnoē, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7 for the breath God breathed into a figure of dust until it became a living man. Ezekiel had watched the breath come into a valley of bones until they stood up, an exceedingly great army (Ezekiel 37:9–14). The same breath is in this room, and what is about to stand up is the church.

And it filled the entire house where they were sitting. Notice the order. It filled the house, and then, in the next verse, the people. God takes the building before he takes the men in it. The glory cloud had once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the temple (1 Kings 8:10–11); now God’s presence fills his new temple, which is his people.

They were sitting. The last thing to see is what the hundred and twenty were doing when it happened. They were sitting. Ten days earlier they had been told to stay in the city and wait (1:4), and they had done that and nothing else: no campaign, no technique, no working up of atmosphere. Whatever else Pentecost is, it is not something anybody in that room produced. Hold onto that if you have been told the Spirit’s work can be triggered by sufficient intensity, have tried it, and concluded that the failure must be yours. It cannot be triggered. It can only be received, in the place obedience has put you, on a morning God has already circled on a calendar you have not been shown.

Should my church pray for another Pentecost? Not for a repeat of this day. Pentecost was the once-for-all arrival of the Spirit to dwell in the church, as the cross was the once-for-all sacrifice, and it no more needs repeating than Calvary does. The Spirit came and has never left. But you may and should pray for what Acts itself goes on to show: that the Spirit already given would fill his people afresh, make them bold, and bring many to Christ (4:29–31). Church history is full of seasons when God did exactly that, through the ordinary preaching of the gospel. Pray for those. Just do not imagine the Spirit is absent until something dramatic happens.

In a sentence. On the day of Pentecost, when they were all together, a sound like a violent wind suddenly came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting.

On a Tuesday. If you have been trying to work up spiritual life by effort and intensity, stop and notice that the hundred and twenty were sitting down when God came. Put yourself where obedience puts you: in the word, in prayer, with God’s people. Then let God be God. And if your church feels dry, do not reach first for a new technique. Pray, together, for the Spirit who has already been given to do what only he can do.

For worship. The first Adam received the breath of God into his dust, and lost the life it gave him. The last Adam went down into death for those who had lost it, and rose to become a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). On this morning the breath that once came down on Eden’s dust comes from his throne, and a room of frightened disciples stands up alive. The wind of the Spirit still blows where it wills, and wherever it blows it carries the life of the risen Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost (“fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, celebrating the wheat harvest. Wind and breath picture the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Weeks

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.

Divided tongues as of fire appeared to them. Fire in Scripture is where God is and where God may not be touched: the bush that burned and was not consumed (Exodus 3:2), the mountain wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18), the fire that fell on Carmel, the coal from the altar at Isaiah’s mouth. Every one of them is a fire kept at a distance, or a fire that would have killed a man who came nearer. Here it comes down and settles on people’s heads, and nobody dies. John the Baptist had promised that the coming one would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). The whole gospel is in that picture: the fire that could not be approached has come to rest on the very thing it should have consumed. And the fire is as of fire, like fire, shaped like tongues: tongues for speaking.

And rested on each one of them. Two details in the sentence carry a great deal. The first is divided. Fire is the one thing that can be shared without being lessened; light a hundred candles from a single flame and the flame you started with is no smaller. The Spirit is not being rationed out in portions, a larger share for the apostles and a thinner one for everybody else. The second is each one of them. In the old covenant the Spirit came on the man with the office: on Moses, on Bezalel to design the tabernacle, on Gideon, on Samson, on Saul, on David. Never on everybody. Now the flame settles on a fisherman, on Mary, on brothers who had once thought Jesus out of his mind, on many whose names Luke does not record. Moses had said out loud that he wished it were so: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:29). It took some fourteen centuries, and it happened on a Sunday morning in a borrowed room. Every believer receives the Spirit (v. 38).

And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. Filled means controlled and empowered, and Luke uses the word again and again for being empowered to speak (4:8, 31; 13:9).

And began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. The Greek word for tongues (glōssai) is the same word Luke has just used for the tongues of fire; the sign was shaped like the gift it announced. And the gift itself is unambiguous in this chapter: other tongues (heterais glōssais) means other languages, real, existing, human languages, because the crowd outside identifies them and says so three times (vv. 6, 8, 11). Nobody here is in a trance. They are speaking the languages of Egypt and Rome and Parthia. And here is the reversal of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9). There God confused the languages and scattered people in judgment; here he gives languages to gather the nations in grace.

The fire he longed to cast. Luke had heard Jesus speak of this fire, and of what it would cost him. I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! (Luke 12:49–50). The baptism he meant was his death. Interpreters read the fire of that saying in more than one way, but whatever else it is, it is fire that only he could cast, and only after he had passed through that baptism. Seven weeks after the cross the fire falls, and it falls from him (2:33). The flames on those heads are the answer to his longing, and the price of them was paid on a hill outside the city.

Is this the gift Paul discusses at Corinth? The two are not obviously identical. What happens here is understood instantly by native speakers; what happens at Corinth needs an interpreter and is unintelligible to the hearer without one (1 Corinthians 14:2). Some conclude they are two gifts sharing a name. Others, more probably, take them as one gift in two settings: a genuine language is a sign to the man who owns it and undecipherable noise to everyone else, and there were no Parthians in the Corinthian assembly. The text does not settle it, and a reader is allowed to leave it unsettled.

Where Christians differ: tongues today. Pentecostals and charismatics teach that tongues continue today, often as a prayer language, and some that it is the sign of Spirit baptism. Verdict: the tongues of Pentecost were known languages, a sign that the gospel was for every nation. Tongues and other sign gifts served to confirm the apostolic message in the founding era (Hebrews 2:3–4; 1 Corinthians 14:22), and the church’s historic testimony is that they ceased. This is the cessationist position, held charitably: we gladly acknowledge that many charismatic believers love Christ deeply. The Spirit himself, and his saving and sanctifying work, continue in full.

Is this the baptism in the Spirit that Pentecostal Christians teach? Pentecostal teaching describes a second experience after conversion, marked by tongues. But Pentecost was the once-for-all outpouring of the Spirit on the church, promised by Jesus (1:5). From now on, every believer receives the Spirit when he believes: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Those who were added later this same day received the gift of the Spirit on repentance and faith (v. 38), and Luke records no tongues among the three thousand.

A test Scripture will not carry. What should not be left unsettled is the pastoral use this verse is put to. It is regularly held over believers as the test of whether the Spirit is truly in them. Scripture will not carry that. Paul asks the Corinthians, in a run of questions built so that the answer to every one of them is no: do all speak with tongues? (1 Corinthians 12:30). He says so to a church that prized the gift above everything. A Christian who has never spoken a syllable of another language is not standing outside anything; he lacks nothing of the Spirit. And the traffic runs both ways: the same chapter forbids the contempt that says I have no need of you.

What do I say to a Christian friend who speaks in tongues? Begin by remembering that he is your brother, and that the things you share, Christ crucified and risen, the authority of Scripture, salvation by grace, are vastly greater than this difference. You can tell him honestly why you believe the sign gifts served the founding of the church and have ceased, and point him to what Acts 2 shows: known languages, declaring God’s mighty works, understood by hearers. But do not mock or question his faith. Ask him what the experience means to him, and listen. Agree together that every gift must build up others and point to Christ (1 Corinthians 14:12), and that love is greater than any gift (1 Corinthians 13). Then pray together. That kind of conversation honours the Spirit far more than winning the argument.

As the Spirit gave them utterance. Luke, for his part, tells us plainly what the fire was for, and it is not an experience. The first recorded act of the Spirit in the church is to make ordinary people talk about God to strangers, out loud, in the street, in words the strangers can understand.

In a sentence. Tongues like fire appeared and rested on each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit gives speech for Christ. You will not speak Parthian today, but you will speak to someone, and the Spirit who filled the mouths of fishermen is in you. Ask him to fill your mouth with the gospel. And if you have ever been made to feel second-class because you have not had a particular experience, put the feeling down: the flame rested on each one, and it has rested on you.

For worship. The God who scattered the nations at Babel has begun, in one morning, to gather them back in their own tongues, and every tongue is being gathered for one confession. The day is coming when every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11). The tongues of fire on a hundred and twenty heads were the first flames of that day: Galilean mouths given foreign words so that the nations might hear, in their own speech, the name that every speech on earth will one day honour.
verseByVerse.note: Fire often signals God’s presence.

parallels.desc: the LORD descended on it in fire

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.

Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. The word Luke uses of these men, dwelling, does not mean visiting. He has a separate word for visitors and uses it five verses later of the Romans. These are residents: Jews born in Parthia or Egypt or Cappadocia who had come back and settled. The Jewish population outside the land, the Dispersion, may have numbered several million across the Roman and Parthian empires, and huge numbers came for the pilgrim feasts. A great many had come home to die.
