It was the deep desire of Diaspora Jews to be buried in the land, and the hills around Jerusalem were quarried with the tombs of men who had crossed an empire in old age to lie there. On this particular morning some of those men, who had organised the whole last chapter of their lives around a grave, stood in a street and heard, in the language they had learned as children, that a man had been raised from the dead.

Devout men. Devout (eulabeis) is Luke’s word for a certain kind of serious Israelite: God-fearing, careful, pious. He uses it of old Simeon waiting in the temple for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and later of the men brave enough to bury Stephen (8:2). These are not sightseers at a festival. They are the people who had been waiting.

The multitude came together, and they were bewildered. Then the sound draws a crowd, and the crowd is bewildered. The Greek verb is the one the Greek Old Testament uses at Babel, where the LORD confused the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9). Luke has reached for Babel’s own word and turned it inside out. At Babel men were thrown into confusion because they suddenly could not understand one another. Here they are thrown into confusion because they suddenly can. The same bewilderment, running the other way.

Because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. And it is a specific bewilderment. They are not staggered by volume or spectacle. They are staggered by intelligibility: each man is hearing his own language, his dialektos, his native dialect. Some suggest the miracle happened in the ears rather than the mouths, but verse 4 has already settled it: the disciples began to speak in other tongues. God did not adjust fifteen nationalities of hearing. He gave a hundred and twenty Galileans fifteen nationalities of speech.

God crosses the room. Consider what that decision discloses about him. He could have done this in Hebrew, the language of the covenant, and required every nation to come and learn it, which is what most religions of that world required of anyone who wanted to approach. He did the exact opposite. The first sermon of the Christian era was delivered in the languages people count money in, swear in when they drop something, and sing over their children at night. He had already done it once, at far greater cost. The eternal Word did not wait for us to climb up into the speech of heaven; he took flesh, learned to talk at his mother’s knee, and spoke the Aramaic of Galilean villages. Pentecost carries the logic of the incarnation into every tongue: the Son who came down into one human language now sends the news of it down into all of them. From the first morning of the church, God has been the one who crosses the room.

Why does God care which language people hear him in? Because he wants to be understood, not merely obeyed. A message in a borrowed language can be followed with the mind; a message in your mother tongue reaches the heart. God’s purpose is not only to save individuals but to gather worshippers from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9), and he does not ask them to become culturally Jewish, or English, or anything else first. That is why the church has always translated the Scriptures rather than requiring people to learn a sacred language, and why missionaries still learn languages with a few thousand speakers. Every translation is a small Pentecost.

In a sentence. Devout Jews from every nation were living in Jerusalem, and when they heard the sound, a crowd gathered, bewildered because each heard the disciples speaking his own language.

On a Tuesday. Think of a neighbour or colleague whose first language is not yours, or whose world is very different from your own. God did not wait for the nations to come to him on his terms; he went out into the street and spoke their language. Ask how you might do something similar: learn their story, use words they understand, cross the room.

For worship. How kind is the Lord who will not be known only in a foreign accent. By the lake he called fishermen in their own Galilean speech, and on this morning he called a Parthian in Parthian and an Egyptian in the words his mother had sung to him. He is the Good Shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and he does not call them in a language they must strain to follow. The voice that reaches a sinner through the gospel is never the voice of a stranger. It is the voice of the one who made his tongue.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews born abroad settled in Jerusalem, and huge numbers came as pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?”

Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? The crowd’s objection is an accent, and everyone in that street knew what a Galilean sounded like. The northern pronunciation was a standing joke in Judea; Galileans were said to swallow their gutturals so badly that a hearer could not always tell which word was meant. It was the accent of the provinces: fishing villages, small farms, no great rabbinic schools within a day’s walk. That makes it all the more astonishing.

The accent that once betrayed him. Which makes the identity of the man about to do the talking almost unbearable. Some fifty days before this, in a high priest’s courtyard, a bystander looked at Peter and said that his accent betrayed him (Matthew 26:73), and he swore he had never met the man. The accent that exposed him as a coward is the accent now filling a public square with the resurrection. God did not give Peter a new voice. He gave him a new message and sent him back out with the same voice that had denied it, into the same city, to be identified by the same sound.

The first Galilean. And the accent was not only Peter’s. Jesus grew up in Nazareth and will have spoken as Galileans spoke. When Pilate heard Galilee mentioned at the trial, he asked whether the man was a Galilean (Luke 23:6), and the Pharisees were sure that no prophet arises from Galilee (John 7:52). The region they dismissed was the region Isaiah had named: in the latter time the LORD would make glorious Galilee of the nations, and the people who walked in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2). When God put the languages of the nations into Galilean mouths, he was honouring the despised country of his Son, and the scorn the crowd aimed at the disciples had first been aimed at him.

The disqualifications we hold against ourselves. Anyone who has kept quiet about Christ because of how they sound should sit with that for a moment. The disqualification this crowd cannot get past is a regional accent. The disqualification most believers privately hold against themselves is of precisely that order: not enough education, the wrong background, a stammer, a criminal record, a voice that goes thin exactly when it matters. The council will lodge the same complaint a few weeks later, that these are uneducated, common men, and will stumble on the answer without meaning to: they recognised that they had been with Jesus (4:13).

What it does not mean. What must not be drawn out of it is the sneer’s mirror image, that learning is a hindrance and ignorance a qualification. Luke writes some of the most polished Greek in the New Testament. The man who will do more preaching than anyone else in this book was trained under Gamaliel. The point is not that God prefers the untaught; it is that he is not confined by the paperwork, and that on this morning a set of credentials which mattered enormously in that street abruptly stopped mattering at all.

How is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? Literally, the language in which we were born. Most of these men could have traded in Greek or Aramaic, but they hear the gospel in their mother tongue, the language of the heart, and this is the root of the long Christian work of Bible translation.

Amazed and astonished. Luke stacks two verbs on the crowd. The first is the word he uses of Jairus and his wife when their dead daughter sat up (Luke 8:56). That is where the chapter stands by verse 8: several thousand religious, sober, widely travelled men in a street at nine in the morning with no category left to put the thing in. It is exactly the right condition in which to hear a sermon.

Should I support Bible translation, and why does it matter if most people speak a trade language? Yes, and it matters for the reason this verse shows. People can do business in a second language and still hear God as a foreigner. Hundreds of millions of people still have no complete Bible in the language they think and pray in. Supporting translation, by prayer, giving, or going, is joining the work God began on this morning. And at home it means taking care to explain the gospel in plain words, not church jargon, to people who do not share your background.

In a sentence. Amazed, they asked how these Galileans could be speaking, so that each heard in his own native language.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you think disqualifies you from speaking about Christ: your accent, your education, your past, your nerves. Then remember Peter’s accent, and speak anyway.

For worship. There is a man at the right hand of God who once spoke with a northern country accent, and he is not ashamed of the voices of his people. He chose the voice that had denied him to announce his resurrection. He chooses stammering tongues, thin voices and plain speech, and he fills them with his own name. The Lord of glory took a voice the world mocked, and now, from a throne no accent can reach, he puts his praise into the mouths of the people the world dismisses.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,

Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia. Luke’s list repays being read as a map rather than as a catalogue. The list runs roughly from east to west. He begins in the far east, outside the empire altogether. Parthia, beyond the Euphrates in what is now Iran, was the one great power Rome never managed to conquer; for a man standing in Jerusalem the Euphrates was the edge of the known world, and Luke opens his list on the wrong side of it. Then Media and Elam and Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers that had been Babylon, and those names are exile addresses. When Assyria carried the northern tribes away it settled them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), and Babylon later took Judah. Centuries later the descendants of the deported are standing in a Jerusalem street. They had trickled back over centuries, and on this morning God gathers a scattering that history never repaired, and preaches to it.

Judea. Judea sits in the middle of the list, between Mesopotamia and Cappadocia, which is strange in a roll-call of foreign parts and stranger still as geography. The simplest explanation is that Luke is tracing the arc of the Fertile Crescent from east to north-west and Judea lies on the arc, perhaps meaning the greater Judea of David’s day, named as territory rather than as a foreign country. Or he includes it to say that even the locals heard their own speech. Either way, a forger would have tidied it.

Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia. From there the list sweeps north and west through Asia Minor, modern Turkey, which is very nearly the route Paul will spend the second half of this book walking. Years later Peter writes a letter to the exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1). Some of the people he addressed may first have heard the gospel in this street.

Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene. Then south to Egypt, whose Jewish community at Alexandria was large enough to have produced its own Greek translation of the Scriptures, and along the coast of North Africa to Cyrene, whose Jews turn up again in this book both as opponents (6:9) and as the men who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (11:20). One of them had carried a cross up a hill outside this city seven weeks earlier: Simon of Cyrene (Luke 23:26).

And visitors from Rome. And the list ends at Rome, which is where Luke’s own second volume ends (28:16). He names his destination on page two. These visitors may well have been among the beginnings of the church in Rome, to which Paul later wrote.

A promise kept in the wrong order. Underneath the geography a promise is being kept in the wrong order. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8). On the first morning, the end of the earth has come to Jerusalem. Before a single missionary has packed a bag, the gospel is being heard by men who will carry it home to Parthia and Egypt and Rome; when Paul writes to the Roman church years later, it is a congregation he did not plant. Somebody in this street was listening.

Gathered to the root of Jesse. Behind the exile addresses stands a promise about the Messiah. Isaiah said that the root of Jesse would stand as a signal for the peoples, and that the Lord would recover the remnant of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Elam and from Shinar, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:10–12). Every one of those names is in Luke’s list or behind it. And John tells us why Jesus died: to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad (John 11:52). This morning the scattered stand in one street, and they are not gathered to a king in a palace. They are gathered to a crucified and risen son of David, who is himself the signal raised for the nations.

Why does a list of places matter to me? Because it is a map of God’s faithfulness and a preview of his plan. Every name on it was a place where God’s people had been scattered by judgment, exile or trade, and every one of them is being gathered back to hear of Christ. If you are a Gentile believer, your own people are somewhere on the long extension of this list, and it reached you because God meant it to. The list also reminds us that the gospel is not owned by any one culture. It belonged to Parthians and Libyans before it belonged to Europeans, and it belongs today to the churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America as much as to anyone.

In a sentence. They came from Parthia, Media, Elam, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, and Rome.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the nations today, by name. Choose one of the places in this list, find out what the church there is facing now, and pray for it. Many of these lands, once full of churches, now have very few believers. The God who gathered them once can do it again.

For worship. The God who scattered Israel for her sins sent the scattered home to hear of her Messiah, and turned the map of her exile into the map of his mission. This street was only the first gathering. Jesus has said that the Son of Man will send out his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven (Mark 13:27). No place on earth is too far from him, and no scattering is too old for him to gather.
verseByVerse.note: The list runs roughly from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates) to west (Rome): the whole Jewish world scattered among the nations.

parallels.desc: the table of nations
Babel, where languages were confused

verseByVerse.quote: both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.

Both Jews and proselytes. The list ends with two words that widen it past nationality altogether. Proselytes were Gentiles who had gone the whole distance into Judaism, and the distance was considerable. A man born in Rome or Cyrene who wanted in did not merely change his opinions. He renounced the gods his family had honoured for generations. He was circumcised as an adult. He was immersed. He brought an offering. And having paid all of it he remained, in many eyes, a second-tier member of the covenant. Such men are in this crowd, hearing the wonders of God in their own language, and within twenty years the church will meet in this same city to decide whether Gentiles need any of that machinery at all (15:1–11). The door they crawled through is about to be taken off its hinges.

Cretans and Arabians. Then Cretans and Arabians, island and desert, west and east, the far margins added as if to say the list could go on. Paul would later leave Titus in Crete (Titus 1:5) and spend time himself in Arabia (Galatians 1:17).

We hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God. And then the sentence that tells us what all these languages were being used to say. The mighty works (ta megaleia) are the great things God has done. The phrase belongs to the Old Testament’s language for the great things God did in bringing Israel out of Egypt: his mighty hand, the signs, the sea (Deuteronomy 11:2–4). The first Christian speech in history was not a body of moral instruction and it was not a report of religious feelings. It was a recital of things God had done, in the same register Israel used for the exodus, now attached to a tomb outside a city wall. Tongues were not gibberish but praise and proclamation.

The exodus he accomplished at Jerusalem. Luke has prepared us for this. On the mountain of transfiguration, he tells us, Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The word for departure is exodos. Moses had led Israel out through the sea; Jesus led his people out through death itself, out of the bondage of sin and the grip of the grave, and came up on the other side alive. The great deed of God that filled the street was the exodus his Son had accomplished in this very city seven weeks before.

News before advice. That order has never changed, and it is worth testing yourself against. Christianity is first news and only afterwards advice. Subtract the announcement, suppose God has not in fact done anything, suppose nothing happened in Jerusalem that spring, and what is left is a philosophy of life. This is not to say a believer’s own story does not matter; Paul tells his three times in this book. But notice what actually filled the street on the first morning. Not a hundred and twenty people describing what had happened to them. A hundred and twenty people describing what God had done.

What are the mighty works of God I should be telling? Start with the ones the apostles told. God created the world and made us for himself. We turned away and came under his judgment. God sent his Son, who lived the life we should have lived, died on the cross in the place of sinners, bearing their punishment, and rose bodily from the dead. He has ascended and reigns, and he has poured out his Spirit. He will come again to judge the living and the dead. Everyone who turns from sin and trusts him is forgiven and made new. Your own story fits inside that one: tell what God has done for you, but make sure the cross and the empty tomb are in it.

In a sentence. Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs, all heard them telling in their own languages the mighty works of God.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone today, in plain words, the mighty works of God. Not first your opinions about morality, or how church makes you feel, but what God has done in Christ. If you cannot yet put it into three or four sentences, write them down tonight and practise them.

For worship. It is a strange and glorious way for God to introduce himself to the nations. He does not open with a demand. He opens by reciting his own acts of rescue, in fifteen languages at once, to men who had crossed an empire in order to worship him at a distance and had no idea he had come out into the street to meet them. The first thing the nations heard about God in their own tongues was not what he required of them but what he had done for them, and at the heart of it was a death his Son had died for them and a grave his Son had left empty.
verseByVerse.note: Proselytes were Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

parallels.desc: Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.”

And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, What does this mean? Every crowd that has ever heard the gospel is inside these two sentences. The first is a real question. These men have no explanation and they say so, and by saying so they hold a door open. It is the right question, and the whole of the rest of the book is an answer to it; Peter begins answering it in the next verse. It is also, in miniature, the difference between the two halves of this crowd: one group has run out of explanations and admits it, the other has run out of explanations and invents one.

But others mocking said, They are filled with new wine. Because the second sentence is not an argument. Notice how poor an explanation it is. The word is gleukos, sweet wine, the juice of a fresh pressing, and Pentecost falls in late spring, with the grape harvest still months away. Nor was there any drinking to be had at that hour on a feast morning, when observant men did not eat or drink before the morning prayer, which is precisely the point Peter makes in his first breath. Perhaps those who heard only languages they did not understand thought it was drunken babble; Paul later warns that uninterpreted tongues make outsiders think believers are out of their minds (1 Corinthians 14:23). But the mockers were not weighing evidence. They grabbed the nearest available insult and did not stop to check whether it fitted the season.

How the quick dismissal works. That is generally how the closed dismissal works. It does not need to be true. It only needs to arrive fast enough to spare a man from standing there with no explanation, which is an uncomfortable place to stand. Anyone who has tried to speak about Christ at work has met the sentence that comes too quickly to be a real reply, that is fine for you, people believe what they need to believe, and has felt how efficiently it closes a conversation that had not yet begun.

What the sneer concedes. There is one thing the sneer concedes without meaning to. Drunkenness was the closest thing these men could find to what they were watching. It looked like people who had stopped guarding themselves. Paul later plays the comparison back the other way and tells the Ephesians not to get drunk with wine but to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), as though the two sit on the same shelf and only one of them delivers what it advertises.

Called a drunkard before them. And the sneer is not new. It had been used on their Master. Jesus himself had said what his generation made of him: the Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard (Luke 7:34). The world that dismissed the Lord with a joke about wine dismisses his Spirit-filled people with the same joke, which is exactly what he told them to expect: a servant is not greater than his master (John 15:20). There is an honour hidden in it. The church on its first morning is mocked in the very words that had been thrown at Jesus, because the life in it is unmistakably his.

Nobody beyond the next twenty minutes. And here is what should stop any believer writing off the scoffer at the back. Peter preaches to both halves of this crowd without distinguishing between them, and by evening three thousand of them have been baptised. The arithmetic makes it very likely that some of the men shouting about new wine at nine in the morning were in the water before dark. Nobody in that street was beyond the reach of the next twenty minutes. The gospel has a long history of being sneered at by people who go on to preach it.

What should I do when someone mocks my faith? Do not answer mockery with mockery, and do not take it as the last word. Peter’s response was calm: he corrected the misunderstanding in a sentence and then told them about Jesus. You can do the same. A light, honest reply, a question back, or a simple statement of what you believe and why, often does more than a long argument. Be gentle and respectful (1 Peter 3:15–16). Remember that the mocker may be closer to faith than he looks, and pray for him by name.

In a sentence. All were amazed and asked what this meant, but some mocked that they were drunk on new wine.

On a Tuesday. Some will always mock God’s work. Let it not stop you, and let it not stop you hoping for the mocker. Think of the person who last dismissed your faith with a quick line. Pray for him today. He may yet be in the water before dark.

For worship. On the cross, with the mocking going on around him, Jesus prayed, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). That prayer did not end at Golgotha. Seven weeks later his Spirit is poured out, the world calls it drunkenness, and the answer from heaven is not fire but a sermon, an offer of pardon to everyone standing there, scoffers included. The mercy that prayed on the cross preaches in the street. His grace is not frightened off by a sneer, because it was never earned by courtesy in the first place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter stood up with the Eleven and addressed the crowd. These men are not drunk, he said; it is only nine in the morning. This is what the prophet Joel foretold: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all people; sons and daughters will prophesy, young men see visions and old men dream dreams, and even slaves, men and women, will receive the Spirit and prophesy. There will be wonders above and signs below, blood, fire and smoke; the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood before the great day of the Lord. And everyone who calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Peter then spoke of Jesus of Nazareth, whom God had clearly approved by miracles, wonders and signs done among them, as they knew. This man was handed over according to God’s settled plan and foreknowledge, and they killed him by having lawless men nail him to a cross. But God raised him, freeing him from death’s agony, because death could not keep its hold on him.
verseByVerse.theology:
How Peter Reads the Psalms

Peter's argument from Psalm 16 is not proof-texting; it is a method, and he shows his working. David wrote you will not let your Holy One see corruption. David died, was buried, and his tomb was a landmark a short walk from where Peter was standing. Therefore the words say more than David's own life could pay, and they are prophecy — and the man they fit is the one whose tomb is empty. He does the same with Psalm 110: David did not ascend into the heavens, so the psalm in which David hears the LORD speak to my Lord must be about somebody else. This is the way the risen Christ himself had taught them to read on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27, 44). The Reformed tradition has taken this sermon as the pattern for reading the whole Old Testament — not squeezing Christ out of texts that will not hold him, but recognising that the Scriptures were written by a Spirit who knew where the story was going and left the shape of it in the words.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who were personally implicated — this Jesus whom you crucified — and he said it to their faces in the seventh week after they had done it. He did not soften the charge in order to get a hearing, and three thousand of them were baptised before dark. Now: A gospel that never implicates the hearer never has anything to forgive him for. The reason this crowd asked what shall we do is that Peter had left them with something that needed doing. Preaching which manages to be about sin in general, committed by people in general, will produce interest, and will not produce that question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day.

But Peter, standing with the eleven. Three details before the sermon starts carry more than they look. Peter is not a solo act, and Luke has counted: eleven beside him makes twelve, the number restored at the end of chapter 1 when the lot fell on Matthias (1:26). The apostolic band is complete and standing together on its first working day: one voice for the twelve. What follows is testimony, not personality.

Lifted up his voice and addressed them. Lifted up his voice is Old Testament language for a solemn public declaration (Judges 9:7). It is also, quite literally, what he had to do: preaching to thousands in the open air meant shouting until the throat tore. And addressed (apephthenxato) is the same word as utterance in verse 4: Peter speaks out boldly, as one moved by the Spirit.

Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem. Note whom he addresses: the settled residents of verse 5, the Diaspora that had come home, alongside the people of the city. He is speaking to the people who had spent their lives waiting, and he opens by telling them the waiting is over.

For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. Then the defence, which is almost dry. The third hour was about nine in the morning, and the point is sharper than a modern reader hears, because on a feast day devout Jews took nothing at all before the morning sacrifice and prayer. What the mockers alleged would have been an act of impiety on a holy day in a city full of people who would have noticed. He disposes of the charge in a sentence and never returns to it. It is not what he came to talk about; it is only the door the mockers accidentally held open for him.

The same voice. But stay with the man a moment longer. This is the same voice. Some fifty days ago, in this city, under pressure from a servant girl with no authority over anybody, it said I do not know the man, three times, the last time with oaths. It is now saying, at the top of its range, to the assembled population of the city and within earshot of the authorities who arranged the execution, that the man they killed is alive and is Lord. Between those two mornings Peter attended no course. Nor did he simply resolve to do better; he had already tried that, had promised out loud that he would die first, and had folded inside a few hours. What came between was the risen Christ, and then Pentecost.

Not more determination. The standard advice to a frightened Christian is to try harder, and Peter’s own history refutes it. He had determination in quantity, and at the point of testing it was worth nothing. What he lacked was the Spirit; and when the Spirit came, the courage came with him, not as a technique to be mastered but as a Person to be received. The church’s boldness has the same source this morning that it had at nine o’clock on that one, which is an enormous relief to anybody who has already found out what his own resolve is worth.

I am timid by nature. Can the Spirit really make me bold? Yes, though boldness may not look like Peter shouting to thousands. In Acts it usually means speaking plainly about Jesus when it would be easier to stay silent, and the Spirit gives it to quiet people as well as loud ones. Ask for it directly; the church prayed exactly this, grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness (4:29), and God answered. Then take one small step in the direction of courage, a sentence, an invitation, an honest answer, and expect his help in the step rather than before it. Remember too that Peter’s past did not disqualify him. Yours does not disqualify you.

In a sentence. Peter stood with the eleven and spoke to the crowd, telling them to listen, for these people were not drunk, since it was only nine in the morning.

On a Tuesday. Where have you been relying on your own resolve to be faithful, and failing? Stop promising God you will do better, and ask him for his Spirit. Then go back to the place where you failed, as Peter did, and speak there.

For worship. On the night of the denials, Luke tells us, the Lord turned and looked at Peter across the courtyard (Luke 22:61). That look did not end the friendship; it began the restoration. The Lord who looked at him then now speaks through him, from the throne, in the same city and at the top of the same voice. He did not replace the apostle who denied him. He kept him, and filled him, and made him the first preacher of the resurrection. Our Lord does not need strong men. He makes weak men strong, and the glory of it is his.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour was about 9 a.m. — far too early for drunkenness.

parallels.desc: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:

But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel. These few words are the hinge of the sermon. This is that. Peter’s first move is not to explain the phenomenon, or defend it, or invite anyone to admire it. It is to open the Bible and say that this was on the schedule. Pentecost is not a strange new thing but the fulfilment of what God promised through Joel centuries earlier. Nothing new has happened. Something promised has happened. And that is the first principle of all true spiritual experience: the Spirit’s work is always in line with Scripture, because he is its author.

A book about locusts. It is worth knowing which book he has reached into, because Joel is not the obvious place to go on a morning of glory. Joel is about locusts. A real swarm had come through a real country and stripped it: what the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten, wave after wave of them, the vine dried up, the fig tree languishing, the grain offering cut off from the house of the LORD, the priests in mourning and the cattle groaning because there was no pasture. The farmers were ruined. Out of that ruin God makes the promise everybody knows: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). And immediately after the promise of the restored years comes the promise of the Spirit.

The years the locust has eaten. That is what Peter reaches for. The outpouring this crowd is watching is the sequel to a promise made to people who had lost everything, and it is the sign that God means to put the years back. Anyone who has lost years, to an illness, to a marriage that came apart, to a decade of his own stupidity, is reading a promise addressed to exactly that condition. The Spirit is not given first to the flourishing. He is promised to a field that has been eaten bare, as the down payment on a harvest that is coming back.

This is that, but not all of it. One honest qualification is needed here, because Peter is about to quote a paragraph containing blood and fire and a darkened sun, none of which happened that morning. This is that does not mean the prophecy was used up before breakfast. It means the age Joel described has begun. Scripture speaks of the last days as a single stretch running from the coming of Christ to his return, and Peter is standing at the front of it, quoting the whole span because the era has opened, not because it has closed. The cosmic signs belong to that same era, partly already seen and wholly certain to come.

A fisherman reading the prophets. What should not be lost in the mechanics is the sheer confidence of the move. A fisherman stands up in front of scholars and tells them what their own Scriptures are about, and he is not guessing. The risen Jesus had taught his disciples to read like this. Luke tells us that, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and then opened their minds to understand (24:45). So this is that is ultimately a sentence about Christ. Joel’s promise has landed this morning because the one it was waiting for has died, risen and been exalted, and the Spirit filling the street is the Spirit he has poured out (2:33).

How do I test a spiritual experience by Scripture? Ask what Peter asked: does this match what God has said? First, does it exalt Jesus Christ as he is presented in Scripture, crucified, risen and Lord (1 John 4:2–3; John 16:14)? Second, does it agree with the plain teaching of the Bible, or does it add to it or contradict it? Third, does it lead to holiness, love and humility, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), or to pride and division? An experience can be intense and still be mistaken; feelings are not the test. And if something is not taught in Scripture, you are not bound to seek it, however many people around you claim it.

In a sentence. Peter declared that this was what the prophet Joel had foretold.

On a Tuesday. Test every spiritual experience by Scripture. Peter’s first move was to open the Bible. Before you trust a dream, an impression, a powerful meeting or a persuasive voice, ask what God has written. And if you have lost years, read Joel 2 tonight, slowly. The promise of restored years was spoken to people exactly like you.

For worship. The God who promised to restore the years the locust had eaten kept his word by pouring out his Spirit, and nothing he did at Pentecost was improvised; it was written down centuries before by a prophet in a famine. And he gives more than Joel could have asked. In Christ he does not only hand back the lost years. He gives eternal life, an age that no locust can strip and no moth or rust can reach, and he gives it first to people whose fields had been eaten bare.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy.

And in the last days it shall be, God declares. Notice first the phrase you may misread: in the last days. Joel 2:28 has afterward; Peter, by the Spirit, interprets it as the last days, and declares them to have arrived at Pentecost. So in the Bible’s reckoning the last days are not only a short future window before the end; they are the whole gospel age, from Christ’s first coming to his return. In these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:2); it is the last hour (1 John 2:18); the end of the ages has come upon us (1 Corinthians 10:11). We have been living in the last days for two thousand years. Scripture does also speak of the days growing harder as the end nears (2 Timothy 3:1), a note dispensational interpreters rightly stress, but the era as a whole is already underway. The effect is urgency, not date-setting: we live in the final act of God’s story, awaiting only the King’s return.

Where Christians differ: when are the last days? Dispensational teaching usually places the last days chiefly in a future period connected with a restored national Israel, a seven-year tribulation and an earthly millennium, with the church age as a parenthesis. Verdict: Peter says the last days began at Pentecost, and the New Testament consistently treats the whole time between Christ’s first and second comings as the last days. This is the amillennial reading: Christ reigns now from heaven, the Spirit has been poured out, the gospel goes to the nations, and the next great event on God’s calendar is the return of Christ, the resurrection and the judgment. Faithful brothers read the prophetic timetable differently, and the difference should be held with patience.

The roll of the Spirit-bearers. Who had the Spirit of God under the old covenant? A very short roll, and nearly every name on it holds an office: Moses and the seventy elders, Bezalel to design the tabernacle, Othniel and Gideon and Samson, Saul and David, the prophets. Almost all of them men, almost all of them leaders, and the Spirit came upon them for the work and could depart again, which is precisely what David is terrified of when he begs God not to take his Holy Spirit from him (Psalm 51:11).

The last name on the roll. The roll ends with one more name, and it changes all the rest. At the Jordan the Spirit came down on Jesus (Luke 3:22) and, as John’s Gospel adds, remained on him (John 1:32); in Nazareth he read, the Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Luke 4:18), and said that the Scripture was fulfilled that day. Peter will later sum up his whole ministry in one phrase: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power (10:38). David feared losing the Spirit. The Son never could. And Pentecost is what happens when the anointed one is exalted: the Spirit who was given to him without measure (John 3:34) flows from him, the head, to all his people.

I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Now read Joel’s list against that. All flesh does not mean every individual without exception, but all kinds of people without distinction. Sons and daughters. Young men and old men. And then, so that the direction of travel cannot be mistaken, male servants and female servants: the word means slaves. The lowest person in the household, with no property, no standing, no vote in the synagogue and in most cases no name recorded anywhere on earth, is written into a promise about the Spirit of God. No social barrier keeps anyone from the Spirit (Galatians 3:28). And before long the promise will reach the Gentiles too (10:45).

What Peter adds. That change of afterward into the last days is the largest of three, and the other two run the same way. Where Joel says simply that God will pour out his Spirit, Peter inserts God declares, so that the sentence is signed. And where Joel’s line about the male and female servants ends without further comment, Peter adds four words, and they shall prophesy. This is not carelessness with a text. It is an apostle saying what the text turned out to mean, and refusing to let the slaves be dropped from the promise on the way past.

Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. In the Old Testament prophecy was rare. Now the Spirit-given knowledge of God and the ability to speak his truth is spread among all his people. Prophecy here, in the setting of this chapter, means speaking God’s word, declaring his mighty works (v. 11). The visions and dreams are poetic parallelism: all will know God directly, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34).

The daughters of Philip. Which raises a fair question: what does it mean that the daughters prophesy? Luke does not leave it hanging. He shows us four of them, the unmarried daughters of Philip the evangelist, prophesying at Caesarea (21:9), and a prophet named Agabus arriving at the same house. Whatever prophecy is in Acts, it plainly includes women. What this verse establishes, and establishes past argument, is that the gift of the Spirit is distributed with no regard whatever to sex, age or social rank. Whatever else is debated, that is not.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Charismatic Christians see ongoing prophecy as new words from God. Verdict: Joel’s promise is fulfilled in the Spirit given to all believers, who all know God and declare his word. In the apostolic era this included revelatory prophecy, which laid the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5). With the canon complete, the prophetic word continues in the Spirit-empowered proclamation of Scripture. Women as well as men proclaim God’s mighty works, while the office of elder and preaching in the gathered church belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7).

Do women, and men, still prophesy today? Joel’s promise was fulfilled at Pentecost: the Spirit is now poured out on all God’s people, men and women, young and old. Continuationists believe the gift of prophecy continues as a gift to be weighed by the church (1 Corinthians 14:29). The more likely reading is that prophecy as new revelation belonged to the founding of the church, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and has ceased with the completed Scriptures. What continues is the Spirit empowering every believer to speak of Christ (1:8): the mother teaching her children, the old man telling his grandson what God has done, the young woman explaining the gospel to a friend at work.

So what may a woman do with this gift? A great deal. She is filled with the same Spirit as any apostle. She may pray and speak God’s truth, tell the gospel to anyone, teach children and other women (Titus 2:3–5), explain the way of God more accurately, as Priscilla did with her husband to Apollos (18:26), counsel, encourage, serve and lead in many ministries. The New Testament restricts one thing: the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church belong to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). That restriction is about order in God’s household, not about worth or gifting, and it is never a licence for men to belittle or silence women. The Spirit came on the daughters as fully as on the sons.

The God who does not run short. Under the old covenant the Spirit came down on one man and Israel gathered round him. Under the new, God has moved into the whole house: the daughters, the old men who assumed their useful years were behind them, the slave girl in the kitchen, each with the same Spirit, entire and undivided, because the God who gives him does not run short.

In a sentence. Joel said that in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on all people: sons and daughters would prophesy, young men see visions, old men dream dreams, and even on slaves, men and women, he would pour out his Spirit.

On a Tuesday. You live in the last days, and the Spirit has been poured out on you. If you are old and think your usefulness is over, or young and think you are too inexperienced, or in a humble job and think God has no use for you, read the list again: old men, young men, servants. Speak of God’s mighty works to someone today.

For worship. Why should the Spirit of God come down on a slave girl in a Jerusalem kitchen? Because the Lord of glory first took the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7). He went to the lowest place in the household of humanity, and from the highest place in heaven he now pours out his Spirit on the lowest people in it. The last days have dawned, and the God who signed the promise has kept it to the letter: sons and daughters, old and young, slaves and free, all who belong to Christ, all filled with the same Spirit who rested on him.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!
Philip’s four daughters prophesied

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day.

I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below. Here is the difficulty every honest reader of this chapter runs into. Peter has just said this is that. He then quotes a paragraph about blood and fire and vapour of smoke, a sun turned to darkness and a moon turned to blood, and none of it had happened in Jerusalem that morning. The sun was up. The crowd could see one another’s faces. If the prophecy was fulfilled at nine o’clock, a third of it was visibly not. Notice first that Peter adds three words to Joel, above, below and signs, linking the passage to the signs Jesus did, which he names in verse 22. Three things go a long way toward resolving the difficulty.

The language of a world ending. The first is that this is simply how the prophets speak of the fall of a power. When Isaiah announces the end of Babylon he says the stars will not give their light and the sun will be dark at its rising (Isaiah 13:10). When he announces the end of Edom the skies roll up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4). When Ezekiel announces the end of Egypt, God covers the sun with a cloud and the moon does not give its light (Ezekiel 32:7). Babylon fell. Edom fell. Egypt was humbled. The sun came up through the whole of it. This is not failed prediction, and it is not a code to be broken; it is the settled idiom of Scripture for saying that a world is ending, which, for the people living inside it, is what the fall of a nation actually is. Jesus used the same language of the destruction of Jerusalem, which arrived inside the lifetime of some of the men standing in that street.

They had stood under a darkened sun. The second is that a piece of it had happened, and they had watched it. Some fifty days earlier, in this city, at midday, the sun’s light failed for three hours while a man died on a hill outside the wall (Luke 23:44–45). Peter is not describing something his hearers have never seen. He is quoting a prophecy about a darkened sun to people who had stood under one, gone home unsettled, and never been given a satisfactory account of it. Part of the reason this sermon lands as hard as it does may be that the crowd is being handed the meaning of something they had already survived.

Before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day. The third is the shape of the whole promise. The day of the Lord is the day of God’s judgment and salvation. With Christ’s first coming it has begun; with his return it will be complete. The whole age of the church lies between the outpouring of the Spirit and that great day, and Peter is standing at the front of it. He quotes Joel to the end of the paragraph because he is opening an era, not closing one. The signs belong to the era. So does the outpouring. So, above all, does the sentence he is driving toward, which is the next verse and the reason he quoted any of it. The rest of the cosmic shaking awaits the final day.

What it does not mean. What the passage will not bear is the industry that has grown up on top of it: the charts, the calculated dates, the eclipse tables, the recurring announcements that some particular sequence of blood moons has started a countdown. Every generation has produced men who were certain, and every one of them has been wrong, and the wreckage is not confined to their own embarrassment. The purpose Joel’s paragraph actually serves is stated in the line immediately after it. The signs are not a timetable to be decoded. They are a reason to call on the name of the Lord while there is still time to call.

Should I be worried when I hear about blood moons or world events as signs of the end? No. Wars, earthquakes, eclipses and disasters have filled every century, and Jesus said such things must take place but the end is not yet (Matthew 24:6). They remind us that this world is passing and that judgment is real. But they are not a code, and no one can read the date from them. The right response to any sign is the one Peter draws: call on the Lord, live faithfully, and tell others. A believer who knows Christ does not need to fear the day of the Lord, because the judge is his Saviour.

In a sentence. God said he would show wonders in heaven and signs on earth, blood, fire and smoke, with the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood, before the great day of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. The day of the Lord is coming. Live today in the light of it: not in fear, not in calculation, but in readiness. Is there anything in your life you would be ashamed to have him find you doing? Deal with it today. Is there anyone you would want to have warned? Speak to them.

For worship. Amos warned an Israel that longed for the day of the LORD what was in it: it is darkness, and not light (Amos 5:18). And at midday on a Friday the darkness of that day came down on one man. The Son of God stood under the judgement the great day will bring, and took its night into himself, so that for everyone who calls on him the day will dawn as light. The judge on the throne of that day will be the one who was judged in their place. There is no darker phrase in the prophets, and none that has been turned more gloriously into an invitation.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: darkness at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’

And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. This is the sentence the whole citation has been climbing toward, and Peter stops here. Joel goes on; Peter does not. He wanted this line, the climax of the quotation and the point of the sermon.

Everyone. Take the three parts in turn. Everyone: with no qualifier of nation, class, sex, age or record, and spoken over a crowd who had between them killed the Son of God.

Calls upon the name of the Lord. The single condition, and it is not a work, an achievement or a standard of behaviour; it is the noise a man makes when he has run out. To call on the Lord’s name is to appeal to him, trusting him for rescue. It is faith expressed in prayer.

Shall be saved. Not may be, not stands a better chance. Peter is quoting a promise, not proposing a scheme.

The name of the LORD, applied to Jesus. But there is something here that ought to stop a reader in his tracks, and it is easy to miss. In Joel it is the LORD in small capitals, the ESV’s sign for the covenant name of God, Yahweh, the name Israel would not say aloud. Peter quotes it; and fifteen verses later he tells the same crowd who the Lord is: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (v. 36). A verse about calling on the name of the God of Israel has just been applied to a Galilean tradesman who was executed outside the city seven weeks ago. To call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh.

Not a slip. Nor is it a slip in the excitement of a first sermon. Once you have seen the move it is everywhere in this book. Peter will say there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (4:12). Saul rides to Damascus with authority to bind all who call on your name, which by then is simply the ordinary description of a Christian (9:14), and at his own baptism is told to be washed, calling on his name (22:16). Paul, writing to Rome, quotes this very line of Joel and applies it to Jesus without pausing to justify himself (Romans 10:9–13). And Stephen dies praying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit: a Jewish monotheist, being executed for blasphemy, praying to Jesus with his last breath (7:59).

How the deity of Christ entered the church. There was no committee, no vote, no slow inflation of a human teacher into a god across three centuries, which is the story usually told. What happened is that Jewish monotheists, men who would sooner have died than pray to a creature, and some of whom did die, began praying to Jesus, and reached for the Old Testament’s texts about the LORD to explain why, within weeks of the resurrection. The doctrine was not invented at a council. It was already sitting in the way a fisherman quoted Joel on the morning the church was born.

What does calling on the name actually look like? It is not a formula and it is not a technique. It is what the tax collector did at the back of the temple when he would not even lift up his eyes, and beat his breast, and said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. No preparation, no cleaning himself up first, no promise of improvement, and he went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). A man who believes he must repair himself before he is entitled to call has the order exactly backwards; calling is what the unrepaired do. If you have never called on Christ, you can do it now, in your own words: Lord Jesus, I have sinned; you died and rose again; save me.

But if salvation is for everyone who calls, how does that fit with God’s choosing? Both are true, and Peter holds them together in this very sermon: the promise is for everyone, and it is for everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself (v. 39). The invitation is genuinely universal, and no one who calls on Christ will ever be turned away. At the same time, no one calls on him unless God first opens his heart (16:14). The two do not compete. God’s choosing is the reason anyone calls at all, and it never makes the offer insincere. You do not need to know whether you are chosen before you call. Call, and your calling will be the evidence that he chose you.

In a sentence. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

On a Tuesday. Call on the name of the Lord Jesus. Everyone who does is saved. Do it today about the sin you are ashamed of, the fear you cannot shake, the person you cannot forgive. And remember that the promise is for everyone: there is no one you know who is outside its reach.

For worship. The name the prophets would not pronounce has been given to a crucified Galilean, and in it the whole world is invited to call for mercy. Jesus is the LORD of Joel, the God of Israel in our flesh, and the promise has never failed: not one sinner who has called on him has been refused. The name the city shouted down at Golgotha is the name by which, seven weeks later, three thousand of its people called for mercy and were saved.
verseByVerse.note: In Joel “the Lord” is the LORD; Peter applies the name to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.

Men of Israel, hear these words. Now the sermon turns from explaining the morning to announcing the man.

Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God. Peter begins where his hearers already are. Jesus was a real man, from a real town, and God showed his approval of him publicly. Attested means publicly displayed, accredited, as a man’s credentials are produced in court. God had put his signature on this man in front of witnesses.

With mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know. He is not introducing a stranger. Jesus had worked in public, in their own country, within the last three years, and no one denied the miracles. And Peter appeals to the memory of a hostile crowd for confirmation, which is a dangerous way to preach unless it is true. Seven weeks after the events, in the city where they happened, a man tells several thousand people what they saw with their own eyes, and nobody laughs.

This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God. Then comes one of the most compressed sentences in the Bible: two claims about one event, welded together, with no attempt to soften either. The first phrase is worth its weight. Definite plan (hōrismenē boulē) is a fixed purpose; the participle is built on the verb for marking out a boundary, the root of our word horizon. The cross was not an accident or a tragedy that took God by surprise. It was not a contingency God accommodated after the fact; it lay inside a line drawn before the world was made (4:27–28; 1 Peter 1:20; Revelation 13:8). And foreknowledge (prognōsis) here is not God peering ahead and noticing what people would decide. When Scripture says God foreknows, he is not a spectator with unusually good eyesight; his foreknowing carries his settled purpose, not merely his advance information.

You crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. The second claim is left every bit as sharp. You crucified him: not events, not circumstances, not the system, but you. And by the hands of lawless men, the men without the law being the Romans, so that Peter distributes the guilt without diluting it. The Jerusalem crowd wanted it done; the empire’s soldiers did it; nobody in the transaction is a mere instrument and nobody’s hands are clean. God’s plan does not cancel human guilt. They did it freely and wickedly; God planned it for good. As Joseph said to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). This is the clearest statement in Scripture of how divine sovereignty and human responsibility relate.

Hold the two together. The moment they come apart something is lost. Take away the plan and the cross becomes a tragedy God salvaged, a rescue improvised after the worst had already happened, which is comfort of a very thin sort. Take away the guilt and the cross becomes theatre in which nobody is responsible, and there is nothing left for it to forgive. Scripture has kept them in one sentence since Isaiah, who watched God send Assyria as the rod of his anger against his own people, though the Assyrian did not so intend and his heart did not so think, and then announced that God would punish the king of Assyria for the arrogance of his heart (Isaiah 10:5–12). The Assyrian was doing God’s work and his own wickedness in the same act, and was judged for the second.

What it does not mean. Two guards are needed here, and both matter. This verse does not make God the author of sin, or say that he forced anyone to sin: Peter charges his hearers with murder in the same breath in which he says it was planned, and no preacher could do that if the real agent of the crime were God. Nor does it mean that the Jews are uniquely guilty. All of us, by our sins, put Christ there, and Gentiles and Jews together crucified him (4:27). The long and wicked history of Christians blaming the Jewish people for the death of Christ has no ground in this verse; Peter is speaking as a Jew to his own people, and offering them pardon within the hour. And this is not a sentence to be handed to a suffering person as a tidy explanation of what has happened to him, because Peter is not explaining a tragedy at all. He is announcing that the worst thing the human race has ever done is the thing God used to save it.

If God planned the cross, why did Jesus have to die at all? Because there was no other way to save sinners justly. God’s plan was not arbitrary. Our sin deserved God’s judgment, and God could not simply overlook it without ceasing to be just. So in love he planned that his own Son would bear our sin and its punishment in our place, that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The plan was the plan of a God who loved sinners enough to give his Son, and who is holy enough that only such a sacrifice would do. That is why the cross is both the greatest crime and the greatest gift.

There has never been a plan B. Which is where the comfort actually lies. If the murder of the Son of God did not fall outside the plan, nothing does. Whatever a reader has done that he believes has put him permanently beyond reach, and whatever has been done to him that looks like the end of every good purpose, is smaller than this and stands inside the same sovereignty. The cross was not plan B. There has never been a plan B.

In a sentence. Peter told the men of Israel that Jesus of Nazareth was approved by God through miracles they knew of, and was handed over by God’s fixed plan and foreknowledge, and they killed him by nailing him to a cross through lawless men.

On a Tuesday. Bring your hardest circumstance to this verse. Not to explain it away, but to set it inside a sovereignty that held even the cross. Then bring your own sin here too, and own it: you were among the reasons he died. The same verse that humbles you comforts you, because the God who planned the cross planned your rescue.

For worship. The worst sin in history was in God’s hands, and he used it for the greatest good. Before the world began, the Father purposed that the Son would be given up for sinners, and the Son came willingly to be delivered into lawless hands. Not one nail was outside his plan, and not one drop of that blood was wasted. He is sovereign over your trials too, and he is the God who turns murder into redemption.
verseByVerse.note: Lawless men are the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.

God raised him up. The heart of the apostolic preaching. You killed him; God raised him. God reversed their verdict.

Loosing the pangs of death. Two things are said about the resurrection in this line. The first is the picture. The word for pangs (ōdinas) is the word for labour pains. The Greek Old Testament uses it where David describes being caught in the cords of death and of Sheol (Psalm 18:4–5), and Peter takes it up and lets it do its work: death is in labour, and it cannot keep what it is carrying. Something is coming out. The language of birth is not a later flourish of the church’s; Paul calls the risen Christ the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18) and John calls him the firstborn of the dead (Revelation 1:5), and the word was chosen because on one particular Sunday a tomb behaved like a womb, and tombs have been unreliable ever since.

Because it was not possible for him to be held by it. The second is the sentence to slow down over. Not unlikely. Not difficult. Not possible. The New Testament gives several reasons why not.

Because of who he is. One is who he is. The men standing at Peter’s shoulder will say a chapter later that Jerusalem killed the Author of life (3:15), and life does not stay dead any more than fire stays cold. What happened in that tomb was less a rescue mounted from outside than a contradiction resolving itself.

Because of what he had not done. Another is what he had not done. Death in Scripture is not a natural process; it is a wage, and wages are paid to those who have earned them (Romans 6:23). Jesus had earned nothing; the ruler of this world had no claim on him (John 14:30). Death is a bailiff who arrives holding a warrant, and when the warrant was read out in that tomb it had somebody else’s name on it. He had gone in voluntarily, carrying other men’s debts; once those were discharged there was no ground in law on which he could be detained another hour. The stone was not rolled back to let him out. It was rolled back to let the world in to look.

Because God had sworn it. The third is that God had promised it. Peter goes straight on to prove it from Psalm 16: the promise had been in writing for a thousand years, in a psalm the crowd had sung, that God’s Holy One would not see corruption. Scripture foretold it, and God’s plan required it, and heaven and earth would pass away before his word failed.

What it does not mean. One guard is needed, because the sentence can be misread in a way that empties the cross. Not possible for him to be held is not not possible to die. He really died. The blood ran out, the body went cold, friends made the arrangements, and women prepared spices for a job that genuinely needed doing (Luke 23:56). Anything less than a real death would leave the human race precisely where it was.

What does Christ’s resurrection mean for my own death? It means that death is not the end for anyone who belongs to him. Because he was raised, those united to him will be raised too, bodily, at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and his body rests until the resurrection. There is no soul sleep and no purgatory in between; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). So you may grieve at a Christian’s graveside, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

In a sentence. God raised him, freeing him from the pains of death, because death could not keep its hold on him.

On a Tuesday. Think of the grave that most frightens you: your own, or that of someone you love. Then say aloud: it was not possible for him to be held by it. If you are in Christ, the same will be true of you. Live today as someone who is not finally afraid.

For worship. What death could not do to him it will not finally manage against those who are in him. A believer standing at a graveside is not looking at a permanent arrangement. He is looking at a room that death has already been made to give up once, by a man who walked out of it and took the keys with him. Death could not hold him, and in him it cannot hold you.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope.

For David says concerning him. Peter now does something a first-century audience found natural and a modern reader often finds baffling: he settles a question about a man who died seven weeks ago by quoting a poem written a thousand years earlier, Psalm 16:8–11. The method is the one the whole New Testament uses. Peter says David spoke concerning him: concerning Christ.

The words fit the writer, and then overflow him. Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust, headed simply as David’s, and it is genuinely his. He is not a ventriloquist’s dummy with an inspired hand working his jaw; the psalm reads like a man’s own settled confidence in God, and he meant every word of it about himself. That is the ordinary way prophecy works in the Psalms. The words fit the writer, and then they overflow him. David could say my flesh also will dwell in hope and mean that he expected God to bring him through the present trouble alive. What he could not do was make the sentence come true in the full sense the words will bear, and Peter is about to point at the man’s grave to prove it.

I saw the Lord always before me. Look at the two lines quoted here. The first is a deliberate act of keeping God in view, not a feeling that he is near; the psalm itself, as the ESV renders it, reads I have set the LORD always before me, which is something a man does whether or not he can feel anything. It describes perfect communion with God, never broken, true of David in part, but fully true only of Christ.

For he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken. A soldier’s shield hung on his left arm, so his right side was the exposed one, and what a man in a battle line wanted above everything was somebody he trusted standing at his right, covering the side he could not cover himself. That is where the psalm puts God. The speaker trusts God completely.

Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope. Then the consequence, and notice its order. Heart, tongue, body: the gladness works outward until even the flesh is included, the part of a man that knows perfectly well it is going to die. This is not stoicism, which teaches a man to expect nothing and so not be disappointed. It is a man expecting his own body to have a future, even as it is laid in the grave.

What held the Son of God steady. And these are the words Peter puts into the mouth of Christ. Which means we are being told what held the Son of God steady on the road to the cross: not the absence of dread, for he sweated in Gethsemane, but the Father in view. He kept looking. That is also what is asked of anyone walking into something he cannot get out of: a diagnosis, a court date, a conversation he has been dreading for a month.

How do I set the Lord always before me when I cannot feel him near? By deliberate attention, not by feeling. Start the day by reading a few verses and turning them into prayer, so that the first voice you hear is his. Through the day, bring your thoughts back to him: before a hard conversation, in the car, at the hospital bed. Remind yourself of what is true whether you feel it or not, that he is at your right hand, that he is for you, that he has promised never to leave you (Hebrews 13:5). Feelings of his nearness come and go, even for mature believers. Setting him before you is something you do, and he honours it.

In a sentence. David spoke of Christ when he said that he always saw the Lord before him at his right hand, so that he would not be shaken, and so his heart was glad and his body would rest in hope.

On a Tuesday. Set the Lord always before you. With him at your right hand, you will not be shaken. Name the thing you are dreading this week. Before you walk into it, stop and say: the Lord is at my right hand. Then walk.

For worship. The Son of God walked to the cross with the Father before his eyes, and his heart was glad even as his flesh went down into the grave in hope. He trusted the Father all the way, and the Father did not fail him. The Lord who was at Christ’s right hand in the valley of death is at the right hand of every believer, and the hope that held his flesh holds ours.

parallels.desc: I have set the LORD always before me

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.’

For you will not abandon my soul to Hades. This is the hinge of Peter’s argument, and it contains a phrase that has troubled readers for centuries. Hades here is not hell. It is the realm of the dead; the psalm Peter is quoting says Sheol (Psalm 16:10), the place where the dead simply are. God would not leave him there.

Or let your Holy One see corruption. First the argument. To see corruption (diaphthora) is to undergo decay. What is being denied is not death but decay. Peter’s hearers knew exactly what the sentence described, because burial in that country was often a two-stage business: the body was laid on a shelf in a rock tomb and left for a year while it decomposed, after which the bones were gathered into a box and stored. Everyone in that crowd had done it for a parent. Martha, at her brother’s tomb, warned Jesus that by the fourth day there would be an odour (John 11:39). The women who went out on the Sunday morning went carrying spices for exactly that reason (Luke 24:1); they were not expecting a resurrection, they were expecting the smell. And when the tomb was opened, nothing had begun. Jesus was raised on the third day, before decay could set in.

He descended into hell. Now the phrase. This verse, with one or two others, lies behind the line in the Apostles’ Creed that has made congregations uneasy for a very long time: he descended into hell. It deserves an explanation. Nobody in the mainstream of the church has ever taught that Jesus went somewhere to be punished further after the cross; the punishment was finished there, and he said so with his last breath: it is finished. Some read the creed’s phrase as meaning simply that he was truly dead and went where the dead go: no swoon, no shortcut, the full distance travelled. Others, in the Reformed tradition especially, have taken it to describe the anguish of the cross itself, the God-forsakenness of those three hours, when he bore the wrath of God in our place. Either reading is honest to the words. And notice that the psalm itself claims something more modest than what people fear: it does not say he would not go there. It says he would not be abandoned there.

Where did Jesus go between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb. His human soul went, as he promised the thief, to paradise: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). He did not go to a place of further suffering, and he did not go to give the dead a second chance; Scripture gives no such chance after death (Hebrews 9:27). His death was real and complete, body and soul truly separated, as ours will be. And because he has walked that road and come back, a believer facing death walks a road with his Lord’s footprints on it.

You have made known to me the paths of life. Then the two clauses that close the quotation, which are pure light after all of that. The word is plural, paths: roads, a whole country to walk in and not a bare survival. The path through death to life is fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection and ascension.

You will make me full of gladness with your presence. In the Greek, the phrase is literally with your face. Run a test on yourself.
