Suppose the resurrection delivered everything except that one thing: a body that never failed again, a world with no funerals in it, the people you have buried handed back to you, and God himself somewhere else, benevolent and absent. Would that be enough? Most of us would take it gladly, and then find out in a century or so what was missing. The psalm does not describe the joy of the risen Christ as a location or a condition. It describes it as a presence. Whatever else the life to come is, it is the end of God being somewhere else; and that, rather than the absence of trouble, is what the church has always sung about.

In a sentence. David continued that God would not leave his soul in the grave or let his Holy One decay, but had shown him the paths of life and would fill him with joy in his presence.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly what you most look forward to in heaven. If God himself is not near the top of the list, ask him to make him so. Then live today as a traveller on the paths of life, toward the face of God.

For worship. The path of life runs through Christ’s empty tomb. The Holy One was not abandoned to the grave, and his body did not see decay, because the Father would not let him go. He has walked the road through death and out the other side into the gladness of the Father’s face, and he has opened that road for all who are his. At his right hand are pleasures for evermore.
verseByVerse.note: Hades (Sheol) is the realm of the dead.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,

Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried. Peter now does the boldest thing in the sermon, easy to walk past because it looks like local history. He appeals to a landmark.

And his tomb is with us to this day. That tomb was a real building on the southern ridge of the city, known to everybody in that street and a fixed point in Jerusalem’s geography for centuries; Nehemiah mentions the tombs of David (Nehemiah 3:16), and Josephus reports that a king had once broken into it looking for treasure. Peter could have raised his arm and pointed at it while he was speaking. And nobody in the crowd said: no it is not.

Two graves in one city. Consider what he has therefore done. He has staked the argument on two graves in one city, both within an easy walk of where he is standing, and made both of them checkable that same afternoon. David’s tomb is occupied: go and see. The tomb of Jesus is empty: go and see that too. This is not how legends are put together. A story that needs distance and time to survive has just been nailed to two addresses in the town where the events happened, seven weeks after they happened, in front of the people best placed to demolish it.

The logic of the occupied tomb. David wrote that God’s Holy One would not see corruption. David saw corruption, and the proof is a sealed door on the ridge. So Psalm 16 is prophecy, and it has been waiting for somebody.

Being therefore a prophet. But Peter adds a step, and the step matters. David is not merely a poet who happened to write past himself without noticing. He was a prophet, speaking by the Spirit (1:16); the Spirit of the LORD speaks by me, he said at the end of his life (2 Samuel 23:2). He knew, at least in part, what he was doing.

And knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne. He knew because he had been given a promise on oath: that God would set one of his own offspring on his throne, and that the throne would have no end (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11). David wrote Psalm 16 as a man who had been told his family would produce a king whose reign would never stop, which is a promise that cannot be kept unless somebody in that family stops dying. David knew that his greater son would come.

The hidden child. And then look at what God had to steer in order to keep it. The royal line ran through adultery and murder in its very first generation; through a son whose folly split the kingdom; through kings who burned their own children as offerings; through exile, when the throne stood empty for centuries and the family ended up as village carpenters. At one point the whole line came down to a single infant. A usurping queen had every royal child she could reach put to death, and one baby was carried out of the killing by his aunt and hidden in the house of the LORD for six years, while the woman who wanted him dead ruled the country (2 Kings 11:1–3). The oath God swore to David hung, for six years, on whether a hidden child would cry at the wrong moment.

Where Christians differ: is Christ on David’s throne now? Dispensational and other premillennial teaching holds that the promise of David’s throne will be fulfilled chiefly in a future earthly reign of Christ from Jerusalem during a millennium after his return. Verdict: Peter says the oath to set David’s descendant on his throne was what David foresaw when he spoke of the resurrection (vv. 30–31), and that Jesus, raised and exalted to God’s right hand, now reigns (vv. 33–36). The throne of David is fulfilled in Christ’s present heavenly reign, which the New Testament calls the kingdom already come (Luke 1:32–33; Colossians 1:13; Hebrews 1:8–13). This is the amillennial reading. Christ reigns now, until his enemies are made his footstool, and his reign will be seen by all at his return, in the new creation. Brothers who expect a future millennium love the same King and await the same return, and the difference is held in charity.

Waiting on a promise that looks past saving. Anybody waiting on a promise of God that looks by now to be beyond rescue should sit with that a while. The promise did not fail while the nation was in exile, or while the throne stood empty, or while the last heir was a toddler hidden in the temple. God keeps his word across a thousand years and through a family history that would have finished any human undertaking, and the promise is kept, in the end, by a man from Nazareth whom this crowd had watched die.

What promises of God can I rely on in my own waiting? Rely on what God has actually promised in Scripture, not on what you wish he had promised. He has promised to forgive all who confess their sins (1 John 1:9), never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), to work all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), to give wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), to complete the work he began in you (Philippians 1:6), and to raise you on the last day (John 6:40). He has not promised every specific outcome you pray for, such as a particular healing or a particular marriage. But every promise he has made is yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the story of David’s line shows how far he will go to keep them.

In a sentence. Peter said David died and was buried and his tomb is still there, but as a prophet he knew God had sworn to set one of his descendants on his throne.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his oaths. Every promise of his is yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Pick one promise from the list above, write it somewhere you will see it, and lean on it this week, especially if the thing you are waiting for looks past saving.

For worship. David’s tomb is still sealed on the ridge, and his greater Son’s is open. But the story does not leave David there. The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come out (John 5:28–29), and on that day the son will call the father out of his grave. The King who now sits on David’s throne will never die and never be succeeded, and among those who rise at his word will be the shepherd king who wrote of him, glad at last in the presence he sang about.
verseByVerse.note: David’s tomb was a known landmark in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: the LORD swore to David a sure oath

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses.

He foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ. Peter will not let the psalm be an accident that happens to fit, a set of old words that turned out to be usable. David looked ahead and wrote of the Messiah’s resurrection, which means the resurrection was not the salvage of a wrecked plan. It was announced in Israel’s hymn book a thousand years before there was a tomb for it to empty. Jesus had taught the apostles to read the Old Testament this way: that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead (Luke 24:44–47).

That he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. Fulfilled in Jesus, and in no one else. Every other son of David lies on the ridge.

This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. Then Peter puts the psalm down and does something quite different. He has argued from Scripture for verse after verse; now he argues from the eleven men standing beside him. We all: not I, and not a report that reached him. The qualification for the vacancy back in chapter 1 was set at exactly this point: a man who had been with them the whole time and had seen the risen Lord (1:21–22). These are not people passing on a rumour from another province. They are named men, in their own city, seven weeks after the event, telling several thousand of their neighbours that they saw it, and inviting cross-examination from a crowd that included the friends and families of the men who had arranged the execution. Scripture foretold it; eyewitnesses confirm it.

Men in a position to know. The argument usually built on this is, in its common form, weaker than it sounds. People say that nobody dies for a lie. In fact people die for lies constantly; the world is full of sincere martyrs for things that are not true, and always has been. The real point is narrower and much harder to get round. These particular men were in a position to know whether it was a lie. A man may well die for a doctrine he was taught and cannot check. He does not ordinarily die for a body he moved himself. And what happened to these witnesses across the next thirty years, floggings, prisons, and for many of them, by early tradition, execution, is not the record of men who had the option of quietly correcting themselves at any point.

An inheritance and a limit. Which leaves the church with an inheritance and a limit, and both should be stated plainly. The inheritance: Christian faith is not a philosophy that would survive the disproof of its own history, and it has never claimed to be. It rests on something that either happened outside a wall in Jerusalem or did not, and Peter is content for it to be tested. The limit: nobody today is a witness in the sense Peter means it here. What the church holds is the testimony of the men who were, written down while people who could have contradicted them were still alive. That is a great deal, and it is enough to build a life on; but the honest name for it is testimony received rather than experience possessed, and no believer should feel awkward saying so.

If I did not see it, how can my faith be certain? Because God has given you something better than a private sighting: the public testimony of chosen eyewitnesses, preserved by the Spirit in Scripture, and the Spirit himself bearing witness in your heart that it is true. Jesus said to Thomas, blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29), and John wrote his Gospel so that you may believe (John 20:31). Your faith rests on the same event the apostles saw, through their words. That is not second-hand faith; it is the faith God intended for every generation after the first.

In a sentence. David foresaw and spoke of the Christ’s resurrection, that he was not left in the grave and his body did not decay, and God raised this Jesus, as they all witnessed.

On a Tuesday. Scripture and eyewitnesses agree: Jesus is risen. Rest your faith on that rock, not on your feelings this morning. If a friend asks why you believe, you do not need to argue from your experience alone. Tell him about the eleven men and the empty tomb in the city where it happened.

For worship. How gracious of the risen Lord to want witnesses at all. He could have risen in secret and reigned unseen. Instead he showed himself to chosen men, ate with them, let them look at his hands, and sent them out with their own eyes for credentials, so that a fisherman’s we saw it could reach a reader twenty centuries later. The grave David described could not hold the Christ, and the Christ would not keep his victory to himself. He rose to be known, and every word of that testimony is an invitation to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,

Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God. Here the sermon turns back on the crowd with one of the neatest arguments in the New Testament. He has told them Jesus was raised and produced eleven witnesses. But a witness can be doubted, and nobody at all saw the exaltation. The right hand of God is the place of highest honour and power, and the risen Jesus now reigns there with the Father. How can a crowd in a street know that?

He has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. Peter does not ask the crowd to take it on trust. He points at the noise. The thing that dragged several thousand people into the street at nine in the morning is itself the evidence. You cannot see a throne in heaven; you can hear a hundred and twenty Galileans speaking Parthian. The argument runs from an audible effect back to an invisible cause. The crowd came out looking for an explanation of a noise, and Peter tells them the noise is the sound of a coronation that has already taken place somewhere they cannot look. Pentecost is proof that Jesus is alive and reigning. And only God pours out God’s Spirit: in Joel it was I, the LORD, who would pour it out (Joel 2:28), and here it is Jesus.

And having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit. Three persons are named in this single sentence, doing three different things. Jesus is exalted at the right hand of God. He receives the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father. He pours out the Spirit. Anyone who reads Father, Son and Spirit as three costumes worn in turn by one person has to get past this verse, where all three are active at once. The Trinity is not a later theory laid over the gospel. It is the shape of the gospel’s first sermon.

The coronation gift. And notice what the risen Christ does first with his authority. An accession in the ancient world was marked by largesse: the treasury opened, gifts scattered, debts remitted, prisoners released, because that is how a new reign announced itself to a city. Psalm 68, which Paul later applies to the ascension, pictures the conqueror going up on high and receiving gifts among men (Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 4:8). The first recorded act of Jesus after his enthronement is to give something away, and what he gives is not a benefit but a Person. The Spirit in the church is not an impersonal force on loan. He is the coronation gift of a King who had nothing left to prove and gave anyway.

A receipt from the throne. Every time a believer understands a verse that was closed to him a year ago, or finds he wants to pray when he does not feel like praying, or discovers that a sin which used to own him has quietly loosened its grip, he is holding a piece of evidence about where Jesus is. That is Peter’s argument, and it did not stop working when the languages did. The Spirit’s presence in an ordinary life is a receipt, and the transaction it records took place at the right hand of God.

For David did not ascend into the heavens. Then Peter reaches for his second psalm and introduces it with exactly the logic he used on the first. David’s body is on the ridge. David did not go up. So whatever the psalm is about, it is not about him; it is about the one he calls his Lord.

But he himself says, The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand. This is Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament text most quoted and echoed in the New, and Jesus used it himself (Luke 20:41–44). In the psalm the ESV prints the first in small capitals, the LORD says to my Lord: the first is the covenant name of God, the second a title for a master, a superior, one to whom a man owes allegiance. So David, the king, with nobody above him in Israel, overhears a conversation and finds God addressing somebody David himself has to call his master. Jesus had put that puzzle to the scholars in this very city a few weeks earlier: if the Christ is David’s son, how does David call him Lord? Fathers do not address their descendants that way. The son of David turns out to be the master of David, and the riddle had been sitting in the temple songbook the whole time. David did not ascend; Jesus did.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Look for the evidence Peter points to: the things only the Spirit produces. Do you confess that Jesus is Lord and mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3)? Do you, however weakly, love God and want to obey him? Do you call God Father with trust (Romans 8:15–16)? Is there some growth, however slow, in love, joy, patience and self-control? Do you love other Christians? These are not achievements that earn the Spirit; they are the fruit of his presence. Nobody has them perfectly, but no unbeliever has them at all. If they are there, even in seed form, the King has given you his gift.

In a sentence. Peter said that Jesus, exalted to God’s right hand and receiving the promised Spirit from the Father, had poured out what they saw and heard, for David did not ascend to heaven, but said the Lord told his Lord to sit at his right hand.

On a Tuesday. The next time you find yourself wanting to pray, or understanding Scripture, or resisting a sin that used to master you, stop and give thanks: that is a receipt from the throne. And when you feel far from God, remember that the Spirit was given as a gift from a King, not earned as a wage. He has not been withdrawn because you had a bad week.

For worship. The hands that were opened on the cross to receive the nails are opened on the throne to give. David’s riddle is answered at last: his son is his Lord, seated where no king of Israel ever sat, and the first thing those pierced hands do from that height is pour. He asked nothing from the city that had killed him before he gave, and what he gave was not a favour or a token but God the Holy Spirit, received from the Father for people who had done nothing to deserve him. Such is the King at the right hand of God.

parallels.desc: “Sit at my right hand”

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
until I make your enemies your footstool.’ Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.

Until I make your enemies your footstool. The picture is concrete and it is not gentle. Ancient kings put their feet on the necks of defeated enemies (Joshua 10:24), and footstools were made with conquered peoples worked into them; one was found in an Egyptian royal tomb with bound captives carved across the surface, so that the king put his feet on the nations every time he sat down. That is the image: not a negotiated settlement with the powers that oppose God, but their subjugation, placed under the feet of a man who is sitting still. Christ reigns now, until every enemy is subdued, the last being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

The King who sits. And the sitting matters. The priests in the temple a few hundred yards from where Peter was preaching never sat down. There were no chairs in the holy place, because the work there was never finished; every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, but Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down (Hebrews 10:11–12). This King sits. Nor does until mean that the reign expires when the job is done; it means the reign is what does the job. He is not waiting for reinforcements. He is waiting for the last of it to be brought in.

Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain. The conclusion of the sermon. For certain (asphalōs) means beyond doubt, securely. It is the same root Luke used in the first line of his Gospel, where he told Theophilus he was writing so that he might have certainty concerning the things he had been taught (Luke 1:4). Peter is not offering a hypothesis for consideration. He is announcing a fact.

That God has made him both Lord and Christ. Then the sermon’s final sentence. Lord was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God, translating the divine name. Christ is the Messiah, the anointed king. Read carelessly the sentence sounds as though there was a time when Jesus was not Lord, and the resurrection promoted him: that a good man was handed a divine job at Easter. That is close to what the adoptionists taught in the second century, and this verse is regularly quoted today by those who say the church made Jesus God. It will not carry the weight, and three things show why.

The verb. The first is the verb. Made, in a sentence of this kind, is appointment language, and Greek uses it that way constantly. The Greek Old Testament says the LORD made Moses and Aaron (1 Samuel 12:6), which English Bibles render appointed, since nobody imagines God manufactured two grown men on the spot. The Gospels say Jesus made twelve, meaning he appointed them (Mark 3:14). To be made Lord in this sense is to be installed in an office, not brought into existence.

The man writing it down. The second is the man writing it down. Luke has already told us, in the first volume of this same work, what an angel said over a newborn at Bethlehem: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11). Both titles, spoken over an infant, some thirty years before this sermon, by the same author who now records verse 36. Whatever Luke meant here, he cannot have meant that Jesus acquired those two titles in the spring of that year, because he had already used both of them of a baby in a manger.

Declared, not created. The third is what the resurrection is actually said to have done. Paul puts it precisely: Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4), and the verb he chooses is built on the same root as the definite plan back in verse 23 of this chapter, the word for marking out and appointing. What is new at Easter is not the nature but the office, publicly entered. The eternal Son, who humbled himself, is exalted in his human nature to the highest place, and given the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). A king’s son is royal from birth and is crowned at thirty; nobody at the coronation supposes the crown created the man. The hall fills, the trumpet sounds, and the herald announces what has been true since the day he was born.

This Jesus whom you crucified. What Peter actually meant is more alarming than the doctrinal difficulty. This is not a statement about promotion. It is the closing move of a prosecution, and the sermon ends with a dagger. A court in this city examined a man, found against him, and had him put to death. Heaven has reviewed the case. The verdict is overturned, and the prisoner has been seated on the bench. Every person in that street stood in some relation to a legal decision that had just been publicly reversed, and the judge under the new arrangement is the defendant from the old one.

What does it mean for me that Jesus is Lord? It means he has the right to rule every part of your life, and that he is able to. Lord is not a title you confer on him when you are ready; it is the office God has given him, and the only question is whether you will bow now, gladly, or later, unwillingly (Philippians 2:10–11). In practice, it means bringing your money, your sexuality, your time, your work, your plans and your fears under his word. But it also means that the one who rules you is the one who died for you. His lordship is not a tyrant’s; it is the rule of the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep. To call him Lord is to be safe.

In a sentence. God will make his enemies his footstool, so all Israel should know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ.

On a Tuesday. Is there an area of your life where Jesus is Saviour but not yet Lord? Name it, and bow to him there today. He is going to reign over it either way; it is better by far to be under his feet as a friend than as an enemy.

For worship. He has been given the name above every name, and his enemies are being gathered under his feet; yet the first exercise of that power is not a reckoning. The crowd that hears what it has done is told that it may repent, be forgiven, and receive the very Spirit whose arrival it had been jeering at an hour before. The man they murdered is Lord of heaven and earth, and the first thing he does as Lord is offer his murderers himself. There is nothing else like it in the history of the world. The footstool is for enemies who refuse him; the throne’s first word to its enemies is peace.
verseByVerse.note: “Lord” was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God’s name; “Christ” means the Messiah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the people heard this, they were deeply moved and asked Peter and the other apostles what they should do. Peter replied that every one of them should repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for them and their children and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord God will call. With many other words he warned them and pleaded with them to save themselves from this corrupt generation. Those who accepted his message were baptised, and about three thousand were added that day. They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs the apostles performed. All the believers were together and shared everything; they sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. Every day they kept meeting together in the temple courts and broke bread in their homes, eating together with glad and sincere hearts, praising God and enjoying the favour of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Verse 42 gives the church four practices, and each is named with its definite article: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. These are not four vague virtues but four definite things a visitor to Jerusalem that summer could have been taken to and shown. Reformed ecclesiology has read them as the permanent shape of church life. The apostles' teaching — which is now the New Testament — norms everything else, so that no experience, however vivid, is permitted to correct it. The fellowship is not sociability but a shared life the Spirit creates, and in this chapter it costs people money within three verses. The breaking of bread is the Supper in which his death is proclaimed until he comes. And the prayers are the church's dependence made audible. A congregation strong in all four will be healthy in almost any circumstances; a congregation that quietly lets one go will be impoverished in ways it may take a generation to notice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? Jerusalem was already equipped. The southern approach to the temple mount was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock, so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; dozens have been excavated and can still be walked into. The infrastructure of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it. Now: God is not in the habit of waiting for ideal conditions, and he has a long record of using whatever is already lying about — a borrowed upper room, a set of ritual baths, and a preacher with a provincial accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” And Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart. The word (katenygēsan) means pierced, stabbed. It is the language of a blade, and the blade is the Spirit’s: when he comes, Jesus had said, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8). The crowd recognises their city’s guilt and their own share in it. They had crucified the Messiah, the Lord of glory. What hope could there be?

They looked on him whom they had pierced. Luke does not cite it, but the scene is written in Zechariah. God promised to pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child (Zechariah 12:10). John applies that verse to the spear at the cross (John 19:37). Here it comes true in order: the Spirit is poured out on Jerusalem, the city is shown the one it pierced, and the piercing turns back on the hearers’ own hearts. Their grief is not the end of the prophecy but the beginning of grace. The pierced one is the one who has sent the Spirit to wound them in order to heal them.

Brothers, what shall we do? It is the right question, the best possible response to the gospel: the response of people who take it seriously enough to ask what it demands. Notice that they call the apostles brothers. An hour earlier some of them were calling these men drunk.

Repent. Peter’s answer comes in two parts, and the first is a single word. Repent (metanoēsate) means to change your mind, to turn around. It is a change of mind about Jesus, and about sin, leading to a change of life. They had rejected him; now they must turn to him. Repentance is not penance, a payment made in tears. It is a turning of the whole self, from sin to God, from trusting yourself to trusting Christ.

And be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ. Baptism publicly marks the turn and identifies the believer with Jesus: his death, his burial, his rising (Romans 6:3–4). In the name of Jesus Christ means by his authority, into union with him and under his ownership. Every one of you: each person who repents, individually. Nobody is baptised by proxy, and nobody comes in by belonging to a nation.

In the name of Jesus, and in the name of the Father, Son and Spirit. There is an apparent tension with Matthew 28:19, where the risen Christ commands baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The two are not contradictory. In the name of Jesus Christ is not a different formula but a statement of whose disciple one becomes: to be baptised into Jesus is to be baptised into the God who raised him, the Spirit he poured out, and the Father who sent him. The Didache, the earliest manual of church practice outside the New Testament, prescribes the threefold name (Didache 7). Oneness Pentecostals have used the Jesus-name passages to argue that Father, Son and Spirit are not three persons but three manifestations of one. The church, East and West, has always read Luke’s phrase as a description rather than a rival formula, and this chapter shows why: Jesus receives the Spirit from the Father and pours him out (v. 33), a scene that requires three persons.

For the forgiveness of your sins. The promise: sins forgiven, all of them, even the sin of crucifying the Messiah. These are people who killed the Messiah a few weeks before, and he offers them full pardon in the same breath in which he charges them.

And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Not the gifts of the Spirit, but the gift who is the Spirit: the same Spirit poured out on the apostles that morning, given to every believer. The three thousand did not have to wait ten days as the hundred and twenty did. The Spirit had come, and he was given to them as they repented and believed.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some read this to mean that baptism itself brings forgiveness (baptismal regeneration), so that forgiveness depends on baptism. Verdict: the preposition for (eis) can mean with a view to or in connection with. Throughout Acts forgiveness is received by faith (10:43; 13:38–39; 26:18), and Cornelius received the Spirit before baptism (10:44–48). Repentance and faith receive forgiveness; baptism is the God-given sign and seal of it, closely linked, normally following at once. It is commanded, and no believer should neglect it, but it is not the cause of salvation.

Does the water wash sins away? No. Forgiveness is by grace through faith in the blood of Christ: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name (10:43; Ephesians 1:7). That is why the dying thief was saved with no baptism at all (Luke 23:43). So we do not rest our hope in the water but in Christ, to whom the water points. Roman Catholic Christians, and some in the Churches of Christ, read the verse differently, holding that baptism actually conveys the new birth; the difference is real, and turns on whether the rite signifies grace or effects it. But notice that Peter does not treat baptism as optional either. It is the first act of obedience of a new believer, the public flag of a changed allegiance.

I trusted Christ years ago but was never baptised as a believer. What should I do? Be baptised. You are not less saved for having waited, but the Lord commands it, and in the New Testament it is the normal first step of every believer (8:36–38; 16:33). Speak to your pastor or elders. If you were baptised as an infant and have since come to personal faith, you will want to weigh this carefully and humbly: we believe the New Testament pattern is baptism after repentance and faith, as here, and so we would encourage baptism as a believer. Paedobaptist brothers and sisters, out of real conviction, would not; respect them, and act on your own conscience before God, from Scripture.

In a sentence. Cut to the heart, they asked what to do, and Peter told them to repent and each be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. No sin is too great to be forgiven. If there is something you have never believed God could forgive, bring it to him today, by name, and turn from it. Repent and believe. And if you have never been baptised as a believer, ask yourself what is holding you back.

For worship. The Lord whom they had crucified offered them forgiveness before the day was out, and poured on them the very Spirit they had mocked. There is no blood on any hand that his blood cannot wash away. He did not wait for them to make amends; he only called them to turn, and gave them everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.

For the promise is for you and for your children. You: those present, the very people who called for his death. Your children: the next generation, their descendants. The promise is the one Peter has just named, forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit.

And for all who are far off. All who are far off came to include the Gentiles. Peter may not yet have understood how far this reached; it will take a vision and a Roman centurion’s house to show him (10:28, 34). But he said more than he knew, and the Spirit meant all of it. Paul takes the same phrase from Isaiah 57:19 and tells us what closed the distance: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13). And it is Christ himself, he says, who came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near (2:17). The promise travels outward from Jerusalem because the one who made peace by his cross is the one doing the preaching, through every mouth that carries it.

Everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself. And here the promise has its boundary, which is not ethnic or geographic but the call of God. The promise is wide, everyone, and it is grounded in God’s effectual call. Those who receive the promise are those whom God calls. Notice the balance: Peter commands all to repent (v. 38) and assures them that the promise rests on God’s call. Human response and divine calling stand together, as Luke will put it later: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (13:48). The gospel is universal in its offer; the Spirit is sovereign in its application.

Where Christians differ: baptism and children. Paedobaptists read for you and your children as a covenant promise to believers’ infants, supporting infant baptism. Verdict: the promise is to children as to everyone, whom the Lord calls: it is received by those who repent (v. 38), and those baptised were those who received the word (v. 41). Believer’s baptism is the New Testament pattern. Children of believers are in a place of great privilege, and the promise is for them as they come to faith. Paedobaptist brothers and sisters hold their view in good conscience, and we hold ours charitably.

The friendly disagreement. This verse stands near the heart of a long, friendly disagreement. The Reformed and Presbyterian reading sees an unbroken covenant pattern: God has always included the children of believers in the covenant and its sign, circumcision in the Old Testament (Genesis 17) and now baptism, so believers’ infants receive the sign as covenant children, awaiting their own personal faith. The Baptist reading, which the 1689 London Baptist Confession expresses, takes your children simply as offspring who, like everyone, must themselves repent and believe to receive the promise, noting the very next clause, everyone whom the Lord our God calls, and so baptises only those who profess faith. Both honour Scripture and the gospel of grace; the difference turns on how much the old covenant sign carries over into the new, and it is held charitably even within Reformed circles, which include both convictions. But the point no one must miss is the one both sides shout together: the promise is sheer grace, and it is offered to you and yours.

What does this mean for my children? It means you may pray for them with great confidence, and raise them with great hope. They are not saved by being born to you, and they will need to repent and believe for themselves. But they live near the promise every day: they hear the gospel at your table, see it in your life, and sit under it in church. God very often calls the children of believers to himself, sometimes so early that they cannot remember not trusting Christ. So tell them plainly that the promise is for them, teach them the Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15), pray with them and for them, and welcome every sign of real faith. When they profess it credibly, rejoice to see them baptised.

In a sentence. The promise is for them, their children, and all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for the children you love, by name, that the Lord would call them to himself. And remember that you were once among the far off. If you trust Christ now, it is because the Lord your God called you.

For worship. Jesus once said that he had other sheep, not of this fold, and that he must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice (John 10:16). The call in this verse is that voice. It went from the men who crucified him to their children, and from Jerusalem to peoples Peter had never seen, and it has never once failed to reach the sheep it was sent for. The far off hear it and come near, the Shepherd counts them in, and the God who calls is the God who keeps.
verseByVerse.note: “All who are far off” came to include the Gentiles.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.

And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them. Two things in these verses are usually read straight past. The first is that we have a digest, not the whole sermon: what survives takes about three minutes to read aloud. Luke says he continued to exhort them. He kept going. Whatever else the first Christian preacher did, he did not stop when he had covered the material.

Save yourselves. The second is the grammar of the famous sentence, and it turns the sentence inside out. Save yourselves from this crooked generation sounds in English like an instruction to perform a rescue: pull yourself together, extract yourself, do something. In Greek it is passive: be saved. Peter is not telling these people to save themselves. He is telling them to let themselves be saved, to stop resisting a rescue that is being carried out on them. A man in a burning building is not told to put the fire out. He is told to stop arguing and be carried down the stairs. And the sermon has already named the one doing the carrying: the Lord on whose name everyone who calls will be saved is Jesus, made Lord and Christ (vv. 21, 36). That is the difference between the gospel and every other religion on earth, sitting inside a verse regularly quoted to prove the opposite.

From this crooked generation. Notice, too, what they are being saved from. Not from hell in the abstract, and not from the world in the sense of leaving town: from this crooked generation. Crooked (skolias) means twisted, perverse, and the phrase comes out of the Song of Moses, where God calls his own covenant people a crooked and twisted generation (Deuteronomy 32:5); Paul uses it of the world around the Philippian church (Philippians 2:15). Peter lays Moses’ description of Israel on the Israel standing in front of him, a hard thing to say to a devout crowd on a feast day. They must break with the generation that rejected the Messiah. A generation is not something a man can resign from. Nobody chooses his parents, his decade, or the assumptions he absorbed before he was old enough to examine them. He can only be taken out.

So those who received his word were baptized. Receiving the word, then baptism: faith first. That is the order Luke gives every time, and it is why the church that holds to believer’s baptism reads this verse as its pattern. The ones who were baptised were the ones who had welcomed the message.

Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? Jerusalem was already built for it. The southern approach to the temple was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; many have been excavated and can still be walked into today, and the great pools of Siloam and Bethesda lay within the city. The apostles did not have to improvise. The plumbing of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it.

And there were added that day about three thousand souls. Then the number, and it carries an echo the crowd’s Bible readers would not have missed. When Moses came down from Sinai and found the nation dancing round a calf, about three thousand men fell that day (Exodus 32:28). The law came, and three thousand died. Here the Spirit comes, and three thousand live. Paul later reduced the principle to a sentence: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6). These are the greater works Jesus had promised his disciples would do because he was going to the Father (John 14:12): not greater miracles, but a greater harvest.

What it does not mean. One guard, because this verse has bruised a great many faithful people. Three thousand in a day is not the measure of a ministry. The same Spirit produced this and produced Jeremiah, who preached for forty years to a nation that would not turn, and was right the whole time. Numbers are God’s business and are not issued as a report card. What is asked of a preacher is what Peter did here: bear witness, keep exhorting, and leave the cutting of hearts to somebody better qualified.

How do I know whether I have truly received the word? Not by remembering a particular moment, though some do, but by what the word has done and is doing in you. Do you believe what it says about Jesus, that he died for sinners and rose again, and are you trusting him rather than yourself? Have you turned, however imperfectly, from the life you lived without him? Do you want to keep hearing his word and obeying it? Those who received the word that day went straight on to devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching (v. 42). The best evidence that the seed has taken root is that it keeps growing.

In a sentence. With many more words Peter urged them to be saved from this crooked generation, and those who accepted his message were baptised, about three thousand that day.

On a Tuesday. If you preach, teach a children’s class, lead a Bible study or simply tell a friend about Christ, do it faithfully and leave the results to God. Some weeks there will be three thousand and some years there will be none. And if you are still standing at the edge, stop resisting the rescue. Let yourself be saved.

For worship. Pentecost was the feast of the wheat harvest, and Jesus had told his disciples what kind of harvest he meant to bring in: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Seven weeks after the grain went into the ground, three thousand are gathered in a single day. Every one of them is fruit of his dying. Between Sinai’s three thousand dead and Pentecost’s three thousand alive stands a cross where the Son of God took the death the law demanded, and the harvest of that death is still coming in.
verseByVerse.note: Three thousand died when Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai; now three thousand receive life.

parallels.desc: a crooked and twisted generation

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.

And they devoted themselves. Luke’s word (proskarterountes) is stronger than devoted may suggest to an English ear. It means to stick at a thing, to hold on, to stay put. It is used of a boat kept standing by ready for Jesus (Mark 3:9), of the apostles refusing to be pulled off prayer and the word (6:4), and, memorably, of Simon the magician attaching himself to Philip and not going away (8:13). It is not the vocabulary of attendance. It is the vocabulary of a man who has got hold of something and will not be prised off it. And Luke puts it in a tense meaning they kept on doing it. These are the marks of a true church, from its first day.

Four things you could be shown. Each has its definite article: the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. Not four qualities to aspire to, but four things you could have been taken to and shown.

To the apostles’ teaching. The apostles’ teaching comes first because everything else has to be measured against it. Three thousand brand-new believers had just witnessed wind, fire and a miracle of languages, and what they were put on was a syllabus. That runs against every instinct: the correction of an overwhelming experience is not more experience but more truth. The apostles taught what Jesus had taught them, and what they taught then is the book a reader has open in front of him now, the New Testament. Which means there is no way to be devoted to the apostles’ teaching and casual about Scripture. A church devoted to the apostles’ teaching today is a church devoted to the Bible.

And the fellowship. Fellowship (koinōnia) is a word worn thin by use. In this chapter it costs money within three verses. It means sharing, partnership, common life. It is not the conversation afterwards over coffee, though it may include that; it is a shared life in Christ, in which what belongs to one is genuinely available to another (v. 44).

To the breaking of bread. The breaking of bread almost certainly covers both ordinary meals and the Lord’s Supper, which in this period were not separated: the table where the bread was broken in remembrance was the table where supper was eaten (20:7; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26). And Luke has used the phrase before, at the most moving table in his Gospel. On the evening of the resurrection two disciples at Emmaus recognised their guest only when he took the bread, blessed and broke it, and they ran back to Jerusalem to tell how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:30–35). That is what these new believers were devoted to. Christ’s chosen memorial of himself is not a monument or a pilgrimage but the most ordinary act of a human day, and at that table he still makes himself known.

And the prayers. The prayers, plural and definite, very likely includes the set hours of prayer at the temple, which the apostles were still keeping a chapter later (3:1), as well as their own gatherings. The first Christians did not invent a devotional life from nothing. They took the one they already had and prayed it to a Lord they could now name.

Not a stick. Any believer can run the list over his own life in half a minute and find out where he actually stands, which is a mercy, because most people’s sense of how they are doing spiritually is governed by how they feel that week rather than by anything checkable. But it is a description of what the Spirit produced in a healthy church, not a set of hoops to be cleared for approval, and it is not a stick. Nobody in this verse is doing these four things in order to be accepted. They had been forgiven that morning. This is simply what forgiven people turned out to want.

What if my church is weak in one of these? Most churches are stronger in some than others: rich teaching but thin fellowship, warm fellowship but little prayer, frequent meetings but shallow teaching. Do not leave at once, and do not grumble. Start by being devoted yourself in the area that is weak: come to the prayer meeting, open your home, take the Supper seriously, read the Scriptures with others. Speak graciously to your elders about what you long to see. And pray for your church. But if a church has abandoned the apostles’ teaching itself, denying the gospel or the authority of Scripture, then it has lost the first mark, and you should find a church that holds it.

In a sentence. They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.

On a Tuesday. Measure your church life by these four: the word, fellowship, the Supper, prayer. Which of them would you be most tempted to drop? Devote yourself to that one this month. Read the Bible, open your home, come to the Table prepared, and pray with others.

For worship. How humble is the Lord of glory, to keep his church alive by things this ordinary: a book read aloud, a shared purse, a loaf passed round, a prayer said together. The flames on the heads lasted a morning. These four have lasted twenty centuries, through persecutions and heresies and dull Sundays, because the one who gave them is faithful to the people he bought. He has never needed anything more spectacular, and he has never once left his church without bread.
verseByVerse.note: “The breaking of bread” likely included the Lord’s Supper within a shared meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.

And awe came upon every soul. The ESV notes that the word can simply be rendered fear (phobos), and it should be heard that way: fear, reverence, a sense of God’s presence. Something was in that city which people did not handle casually. The same reaction runs through the church again in chapter 5, on a far darker morning: a community genuinely aware that God is present does not become breezy about it.

Joy and fear together. A good deal of modern Christian atmosphere is engineered to keep everyone comfortable. The first church was joyful; Luke says so explicitly three verses later. It was also afraid. It did not experience the two as being in competition, and any picture of God that has to shed one in order to keep the other has quietly lost him.

And many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. Were being done, so this is a season rather than a single burst. And the preposition is doing work: through. The signs were done through the apostles specifically: they marked them as Christ’s authorised messengers (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

Jesus Christ heals you. And the apostles knew whose power it was. A chapter later Peter takes a lame man by the hand in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and then tells the staring crowd not to look at him as though he had done it: the name of Jesus, by faith in that name, has made this man strong (3:6, 12, 16). Later still he says to a paralysed man at Lydda, Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you (9:34). The wonders in this verse are not the apostles’ achievements but the risen Lord’s own works, continued from heaven, the same works he did in Galilee now done through his messengers. The awe that fell on every soul was awe at him.

Do such signs continue? Luke ties them to the apostles (5:12), and Paul calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). Continuationist Christians believe they continue in the church. The more likely reading is that they confirmed the apostles’ message and ceased with the apostolic age, which is the cessationist position, held charitably toward brothers who see it otherwise. God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills, and we should pray for the sick with faith (James 5:14–15).

And all who believed were together and had all things in common. In common (koina) means shared: they treated their possessions as available to one another. Three things need saying, and the third is the one usually skipped.

It was not compulsory. First, it was not compulsory. Peter says so outright a few chapters on, when Ananias sells a field and lies about the price: while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? (5:4). The property was theirs. Nobody was assessed. Luke is not describing a system imposed on a community; he is describing something a community did.

It did not abolish ownership. Second, it did not abolish ownership as such. They still had homes to break bread in two verses later, and Mary the mother of John Mark still has a house with a gate and a servant girl in chapter 12. This is selling as needs arose, not the founding of a commune.

None of that lets the reader off. Third, and this is the part often skipped: none of that lets the reader off. The text still says that these people held what they owned so loosely that men sold land in order to feed fellow believers they had met that month, and that in consequence there was not a needy person among them (4:34). Whatever the arrangement was not, that is what it was. A church can be perfectly orthodox about private property and completely unlike this.

Would anyone know? Which suggests a test, and it is narrower and less comfortable than the one people usually apply. The question is not whether a Christian would give if he were asked. It is whether he would know. In a congregation of any size, is there anyone quietly going without whom nobody has noticed? The Jerusalem church knew, which means somebody had asked, and the asking is where the whole thing begins.

In a sentence. Awe came over everyone, many wonders and signs were done by the apostles, and all the believers were together and shared everything.

On a Tuesday. Ask someone in your church this week how they are really managing, and listen to the answer. If there is a need you can meet, meet it quietly. And next time you come to worship, come with a little holy fear: the living God is present.

For worship. Holy is the Lord who came so near that a whole city trembled, and kind is the Lord whose nearness made people open their hands. The risen Christ walked again, by his Spirit, among the people of Jerusalem, and those who belonged to him found that they could no longer call anything simply their own, because they had been given everything in him. He is to be feared because he is holy, and loved because he is generous, and in him the trembling and the gladness have never been enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.

And they were selling their possessions and belongings. The tenses carry this verse. Luke does not describe one great liquidation on a particular afternoon. They were selling and distributing: continuous, repeated, as needs came up. Somebody’s situation became known, a field was sold, the money went where it was needed, and a month later it happened again. That makes it harder, not easier. A single dramatic renunciation has the great advantage of being over. What Luke describes is the far more expensive business of remaining permanently available.

And distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. Then the criterion, and it should be read precisely. Not equally. Not by formula. The measure is need, which means somebody had to know what the needs were and exercise judgement about them, and that requires a community close enough that a widow’s circumstances are not a private matter she has to raise herself. It also means the money did not go where it was not needed, which is worth saying to anyone who has watched generosity administered by people who never met the recipient. Believers still owned homes (v. 46; 12:12); Peter tells Ananias that his property was his own to keep (5:4).

The arrangement was not perfect. And Luke does not conceal that it was not perfect. Within four chapters the distribution has broken down along language lines: the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution, and the apostles had to restructure the leadership of the church to put it right (6:1). Luke could have left that out. The first congregation, filled with the Spirit and running on extraordinary generosity, still developed a problem that fell along ethnic lines within a few years. Radical love does not exempt an institution from needing structures, and the people who complained were right to complain.

Where Christians differ: was this communism? Some have seen here a model for Christian communism, or a rule that all Christians must give up private property. Verdict: it was a spontaneous, voluntary expression of love, not a compulsory system imposed by any authority. It met real needs, perhaps of pilgrims who stayed on in Jerusalem. The abiding principle is generous, sacrificial sharing with fellow believers in need (2 Corinthians 8:13–15; 1 John 3:17), not a particular economic model.

Generosity as a symptom. This verse is often preached in a way that leaves Christians vaguely guilty about owning a house, which produces unease and no actual giving. These people did not resolve to become generous. They had, that spring, been forgiven an unpayable debt by a man they had helped to kill, and had been handed the Spirit of God as a free gift when what they had coming was judgement. Money went out of their hands because something enormous had come into them. Generosity here is a symptom, and symptoms are not produced by being scolded about symptoms.

How much should I give, then? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage for believers, but it sets the bar by grace, not by law. Give regularly, as the Lord has prospered you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give proportionately, more as you have more. Give cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the needs of your own church family and its ministry, and then more widely. Many Christians find a tenth a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. And keep some margin in your life so that you can respond when a real need appears, as the Jerusalem church did. Above all, look at the cross first: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In a sentence. They were selling their property and possessions and giving to anyone who had need.

On a Tuesday. Is anyone in your church in need? What could you give? Not only money: a meal, a lift, an evening’s help, a spare room. Look at your diary and your bank statement this week as a disciple, and ask whether they show a person who is permanently available.

For worship. As any had need: that is how the church distributed, and it had learned it from its Lord. Jesus never handed out mercy by merit. He gave sight to the blind because they were blind, bread to the hungry because they were hungry, and forgiveness to sinners because they were sinners. And from his riches in glory God still supplies every need of his people in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19). The church that sold a field to feed a widow was doing on a small scale what its King does on the scale of eternity, giving to the need, at his own cost, and never running short.
verseByVerse.note: Selling was voluntary and as needs arose, not the abolition of property.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.

And day by day, attending the temple together. Two settings in one sentence, and the church has needed both ever since. The temple was the largest sacred enclosure in the ancient world, some thirty-five acres of stone, where a man stands in a crowd of thousands and is one voice in it. They met in Solomon’s Portico, the colonnade along its eastern side (5:12). And notice that the temple is still in use. These are not people who have walked out of Israel’s worship. They are Jews who have found in the Messiah what the temple was for. The break comes later, and when it comes it is forced on them.

Where he had taught daily. Luke has a reason to point us to the temple courts. That is where Jesus himself had taught every day in his last week, while the leaders looked for a way to destroy him (Luke 19:47); he said at his arrest that he had been with them day after day in the temple (Luke 22:53). And Luke’s Gospel ends with the disciples continually in the temple blessing God (Luke 24:53). Now, day by day, the church is back in those courts, because the Lord who taught there is still teaching there, through them. It is the risen Christ who fills his Father’s house again.

And breaking bread in their homes. A room where the loaf has to be passed from hand to hand and everybody present is known by name. Meals together, including the Lord’s Supper. The house church was the basic unit. Nothing the temple does can be done in the kitchen, and nothing the kitchen does can be done in the temple. Congregations tend to be strong in one and thin in the other, and to make a virtue of whichever they happen to have.

Day by day. The phrase appears twice in these two verses, once of their meeting and once of the Lord’s adding. It is not a rule for a modern week, but nobody had instructed them to meet every day.

They received their food with glad and generous hearts. Glad (agalliasis) is exultant joy, the leaping kind. Generous (aphelotēs) is an unusual word that appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It means something like singleness, simplicity, sincerity: the absence of a hidden agenda. Set beside gladness, it describes a table at which nobody is angling for anything, and anyone who has sat at the other kind of table will recognise that as rarer than it sounds.

Praising God and having favor with all the people. At first the ordinary people respected them. It does not last. Within two chapters the apostles are under arrest; within five, one of their number is dead; within six, a persecution has scattered the church out of the city. Luke is describing a season, not issuing a promise. It is a mistake to read this line as though a faithful church will always be liked, for Jesus said plainly that it would not be, and it is an equal mistake to treat unpopularity as evidence of faithfulness. Sometimes a church is disliked because it is faithful and sometimes because it is unpleasant, and the two are not told apart by measuring how disliked it is.

And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. And then the last clause, which is where Luke chooses to set the chapter down. Not the apostles added. Not the preaching added. The Lord added, and in this chapter the Lord is the one God has made both Lord and Christ (v. 36): church growth is the risen Jesus’ own work. The apostles preached and the church lived out its life; the Lord saved. And being saved is in the present tense: a continual stream, day by day, so he kept on doing it. Peter had preached the sermon of his life, and when Luke summarises what was happening, the credit goes elsewhere.

If the Lord adds, what part do we play? The part he has given us, done faithfully. We preach the gospel, pray, welcome, love, and live in a way that commends Christ. The Lord uses all of it, and he usually saves people through the words and lives of ordinary believers. But we cannot make anyone a Christian; only he can open a heart. That frees us from two errors. One is laziness, as if God’s sovereignty meant we need do nothing; the Jerusalem church did a great deal. The other is anxiety and manipulation, as if growth depended on our technique. Plant and water faithfully, and pray for the Lord of the harvest to do what only he can do.

In a sentence. Every day they met together in the temple and broke bread in their homes, eating with joyful, sincere hearts, praising God and enjoying the people’s goodwill, and every day the Lord added to them those who were being saved.

On a Tuesday. Do you have both the temple and the kitchen in your Christian life: the large gathering where you worship with many, and the small table where you are known by name? If one is missing, take a step toward it this week. Invite someone from church for a meal. And pray for the Lord to add to your church those who are being saved.

For worship. Everything in this chapter comes down from somewhere else: the wind, the fire, the languages, the Spirit poured out, the cutting of three thousand hearts, and now the daily arrival of people who were being saved. The church did not launch itself and has never once grown itself. Its Lord’s mercies are new every morning, and so are its members: day by day, as surely as the sun came up over the Mount of Olives, he brought in someone else he had chosen and bought. He was adding on the first morning of the church, and he has not missed a morning since.
verseByVerse.note: The believers still worshipped at the temple while meeting in homes.

2.theology: The Sovereignty of God at the Cross. Acts 2:23 is the Reformed doctrine of divine sovereignty distilled to a sentence. The cross happened “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.” The “definite plan” is God’s eternal counsel, his settled, unalterable purpose. This is not foreknowledge in the Arminian sense of God merely looking ahead and seeing what humans would choose. This is foreordination: God planned the cross before the world began (1 Peter 1:20, Revelation 13:8). Total depravity and sovereign grace appear in one verse: the guilt is wholly human, the purpose is wholly divine. The cross is the intersection of man’s worst deed and God’s greatest gift.
2.examples:
Then: The feast of Pentecost was transformed on this day from an agricultural harvest festival into the birthday of the church. Devout Jews from fifteen regions of the empire heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in their mother tongues and were cut to the heart. The harvest that day was three thousand souls.

Now: Every Lord’s Day is a Pentecost echo. The same Spirit, the same Word, the same call to repentance — and the same Lord who adds to his church those who are being saved. The question for every preacher and every congregation is whether we are as devoted to the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers as that first gathering was. The form has not changed. The power has not diminished.

3.title: The Lame Man and the Living Lord
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. <sup>2</sup>And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple. <sup>3</sup>Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. <sup>4</sup>And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” <sup>5</sup>And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. <sup>6</sup>But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” <sup>7</sup>And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. <sup>8</sup>And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. <sup>9</sup>And all the people saw him walking and praising God, <sup>10</sup>and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. <sup>11</sup>While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. <sup>12</sup>And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? <sup>13</sup>The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. <sup>14</sup>But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, <sup>15</sup>and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. <sup>16</sup>And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. <sup>17</sup>“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. <sup>18</sup>But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. <sup>19</sup>Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, <sup>20</sup>that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, <sup>21</sup>whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. <sup>22</sup>Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. <sup>23</sup>And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’ <sup>24</sup>And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. <sup>25</sup>You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ <sup>26</sup>God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.”
3.overview:
Luke now shows one of the “wonders and signs” of 2:43 in detail. Peter and John go up to the temple for the afternoon prayer, at three o’clock, when the evening sacrifice was offered. At the gate called Beautiful sits a man lame from birth, over forty years old (4:22), carried there daily to beg. Peter has no money, but in the name of Jesus of Nazareth tells him to walk, and the man leaps up and goes into the temple courts walking, leaping and praising God, a living fulfilment of Isaiah’s promise that the lame would leap like a deer when God came to save.

A crowd gathers at Solomon’s Portico, and Peter preaches his second sermon. The healing was not their power but Jesus’ name. The God of Abraham has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom they handed over and disowned before Pilate, asking for a murderer instead and killing the Author of life; but God raised him. They acted in ignorance, yet God used it to fulfil what the prophets foretold, that the Messiah would suffer. So they must repent and turn back, so that their sins may be wiped out, refreshing may come from the Lord, and he may send the Messiah, who must remain in heaven until the time when God restores everything. Jesus is the prophet like Moses whom everyone must hear, and the offspring of Abraham through whom all nations will be blessed; God sent him first to Israel, to bless them by turning them from their wickedness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Healing at the Beautiful Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One afternoon at three, the hour of prayer, Peter and John were going up to the temple. A man lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those going into the temple courts. When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. Peter looked straight at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us!” The man gave them his attention, expecting a gift. Peter said he had no silver or gold, but what he had he would give: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.” Taking him by the right hand, Peter helped him up, and at once his feet and ankles became strong. He jumped to his feet, began to walk, and went with them into the temple courts, walking, jumping and praising God. All the people saw him and recognised him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
Signs, and What They Are Signs Of

The healings in Acts are called signs, and a sign is not the destination; it is a board at the roadside with the name of the destination written on it. These are not displays of power for their own sake, and they are certainly not the working of impersonal forces — Luke will show us in this same book what happens when men try to use the name as a technique (19:13–16). They are the personal act of a risen King through men he has authorised, and what they point to is the repair of a world that has been broken since Eden. A man's ankles are made whole in the middle of Jerusalem, and the thing being said is about everything: a day is coming when the whole creation will be put right, and here is a down payment on it, walking about in the temple courts and making a good deal of noise. Reformed theology has also read the apostolic signs as authenticating the apostolic message, which is why Scripture ties them so closely to the apostles themselves, and why the long argument over whether such things continue is an argument about their function and never about whether God is able.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The man asked for alms and got his legs. But Luke is careful about what else he got: he went into the temple, through the gate that had been the limit of his days. The gate he sat at was the boundary of his whole life, and he had spent forty years on the wrong side of it with his hand out. He received his body back, and his place with it.
