Now: The church still meets people asking for the small thing because it is the only thing they know how to ask for, and it still has no silver worth mentioning. What it has is a name. The temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by that and to offer something more respectable instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.

Meaning first. Acts 3 gives one example of the wonders and signs done through the apostles (2:43). A man lame from birth is healed in Jesus’ name, a crowd gathers, and Peter preaches his second sermon. The healing is a sign of what Jesus does for all who believe: those who could never walk into God’s presence are made whole and enter, praising God. And it sets off the first persecution (chapter 4).

Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. Three details in this opening sentence are doing quiet work. The first is the time. The ninth hour was about three in the afternoon, when the evening lamb was offered on the great altar and the incense went up, and the whole city knew the hour by it. The first Christians kept the Jewish hours of prayer. It is also, as any reader of Luke’s first volume knows, the hour at which Jesus died (Luke 23:44–46). Peter and John are going up to pray at the hour of the sacrifice, into a building where a lamb is being offered, not long after the real Lamb died at that same hour. Luke makes nothing of it. He simply tells us the time.

Peter and John. Luke keeps putting these two together: partners in fishing (Luke 5:10), sent ahead to prepare the Passover (Luke 22:8), and later sent down together to Samaria (8:14). On paper it is an odd pairing, the loud one and the quiet one, and it lasted for years. Whatever else the church is, it is not an arrangement in which everybody has to be the same shape.

A man lame from birth. Not an accident, not an illness he might have recovered from; he had never taken a step. The next chapter tells us he was over forty years old (4:22), which turns a phrase into a life. Somebody carried him out every morning and home every night for something like twelve thousand days. Luke does not name them. There is a family in this story doing forty years of unrecorded lifting.

Whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate. Where they set him down is the point. The Beautiful Gate was most likely the great doorway of Corinthian bronze, often identified with the Nicanor Gate, between the Court of the Gentiles and the Court of the Women. Josephus says it took twenty men to close it and that it far surpassed the gates plated with silver and gold. So he sat at the most magnificent doorway in the Jewish world, and could not go through it. The law barred a lame priest from the altar (Leviticus 21:18); an old saying from David’s capture of the city kept the blind and the lame out of the house (2 Samuel 5:8); Qumran excluded the lame from its assembly outright. Whether or not any rule formally shut this man out, everyone knew where he belonged: outside, at the door, with his hand out.

To ask alms of those entering the temple. It was a good spot for begging: people on their way to pray are at their most generous. So a man is carried daily to the threshold of the place where God had promised to meet his people, and set down in the last position from which he can see in without going in. If a picture were wanted of religion at its most exquisite and least useful, it would be hard to improve on this: the most beautiful gate in the world, a man who cannot walk through it, and a system with nothing to offer him but the small change of the people who can.

What it does not mean. One thing should be said before the miracle, because this chapter is sometimes read in a way that quietly insults people. Nothing here suggests the man’s condition was a punishment, or that it revealed anything whatever about him personally, and Jesus had already refused that entire way of thinking: it was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:3). What the exclusion at the gate exposes is not a defect in the man. It is a limit in the arrangement, and within a few verses the arrangement is going to be walked straight through by somebody it had shut out.

Outside the gate. The one who will open this gate was himself put outside one. Hebrews draws the line from the old sacrifices: the bodies of the animals were burned outside the camp, so Jesus also suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). The lame man sat at the edge of the holy place because the system had no room for him; the Son of God was led out to the edge of the city to make room for people like him. Matthew tells us that in his last week the blind and the lame came to Jesus in the temple and he healed them (Matthew 21:14). This afternoon he does it again, from heaven, through two of his men.

Why were Peter and John still going to the temple? The first Jewish believers kept the temple’s hours of prayer, both from habit and because it was the place to reach their people. They had not left the faith of Israel; they had found its fulfilment. The break came gradually, through Stephen’s preaching, the persecution, and finally the destruction of the temple in AD 70. Hebrews explains that the old system had become obsolete and was ready to vanish away (Hebrews 8:13), because Christ is the true temple, priest and sacrifice. Christians are not bound to Jewish worship practices, though there is wisdom in keeping regular times of prayer.

Who are the people at the gate today? Look for those who are near the church but cannot get in: the disabled person who cannot climb the steps or follow the service, the visitor who does not know the songs, the mentally ill man who makes people uncomfortable, the single mother who cannot manage the children alone in the pew, the elderly widow nobody visits. Many of them are carried to the door by someone else and left there. A church that loves Christ will notice them, make room for them, and above all bring them the gospel, which is the one thing that gets anyone through the gate.

In a sentence. Peter and John were going up to the temple for the three o’clock prayer, as a man lame from birth was being carried to the Beautiful Gate, where he was laid each day to beg from those going in.

On a Tuesday. Notice the people at the gate, who cannot get in. Christ came for them. Ask who in your church or street has been carried to the edge and left there, and do one thing this week to bring them nearer: a lift, a visit, a seat beside you, an explanation of what is going on.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the true door of the house of God, and he is not a door of bronze that takes twenty men to shut. He opens, and no one can shut. The most beautiful gate in Jerusalem could only be admired from outside; he is the gate the lame walk in by. Every one of his people once sat where this man sat, near enough to see in and unable to enter, and he did not toss us a coin. He gave us himself, and brought us home.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer. The Beautiful Gate is not named elsewhere; it was probably a great bronze gate into the temple courts.

parallels.desc: the evening offering

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.

Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. A single verse, and the most ordinary sentence in the chapter. He sees two men about to go in, and he asks for money. Beggars sat where worshippers passed, since giving alms was a religious duty, especially on the way to prayer (Matthew 6:2). He has asked ten thousand times; there will be a way of saying it, a pitch worn smooth with use, and the words will be out before he has properly looked at them.

Reasonable and enormously too small. Notice what he does not ask for. It does not occur to him to ask to be healed. Why would it? He was born like this, nothing in forty years has ever suggested another possibility, and the two men in front of him look poorer than most of the crowd going past. He asks for what he expected: money. The request is entirely reasonable and enormously too small. He got far more.

Our prayers are not the ceiling. There is something here worth taking personally, with a guard round it first. This is not an argument for asking God for larger things on the theory that he is then obliged to produce them, a doctrine with a great deal of wreckage behind it. The thing worth taking is quieter. We do not know what to pray for as we ought (Romans 8:26), which is not a rebuke but a mercy, because it means our prayers are not the ceiling. God is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). This man was still expecting coins when Peter took hold of his hand.

Why was he still lame? But a harder question sits in this verse, and it should not be walked past, because a suffering reader will find it whether or not anyone points at it. This man was carried to that gate every day for decades. Jesus of Nazareth went in and out of that temple repeatedly, feast after feast, for three years. He may have passed him. And the man was still lame on the afternoon Peter came by.

Healing is not delivered evenly. There is no way of making that comfortable, and an attempt would be worse than silence. What can be said is that Scripture never presents God’s healing as a service delivered evenly. At a pool in this same city a multitude of sick people lay in five colonnades, and Jesus healed one man and left (John 5:2–9). Elisha cleansed a foreign general and left many lepers in Israel uncleansed, and Jesus said so in his first sermon, to a congregation that tried to throw him off a cliff for it (Luke 4:27). The pattern is not concealed. The Lord himself stated it to people who did not want to hear it.

Kept for an afternoon. Look at the timing squarely. Forty years at a gate looked, from inside, like forty years of nothing happening. It turns out to have been forty years of a man kept for an afternoon when his healing would be seen by the whole city, admitted as undeniable by the highest court in the nation, and followed by a sermon after which the men alone numbered about five thousand (4:4). He had not been overlooked. That is said about this man, and it is not a formula to lay over anyone else’s forty years: Luke tells us what God did here, not what he is doing in every case. But this delay had a shape, and from inside a delay there appears to be none.

Healed by a living Lord. Notice who is honoured by the waiting. Had this man been healed on one of the days Jesus taught in the temple, it would have been one more wonder in a ministry that ended on a cross, and the city could have buried it with him. Luke does not tell us why the healing waited, but he shows us what it proved. Done weeks after the crucifixion, by two men with nothing but a name, it could mean only one thing, and Peter draws it out at once: the Jesus they killed is alive, and his name has made this man strong (3:15–16). The beggar’s new legs became a witness to an empty tomb.

Should I keep praying for a healing that has not come? Yes, unless God has made it plain that the answer is no, as he did to Paul about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus told a parable so that his people would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1), and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). Pray honestly, and keep praying. But pray as a child, not as a negotiator: ask for healing, and ask also for what God may be giving instead, endurance, his nearness, a deeper trust. And hold on to the certain promise behind all the uncertain ones. Every believer will be healed completely at the resurrection, when he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

In a sentence. When he saw Peter and John about to enter the temple, he asked them for money.

On a Tuesday. Look at what you most often ask God for. Are your prayers all coins: a better week, a smaller bill, a problem gone? Keep asking for those; he is your Father. But ask also for the larger things he delights to give: a heart that loves him, a family turned to Christ, a sin finally broken. He may surprise you as he surprised this man.

For worship. A man held out his hand for coins, and the risen Lord filled it with more than it could hold. Christ does not measure his gifts by the size of the hand stretched out to him, but by the riches of his own glory. He gave this beggar legs, a place in the house of God, and a song, when all he had asked for was the price of a meal. That is the generosity of the Son of God, who gave his life for people who did not know to ask, and who still gives far beyond our asking.
verseByVerse.note: Beggars sat where worshippers passed, since giving alms was a religious duty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, "Look at us." And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.

And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John. Before the word of power there is a look, and Luke spends two verses on it: Peter fixes his eyes, John does the same, the man is told to look, and he fixes his attention. Nothing has happened yet except that two men and a beggar are looking at each other, and Luke thought it worth the ink. The verb (atenisas) is a strong one: a fixed, deliberate stare, the same word used later of Stephen gazing into heaven (7:55) and of Paul looking intently at the council about to try him (23:1). It is not a glance. Peter stops, and locks on. Most people avoided looking at beggars. Peter looks him in the eye.

How the beggar’s pitch works. Consider what that interrupts. A beggar’s pitch is arranged so that nobody has to look at anybody. The hand goes out, the eyes go down, the coin drops from above, and the giver walks on without meeting a face. Both parties are protected by it: the giver from the person, and the beggar from the humiliation of being seen.

Look at us. Peter dismantles the arrangement before there is any healing on offer, so that for a moment the man is simply a person being addressed, perhaps for the first time that day. The command is not for attention, but to direct his expectation.

Looked at by the Lord. Peter had learned this look somewhere. On the night of his denial, as the rooster crowed in the high priest’s courtyard, the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61), and Peter went out and wept bitterly. That look did not finish him; it brought him back. The man who now fixes his eyes on a beggar has himself been looked at by Jesus at his worst and not discarded. And the look serves a name: Peter draws the man’s eyes to himself only so that, a moment later, he can turn them past himself to Jesus of Nazareth.

Attention before help. It should be said that this is not a method to be copied in the hope of results; Peter is not doing a thing that works. But there is an order in it that does travel. Attention comes before help. Whatever else the church has been given to do, it cannot do any of it for people it will not look at, and a great deal of Christian charity is organised, with the best intentions in the world, so that nobody has to. Every person at the gate is made in the image of God.

And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. And notice what the man is doing at the end of verse 5. He is wrong about what and entirely right about who. He is looking at the right men with far too small a hope, which is a more promising position than the alternatives, and God has a long record of meeting people exactly there. Expectation is the first step.

Should I give money to people who beg? Scripture commands generosity to the poor (Proverbs 19:17; Galatians 2:10), and it also calls for wisdom, because some gifts help and some harm. There is no single rule. Sometimes giving a little money is right; sometimes buying food, sharing a meal or pointing someone to a church mercy ministry or local shelter does more good; sometimes the most loving thing is to give through an organisation that knows the person’s situation. What is never right is contempt, or walking past as if the person were not there. Whatever you give or do not give, look the person in the eye, speak kindly, and if you can, ask his name.

In a sentence. Peter and John looked straight at him, and Peter told him to look at them, and he gave them his attention, expecting to receive something.

On a Tuesday. Look people in the eye. Treat the overlooked as people, made in God’s image: the cleaner, the checkout assistant, the man outside the station, the child nobody listens to. Learn one new name this week, and use it.

For worship. A beggar looked up expecting a coin from two strangers, and what was coming toward him was the name of the Son of God. That is the way of our Lord: he meets a small hope with a great gift. His eyes were on his people before the world was made, and they did not turn away when he hung on the cross with the rulers scoffing at him. One day we shall see his face, and the gaze that meets ours will be the gaze of the one who loved us there.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!" And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.

I have no silver and gold. Do not hurry past the first half of what Peter says, because it is the half people forget. The leading apostle of the church, in the days of its greatest power, is standing at the temple gate without money. He is not withholding it on principle; he does not have it. What money was given went to the needy (2:45; 4:35). And he does not brush the man’s need aside either. But what I do have I give to you: he gives what he has, and it is far more than was asked for.

In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk! A name in that world was not a label. It stood for the person and everything he was: his authority, his standing, his will. That is why a king’s officer acted in the name of the king and expected to be obeyed as though the king were present in the room. Peter is not reciting an incantation. He has no power of his own, and he will say so (v. 12). He is standing at a temple gate as the accredited representative of somebody who is not visibly there, and doing exactly what such a man does: acting on his master’s authority, in his master’s name, in public. Jesus is the healer, from heaven.

Of Nazareth. And notice which name he uses. Of Nazareth: the address, the sneer, the thing written on the board over the cross not long before for the whole city to read on its way past (John 19:19). Peter does not reach for a dignified title. He uses the one that had been used to dismiss the man and to execute him, and it puts a cripple on his feet. The despised man from the despised town is the Lord of all.

And he took him by the right hand and raised him up. Then the touch. Peter does what Jesus did, taking Peter’s own mother-in-law and Jairus’s daughter by the hand (Mark 1:31; 5:41). And raised him up (ēgeiren) is the word this same chapter uses of the resurrection (3:15). The gesture is a small enactment of the thing being announced: a man who cannot get up is pulled upright by somebody who has met the one God raised.

And immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. Luke, whom Paul calls the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), gets specific, using a term for the ankle bones found nowhere else in the New Testament. He is telling us which joints took the weight. The healing was instant and complete, of a condition from birth: muscles that had never been used, in a man who had never learned to walk.

Silver and gold have I none. An old story tells of a medieval pope showing a visitor the treasures of Rome and remarking that the church could no longer say silver and gold have I none, and being answered, neither can she now say rise up and walk. Whether it happened or not, the point is worth keeping. Power in the church has never been carried in its purse.

What it does not mean. It is also worth setting beside the teaching that God’s favour shows itself in wealth, and that a believer who lacks money is short of faith. Here is the man through whom this miracle came, and he has nothing in his pockets. On that account he was either the least favoured man in Jerusalem or the doctrine is wrong. Not that poverty is holiness: this same church will take up collections and handle money carefully. But what Peter had to give was not for sale, and no amount of silver would have bought it.

The name is not a lever. One guard, and Luke himself supplies it later in this same book. There were men at Ephesus who heard about the name and tried to work it as a formula, adjuring evil spirits by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims, and it went extremely badly for them (19:13–16). The name works here because Peter belongs to the one who owns it, and it has never once worked for anybody who wanted the effect without the allegiance.

Do healings like this still happen, and should churches have healing ministries? God still heals, in answer to prayer and by ordinary means such as medicine, as he wills. But this healing was a sign that confirmed the apostles’ message about the risen Christ. Many Christians believe such gifts continue in the church; the more likely reading is that healings of this apostolic kind, instant, complete, at a word, belonged to the foundational age, and that position, cessationism, is held charitably toward those who see it differently. The church today prays for the sick (James 5:14–15), and expects God to answer; but no one holds the apostles’ gift.

What does it mean to pray in Jesus’ name? It is not a phrase to add at the end like a password. It means coming to God on the basis of who Jesus is and what he has done, not your own worthiness; asking as his representative, for things that fit his character and purposes; and trusting his authority, not your technique. That is why Jesus promised that whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son (John 14:13). A prayer that is truly in his name is a prayer he would sign, and you can pray it with great boldness.

In a sentence. Peter said he had no silver or gold, but gave what he had, commanding him in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth to get up and walk, and taking his right hand he raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles grew strong.

On a Tuesday. You may not have much money to give, but if you know Christ you have something worth more: his name and his gospel. Give what you have. Pray for someone by name today, and if the moment comes, tell them about Jesus of Nazareth.

For worship. A man asked two strangers for the price of a meal, and was answered from the throne of God. The power that raised Christ from the dead came down to a pair of ankle bones, at three in the afternoon, at the door of a building he had sat outside for years. That is how near the risen Lord’s reign comes, and how low it stoops. He holds the treasuries of heaven and earth, and what he gives the poor is not silver or gold but his own strength, put into their feet.
verseByVerse.note: “In the name of” means by his authority and power.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.

And leaping up, he stood and began to walk. Luke piles up the verbs, and the pile is the point: leaping up, standing, beginning to walk, entering, walking, leaping, praising. Seven actions in one sentence, from a man who had never performed any of them.

A man who never learned to walk. Stop on the leaping, because it is stranger than it looks. A man lame from birth has never learned to walk. Even supposing the legs were suddenly sound, balance and coordination and the whole unconscious skill of putting one foot in front of the other are learned in infancy over months of falling down. He does not fall down. He is given the legs and the use of them in the same instant, and his first instinct with a working body is to jump.

Then shall the lame man leap like a deer. Isaiah had used that very picture: then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6). Isaiah 35 is not a list of medical predictions. It is a poem about a desert that blossoms, a highway running through it, and the ransomed of the LORD coming home to Zion with everlasting joy upon their heads. The leaping man is one line in a song about the end of exile.

The lame walk. And Jesus had already claimed that song as his own. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether he was the one who was to come, Jesus answered with Isaiah’s list: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk (Luke 7:22). The healings were his credentials as the Messiah. So when a lame man leaps in the temple courts weeks after the crucifixion, the sign says what it said in Galilee, with one addition: the one who was to come has not stopped coming. He has died, risen and ascended, and his works go on. What breaks out at the Beautiful Gate is a fragment of Isaiah’s homecoming arriving early, under the name of the King who leads it.

And entered the temple with them. Set down at that gate morning after morning for forty years and never once through it, he now walks in with the two men, on his own feet, making a scene. The place of worship, which for his whole life had been the building he was carried to and not into, is the first place he goes. It is a picture of salvation: Christ brings those who were shut out into the presence of God. You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ, and through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:13, 18).

Walking and leaping and praising God. What he does with the new legs is not what most people would predict. He does not go home, or look for work, or walk the streets of a city he had only ever seen from a sitting position. He goes into the house of God and praises, and Luke says it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9). Not praising Peter, but God.

The praise of those who remember. Anyone who has had a prayer answered knows how quickly an answer becomes the new normal. This man’s gratitude is loud, immediate, physical and entirely undignified, and nobody asks him to keep it down. There is a kind of praise that only comes from people who remember exactly what they were like before, and a church is poorer in proportion to how fast it forgets.

Why don’t I feel like leaping any more? Because joy fades when memory fades, and familiarity dulls even the greatest gifts. The answer is not to manufacture excitement but to remember. Go back over what you were without Christ: guilty, far off, without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). Recall specific mercies, the answered prayer, the sin forgiven, the dark year he carried you through. Read the Gospels and watch what he did for you. Sing truths, not just feelings. And sit near those who have just come to faith; their wonder is contagious. Joy in God is not always loud, but it grows wherever grace is remembered.

In a sentence. He jumped up, stood and started walking, and went into the temple with them, walking, leaping and praising God.

On a Tuesday. Write down three things God has done for you that you once could not have imagined. Thank him for each one out loud. Then go to church on Sunday as someone who has been carried in from the gate.

For worship. A man who had never taken a step went in leaping, and the first thing he did with his new legs was to praise God. The Lord Jesus gives his people more than strength: he gives them somewhere to go and someone to praise. He opened the way into the holiest place by his own blood, and every one of his redeemed will one day walk into the Father’s presence on legs that will never fail, and find the house full of others who were once carried to the gate.

parallels.desc: then shall the lame man leap like a deer

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

And all the people saw him walking and praising God. These two verses look like scene-setting. They are in fact the hinge on which the next chapter turns. It was a public miracle, at the busiest hour, in the busiest place.

And recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. That word recognised carries the whole evidential weight of the chapter. He was not a stranger who might have been anybody. He had been at that gate every day for decades, part of the furniture of the place; every worshipper going up to pray had stepped round him, and a great many had put something in his hand. There was no room for a substitution or mistaken identity. Everyone knew him. There could be no fraud.

We cannot deny it. The council runs into this the following morning. Hostile, with every motive to find a hole in the story, it examines the case and concludes that a notable sign has been done, that all Jerusalem knows it, and that we cannot deny it (4:16). It then forbids the apostles to speak, which is not what men do when they have exposed a fraud. It is what they do when they have run into something true that they did not want.

The same Jesus, still at work. Luke opened this book by calling his Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1), and here is what he meant. The scene at the gate has happened before. When Jesus healed a man born blind, his neighbours said, Is this not the man who used to sit and beg? (John 9:8). The same question, the same kind of man, the same unarguable recognition. The hands are different now, Peter’s instead of his, but the work is the same work, because the worker is the same. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Hebrews 13:8), and the risen Lord is still straightening legs from the right hand of God.

And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. Luke gives the crowd two words for their reaction. The first means a stunned, arrested wonder; the second (ekstasis) is the word for being put out of one’s own mind. Neither is faith. This is the condition a person is in when the shape of the world has just changed and nothing has yet replaced it, and it is exactly the condition Peter is about to preach into. Astonishment is not conversion, and Luke never confuses the two: a crowd can be amazed at an act of God and still need telling what it means. Which is why the miracle takes ten verses and the sermon takes sixteen. The sign draws a crowd, and opens the way for the word.

Where it cannot be filed away. Notice how the whole thing was arranged. God healed the one man in Jerusalem whose condition everyone could verify, at the busiest hour, at the most public gate of the temple. He is perfectly capable of working where nobody sees, and does so constantly; but when he intends a thing to stand as evidence, he puts it where it cannot be filed away, and lets his enemies examine it at their leisure.

Why doesn’t God do public miracles today to convince sceptics? Partly because miracles do not by themselves produce faith: the council saw this one, admitted it, and still refused to believe. Jesus said that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And partly because the great public signs have already been given and recorded. The healing at the gate, and above all the resurrection, were done in the open and written down so that you may believe (John 20:31). God now works chiefly through his word and Spirit, and his most persuasive evidence today is often a changed life: a man who was known for one thing and is now known for Christ.

In a sentence. All the people saw him walking and praising God and recognised him as the beggar from the Beautiful Gate, and were filled with wonder and amazement.

On a Tuesday. A changed life opens doors for the gospel. Let yours be seen. The people who knew you before Christ are the ones best placed to notice what he has done, and they are also the ones you are most tempted to hide it from. Do not hide it.

For worship. A city that had stepped round this man for forty years now stood and stared at him, and he was praising God. The Lord Jesus delights to turn the most familiar figures in a town into trophies of his grace, so that the people who knew them best are the first to wonder. He has done it with tax collectors and persecutors, with beggars, and with us. Every saved sinner is somebody’s neighbour, recognised and changed, walking where he could not walk before, with the name of Jesus written over the change.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While the man held on to Peter and John, the astonished crowd ran to them at Solomon’s Colonnade. Peter asked why they were surprised and why they stared as if he and John had made the man walk by their own power or godliness. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they handed over and rejected before Pilate when Pilate had decided to release him. They disowned the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer instead; they killed the author of life, but God raised him from the dead, and the apostles are witnesses. By faith in Jesus’ name this man, whom they know, has been made strong; the faith that comes through Jesus has given him complete healing. Peter knows they acted in ignorance, as their leaders did, but this is how God fulfilled what all the prophets had said, that his Messiah would suffer. So they must repent and turn to God, so that their sins may be wiped out, times of refreshing may come from the Lord, and he may send the Messiah appointed for them, Jesus. Heaven must receive him until the time comes for God to restore everything, as he promised long ago through the prophets. Moses said God would raise up a prophet like him, whom they must listen to in everything, and anyone who will not listen will be cut off. All the prophets from Samuel on foretold these days. They are heirs of the prophets and of the covenant God made with Abraham, when he said that through Abraham’s offspring all peoples on earth would be blessed. God raised up his servant and sent him first to them, to bless them by turning each of them from their wicked ways.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus as the Fulfilment of the Covenant with Abraham

Peter closes on the promise to Abraham — in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed (v. 25; cf. Genesis 22:18; 28:14) — and it matters a great deal where that promise was sworn. It is repeated on the mountain, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught in the thicket: the promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham's line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided. The gospel, on this reading, is not the abandonment of God's promises to Israel but their arrival — not a second plan drawn up after the first failed, but the first plan reaching the date it had been set for. Reformed biblical theology insists that the covenant of grace runs unbroken from Genesis to Revelation and finds its definitive form in Christ, which is why Peter can preach this to Jews in the temple courts without once suggesting that they should change religion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who bore the most direct responsibility there was — you denied the Holy and Righteous One — and then called them brothers three verses later and told them the blessing was coming to them first. Now: The order has never changed. A gospel that cannot name what a man has actually done has nothing to forgive him for; a gospel that names it and leaves him standing there is not the gospel at all. Peter does both in one sermon, and the second half is longer than the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon's. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?

While he clung to Peter and John. The first thing Luke tells us about the healed man is that he would not let go. The word means gripping, holding fast. A man who has been dependent his whole life has just been made independent, and his instinct is to hang on to the two people who did it. It is a small, entirely human detail, and Luke keeps it.

All the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. The location is worth knowing. Solomon’s Portico was the long covered colonnade running down the eastern side of the temple platform, popularly believed to have survived from Solomon’s original building: a sheltered walkway of columns where people gathered out of the weather. It is where Jesus was walking at the Feast of Dedication when the crowd gathered round him and demanded that he tell them plainly whether he was the Christ, and where they picked up stones to kill him for the answer (John 10:23–31). It is also where the church will later meet as a matter of habit (5:12). Peter is preaching Christ on the very stones where Christ was nearly stoned for preaching himself.

Why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us? Peter refuses the attention, and the refusal repays taking word by word. As though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? He disclaims two things, and the second is the one people miss. He disclaims the power, which anybody would expect. He also disclaims the piety: the word means godliness, personal devotion, and that is the harder disclaimer, because it is the flattering one. A crowd watching a miracle will always conclude that the men involved must be unusually holy, and that is a conclusion which is extremely pleasant to leave uncorrected. Miracles were not rewards for holiness.

A matter of information. Remember who is speaking. This is the man who, a few hundred yards from where he now stands, told a servant girl that he did not know Jesus (Luke 22:57). If any man in Jerusalem had reason to know that his own godliness was not the operative factor in anything, it was Peter. The deflection is not modesty. It is a matter of information.

Who are people looking at? Notice what kind of deflection it is, because there is a counterfeit that achieves the opposite. Peter does not say it was nothing, and he does not perform the shuffling embarrassment that draws as much attention as accepting the credit would have done. He redirects. He names somebody else, immediately and at length, and the crowd’s attention goes where he sends it. False modesty keeps the light on the man by making him interesting; genuine deflection moves it. The test of true ministry is simple enough: when the sentence is finished, whom has it made much of?

Because he went to the Father. Peter can deflect so completely because he knows where the power came from. On the night before he died Jesus had told them that whoever believes in him will do the works he does, and greater works than these, because I am going to the Father (John 14:12). The healing at the gate is not Peter’s achievement, nor the leftover glow of three years in Jesus’ company. It is that promise beginning to be kept: the work of a Lord who has gone to the Father and acts from there through the men he left behind. Peter is not stepping out of the light from good manners. He is pointing to the one who is actually doing it.

What it does not mean. None of which forbids ordinary gratitude to people who have helped us; Paul thanks his fellow workers by name all over his letters. What it forbids is the transfer of a debt. This crowd was about to pay Peter for something he had not done, in a currency he had no right to accept, and he would not take it.

How do I accept thanks without stealing glory? Simply and honestly. When someone thanks you, you need not deny that you did anything; say thank you, and where it is true and natural, say who really did it: I am so glad God used it, or the Lord was kind to us. Do not fish for more praise, and do not perform humility. Then, privately, hand the compliment straight on to God in prayer. Keep a short memory of your successes and a long memory of his mercies. And watch your heart when you are not thanked: if that stings badly, it is a sign you were collecting the glory for yourself.

In a sentence. As the man held on to Peter and John, the astounded crowd ran to them at Solomon’s Portico, and Peter asked why they stared, as if the apostles had made him walk by their own power or godliness.

On a Tuesday. All glory to Christ. When God uses you, point away from yourself. Next time someone praises you for something good, notice how your heart responds, and practise sending the attention where Peter sent it: to Jesus.

For worship. All the people ran together to Peter and John, and Peter sent them on to Jesus. The glory of the church has never been its own shine, only its pointing. The Lord Jesus is the healer and the giver, at work from the Father’s right hand, and he shares his work with his servants without ever sharing his glory, because there is no one else worthy of it. Every crowd that has ever gathered round a servant of his was, in the end, meant for him.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s portico was a covered colonnade along the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him.

The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers. Peter opens with the oldest name in Israel’s vocabulary. It is the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6, 15), and Peter chooses it deliberately. He is not announcing a new God, a new religion, or a break with anything at all. He is telling a Jewish crowd in the Jewish temple that the God they have worshipped all their lives has just acted in Jesus.

Glorified his servant Jesus. Then a word a first-century congregation would have caught at once and which passes most modern readers by. The term (pais) is not the ordinary word for a slave, and the phrase sits very close to the opening line of the last of Isaiah’s Servant Songs in the Greek Old Testament: behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted (Isaiah 52:13). That is the sentence that begins the passage running straight on into Isaiah 53: the wounds, the silence before the shearers, the grave made with the wicked, the Servant bearing the sin of many. Peter has said one word and put the whole of Isaiah 53 into the air. His hearers knew that chapter. He does not have to explain it. Jesus is the Suffering Servant, now glorified by God in his resurrection and in the healing done in his name.

Whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. Then the charge, delivered without any softening. The contrast: God glorified him; you denied him. And the comparison with Pilate is deliberate and it is brutal. A pagan governor with no covenant, no Scriptures, no promises and no particular appetite for justice had worked out that the prisoner ought to be let go (Luke 23:4, 14–16, 22). The covenant people, standing in front of him, insisted otherwise. Peter is not scoring a rhetorical point. He is describing what happened in that courtyard, and every person listening remembered it, because it had been a matter of weeks.

Denied. One word in the charge changes the temperature of the whole sermon. Denied is the word Luke used of Peter himself in the high priest’s courtyard: but he denied it, saying, Woman, I do not know him (Luke 22:57). Peter is accusing a crowd of a sin whose exact name is written against him. He is not throwing a stone from a safe distance. He has been forgiven for it by the man he is now preaching, which is why he can say this to their faces and call them brothers four verses later. It is the severity of a man who has done it, and who knows what was done about it.

Is the God of the Old Testament the same as the Father of Jesus? Yes, and this verse says so as plainly as anything in Scripture. Some, from the ancient heretic Marcion to modern writers, have set an angry Old Testament God against a loving New Testament Jesus. Peter knows nothing of it. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God who glorified Jesus. The same God shows mercy and judgment in both testaments: the Old Testament is full of his steadfast love, and the New Testament speaks of his wrath as plainly as the Old. Jesus himself said the Scriptures bear witness about me (John 5:39). Read your whole Bible as one story, told by one God, about one Saviour.

In a sentence. Peter said the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they handed over and rejected before Pilate, though Pilate had decided to release him.

On a Tuesday. The God of the Old Testament is the God who raised Jesus. Read your whole Bible as one story. If you have been avoiding the Old Testament, start this week with Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12, and read it with the cross in view.

For worship. The God who spoke to Moses from the burning bush is the God who glorified his Servant after the cross. He promised a Servant who would be wounded for our transgressions, and he kept the promise in his own Son. The covenant God of the fathers has not changed his name or his heart: he is still the God who comes down to rescue, and his Servant is lifted up and exalted for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “His servant” echoes Isaiah’s Servant, who would be “lifted up” and glorified.

parallels.desc: my servant shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.

But you denied the Holy and Righteous One. Peter now stacks three titles, and each is chosen to make the crowd feel the shape of what was done. The Holy One (Psalm 16:10; Mark 1:24) and the Righteous One (Isaiah 53:11; 7:52; 22:14) were both recognised descriptions of the Messiah, and both are the opposite of what a court is supposed to condemn. They rejected the only sinless man who ever lived. You denied him: the second time Peter uses that verb in two verses, and he presses it because the denial was not an accident of a chaotic morning. It was a choice, made out loud, in a public square, in daylight.

And asked for a murderer to be granted to you. That is Barabbas (Luke 23:18–19, 25), and Peter does not name him, because nobody needed reminding. Sit with the transaction a moment. A guilty man was released and an innocent man was executed in his place, at the direct request of the crowd. Barabbas is the first human being for whom Jesus of Nazareth demonstrably died in the plainest sense the words will bear: the death the law had coming for him fell on another man. What the crowd arranged that morning as a miscarriage of justice turned out to be a working picture of the atonement, and they built it themselves without the faintest idea what they were making.

And you killed the Author of life. The word is one Luke likes (archēgos): the founder, the originator, the pioneer and prince, the one who goes first and opens a way. It turns up again at 5:31 of the Leader and Saviour, and Hebrews uses it of the founder of our salvation and of our faith (Hebrews 2:10; 12:2). He is the one through whom all life came, and who leads his people into life. Peter sets it directly against killed so that the absurdity cannot be missed. You murdered the source of life. It is a sentence with a contradiction built into it, like drowning water, and Peter states it flatly and lets it stand there. They spared the murderer and killed the life-giver.

Whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. Then, in a handful of words, the reversal, and then the apostolic signature. Again, eyewitness testimony: we saw him alive.

What it does not mean. A guard is needed here and should not be skipped, because these are among the verses that have been used to do enormous harm. You denied, you killed: sentences of this kind have been read out from pulpits in Christian Europe and followed within days by violence against Jewish neighbours. Anybody tempted to use them so should read the paragraph they sit in. The speaker is a Jew. The audience is Jewish. The setting is the Jewish temple at the hour of Jewish prayer. He calls them brothers; he says in the next breath that they acted in ignorance; he tells them God sent his servant to you first; and the entire sermon is a plea that they should be blessed. What is happening here is what has always happened when a prophet of Israel addresses Israel: Isaiah called its rulers the rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:10), and nobody has ever thought Isaiah an enemy of the Jews. Peter is not indicting a people across the centuries. He is telling the men in front of him what they did, in order to tell them what may now be done about it. And the verse that answers the misuse most completely is the one the sermon ends on: God sent his Servant to bless you.

Am I like Barabbas? In the way that matters most, yes. Every believer is a guilty person set free because an innocent one took his place. Scripture says Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18), and that God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). He bore the penalty our sins deserved, the wrath of God against sin, so that we would never have to bear it. Barabbas walked out of prison with nothing to do but go home. You walk out with everything to live for, and a Saviour to thank.

In a sentence. Peter said they rejected the Holy and Righteous One, asked for a murderer instead, and killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead, as the apostles had witnessed.

On a Tuesday. Think of yourself today as Barabbas set free. When you are tempted to think God owes you something, or to look down on someone else, remember whose place you are standing in and whose death set you loose.

For worship. Men took the one through whom all life came, and killed him, and God answered by raising him from the dead. Death held the Author of life from Friday to the first day of the week and could not keep him, because the life was his own. That is the Lord his people worship: the Holy One who stood condemned, the Righteous One numbered with transgressors, the Prince of life who walked out of the grave as its master, and who leads everyone who belongs to him out after him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all.

And his name, by faith in his name, has made this man strong whom you see and know. This is the most tangled sentence in the book of Acts, and it is worth saying so, because a reader who finds it hard to follow is not being slow. Peter doubles back on himself twice: his name, by faith in his name, has made this man strong, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health. It reads like a man tripping over his own words in his hurry to make sure the credit lands in the right place. He gets the name in twice and the faith in twice, and the grammar takes the damage. The name of Jesus, his person and power, made the man strong; faith in his name was the means. The power is Christ’s; faith is the hand that receives it.

Whose faith? Underneath the tangle is a question that has to be settled, and it is a pastoral question of the first order. It cannot straightforwardly be the man’s, at least not before the healing. Look back at verse 5. He was expecting to receive something from them: a coin. He had no expectation of healing, had not asked for it, did not know it was available, and had, as far as Luke tells us, no opinion whatever about Jesus of Nazareth. He was not healed because he believed hard enough. The faith in view is most probably the apostles’, and perhaps the man’s as he responded when Peter took his hand.

And the faith that is through Jesus. And Peter’s own phrasing points the same way. Whatever faith is operating in this verse comes through Christ. It is not a substance the man manufactured out of himself and presented at the gate. Even the faith is his gift: by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29). Faith here is something handed down, not a fee paid up.

What it does not mean. That matters far more than a point of grammar, because there is an entire style of teaching built on the opposite reading, and it wounds people badly. It tells the sick that they are not healed because their faith was insufficient; it sends them home from a meeting worse off than they came, carrying the illness and an accusation on top of it. It should be said plainly that this verse cannot be used that way. The one man in Scripture whose healing is most explicitly credited to faith in the name of Jesus had shown no interest in the name an hour earlier.

Has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. Then the word Peter picks for the result (holoklēria), which appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It means wholeness: sound in every part, nothing left over, nothing half-finished. Not managed, not stabilised, not improved: whole, and in the presence of you all. The healing is complete, public and checkable, and Peter effectively dares the crowd to check it, since the man is standing there still holding on to him.

What part does faith play when I pray for healing? Pray in faith, trusting that God is able and good, as James tells us to (James 5:15). But faith is trust in God, not a force that guarantees a particular result. Paul had great faith and was not healed of his thorn; Timothy had a weak stomach and was told to take a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23); Trophimus was left ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). So never conclude that someone remains ill because they did not believe enough, and never say it to them. Ask boldly, submit humbly, and keep trusting God whatever the answer, because his love is proved at the cross, not by the outcome of a particular prayer.

In a sentence. Peter said it was Jesus’ name, through faith in his name, that made this man strong, and the faith that comes through Jesus gave him complete health in front of them all.

On a Tuesday. Even your faith is Christ’s gift. Thank him for it, and use it. And if you know someone who has been told they are still sick because they lack faith, go and tell them what this verse really says.

For worship. The name of Jesus took a man who had never stood and made him sound in every part, with nothing left over and nothing half-done. That is how our Lord saves: not by patching, but by making new. What he did for one man’s ankles in the presence of all, he will do for the whole body of every believer on the day of resurrection, when his people stand before the Father without spot or blemish, and the glory of every part of it will be his.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled.

And now, brothers. Here the sermon turns, and it turns on one word. Two verses ago they were the people who denied the Holy One and killed the Author of life. Now they are family, fellow Jews, brothers. Nothing has changed about the facts. Peter has simply arrived at the reason he was reciting them. His tone softens.

I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. This is not an acquittal, and Peter does not present it as one; he has just spent three verses establishing precisely what they did. It does not mean they were innocent, but that they did not know who Jesus truly was. And to feel its force you have to know how Israel’s law handled the distinction.

Two kinds of sin. The law separated two kinds of sin sharply. For sin committed unintentionally, through ignorance, there was a sacrifice and atonement: the offender brought his offering and was forgiven. For sin committed with a high hand, in open defiance, the law made no provision; that man was to be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:27–31). So when Peter says you acted in ignorance, he is not being generous with the truth. He is telling a crowd who have just realised they killed the Messiah which side of that line they stand on, and handing them the only door the law of Moses ever left open.

Father, forgive them. Peter did not invent the assessment. Paul makes the same judgement: none of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). And Luke alone records the prayer from the cross that says it first and most simply: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Some early copies lack the sentence, and most Bibles note it, but it is very old and it is exactly what the rest of the New Testament assumes. Peter is preaching his master’s own prayer back over the heads of the men it was prayed for.

Ignorance is not innocence. Two guards. First, ignorance is not innocence. Paul says of his own persecuting years that he received mercy because he had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13), which is a sentence about mercy, not about acquittal; he still called himself the foremost of sinners. Second, Scripture is perfectly capable of condemning sincere ignorance, saying elsewhere of Israel that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2). Ignorance opens a door. It does not walk anybody through it.

But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. Then verse 18 sets the other half beside it. All the prophets: the whole Old Testament points to a suffering Messiah (Luke 24:25–27; 1 Peter 1:10–11). The worst thing they ever did is the thing God had been announcing through every prophet since Samuel. God fulfilled his own word through their ignorant wickedness. Both are true at once, and Peter does not choose between them.

The man who fears he cannot be forgiven. Here the passage becomes something to hold on to. A reader frightened that he has done the thing which cannot be forgiven should look hard at who is being addressed. These people had arranged the judicial murder of the Son of God and chosen a murderer over him. And they are being called brothers, and offered forgiveness weeks later, by one of his friends. Whatever the unforgivable sin may be, it is evidently not this.

What is the unforgivable sin, then? Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–30), when religious leaders, faced with his plain works of power, attributed them to Satan. It is not a single careless word or a terrible deed done in weakness. It is a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, persisted in until the heart no longer wants forgiveness at all. That is why it cannot be forgiven: not because Christ’s blood is too weak, but because the person refuses the only remedy. If you are worried that you have committed it, your worry is itself strong evidence that you have not. Come to Christ: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Peter acknowledged that they and their rulers had acted in ignorance, but God had fulfilled what all the prophets foretold, that his Christ would suffer.

On a Tuesday. If there is a sin in your past you are convinced is too great, read these verses again and see who was being offered mercy. Then take your sin to God by name and receive his forgiveness. And when someone wrongs you, consider whether they truly knew what they were doing; pray for them as Jesus prayed for his executioners.

For worship. Every prophet had said it, and hardly anyone had understood it: the Christ would suffer. God wrote the sufferings of his Son into the Scriptures centuries before the nails, and then fulfilled them through the very hands that rejected him. Nothing in that dark week caught him unprepared. The crime that seemed to end everything was the promise coming true, and the men who carried it out were among the first to be offered its mercy. Such is the wisdom of God, who brings our salvation out of the worst thing we ever did.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,

Repent therefore, and turn back. Two commands, and they are not one command said twice. Repent (metanoēsate) names what happens in the mind: a change of thinking, a reversal of judgement, a man coming to see a thing the opposite way round from the way he saw it yesterday. Turn back (epistrepsate) names what happens to the feet: to turn around, return, convert, the thing a man does in a street when he realises he has been walking the wrong way. Peter asks for both, and the order is instructive: the mind changes, and then the body goes somewhere different, away from sin and towards God in Christ. A repentance that never reaches the feet has stopped halfway; and a change of direction with no change of mind is only a new set of habits, and will not last the winter.

What it does not mean. Neither word means feeling bad. Sorrow often comes with repentance and there is nothing wrong with it, but a man can be extremely sorry and turn round nothing at all, and Scripture has a name for that: worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Nor is this penance, the working off of a debt by suffering something. Peter is not asking them to pay for the crucifixion. He is telling them to change their minds about the man they crucified and to walk the other way.

That your sins may be blotted out. Then what it is for. The word (exaleiphthēnai) means wiped away, erased, and the picture is exact. Ancient ink did not sink into papyrus and stain it the way modern ink stains paper; it sat on the surface, and a wet sponge took it off and left the sheet clean and usable. That is the picture. Not the debt reduced. Not the record sealed. Not the file marked closed and put in a drawer it can be fetched out of. Wiped off, and the page is the same page. David prayed for it: blot out my transgressions (Psalm 51:1, 9). God promised it: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isaiah 43:25). And at the cross he did it, cancelling the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14).

Wiped by the death they demanded. Notice what Peter is offering, and to whom. The record that is wiped away was nailed to a cross, and it was the cross their own city had shouted for in front of Pilate (Luke 23:21). The death they caused is the death that cleans their page. Peter does not say their sin against Jesus will be overlooked; he says that Jesus himself, crucified at their demand, is the way it is removed. There is no forgiveness anywhere except through the man they rejected, and no rejection of him so complete that his blood cannot wipe it out.

The private file. This is where an ordinary Christian most often fails to believe what he says he believes. Ask a man at eleven in the morning whether his sins are forgiven and he will say yes. Ask him what happens at three in the morning, when a particular memory arrives, the thing he said, the person he damaged, the year he does not talk about, and a different answer comes out. He keeps his own copy. He agrees that God wiped the record, and goes on consulting one he maintains privately, and calls it humility. It is not humility. It is a quiet insistence that the sponge did not work. If the record can come off the page for a crowd who murdered the Son of God, the private file a believer keeps on himself proves nothing except that he has not yet believed the sentence.

How do I stop keeping my own copy? Start by naming the thing to God plainly, once more if you need to, and then thank him that it is gone: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Where you can, put right what you damaged, because restitution is part of repentance. Then, when the memory comes at three in the morning, answer it with Scripture rather than argument: as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12). Remember that your accuser is not God; the Lord’s verdict on you in Christ is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Regret may remain for a while; guilt has been wiped off the page. If the memory still crushes you, speak to a pastor or a mature friend. You were not meant to carry it alone.

In a sentence. Peter told them to repent and turn back so that their sins would be wiped out.

On a Tuesday. Your sins can be wiped out, completely. Repent and turn to Christ, and the slate is clean. Is there something you have repented of in your mind but not yet with your feet: a habit, a relationship, a way of speaking? Turn today. And is there something already forgiven that you keep fetching out of the drawer? Leave it where God put it.

For worship. The Lord Jesus does not forgive his enemies from a safe distance; he forgives them with his own wounds. God took everything written against his people and fixed it to his Son, so that the place where our guilt was put on show is the place where it was taken away for ever. He blots out transgressions for his own sake, not ours, which is why he never regrets it and never takes it back. There is no forgiveness anywhere like his.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: "that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago."
verseByVerse.commentary:
that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago.

That times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord. Two promises come out of that turning, and both are worth slowing down over. The first is times of refreshing. The word (anapsyxis) means a breathing space, a let-up, relief from pressure, revival. In the Greek Old Testament its relative turns up in an unlikely place: when the plague of frogs stopped and Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart (Exodus 8:15). It is the word for getting your breath back. And notice where the relief comes from. Not from a change in the circumstances but from the presence of the Lord, which is the difference between a man whose troubles have lifted and a man who has stopped being alone inside them. The blessings of salvation come now, in measure, and finally at Christ’s return.

And that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus. This is the second coming: the one appointed beforehand as their Messiah will be sent from heaven again.

Whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things. The second promise is about where Jesus is now, one of the very few sentences in the New Testament that says. The must is not a restraint laid on him; it is the word of divine necessity, the same sort of must that stood over the cross. There is an appointed span and he is keeping it, which settles what to make of every claim that he has quietly returned already or is on earth in some concealed form. He stays where this sentence says until a fixed date. Then comes the restoring of all things (apokatastasis): the renewal of all creation, which Jesus called the new world (Matthew 19:28), Paul the freeing of creation from its bondage (Romans 8:19–21), and John the making of all things new (Revelation 21:5).

About which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. Isaiah, among many: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). The restoration is not a new idea of the apostles. It is the old promise of the prophets, now attached to the return of Jesus.

Will everyone be saved in the end? That phrase, restoring all things, deserves a note, because it is the anchor text of those who teach that in the end everyone will be saved and hell will empty. The Greek behind it gave the doctrine its historic name, and it has been pressed into service from Origen’s day to our own. The hope is understandable; more than one Christian has privately wished it were so. But Peter defines his own term two verses later, and he leaves no room for it: every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people (v. 23). A man does not promise universal salvation and then, in the next breath, warn of being cut off. The restoration he means is the one the prophets promised: the renewal of a broken creation, the world put right. It is the healing of the world, not the reversal of the judgment; and this whole sermon is a plea to repent precisely because that judgment is real.

Where Christians differ: restoration of all things. Some (universalists) take restoring all things to mean that every person will eventually be saved. Others (dispensationalists) take it as an earthly millennial kingdom for Israel. Verdict: the restoration is of all things about which God spoke by the prophets, the renewal of creation, which the prophets also say includes judgment on the wicked (Isaiah 66:24). And the next verses warn that those who refuse Christ will be destroyed (v. 23). It is the new creation at Christ’s single return, not the salvation of all, nor an interim kingdom.

Does Christ’s return depend on Israel’s repentance? Dispensational Christians read Peter as offering the kingdom to Israel, postponed when they refused. But Peter is calling his hearers to repent so that they may share in the times of refreshing when Christ comes. The day of his return is fixed by the Father (1:7), and it does not wait on any nation’s response. What depends on their repentance is whether they will be ready.

What will the restoration of all things look like? Scripture gives us real glimpses, not a full map. It will be a renewed creation, not an escape from creation: new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). God’s people will have resurrection bodies, like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21). There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4), no more curse (Revelation 22:3), and no more sin. The nations will bring their glory into it. And at its centre will be God himself: the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3). It will be everything good in this world, healed, and far more besides.

The not-yet. A reader is left holding both halves at once, and Peter does not pretend the not-yet is easy. The restoration is certain, it is dated, and it is not here. The refreshing is available now, and it is not the same thing: a breathing space in a world still broken, from the presence of a Lord still in heaven. Anybody told that the Christian life ought to feel like the new creation already has been sold something Peter did not offer. What he offers is enough air to keep going, a fixed point on the calendar, and the certainty that the one who fixed it is coming back.

In a sentence. Repentance would bring times of refreshing from the Lord, and he would send Jesus, the appointed Christ, who must remain in heaven until the time when God restores everything, as the prophets foretold long ago.

On a Tuesday. If you are worn down, seek refreshing where Peter says it comes from: the presence of the Lord, in his word, in prayer, among his people. And when the brokenness of the world presses on you, lift your eyes to the fixed date. Christ will return and make all things new.

For worship. Heaven has received the Lord Jesus, and holds him only until the appointed day. He is not lost to his people; he is at the Father’s right hand, keeping a date the Father has fixed. And when the time for restoring all things comes, it will be his coming that brings it: the same Jesus, sent again, with the groaning creation set free at his feet and his people seeing his face. Every prophet spoke of that morning, and not one word of it will fail.

parallels.desc: new heavens and a new earth

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.’

Moses said, The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. Peter now reaches for the only promise in the books of Moses that says another prophet like Moses is coming (Deuteronomy 18:15–19), and it is worth knowing the circumstances in which it was given, because they are heartbreaking. Israel waited for that prophet; crowds would later ask whether Jesus was the one (John 1:21; 6:14; 7:40). Peter says he is.

A voice they could live through. At the foot of the mountain the people had heard God speak out of the fire, and could not bear it. They begged Moses: let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die. God did not rebuke them. He said they were right, and made the promise Peter is quoting: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth (Deuteronomy 18:16–18). They asked for a voice they could live through, and he promised one: a man from among themselves with God’s own words in his mouth. What he finally sent was his Son, who could be listened to for three years by fishermen on a hillside without anybody dying of it.

A prophet like me. The likeness is specific. Moses spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks to his friend; Moses mediated a covenant; Moses did signs; Moses brought a people out of slavery and led them toward a country they had never seen; Moses gave them God’s word. Every one of those is true of Jesus and truer, which is exactly how the New Testament handles the comparison: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6).

You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. Not consider him, not weigh him against other authorities. Listen. The Father said the same at the transfiguration, with Moses himself standing there: this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him (Luke 9:35). Peter is pointing out to a temple crowd that the obligation to obey Jesus does not originate with Christians. It was laid on Israel by Moses, in the law they revere, centuries before anybody had heard of Nazareth.

Does this verse point to Muhammad? One question a reader may well have met should be answered briefly, since it is pressed with some force. Islam claims this verse for Muhammad, on the ground that he came from among the brothers of Israel, that is, from Ishmael’s line. The text will not carry it. In Deuteronomy the phrase from among your brothers is used repeatedly of a fellow Israelite and is set directly against the foreigner: Israel’s king must be one from among your brothers; you may not put a foreigner over you (Deuteronomy 17:15). The prophet is promised from inside Israel, as the answer to Israel’s own request at Israel’s own mountain. And the New Testament shows the question being asked in precisely those terms in the first century, crowds asking whether Jesus is the Prophet (John 7:40), and priests sending men to ask John the Baptist the same thing (John 1:21). Peter is settling a question his hearers already had, not inventing one.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Chiefly by listening to Scripture, because the Prophet speaks there. The words of Jesus in the Gospels, the teaching of the apostles he sent, and the Old Testament he said testified about him are all his voice.
