So read the Bible as his word to you, and sit under faithful preaching of it. Listen to all of it, not only the parts you like: whatever he tells you. Do not look for him in inner impressions that go beyond or against what he has said in Scripture. And listening in the Bible always means obeying: be doers of the word, and not hearers only (James 1:22).

In a sentence. Moses said God would raise up a prophet like him from among their brothers, to whom they must listen in everything.

On a Tuesday. Listen to Jesus, in whatever he tells you. Not selectively, but in everything. Is there a command of his you have been politely ignoring because it is inconvenient? Take it out today, read it again, and do it.

For worship. Moses once begged to be blotted out of God’s book for the sake of his sinning people, and God would not take him in their place (Exodus 32:32–33). The prophet like Moses gave himself for his people, and the Father accepted the offering. He is not only the voice they could bear to hear; he bore what they could never have borne, and rose to speak peace to them. There has never been a prophet like him, and there will never need to be another, because in his Son God has said everything.

parallels.desc: a prophet like me from among you

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days.

And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. Verse 23 is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and Peter puts it in deliberately. It is also, strictly speaking, not a quotation of Deuteronomy 18 alone. There God says of the man who will not listen, I myself will require it of him (Deuteronomy 18:19). Peter sharpens it by finishing the sentence with Leviticus in mind: shall be cut off from his people, the fate Leviticus pronounces on anyone who refuses to afflict himself on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 23:29). The two passages are welded together, and the effect is intended. To refuse the Prophet is not a difference of opinion. It is the same category of thing as standing outside on the one day in the year when the nation’s sin was dealt with. And the sacrifice of that day has now been offered once for all in Jesus (Hebrews 9:11–12), so that to refuse him is to refuse the only atonement there is. Rejecting Jesus is not a neutral option. Those who refuse him are cut off from God’s people, and the true Israel is defined by its response to Jesus.

Restoring all things, and then the warning. The verse also does something else, and it is the reason it should be read alongside the promise just before it. The time for restoring all the things in verse 21 has been made to carry the hope that in the end nobody is lost. Verse 23 stands two verses away, in the same breath of the same sermon, and rules it out. Peter does not restore all people. He restores all things, and then he warns.

Why the warning is not cruel. It is worth being clear-eyed about why that is not cruelty. A warning is cruel if it is false, or if it arrives too late to act on, or if there is no way out of what it threatens. This one is true, it is early, and Peter has just spent several verses describing the way out. Nobody in that colonnade is being frightened without being handed a door in the same paragraph. The unkind thing would have been to leave the sentence out, which is generally what people are asking for when they ask for a gentler gospel.

What about people who have never heard of Jesus? This verse speaks of those who hear the Prophet and refuse him, and they carry the greater guilt (Luke 12:47–48). But Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12), and how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? (Romans 10:14). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a gospel they never knew, but for their sin against the light God gave them in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and God judges them justly. We hold, with many in the Reformed tradition, that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. The answer to this question is not speculation but mission: it is why the church sends and goes.

And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. Then a small detail with a long reach. Why Samuel? Because with Samuel the line of the prophets properly begins after Moses, and because Samuel is the man who anointed David, so that the prophetic succession and the royal line start on the same page of the same book. Through Nathan, the next prophet, came the promise of David’s eternal son (2 Samuel 7). Peter is saying that the whole tradition, prophets and kings together, has been pointing down a corridor toward these days, the messianic age.

These days. These days: the ones his hearers are standing in, on an ordinary afternoon, having come up for the three o’clock prayers. Every prophet from Samuel onward had been talking about these days. A Christian in a life that feels entirely unremarkable is living inside the period the prophets strained forward to see. The prophets searched and inquired carefully about this grace, and the angels long to look into it (1 Peter 1:10–12).

In a sentence. Everyone who would not listen to that prophet would be cut off from the people, and all the prophets from Samuel on foretold these days.

On a Tuesday. If someone you love has heard the gospel and is still refusing it, do not stop warning them, and do not stop loving them. Warn with tears, not with triumph. And give thanks that you live in the days the prophets longed to see: open your Bible today as a privilege they never had.

For worship. From Samuel onward the prophets leaned forward, and what they were straining to see was one man. Every anointing of a king, every promise to David’s house, every warning and every comfort pointed down the corridor to Jesus, and he has come. The Prophet whom it is death to refuse is the Saviour who died for those who had refused him, and the God who speaks the warning has already provided the way out of it. He did not leave us without a warning, and he did not leave us without a Saviour.

parallels.desc: Nathan’s prophecy in Samuel’s days

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, 'And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.

You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers. Peter ends the sermon by telling them who they are. Not spectators at somebody else’s story, not late arrivals to a religion, but heirs. Everything he has been quoting at them is family property. The promise was given to them.

And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Then the covenant text itself (Genesis 22:18; 12:3), the promise to Abraham of blessing for all nations through his offspring. Paul says the offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The gospel to the Gentiles is no departure from the Old Testament; it is its fulfilment.

On the mountain of the substitute. It matters enormously where that promise was sworn. It is repeated on a mountain in Genesis 22, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught in a thicket by his horns. The promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham’s line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided, and no ram was found, and the knife was not stopped. Abraham got his boy back down the mountain. God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first. And then the last sentence, which is where the whole chapter has been going. Take the two halves in turn. To you first: to Israel first, then to the nations (13:46; Romans 1:16). In the city that killed him, to the crowd that asked for a murderer instead, the offer arrives before it goes anywhere else in the world. That is the pattern of the whole book, to the Jew first, city after city, long after the doors start closing. And it is a window onto the character of God, who deals with the people who have wronged him worst by putting them at the front of the queue.

To bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness. Then the definition, and it is not what most people mean by the word. Ask a room of ordinary people what a blessing is and the answers will be about health, safety, provision, children doing well, a scan that came back clear; a congregation will say much the same with a religious accent. Here an apostle, at the climax of a sermon, defines the blessing promised to Abraham for the whole world, and it is being turned away from your own wickedness. The blessing of Abraham is not first prosperity but forgiveness and transformation. Jesus saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), not in them.

A test of blessing. Suppose a man were given a long and easy life, well provided for, with everyone he loves kept safe, and arrived at the end exactly as he began, still governed by the temper, the appetite, the coldness or the dishonesty he had at twenty. Was he blessed? By this verse he was never touched. And suppose another man loses most of what he owned and half of what he hoped for, and is prised loose over thirty years from the thing that was quietly destroying him. Peter says God blessed the second one.

So is it wrong to pray for health and provision? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread, and God delights to give good gifts to his children (Matthew 7:11). Health, work, safety and family are real blessings, and we should ask for them and thank him for them. But they are not the greatest blessing, and they are not the measure of God’s favour. Pray for them, and pray more for the blessing Peter names: that God would turn you, and those you love, from sin and toward himself. If he grants the lesser gifts, receive them gladly. If he withholds them, he has not withheld the greater one.

In a sentence. Peter said they were heirs of the prophets and of God’s covenant with Abraham, that all families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring, and God raised up his servant and sent him first to them, to bless them by turning each of them from wickedness.

On a Tuesday. The greatest blessing God can give you is to turn you from your sin. Pray for it. Name the sin that has governed you longest, and ask God this week to begin turning you from it. Count that as blessing, even if it costs you something.

For worship. God raised up his Servant and sent him first to the people who had killed him, not with a bribe or an amnesty on the old terms, but to change them: to take hold of them one at a time and turn every one of them from their wickedness. The Son who was not spared is the Son who was raised, and he comes carrying the blessing he bought with his blood. In Abraham’s offspring all the families of the earth are blessed, and the blessing has reached even us.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. “His name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong” (v. 16). This verse is not about a formula but about a person. The name in the ancient world carried the authority and presence of the one who bore it. When Peter speaks the name of Jesus, he is not invoking magic; he is acting in the delegated authority of the reigning Christ. The healing is an act of the risen Lord performed through his servant. Faith is the hand that reaches for what the name offers. And what the name offers is the full power of the one who conquered death — resurrection life, flowing through a living faith, into a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth, set daily at the gate of the temple he could not enter, excluded by his condition from the presence he longed for. His whole life had been one long reaching-out of an empty hand. And then, in the name of Jesus, he entered the temple walking.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. No program, no therapy, no government initiative can do what the name of Jesus does — not because those things are worthless, but because they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and to offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
The healing and Peter’s sermon bring the first persecution. The temple authorities were dominated by the Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple, cooperated with Rome to keep order, and denied the resurrection of the dead. Two Galileans proclaiming in the temple courts that Jesus had been raised were a threat on every count. Peter and John are arrested and brought before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, with the former high priest Annas, his son-in-law Caiaphas and the high priestly family, the very men who had condemned Jesus weeks earlier. Filled with the Spirit, Peter tells them the man was healed by the name of Jesus, the stone they rejected who has become the cornerstone, and that there is salvation in no other name.

The council is astonished at the boldness of these untrained men, recognises that they had been with Jesus, and cannot deny the miracle, so it orders them to stop speaking in his name. Peter and John reply that they must obey God and cannot stop speaking of what they have seen and heard. Released, they return to the believers, who pray using Psalm 2: the nations and rulers raged against the Lord’s Anointed, just as Herod and Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel had done, but only to carry out what God had planned. They do not ask for safety but for boldness and for God to stretch out his hand to heal. The place shakes, they are filled with the Spirit and speak boldly. The chapter ends with the church’s generosity: no one in need, owners selling property for the poor, and a Levite from Cyprus, Joseph, nicknamed Barnabas, “son of encouragement”, selling a field and laying the money at the apostles’ feet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up, greatly disturbed that the apostles were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. They seized them and, since it was evening, put them in jail until the next day. But many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand. The next day the rulers, elders and teachers of the law met in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and others of the high priest’s family. They had Peter and John brought before them and asked by what power or name they had done this. Filled with the Spirit, Peter replied that if they were being questioned about an act of kindness to a disabled man, everyone in Israel should know it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised, that this man stood there healed. Jesus is the stone the builders rejected, now the cornerstone, and salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven by which people must be saved. Seeing the courage of Peter and John and realising they were ordinary men with no formal training, the council was astonished and recognised that they had been with Jesus. With the healed man standing there, they had nothing to say. They sent them out, conferred, and admitted that an undeniable miracle had happened which everyone in Jerusalem knew about. To stop it spreading, they warned the apostles not to speak or teach in Jesus’ name. Peter and John answered that the council must judge whether it is right before God to obey them rather than God; as for themselves, they could not help speaking about what they had seen and heard. After further threats the council let them go, because they could find no way to punish them without upsetting the people, who were all praising God for the healing of a man over forty years old.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exclusivity of Christ

Peter's declaration in v. 12 — there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved — is among the clearest statements of Christ's exclusive lordship in salvation anywhere in Scripture, and it is worth noticing that it is spoken in a courtroom, to men who could imprison him for it. Reformed theology has always held this exclusivity to follow from the incarnation itself: if God became flesh in one particular person, in one particular place, at one particular hour of history, then salvation is tied to that person and cannot be detached from him. A plurality of saviours would require a plurality of incarnations, which is not a thing the gospel can be stretched to accommodate. And the same logic that makes the claim exclusive makes it universal: the name is given among men, offered, held out — the door is single and it is not shut.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter and John were laymen without rabbinic training, standing in the middle of the supreme court of Israel, and their boldness astonished the men trying them — parresia, a word that in Greek public life meant the free speech of a citizen in the assembly, the very thing a slave did not have. Now: The same Spirit who supplied it is given to every believer, and the church prays for more of it in this very chapter (v. 29). Boldness in the New Testament is not a temperament. It is a gift, asked for and granted, and it is perfectly compatible with being frightened.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.

Meaning first. Acts 4 tells of the first persecution of the church. Peter and John are arrested, tried before the same council that condemned Jesus, and forbidden to speak in his name. They refuse, are released, and the church prays not for safety but for boldness. The chapter shows the pattern of the whole book: opposition cannot stop the word of God; it only spreads it.

And as they were speaking to the people. Note the timing. They do not wait for the sermon to finish. Whatever else this is, it is not a considered response to a case that has been heard out.

The priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them. Three groups come down on them. The priests were the men on duty. The captain of the temple commanded the temple police and ranked next to the high priest: not a verger, but the head of a police force with the power of arrest. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and cooperated with Rome to keep their power. They accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative and, as Luke says later, denied that there is any resurrection, or angel, or spirit (23:8). Their whole position rested on the temple continuing as it was.

Greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people. Luke says they were greatly annoyed: worked up, exasperated, thoroughly put out. And he tells us exactly what put them out, in two parts. The first is that the apostles were teaching the people. Two laymen with no standing whatever were instructing a crowd, in the temple, on the priests’ own premises, without anybody’s permission. Unauthorised teachers drawing crowds were an affront to a body whose authority rested on being the only legitimate interpreters of these things.

And proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. The second is the content. This is the doctrine the Sadducees had built a career on denying, and the apostles are not arguing it in the abstract. They are naming the man. In Jesus: his resurrection is the proof and the guarantee of the general resurrection, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). Only weeks earlier these officials had believed the matter closed: a stone and, as Matthew records, a seal and a guard (Matthew 27:62–66). Now the claim is back, in their own courtyard, with a healed cripple standing next to it and thousands listening.

He had answered them once already. The Sadducees had tried this argument on Jesus himself, in these same courts, with a riddle about a woman married to seven brothers in turn. He answered them from the books of Moses they accepted, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:27–38). They had no reply, and within days their party had helped to kill him. Now the argument has been settled in a way no riddle could answer. The man who told them that God is the God of the living is himself alive, and his name has just made a lame man walk.

The third irritant. There is a third irritant Luke does not need to state, because the previous chapter supplied it: the apostles were telling Jerusalem that its rulers had handed the Messiah to Pilate and killed him.

What it does not mean. It is tempting to draw from this the tidy conclusion that opposition to the gospel is never really intellectual and always about protecting an interest, and that conclusion should be resisted, because it is not always true and it is a lazy way to avoid an argument. Some people object to the Christian faith because they have thought about it and find it incredible, and they deserve to be answered rather than psychoanalysed. But it is worth noticing what actually triggered the first arrest in Christian history. Not a doctrine as such. A doctrine that, if true, cost a group of powerful men everything they had.

Should I expect opposition if I speak about Jesus? Some, yes, though not always and not usually in this form. Jesus said, if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20), and Paul that all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). In many places that means prison or death; in others it means mockery, exclusion, a lost promotion or a cold family. Do not go looking for it, and do not provoke it by being needlessly offensive. But do not be surprised by it, and do not take it as a sign that you have done something wrong. Often it is a sign that the gospel has touched something people would rather not have touched.

In a sentence. While they were speaking, the priests, the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them, angered that they were teaching the people and proclaiming the resurrection of the dead in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection offends those whose power depends on this world. Proclaim it anyway. Ask yourself what in your own life the resurrection threatens: what comfort, what ambition, what way of keeping control. The truth that unsettled the Sadducees should unsettle you too, and then set you free.

For worship. The doctrine the most powerful men in Jerusalem had built their careers on denying walked out of a tomb and stood in their courtyard. The risen Lord does not ask permission to be proclaimed. His resurrection is the firstfruits of a harvest, and every grave of every believer will one day be emptied by the same power that emptied his.
verseByVerse.note: The captain of the temple commanded the temple police and ranked next to the high priest. The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.

And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. Two sentences side by side, put together on purpose. In the first, the authorities do the only thing they can think of. In the second, it turns out to have been beside the point. Hearings of this kind were not normally held after dark, which makes the night trial of Jesus all the more irregular. So the two men spend the night in custody: the first Christian imprisonment. By the end of this book it will be so routine that Luke barely stops to comment on it. Everything that would happen to the church for the next three centuries began on an ordinary evening with a locked door and two tired men who had been to a prayer meeting.

Along the master’s road. Luke has walked this road before. Jesus too was seized at night by the temple authorities and held until morning, and when day came the council of the elders gathered and he was led before them (Luke 22:54, 66). His apostles now take the same steps: arrest at evening, a night in custody, the council at daybreak. He had told them it would be so, that they would be seized and delivered up for his name’s sake, and that it would be their opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). But the roads part in the morning. His night ended at a cross; theirs ends in release and a sermon, and the master who walked the road first walks it now beside them.

But many of those who had heard the word believed. The sentence is built to defeat the one before it. But. They can stop the speaker; they cannot retrieve what has already been said. The word was out of the building before the guards arrived, working in several thousand people they could not arrest and did not know how to find. They took the preachers into custody and left the sermon at large. Paul would write the same from his own chains: I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound! (2 Timothy 2:9).

And the number of the men came to about five thousand. The word (andrōn) is the one for adult males, perhaps heads of households. So five thousand is not the size of the church; it is one column in the register. Add wives and households, and the community in Jerusalem may already be well past ten thousand. From a hundred and twenty, to three thousand, to this, within weeks. No wonder the temple authorities were alarmed: from where they sat, this was a movement that had taken a visible share of the city while they were deciding what to do about it.

What it does not mean. Preachers often turn this passage into a promise, and it needs a guard. Luke does record a pattern in Acts in which pressure and growth run together, and it is real. But it is a pattern, not a law, and Scripture nowhere guarantees that opposition will produce numbers. There have been faithful churches that were persecuted and shrank, and faithful men who preached for forty years to a nation that never turned. What this passage promises is not that the church will grow under pressure. It is that the word, once spoken, is no longer under the control of the people who object to it.

My church is small and getting smaller. Has God failed? No. God has promised to build his church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18), but he has not promised that every congregation will grow, or grow now. Churches rise and fall; whole regions once full of believers now have few, and others that had none now have millions. Ask honestly whether your church is faithful to the gospel, prayerful, loving and outward-looking, and repent of anything that is not. Then keep sowing, and leave the harvest to the Lord. Faithfulness, not size, is what he asks of you, and a small faithful church is precious to him.

In a sentence. They arrested them and held them overnight, but many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand.

On a Tuesday. If you have spoken about Christ to someone and seen nothing, remember that the word is out of your hands now and into God’s. It is still working. Pray for that person today, and trust that you cannot lock up what God has sent.

For worship. Two men were locked in for the night, and outside their cell the church grew to five thousand men. The word of the risen Christ was loose in the city before the door of the cell was shut. That is the freedom of our Lord’s word: no guard can stand over it and no seal can hold it, because the one who speaks it broke the seal on his own grave. Councils have come and gone, and the word he sent out that evening is still running.
verseByVerse.note: Hearings were not normally held at night.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.

On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem. The full apparatus assembles. Rulers, elders and scribes is Luke’s shorthand for the Sanhedrin: seventy-one men, the supreme Jewish council, with authority over religious law, over the temple, and, within the limits Rome allowed, over life and death. The rulers were the chief priests; the elders, the leading lay aristocrats; the scribes, the experts in the law. This is the body that had condemned Jesus a few months earlier. The room, the procedure, and most of the faces are the same. Only the defendants have changed.

With Annas the high priest and Caiaphas. Then Luke names names, and one of them raises a question a careful reader is entitled to ask. He writes Annas the high priest and Caiaphas, but Caiaphas was high priest. He held the office from about AD 18 to 36, and the events of this chapter fall squarely inside that. Luke appears to have given the title to the wrong man, and this has been produced more than once as evidence that he did not know the Jerusalem he was writing about.

The family firm. The explanation tells you something about the city. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until a Roman prefect removed him. But by the law of Moses the high priesthood was for life, and to many Jews a pagan governor deposing Israel’s high priest acted with no authority. Five of Annas’s sons held the office after him, and so did his son-in-law Caiaphas. It was a family firm, and Annas ran it as a patriarch runs a business through his children: out of the chair, and in charge. That is why the arrested Jesus was taken to Annas first, before being sent on to the man who held the title (John 18:13, 24). Luke, who dates John the Baptist’s ministry to the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas together (Luke 3:2), is not confused. He names both the office-holder and the power.

And John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. John and Alexander were probably members of the family; a Jonathan son of Annas later became high priest, and some manuscripts read Jonathan here. Otherwise they are unknown, and that is itself worth a moment. A writer inventing a scene does not clutter it with two names that do nothing and lead nowhere. Luke includes them because they were in the room and somebody who was there remembered.

The arithmetic of the morning. Stand back and look at the arithmetic of the morning. On one side: the high-priestly dynasty, the aristocracy of the nation, the men who controlled the temple, its treasury, its police and its courts, seated in the chamber where they had sentenced a man to death. On the other: two fishermen from a lake far to the north, who had spent the night in a cell, with no lawyer, no credentials and no allies in the building. The odds are not close. And by the end of the session it will be the seventy-one who cannot think what to do.

Seated at the right hand. The last time Jesus stood before this council, at daybreak, they asked whether he was the Christ, and he told them: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69). They called it blasphemy and sent him to Pilate. Now they sit again, and the evidence for that sentence is about to be brought in: a man who could not walk, standing on his own feet by the name of the one they condemned. The prisoner of that morning has taken his seat, and this morning’s session is being held in his sight.

How should I think about powerful people who oppose the faith? Neither with fear nor with hatred. Not with fear, because they are men, and the Lord laughs at the rulers who take counsel against him (Psalm 2:4); their power is real but borrowed and temporary. Not with hatred, because Jesus told us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and because some of them will be converted: within a few chapters a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (6:7), and Saul of Tarsus was trained by this council. Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), honour their office where you can, and keep speaking the truth.

In a sentence. The next day the rulers, elders and scribes gathered in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and the whole high-priestly family.

On a Tuesday. Name the person or institution that most intimidates you as a Christian. Pray for them by name today, for their good and for their salvation. Then remember the arithmetic of this morning in Jerusalem, and whose side the odds were really on.

For worship. Seventy-one men sat in judgement, and above them sat one man at the right hand of God, and the session was his. Our Lord stood silent before these judges once and let them condemn him, because he had come to be condemned for us. He does not stand before them now. He reigns, and the councils of the earth meet, scheme and adjourn beneath his throne. Two fishermen in the dock were safer than every judge in the room, because they belonged to the King.
verseByVerse.note: The rulers, elders and scribes made up the Sanhedrin. Annas had been high priest earlier and remained head of the family; Caiaphas was the serving high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?”

And when they had set them in the midst. The phrase is describing the furniture. The Sanhedrin sat in a semicircle so that every member could see every other, with the accused placed in the open space at the centre. There is nowhere to look that is not a face, and every face belongs to somebody who can ruin you. It is a room designed to make a man feel the weight of the institution before a word is spoken.

By what power or by what name did you do this? The question sounds neutral and is not. They do not deny the miracle; they want its source. Naming the power and the name behind a wonder is the language of magic and exorcism, where everything depended on which being you had invoked. And there is a trap under it. Israel’s law prescribed death for a man who worked a sign or wonder to draw the people after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Give the wrong answer here and the charge is not disorderly preaching. It is capital.

The old move. They had used the same move on his master. When Jesus cast out demons, the accusation was not that nothing had happened; it was that he did it by Beelzebul, the prince of demons (Luke 11:15). It is a durable tactic, because it concedes the event and poisons the source, and it does not require the accuser to explain anything.

The small contempt. Notice also the small contempt in the wording. Not by what power did you heal this man, but did you do this: an unnamed this, a thing, an incident. And the you is emphatic and scornful: people like you? The court has forty years of a man’s life in front of it and refers to the whole business as this. Peter is about to make them say what it was.

The right question. Without meaning to, the council has asked exactly the right question, and they have asked it before. In these same courts the chief priests, scribes and elders had put almost the same words to Jesus: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority (Luke 20:2). He answered with a question about John the Baptist, and they would not reply. Now they ask his servants, and this time they will get a straight answer. By what power and by what name: that is the question the whole book of Acts exists to answer, and its one answer is the name of the man they asked first.

How do I answer when someone asks why I believe? Be ready, as Peter tells every Christian to be, to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). You do not need to be an expert. Start with the person of Jesus: who he is, what he did, and that God raised him from the dead. Then say honestly what he has done for you. If you do not know the answer to a hard question, say so, and offer to find out. Think through, before you are asked, three or four sentences that explain the gospel and why you trust it. The question by what name is still the right one, and Jesus is still the answer.

In a sentence. They stood them in the middle and asked by what power or in whose name they had done this.

On a Tuesday. When asked about the source of your hope, be ready to answer (1 Peter 3:15). Write down tonight, in plain words, why you believe in Jesus. If someone asks you this week, you will have something to say.

For worship. The council asked by what name, and heaven had already answered: the name above every name, given to the crucified Jesus. There is no power behind the church’s life but his, and no name under which it works but his. The question his enemies asked as a trap is the question every soul must one day answer, and the answer is the glory of God.

parallels.desc: by what authority?

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,

Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them. This is the second time Luke has said it of Peter, and it will be said again of the whole church before the chapter is out (2:4; here; 4:31). The point is not that Pentecost has worn off and needed topping up. It is that Luke’s filling language describes a repeated equipping for particular moments, and this is one of them: a man who is about to speak for his life is given what he needs at the hour he needs it and not before. A fresh filling for a fresh need.

The promise kept. Which is exactly what had been promised. When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11–12; 21:12–15). Peter is standing in the sentence. He had heard it on the road to Jerusalem not long before, and he is now in a room with rulers and authorities finding out that it was not a figure of speech.

What it does not mean. A guard is needed on that promise, because it gets misapplied. It is not a general licence to go into the pulpit unprepared and call it faith; the setting Jesus specified is the dock, not the desk, and the same New Testament tells a teacher to do his best to present himself to God as a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). What is promised is that when a believer is put on the spot for Christ, in a courtroom, a hostile family, an interview, he will not be left to improvise alone.

Rulers of the people and elders. Then watch what Peter does with his first sentence. He is courteous: the proper address, no sneering. Boldness in this chapter never once shades into rudeness, and that is worth registering by anyone who has met the sort of Christian who mistakes being obnoxious for being faithful.

If we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man. And then he takes the vague this of the council’s question and gives it a name. Examined is courtroom language, so he is granting the proceedings their full formality, and then reading the charge sheet aloud in language nobody in that chamber would want in the minutes. We are on trial for making a cripple walk. There is a touch of irony in it: they are on trial for an act of kindness. He has not raised his voice, and he has already made the court’s position sound absurd, which is what it was.

By what means this man has been healed. One word in that sentence is the hinge of the whole speech, and English hides it. The verb Peter uses for healed (sesōstai) is the ordinary Greek word for saved. He uses it here of a man’s ankles. Three verses later he will use it of the whole world’s only hope (v. 12). The council asked him about a body, and he is going to answer about a soul, and he does it by keeping one word running through both. Physical healing points to the greater salvation.

What if I freeze when I am put on the spot? Most of us have, and Peter himself once did, beside a fire, in front of a servant girl. The promise is not that you will never feel fear but that you are not alone in it. Pray before hard conversations, even a sentence under your breath. Say less rather than more: one true, kind sentence about Jesus is better than a flustered argument. If you fail, do what Peter did after the courtyard: go back to the Lord, receive his forgiveness, and try again. The Spirit who filled Peter in the council is the same Spirit who lives in you, and he delights to help weak people speak.

In a sentence. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answered that if they were being questioned about a good deed to a crippled man and how he was healed...

On a Tuesday. The Spirit gives words in the hour of need. Trust him when you are put on the spot for Christ. And practise courtesy: the next time you speak about your faith to someone who is hostile, speak to them with the respect Peter gave the men who could have had him flogged.

For worship. The Lord Jesus promised his frightened friends that in the hour of trial the Spirit would teach them what to say, and in the high priest’s court the promise came true to the letter. He does not send his people into the dock and leave them there. He goes with them by his Spirit, and puts into weak mouths the calm and the courage he himself showed before the same judges. That is what the Spirit of Christ does with cowards, and he has kept that promise in courtrooms and prisons for two thousand years.

parallels.desc: I will give you a mouth and wisdom

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.

Let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel. He answers the question exactly and without a syllable of diplomacy. They asked for a name; they get the name, with the address attached and the crucifixion attached and the resurrection attached, in one clause.

By the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. Two verbs, two subjects, side by side: what you did, and what God did about it. It is the gospel in one sentence. You crucified him; God raised him. And he is saying it to the men who did the first one, in the room where they voted for it.

By him this man is standing before you well. Peter can point while he says it, because the healed man is in the chamber; verse 14 tells us so. The court’s exhibit walked in on his own feet and is standing there for the duration of the hearing. The proof is visible. For forty years he could not get through the door of the temple; this morning he is inside the supreme court of Israel.

This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. Then Peter quotes Scripture at them, and the choice of text is not casual. It is Psalm 118:22, and every man in that room could have finished the psalm from memory, because it is the last of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover, and because a crowd had shouted its lines about the one who comes in the name of the Lord at a man riding into this city on a donkey a few months before.

Finishing his master’s sentence. There is a sharper reason it lands. Jesus had quoted this identical verse to these same men, in the temple, at the end of the parable of the tenants who killed the owner’s son, and they perceived that he had told it against them and sought to lay hands on him at that very hour (Luke 20:17–19). Peter is finishing his master’s sentence in front of the same audience, and they know which conversation he is resuming. He also adjusts the psalm deliberately, putting in by you, so that the builders have faces. The charge is not a technical error, but that they looked at him and judged him worthless.

The spoil heap and the corner. The image is a working man’s picture, and it is savage. Judging which block goes where is the whole of a builder’s competence. These men examined this stone with the best professional judgement in the nation and threw it on the spoil heap. God took it off the heap and set it at the corner, where every line in the building is measured from. Jesus is the cornerstone of the new temple, the church, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

Wrong about the most important thing. There is something in that worth carrying about. The judgement of the most qualified people in the world, delivered unanimously, in the proper forum, after due process, was wrong about the most important thing that has ever happened, and God overturned it without consulting them. It is a caution against being impressed by consensus, and it is a comfort to anybody who has been weighed by people with every right to weigh him and found to be of no value.

What does it mean to build my life on the cornerstone? It means taking your measurements from Jesus rather than from anyone else. Your worth is set by what he says about you, not by the verdict of employers, family or friends. Your choices are lined up with his word. Your hope for the future rests on his promises, not on your plans. And when other supports give way, health, money, reputation, relationships, you discover what the whole building was really resting on. Practically, that means returning to him daily in Scripture and prayer, and asking of each decision: does this fit the line of the cornerstone?

In a sentence. Peter told them and all Israel that this man stood healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised, the stone the builders rejected that has become the cornerstone.

On a Tuesday. If you have been rejected by people whose opinion matters to you, remember who else was thrown on the spoil heap by experts. Bring that rejection to him. And check where you take your measurements from this week: the cornerstone, or the crowd.

For worship. Rejected by men, but chosen and precious in the sight of God: that is the Lord Jesus, and the Father has never once changed his mind about him. The stone the builders discarded is alive, and everyone who comes to him is made alive and laid beside him, living stones in a house God himself is building. The judges of Israel thought they were finished with him. They were standing, without knowing it, at the foot of the one building in the world that will never fall.

parallels.desc: the stone the builders rejected

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.

And there is salvation in no one else. Now the sentence the chapter is famous for, and the first thing to see is that it is an answer to a question about a pair of ankles. The council asked how a crippled man came to be walking. Peter used the ordinary Greek word for saved to describe the healing in verse 9, and he now runs that same word straight on into its largest possible meaning. He has taken the small case in front of the court and enlarged it until it covers everything. You want to know how one man got his legs back. I will tell you how anybody gets anything back. Not only was this man healed by Jesus alone; all salvation is in Jesus alone.

For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. Every clause tightens it. No other name: no other person, no other way. Under heaven: anywhere in the world, not merely nowhere in Israel. The name is given, by God, a gift handed down rather than a prize achieved. And the last phrase carries a quiet necessity: by which we must be saved. It is God’s appointed way, and it is necessary. Peter includes himself in that we, which is worth noticing. He is not standing over the council as a man who found the way; he is standing beside them as a man who needed it. This is the exclusive claim of the gospel, spoken to the highest religious court of the only nation that knew the true God.

How can Jesus be the only way? This is also one of the great apologetic verses, for the world calls it narrow and arrogant. Three things help. First, it is not a boast about Christians but a confession about Christ: if God himself became man and died and rose to save sinners, then salvation simply is found in him and nowhere else, not because we are better, but because there is only one Saviour who did this. Second, the one narrow door opens to all: narrow in the way, one Saviour, and infinitely wide in the welcome, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). Third, sincerity cannot save. A man can be sincerely wrong, as one who sincerely drinks poison thinking it medicine; salvation rests on the truth of who Christ is, not the earnestness of the seeker.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways of salvation? Pluralists hold that all religions lead to God; inclusivists that people may be saved by Christ through other religions, without knowing him. Verdict: no other name is unmistakable. Even Israel’s religion, without Christ, could not save. Salvation is found in Jesus alone, through faith in him (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). This is why the gospel must be preached to every nation (Romans 10:13–15). It is said not with arrogance, but with urgency and love.

Could people be saved through Christ without ever knowing him? Inclusivist Christians think so: they point to Old Testament believers saved before Christ came, to Cornelius before Peter arrived (10:1–4), and to Romans 2:14–16. But Old Testament saints trusted the promise God had given about the coming Saviour; Cornelius was told to send for Peter to hear a message by which he would be saved (11:14); and Romans 2 is about how all are judged, not how any are saved. The more likely reading is the plain one: there is salvation in no one else. As for those who never hear, Scripture’s answer is honest and sobering: all are accountable for the light they have (Romans 1:20), none seek God on their own (Romans 3:11), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. And therefore we must go and tell (Romans 10:14), leaving the secret things to God (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Said by a prisoner. Remember where Peter is standing when he says it. Not in a lecture hall, but under arrest, before a court that could flog him and had recently arranged an execution, answering a question designed to trap him into a capital charge. A man in that position has every incentive to find a broader formula: Jesus as one road among several, and the council not implicated. Peter tells them instead that the man they threw away is the only name there is, and that they too must be saved by it. The narrowness people object to was spoken by a prisoner who gained nothing by it, to the men holding the keys, and it included an invitation to them. Far from cruel, this is the most loving truth there is: if Jesus really is the only Saviour, then telling people is the kindest thing we could ever do.

How do I say this to friends of other faiths without arrogance? By remembering that you are a beggar telling other beggars where you found bread, not a winner looking down on losers. Listen first, and understand what your friend actually believes; respect his sincerity and the good in his life. Speak of Jesus himself, not of your religion’s superiority. Admit your own sin and need. Be honest that you believe Jesus is the only Saviour, because he said so (John 14:6), and explain why that is good news, not bad: God has provided the way himself. Let your life show the love you speak of. And pray, because only God can open a heart.

In a sentence. There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to people by which we must be saved.

On a Tuesday. One name saves. Make it known, because there is no other. Think of one person in your life who does not know Jesus. If this verse is true, what is the most loving thing you could do for them this week? Do it.

For worship. There is one name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, and God gave it. He did not leave the world to find its own way back to him; he came himself, in his Son, and died and rose, and wrote his name over the only door. The name Jesus means the LORD saves, and he has never failed to save anyone who called on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.

Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John. The word Luke uses is parrēsia, and it carried weight in the Greek world. It meant the right to say everything: the free speech of a citizen standing up in the public assembly. A slave did not have it; a foreigner did not have it. So the Sanhedrin is watching two men with no standing in that room exercise the freedom of men who own the place. They are prisoners, fetched up from a cell, and they are talking like free men.

The theme word of Acts. Luke uses this word all through his book. The church prays for it in this chapter (v. 29) and receives it (v. 31), and the very last line of Acts leaves Paul in Rome under house arrest, proclaiming the kingdom of God with all boldness (28:31). It is a fair candidate for the theme word of the whole book, and it always belongs to somebody who has no business being that free. It is the Spirit’s gift.

And perceived that they were uneducated, common men. The council’s own description is worth getting right, since it is often misheard. Uneducated does not mean illiterate; it means without formal training in the rabbinic schools: no letters after the name. And common men (idiōtai) means laymen, private persons, amateurs as opposed to professionals. The Sanhedrin is not saying that Peter and John cannot read. It is saying they have no credentials: they have not sat at the feet of a Gamaliel, as the young Saul of Tarsus had. Galilean fishermen are arguing from Scripture with the scholars of Israel.

What it does not mean. This is not an argument against learning: Luke writes careful Greek, Paul was thoroughly trained, and the church has needed both kinds of men ever since. It is a note about where the power was not coming from. The council looked for a qualification that would explain what they were seeing, found none on paper, and then named the real one without meaning to.

And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. Then the sentence that has outlived everything else in this chapter. It is the word Luke used of the crowd recognising the beggar at the gate (3:10): not a guess but an identification. Something in the bearing of these two men made a hostile court think of a prisoner it had condemned. Jesus too had astonished them without formal training: how is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied? (John 7:15). Whether this was memory of a face or recognition of a manner, Luke does not say. But the sentence is not really about faces. Time spent with Jesus leaves a residue which outlasts any argument, and the people who dislike him are often the first to spot it.

A test that does not run on self-assessment. Which yields a test, and it is uncomfortable precisely because it does not run on self-assessment. Not: do I consider that I am walking closely with Christ? But: if somebody who wanted to find fault with me had to account for me, what would they reach for? The council reached for the only explanation available to it, and it was not education, temperament, social position or nerve. It was company.

But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. And then verse 14 supplies the last piece. You cannot argue with a walking man. He was there, and Luke gives no hint that anyone made him come. A man with forty years’ experience of staying out of trouble stood in the highest court in the land and stood next to the accused, and by doing it he ended the prosecution. Luke gives him not one line of dialogue. He did not need one. He stood where everybody could see him, which is very largely what the church has been asked to do ever since.

How do I spend time with Jesus, now that he is in heaven? The apostles had walked with him for three years; we meet him now by his Spirit through his word. Read the Gospels slowly and often, watching how he speaks, treats people and prays. Pray to him, honestly and regularly, not only in emergencies. Meet him at the Lord’s Table with his people. Obey what he says, because he said that whoever keeps his commandments is the one who loves him, and he will manifest himself to him (John 14:21). And keep company with others who love him. The residue the council noticed was not produced in a weekend, and it will not be in you either; it grows by daily nearness.

In a sentence. The council was astonished at the boldness of Peter and John, seeing that they were ordinary men without training, and recognised that they had been with Jesus, and with the healed man standing there, they could say nothing against it.

On a Tuesday. Spend time with Jesus. People will notice. And if you have been changed by him, do not hide it: stand where you can be seen, like the healed man in the council. Your presence beside other believers under pressure may say more than any speech.

For worship. The Lord Jesus took fishermen with no credentials and made them so like himself that his enemies recognised him in them. That is what his company does. He gives his own freedom to those who have no right to it, his own boldness to those who once ran, and his own likeness to those who stay near him, until the world looks at ordinary believers and sees their Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Uneducated, common men” means they had no formal training in the law under a rabbi — not that they were illiterate.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.

But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another. Luke now takes us into a closed session, which raises a fair question: how does he know what was said? This council was not sealed. Nicodemus was a member (John 3:1–2); Joseph of Arimathea was a member and had not consented to their decision (Luke 23:50–51); Gamaliel sat on it (5:34). Within two chapters a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (6:7), men who had sat in meetings like this one. By the time this account was written, the private deliberations of the Sanhedrin were not private any more, because some of the men in the room had changed sides.

What shall we do with these men? It is the question this council had asked about Jesus himself. John tells us that after the raising of Lazarus they gathered and said, What are we to do? For this man performs many signs (John 11:47). That meeting ended with Caiaphas advising that one man should die for the people, and John adds that he spoke better than he knew: Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:50–52). Their worst decision became the means of the world’s salvation. Now the same men meet over the same problem, and the problem is still Jesus. The fishermen are only the latest sign that he is alive.

For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. Consider who is speaking. Not a sympathetic witness, but a hostile court in closed session, with no audience to perform for, every motive to find a flaw, and the resources of the nation at its disposal. They have the man, the history, and forty years of testimony from every worshipper who ever stepped round him at the gate. They examine the case intending to destroy it, and their finding is that a notable sign has been performed, that everybody in Jerusalem knows it, and that denial is not available to them. And in the next breath they resolve to shut it down.

The obstacle was never the evidence. This is the passage to put in front of anyone who assumes that unbelief is fundamentally an information problem: that if only the case were laid out clearly enough, people would believe. Here is a case laid out with total clarity and conceded in private by qualified and hostile investigators, followed immediately by a decision to suppress it. The obstacle was never the evidence. Their problem was not proof, but unwillingness.

What it does not mean. Which does not make evidence worthless, and the opposite error does just as much damage. Peter’s entire speech is an appeal to evidence. The healed man is standing in the room precisely because he is evidence. Luke wrote two volumes so that his reader might have certainty about the things he had been taught (Luke 1:4). Christians are not asked to believe without grounds, and they are not asked to argue without facts. What this passage shows is that facts are necessary and not sufficient: a man may be persuaded in his understanding and remain unwilling in his will, and the second is where the real business is transacted.

With these men. The proof of it lies in a comparison Luke almost certainly intends. At Pentecost a crowd that had just been told they crucified the Messiah cried out, Brothers, what shall we do? (2:37). Here a council that has just been told the same thing asks, What shall we do with these men? Nearly the same words. One is asking to be changed; the other is asking how to make the problem go away. Everything turns on three words: with these men.

Why won’t my friend believe when the evidence seems so clear? Because, as this passage shows, unbelief is not only in the head. Pride, fear of what others will think, love of a way of life, or simple unwillingness to bow to God can all hold a person back when the arguments are answered. Jesus said that people loved the darkness rather than the light (John 3:19). So keep giving reasons, patiently and kindly, because God uses them. But do not imagine that the right argument will do what only God can do. Pray for your friend’s heart, not only his mind, that God who said let light shine out of darkness would shine in his heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). And keep loving him, whatever he decides.

In a sentence. After sending them out, the council discussed what to do with them, since all Jerusalem knew they had performed a notable sign that could not be denied.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself the council’s question, and Pentecost’s. When God’s word confronts you with something uncomfortable, are you asking what shall I do, or what shall I do with this? The first leads to life. The second leads to the closed door of verse 17.

For worship. The council could not deny the sign and would not bow to it, and their will held out against the plainest evidence in Jerusalem. Only God can change a will like that, and he does. The risen Lord who was condemned in that chamber went on to win men out of it: a great many priests, and a young Pharisee trained by Gamaliel who would one day call himself the foremost of sinners. No heart is so closed that Christ cannot open it, and every believer is someone whose unwillingness he overcame.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name. So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

But in order that it may spread no further among the people. The plan tells you they had run out of arguments. No attempt to explain the healing, no rival account, no enquiry into fraud: they go straight to damage control, treating the message like stock in circulation that has to be withdrawn. It is an administrative answer to a theological problem, which is what institutions reach for when they have lost the argument and kept the power. And Luke will not have missed the irony: the measure taken to stop the name travelling is recorded in a book that carried the name to Rome.

Let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name. Look at what they prohibit. Not healing, gathering, charity or prayer. They ban a name. Jesus had told them it would come to this: you will be hated by all for my name’s sake (Luke 21:17). The council had grasped the essential point better than some of the church’s friends have since. Everything in this movement is carried in a person; make the person unmentionable and the remainder is harmless. And there is a small tell in their words. They say this name. In a private session, with nobody listening, seventy-one men discuss the problem of Jesus of Nazareth without once pronouncing it.

So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. A direct order from the highest religious authority in Israel: the first ban on evangelism. Many have followed.

Soup without the sentence. The modern shape of this is recognisable enough to be worth naming, and worth naming carefully. Christian activity of most kinds is welcome nearly everywhere: the food bank, the night shelter, the hospice, the school. It is the speech that draws the objection: the naming of the name, the claim that this particular man is Lord and that what anyone does about him matters. Institutions perfectly happy to fund the soup will often ask, in so many words, that the sentence not be said. That is the council’s exact position, and the church’s answer to it has been on the record since the next verse.

What it does not mean. But it should be said plainly, and by comfortable Western Christians most of all, that there is an enormous distance between being thought awkward at work and a night in a cell under the temple, and a further distance again between either of those and what believers in a good many countries will face this week. Peter and John are flogged for this in the next chapter. A man who finds a conversation uncomfortable and calls it persecution has not read the passage he is quoting.

My employer has told me not to talk about my faith at work. What should I do? Think carefully about what is actually being asked. A reasonable rule about how you use working time, or a ban on pressuring colleagues or customers, is not the same as a command to deny Christ, and you can obey it gladly while being honest when someone asks you a direct question in a break or outside work. Be a diligent, kind and truthful worker; that itself speaks. But if you are told to lie, to affirm what Scripture calls sin, or never to admit that you are a Christian, then you have reached the line in the next verse, and you must obey God, respectfully, and accept the cost. Seek advice from your pastor and, where needed, from Christian legal organisations.

In a sentence. To stop it spreading, they decided to warn them, and called them in and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The world often says: believe what you like, but don’t speak in Jesus’ name. Be ready for that pressure. And notice whether you have already given in to it without anyone asking, by doing the good works and quietly leaving out the name.

For worship. They forbade the name, and the name has gone to the ends of the earth. The Lord whose name his enemies would not even say has been given the name above every name, and every tongue will one day confess it. No ban has ever silenced it, because it is the name God himself has spoken over his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.”

But Peter and John answered them. The most quoted sentence in the chapter, and what is usually missed about it is the form. Peter does not make a declaration. He asks the court a question and leaves it with them.

Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge. He could have said: we will not obey you. Instead he puts the case to the men trying him and invites them to deliver the verdict, and they cannot deliver it, because there is only one answer and it dismantles their own order. A body whose entire authority rests on claiming to represent God has just been asked, on the record, whether God ought to be obeyed. It is a respectful but firm refusal, an appeal to a higher court. It is the most respectful thing Peter could have said, and the most devastating.

For we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard. Then the second half, and the wording repays attention. Not we will not stop. We are not able. It is a statement of incapacity rather than defiance: the position of a man who has seen something and cannot arrange to un-see it. Jeremiah knew it: there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in (Jeremiah 20:9). Paul knew it: necessity is laid upon me (1 Corinthians 9:16). You may forbid a man to mention it; you cannot make him not know it. A witness can be silenced and cannot be un-witnessed, and that is the whole of Peter’s case.

What we have seen and heard. Notice too how modest the claim is. He does not say they cannot stop because they are courageous, or called, or full of conviction. He says they cannot stop reporting what they have seen and heard. The apostles are not claiming a temperament. They are claiming an experience: that a man they watched die was afterwards alive in front of them, and that they had eaten with him. Everything the church has ever said rests on that being either true or false.

Where Christians differ: civil disobedience. Some say Christians must always obey the government; others that they may resist any unjust law.
