Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length. The measurement is the argument. The man to whom the entire country was promised died holding title to one thing in it: a cave with his wife buried in it, bought from a Hittite at a price he did not trouble to haggle over (Genesis 23). He lived in tents, a stranger in a land that was his by promise and nobody else’s by law (Hebrews 11:9). Stephen says this to men whose case rests on a plot of land and a building on it. The founder of their nation had neither, and the lack of them made him not less the friend of God but the pattern. God’s promises were never exhausted by the land.

But promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. Abraham had no land and no child, only God’s word, and he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6).

The heir who owned nothing. The promise was to Abraham and to his offspring, and Paul insists the word is singular: it means one, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). So the strange shape of Abraham’s life, heir of a whole country without a foot of it, is repeated in the true Offspring. The Son whom God appointed heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2) had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and died owning the clothes the soldiers divided. Then God raised him and gave him the nations for his inheritance (Psalm 2:8). Abraham’s waiting was not wasted: the promise was always heading for Christ, and those who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29).

Is the land of Israel still promised to the Jewish people? Christians answer differently, and this app presents the views fairly. Some believe God’s promise of the land to Abraham’s physical descendants still stands and will have a future fulfilment, and they point to the unconditional language of the promise and to Romans 11. Others believe the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs themselves were looking for a better country, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13–16). All agree on what Stephen shows here: that Abraham’s true hope was never a piece of real estate but God himself and the city he has prepared, and that every Christian shares that hope with him.

In a sentence. Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran, and after his father died God brought him to this land, though he gave him none of it, not even a foot’s length, but promised it to him and his descendants, though he had no child.

On a Tuesday. Live by God’s promise even when you have nothing to show for it. Abraham did. Name one promise of God you are clinging to with nothing yet in your hand, and thank him for it today as though it were already kept.

For worship. Abraham died owning a grave, and he died rich, because he had God’s word, and God’s word is as good as the thing itself. The Lord who promised a country to a childless wanderer was never short of time or of means. He gave the son when Abraham was a hundred, and he is giving the inheritance at the end of the ages, larger than every hill Abraham walked: the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). This God counts a promise kept on the day he makes it, and not one of his children will find that he gave them less than he said.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. ‘But I will judge the nation that they serve,’ said God, ‘and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’

And God spoke to this effect, that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. The promise as God actually gave it (Genesis 15:13–14) contained something people rarely notice when they quote it: four centuries of slavery, announced in advance. Abraham was told that his great-grandchildren’s great-grandchildren would be born in chains, and that this was not a failure of the plan but part of it.

The gap between word and fulfilment. Stephen includes it because his hearers need to see how God’s promises run. There is a gap between the word and the fulfilment, and God fills it with things nobody would have chosen. The four hundred years are not an interruption in this story; they are the story. Anyone who concludes from four months of silence that God has changed his mind should look at the arithmetic Abraham was handed, and still believed.

Four hundred or four hundred and thirty? Stephen is quoting God’s word to Abraham, which says four hundred. Exodus gives the sojourn as four hundred and thirty years (Exodus 12:40), and Paul uses that longer figure too (Galatians 3:17). There is no conflict. Four hundred is the round number for the affliction, spoken to Abraham in the shape a promise takes rather than a ledger; four hundred and thirty is the precise span, counted from a different starting point. Scripture is quite capable of giving a figure to the year in one place and rounding it in another, exactly as we do.

But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God. The plagues on Egypt, foretold centuries before Pharaoh was born. The oppressor is not out of God’s reach, even when he is out of the oppressed people’s sight.

And after that they shall come out and worship me in this place. Then the clause Stephen is steering toward. Which place? Stephen blends Genesis 15:14 with Exodus 3:12, where God says these words to Moses at the burning bush, and this place means the mountain in the desert where he is standing. The first act of national worship God ever promised his rescued people was to take place at Sinai, several hundred miles from the building these men are prosecuting Stephen to protect. Worship, not land, was the goal of the exodus.

Something greater than the temple. The place where God’s rescued people would worship was first a mountain in the desert, then a tent, then a house in Jerusalem. Stephen’s accusers thought the line ended at the house. Jesus said it ends in him: something greater than the temple is here (Matthew 12:6), and he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with him about his departure, the word is exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). That greater exodus brings a people out of a worse slavery than Egypt’s, and the place where they come to worship God is Christ himself.

How do I keep trusting when God’s promise seems delayed? Remember that delay is not denial. God told Abraham about the four hundred years in advance precisely so that later generations would not mistake the waiting for abandonment. Fill the waiting with what you know: his character, his past faithfulness, his written promises. Keep obeying in the meantime, as Israel kept having children in Egypt. Bring your impatience honestly to him, as the psalmists did: how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1). And remember that the greatest delay in history, the long wait for the Messiah, ended exactly on time, when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4). He is not late with you either.

In a sentence. God told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in another land, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, but that God would judge that nation, and afterwards they would come out and worship him in this place.

On a Tuesday. God redeems his people so that they will worship him. When you wonder what your salvation is for, the answer is here: you were brought out to worship. Begin this week by thanking him for one specific way he has brought you out.

For worship. He named the slavery before it began and the rescue before it came, and set the judgment of Egypt on his calendar centuries before Pharaoh was born. No oppressor has ever outrun this God, and no suffering of his people has ever fallen outside his count of years. He did it because he had already set his love on a people who did not yet exist, and the whole long story was aimed at one thing: that they should stand before him and adore. The worship first promised at the foot of a desert mountain will end before his throne, in a multitude no one can number.

parallels.desc: your offspring will be sojourners, afflicted four hundred years
you shall serve God on this mountain

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. Notice where the covenant sign is given (Genesis 17:9–14). Abraham has no land, no city, and not yet the son of the promise, and God hands him a sign to be cut into his own body. Given before the law, and long before the temple. And Stephen honours it: he is not against Moses or the covenant.

A sign that travels. The mark of belonging to God is put on the flesh, not on a plot of ground, and so it travels. Jacob’s sons carried it into Egypt, their descendants carried it through slavery and out again, and every Israelite in Babylon carried it through seventy years with no temple to go to. God chose the one mark his people could not be separated from or leave behind when they were deported.

Why call it the covenant of circumcision? The phrase names the covenant by its sign. The covenant itself was God’s promise to Abraham: a people, a land, and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12; 15; 17). When God formalised it, he gave circumcision as its token: this is my covenant, every male among you shall be circumcised, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you (Genesis 17:10–11). Sign and covenant became so bound together that the whole could be called by the sign. And two things are worth holding. The sign sealed a promise already received by faith: Abraham was counted righteous before he was ever circumcised (Genesis 15:6; 17), so circumcision was a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith (Romans 4:11). The mark never earned the promise; it pointed to it.

And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day. God kept his promise of a son. And Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs, the heads of the twelve tribes. Three generations in a single sentence, and a nation exists by the end of it. Stephen is moving fast, but he is establishing something no one in that room can dispute: that everything essential to being the people of God was in place and working generations before there was a land to live in or a house to worship in.

The son circumcised on the eighth day. The sign Abraham gave Isaac on the eighth day was given to another son of Abraham. Luke has already told us that when eight days were completed Jesus was circumcised and given his name (Luke 2:21). The Son of God took the covenant mark in his own flesh, born under the law to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). The sign that pointed forward was borne by the one it pointed to: the Offspring to whom the promise had been made (Galatians 3:16), keeping the covenant his people had broken, so that the blessing promised through Abraham could at last flow out to the nations.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Our paedobaptist brothers in the Presbyterian and Reformed churches see baptism as the new covenant sign that takes the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12), and so give it to the infant children of believers, as circumcision was given to Isaac on the eighth day. They do so out of a sincere conviction about God’s covenant faithfulness to families, and we honour them for it. Credobaptists answer that the new covenant is different in its membership: all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and its true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29). In Colossians 2 the circumcision that answers to baptism is the one made without hands, the new birth, and in Acts baptism follows repentance and faith (2:38, 41; 8:12). Verdict: baptism is for those who profess faith in Christ (1689 London Baptist Confession 29.2). Circumcision marked out a physical family through whom Christ would come; baptism marks out those who have been united to Christ by faith. Both sides agree on what matters most here: the sign never saves, and the promise is received by faith alone.

In a sentence. God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and so Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his promises across generations. Trust him for your children and grandchildren, pray for them by name, and teach them the promises. And if you have been baptised, remember this week what it signified: not something you achieved, but your union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4).

For worship. The covenant God gave Abraham was always too large for one family. It reached past Isaac, past the twelve patriarchs, past the borders of the land, toward the blessing of all the nations (Galatians 3:8). Men and women who never bore the old mark, from places Abraham never heard of, have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13), and given the circumcision that was always the point, of the heart, by the Spirit. The God who began with a single household in a tent has kept his word to the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.

And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. Consider whom Stephen is saying that to. In front of him sits the high priest, and on the high priest’s chest, when he is robed, is a breastpiece set with twelve stones, and on those stones are engraved twelve names: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah and the rest (Exodus 28:21). The founding fathers of the nation, worn over the heart of the man presiding at this trial. Stephen has just described them, accurately and without softening, as men who sold their brother into slavery because they could not stand him. This is the first rejection. The fathers of Israel rejected the one God had chosen to save them, out of jealousy, the same motive as the leaders who handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10; Acts 5:17).

The pattern appears. Stephen does not linger, but the pattern that will run through the whole speech is now visible: the man his brothers got rid of turns out to be the man they cannot live without. Joseph goes down into Egypt in a slave train and comes up as the only source of food in the world, and the brothers who sold him arrive at his door to beg.

But God was with him. Then the other half of Stephen’s case. Where was God with him? Not in the promised land, not at a shrine or a festival, but in a slave caravan, in an Egyptian official’s household, and in a prison cell on a false accusation, for some thirteen years between the pit and the palace. Joseph had no priest, no place of worship, none of the things his descendants would one day kill a man for defending, and God was with him, outside the land.

And rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. God’s presence did not keep him out of prison. God rescued him out of all his afflictions, which means he was in them first, one after another. The rescue ran through the trouble rather than round it, and at no point in those years could Joseph have told you it was working. Then God exalted the rejected one, and he became the saviour of his brothers: God sent me before you to preserve life; you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 45:5–8; 50:20).

What it does not promise. There is a version of this story preached as a guarantee: hold on, because your Egypt is preparing you for a throne. Scripture does not promise that. Joseph received a visible reward within his lifetime; a great many faithful people do not, and the letter to the Hebrews says plainly of a long list of them that they died still waiting. What this passage does establish is the thing Stephen needs, and it is enough to build a life on: there is no place a believer can be taken, sold, imprisoned, deported, forgotten or simply stuck, where God is not already there ahead of him, and no institution whose absence can put him out of reach.

Is it right to see Joseph as a picture of Jesus? Yes, because Stephen does, and because the shape is unmistakable. The beloved son of his father, hated by his brothers, sold for silver, falsely accused, brought down into the depths, then raised to the right hand of the throne, and from there giving bread to the very people who betrayed him. The Old Testament is full of such patterns, which the New Testament calls types: real events and people that God shaped to point forward to Christ (Romans 5:14; Hebrews 10:1). We should not invent fanciful links, but where Scripture itself draws the line, as here, we should follow it with joy.

In a sentence. The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt, but God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles, and gave him favour and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.

On a Tuesday. If you are in your own pit or prison this week, the promise is not that you will be out by Friday but that God is with you there. Say it to yourself aloud: God is with me here. Then do the next faithful thing, as Joseph did in Potiphar’s house and in the jail.

For worship. God was with Joseph in the pit, the caravan and the cell. The greater Joseph went further down, to the one place where even that comfort was withdrawn, and cried out that God had forsaken him (Matthew 27:46). He was abandoned so that his brothers never will be, and now he is Immanuel, God with us, in every Egypt they are carried to. He has been raised to the right hand of the Majesty on high, and the people who sold him are the people he feeds, and forgives with tears, and calls to come near.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit.

Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. A famine in the ancient world was not a disruption to the food supply. There were no reserves worth the name, no imports, and nobody to appeal to. A household ate its stores, then its breeding animals, then the seed corn it needed for the next year, and once the seed was gone, next year had been decided as well. After that it moved, or it died (Genesis 41:54–57).

And our fathers could find no food. Notice where this one strikes. The chosen family, standing in the land of promise, holding the covenant, descended directly from Abraham, could find no food. The country God had sworn to give them could not feed them, and the grain was in the pagan empire down the road. Stephen is still quietly dismantling the same equation. His accusers hold that God’s favour and God’s land belong together, so that possessing one proves the other. He observes that the covenant family’s first great crisis was solved by leaving.

But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. Look at the machinery of it. A rumour reaches an old man in Hebron that there is wheat for sale in the south, and he sends his sons to buy some. There is no vision, no angel and no word from God. A man acts sensibly on a piece of market news, and sets in motion the descent into Egypt, the four hundred years, the exodus, Sinai and the whole national existence of Israel. And on that first visit they did not recognise Joseph (Genesis 42:8).

How providence usually works. A great deal of Christian anxiety is spent looking for the other sort. Very little of what God does in a life arrives labelled. It arrives as the price of wheat, a conversation that ran long, a job that fell through, a piece of news somebody happened to mention. Jacob was being practical, not spiritual, and without the faintest suspicion of it he was delivering his household into the hands of the son he had spent twenty years mourning.

Not fatalism. One guard, because this can slide into fatalism. That God governs the ordinary does not mean ordinary decisions are unimportant. Jacob still had to weigh the risk and send the boys, and if he had not, they would have starved. What it means is that a man doing the sensible next thing in front of him, with no sense of destiny about it whatever, may be doing something that is still being discussed thousands of years later.

Bread only in the hands of the rejected. Follow Stephen’s pattern one step further. The brothers have no bread, and the only bread in the world is in the hands of the brother they sold, though they do not know it. Stephen’s hearers stand in the same place. The Jesus they handed over is now the one through whom alone God gives life, and there is salvation in no one else (4:12). Jesus called himself the bread of life, and promised that whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35). Every sinner who comes to Christ comes the way Jacob’s sons came to Egypt: hungry, empty-handed and unaware, to find that the one they wronged has been ready for them all along.

Does God send famines and disasters? Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including famines, storms and pandemics, and that nothing happens outside his wise and holy providence (Westminster 5.1; Amos 3:6). Genesis says plainly that God sent the famine as part of his plan to save many lives (Genesis 45:5–7). But God is never the author of sin, and his purposes in a disaster are usually hidden from us. Jesus forbade us to read a disaster as proof that its victims were worse sinners (Luke 13:1–5). The right response is not to explain other people’s suffering, but to humble ourselves, help the hungry, and trust that the God who governed Joseph’s famine is governing ours for the good of his people.

In a sentence. A famine came over all Egypt and Canaan, bringing great hardship, and their fathers could find no food, but when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent them on their first visit.

On a Tuesday. God uses hunger to bring people to the one they rejected, and your need may be his call. Look back over the last year at one ordinary event, a chance meeting, a closed door, a piece of news, and thank God for the hand you can now see was in it.

For worship. The God of the famine is also the God of the granary. Seven years before the first field failed in Canaan, he was filling storehouses in Egypt through a slave who had been sold for silver. He is never surprised by his people’s hunger; he is always further ahead of it than they can see. And the grain he stored then for one family was a small gift beside the bread he has given since: his own Son, sent down from heaven and given for the life of the world (John 6:51).

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all.

And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers. Everything turns on the second visit (Genesis 45:1–4). Genesis gives the moment four chapters, a room emptied of Egyptians, and a man weeping so loudly that the household heard it through the wall. Stephen gives it a single clause, because he needs the shape rather than the detail. The brothers had assumed for twenty years that they had got away with it, and the man they had wronged had meanwhile been put in charge of the only food in the world, and could have done anything he liked with them.

Recognised the second time. On the first visit the brothers did not recognise Joseph; on the second he made himself known. Many see a hint that Stephen means his hearers to catch, and the speech supports it: later Moses too is not understood when he first comes to his brothers (7:25), and returns as ruler and redeemer. Israel did not recognise Jesus when he came, and acted in ignorance, as Peter told them (3:17). Now, risen and exalted, he is making himself known through the preaching of men like Stephen. The scene in Genesis, with Joseph weeping and telling the men who sold him that he is their brother, is the gospel in miniature: the wronged one reveals himself in order to save.

And Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. This clause is easy to skim, and it decides what follows. A household of shepherds was presented at court, and the king assigned them the best of the land in Goshen. Israel came to Egypt by royal invitation, under the protection of the second man in the kingdom. That is why the new king of verse 18 is such a catastrophe: everything had rested on one man’s standing at court, and courts forget.

And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. The whole covenant family, counted, packed and moved out of the land of promise into the land of the Nile. On the face of it, it is the end of the story. It is in fact the mechanism of the next act. A household goes down, and a nation comes up.

Seventy or seventy-five? Genesis puts the number at seventy (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5). Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which Greek-speaking Jews used everywhere in his day, and which reads seventy-five, counting several more of Joseph’s descendants born in Egypt. A difference in counting between two textual traditions, not an error. Either way Stephen’s point holds.

Will Israel recognise Jesus at a second visit? Christians hold different views about Israel’s future, and this app presents them fairly. Many believe Romans 11 foretells a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others read all Israel as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, gathered in through the gospel age. All agree that God has not cast away his people, that Jewish men and women are coming to Christ now as they did in Acts, and that the church should pray and long for Jewish people to see in Jesus the brother they did not recognise.

In a sentence. On the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh, and Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people in all.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you wronged long ago and have avoided ever since? Joseph’s brothers found that the one they feared most was the one who forgave most freely. Pray about whether it is time to seek that person out and put it right.

For worship. The brothers spent twenty years dreading the face of the man they had wronged, and when at last they saw it, it was wet with tears and turned toward them in welcome. Christ has a face like that. The one with every right to condemn us is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and he gives his people more than Goshen: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading (1 Peter 1:4). On the day he shows himself fully, those who once looked straight at him without knowing him will see him as he is, and the seeing will be their joy.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text counts seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.

And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers. A single clause for the death of an entire generation, and Stephen keeps moving. But he stops for one thing, and it is the burial. These men died outside the land, every one of them, patriarchs of a people who had been promised a country, and their bodies were carried back across the desert so that they could lie in ground they had never owned. Joseph made his brothers swear to it on his deathbed, and four hundred years later a nation walking out of Egypt in a hurry took his coffin with them (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19).

A tomb as evidence. The only real estate any of the patriarchs held in the promised land was a grave and a field. They believed the promise so completely that they arranged their own funerals around it, and so patiently that not one of them expected to see it kept in his lifetime. Stephen’s accusers hold the land, the city and the temple, and are about to kill a man over a building. The founding fathers held a tomb, and held on to God.

Two purchases in one clause. A careful reader will stop here, and should. Genesis records two separate transactions: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), and Jacob bought the plot at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). Jacob himself was buried at Machpelah (Genesis 50:13); Joseph’s bones were laid at Shechem, in Jacob’s plot (Joshua 24:32). Stephen has folded two purchases and two burial grounds into a single clause.

If Stephen compressed the history, can I trust the Bible? Yes. The natural explanation is compression. Stephen is racing through more than a thousand years in one speech, on trial for his life, and he telescopes the patriarchal burials into a summary phrase, as speakers often did; he is not filing a title deed. His hearers knew the law better than we do, and they do not challenge a syllable of his history. They rage at his conclusion, not his facts. A few have suggested Abraham made a further, unrecorded purchase at Shechem, where he built his first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7): possible, but speculative. And notice what Scripture is doing. Luke’s task is to report the sermon faithfully, and he has. Inspiration guarantees a true record of what Stephen said, as it guarantees a true record of what Job’s friends said. Nothing hangs on this detail. What Stephen came to say, that God was never confined to this land or that building, stands untouched.

Why did the patriarchs care so much where they were buried? Because their burial was an act of faith in God’s promise and, at its deepest, in the resurrection. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus and gave directions concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22). He wanted to be where God’s promise would be kept, because he expected to share in it. Christians bury their dead with the same hope, not because the place saves, but because the body matters to God and will be raised. A Christian funeral is a statement of faith about the future, made beside a grave.

Joseph’s field and Jacob’s well. The patriarchs lie at Shechem, in Samaria, the region Jerusalem despised, and that ground turns up again in the Gospels. John tells us that Jesus, tired from his journey, sat by Jacob’s well at Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph (John 4:5–6). Beside the burial ground of the patriarch who died waiting, the one he waited for told a Samaritan woman that he was the Messiah (John 4:26). And in the very next chapter of Acts, scattered by the persecution that begins at Stephen’s death, Philip preaches Christ in Samaria and the Samaritans believe (8:1, 5–12). The fathers were buried in Samaritan ground in hope, and their hope came and sat down beside them.

In a sentence. Jacob went down to Egypt and died there, as did their fathers, and they were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb Abraham had bought for silver from the sons of Hamor.

On a Tuesday. The patriarchs died in faith, not having received what was promised (Hebrews 11:13). So may we. Ask yourself what your plans for the end of your life say about your hope, and whether the people who will one day bury you know what you believe about the resurrection.

For worship. The patriarchs lay in ground they never owned, and they lay there waiting. Christ was laid in a tomb cut for someone else, Matthew tells us (Matthew 27:60), and on the third day he handed it back empty. Because he lives, every grave his people lie in has become a bed with an appointed morning. The God who kept his word over the bones of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph will keep it over all who die in his Son, and he will call them, every one by name, out of the dust.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron, and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph.

But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham. Stephen has been counting. Four hundred years were named to Abraham back in verse 6, and God’s clock has been running ever since. It is now nearly up, and what happens as it runs out is not a softening of Israel’s circumstances but a hardening of them.

The people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. Put the two halves together, because Stephen has welded them deliberately (Exodus 1:7–8). The people increased: the promise working, outside the land, God blessing them in a foreign country. Until there arose another king: the terror beginning. Blessing and persecution arrive in the same sentence, and the second is a direct consequence of the first: a rapidly growing foreign population in the delta is precisely what alarms a new dynasty.

Did not know Joseph. A man had once saved the country from starvation, reorganised its agriculture and been made second in the kingdom, and within a few generations the palace has no idea who he was. It is a small, cold observation about the memory of nations: whatever a man does for a country, it forgets him faster than he would believe, and his descendants are assessed on their usefulness this year.

The whip and the promise. The harder thing here should be said carefully. Israel in Egypt before this king was doing well: land in Goshen, growing numbers, standing because of Joseph, and no recorded sign of wanting to leave. The promise required them to go, and what finally made them willing was the whip. It does not follow that every hardship is God prising somebody loose from a comfort, and it is never a thing to say to a person in the middle of one; a friend who explains your suffering to you has stopped being a friend. What can be said is only what the text says: this affliction fell inside a promise made four hundred years before, and the people groaning under it could not see that, and found out afterwards. Most people do.

Settled where we were never meant to settle. There is a plainer application, and it cuts close to home for readers in comfortable countries. It is entirely possible to be a member of the covenant people, prospering quietly, in a place you were never meant to settle, for a very long time, with no intention whatever of moving. Christians are sojourners and exiles (1 Peter 2:11), and the danger of comfort is that we forget it.

When the fullness of time had come. Stephen’s phrase, the time of the promise drew near, is the language of the whole Bible’s waiting. The first deliverance came when God’s appointed years ran out in Egypt. The greater one came the same way: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4), into a land ruled by a foreign emperor whose census decided where he was born (Luke 2:1–7). Before he finishes, Stephen will name the goal of all this waiting: the prophets announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One (7:52). Every promise that drew near in Egypt was drawing near to him.

How do I wait for God’s timing without becoming passive? Waiting on God in Scripture is never idleness. Israel waited in Egypt by having children, working, and keeping the memory of the promise alive; Joseph had made them promise to carry his bones out, so every generation knew they were not home. Wait like that. Do your work well, raise your children in the faith, pray for what God has promised, and hold your present comforts loosely, ready to move when he moves you. Waiting is active trust: doing today’s duty while looking for tomorrow’s fulfilment.

In a sentence. As the time drew near for God to fulfil his promise to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, until another king came to power who did not know Joseph.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether there is anywhere in your life you have settled that God never meant to be home: a comfort, a pattern, a security you would not let go of if he asked. Hold it more loosely this week.

For worship. Kings rise who forget the servants of God, and dynasties fall that never knew his name, but God forgets no one. He remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob (Exodus 2:24), and the remembering was no sudden recollection: every one of the four hundred years was already counted. His people multiplied under his blessing in a land not their own, and even the whip that fell on them fell inside his promise. His memory outlasts every throne, and his appointed hour arrives exactly when he said.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house,

He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. He outwitted them, out-thought them. The persecution was not a spasm of temper. It was policy: drafted, revised when it failed, and escalated by stages (Exodus 1:10, 22). First the forced labour to break them; then a quiet instruction to the midwives; then, when the midwives would not do it, the open decree that every son be thrown into the Nile. It is the coldest thing in the chapter, and it was arrived at in meetings.

Our fathers. Stephen puts the horror exactly where it belongs: Pharaoh forced our fathers to expose their infants. To expose was to abandon a baby to die, common in the ancient world, and later opposed by Christians who rescued abandoned babies from the rubbish heaps of Roman cities. The parents were made to give up their own children, which is why such a programme takes something out of a people that a massacre does not.

At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. That is God’s answer to the machinery of a superpower, and it is very small. No plague yet, no army, no uprising: a baby, born to slaves, in the middle of the programme designed to kill precisely him. Beautiful in God’s sight is a Hebrew way of saying exceptionally fine, pleasing to God (Exodus 2:2). God had his hand on him.

And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house. Hidden in a house where one cry at the wrong moment would have finished the whole family. Hebrews picks up the detail: by faith Moses was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict (Hebrews 11:23). The first act of faith in Israel’s deliverance was performed by a mother and a father with a basket.

The other babies. This must be said, because rescues are not universal. The other babies died. Stephen does not mention them and Exodus does not name them, but they were there: households whose sons were not hidden or were found, and for whom the deliverer born down the street was, at the time, no help at all. Scripture neither explains them nor pretends they were not there. Any reading of this passage that suggests God protects the children of the faithful as a general rule must be kept well away from anyone who has buried one. What the passage does say is that a state which had decided to end a people could not kill one particular child, and ended up paying for his upbringing. That is not an explanation of the others. It is a statement about who was in charge of the outcome, made to a court that thought it was.

Another child under a king’s decree. Matthew tells the birth of Jesus in words chosen to recall this one. A king hears of a child who threatens his throne and orders the boys of a whole district killed; the child is carried to safety; and then the angel tells Joseph to return, for those who sought the child’s life are dead (Matthew 2:16, 20), almost the words God spoke to Moses in Midian (Exodus 4:19). The deliverer born under a death sentence was a preview of a greater one. And the greater one did more than escape the decree as a baby. At the end he walked into the death sentence on purpose, so that it would fall on him and not on his people.

What does this say about the value of unborn and newborn children? That every child is precious to God, including the ones the powerful find inconvenient. Each is made in his image and known by him before birth (Genesis 1:27; Psalm 139:13–16). Pharaoh’s policy was condemned by God, and so is every modern equivalent, including abortion and the abandonment of the unwanted. Christians should speak for the voiceless (Proverbs 31:8), and should do it as the early church did, by caring practically for mothers and children. And to anyone carrying the grief or guilt of an ended pregnancy: there is full forgiveness in Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). The church is meant to be a place of refuge for you, not judgment. And Scripture gives grieving parents real hope: we believe that God in his mercy saves the elect infants who die in infancy (Westminster 10.3; 2 Samuel 12:23).

In a sentence. The king dealt cunningly with their people and forced their fathers to abandon their babies so that they would die, and at that time Moses was born, a child beautiful before God, who was cared for three months in his father’s house.

On a Tuesday. God saw and valued an infant marked for death, and every child is precious to him. Do one concrete thing this month for a child or a struggling parent: a meal, an hour of help, a gift to a pregnancy support centre, a prayer said with them.

For worship. Pharaoh saw a Hebrew boy as a problem to be drowned; God saw a child beautiful in his sight, and the whole might of Egypt could not reach him. The Father has looked on another child that way. Over the waters of the Jordan he said of Jesus, You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (Luke 3:22), and no ruler on earth could take that life until he laid it down himself. Every child the powerful count as disposable is seen by this God, and not one of the little ones Pharaoh drowned was ever out of his sight.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds.

And when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. The rescue is arranged by the daughter of the man who signed the death warrant, and the child is brought up in the palace of the regime that wanted him dead (Exodus 2:5–10). Rescued by the enemy’s own household. Stephen does not comment on the irony. He does not need to.

What it cost him. He was taken out of a Hebrew house and raised as an Egyptian prince, eating at the table of the people who had enslaved his family, speaking their language, learning their gods, and addressed by a name that was not the one his mother used. Whatever else that childhood was, it was not simple.

And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Egypt was the great seat of learning in the ancient world; even of Solomon it is said that his wisdom surpassed all the wisdom of Egypt (1 Kings 4:30). It embraced mathematics and geometry, astronomy and the calendar, a famed medicine, architecture, the scribal art, statecraft, a large body of moral instruction, and the lore of the priests. As the adopted son of Pharaoh’s daughter, Moses would have received a prince’s education. Exodus does not say this; it is the natural inference from his upbringing, preserved also in Jewish tradition, for Philo and Josephus describe his education at length. God prepared him in a pagan court.

And he was mighty in his words and deeds. Moses would later say he was not eloquent (Exodus 4:10), but his words carried power. Stephen’s point in this stretch is aimed at the temple charge again: God’s man is formed entirely outside the covenant community, in a pagan palace, by a pagan education, at the expense of the pagan state.

A prophet mighty in deed and word. Luke chooses the phrase with care. In his first volume, two disciples on the Emmaus road described Jesus of Nazareth as a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people (Luke 24:19), and the risen Jesus then showed them from Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (24:27). The echo is hardly accidental, and the difference is as telling as the likeness. Moses was a son adopted into a palace that was not his; Jesus is the Son who came from the Father into a world he had made. Moses learned all the wisdom of Egypt; in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

Equipped, but not the deliverer. Stephen’s deeper point soon follows. For all his Egyptian learning and natural greatness, Moses’ first attempt to deliver Israel in his own strength failed (vv. 23–29), and he had to wait forty years in the desert for God’s call. The world’s finest wisdom equipped him, but it did not make him the deliverer. God did.

Should Christians pursue a secular education? Yes, with open eyes. Moses learned the wisdom of Egypt, Daniel the literature of Babylon (Daniel 1:4, 17), and Paul quoted pagan poets (17:28). All truth is God’s truth, and learning is a gift to be used for his glory and our neighbour’s good. But neither Moses nor Daniel let the school decide who they were. Daniel resolved not to defile himself; Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter (Hebrews 11:24). So study hard, and study well, and take your faith into the classroom with you. Learn everything you can, and let God’s word judge it all.

In a sentence. When he was abandoned, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son, and Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was mighty in his words and deeds.

On a Tuesday. God prepares his servants in unlikely places, and your training may be his preparation. Look at the job, the course or the experience you think is wasted, and ask how God might use it for his kingdom.

For worship. The Lord used Pharaoh’s own daughter to raise the man who would bring Pharaoh down, and Egypt’s treasury to pay for the schooling of Israel’s deliverer. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10). No palace is closed to him, and no enemy’s resources finally belong to the enemy. He did it again, on a scale that dwarfs Egypt, at the cross: the rulers who gathered against his Son did only what his hand and his plan had predestined to take place (4:28), and their worst became the rescue of the world.
verseByVerse.note: Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian.

When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. Something rose in him, and it was a decision about who he was: a man raised as an Egyptian must eventually settle which of the two peoples inside him will win. Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ hundred and twenty years into three forties: forty in Egypt, forty in Midian (v. 30), forty in the wilderness (v. 36; Deuteronomy 34:7).

A renunciation. The letter to the Hebrews describes the moment as a refusal: he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin (Hebrews 11:24–26). So this is not a young man’s impulse. He chose to identify with his oppressed people, and it cost him a kingdom.

The reproach of Christ. In the same breath Hebrews adds a startling phrase: Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:26). He suffered as one of the people through whom the Messiah would come, and his choice had the shape of Christ’s before Christ came. The contrast tells as much as the likeness. Moses left a palace and took a life; the Son left glory and gave his. He too saw his brothers wronged, by sin and death and the devil, and came down to defend them, but he struck down no one. He let himself be struck, and by his wounds we are healed (1 Peter 2:24).

And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. And then he kills a man (Exodus 2:11–12). Stephen neither condemns nor approves. Exodus supplies two details that settle the moral question: Moses looked this way and that, and seeing no one, struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Those are the movements of a man who knows exactly what he has done.

Right about the cause, wrong about the method. The loyalty was right and the hands were his own. God had not sent him; there is no word from God anywhere in these verses. The deliverer who eventually stands before Pharaoh will do it with a staff and a message and no violence of his own. Moses was right about the cause and wrong about the method, and the method cost him forty years. The pattern is common and does not look like sin from the inside: a man is right about the need and the injustice, then forces the issue in his own strength, and the result is a body in the sand and a career in the desert. The wrongness is not in the caring but in the assumption that being right about the cause authorises whatever gets it done.

Forgiven, but not spared. And then the mercy, which should not be hurried. God did not discard him. The man who buried an Egyptian at forty was standing before a burning bush at eighty, and the intervening decades turned out to be preparation rather than punishment. But they were real decades. He lost forty years, a nation waited forty years longer in slavery, and being forgiven was never the same thing as being spared the consequences.

When should a Christian step in to defend someone being wronged? Often, and gladly, by right means. Scripture commands us to open our mouths for the mute and defend the rights of the poor and needy (Proverbs 31:8–9), and Moses’ instinct to stand with the oppressed was right. But we act within the law and through proper channels: we report abuse to the authorities, speak up at work, give evidence, support the vulnerable, and in an emergency we protect life. What we do not do is take private vengeance; vengeance belongs to God and to the authorities he has appointed (Romans 12:19; 13:4). Care deeply, act wisely, and do not let zeal for justice become an excuse for sin.

In a sentence. When Moses was forty, he decided to visit his fellow Israelites, and seeing one being mistreated, he defended him and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian.

On a Tuesday. Moses chose God’s suffering people over Egypt’s comforts. What will you choose? Ask where in your life you are tempted to force God’s work forward by your own methods, and hand it back to him.

For worship. Moses looked this way and that before he struck, because he knew he was alone and in the wrong. The Son of God did his saving work in full view, lifted up outside the city, with nothing to hide and no blood on his hands but his own. One blow cost Moses forty years in the desert; one offering of Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). Every human deliverer forces the issue and falls short somewhere. This one was never too early, never too late, and never once wrong in his method.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’

He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. Verse 25 is not in Exodus. Stephen is telling us what Moses was thinking, a preacher interpreting, and the interpretation unlocks the whole speech. God was giving Israel salvation (sōtēria) by Moses’ hand: that is stated as fact. What was Moses’ own opinion was that they would grasp it. They did not. God was genuinely at work in him, and the people he had come to rescue saw a palace-raised Egyptian who had killed a man.

The failure is in the seeing. The failure is not in the sending; it is in the seeing. The phrase Stephen chooses, they did not understand, hangs over everything that follows. Twenty-seven verses later he will tell these men that they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, and he does not have to draw the line between the two statements. God giving salvation by the hand of a deliverer his people did not recognise is the story of Jesus before it is the story of Moses. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11); the rulers acted in ignorance (3:17); and yet God was giving salvation by his hand all the same. The cross they did not understand was the salvation itself.

And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them. The second scene is harder than the first. Yesterday he stepped between an Egyptian and a Hebrew, the easy kind of intervention, with an obvious oppressor and victim. Today he steps between two Hebrews, where both men have a grievance and neither wants him there. Anyone who has tried to make peace inside a family or a congregation knows which day is harder, and what tends to happen next: two parties who agree about nothing else unite instantly against the man who came to help.

Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other? A plea for unity. The sentence is true, and is the only reason Moses had any business being there, and is precisely the thing that neither of them wished to hear.

How should I try to make peace between two people? Carefully, prayerfully and humbly. Begin by praying for both. Go to each privately before bringing them together, and listen far more than you speak. Remind them, as Moses did, of what they share: if they are believers, they are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died. Do not take sides before you understand, and do not carry tales between them. Be ready to be resented; peacemakers often are. And know your limits: serious conflict, especially where there is abuse or law-breaking, belongs with elders and sometimes with the authorities. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9).

In a sentence. Moses thought his brothers would realise that God was rescuing them through him, but they did not, and the next day he came upon two of them fighting and tried to reconcile them, asking why brothers would wrong each other.

On a Tuesday. Think of two people in your church, family or workplace who are at odds. Pray for them by name this week, and ask God whether you are meant to be a peacemaker between them.

For worship. Moses could only plead with two brothers to stop wronging each other, and was pushed away for it. Christ did what no plea could do. He made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), reconciling sinners to God and, in the same act, to one another, breaking down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The quarrels of Hebrew slaves, of Jews and Gentiles, of families and congregations, all lie within reach of that blood. The peacemaker whom his brothers thrust aside has become the peace of everyone who comes to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’

But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside. The word for thrust aside (apōtheō) is pushed away, rejected, and it is a key word, for Israel will thrust Moses away again (v. 39). The guilty one rejects the peacemaker.

Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Stephen has included the question for a reason, and the reason arrives eight verses later. At verse 35 he says: this Moses, whom they rejected, saying, Who made you a ruler and a judge, this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. The question receives its answer in its own words. Israel demanded to know who had made him a ruler. The answer, which took forty years to become visible, was God (Exodus 2:14).

The question asked again. That is the spine of the Moses section, and Stephen leaves its third instance unspoken. The men in front of him had put the identical question to Jesus in the temple courts: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority (Luke 20:2). God has since answered it for them, in Peter’s words at Pentecost: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (2:36).

Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? The second half of the taunt is the sting, and a threat. Moses had looked round and seen nobody. Somebody had seen. And the man who tells him so is one of the two he has just tried to reconcile: the secret is out, and it is out through the people he was trying to help.

Israel had some reason. The rejection establishes Stephen’s pattern, the rescuer refused by the rescued on the question of his standing. But in fairness, consider how it looked from the labour camp. A man who has spent forty years in the palace, who has never carried a brick, turns up, kills a foreman, and expects to be recognised as the nation’s deliverer. The reprisals would fall on them and not on him. Their failure was genuine, and Stephen names it. But it was not stupidity. It was the ordinary difficulty of recognising a deliverer who does not look like one, the very difficulty the men listening had lately failed to overcome with a carpenter from Nazareth.

How do I respond when my help is thrown back at me? First, do not be surprised; Moses was rejected for trying to make peace, and Jesus for far more. Second, examine yourself honestly, as Moses had reason to: was there something in my manner or method that made the help hard to receive? Third, do not retaliate or become bitter; commit the matter to God, who sees. And fourth, do not conclude that you must never help again. Moses was rejected at forty and sent back at eighty. Sometimes the timing was wrong, not the love. Keep your heart soft, and wait to see whether God reopens the door.

In a sentence. The man in the wrong pushed Moses aside, asking who had made him ruler and judge over them, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian the day before.

On a Tuesday. When the guilty resist correction, do not be surprised. And when you are corrected, notice whether your first response is to ask who gave them the right. Listen before you answer.

For worship. Who made you a judge over us? Every time the question has been put to God’s deliverer, the one asking it has been in the wrong. God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (17:31). The one men pushed aside will be the judge of those who pushed him. And the wonder is that his judgment seat is the one place where the guilty can still find mercy, because the judge has already borne their sentence.

parallels.desc: who made you a prince and a judge over us?

verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.

At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. One sentence, and forty years disappear into it. Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in north-west Arabia. Exile (paroikos) is a sojourner, a resident alien, like Abraham.

Three forties. This speech is the only place in Scripture where the arithmetic of Moses’ life is spelled out: forty years in Egypt (v. 23), forty in Midian (v. 30), forty in the wilderness (v. 36), making the hundred and twenty at which Deuteronomy says he died. Two-thirds of that life was over before God said anything to him at all.

What the middle forty contained. He married a Midianite priest’s daughter and kept another man’s sheep in another man’s country. He named his first son Gershom, which Exodus explains as I have been a sojourner in a foreign land (Exodus 2:22), and a man who names his child after his own homelessness is telling you how the years were going. Nothing in the record suggests he expected to go back.

God waited for the second man. The contrast between the men at either end of the gap is the point. At forty he was a prince with an education, a position and a plan, convinced that God was going to save Israel by his hand and that everyone would see it. At eighty he was a shepherd standing before a burning bush producing five separate excuses why God ought to send somebody else. God waited for the second man.

The fallow years. This is the passage for a reader in a long fallow stretch: the years after the thing that was supposed to happen did not, the ministry that closed, the plan that came to nothing. Scripture shows the shape repeatedly: David between the anointing and the throne, Paul in Arabia and Tarsus until Barnabas came looking for him. But the pattern is easily turned into a promise it does not make. Not every fallow decade is preparation for something visible, and telling somebody in year twelve that God is getting them ready is a guess dressed up as a word from the Lord. Moses did not know. What can be said is that the desert was not wasted and God had not finished, and nobody in Midian could have told you either thing at the time.

The rejected one who went away. Stephen’s story has a shape worth holding. The deliverer is refused, goes away into a far country, and comes back with God’s authority to the people who refused him. It is the shape of what Peter had preached in the temple: the Jesus they denied, God has raised, and heaven must receive him until the time for restoring all things (3:13–15, 21). Between the rejection and the return there is a long middle, and in it the deliverer is not idle and the people are not forgotten. Moses kept sheep in Midian. Christ, risen and ascended, is gathering his flock from every nation, and he will come back.

Is it wrong to run from danger? No. Moses fled for his life, and so did David, Elijah, Joseph and Mary with the infant Jesus, and Paul over the Damascus wall. Jesus told his disciples, when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Fleeing is not cowardice when it preserves life and does not require denying Christ. What a Christian must not do is run from a clear duty, or deny the Lord to save his skin. Where faithfulness and safety can go together, take the safe road with a clear conscience. Where they cannot, stand.

In a sentence. At this retort Moses fled and lived as a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he had two sons.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a Midian season, do the ordinary work in front of you faithfully, the sheep, the job, the family, and keep your heart open to God. He spoke to Moses in the middle of a working morning.

For worship. The Lord took a prince with a plan into the desert and brought out a shepherd who trembled, and he lost nothing in the exchange. Forty years of sheep and silence lay in the same hand that held the four hundred years of Egypt. He is never in a hurry and never late, and the long middles of his people’s lives, which look like nothing from the inside, are where he does some of his deepest work. He hears what Gershom’s name confesses, he names his exiles as his own, and he has never forgotten the way home.
verseByVerse.note: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:

Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. Stephen puts the silence in first. Whatever else the burning bush is, it is the end of four decades in which God said nothing whatever to the man he intended to use (Exodus 3:1–2). In the wilderness, outside the land, far from any temple: God revealed his name there.

What stopped Moses was not the fire. In the Sinai, among bare rock and thorn scrub, a burning bush is a commonplace and a nuisance, a handful of ash a minute later. Exodus tells us what arrested him: I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned (Exodus 3:3). It was the duration. He looked, and it was still there, and at some point he understood that he was watching something that was not obeying the rules.

When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord. Exodus gives the order: when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush (Exodus 3:4). God spoke to a man who had stopped. It would be a mistake to make that a technique, as though attentive people could produce revelations by noticing harder; God was in that bush whether Moses looked or not. But much of what God does is available to anybody prepared to stop and look twice, and a life can be spent walking briskly past. Moses was eighty, minding animals that were not his on an ordinary working morning, and the rest of the Bible turns on his going to have a proper look at something odd.

Was it an angel or God himself in the bush? Exodus says the angel of the LORD appeared, and then that God spoke from the bush, saying, I am the God of your father (Exodus 3:2–6). The angel of the LORD speaks as God and is called God. Many Christians, from the early church onward, have understood him as the Son of God appearing before his incarnation, and that is a reasonable reading. What is certain is that Moses met the living God himself, and that the God who spoke from the bush is the God revealed in Jesus Christ (John 8:58).

In the wilderness. This is Stephen’s real interest. Where does this happen? In the wilderness of Mount Sinai: not in Egypt, where God’s people were, nor in Canaan, which God had promised them, but in desert belonging to nobody, with one man and a flock of sheep for a congregation. Stephen is on trial for saying that God is not confined to a building, and he walks the court through the places their own Scriptures record him turning up. And the one who spoke from that bush did not stay in deserts. He came to his own in flesh, and before Stephen finishes the court will hear where he stands now.

Should I expect God to speak to me in a burning bush? No; the bush was a unique moment in the history of redemption, when God was giving new revelation. Now God has spoken to us by his Son, and his word is complete in Scripture (Hebrews 1:1–2). But the lesson of turning aside still holds. God speaks to us whenever we stop and attend to his word, and he often draws our attention through ordinary things: a verse that will not let go, a sermon that lands, a providence that makes us look twice. Do not rush past. Make room in your day to stop, read, and listen.

In a sentence. After forty years an angel appeared to Moses in the wilderness of Mount Sinai in a flame of fire in a bush, and when Moses saw it he was amazed, and as he went closer to look, the voice of the Lord came.

On a Tuesday. God can meet you in the wilderness, in the most ordinary place. Stop and look. Choose one quiet ten minutes this week, put your phone in another room, and read a passage of Scripture slowly, twice.

For worship. The bush burned and was not consumed, because the God who was in it needs nothing to keep him burning; he is not fed by the wood and does not use it up. After forty years of silence he still knew the name of a fugitive shepherd, and he called it twice (Exodus 3:4). The God who spoke from that fire came nearer still in his Son, and the sinners he came among were not consumed: he ate with them, touched them, and gave himself for them. The holy one of the burning bush has drawn near without destroying, and his nearness is our life.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’

I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob. Four hundred years of silence, and the first thing God says is that he is the same (Exodus 3:6). No explanation of the delay; he names himself by three men dead for centuries, and so tells Moses that nothing has been dropped: the promise made in Mesopotamia to a childless man is being kept this morning in a desert. And Jesus would later draw out of this very sentence the proof of the resurrection: he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:37–38).

And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Holy fear. Set that beside the man of verse 24. At forty he was ready to take on Egypt single-handed; at eighty he cannot raise his eyes to a bush. Whatever the desert did to him, it did not leave his nerve where it found it, and this is the man God has decided to send.

Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. Then the sentence Stephen has been building toward (Exodus 3:5). This is the first time in the Bible that any ground is called holy, and it is a patch of dirt in a foreign desert with a thorn bush on it: no altar, no priest, no ark, no temple, no city, no ceremony. When God had finished speaking and Moses walked back to his sheep, it was scrub again. What made it holy was that God was there. Nothing else did, and nothing else ever has.

The sandals. In that world a man took his shoes off at the door of a house, and by long tradition the priests served barefoot in the sanctuary. God is telling Moses that this hillside is his house. Now hold that against the charge sheet. Stephen has shown the court, out of the law they revere, that the first ground God ever called holy was unmarked desert, holy for exactly as long as he stood on it, and not one man in that room can dispute it, because Moses wrote it down.

Where God now stands. If ground is holy only because God is there, then the holiest place on earth in Stephen’s lifetime was wherever Jesus stood, for in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). Moses took off his sandals before a bush. This council had condemned the one who was God with us, after witnesses accused him of saying he would destroy the temple made with hands and build another not made with hands (Mark 14:58). Within minutes Stephen will see where he stands now, at the right hand of God (7:56). The holy ground of the desert has become the throne of heaven, and it is open to a man about to be stoned.

Is my church building holy ground? Not in itself. No place under the new covenant is holier than another; Jesus said that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). A church building is a useful room, to be cared for well and used reverently, but it is not a temple. What is holy is the presence of God among his gathered people, and that is why public worship should be reverent: not because of the bricks, but because the Lord is in the midst of his assembly (Matthew 18:20). Wherever God’s people meet in his name, whether a cathedral, a school hall or a living room, take off your sandals in your heart.

In a sentence. God said he was the God of their fathers, of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses trembled and did not dare to look, and the Lord told him to take off his sandals, for the place where he stood was holy ground.

On a Tuesday. Wherever God meets you is holy ground. Before you open your Bible or begin to pray today, pause for a moment and remember who you are speaking with. Let reverence and nearness go together.

For worship. Moses could not lift his eyes to a bush. The God who burned in it has since let himself be looked on, in the face of his Son, and the looking does not kill but heals. He still names himself by the men he made promises to and kept, and he is pleased to add to that list the name of everyone who trusts his Son. The barefoot fear of the desert has not been cancelled. It has been taken up into something greater: the bold nearness of children who are welcome in their Father’s house.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; take off your sandals

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’

I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. Three verbs, in an order worth following: I have surely seen, and have heard, and I have come down (Exodus 3:7). The first is doubled in the Hebrew: seeing I have seen. Not glanced at; looked at steadily, the whole way through, for four hundred years.

God hears groaning. Exodus, describing the same moment, does not say that Israel prayed. They groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help, their cry rose up to God, and God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant (Exodus 2:23–24). No national repentance, no prayer meeting, no petition properly worded: a noise made by people at the end of their strength, and God treats it as a communication. That is worth knowing by anyone who has sat with something so heavy that the words would not come, and concluded that it did not count. Paul says that when we do not know what to pray for as we ought, the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Whatever reaches God, it is not the wording.

And I have come down to deliver them. Then the strangest verb. God does not explain. Four hundred years have passed exactly as he told Abraham, and he offers no reason for the timing and no answer to the question every Hebrew slave must have asked in the dark. He has seen, he has heard, and he has come down. Israel received a rescue and never an explanation. Much Christian energy goes into demanding from God the reason for a silence, and Scripture’s most sustained example of a long silence ends without one. What was given instead was God himself, in motion, on the way.
