And now come, I will send you to Egypt. The last clause turns the whole thing over. God says he has come down to deliver them, and then sends a man. The coming down and the sending are one act. It is how he has always worked. And the men listening to this speech had lately watched him do it in a form so complete that they killed the messenger, for the true coming down of God was in his Son, and they are about to kill the next messenger too.

How can God come down, if he is everywhere already? God is everywhere present, filling heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24). When Scripture says he came down, it means he acted in a new and particular way: he drew near in saving power to a specific people in a specific place. It is language suited to us, but it describes something real. And it reaches its full meaning in the incarnation, when the eternal Son literally came down from heaven and became flesh (John 6:38; 1:14). The God who said, I have come down, in Exodus, said it again in Bethlehem, and this time he stayed.

In a sentence. God said he had surely seen his people’s suffering in Egypt and heard their groaning, and had come down to rescue them, and now he was sending Moses to Egypt.

On a Tuesday. God sees your affliction and hears your groaning. If you cannot find words to pray today, groan before him. He hears that too. And then look for whom he might be sending to help you, or whom he might be sending you to help.

For worship. God heard the groaning of slaves who could not frame a prayer, and counted it as speech. Then he did more than hear. In his Son he entered the groaning himself: in the days of his flesh Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7), and on the cross he cried out in the words of a psalm. The God who saw, and heard, and came down has been seen with human eyes and touched with human hands (1 John 1:1), and the cry of every afflicted child of his now goes up to one who has cried the same way.

parallels.desc: I have surely seen the affliction of my people

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’ — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.

This Moses, whom they rejected. Something changes in the rhythm here, and it is audible even in English. Stephen begins hammering the same word at the head of each sentence: this Moses, this man, this man, this is the Moses, this is the one (vv. 35, 36, 37, 38). He has stopped narrating. He is pointing, and this is the heart of the speech: Stephen is drawing a portrait of Jesus.

This man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. What he points at is a contradiction his hearers have never resolved. Israel demanded to know who had made Moses a ruler and a judge; God made him a ruler and a redeemer. The very office they refused him is the office he was given, and the men who asked the question spent the next forty years being led by him. So with Jesus: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (2:36); the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (4:11).

Redeemer. The second title is worth a moment: redeemer (lytrōtēs), a word that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It is the one who buys a man out of slavery or debt, the deliverer and ransomer, the man with both the right and the resources to pay what you cannot pay yourself. Stephen is describing Moses, and he has chosen a word his hearers will not be able to keep at a comfortable distance.

This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. Verse 36 spreads the vindication over forty years. Signs confirmed him, as they confirmed Jesus (2:22). And it is worth noticing that this is the phrase Luke has been using of the apostles in this book, and used in the previous chapter of Stephen himself (6:8). Moses, the Twelve and the man now on trial are being set in a single line: all sent, all attested, and all disbelieved by the same institution.

The pattern fully drawn. The pattern is now complete, though Stephen still refuses to name it. Joseph, sold by his brothers, fed them. Moses, thrust aside by his people, brought them out. Twice God sent Israel a deliverer, twice Israel refused him at first sight, and twice God sent him anyway. One question now hangs in that chamber, and every man on the council can hear it.

What does it mean that Jesus is my redeemer? It means you were a slave, and he paid to set you free. Not with silver or gold, Peter says, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). You were in bondage to sin, under the law’s curse and the fear of death (Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 2:15), and you could not buy yourself out. Christ had the right, as your kinsman in our flesh, and the resources, as the Son of God, and he paid it all. So you belong to him now, not as a slave in fear but as a ransomed child, and the life you have is no longer yours to spend as you please, because it was paid for (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

In a sentence. This Moses, whom they rejected by asking who made him ruler and judge, God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the angel who appeared to him in the bush, and he led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.

On a Tuesday. When someone rejects you for Christ’s sake, remember that rejection by men has never been the final verdict on God’s servants. And when you are tempted to think little of Jesus, say aloud the titles God gave him: Ruler, Redeemer, Lord.

For worship. Redeemer is a costly word. Moses paid nothing for Israel’s freedom; he led slaves out with a staff, and they went free under the blood of lambs on the doorposts. The Redeemer Moses foreshadowed paid in his own blood, and paid it for the very people who thrust him aside. He is Ruler and Redeemer at once, the King who owns his people because he bought them, and the ransomed of every nation follow him out of a bondage deeper than Egypt’s, all the way home.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us.

God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. Stephen now plays what looks like his strongest card. The promise (Deuteronomy 18:15) is the text Peter preached from in the temple courts (3:22), and Stephen means Jesus, as Peter did. Here it goes straight at the second charge, that Jesus would change the customs Moses delivered. Moses himself told Israel to expect somebody else and to listen to him when he came. The man they accuse Stephen of dishonouring pointed beyond himself to Jesus. To honour Moses is to listen to Jesus.

This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness. The description in verse 38 is extravagant. The word for congregation is ekklēsia, the Old Testament’s term for the assembly of Israel and the New Testament’s word for the church. Israel in the wilderness was God’s assembly, the church of the old covenant.

With the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. Stephen says the law came through angelic mediation, as the New Testament says elsewhere (v. 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). He is not diminishing the law by saying so. He is about to use it, at verse 53, as the aggravating factor in the charge he brings against them.

He received living oracles to give to us. Living oracles: not a dead code or an antique, but words of God with life still in them, still speaking. It is one of the highest things anyone in the New Testament says about the law of Moses, and it is said by the man on trial for despising it. And note the last word. Not to you but to us: he claims the law as his own inheritance, in a hearing convened on the charge that he has thrown it away.

A demonstration, not a denial. The instinct under a false accusation is to deny, and denial always sounds like a man on the back foot. Stephen states what he actually believes, in terms so high that the accusation collapses. The best answer to being misrepresented is usually not a correction but a demonstration.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians? Entirely. It is the Bible Jesus read, quoted and called the word of God, and he said it bears witness about him (John 5:39). Paul says the Scriptures, meaning the Old Testament, are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and that all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable (2 Timothy 3:15–16). We read it through Christ, so that its sacrifices point us to his cross and its ceremonies are fulfilled in him rather than kept by us. But its stories, laws, psalms and prophets remain living oracles for us. If you have neglected it, start with Genesis, the Psalms or Isaiah, and read looking for Christ.

In a sentence. This is the Moses who told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from among their brothers, who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Sinai and with their fathers, and who received living words to give to us.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is living. Read it as such: not as a duty to tick off, but as a voice speaking to you today. Before you read tomorrow, pray, Lord, speak; your servant is listening.

For worship. The living oracles given at the mountain were never meant to stay on stone. The God who spoke through angels and through Moses has now spoken in a Son, who is himself the Word, full of grace and truth, and whose words are spirit and life (John 6:63). At Sinai the congregation heard the voice and begged not to hear it again (Deuteronomy 18:16), and the promise of a prophet like Moses was God’s answer to that fear. The same God now speaks through one of our own brothers, and the word that once thundered from the fire calls sinners by name and gives them life.
verseByVerse.note: “The congregation” is the same word as “church.”

parallels.desc: a prophet like me

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’

Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside. Thrust aside is the word he used at verse 27, where the quarrelling Israelite shoved Moses away. Israel pushed Moses aside before the exodus, and again at the foot of the mountain, after the sea had opened. They had the living oracles, and refused them. The rescue made no difference to the reflex.

And in their hearts they turned to Egypt. They had walked through a sea on dry ground and watched an army drown, and within months they wanted to go back (Numbers 14:3–4), not because slavery was preferable but because Egypt was familiar and the food arrived. Numbers records what they missed: the fish, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic (Numbers 11:5). They remembered the menu and forgot the whips. The heart turned back before the feet did.

The homesickness of the redeemed. This is not about somebody else. A man is genuinely delivered, the thing that owned him is broken, and he would not go back if asked outright. Yet there is a homesickness in him for the country he was rescued from: not for its misery but for its familiarity, the not having to trust anybody for tomorrow. Egypt fed you every day and asked nothing of you except your life.

Make for us gods who will go before us. The request came while Moses was up the mountain receiving the law on their behalf (Exodus 32:1); they gave him about forty days before replacing him. Idolatry is wanting a god you can see and control, one who goes where you want to go. And the complaint is a small masterpiece of contempt: not our leader, not the man God sent, but this Moses, of whom we do not know what has become.

The mediator out of sight. The calf was made while Moses was out of sight on the mountain, doing for the people what they could not do for themselves. The church lives in the same situation. Our mediator has gone up, out of sight, and the world asks what has become of him. He is not idle: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). And the comparison runs deeper. When Moses came down he offered to be blotted out of God’s book for the people’s sin, and God would not accept the offer (Exodus 32:30–33). Christ’s offering was accepted. He became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and bore the sin of the very people who were so quick to replace him.

A trap closing. This passage is easily turned into a lash. The people who did this had seen the sea open and eaten manna that morning, so witnessing miracles does not make anybody faithful, and a Christian who assumes he would have done better is the sort of person Stephen has in front of him. Every man on that council would have agreed that their ancestors were a disgrace. That is the trap, and it closes in twelve verses.

What do I do with the longing for my old life? Name it honestly, and do not be shocked by it; Israel felt it, and so do most believers at some point. Then remember accurately. Egypt was not garlic and melons; it was whips and dead babies. Ask God to show you the truth about what you were rescued from. Feed on what he has given now: his word, his people, the manna of each day’s grace. Remove what makes the road back easy. And look forward, as Moses did, to the reward (Hebrews 11:26). The longing for Egypt fades fastest when the heart is fixed on the promised land.

In a sentence. Their fathers refused to obey Moses and pushed him aside, turning back to Egypt in their hearts and asking Aaron to make them gods to lead them, since they did not know what had become of this Moses.

On a Tuesday. Idolatry begins in the heart. Guard yours. Notice this week what you reach for when God seems slow or distant, the comfort food of the soul, and bring that longing to him instead.

For worship. Within months of the Red Sea they wanted Egypt back, and God did not give them up. He kept the manna falling, forgave them again, and carried their children into the land. His patience outlasts our homesickness for the old country, and his grip is stronger than our looking back. The Shepherd who led Israel through the wilderness leads his flock still, and no one will snatch out of his hand those the Father has given him (John 10:28–29).

parallels.desc: make us gods who shall go before us

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: “‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?

And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. This phrase explains why Stephen dies (Exodus 32:4–6). Its twin arrives at verse 48: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. In the Greek Old Testament, made by hands is very largely a word for idols, the contemptuous term for things people carve and then bow down to (Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 2:18; 46:6). Idolatry is worshipping what we make.

The temple in the same category. So when Stephen applies it to the temple, a Jewish ear does not hear a remark about architecture. It hears the temple put into the same category as the golden calf. That is the offence: not that he disparaged a building, but that he used the vocabulary of idolatry about the house of God, having just established that Israel has a very long history of rejoicing in things it made itself. Even a God-given building can become an idol when it takes God’s place.

But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, the stars worshipped as gods. This is the most frightening judgment there is. He did not strike them; he let them have it. Paul uses the language three times in Romans 1: God gave them up (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). From the inside it feels like nothing happening at all. A man insists on his idol, and God stops arguing with him.

Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? Stephen quotes Amos (Amos 5:25), and the question is extraordinary, because of course they did; Leviticus is the paperwork for it. Amos is not denying that the ritual happened. He is denying that it arrived.

Who is hearing this. Stephen stands before the men who run the sacrificial system and quotes a prophet asking whether Israel’s sacrifices were ever for God at all. He is not merely saying the building cannot contain God; he is putting the offerings in question, a far more dangerous thing in that room. And the question reaches anyone who does religious things: not whether the activity is happening, or correct, or sincere-feeling, but whether it is being brought to God or merely performed in his vicinity.

The one offering that arrived. Amos’s question hangs over every altar in Israel’s history: forty years of offerings, and did any of them truly reach God? The New Testament gives the answer the whole sacrificial system was waiting for. It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). But one offering did arrive. Christ, through the eternal Spirit, offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14), and God accepted it, as the empty tomb and the ascension declare. Stephen is speaking to the men who run the altar, and they have just condemned the one sacrifice to which every altar pointed.

Could God give me over like that? If you are worried that he might, that worry is good evidence he has not. Those whom God gives over do not tremble about it; they rejoice in the works of their hands and want nothing more. The believer who sins and is grieved, who wants to be rid of his idol and cannot yet see how, is being pursued by God, not abandoned. God disciplines the children he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and his discipline hurts precisely because he has not let go. The danger is not in the struggle. It is in the settled, contented refusal to be turned. If you can still hear his objection to your idol, thank him, and listen.

In a sentence. They made a calf, offered sacrifice to the idol and celebrated what their hands had made, so God turned away and gave them over to worship the stars, as Amos wrote, asking whether they had really brought him sacrifices in the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. What have your hands made that you are tempted to worship: career, home, reputation, a family image? And in your religious life, ask Amos’s question: is my worship being brought to God, or only performed near him? Turn from the idol, and bring the next prayer to God himself.

For worship. The most terrible judgment is to be handed over to what we wanted. The wonder of the gospel is that God handed someone else over: he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), so that people who had rejoiced in the works of their own hands might rejoice for ever in the work of his. The living God will not share his glory with a calf, and yet he shares his Son with those who made one.

parallels.desc: did you bring me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?
the host of heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship. The quotation from Amos runs on (Amos 5:26), and it means that Israel in the wilderness had two tents. One was the tent of witness, built to the pattern God showed Moses, with the ark inside and the cloud over it. The other was the tent of Moloch, carried through the same camp by the same people. Stephen’s accusers have built their case on the sanctity of the sanctuary; he tells them that from the first generation it had a rival travelling beside it in the baggage, and that the golden calf was the visible part of something the nation never put down. And note the word again: the images that you made.

Who were Moloch and Rephan? Moloch (or Molech) was a pagan deity, named as the abomination of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7) and notorious across the region for child sacrifice: children were made to pass through the fire to him (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35). The tent of Moloch is a portable idol shrine carried in procession, a grim parody of the tabernacle. Rephan is the star of your god: an astral deity, probably the planet Saturn worshipped as a god. This is star worship, the bowing to the host of heaven that Scripture repeatedly condemns (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3–5).

An honest word on the names. Stephen is quoting the Greek Old Testament of Amos 5:25–27, and its wording differs from the Hebrew, which at this point is genuinely obscure. Where the Hebrew has Sikkuth and Kiyyun, probably names of Mesopotamian astral gods (Saturn again), the Greek rendered them Moloch and Rephan. So the exact identifications are the best scholarly reconstruction, not certainty; but the sense is plain, and it is Stephen’s point. Even in the wilderness, the very generation that carried God’s tabernacle was also carrying the shrines of pagan star gods.

And I will send you into exile beyond Babylon. Amos wrote beyond Damascus. Stephen extends it to the exile that actually came, which is not carelessness but the ordinary freedom of a preacher pressing a prophecy to the event it reached. The end of persistent idolatry was exile from the land. The land did not protect them. The judgment threatened by the prophet is the judgment their ancestors received, and Stephen is placing the court he stands in inside the same sentence.

Exile borne outside the gate. The end of the rival tent was exile, and Israel went into it. The prophets also promised a return, and the New Testament shows how God brings home a people who deserve to be sent away. Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). He was led out of the city, cut off out of the land of the living (Isaiah 53:8), carrying the banishment that idolatry earns, so that those whose fathers had carried Moloch’s tent could be brought near. And Stephen, about to be dragged outside the same city, will follow him there.

Do people still worship Moloch and the stars? In other forms, yes. Moloch was the god to whom children were sacrificed for the sake of prosperity and security, and every age finds its own ways of sacrificing children to the adult’s comfort, career or convenience. The star of Rephan is the old ancestor of astrology, the belief that our lives are ruled by the heavens rather than by the God who made them. Horoscopes may seem harmless fun, but Scripture treats looking to the stars for guidance as turning from God (Isaiah 47:13–14). The Christian looks past the stars to their Maker, who calls them all by name (Isaiah 40:26), and who holds our times in his hand.

In a sentence. Amos said they had taken up the shrine of Moloch and the star of their god Rephan, the idols they made to worship, and so God would send them into exile beyond Babylon.

On a Tuesday. Is there a second tent in your baggage, something you carry alongside your faith that has never been surrendered? Name it before God today. And if you have dabbled in horoscopes or similar things, set them aside, and trust your future to the Lord.

For worship. Israel bowed to a planet. The God who made it has never given his glory to it, and he has given his people something brighter to look to: his Son, the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16), risen over a people who once worshipped what he had made. The shrine of Moloch demanded children; this God gave his own Son. The exiles who carried rival tents have been welcomed home by the God they betrayed, and the star gods of their fathers are now only lamps hung in his sky.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was the god of child sacrifice, and Rephan probably an astral god (Saturn). Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” where the exile actually went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,

Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Stephen now turns to the sanctuary, and first he defends it. God ordered it and specified it; there is not a syllable of criticism here. The tent of witness is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the law, the testimony (Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:7). The fathers carried the tent of Moloch; God gave them the tent of witness.

A tent. Not a house or a temple: a tent, with pegs and ropes and curtains and poles, struck in a morning and standing again by evening. The one dwelling God ever designed for himself was portable, every piece of its furniture fitted with rings so that poles could be run through and men could pick it up and walk.

According to the pattern. So even the tent was a copy, a model of something Moses was shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), a copy and shadow of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8:5). Hebrews says what it pointed to. Christ is a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man (Hebrews 8:2). He entered through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:11–12). Every peg and curtain Moses fixed to the pattern was a sketch of Christ going into the presence of God for us.

Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. And it kept moving: into Canaan, then round the country for centuries, to Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob and Gibeon. For Greek readers there is a glint of something more: the name Joshua in Greek is Jesus (Iēsous). The first Jesus brought the tent into the land; the second would bring the true dwelling of God among men.

So it was until the days of David. That is the hinge, and everything after it concerns what happened when somebody decided the arrangement ought to be permanent.

Then should churches not own buildings? They may, and many should; a building is a tool, and a good one. Stephen thought the tabernacle mattered enormously, and God designed it. The question is not whether a church has a building but whether it could lose one and still be a church. The early Christians met in homes, in rented halls (19:9) and in the open air, and the church grew. A congregation that would collapse if its building were taken away has put its weight on the wrong thing. Use your building gladly, keep it modest and useful, and keep your heart in the people and the word.

In a sentence. Their fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, made just as God had directed Moses according to the pattern he had seen, and they brought it into the land with Joshua when God drove out the nations, and it remained until David’s time.

On a Tuesday. God moved with his people in a tent, and he still goes with you wherever you go. Ask whether your church, and your faith, could move if God called: whether what you run on is the sort of thing that can be picked up and carried.

For worship. The God who let men carry his dwelling on poles across a desert did not wait for a house before he came to live with his people. In the end he came in the flesh of his Son: the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally pitched his tent, among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). That tent was struck down on a cross and raised again in three days, and it will never be folded away. The pilgrim God still travels with his church, through every wilderness, to the end of the age.
verseByVerse.note: The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him.

Who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. David comes off well here, and Stephen means him to (Psalm 132:5). He found favour in the sight of God, and what he wanted was to build God a house (2 Samuel 7:2). It was a generous impulse in a man who had noticed that he was living in a palace of cedar while the ark of God sat under canvas, and Scripture never suggests the motive was wrong.

But it was Solomon who built a house for him. That but carries a great deal, and to feel it you need what God said through Nathan when David proposed the idea. Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt, but I have been moving about in a tent. Did I ever ask any of the judges of Israel why they had not built me a house of cedar? (2 Samuel 7:5–7). Since the exodus God had never asked anybody for a building, nor once complained about not having one.

I will build you a house. When David offered, God turned the offer round. You will not build me a house; I will build you a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11–13). The play on the word is the point of the whole passage: David offered God a building and God gave David a dynasty.

The greater Son of David. God promised David a son who would build a house for his name, and whose throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:13). Solomon built a house of stone, and his kingdom was torn in two soon after he died. The promise was waiting for a greater Son. The angel told Mary that the Lord God would give her child the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32–33). The house he builds is not cedar but living stones, his people (1 Peter 2:5). And the heir of that dynasty is the one these men had lately helped to nail to a cross outside the city wall.

Even the builder knew. None of which makes the temple illegitimate. God permitted it, filled it with his glory on the day it opened, and Jesus called it his Father’s house. Stephen does not condemn it. And the man who built it said at the dedication, before the whole nation, that heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built (1 Kings 8:27). Even the builder knew.

A short and nearly invisible step. What the passage exposes is a very ordinary religious mistake, and sincere people make it almost invariably. David’s desire was good. The impulse to do something substantial for God is good. But there is a step from I want to honour God with this to God requires this, and must be honoured here, and the step is short and very nearly invisible. A thousand years after Solomon, a man is on trial for his life because a building God never asked for had become the thing his people could not imagine him without.

How do I know whether my good plan for God is what he wants? Hold it with open hands, as David did. David told Nathan, and when God said no, he did not sulk; he sat before the LORD and gave thanks for what God would do instead (2 Samuel 7:18–29). So test your plan against Scripture, pray over it, ask the counsel of godly people, and watch how God opens or closes the way. Above all, notice if the plan has become something you cannot imagine God without. That is the sign a good desire is turning into an idol. God may give you something better than you asked: not the house you wanted to build him, but the house he builds you.

In a sentence. David found favour with God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob, but it was Solomon who built a house for him.

On a Tuesday. Think of a good thing you want to do for God. Offer it to him this week with a genuine willingness to hear no, and thank him in advance for whatever better thing he may give instead.

For worship. David looked at his cedar palace and the ark under canvas and wanted to do something for God. God answered by doing something for David that made the offer look small: not a building for a season but a house for ever, a Son on the throne whose reign will not end. That is how this God answers the generosity of his servants. He takes the cup they hold out and fills it until it runs over, and every believer gathered into the house of David’s Son is part of the overflow.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, ‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?

Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says. Here is the sentence they kill him for. Made by hands (cheiropoiētos) is idol vocabulary, the standard term in the Greek Old Testament for the manufactured objects the prophets pour contempt on, and Stephen has already used its twin of the golden calf. Now he fastens it onto the temple. His point is not that the temple was wrong, but that treating it as the place where God was contained was idolatry. Paul says the same in Athens (17:24).

The Most High. The second is the title he chooses. The Most High is a title for the God of Israel that outsiders often use: it is on the lips of Melchizedek, of Nebuchadnezzar, of a demoniac in the Gospels, and of a fortune-telling slave girl later in this same book (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 4:34; Mark 5:7; Acts 16:17). It is the God of Israel described from beyond the boundary, and exactly the right title for a speech about a God who declines to be kept inside one.

Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. So that nobody can accuse him of inventing the idea, he quotes Isaiah (Isaiah 66:1): God seated with the sky for a chair and the planet under his feet for a stool.

What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Describe the building, says the prophet; give the dimensions. The question answers itself the moment anyone tries. No house can hold him.

The throne Stephen is about to see. Stephen quotes God saying that heaven is his throne, and within minutes he will look into that heaven and see who stands at the right hand of God (7:55–56). The council thinks God is to be found in the building down the hill. Stephen is about to tell them, from the evidence of his own eyes, that God’s dwelling is where Jesus is. The man from Nazareth they condemned for threatening their temple is at the right hand of the only throne Isaiah says God has. No house can hold the Most High; but the Most High has a Son, and in him God came close enough to be crucified and has been raised high enough to rule.

The line he leaves out. His hearers knew the passage well enough to supply Isaiah’s very next sentence: but this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isaiah 66:2). So Isaiah does say where God dwells: not in a structure but in a certain sort of person. Stephen stops one line short, and the line describes precisely what the men in front of him are not. They are proud of their building, unmoved by their guilt, and about to show what they think of the word of God by killing the man reciting it. Every man in the room can hear the missing sentence, which is worse.

If God is everywhere, why should I go to church? Because the church is not a building but a people, and God has promised to be present among his gathered people in a special way (Matthew 18:20; 1 Corinthians 14:25). Scripture commands us not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), because we need the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, the prayers and the fellowship of the saints. You can pray alone anywhere, and you should. But the living stones are meant to be built together into one house, not scattered across the field. Going to church is not visiting God’s building; it is joining God’s temple.

In a sentence. The Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says: heaven is my throne and earth my footstool; what kind of house will you build me, says the Lord, or where is my resting place?

On a Tuesday. Church buildings are useful, but God does not live in them. He lives in his people. Be his temple: this week, treat your body, your home and your congregation as the places where God has chosen to dwell.

For worship. The high and lofty one, whose chair is the sky and whose footstool is the earth, bends down to look at a person who trembles at his word. He passes over palaces and temples to find a contrite heart. And he has done more than look: in his Son he stooped all the way down, was laid in a manger, and died outside the city. The God too great for any house has made himself at home among the broken-hearted, and the only dwelling he asks of us is a humble one.

parallels.desc: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Did not my hand make all these things?’

Did not my hand make all these things? Eight words close the argument (Isaiah 66:2). The temple was built by human hands, and human hands were made by God. The stone came out of ground he made, cut by men whose lungs he kept full while they worked. A man cannot house his maker in materials his maker supplied. The Creator cannot be confined by what creatures make.

A question to end on. Stephen ends this whole section with a question rather than a statement. He has been quoting Isaiah for two verses, and the last thing the council hears before he turns and faces them is God’s own voice asking whether they had ever stopped to consider who made the quarry.

Where God dwells now. If God never truly dwelt in the building, where is his dwelling now? In Christ first of all. Jesus called his own body this temple (John 2:19–21), and in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). And through him, in his people: you are God’s temple and God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22). Stephen’s point is not that buildings are wrong, but that we must never trap the living God in a place or a thing while missing him where he truly dwells.

A question to put to oneself. It is possible to know perfectly well that God is not contained in a building and to have quietly relocated him somewhere just as manageable: a style of service, an hour of the week, a way of feeling when the music is right. The test is what a man would have left if the thing were taken away.

What does it mean to tremble at God’s word? Not to be terrified of the Bible, but to take it with utter seriousness, as the voice of the living God. The one who trembles at God’s word lets it correct him rather than correcting it. He reads it expecting to be addressed, obeys what it says even when it costs, and is moved by its promises as well as its warnings. Josiah tore his clothes when he heard the law read (2 Kings 22:11–19), and God looked on him with favour. Trembling at the word is the opposite of the council’s stopped ears. It is a soft heart that hears God speaking and bows.

In a sentence. God asks whether his hand did not make all these things.

On a Tuesday. God made everything. He does not need our buildings, but he seeks our humble hearts. Ask yourself what you would have left of your faith if your favourite form of it, the music, the building, the routine, were taken away. Then make sure your hope is in God himself.

For worship. All things were made through the Son (John 1:3), and the hand that shaped the quarries and the stars was one day stretched out on a cross and pierced with nails. God, who needs nothing from us, since everything we could bring him came from him first, gave everything for us. The Maker would not be housed in a building of his own stone. He chose instead to be laid in a tomb cut from his own rock, and to walk out of it, and now he makes his home with the humble who tremble at his word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen turned the charge back on his accusers: they were stubborn, with hearts and ears uncircumcised, always resisting the Holy Spirit just as their ancestors did. Their ancestors persecuted every prophet and killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, and now they had betrayed and murdered him. They had received the law through angels and had not kept it. Hearing this, they were furious and ground their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He said he could see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. At this they covered their ears, shouted, rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. While they stoned him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he knelt down and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” With that he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the Pattern of Martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it did not come to mean somebody killed for the faith until enough witnesses had been. Stephen is where the shift begins, and the shape of his death is the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. Reformed theology has been careful about what this is and is not. It is not heroism and it is not an achievement that earns anything — Luke states plainly that Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit at the moment he looked up, which is to say that the courage and the vision and the forgiveness were all supplied to him. What this passage exhibits is not a strong man but a sustained one. And it should be added, because the church has periodically forgotten it, that martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for this. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: Nobody watching that morning could have identified what was actually happening. The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed scattered most of the Jerusalem church; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.

You stiff-necked people. The turn is abrupt, and it lies in a single pronoun. Again and again Stephen has said our fathers: our father Abraham, our fathers could find no food, our fathers had the tent of witness. He has argued as a member of the household about the household’s own history. Now he says your fathers, and says it again in the next verse. The defence has become a prosecution, and every man in that chamber feels the floor shift.

A farming word. Then three charges, and every one of them is a quotation. Stiff-necked describes an ox that sets its neck against the driver’s hand: not an animal that bolts, but one that simply refuses to go the way the plough needs to go. It is the word God himself used of Israel at Sinai after the golden calf (Exodus 32:9; 33:3, 5).

Uncircumcised in heart and ears. To that audience this is the deepest insult the language holds: telling circumcised men, in the covenant’s own vocabulary, that the mark cut into their bodies never reached the place it pointed to. And it is not his coinage. Moses, the law and Jeremiah all said it (Deuteronomy 10:16; Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 4:4; 6:10; 9:26), the prophets’ language for those who will not listen to God. True circumcision is of the heart (Romans 2:28–29). Stephen is quoting their Scriptures at them and letting the Scriptures do the accusing.

You always resist the Holy Spirit. To resist is to fight, to shove back against something coming toward you. The Spirit is the one who spoke through the prophets, against whom Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit (Isaiah 63:10). And always is the sting: not sometimes, not in the bad generations, but as a continuous habit running from the wilderness into this room.

The Spirit of Christ in the prophets. Whom were they resisting? Peter says that the Spirit who spoke through the prophets was the Spirit of Christ in them, predicting the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow (1 Peter 1:10–11). So to resist the Spirit in Moses and the prophets was already to resist Christ, and when the Son came, anointed with that same Spirit (Luke 4:18), the old resistance found its final object. The neck that would not bend to the prophets would not bend to him either. The apostles had told this very council that the Holy Spirit is a witness to Jesus, given to those who obey him (5:32).

As your fathers did, so do you. The recital of the last fifty verses was the evidence for this sentence: rejecting Joseph, rejecting Moses, worshipping idols, and now rejecting Jesus.

A word of care. Sentences like this one have been lifted out and used as a weapon against Jewish people for the better part of two thousand years, and that must be named. Notice the speaker and the setting. This is a Jew, in the Jewish council, quoting Moses and the prophets, saying to the leadership of his own nation what Isaiah and Jeremiah had said to the leadership of theirs. It is prophetic speech inside a family, the oldest and most Jewish form of address in the Bible. A man does not get to borrow Stephen’s sentence unless he is standing where Stephen was standing, and almost nobody who has quoted it has been.

If the Spirit can be resisted, is grace not irresistible after all? Both truths are taught in Scripture, and they fit. The Spirit’s outward call through the preaching of the word comes to many, and those left to themselves resist it, always, as Stephen says; that is what fallen hearts do. But when God effectually calls his elect, he does not merely invite; he gives a new heart that gladly comes (Ezekiel 36:26; John 6:44; Westminster 10.1). The resistance is real, and God overcomes it, not by forcing an unwilling man but by making him willing. The proof is standing at the edge of this very scene, holding coats. Saul resisted the Spirit as hard as any man in Jerusalem, until the risen Christ called him by name, and he could resist no longer.

In a sentence. Stephen said they were a stubborn people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, who always resisted the Holy Spirit, just as their fathers had.

On a Tuesday. The resistance Stephen names is not an ancient national peculiarity. It is the ordinary daily possibility of hearing something true from God and setting the neck against it. Is there a word of God you are resisting? Soften your neck and listen, today.

For worship. The God whom Israel resisted did not stop sending: prophets, then his Son, then his Spirit poured out on all flesh. He met the stiff neck not with a heavier yoke but with a new heart. He is the God who circumcises hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6), who takes out the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, and the mark that never reached the place it pointed to he now writes there himself. The necks that bow to Christ bow not because they have been broken but because they have been made new, and they bow gladly.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for stubborn refusal to listen.

parallels.desc: a stiff-necked people

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.

Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? A question with no available answer. Jeremiah was imprisoned and dropped into a cistern; Isaiah, by tradition, was sawn in two; Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:21). It was not the pagans who did it: the men who suffered most at Israel’s hands were the men God sent to Israel. Jesus had said the same (Matthew 23:29–37; Luke 11:47–51).

And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One. Stephen chooses his title with care. The Righteous One is the title Peter used in the temple courts (3:14), the one Paul will hear applied to Jesus at his conversion (22:14), and it reaches back to the righteous Servant of Isaiah (Isaiah 53:11). It is exactly what a court exists to protect. The supreme judicial body of the nation is being told that it condemned the one genuinely innocent man in its history, Jesus, the sinless one.

Whom you have now betrayed and murdered. The climax of the pattern. The Greek does not say they committed betrayal and murder; it calls them betrayers and murderers. He has turned the verbs into nouns and hung them round their necks as titles.

You who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it. Then the answer to the charge that began all this. Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law (Deuteronomy 33:2; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). On trial for speaking against the law, Stephen closes by saying that it came to them by the hand of angels, an honour he praised at verse 38, and that they broke it. He never denies the charge; he changes who is being examined. The question is no longer whether Stephen kept the law, but whether they did.

The most conservative accusation. He does not say the law is finished or mistaken. What he says is that they had it and did not do it, the most conservative accusation available and the hardest to answer. The last word on the law of the first Christian to die for the faith was not an attack on Israel’s Scriptures but a charge that Israel’s leaders had not obeyed them.

Was Stephen being unloving? No. Love sometimes has to say the hardest thing, and Stephen said it as a member of the family, in the words of the family’s own prophets, to people he wanted to see saved. His last breath proves it: he prayed for these very men. The prophets spoke like this because they loved Israel, and Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the same week he pronounced its judgment (Luke 19:41–44). We should be slow to imitate Stephen’s sharpness, because we rarely have his clarity, his Spirit-filled courage or his love. But when the truth must be spoken, it is not unloving to speak it plainly, as long as we would gladly die for the people we are speaking to.

In a sentence. Stephen asked which prophet their fathers had not persecuted, for they killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, whom they had now betrayed and murdered, though they had received the law delivered by angels and had not kept it.

On a Tuesday. Before you criticise anyone for failing to keep God’s law, ask honestly whether you keep it. And thank God that the Righteous One kept it perfectly in your place.

For worship. The Righteous One was betrayed and murdered by the court that existed to protect the righteous, and in that unrighteous verdict God did the most righteous thing ever done: he made the guilty right with himself. By one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). Every persecuted prophet was announcing him, and every one of them is vindicated in him. The judges of that day called him a criminal; now he is the advocate of the very people who broke the law, pleading his own righteousness for them before the Father (1 John 2:1).
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. The council is enraged, the word Luke used at 5:33 of this same body hearing Peter: cut to the quick, sawn through. Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury (Psalm 35:16; 37:12), and Jesus uses the phrase of the lost in outer darkness (Matthew 8:12). Fury has gone past words: seventy-one of the most dignified figures in the nation, in session, in robes, making a noise with their jaws.

But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven. While they glare at him, he looks up. Luke’s verb is the fixed gaze (atenizō) he used at the end of chapter 6, when this council stared at Stephen and saw a face like an angel’s. Now the staring runs the other way, and what he is looking at is not in the room.

Full of the Holy Spirit. Luke has already used the phrase of Stephen (6:3, 5): a person so yielded to the Spirit that his presence and power are evident. At this moment it brings two things. First, sight: the Spirit gives eyes for the unseen, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10). Second, strength for the supreme test, so that he dies like his Lord, committing his spirit to Jesus and forgiving his killers. It is what Jesus promised witnesses dragged before councils: the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11–12). Stephen was already full; this is a fresh filling for a decisive moment, as when Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answered the council (4:8).

And saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. The God of glory who appeared to Abraham (v. 2) now appears to Stephen at the end of the same speech, and Jesus is at his right hand, the place of honour and power. The speech opened with glory appearing to the father of the nation in Mesopotamia; it closes with glory opened to the first martyr outside Jerusalem, and in the middle of the glory, a man.

Can I be filled with the Spirit? Yes; every Christian is commanded to be: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). The verb means keep on being filled. It is not a one-off experience for the spiritual elite, but the ordinary Christian life lived under the Spirit’s control. And its truest evidence is not ecstatic feeling but a man who sees Christ clearly and lives and dies like Christ graciously. Paul follows the command with singing, thanksgiving and humble submission to one another (Ephesians 5:19–21). So ask God for it daily, feed on his word, confess sin quickly, and obey what you know. The Spirit did not spare Stephen the stones. He filled him to face them.

In a sentence. When they heard this they were furious and ground their teeth at him, but Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked steadily into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God’s right hand.

On a Tuesday. When the world grinds its teeth at you, look up. Jesus is there. Before the meeting, the confrontation or the bad news this week, lift your eyes, and remember who stands at the right hand of God.

For worship. While men grind their teeth on earth, heaven stands open, and the glory that once filled a tent and a temple rests on the face of a crucified man. That is where the glory of God now lives. The Spirit who filled Stephen did not lift him out of the hail of stones; he lifted his eyes above it, to the Lord who had gone ahead. The exalted Christ is not absent from his suffering people. He is above them and for them, and at the last he lets them see the glory they were made for.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

Behold, I see the heavens opened. As at Jesus’ baptism, when the heavens were opened and the Spirit descended (Luke 3:21). The barrier between earth and the throne room is drawn back, and a dying man is allowed to see.

And the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Two things here are extraordinary, and the first is the title. Son of Man is how Jesus habitually spoke of himself, some eighty times in the Gospels, and almost nobody else uses it; once a puzzled crowd throws it back at him (John 12:34). Outside the Gospels this is the only place anyone calls Jesus the Son of Man, apart from the visions of Revelation. Stephen calls Jesus what Jesus called himself, in the very chamber where Jesus had told this council: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69). Stephen says: I see him. He confirms the very claim for which they condemned Jesus, and they have now heard it twice, from two men, in the same room. The second time, they do not wait for a verdict.

Standing. The second is the posture. Everywhere else in the New Testament Christ at the Father’s right hand is seated. Psalm 110 says sit, and Hebrews builds an argument on the fact that this priest sat down, because his work was finished (Hebrews 10:12). Stephen sees him standing. Why? Perhaps to welcome his servant home; or as a witness standing to testify for him in the heavenly court, as Stephen testifies for him on earth; or as a judge rising to pass sentence. All may be true.

Two courts. The setting suggests the strongest answer. Two courts are sitting that morning. In the lower one a man is tried on the evidence of witnesses put up to lie, the outcome settled before he opened his mouth. In the higher one, as the accused is about to be condemned, his advocate rises to his feet. Jesus had promised it in Luke’s first volume: everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God (Luke 12:8). Stephen is acknowledging him before men at the highest cost, and Luke shows the promise being kept while it is still being paid for.

The court at three in the morning. Most Christians will never stand before a council, and will nevertheless be judged: by an employer, a family, a country, or their own conscience convening a court at three in the morning with the evidence stacked and no defence prepared. This verse says there is another court in session, and it never lets the testimony go unanswered. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Christ Jesus is the one who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34).

Will I see heaven opened when I die? Scripture does not promise every believer a vision like Stephen’s, and many faithful Christians die without one, some peacefully and some in confusion or pain. What it promises is better than a vision: presence. To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Whether your eyes see anything at the end or not, the Lord Jesus will be there to receive you. Stephen was allowed to see beforehand what every believer will see immediately afterwards.

In a sentence. Stephen said, Look, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.

On a Tuesday. When you feel condemned, by others or by your own conscience, remember the other court. Say it aloud: Christ is at the right hand of God, interceding for me. Then go on with your day as one who has an advocate.

For worship. The Son of Man whom the council condemned is the one to whom the Ancient of Days has given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him, with a dominion that will never pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). The council had the last word on earth for about an hour. He has it for ever. And the King of that everlasting kingdom is on his feet for one dying servant in a field outside Jerusalem, because no one who confesses him is too small for him to rise for.
verseByVerse.note: Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he stands — perhaps to welcome Stephen or to plead as his witness.

parallels.desc: I will acknowledge him before the angels of God

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Picture it: seventy-one of the most dignified men in the nation, in session, with their fingers in their ears, shouting so as not to hear. To them it was blasphemy. Luke reports it without comment. It is also the exact fulfilment of Stephen’s charge six verses earlier: he said they were uncircumcised in their ears, and they stopped them with their hands.

With one accord. The word Luke uses for rushed together (homothymadon) is the word he used of the church’s unity, with one accord in prayer and in the temple (1:14; 2:46). Now it describes a mob’s rage. There is a unity of the Spirit, and there is a unity of the mob, and they look alike for a moment from a distance.

A lynching by a court. No verdict is recorded, no sentence pronounced, no vote taken; they simply rushed at him. Whether the council even had the power to execute is doubtful: Rome reserved capital punishment, and John records them telling Pilate that it was not lawful for them to put anyone to death (John 18:31). It was probably a lynching, perhaps in a gap when no Roman governor was watching closely. Luke does not say. He is describing a proceeding that had stopped being a proceeding.

Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. Yet the form is kept wherever it suits them. They cast him out of the city, because the law required a stoning to take place outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). They keep the geography of Leviticus and abandon everything else in it.

Outside the gate with his Lord. The disciple follows his Lord out of the city. Jesus had been led out of Jerusalem to die, suffering outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12), and false witnesses had stood up at his trial too (Mark 14:56–57). Stephen’s death has the shape of his Master’s because he belongs to him. But the likeness stops at the decisive point. Stephen’s blood sanctifies no one. He goes outside the camp bearing the reproach that Christ endured (Hebrews 13:13), because Christ had already gone there bearing his sin.

And the witnesses laid down their garments. Then a detail that ought to stop a reader cold. Luke mentions the witnesses because the law of Moses required that in a stoning the witnesses throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7), so that any man who had sworn a life away had to be the one to take it. These are the witnesses of chapter 6: the men who were suborned, planted and briefed. The men who lied about Stephen are the men who killed him with their own hands, and they took their coats off in order to do it properly.

At the feet of a young man named Saul. In a single sentence, with no introduction, the New Testament brings in the most important man of its second half. A young man (neanias), perhaps in his twenties or thirties, minding the coats: the respectable part, the part that gets no blood on it, the part a man can afterwards tell himself was not really participation. Luke says at the start of chapter 8 that he approved, and Paul never let it go. Years later in this same city he described how he stood by approving and watching over the garments of those who killed Stephen (22:20); elsewhere he admits he cast his vote against the believers (26:10). Every man who threw a stone is anonymous. The one Luke names is holding the coats.

Is holding the coats really so bad? Yes, and that is why Paul never forgot it. Most of us will never throw a stone, but most of us have held a coat: laughed along with the cruel joke, stayed silent while someone was slandered, approved in our hearts what we would never have done with our hands. Scripture treats approval as participation; Paul says those who give approval to evil share in its guilt (Romans 1:32). The good news is in the same verse. The man who held the coats became the apostle who wrote, Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:15). There is forgiveness for the coat-holders too.

In a sentence. They shouted, covered their ears, rushed at him together, dragged him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.

On a Tuesday. When something cruel happens near you this week, a mocking conversation, an unjust decision, a person being shut out, refuse to hold the coats. Say a quiet word, or at least decline to approve. And pray for anyone you know who is fighting Christ hard. They may be Saul.

For worship. The stones were thrown by men who thought they were silencing a witness, and the coats were held by the man who would carry that witness to Rome. The Lord who stood over that field outside the wall was not losing that morning. In the very fury of his enemies he was preparing his chosen instrument, who would carry his name before the Gentiles and kings (9:15). The one whose name the council stopped its ears against has been turning persecutors into preachers ever since, and his grace has a way of running first toward the people standing nearest the stones.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones. This is the first mention of Saul, later Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Two prayers, and the order of them is the last thing Luke wants the reader to notice. The first is for himself, and it is a quotation. Psalm 31:5 says into your hand I commit my spirit, and it is addressed to God. Jesus prayed it from the cross, addressed to the Father: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays it to Jesus.

Dying on the assumption of his deity. Consider what that is. A Jewish man, being killed for blasphemy by the highest religious authority in Israel, spends the last moments of his life praying a psalm addressed to the God of Israel, and addresses it to Jesus of Nazareth. He is not constructing an argument for the deity of Christ. He is doing something far more telling: he is dying on the assumption of it. Nobody commends his soul to a creature. The first Christian martyr dies praying to Jesus as Lord. And he expects his spirit to go at once to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

And falling to his knees. Falling to his knees is a decision. A man under a hail of stones does not kneel by accident. Standing, he might have lasted longer; turned away, he might at least have covered his head. He knelt because he was going to pray, and he wanted his whole body to say so.

Lord, do not hold this sin against them. The second prayer is not for himself. And Luke notes that he cried this one out with a loud voice. The request for his own soul was spoken. The request for his murderers was shouted. He spent the last breath he had on the men who were taking it, and he made certain they heard him do it. It is Jesus again: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Stephen loves his enemies to the last.

The order reversed. The parallel with the cross is exact, and the order is reversed. Jesus prayed first for his killers and then committed his spirit. Stephen commits his spirit and then, with whatever he has left, prays for his killers. The first Christian death is shaped like the death of Christ, and the disciple takes the sequence the other way round because he was running out of time and would not go without saying it.

What it does not mean. A guard belongs here, because this verse has been used to lay a burden on people that Scripture does not lay. It is not a rule that a Christian must feel forgiving at the moment of injury, or that failure to produce this prayer at the graveside of a murdered child is a failure of faith. Luke has already told us where it came from: Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit. The forgiveness in this verse is not an achievement modelled for imitation by willpower. It is a gift being reported. What is asked of ordinary Christians is that they should want to get there, and be willing to be taken there slowly, which for most people is the work of years and not of minutes.

Must I forgive someone who is not sorry? Stephen prayed for men who were still throwing stones, so the heart of forgiveness does not wait for an apology. It lets go of revenge, hands the wrong to God, and genuinely desires the other person’s good, even their salvation (Romans 12:17–21). But full reconciliation, the restoring of trust and relationship, does require repentance (Luke 17:3–4), and forgiveness never means pretending a wrong was not wrong, or staying exposed to someone dangerous, or not reporting a crime. You can forgive an abuser in your heart and still go to the police. Begin, as Stephen did, by praying for them. The feelings often follow the prayers, slowly.

And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Luke’s last word is the gentlest verb in the language attached to the most violent death in the book. A man has just been beaten to death with rocks in a field outside the wall, and Luke writes it as though somebody had nodded off in a chair. It is neither euphemism nor sentiment. It is the New Testament’s word for the death of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:18, 20), a statement about what death now is for those who belong to Christ: sleep, from which the body will wake in resurrection.

Does fell asleep mean the soul is unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes the body, which lies in the grave and will be woken. Stephen’s spirit did not sleep. He had just prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and the Lord did. Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Paul says that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The souls of believers at death are made perfect in holiness and pass immediately into glory, while their bodies rest in their graves until the resurrection (Westminster 32.1).

The prayer answered. And one thing more, which Luke leaves the reader to assemble. Stephen asked that this sin not be held against them. A few feet away, holding the coats and approving, stood a young man who would be struck down on the road to Damascus, would spend the next thirty years telling anyone who would listen that he was the foremost of sinners, and would write more of the New Testament’s letters than any other man. Augustine is said to have put it this way: if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. The prayer was answered, and it was answered first in the person who, that morning, would have been the very last to expect it.

In a sentence. As they stoned him, Stephen called out, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, Lord, do not hold this sin against them, and when he had said this, he fell asleep.

On a Tuesday. Learn to forgive like Stephen, who learned it from Jesus. Name one person who has wronged you, and pray for their good today, even if you have to start with a single sentence. And learn to die like him: each night as you lie down, commend your spirit to the Lord Jesus, so that when the last night comes, the words are already familiar.

For worship. Stephen died like his Master because his Master had died for him, and had already taken out of death the sting that made it terrible (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). The Lord Jesus received his spirit, as he will receive the spirit of every one who trusts him. The body left broken in the field was only asleep, and its waking is fixed. The one who heard a dying man’s two prayers and answered both is Lord of the dead and of the living (Romans 14:9), and into his hands his people may let go of everything, even their last breath.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross. “Fell asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of a believer’s death.

7.theology: The Pattern of Rejection and Vindication. Stephen’s survey of Israel’s history reveals God’s way in the world: the one God sends is always rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One himself. And in each case, God vindicates the rejected one and uses that rejection as the means of redemption. This is not historical accident; it is divine pattern — the pattern of the cross. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die (John 12:24). The stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone. And the martyr who follows the rejected-and-vindicated Lord shares the same arc: killed by men, received by God, his prayer answered in the conversion of his chief persecutor. Saul of Tarsus is Stephen’s greatest vindication.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, and preaches them their own history. He is the first Christian martyr, and he dies as he lived — full of the Holy Spirit, full of faith, his face like an angel’s. His death scatters the seed further than his life could have planted it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces Stephen’s question: what do you do when you cannot be silenced by argument and so are silenced by violence? Stephen shows us: you look up, you see the glory of God, you commend your spirit to Christ, and you pray for those who kill you. This is not heroism; it is the overflow of a life lived so close to Christ that even death cannot separate you from him — and cannot stop the gospel.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution.
