And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Stephen’s death sets off the first great persecution, led by Saul, who goes from house to house dragging believers to prison. The church in Jerusalem is scattered, except the apostles, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. So the second stage of Jesus’ plan in 1:8 begins: Judea and Samaria. The Samaritans were descendants of northern Israelites who had intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest; they accepted only the five books of Moses, worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and were despised by Jews, and the feeling was mutual (John 4:9). Philip, one of the seven, preaches Christ there with signs, and many believe, including a famous magician named Simon. The apostles send Peter and John, and only when they pray and lay hands on the Samaritans do they receive the Spirit, a sign to everyone that Samaritans and Jews are one church. Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, and Peter sternly rebukes him.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where he meets a high official of the queen of Ethiopia, the kingdom of Meroë on the Nile far south of Egypt. The man is a eunuch who had come to worship in Jerusalem, and he is reading aloud from Isaiah 53 about the lamb led to the slaughter. Philip explains that the passage is about Jesus, and when they come to water the Ethiopian asks to be baptised. Philip is then taken away by the Spirit, and the Ethiopian goes home rejoicing, the gospel already heading towards the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul approved of Stephen’s killing. That day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered through Judea and Samaria. Devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him. Saul set out to destroy the church, entering house after house and dragging men and women off to prison. Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there. When the crowds heard Philip and saw his signs they all paid close attention: impure spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many paralysed and lame people were healed, so there was great joy in that city. A man named Simon had practised sorcery there for some time and amazed the Samaritans, claiming to be someone great; everyone, high and low, called him the great power of God, because he had astonished them with his magic for so long. But when they believed Philip’s good news of God’s kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptised. Simon himself believed and was baptised, and followed Philip everywhere, astonished by the signs and miracles. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God’s word, they sent Peter and John, who prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had simply been baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John laid hands on them and they received the Spirit. When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ hands, he offered them money to give him the same power. Peter told him to take his money to destruction with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift; he had no share in this ministry, because his heart was not right before God. He must repent and pray that the Lord would perhaps forgive him for such a thought, for Peter could see he was full of bitterness and captive to sin. Simon asked them to pray for him that none of this would happen to him. After testifying and proclaiming the Lord’s word, Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages on the way.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Scattering as Mission Strategy

Reformed theology has read Acts 8 as the clearest narrative demonstration that God's purposes are not merely undamaged by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and for perhaps two years nothing had moved; the church was large, joyful, generous and entirely stationary. It took a murder and a persecution to get it out of the city. The point is not that God needed the persecution, nor that the suffering was anything other than real — Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It is that the machinery of opposition turned out to be the machinery of expansion, and that the man superintending the destruction was, without the faintest idea of it, dispersing the gospel across two provinces. The kingdom advanced that year in the shape of a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding — it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.

Meaning first. Acts 8 is the turning point when the gospel leaves Jerusalem. Persecution scatters the church, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, where many believe, a sorcerer is exposed, and the apostles confirm the work. Then Philip meets an Ethiopian official on a desert road and leads him to Christ from Isaiah 53. The gospel is moving outward, as Jesus said it would (1:8): to the half-Jewish Samaritans, and to a Gentile from the ends of the earth. The chapter that opens with a grave ends with a man going home rejoicing.

And Saul approved of his execution. The chapter division cuts a sentence in half. This line belongs with the stoning at the end of chapter 7, and Luke wrote it as the last word on that scene. The young man holding the coats was not a bystander who happened to be present. He approved. The word (syneudokōn) means he consented, thought well of it, was pleased; and Paul spends the rest of his life saying so, with shame (22:20).

And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem. On that day. Stephen’s death was not merely the first casualty; it was the starting gun of the first general persecution, aimed probably at the Hellenists, Stephen’s circle. Once somebody had been killed and nothing happened to the killers, the restraint was gone and the whole thing came down at once.

And they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. The church had not left Jerusalem by choice; God used persecution to push them out. The word for scattered (diesparēsan) is a sowing word: seed thrown across a field. And then a puzzling detail: except the apostles. The twelve men most identified with the movement, already arrested twice and flogged once, stayed in the city everybody else was fleeing. That was not caution. Perhaps the shepherds would not be first out of the field, or Jerusalem had to keep a centre; Luke does not say. The consequence is clear: the people who took the gospel to Samaria were not the apostles but the ordinary members who ran.

Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. The burial is braver than it looks. Jewish practice withheld public mourning from a man executed by the court; part of the punishment was that he went into the ground without honour. These men did the opposite, loudly, in a city where a persecution had begun that morning. Luke’s word for them is the one he used of old Simeon and of the pilgrims at Pentecost (Luke 2:25; Acts 2:5). They may have been believers, or devout Jews who would not let the man be shovelled away. Either way, somebody with something to lose stood at that grave and wept aloud on purpose.

Grief is not a lapse. Christians are sometimes given the impression that a believer with a firm grasp of the resurrection should bury somebody without much noise. The first Christian response to the first Christian martyrdom was a great lamentation. Paul’s instruction to a grieving church is not that they should not grieve but that they should not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), which assumes the grief and changes its quality. Stephen had seen heaven opened moments before he died, and they still stood over the body and wept loudly, and Luke records it without a word of correction. Jesus himself wept at a graveside he was about to empty (John 11:35).

The Lord who stood for Stephen. Stephen’s last sight on earth was the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (7:56), and what follows is not the collapse of Christ’s cause but its next step. At his ascension the Lord had said his people would be his witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria (1:8), and on the day of the first martyr’s death he begins to keep that word, using the stones as his means. Luke also shapes the burial to recall another. In his Gospel a good and righteous man took down a body the council had condemned and laid it in a tomb (Luke 23:50–53). The servant is buried as his Master was. But the Master’s tomb was empty on the third day, and that is why devout men can weep loudly over Stephen and still not weep without hope.

Why does God allow his church to be persecuted? Scripture gives us part of the answer, though not all of it. Persecution purifies the church, as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It joins us to Christ, who was persecuted first (John 15:20; Philippians 3:10). And, as here, God uses it to spread the gospel: the seed is scattered and grows in new fields. The church historian’s old saying, that the blood of the martyrs is seed, began in this verse. None of that makes persecution good, and we should pray for persecuted believers and work for their relief (Hebrews 13:3). But it means that no persecution is outside God’s purpose or beyond his power to turn to good.

In a sentence. Saul approved of Stephen’s killing, and that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, scattering everyone except the apostles through Judea and Samaria, while devout men buried Stephen and mourned him deeply.

On a Tuesday. God can use what looks like disaster to spread his word. Trust him in your scattering: the move you did not want, the job you lost, the church that broke up. And when someone you love dies, grieve honestly. Hope does not forbid tears; it gives them a future.

For worship. Our God wastes nothing that is laid in the ground for his sake. The stones that killed Stephen scattered a church, and the scattering was a sowing: every refugee on the roads out of Jerusalem was seed in the hand of the Lord of the harvest, falling on Judea and Samaria where he meant it to fall. What Saul intended for the destruction of the church, God intended for the salvation of Samaria and Ethiopia. He holds the grief of those devout men as surely as he holds the harvest, and on the last day he will wipe from his people’s eyes every tear they shed over his martyrs.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.

But Saul was ravaging the church. Luke picks a violent word, and he picks it deliberately. Ravaging (elymaineto) is the word the Greek psalm uses of a wild boar getting into a vineyard and wrecking it (Psalm 80:13): an animal in an orchard, tearing at roots, ruining in an afternoon what took years to grow. Luke had a perfectly good word available for official persecution. He used this one instead. Saul later admitted it all, calling himself a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent (22:4; 26:10–11; Galatians 1:13; 1 Timothy 1:13).

And entering house after house. There were no church buildings; the church met in people’s homes, ate in them, broke bread in them. So persecuting the church meant going through front doors. Someone had to compile the list of addresses, and somebody in the neighbourhood had to supply it. The scene is domestic and squalid: men coming into a kitchen where a family has been praying, and taking people out of it.

He dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. Women too; he spared no one. Paul later confirms it in his own words: he bound and delivered to prison both men and women (22:4), and cast his vote against the saints when they were put to death (26:10). Dragged off is the word Luke will later use of Paul himself being dragged out of a city and left for dead (14:19), a small piece of irony he leaves the reader to find.

Every door he broke was Christ’s. Saul thought he was clearing heretics out of Israel’s vineyard. In fact he was laying hands on the Lord himself. When the risen Jesus stops him on the road, he does not ask why Saul is persecuting his followers. He asks, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4). The Lord counts his people’s injuries as his own, so that every kitchen Saul entered was a room from which Christ was being dragged. And the psalm whose word Luke borrowed already pointed to the remedy. After the boar has ravaged the vine, Israel prays, let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself (Psalm 80:17). Stephen had just seen that Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. The vine had a keeper, and the ravager was about to meet him.

The man who wrote about love. This verse is written about the man who wrote that love is patient and kind and bears all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). The most tender pastoral writing in the Bible came from a man who had gone door to door arresting mothers.

Grace did not give him amnesia. Thirty years on he still calls himself the foremost of sinners, in the present tense (1 Timothy 1:15), unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church of God (1 Corinthians 15:9). Grace did not erase his memory. It let him carry an accurate, unbearable memory without despair, which is more remarkable than forgetting.

Not a guarantee. Saul’s story is sometimes preached as a pledge that every persecutor will be converted, and it gives no such pledge. Most of the men who arrested Christians in the first century died as they had lived, and the same is true in every century since. What it is, is a demonstration that nobody is disqualified by the record, which is a different and better thing to know, and which is what Paul himself says it was given for: that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16).

How should I pray for those who persecute Christians today? As Jesus told us: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). Pray for their conversion, by name if you know them, remembering Saul. Pray that God would restrain their violence and protect his people (4:29–30). Pray for justice, for governments to protect religious freedom, and for persecuted believers to stand firm and be comforted. It is not wrong to ask God to stop evil men, as the psalmists did. But let the first prayer be Stephen’s: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. God has answered that prayer before.

In a sentence. But Saul was trying to destroy the church, going from house to house, dragging off men and women and putting them in prison.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in public life or in your own life whom you find hardest to imagine as a Christian, perhaps someone hostile to the faith. Pray for them today, as for a future brother.

For worship. The Lord Jesus watched a young man breaking into Christian homes and did not strike him dead. He let the ravager run his course until the appointed day, and then he met him, not to destroy the vineyard’s enemy but to make him a planter of churches. The hands that dragged off men and women would be laid on the sick in Malta and lifted in prayer for every church from Rome to Colossae. Such is the patience of Christ: longer than the cruelty of his enemies, and wide enough to hold the worst record a sinner can bring.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.

Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Everybody was scattered except the apostles (8:1), so the people now preaching across two provinces are precisely the ones with no office, no ordination and no commission. The twelve stayed in Jerusalem. The gospel went to Samaria carried by refugees, and the scattering became sowing.

The ordinary word. And the verb Luke chooses (euangelizomenoi) is not the formal one for public proclamation. It is the ordinary word for telling good news. They arrived in strange towns with whatever they could carry, and when people asked why they had left Jerusalem, they told them. The first missionary expansion of the church was carried out by amateurs, under duress, with no strategy, because they could not stop talking about the reason they had been driven out.

Philip went down to the city of Samaria. This Philip is one of the seven (6:5), not the apostle: one of the men appointed to make sure the widows were fed. Stephen, another of the seven, has just been killed for his preaching. It is the table-servants who are breaking the boundaries in this book while the apostles hold the centre.

A feud five centuries old. The boundary he breaks is not a small one. Samaria was not simply an unevangelised region; it was the object of a feud five centuries old. After Assyria deported the northern tribes, it resettled the territory with foreign peoples, and the mixed population that resulted claimed the God of Israel, kept only the five books of Moses, and worshipped at a rival temple on Mount Gerizim (2 Kings 17:24–41). About a hundred and fifty years before this, a Jewish army pulled that temple down. In Jesus’ day Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and calling a man a Samaritan was an insult (John 8:48).

And proclaimed to them the Christ. Philip walks into that, and he preaches a person. He does not open with an argument about the temple, or about which mountain was the right one, or about whose copy of the law was correct, all of which were live and available. The Samaritans expected a Messiah too, the restorer (John 4:25), and Philip tells them he has come. The quarrel that five hundred years of argument had not settled was left where it was, and something was announced that made it irrelevant.

Am I meant to share my faith if I am not a pastor? Yes. The people in this verse had no office at all, and they spread the gospel across two provinces. Pastors are called to preach and teach publicly, and that is a particular calling (Ephesians 4:11). But every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done, and every Christian can tell someone why he believes. You do not need to preach a sermon. You need to be ready to give a reason for your hope when asked, gently and respectfully (1 Peter 3:15), to invite people to hear the word, and to speak naturally of Christ in the places where life has put you. The gospel has always travelled furthest in ordinary conversations.

In a sentence. Those who had been scattered went about telling the good news of the word, and Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.

On a Tuesday. Wherever life scatters you, take the gospel with you. When someone this week asks about your weekend, your values or your hope, tell them honestly, and let Christ be in the answer.

For worship. The Lord Jesus once sat tired by a well in Samaria and offered living water to a woman from whose jar no Jew would drink (John 4:7–10). Now his scattered people carry that same water into the same country. The Samaritans of Sychar called him the Saviour of the world (John 4:42), and here he proves the title, not of one nation only. A wall of five hundred years falls at the sound of his name, carried there by refugees who had lost everything except him, and found that he was enough to give away.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.

And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. With one accord: the phrase Luke used of the hundred and twenty in the upper room (1:14), now used of a crowd of Samaritans, a small shock deliberately given. And what they did with one accord was pay attention to what was being said. The signs are in the sentence, in second place. The miracles got Philip a hearing; the message held the crowd.

For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them. Unclean spirits are demons, fallen angels who torment and bind people, and here they cry out as they did before Jesus (Mark 1:26). The list ties Samaria to Jerusalem on purpose: spirits coming out, the paralysed and the lame healed, as in the earlier chapters, now in a despised half-Jewish city through a man appointed to hand out bread. There is no reduced edition of the kingdom for people on the wrong side of a border.

And many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. Paralysis and lameness are not ailments a man recovers from quietly. They are chronic and visible, and in a town that size everybody knew who was carried where. As at the Beautiful Gate, a healing the whole neighbourhood can verify becomes an argument nobody can answer (3:1–10; 4:16).

Many, not all. One small honesty in the wording belongs to anybody who has prayed a long time and not been healed. Luke writes that unclean spirits came out of many, and that many were healed. Even in a chapter of undisputed power, at the height of an outpouring, with a Spirit-filled messenger in the town, Luke reaches for a word that may leave somebody still on the mat. He does not explain it and he does not hide it.

The lame walk. These are not random wonders. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus answered by pointing to exactly these things: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor have good news preached to them (Luke 7:22). Isaiah had said that when God came to save his people, the lame man would leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:4–6). So when paralysed Samaritans stand up under Philip’s preaching, the answer Jesus gave John is being given again, in a city Jerusalem despised. Luke began Acts by calling his Gospel the account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1). The healer has gone up to heaven, and his work goes on in Samaria under his name.

Philip was not an apostle, so why could he do signs? Like Stephen, he was one of the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands (6:6), and his signs belong to the same founding ministry. Even so, the Samaritans received the Spirit only when the apostles came (vv. 14–17), which shows how closely these gifts were tied to the apostles. On the cessationist reading, held charitably, such sign gifts belonged to the foundation age and are not a standing pattern for today. God still heals in answer to prayer; what has ceased is the apostolic sign gift attesting new revelation.

Why does God not heal everyone I pray for? Scripture does not give us a full explanation, and we should beware of anyone who claims to. It is not because your faith was too small; Paul prayed three times for his own thorn to be removed, and God said no, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God heals some now as a foretaste of the new creation, and he will heal all his people in the resurrection, when there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Until then, keep praying, use the means he gives, and trust that his no is never a lack of love.

In a sentence. The crowds all listened intently to what Philip said as they heard him and saw the signs he did, for unclean spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many who were paralysed or lame were healed.

On a Tuesday. When you pray for the sick this week, pray boldly and leave the answer with God. And notice what grips you most in church: the remarkable things that happen, or the message about Christ. Give your attention, as the Samaritans did, to what is being said.

For worship. In the city Jerusalem despised, men carried for years on mats walked home, and the demons that had owned others went out shrieking at the name of Jesus. That name has lost none of its authority since he ascended. The King who healed many in Samaria as a sign of his kingdom has promised a day when none of his people will be carried anywhere, and those of every century who prayed and still sat on the mat will rise whole on the last day, to walk with him in a city with no sickbed in it.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.

So there was much joy in that city. One of Luke’s markers, and he uses it carefully. Joy in a city, not merely in individuals: something had changed in the public atmosphere of the place. The gospel brings joy (v. 39; 13:52; 16:34). He will use the same note at the end of this chapter of a single man on a desert road, and the two are the same fact at different scales.

But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city. Without a paragraph break Luke introduces the man who will show what the gospel is not. Magic (mageuōn) meant more in that world than the modern word suggests. This was not entertainment or conjuring. A practitioner claimed real access to powers, and people paid him for results: a curse on a rival, a charm against illness. Surviving spells from the period are long lists of divine names gathered from every religion, in case one of them worked. The man who could operate that machinery was feared, consulted and rich. Later Christian writers regarded this Simon, often called Simon Magus, as the father of heresies, especially of Gnosticism, and Justin Martyr, himself a Samaritan, wrote that the Samaritans honoured him as the first god.

And amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. Luke’s summary of Simon’s message is devastating. That is the entire content. Not a doctrine, not a God, not a promise: a claim about the speaker. Everything Simon offered was ultimately about Simon.

The one who is great. Simon’s claim has an answer in the one Philip preached. In the first chapter of his Gospel Luke recorded an angel’s word to a young woman about her son: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:32). The greatness Simon claimed for himself God had already given to someone else. And the one who truly is great never once said so to gather a crowd. At the table on the night he was betrayed he said, I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:27), and the next day he died for the people he served. Simon took a city’s worship and gave it nothing. Christ takes nothing from us and gives himself, which is why Philip had only to proclaim him.

The test of a ministry. The collision is not between power and no power; Philip has just been casting out spirits and healing paralytics. The difference is what the power points at. Simon amazed people, and they concluded that Simon was great. Philip did signs, and the crowds ended up listening to a message about somebody else. The test in any century is not whether remarkable things happen around a person, but what the watchers end up attached to. If a ministry produces crowds who are knowledgeable about the minister, something has gone wrong that no amount of orthodoxy in the statement of faith will correct.

Is magic real, and is it harmless to dabble? Scripture treats sorcery and the occult as real and as forbidden, not as harmless fun (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Galatians 5:20). Some of it is trickery and some of it may involve real spiritual powers, and both are dangerous: the one deceives, the other enslaves. So a Christian should have nothing to do with fortune-telling, séances, spells, tarot or any attempt to gain hidden knowledge or power apart from God. If you have been involved, confess it, renounce it, get rid of the objects, as the Ephesians burned their magic books (19:19), and rest in Christ, who has disarmed every power (Colossians 2:15). You do not need to be afraid. You need to be finished with it.

In a sentence. There was great joy in that city, but a man named Simon had been practising magic there, amazing the people of Samaria and claiming to be someone great.

On a Tuesday. Beware of spiritual leaders who proclaim themselves; true servants proclaim Christ. And check your own speaking about your faith: when you talk about what God has done in your life, who comes out of the story looking great?

For worship. Joy came to a Samaritan city that no magician’s wonder had ever brought, because the good news of great joy announced over a manger in Bethlehem was for all the people (Luke 2:10), and Samaria was among them. Simon’s amazement wore off and had to be renewed. The joy of Christ does not wear off, for it rests on what he has done and not on what anyone has seen. The God who first sent that news by angels still delights to send it by ordinary men, and wherever his Son is named, a city can be glad.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest. Luke means the whole social range: the labourer and the magistrate, the woman at the well and the man who owned the well. Simon’s hold on that city was not confined to the credulous poor, which is the comforting assumption people make about this kind of thing. It reached the top. His influence was enormous.

This man is the power of God that is called Great. They had a formula for him. The odd, half-technical phrase shows that Simon had not merely impressed people; he had supplied them with a theology. They thought him a divine power, an emanation of God, as pagan religion spoke of such powers. He was not a street performer with a following but a religious institution with a creed. Simon was worshipped.

And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. Luke gives the mechanism: two ingredients, and neither is truth. Amazement, the experience of watching something you cannot account for; and a long time, the sheer weight of years in which everybody grew up with it. That is the anatomy of most religious authority not from God. Nobody has to be persuaded of anything. It only requires that nobody can explain what is happening, for long enough that it becomes normal.

The stronger man. Jesus once described his own work in words that fit this city. When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks and overcomes him, he takes away the armour he trusted in and divides the spoil (Luke 11:21–22). Samaria had been held a long time, by fear and wonder, under powers Scripture does not treat as a game. Jesus does not send a cleverer magician against them. He comes in his word, by an ordinary preacher. Simon is a man, not the devil, but the powers behind magic are real, and in Samaria the stronger one walked in and took his spoil: men and women set free and baptised into his name.

How was anyone to tell the difference? Philip’s ministry looks, from outside, remarkably similar: crowds, signs, amazement. Luke’s answer is not about the phenomena. The Samaritans turned when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Simon offered an experience and a claim about himself; Philip offered a message about a King, and people believed it. The signs got him a hearing. The content held them, and the content was somebody else’s name. Signs alone do not prove truth; the message must be tested (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

Not a reason for cynicism. The lesson is not that anything remarkable is suspect and the safest ministry is one where nothing happens. Luke has just described genuine healings and deliverances with approval, and the joy in that city was real. The test is not whether power is present. It is whose name is left standing at the end of the meeting.

Can Satan really do miracles? Scripture warns that he can produce counterfeit signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13; Matthew 24:24), though his power is limited and always under God’s control (Job 1:12). That is why a miracle is never enough by itself to prove a message true. Moses told Israel that if a prophet gave a sign that came to pass but led them to other gods, they were not to listen (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). So the question to ask of any wonder is not merely whether something happened, but what it is being used to teach, and whether it leads you to the Christ of Scripture.

In a sentence. Everyone from the least to the greatest followed him, calling him the power of God that is called Great, because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

On a Tuesday. Not every wonder is from God, and not every long-standing religious habit is true. Test what you hear, from any pulpit, book or screen, by the plain message of Christ and his word.

For worship. The true power of God was never a man in Samaria with a title and a following. It is the crucified Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), whose strength was shown at its height when he hung weak on a cross and then rose from a sealed tomb. Simon amazed a city and left it bound. Christ was despised by a city and set the world free. His power is truth and love together, and it holds no one by fear.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.

But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Watch what displaces Simon, because it is not a stronger performance. A city held for years by amazement is released by a message. The gospel content is given in two phrases: the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ. The kingdom has come in Jesus.

What is it to preach the kingdom of God? The kingdom is God’s saving reign, his kingly rule breaking in through Jesus the Messiah to rescue and to rule. Notice that Philip preached the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ in one breath: you cannot proclaim the kingdom without the King. To preach it is to announce that God’s long-promised reign has arrived in Christ, who died, rose and reigns, and to call people to repent, believe and bow to him as Lord, entering his kingdom now and for ever (28:31). Why is the phrase on nearly every page of Matthew, Mark and Luke, and rare in John and the letters? Not because the truth fades, but because the vocabulary shifts. Jesus preached the kingdom to Jewish hearers, steeped in Israel’s hope (Matthew 4:17; Daniel 7:13–14). John says the same thing with a different word, eternal life (John 3:3, 5). The apostles, writing after the resurrection, put the focus on the reigning King: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9). Same kingdom throughout.

They were baptized, both men and women. Believers’ baptism: they believed, then were baptised. And both men and women: Luke keeps saying this, the phrase he used of the Jerusalem church and, grimly, of Saul’s arrests nine verses earlier. In a world where a woman’s religious standing generally travelled through her husband, Luke records the women being baptised on their own account, on their own faith.

Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And then Simon. Luke states it without qualification: he believed, he was baptised, he attached himself to the preacher. Nothing in the sentence is flagged as false, and a reading which has Simon play-acting from the start reads something Luke has not written. Like the seed on rocky ground that believes for a while (Luke 8:13), he believed something, for a time, without new birth. Baptism did not make him a Christian.

And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. Amazement has followed Simon through this whole passage: he amazed the Samaritans, they were amazed by him, and now the amazer is amazed. He has changed places in the sentence without changing his interest. He was drawn by power, not by Christ, and five verses later he will try to buy it.

Was Simon truly saved? Luke says he believed and was baptised, and some take him as a true believer who fell into serious sin. But Peter’s words say his heart was not right before God, that he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, and that he had neither part nor lot in this matter (vv. 20–23). The more likely reading is that his faith was the kind that is impressed by miracles but has never turned from self. That fits what Scripture teaches about perseverance: those whom God truly saves, he keeps, and those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

Can I be baptised and still not be a Christian? Yes, sadly; Simon was. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, commanded by him, and believers should be baptised. But the water does not save. What saves is Christ himself, received by true faith, which the Spirit works in the heart (Ephesians 2:8–9). So the question is not, was I baptised, but, do I trust Christ, love him, and want to turn from my sin? If you find those things in yourself, however weakly, they are the marks of the new birth. If you do not, do not rely on your baptism. Come to Christ today.

In a sentence. When the people believed Philip as he preached the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, both men and women were baptised, and even Simon believed, was baptised, stayed close to Philip, and was amazed by the signs and great miracles.

On a Tuesday. Being baptised and amazed by God’s power is not the same as being born again. Make sure your faith is in Christ himself. Ask yourself one honest question this week: what draws me to church, what God gives, or God himself?

For worship. The name of Jesus Christ opened a city that a magician’s name had shut for years, and his kingdom took in men and women alike, each on their own faith, through the same water. He is a King who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). He sees through amazement to the heart, he is not deceived by a baptism without faith, and he never loses one whom he has truly made his own. His kingdom is entered not by being dazzled but by trusting the King.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,

Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John. The sentence is remarkable for what is not in it: no debate, no committee, no summons for Philip to explain himself. A city of Samaritans has believed, and the response is to send two men down to pray for them. Yet nobody had authorised this. Philip had been appointed to a food distribution, and the converts were on the far side of a five-century quarrel. An institution faced with an unauthorised expansion into disputed territory has its reflexes, and Luke records none of them.

Peter and John. Then the names, and they are the best thing in the verse. John. Luke’s own Gospel records that when a Samaritan village refused Jesus hospitality, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven to consume them, and were rebuked (Luke 9:52–55). Now the same man walks into the same territory, and his errand is to put his hands on Samaritans and ask God to give them the Holy Spirit. Luke, who wrote the other story himself, simply puts the name in. What grace had done to John in the intervening years is described nowhere; it is visible in the fact that he made the journey.

Who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Note what they came to do. Not to inspect, not to regularise, not to take charge of somebody else’s work. Prayer is the first thing. The two senior apostles arrive at a revival they had no part in starting, and their first act is to ask God to give those people more.

Reaping where Jesus sowed. This was not the first time Jesus’ disciples had seen a harvest in Samaria. At a well outside the Samaritan town of Sychar, Jesus had told them to lift up their eyes and see that the fields were white for harvest, and then said: I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour; others have laboured, and you have entered into their labour (John 4:35–38). The apostles now arrive at a work they had no part in starting, exactly as their Lord had told them they would. He had sown in Samaria himself, by a well, with one woman. Philip had now preached in that country. The harvest the apostles came to bless was the Lord’s before it was anyone else’s.

How can I lose a prejudice I have had all my life? Probably not by arguing yourself out of it in an afternoon. John’s instinct about Samaritans was to incinerate them. The instinct was not argued away. It was replaced, slowly enough that nobody recorded the process, by walking with Jesus. So bring the prejudice to Christ honestly, as sin. Pray for the people you find it hardest to love. Get to know some of them as people, especially fellow believers from that group. Serve them. And remember that Christ died for them as he died for you, and that they will share heaven with you (Revelation 7:9). Feelings follow faithfulness, and the Spirit who changed John can change you.

In a sentence. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John, who went down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Think of a group of people toward whom you carry a settled contempt: a nation, a class, a political tribe, a kind of Christian. Pray for them by name this week, and ask God to replace the reflex with love.

For worship. John once asked for fire from heaven on Samaria, and Jesus said no. Now John asks heaven for a gift on Samaria again, and this time the answer is yes, and what comes down is the Spirit. Between the two prayers stands a cross, where the judgment those villages deserved, and John deserved, fell on the Son of Man himself. That is why heaven can send blessing where it might have sent fire. The Lord who came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them (Luke 9:56, in some manuscripts) still answers prayers for former enemies with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.

For he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Luke states the anomaly flatly. These people had believed and had been truly baptised, and the Spirit had not come. He knows how strange that is, which is why he stops the narrative to say so. Normally the Spirit comes with faith (2:38); in chapter 10 he interrupts Peter before anybody has been baptised at all (10:44). Here there is a gap. Why the delay?

Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. The answer that best fits Luke’s own narrative is that this was a hinge in the history of salvation rather than a pattern for individuals. After centuries of hatred and rival temples, there was a real danger of two churches: a Jewish one and a Samaritan one. God held back the Spirit until the apostles came, so that the Samaritans received the Spirit through Jewish apostles, and the church remained one. Five hundred years of schism were repaired in public, by two Jewish pairs of hands on Samaritan heads. Something visible probably happened, since Simon saw it (v. 18).

The great crossings. The pattern across Acts supports this. As the gospel crossed each great barrier, God marked the crossing with a visible coming of the Spirit: on Jews at Pentecost (chapter 2), on Samaritans here, on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10), and on the disciples of John at Ephesus (chapter 19). Each was a once-for-all moment in the spread of the one church to all peoples, as Jesus had mapped it: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the end of the earth (1:8).

The gift of the ascended Christ. Whoever lays hands on whom, the giver in this scene is the Lord Jesus. Peter had told the crowd at Pentecost that Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, had poured out what they saw and heard (2:33). John the Baptist had said the coming one would baptise with the Holy Spirit (Luke 3:16). So the Samaritans had not been baptised into a lesser Lord. The one in whose name they were baptised is the very Lord who, from his throne, now gave them his Spirit in a way the whole church could see. The apostles prayed; Christ answered.

Where Christians differ: a second blessing, or a sacrament? Pentecostal and charismatic brothers often see here a two-stage pattern: conversion, then a distinct baptism in the Spirit, and they read Acts 19 the same way. Roman Catholics and others see the basis for confirmation, a sacrament in which a bishop’s hands confer the Spirit. Verdict: this was a unique moment in salvation history, as the gospel crossed a great barrier, like the Gentiles in chapter 10 and John’s disciples in chapter 19. It was a once-for-all bridging, not the normal pattern. Romans 8:9 says anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, without a second stage or an apostle’s hands. This is said with real respect for brothers who differ, many of whom love the Spirit and the Scriptures deeply.

The apostles’ hands. The same reading explains why no one today should claim to give the Spirit by laying on hands. The gift came through the apostles because it was the apostles’ foundational work to join each new people into the one church (Ephesians 2:20). That role was not passed on. On the cessationist reading, held charitably, the visible signs that accompanied these moments, very likely tongues or prophetic praise as in chapters 2, 10 and 19, belonged to the foundation age and are not a pattern to seek now. The regular doctrine of how we receive the Spirit is taught in the letters: when you believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13; Galatians 3:2).

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit? No. If you belong to Christ, you already have the Spirit, all of him, from the moment you believed (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). You are not a half-Christian waiting for a second gift. What you do need, every day, is to walk by the Spirit and be filled with the Spirit (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 5:18): to yield more of yourself to the one who already lives in you. Many believers have seasons when God makes his presence and love unusually vivid, and those are precious gifts. But they are fresh fillings of the Spirit you have, not the arrival of a Spirit you lacked.

Should I seek to speak in tongues as proof that I have the Spirit? No. Even in the apostolic church, Paul asked, do all speak with tongues? and expected the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). The proof of the Spirit’s presence is that you confess Jesus as Lord, cry to God as Father, and bear the Spirit’s fruit (1 Corinthians 12:3; Romans 8:15; Galatians 5:22–23). Many Reformed Christians believe the gift of tongues ceased with the apostolic age; continuationist brothers disagree, and we hold our view charitably. But on any view, no believer should be told that he lacks the Spirit because he has not spoken in tongues.

In a sentence. The Spirit had not yet come upon any of them, for they had only been baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus; then the apostles laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his church one. Work for the unity of believers across old hostilities: the church down the road with a different style, the Christians of another nation or background. Pray for them this week, and if you can, worship with them once.

For worship. The rival mountains, Gerizim and Jerusalem, were both left behind that day. The true temple was now a people, indwelt by one Spirit and built on one foundation, the Christ whom both had waited for. There is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Ephesians 4:4–5). The Spirit given to every believer is still at the work he began in Samaria, binding Jew and Samaritan, Jew and Gentile, into one holy temple in the Lord, where the Father is worshipped in spirit and truth.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.”

Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money. Saw. Whatever happened when Peter and John laid hands on those Samaritans was visible, perhaps tongues or praise; Luke, normally happy to describe wind and fire and shaking buildings, declines to say. Then the offer, the first attempt in Christian history to purchase a spiritual gift.

Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit. Look carefully at what he asks for. He does not ask to receive the Spirit, but for the power to lay his own hands on somebody else and have the Spirit come. He is not applying for a blessing. He is applying for a franchise. He wanted to be the dispenser, to be somebody great again (v. 9).

Doing business the only way he knew. By the standards of Simon’s old profession the request is reasonable, even courteous. Names, formulas and techniques were commodities, bought from a practitioner at the going rate and used on paying customers. Simon is doing business the only way he knows, with a product he has just watched being demonstrated. He has failed to notice that he has changed worlds. In this one there is no going rate, because the thing on offer was never for sale, and the men holding it did not buy it either. Simon thinks the Spirit is a power to be bought and used. But the Spirit is God.

The Spirit for the asking. Simon wanted to buy what Jesus had promised to give for the asking. If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, Jesus said, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13). The Samaritans did not pay for the Spirit; the apostles prayed and the Father gave. And the one who dispenses the Spirit is the Son, who received him from the Father without measure (John 3:34) and pours him out on his people. Simon wanted to stand where only Christ stands. The power to give the Spirit belongs to the Lord Jesus, and he gives freely to beggars, never to buyers.

Simony. His name has been attached to the sin ever since. Simony, the buying and selling of church office and spiritual privilege, became one of the great scandals of the medieval church, with bishoprics sold to the highest bidder. It took a Reformation to prise it loose, and every tradition since has found its own way of putting a price on something God gives away.

The quieter modern shapes. The modern forms are quieter: treating a relationship as a transaction. The giving that expects a return in blessing, the service undertaken with an eye on what it buys, the prayer offered as a lever. In each the assumption is Simon’s: that there is a rate, and a man who pays it is entitled to the result. It is how nearly everything else in life works. It is not how this works, and Peter’s reply explains why not.

Is it wrong to pay ministers, or to give expecting God to bless me? Paying ministers is right: the labourer deserves his wages, and those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). That is support for work, not a purchase of grace. And God does promise to bless generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–11). What is wrong is giving as a transaction to obtain spiritual power or material reward, the seed-faith teaching that a gift to a preacher will make God pay you back with money or healing. That is Simon’s error dressed up as faith. Give because God has given to you, freely and cheerfully, and leave the blessing to him.

In a sentence. When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ laying on of hands, he offered them money, asking them to give him this power too, so that anyone he laid hands on would receive the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week where you treat God as a vending machine: if I pray this, if I give this, if I serve here, then he owes me that. Repent of the bargain, and thank him instead for what he has given freely.

For worship. The Spirit is God, and God is not for sale. He blows where he wishes (John 3:8); no hand can hold him and no coin can summon him. Yet this sovereign Spirit, whom Simon thought he could buy, gives himself away to sinners who bring nothing, makes his home in them, and never moves out. What could not be purchased at any price has been given at no price, because the Father and the Son delight to give him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.

May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! It is among the harshest things Peter says to anybody. Literally, your silver be with you to destruction; J. B. Phillips rendered it, to hell with you and your money. Yet Peter is not so much laying a curse as naming the direction the man is travelling: your money is going to destruction, and on present course you are going with it. He describes the trajectory because he wants it changed, and he goes on to tell Simon to repent.

The gift of God. Then the reason, the theology of the whole passage in one clause. It is the word Peter used at Pentecost: repent and be baptised, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (2:38). The gift of God is free (Isaiah 55:1; Romans 6:23), and a gift is not a cheap kind of purchase but a different kind of thing. The moment a price is paid, it has stopped being a gift. That is why the answer is so severe. Simon has proposed an arrangement under which grace would cease to be grace, and if it were available on those terms, nobody in that room would have had any, Peter included.

Not with silver. Simon offered silver for something already paid for. Years later the same Peter wrote to scattered Christians that they were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). That is why the gift is free. It is not free because it is cheap; it is free because the whole price was paid by another, and paid in full. To offer money for it is not only crude. It treats the blood of Christ as a deposit that needs topping up. Peter’s horror is the horror of a man who knows what the Spirit cost.

You have neither part nor lot in this matter. No share at all. The phrase echoes the law of Moses, where the Levite has no portion or inheritance when the land is divided (Deuteronomy 12:12). Peter is telling Simon that when the ground is measured out, his name is on none of it. He has no part in the gospel, nor in the Spirit.

For your heart is not right before God. Then the diagnosis, echoing Psalm 78:37: their heart was not steadfast toward him. Something in him does not run true. Outward faith, inward crookedness.

Simon believed and was baptised. Could that be me? Verse 13 said Simon believed and was baptised; verse 21 says he has no share in this at all. Scripture is not embarrassed by the category. It says the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). It records a crowd who believed when they saw the signs, to whom Jesus did not entrust himself, for he knew what was in man (John 2:23–25). And John, writing to a church that had watched people walk out, says they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). There is a kind of believing which is real as far as it goes and never goes as far as Christ. Simon is its portrait: gripped, impressed, attached to the preacher, and interested from first to last in what he could get. But the reader who finds this passage frightening, who has read verse 13 and thought, that could be me, is displaying the one symptom Simon never displays anywhere in this story. Simon is not worried about his heart. He is worried, as his reply to Peter shows, about what might happen to him. A man anxious about whether he truly loves Christ is asking a question that never entered Simon’s head, and the anxiety is itself evidence of an interest Simon did not have. God gives his children assurance through his promises, the inner witness of the Spirit, and the fruit of a changed life (Westminster 18.2).

In a sentence. Peter told him that his money could perish with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift, and that he had no part or share in this, for his heart was not right before God.

On a Tuesday. Grace cannot be bought. Do not try to purchase God’s favour with gifts or good works or religious effort. Receive it freely, and then live as one who has been given everything.

For worship. The Lord is the portion of his people, and he will not be bought as if he were a field. Simon had neither part nor lot in the matter, but every beggar who comes empty-handed is given a share in the inheritance of the saints in light (Colossians 1:12), with the Spirit himself as its guarantee (Ephesians 1:14). God does not sell himself to the highest bidder. He gives himself, wholly and freely, to those who have nothing to offer, and makes them heirs of everything.

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.

Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord. Peter, having said one of the severest things he ever says, immediately tells the man what to do about it. Even for Simon the door is not shut. The prescription follows the diagnosis in the same breath, which is what distinguishes a rebuke from a dismissal. Some will say the hard thing and leave the man standing in it; others will not say it at all and call the omission kindness. Peter does both inside two sentences, and the second is the reason for the first.

That, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. The phrase troubles readers. Read carelessly, it sounds as though Peter were unsure whether God would forgive a sin of this size. But the uncertainty does not attach to God’s willingness. It attaches to Simon. Peter cannot know whether this man will actually turn, and he is honest about it rather than issuing a guarantee. It is the difference between God may not forgive you and you may not repent, and the distinction matters to anyone carrying something he fears is too large.

Pray to the Lord yourself. Notice what Peter tells him to do: pray to the Lord. Not, ask me to pray. The man who has just tried to buy access through an intermediary is told to go directly and ask for himself. In one sentence Peter refuses both the money and the role of broker.

For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity. The diagnosis is built from two Old Testament phrases. The gall of bitterness reaches back to Moses’ warning about a root among Israel bearing poisonous and bitter fruit (Deuteronomy 29:18): a thing growing underground and out of sight, exactly right for a man whose problem nobody could see until money was mentioned. The bond of iniquity is the language of chains, from Isaiah’s passage about the fast God wants: to loose the bonds of wickedness and let the oppressed go free (Isaiah 58:6). Simon is not a believer who has slipped but a man still tied up, never released. So Peter prescribes not effort but repentance and prayer, because a man in chains cannot untie himself.

The chains Jesus came to loose. That second phrase has a history in Luke’s own Gospel. When Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth and read from Isaiah, the reading as Luke records it includes a line drawn from this same passage about the bonds of wickedness: to set at liberty those who are oppressed (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 58:6). Then he rolled up the scroll and said the Scripture was fulfilled that day. So when Peter tells a man bound in iniquity to pray to the Lord, he is sending him to the one person who announced, as the very programme of his ministry, that he had come to undo exactly this kind of knot. The chains are real. So is the Liberator.

Is there any sin too big to be forgiven? No sin is too big for the blood of Christ, which cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Jesus does speak of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as unforgivable (Mark 3:28–30), but that is the settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work the devil’s, not a single terrible act a person regrets. Those who have committed it do not fear they have; they do not care. If you are troubled that your sin may be too great, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Do what Peter told Simon: repent, and pray to the Lord. Whoever comes to Christ, he will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Peter told Simon to repent of his wickedness and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of his heart might be forgiven, for he saw that Simon was full of bitter poison and chained by sin.

On a Tuesday. If someone needs to hear a hard truth from you, do not say it without also showing the way back. And if you have heard one, do not stand in it. Go straight to the Lord, yourself, today.

For worship. The Lord to whom Peter sent a bound man is the Lord who prayed for the men driving nails into his hands, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). If possible, said Peter, and the only doubt in it was Simon’s heart, never the mercy of Christ. There is no root of bitterness so deep that his blood cannot reach beneath it, and no knot of iniquity he cannot untie. He has never yet turned away a sinner who came to him in chains and asked to be set free.
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.

Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me. Simon’s answer is a small masterpiece of missing the point, and two things are quietly wrong with it. The first is what he asks about. Peter had named a crooked heart, a buried bitterness, a bond of iniquity. Simon asks about the consequences. He is not asking to be changed; he is asking not to be hit. That is the difference between a man who is sorry and a man who is frightened, and the two make very similar noises. It is Pharaoh asking Moses to plead with the LORD to take away the frogs (Exodus 8:8).

Whom he asks. The second is whom he asks. Peter had told him to pray to the Lord himself. Simon’s reply is: you pray for me. He is still in his old trade, still assuming that the power belongs to the practitioner and that a layman’s best move is to hire the man who has it. He has been rebuked for treating the Spirit as a commodity, and his instinctive next move is to treat Peter as one.

The prayer behind Peter. Simon wanted Peter to stand between him and God. Peter knew, better than anyone, what he himself stood on. On the night of the betrayal Jesus had said to him, Simon, Simon, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). Peter denied his Lord three times before morning, and his faith did not fail, because the prayer that held him was Christ’s. That is the intercession every sinner needs, and it is not for hire. The risen Jesus always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and the way to be covered by his prayer is to come to him oneself.

Luke stops. We hear no more of Simon in Scripture. He neither repents nor refuses. The later church filled the gap with legends about Simon Magus, most of them lurid and none of them in Scripture. Luke leaves him under a question mark: a warning delivered, a door held open, no answer recorded. Perhaps Luke did not know. But a resolved ending would let the reader off. If Simon repents, the reader relaxes at the long reach of grace; if he is damned, the reader relaxes in the other direction. Left open, the question was never really about Simon.

Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. Then verse 25, the loveliest note in the chapter. The apostles themselves now evangelise Samaritan villages. Sent to look into a revival in one city, they went home seeding a whole region on foot, village by village, having become part of what they came to see. The barrier has fallen.

Is it wrong to ask others to pray for me? Not at all. Scripture tells us to pray for one another (James 5:16), and Paul constantly asked churches to pray for him (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19). The problem with Simon was not that he asked for prayer but that he asked for it instead of repenting, and instead of going to God himself. Ask your friends to pray for you, and pray for them. But never let someone else’s prayers become a substitute for your own coming to Christ. No one can repent for you, and no one needs to stand between you and God: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

In a sentence. Simon asked Peter to pray for him that none of these things would happen to him, and the apostles, having testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages on the way.

On a Tuesday. Fear of consequences is not repentance. True repentance hates the sin itself. Next time you are sorry for something, ask yourself honestly: am I sorry I did it, or sorry about what it might cost me? Take the real thing to God.

For worship. Jesus once sent messengers ahead of him into a village of the Samaritans, and it would not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:52–53). He went on to Jerusalem and died there, for them among others. Now his apostles walk back through Samaritan villages, and village after village hears his word. The patience of the Lord outlasted the shut door. The one refused at a Samaritan gate is proclaimed at many, and no village is too small, and no old refusal too final, for his mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. On the way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a senior official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit told Philip to go to that chariot and stay near it. Philip ran up, heard the man reading Isaiah and asked whether he understood it. He replied that he could not unless someone explained it, and invited Philip to sit with him. He was reading the passage about one led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, humiliated and denied justice, whose life was taken from the earth. The eunuch asked whom the prophet meant, himself or someone else. Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus. As they travelled they came to some water, and the eunuch asked what stood in the way of his being baptised. He ordered the chariot to stop, and both went down into the water and Philip baptised him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the passage in the Old Testament that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. Notice the grammar, because the Reformed tradition has always insisted that everything turns on it: the transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the entire point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering, of which the world has always had an ample supply. He is a substitute — the guiltless one bearing what the guilty had coming, so that the guilty go free. That is what Philip preached from. And it is worth noticing that he did not have to argue his way to Christ across a long distance. He started at Isaiah 53 and the road was short.
