After he gave sight to a man born blind, he said, For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind; and some Pharisees standing near asked, Are we also blind? (John 9:39–40). Saul was a Pharisee of Pharisees, as certain of his sight as any man in Jerusalem, and on this road the word of Jesus comes true in his own body. The blindness that strikes him is the outward form of the blindness he already had. And because the same Lord came to make the blind see, the darkness on the road is not the last word over him. It is the first stage of the miracle.

So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. That is the detail to keep. The last time we saw Saul he was dragging people through doorways. He meant to lead prisoners out of Damascus; he is led into it, helpless, dependent, going wherever somebody else takes him, in the position of the people he came to arrest.

Was the blindness a punishment? It was more a mercy and a sign than a penalty. A punishment would have fitted the crime, and nothing in this chapter does. The blindness was the natural effect of the glory he had seen, and it gave him three days in which the whole world he had lived in could be taken down. It was also a living picture: the man who had been spiritually blind was made to feel his blindness so that he would know his sight, when it came, was a gift. Compare the sorcerer Elymas, who is struck blind for a time as a judgment for opposing the gospel (13:11). Saul was blinded on the way into the gospel, and his sight was given back with the Spirit.

In a sentence. His companions stood speechless, hearing the sound but seeing no one, and Saul got up from the ground but could see nothing, so they led him by the hand into Damascus.

On a Tuesday. Pride is the feeling of seeing perfectly well. If there is a subject on which you are completely certain and have stopped listening to anyone, it is worth asking God whether that is where you are blind. And if he has recently taken something from you, a confidence, a reputation, a plan you could see clearly, do not assume he is finished with you. Sometimes he has to put out the old light before the new one can be seen.

For worship. Christ did not argue Saul out of his blindness; he shone on him, and the man who had seen everything saw nothing. Then the Lord who is the light of the world had him led by the hand into the city like a child. That is how the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, shines in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Paul wrote that sentence, and it is hard to believe he wrote it without remembering this road.
verseByVerse.note: In 22:9 Paul says his companions did not understand the voice; they heard a sound but not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.

For three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. Three days of nothing. No sight, no food, and, the detail people skim, no water. Three days without drinking is not a devotional exercise; in that climate it is the edge of what a body will take. This is not a man keeping a fast. It is a man who has stopped functioning, in shock, in repentance, and, as the Lord will tell Ananias, in prayer.

The room in the dark. Try to picture it. He is in a strange city, in a borrowed house on a street called Straight, in the dark, with an escort outside who do not know what to do with him and a set of arrest warrants in a bag that nobody is going to use. Every certainty he possessed on the morning he left Jerusalem is gone, not weakened but gone, and the one thing he now knows for certain is that the people he was travelling to imprison were right about everything, and that he has spent his best years and his considerable gifts hunting the Messiah of Israel. He had much to think about: everything he had believed about Jesus, and everything he had done to Jesus’ people. And what he did with the time was pray: not, one imagines, in the well-formed manner of a Pharisee who had prayed every day of his life, but in a dark room, with no idea what to say.

A death and a rising. Luke does not press the number, and we should not build on it. But the shape is unmistakable: he goes into darkness, everything he was dies there, and then a man comes and he is raised up and washed. It is the shape of the gospel itself, the death and resurrection of the Lord into which every believer is baptised. Paul would spend the rest of his life writing about being buried with Christ and raised with him (Romans 6:4), about the old self having been crucified, and about a new creation in which the old has passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17). He had lived it before he wrote a word of it, on the floor of somebody’s guest room.

For anyone in a collapse of certainty. There is something here for the person whose faith has come apart in his hands, or who has discovered that a thing he built a life on was not true, or who has been shown something about himself he cannot unsee. Saul’s three days were not the end of him, and they did not feel like anything but an end at the time. It is worth knowing that Scripture’s most spectacular conversion has a dark room in the middle of it, and that nobody in the house had the least idea what was going on.

What it does not mean. This sort of passage attracts imitators. Luke is not recommending three-day fasts, and there is no suggestion that Saul’s abstinence achieved anything or earned him his sight. The man was in shock. What the verse describes is a condition, not a technique.

Does God always bring people through darkness before conversion? No. Some, like Saul, are broken before they are healed. Others are drawn quietly: of Lydia Luke says simply that the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (16:14), and the Ethiopian went on his way rejoicing within an hour of meeting Philip (8:39). The darkness is not a stage that has to be passed through, and nobody should feel his conversion is suspect because it lacked one. What every conversion has in common is that the old self is put to death and a new one is raised by Christ. In some lives that takes three days on a floor; in others it happens over a cup of coffee and an open Bible.

In a sentence. For three days he was blind and neither ate nor drank.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a dark room of your own just now, do what Saul did: pray, even if the prayer has no shape and you do not know what to say. You do not need to understand what God is doing to keep talking to him. And if you know someone in that room, do not rush him out of it with explanations. Be the person who brings food on the third day.

For worship. The risen Christ was in that silent room, listening to prayers that had no shape and needed none. He was taking a man apart in order to make him new, and not one hour of the three was wasted. The Lord who struck Saul down on the road had already chosen the hour of the knock at the door. He still keeps watch over every dark room where a sinner lies undone before him, and he never leaves anyone there a day longer than his love intends.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,

Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. Luke introduces the most important minor character in the New Testament with six words. No office. No title. He is not an apostle, not one of the seven, not an elder, not a prophet. He is a Christian who lives in the city, and God has decided to hand him the most consequential errand of the first century. (He is not the Ananias of chapter 5; the name, meaning the LORD is gracious, was common.)

A man with something to lose. Paul fills in what Luke leaves out, when he tells the story in Jerusalem years later: Ananias was a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there (22:12). That is a description of a man with a standing in the Jewish community of Damascus, and the errand he is about to be given would end it.

Here I am, Lord. The Lord calls him by name in a vision, and this is the reply. It is the answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Jacob, and Moses at the bush, and Samuel in the dark, and Isaiah in the temple (Isaiah 6:8). It is not a promise to do the thing; Ananias has not been told what the thing is, and he will argue about it once he hears. It is simply the reply of a man who is available before he knows the assignment, which is a different and rarer disposition than willingness after the details are in.

Rise and go to the street called Straight. Then the directions, and their ordinariness is the point. It was a real road, the long colonnaded thoroughfare that ran east and west through Roman Damascus, and it runs through the old city to this day.

At the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul. A street, a householder, a name and a home town. Tarsus was Saul’s birthplace, a proud university city in Cilicia, no mean city as he would later call it (21:39). God’s guidance in this passage has an address on it.

For behold, he is praying. And then the one piece of information the Lord offers about the man Ananias is being sent to. It is worth noticing what is not said. Not, he is safe now. Not, he has repented and you will find him much changed. Not, I have dealt with him. The single credential given for the most dangerous man in the province is that he is at that moment praying, which from anybody else would be no proof of anything at all. Saul had prayed every day of his life as a Pharisee. Now he prays as a broken man to the risen Jesus. From the Lord who is speaking, that is the whole case. A man who has begun to pray to Christ is a man Christ has already taken hold of.

Does God still guide his people by visions like this? God is free to do as he pleases, and Christians who believe he still sometimes speaks in dreams and visions are our brothers. But even in Acts such visions were rare and came at turning points in the founding of the church, and the more likely reading is that this kind of direct revelation belonged to that apostolic age. Ananias’s vision was not the normal way God guided his people then, and it is not the normal way now. We are guided by Scripture, which is sufficient for everything we need for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17), and by prayer, wise counsel and the ordinary providences that open and close doors. Any impression that pulls against the plain teaching of Scripture is to be refused, however vivid. And the good news is that we do not need a vision to obey. Ananias’s great act was simply going to a house and loving a man. That is guidance anyone can follow today.

In a sentence. There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord called him in a vision, and he answered, and the Lord told him to go to Straight Street, to the house of Judas, and ask for a man of Tarsus named Saul, who was praying.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary believers for extraordinary tasks, and almost always the task is a person at an address. Ask whether there is someone you have been sent to without a vision: the neighbour who has just lost her husband, the colleague who asked a question about church and was never followed up, the young man at the back who has stopped coming. Be ready to say, Here I am, Lord, before you know what it will cost.

For worship. The ascended Christ, who holds the universe together, knew the name of a street in Damascus and the name of the man whose house was on it. He knew which of his disciples lived nearby and what he was afraid of. That is the Lord of the church: not a remote power issuing general policy, but a Shepherd who knows his sheep and the doors they live behind, and who sends one of them to fetch another home.
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.”

And he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight. God has been at both ends of this the whole time. While Ananias is being given a street name in one part of Damascus, Saul has already been shown a picture of a man called Ananias coming through a door and putting his hands on him. Neither of them arranged it. Neither of them knew the other existed a week ago. And when Ananias finally walks into that room, the blind man on the other side of it will have been expecting him by name. Two visions, matching, just as God will prepare both Peter and Cornelius in the next chapter.

A kindness to both. It is worth seeing which way it runs. For Saul, three days into the dark with nothing to hold, it is the first concrete thing he has been given: somebody is coming, and here is his name. For Ananias, it means he is not walking in cold. The man he is dreading has been told he is on his way and what he is coming to do. And the sight to be restored is more than physical. It is a sign of the spiritual sight Saul is about to receive.

The door opened from the inside. This verse is still part of what the Lord says to Ananias, the last thing before he objects, and it is offered as a reason: go, he is expecting you, and he already knows your name. The Lord is reasoning with a frightened man, and his argument is that the door has already been opened from the inside. The same is often true of the conversation a Christian quietly dreads: the apology owed, the subject that has to be raised. Sometimes a great deal has been done at the other end, by somebody with access to both sides of the door.

What it does not mean. A promise can be manufactured out of this that Scripture does not make. It is not a guarantee that every difficult conversation has been divinely prepared, or that obedience will always turn out to be safer than it looked. Ananias’s errand was genuinely dangerous and he was right to say so. What the verse establishes is narrower: that the God who sends people is already at work on the far side, and that the messenger is very rarely the first one there.

Why did the Lord not simply heal Saul himself? He could have, of course. The light that blinded him could have restored him on the spot. But Christ chose to give Saul his sight, his welcome and his baptism through a member of the church he had been persecuting. Saul needed to receive mercy from the hands of the people he had hunted, and to be taken into their family, not merely converted on his own. That is how the Lord ordinarily works still. He saves people by himself alone, but he brings them to faith through the word spoken by other believers (Romans 10:14), and he gathers them into a church. Nobody is meant to be a Christian by himself.

In a sentence. Saul had seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he would see again.

On a Tuesday. If there is a conversation you have been avoiding because you are afraid of how it will go, pray for the other person before you pray for yourself. Ask God to be at work in him before you arrive. Then go. You may find, as Ananias did, that you are expected.

For worship. Christ works on both ends: preparing hearts to hear, and messengers to speak. He was in a dark room on Straight Street and in a believer’s house across the city at the same hour, arranging a meeting that neither man could have imagined. Nothing in his church happens by accident. The one who sits at the right hand of the Father is the Lord of every appointment, and he loves to bring his enemies and his friends into the same room and make them brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

Lord, I have heard from many about this man. Ananias argues with God, and God does not rebuke him for it. That is the first thing to notice, and Luke reports the exchange without a syllable of disapproval. He is not being difficult. He is stating the case as any sane member of that congregation would state it. Reports have been coming up the road from Jerusalem for months: houses entered, people taken, a young man from Tarsus at the centre of it. Ananias almost certainly knew names. Some of the refugees who had run to Damascus were sitting in his own meetings, and they had told him what they had seen. Saul’s reputation had arrived well before Saul.

How much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. One phrase in the objection is worth a moment on its own: your saints. It is the first time in Acts that Christians are called this, and it means simply the holy ones, hagioi, the people set apart for God. It is not a special class of especially pious believers; it is the ordinary name for all of them (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Your saints: they belong to Jesus, which is why harming them is harming him (v. 4). Ananias uses it of the men and women Saul had been hunting. Within a few years the man he is being sent to will be using the same word in letter after letter to describe ordinary congregations of fishermen and slaves and tradespeople, and once, describing himself, will say he is the very least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8).

And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name. The second half of the objection is the sharper one. All. Ananias is describing a warrant that has his own name inside it. He is not being asked to visit a difficult man; he is being asked to walk into a house and identify himself, by name and as a Christian, to the officer sent to arrest him. And notice how he describes the believers: those who call on your name. That was the mark of a Christian from the beginning (2:21; Romans 10:13; 1 Corinthians 1:2). They called on Jesus as Lord, and they prayed to him. That phrase comes from the prophet Joel, where everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved (Joel 2:32), and Peter and Paul both apply it to Jesus (2:21, 36; Romans 10:9–13). The name on which Israel called for salvation is now the name of Jesus.

Arguing with God. Scripture has a small tradition of people who answered God back at the moment of calling. Moses produced five separate objections at the bush, and God dealt with each. Gideon asked for the fleece twice. Jeremiah said he was too young. What distinguishes Ananias from Jonah is not that he kept his doubts to himself (he did not) but that he raised them in God’s presence and then did what he was told. Jonah raised nothing and went to the harbour.

Fear in better clothes. A certain kind of piety teaches people to suppress the objection and calls the suppression faith. It is usually fear wearing better clothes, and it tends to come out sideways later. Ananias tells God exactly what he thinks of the assignment, in plain words, with the reasons, and God answers him with an explanation rather than a reprimand. There is room in that conversation for a man to say what he actually thinks. The Psalms are full of it.

Where Christians differ: who are the saints? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches use “saints” mainly for specially holy people, canonised after death, whose prayers are sought. Verdict: in the New Testament every believer is a saint, set apart by God in Christ (Ephesians 1:1; Philippians 1:1). Holiness of life should follow, but the title is given by grace, not earned. We pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

Is it right to pray to Jesus himself? Yes. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18), and that is how Jesus taught us to pray. But the first Christians also called directly on Jesus, as Stephen did while the stones were falling: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (7:59). Ananias is talking to Jesus in this very verse. That is one of the clearest signs in the New Testament that the church worshipped Jesus as God, because a devout Jew would never pray to anyone less. So you may speak to the Lord Jesus freely, as to the Father, and you are not praying to a different God when you do. The three persons are one God, and every prayer offered in Christ’s name reaches him.

In a sentence. Ananias answered that he had heard from many people how much harm this man had done to the Lord’s saints in Jerusalem, and that he had come with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on the Lord’s name.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are a saint, not because you feel holy but because he has set you apart for himself. Live like one, in the ordinary places where nobody calls you anything. And if you are carrying an objection to something God has plainly asked of you, do not bury it. Bring it to him in so many words. Then, like Ananias, get up and go.

For worship. Christ calls his people his saints, and he calls them that while they are still frightened, still arguing and still very far from finished. He did not wait for Ananias to stop objecting before he answered him; he reasoned with him, patiently, as a friend. That is the Lord we pray to: holy enough to set us apart, and gentle enough to hear our fears in full.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine. God answers the objection, and the answer is not reassurance. It is information. The word for chosen, eklogē, is the word of election, the same that Paul will use of God’s choosing grace in Romans 9 and 11. Saul was chosen by Christ before he knew it, before he was born (Galatians 1:15), and long before he deserved anything except judgment. Not because he was good, but because God chose him: by the grace of God I am what I am, he would write (1 Corinthians 15:9–10).

A chosen vessel. The word behind instrument, skeuos, is the ordinary one for a container or a piece of equipment: a jar, a pot, a vessel, the sort of word that turns up in an inventory. Saul is not being described as a hero, a champion or a great man. He is a receptacle that has been picked out, and the value is entirely in what it is for and who chose it. Paul evidently never forgot the word. Writing to Corinth years later about the ministry he had been given, he says we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7). He is using the same term about himself, and he had heard it first in a sentence he was not present for.

To carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. Then the destinations, and they are the table of contents for the rest of the book. The Gentiles are named first, which would have been an extraordinary thing to say in those first years (13:46–48); the kings are Agrippa in chapter 26 and, by the end, Caesar himself; the children of Israel are the synagogue in every city, which is where Paul begins every time. And he is to carry the name, as one carries something precious through a crowd. It is the name, not his own, that he is entrusted with.

A share in the Servant’s work. The commission is not Saul’s invention, nor even quite his own. Isaiah’s Servant was told that it was too light a thing to raise up the tribes of Jacob only; he would be a light for the nations, that God’s salvation might reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6). Simeon held the infant Jesus and called him exactly that, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). And years later Paul and Barnabas quoted the same verse of Isaiah to explain why they were turning to the Gentiles (13:47). Saul is not being sent on an errand of his own beside Christ’s. He is being drawn into the Servant’s own mission, as a vessel through which the light of the nations will shine.

For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name. And then the sentence which is the reason this passage cannot be preached as a success story. It is joined to the commission by a conjunction, not separated from it by a paragraph. The calling and the cost arrive in the same breath, spoken to a third party before the man himself has been told anything. The little word must, dei, is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 9:22). And there is an exchange in it that is hard to miss: Saul had spent a year making people suffer on account of that name, and the first thing said about his future is how much he will suffer for it. Not as punishment, because his sins were forgiven, but as the cost of carrying the name of a crucified Lord.

What that meant in practice. It is not left to the imagination, because Paul eventually listed it (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). Five times he received thirty-nine lashes from his own people; three times he was beaten with Roman rods; once he was stoned and left for dead; three times shipwrecked, and a night and a day adrift at sea. Add hunger, cold, sleeplessness, and the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches. That is the career being announced here, and the Lord gives it to Ananias as part of the reason to go.

What it does not mean. This can be turned into a formula. Not every calling carries this measure of suffering, and a Christian whose life has been comparatively gentle has not been overlooked or given a second-rate commission. Scripture nowhere makes hardship the proof of authenticity, and men have done real damage by implying it. But the verse is a permanent corrective to a way of speaking about the Christian life that has become almost standard: the presentation of Christ as the route to a better, smoother, more successful version of the life one already has. The Lord’s own summary of what he was calling his greatest servant to was: he will carry my name a very long way, and it will cost him everything he has.

Was Saul chosen only for service, or for salvation too? Both, and they cannot be pulled apart. In this verse the emphasis falls on service: Saul is chosen as an instrument for a task. But Paul himself traced his salvation back to the same choosing grace. God set him apart before he was born and called him by grace (Galatians 1:15), and he received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience in him as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). The same is true of every believer: chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), and created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). You were not chosen because you were useful. You were chosen in love, and then made useful.

In a sentence. The Lord told Ananias to go, for Saul was his chosen instrument to carry his name before the Gentiles and kings and the people of Israel, and he would show Saul how much he must suffer for the sake of his name.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ is costing you something this week, a friendship, a promotion, a reputation, do not conclude that you have taken a wrong turning. The cost was in the calling from the start, and your Lord said so. And if you have been treating your faith as a way of getting a smoother life, let this verse reset the expectation gently: he promises himself, and his presence in the suffering, not an easy road.

For worship. Christ chooses his instruments by grace, the clay jars nobody else would have picked, and he fills them with a treasure that is not theirs. He chose the man who had shed his people’s blood and made him the herald of his name to the nations. And when he called him to suffer, he was calling him to walk the road he himself had walked first, all the way to the cross. To bear the name of such a Lord is not a burden borne grudgingly. It is the highest honour a sinner can be given.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;

So Ananias departed and entered the house. Seven words for the bravest thing anybody does in this chapter. Obedience despite fear. He had said what he thought, been answered, and gone.

Brother Saul. Ananias lays his hands on him, and the first word out of his mouth is brother. Two of the most beautiful words in Acts. In the room is a blind man from Tarsus who arrived in Damascus with a warrant that covers Ananias by name, and somewhere in the house is a bag of letters from the high priest. Ananias belongs to a congregation swollen with refugees who ran from this man, some of whom may have lost somebody. He has every reason to open with a question, or a condition, or at the very least a wary silence. He opens with a family word, and he uses it before Saul has said anything at all. He can say it because Christ had said it first: the one who sanctifies is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

The Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me. What follows is careful and generous. Ananias tells him he knows, and specifies the road, so that Saul understands he is not being humoured. He confirms that the one who met him was Jesus. Then the two things he has come for: sight, and the Holy Spirit.

So that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Notice who is doing this. Not Peter, not John, not an apostle at all. The man who lays hands on Paul, restores his sight, tells him he will be filled with the Spirit, and very probably baptises him, is a disciple in a provincial city about whom nothing else is known beyond Paul’s own retelling (22:12). There is no fixed pattern here requiring an apostle for the Spirit to be given. Paul would insist for the rest of his life that he had not received his gospel from any man (Galatians 1:11–12), and it is perfectly consistent, because what Ananias gave him was not a gospel. It was his eyes, a welcome, and water.

Was this a second blessing after conversion? No. The filling with the Spirit came as part of Saul’s conversion; Ananias came to him within days of the road, and the Spirit came with the restoring of his sight and his baptism. It was not a later stage that every Christian must seek.

And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. The doctor writing this reaches for the nearest physical comparison and marks it as a comparison: something like. Whatever came away, Luke will not pretend to know exactly what it was. We still say the scales fell from my eyes, and we have this verse to thank for it. And the miracle has a pedigree. At Nazareth Jesus had read out his own programme from Isaiah, and it included recovering of sight to the blind (Luke 4:18). Here the risen Lord keeps that word for the man who had fought him hardest.

Then he rose and was baptized. With his sight barely back, he got up and was baptised. There is no interval, no probation while the church works out whether it can trust him. He had been in the dark for three days, and the moment the light came back he went and was washed. Baptism follows faith, at once.

Was Saul converted on the road, or at his baptism? He was Christ’s from the road: he called Jesus Lord, he prayed, and Ananias greets him as Brother (v. 17). Baptism was the outward sign and public confession. When Ananias later says be baptized and wash away your sins (22:16), he joins the sign to what it signifies, as Scripture often does; the washing is by faith in Christ, calling on his name.

Should we baptise people as quickly today? In Acts, those who professed faith were baptised promptly, usually the same day (2:41; 8:38; 16:33), and that pattern should shape us: baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, not as a reward at the end of a long course. We hold, with the London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ (London Baptist Confession 29.2), so a church rightly asks for a credible profession first and takes time to hear it. Our paedobaptist brothers baptise the children of believers as well, and we honour them as faithful Christians while we differ. But no one should be kept waiting for years to prove himself. If you trust Christ and have not been baptised, speak to your pastor this week.

How could God forgive a man like this? Saul had approved of murder and dragged families to prison. Many people quietly wonder whether some sins are too great. Paul answered the question himself: though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent, I received mercy, and Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:13–15). He adds that he was shown mercy precisely as an example, so that no one would ever think himself beyond it (1:16). The blood of Christ is enough for the worst thing you have done. The only sin that is never forgiven is the one never brought to him.

In a sentence. Ananias went into the house, laid his hands on him and called him Brother Saul, saying the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road had sent him so that Saul would see again and be filled with the Spirit, and at once something like scales fell from his eyes, he could see, and he got up and was baptised.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you find it hard to call brother or sister: a person who hurt you, a believer from a background you distrust, a new convert with an ugly past? Grace calls you to say the family word first, before he has proved anything. That does not mean pretending nothing happened or setting aside wise safeguards. It means meeting a person Christ has received as Christ received you.

For worship. Brother Saul. In those two words the whole gospel stands in a doorway. The Lord Jesus had forgiven his persecutor before a single apology was offered, and sent one of the persecuted to say so. The blood that cleanses the sinner also makes him a son, and every son a brother. That is what the risen Christ does with his enemies: he gives them eyes, he gives them his Spirit, and he gives them a family.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.”

And taking food, he was strengthened. Luke has not forgotten that this man has not eaten for three days. Before the theology there is a meal, and somebody in that house made it. The Lord who restored his eyes also cared that he was hungry.

For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. The people he came to arrest became his family. He sat at their tables, slept under their roofs and learned their hymns, and some of them will have been the very refugees whose names were in his letters.

And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues. Then the sentence, and the geography in it is the irony Luke has been setting up since verse 2. Saul had carried letters addressed to the synagogues at Damascus, authorising him to search them for followers of the Way. He now walks into those same synagogues, with the same letters presumably still in his luggage, and preaches the thing he came to stamp out. One imagines the faces. (Paul tells us that at some point in these years he also went away into Arabia, the Nabataean kingdom to the south and east, and then returned to Damascus, Galatians 1:17. Luke compresses the time.)

He is the Son of God. What he preaches is worth weighing, because of how soon it is. Not: this man was a prophet, or a teacher, or even the Messiah; that comes two verses later. The very first recorded sermon of the apostle Paul, preached within days of his baptism by a man who had spent his adult life defending the oneness of God against every blasphemy, is that Jesus of Nazareth is God’s Son. It is the only time in Acts that the title is used in preaching like this (but compare 13:33), and it is exactly the claim for which the council had condemned Jesus (Luke 22:70–71). Whatever else his conversion did, it did not leave him working his way toward that conclusion gradually. He had met the person and drawn the only possible inference on the road (compare Galatians 1:16; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

What did Saul mean by “Son of God”? The title gathers up two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it is a claim to full deity. To call Jesus God’s own Son, in the unique sense, is to say he shares the very nature of God, which is exactly how his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with “making himself equal with God” because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). “Son” here speaks not of a beginning or of a lesser rank but of sameness of nature and eternal relation: as an earthly son shares his father’s humanity, the divine Son shares the Father’s deity, eternally, of one substance with him, “begotten, not made.” Second, “Son of God” was a royal, messianic title: the promised king of David’s line was called God’s son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), so to say “Jesus is the Son of God” is also to say he is the Christ, the anointed King, which is just where Saul’s preaching goes next, “proving that Jesus was the Christ” (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers “sons of God” (Job 1:6; John 1:12), but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the Son, the “only-begotten” (monogenēs, John 3:16), Son by eternal right and by nature, not made a son and not adopted. We become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the man Jesus, crucified and risen, is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust, worship, and obedience, and it is the very confession that saves, “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31; compare 1 John 4:15). And here is the wonder of the moment: the man who had set out to destroy everyone who made this claim is now the first in Damascus to make it.

Should a new believer start speaking about Christ straight away? Yes, in the sense Saul did: telling people who Jesus is and what he has done. You do not need a theology degree to say that Jesus is the Son of God and that he has changed your life; the man born blind in John 9 had been a believer for an afternoon when he said, I was blind, now I see. What a new believer should not do is rush into teaching or leading others, and the church kept that distinction even with Saul, who spent years out of the limelight before he was given leadership. Speak of Christ freely and early. Take on responsibility slowly.

In a sentence. He ate and regained his strength, stayed some days with the disciples in Damascus, and at once began proclaiming Jesus in the synagogues, saying that he is the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. If someone asked you today who Jesus is, what would your first sentence be? Saul’s was not about himself, his experience or what Jesus could do for his listeners. It was about the person. Practise saying it plainly, in your own words, so that when the moment comes you are not fumbling. And if you have a past that people know about, do not hide from it. A changed life is the loudest sermon in the synagogue.

For worship. Jesus is the Son of God. The Pharisee who had defended the oneness of God against every blasphemy now bowed before the eternal Son, of one nature with the Father, who had come down into David’s line, died under the curse and risen in power. And that confession is the very centre of heaven’s worship: the Son who was with the Father before the world began, who shares his glory, who reigns now as the anointed King. The first words of the converted persecutor are the words every redeemed voice will be singing for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.

Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? All who heard him were amazed, and the synagogue’s reaction is one of the more understandable in Scripture. They know exactly who this is and exactly what he came for, because the letters had been announced in advance and arrangements had presumably been made. And here he is, in the seat, saying the opposite of what he was sent to say. The word they use of his career, porthēsas, is a violent one: made havoc, the language of sacking a city or laying waste to a country. It is not their invention either. Paul takes the same word and uses it of himself, twice, when he writes to the Galatians (Galatians 1:13, 23). He never softened the vocabulary. Whatever else he became, he did not become a man who described his past in careful language.

But Saul increased all the more in strength. Then two verbs describing what he did next, and both are worth having. The first is the one Paul later uses of being strengthened by Christ, the word behind I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13). He is not describing natural confidence returning. Something was being supplied.

And confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. The Greek word for proving, symbibazōn, means to bring things together, to knit or join them side by side; the image is of laying two things next to each other until the fit is obvious. That is precisely what Paul does in every letter and every sermon recorded of him: this text and that event, laid alongside one another, the promise beside the fulfilment, until the listener can see they belong together. And the hardest piece he now fitted was the one that had kept him from Christ: a Messiah hanged on a tree, under the curse of the law (Deuteronomy 21:23). He had thought the cross disproved Jesus. He came to preach that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The method of a lifetime was operating from the first days, because a first-class rabbinic training in the Scriptures was now pointing the other way. God does not throw away the gifts and training of the people he converts. He turns them round.

Ability arrived at once; deployment did not. There is a caution here that the passage itself supplies if one keeps reading. Saul is formidable immediately, and he is also, within a few years, sent quietly home to Tarsus and not heard of again for the best part of a decade. The New Testament elsewhere warns against putting a recent convert into leadership, lest he become puffed up with conceit (1 Timothy 3:6), and the most gifted convert in the history of the church spent something like ten years in obscurity before anybody came to fetch him. The interval was not an accident.

How can I show someone that Jesus is the Christ? Do what Saul did, on a smaller scale: lay the Scriptures and the facts side by side. Read Isaiah 53 with a friend and ask whom it describes. Read Psalm 22 next to the crucifixion. Show how the promises to Abraham and David land on Jesus, and how the empty tomb is the hinge of it all (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). You do not need to win every argument, and you will not convert anyone by cleverness, because only the Spirit opens blind eyes. But God uses honest explanation of his word, and it is far better to open the Bible with someone than to argue round it.

In a sentence. Everyone who heard him was amazed, asking whether this was not the man who had ravaged those in Jerusalem who called on this name and had come here to take them back as prisoners, but Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

On a Tuesday. God can use your training, your mind and your past for his glory, including the parts of your past you are ashamed of. Write down one skill or piece of knowledge you have that could serve Christ’s people, and offer it to your church. And if you are newly converted and gifted, be patient with those who ask you to wait before you lead. The waiting is part of the training.

For worship. The Christ whom Saul had denied was the one to whom all his Scriptures pointed, and now every text he had memorised as a boy lit up with the face of Jesus. That is the glory of the Old Testament: it is not a collection of separate stories but one long promise, and Christ is its yes and amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who wrote the promise has kept it, and he gave the persecutor eyes to see it fit.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,

When many days had passed. Luke’s phrase is doing a great deal of quiet work. Laid against Paul’s own account, those days include a departure into Arabia and a return to Damascus, and the whole stretch comes to about three years (Galatians 1:17–18). Luke is not concealing it; he is writing the story of a movement and moving at the movement’s pace.

The Jews plotted to kill him. The hunter becomes the hunted. Paul describes the same episode in a letter and adds a detail Luke omits: the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city in order to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Aretas was the Nabataean king whose territory ran south and east of Damascus, and his official was involved in the watch on the gates. So this was not merely a synagogue quarrel that turned nasty. Within three years of his conversion, Saul’s preaching had become a matter for the civil authority of a neighbouring kingdom. The suffering Jesus promised (v. 16) has begun.

Charge and muscle. The two accounts fit together without strain, and the shape is familiar from this whole book: the complaint comes from one quarter and the force from another. It happened to Jesus in front of Pilate, to Paul again at Philippi and Thessalonica and Corinth. Religious objection supplies the charge; the state supplies the soldiers.

But their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him. Damascus was a walled city with a limited number of gates, and a watch on all of them, around the clock, is not a gesture. Somebody was paying for it. The city was sealed. And set this beside chapter 8, three years earlier, and notice what has happened to the man. There, he was the one going house after house. There, he was the one with the authority, the letters and the men. Here he is the one being hunted through a city, unable to use the gates, dependent on a handful of disciples to get him out alive. The exchange was quick and it was complete, and it is the pattern of everything that follows: for the next thirty years Paul is on the receiving end of precisely what he used to administer.

Why did God let his new servant be hunted so soon? Because this is what the Lord had said would happen (v. 16), and because the servant is not above his master (John 15:20). Persecution was not a sign that something had gone wrong with Saul’s conversion; it was a sign that it was real. Notice, too, that the plot became known to Saul. God did not prevent the danger, but he watched over his man in the middle of it and kept him until his work was done. That is how he usually protects his people: not always from trouble, but always through it, and never one day beyond his appointed time.

In a sentence. After many days had gone by, the Jews plotted to kill him, but Saul learned of their plan; they were watching the city gates day and night so that they could kill him.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for your faith this week, at work, in your family, online, do not be surprised and do not take it as proof that you have failed. Ask instead whether you have given offence by Christ or only by your manner. If it is by Christ, rejoice quietly. You are in good company.

For worship. The persecutor became the persecuted, and so began to share in the sufferings of the Lord he had hunted. Christ himself was watched, plotted against and handed over by religious men to the soldiers of the state. Every servant who walks that road walks in his footsteps, and the Lord who was raised from the dead watches the gates of every city where his people are hunted. Not one of them is taken a moment before he says.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.

But his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. The most famous escape in the New Testament, and it is entirely undignified. Picture the mechanics. The house is built into the city wall, with an opening, probably a window. The basket is a large woven hamper for produce, big enough to hold a man with his knees drawn up. It is dark. A rope is tied on. And the future apostle to the Gentiles, the man who will stand in front of kings, is folded into a fruit basket and let down over a wall by people who are hoping the rope holds. The great Pharisee, who came with letters of authority, leaves in a basket in the dark, like the spies Rahab let down from her window at Jericho (Joshua 2:15).

The boast of a basket. He never forgot it, and what he did with the memory is the remarkable part. Years later, writing to the Corinthian church about the men who were undermining him with their credentials, he says that if he must boast he will boast of the things that show his weakness, and then he gives a list: labours, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, hunger, the pressure of the churches. And the item he chooses to end on, the climax of the whole catalogue, is the basket (2 Corinthians 11:30–33). Of everything in a life that included being caught up into the third heaven, he selected as his boast the night he was lowered out of a window like a sack of figs.

The destruction of a category. That is not false modesty and it is not a joke. His rivals were competing on the strength of their standing; Paul answers by putting the single most humiliating moment of his career at the top of his own list of qualifications. He had understood something they had not: my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Those words were the risen Christ’s, spoken to Paul when he begged to be rid of his thorn, and they describe Christ before they describe Paul: he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). The basket was where the servant began to learn the shape of his Master’s glory.

Is it cowardly to run? One thing should be said plainly, because it releases a great many people from an unnecessary burden. Saul ran away. He did not stay and preach and take what came; he went over the wall at night and left the city. There is no hint of reproach in the text, and the Lord himself had told his disciples that when they were persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Courage in Scripture is not the refusal to leave. Paul stood his ground on plenty of occasions and left quietly on others, and he seems to have had no rule about it beyond the work continuing.

So when should a Christian flee, and when stay? A rough guide from Scripture: it is right to flee when staying would achieve nothing but your death or imprisonment and the work can go on elsewhere, as here, and as when Jesus himself withdrew from those who sought to kill him before his hour had come (John 8:59; 10:39). It is right to stay when leaving would mean denying Christ, or abandoning people in your care who cannot leave with you; a shepherd who runs and leaves the sheep is a hired hand (John 10:12–13). Between those two, pray, take counsel from your church, and do not despise yourself for choosing life. The Lord wants living witnesses as well as faithful martyrs.

His disciples. And note who did it. He has been a Christian for perhaps three years and there are already people in Damascus who are his, men and women he has won to Christ. They put him in the basket, and they held the rope.

In a sentence. But his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.

On a Tuesday. Think of your most humiliating moment as a Christian, the time you looked weak, foolish or out of your depth. Instead of burying it, thank God for it, and ask what it taught you about his strength. God’s servants are not too proud for the basket. And if someone you know is in danger or distress, be one of the people who holds the rope.

For worship. The Lord who would one day send Paul before Caesar first sent him over a wall in a basket, and both journeys were equally in his hand. The disciples held the rope; Christ held the man. He is not embarrassed by the undignified ways he rescues his servants, and he does not need them to look impressive. The King of glory, who once let himself be bound and led out of a city to die, keeps the lives of his people until their work is done, and when he lowers them into the dark, his own hand is beneath them.

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.

And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him. It is the loneliest sentence in the chapter. The last time Saul was in Jerusalem he was emptying houses; the people now shutting their doors are the ones who got away, or whose relatives did not. Their fear is not weak faith. It is arithmetic. A man with his record turning up claiming to be one of them is exactly what an informer would do. Was it a trick? Luke says they did not believe that he was a disciple, which is put charitably. They thought he was lying. So here is Saul, three years after the road, no longer welcome in the synagogue and not admitted by the church, with a price on him in Damascus and nowhere at all to stand.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. And then one man crosses the room. Took him means took hold of him: he laid hands on the man everybody else was backing away from, walked him in, and vouched for him out loud. Barnabas was a respected believer, a Levite from Cyprus whose name meant son of encouragement (4:36), and it is the second time Luke has shown us this man doing the same kind of thing. The first was a field sold and the money laid down without a speech; this is a reputation put at risk on behalf of somebody with none. If Barnabas was wrong, he had just introduced an assassin to the entire leadership of the church. Years later he would take the same kind of risk on John Mark (15:37–39), and be proved right again.

The door the Gentile mission came through. It is worth saying plainly what the New Testament would look like without this paragraph. Nobody else moved. There is no indication that the apostles sent for Saul, or that the church debated it and came round. One man with no office beyond a nickname decided to believe a story that everybody else found incredible, and the entire Gentile mission came through that door.

And declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord. Barnabas tells how the Lord had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. He tells the two things that mattered: that Saul had met the risen Lord, and that his life since had matched his claim. A testimony and a track record. The first was the heart of it: Paul would later rest his whole apostleship on that sight, Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8). The Lord who had met him on the road was now, through Barnabas, opening the church’s door to him.

The apostles, or two of them? Set this beside Paul’s own account of the same visit and a question surfaces. Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Paul says that when he finally went up to Jerusalem he saw Cephas, and stayed fifteen days, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:18–19). Plural in one, and pointedly not plural in the other. They fit once you see what each writer is doing. Luke is describing Saul’s reception by the church’s leadership and uses the collective term, as we might say a man was taken to meet the board when two directors were in the office that week. Paul is arguing to the Galatians that he did not get his gospel secondhand from Jerusalem, so he counts heads with deliberate precision. And Paul’s two names are exactly the two who mattered: Peter, the leading apostle, and James, the head of the Jerusalem church.

The timing. Read alone, Luke’s account sounds swift, and he does not pause to say that about three years in Arabia and Damascus lie between the road and this doorway (Galatians 1:17–18). Luke moves at the pace of the movement; Paul, writing his own defence, needs the calendar. Neither tells you something the other denies.

How can I be a Barnabas without being naive? Barnabas did not simply feel generous; he knew the facts. He had evidently heard Saul’s story, checked what had happened in Damascus, and judged it true before he put his name to it. So take time to listen to the person others are wary of, find out what has actually changed, and then speak up for him. At the same time, welcoming a repentant sinner never means ignoring real dangers. Where someone has abused or harmed others, a church must keep proper safeguards in place and protect the vulnerable, while still offering the gospel and fellowship. Grace and wisdom are not opposites. Barnabas had both, and the church was safer for it, not less safe.

In a sentence. When Saul came to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, they were all afraid of him, not believing he was a disciple, but Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Be a Barnabas. Think of the newcomer at church whom nobody quite knows what to do with, the person with the awkward history, the believer from a background that makes others uneasy. Find out his story. Sit with him. Introduce him to someone. One person crossing the room can change the course of a life, and occasionally of the whole church.

For worship. Christ has an advocate before the Father for every one of his people (1 John 2:1), and he took the far greater risk. He did not merely vouch for sinners; he put his own name and his own blood on the line for people with records far worse than their reputations. Barnabas walked Saul into a room of frightened apostles. Jesus Christ brings us into the presence of the holy God and says, this one is mine. Every Barnabas in the church is a small picture of him.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.

So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. The phrase in and out is an Old Testament way of describing somebody’s ordinary comings and goings (Deuteronomy 28:6; 1 Samuel 18:16). It means he was simply part of the household now, moving about the city with them, no longer at the door. And he was bold. Boldness, parrēsia, plain and fearless speech, is Luke’s mark of the Spirit-filled witness all through this book (4:13, 29, 31).

And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. Then Luke names the people he argued with, and the choice ought to stop a reader. These are the Greek-speaking Jews of the Jerusalem synagogues: the same circle Stephen had argued with in chapter 6, who could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke, and whose response was to plant false witnesses and have him killed. Saul had been at that killing, holding the coats and approving (7:58; 8:1). So he has walked straight back to the room where it happened and taken up the argument that got Stephen stoned, on Stephen’s side, against Stephen’s opponents. Stephen’s mantle has fallen on the man who held the coats. Luke does not comment.

A word on who the Hellenists were. The term, as the ESV notes, means Greek-speaking Jews, men of the diaspora raised in Greek language and culture, many with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem, such as the Synagogue of the Freedmen with its members from Cilicia (6:9). The word names a person’s language and culture, not his faith: in 6:1 it labels Greek-speaking Jewish believers, but here it means unbelieving Greek-speaking Jews. And Saul, a man of Tarsus in Cilicia, was himself a Hellenist, very likely once standing with this circle against Stephen. Now he pleads the name of Jesus among his own former camp, and meets the answer Stephen met.

But they were seeking to kill him. The last clause deserves counting. That is the second organised attempt on Saul’s life in this one chapter, the Damascus gates and now Jerusalem, and he has been a Christian for about three years. He had been warned. What was said to Ananias about him was not that he would be protected but that he would be shown how much he must suffer for the name, and the instalments have started arriving before he has preached outside two cities.

Was Stephen’s death wasted, then? It looked like it at the time: a brilliant young preacher silenced in his first public season, and the church scattered. But Stephen died praying for the men who stoned him, Lord, do not hold this sin against them (7:60), and one of those men is now preaching Stephen’s message in Stephen’s synagogue. Augustine said that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. Whether or not one can draw the line so straight, the pattern is plain: no faithful witness for Christ is ever wasted, even when it seems to end in failure. God answers prayers in ways the one who prayed may never see this side of glory.

In a sentence. So Saul stayed with them and moved freely about Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord, and he talked and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they were trying to kill him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a place, a family, a workplace, an old circle of friends, where you used to stand on the other side? That may be exactly where God wants you to speak now. Not with a sense of superiority, but as one who knows from the inside what they believe and why. Your history may be the key to their door.

For worship. The name Saul once tried to erase from Jerusalem he now spoke boldly in its streets, and in the very synagogues that had silenced Stephen. Christ is never short of witnesses. When his enemies stop one mouth he opens another, and sometimes he opens it in the throat that cried loudest against him. His name has outlived every council that forbade it and every plot laid against those who carry it, and one day every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews — the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. The church takes charge of him and removes him: down to the coast, to the port at Caesarea, onto a boat, and home to Cilicia. The man who had just been prepared to argue himself to death in Jerusalem does not appear to have resisted. He went where the brothers put him. Paul later adds that the Lord himself had told him in a vision in the temple to leave Jerusalem quickly, because they would not accept his testimony, and that he would be sent far away to the Gentiles (22:17–21). So the church’s decision and Christ’s command pointed the same way.

The hidden years. And then the narrative simply stops carrying him. Saul does not appear again until chapter 11, when Barnabas travels to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (11:25–26), and depending on how the years are counted, the gap is something in the region of eight to ten. Luke covers a decade of the most important life in the early church with half a sentence.

What was he doing? Not nothing. Paul says in his own account that he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, and that the churches of Judea kept hearing that the man who used to persecute them was now preaching the faith he had once tried to destroy (Galatians 1:21–23). Several of the beatings in his later catalogue have to fall somewhere, and this is the most likely stretch of road for them; so does the vision he describes as having happened fourteen years before he wrote about it (2 Corinthians 12:2). He was working. Nobody was writing it down.

The arithmetic of a life. Do the sums. Converted at perhaps thirty, he goes home at about thirty-three, the most formidable mind in the movement, commissioned by the risen Christ to carry the name to the Gentiles, and spends roughly his mid-thirties to his mid-forties in a province nobody was watching, doing work that has left almost no record. The decade was not a waiting room: he was preaching, the churches in Judea heard about it, and it counted. But if Barnabas had not remembered where he lived, those years would have been all we ever had of Paul.

Thirty years in Nazareth. Saul’s hidden decade follows the shape of his Lord’s life. Jesus was about thirty when he began his ministry (Luke 3:23), and of the years before it the Gospels tell us almost nothing: a carpenter’s son in a town nobody thought would produce anything good. Yet it was at the end of those unrecorded years, before he had preached a sermon or healed anyone, that the Father spoke from heaven: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (Luke 3:22). The years nobody wrote down had pleased God. The servant sent home to Tarsus was walking where his Master had walked.

Was the church wrong to send its best preacher away? No. They were protecting his life, and the Lord himself had told him to go (22:18). There is no failure here, either of courage on Saul’s part or of love on the church’s. Sometimes the wisest thing a church can do for a gifted and endangered young man is to take him out of the spotlight. And if you are the one who has been moved on, out of a role, a city or a ministry you loved, it may not be a demotion. It may be the Lord’s way of preparing you for the work he actually has in mind.

In a sentence. When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season where nothing you do seems to be noticed, the ministry is small, the work is unseen, the years are passing, do the work in front of you as though Christ were watching. He is. Write down what you are doing for him this week that nobody else will ever know about, and offer it to him alone.

For worship. Nothing done for Christ in Tarsus was lost to him. The Lord of the church kept the record no historian kept: the sermons in Cilician towns, the beatings nobody listed at the time, the slow years of a servant learning his Master. He sees what is done in secret, and he is the one who rewards it (Matthew 6:4). The call to the nations and the quiet years at home were both his good gift, and on the last day he will bring into the light every cup of cold water ever given in his name.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.

So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace. One of Luke’s hinge sentences, closing a section and opening the next, and there is a quiet irony in its placing. The church gets its peace in the paragraph immediately after its chief persecutor has been converted and shipped home. The man whose arrival scattered it is gone, and the persecution he was driving has gone with him. And notice church, singular: one church across three regions, not a federation of separate movements. Luke sees all the congregations of the land as one people under one Lord.

The peace Christ made. The church’s peace did not come from a change of policy in the council or a change of mood in the city. It came because the risen Lord had gone out to meet the man driving the persecution and made him his own. No treaty could have done it; the enemy was not pacified but converted. And the building that follows is the work of the same hands. Matthew records Jesus’ promise, I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). In Judea, Galilee and Samaria the church is being built up, and the builder is the one who had just stopped its fiercest opponent on the road.

A target hit. Note the geography as well, because Luke is quietly marking a stage completed. Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria: that is the second and third stage of the commission given in the first chapter of this book (1:8), and it has now happened, largely by accident, through a persecution nobody wanted. Only the end of the earth is outstanding, and the man who will take it there has just gone home to Tarsus to wait.

And was being built up. Peace was not used for idleness. The church was strengthened, edified, built like a house, the word Paul would later use for the growth of the body in love (Ephesians 4:12–16).

And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. And then the two phrases in which Luke chooses to describe a healthy church. Not its numbers, not its organisation, not its preaching: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit. It is an unexpected pairing, and it is the whole character of the thing.

The comfort of the Holy Spirit. The fear of the Lord is the reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness, like a man who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it. Its companion is richer than our word comfort suggests. Paraklēsis belongs to the same family as paraklētos, the name Jesus gave the Spirit: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16). The root means called alongside to give aid, and it sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted, and, as the old English word from the Latin for with strength reminds us, to make strong. It is God’s own Spirit coming alongside his people to console them, embolden them and strengthen them to stand.

Fear and comfort together. Fear and comfort are not rivals but partners; the same church that fears God is upheld by his Helper, and out of the two together it multiplied. A church with fear and no comfort becomes harsh and anxious. A church with comfort and no fear becomes careless and soft. A healthy church has both, and it grows. This is another of Luke’s progress reports (6:7; 12:24).

Does a church grow only when there is no persecution? No. The church had grown explosively under persecution too: those who were scattered went about preaching the word (8:4). God uses both seasons. Persecution scatters the seed; peace lets it root and be built up. Neither is a sign of his absence. If your church is in a quiet season, the question is not whether God is at work but whether you are using the peace to be built up in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit, or simply to rest.

In a sentence. So the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed a time of peace and was strengthened, and living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers.

On a Tuesday. Take the two phrases as a check on your own walk this week. Where have you been treating God casually, as if his holiness did not matter? That is a lack of fear. Where have you been carrying anxiety alone, as if there were no Helper beside you? That is a neglect of comfort. Ask the Spirit for both, and pray for your church by name to walk in them together.

For worship. The God who is a consuming fire is also the God of all comfort, and he gives his church both at once: the awe that bows before his holiness, and the Helper who comes alongside to hold us up. In the house Christ is building, trembling and consolation live under one roof. That is the life of his church in every age: humbled and strengthened, fearing and comforted, and growing, because its Lord walks in the midst of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Peter travelled about the country, he went to visit the Lord’s people in Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years. Peter told him that Jesus Christ was healing him and to get up and roll up his mat, and Aeneas got up at once. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek, Dorcas), always doing good and helping the poor. She became ill and died, and her body was washed and laid in an upstairs room. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples sent two men to urge Peter to come at once. When he arrived he was taken upstairs, where all the widows stood around him crying and showing him the robes and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out, knelt and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, saw Peter and sat up. He took her hand and helped her to her feet, then called the believers, especially the widows, and presented her to them alive. This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha is told in a way that deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter — the mourners put outside, the taking of the hand, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter is not improvising, and he is not exercising a power of his own; he is doing what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it and who was himself raised afterwards. That is why he kneels first. Reformed theology has read every healing and raising in Acts as a sign rather than a policy: a working sample of the new creation, offered in advance and on a small scale, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right permanently. Which is also why these events are rare rather than routine even in Acts. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign; it would be the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and the dresses she had made, and Luke notes that she had made them while she was with them.
