That is what her ministry consisted of, and it is what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up. Not what would be said at the service, which is a different question and easier — but what could be carried into the room and shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.

Now as Peter went here and there among them all. Luke’s phrase describes a circuit: the apostle out of Jerusalem, going round from congregation to congregation on the coastal plain. It is the first glimpse in this book of what most Christian ministry actually consists of: travelling to see people who are already believers, in unremarkable towns, and staying a while. Peter the fisherman has become Peter the shepherd, doing what his Lord told him on the shore of Galilee: feed my sheep (John 21:17).

Whose churches these were. Peter did not plant them. Lydda and Joppa lie in exactly the stretch of country the scattered believers of chapter 8 ran into, and Philip had preached his way through this plain from Azotus to Caesarea (8:40). The saints Peter is visiting are the fruit of a persecution and of refugees who could not stop talking. He arrives as a visitor to work somebody else began.

He went about doing good. Peter’s circuit has a model, and Peter himself would soon describe it, in Cornelius’s house: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him (10:38). The apostle going here and there among the towns of the plain is walking the way his Master walked through Galilee, and the healing about to happen in Lydda is the same Jesus still doing good, now from heaven, through the man he had told to feed his sheep. The ministry of Acts is not Peter’s ministry replacing Christ’s. It is Christ’s, continued.

He came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. Lydda is the old town of Lod, about twenty-five miles north-west of Jerusalem, sitting on the main road down to the sea and about eleven miles from the port at Joppa. It was a market town on a trade route, which means that whatever happened there would be discussed by carriers and travellers within a day.

There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. He has a Greek name, and Luke does not say that he was a Christian; the phrase is that Peter found him, which is what you say about somebody you were not looking for. Eight years is the detail to hold, because Luke gives numbers of this kind for a reason. It is long enough that everybody in a town that size knows the house and has stopped expecting anything. Somebody had been washing him and turning him and carrying him for eight years, and had long since stopped mentioning it.

Mercy before confession. One more thing about Aeneas is worth registering because of where this book is going. Luke tells us his name, his condition and the length of it, and says nothing whatever about his faith. He is not called a disciple, not said to have believed, and not recorded as speaking. He is simply a man Peter found. In two verses the mercy will arrive before any confession does, and within two chapters Peter will be standing in a Gentile house watching the same thing happen on a very much larger scale.

In a sentence. As Peter travelled about the country, he went down to visit the saints in Lydda, where he found a man named Aeneas, who was paralysed and had been bedridden for eight years.

On a Tuesday. Visit the sick and the shut-in. Peter went to them. Think of someone in your church or street who has been ill or housebound so long that people have stopped calling, and go this week. And remember the carers too: the person who has been doing the lifting and washing for years without anyone mentioning it. A meal, an afternoon off, or simply asking how they are may be the first kindness anyone has shown them in months.

For worship. The risen Christ notices the man nobody is looking for any more. Eight years on a mat in a market town, eight years of a family’s lifting and washing, and none of it was hidden from the Lord of glory. He who numbers the hairs of our heads had numbered those years, and on the day he had appointed he sent his apostle down the road to find the one he had never lost sight of.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Peter says the name before he says anything else, and the tense is present: not will heal, not can heal, but is healing you, now, as I speak. Not I heal you: Jesus Christ heals you. Peter is only the messenger. He had learned this at a temple gate years earlier, when a crowd came running to stare at him and he had to tell them it was not by his own power or piety that the lame man walked (3:12–16). He does not wait to be misunderstood a second time.

Rise and make your bed. Then the strangest instruction in the chapter. The Greek can also mean, prepare a meal for yourself, spread your own table, and either way the point is the same. Consider it as the first command given to a man who has not stood up for eight years. Not run, or leap, or go and tell somebody, but make your own bed: do for yourself what others have done for you all these years. It is the ordinary domestic gesture by which a man signals that the illness is over. There is nothing to arrange around any more. And immediately he rose.

And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. Then Luke widens the shot. Sharon is not a town but the whole fertile coastal plain running north, so this is a district-wide result from one man getting off a mat in a market town on a main road. Luke is describing a movement across a region, not conducting a census. But the mechanism is easy to see. Everybody within a day’s travel had known about Aeneas for eight years. He was the case that could not be argued with, and he was standing in the street. The sign led to faith, and the faith was in the Lord, not in Peter.

Does Christ still heal like this through his ministers? Christ still heals and answers prayer as he wills. But healings like Aeneas’ and the raising of Dorcas at Joppa were apostolic signs confirming the gospel as it spread. Many Christians believe such gifts continue; the more likely reading is that they belonged to the apostolic age, and that no minister today may claim them.

A word to the reader still on the mat. A passage like this can be quietly cruel if it is left to speak alone. Aeneas was healed after eight years; a great many faithful people are not healed after eighty. Paul, whom Luke the physician travelled with, left a colleague behind ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and carried a thorn in the flesh that was never removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Nothing in this chapter suggests that Aeneas had more faith than anybody else on the plain, or indeed any faith at all; he is not recorded as saying a word. What the passage establishes is not a method but an authority, and the authority has not diminished. The timing is not ours to hold, and the day is coming when the whole plain of Sharon gets up.

Then should I still pray for healing? Yes, and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them (James 5:14–15), and God often heals in answer to prayer, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them. What we may not do is claim a guarantee, or tell a sick believer that his illness continues because his faith is weak. Pray as Jesus did in the garden: ask plainly for what you want, and add, not my will, but yours, be done. If healing comes, give Christ the glory. If it does not, he has promised grace sufficient for the weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), and a resurrection body that will never be ill again.

In a sentence. Peter said to him that Jesus Christ was healing him and told him to get up and make his bed, and at once he got up, and everyone who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. When something good happens to you, a recovery, an answered prayer, a crisis averted, say out loud whose doing it was, as Peter did. Jesus Christ did this. And if you are still waiting on a healing that has not come, keep bringing it to him, and let the church carry you in prayer as Aeneas’s family carried him for eight years.

For worship. Jesus Christ heals. He healed then by a word through his apostle, and he heals now as he wills, in answer to his people’s prayers. And every healing in this age is a down payment on the morning when he will make all things new, when every invalid will rise and make his bed for the last time, and there will be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain. He is the Lord of the body as well as the soul, and he will raise every one of his people whole.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.

Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha. Luke does something here that he does nowhere else in the New Testament, and the Greek shows it where English cannot. He calls her a disciple, and he uses the feminine form of the word, mathētria, which occurs in no other verse of the Bible. There was a perfectly serviceable masculine term he could have used, as he does of everybody else. For Tabitha he reached for a form nobody else ever needed. And Joppa, modern Jaffa, is a town with a history: it was the port from which Jonah sailed to flee from God’s call to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3).

Which, translated, means Dorcas. Her name is given twice because she lived in a port. Tabitha in Aramaic and Dorcas in Greek both mean gazelle, and a woman with a working name in each language is a woman known in both halves of a mixed town.

She was full of good works and acts of charity. Then the description, and it is worth weighing what Luke has decided to say about her. Full of is his own particular phrase, and he has used it in this book of Stephen: full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (6:5), full of grace and power (6:8). He now uses the same construction of a woman whose recorded output is coats. Luke evidently did not consider these to be different orders of achievement. She overflowed with practical kindness: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17).

In those days she became ill and died. In half a sentence she is gone, in the middle of a chapter full of healings, with an apostle eleven miles away. Luke does not soften it or account for it. The New Testament, often accused of promising too much, records the sudden death of its most useful woman in a few words and moves on.

Her Lord’s compassion, stitched. Tabitha’s needle was doing in Joppa what her Lord had done in Galilee and Jerusalem. Luke’s Gospel is full of widows and of Jesus’ care for them: he saw the two small coins a poor widow dropped into the offering and praised her above the rich (Luke 21:1–4); he condemned the teachers who devoured widows’ houses (Luke 20:47); and John records that from the cross he provided for his own mother (John 19:26–27). The God of Israel had always called himself father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). Her coats were not a side-activity of discipleship. They were the likeness of Christ, made in cloth.

And when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. The last detail is the one to notice. In that climate burial followed death within the day; washing the body and laying it out was the first act, and interment ordinarily came next. They did the first and stopped. They put her upstairs, and they sent two men down the road. Nobody says why, and everybody knows why. They were hoping.

Why does God take his most useful servants? Scripture does not give us the reason in Tabitha’s case, and it would be presumption to invent one. What it does tell us is that our days are written in God’s book before one of them comes to be (Psalm 139:16), and that usefulness is not a shield against death. Godly people die young, and wicked men sometimes live long. The comfort is not that we can explain it but that the one who holds the days is good, and that for the believer, to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). The church in Joppa grieved as people who loved her, and they were right to. But they did not grieve as those who have no hope.

In a sentence. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which in Greek is Dorcas, who was always doing good and helping the poor, but at that time she became ill and died, and they washed her body and laid it in an upstairs room.

On a Tuesday. Be full of good works. Not famous ones, but the kind that can be held up in a room after you are gone: the meal, the coat, the visit, the note. A life of quiet kindness is precious to God. Ask what one thing you could make or do this week for someone who has no one to provide for them.

For worship. Christ sees the needle and thread. The Lord who will judge the world by what was done for the least of his brothers counted every garment Tabitha stitched as made for him. He does not rank his servants by the size of their stage, and he names a seamstress in a port town in the same breath as the first martyr. Our God is the God of small and faithful things, and nothing done in love for him is ever lost.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.”

Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him. Eleven miles between Lydda and Joppa: a few hours on foot each way, which means the messengers have a long day’s round trip and a body upstairs in a warm climate. They send two men, which is the formal number for a delegation and also the practical number for a road.

Please come to us without delay. The message they carry is six words long. Now notice what it does not say. It does not say what for. It does not ask Peter to raise her; it does not mention prayer, or even name the woman. They have washed a corpse, declined to bury it, and sent for an apostle with an urgent request that says nothing about what they want him to do when he arrives. They had heard of Aeneas. Luke, who could easily have told us what they were thinking, leaves the sentence exactly as short as they sent it.

How people pray at the worst moments. Not with a clear petition properly framed, but with an urgent, half-formed sentence that cannot bring itself to ask for the thing it wants, because the thing is too large to say out loud. Come quickly is very often the whole of it. God is not put off by a badly drafted request. He had already told Moses that he heard the groaning of people who had not managed to compose a prayer at all (Exodus 2:23–25), and Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). What these disciples had was a dead friend, a road, and a conviction they could not articulate that it was worth fetching the man who knew Jesus. That turned out to be sufficient.

Joppa again. Luke’s readers would have known the town’s one famous story. Joppa is the port where a prophet, ordered to preach to Gentiles, went down to the harbour and took ship in the opposite direction. Peter is about to spend many days there, and on a roof in that town he will be told three times to take and eat what he has spent his life refusing, and will say no, before getting up and going to a Gentile house. Luke does not point at the parallel. But of all the ports on that coast, the call to the nations comes a second time at Joppa, and this time the man goes.

Something greater than Jonah. What makes the difference is not that Peter is braver than Jonah. It is that the greater Jonah has come. Jesus called himself the sign of Jonah to his generation and said, something greater than Jonah is here (Luke 11:29–32). The prophet who sailed from Joppa went down into the deep against his will, came up, and preached to Gentiles grudgingly. The Son of Man went down into death willingly, rose on the third day, and sent his own message to the nations with joy. The call that goes out from Joppa a second time is his call, and the one who now gives it has already been to the depths and back for the people he is calling.

In a sentence. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him to urge him to come to them without delay.

On a Tuesday. In your grief, send for help. Do not wait until you can pray properly or explain what you need. Call a friend, call your pastor, call on the Lord with the six words you have. And if you are the one sent for, go without delay, even if you do not know what you will say when you get there.

For worship. The Lord hears the prayer that cannot finish its own sentence. Come to us without delay was all a frightened church could manage, and it was enough, because the one they were really sending for was not Peter but the Lord who had stood at other deathbeds and spoken. Our Saviour does not wait for us to pray well. He knows what the half-sentence means, and he answers the longing beneath the words with more than anyone in that house had dared to ask.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.

So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. He goes, and the scene that meets him upstairs is the most affecting in the chapter.

All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. They are holding up the clothes. Not describing them; holding them out for Peter to look at, one after another, while they cry. It is the sort of detail nobody invents, and it is almost certainly what somebody in that room remembered decades later when Luke asked. Her love had been made visible in cloth. Many a church sewing circle since has been named after her.

Who these women were. Consider them. A widow in that world without a son had no income, no legal standing to speak of, and nothing between her and destitution but charity. They are the same class of people whose neglect had caused the first crisis in the church three chapters back, when the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution (6:1). Here in a port town a woman had made it her business, personally, with her own hands, and the evidence is being waved in an upper room. Luke recorded the failure. He records the remedy too, and the remedy has a name.

But Peter put them all outside. Then Peter clears the room, and every move he makes is one he has seen before. He put them all outside, as his Lord had done in a house in Galilee where a twelve-year-old girl lay dead and the mourners laughed at him (Mark 5:40). Peter had been there, one of only three disciples allowed in.

Tabitha, arise. He turned to the body and spoke to it. And what he said, very likely in Aramaic, was Tabitha, koum, one letter away from Talitha koum, the two words Jesus had said to Jairus’s daughter with Peter standing in the room (Mark 5:41). He is doing what he watched being done. That is not imitation in any hollow sense; it is a man reaching for the only precedent he has, in the same language, in almost the same words, because he was there when it worked.

And knelt down and prayed. But one thing he does that his Lord did not, and it is the difference between them. Jesus put the mourners out and took the child’s hand and told her to get up; there is no prayer in that account because there did not need to be. Peter has to ask. He kneels on the floor of a room containing a dead woman and requests something he has no power whatever to perform, and only then turns round and speaks. It is a small distinction and the whole of apostolic ministry sits inside it. The words are nearly identical and the authority is entirely borrowed.

And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. Simple, vivid detail. The first face she sees is not the one she might have expected, and Luke, who loves such touches, lets us see it through her eyes.

In a sentence. Peter went with them, and when he arrived they took him upstairs, where all the widows stood around him weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them, but Peter sent them all out, knelt down and prayed, and turning to the body said, “Tabitha, arise,” and she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.

On a Tuesday. Before you try to help anyone in a crisis, kneel. Peter, who had seen Jesus raise the dead, still knew he had nothing of his own to give. Whatever room you are walking into this week, a hospital ward, a difficult meeting, a grieving home, pray first and speak second, and remember that every good thing you bring is borrowed.

For worship. The Lord of life works through his servants’ prayers. He is the one who said to a dead girl, Little girl, arise, and to a widow’s son at Nain, Young man, I say to you, arise, and to a friend four days in the tomb, Lazarus, come out. When Peter knelt in Joppa he was kneeling before that Lord. Death has no word that Christ cannot answer, and every resurrection in his name is an echo of his own.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.

And he gave her his hand and raised her up. The last thing Peter does is the most ordinary: she has been dead and is now sitting on a bed, and a man puts out his hand and helps her to her feet, exactly as anyone would. It is what Peter did for the lame man at the temple gate (3:7), and what Jesus did for Peter’s own mother-in-law (Mark 1:31).

Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. Then he opens the door. They had been put outside a few minutes earlier in tears with an armful of clothes. Luke does not describe what happened next, and there was no need. And the phrase he uses is worth noticing. Presented her alive is the language Luke used of Jesus presenting himself alive to his apostles after his suffering (1:3). It is a picture of resurrection, and of whose resurrection lies behind this one.

The hard thing. Something has to be said, or the passage becomes an instrument of cruelty. Tabitha was raised. Every other Christian who died in Joppa that year stayed dead. Luke records two resurrections in the whole of Acts (here and Eutychus, 20:9–12) and the deaths of many believers, including James, one of the Twelve, executed by Herod with no rescue, in the same chapter in which prayer brought Peter out of prison (12:1–11). Whatever this passage is, it is not a description of what God routinely does when his people ask, and no one should be handed it as though it were.

A sign, not the destination. What it is, is a sign: not the destination but a board at the roadside with the destination’s name on it. Tabitha herself proves it, because she died again, and at her second funeral nobody sent to Lydda. What she was given was not immortality. It was a few more years of making coats, and a demonstration, in one upper room on one afternoon, of what the God of the resurrection intends to do universally and at once.

Where the comfort lies. That is where the comfort lies. The point is not that God might do this again for the person you have lost. The point is that he has announced, in a room in a port town, in front of witnesses who told a doctor about it, what he means to do for everybody who belongs to him. The widows got their friend back for a while. They will get her back for good.

Will we know our loved ones again? Scripture gives good reason to think so. Paul comforts grieving Christians not with a vague hope but with a reunion: the dead in Christ will rise, and we will be caught up together with them, and so we will always be with the Lord, therefore encourage one another (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). That comfort would mean nothing if we did not know each other. Moses and Elijah were known on the mount of transfiguration, and the risen Jesus was recognised by his friends. We will be changed, made like Christ, but not made into strangers. The widows of Joppa will hold Dorcas’s hands again, and they will know whose hands they are.

In a sentence. He gave her his hand and helped her to her feet, and then, calling the saints and the widows, he presented her to them alive.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving a believer who has died, do not let this story become a reproach, as though you had not prayed hard enough. Let it become a promise. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 aloud this week, and say the name of the one you have lost alongside it. One day Christ will take your hand and raise you, and present you alive to all his people.

For worship. The Lord Jesus presented himself alive after his suffering, by many proofs, and because he lives, we shall live also. The hand Peter held out in Joppa was a picture of a greater hand, the pierced hand of the Son of God, which will reach into every grave where his people lie and raise them up. On that morning he will call the saints and widows of every age and present them alive, all of them together, for ever. Death will be swallowed up in victory, and the God who did it in one upper room will do it for the whole creation.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.

And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. The pattern of the whole section: the sign is not the point, the sign gets a hearing, and what people believe in is the Lord rather than the apostle.

And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner. The last verse of the chapter reads like travel administration and is nothing of the sort. A tanner turned the hides of dead animals into leather, curing them in solutions that included urine and dung. The work brought him into constant contact with carcasses, which under the law of Moses made a man unclean (Leviticus 11:39–40), and the stench carried; later Jewish law required tanneries to stand outside the town, downwind. A tanner’s house was where the town ended. And Peter, an observant Jew who will shortly tell the Lord that he has never eaten anything common or unclean (10:14), moves in and stays for weeks.

The touch that cleanses. Peter is learning the way of his Master. In Luke’s Gospel Jesus stretched out his hand and touched a leper (Luke 5:13), and he touched the bier of a dead young man at Nain (Luke 7:14), both things the law said would make a man unclean. But when Jesus touched the unclean, the uncleanness did not pass to him; his cleanness passed to them. The leper was cleansed, and the dead man sat up. Peter, lodging among carcasses, is not compromising the holiness of God. He is following the Holy One who came to the unclean, and who is about to send him into a Gentile house to do the same.

The house before the roof. Luke has put the tanner’s address at the end of the chapter deliberately, because of what happens at the beginning of the next. On the roof of that house, over that smell, Peter will fall into a trance and see a sheet let down full of every kind of animal, and be told to kill and eat, and will refuse, and be told not to call common what God has made clean. The vision that opens the door to the Gentile world is given to a man who is already, without quite having noticed it, sleeping under a roof no scrupulous Pharisee would have entered. Cornelius’s messengers will find him at exactly this address (10:6). That is generally how God moves people. Not by winning the argument first and relocating them afterwards, but by getting them into the house, and then asking the question, on the roof, at midday, when the answer has already been half-conceded by the address on the letter.

Whose house would you not stay in? It is worth asking. Not in theory, where everybody is generous, but in practice: the address that would need explaining, the household whose habits or history or trade would make it awkward. Peter had not yet worked out his theology of clean and unclean; he had merely accepted an invitation from a man who worked with dead animals. The theology came later, on the roof, and it came to a man who was already in the building.

Does this mean every scruple is just prejudice? No. Some lines are drawn by God’s word, and those we must keep whatever it costs: Christians may not join in idolatry or sexual sin, however welcoming the house. But many of our lines are drawn by custom, class, culture or temperament, and Christ is constantly stepping over them. The test is to ask, honestly and with an open Bible, whether a thing you avoid is forbidden by God or merely unfamiliar to you (Romans 14:1–4, 14). Peter’s food laws had once been God’s command, and in Christ they had been fulfilled and set aside (Mark 7:19). How much more should we hold loosely the barriers that were never commanded at all.

In a sentence. This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord, and Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.

On a Tuesday. Accept the invitation you would normally find a reason to decline: the meal with the neighbour whose life is a mess, the coffee with the colleague from a different background, the visit to the household the church tends to forget. You do not need to have worked out a theology of it first. Go in, and let the Lord teach you on the roof.

For worship. The bodies of the animals whose blood was brought into the holy place were burned outside the camp, and so Jesus also suffered outside the gate, to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). The Son of God went to the place where the town ended, the place of carcasses and shame, and made it the door into the household of God. The Lord who led Peter to a tanner’s house at the edge of Joppa was leading his gospel to the Gentiles, and to us. Blessed be the one who went outside so that outsiders could be brought in.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean — a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
This is one of the turning points of Acts, so important that Luke tells it twice (again in chapter 11) and Peter retells it at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11). The gospel has reached Samaritans and one Ethiopian; now it reaches Gentiles as Gentiles. Cornelius is a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, a “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God, prayed at the Jewish hours of prayer and gave generously to Jewish causes, but had not become a Jew by circumcision. In a vision at three in the afternoon an angel tells him that God has noticed his prayers and gifts, and that he should send to Joppa for Simon Peter.

The next day at noon, on a flat rooftop in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet let down from heaven full of animals the law of Moses called unclean, and hears a voice telling him to kill and eat. He refuses, and the voice answers: “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happens three times. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius’s messengers arrive, and the Spirit tells him to go with them. Peter, who earlier would never have entered a Gentile’s house, goes to Caesarea, finds a house full of Cornelius’s relatives and friends, and declares that God shows no partiality. He preaches Jesus: anointed with the Spirit, doing good and healing, killed on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles, they speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter’s Jewish companions are astonished. Peter asks who could refuse them water for baptism, and they are baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion at Caesarea, is told by an angel to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day Peter, praying on a rooftop at noon, sees a sheet full of animals the law called unclean and hears a voice telling him to eat; when he refuses, the voice says three times that he must not call unclean what God has made clean. Cornelius’s messengers arrive, the Spirit tells Peter to go with them, and he travels to Caesarea, where he enters a Gentile home full of people waiting to hear him. Peter declares that God shows no favouritism and accepts people from every nation who fear him. He tells them about Jesus: anointed by the Spirit, doing good and healing, put to death on a cross, raised on the third day, seen by chosen witnesses, appointed judge of all, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on all the Gentiles listening, to the astonishment of Peter’s Jewish companions, and Peter has them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The food laws had never been about digestion. They were about difference — a daily, three-times-a-day mechanism for keeping Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, and they worked, which is why a devout Jew could not eat at a Gentile table without the whole arrangement collapsing. Reformed theology has read the vision as the retirement of a shadow rather than the repeal of a word: the separation was always temporary, always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled the moment the dividing wall of hostility came down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). What is striking is the order in which Peter learned it. He did not reason his way from Christology to table fellowship. He was given a command he found repellent, obeyed it under protest, and worked out the theology afterwards — which is worth remembering by anyone who assumes conviction always precedes obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a direct instruction from the Spirit, three men at the gate and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. And even then the church argued about it for a chapter and a half. Now: The instinct to take the gospel to people like ourselves is not usually held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter did not have an opinion about Gentiles that could be corrected. He had a lifetime of habit, and it took God three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.

Meaning first. Acts 10 is the great turning point of the book: the gospel goes to the Gentiles. God prepares both sides: Cornelius, a Roman officer, through an angel; Peter, a Jewish apostle, through a vision. Peter preaches Christ, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles as he did at Pentecost, and they are baptised. Luke tells the story at length, and Peter retells it twice (11:1–18; 15:7–11), because it settles for ever that Gentiles are welcomed into God’s people by faith in Christ, without becoming Jews first. Over the whole chapter stands one sentence of Peter’s: Jesus Christ is Lord of all (v. 36).

At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius. Luke introduces the man carefully, and every detail is chosen to make him the hardest possible case in the best possible way. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod the Great with a harbour, a theatre and a temple to the emperor, and named after Caesar Augustus. Pilate governed from there; a stone bearing his name was found in its theatre in 1961. It was the most Roman city in the land.

A centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort. A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers and in practice about eighty: the professional backbone of the Roman army. Cornelius is the occupation. Whatever a Jewish reader felt about Rome, the taxes, the standards, the crucifixions, this is the man who enforces it. And yet the centurions of the New Testament are consistently portrayed well, like the one whose faith astonished Jesus (Luke 7:2–10).

A devout man who feared God with all his household. Then four things which make him, by any standard of first-century Judaism, an exemplary man. He is devout. He fears God with all his household, having brought his family and servants with him into it. He gives alms generously to the people, which in Luke means the Jewish people, so a Roman officer was funding the poor of the nation he garrisoned. And he prays continually to God.

A God-fearer. What he is not is a convert. He belonged to a recognised category: the God-fearer, the Gentile who attached himself to the synagogue, believed in the God of Israel, kept what he could of the moral law and gave to the poor, but had not been circumcised and so remained, formally, outside. There were many such men around the synagogues of the empire, and they occupied an uncomfortable middle ground: too Jewish for their Roman friends, never quite Jewish enough for the congregation.

The best Gentile in the empire. So Luke has assembled him: sincere, generous, prayerful, respected by the people he had power over, and bringing his whole household with him. If moral seriousness and religious sincerity were enough, this is the man they would be enough for. Yet the angel does not tell him he is fine. He tells him to send thirty miles down the coast for a fisherman with something to say. That cuts two ways at once. Nothing Cornelius had done had earned him anything, and God had noticed every bit of it, and was already moving.

The rank that stood at the cross. Luke’s readers have met this rank before, at the foot of a cross. A centurion oversaw the crucifixion of Jesus, watched him die, and praised God, saying, Certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47). Now, in the capital of the province that executed him, another centurion is praying to the God of Israel without knowing the name of the man his fellow officer saw die. Before the chapter ends he will hear that the man hanged on a tree is Lord of all, Judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness (vv. 36–43). The best Gentile in the empire needed exactly what the worst needed: not more devotion, but Christ.

In a sentence. In Caesarea lived Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian Cohort, a devout man who with his whole household feared God, gave generously to the people and prayed to God constantly.

On a Tuesday. God sees those who seek him, even outside the church: the colleague who asks careful questions, the neighbour who says she prays but has never heard the gospel, the decent man who gives more to charity than you do. Do not assume they are fine, and do not assume they are far away. Pray that God will send them the gospel, and be ready to be the one he sends.

For worship. The God of Israel saw a Roman soldier praying in a garrison town and did not despise his reaching. He is the God who made of one blood every nation of men, who is not far from each one of us (17:26–27), and who had already purposed, before the foundation of the world, to gather a people from every tribe and tongue. Cornelius was groping in the half-light. The Lord of all was coming to meet him.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.

About the ninth hour of the day. Three in the afternoon, which is one of the Jewish hours of prayer: the hour of the evening sacrifice, when the smoke went up in Jerusalem and devout men everywhere turned toward it (3:1). A Roman officer in a Roman garrison town was keeping Jewish prayer times, and the angel arrived while he was doing it.

He saw clearly in a vision an angel of God. Luke is careful: not a dream, not an impression. And Cornelius’s reaction is not devotional pleasure. He stared at him in terror, as every person in Scripture does who meets an angel. A professional soldier was frightened rigid, and he asked what it was, and called the messenger Lord.

Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. The message has been misread in both directions, so read it slowly. The vocabulary is taken from the sacrificial system. A memorial, mnēmosynon, was the portion of the grain offering that the priest burned on the altar, the token by which the whole offering came before God (Leviticus 2:2). So the angel tells an uncircumcised Roman soldier, who could not have carried a sacrifice past the outer court, that his prayers and his money have gone up like an offering God has noticed. The psalmist had prayed that his prayer would be counted as incense before God (Psalm 141:2). Cornelius’s had been.

The hour Jesus died. The ninth hour had gained a new meaning, though Cornelius did not know it. A few years earlier, about the ninth hour, Jesus had cried out with a loud voice and breathed his last outside Jerusalem (Luke 23:44–46). So a Gentile was keeping the hour of the evening sacrifice without knowing that the true sacrifice had already been offered. His prayers rose like the memorial portion; but a memorial is only a token, and it is the sacrifice that atones. The angel sends him to a man who will tell him of the Lamb whose once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:10) is the reason any sinner’s prayer can be welcome before God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean his prayers and alms earned salvation. If they had, he would not need to send for Peter to hear the message by which he would be saved (11:14). The chapter exists precisely because he still needed a preacher. God honoured his seeking by sending him the gospel. Those who seek God sincerely will find him, through Christ (Hebrews 11:6; Jeremiah 29:13).

Nothing is lost. But neither is God indifferent to the groping of an honest man. The prayers of a Gentile who did not know the gospel went up, were noticed and were remembered, and God answered them by arranging a journey. That is a comfort to anyone praying for someone nowhere near the faith, or who fears that his own years of half-informed prayer, before he understood anything, have simply evaporated. Cornelius’s had not.

Does God hear the prayers of people who are not yet Christians? The Bible says plainly that no one comes to the Father except through Christ (John 14:6), and that the prayers of the wicked who despise him are an abomination (Proverbs 15:8). But God is not deaf to the cry of a person whom he is drawing to himself, and this verse shows him hearing such a cry and answering it, by sending the gospel. He does not answer it by saving the man without Christ; he answers it by bringing him to Christ. So if you are not yet a believer and have been praying in the dark, keep seeking. The answer God gives to that kind of prayer is himself, in his Son, through his word.

In a sentence. About three in the afternoon he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God come in and call his name, and staring at him in terror he asked what it was, and the angel said his prayers and gifts to the poor had gone up as a memorial before God.

On a Tuesday. Keep praying for the person who seems furthest from God. You may never see the answer arrive, and it may come by a road you would not have chosen, but nothing offered in faith is wasted. And if you have a time of prayer, keep it as Cornelius kept his, even on the days when nothing seems to happen. The angel came at the ninth hour.

For worship. God remembers. The God who counted the tears of David, who heard Hagar in the wilderness and Hannah at the door of the tabernacle, saw the prayers of a Roman soldier rising and kept every one. He answers in his time, and by his gospel, and his answers are always better than the prayers that asked for them. Cornelius asked for light. God sent him Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.

And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. An angel is standing in the room, and what he brings is an address. Here is a genuine messenger from heaven, speaking to a man who wants God, and he does not preach the gospel. He does not explain about Jesus, or the cross, or forgiveness. He gives a name, a town, a householder and a street.

On human breath. Angels in Scripture announce, warn, guide and rescue. They do not evangelise. God’s settled arrangement is that the news of salvation travels on human breath, from someone who has it to someone who has not (Romans 10:14). It would have been simpler to let the angel say it; instead the whole apparatus of heaven is deployed to get a fisherman onto a road. We have this treasure in jars of clay (2 Corinthians 4:7). That is a great dignity conferred on ordinary Christians, and a great responsibility.

The name Jesus gave him. The angel uses the name Jesus had given. Simon was called Cephas, Peter, the rock, by Christ at their first meeting (John 1:42), and to this man, after he confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, the Lord promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:16–19). Those keys are turned by the preaching of the gospel. Peter turned them for Jews at Pentecost (2:14–41), and he is about to turn them for Gentiles in Caesarea. So even the address points to Christ: Cornelius is to send for the man whom Jesus named and commissioned, and what that man carries is the confession on which Christ builds his church.

He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea. The directions are almost comic in their precision. The angel distinguishes the two Simons, knows the second one’s trade, and knows the house is by the sea, as tanneries were, needing water and keeping their smell downwind of the town. God’s guidance in this chapter has a postcode.

Enough to act on. And Cornelius is not told why, or what Peter will say, or that this errand will open the whole future of the church. He is told to send for a man, and he sends. Most obedience arrives in that condition: enough instruction to act on and no explanation at all.

Why did God not just let the angel tell him the gospel? Because God has chosen to spread the news of his Son through people who have received it themselves. A preacher who has been forgiven speaks of forgiveness as no angel can, for angels have never needed a Saviour. And the message binds the church together: the Gentile is brought in by the Jew, the hearer by the speaker, so that no one can boast of having found the way alone. It also means the job is yours. If an angel would not do it in Caesarea, an angel will not do it in your street.

In a sentence. The angel told him to send men to Joppa to bring back Simon called Peter, who was staying with Simon, a tanner, whose house was by the sea.

On a Tuesday. God has given the gospel to people like you to tell. Angels cannot do it for you. Think of one person who may be waiting for exactly what you know, and ask God for an opening to say it this week. You do not need the whole plan; you need the next address.

For worship. The Lord of hosts, who commands myriads of angels, has chosen to send the best news in the universe by fishermen, tentmakers and ordinary church members. He is not short of messengers. He delights to honour weak servants with the greatest errand there is, so that the glory belongs to him and the power is plainly his.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.

When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier. Then, immediately, action. Cornelius does not sleep on it or wait to see whether the impression fades by morning. The angel goes and he calls for staff.

A devout soldier from among those who attended him. Luke troubles to tell us the soldier was devout, a small window into this household. Verse 2 said Cornelius feared God with all his household, and here is the corroboration: a man under his command shared his faith closely enough to be trusted with an errand of this kind.

And having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. He did not send them with an instruction; he sent them with the whole story. The angel, the hour, the message, the fear: a senior officer in a rigidly hierarchical profession sat his subordinates down and told them what had happened to him while he was praying.

Why it mattered. It is a small thing, and it explains a great deal about the welcome Peter gets four days later. The men can give an account of Cornelius that persuades an apostle to travel, and Peter arrives to find a room full of relatives and friends already assembled and briefed. That happened because a man who had received something extraordinary told the people around him. Joppa lay about thirty miles down the coast, a day and a half on foot, and Cornelius staked four days of waiting, and his reputation, on one conversation with a stranger in bright clothing.

As the other centurion sent. Luke’s readers have seen a centurion send messengers before. At Capernaum a centurion with a dying servant sent elders, and then friends, to Jesus, saying he was not worthy to have him under his roof and asking him only to say the word (Luke 7:3–7). Jesus marvelled at him and healed the servant from a distance. Cornelius sends for the same reason: he needs what only Jesus can give. But Jesus is no longer on the road to Capernaum. He is risen and reigning, and he comes to a Gentile house now in the word his servants preach. That is how the Lord of all will enter Caesarea, and it is enough, because the word is still his.

In a sentence. When the angel who had spoken to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from his attendants, told them everything that had happened, and sent them to Joppa.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks to you through his word, do not delay, and do not keep it to yourself. Tell the people closest to you what he has been showing you: your spouse, your children, the colleague who shares your faith. Obedience that is spoken about tends to spread.

For worship. Cornelius obeyed at once, and behind his obedience stood the God who had made him willing. The Lord who sent an angel to a soldier was also at work in his servants and in the devout man under his command, building a household that would be ready for the gospel. He prepares whole families for his grace, and he loves to save them together.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance

The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city. Luke does something here that he does all through this chapter: he cuts between the two ends of the story and lines up the timing so the reader can see the machinery. The messengers are perhaps an hour away, and Peter’s vision comes just as they arrive. God’s timing is not approximate.

Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. The roof was the coolest and most private place in an eastern house: flat, reached by an outside stair, used for sleeping in hot weather and for drying things, often shaded with an awning. It was where a man went to be alone. And the sixth hour is noon. The fixed hours of prayer at the temple were the morning and the afternoon sacrifices, but the devout also prayed at midday (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10). Peter has gone up to pray in the middle of the day, as he did most days.

And he became hungry and wanted something to eat. Then the unspiritual detail that Luke refuses to leave out. It is noon, the meal is cooking downstairs, and in the gap between the hunger and the food, God speaks. It would be easy to make too much of that and a pity to make nothing of it. A hungry man waiting for lunch already has food on his mind, and what is about to come down is a sheet full of animals with an instruction to kill and eat. The revelation arrives in the vocabulary Peter’s body has just supplied.

But while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance. The word is ekstasis, a state in which ordinary perception is suspended and God communicates directly, as he did with Paul in the temple (22:17). The most consequential vision in Acts, the one that opens the church to the whole non-Jewish world, is given to a man on a roof, in a borrowed house that smelt of tanning, at midday, while he waited for lunch. Nothing had been arranged. He had simply gone up to pray.

What Jesus went on doing. Luke opened this book by calling his Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1), which means that Acts is what he goes on doing from heaven. That is the hand behind the timing here. The Lord who told these apostles they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8) is now moving the last stage himself, setting a hungry apostle on a roof as the Gentiles reach the gate. Not long before, Peter had told a paralysed man at Lydda, Jesus Christ heals you (9:34). The same Jesus is at work in Joppa, keeping his word to the nations.

In a sentence. The next day, as the messengers were nearing the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray at about noon, and he became hungry and wanted something to eat, and while the food was being prepared he fell into a trance.

On a Tuesday. Peter was praying when God spoke. Keep your times of prayer, especially the unremarkable ones in the middle of a working day. You are not waiting for a vision; you are keeping company with the God who speaks through his word, and he often meets his people in the most ordinary hour.

For worship. The God who rules the timing of the universe arranged that a sheet would come down from heaven over a tanner’s roof at the very hour three Gentiles reached the gate. He works on rooftops and on roads at once. Not a sparrow falls without him, and not a lunch is cooked in Joppa outside his care, and every one of those threads was being drawn toward the cross of his Son and the gathering of the nations.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for prayer and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.

And saw the heavens opened. Luke uses that phrase very sparingly and always at a moment when something changes permanently: at the Jordan when the Spirit came down on Jesus (Luke 3:21), and in a council chamber when Stephen looked up and saw the Son of Man standing (7:56). It is not decorative language. It means the boundary has been crossed from the other side. The vision comes from God.

Something like a great sheet descending. What comes through is a household object. The something like is Luke’s habitual honesty when a witness describes an unfamiliar thing by the nearest familiar one: a large square of cloth, such as would lie about on that roof, or a sail like those in the harbour below.

Being let down by its four corners upon the earth. Four corners is a phrase with a history. The prophets speak of God gathering the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12), and the four corners are a standard way of saying everywhere, from every direction, the whole inhabited world. Peter is watching something being lowered toward him that is held at the four points of the compass, and it will be full of every kind of living creature. The shape of the vision is announcing its subject before a word is spoken: all nations.

It comes down. The direction of travel is the thing to hold. Peter does not go up, is not caught away, is not given a tour of anything. He is on a roof and heaven descends to where he is standing, which is exactly what the rest of the chapter is about: God moving toward people who could not have come to him, and doing it on their own roofs, at lunchtime.

Why heaven stands open. Every other opened heaven in Luke’s two books has Jesus at its centre: the Spirit descending on him at the Jordan, the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand for Stephen. Jesus had told Nathanael that he would see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man (John 1:51). He is Jacob’s ladder, the one way between heaven and earth. So when heaven opens over a roof in Joppa, it is open because of him. The barrier between a holy God and the unclean nations was not lifted by a change of policy. It was removed by the Son who came down, died and ascended, and the sign that the nations are now to be gathered comes down by the way he opened.

In a sentence. He saw heaven opened and something like a great sheet coming down, being let down to earth by its four corners.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word opens something to you that you did not expect, do not reach first for the reasons it cannot mean what it says. Let it come down to where you are. The vision was not given for Peter to study from a distance; it was let down to his feet.

For worship. The Son of God is the true meeting of heaven and earth. He came down from the Father’s side without ceasing to be God, he was lifted up on a cross to draw all people to himself (John 12:32), and he went up again with a way behind him that no one can shut. Four corners held that sheet, and from the four corners of the earth he is gathering a people who could never have climbed to him. Heaven did not open for one afternoon over Joppa. Through him it stands open still.

parallels.desc: the heavens were opened

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. The three categories are the ones Genesis uses at the creation and Leviticus uses when it draws the lines (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14), and the sheet is not a selection. It is the whole zoo: clean and unclean together, the pig beside the sheep, the vulture beside the pigeon, and creeping things which were unclean without exception. Contact with unclean creatures defiled a Jew; eating them was unthinkable.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. Then the voice, and it gives an order. Kill: not merely eat what is put in front of you, but do the butchering yourself, and from the mixed sheet. He is told to get up, take a knife and prepare a meal out of creatures he had been taught before he could walk were an offence to God.

What martyrs had died for. And it was not a marginal scruple. Under the Greek persecution two centuries earlier, mothers had watched their sons killed rather than eat pork, and the books that recorded it were treasured. Refusing unclean food was what martyrs had died for, and everybody knew the stories. So the command is an instruction to do the very thing faithful Israelites had gone to their deaths refusing to do, and it comes from heaven, from a voice Peter will call Lord. That is why the next verse holds one of the most understandable refusals in Scripture, and why God has to say it three times.

The one whom uncleanness could not touch. The command makes sense only because of who had come. Under the law, uncleanness spread: touch a leper or a corpse and you were defiled. Then Jesus touched a leper, and the leprosy left him (Luke 5:13). He took a dead girl by the hand, and she rose (Luke 8:54). A woman unclean for twelve years touched his garment, and she did not make him unclean; he made her whole (Luke 8:43–48). In him holiness ran the other way. The food laws had trained Israel to guard the clean from the unclean. Now the Holy One himself had come, and his cleanness was the stronger.

The animals were the vehicle; the freight was people. One guard, because this passage is pressed into service for arguments it was not given for. It does bear on what Christians may eat: the New Testament is clear that no food is unclean in itself, and Mark says so in an aside (Mark 7:19). But Peter himself tells us what the vision was for, and it is not a menu: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean (v. 28). The passage is used most faithfully when it dismantles the habit the food laws had come to enforce, the sorting of human beings into those one can sit down with and those one cannot. That habit long outlived the dietary code, and it has never needed a Bible verse to keep it going.

In a sentence. In the sheet were all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles and birds, and a voice told Peter to get up, kill and eat.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes God’s word shocks our habits. Listen anyway. Ask yourself which people you instinctively sort into the category of those you would not sit down with: a class, a nationality, a political tribe, a lifestyle, a church tradition. That is where this vision is aimed in your life.

For worship. The God who drew the lines in Leviticus is the God who erased them in Christ, and he is the same God, faithful in both. He gave Israel the food laws to keep her distinct until the promised Seed came, and when Christ had come and died, he lowered a sheet over a roof in Joppa and declared the meaning fulfilled. His purposes run straight through the centuries, and they were always heading for a table with every nation at it.
verseByVerse.note: The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all of which Peter is told to eat.

parallels.desc: clean and unclean animals

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”

By no means, Lord. Two words that will not go together. The first is as strong a refusal as can be made: not I would rather not, but absolutely not, under no circumstances. The second is Lord. Peter has said, in a single breath, never and master, and the sentence contradicts itself before he has finished it. He stands where Ezekiel stood when he protested against eating defiled food (Ezekiel 4:14).

A recognisable habit. It is not the first time. In a boat on Galilee, after a catch of fish, Peter begged the Lord to depart from him, for he was a sinful man (Luke 5:8). At a supper table he said, You shall never wash my feet (John 13:8). On the road, when Jesus told him what would happen in Jerusalem, he said, Far be it from you, Lord (Matthew 16:22). He is the disciple who tells Jesus what will not be happening, and calls him Lord while doing it.

Jonah’s port. There is a precedent for this refusal in this very town. Joppa was where Jonah went down to find a ship going the other way when God sent him to Gentile Nineveh (Jonah 1:3). Centuries later a Jewish prophet in Joppa is again told to go to the Gentiles, and again his first word is no. What lies between the two men is Christ. Jesus called his own death and resurrection the sign of Jonah, three days in the heart of the earth, and said that something greater than Jonah is here (Matthew 12:39–41). The greater Jonah went down into death willingly, for the nations, and came up again. Because he did, this reluctant prophet needs no storm and no fish, only a word repeated three times.

For I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean. And the reason is not stubbornness. Common means ritually unfit, profane, for ordinary use rather than for God. Peter lays out a lifetime’s record as evidence, and every word of it is to his credit: in poverty, travelling, working as a fisherman on a lake with a mixed shoreline, he has never once done it. He is defending God’s own law, which he has kept at cost, and he is defending it against God. Even after Jesus had declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), he had not grasped it.

Holding the scaffolding. That is worth sitting with, because it is more common than it looks. What Peter cannot let go of is not a sin but an obedience, a genuine one, kept faithfully for decades. God has not grown lax; the command had a purpose, the purpose has arrived, and Peter is holding on to the scaffolding after the building is up. Most Christians who are stuck are stuck on something that was once right, was kept at cost, and has quietly become the thing they will not let God touch. Peter’s by no means, Lord is not a rebel’s sentence. It is a good man defending a good thing at the moment God is moving past it.

How do I tell a good conviction from a scaffold I should take down? Ask where it comes from and what it is for. If a conviction rests on a plain command of Scripture that still applies to Christians, keep it, whatever it costs: no vision overturns the moral law. But if it rests on a custom, a tradition, or an Old Testament ceremony that the New Testament says has been fulfilled in Christ, hold it loosely, and be ready to let it go when it starts to keep people at a distance whom Christ has welcomed. Peter did not change his mind because he felt like it; he changed because God himself spoke. We have the finished word of God for that, not new visions, and the New Testament is clear on which lines have been taken down (Colossians 2:16–17).

In a sentence. Peter replied, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”

On a Tuesday. You cannot say no and Lord in the same breath for long. Ask whether there is an area of your life where you have been saying both: a good habit that has become a wall, a preference you defend as if it were Scripture, a way of doing church that you will not let anyone question. Bring it to the word of God honestly, and let him be Lord of it.

For worship. Peter put never and Lord into one sentence, and the Lord answered the second word, not the first. That is the mercy of Christ with his servants. He hears our protests and outlasts them, not by crushing the protester but by speaking again. He had bought this man with his blood, and he would not lose him over a sheet of animals. Every believer who has argued with God and been brought round owes it to the same patient Lord, who is more determined to bring us to his yes than we have ever been to keep our no.
verseByVerse.note: “Common” means ritually unfit, profane.

parallels.desc: “I have never defiled myself”

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
