And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.

What God has made clean, do not call common. Note the tense and the agent. Not what I am now permitting, but what God has made clean: the thing has already been done, and Peter’s part is simply to stop describing it wrongly. He is not being asked to change a rule. He is being told that a fact has altered and his vocabulary is out of date.

Aimed at his mouth. And the correction is aimed at his speech: do not call common. The problem the voice addresses is not only what Peter eats but what he says about people, and within thirteen verses he will have made the translation himself in front of a room full of Gentiles: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean (v. 28). Not food only, but people. Gentiles are not unclean.

Made clean at Golgotha. The tense is past because the work is finished. The food laws had separated Israel from the nations (Leviticus 20:24–26), and Paul says that Christ abolished the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, to create in himself one new man in place of the two, and to reconcile both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). The line was not worn away by time or repealed by a council. It was fulfilled and taken down by a death, and what it had pictured is now the substance, which belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The voice on the roof is announcing an accomplished fact, and the fact has a name: Jesus Christ crucified.

Heard but not grasped. Nor is this the law being contradicted. Jesus had already said that what goes into a man cannot defile him, and Mark adds the note that in saying so he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:18–19). Peter had been standing there. He had heard it and not drawn the conclusion, which is worth knowing by anyone who assumes that hearing good teaching is the same as being changed by it. He needed it said again, from heaven, three times, with livestock.

This happened three times. It is the same number as a charcoal fire in a courtyard and three questions on a beach, and it is hard to believe Peter missed the resonance. Three times he had denied; three times he had been restored (John 21:15–17); three times now the vision comes and the command is repeated. God appears to know exactly how many repetitions this particular man requires.

And the thing was taken up at once to heaven. Then, abruptly, it is gone. The vision does not end with an application. It simply stops, leaving a man on a roof with a command he has refused, a sentence he cannot argue with and no idea what it is for. A great deal of Christian experience happens there: the instruction received and the meaning not yet arrived, and nothing to do but wait until somebody knocks at the gate.

Where Christians differ: are the food laws binding today? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jews, still keep the Old Testament food laws. Verdict: Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); this vision confirms it; Paul teaches that food is a matter of freedom (Romans 14:14, 20; 1 Timothy 4:3–5). The food laws were shadows fulfilled in Christ. Christians are free to eat anything with thanksgiving, though they should be considerate of the weaker conscience (Romans 14:15).

Then why did God give the food laws at all? Not because pork was wicked or sheep were holy, but to teach and to protect. Day by day, at every meal, the food laws taught Israel that she was set apart for a holy God, and that holiness means distinction (Leviticus 11:44–45; 20:25–26). They also kept her from being swallowed by the nations around her until the Messiah came. When Christ came, the true holiness they pictured arrived in him, and the people of God was no longer to be marked by a diet but by faith in him, gathered from every nation. The laws were not a mistake that God corrected. They were a signpost, and Peter was standing at the place it pointed to.

In a sentence. The voice spoke to him a second time, telling him not to call common what God had made clean, and this happened three times, and the sheet was taken back up to heaven at once.

On a Tuesday. Do not call unclean anyone God has made clean in Christ. Think of a Christian whose background, culture or past makes you uneasy, and ask whether you treat him as a full brother. Then do one concrete thing about it: an invitation, a phone call, a seat beside him on Sunday.

For worship. What God has made clean is clean indeed. The blood of Christ cleanses from all sin, and no one it has washed can ever be called common again. The Father declared it from heaven three times over a tanner’s roof, and he declares it still over every sinner who comes to his Son: clean, accepted, mine. Blessed be the God who does not leave us to define who is fit for him.

parallels.desc: he declared all foods clean

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.

While Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean. Thoroughly at a loss. Luke describes not a man savouring a great truth but bafflement, and he says it twice, adding a moment later that Peter was still pondering when the Spirit spoke. The apostle received a revelation from heaven, repeated three times, and did not know what it meant. He was not being slow. The vision was about food and not about food, and there was no way to get from the sheet to the Gentiles by thinking harder. The interpretation would arrive by other means.

Perplexed before. It was not the first time. Luke’s Gospel records the disciples failing again and again to understand what Jesus told them about his death: the saying was hidden from them (Luke 9:45; 18:34). The women at the empty tomb were perplexed (Luke 24:4), and the meaning came only when the risen Lord opened the disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). The same Lord is at work on this roof. He does not leave his servants holding riddles. He explains himself in his own time, and the explanation always leads back to him: the sheet will make sense in a Gentile house, while Peter is telling them about Jesus.

The men who were sent by Cornelius stood at the gate. Having asked their way to Simon’s house, they call out to ask whether Simon called Peter is lodging there. Luke wants the timing noticed: while the vision is still unresolved, its answer is standing in the street asking for Peter by name.

Understood by obeying. The meaning is delivered not by further revelation, nor by a better idea occurring to Peter on the roof, but as three men with a message: as circumstances. Peter will understand the sheet by obeying the knock, and not before. That is worth holding by anyone wrestling with a passage he cannot yet see how to apply. Peter was perplexed on a roof and the explanation was downstairs. Some things are understood only when they are acted on, and God often explains his word by his providence.

In a sentence. While Peter was wondering what the vision might mean, the men sent by Cornelius, having asked their way to Simon’s house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was staying there.

On a Tuesday. If you are puzzled by something God has plainly told you in Scripture, do not wait until you understand all of it before you obey the part you do understand. Watch for the knock at the gate: the person who arrives, the need that appears, the door that opens. The meaning is often on the other side of the next step.

For worship. The God who spoke on the roof had already sent the answer up the road. He is never late with his explanations and never early with his providences. His word and his works fit together like a key and a lock, because the same Lord governs both, and he is leading his people step by step into purposes far larger than they can see from where they stand.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.”

And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him. Three parties are being moved in this chapter, and none can see the others. Cornelius has an angel and an address; the messengers have a road and an errand; Peter has a sheet of animals and no idea what it is for. Here the wiring becomes visible. And it is not an angel who speaks now, but the Spirit himself, a person who directs, sends and commands.

Behold, three men are looking for you. The Spirit gives the number, two servants and a soldier (v. 7), and then the instruction: rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation. That phrase does more than steady Peter’s nerves. The Greek, mēden diakrinomenos, can also be rendered making no distinction. The verb means to divide, to sort one thing from another, and it is the verb Peter uses in his report at Jerusalem (11:12) and the idea he returns to at the council, where he says God made no distinction between us and them (15:9). So the Spirit’s word is not merely do not dither. It is do not sort these men into a category, and it forbids the reflex before it can operate.

For I have sent them. That last clause is the hinge of the chapter, and Peter never lets go of it. He is not told who Cornelius is, or what the vision meant, or what will happen in Caesarea: only that three men are downstairs, that he is to go with them, and that they were sent. When the Jerusalem church calls him to account a chapter later, this is what he produces: the Spirit told me to go with them. The briefing is enough because of its last clause.

The Spirit of Jesus. The Spirit who speaks on the stairs is not a free-floating influence. Peter had told the crowd at Pentecost that Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (2:33), and Luke will later call him the Spirit of Jesus (16:7). So the voice that sends Peter downstairs carries on the risen Lord’s own commission: you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses (1:8). The Spirit sends Peter to Gentiles because Christ has already claimed them, and his work, as Jesus promised, is to bear witness about Christ (John 15:26).

How does the Spirit lead Christians today? Here the Spirit spoke directly to an apostle at a turning point in the founding of the church, and we should not expect such words as our normal guidance. Today the Spirit leads us chiefly through the Scriptures he inspired, which are complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17), by opening our understanding of them, by working in our hearts a desire to obey, and by ordering our circumstances in his providence. And the direction he gives in Scripture is unmistakable on this very point: we are to make no distinction among those Christ has received. You do not need a voice on the stairs to know you should welcome the stranger at the gate.

In a sentence. While Peter was still thinking about the vision, the Spirit told him that three men were looking for him, and that he should get up, go down and go with them without hesitation, for the Spirit himself had sent them.

On a Tuesday. When the Spirit, through his word, leads you toward someone different from you, go without hesitation and without sorting. The next person who knocks at your gate, literally or otherwise, may have been sent.

For worship. The Holy Spirit is not a force but the living God, who speaks, sends and directs his church. He moved on the waters at creation, overshadowed the virgin, descended on the Son at the Jordan, and here he sends Gentiles to fetch an apostle. The whole mission of the church is his work, and he never sends his servants anywhere he has not already gone ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.”

I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming? Peter goes down and opens with a flat, practical sentence. The Spirit gave him the instruction and withheld the explanation, and he is about to get it from three strangers at a gate.

Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man. Their answer is a small masterpiece of diplomacy. Cornelius, a centurion: they lead with the awkward fact. An upright and God-fearing man: what a Jewish hearer would most want to know. Well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation: the people you fear offending already think highly of him. And the clincher: directed by a holy angel to send for you. Not, he would like a word; he was told to fetch you, from heaven. The case is made so well that they had probably rehearsed it on the road, knowing how unlikely their errand sounded.

To come to his house and to hear what you have to say. That is the whole invitation: not to be healed, advised or impressed, but to hear. A household has been assembled thirty miles away, and what it wants is words. Cornelius needs Peter’s message to be saved (11:14): not his prayers, not his alms, but the gospel. Most preachers spend their lives trying to get people to listen; here is a man who sent servants on a journey of days to secure a hearing for a message he could not yet describe. Peter was walking toward the most willing audience of his life.

The voice of the Shepherd. What Peter has to say is not a set of ideas but a person. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), and Peter’s message will be a man: anointed, crucified, raised, appointed Judge, offering forgiveness in his name (vv. 38–43). Jesus had said that he had other sheep, not of this fold, whom he must bring also, and that they would listen to his voice, so that there would be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). Some of those sheep were waiting in Caesarea. The servants at the gate were fetching more than a preacher. They were fetching the voice of the Shepherd.

In a sentence. Peter went down and told the men he was the one they were looking for and asked why they had come, and they said that Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man respected by the whole Jewish nation, had been told by a holy angel to invite Peter to his house and hear what he had to say.

On a Tuesday. The world around you is often more ready to hear about Christ than you think, and what people need from you is not your opinions but his word. If someone asks you a question about your faith this week, do not change the subject. Say what you have to say, simply and kindly.

For worship. God was gathering an audience for his Son in a Roman officer’s house before Peter had heard of it. The Father has always been drawing people to the Son (John 6:44), in places the church has not thought to look. The harvest is plentiful, and the Lord of the harvest is already at work in the field.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.

So he invited them in to be his guests. Three things happen in this verse, and two are quietly enormous. First, Peter takes two Gentile servants and a Roman soldier into the house for the night. That means beds and a meal, and a meal means a table, precisely what a devout Jew did not share with Gentiles and precisely what the vision had been about an hour earlier. Luke does not comment. The man who had said by no means, Lord before lunch had Gentiles eating in his lodgings by supper.

Obedience before understanding. Peter did not resolve his theology first and act on it afterwards; that does not come until verse 28. He obeyed a plain instruction one step at a time, and the first step was not preaching to Gentiles. It was having them in the house.

The table Jesus kept. Peter had learned this from his Master. He had watched Jesus go in to Zacchaeus while the crowd grumbled that he had gone to be the guest of a sinner (Luke 19:5–7), and recline at Levi’s feast among tax collectors, saying, I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Luke 5:29–32). Hospitality in the church is not good manners added to the gospel; it is the gospel acted out, because Christ welcomed us when we were strangers to God (Romans 15:7). The man who said by no means at noon is, by supper, doing what his Lord did.

The next day he rose and went away with them. Not that afternoon. Joppa to Caesarea is about thirty miles and the men had already walked it. He gave them a night’s rest first, which is a small kindness Luke did not have to record and did.

And some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. The third thing is the shrewdest in the chapter. At Jerusalem we learn there were six of them (11:12), and we learn it because Peter had them beside him when the church demanded an explanation. A man does not take six witnesses on a pastoral visit. Peter knew that whatever happened in Caesarea would be examined and possibly disbelieved, and that his word alone would not be enough, so he arranged in advance for six others to see it. It is not timidity or politics. It is a leader making his account checkable before anyone has asked.

Why does it matter that Peter brought witnesses? Because the gospel is not a private experience but public truth, and God wanted the church to receive the Gentiles on the basis of evidence, not on one man’s say-so. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Peter brought six. There is wisdom here for any Christian or leader involved in something sensitive: act in the open, bring others with you, keep your conduct checkable. Integrity that welcomes scrutiny protects both the leader and the people he serves.

In a sentence. So Peter invited them in as his guests, and the next day he got up and set out with them, and some of the believers from Joppa went along with him.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality often comes before the gospel. Open your home this week to someone outside your usual circle: a meal, a coffee, a bed for the night. And in any matter where your conduct might later be questioned, bring a trusted brother or sister with you, not out of suspicion, but out of love for the truth.

For worship. Christ is the host of a supper so large that his servants are sent into the roads and lanes to compel people to come in, until his house is filled (Luke 14:23). Two servants and a soldier asleep in a tanner’s house in Joppa were among the first guests brought in from the lanes of the Gentile world. He has been filling his house ever since, from every coast and every language, and he will not stop until the hall is full and the Lamb sits down with his bride at the marriage supper.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

parallels.desc: six brothers accompanied me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.

And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. He has spent four days on this: the angel, the messengers’ day and a half on the road, a night in Joppa, the walk back. Meanwhile Cornelius has been going round Caesarea inviting people to hear a man he has never met say something he cannot describe.

What it took. He is a serving officer in a garrison town, and he has told his family and friends, probably including brother officers, that an angel appeared to him at prayer and told him to send for a Jewish fisherman. If nothing came of it he would look ridiculous for years in front of everyone whose opinion mattered to him. That is faith expecting something, and love too: he wanted the people he loved to hear.

He filled a room. The first thing this man does with something from God is gather a congregation. He assumes from the outset that whatever is coming is too large to keep. The Gentile mission begins in a house full of somebody’s relatives, because a Roman soldier could not think of a reason to hear this alone.

A light for the Gentiles. Luke began his Gospel with people waiting in the temple. Simeon, waiting for the consolation of Israel, took the infant Jesus in his arms and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:25–32). Now, in the most Gentile house in Judea, a room full of people is waiting too, without knowing for what. They are waiting for the same light. Simeon held the child; this household will hear of the man he became, crucified, risen and Lord of all. Cornelius goes to the floor because he takes the messenger for the thing itself. But something worthy of worship has indeed come to his door, carried in Peter’s mouth.

Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. Then Peter arrives, and Cornelius does the wrong thing. The verb, prosekynēsen, means to prostrate oneself in reverence, the ordinary word for worship. Be fair to him. Four days ago an angel stood in his house and told him to send for this man, and in the world Cornelius grew up in, when something from heaven turns up you get on the floor. His is an error of reverence, made by a man who does not yet know what he is dealing with, and it is corrected in the next verse, immediately and kindly.

In a sentence. The following day they arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was waiting for them with the relatives and close friends he had invited, and when Peter came in, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet in worship.

On a Tuesday. Gather your family and friends to hear the gospel. Invite one person this week to come with you to church, or to a meal where Christ will be spoken of. And when you bring them, let them see that you are expecting God to speak.

For worship. The God who gathered a household in Caesarea is the God who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6). He does not save people only one by one, in isolation; he gathers them into homes and congregations, and he delights when the first thing a seeker does is call his loved ones to come and hear. The gospel was always meant to fill a room.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.”

But Peter lifted him up, saying, Stand up; I too am a man. A single sentence, and it is the whole of Christian ministry. Not, you are embarrassing me; not, this is inappropriate. I too am a man: the same kind of thing you are, on the same side of the floor, made of the same material.

He lifted him up. And he does not simply say it. He reaches down, takes hold of a Roman centurion lying on the ground, and puts him back on his feet. The first thing Peter does in the first Gentile home to hear the gospel is pick a man up off the floor.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Luke sets scenes like this against each other. Two chapters later a king in this same city will accept exactly the acclaim Peter refuses: the crowd will shout that it is the voice of a god and not of a man, Herod will take it, and Luke records his end in one unsparing verse (12:21–23). A fisherman on his feet saying I too am a man; a king on a throne saying nothing at all. Paul and Barnabas will refuse worship at Lystra (14:14–15), and the angel in Revelation refuses it from John (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9).

Harder than it looks. Cornelius’s reverence was genuine, directed at a man who had walked thirty miles to help him, and refusing it risked chilling the room. There is a false humility that deflects with one hand and enjoys the compliment with the other. Peter ends the transaction on the spot. Every ministry that lasts is built on this refusal, and every one that collapses has stopped making it somewhere.

What Jesus did not refuse. And notice the difference that shows who Jesus is. The apostles and angels refuse worship. Jesus accepted it: from the disciples in the boat who said, Truly you are the Son of God (Matthew 14:33), and from Thomas, who called him my Lord and my God (John 20:28). He never once said, Stand up; I too am a man. Either he was the most dangerous blasphemer who ever lived, or he is God.

Where Christians differ: veneration of saints and leaders. Some traditions bow before popes, saints or images. Verdict: Peter, whom Rome calls the first pope, refused to let anyone bow before him. No servant of Christ should receive the reverence due to God.

Is it wrong to honour Christian leaders? No. Scripture tells us to respect and esteem those who labour among us and are over us in the Lord, very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). The line is crossed when honour becomes reverence, when a leader is treated as beyond question, his words as equal to Scripture, or his presence as bringing us nearer to God. Healthy honour says, thank God for this man. Idolatry says, I cannot do without him. A good pastor will do what Peter did and lift you back on your feet.

In a sentence. But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.”

On a Tuesday. Do not put any Christian leader on a pedestal. They are only men and women, and the pedestal is bad for them and worse for you. And if you are the one people look up to, a parent, a teacher, a pastor, notice when you are enjoying it, and lift them up. Point them past yourself to Christ.

For worship. There is one before whom falling down is right, and he too lifts the fallen. When John fell at his feet as though dead, the risen Christ laid his right hand on him and said, Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one (Revelation 1:17–18). The servant raises us by refusing our worship. The Lord raises us while receiving it, because he is God, and his hand on the shoulder of a terrified sinner is pure kindness. Glory to the one at whose feet it is safe to fall.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.

And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. Peter walks into a Gentile house, a huge step for a Jew, sees a room full of Gentiles, and opens by naming the barrier. He does not pretend the difficulty is not there, or begin with something warm and general and hope nobody raises it.

You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation. He says it in the first sentence, to a roomful of people it applies to. They did know. Every person in that house had lived with it, and the God-fearers among them had felt it most: welcome at the synagogue door and not past it. The word athemiton means taboo, against custom, not done.

Two things about the barrier. First, the law of Moses nowhere forbids a Jew to enter a Gentile house. What had grown up was a dense hedge of custom around the purity laws, hardened by centuries of pressure, until strict Jews would not enter Gentile homes or eat with Gentiles (John 18:28; Galatians 2:12). That is why Peter can call it unlawful in ordinary speech and be understood. Second, it had once had a real purpose: a people surrounded by empires that swallowed nations whole survived by not eating with them.

But God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. Then the pivot, and Peter makes the translation himself. The vision was about animals; Peter says it was about persons, and nobody had told him that. Between the roof and this doorway, on thirty miles of coast road with three Gentiles for company, he worked out what he had been shown. Obedience came first, at the gate in Joppa; understanding caught up on the journey. No human being is unclean in God’s sight because of race or nation.

The doorway Jesus was led through. John’s Gospel gives this custom a sharp edge. On the morning of the crucifixion the chief priests would not go into the Roman governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled but could eat the Passover (John 18:28). They stood outside. Jesus was taken in. The true Passover Lamb was led across the threshold they would not cross, condemned in a Gentile house by a Gentile judge, and crucified by Gentile soldiers, for Jew and Gentile alike. Peter steps through a Roman doorway now because his Lord went through one first, and went through it to die.

Naming the barrier. Imagine a congregation that did this: named its own barrier aloud, in front of the people on the other side of it, before saying anything else. Peter’s honesty is the reason the room believed him. He had not come to tell them the division never existed. He had come to tell them who had ended it.

Does this mean every human being is already clean before God? No. Peter is speaking about race and nation, not about sin. No one is unclean because he is a Gentile, a Roman, or anything else he was born. But every one of us, Jew and Gentile alike, is unclean because of sin, and needs to be washed (Romans 3:23). That is why Peter goes on to preach forgiveness through Christ (v. 43). The barrier of nationality has been removed so that the gospel can reach everyone; the barrier of sin is removed only by the blood of Christ, received by faith. Both truths have to be held together, or we end either with racism or with universalism.

In a sentence. As he talked with Cornelius, Peter went in and found many people gathered, and told them that they knew it was against Jewish custom for a Jew to associate with or visit a foreigner, but God had shown him that he should not call any person common or unclean.

On a Tuesday. Name your own barrier. Is there a group of people you were raised to look down on, or simply to avoid? Say it honestly to God, and then cross the room. In Christ, no one is unclean because of race, class or background. Tear down your walls, starting with the one nearest you.

For worship. The dividing wall that stood for centuries came down at the cross, where Christ made peace by his blood and created in himself one new humanity in place of two (Ephesians 2:14–16). What custom, history and fear had built, he demolished in a single afternoon outside Jerusalem. And he sent a fisherman through a Roman doorway to announce it. Glory to the Lamb, who has ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.

So when I was sent for, I came without objection. It is not quite the whole truth, and Peter knows it. He had objected: he had said by no means, Lord, until God repeated himself three times (v. 14). He means that once he was actually sent for, once the men were at the gate and the Spirit had spoken, he raised nothing. The arguing was finished on the roof.

The one who came without objection. Peter’s thirty miles, walked after three refusals, sit inside a far longer journey made with none. The Son of God came from the Father’s side into a world that was not merely unclean but hostile, and the letter to the Hebrews gives his words on coming as, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7). He needed no vision repeated three times. He came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10), and he went further than any centurion’s parlour: to a cross. Every servant who goes without objection follows, at a great distance, the Lord who came without one.

I ask then why you sent for me. Then a question, more courteous than it looks. He has a vision, a word from the Spirit and the authority of an apostle, and the first thing he does in that house is ask and wait. He gives Cornelius the floor in his own home, in front of the relatives and friends he has assembled.

Letting his host establish it. What follows is Cornelius’s account of the angel, told aloud to a room that has waited four days for it, so that when the sermon comes everyone present knows the meeting was arranged from heaven at both ends. Peter could have asserted that. He asked, and let his host establish it. The apostle with the revelation began by asking the Roman soldier to explain himself, and listened, and only then opened his mouth.

In a sentence. Peter said that when he was sent for he came without objection, and asked why they had sent for him.

On a Tuesday. When God calls you to cross a boundary, go without objection. And when you arrive, ask before you tell. The next time you have a conversation about faith, begin by asking the other person what has been happening in his life, and listen properly before you speak.

For worship. The Lord who turned Peter’s by no means into without objection is the God who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). He does not merely command; he changes the heart that hears the command. Every objection silenced in his servants is a monument to his patient grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.’

Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour. Cornelius tells it back, so the angel’s message appears twice in one chapter, once as it happened and once in the man’s own words, and a third time in the next chapter when Peter reports in Jerusalem. Luke repeats what matters.

A man stood before me in bright clothing. The angel of verse 3, and Luke’s description is not idle. Two men in dazzling apparel stood by the women at the empty tomb and asked why they sought the living among the dead (Luke 24:4–5), and two men in white robes stood by the apostles as Jesus was taken up (1:10). Wherever such messengers appear in Luke’s two books, the news is about Jesus: risen, ascended, coming again. This one comes with only an address to give, but he belongs to the same story, and the message he is sending for is theirs: the crucified man is alive, and he is Lord.

Your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. Both here and at verse 4, the angel’s message is that Cornelius’s prayers and alms have been remembered, and that he should send for Peter. That is all. Reporting to Jerusalem, Peter adds the clause the reader has not yet been given: the angel said Peter would declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household (11:14).

The question the third telling settles. That clause settles the question this chapter otherwise leaves open, and it is the question every thoughtful reader asks about Cornelius. He was devout, God-fearing, generous and prayerful, and his prayers went up before God like an offering. Was he then already saved, and was Peter merely bringing information? The angel’s own words say no. He was told to send for a man who would tell him how to be saved, which means that on the day the angel appeared, with all that piety behind him, he was not.

Hard and kind. It is a hard sentence and a kind one. Hard, because it will not allow the comfortable conclusion that sincerity is enough and the gospel an optional refinement. Kind, because of what God did about it. He did not leave the honest seeker to his sincerity. He sent an angel and a vision, and moved an apostle thirty miles against every instinct he had, to get the message to one Roman officer and his household. God is so far from indifferent to the man reaching after him in the dark that he will rearrange the church to reach him.

In a sentence. Cornelius said that four days earlier, at this very hour, three in the afternoon, while he was praying at home, a man in bright clothing stood before him and told him his prayer had been heard and his gifts to the poor remembered before God.

On a Tuesday. Tell what God has done for you. Your story, told simply and honestly, can open hearts that an argument would close. Practise telling it in two minutes: what you were, how Christ met you, what he has done since.

For worship. The God who hears prayer heard a soldier asking for he knew not what, and answered with the one thing he needed: the news of his Son. He did not send an improvement on Cornelius’s religion. He sent the risen Christ in the mouth of a witness. That is how the Father answers an honest cry from the dark: not with a brighter lamp, but with the Light of the world himself, carried to the door by someone who has seen him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.

So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Gratitude, and a courtesy that a Roman officer did not owe a Jewish fisherman. Cornelius thanks him for coming, which is a recognition that Peter crossed something to get here.

Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord. The last sentence of Cornelius’s speech is worth learning by heart, phrase by phrase. We are all here: nobody is missing. In the presence of God: they are not primarily aware of Peter; they know whose house this has become. To hear all: not the parts that suit them, all of it. That you have been commanded by the Lord: they do not expect Peter’s opinions. They assume he is under orders and that they are about to hear what the orders were.

Commanded by the Lord. Cornelius cannot have known how exactly he had put it. Peter had indeed been commanded, by the risen Lord Jesus, who gave commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen (1:2) and sent them to make disciples of all nations, teaching them to observe all that he had commanded (Matthew 28:19–20). Within minutes Peter will say so: he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify (v. 42). The room is right about whose orders are coming. The preacher stands under the Lord Jesus, and the sermon is Christ’s own message about himself.

A model congregation. No preacher ever walked into a better room: no resistance to overcome, no attention to win, a congregation that has prepared itself and said in advance that it means to obey. It did not happen by accident. Behind that sentence lie four days of a man telling a garrison town what had happened to him while he prayed, and behind those, the years of praying and giving in verse 2. This is what the preparation of a heart looks like when it has spread to a household.

Turning the sentence round. Let it look at us. Most Christians hear preaching expecting some of it to be interesting, and respond by assessing it. Cornelius’s household came expecting to be commanded by God through a man, said so before he opened his mouth, and the Holy Spirit fell on them before he had finished. Those two facts may not be unrelated.

What if the preaching at my church is poor? Then pray for your preacher, and come anyway in the presence of God. Cornelius’s words do not depend on the preacher’s eloquence but on the hearer’s expectation that God will speak through his word. Where a sermon faithfully opens Scripture, God is speaking, even if the delivery is plain. You can help by preparing: read the passage beforehand, pray for the preacher, arrive in time, and listen for what God is commanding rather than for what entertains. If the preaching is not faithful to Scripture, that is a different and more serious matter, to be raised lovingly with the elders. But most of us need to bring more to church before we complain about what we take away.

In a sentence. Cornelius said he had sent for Peter at once and thanked him for coming, and said they were all there in the presence of God to hear everything the Lord had commanded him to say.

On a Tuesday. Come to church like this: in God’s presence, all of you, ready to hear all he has commanded. On Saturday night, pray this sentence for Sunday, and see whether it changes the way you listen.

For worship. Every faithful sermon is a meeting with the living God, because he has chosen to speak through his word preached by men. The Lord who commanded Peter commands his servants still through the Scriptures, and where his word is opened, he is present. What a wonder that the God of heaven should take his seat among an ordinary congregation and speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

So Peter opened his mouth and said. A solemn beginning, the formula Luke uses for a weighty speech (8:35), and this is the first sermon ever preached to a Gentile household. Its first words are an admission: truly I understand that God shows no partiality. Not, as I have always taught, but, I am now getting it. It begins with a man saying aloud that he has just changed his mind.

The face-receiver. The Greek word, prosōpolēmptēs, is a vivid compound meaning one who receives the face: who judges by who somebody visibly is. It is courtroom language for a judge who decides by looking at the parties, and the Old Testament uses it of exactly the magistrate God is not (Deuteronomy 10:17). He does not take the face. And Peter says it while looking at a room of faces he had been raised to sort. He had known the principle all his life; he is saying that he has finally seen where it goes. Paul builds on the same truth: God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11), and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28).

Even his enemies said it. Peter had watched this impartiality walking about. In the last week in Jerusalem, spies sent to trap Jesus opened with flattery that was nonetheless true: Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality (Luke 20:21). He had touched lepers and dined with Pharisees, healed a centurion’s servant and a synagogue ruler’s daughter. The God who does not take the face had shown his own glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and that face turned toward the poor, the foreign and the despised as readily as toward anyone. What Peter now understands about God, he had watched for three years in the Son.

But in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. Acceptable, dektos, means welcome. Nationality is no barrier. God welcomes the one who fears him, from any nation.

Where Christians differ: are sincere seekers saved without the gospel? Inclusivists read this verse to mean that people who fear God and do right in any religion are saved, even without hearing of Christ. Verdict: Cornelius was not yet saved: the angel said Peter would bring a message by which he would be saved (11:14). “Acceptable” means acceptable as a candidate, someone God welcomes to hear the gospel, regardless of nation. The verse removes ethnic barriers, not the need for Christ. Peter goes straight on to preach that forgiveness comes through faith in Jesus (v. 43).

One clarification. The passage itself rules out the idea that sincere people of any religion are saved without Christ. God plays no favourites by nation: he welcomes seekers from every people, not Jews only. But acceptable does not mean already saved apart from the gospel. Devout, praying Cornelius still needed to hear and believe, for the angel said Peter “will declare to you a message by which you will be saved” (11:14), and Peter preached that “everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness” (10:43). God accepted Cornelius’s search by sending him the gospel, not by counting him saved without it. The precious missionary truth is that God will see to it that the gospel reaches the honest seeker in any nation; yet salvation remains through Christ alone, received by faith.

What about those who never hear? It is the question behind the question, and it is asked with real anguish. Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (4:12; Romans 10:13–17), and that everyone has enough light in creation and conscience to be without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). It also tells us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and that infants dying in infancy who are among God’s elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3). What Scripture never does is offer the unevangelised as a reason for the church to relax. Its answer to the question is this chapter: God moved heaven and earth to get the gospel to one man. The right response to the question is not speculation but mission.

In a sentence. Peter began by saying he now truly understood that God shows no partiality, but that in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

On a Tuesday. God shows no partiality. Neither should you. Notice this week whose company you seek out and whose you avoid, whom you listen to with interest and whom you dismiss, and ask whether the face is deciding for you. Then pray for one missionary or gospel work among a people who have little access to the Bible.

For worship. The God who does not receive faces looked on the human race, Jew and Gentile alike, and saw sinners all. And then, without partiality, he sent his Son for people from every nation. He did not choose us because of our faces, our families or our virtues. He chose us in love, and the welcome he extends in the gospel is as wide as the world. Peter only understood it that afternoon. The Father had purposed it from eternity.

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),

As for the word that he sent to Israel. Peter begins the story where it began, and he does not apologise for it. The gospel came to the Jews first; that is simply the history, and Peter states it in a Gentile drawing room without embarrassment. This message has an address it started from, as Paul would say: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16).

Preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ. The phrase is out of Isaiah, where a runner comes over the hills with news that the war is over: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace (Isaiah 52:7). Peter stands before a professional soldier using the vocabulary of a herald announcing the end of hostilities. And the peace is double: peace with God, for sinners who were his enemies (Romans 5:1), and peace between Jew and Gentile, who were enemies of each other (Ephesians 2:14–17).

He is Lord of all. Then, dropped into the sentence like a bracket, the largest claim in the chapter. Not Lord of Israel, or of the church, or of those who acknowledge him. The Greek puts all first: of all, he is Lord. Peter is speaking to an officer of an empire whose creed was that Caesar is lord, in a city named after Caesar with a temple to Caesar on the seafront, and he says it in an aside. Paul says the same: the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him (Romans 10:12).

Why it matters here. But it is not mainly a political sentence. Peter has just said that God shows no partiality, and a hearer might ask on what grounds. Here is the ground. The gospel cannot be kept inside one nation, not because God has become broad-minded, but because the man at its centre owns everything. A local Lord may have a local people. A Lord of all has no outsiders, only subjects who have not yet been told. And it explains the last two chapters: Peter was brought up a coast road against his instincts to a house he would never have entered, because the one who sent him already owned the address.

What does it mean in practice that Jesus is Lord of all? It means there is no part of the world, and no part of your life, outside his rule. He is Lord of the nations, so no people is beyond the reach of the gospel. He is Lord of governments, so rulers are accountable to him and Christians obey them under him, not instead of him (4:19). He is Lord of your work, your money, your body, your evenings and your relationships. The confession Jesus is Lord was the earliest Christian creed (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), and it was dangerous precisely because it left Caesar no room to be ultimate. It still leaves nothing else room: not career, not comfort, not self.

In a sentence. Peter said that God sent the message to the people of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.

On a Tuesday. Take one area of your life you tend to keep to yourself, your finances, your screen time, your ambitions, and say aloud, Jesus Christ is Lord of this. Then ask what one change that confession would make this week.

For worship. The Lord of all could have come to Caesarea as Rome had come, with standards and a garrison. He came preaching peace, and he paid for the peace himself, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). Every other lord of the earth has made his peace by killing his enemies. This one made it by dying for them. The soldier in that room served a Caesar whose peace was enforced. He was about to meet a King whose peace is given, and whose rule no border, no legion and no grave can ever end.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.

You yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed. Peter takes it for granted that a Roman household in Caesarea has followed the story of a Galilean preacher, and they had: it had been in every town of the province for three years and had ended in a public execution sixty miles away. So he starts where the public record starts. This is the shape of the earliest Christian preaching in Acts: not a philosophy but an account of what a particular man did, within living memory, offered to people who could check it. Peter’s outline, from Galilee and John’s baptism through the ministry to the death and resurrection, is the very shape of Mark’s Gospel, and early church tradition says that Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching. Here, perhaps, we hear it in miniature.

How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. The word anointed is the verb behind Christ, so Peter is explaining the title rather than just using it, a courtesy to a room that has not grown up with the vocabulary. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; this one was anointed with the Spirit, at his baptism (Luke 3:22; 4:18). And here again is the Trinity in a single clause: God the Father anointed Jesus the Son with the Holy Spirit.

He went about doing good. And then the summary of a whole life, which is as good a sentence as exists in the New Testament: he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. A beautiful summary of Jesus’ life, and no one who knew him ever contradicted it.

Oppressed by the devil. To be oppressed is to be tyrannised, held down under a cruel power. Peter sums up Jesus’ whole ministry of healing and deliverance as a rescue operation, prising people loose from the devil’s grip. The phrase reaches wider than open demon-possession, though not every illness is a direct demonic act. It gathers up all whom the devil’s dark dominion held, for behind the reign of sickness, bondage and death in a fallen world stand “the works of the devil,” and “the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy” them (1 John 3:8). Jesus himself called a crippled woman one “whom Satan bound for eighteen years” (Luke 13:16).

The great Liberator. So every healing was a liberation and a preview of total victory. Jesus came as the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27): “if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). And he pressed it to the end: at the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15), and through death destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Whatever cruel power has held a person down, Jesus is mightier, and he rescues us “from the domain of darkness” into his own kingdom (Colossians 1:13; Acts 26:18).

For God was with him. The explanation of his power. Peter speaks here of Jesus’ true humanity: a man anointed and empowered by the Spirit, in whom the Father was at work. That is not the whole truth about him, and in the same sermon Peter calls him Lord of all and Judge of all (vv. 36, 42). But it is a real truth. The eternal Son did not lay aside his deity when he became man; he lived his human life in dependence on the Spirit, as the true and perfect man, which is why he can be our pattern as well as our Saviour.

In a sentence. Peter reminded them of what had happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee after the baptism John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.

On a Tuesday. Go about doing good today, as Jesus did. Not grand deeds, but the next good thing: the visit, the repair, the meal, the word of comfort. And if you feel held down by something you cannot shake, a habit, a fear, a darkness, bring it to Christ by name. He came to set captives free.

For worship. He went about doing good. The Son of God walked the dusty roads of Galilee with the Spirit upon him, touching lepers, opening blind eyes, freeing the oppressed, and then went to the cross to break the devil’s power for ever. There has never been a life like his. Every act of mercy he performed was the kingdom of God breaking in, and every one was a promise of the day when the oppressor will be cast down and his people set free completely.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,

And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. Peter says it before he says anything about the cross, and he will say it again in the next verse. Everything in this sermon rests on the claim that the men saying it were there. Eyewitness testimony again, as throughout Acts (1:8; 2:32; 3:15).

They put him to death by hanging him on a tree. Then the death, and the way he puts it would have made a Jewish hearer flinch. He does not say crucified, which is the ordinary word and the one Cornelius would have expected from a Roman perspective. He reaches instead for a phrase out of Deuteronomy, a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23): the law about a body left on a tree, which every Jew knew and which was the standing objection to the whole Christian claim. A crucified Messiah was a cursed Messiah, and that was the end of the argument.

The objection as the description. Peter does not avoid the scandalous word; he puts it in the sermon. Paul later takes the same verse and shows what it is for: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). So the church understood from very early on that the worst thing about the crucifixion was the point of it. He bore the curse that was ours.

But God raised him on the third day. One conjunction carries the whole gospel. They put him to death; God raised him. Two subjects, two verbs, and the second reverses the first. In these early sermons the resurrection is consistently something done to Jesus by God. Not only that he rose, though that is true, but that God raised him, which is the language of a verdict. A court had ruled; a higher court has set the ruling aside. What men called a curse, God called his Son, and said so by emptying the grave. And he made him to appear, literally gave him to become visible: real appearances, to real people, which leads straight into the strangest sentence in the sermon.

What does it mean that Jesus became a curse for us? The curse is God’s just sentence on sin, the opposite of his blessing (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10). Everyone who breaks his law is under it. On the cross, Jesus, who had never sinned, took that sentence in our place: God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: the penalty was real, the substitute was Christ, and the debt was paid in full. So if you trust in him, there is no curse left for you. It fell on him at Golgotha, and the empty tomb is God’s announcement that it has been exhausted.

In a sentence. Peter said the apostles were witnesses of everything Jesus did in the Jewish countryside and in Jerusalem, and though they killed him by hanging him on a tree, God raised him on the third day and made him appear.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think that God is against you because of your sins, look at the tree. Say to yourself, slowly: he became a curse for me. Then live this week as someone who has been blessed instead.

For worship. He hung on the tree under the curse, and rose on the third day. That is the whole gospel in two clauses. The holy Son of God was counted cursed so that cursed sinners might be counted sons, and the Father who laid the curse on him raised him in glory. Blessed be the Lamb who was slain, and the God who vindicated him.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses. It is an odd thing to volunteer, and it is the last thing an inventor of a story would include. If a man is fabricating a resurrection, he does not pause in the middle of the account to concede that the risen figure was not shown to the general public. Peter raises the difficulty himself, unprompted, in front of an audience that had not asked.

Why not to everybody? Scripture does not fully explain it, and it is honest to say so. But the logic is not hard to see. A public appearance in the temple courts would have compelled belief of a kind, the kind a man cannot get out of, and God’s consistent way is to give sufficient evidence to those who will testify rather than overwhelming evidence to those who will not. And there was to be a definite, nameable, countable body of witnesses, so that the church’s claim would rest on people who could be found and questioned rather than on a rumour that everybody had heard from somebody (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). God chose to spread the news by witness, not by spectacle, because faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29).

Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. Then the proof Peter chooses, which nobody would predict. Not: we saw him, we touched him. We had meals with him. It is the most ordinary evidence there is and the hardest to explain away. A vision does not ask for something to eat. A hallucination shared by a dozen men does not take bread and hand it round. Luke’s Gospel records the risen Christ asking for food and eating broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:41–43), and John records breakfast on a beach (John 21:12–13). Ghosts do not eat.

A man at supper. The resurrection Peter preaches is not a survival of the spirit or a continuing influence. It is a man who was dead, sitting down to supper. That is what the apostles said they had seen, and no lash or sword could talk them out of it.

Does it matter whether the resurrection was physical? Everything depends on it. If Christ was raised only as a spirit, then death has not been defeated, only survived, and our bodies have no future. But the New Testament insists that the same body that was laid in the tomb came out of it, transformed and glorified, with the marks of the nails still in its hands (John 20:27). That is why Christians bury their dead in hope, and why Paul could say that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). Because he rose bodily, we will too.

In a sentence. He appeared not to all the people but to witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

On a Tuesday. You believe on the testimony of chosen witnesses, and their word is enough. When doubts come, go back to the evidence they gave: read Luke 24 or 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as testimony from men who had breakfast with the risen Lord.

For worship. The Lord of glory, who has conquered death, kept the habits of friendship on the far side of the grave. He asked for food in Jerusalem and served it by the lake, and the hands that passed the bread still bore the marks of the nails. His resurrection is not a rumour of survival but a body at a table, and the table is not finished. He has promised to drink the fruit of the vine new with his people in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29), in bodies raised like his, with every death and every parting behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

He is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify, Peter says, and his last two sentences hold the whole of what the church has to say. The first is the harder. Peter has told them who Jesus was, what he did, how he died and that God raised him, and the conclusion he draws is that this man will judge the human race (17:31; John 5:22; 2 Timothy 4:1). The living and the dead is a phrase that closes every exit: nobody is too long buried to be included and nobody too much alive to be exempt. Every person will stand before him. The gospel includes the warning of judgment.

Good news, not only threat. This is presented as part of the good news, and it is, when you consider the alternative: a universe in which nothing is ever finally called what it is, where the killer and the killed go into the same silence. A judgment guarantees that the accounts will be settled. What makes it terrifying is not that there is a judge; it is that we are in the dock.

To him all the prophets bear witness. Which is why the second sentence has to come immediately, and does. The whole Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27). So this is not a novelty; it is what Israel’s Scriptures were for.

That everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. The judge and the Saviour are the same person. That is the whole architecture of the gospel in one movement, and it is the only arrangement under which anybody could survive the first sentence. The one appointed to assess the living and the dead is the one on whose name a man may call and be forgiven, and he is offering it now, in a front room in Caesarea, before the bench is ever taken. This is the climax of Peter’s sermon, and the answer to Cornelius’s prayers.

Every word chosen. Look at the width of the last sentence. Everyone: not every Jew, not every circumcised person, everyone. Who believes in him: not achieves, not qualifies, not is born into; faith alone, not circumcision, law-keeping or good works. Receives forgiveness of sins: a gift received, not a wage earned. Through his name: on his account and not on ours. That word everyone is very nearly the last thing Peter says before the Holy Spirit interrupts him, and the interruption is God’s way of saying that the word meant what it said.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Some teach that forgiveness comes through faith plus sacraments, or faith plus works. Verdict: Peter says forgiveness is received by everyone who believes, and the Spirit falls before any baptism or work is done (v. 44). This is justification by faith alone, through Christ alone, by grace alone.

How do I know if I have really believed? Believing in Christ is not a feeling to measure but a trust to place. Ask yourself: Do I rely on Jesus alone, and not on my goodness, to be accepted by God? Do I believe he died for my sins and rose again? Am I turning from sin to follow him, however falteringly? If the answer is yes, then the promise of this verse is yours: everyone who believes receives forgiveness. Assurance does not rest on the strength of your faith but on the faithfulness of the one you trust. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves as surely as strong faith does. And the evidence that it is real will grow: love for Christ, a hatred of sin, and a desire to obey him (1 John 5:13).

In a sentence. Peter said Jesus had commanded them to preach to the people and testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead, and that all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

On a Tuesday. Hold both truths together this week. When you are careless about sin, remember that Jesus is the Judge. When you are crushed by guilt, remember that the Judge is the one who forgives. And if you have never put your trust in him, there is no reason to wait: everyone who believes receives forgiveness.

For worship. All the prophets bore witness to him, and on the last day all the nations will stand before him. Between those two lies a front room in Caesarea, and every room like it, where the Judge sends his heralds ahead of the court to offer pardon in his own name. No earthly judge has ever done such a thing: borne the sentence of the accused himself, risen from it, and sent out word that the case may be settled now, freely. Blessed be his name, the only name a sinner ever needs to plead.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.

While Peter was still saying these things. He is interrupted. The most important sermon of his life is cut off in the middle by the Holy Spirit, and Luke evidently thought the timing worth recording precisely. As soon as they heard that everyone who believes receives forgiveness, they believed, and God sealed it.

The Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. Notice what is not in this account. No appeal, no call to respond, no prayer to repeat. Nobody is baptised first; the water does not appear until verse 47, and Peter has to ask for it. Nobody is circumcised or has agreed to keep the law. God simply does not wait. Faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit with it (Galatians 3:2).

Sealed in his name. The Spirit fell at a precise point in the sermon: the moment the name of Jesus had been offered to everyone who believes in him. Jesus had sent his apostles to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (Luke 24:47), and had said that the Spirit would glorify him, taking what was his and declaring it (John 16:14). In Caesarea the two promises met. Forgiveness was offered in Christ’s name to Gentiles, and Christ’s Spirit, poured out from his throne (2:33), came down on them before the sentence was finished. The interruption was the risen Lord setting his own seal on his own gospel.

The believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed. Then Luke turns the camera on the men Peter had brought with him. These are the six from Joppa: Jewish Christians, brought along as witnesses, who had walked thirty miles for exactly this purpose. And what they feel is not delight. It is astonishment: the word means they were standing outside themselves, knocked out of their own minds. They had believed for some time that Jesus was the Messiah. They had not remotely believed this.

Because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. Even on the Gentiles: unthinkable, but undeniable. God accepted them as they were, uncircumcised. It is an honest sentence, and a mercy that Luke left it in. The first Christians did not arrive at the inclusion of the Gentiles by reflection, nor welcome it warmly. Their own Scriptures had foretold it and their Lord had sent them to the ends of the earth, and when God did it in front of them they stood with their mouths open.

Is this a second experience after conversion? The Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking, the moment they believed; there was no second step. This was the Gentile Pentecost, the moment God showed the church that Gentiles too received the Spirit on believing, and as an event it was unrepeatable. Pentecostal Christians read it as a pattern for a later baptism in the Spirit; but Peter himself later says that God gave them the same gift when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ (11:17).

Bewildered witnesses. That is a comfort to anybody who has watched God do something they had no framework for and found that their first reaction was not faith but bewilderment. It was the reaction of the six men brought specifically as witnesses, and it neither stopped God nor disqualified them; they went back to Jerusalem and told the church what they had seen.

In a sentence. While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the message, and the circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. Expect God to be at work when his word is spoken, even before the speaker has finished. When you share the gospel, you are not the one who makes it effective; the Spirit is. And if God does something in your church you did not expect, a conversion from an unlikely quarter, a newcomer you would not have chosen, let your astonishment turn into praise.

For worship. The Father promised through Joel that he would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and in a Roman parlour all flesh came to include soldiers, servants and a centurion’s relatives. He gave the gift before anyone could earn it, examine it or argue about it, and he gave it whole. That is what his grace is like. It falls on the undeserving while the preacher is still talking, and it leaves the most careful believers in the room standing amazed. Glory to the God who does not wait for us to finish.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,

For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. How did anybody know the Spirit had fallen? Luke answers directly, because the argument of the next chapters depends on its being checkable. The sign is the same as on the first morning in Jerusalem (2:4, 11), recognisable at once by a man who had been there. Peter will tell the Jerusalem church that the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning (11:15), and the council that God gave them the Spirit just as he did to us, and made no distinction (15:8–9).

The demonstration was for Jerusalem. God could have converted that household quietly; the sermon was believed and Peter could have baptised them and gone home. Instead he gave a sign that could only be described in the words already used of Pentecost, in front of six Jewish witnesses who would have to give evidence. The tongues served as proof at a turning point in the church’s history. The demonstration was not for Cornelius. It was for Jerusalem.

No two-tier church. And it settled the question before the argument began. Once the Spirit had been given on the same terms as at Pentecost, there was no case left for Gentile believers as associate members, on probation, conditional on circumcision, at a separate table. God had decided publicly, and the church spent years catching up with a decision it had not been consulted about.

Were these tongues real languages, and is speaking in tongues the evidence of the Spirit? Peter says the Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning (11:15), so they were likely the same as at Pentecost. The tongues were a sign for the Jewish believers that God had accepted Gentiles; they are not presented as the proof of the Spirit for every later Christian. Many Christians believe the gift continues today; the more likely reading is that it belonged to those foundational moments.

Extolling God for his Son. The word, megalynontōn, means magnifying, making great, and as at Pentecost they declared the mighty works of God. Luke does not record the words, but their subject is not hard to find. Moments earlier this household had heard for the first time that a man anointed by God had been hanged on a tree, raised on the third day and appointed Judge of all, and that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness (vv. 38–43). Their first praise, in languages nobody had taught them, was praise for that. Mary had magnified the Lord when the Son of God was conceived in her (Luke 1:46). A Roman officer’s household, minutes into the faith, was magnifying the God of Israel for the same Christ.

Then how do I know I have the Spirit if I have not spoken in tongues? By the signs Scripture gives every believer, not the special sign given at this turning point. The Spirit is present wherever a person confesses from the heart that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), cries out to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16), loves other Christians (1 John 4:13), and bears his fruit: love, joy, peace, patience and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). Paul asks the Corinthians, do all speak with tongues? and expects the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). If you trust Christ, you have the Spirit. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so the reverse is also true: if you belong to him, the Spirit is yours.

In a sentence. They heard them speaking in tongues and praising God, and then Peter spoke up.
