On a Tuesday. The Spirit’s gift always leads to praise of God. If you are a believer, the same Spirit lives in you, so let him do in you what he did in Caesarea: magnify God. Take five minutes today simply to tell God what he has done, without asking for anything.

For worship. The Spirit of God took the tongues of Gentiles and filled them with the praises of the God of Israel. It was a foretaste of the great multitude that no one can number, from every nation, crying out with a loud voice, Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10). Every language that learns his praise is a pledge of that day, and the God who gave the first of them in Caesarea will not rest until the last language on earth has learned to sing of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.

Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have? The question is addressed less to the room than to the six men behind Peter, and through them to the church in Jerusalem, and it is unanswerable. Withhold, kōlysai, means prevent, hinder: the word of the eunuch’s question by the roadside, what prevents me from being baptized (8:36). The argument runs back from a fact nobody can dispute: these people have received the Holy Spirit just as we have. No second-class Gentile believers. If God has given the reality, who can refuse the sign?

Not more cautious than God. It is worth noticing what Peter does not do. He does not send to Jerusalem for a ruling, though the question is momentous and he will certainly be answering for it later. He does not impose conditions or a probationary period. He does not require circumcision, which is what the whole church will be arguing about for the next several years. He watches what God has plainly done and refuses to be more cautious than God.

And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. And then, having asked whether anyone can withhold it, he commanded them to be baptised. Not invited, not offered: the language of an order, which the head of that household would have recognised. The question was for the Jewish witnesses; the command was for the Gentile believers. Baptism follows faith and the Spirit.

In the name of Jesus Christ. The apparent tension with Jesus’ own command to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) is not a contradiction, and it gives no support to the Oneness or Jesus Only teaching, which treats the phrase as a rival formula and denies the Trinity. Luke is not recording the exact words spoken over the candidate; he is describing the baptism’s character. It was Christian baptism, baptism that belongs to Jesus and marks a person out as now his, as distinct from John’s baptism or any other washing. To be baptised into the name of Jesus is to be baptised into the whole triune God, for you cannot have the Son without the Father who sent him and the Spirit he gives, and this very scene proves it, with the Father anointing (10:38), the Son saving, and the Spirit falling on the household (10:44).

The Spirit before the water. These people received the Spirit before they were baptised. That shows that the Spirit and forgiveness come by faith, and that baptism follows as the sign and the Lord’s command, not as the means. Christians who see baptism as the instrument of new birth must explain why these had the Spirit already; Peter’s reasoning is that those who have received the Spirit should not be refused the sign.

And does all his household support infant baptism? The household here were those who heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (vv. 44, 46), so all were believers. Christians who baptise infants see in household baptisms a covenant pattern including children; but this household, at least, was made up of believers.

The way we should do it. So we follow Jesus’ own explicit instruction and baptise in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), as the church has done from the earliest days (the Didache, around AD 100, already prescribes the words). The Acts phrase names whose baptism it is; the Lord’s formula names the God into whom the baptised are brought. Both say that to belong to Jesus is to belong to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Under a new name. Whatever words were spoken over the water, the name that mattered was the one Peter had just preached: the anointed man, hanged on a tree, raised on the third day, Judge of the living and the dead. Roman soldiers swore their military oath in the name of the emperor, and Cornelius had served for years under Caesar’s name. Now he went down into the water under another, and came up owned by a better Master, who had bought him not with wages but with his own blood (20:28). From that afternoon the first thing to be said about him was not his rank but his Lord.

Then they asked him to remain for some days. The quiet triumph of the chapter. A Jewish apostle who days earlier had never entered a Gentile house stays on as a guest in one, eating at that table and sleeping under that roof. The Jerusalem church will complain of exactly this: you went to uncircumcised men and ate with them (11:3). The man who said by no means, Lord over a sheet of animals had stopped arguing. The wall is truly down.

If baptism does not save, why does it matter so much? Because Christ commanded it, and obedience to him is never optional (Matthew 28:19). Baptism is his appointed sign of union with him in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4), a public confession that you belong to him, and the doorway into the visible fellowship of his church. It does not make you a Christian; it marks you as one. Peter did not treat it as a formality to be skipped once the Spirit had come. He commanded it at once. A believer who has never been baptised is not lost, but he is living in disobedience to a plain command of his Lord, and missing a means of grace by which Christ strengthens faith.

In a sentence. Peter asked whether anyone could withhold water for baptising these people who had received the Holy Spirit just as they had, and he commanded them to be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ, and then they asked him to stay on for a few days.

On a Tuesday. If God has accepted someone, so must you. Welcome every believer as a brother or sister, whatever his background, and refuse to create second-class Christians in your church by look, tone or seating plan. And if you have trusted Christ but never been baptised, do not withhold the water from yourself any longer. Speak to your pastor this week.

For worship. The Father anointed, the Son saved, and the Spirit fell, and a Roman household went down into the water in the name of the triune God. The promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, was kept that afternoon in one Gentile family, and it has been kept in every family gathered in since. Every believer from every nation who has been welcomed into Christ’s church stands in a line that runs back through that house by the sea. Glory to the God who swore an oath to Abraham, and kept it in Abraham’s greater Son.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home — brought together by two visions, thirty miles apart, orchestrated by the God who wastes nothing and plans everything. The Spirit fell. The barriers fell. The church was never the same.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to build walls that God has torn down. The divisions that seem most natural — racial, cultural, economic, denominational — are the ones most likely to be the new versions of the Jewish-Gentile divide. What God has made clean, do not call common. The community of the Spirit is wider than our instincts, and deeper than our categories.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
News that Gentiles have received the word reaches Jerusalem, and when Peter returns, Jewish believers who insisted on circumcision criticise him: he went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them. Table fellowship meant full acceptance, and that was the offence. Peter tells the whole story step by step, with six witnesses, and ends with the decisive fact: God gave the Gentiles the same gift of the Spirit he gave the apostles, so who was Peter to stand in God’s way? The critics fall silent and praise God that he has granted repentance leading to life even to the Gentiles.

Meanwhile, believers scattered after Stephen’s death reach Antioch in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, a great trading centre on the Orontes river, with a large Jewish community and a reputation for luxury and loose living. Some of them, from Cyprus and Cyrene, begin preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and many believe. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who is delighted by what he sees, and fetches Saul from Tarsus to help him; for a whole year they teach the new church, and it is at Antioch that the disciples are first called “Christians”. When the prophet Agabus predicts a severe famine, which came in the reign of the emperor Claudius, the Antioch church sends relief to the believers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul, a first sign of the Gentile churches caring for the mother church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles and believers in Judea heard that the Gentiles had received God’s word. When Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers criticised him for going into the house of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter explained everything in order: the vision at Joppa of the sheet with animals, the voice telling him to eat, his refusal, the voice saying three times not to call unclean what God has made clean, and the arrival at that moment of three men from Caesarea. The Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation, and six brothers went with him into the man’s house. The man told them how an angel had told him to send for Peter, who would bring a message through which he and his household would be saved. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit came on them as on the apostles at the beginning, and Peter remembered the Lord’s words that John baptised with water but they would be baptised with the Spirit. If God gave them the same gift he gave those who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was Peter to stand in God’s way? When they heard this they had no further objections and praised God, saying that God had granted even the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel's Reach and the Church's Lag

What this passage shows is not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken. The men who met Peter at the door were not bigots inventing a rule; they were holding to a boundary God himself had drawn, for reasons he himself had given, which had been kept at enormous cost for centuries. Their difficulty was that the boundary had done its work and been retired, and nobody had told them. Reformed theology has taken the episode as the clearest case in Scripture of the Spirit going ahead of the church's understanding — and of how he settles such questions. Not by a decree, not by a text, and not by an apostolic ruling: by doing the thing in public, in front of witnesses who could be cross-examined, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct. The Jerusalem church conceded the principle in verse 18 and was still arguing about the practice at a council several years later, and Peter, who won this argument, later behaved as though he had lost it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter's answer to a hostile hearing was to narrate what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He produced no proof text and pulled no rank. Now: That is still the strongest thing available in a disputed matter, and the rarest. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is very hard to answer — and a man who says only that God told him, with nothing checkable attached, has said nothing anybody can test.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,

Meaning first. Acts 11 has two halves. First, Peter defends himself in Jerusalem for eating with Gentiles, and the church accepts that God has given the Gentiles repentance that leads to life. Second, the gospel reaches Gentiles in Antioch, the great city of Syria, where a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles grows under Barnabas and Saul, and where believers are first called Christians. Antioch will become the base for the mission to the world. Over both halves stands the same truth: the turning of a sinner to God is God’s own gift, and he gives it to whom he pleases, from every nation, so that his people come to be known simply by the name of his Son.

Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. Two sentences, and a great deal happens in them. The first is that the news travelled faster than the man. Not just Jerusalem but the whole province heard; six men had walked home from Caesarea with a story, and by the time Peter came up to the city everybody had heard a version.

The circumcision party criticized him. The second is that Luke names a faction, literally those of the circumcision, the first group inside the church identified in this book as a party with a position. They are believers in Jerusalem who hold that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people (15:1, 5). Paul uses the same phrase of the men whose arrival at Antioch made Peter get up from a Gentile table (Galatians 2:12). This is a standing party with a policy, and it runs through the next four chapters and into the epistles.

The verb Luke chooses. They criticised him, diekrinonto, took issue with him, and it is the verb the Spirit had used on the stairs at Joppa when Peter was told to go with the three men making no distinction (10:20; v. 12). It means to separate, to sort, to discriminate between one thing and another. So, to anyone with the Greek: the Spirit told Peter not to discriminate, and here are the brothers, discriminating. Luke does not comment. He uses the word twice, ten verses apart, and lets the reader find it.

Being fair to them. These men were not inventing a prejudice. They were defending a boundary God had drawn himself, in writing, which faithful Israelites had died rather than cross. From where they stood Peter had done something indefensible, and that it had gone well was no argument; plenty of wrong things go well. Their instinct was not that of small men but of serious ones who had not yet been told what God had decided.

The circumcision made without hands. Their question is answered, in the end, by Christ himself. Circumcision was the sign that a man belonged to the covenant people. Paul would later tell Gentile believers that in Christ they had been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:11–12). What the knife had marked on the outside of Abraham’s sons, Christ accomplishes within every believer by his death and resurrection. The Gentiles in Caesarea were not lacking what the sign pointed to. They had been given the reality, because they had been given Christ.

Is it wrong to question a Christian leader? No, and this passage shows it can be right. The Jerusalem believers did not gossip about Peter behind his back or split the church; they raised the matter with him directly, and he answered them patiently. The Bereans were praised for checking even Paul’s teaching against the Scriptures (17:11). What matters is the spirit and the standard. Question openly, not in whispers. Question by Scripture, not by preference. And be ready, as these men were in the end, to be persuaded and to praise God when you are shown to be wrong.

In a sentence. The apostles and believers throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God, and when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticised him.

On a Tuesday. Even true believers can resist what God is doing when it breaks their habits. Be teachable. Ask yourself where you might be defending a good thing past the point where God has moved on, and where your first instinct when something new happens in the church is to look for the fault.

For worship. The word of the Lord ran from a front room in Caesarea to every town in Judea faster than the apostle who had preached it, and no faction could call it back. Such is the God who speaks. His word does not wait for permission, it is never bound (2 Timothy 2:9), and it does not return to him empty but accomplishes what he purposes (Isaiah 55:11). He spoke Christ into a Gentile house, and the house believed. He is speaking him still into houses the church has argued about.
verseByVerse.note: The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”

You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them. Here is the charge, and the first thing to notice is what it is not. They do not say, you preached to Gentiles. They do not say, you baptised uncircumcised men, which is the far larger question and the one that will dominate the council in chapter 15. They say: you went to uncircumcised men and ate with them. The complaint is about a meal.

Eating as a verdict. That looks trivial to a modern reader, and it was nothing of the sort. In the ancient world a shared table was the plainest public statement two people could make about each other. A Jew could trade with a Gentile, serve under one and argue with one; sitting down to supper said, in front of everybody, that you belonged to one company. So the circumcision party have gone straight to the real issue. Preaching to Gentiles could be a mission. Eating with them is a verdict. If Peter can sit at Cornelius’s table, the wall is down, and everything else follows.

The charge laid against his Master. The complaint has a history, and Peter had heard it before. The Pharisees and scribes grumbled at Jesus in almost the same words: this man receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2). Jesus answered with three parables about a shepherd, a woman and a father who go after what is lost and rejoice when it is found. So the charge brought against Peter is the charge brought against his Lord, and it is the best thing that could be said of either. The table Peter sat at in Caesarea was set by Jesus long before, at the house of Levi and the house of Zacchaeus. A church that is never accused of this has stopped doing what Jesus did.

The same man, later. And this must be said, because it makes the passage honest rather than triumphant. Peter wins this argument completely; the room falls silent and praises God. Some years later, at Antioch, he is eating with Gentile believers as a matter of course when men arrive from this same party, and he gets up from the table. The other Jewish believers follow, even Barnabas, until Paul confronts him in front of everybody because his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11–14). Having told them in Jerusalem why the wall was down, he later left a table because he was afraid of them.

Where Christian failure lives. There is no comfort in that and there is a great deal of use. A conviction can be argued to a conclusion, defended in public, praised by the church, and still not have reached the part of a man that decides where he sits at dinner. Peter’s theology was right in chapter 11 and his feet were wrong in Galatians, and the gap between the two is where most Christian failure actually lives.

If Peter could fail like that, how can I hope to stand? By the same grace that restored Peter every time he fell. He denied Christ three times and was restored; he withdrew from the Gentiles and was corrected, and he received the correction, for years later he calls Paul our beloved brother (2 Peter 3:15). Your standing does not depend on never failing, but on Christ, who keeps those the Father has given him (John 10:28–29). What you can do is close the gap between belief and practice deliberately: notice where your table, your friendships and your diary contradict what you say you believe, and let a faithful friend tell you when they do.

In a sentence. They accused him of going to uncircumcised men and eating with them.

On a Tuesday. Who would you be uncomfortable being seen eating with? Not in theory, but in your actual town, with your actual friends watching. That is the person to invite.

For worship. On the night he was betrayed, Christ took bread and gave it as his body, given for men who would all desert him before morning. He does not merely eat with sinners. He gives himself to be their food, and now he spreads his table for people from every nation, circumcised and uncircumcised, who come with nothing but their hunger. No one has ever been worthy to sit there, and no one who came in his name has ever been turned away. That is why it is grace.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter began and explained it to them in order: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me.

But Peter began and explained it to them in order. The word for in order, kathexēs, is the one Luke used when he told Theophilus he had written an orderly account (Luke 1:3): one thing after another, nothing left out, nothing rearranged. Peter is not making a case. He is giving evidence.

What is absent. Look for what is missing from this defence. He does not quote Scripture, though Isaiah has much to say about the nations. He does not appeal to his office, or to the commission to go to the ends of the earth, which every man there had heard from the Lord’s own mouth. He does not argue or pull rank. He tells them what God did, in the order it happened.

Why an account works better than an argument. An argument meets a counter-argument, and both sides go home unmoved. An account of events, given in order, with witnesses present, must be either accepted or called a lie, and with six men from Joppa in the room the second is not available. The best answer to criticism is often a patient, honest account.

A witness, not an advocate. Peter is doing exactly what Jesus appointed him to do, without needing to say so. You will be my witnesses, the Lord had told him (1:8), and a witness does not argue a case; he says what he saw. All through Acts the apostles’ authority rests on that: they testify to what the risen Christ has done, so that their hearers must deal with him and not with them. Even this report, though it begins with a sheet, is about Christ’s work. It ends with the Lord’s remembered word (v. 16), with faith in the Lord Jesus Christ (v. 17), and with Gentiles given repentance that leads to life. The sequence Peter keeps so carefully is the sequence of the risen Lord at work.

I was in the city of Joppa praying. He starts where the story starts: not with the Gentile question, but on a roof at midday doing what he did most days, when the whole thing came down on him from outside. That matters to his case. If this had begun with an idea of Peter’s, the circumcision party would be entitled to their objection. It began with a sheet.

Something like a great sheet descending. And he says so with the same phrase Luke used in chapter 10 (10:11). Even under pressure, defending himself in front of a hostile room, Peter will not describe the thing more definitely than he saw it. And he adds one small detail: it came down to me. Heaven came to where he was.

In a sentence. Peter explained everything to them step by step: while praying in the city of Joppa he saw in a trance a vision, something like a great sheet let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came right down to him.

On a Tuesday. When you are criticised, resist the urge to defend yourself with heat or with your credentials. Tell the story patiently and honestly, in order, and let the facts speak. And when you tell anyone what God has done in your life, begin where it actually began: with him.

For worship. The Lord comes down. He came down to a roof in Joppa with a vision Peter had not asked for, as the Son once came down to a manger and a cross, unbidden and unearned, and every work of grace since has had the same direction. Sinners do not find him by searching the heavens. He finds them where they are, praying or not praying, and leaves them with nothing to say for themselves except to tell, in order, what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’

Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. Peter’s retelling is harder than Luke’s own account of the vision, which listed animals, reptiles and birds. Reporting to law-observant Jews already angry with him, Peter adds a category: beasts of prey, wild carnivores, the creatures furthest from anything a Jew would put on a plate. He has volunteered the most repellent item on the list.

He studied it. He adds something else: looking at it closely. He did not glance at the sheet and recoil. He examined it item by item, and knew exactly what he was being asked to do before he refused.

Making his own case worse. This is a man under examination making his case worse on purpose, and it is why the defence works. Every instinct would shade the account: leave out the beasts of prey, imply that the contents were unclear. Peter tells them precisely how offensive the command was, because his case rests on its having come from God, and a softened command is no longer the one that came. A man defending something God has done does not need to make it palatable. The offensiveness of the instruction is part of the evidence that it was not his idea.

The hardest fact in the apostles’ message. Peter had done this before, in a far greater matter. Preaching in Jerusalem, he did not soften the death of Jesus into a misfortune. He told the crowd that they had crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men, and that God had made him both Lord and Christ (2:23, 36). The apostles always led with the most repellent fact in their message, a Messiah executed on a tree, because it was the fact that saves, and no one inventing a religion to please Jews or Greeks would ever have chosen it. The beasts of prey in Peter’s report are a small instance of an honesty he had learned from the cross itself.

And I heard a voice saying to me, Rise, Peter; kill and eat. He quotes the words unaltered, including his own name in them. The command he resisted is reported as it came. Whatever else the men in that room concluded, they could not conclude that Peter had drifted into this.

Should we soften the hard parts of the gospel to make it easier to accept? No. The gospel has an offence that cannot be removed without destroying it: the cross is a stumbling block and folly to the world (1 Corinthians 1:23). We should remove every unnecessary offence, our rudeness, our jargon, our cultural baggage, so that the only stumbling block left is Christ himself. But we may not trim what God has said about sin, judgment, the uniqueness of Christ or the call to repent, because it is the very hardness of these truths that shows they did not come from us. People are not won by a gospel made comfortable. They are won by a gospel made clear.

In a sentence. Looking at it closely, he saw four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles and birds, and heard a voice telling him to get up, kill and eat.

On a Tuesday. When you speak about your faith this week, resist the temptation to leave out the part you think will offend. Say it kindly, say it carefully, but say it. The truth told whole is more persuasive than the truth made convenient.

For worship. The wisdom of God has never needed to be made palatable. He lowered a sheet of unclean beasts over a roof and built his church out of the people it stood for; he sent his Son to a cross and made the place of the curse the fountain of blessing. Every time, what looked like foolishness has proved wiser than men. There is no part of his way with us that he is ashamed of, and no part of it that will not, at the end, be seen to have been glorious.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’

But I said, By no means, Lord. Now the shrewdest thing in the speech, and it is simply honesty. Peter tells them he refused: for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth. He puts his own objection into the record in the words he used, the words every man in that room would have used. When God gave him this command, his first reaction was theirs.

What it does to the argument. They came believing Peter had gone soft on the law, and here he is testifying that he defended it to God’s face. There is no version of the story now in which Peter was a man with loose views looking for an excuse. He was the man who said no. Whatever changed his mind was not in him.

How to move people who disagree. Most persuasion begins by explaining why the other man’s position is inadequate, and most persuasion fails, because a man defending a position hears only that he is under attack. Peter shows that he held their position, understood its reasons and stated it more strongly than they had. Only then does he say what happened next.

But the voice answered a second time from heaven, What God has made clean, do not call common. That is the sentence that ends the matter, and Peter does not paraphrase or apply it. He reports it and lets it sit in the room. It had been said to him and is now said to them, in the same words, by the same voice, and it is as unanswerable the second time. The only reply open to the circumcision party is the one Peter had already tried, and they have just heard how it went for him.

With the blood of a spotless lamb. Peter would come to say how God makes people clean. At the council he said that God had cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts by faith (15:9), and in his first letter he told Gentile Christians that they had been ransomed from their futile ways not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). The voice that overruled him on the roof was not announcing a relaxation of standards. It was announcing that the Lamb without blemish had been sacrificed, and that the cleansing he purchased reached Gentiles too.

Does the vision abolish the Old Testament food laws? Its first point is about people: Peter concludes that he should not call any person common or unclean (10:28). But it also reflects what Jesus had already declared (Mark 7:19): the food laws, which separated Jew from Gentile, are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and Christians are free to eat any food (Romans 14).

In a sentence. Peter said he had refused, since nothing common or unclean had ever entered his mouth, but the voice from heaven answered a second time that he must not call common what God had made clean.

On a Tuesday. Admitting your own resistance can help others accept what God is doing. The next time you need to persuade a fellow Christian of something, begin by stating his view fairly and saying honestly where you once stood. Then tell him what changed you.

For worship. The voice from heaven had the last word, and it always will. God does not need our permission to cleanse what he chooses to cleanse, and his declaration over a sinner washed in Christ cannot be overturned by any accuser. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven.

This happened three times. Peter produces it as evidence, and in that room it was strong. A single extraordinary experience can be doubted: a dream, a mood, something misremembered. A thing repeated three times, with the same voice, command and correction, has moved out of the category of impressions. God said it until it could not be mistaken.

The Lord who asks three times. Three is Peter’s number. Three denials by a charcoal fire; then, on a beach, the risen Jesus asked him three times, Simon, son of John, do you love me? and three times gave him his sheep to feed (John 21:15–17). The Lord did not restore him with one question and leave him to wonder whether it had taken. He met each denial with a question of its own. Now the same Lord speaks three times on a roof, with the same kindness, not exasperation. He knew how many times this man would need to hear it, and said it that many times. Christ’s patience is measured not by what we deserve but by what we need.

And all was drawn up again into heaven. Then it stopped: no interpretation, no application, no instruction. Peter was left with a command he had refused and a sentence he could not argue with. Anyone shown something in Scripture with no clear next step attached may take heart. The application was already walking up the road and would be at the gate within the hour. Peter did not have to work it out. He had to answer the door.

In a sentence. This happened three times, and then everything was drawn back up into heaven.

On a Tuesday. Is there a lesson God keeps teaching you, through sermons, through Scripture, through circumstances, that you keep failing to learn? Do not read the repetition as anger. Read it as love, and this time, act on it.

For worship. The patience of the Lord is not a reserve that runs down. He is the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine for the one, and goes out again when the one wanders again. His mercies are new every morning because his people need them every morning, and the sheet was drawn back into heaven only when the lesson had been given in full. His patience is longer than our stubbornness, and it is the patience of one who has already borne our sins and will not lose what he has paid for.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house.

And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were. Peter’s case rests on timing. The sheet has just gone back up, and at that instant three strangers are at the door asking for him by name, sent from thirty miles away by a man he has never met, who had sent them the day before the vision was given. Nobody arranged that. God’s timing confirmed the vision.

And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. That phrase is the hinge of the defence, and in Greek, mēden diakrinanta, it is the same verb Luke used in verse 2 of the men now questioning him: they criticised Peter; the Spirit told Peter to make no distinction. Peter is quoting the instruction back to a room full of people doing the very thing it forbade. He does not point it out. He does not have to. The Spirit forbade distinction between Jew and Gentile.

All authority, down to the minute. The Lord who sent Peter had told his apostles on what ground he sent them: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; go therefore and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18–19). Three men arriving at the moment the sheet withdrew is that authority at work in small things. The risen Christ, who upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), also governs the pace of travellers on a coast road, so that his word and his messengers meet at a door. And the Spirit’s instruction to make no distinction is the same commission in its plainest form: all nations, without exception.

These six brothers also accompanied me. These: they are in the room. Peter brought his witnesses back to Jerusalem and up to this meeting, and at the critical moment he can point to six men who saw it all. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). He has brought double, and with himself they make seven; Roman law, it has often been noted, had important documents such as wills sealed by seven witnesses. Ask them, Peter is saying.

The foresight. On the morning he left Joppa, Peter had a vision he did not understand and an instruction without a reason, and he still thought: whatever happens at the end of this road, I will have to account for it, and my word alone will not be enough. That is a leader who knows that being right is not the same as being believed, and that the honest way to handle a claim nobody wants to hear is to make it checkable in advance. And then, plainly: we entered the man’s house. The very thing he is accused of, he states as a fact.

In a sentence. At that very moment three men sent from Caesarea arrived at the house where Peter was, and the Spirit told him to go with them, making no distinction, and these six brothers went with him, and they entered the man’s house.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit makes no distinction among those who believe, and neither should the church. Look around your congregation and ask whether any group is quietly treated as second-class: the poor, the new, the foreign, the young, the old. Then do something to bring them in.

For worship. The Lord of history is never early and never late. He timed a knock at a tanner’s door as he timed the fullness of time, when he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). The hand that brought Christ into the world at the appointed hour brought three Gentiles to Peter’s gate at the appointed minute, and it governs every hour of ours with the same wisdom and the same love.
verseByVerse.note: Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’

And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house. Here Peter supplies Cornelius’s side of the story, and with it a piece of information that Luke’s earlier account twice held back (10:4–6, 30–32). Both times the angel’s message ran the same way: your prayers and alms have been remembered; send to Joppa for Simon called Peter. Both times it stopped there.

He will declare to you a message by which you will be saved. Now, reporting to Jerusalem, Peter finishes the sentence. That clause is the whole reason Peter can stand in that room. Think about what he is demonstrating with it. Before he ever left Joppa, before the vision on the roof, before the knock at the gate, God had already told a Gentile that a message was coming by which he would be saved. Peter did not go to Caesarea and then decide that Gentiles could be saved. He was sent as the delivery of a promise that had already been made without him.

What the message was. The angel did not say what the message would be, but Peter had preached it in Caesarea: Jesus of Nazareth, anointed with the Spirit, hanged on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed Judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness (10:38–43). That is the message by which a man is saved, because it is the announcement of the only Saviour. Cornelius’s prayers could reach God’s notice; only Christ could reach his guilt. Peter had already told the council in Jerusalem that there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12).

It settles the question about Cornelius. And it settles the question the story otherwise leaves open. Cornelius was devout, generous and prayerful, and God had noticed all of it. He was also, on the day the angel came, not saved, because the angel told him a message was coming by which he would be. No reading of that sentence allows his piety to have been sufficient in itself, or the gospel to have been an optional enrichment for a man already safe. Salvation comes through the gospel (Romans 1:16; 10:14–17).

Hard and kind together. The hard half: sincerity does not save, and God does not pretend it does. The kind half: God’s answer to a sincere man was not to leave him with his sincerity but to send an angel, arrange a vision, override an apostle’s lifelong conviction and move him thirty miles up the coast, to bring him the message.

You and all your household. And note the last five words. The promise arrives with a family attached to it, the servants, the soldiers, the relatives Cornelius had gathered, which is how God had been speaking to households since Abraham, and which Peter had already announced at Pentecost when he said the promise was for them and for their children (2:39). The whole household heard and believed (10:44), and household salvation in Acts follows household hearing and believing (16:31–34; 18:8).

Does you and all your household mean that a family is saved together, or support infant baptism? Cornelius’ household heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (10:44–46), so they were believing hearers. The verse does not teach that faith passes to children automatically; each was saved by hearing and believing. Christians who baptise infants see a covenant pattern in household baptisms; but the households in Acts are described as hearing and believing.

Can I trust God for my family’s salvation? You can pray for it with great confidence, because God loves to work in families and has often saved whole households. But Scripture does not promise that every member of a believer’s family will be saved, and each person must come to Christ himself. What you can do is what Cornelius did: bring your family under the word, gather them where the gospel is preached, live the faith in front of them, and pray for them by name, every day. Then leave them in the hands of the God who is more willing to save than you are to ask.

In a sentence. Cornelius told them how he had seen the angel standing in his house and telling him to send to Joppa for Simon called Peter, who would declare to him a message by which he and all his household would be saved.

On a Tuesday. Good people still need the gospel. Do not assume your decent friends and relatives are fine without Christ. Think of the most moral unbeliever you know, and ask God for an opportunity to speak to him about the message by which he can be saved.

For worship. The Father kept a Roman soldier waiting four days for news of his Son, and it was worth every hour. He could have sent anything to Caesarea. He sent the only thing that saves: Jesus Christ, offered freely to a Gentile and all his house. That is the love of God, which is never content to admire our sincerity from a distance, but comes all the way to us with the Saviour in its hands.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’

As I began to speak. Peter is being precise, and the precision is his argument. Luke’s account in chapter 10 says the Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking; Peter’s own account says it happened as he began. He felt he had only just started. He wants the room to understand how little of the work was his. He had not finished. He had not called for a response. He had barely got going, and God did not wait for the rest of it.

The Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. Then the comparison that ends the debate. Not something similar. Not a lesser gift, or a partial one, or an unusual religious experience which might be interpreted in various ways. The same thing, and the apostles in that room had been there for the first one and could judge for themselves. Peter calls Pentecost the beginning, which is how the church had come to date itself, the start of a new era, and he is saying that what happened in a Roman officer’s front room was the beginning happening again to different people. The Gentile Pentecost was the same gift.

And I remembered the word of the Lord. Then the loveliest detail in the speech: the theology arrived as a memory. Watching Gentiles speak in tongues, Peter did not reason his way to a conclusion; a sentence came back to him, spoken by Jesus just before the ascension: John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit (1:5). It had sat in him for years, and it came up at the exact moment it was needed and explained everything he was seeing. The promise applied to the Gentiles too. The words of Jesus interpret events, and not the other way round.

The worth of memorising Scripture. Anyone who wonders whether getting Scripture into the memory is worth the trouble should notice that Peter could not have looked it up. What he had was what he had heard and kept, and when the moment came the sentence was there, as Jesus had promised: the Spirit will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (John 14:26).

What is the baptism with the Spirit? It is Christ’s act of pouring out his Spirit on his people, uniting them to himself and to one another. John the Baptist could only apply water to the outside; Jesus gives the Spirit himself, who cleanses and renews from within. Paul says that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free (1 Corinthians 12:13). So every believer has been baptised with the Spirit, and the proof is not a particular experience but faith in Christ and a life being changed by him. If you trust in Jesus, the promise of Acts 1:5 has been kept in you.

In a sentence. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them as he had on the apostles at the beginning, and Peter remembered the Lord’s words, that John baptised with water, but they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Learn one verse of Scripture by heart this week, and say it over to yourself each morning. You do not know when you will need it, but the Spirit does, and he works with what you have stored.

For worship. The same Spirit, the same gift, for every believer. There is one baptism of the Spirit into one body, and the risen Christ who promised it on the Mount of Olives kept his word in Jerusalem and again in Caesarea. He does not give his Jewish people one Spirit and his Gentile people another. He gives himself, wholly, to all who believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?

If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. The same gift: no difference. The gift came with faith, for Jews and Gentiles alike. Not with circumcision, not with law-keeping. He gave it when we believed; he gave it when they believed. The only variable that has been removed is the one the circumcision party was standing on.

When we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. Notice the full title. The one thing the apostles and Cornelius’s household had in common was not a nation, a law or a history, but a Person believed in. Jews who had walked with Jesus for three years and Gentiles who had first heard of him that afternoon received the identical gift on the identical ground, because the gift does not come from the believer’s past but from the Lord he trusts. That is why Peter cannot stand in God’s way. To refuse those who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ would be to refuse the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who had given them his Spirit.

Who was I that I could stand in God’s way? It is the last sentence of the defence, and it is worth noticing what kind of sentence it is not. Peter does not say he was right. He does not say he had authority, or that he had weighed the matter and reached a considered view, or even that he had obeyed. He pleads incapacity. The leading apostle of the church, answering the church, says in effect: what was I supposed to do, stop him? Stand in God’s way is kōlysai, hinder, prevent: the same word as withhold the water (10:47). To refuse those whom God has accepted is to fight God (5:39).

Airtight. The logic has no moving parts. If God has done the identical thing on identical terms, the question is no longer whether Gentiles may be admitted, but whether anyone proposes to overrule God on a matter he has settled in public. Nobody does, and the next verse records silence.

What it does not mean. A guard is needed here, because this verse is quoted in church disputes far more often than it is examined, and in the wrong hands it becomes a way of ending discussion rather than resolving it. Who was I that I could stand in God’s way is not a formula for winning arguments by asserting divine backing. It works in this passage because of everything attached to it: a vision that was repeated three times, an independent vision given to a man thirty miles away, three messengers who arrived at the precise moment, an explicit word from the Spirit, six witnesses who can be questioned, and a public sign identical to the one the apostles had seen at the beginning. Peter is not merely saying, God told me. He has just spent thirteen verses laying out the evidence, and only then does he draw the conclusion. A man who says God told him and produces none of that has said something quite different, and the church has been damaged by people who learned Peter’s last sentence without noticing that it came at the end. And today, with the apostolic witness complete, the test of any claim is the written word of God.

So is the baptism with the Spirit a second stage after conversion? Peter equates what Jesus promised (1:5) with what Cornelius received when he believed: the same gift. Pentecostal Christians point to the Samaritans (8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (19:1–7), who received the Spirit after believing. But those were moments when the gospel crossed new boundaries, and Paul teaches that every believer has been baptised in the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). The more likely reading is that the baptism with the Spirit is given to every believer at conversion.

In a sentence. Peter asked that if God gave them the same gift he gave the apostles when they believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was he to stand in God’s way?

On a Tuesday. Do not stand in God’s way. If he has accepted someone, accept him. Ask whether there is a believer you have been holding at arm’s length, not because of his sin, but because he does not fit your expectations, and close the distance.

For worship. The same gift, to all who believe. God does not ration his Spirit by nationality, or measure out his grace by pedigree. The Father who gave his only Son gives with him all things freely, to Jew and Gentile alike, and the gift is nothing less than himself dwelling in us. Who could stand in the way of such a God, and who would want to?

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.

When they heard these things they fell silent. Silence first, and the order matters. Before there is any praise there is a roomful of men with nothing to say: the objection simply runs out. Luke does not record anyone conceding, or apologising, or explaining how they had come to see it differently. The argument stops because there is no longer anything on the other side of it.

Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life. Then the praise, from criticism to worship, the best possible response to correction, and a well-judged sentence from men who have just lost a debate. Note the verb. Not, the Gentiles have repented, which would be a report, but God has granted. They name the giver in the same breath in which they concede the point. Repentance is God’s gift (2 Timothy 2:25), not something we produce, and what they praise him for is not that a barrier fell but that people were given eternal life. Gentiles are saved the same way as Jews, by God’s grace, through repentance and faith.

The gift from the throne. The church in Jerusalem knew through whose hands the gift came. Peter had told the Sanhedrin that God exalted Jesus at his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins (5:31). Now the church hears that the exalted Christ gives the same thing to Gentiles. Repentance that leads to life is not a mood a sinner works up. It is a gift given from a throne by the Saviour who died, and the life it leads to is his own risen life. The silence in Jerusalem breaks into praise because the church sees its Lord giving to the nations what he had first given to them.

One part for the whole. There is a useful lesson in reading the Bible here. Only repentance is named, not faith; yet faith is plainly implied, for these Gentiles had believed (vv. 17, 21). Scripture often names one part of a thing for the whole (a figure called synecdoche). Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning to Christ: repentance turns from sin, faith turns to the Saviour, and you cannot truly do one without the other. So Scripture sometimes names both, “repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15), “repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21); sometimes only repentance (here; Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19); and sometimes only faith (“believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,” Acts 16:31; John 3:16). Whichever is mentioned, the other comes with it, as with calling on the name of the Lord (Romans 10:13) and confessing that Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9).

Two cautions. First, never build a doctrine on the absence of a word: it would be a serious mistake to read this verse as though faith were unnecessary, or Acts 16:31 as though repentance were. Scripture everywhere joins the two. Second, savour what the verse says: God granted repentance. The turning itself is his gift, as faith is also called “the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8; compare Philippians 1:29). So when you read repent or believe standing alone, hear the whole: turn to Christ, from sin and unto the Saviour, and give thanks that even the turning was granted from above.

Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen. Then Luke drops the scene, goes back several years to the persecution that killed Stephen, and picks up a thread left in chapter 8 (8:1–4). The scattered believers travelled as far as Phoenicia, the coast around Tyre and Sidon, and Cyprus, and Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire after Rome and Alexandria, with perhaps a quarter to half a million people and a large Jewish community.

Speaking the word to no one except Jews. After verse 18 it lands like a cold draught. The church has just agreed, with praise, that God has granted repentance to the Gentiles, and Luke’s next sentence reports that for years believers had carried the gospel across three provinces and told nobody but their own kind. Luke makes no comment, but the gap between the two sentences measures how long it takes a settled conviction to reach the street. The principle was conceded in a meeting. The practice changed in Antioch, almost by accident, in the hands of men whose names nobody wrote down.

If repentance is God’s gift, what am I supposed to do? Repent. God’s gift of repentance does not happen around you but in you: he gives it by working in your heart so that you yourself turn from sin, freely and genuinely. You are never told to wait passively until you feel repentant. You are commanded to repent and believe (17:30), and the very desire to obey that command is the first sign that God is granting it. And if you are praying for someone who shows no sign of repentance, this verse is your warrant. You cannot argue anyone into it, but you can ask the God who grants it to grant it to them.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying that God had granted the Gentiles too repentance that leads to life; meanwhile those scattered by the persecution after Stephen had travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word only to Jews.

On a Tuesday. Is there a gap between what you believe about the gospel and whom you actually speak to about it? Write down the names of three people outside your usual circle, a different background, a different language, a different generation, and pray for an opening with one of them this week.

For worship. The turning of a heart is the gift of God. The tears a sinner sheds over his sin, the first turn of his face toward Christ, the whole road from death to life: all of it is granted, from the throne of the one who died. He gave it in Jerusalem, and in Caesarea, and soon in Antioch, and he is giving it still. There is no heart so hard that he cannot give it repentance, and no nation he has not purposed to give it to.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee. Antioch in Syria was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those scattered by the persecution after Stephen’s death travelled to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, telling the message only to Jews. But some from Cyprus and Cyrene went to Antioch and began speaking to Greeks as well, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus. The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord. When news reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Arriving and seeing what God’s grace had done, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord. Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, found him and brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught great numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. During this time some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, Agabus, predicted through the Spirit that a severe famine would spread over the entire Roman world, which happened during the reign of Claudius. The disciples, each according to their ability, decided to provide help for the believers living in Judea, and sent their gift to the elders by Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the model the New Testament actually gives us for a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with unnamed laymen doing the obvious thing; it was recognised rather than authorised; it was established by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first corporate act was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them. Reformed missiology has drawn the pattern out: rooted in the word, generous beyond its own borders, and willing to give away its best men — for within two chapters Antioch will send Barnabas and Saul off on the first missionary journey, which is to say it exported its two finest teachers and kept none of them. A church is not measured by what it gathers. It is measured by what it is prepared to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The single most important barrier in Christian history was crossed by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Luke knows their home towns and not their names, which tells you they were never anybody's leadership. Now: The work that turns out to have mattered most in any generation is very often done by people who will not appear in an account of it — who simply spoke to whoever was in front of them, because it did not occur to them to check first whether they were allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene. Everything turns on a small word at the start of the sentence: but. Verse 19 said the scattered believers spoke to nobody except Jews. But there were some of them, and the whole future of the church is in that exception.

Nameless men. Luke tells us where they came from and not who they were: Greek-speaking Jews from the island of Cyprus and from Cyrene in North Africa, used to living among Gentiles and less scandalised by them than a man raised in Judea. Not apostles. Luke, a careful historian who names dozens of minor figures, evidently could not find out their names. The first deliberate preaching to Gentiles in a Gentile city was done by ordinary, nameless Christians. God uses ordinary people.

Cyrene again. Men of Cyrene had a synagogue in Jerusalem and were among those who argued with Stephen and could not withstand him (6:9–10). Luke does not say these are the same men, and it would be wrong to assert it. But the city that supplied some of Stephen’s opponents also supplied some of the first men to do what Stephen had been killed for pointing toward.

Who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also. There is a genuine question about the word here. The manuscripts divide between Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews, and Greeks, meaning Gentiles proper, and your Bible probably has a footnote. The sense of the passage requires Gentiles: verse 19 has just said to no one except Jews, and this sentence is the contrast to it. Whatever the copyists made of the word, Luke’s argument is unmistakable.

Preaching the Lord Jesus. Notice what they led with. To Gentiles they did not start with Jesus is the Messiah, a Jewish title that meant little in a Greek city, but with Jesus is Lord, which every Greek understood and which claimed everything. Antioch was full of lords: Apollo in his famous grove at Daphne outside the city, the mystery cults, the emperor himself. Into that city these men carried one name, and when Luke says a great number turned to the Lord, the Lord is the one they preached. Jesus had never walked the streets of Antioch. He went there in the mouths of his people, and he was with them as he had promised, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). Wise evangelism adapts its words, not its message.

No vision, no angel. And notice what is absent: no vision, no angel, no word from the Spirit, no instruction from Jerusalem, no debate, no record that anybody asked permission. Peter needed a sheet let down three times before he would enter a Gentile house. These men reached a Greek city and talked to Greeks because there were Greeks there. They already had their commission (1:8), and they obeyed it.

And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. The hand of the Lord is an Old Testament phrase for God’s power actively at work (Isaiah 59:1). And notice the pairing: they believed and turned, faith and repentance together, as in verse 18. Heaven’s verdict on the initiative of unnamed men was to bless it enormously.

Do I need a special call to tell people about Jesus? No. Every Christian already has one. The command to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19) and the promise of the Spirit for witness (1:8) belong to the whole church, not to apostles alone. Some are called and gifted to preach and to lead, and the church should recognise them. But speaking of Christ to your neighbour needs no ordination. These men had no title, no training we know of and no instructions, and they started the church that evangelised the world.

In a sentence. But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and spoke to the Greeks too, preaching the Lord Jesus, and the Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a title to share Christ. Think of one person you meet regularly who does not know him, and this week tell him one thing about Jesus as Lord: what he has done for you, or what he claims. Leave the results to the hand of the Lord.

For worship. The hand of the Lord was with nameless men in a pagan city, and a great number turned to him. God does not need famous servants to do his greatest works; he delights to use the unknown, so that the glory is plainly his. Their names are not in Acts, but they are written in heaven, and on the last day the Lord Jesus will call them by name.
verseByVerse.note: “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,

The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Jerusalem hears, and Jerusalem sends somebody. It is the second time in three chapters that news of an irregular advance has reached the mother church and produced a delegation: they sent Peter and John down to Samaria (8:14), and now they send a man to Antioch.

The man they chose. The choice settles the outcome. There were men in Jerusalem who would have arrived with the circumcision party’s questions in their pocket, and the first Gentile congregation in history would have had its foundations examined by somebody looking for a fault. They sent Barnabas, a Cypriot like some of the evangelists, and the son of encouragement (4:36).

When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad. What did he actually see? A room full of uncircumcised Greeks with pagan backgrounds and no synagogue training, worshipping the God of Israel, taught by nobody in particular. There was plenty for a careful man to worry about, and Barnabas saw the grace of God. He looked at an untidy, unauthorised, doctrinally unformed crowd of new believers and identified the one thing that was really going on.

Glad. Not relieved, not cautiously satisfied: glad, a word from the same family as the grace he saw (chairō, charis). His name meant son of encouragement, and he had earned it twice already, selling a field for the poor and vouching for Saul when nobody else would go near him. Here he earns it a third time simply by being pleased, and a great deal turned on it. The Gentile mission survived its inspection because the inspector was a man capable of being delighted.

And he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose. Then he does the work. Exhorted, parekalei, is the root of his nickname: he encouraged them. With steadfast purpose is literally with purpose of heart, a settled inward intention. He does not begin by correcting them. He tells a young church in a pagan city the one thing it will most need, which is to stay put, and he tells them to do it from the inside out. New believers need encouragement to keep going.

Holding fast to the Lord. The Lord they are to remain with is the Lord Jesus they had just turned to (v. 21), and the charge is the one Jesus gave his own disciples on the night before he died: abide in me, and I in you, for apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:4–5). Barnabas does not give a young church a programme. He points it to a Person and tells it to hold on. And the grace he saw was Christ’s too: Peter would soon say that Jew and Gentile alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus (15:11). What Barnabas saw in Antioch was Christ at work, and what he urged was Christ held fast.

How do I see the grace of God in other Christians? Look for what only God could have done. A new believer’s doctrine may be muddled and his habits rough, but if he loves Christ, wants to hear the word, is beginning to hate his sin and loves God’s people, you are looking at the grace of God. Name it to him, and thank God for it aloud. Then, when correction is needed, it will come from someone he knows is on his side. Barnabas did not ignore what needed teaching; he and Saul spent a year teaching (v. 26). But he started with gladness.

In a sentence. When news of this reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch, and when he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with steadfast hearts.

On a Tuesday. The next time you visit another church, or meet a Christian from a different tradition, look first for the grace of God and say what you see. Then encourage one person this week to keep going with Christ, specifically and by name.

For worship. The grace of God has a face. It shone in Antioch on the faces of former pagans because it had first shone in the face of Jesus Christ, and it is his grace that saves, keeps and makes a church out of strangers. He gives it to the untidy and the untaught, and he gives eyes to see it to men like Barnabas, so that the joy in heaven over sinners who turn is echoed, here and there, by gladness on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.

For he was a good man. Luke stops the narrative to explain the previous verse, and the explanation is a character reference. Good. Not brilliant, strategic, eloquent or well connected: Luke had those words available and did not reach for them. It is the plainest commendation in the New Testament and one of the rarest, offered as the reason a whole city came to Christ. A good man sees good.

No jealousy in him. And notice where Luke has placed the sentence. It sits between Barnabas being glad at what he found and Barnabas going to fetch Saul: that is, in the middle of an account of a man rejoicing over somebody else’s work and then going to get somebody better at teaching than himself. Luke’s portrait of goodness is not abstract. It is a man with no jealousy in him.

Full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. It is one of the loveliest things Scripture says of anyone. Luke uses the phrase not for a momentary filling for a single task (Acts has those too, a sudden filling for boldness or speech, 4:8, 31; 13:9) but for a settled condition: a man so yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit governs his character, words and deeds, and the church can see it in the fruit. The same is said of Jesus himself (Luke 4:1) and of Stephen (6:5), so to be full of the Spirit is simply to be deeply like Christ. In Barnabas it is concrete: the giver who sold his field (4:36–37), the big-hearted man who vouched for the feared new convert Saul (9:27), the encourager who was glad to see God’s grace in Antioch (11:23).

Borrowed from the Good Shepherd. Every goodness Luke can find in Barnabas is borrowed. Jesus called himself the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and the marks of Barnabas’s goodness are the marks of that Shepherd in miniature.
