The shadow in the verse. Luke reports it in half a sentence and offers no comment, and it would be dishonest to supply the comfort he withholds. Peter’s deliverance cost other men their lives. That is in the text, and a reading of this chapter which celebrates the falling chains and skips verse 19 has read half of it. Two things can be said, and neither is a full resolution. The first is where the moral weight actually sits. God opened a door; Herod gave the order. The king who had already killed an apostle because it was popular now executes his own soldiers to cover an embarrassment, and Luke has arranged this chapter so that four verses later God deals with him. The blood of those guards is on the account of the man struck down at Caesarea in the twenty-third verse. This is the kind of king he was. The second is that this is what the world is like, and Scripture will not pretend otherwise. Deliverances happen inside a fallen system, and the system exacts a price somewhere. The Bible reports it rather than tidying it, which is one of the reasons it can be trusted about the rest. A book written merely to encourage the church would have ended verse 19 after the words did not find him.

Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. And then the last clause, which reads like an administrative detail and is in fact the end of a man. Herod leaves Jerusalem for his coastal capital, and never comes back. His final recorded act in the holy city, the place where he had been so careful to appear devout, was to have his own men executed for something none of them had done.

Was God unjust to let the guards die? No. God did not kill the guards; Herod did, and Herod answered for it. God is under no obligation to prevent every evil act of wicked men, and he often allows them to show what they are before he judges them. His ways in such things are often hidden from us, and Scripture does not invite us to explain them all. But it assures us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), that no innocent blood is forgotten by him, and that every tyrant will give account. The cross itself is the ultimate proof: the most unjust act in history, done by wicked men, was the means by which God saved the world, and the men who did it will answer to him.

In a sentence. When Herod had searched for him and could not find him, he cross-examined the guards and ordered them to be executed, then went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

On a Tuesday. Cruel power destroys even its own servants. Pray for those who live under such rulers today, and for those who serve them in fear. And pray for rulers themselves, that they would come to fear God before it is too late.

For worship. The God who hides his own also sees everything done in the dark by those who hate them. He is not mocked. The blood of James and the blood of sixteen soldiers cry out to him, and he hears. And the blood of his own Son speaks a better word than all of them, offering pardon even to the violent, while the unrepentant tyrant runs out of time.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.

Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. Luke turns to a piece of provincial diplomacy, and the reason he includes it becomes apparent two verses later. Tyre and Sidon are the two Phoenician ports up the coast. The quarrel itself is not explained, and we do not know why he was angry, but the leverage is plain: their country depended on the king’s country for food. Those cities sat on a narrow strip between mountains and sea with almost no farmland, and had imported their grain from the fields of Galilee since Solomon’s day (1 Kings 5:11; Ezekiel 27:17). Herod could not conquer them. He could starve them, and they knew it.

Having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain. So they come to terms, and Luke records how it was arranged. The chamberlain was the man in charge of the king’s private rooms, controlling access to the royal bedchamber and therefore to the king, and persuaded is doing a certain amount of work; men in that position were not usually persuaded by argument alone. Probably a bribe. Two ancient cities had to win over a courtier, very possibly with money, in order to get permission to eat.

On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. Then the day itself: power on display. It is worth knowing that we have a second account of this occasion from outside the New Testament. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing for a Roman audience some fifty years later and with no interest whatever in defending Luke, describes Agrippa at Caesarea at games held in honour of the emperor, coming into the theatre at daybreak in a robe woven entirely of silver, so that when the early sun struck it the garment blazed and the onlookers were dazzled, and then flatterers in the crowd calling out to him as a god. He records that the king was seized almost at once with violent pain in his belly, was carried out, and died after five days.

Two independent witnesses. Two writers, working independently and for different readerships, describe the same king, in the same city, on the same public occasion, in the same royal display, receiving the same acclamation and dying of the same sudden illness. Luke says an angel of the Lord struck him and Josephus does not, which is exactly the difference one would expect between the two. On everything a historian can check, they agree.

Why does it matter that Josephus confirms Luke? Because the Christian faith rests on things that really happened, not on myths or private visions. Luke told Theophilus he had written so that he might have certainty concerning the things he had been taught (Luke 1:4), and he wrote as a historian, naming rulers, cities and dates that could be checked. Again and again, outside sources and archaeology have confirmed his accuracy in detail. That does not prove every miracle, but it shows that Luke was a careful and truthful witness, and it gives good reason to trust him when he tells us what only the eyewitnesses saw: an empty tomb, an angel in a cell, and a church that turned the world upside down.

In a sentence. Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him together, and having won over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food, and on an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat on the throne and delivered a speech to them.

On a Tuesday. Notice how much of your life depends on things you cannot control: food, health, employment, the decisions of powerful people. Thank God this week for daily bread, and remember that every earthly supply comes ultimately from his hand, not from any king’s.

For worship. The world’s power dazzles for a moment. Herod’s silver robe blazed in the morning sun, and within a week he was in the grave. Christ’s glory is for ever. His face shines like the sun in its strength, his garments are white as light, and his throne is established for ever and ever. The kingdoms of this world are lit by borrowed light. The Lamb is the lamp of the city of God.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.

The voice of a god, and not of a man! The crowd kept shouting it. It is flattery from men who had just won over a courtier and needed the grain to keep coming, and Herod knew exactly what it was worth. Ancient rulers were often hailed as gods. That is not the point. The point is what he did with it, which was nothing. He did not correct it.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Set that beside a scene two chapters earlier in this same city of Caesarea. A Roman centurion fell at Peter’s feet, out of genuine reverence rather than calculation, and Peter reached down and pulled him up and said, Stand up; I too am a man (10:26). Same town, same kind of moment, and the two men in it do opposite things. Luke has put them a few pages apart on purpose, and only one of them is alive at the end of this chapter. Paul and Barnabas will do as Peter did at Lystra (14:14–15).

Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down. And there is the verb again, the one Luke used at verse 7, when an angel of the Lord struck Peter on the side to wake him. Two blows in one chapter from the same order of being: one to rouse a prisoner who was about to die, and one to end a king who thought he was a god. Luke never remarks on it. He simply uses the word twice.

Because he did not give God the glory. Now the reason given, and it is not the one a reader expects. Not because he executed James. Not because he imprisoned Peter, or killed his own guards, or played politics with people’s lives to keep a crowd happy. All of that stands on the record, and none of it is cited. The charge God brings against Herod Agrippa is that a man let himself be called divine and did not hand the honour back. I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8).

The sin underneath the others. That is worth sitting with, because it rearranges most people’s instinctive scale of sins. The murders were real and will be dealt with. But the thing named in the indictment is the theft of something that belongs to God alone, which is, when you think about it, the sin underneath all the other ones. A man who is willing to be worshipped will do anything at all to the people underneath him.

And he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. Josephus, independently, records five days of agonising pain in his belly before his death in AD 44. Luke gives it a single sentence. The grandson of Herod the Great, in silver, on a platform, with a crowd calling him a god, and within the week a burial. The man who was hailed as a god was eaten by worms. Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18), as Nebuchadnezzar learned when he boasted on his palace roof and was driven out to eat grass like an ox until he acknowledged that the Most High rules (Daniel 4:30–37).

What it does not mean. One guard is needed, and it matters. This is not a template for reading illness or sudden death as divine judgment, and it has been misused that way with great cruelty. Luke tells us the reason here because it was disclosed to him. In almost every other case nobody has been told anything, and the man who claims to know why somebody is ill has appointed himself to a bench he has not been called to. Jesus himself warned against the assumption that those who suffer disaster were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1–5).

How do I give God the glory when I am praised? Receive the kindness graciously, without false modesty, and then turn it quickly toward God, in your heart and, where it is fitting, in your words. You might say, thank you, God has been very kind, or, I am grateful it helped. More important is what happens inside: remind yourself that every gift you have was given (1 Corinthians 4:7), and refuse to feed on the praise in private afterwards. Herod’s danger was not that people admired him but that he kept what belonged to God. The test is whether, when praised, you feel larger, or more grateful.

In a sentence. The people kept shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” and at once an angel of the Lord struck him down because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died.

On a Tuesday. When praised, give God the glory. Quickly. And watch the subtler forms of Herod’s sin: the secret pleasure in being thought indispensable, the irritation when someone else gets the credit. Bring them to God as soon as you notice them.

For worship. To God alone belongs the glory. He will not share it with kings in silver robes, nor with apostles, nor with angels, nor with us. And yet the eternal Son, who alone deserves the worship Herod stole, humbled himself to the death of the cross, and therefore God has highly exalted him. The crowd at Caesarea gave a man the honour due to God. One day every tongue will give it to the right Man: Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, in AD 44.

parallels.desc: my glory I give to no other

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.

But the word of God increased and multiplied. Put that sentence immediately after the one before it and feel the size of the contrast. A king in cloth of silver, hailed as divine by two cities, is dead and buried. And the next thing Luke writes is a sentence about a message spreading, with a but in front of it, as though the death of a king were the sort of thing that might have been expected to slow it down and did not. This is the point of the whole chapter. Herod killed, imprisoned, persecuted, and was worshipped; now he is dead. The word of God grows.

The language of living things. The verbs are the ones used of living things: increased and multiplied, the language Genesis uses of creatures filling the earth (Genesis 1:22). Luke has used this kind of progress report before, at the end of the Jerusalem years (6:7) and after the conversion of Saul (9:31), and each time it marks the close of a movement and the opening of the next. Here it is doing something more pointed. To most readers today Herod Agrippa is known for one thing: he appears in this chapter. The movement he set out to destroy wrote him into its records as an illustration. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of our God will stand for ever (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:24–25).

And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service. Then the last verse, which is housekeeping and is also the assembling of a team. The famine money from Antioch has been delivered (11:29–30), and the two of them turn for home. Some manuscripts read to Jerusalem, but from Jerusalem, back to Antioch, fits the story.

Bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark. He is Mary’s son, and Mary’s house is where the prayer meeting was. Which means that on the night Rhoda left Peter standing at the gate, this young man was very likely in that house. He had watched the church pray all night for a man, and had watched it refuse to believe the man was at the door.

The boy in the luggage. He is now going to Antioch, and from Antioch he will go out on the first missionary journey (13:5), and at Pamphylia he will turn back and go home (13:13), which will cause the sharpest quarrel recorded between two Christians in the New Testament and split Paul from Barnabas (15:37–39). And years later Paul will write from a prison cell asking for him, because he is useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). And somewhere in those years, by the church’s earliest tradition, he wrote down the recollections of Peter, and the church has been reading them as the Gospel of Mark ever since. All of which is in front of a young man who, at the end of this chapter, is simply a name added to somebody else’s luggage. Luke closes an account of an executed apostle, a miraculous deliverance and the death of a king by mentioning, almost in passing, a young man going along with his cousin, and it turns out to be one of the most consequential sentences in the paragraph.

If a Christian has failed badly, can God still use him? Mark is the answer. He deserted the mission, became the cause of a painful split, and might easily have been written off for good. Barnabas did not write him off, and in the end neither did Paul, who came to count him useful. And God used him to write the earliest Gospel. Failure is not the end of usefulness for a believer who repents and keeps going. The same is true of Peter, who denied his Lord and was restored to feed his sheep. If you have failed, confess it, receive Christ’s forgiveness, accept the consequences humbly, and get back to work. The Lord is not finished with you.

In a sentence. But the word of God kept increasing and spreading, and Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had finished their service, bringing with them John, also called Mark.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of powerful people doing terrible things, read Acts 12 again, and remember who has the last word. Then do something small for the word of God this week: give to a missionary, invite a friend to church, teach a child a verse. That is the work that outlasts every king.

For worship. Tyrants die, but the word of God grows. Herod is dust, and the gospel he tried to silence has gone to the ends of the earth and is still increasing and multiplying in every nation. The kingdom of our Lord is not shaken by the rage of rulers or the death of apostles. Christ reigns, and he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. Take heart. The word of the Lord endures for ever, and so does every soul it has made alive.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 is a meditation on what it means to live under the providence of a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies; Peter lives — both by divine appointment. The church prays; the answer comes — and still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour; he is given worms and silence. This is the world the New Testament describes: not a world where God occasionally intervenes, but a world where God is always governing — every chain, every gate, every angel, every worm. The appropriate response is not to explain his ways, but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the Word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no political recourse, no legal protection, and no army — meeting in a house and praying with everything they had. Their prayers opened a prison door a few streets from where they sat. They did not know it would happen that way. They prayed because there was nothing else to do, and because the God they prayed to had not changed.

Now: The church in every hostile political environment must learn the same calculus: Herod has soldiers; God has angels. Herod has chains; God has the Word. The appropriate response to power arrayed against the gospel is not despair and not political calculation — it is earnest, persistent, expectant prayer to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And then, when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>18</sup>And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. <sup>19</sup>And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance. <sup>20</sup>All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. <sup>21</sup>Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>24</sup>Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <sup>25</sup>And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>34</sup>And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ <sup>35</sup>Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ <sup>36</sup>For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, <sup>37</sup>but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The third stage of Acts 1:8, “to the end of the earth”, begins in earnest. The church at Antioch, led by a strikingly mixed group of prophets and teachers, is worshipping and fasting when the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special work. With prayer and the laying on of hands they send them off, with John Mark as their assistant. They sail to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island, preach in synagogues from Salamis in the east to Paphos in the west, and there meet the Roman governor, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet, Elymas, who tries to turn him from the faith. Saul, from now on called by his Roman name Paul, rebukes Elymas, who is struck blind, and the proconsul believes.

They sail to Perga on the south coast of modern Turkey, where Mark leaves them, and travel inland over the Taurus mountains to Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony on the high plateau. In the synagogue Paul is invited to speak and gives the first of his sermons recorded in Acts: God chose Israel, brought them out of Egypt, gave them the land, judges and kings, and from David’s line has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. The people of Jerusalem condemned him, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is proclaimed and everyone who believes is freed from everything the law of Moses could not free them from. The next Sabbath nearly the whole city gathers. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas announce that they are turning to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. Opposition drives the missionaries out, and they shake the dust off their feet, while the new disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he had called them. After more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on them and sent them off. Sent out by the Spirit, the two went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus. At Salamis they proclaimed God’s word in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper. They travelled through the whole island to Paphos, where they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, an intelligent man, sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer, as his name was translated, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. Then Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Spirit, looked straight at Elymas and called him a child of the devil, an enemy of everything right, full of deceit and trickery, who would not stop perverting the Lord’s right ways. The Lord’s hand was against him, and he would be blind for a time. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit does not speak to Barnabas and Saul privately and send them to inform the church. He speaks in the assembly, to the assembly, about two men who are standing in it — and the church then fasts, prays, and lays hands on them before letting them go. Reformed ecclesiology has taken this as the pattern: an individual sense of call confirmed by a congregation, and a congregation's judgement confirmed by the Spirit, with neither operating alone. Notice also what the sending cost. Barnabas had been sent to build up that church and Saul was its finest teacher, and Antioch gave away both on the strength of one sentence in a prayer meeting. A church's seriousness about mission is not measured by what it collects for it but by whom it is willing to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in verse 1 is the most cosmopolitan leadership team in the New Testament, and it was assembled by a persecution. Every man on it was in Antioch because something had gone wrong somewhere else. Now: Congregations tend to produce leaders who resemble each other, and to regard that as normal rather than as a symptom. Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what the room looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”

Meaning first. Acts 13 begins the third part of the book: the gospel to the ends of the earth (1:8). The church in Antioch, prompted by the Spirit, sends out Barnabas and Saul on the first deliberate missionary journey. In Cyprus a Roman governor believes; in Pisidian Antioch Paul preaches his first recorded sermon, the gospel of forgiveness and justification through Jesus; many Gentiles believe, “as many as were appointed to eternal life”; and the pattern of Paul’s mission is set: to the Jew first, then to the Gentile. Behind every step stands the risen Christ, sending his Spirit, keeping his ancient promises to David, and gathering a people he chose before they had heard his name.

Prophets and teachers. These are the leaders of the church: prophets who brought a word from God before the New Testament was written, and teachers who explained the Scriptures. A young church in a pagan city, and God had given it both.

Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul. Read the list of names slowly, because Luke did not have to give it and it tells you what had happened to the church in about fifteen years. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, the man who sold a field and vouched for Saul. Simeon who was called Niger: Niger, the ESV notes, is a Latin word meaning black, or dark, very likely a description rather than a family name, so Simeon may well have been from Africa; some suggest he was Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross (Mark 15:21), though no one can be sure. Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa, and men of Cyrene were among the unnamed pioneers who first preached to Greeks in this very city (11:20). Manaen, a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch: the word (syntrophos) means he was brought up with him, a foster brother at court. This man had shared a nursery with the Herod who beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Jesus. And Saul, last on the list, who had gone through Jerusalem dragging believers out of houses.

What a church looks like. Five men, four countries, two continents, an African, an aristocrat and a former persecutor, and not one of them from Jerusalem. Nobody designed that. It is what a church looks like when it has been assembled out of a scattering and has stopped asking who is allowed in. Two boys grew up in the same palace; one became the murderer of the Baptist and the other a teacher of the church of Christ. Grace took one and passed the other by, and the one it took never forgot it.

While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting. The word for worshipping (leitourgountōn) is the word for priestly service, ministering before God; it gives us our word liturgy. These men were not in a planning meeting. They were before the Lord, and the church’s great missionary step came out of worship and prayer, not out of a strategy paper.

Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. And then, while they are worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Spirit speaks and asks for the two best men in the room. Notice the pronouns. For me: they belong to him before they belong to Antioch. I have called: the call had already been given; the church only recognises it. The Holy Spirit speaks in the first person, as one who calls and claims servants for himself, which is how only God speaks. Mission is the Spirit’s initiative from first to last. Paul uses the same phrase of himself when he writes to Rome, saying he was set apart for the gospel of God (Romans 1:1). And note too that the church is asked for its best two leaders, not those it can spare.

What is fasting? Fasting is worth pausing on, since many believers today have never done it. To fast is voluntarily to go without food (for part of a day, a day, or longer) to seek God. It is not dieting, nor a hunger strike to twist God’s arm, nor the self-punishment Scripture warns against (Colossians 2:23). The empty stomach drives the soul to God, saying with the body what the heart means: Lord, I want you more than my daily bread. In Scripture it goes with earnest prayer and attends the great seekings of God: guidance and the sending of missionaries (here; 13:3; 14:23), repentance (Joel 2:12; Jonah 3), grief (2 Samuel 1:12), crisis and intercession (Esther 4:16; Ezra 8:21–23), and steady devotion (Anna, Luke 2:37). Jesus himself fasted forty days (Matthew 4:2).

Is it commanded of Christians, and is it in the Epistles? Honestly, no: fasting is nowhere laid on believers as a law, and the letters mention it barely (2 Corinthians 6:5; 11:27 may even be involuntary hunger). So no one sins by not fasting, and no one earns anything by it. And yet Jesus plainly assumed his people would fast: when you fast, he said (not if), warning only against doing it for show (Matthew 6:16–18); and asked why his disciples did not fast, he said the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, but the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast (Matthew 9:15), this present age between his ascension and return. So fasting is not a rule to keep under compulsion, but a privilege and means of grace the Lord expects his church to use.

How did the Spirit say this? Luke does not say. The likeliest answer is through one of the prophets named in v. 1, speaking in the gathered church (compare 11:28). Today, with the Scriptures complete, the Spirit guides churches through his word, prayer, and the wisdom of the church and its elders, not by new revelations.

How does a person know whether he is called to such work? Notice that the call here was heard by the church, not by Barnabas and Saul alone, and confirmed with fasting, prayer and the laying on of hands (v. 3). A call to missionary or pastoral work is not a private impression; it is tested by gifts, character, the desire to serve, and the recognition of the church and its leaders.

So should you fast? Gently, yes: not from guilt or to score points, but as a gift worth taking up; you are missing a help your Master meant you to have. Why? Because in some seasons, a weighty decision, a heavy burden in prayer, sorrow over sin, a longing to seek God afresh, setting aside even food to give that time and hunger to God focuses and humbles the heart and intensifies prayer; and the very hunger preaches that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). How? Start small: skip a meal or a day, and spend the time in prayer and the Word; always tie the fast to a purpose and to prayer (fasting without praying is merely going hungry); keep it secret, never paraded (Matthew 6:17–18). Two cautions: guard against pride, for the Pharisee boasted that he fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and Isaiah 58 shows God despising a fasting joined to hard-heartedness; and use ordinary wisdom about health (the unwell, pregnant, or medicated should take care, and abstaining from water is only ever brief). Fasting earns nothing; but as a humble, hungry way of seeking the God who satisfies, it is worth recovering, for out of one such fast at Antioch the Spirit launched the gospel to the nations.

Does the Holy Spirit still call particular people to particular work? Yes, though not usually by a voice in a meeting. He still gives gifts, lays burdens on hearts, opens doors and moves churches to recognise and send. What has changed is the means, not the Sender. If you sense a pull toward some work for Christ, do not keep it private and do not wait for a voice. Tell your elders, serve where you are, let others test whether the gifts are there, and pray with them. The Spirit who called Barnabas and Saul called them in company, and he still does.

In a sentence. In the church at Antioch were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen who grew up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul, and while they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work he had called them to.

On a Tuesday. Be willing to send your best for the gospel, whether that is a person from your church, a child from your home, or the hours you most value. And listen for the Spirit in worship and prayer: the guidance of Antioch came to people who were already on their knees, not to people waiting for a sign before they would kneel. If you have never fasted, choose one meal this week, give its time to prayer for the spread of the gospel, and tell no one.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest does not wait for his church to have a missionary strategy. He has one, and he has had it since he promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him. He gathered an African, a courtier and a converted persecutor into one room, and out of their worship he launched the nations’ hope. The Spirit who says for me is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who owns every servant he sends, and who has never once called a man to a work without going with him into it.
verseByVerse.note: Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa, like Lucius of Cyrene. Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas. Here begins Paul’s first missionary journey (13–14).

parallels.desc: set apart for the gospel of God

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.

Then after fasting and praying. Four verbs, and the whole of a sending is in them: they fasted, they prayed, they laid hands on them, and they let them go. Notice that they fast again. They had been fasting when the Spirit spoke; now, having heard him, they fast a second time. There is no suggestion that the word settled the matter and the rest was administration. Between the call and the departure there is another season of going without food and asking God about it, which is not doubt, and is what serious people do before an irreversible step.

They laid their hands on them. The laying on of hands here is not ordination to an office and does not confer anything Barnabas and Saul did not have; the Spirit had already called them, and both had been in ministry for years. It is not promotion to a higher rank. It is the congregation’s public act of identification and blessing, as with the seven (6:6): these are our men, this is our work, and we are putting our hands on it in front of everybody. Whatever happens in Cyprus and Galatia, Antioch has signed for it.

And sent them off. And then the last words, which are the costly ones. The verb means literally they released them, let them go. The Spirit sent them (v. 4); the church released them. Both are needed. Consider the arithmetic from Antioch’s side. Barnabas is the man Jerusalem had sent to establish them, who had seen the grace of God among them and been glad, and who had then travelled to Tarsus to fetch the teacher. Saul is that teacher, who had spent a year instructing them. They are the two most valuable men the congregation possesses, and the church has had them for perhaps two years, and it lets them both walk out of the door at once.

The actual test. Every church knows how to pray for missions and most know how to fund it. The thing this verse describes is rarer and is the actual test: a congregation giving away the people it can least afford to lose, to work it will not see, on the strength of a conviction that God has asked for them.

Does laying on of hands give the Spirit or special power? Not here. Sometimes in Acts the apostles laid on hands and the Spirit came in a special way (8:17; 19:6), marking key moments as the gospel crossed new boundaries. But this act at Antioch is done by the church, for men who already had the Spirit and the call. It is a solemn, prayerful setting apart, much as a church today commissions missionaries or ordains elders. Nothing magical passes through the hands. What passes is the church’s blessing, its recognition and its pledge to stand behind those it sends.

What does it mean to share in a missionary’s work? It means more than an occasional prayer. Antioch put its hands on these men, and that meant owning them: praying by name, sending money, writing, welcoming them back and hearing their report (14:26–27). Paul calls such churches partners in the gospel (Philippians 1:5). In practice, know the names of the missionaries your church supports, pray for one of them each week by name, find out what they actually need, and when they come home, give them a meal and an evening, not a five-minute slot.

In a sentence. After fasting and praying, they laid hands on them and sent them off.

On a Tuesday. Ask what in your life you would find hardest to release to God’s work: a son or daughter abroad, a favourite colleague in the church called elsewhere, your evenings, your savings. Antioch held its best people with an open hand. Hold yours the same way, and pray for the missionaries your church has sent: you share in their work.

For worship. The Father did this first and at infinitely greater cost. He did not send what he could spare. He sent his only Son, the one he loved before the foundation of the world, out of the glory of heaven and into a hostile world, knowing what it would cost. Every church that releases its best for the gospel is only tracing, faintly, the outline of the gift at the centre of the gospel: God so loved the world that he gave.
verseByVerse.note: Laying on hands commissioned them for the task.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.

So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit. Luke has just told us in the previous verse that the church sent them off. Both are true and he sets them side by side without the slightest awkwardness. The congregation released them and the Spirit sent them, and it is one act described from two sides. The Spirit is the sender. Mission belongs to God.

They went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. They go down to Seleucia, the port for Antioch, sixteen miles down the Orontes, and take ship for Cyprus, which is a hundred miles across open water and, on a clear day, visible from the Syrian coast. It is worth registering how modest the first stage is. The first missionary journey in the history of the church begins with a day’s sail to an island you can see from the beach, in the direction of the place one of the two men grew up. That is not a criticism; it is how sensible mission usually starts. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island (4:36), and he had family and contacts there; the island had a substantial Jewish population and a settled community of believers already, since some of the refugees of chapter 8 had gone there (11:19). They begin where they have a reason to begin.

When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. Salamis was the main city on the east coast, and at Salamis they establish the pattern that will govern the next fifteen years. Synagogues, plural: Salamis was large enough to have several. Jews and God-fearers there knew the Scriptures and were waiting for the Messiah. To the Jew first (Romans 1:16). Paul will do this in every city he enters, right through to the end of the book, and he will do it in cities where the synagogue has already thrown him out of the last one.

And they had John to assist them. Then the last sentence, dropped in without emphasis. The word (hypēretēs) is the assistant, the subordinate who does the practical work: the man who handles the arrangements, the money, the baggage, the copies of the Scriptures, perhaps some teaching of new converts. John Mark is not on the platform. He is carrying things. Luke mentions him here so that the reader will notice his absence eight verses later.

Why go to the synagogue first if they were sent to the Gentiles? Because God’s promises came through Israel, and the gospel is the fulfilment of those promises. It would have been strange to announce that Israel’s Messiah had come and skip Israel. The synagogue was also where people already knew the Scriptures, and where God-fearing Gentiles gathered, so it was the natural first door. Paul never saw Jew and Gentile as rival audiences. One Christ, promised to the one and given to both.

Is it wrong to start where you have connections? No. Barnabas began on his own island, among his own people, and Luke records it without a hint of reproach. God usually spreads the gospel along existing lines: families, friendships, workplaces, home towns. Andrew brought his brother; the Samaritan woman told her village. Start with the people God has already put near you. Just do not stop there. The same journey that began in Cyprus went on over the Taurus mountains to towns where they knew no one.

In a sentence. Sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, and at Salamis they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper.

On a Tuesday. Start your witness where you have connections. God uses relationships. Name three people you already know who do not know Christ, and pray for an opening with one of them this week. And if your part in the work is carrying the bags, carry them gladly: John Mark’s first job was luggage, and the Spirit wrote him into Scripture.

For worship. The Spirit of God does not drift. He sends, and he sends with precision: to a port, an island, a city, a synagogue, a particular Sabbath. The same Lord who prepared Cyprus long before Barnabas set sail goes ahead of every messenger he sends. The mission is his before it is ours, and it will be his when ours is over.
verseByVerse.note: Seleucia was Antioch’s port. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island; Salamis was its main city in the east. John is John Mark.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.

When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos. A hundred miles or so on foot, east to west, coast to coast, town by town. Luke covers it in a clause. There is a great deal of ordinary walking in the missionary journeys and almost none of it gets a sentence. Paphos was the Roman administrative capital, at the western end, so this is the seat of government, and what they find there is a study in contrasts that Luke sets out with some care.

A certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. On one side, a magician. Note the combination, because it is a peculiarly ugly one: a Jew, with access to the Scriptures, trading in the magical arts that those Scriptures forbid absolutely (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), attached to a Roman household as a resident specialist in the supernatural. His name means son of Joshua, or son of Jesus. Like Simon in Samaria (8:9), he is an occult figure attached to the powerful.

He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence. On the other side, the proconsul, a man of intelligence: shrewd, perceptive, a man who understands things. And what this shrewd man does is send for two travelling Jewish preachers, because he sought to hear the word of God. Not all the powerful are closed to the gospel.

The proconsul and Luke’s accuracy. It is worth pausing on the title, because it is one of the small marks of Luke’s accuracy that has been tested and held. A proconsul governed a senatorial province on behalf of the Roman Senate. Cyprus had been an imperial province governed by a legate, and was transferred to the Senate in 22 BC, after which its governor was a proconsul. Luke uses the correct term for the correct decade in the correct province, a thing he does repeatedly, and which has been vindicated by inscriptions again and again; an inscription mentioning a Paulus as proconsul has been found. The fuller defence of Luke as a historian is set out at 5:37–38 and need not be repeated; it is enough to note that this is another instance.

The man at his elbow. And the human situation is one every evangelist recognises. There is an intelligent man who genuinely wants to hear, and there is somebody at his elbow whose whole position depends on his not hearing it.

Is magic or the occult real, and should Christians be afraid of it? Scripture treats the occult as real enough to forbid and false enough to despise. Behind it stand real spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12), but they are creatures, and they are defeated ones: Christ disarmed them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). So a Christian should neither dabble nor dread. Keep away from horoscopes, mediums, spells, charms and anything that promises hidden power or knowledge apart from God. But if you belong to Christ, you are not at the mercy of any of it. Greater is he who is in you.

In a sentence. When they had travelled across the island to Paphos, they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, an attendant of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man who sent for Barnabas and Saul wanting to hear the word of God.

On a Tuesday. Do not assume that the clever, successful or powerful person in your life is closed to Christ. Sergius Paulus sent for the preachers. Some of the people you are most nervous of speaking to are quietly wanting someone to speak. Pray for leaders to hear the word, and pray by name for one person in authority you know.

For worship. God reaches into governors’ houses. No office is too high for his grace, no court too guarded, no man too intelligent for the word to astonish him. The Lord who rules the rulers of the earth had his eye on a proconsul in Paphos and sent two tired walkers a hundred miles to find him.
verseByVerse.note: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end. A proconsul governed a province for the Roman Senate. Bar-Jesus means “son of Joshua.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.

But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name). Luke gives us two names for this man in three verses, Bar-Jesus in the Aramaic and Elymas in whatever language the parenthesis is explaining, and then tells us plainly what he was: a magician. Elymas may come from an Arabic or Aramaic word for a wise man or sorcerer, more a title than a name. The trade has been described at Samaria in chapter 8, and it was not entertainment; it was the sale of access to power, and it paid well when the customer was a Roman governor.

Opposed them. Which is exactly what is at stake, and it is worth naming without pretending the man’s motives were purely theological. Elymas has a position. He is the resident authority on the invisible in the household of the most powerful man on the island, and two Jewish preachers have just been invited in to talk about God. If the proconsul believes them, Elymas is finished: not damned, merely unemployed. A great deal of opposition to the gospel has looked exactly like this, and very little of it has ever announced itself in those terms. And behind the man’s interests stood darker powers, for the occult resists the gospel (Ephesians 6:12).

Seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Note also his method, because it is the shrewd one. He does not challenge Paul to a debate and he does not attack the doctrine. The work is done sideways, in private, through the relationship he already has. A man with the governor’s ear does not need to win an argument. He needs only to keep the argument from being properly heard, and he has all the time in the world to do it. That is worth recognising because it is still the commonest shape of the thing. The gospel is rarely refuted in front of the person who was about to believe it. It is undermined afterwards, quietly, by somebody they trust, who says nothing that could be written down and answered.

Away from the faith. And the last phrase tells you how close the man was to being lost. Sergius Paulus was not on the edge of an interesting conversation. He was on the edge of believing, and Elymas could see it.

What if someone close to the person I am praying for is working against the gospel? Expect it, and do not be thrown by it. Pray specifically, both for your friend and for the one turning him away, because Elymas too was within reach of mercy (v. 11). Keep the conversation open and honest, so that quiet undermining has something plain to be measured against. And remember that no adviser, spouse or friend can finally keep away from Christ someone God is drawing. The proconsul believed with Elymas standing in the room.

In a sentence. But Elymas the sorcerer, as his name means, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith.

On a Tuesday. When someone is close to faith, expect opposition, and pray. Then turn the light on yourself: is there anyone whose drift toward Christ, or toward deeper obedience, you are quietly discouraging because it would cost you something if they changed? A raised eyebrow, a joke at the right moment, a warning about getting too religious. That is Elymas’s method, and it can be used by church people too.

For worship. The enemy works sideways, but the Lord works in the open, and his purposes are not at the mercy of anyone’s influence. Every whisper at the governor’s elbow was heard in heaven, and none of it could unwrite the name the Father had written. Christ holds his sheep, and no one, not the most trusted adviser in the most powerful house, can snatch them out of his hand.

parallels.desc: the magicians of Egypt oppose Moses

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?

But Saul, who was also called Paul. It happens in the middle of a sentence and Luke never explains it. From this verse to the end of the book the man is Paul, and the name Saul appears again only when he is retelling the Damascus road and quoting the voice that used it. The change is not a conversion souvenir; converts in the New Testament do not get new names, and he had been a Christian for well over a decade by now. Like a great many Jews of the Diaspora he simply had two, as John Mark did (12:12): a Hebrew name for the synagogue and a Roman one for everywhere else, and Paulus was a common Latin family name. What changes here is not the man’s name but his world. He has walked into the household of a Roman proconsul, and from this point onward his life is spent among Gentiles, and Luke starts calling him what those Gentiles called him.

Paul now leads. From here on Paul usually leads as well: Paul and Barnabas, not Barnabas and Saul (v. 13). There is one further touch, and it is either a coincidence or a very dry joke: the proconsul’s name is Sergius Paulus. Luke introduces the Roman Paulus and switches to the Jewish Paul in the space of three verses. Some note that the Latin name means small, and the man who called himself the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9) carried it well.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him. Luke is careful to tell us where the words came from: Paul was filled with the Holy Spirit when he said them. The steady gaze is Spirit-filled discernment, seeing through the man to what he was doing.

You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy. Then the confrontation, and it is ferocious. There is a play on his name: Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus (or Joshua, meaning the Lord saves), is really a son of the devil (John 8:44), not the son of any man of God, but of the other one. Strong words, exposing evil.

Will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? And then the charge itself, which echoes Scripture. The prophet’s cry was to make straight in the desert a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3), and John the Baptist came to prepare those straight paths (Luke 3:4). Elymas has been doing the reverse, putting bends in a road God was building toward a man’s soul.

Not a model for ordinary conversation. It should be said that this is not a model for how to talk to opponents generally, and Paul elsewhere instructs Timothy to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). This is not temper. It is a prophetic sentence, and the man it was spoken to had a governor’s ear and was using it to shut a door.

So when, if ever, should a Christian speak this sharply? Rarely, and almost never in our own cause. The ordinary pattern is gentleness, patience and respect (1 Peter 3:15–16), even with people who mock. Scripture keeps its severest words for those who deliberately twist God’s truth to keep others from it, false teachers and spiritual manipulators, and even then they are spoken to protect the vulnerable, not to win an argument. Paul here was filled with the Spirit and spoke with apostolic authority. An ordinary believer’s plain duty, when someone is leading others astray, is usually to say clearly that it is false, warn those at risk, and leave the judgment to God.

In a sentence. But Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, stared at him and called him a son of the devil, an enemy of all righteousness, full of deceit and trickery, who would not stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Ask the Spirit for discernment to recognise what is really going on when someone stands between another person and the gospel. And watch your own motives when you feel the urge to speak sharply: the test is whether you are protecting the straight paths of the Lord or your own reputation.

For worship. The Lord’s ways are straight. Every road he builds toward a sinner runs true, and no crookedness of men or devils can bend it for long. The Spirit who filled Paul is the same Spirit who once pinned Saul to the dust on another road, and who knows exactly when a word must be gentle and when it must be fire.
verseByVerse.note: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul.

parallels.desc: the ways of the LORD are right

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

The hand of the Lord is upon you. In judgment. The same hand that leads his people out of Egypt (13:17) can fall on those who oppose him. It is the Lord’s hand, not Paul’s.

And you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time. Read the next clause and then remember who is watching it. Some dozen years earlier a man had been travelling to Damascus, certain he was doing God’s work and standing between the gospel and everybody he could reach, and a light had struck him blind, and he had gone into the city groping, led by the hand: Luke’s phrase in chapter 9 and his phrase again here (9:8). Paul is looking at a man going through the exact thing that happened to him. He is not enjoying it. He is recognising it.

For a time. Which explains the three words that turn the whole judgment round. It is a sentence with an end date, a judgment with mercy in it, room to repent. Paul had been blind for three days, and at the end of them a man had come and put hands on him and called him brother. There is no suggestion anywhere in this passage that Elymas is beyond hope, and the one man in the room who knew what that darkness was like is the one who set a limit on it. Luke never tells us what became of him. Given who is speaking, the silence is not a bad sign. Perhaps Paul hoped Elymas would find the same grace.

Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Luke the doctor describes a progressive blindness: mist first, then darkness. The man who had been leading a governor by the ear now needs a stranger to lead him by the hand. He had been making the Lord’s straight paths crooked; now he cannot find any path at all.

Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. And notice what Luke says actually converted the proconsul. The sign got his attention, but he was not astonished at the miracle. He was astonished at the teaching. The blindness cleared the obstruction; what a shrewd Roman administrator actually found overwhelming was the content of what these men were saying. Luke has been careful about this all through his book, and he is careful here: the sign opens the door and the word does the work, and a man who believes because he was impressed has not yet believed anything. Sergius Paulus is the first named Gentile ruler in Acts to believe.

Did the proconsul really become a Christian? Luke says plainly that he believed, and in Acts that word means saving faith, not polite interest. Some have doubted it because Luke does not mention his baptism, but Luke often leaves such details out, and his point is clear: the governor of Cyprus put his trust in the Lord Jesus. It is a fine thing to notice that the first convert of Paul’s Gentile mission was a Roman of the highest rank, and that one of the next would be a slave girl at Philippi. The gospel came for both.

Why are such miracles not common today? Signs like this blindness accompanied the apostles, marking them out as Christ’s authorised messengers while the new covenant word was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and Scripture complete, that particular ministry has ceased. God has not changed, and he still answers prayer, heals and judges as he wills. But the ordinary means he now uses to astonish people is the one that did the real work in Paphos: the teaching of the Lord, faithfully spoken.

In a sentence. Paul said the Lord’s hand was against him and he would be blind for a while, and at once mist and darkness came over him and he groped for someone to lead him, and when the proconsul saw this, he believed, astonished at the Lord’s teaching.

On a Tuesday. Signs point to the word. It is the teaching of the Lord that saves. When you speak to someone about Christ, do not rely on dramatic stories or arguments alone; open the Bible and let the teaching of the Lord do its own astonishing. And if you have ever been led by the hand out of your own darkness, let that make you merciful toward people still groping in theirs.

For worship. Even the Lord’s judgments are shot through with mercy. He struck the persecutor blind and then sent Ananias; he struck the sorcerer blind for a time and left the door open. And the teaching that astonished a Roman governor is the teaching that still astonishes: that the Judge of all became the one judged, that the Light of the world went into the dark at Calvary, so that the blind could be led by the hand into his marvellous light.

parallels.desc: Paul himself led by the hand

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The missionaries sail to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and go inland to Pisidian Antioch. Invited to speak in the synagogue after the Scripture readings, Paul retells Israel’s story from the exodus to King David, and announces that from David’s line God has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. Jerusalem’s leaders condemned him, unknowingly fulfilling the prophets, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is offered: everyone who believes is set free from everything the law could not free them from. Many want to hear more, and the next Sabbath almost the whole city comes. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas declare that, since the word has been rejected, they now turn to the Gentiles, as Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations require. The Gentiles rejoice, those appointed for eternal life believe, and the word spreads, until opponents stir up the city’s leading people and expel the missionaries. They shake the dust from their feet and go on, leaving disciples full of joy and the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. The ESV notes that freed can be rendered justified — a courtroom word, the word for a judge declaring a man to be in the right. The law cannot issue that verdict; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives it. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans. And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends on Habakkuk's word to scoffers, be astounded and perish (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.

Paul and his companions. Something has changed that Luke does not stop to explain. Until this point it has been Barnabas and Saul, in that order, every time: the church set apart Barnabas and Saul (v. 2), the proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul (v. 7). From here on it is Paul, and the man who fetched him out of obscurity in Tarsus, who vouched for him in Jerusalem when nobody else would touch him, and who was the senior partner in every earlier sentence, has become part of the phrase and his companions.

Overtaken and content. Luke records the change and passes no comment on it. There is no meeting, no vote, no explanation. The gifts sorted the order out, and Barnabas, who had every reason to mind, appears not to have minded. It is one of the quietest and hardest things in the New Testament: a man overtaken by somebody else’s growth, who goes on walking beside him.

Came to Perga in Pamphylia. Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor, modern Turkey, a few miles inland from the sea.

And John left them and returned to Jerusalem. Eight words, and no reason given. It is worth saying plainly that we do not know why, because a great deal of confident guessing has been done here. The suggestions are reasonable and not one of them is in the text: homesickness; the road ahead was hard and dangerous; the coastal plain of Pamphylia was malarial, and Paul later reminds these very churches that it was a bodily ailment that brought him to them in the first place (Galatians 4:13); his cousin Barnabas had just slipped to second place; the mission was turning toward Gentiles faster than a Jerusalem boy had bargained for. Take your pick. Luke will not help you.

What it cost. What Luke does record is the cost. Two chapters on, this departure, which Paul regards as desertion (15:38), breaks up the partnership. Paul will not take him, Barnabas will not go without him, and the two men who walked out of Antioch together in verse 3 separate over it (15:36–41). One young man goes home early, and the consequences are still running two chapters later.

Failure need not be final. And then the end of the story, which is the reason to be careful how we read the middle of it. Mark reappears in Paul’s letters, and in the last letter Paul ever wrote, from a Roman prison with his own execution close, he asks for him by name: Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11; see also Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). The man who could not be relied on for one journey became the man the apostle wanted with him at the end, and the writer, as the early church held, of the second Gospel. If you have a Perga in your own history, a work you began and did not finish, a post you left, a moment when you simply went home, notice that Luke puts it in verse 13 and does not close the file. The record of the desertion is in Scripture forever. So is the request for him at the end.

But they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. The two who remain go up. Perga is on the coast; Pisidian Antioch is about a hundred miles inland and three and a half thousand feet up, over the Taurus mountains, a hard and dangerous road with bandits, which Paul later summarises in a few words: danger from rivers, danger from robbers (2 Corinthians 11:26). Luke gives the crossing half a sentence. Most of the cost of the missionary journeys is in the half-sentences. Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony, a different city from Syrian Antioch where they had started.

And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. And then a clause smaller still, which matters more than it looks. This was Paul’s usual practice (17:2). They sent no word ahead. They asked for nothing. Two travel-stained strangers came in, found a place, sat down among the congregation like anybody else, and waited to see whether they would be asked. The most consequential sermon of Paul’s recorded ministry begins with two men sitting down and keeping quiet.

I gave up on something God gave me to do. Can I come back? Yes, and Mark is your proof. His failure was real, it was public, and it hurt people he loved. Scripture does not pretend otherwise. But the same Scripture shows him restored, trusted and useful. Coming back usually means owning the failure honestly, without excuses, and then simply taking up faithful work again, often smaller work, alongside people who will help you. You will not undo Perga. You do not need to. The Lord who restored Peter after his denials restores deserters still.

How should I treat someone who let the team down? Paul and Barnabas both had a point. Paul saw that the work needed reliable men; Barnabas saw that a young man needed a second chance. In the end both were vindicated, and Paul himself came to value Mark. So take failure seriously, and do not pretend it does not matter, but do not write the person off. Give him a smaller task, an older friend, and time. Many of the most useful servants in the church were once somebody’s disappointment.

In a sentence. From Paphos Paul and his companions sailed to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them and went back to Jerusalem, while they went on to Pisidian Antioch, and on the Sabbath they went into the synagogue and sat down.

On a Tuesday. If you have been overtaken by someone else’s gifts, walk beside him gladly, as Barnabas did. If you have a Perga in your past, ask whether the Lord is calling you back to some piece of faithful work. And next Sunday, go in and sit down: be present, unhurried and available. God opens most of his doors to people who have simply turned up.

For worship. If you have turned back from God’s work, he can restore you, as he did Mark, and he restores because his faithfulness never depended on ours. The Lord Jesus never once left the road. He set his face to go to Jerusalem, and he climbed the hill and did not come down until the work was finished. Because he did not turn back, deserters can be brought home and made very useful for ministry.
verseByVerse.note: Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor; Pisidian Antioch lay about 100 miles north, up in the mountains. Mark’s departure later divided Paul and Barnabas.

parallels.desc: Mark is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.”

After the reading from the Law and the Prophets. The service runs its course: the prayers, the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), the scroll of the Law lifted and read, the passage from the Prophets after it. Then the rulers of the synagogue notice the two visitors and send a message down to them. These rulers were lay leaders who organised the service, and visiting teachers were often invited to speak (Luke 4:16–17).

The reading and its history. A word on the reading from the Law and the Prophets, since it shaped the scene.
