The service centred on two readings: one from the Law (the five books of Moses) and one from the Prophets (a chosen passage, the Haftarah, the reading Jesus stood to give from Isaiah, Luke 4:16–20). After them came a word of exhortation, open to any competent man present, exactly the door opened to Paul. Its roots run to Moses, who commanded the Law be read aloud to the people (Deuteronomy 31:10–13), and to Ezra, who read it to the gathered nation and gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8). The synagogue itself grew up during and after the Babylonian exile: with the temple gone and the people scattered, Jews met locally to hear and study God’s Word. The Law was read in order over a fixed cycle, the prophetic reading chosen to match, often with an Aramaic paraphrase for those who no longer spoke Hebrew.

And do Jews still do this? Yes, with striking continuity. To this day the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on the Sabbath (and Mondays, Thursdays, and festivals), on the annual cycle that ends and begins again each year at Simchat Torah (rejoicing in the Torah), still paired with a prophetic reading and a teaching: the very practice Luke describes, kept now as two thousand years ago. And it is the church’s inheritance too: the public reading of Scripture followed by exposition is the pattern Paul charged Timothy to keep, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching (1 Timothy 4:13), the shape of Christian worship ever since. The deep irony here: the Law and the Prophets had just been read aloud, and Paul rises to show that every line was pointing to the Jesus he is about to preach (Luke 24:27, 44). The reading set the table; Paul served Christ from it.

If you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it. The phrase is worth holding for a moment. A word of encouragement, in Greek a logos paraklēseōs, is the very phrase the writer to the Hebrews uses of his own long letter (Hebrews 13:22). It means a word that comes alongside and strengthens. It is what a synagogue expected from a visitor, and it is the ancestor of the sermon. The rulers are being generous, and they are being entirely routine. They are asking for a few warm words on the readings.

They have no idea what they have asked for. Within a fortnight this congregation will have split, the whole city will be at the door, and the two visitors will have been run out of the district by the leading families of the colony. Nobody in the room plans any of it. A polite formality, offered to strangers as a matter of form, is the hinge the entire chapter turns on, which is very often how God gets a door opened, and is worth remembering the next time you are handed something small and routine to do.

Is a sermon really encouragement, even when it is hard? Yes. The word Paul was invited to give was a word of encouragement, and the sermon that followed contained a sharp warning (vv. 40–41). Biblical encouragement is not flattery. It is the word that comes alongside you and puts strength into you, and sometimes that strength comes through a rebuke, sometimes through comfort, always through Christ. A sermon that only made you feel good about yourself would not have encouraged you; one that brought you to Christ always does, even when it hurts on the way.

In a sentence. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders invited them to speak a word of encouragement to the people.

On a Tuesday. When an opportunity opens to speak of Christ, take it, even when it comes dressed as a formality: a request to say grace, a card to sign, a question asked out of politeness. And value the public reading of Scripture in your own church. Listen to it as though it were the main event, because it is.

For worship. For centuries the scrolls had been unrolled, Sabbath after Sabbath, in a thousand synagogues across the world, and every one of those readings had been carrying a name the readers did not yet know. God had been setting the table for his Son in every town of the empire, and when the time was full he sent his messengers to sit down at it. The Word read and the Word made flesh were always meant to meet, and on that Sabbath in Pisidia they did.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it.

So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand. He stands up. In a synagogue the teacher normally sat to expound (Jesus sat down in Nazareth before he began, Luke 4:20), and Paul stands, motioning with his hand, which is the posture and the gesture of a public speaker in the Greek world. Luke notices that hand twice more before the book ends, on the barracks stairs and in front of Agrippa (21:40; 26:1). It is a small thing, and it tells you what kind of man is about to speak: a Jew of the Scriptures who has spent his life in Greek cities and knows how to hold a room. This is his first recorded sermon. Like Stephen’s, it retells Israel’s history, but its aim is to show that God’s promises are fulfilled in Jesus.

Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. His first sentence names two congregations, not one. The second group needs explaining, because they are all over this chapter and much of this book. The God-fearers were Gentiles who had attached themselves to the synagogue. They believed in the God of Israel, kept the Sabbath, came to the readings, tried to live by the moral law, and had not been circumcised, and so had not become Jews. They were the most sympathetic hearers in the ancient world and the most frustrated. Picture a man who has been coming to that building for twenty years. He knows the psalms by heart. He has heard the promises to Abraham read aloud perhaps a thousand times, and every one of those times he has understood that they were being read out to somebody else’s family and that he was welcome to listen. Cornelius was one of these men (10:2). So was Lydia (16:14), and Titius Justus, whose house stood next door to the synagogue in Corinth (18:7).

The back of the room. Paul puts them in his opening sentence. Before a word of the sermon proper, the man on his feet has told the back of the room that this is addressed to them too. So when the Gentiles of this city respond as fast as they do in verse 48, it is not a sudden lurch. The ground had been ploughed for years by the synagogue itself, and Paul knew it.

The God of this people Israel chose our fathers. Then the history begins, and notice the verb it begins with. The sermon opens on God’s choosing, election. Israel was chosen not for its greatness but because the LORD set his love on them (Deuteronomy 7:6–8). It will also end on God’s choosing: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (v. 48). Every man in that room would have said amen to the first without blinking. What split the congregation a week later was not whether God chooses. It was whom.

And made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt. And where did the choosing get them? Read that slowly. The multiplying of the promised family did not happen in the promised land. It happened in a foreign country, under a king who was trying to stop it, through years the Bible describes as bitter with hard service: the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exodus 1:12). God’s promise to Abraham made its greatest visible progress during the four centuries that looked, from the inside, like the promise having been forgotten. If you are in a season you did not choose and would not have chosen, that is not a decorative thought. It is the shape of the first thing Paul says about God in the first sermon of his we possess.

And with uplifted arm he led them out of it. The exodus, God’s great act of salvation in the Old Testament (Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 4:34), the arm bared and raised, the way a man raises his arm to strike. Israel did not slip out of Egypt unnoticed in the night. God took his people out with his sleeve rolled up.

Why does Paul start so far back? Because he wants them to see that Jesus is not a new idea but the point of the whole story. Every hearer knew this history; Paul retells it so that, when he reaches Jesus, they will see the story landing where it was always heading. It is also a lesson in how to read the Old Testament. It is not a collection of moral examples; it is one long account of God choosing, rescuing, enduring and promising, all of it leading to his Son (Luke 24:27).

In a sentence. Paul stood, gestured, and addressed the men of Israel and the God-fearers, saying that the God of Israel chose their fathers, made the people great in Egypt, and led them out with his mighty arm.

On a Tuesday. If you are in an Egypt of your own, a job, a family situation, an illness you would never have chosen, do not conclude that God’s purposes for you have stalled. His people grew most where it looked least likely. Ask him what he is doing in this season, and thank him for one thing that has grown in you because of it.

For worship. Salvation always begins with God’s choice. He chose his people, and he chose you, before you could choose anything. And the God who chose is the God who acts: he does not merely sympathise with slaves, he bares his arm and brings them out. The greater exodus was won on a cross, where the same arm was bared to save (Isaiah 53:1), and no Pharaoh, no sin and no grave could hold the people he redeemed.
verseByVerse.note: “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God.

parallels.desc: with an outstretched arm

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance.

And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. It is a blunt rendering, and very probably the right one. The word (etropophorēsen) means he bore with their ways. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read he carried them (etrophophorēsen, a difference of one letter), and points to what Moses said of these same forty years: the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son (Deuteronomy 1:31). Translations divide here, and honest scholars divide with them. What is worth noticing is that both are true of that wilderness, and neither is flattering to Israel. Either God spent forty years enduring them or he spent forty years carrying them, and the reason he had to do either is the same reason.

Measure the forty years. Put up with is not a compliment and the Bible does not intend it as one. Within weeks of hearing God’s own voice at Sinai they were dancing round a golden calf. They complained about the food and the water, wept for the fish and the cucumbers of the country where they had been slaves, and proposed choosing a leader to take them back to it (Numbers 14:4). God’s own summary is that they put him to the test ten times (Numbers 14:22). The generation that saw the sea open died in the sand.

He did not leave, and he did not pretend. And here is the thing to sit with. God is nowhere recorded as saying that they were doing rather well under the circumstances. He put up with them. If you have ever suspected that God stays with you only because he has not looked closely, this verse is better news than that. He has looked, the assessment is in, and he is still walking at the pace of the slowest man in the column.

He gave them their land as an inheritance. Then, in the next breath, a gift, not an achievement. An inheritance is not a wage. Nobody in Scripture earns an inheritance; it comes to you because of who your father is. Moses made sure they could not misunderstand it: not because of your righteousness (Deuteronomy 9:5). Forty years of being put up with, and then a country, handed over.

After destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan. Paul passes over it in a phrase (Deuteronomy 7:1), but it is one of the hardest things in Scripture, and an honest reader feels its weight: how could a good God order the destruction of the Canaanites? We must not be glib; the loss of life is real and grievous. But several truths, held together, show this is not the arbitrary cruelty it is often imagined to be.

First, it was judgment, not ethnic hatred. Israel had no general warrant to harm Gentiles; she was even to offer peace to distant cities (Deuteronomy 20:10). This was a bounded act of justice on particular nations for particular, appalling sin. God said so: four centuries earlier he told Abraham his descendants would wait, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Genesis 15:16), holding back judgment four hundred years. And the sin? Among other things, burning their own children alive in sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; Leviticus 18:21), with entrenched idolatry and cultic prostitution, until the land itself, defiled, vomited out its inhabitants (Leviticus 18:24–25). This is the wrath of a holy God against great and violent evil, long endured.

Second, it was not favouritism toward Israel. God twice tells them this is not because of your righteousness but because of the wickedness of these nations (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), warning that if Israel does the same, the land will vomit them out too (Leviticus 18:28), and centuries later it did, in the exile. The standard is God’s holiness applied impartially, not ethnic preference; that dismantles the charge of tribal genocide. And mercy stood open throughout: Rahab the Canaanite was spared through faith and stands in the Messiah’s own bloodline (Joshua 6:25; Matthew 1:5). The issue was never race but allegiance.

Third, underneath the objection lies a question it skips. We assume the Canaanites had a right to life that God violated. But Scripture holds that God is the Author and rightful Lord of all life (Deuteronomy 32:39), and that every one of us has already forfeited life through sin (Romans 6:23). On that reckoning, what needs explaining is not that God judges sin, but that he is so patient, and that anyone is spared at all. The Canaanites were not innocents struck down by a capricious deity but guilty people under the just sentence of a Judge who had waited centuries. (On the hardest part, the children, Scripture gives no glib answer; we rest in the One of whom Abraham asked, Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25), trusting his mercy toward little ones, as David did for his own child (2 Samuel 12:23), and refusing to pretend we see more than we do.)

And finally, a unique event. Most importantly for a Christian: this was a unique, one-time event, Israel as a covenant nation executing God’s judgment in a particular land. It is emphatically not a model for today. Jesus refused the sword (my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting, John 18:36); the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:4); we love our enemies and leave vengeance to God (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:19). No one may invoke Joshua to justify violence in Christ’s name. Rather, the conquest is a sober, localised preview of the final judgment. And here the gospel speaks its deepest word: at the cross the judgment we all deserve fell on Jesus. The same holy God who judged Canaan did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32) but laid our condemnation on him, so that wrath and mercy met. The only refuge from judgment, as for Rahab, is faith in the God of Israel, now revealed in Christ. That is just where Paul’s sermon is heading: all this history runs to a Saviour (v. 23).

Does God still put up with his people today? Yes, and every honest Christian depends on it. The patience that bore with Israel in the wilderness bears with the church now: our grumbling, our forgetfulness, our small idolatries. But patience is not approval. The wilderness generation also shows that God’s patience is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), and Hebrews uses this very forty years as a warning not to harden our hearts (Hebrews 3:7–19). So take comfort that he bears with you, and take care not to treat his bearing as permission.

In a sentence. God put up with them for about forty years in the wilderness, and after overthrowing seven nations in Canaan, gave them their land as an inheritance.

On a Tuesday. God bears with his people patiently. He has borne with you. Bear with others. Think of the person in your church or family whose slowness tries you most, and remember how many times God has walked at your pace. And if grumbling has become your habit, name the complaint you most often repeat, and turn it, today, into a request or a thanksgiving.

For worship. For forty years the Holy One walked through the sand with a complaining people and did not walk away. He fed them bread from heaven and water from the rock, and that rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The same Lord bears with us still, carrying us as a man carries his son, and he will not set us down until he has brought us into an inheritance we never earned and could never deserve.

parallels.desc: seven nations greater than you

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.

All this took about 450 years. A reader with a study Bible will already have seen a footnote, because this is one of the well-known chronological knots in the New Testament, and it is better untied than stepped over.

The difficulty. If the 450 years covers the period of the judges, which is how the older printed Greek text reads, and how the King James renders it (after that he gave unto them judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years), then the sum will not come out. First Kings 6:1 puts 480 years between the exodus and the fourth year of Solomon, and 450 years of judges alone leaves no room for the wilderness, the conquest, Samuel, Saul, David, and the first four years of Solomon on top.

The better reading. The better attested reading, which is what the ESV translates, attaches the number to what has just been said rather than to what follows: all this, the growth in Egypt, the exodus, the wilderness, the dividing of the land, took about 450 years. Then the sum works, and works neatly: about four hundred years in Egypt (Genesis 15:13; Acts 7:6), forty in the wilderness, and roughly seven to ten to take and divide the land. Four hundred and fifty, near enough. The apparent contradiction turns out to be a question of which clause the number belongs to.

About. And note the word Paul actually uses. He is a preacher giving a congregation the shape of their own history, not a chronicler filing dates. It is a round number. The wider case for Luke’s care as a historian was set out at 5:37–38 and does not need repeating here; this is simply another place where a charge dissolves on inspection.

And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. Now the sentence that follows, which is easy to read past. He gave them. The judges were God’s gift of deliverers. Consider what that word means, given what the book of Judges actually contains. This is the bleakest stretch in Israel’s history: a spiral in which the nation goes after other gods, is handed over to an oppressor, cries out, is rescued, and then does the whole thing again, round after round, each one worse than the last, until the book’s own closing verdict is that everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25). And God’s response, through three centuries of it, was to go on giving.

Look at what he gave. It is not a roll of heroes. A left-handed assassin. A woman, with a general who would not go without her. A frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the enemy. The son of a prostitute, thrown out by his own family. A strong man who could not govern his own appetites and ended blind, grinding grain in his enemies’ prison. That is God’s provision for the worst period of Israel’s life: not better men, but the men who were there, taken up and used.

The deliverance never depended on the deliverer. If you have ever looked at the leadership God has actually provided you, in your church, in your family, in the mirror, and privately concluded that he could have done better, the book of Judges was written for you. He was not doing his best with poor material. He was demonstrating, over three hundred years, that the deliverance never depended on the deliverer. And then, until Samuel the prophet. Paul disposes of three centuries in eleven words, because he is in a hurry. The whole recital has been running downhill toward one name, and it is not Samuel’s.

Does a chronological puzzle like this undermine the Bible’s reliability? No. A difficulty is not a demonstrated error. Here the problem disappears once you notice which clause the number belongs to, and that Paul says about. Many such puzzles have clear answers; a few still lack a certain one, and an honest reader can say so without alarm. Scripture is true in all it affirms, and our understanding of ancient numbering, manuscripts and summaries is what needs patience. A book that had been tidied up by later hands would have fewer such knots, not more.

In a sentence. All this took about 450 years, and afterwards God gave them judges until the prophet Samuel.

On a Tuesday. Look at the imperfect people God has put over you, your pastor, your parents, your manager, and thank God for one specific good he has done you through one of them. Then look at yourself, and take heart: God uses the men and women who are there.

For worship. God works across centuries. His plans are never late. Through four hundred years of slavery and three hundred years of chaos he kept giving, kept raising up, kept rescuing, and every flawed deliverer was a signpost toward the Deliverer who would not fail. The Judge of all the earth became the Judge who saves, and in him the long cycle of sin and rescue finally ends in a salvation that does not need to be repeated.
verseByVerse.note: The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’

Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul. Two clauses, and the whole tragedy of 1 Samuel 8 is folded into the space between them. They asked. God gave. And what the older account tells us, which Paul’s sentence does not, is that the asking was itself the sin: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7). Samuel told them in advance what a king would cost: your sons for his army, your daughters for his kitchens, a tenth of everything, and one day you will cry out because of the king you chose, and the LORD will not answer you. They heard the whole list and said: no, we will have a king.

Answered prayer is not always approval. So God gave them one. He gave them precisely what they insisted on, and the giving was not approval. There is a verse elsewhere that says it exactly: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Psalm 106:15). That is worth stopping on, because most of us have quietly learned to read an answered prayer as a divine endorsement, and Scripture will not let us. Some of what you have been given, you were given because you would not stop asking for it. The test is not whether the door opened; some doors open because you leaned on them. Before you take an opening as approval, ask whether you would still have wanted this if God had said no first, and whether you gave him a real chance to.

The son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. The forty is Paul’s, not the Old Testament’s. The text of 1 Samuel 13:1 is incomplete, as the ESV’s footnote there shows, and gives no reliable figure for Saul’s reign. Josephus, writing a generation after Paul, also reckons forty, so Paul is repeating the received figure of his day rather than inventing one.

A Saul of the tribe of Benjamin. And there is something in that verse the men in the synagogue would have caught instantly, though Paul says nothing about himself and does not need to. A Saul. Of the tribe of Benjamin. Standing in front of them, a dozen verses after Luke told us his name is now Paul, is a Saul of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5; Romans 11:1) who spent his early career being everything a tall, impressive, self-directed Benjamite could be, and was removed from it on a road. He does not draw the line. He tells the story of the first Saul and moves on to David, and every man in the room knew the preacher’s name.

And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king. Raised up is the same verb Paul will use of the resurrection (vv. 30, 37). God raises up his king. The commendation Paul quotes is Scriptures joined: a man after his own heart from 1 Samuel 13:14, I have found David, my servant from Psalm 89:20, and the words about doing all my will echo what God says of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28. And it raises the question every honest reader of the Old Testament ends up asking out loud.

How can God call David a man after his own heart? This is the man who took another man’s wife; who, when the pregnancy could not be hidden, tried to manoeuvre the husband home to cover it; and who, when the husband proved too loyal to go, had him posted where the fighting was heaviest and the line pulled back from him. Adultery finished off by murder by memorandum. And this is God’s man? Three things, and they matter.

First, the sentence describes God’s choice. It was spoken long before Bathsheba, and it is not a character reference. God says it in 1 Samuel 13, at the moment Saul is rejected, and its emphasis falls on the seeking rather than on the man found: the LORD has sought out a man after his own heart. I have found in David: the finding is God’s verb, and David is its object.

Second, what each did when he was caught. What actually separates the two kings is not that one sinned and the other did not. Saul, confronted over Amalek, argued: the people did it, the animals were meant for sacrifice, and in any case he had obeyed. He was still explaining when Samuel walked away. David, confronted by Nathan with a story and one sentence, you are the man, answered: I have sinned against the LORD (2 Samuel 12:13). No lawyer, no context, no blame shifted. And then he wrote it up, set it to music, and handed it to the choirmaster, so that the whole nation could sing his worst hour back to him forever (Psalm 51). That is not a man protecting his reputation. That is a man who cared more about being right with God than about being thought well of.

Third, the direction of a life. Who will do all my will is measured against the man he replaced. Saul had one plain instruction at Amalek and kept the best of the livestock. David’s life, for all its wreckage, ran in the direction God pointed; he never went after other gods, and that is precisely the measurement the books of Kings apply to every later king in the line.

God’s man cannot stay down. So if you are afraid your failures have disqualified you, notice that God’s chosen king has a murder in his file. And if you are tempted to use that as cover, notice what it cost him: a dead child, a fractured house, a son in armed rebellion, and a psalm he had to sing in public for the rest of his life. God’s man is not the man who never falls. He is the man who cannot stay down, because God will not leave him there. The question this verse puts to you is not whether you have sinned. It is narrower than that, and you can answer it from this week: what did you do the last time you were found out?

What does it actually mean to be after God’s heart? It means to want what God wants and to love what he loves. In David’s case that showed in his delight in God’s presence, his hunger for God’s honour, his refusal to touch the Lord’s anointed even when Saul hunted him, and his readiness to be broken over sin. It is not a temperament or a talent. It is a direction of the heart that only grace produces, and it is visible most clearly not in success but in repentance. You can ask God for it today: create in me a clean heart, O God (Psalm 51:10).

In a sentence. When they asked for a king, God gave them Saul son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years, and after removing him he made David their king, of whom he said he had found in David son of Jesse a man after his heart who would do all his will.

On a Tuesday. Pray to be a person after God’s own heart, who does all his will. Then answer the question honestly: the last time you were confronted with a fault, by your spouse, a friend, your own conscience, did you argue like Saul or confess like David? If it was Saul, go back to that person this week and say the plain words: I was wrong.

For worship. God sought out a king, and then, a thousand years later, he gave the true King, great David’s greater Son, who alone did all his Father’s will without a single failure. David needed a Psalm 51; Jesus never did. And because the Son after God’s heart was crushed for the sins of a David, every broken sinner who comes to him is welcomed as a son and made a man after God’s heart.
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the historian Josephus also gives forty years.

parallels.desc: a man after his own heart

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.

Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. This is the sentence the whole recital has been walking toward, the climax of the history, from David to Jesus, and the last three words carry the weight: as he promised.

The promise made. Set the promise where it was made. It is night, and David is settled at last: the wars are over, he is living in a house of cedar, and it strikes him that the ark of God is still under canvas. He proposes to build a temple. God’s answer, through Nathan, declines the offer and returns it multiplied: you will not build me a house; I will build you one. I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever; your throne shall be established forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus is that son.

The promise buried. Now measure that promise against what had actually become of it by the time Paul stood up in Pisidia. Four hundred years after Nathan, Nebuchadnezzar’s army broke into Jerusalem. The last king of David’s line, Zedekiah, was caught fleeing and brought to Riblah. They killed his sons in front of him, and then they put out his eyes, so that the last thing he ever saw was the end of the dynasty (2 Kings 25:7). He was led away in chains, and no son of David sat on a throne in Jerusalem again. Not under the Persians. Not under the Greeks. Not under the Maccabees, who were priests and not David’s house. Not under Herod, who was an Idumean and knew it, and killed his own family to keep what he had taken. Some six hundred years, and the royal line had run down into a carpenter’s shop in a village of a few hundred people in the hills of Galilee.

As he promised. Any reasonable observer would have called that promise dead. It had not merely been delayed. It had been publicly falsified, on a scale everybody could see, for two dozen generations. And a travelling tentmaker stands up in a provincial synagogue and says: as he promised. Not as he intended. Not as we still hope. As he promised, and here he is. The whole of Israel’s history was leading to him.

God has brought. Notice the verb, too. God brought a Saviour to Israel. He did not offer them the possibility of one, or make salvation available in principle. He led one in, in a body, to a particular people, at a particular date, under a named governor.

A Savior. And notice the title, which had a rival in that town. The word (sōtēr) means rescuer, deliverer. Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony, refounded by Augustus and settled with discharged legionaries, and Saviour was a word the empire used of its emperor on inscriptions and coins: the man who ended the civil wars and gave the world peace. Paul walks into a town full of old soldiers and old loyalties and hands the title to a crucified Galilean. Everyone in the room understood that there was only room for one.

What exactly does Jesus save us from? From the guilt of our sin and the wrath of God it deserves, from the power of sin that enslaves us, and in the end from the very presence of sin and death. Matthew puts it plainly: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). He is not first a helper for people who are mostly managing; he is a rescuer for people who are lost. That is why the name and the title belong together: Jesus means the LORD saves, and the Saviour is the LORD himself come to do it.

In a sentence. From David’s descendants God has brought Israel a Saviour, Jesus, as he promised.

On a Tuesday. What this verse asks of you is simple and rather searching. Name the promise of God you have quietly written off: not denied, just shelved, because of how long it has been. Then look again at how late this one was, and how completely kept. And take one of his promises with you into the day, written down, where you will see it.

For worship. All of history leads to Jesus. He is the Saviour God promised. Six hundred years of silence could not cancel one word God spoke to David in the night, and the stump of Jesse put out a shoot that will never be cut down. Every promise God has made finds its Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who kept this one keeps them all, and the King he brought sits now on a throne no Babylon can break.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’

Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. Why does John the Baptist appear in a sermon preached some five hundred miles from the Jordan, to a congregation of Anatolian Jews and Gentile God-fearers, some fifteen years after John was executed? Because they had heard of him. That is not a guess: Luke shows us the evidence twice, both times in this same mission field. At Ephesus Paul finds twelve men who had received John’s baptism and had never so much as heard that there is a Holy Spirit (19:1–7); and Apollos turns up in the same city, a learned Alexandrian Jew, accurate about Jesus as far as he went, knowing only the baptism of John (18:25). John’s movement had travelled the trade routes into the Dispersion and arrived without its ending. There were synagogues across the empire where the Baptist was honoured as the last of the prophets and nobody knew what had happened next.

Closing a real gap. So Paul is not padding a sermon with background. He is standing exactly where a real gap in his hearers’ knowledge sits, and closing it: yes, John, and here is what John himself said he was for.

As John was finishing his course. Then look at what Luke chose to preserve. The word is dromos, a runner’s track, the distance a man has been set to cover. Paul will use it of himself twice: if only I may finish my course (20:24), and at the very end, I have finished the race (2 Timothy 4:7). Now put that word against the facts. John’s course finished in a cell in Herod’s fortress, cut short in the dark because a girl danced well at a birthday party and her mother wanted a head on a dish (Mark 6:21–28). He had been left in that cell long enough to send word out asking whether he had backed the right man after all (Luke 7:19). By every measurement we normally use, it was a wasted, unfinished, humiliating end.

Finishing a course. Scripture calls it finishing his course. That is not sentiment; it is a different way of measuring. A course is finished when the distance you were given has been run, not when you have arrived somewhere impressive. If you are afraid that your life is going to end mid-sentence, a work half done, a family not yet safe, something somebody else will have to pick up, this is the word you need. God does not measure a life by where it stopped. He measures it by whether the ground assigned to you was covered.

I am not he. And what did John say at the height of his influence, with crowds coming out to him and delegations sent to ask who he was? He refused to be thought the Messiah (John 1:20). He spent his greatest capital on a denial.

After me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie. And then the picture. Untying sandals was a slave’s job (Luke 3:16). The rabbis had a saying that a disciple should do for his teacher anything a slave would do, with one exception: he must not loosen his master’s sandal, because that was too degrading a thing to ask of a free Israelite. John reaches for the one job a disciple was excused and says he is not fit for it. The greatest prophet was not worthy to be Jesus’ slave.

The pattern for preparatory work. This is the pattern for everybody whose work is preparatory, which is to say nearly everybody. The parent whose child will go further. The teacher whose pupil will be the better preacher. The man who trained his own replacement and now watches him do it better. I am not he is not false modesty. It is accuracy, and it is the most liberating sentence a servant can say, because the moment you stop being the point you stop having to be impressive. Ask yourself honestly which you would find harder: to be told your ministry had failed, or to be told it had succeeded and that its entire value lay in making somebody else visible. John was told the second, and called it his joy (John 3:29–30).

What was John’s baptism, and how is it different from Christian baptism? John’s baptism was a sign of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming Messiah. Christian baptism is baptism into the name of the Lord Jesus, after he has come, died and risen, and it signifies union with him and the gift of the Spirit. That is why the men at Ephesus who knew only John’s baptism were baptised again in Jesus’ name once they believed (19:4–5). John pointed forward; Christian baptism looks back to a finished work and confesses it.

In a sentence. Before Jesus came, John preached a baptism of repentance to all Israel, and as he finished his work, said he was not the one they thought, but one was coming after him whose sandals he was not worthy to untie.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Christ. In the conversation, the project or the ministry where you are tempted to be the centre this week, look for one concrete way to make Jesus more visible and yourself less. And if you fear your life will end unfinished, give today’s stretch of the course to God and leave the finishing line to him.

For worship. The greatest man born of woman knelt in his mind before the sandals of Jesus. And the One whose sandals he was not worthy to untie took off his own outer garment, knelt, and washed the feet of his disciples, and then went to the cross to wash them entirely. He must increase. He has, and he will, until every knee bows.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation.

Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God. Something happens to the pronouns here, and it is the moment the sermon stops being a history lesson. For ten verses Paul has spoken in the third person. God chose our fathers; he brought them out; they asked for a king; he raised up David. Now he addresses them directly and warmly: brothers. And he names both groups again, Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, in the same order as verse 16. He opened with them both, and now, at the point of application, he names them both and puts them inside a single word.

To us has been sent the message of this salvation. To us. Not to them, back there. To the people in this room, this morning. This message is for you, here, now; not for someone else. Every sermon has to make that turn or it is a lecture, and this is how Paul makes it: not by raising his voice, but with a pronoun. There is no smaller circle for the Gentiles at the back. Nothing in this sermon has been for the born Israelites only.

Consider what that does to a God-fearer. He has spent years in the position of a guest at somebody else’s family reading of a will. The promises were read aloud in his hearing every Sabbath and were addressed to a household he could not enter without a knife. And now a visiting rabbi, speaking with the full authority of the Scriptures that have just been read, says: to us. Not you may listen. Not you may hope. Sent to us.

Has been sent. Look at the verb, too. The message has been sent, passive, and the sender is not named for the good reason that no naming is needed. It did not develop. It was not discovered by clever men, or arrived at by anyone thinking hard about God. It was dispatched. The word behind our word apostle is inside that verb. Somebody sent this, deliberately, to a particular address.

This salvation. Not salvation in general, not a religious idea of rescue, but this one: the specific, dated, local thing that happened to a named man under a named governor, which Paul is about to describe in five verses. Christianity is not a theory about how people get saved. It is a report of something done.

How can I know the message is really for me? Because it is addressed to everyone who hears it, without exception and without a qualifying test. You do not need first to prove that you are chosen, or good enough, or sorry enough. The gospel comes to you as a sinner and says: this is for you; come. Election is God’s secret business, and it is discovered by believing, not before believing. If you have heard this message, it has been sent to you, and the right response is not to wonder whether you are allowed to take it but to take it.

In a sentence. Paul told the descendants of Abraham and the God-fearers that the message of this salvation had been sent to them.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test. If somebody asked you who the gospel was sent to, you would probably answer, without thinking, something like everyone, or people who need it. Both true, and both a way of standing at a polite distance from it. Paul’s sentence is narrower and much harder to get out of: it was sent to us. Which means it was put into your hands, addressed, by name, and you have signed for it. Then pass it on: name one person to whom you will say, this week, that it was sent to them too.

For worship. The message of salvation has been sent to you. God did not wait for us to find our way to him; he addressed the good news to sinners by name, and sent it across mountains and seas, carried by tired men on foot, until it reached the back row of a synagogue in Pisidia and, at length, your own door. The Father is the sender, the Son is the message, and the Spirit is the one who puts it into the hand of the one it was meant for.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed.

Because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath. Read the middle clause again, and then look around the room Paul is standing in. The prophets had been read aloud in that synagogue perhaps twenty minutes earlier. It is what got Paul on his feet in the first place (v. 15). He is not offering the congregation a general fact about Jerusalem’s religious habits. He is describing them. The men who missed the Messiah were men who did exactly what this congregation had done before he stood up, in a building like this one, on a day like this one. That is the sting, and Paul does not have to point it out. It is the tragic irony Paul later describes as a veil lying over the heart whenever Moses is read (2 Corinthians 3:14–15).

Fulfilled them by condemning him. Then the sentence that ought to stop anyone who reads it carefully. They did not understand the prophets, and so they fulfilled them. Their blindness did not frustrate the Scriptures. It carried them out. Every step the authorities took to shut this business down had been written down centuries earlier: the betrayal price, the false witnesses, the silence under accusation, the sentence, the cross, the tomb (Isaiah 53). They were not derailing God’s plan. They were the instrument of it, and they did not know.

And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. Which raises the obvious question, and Scripture does not dodge it. If they were fulfilling prophecy, were they guilty? Paul answers in this very breath, and the answer is yes. Two clauses, and everything is in the gap between them. This was not a court that got it wrong. This was a court that got it right and asked for the execution anyway. Luke’s Gospel has Pilate say three separate times that he finds no guilt in the man (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). The innocent was condemned.

Ignorant and answerable. So both things stand: they acted in ignorance, and they are answerable. Peter had already held those two together in Jerusalem itself, and that ground was covered at 3:17; it does not need going over again. But notice that Paul does not use their ignorance to excuse them, and he does not use God’s sovereignty to either. He says they did not know, and he says they had no case and asked for the death anyway, and he lets the two sentences stand side by side without softening either one.

Would we have known better? Now the part aimed at us. Almost everyone reading this quietly assumes he would have known better. It is very hard not to; we have the end of the story and they did not. So be exact about who these people were. They were the most Scripture-soaked population on earth. They read it in the language it was written in. They had it read publicly every week of their lives. They lived in the city where it was kept and worked in the building where the promises were housed. And they looked straight at the fulfilment and saw a blasphemer. Familiarity with the Bible is not the same thing as recognition of Christ. You can read a chapter every morning for thirty years and be no nearer. That is not an argument for reading less; it is a reason to pray before you read, because the difference between them and us was never that we are cleverer.

If God planned it, how can people be blamed for it? Because God’s plan does not force anyone to act against his own will. The rulers did exactly what they wanted to do, from motives that were their own: envy, fear, the love of power. God, in his wisdom, ruled over their wickedness and turned it to the salvation of the world (2:23; 4:27–28). Scripture never lets God’s sovereignty excuse human sin, and never lets human sin escape God’s sovereignty. Both are taught; we are to believe both, and to be glad that even the worst crime in history could not slip out of the hands of a good God.

In a sentence. The people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognise Jesus or understand the prophets read every Sabbath, and fulfilled them by condemning him, asking Pilate to execute him though they found no grounds for death.

On a Tuesday. You can hear the Bible every week and miss Christ. Ask God to open your eyes as you read. And here is a test you can actually run, because it exposes the mechanism. The rulers had a reason to misread the prophets: recognising this man would have cost them their standing, their income and their control of the temple. So ask what a plain reading of Scripture would cost you, in your marriage, your money, your reputation among people whose good opinion you value. And then ask, honestly, whether that happens to be a passage you have found unusually difficult to be sure about.

For worship. The wisdom of God is deeper than the wickedness of men. The rulers meant to silence him, and in silencing him they spoke every line the prophets had written. The Lamb was led to the slaughter by men who did not know they were leading a Lamb. And the innocent one, condemned without a case, went willingly, because the guilt he died for was not his but ours.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.

And when they had carried out all that was written of him. All of it, and it is worth refusing to leave that vague, because Paul certainly did not. Everything Scripture foretold happened. Nothing was left undone (John 19:28, 30). Sold for thirty pieces of silver, which were flung down in the temple and spent on a field (Zechariah 11:12–13). The shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zechariah 13:7). Silent in front of his accusers, like a sheep before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). Hands and feet pierced, his clothing divided by lot while men stood and stared (Psalm 22:16–18). Numbered with transgressors, one on either side (Isaiah 53:12). Given sour wine for his thirst (Psalm 69:21). Not one of his bones broken, like the Passover lamb (Psalm 34:20; Exodus 12:46). And a grave with a rich man (Isaiah 53:9), which is exactly where this verse ends up. These were not obscure texts that could be bent into shape afterwards. They were in the scrolls in that synagogue’s own cupboard, and Paul is preaching to men who could go and check him.

They took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. There is a small thing in the grammar worth clearing up, since a careful reader will trip on it. Paul says they took him down and they laid him in a tomb, and the they of the previous verse were the rulers who asked Pilate to have him killed. In fact it was Joseph of Arimathea who went and asked for the body, with Nicodemus and about seventy-five pounds of spices, and a tomb Joseph had cut for himself (Luke 23:50–53; John 19:38–42). Paul is compressing, speaking of Jerusalem as a single actor, the way we say that a city did something. He is not correcting the Gospels; he is summarising in one clause what took them a paragraph.

Do not hurry past the burial. It is in the sermon, and it is in the creed, crucified, dead, and buried (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), and it is there because the burial is the notary’s seal on the death. He truly died and was buried. A man who is buried has been handled, examined, wrapped, carried and shut in by people with no interest whatever in pretending. Every theory that Jesus merely fainted on the cross and revived in the cool of the tomb has to explain how a man in that condition, sealed behind a stone he could not have reached from the inside, presented himself three days later as the conqueror of death. The stone was moved from the outside. Somebody had to move it, and it was not the occupant working the door.

Why the tree here, and not the cross? The word is xylon, which means simply wood or timber: a beam, a stake, a tree. The apostles use it of the cross on purpose (also 5:30; 10:39; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24), to sound a deliberate echo of the Law: if a man is hanged on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). To call the cross a tree is therefore to load the word with meaning: Jesus hung where the accursed criminal hung, bearing the curse of God in our place, as Paul spells out: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). And notice the precise fit right here: they took him down from the tree and buried him at once, fulfilling that very command not to leave the body on the tree overnight. The word is no loose synonym; it preaches the heart of the cross: he took our curse. (Some also hear a quiet echo that the curse which entered the world by a tree in Eden was undone on a tree at Calvary, a lovely thought, though the plain reference is Deuteronomy’s curse.)

Why does it matter so much that prophecy was fulfilled in detail? Because it shows that the cross was not an accident God later made the best of. It was the plan, announced centuries ahead and carried out to the letter. That matters for your faith: Christianity rests on events God foretold and then did, which you can check. And it matters for your comfort: if God kept every word about his Son’s suffering, down to the dice and the vinegar, he will keep every word about your salvation and your future too.

In a sentence. When they had done all that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.

On a Tuesday. Choose one of the prophecies listed above, read it in its Old Testament setting this week, and then read its fulfilment in the Gospels. Let it steady you in whatever promise you are finding hardest to believe. And when you recite crucified, dead and buried, slow down at the last word.

For worship. Every prophecy fulfilled, to the last detail. Your Saviour’s death was no accident. He hung on the tree of the curse so that the curse would never hang over you, and he lay in a borrowed tomb because he needed it only for a short while. The God who wrote the story wrote himself into its darkest chapter, and the tomb that closed over him is the measure of how far he came for us.

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people.

But God raised him from the dead. Track the subjects of the verbs for a moment, because Paul has built this. In verses 27 and 28 the subject is they: they did not recognise him, they did not understand, they condemned him, they found no guilt, they asked Pilate. In verse 29 it is still they: they carried it out, they took him down, they laid him in a tomb. Men are doing everything, and what men do reaches its natural end in a sealed tomb, which is where every human story has always finished.

But God. Then the subject changes. Two words, and the direction of the whole history reverses. The great reversal, again, as at every apostolic sermon in this book (2:24; 3:15; 4:10). The tomb is the last place in the paragraph where men are the subject of the verbs.

And for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. Now the evidence, and notice how careful Paul is with it. He does not say the resurrection was felt, or that the disciples came to a new understanding of things. He gives duration, movement, and named witnesses. For many days: Luke has already given us the number, forty (1:3). This was not one shattering moment in a garden at dawn that could be put down to grief and poor light. It was six weeks. And to those who had come up with him: the same men, the whole way. They were with him in the north, they walked south with him, they were there when it went wrong. Their testimony spans the entire story; they are not late arrivals who turned up after the interesting part.

Who are now his witnesses to the people. And then the phrase that carries the argument. Now. Present tense. Paul is speaking some fifteen years after the event, in a city a long way from Judea, and the men he is citing are alive at that moment and can be found and questioned. It is exactly the move he makes in writing to Corinth: more than five hundred saw him at one time, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6). That is a strange sentence to write unless you positively want your readers to go and check.

Witnesses rather than experience. There is something else here worth noticing. Paul had his own encounter with the risen Christ, and it is the best story he owns; Luke tells it three times in this book (chapters 9, 22, 26). He does not use it. He rests the resurrection on the testimony of the Twelve, men he had been hunting at the time, and puts the weight on witnesses rather than on his own experience. That is the right way round, and it is the opposite of how most of us argue for our faith.

My own experience of God feels thin. Is my faith on weak ground? No. Your assurance does not stand on the vividness of what happened to you. It stands on what happened to Jesus, in public, in front of people who could be named, in a city where the authorities had every motive to produce a body and never did. Feelings rise and fall; the empty tomb does not. Experience matters, and the Spirit does give his people a living sense of God, but the foundation is history. On grey days, go back to the witnesses, read the resurrection chapters, and stand where they stood.

In a sentence. But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses.

On a Tuesday. Write down the two words but God, and put them where you will see them today, over the thing that seems finished: a marriage, a prodigal, a diagnosis, your own sin. Then, if someone asks why you believe, start where Paul started: not with how you feel, but with what happened.

For worship. But God raised him. Two words that change everything. Men did their worst and sealed the stone, and the Father answered with life. The Son who was obedient to death was raised in triumph, death’s claim on him broken from the inside, and he lives as the firstborn from the dead. Every but God in the life of a believer flows from this one, and the God who reversed the verdict of Calvary will reverse the grave for all who are his.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’

And we bring you the good news. This is the first time in Acts we hear Paul use gospel language of his own preaching. Notice what its content turns out to be. Not advice, not a philosophy, not a technique for living better: a report that a promise has been kept.

That what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus. And kept to whom? The fathers were given the promise. The children were given the thing. Abraham died holding a word from God about a family he could not see; a man sitting in the third row of a synagogue in Asia Minor is handed the fulfilment. Hebrews puts it exactly: these all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40). We are the generation that took delivery of what they signed for. The gospel is the fulfilment of the Old Testament promises: not a new religion, but the completion of the old.

As also it is written in the second Psalm. Then the proof text, and it needs a guard, because read carelessly it will teach a reader something the Bible does not: You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Psalm 2:7), applied to the resurrection. Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm for the king of David’s line, on the day he was enthroned. Paul applies it to the resurrection: the day God installed Jesus as king, declaring him Son with power (Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:5; 5:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God’s Son at the resurrection, as if he were not his Son before. He is the eternal Son (John 1:1, 18; 17:5). The resurrection publicly declared and installed him as the messianic Son and King. Begotten here is the language of royal enthronement. Taken flatly, the verse sounds as though Jesus became the Son of God on Easter morning, that he was a man whom God promoted, adopted, upgraded. That teaching has a name and a long history (it is called adoptionism), and it is wrong. Four things put it out of court.

First, look at the psalm Paul is quoting. Its scene is a king being installed while the nations rage, and the today in it is the day of enthronement, not the day of anybody’s conception. Israel’s kings were addressed as God’s son at their accession: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:14); I will make him the firstborn (Psalm 89:27). The language is throne language from the start.

Second, declared, not created. Paul says elsewhere precisely what the resurrection did to Jesus’s sonship, and he chooses his verb with care: he was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). The resurrection published a fact; it did not manufacture one.

Third, the Son before the raising. The New Testament has the Son in place long before there was anything to raise him from. God has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world (Hebrews 1:2), and Hebrews then quotes this very psalm three verses later (Hebrews 1:5) without the least embarrassment. God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4), which is not something anyone can do with a son he does not yet have.

Fourth, the same guard at Pentecost. The identical guard is needed at Peter’s Pentecost sermon, where God has made him both Lord and Christ (2:36), and it is worked out at that verse. The two stand or fall together, and the answer in both places is the same: enthronement, not manufacture.

So what changed on the third day? Not who Jesus is. What changed is who knows it. On the Friday the public verdict on him was that he was a blasphemer, justly executed, and heaven had said nothing. On the Sunday God said something, and what he said was: this is my Son, here is the proof, and I am putting him on the throne. If you have ever wondered what God thinks of Jesus, you are not left to guess. He said it out loud, in an empty tomb, in a way that cannot be argued with, and the sentence he used was: You are my Son.

What does this mean for me if I am in Christ? It means you belong to a King who is already reigning, not to a cause that might one day win. Psalm 2 goes on to promise the Son the nations as his heritage and the ends of the earth as his possession, which is exactly what is beginning to happen in this chapter. And because you are united to the Son, the Father’s pleasure in him reaches you too: you are adopted, a child of God (Galatians 4:5–7). The verdict of the empty tomb is the verdict over your life.

In a sentence. Paul announced the good news that what God promised the fathers he has fulfilled for their children by raising Jesus, as the second Psalm says: you are my Son, today I have begotten you.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 2 slowly today, and notice its last line: blessed are all who take refuge in him. Where in your life are you treating Jesus as a candidate for the throne rather than the King on it? Bring that area to him and acknowledge his rule there in plain words.

For worship. The risen Jesus is the King on David’s throne. Bow before the Son (Psalm 2:12). The nations raged and the rulers plotted, and the One enthroned in the heavens laughed, and set his King on Zion. The eternal Son, begotten before all worlds, took flesh, died, and was raised and crowned, and the Father has spoken over him the word that ends every argument: You are my Son.

parallels.desc: you are my Son; today I have begotten you

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’

No more to return to corruption. Paul now sets two Old Testament texts side by side, and to a modern reader the join looks arbitrary: a line from Isaiah about David’s blessings, then a line from a psalm about a body that does not decay, and somehow the two are supposed to prove a resurrection. It is worth seeing what he is actually doing, because it is not sleight of hand. But first hold on to the phrase he puts in front of them both. That is the clause which separates Easter from every other raising in the Bible, and it is a distinction most Christians have never been taught to make. Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). Unlike Lazarus.

Reprieve or resurrection. The widow’s son at Nain sat up and spoke, and one day was buried again. Jairus’s daughter got up and was given something to eat, and grew old, and died. Lazarus came out of the tomb still bound in his grave clothes, and somewhere in Judea there is dust that used to be Lazarus. Every one of those was a reprieve, a postponement, a body handed back on loan. Death let them go and then took them. Jesus was not resuscitated. He was raised, no more to return to corruption, out the far side of death and beyond its reach, into a body that will not wear out and cannot be reclaimed. Death has no second claim on him.

I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David. This is Isaiah 55:3, God’s everlasting covenant of steadfast love to David. The two texts share a word. Isaiah promises the holy and sure blessings of David; Psalm 16:10 says you will not let your Holy One see corruption. In the Greek Bible these congregations used, the same root stands behind holy in both places: hosios. Linking two passages by a shared term was a recognised method of Jewish exposition, and every trained man in that synagogue would have followed the move without needing it explained. Paul is not lifting verses out of context. He is arguing in the way his hearers had themselves been taught to argue, and inviting them to go and read both passages.

Sure blessings need a living King. And the argument itself is tight. God swore David an everlasting covenant, and Isaiah calls its benefits sure: the word means reliable, guaranteed, the sort of thing you could take into a court. But how sure can a covenant be if the man it was made with is in a tomb, and everyone who inherits it ends in a tomb as well? A dynasty of corpses is not an everlasting kingdom. If the promises to David are to be sure, at some point somebody in that line has to stop dying. The blessings promised to David are given to us through his risen Son. They are sure because he lives for ever.

You will not let your Holy One see corruption. Which is why Paul reaches for the second text, Psalm 16:10, as Peter used it at Pentecost (2:27).

What are the blessings of David that come to us? Everything God promised to David’s house: a King who reigns for ever, God’s steadfast love that will not be withdrawn, a people secure in his kingdom, and, in Isaiah 55, an open invitation to everyone who thirsts to come and receive it without money. In Christ these become ours: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, an eternal inheritance. They are holy because God gives them, and sure because the King through whom they come can never die again and lose them.

In a sentence. As for raising him from the dead never to decay, God said he would give them the holy and sure blessings of David, and in another psalm, that he would not let his Holy One see decay.

On a Tuesday. God’s blessings are sure because Christ lives for ever. Rest on them. When you think of your own death, or stand at a believer’s grave, say to yourself what this verse says: not a longer loan, but a body given outright. And read Isaiah 55 this week, and accept its invitation again.

For worship. And that is why the Christian’s grave is not a postponement either. What is promised to us is the same kind of thing: this perishable body must put on the imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:53–54). If Jesus had merely been revived, the best any of us could hope for would be more time. Because he was raised past corruption, what waits for the believer is not a longer loan but a body given outright. Death had one claim on the Holy One, and lost it for ever; and in losing it, it lost its claim on everyone who is his.

parallels.desc: the steadfast, sure love for David

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption.

For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation. Here is the argument’s last step, and it is an argument, not an assertion: Psalm 16 cannot be about David, because David decayed. Peter had made the identical point at Pentecost, and he made it with a piece of evidence lying on the ground in front of him: his tomb is with us to this day (2:29). You could walk to it. Paul, hundreds of miles away, has nothing to point at, so he argues it from the text and from a fact nobody in the room would dispute. Two apostles, the same psalm, the same conclusion, each preaching it to the congregation actually in front of him. The gospel does not change between Jerusalem and Pisidia, but the way of putting it does.

A beautiful epitaph. Do not rush past the description of David’s life, though, because it is one of the quietly weightiest sentences in the New Testament. The older versions turn the sentence the other way, that David served his own generation by the will of God. Both readings are true and both are humbling, and either way the boundary in the sentence is the same: in his own generation. Not in every generation. Not in ours. Every believer has a generation to serve. We cannot serve every age, but we can serve ours.

Enough. David did not fix Israel. He left a divided family, an unbuilt temple, a census plague, and a son who would undo a good deal of what he had built. He did what God gave him to do in the years he was given, and then he stopped. That was enough, and it is recorded as enough. If your own work feels small and local, a congregation of forty, a family, a class of children, one difficult relative, this is the sentence to keep. You are not asked to serve the purpose of God in history. You are asked to serve it in your own generation, which is the only one you have been issued with. Nobody in Scripture is ever commended for the size of his sphere.

Fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption. And then Paul refuses to be sentimental about the end of it. David died and decayed. The man after God’s own heart rotted in the ground. Scripture does not flinch and does not decorate. The psalm cannot be fully about him.

But he whom God raised up did not see corruption. Jesus did not. So the psalm is about Jesus. Now notice what that does to the gentle word Paul used a moment earlier. Christians call death sleep. We put it on gravestones. It is a lovely word, and it is only usable because one body in the history of the world went into a tomb and did not decay. Take verse 37 away and fell asleep is a euphemism. Leave verse 37 where it stands and it is a description.

Does fell asleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes how death looks from this side and what it is for the believer: temporary, peaceful, with a waking to come. It does not mean the soul is switched off. Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43); Paul said to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). The believer’s soul goes at once into the presence of the Lord, conscious and at rest, while the body sleeps in the ground awaiting the resurrection (Westminster 32.1).

What does serving my generation look like in practice? It means taking the people, place and years God has given you as your actual assignment, rather than waiting for a bigger one. Ask: who has God put within my reach that no one else is placed to serve? Your children or grandchildren, your neighbours, your colleagues, the congregation you belong to, the needs of your town in your lifetime. Be faithful there, in the ordinary means: prayer, the word, hospitality, honest work, mercy. Then leave the next generation to the God who will raise up its servants too.

In a sentence. David served God’s purpose in his generation, then died, was buried with his ancestors and decayed, but the one God raised did not see decay.

On a Tuesday. Write one sentence describing your generation as God has given it to you: the people and place within your reach. Then do one thing today that serves God’s purpose there. Do not compare it with anyone else’s sphere.

For worship. Serve God’s purpose in your own generation. That is your calling. And the One you serve is not bound by generations. David served his and fell asleep; the Son of David serves the purpose of God in every generation, and he did not see corruption. He holds the keys of death, and because he lives, the word asleep on a Christian’s grave is not a kindness but a promise.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.

Let it be known to you therefore. Everything up to this point has been argument: the history, the promise, the death, the witnesses, the two psalms. This is the conclusion drawn from it, and the whole sermon has been climbing toward these two verses. This is its heart.

Through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. And the first thing to notice is the verb. Forgiveness is not offered on conditions. Not made available to suitable applicants. Proclaimed: the word for a herald standing in a public square reading out what the king has decided. There is a world of difference between a notice explaining how to apply for a pardon and a herald announcing that one has been granted. Paul is not describing a process the synagogue might enter. He is reading out an amnesty, through Jesus, offered to you.

And by him everyone who believes is freed from everything. Then the sentence that will fill two of his letters. The English says freed; the ESV notes that it can be rendered justified, twice in the verse. The word is dikaioutai, and this is the first time Acts uses Paul’s great word. It is a courtroom word. To be justified is not to be improved, cleaned up, or given a fresh start. It is to have a judge declare, formally and on the record, that you are in the right. Everyone who believes: by faith alone. From everything: every sin, completely.

The courtroom. Stage it, because the picture is what makes it land. A man is in the dock. He did it. The evidence is in, the witnesses were credible, his own counsel has stopped pretending. And the judge, who has read every page of it, says: not guilty. And the reason is not that the file was thin, and not that the judge is easy-going, and not that the offence turned out to matter less than it seemed. The reason is that the sentence has already been served by somebody else, and the court holds the receipt. That is justification. It is why Paul can put everyone who believes in the same sentence as freed from everything, and it is what the Reformers spent their lives on.

From which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. Now the other half, which the men in that synagogue felt far more sharply than we do. The law could not justify. It showed sin but could not remove it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). The sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). What the law could not do, Christ does. But be specific here, because the general answer, that nobody keeps it perfectly, is true and is not the whole of it.

The limit written into the law. The law had an elaborate machinery for sin: sacrifices, washings, a priesthood, a day of atonement once a year. But that machinery had a limit written into it, and every Israelite knew exactly where the limit was. The offerings covered sins committed unwittingly, in ignorance, by mistake.
