For the sin done deliberately, with the eyes open and the hand raised, the law made no provision whatever: the person who does anything with a high hand shall be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:30–31). There was no offering to bring. A man could stand in the temple courts with his best lamb and there was nothing in the book that would take it.

David knew. David knew that better than anybody. He had committed adultery and arranged a killing, both with his eyes wide open, and when he came to write it up he said so out loud: you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering (Psalm 51:16). He was not being poetic. He was a king with unlimited access to the altar, saying that the altar had nothing for him. And now look at what Paul has just spent ten verses doing. He has walked this congregation through the story of David, chosen, commended, the man after God’s own heart, the man the promise was made to, and then says, at the top of his voice, that in Jesus there is a freeing from precisely the things the law of Moses could not free you from. He never draws the line between the two. He does not have to. He has told them the story, they know the psalm, and they can hear a thousand-year-old question being answered in their own synagogue.

The high-handed sin. So the offer here is not for tidy people who have fallen a little short. It is aimed at the high-handed sin: the one you did not drift into, the one you chose. The one nothing has ever touched: not resolutions, not service, not an unbroken run of Sundays, not a hundred confessions of the same thing. Name it, privately, now. That is what Paul means by everything from which you could not be freed.

Everyone who believes. And note the width of the door. Not everyone who improves, or qualifies, or has the right ancestry, which is a startling thing to say in a room half full of men who had been told for years that their ancestry was the problem. Believes. That is the whole entry requirement, and it is deliberately the one thing a beggar can do as easily as a benefactor.

Galatians and Romans in embryo. This is Galatians and Romans in embryo, in the first sermon of Paul’s that we possess, years before either letter was written. He did not develop this doctrine under pressure from opponents. He preached it the first time he opened his mouth in a synagogue, because it is not his theory. It is the gospel.

Where Christians differ: justification. Some teach that justification is a process in which faith and works, or faith and sacraments, together make us righteous. Verdict: Paul says everyone who believes is justified, declared righteous, from everything, through Christ, not by the law. Justification is God’s legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness credited to us (Romans 4:5; 5:1; Philippians 3:9). Good works follow as fruit, not as ground.

If I am justified by faith alone, does it matter how I live? It matters enormously, but not as the ground of your acceptance. The faith that receives Christ for pardon also receives him as Lord, and the Spirit who gives that faith begins at once to change the believer (Ephesians 2:8–10). So a justified person will fight sin and grow in good works, not to earn God’s verdict but because he already has it. Someone who says he trusts Christ and is content to go on in deliberate sin should not comfort himself with this verse; he should ask whether he has believed at all (James 2:17).

What if I do not feel forgiven? Then rest on what has been proclaimed rather than on what you feel. A herald’s announcement is true whether or not the prisoner believes it at first; the gates are open either way. Feelings of guilt often linger after a sin has been forgiven, especially for the high-handed sins. Take them back to the word: everyone who believes is freed from everything. Thank God for it in so many words, even before the feelings follow. They usually do, but your pardon does not wait for them.

In a sentence. Paul declared that through this man forgiveness of sins was proclaimed to them, and through him everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses could not justify them from.

On a Tuesday. Name the sin nothing has ever touched, and bring it, by name, to the One through whom forgiveness is proclaimed. Then, when the memory of it accuses you this week, answer it with this verse rather than with a promise to do better. And treat someone who has wronged you as one who has been freed from everything: forgive as you have been forgiven.

For worship. Everyone who believes is justified from everything. Everything. Rejoice in it. The Judge of all the earth looked at the whole file, the sins done in ignorance and the sins done with a high hand, and declared believing sinners righteous, because his own Son had stood in the dock in their place and served the sentence to the last stroke. There is no sin so deliberate that his blood cannot cover it, and no beggar so poor that he cannot take it with an empty hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: ‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’

Beware, therefore. He has just announced an amnesty. He ends by telling them what happens to men who laugh at one, as Peter did (3:23).

Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish. The quotation is Habakkuk 1:5, and its original setting is what gives it teeth. Habakkuk had been complaining, properly, out loud, in the way the Bible permits, that God was doing nothing about the corruption of Judah. O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? God’s answer is not comfort. It is this verse: look, be astounded, for I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told. And what was the work? Babylon. God’s answer to Judah’s wickedness was to raise up the Chaldeans and let them come, and Habakkuk was so appalled by the answer that he spends the rest of the chapter arguing with it. The unbelievable work in the original was a judgment nobody would credit until the siege ramps were up against their own walls.

Paul’s use of it. Now hear Paul use it. God has done another unbelievable thing in your days, this time a rescue and not a ruin, a crucified man raised and forgiveness proclaimed in his name: salvation through a crucified Messiah, and judgment on those who scoff at it. The warning is not: this might be true, so do be careful. It is: your fathers were told in advance about a work of God they refused to credit, and it arrived anyway, and it flattened the city. Do not make that mistake twice. And do not assume that because this word is good news it can safely be laughed at. Notice too that Paul is quoting the Greek Old Testament his hearers used, which reads you scoffers, where our Old Testament reads look among the nations (Habakkuk 1:5). He preaches from the Bible that is on the table in front of them, which is what a good preacher does.

For I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you. A warning against unbelief. The gospel is too wonderful for some to believe. And then the word he chooses to end on: perish. That is where the first recorded sermon of the apostle to the Gentiles lands. Not on an invitation to consider the claims of Christ at one’s leisure. On astonishment and perishing. A gospel that has lost the ability to say that word is not the gospel Paul preached, and the kindness of a warning is exactly proportional to the danger it names. Nobody shouts at a man about a fire that is not burning.

Who the warning is aimed at. But be careful who this is aimed at, because the wrong reader will take it home. It is a warning to scoffers: men who hear, understand, and treat the thing as beneath serious attention. The frightened Christian who reads this verse at midnight and wonders whether it describes him should notice something simple: a scoffer is not troubled by warnings. That is what makes him a scoffer. The alarm you feel is itself evidence that the description has not fastened on you. So the real question the verse puts is not whether you feel certain. It is whether you have been told and are declining to act on it. And if you have read this far, the first half of that is already settled.

Is it loving to end a gospel message with a warning? Yes. Jesus warned more often about judgment than anyone else in Scripture, and he was love made visible. A warning is not the opposite of good news; it is what makes good news urgent. If perishing is real, then a preacher who never mentions it is not being kind, only quiet. The aim is never to frighten people away but to frighten them toward the only refuge. Paul’s warning comes straight after the widest offer imaginable, and that order is the pattern: the door first, then the reason to go through it now.

In a sentence. Paul warned them to beware that the prophets’ words not come true of them: look, you scoffers, marvel and perish, for God is doing a work in your days you would not believe even if told.

On a Tuesday. Do not scoff at the gospel because it seems too simple or too good. Believe it. And watch for the quieter scoffing that creeps into Christians: the shrug at a sermon, the joke that makes holy things small, the habit of hearing warnings as meant for other people. When you speak of Christ to someone, have the courage, gently, to say why it matters now.

For worship. God is still doing a work in our days that the world would not believe if it were told: raising the dead in sin to life, gathering a people from every nation, building a kingdom out of a crucified man’s followers. It is the most astonishing thing that has ever happened, and it is happening now. Blessed be the God whose works are too great for scoffers and exactly the right size for sinners who believe.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians.

parallels.desc: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.

As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. They begged, all the way out of the door, a crowd of them, hungry for more; and what they asked for was not a discussion or a private word but the same thing again. Say it to us again next week.

They could not take a copy home. Sit with what that meant. There was no record of the sermon, no way to hear it a second time, no Gospel to read it against; the New Testament did not exist and would not for years. They had heard the most important thing they would ever hear, once, and now they had seven days to hold it in their heads with nothing but memory and each other. That is why they begged. We carry more sermons in our pockets than we will ever listen to, and beg for none of them, and it is worth asking honestly which of us is in the worse position.

One week apart. And keep this verse where Luke put it, because he is setting something up. This is the same congregation that will be filled with jealousy two verses from now. Between the begging and the jealousy lies one week, and Luke does not tell us what happened in it. He tells us only two things: that a great many people wanted to hear more, and that when the next Sabbath came the crowd was too large and too Gentile. Enthusiasm for the word of God and hostility to it can live in the same building seven days apart, and sometimes in the same person.

Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas. Meanwhile, some did not wait for next week. Note who these are: not the Gentile God-fearers at the edge of the synagogue but people from inside it. Born Jews, and proselytes, Gentiles who had gone the whole way into Judaism, circumcision included. The first fruit of this mission comes out of the synagogue, not around it.

Who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. And what did the two missionaries say to their brand-new converts, walking along the street with them? Not a programme. Not a list of things to start doing. Not in the law, not in their own efforts, but in grace. The first pastoral instruction ever given in that city was not do more. It was: stay. The Christian life begins and continues by grace (Galatians 5:4; Colossians 2:6).

What does it mean to continue in the grace of God? Grace is God’s free, undeserved kindness to sinners in Christ: salvation as a gift, never a wage, never earned. To continue in it, to remain, to abide, to hold fast, is to go on living every day on that same footing of free grace on which you first came in. You were welcomed home freely, with empty hands; continuing in grace means staying there: not slipping back onto the treadmill of trying to make God love you by being good enough, and not despairing when you fail, as though grace had run out. It is the very thing Paul urges on the Colossians: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6). The way in is the way on.

Picture the prodigal son. He came home expecting to earn his keep as a hired servant, and instead the father ran to him, put the robe on him, and welcomed him as a beloved son: sheer grace. Now imagine that son, a week later, quietly slinking off to the servants’ quarters to start earning his place after all. That is exactly what it looks like to drift out of grace. Continue in the grace of God means: stay at the Father’s table as a freely loved child. Keep coming to Christ with empty hands; keep drawing on his daily mercy for strength, forgiveness, and growth (grace is not just the door you enter by but the room you live in: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, 2 Peter 3:18). And keep going: persevere, do not give up. Lest this make you anxious about whether you can hold on, remember what was said at Colossians 1:23: the call to continue is real, yet the God who began this grace is the one who keeps us in it; we persevere because he preserves us. Even our continuing is grace.

How can I tell if I have drifted onto the treadmill? Watch for the signs. You feel closer to God on days you performed well and distant on days you failed. You put off praying after a sin until you feel you have done enough penance. You resent other Christians who seem to get away with less effort. You serve out of fear of disapproval rather than gratitude. The cure is not to try less but to go back to the gospel: confess the sin, receive the forgiveness Christ has already won, and serve from his acceptance rather than toward it.

In a sentence. As they left, the people asked them to speak again the next Sabbath, and after the meeting many Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas, who urged them to continue in the grace of God.

On a Tuesday. Go back to last Sunday’s sermon, from memory or from a recording, and hear it again as if it were the only one you would ever hear. And today, when you fail, do not slink off to the servants’ quarters. Go straight back to the Father’s table and thank him that your place there was never earned.

For worship. Continue in the grace of God. You began by grace; go on by grace. Grace is not the porch of the Father’s house but every room in it. The Lord who welcomed you in with empty hands keeps you in with the same hands, holding you when you cannot hold on, and he will present you blameless at the end, not because you kept yourself, but because he kept you.
verseByVerse.note: Converts to Judaism are proselytes.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.

The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony of some size, and whatever building the synagogue occupied, it did not hold the town. Picture the courtyard full, the street outside full, people standing on walls. And understand where they came from, because nobody organised this. The news spread through the week. There was no advertising and no second meeting arranged. What there was, all week, was a few hundred God-fearers going home to Gentile neighbours and Gentile relatives and saying: you will not believe what a man said in the synagogue on Saturday. That is still how it happens, and it is worth noticing that the largest response in this chapter came through people whose names Luke never gives, doing something nobody commissioned them to do.

But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy. Two things must be said about that sentence, and neither cancels the other. The first is that Luke cannot possibly mean the Jewish people as such. The preacher is a Jew. So is Barnabas. So are the converts of verse 43, and so are most of the Christians in the story so far. Luke means, as the ESV’s note puts it, the Jewish religious leaders and those under their influence, in that city, on that morning. The church’s long and shameful habit of reading sentences like this one as a verdict on a race is a misuse of Scripture that has cost innumerable lives, and the man speaking here is the man who wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Romans 9:3).

The jealousy is not alien to us. The second is that the jealousy is not hard to understand, and we should not pretend it is alien to us. Jealousy has appeared before in this book (5:17). These were men who had kept a minority faith alive in a pagan colony, at real cost, for generations. They had built the congregation, maintained the scrolls, and taught the God-fearers whatever those Gentiles knew about the true God. Last Sabbath the synagogue was theirs. This Sabbath it is full of people who have come to hear two strangers who arrived on foot a fortnight ago with nothing. Perhaps it galled them that Gentiles were being welcomed without becoming Jews; perhaps it was Paul’s popularity. And notice what they were jealous of. Not error: they never do answer Paul’s argument, then or later. They were jealous of a crowd. Luke says precisely what set it off: they saw the crowds.

And began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. And watch how the opposition degrades. First they contradict: that is at least an argument, and an argument can be answered. Then they are reviling him (blasphēmountes, blaspheming, slandering): abuse, the tearing down of a man instead of an answer to what he said, and in opposing the messenger they are opposing the word of the Lord. It is a reliable sign, and you can use it in both directions. When a case moves from the argument to the man, the argument has been lost. And when it is your own tone that has moved from the argument to the man, it is worth asking what you are actually defending.

Why would religious people oppose a work of God? Because religion can become a possession rather than a surrender. When people come to feel that God’s work belongs to them, his blessing on outsiders feels like a loss. That is how the elder brother felt when the prodigal was welcomed (Luke 15:28–30). The danger is greatest for those who have served longest. The protection is to remember that we were outsiders too, brought in by grace, and that the work was never ours to own.

In a sentence. The next Sabbath almost the whole city came to hear the Lord’s word, but when the Jews saw the crowds, they became jealous and contradicted what Paul said, abusing him.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is a nasty one to run honestly. Think of the last time God did something obviously good through somebody whose success made your own work look small: the neighbouring church that grew while yours did not, the younger man who preaches better than you, the colleague who was handed the thing you had been quietly working toward. What was the first thing you felt, before you corrected it? Not what you said. What you felt. That feeling is in this verse, and in this verse it ends with a man being driven out of a city. Beware of jealousy when God blesses others, even outsiders. It is the opposite of love. Pray for that church, that person, by name, and ask God to bless them more.

For worship. The word of the Lord drew a city out of its houses, and the Lord of the word was not threatened by a crowd; he had come for crowds. He is the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine, who fills his house with guests from the highways, who rejoices over one sinner and over a whole city. His heart is bigger than all our jealousies, and the feast he is spreading has room for every outsider he calls.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’”

And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly. Boldness is the great Acts virtue: open, unguarded, free speech, the thing the church prayed for when the threats started in Jerusalem and was given on the spot (4:29–31). It does not mean loudly. It means without editing.

It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. This order was not tact, and not a strategy for finding sympathetic hearers. It was owed. It was God’s order. The promises were made to this people; the Messiah came from them; the Scriptures were kept by them. Israel had the first right to the gospel. To have gone anywhere else first would have misrepresented what God had actually done. It is what Paul later compressed into a single phrase: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16).

Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life. Then the sentence that ought to be uncomfortable. Thrust aside is the word Stephen used of Israel rejecting Moses (7:27, 39). And look at who does the judging. Not Paul. Not God, not yet. You judge yourselves. God did not shut them out; they shut themselves out. Nobody in that synagogue stood up and said, I am unworthy of eternal life. What they said was something far more ordinary: not from him; not on those terms; not now. Paul tells them that this is the same sentence, written out in full. A refusal is a verdict, and the man who gives it has passed it on himself.

Polite refusals. That is worth carrying out of the first century, because most refusals of Christ are not defiant. They are polite, reasonable and postponed. And Paul’s point is that the politeness does not alter what has been decided. If a man is handed the only bread there is and says, thank you, not just now, he has settled the question of whether he will eat, however courteously he put it.

Behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. And here a guard is needed, because these words have been read for centuries as though God had finished with Israel on that Sabbath in Pisidia. He had not, and Paul demonstrates it with his feet. He is not abandoning Jews everywhere; in the next city, they go to the synagogue again (14:1). He says this here; he says it again in Corinth (18:6); he says it again in Rome, in the closing scene of the book (28:28), and in between, on arriving in each new city, the first place he goes is the synagogue. He said it three times because each time it was a local verdict on a local refusal, not a final verdict on a people. His own answer to the question is flat: has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Romans 11:1). What God intends for Israel’s future Christians have read in more than one way, and Romans 11 is the place to weigh them; but no reading permits a Christian to treat the Jewish people as written off.

I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth. Then the Scripture, and this is the most remarkable move in the chapter. That is Isaiah 49:6, and in Isaiah it is spoken to the Servant, that is, to the Messiah. Simeon understood it that way when he held the baby in the temple and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). And Paul takes a text about Christ and says the Lord has commanded us, meaning himself and Barnabas, two tired men who have just been shouted down in a provincial synagogue. The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out by Christ through his messengers.

A share in his mission. He is not confusing himself with the Messiah. He is saying something that ought to steady every ordinary Christian who has ever felt that mission is somebody else’s department: the church’s task is not a separate assignment running alongside Christ’s. It is a share in his. What the Servant was sent to do, his people are now doing in him, which is why Paul can call himself an ambassador and say that God makes his appeal through us (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Too light a thing. And notice which verse of Isaiah he chose, because it is precisely the one that carries the argument. The full sentence runs: it is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob; I will make you as a light for the nations. God himself says that restoring Israel alone would be too small a commission. Paul has just been accused of abandoning his people’s hope. He answers by producing the one verse in which God calls that hope, taken by itself, not big enough.

If God appoints people to life, how can people judge themselves unworthy? Both are true, and Luke sets them two verses apart on purpose. Those who reject the gospel do so freely and are fully responsible; no one is lost who wanted Christ and was refused. Those who receive it do so because God has worked in them (v. 48). Unbelief is ours; faith is God’s gift. We do not need to explain how the two fit to believe both, and we must not let either cancel the other.

In a sentence. Paul and Barnabas answered boldly that they had to speak God’s word to them first, but since they rejected it and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, they were turning to the Gentiles, as the Lord commanded: I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.

On a Tuesday. If you have been saying not now to Christ, hear Paul: a polite postponement is still a verdict. Settle it today. And if you are a Christian, take the commission as yours: you are part of the light God sends to the nations. Find one way this week to pray for, give to or speak to someone from another people or culture with the gospel.

For worship. The light of Christ is for every nation. Shine it where you are. God’s heart was always bigger than one people. He made a Servant whose light would reach the ends of the earth, and that Servant was pierced for our transgressions and raised to be the Light of the world. From a rejected synagogue in Pisidia the beam swung out across the nations, and it has not stopped moving since. One day the whole earth will be full of the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out through the apostles.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.

When the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord. Heard what, exactly? That the door stood open to them, by name, from a Jewish preacher, out of a Jewish prophet, in a Jewish building, on the very morning the leadership of that building was in the act of shutting them out. These were people who had spent years at the edge of somebody else’s promise. Now a man with the Scriptures open has told them that the promise was addressed to them all along, and that God said so seven hundred years ago. They began rejoicing: joy at being included.

Glorifying the word. And notice what they glorified. Not Paul, whom they had every reason to make much of: the word of the Lord. Glorifying is normally kept for God himself, and Luke lets it fall on the message. When people are genuinely converted, the thing they cannot stop praising is what they heard, not the man they heard it from.

And as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. But between the rejoicing and the spreading Luke sets down a single clause, without explanation and without apology, and Christians have been arguing about it ever since. It is one of the clearest statements of election in Scripture. Appointed (tetagmenoi) means ordained, assigned; it is a perfect passive participle, meaning they had been appointed already, by God. Luke does not say as many as believed were appointed, but as many as were appointed believed. God’s appointment came first; their faith followed as its result. Those who rejected the word judged themselves unworthy (v. 46); those who believed did so because God had appointed them to life. Both are true.

Why is this one of the strongest verses in Scripture for election? Three things give it force. Appointed (tetagmenoi) is a perfect passive participle, a completed action done to them by another, and the unnamed agent, as so often, is God (the divine passive): as many as had been appointed by God to eternal life believed. The order is decisive: the appointment comes first and the believing follows; faith is the fruit, God’s prior choice the root. And the context sharpens it: two verses earlier the unbelieving Jews judge themselves unworthy of eternal life (v. 46), rejection at their own door, while the believing Gentiles are those appointed to eternal life. Luke sets the two side by side without embarrassment: responsibility in unbelief, grace in belief. It fits a steady pattern: all that the Father gives me will come to me (John 6:37); you do not believe because you are not among my sheep (John 10:26); the Lord opened her heart (Acts 16:14); Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 8:29–30.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians read this as disposed to eternal life, by their own inclination, or say God appointed those he foresaw would believe. Verdict: the passive voice points to an outside agent, God; and the word is used elsewhere of being appointed by authority (Romans 13:1, “instituted”). God’s sovereign choice is the cause of faith (Ephesians 1:4–5; John 6:37). It is a reason for joy and humility, not pride: they believed because grace chose them. And it fuels mission: God has his people in every city, waiting to hear (18:10).

How do our non-Reformed brothers read it? Godly, Bible-loving Christians who are not Calvinist honour this verse and read it mainly two ways. First, some take the participle as middle voice, as many as had disposed themselves toward eternal life, describing the people’s own receptivity rather than a prior decree. (The form can be middle or passive; Reformed readers answer that, given Luke’s usage and the contrast with v. 46, the passive with God as agent is far more natural, but the middle is honestly held.) Second, the classic Arminian reading affirms a genuine appointing grounded in God’s foreknowledge: foreseeing who would freely believe, God appointed those to eternal life (Romans 8:29). Election is real, but conditioned on foreseen faith, so free will is preserved. A few read it corporately: the destiny of the believing people as a body, entered by faith.

And it must be held in charity. What unites us comes before what divides: every side believes salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, that God is sovereign and good, that sinners are truly responsible, and that the gospel must be freely offered to all, exactly what Paul is doing here. The difference is over how God’s sovereignty and our believing fit together. In honesty, many even non-Calvinist scholars grant the plain passive is the most natural sense of the Greek; but this is an in-house disagreement among brothers who love the same Lord and Bible, to be carried with humility, not point-scoring. And note what the verse does not do: it does not make God the author of anyone’s unbelief (v. 46 lays that on the rejecters), nor does it dampen evangelism; in Acts, election runs right alongside the most tireless preaching the world has seen. Rightly held, it humbles the believer, banishes boasting, and turns assurance into worship: if I believe, it is because grace appointed me, sought me, and opened my heart.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God chose these Gentiles because he saw something good in them, or because he foresaw their faith; the faith itself is the fruit of the appointing (Ephesians 2:8). It does not mean anyone who wants to come to Christ will be turned away for not being on a list; Jesus says whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). And it does not mean we can know in advance who is appointed. The list is God’s, and it is read only in the believing.

How can I know if I am one of those appointed to eternal life? By looking where Luke looks: as many as were appointed believed. You do not discover your election by peering into God’s secret counsel but by trusting Christ. If you have come to him, resting on him alone for forgiveness, that faith is the evidence of your appointment, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). If you are not sure you have come, do not puzzle over decrees; come now. No one who comes is ever told he was not chosen.

Then why preach or pray, if God has already appointed? Because God appoints the means as well as the end. He has chosen to bring his people to faith through the preaching of the word and the prayers of his church (Romans 10:14–17). Look at this very verse: the appointed believed when they heard. Paul was told later in Corinth to keep speaking precisely because the Lord had many people in that city (18:9–10). Election does not make evangelism pointless; it makes it hopeful. We go knowing that God has people out there who will believe.

Is it unfair that God chooses some and not others? Fairness would leave us all under judgment, for all have sinned. Election is not God treating innocent people unjustly; it is God showing mercy to guilty people who deserved none. No one in hell will be able to say he wanted Christ and was refused; no one in heaven will be able to say he earned his place. Paul faces the objection directly and answers with worship, not with a formula (Romans 9:14–24; 11:33–36). We may not understand everything, but we know the Judge of all the earth does right.

And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. And the result: the word went on spreading. Election never stops evangelism; it powers it. Which is worth pausing on, because in two verses’ time Paul and Barnabas are expelled from that district. They are not the ones spreading it. Pisidian Antioch sat on a Roman road at the head of a wide upland region of villages and market towns that Paul never visited, and the gospel reached them anyway, carried by people whose names nobody wrote down, going home and telling their families. The missionaries were removed. The word was not.

In a sentence. When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and honoured the Lord’s word, and all who were appointed to eternal life believed, and the word of the Lord spread through the whole region.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, thank God today, in so many words, that your faith was his gift and not your achievement. Then let it make you humble toward those who do not yet believe, since you were no better, and bold to speak to them, since God has his people still waiting to hear. Pray for one unbelieving friend, asking God to do for them what he did in Pisidian Antioch.

For worship. If you believe, it is because God appointed you to eternal life. Bow in gratitude, and go tell others. Before Pisidian Antioch was founded, before Abraham was called, before the world was made, the Father set his love on a people and wrote their names in the Lamb’s book of life. On one ordinary Sabbath in an upland colony some of those names heard the gospel and believed, and rejoiced. Salvation from first to last belongs to our God: chosen by the Father, redeemed by the Son, called by the Spirit, and every one of them kept to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.

But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city. Luke is being precise, and the precision tells you exactly how it was done. The synagogue could not touch Paul and Barnabas directly; they had broken no law, and in a Roman colony you do not simply remove people. So the pressure went round another way. Women of rank held a genuinely prominent place in the civic and religious life of the cities of Asia Minor, and a good number of them were the synagogue’s own God-fearers: devout, respected, and married to the men who ran the colony. The opponents worked on these women, to act through their husbands, and on the leading men of the city.

Influence, not a mob. Not a mob, then. A word in the right drawing rooms, and soon the missionaries were put out of the district by due process. That is what most opposition to the gospel has actually looked like down the centuries: not violence but influence, applied quietly by people who never have to raise their voices, arriving as a decision from an office that never explains itself. There is a small, hard irony in it as well. The women are called devout. They were the fruit of the synagogue’s own patient work among the Gentiles, and they were used to expel the men who had just told them the promises were theirs.

Stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. Persecution follows fruitfulness. Perhaps this is when Paul was beaten with rods (2 Corinthians 11:25), and this town stayed with him. Twenty years later, writing his last letter from a Roman cell to a young man who had grown up further down that same road, he lists it by name: my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11). He never forgot it. He also never once suggested it had been a mistake to go.

But they shook off the dust from their feet against them. This is not a gesture Paul invented in temper. It is an instruction, given by Jesus to his own men when he sent them out: if a town will not receive you, shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them (Luke 9:5; 10:11). It was a sign that a town was being left to its own responsibility. And it carried a meaning everybody present would have caught. A Jew returning from Gentile territory would shake the dust off at the border, refusing to carry pagan soil into the holy land. To do it to a Jewish community was to say something very hard indeed: in this matter, you are the ones on the outside. A solemn warning.

Two guards. Two guards are needed here, because the verse gets misused. First, it is not permission for an ordinary Christian to write people off in a huff. It was done by apostles, under an explicit command from Christ, after a full and public hearing, and only when the answer had become a settled and organised refusal. Second, look at what they did not do. They did not curse anybody. They did not organise resistance, appeal to Rome, or write to the colony. They did not stay to have the last word. The gesture is not revenge; it is a transfer of responsibility: you have been told, and it is now yours.

And went to Iconium. Eighty miles or so east down the road, and they start again. Persecution moves the gospel on (8:4). Which is the whole answer to the question of what a Christian does when a door is shut in his face. You do not stop; you relocate. An expulsion from one town has never yet been anything but the introduction of the gospel to the next.

When should I stop sharing the gospel with someone who keeps refusing? Rarely, and usually not at all in the sense of giving up on them. Paul left a city, not a person, and only after an organised, public rejection. With family, friends and neighbours, keep loving them, keep praying, and keep the door open, even if you stop raising the subject for a season because it has become an argument. Jesus told us not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), but he also kept eating with sinners. Change your approach if you must; do not change your love.

In a sentence. But the Jews stirred up devout, prominent women and the city’s leading men, started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of the region, so they shook the dust off their feet as a warning and went to Iconium.

On a Tuesday. When doors close, move on. God has other doors open. If a plan for serving Christ has been blocked this year, do not sulk at the closed door; ask where the next road leads. And if you have suffered for the gospel, remember it as Paul did, without bitterness, and with thanks that the Lord rescued you from it all (2 Timothy 3:11).

For worship. No closed city has ever closed the kingdom. The Lord who was himself driven out of Nazareth and led outside Jerusalem’s gate turns every expulsion of his servants into a sending. Antioch drove the messengers out, and the Lord simply carried his word down the road to Iconium. He is never shut out, never at a loss, never without a next town where his people are waiting.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment. Iconium lay about 80 miles to the east.

parallels.desc: persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. The chapter’s last sentence, and look who it is about. Not Paul. Not Barnabas. The disciples are the ones left behind, the new believers, without their teachers, in a hostile city. Take stock of their position. They are converts of a few weeks in a Roman colony that has just formally expelled their teachers. The synagogue, which for the Gentiles among them was the only religious home they had ever known, is now closed to them. The leading families of the city have shown what they are prepared to do. There is no church building, no elder, no letter from Paul, and no New Testament to read. They have a few weeks of teaching, each other, and God.

Filled. And they were filled with joy. Not coping. Not bearing up. Not relieved it had not been worse. Filled, and the tense says they went on being filled, not that it happened once on the day the apostles left. Persecution could not take it away (John 16:22). The Spirit gives joy in suffering (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The apostles left, but the Spirit stayed.

Joy with a source. Notice how the sentence is built, because the order explains it. Joy first, then the Holy Spirit, but the second is the source of the first. If Christian joy were a mood produced by circumstances, this verse could not exist; the circumstances here are unambiguously bad. It is not manufactured out of the situation. It arrives with a Person.

What it does not mean. And that has to be guarded, or it will be used to beat people. This is not a command to feel cheerful, and it is not a denial of grief. Paul knelt on a beach and wept with the Ephesian elders (20:36–38). Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). The Christian position is not joy instead of sorrow but, as Paul put it, sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10): two things at once; and anyone who has buried a believer knows exactly what that means and how it is possible.

What if I am a Christian and do not feel this joy? Then you are not alone, and you are not disqualified. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, and fruit grows; it is not switched on. Seasons of depression, grief, illness or spiritual dryness come to genuine believers, as the Psalms show again and again (Psalm 42; 88). Do not try to manufacture joy; go to its source. Keep near the means God uses: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the company of his people. Tell a mature Christian how you are. And if your low mood is deep or long, seek medical help too; that is not a lack of faith.

In a sentence. The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. So do not test yourself by asking whether you are happy. Ask a narrower question, which is actually answerable: is there anything in your life at the moment that is gladness you cannot account for from your circumstances? Any residue of contentment your situation does not explain and does not deserve? That, and not cheerfulness, is what this verse is describing, and it has a name and an address: filled with the Holy Spirit. Ask him to fill you.

For worship. The Spirit gives joy no one can take away. Antioch got rid of the preachers. It could not get the joy out of the town. The risen Christ promised that he would not leave his people as orphans, and he did not: he left them his Spirit, the Comforter, who fills the abandoned, the expelled and the bereaved with a gladness that circumstances cannot give and cannot take. The joy of the Lord is our strength, because the Lord of the joy is with us.

parallels.desc: joy of the Holy Spirit in much affliction

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 is the Reformed doctrine of election stated with apostolic directness: the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch is grounded in their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism — it does not prevent preaching; it undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach with everything they have, to everyone who will listen, in the synagogue and in the streets. They do not know who is appointed; they preach to all. And God, through the preaching, brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the guarantee that the mission will not ultimately fail: there are sheep in every flock that God is calling, and the voice of the gospel will reach them. This is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from a worshipping, fasting, praying church, arriving in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit — and the word going out, and the appointed ones believing, and the disciples filled with joy even when expelled. The first missionary journey is a portrait of how the kingdom advances: through weakness and proclamation and sovereign grace.

Now: The church sends when it worships. Mission flows from the presence of God, not from strategic planning. The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; they were seeking God — and God spoke. The question for every congregation is not “what is our mission strategy?” but “are we in the kind of sustained, attentive, fasting prayer in which the Spirit can speak?” When he speaks, we must be ready to send our best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The first missionary journey continues through the cities of southern Galatia, in the heart of modern Turkey, and the pattern of chapter 13 repeats: preaching in the synagogue, many believing, opposition, and moving on. At Iconium a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, and the Lord confirms the message with signs, but the city divides and a plot to stone the apostles drives them to Lystra and Derbe, small towns in the district of Lycaonia. At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd, shouting in their local language, decide that the gods Zeus and Hermes have come down in human form. A Roman poet, Ovid, tells a local legend that the two gods once visited this region in disguise and were turned away by everyone except an old couple; the people of Lystra were not going to make that mistake again. The priest of Zeus brings bulls and garlands to sacrifice, and Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes in horror and rush into the crowd. In a short sermon Paul tells these pagans about the living God, Creator of heaven and earth, who in past ages let the nations go their own way but left evidence of his goodness in rain, harvests and gladness.

Opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, turn the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city as dead, but he gets up and goes back in, and the next day leaves for Derbe. After making many disciples there, Paul and Barnabas courageously retrace their steps through the cities that had persecuted them, strengthening the believers, warning that we must enter God’s kingdom through many hardships, and appointing elders in every church with prayer and fasting. Finally they sail back to Syrian Antioch and report to the church all that God had done, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Iconium Paul and Barnabas spoke so effectively in the synagogue that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed. But Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the believers. The apostles stayed a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who confirmed his message of grace by enabling them to do signs and wonders. The city was divided, and when Gentiles and Jews with their leaders plotted to mistreat and stone them, they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding country, and kept preaching the gospel. At Lystra sat a man lame from birth who had never walked. He listened to Paul, who looked at him, saw he had faith to be healed, and called out to him to stand up on his feet. He jumped up and began to walk. When the crowd saw this, they shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down in human form. They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because he did the speaking. The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the gates, wanting to offer sacrifices with the crowd. When Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting that they were only human, like them, bringing good news that they should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven, earth, sea and everything in them. In the past he let all nations go their own way, yet he did not leave himself without testimony: he showed kindness by giving rain and crops in their seasons, and filled them with food and joy. Even with these words they had difficulty stopping the crowd from sacrificing to them. Then Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won the crowd over. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead. But after the disciples gathered round him, he got up and went back into the city, and the next day left with Barnabas for Derbe. They preached there and made many disciples, then returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples, urging them to remain true to the faith, and telling them that we must go through many hardships to enter God’s kingdom. They appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord in whom they had put their trust. After passing through Pisidia they came into Pamphylia, preached in Perga, went down to Attalia and sailed back to Antioch, where they had been commended to God’s grace for the work they had now completed. On arriving they gathered the church and reported all that God had done through them and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they stayed there a long time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the Path into the Kingdom

Paul and Barnabas's declaration in v. 22 — 'through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — is not pessimism but theology: the path of the crucified Lord is the path of his followers. Reformed theology insists that suffering is not a sign of God's absence but often a sign of his presence and approval: the servant who shares his Lord's cross shares his Lord's resurrection. The 'must' (dei) is the divine necessity — the same 'must' applied to Christ's suffering in Luke 24:26. The pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, then got up and went back into the city, and left for Derbe the next day. The courage required to re-enter the city where you were nearly killed is the courage of the man who has nothing to fear from death. Now: The willingness to re-enter dangerous territory — to continue faithful witness after suffering for it — is the distinctive quality of those whose security is not in this world's preservation of their lives but in Christ's resurrection that awaits them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.

Meaning first. Acts 14 completes the first missionary journey. In Iconium, many believe and the city is divided. In Lystra, a lame man is healed, the crowd tries to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, and Paul preaches to pagans who have no Bible: the living God who made all things and gives rain and harvests. Then Paul is stoned and left for dead. Yet the missionaries go back through every city, strengthening the believers, appointing elders, and teaching that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom. They return to Antioch and report that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. It is a chapter about the living God who will not share his glory with idols or with preachers, who feeds the nations while they ignore him, and who keeps the churches his Son has bought.

Now at Iconium. Iconium (modern Konya) was a city in the Roman province of Galatia, a substantial Greek-speaking city some eighty miles east of Pisidian Antioch. Paul’s letter to the Galatians was probably written to these churches.

They entered together into the Jewish synagogue. Two things in that sentence. The first is that they went to the synagogue, in Iconium, eighty miles after the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch had had them expelled from the district. Paul had announced there, publicly and with a prophet’s text behind him, that he was turning to the Gentiles (13:46). And the next building he walks into is a synagogue. Despite what happened in Antioch, they go to the synagogue first again. That is what the turn to the Gentiles actually meant in practice, and anyone who reads 13:46 as a resignation from his own people should read this verse straight afterwards.

And spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. The second is Luke’s curious phrase. He does not say they spoke faithfully, or at length, or with power. He says they spoke in such a way: a comment on the manner of it, on how the thing was put. How we speak matters. There is such a thing as saying true things badly, and these two did not. God uses clear, persuasive, Spirit-filled preaching. Faith is God’s gift, but he uses means.

But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. Poisoned (ekakōsan) means embittered, made hostile. Luke’s picture is of an audience being made bitter, worked on, over time, by people with access to them. Slander turns people against the gospel. And notice what the opposition does not do. It does not answer the preaching. It goes round it, to people who have not heard it yet, and gets there first.

The injury of slander. That is a particular kind of injury, and it is worth naming for the reader who has suffered it, because most of us have. There is no defence against it, because it does not happen where you are. You discover it only in its effects: rooms that go quiet, an invitation that stops coming, a coolness in somebody who used to be warm and will not say why. You cannot answer a charge that was never put to you, and the attempt to try makes you look exactly like the man they were warned about.

Outliving it. So what did these two do about it? Nothing, so far as Luke records. No defence, no letter to the synagogue, no month spent repairing the damage. The next verse tells you what they did instead: they stayed, and went on speaking, for a long time. Some slander can only be outlived, and the outliving is done by going on doing the work in front of everybody, for years if necessary, until the account people were given stops matching the man they can see.

If faith is God’s gift, why does it matter how we speak? Because God gives faith through means, and our words are among them. Faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit is pleased to use speech that is clear, honest, warm and well put. Careless, confusing or unkind speech can put real obstacles in a hearer’s way. None of this means clever words can produce faith; only God opens hearts (16:14). But it does mean we should take care to understand the gospel, explain it plainly, answer questions honestly and speak with love. Paul asked for prayer that he would make it clear, as he ought to speak (Colossians 4:4).

In a sentence. At Iconium Paul and Barnabas went into the synagogue and spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed, but the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and turned them against the believers.

On a Tuesday. Think about how you speak of Christ. God uses words well chosen. Before your next conversation about faith, think through how you would explain the gospel in two minutes, in plain words, to someone with no church background. And if you are being quietly talked about, resist the urge to chase every rumour. Go on doing the good work in front of everybody, and leave your reputation with God.

For worship. The God who opens hearts is pleased to use human mouths, and he takes the poor words of his servants and makes them the means of eternal life. Slander could poison minds in Iconium, but it could not stop a great number of Jews and Greeks from believing, because the Lord of the harvest was at work beneath the noise. Christ himself was slandered and did not revile in return; he entrusted himself to him who judges justly, and the Father vindicated him.
verseByVerse.note: Iconium (modern Konya) was a city in the Roman province of Galatia; Paul’s letter to the Galatians may be to these churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.

So they remained for a long time. Read that against the verse before it. The city has just been deliberately turned against them. And the word Luke uses to join the two sentences is so: therefore. The poisoning of the city is given as the reason they stayed. Opposition was a reason to stay, not to leave. That is the reverse of the instinct. When a place goes cold on us we start looking at the timetable. These men treated the hostility as evidence that something was happening worth opposing, and dug in.

Staying and leaving. Be careful with it, though, because the same chapter has them running from this same city three verses later, and a reader could take either verse as the rule. Neither is. What decided it was not their comfort but the state of the work: while there was preaching to be done they stayed under pressure, and when the pressure became a plot to kill them they left, on Jesus’s own instruction. Courage is not the same thing as staying, and prudence is not the same thing as leaving. The question in both verses is what serves the work.

Speaking boldly for the Lord. Boldness again (4:29, 31): open, unguarded speech, the thing the church had prayed for in Jerusalem.

Who bore witness to the word of his grace. Notice which way round that sentence runs. It is not that the apostles bore witness to the Lord, though of course they did. It is that the Lord bore witness to them, or more exactly, to the word they were preaching. They spoke; he testified that what they said was so. And notice the name Luke gives the message. The gospel is the word of his grace (20:24, 32), named by its content: that God gives what nobody has earned. The Lord himself confirmed it.

Granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. Signs confirmed the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4; Mark 16:20). Paul refers to these in Galatians 3:5, reminding these same churches of the miracles worked among them. And notice precisely what the signs are said to authenticate. Not the men. The word of his grace. The wonders are attached to that and underwrite that. Which is worth holding on to in a Christian world where the miraculous is sometimes offered as a credential on its own. A ministry full of wonders and empty of grace is not the thing this verse describes; the signs here are a signature at the bottom of a particular document.

Should we expect signs and wonders in ministry today? Here the Lord granted them to confirm the word of his grace through the apostles (v. 4). Continuationist Christians believe such signs continue as the gospel goes to new places. The more likely reading is that they belonged to the apostolic witness of the founding era (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). What continues is the Lord bearing witness to his word as it is preached.

How does the Lord bear witness to his word now? By the Holy Spirit, who takes the preached word and presses it home to the conscience: convicting of sin, opening blind eyes, giving faith, changing lives (1 Thessalonians 1:5). That is still a wonder, and in some ways the greater one. A man whose bitterness melts, a family that begins to pray, an addict who walks free, a proud heart that bows to Christ: these are the Lord’s signature on his word today. So when you speak the gospel, you are not on your own. The same Lord stands behind it.

In a sentence. So they stayed a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who confirmed the message of his grace by enabling them to do signs and wonders.

On a Tuesday. If you are facing coldness where you serve, ask the question this chapter asks: not what is comfortable, but what serves the work. And when you speak for Christ, ask him to bear witness to his word, then speak plainly and leave the results to him.

For worship. There is a quiet comfort in it for anyone who has felt the loneliness of saying something true that nobody wants to hear. Two men were being systematically discredited in Iconium, and the record says the Lord Jesus went on publicly backing what they said. He is not neutral about his own word. He may not vindicate it on the timetable you would choose (Paul is stoned at Lystra, the next town, and no sign prevents it), but the word of his grace has never yet gone out unattended. The gospel is the word of his grace. Speak it boldly, and trust him to confirm it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them,

But the people of the city were divided. Luke is unembarrassed about this, and it is worth stopping on, because it is not a result any of us would put in a newsletter. Two good men preached the gospel in Iconium with great effect, and the measurable outcome was that the town split in half. The gospel does that, and Jesus said it would, in terms nobody has ever found comfortable: do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division (Luke 12:51). Not because Christians are quarrelsome, though we often are, but because the message puts a question that cannot be left lying. A man can be neutral about most claims. He cannot be neutral about the claim that a particular executed Jew is the Lord of his life.

Some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. Then a small word with a long argument behind it: the apostles. Luke calls Paul and Barnabas both apostles here, and he does it again at verse 14. Everywhere else he keeps the word for the Twelve. They are men sent out on mission by the church in Antioch (vv. 4, 14). Not apostles in the sense of the Twelve, or of Paul as an eyewitness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 9:1), but sent ones, missionaries (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25). The word has a narrow and a wider sense.

Two senses of apostle. It repays a moment, because Christians are told confidently both that there are no apostles now and that there are, and the word is doing two different jobs in the New Testament. In its strict sense an apostle is one of the men who had seen the risen Christ and been commissioned by him personally as an eyewitness and a layer of foundations: the Twelve, with Paul added as one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8). That office cannot be repeated, and the reason is built into the qualification: the man had to have seen him (1:21–22), and a foundation is laid once (Ephesians 2:20). In its wider sense the word simply means one who is sent, and the New Testament uses it freely: of Barnabas here, of Epaphroditus, whom Philippi sent to Paul (Philippians 2:25), of the men Paul calls the messengers of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). In that sense the church has always had them, and mostly calls them missionaries, which is the same word arriving through Latin instead of Greek.

When someone claims the title today. So when somebody claims the title today, the useful question is not whether the word may be used but which of the two things is being claimed. A sent one, yes, and thank God for them. A man whose word stands beside Scripture because he saw the risen Christ, no. That door closed when the last of them died, and it is a mercy that it did: a church that can still be given new foundational revelation is a church that can be told anything.

When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them. A plot to lynch them. And the alliance is the thing to see. Two communities that agreed on almost nothing found something they could agree on. It is the pattern of the trial itself, where Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day (Luke 23:12). Opposition to Christ has a remarkable power to unite people who would not otherwise sit in the same room, and it is one of the stranger backhanded testimonies to who he is.

What if following Christ divides my own family? Then you are walking a road Jesus described in advance, and he walked it first: even his brothers did not believe in him for a time (John 7:5). Do not provoke division needlessly; be the kindest, most honest and most dependable member of your family. Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ. Keep loving those who disapprove, and keep praying. But do not buy peace by denying him. Many families that were split by the gospel have later been reunited in it, as Jesus’ own brothers were (1:14).

In a sentence. The city was divided, some siding with the Jews and some with the apostles, and Gentiles and Jews together with their leaders plotted to mistreat and stone them.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be surprised if the gospel divides your family or workplace. It always has. Make sure, though, that what divides people is Christ and not your manner. Ask honestly whether anyone keeps their distance because of your tone rather than your Lord.

For worship. Christ is the stone that no one can be neutral about: a sure foundation for those who believe and a stone of stumbling for those who will not. He came to bring a sword that divides, and yet the division serves the deepest peace, for those who come to him are reconciled to God and to one another. The Prince of Peace was rejected by an alliance of enemies, and through that rejection he made peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Barnabas are both called apostles — men sent out on mission.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.

They learned of it and fled. Somebody told them. A plot involving the rulers of a city and both its communities was known in advance to two travelling preachers, which means that among the divided people of verse 4 there was at least one person on the inside who got word out. Luke does not name him, and never finds out what it cost him. This book is quietly full of people like that.

Fleeing is not cowardice. And they ran. It is worth saying plainly that this is not a lapse. Jesus commanded it, saying that when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and did it himself more than once (Luke 4:30; John 8:59). There is a strain of Christian thinking in which leaving is always weakness and staying is always faith, and this verse is flatly against it. There is a time to stay and a time to go. The mission is the point, not the missionary’s reputation for nerve.

What decides it. But now hold verse 6 next to verse 20, where the same man, having been stoned and dragged out of Lystra as a corpse, gets up and walks straight back into the town. One chapter, one apostle, two opposite decisions. So the rule cannot be flee, and it cannot be stay. What decides it in both places is the work. He leaves Iconium because staying would end the preaching; he re-enters Lystra because there are new disciples in it who have just watched their teacher killed and need to see him on his feet. So if you are weighing whether to leave something hard, a post, a church, a situation, the question this chapter puts is not whether you would be braver to stay. It is what happens to the work if you go, and what happens to it if you do not. That is a question you can answer without having to grade your own courage, which is just as well, because nobody grades his own courage accurately.

To Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia. Then the destination: Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding country. Lystra and Derbe were smaller towns to the south and south-east, in the region of Lycaonia. Lystra is only about twenty miles from Iconium, but Luke’s phrase marks the thing that mattered: it was over a boundary, in Lycaonia, and therefore outside the reach of the Iconian magistrates. Twenty miles was enough, provided they were the right twenty miles. Lystra was a Roman colony; Timothy came from there (16:1).

A step down in the world. And it is a step down. Iconium was a substantial Greek-speaking city; Lystra was a small Roman colony in rough hill country whose people, as verse 11 will show, still shouted in Lycaonian when they were excited. Paul is moving steadily away from the places where his education is worth anything.

And there they continued to preach the gospel. Then the clause that carries the weight. They fled, but they did not stop. They arrive as fugitives from a stoning, in a backwater whose language they do not speak, and they start again. Not recovered, and then preached. Fled, and preached.

Is it ever right for a Christian to flee persecution today? Yes. Believers in hostile countries sometimes face a real choice between staying and leaving, and Scripture gives freedom for both. Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt; the church scattered from Jerusalem (8:1–4); Paul was let down the wall at Damascus (9:25). What is never permitted is to deny Christ to stay safe. So pray, seek counsel, think of those who depend on you and of the work, and then act in faith. And churches in safer places should pray for, welcome and support those who have had to flee.

In a sentence. They found out and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding region, where they kept preaching the gospel.

On a Tuesday. If circumstances have moved you somewhere you did not choose, a new town, a new job, a smaller place, ask what gospel work is waiting there. Paul’s instinct on arriving anywhere was to begin again. Make it yours.

For worship. Persecution can move you, but it should never silence you. The Lord who scatters his servants is sowing them like seed. He led his people out of Egypt and he led his apostles out of Iconium, and every road they fled down became a road for the gospel. Nothing in the hand of his enemies can stop the word; it can only send it further.
verseByVerse.note: Lystra and Derbe were smaller towns to the south and south-east, in the region of Lycaonia.

parallels.desc: Timothy of Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary:
