Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,

A man sitting who could not use his feet. Luke slows right down for this man and gives three descriptions where one would have done: he could not use his feet, he was crippled from birth, and he had never walked. The last is the one that costs something. Not injured, not declining: a man who had never in his life taken a step, and had spent all of it watching everybody else do it. The healing closely resembles Peter’s healing of the lame man in 3:1–10. Luke shows that Paul’s ministry has the same marks as Peter’s.

He listened to Paul speaking. A man hearing a preacher in the open air of a town with no synagogue and no Scripture in it. Whatever he was making of it, he wanted more of it. Faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17).

And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well. Made well (sōthēnai) is the word for being saved. His faith reached out to the Christ Paul preached. This sentence has done a great deal of damage in the church, and it has to be handled carefully, because a wounded reader will get it wrong in one particular way. Read carelessly, it says the healing happened because the man’s faith was sufficient, from which it follows, with awful logic, that where healing does not happen the faith was not sufficient. That is what people are told. It is told at bedsides. And it is not what this verse says.

Who is doing the seeing. Look at who is doing the seeing. Paul, looking intently at him, the same verb Luke used of him a chapter ago, staring at Elymas, and seeing. What Paul saw was not printed on the man’s face for anyone to read. It was shown him. This is not an apostle assessing a candidate’s spiritual performance and finding it up to standard; it is an apostle being given to know, in that moment, what God intended to do in that man. And the faith he sees is itself something God has been producing through the preaching the man had been hearing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean healing always depends on the sick person’s faith, so that those not healed lacked faith. Jesus sometimes healed those with no faith at all (Luke 22:51; John 5:13). Paul himself was not healed of his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and he left Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20). God heals as he wills.

Test it against the rest of the book. That is the surest way to settle it. The man at the temple gate asked for money and expected nothing else, and was healed anyway (3:6). Aeneas had been bedridden eight years and is not recorded as saying a word (9:34). Dorcas was dead (9:40). The high priest’s servant (John names him Malchus) was in the act of helping to arrest Jesus when his ear was healed, and it is Luke who tells us so (Luke 22:51). If healing ran on the sufferer’s faith, half the healings in Scripture could not have happened.

The hardest evidence. And then the hardest evidence of all, which ought to settle it for good. Paul himself asked three times to be relieved of something and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). He left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). He told Timothy to take a little wine for his frequent ailments rather than healing him (1 Timothy 5:23). The apostle who read this man’s faith in a Lystran street could not read his own way out of a thorn.

So if you are ill. So if you are ill, or someone you love is, and you have been made to feel that the failure is yours, that if you could only believe harder the thing would lift, put this verse down and pick it up the other way round. It does not say that faith produces healing. It says that on one particular afternoon in one particular town, God let his apostle see what he was about to do. Your not being healed is not a report card on your faith. If it were, Paul failed his.

Should I still pray for healing? Yes, gladly and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them. Pray as a child asks a father, honestly naming what you want, and then rest the answer in his wisdom, as Jesus did in Gethsemane: not my will, but yours. If healing comes, give thanks. If it does not, his grace is sufficient, and the full healing is certain at the resurrection, when the lame will leap and the body will be raised imperishable.

In a sentence. In Lystra there sat a man crippled from birth who had never walked, who listened to Paul, and Paul looked straight at him and saw that he had faith to be healed.

On a Tuesday. Faith comes by hearing. Keep speaking of Christ; someone is listening. And if you know someone who has been wounded by the teaching that their illness reflects weak faith, read them this passage, and tell them about Paul’s thorn.

For worship. The Lord who saw this man in the crowd sees every sufferer, and he knows the whole story of every body. He gives faith, he heals as he wills, and he holds back healing for reasons of love we will one day understand. In the end he will heal entirely: the Saviour who bore our griefs and carried our sorrows will wipe every tear from every eye, and no one who trusts him will be left sitting at the gate.
verseByVerse.note: The healing closely resembles Peter’s healing of the lame man at the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he sprang up and began walking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking.

Said in a loud voice, Stand upright on your feet. A command in a loud voice. Consider what is actually being asked of the man. He has never stood. He has no idea what standing feels like: no learned sense of balance, no memory of how weight shifts from one leg to the other, none of the ten thousand small corrections a body makes without being told. Somebody who has been off his feet for a single year needs months to walk again after the cause is removed, because walking is a skill and the body forgets it. This man had never had the skill to forget.

And he sprang up and began walking. Sprang up (hēlato) means leapt, like the lame man of 3:8. Not stood carefully. Not was helped upright and shuffled a few steps between two men. He jumped. What he was given in that second was not a repair to a mechanism; it was everything a person normally acquires over the first two years of his life and then practises for the rest of it, handed over complete. It is Isaiah 35:6 again: then shall the lame man leap like a deer. The prophet promised it of the days when God comes to save, and in a town with no Bible, the sign of the messianic age walked on new legs.

What is not in the sentence. Now notice something that is not in the sentence, because it explains everything that goes wrong next. Peter, at the temple gate, said, in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk (3:6), and the crowd that came running was preached at about the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob before anybody had time to misunderstand. Here Luke records no name at all. Paul says a few words in a loud voice, and a town with no Scripture in it is left to interpret what it has seen out of the only religious vocabulary it possesses.

A miracle by itself teaches nobody anything. Which is why the next verse goes so badly wrong, and it is a lesson worth carrying well beyond Lystra. A miracle compels attention, and then people explain it with whatever they already believe. Jerusalem had the Scriptures and reached for the God of Israel. Lystra had Zeus and reached for him. The event was the same; the two towns drew opposite conclusions from it, and neither drew a conclusion the event had supplied. So a remarkable thing happening is not, on its own, evidence that God has done it, nor evidence of what he meant by it. The apostles never once treat a sign as self-explanatory; again and again in this book one is followed by somebody standing up and saying what it meant. Where that explanation does not follow, the crowd supplies its own, and this crowd is already sending for oxen.

How should I respond to stories of miracles today? With openness and with care. God is able to do anything, and he does answer prayer in ways that leave doctors puzzled. But a remarkable event does not interpret itself, and it does not prove the teaching of whoever was standing nearby. Ask what is being taught, and whether Christ and his gospel are being honoured, because Scripture warns that false teachers can come with signs (Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9). The test of any ministry is not whether wonders are reported but whether it agrees with the word of God.

In a sentence. Paul called out loudly for him to stand up on his feet, and the man jumped up and began to walk.

On a Tuesday. When God does something good in your life, do not leave it uninterpreted. Say plainly, to yourself and to others, who did it and what it shows about him. Unexplained blessings drift into being called luck, or are credited to the wrong source.

For worship. The Christ who healed in Jerusalem healed in Lystra. He is Lord of every place. The man who had never walked leapt, and his leaping was a preview of the new creation, when every crooked thing will be made straight and every body made whole. The voice that called him to stand is the voice that will call the dead from their graves, and they too will rise.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.

Saying in Lycaonian. Luke’s ear is exact here. They cried out in Lycaonian, the old country language, not the Greek Paul had been preaching in, which Paul and Barnabas did not understand. Under strain people revert to the tongue they think in. And the detail quietly explains the delay: Paul and Barnabas go on standing there while a sacrifice is organised around them, because they cannot understand a word of it. That is why they took a while to realise what was happening. They find out when the animals appear.

The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men! The reaction looks wild until you know the local story, and then it becomes almost inevitable. There was a legend attached to these hills, and the Roman poet Ovid had written it up a generation before Paul walked into the town. Zeus and Hermes came through this country disguised as travellers, looking for somewhere to stay, and were turned away from a thousand doors. One household took them in: an old couple, Philemon and Baucis, poor enough to have almost nothing to offer, who were ready to kill their only goose for the strangers. The gods revealed themselves, turned the couple’s cottage into a temple, and drowned the entire district that had refused them.

Fear with a long memory. That is the story these people grew up on. It is set in their own countryside. And it has a moral with teeth: when two strangers turn up and something impossible happens, you do not want to be the household that got it wrong. The people of Lystra did not want to miss the gods a second time. So the shouting is not simple enthusiasm. It is fear with a long memory, and it explains why the priest comes at a run with cattle instead of convening a meeting about it.

An irony. And there is an irony under the error. God did come down in human likeness, in Jesus (Philippians 2:7), and Paul is there to tell them. The crowd had the right longing and the wrong gods.

Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. Then the roles, which are worth having. Zeus was the chief god: the senior presence, the one you do not address directly. Hermes was his messenger, the god of speech, who runs the errands. Barnabas perhaps looked more dignified; Paul did the talking. Inscriptions linking Zeus and Hermes have been found near Lystra. So the man doing all the talking is taken for the junior deity, and the quiet one beside him for the god. Luke, who has spent the previous chapter recording that Paul had taken over the leadership of this mission, does not comment. He simply lets you notice that a crowd looking for greatness looked straight past the man in the middle of it.

Sized up wrongly. There is something in that for anyone who has been sized up wrongly, passed over on the strength of a manner, or promoted on one. The people of Lystra got both men wrong, in opposite directions, on the same afternoon. Neither verdict survived the week.

How is the incarnation different from the Lystrans’ idea of gods coming down? Utterly. In the myths the gods only looked human for a while, in disguise, to test people and then punish them. In Jesus the eternal Son truly became man, taking a real human body and soul, permanently, without ceasing to be God (John 1:14). He did not come to inspect our hospitality but to receive our rejection, and instead of drowning those who turned him away, he died for them. The Lystrans feared gods who came down to judge. The true God came down to save.

In a sentence. When the crowds saw what Paul did, they shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down in human form, and called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, since he was the main speaker.

On a Tuesday. Many people around you have a picture of God shaped by stories, films or childhood fears rather than by Scripture. Ask a friend this week what they think God is like, listen well, and then tell them about the God who came down in Jesus.

For worship. God truly came down in human likeness in Jesus. Tell people the real story. He did not come in disguise but in flesh; not for an afternoon but for ever; not to test the hospitality of a village but to be turned away from the inn and from the world, and to open his own house to those who turned him away. That is the coming down the gods of Lystra could never have imagined.
verseByVerse.note: A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes visiting the region in human form unrecognised. Hermes was messenger of the gods, so the speaker, Paul, was taken for him.

parallels.desc: they said that he was a god

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.

And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city. Set the scene properly, because this is where a misunderstanding turns into a crisis. Literally the phrase means Zeus-before-the-city, the city’s patron god: the town’s own guardian, whose shrine stood outside the walls, watching the road, so that every trader and traveller passed him on the way in. He was not an abstraction to these people. He was the local authority responsible for the weather, the harvest, and whether Lystra had a good year.

Brought oxen and garlands to the gates. And his priest is now at the gate with oxen, full-grown cattle, the most expensive offering the town could make, not a pair of pigeons, and with garlands, the woollen or flowered wreaths wound about the animals’ heads and horns before they were killed. The garlands mean the beasts are already dedicated. This is not under discussion. It is under way.

And wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. Two men have been preaching in that town for a few days about the true God. In the space of about ten minutes, the most impressive religious act in the town’s calendar is being arranged in their honour, by the professional in charge of it, at public expense, with the whole population delighted about it. Worship of men as gods. A great temptation for any preacher: to accept the praise of men.

Why this moment is dangerous. It is worth asking what makes this moment so dangerous, because on the face of it a misunderstanding by ignorant people looks harmless enough: embarrassing, but correctable. It is dangerous because it is flattering, and because it is sincere. Nobody here is working an angle. These people are grateful, and frightened, and they have brought the best they have. And that is the easiest thing in the world to let run. Not to endorse it; nobody endorses it. Simply to be slow about correcting it. To reflect that they will understand better in time, that this is not the moment, that the crowd is finally listening and it would be a pity to lose them. Very nearly every scandal of Christian celebrity has begun in a version of this room: not a man claiming to be more than a man, but a man declining, for a while, to interrupt people who were treating him as though he were. What happens next takes a handful of words, and it is a large part of the reason we are still reading about these two.

Is it wrong to admire or thank a pastor or Christian leader? No. Scripture tells us to esteem our leaders very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and gratitude is right. The danger begins when admiration turns into dependence or exemption: when a leader is treated as beyond question, when his words carry more weight than Scripture, or when his failings are hidden to protect his image. Thank your leaders, pray for them, and hold them to account. And leaders should be quick, like Paul, to deflect the glory to Christ.

In a sentence. The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood outside the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates, wanting to offer sacrifice with the crowds.

On a Tuesday. Watch out for the subtle ways people want to put leaders on pedestals. And don’t climb onto one. If you have any influence, at work, at home, in church, notice when you enjoy being admired a little too much, and interrupt it: pass the credit on, quickly, to the one it belongs to.

For worship. The LORD says, I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other. There is one God to whom every sacrifice belongs, and one sacrifice that was ever enough: not oxen garlanded at a city gate, but the Lamb of God offered outside the gate of Jerusalem. He alone is worthy, and every honour pressed on his servants is meant to be laid at his feet.
verseByVerse.note: Garlands were wreaths placed on sacrificial animals.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them.

They tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd. Take the two actions separately, because both are deliberate and both cost something. Tearing your clothes was the Jewish sign of unbearable grief, or of horror at blasphemy: it is what the high priest did at what he took to be blasphemy from Jesus (Mark 14:63). Paul and Barnabas are not making a gesture the Lystrans will understand; nobody in that crowd knows what a torn robe means. They are doing what a Jew does when he hears God insulted, in a town where it will simply look odd. That is what they thought of the honour being offered them. And they rushed out into the crowd. Not onto a platform, and not away. Into it, shoving into a mass of excited people in order to get physically between them and the altar.

We also are men, of like nature with you. Then the sentence itself. The Greek is homoiopatheis, of the same feelings, the same sufferings, the same weaknesses and passions, the word James uses of Elijah (James 5:17). Not merely the same species: the same aches, the same fears, the same capacity to be hurt. Within a few days Paul will be lying outside that same gate under a heap of stones, and the town will have its proof. Paul and Barnabas refuse divine honour, at once and loudly.

Harder than Caesarea. The question of what a man does when he is offered honour that belongs to God has already been put in this book, and it was answered the other way by a king in Caesarea who kept his robes on and said nothing (12:22–23); the working of it out is there and does not need repeating. But notice what makes Lystra harder than Caesarea. Herod’s flatterers were buying grain and everybody in the theatre knew it. These people mean it. They are not manipulating anybody; they are overwhelmed with gratitude and have brought oxen. It is far easier to refuse worship from a man working an angle than from a man who simply wants to say thank you in the only currency he has, and who will be hurt when you will not take it.

Preaching with no Bible to quote. Then look at how they preach, because this is the first sermon in Acts addressed to people with no Bible at all. No Abraham, no Moses, no exodus, no prophets: not even one God to start from. Peter at Pentecost could quote Joel. Paul in the synagogue could quote the Psalms and expect the room to follow. Here there is nothing to quote. So they begin where these people actually are.

And we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God. Vain things (mataiōn) are empty, hollow, worthless, with nothing there, which is the Old Testament word for idols (Jeremiah 2:5; 10:15; 1 Thessalonians 1:9). And living is the whole contrast: the gods of Lystra had to be fed by a priest. The living God, against dead idols.

Who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. That last phrase is straight out of Scripture (Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6), and they do not say so, because saying so would have meant nothing here. They just say the thing. To pagans, Paul does not begin with Scripture they do not know, but with God as Creator. He starts where they are.

A note on apostle. Barnabas is called an apostle here in the wider sense of one sent out by a church as a missionary (compare v. 4; 13:2–3), not in the office of the Twelve and Paul, which has no successors.

Where they start, and what they demand. Which is the model, and it is more demanding than it looks. They did not open with justification and they did not open with Genesis 12. They took the one real point of contact a pagan farming town had, the sky, the fields, the food on the table, and they used it. And having found the point of contact, they did not soften the demand by a syllable: turn. It is the same word Peter used in Jerusalem. The starting place moved. The call did not.

How do I talk about Christ with someone who knows nothing of the Bible? Start where Paul started: with what they already know and experience. Creation, conscience, the goodness of ordinary life, the longing for meaning, the reality of death. Speak of the God who made all this and who is not like the idols of our age, money, success, pleasure, image. Then move to the heart of it: he has come in Jesus, died and risen, and calls us to turn to him. Avoid church jargon, explain terms, ask questions, and be patient. The starting point can change. The message and the call to turn must not.

In a sentence. When Barnabas and Paul heard, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting that they were only men like them, bringing good news that they should turn from worthless things to the living God, who made heaven, earth, sea and everything in them.

On a Tuesday. Name the vain things you are tempted to look to for security or joy: your bank balance, your reputation, a relationship, a screen. Turn from one of them deliberately today, and thank the living God for something he made. And if anyone treats you as more than you are, be quick to say: I too am only a man.

For worship. Turn from empty things to the living God. He made everything, and he is worth everything. The idols must be carried and fed; the living God carries his people and feeds the world. Heaven and earth and sea and everything in them are his, and he who made them all came down in Christ, of like nature with us in everything except sin, so that empty-handed idolaters could be brought home to him.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: turned to God from idols

verseByVerse.quote: "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways.

In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. That is a stark sentence, and it raises the question this whole scene has been circling: what about all the people who never heard? Before Christ, God let the nations go their own way, without special revelation, as he gave his law only to Israel (Psalm 147:19–20). Not that he approved, but that he was patient (17:30; Romans 3:25). Now the times of ignorance are over: God calls all to repent.

Not an abstract question. It is not an abstract question here. Lystra is standing in front of Paul as an instance of it: a town that has been sacrificing to Zeus for centuries with no prophet, no Scripture and no summons. And it is one of the two or three questions most likely to be put to a Christian by somebody he loves. Take what Scripture actually says, and refuse both of the comfortable answers.

First, nobody is judged against a light he was never given. Paul’s own developed argument is that Gentiles who do not have the law are judged by what they did have: the work of the law written on their hearts, their conscience accusing or else excusing them (Romans 2:14–16). Whatever the outcome in any individual case, God is not weighing a man against a revelation he withheld from him. That is worth saying to anyone whose real fear is that God is unfair.

Second, they are not innocent. Paul is equally firm that what can be known about God is plain from what has been made, so that people are without excuse, and the charge he brings is not ignorance but suppression: knowing something of God and not honouring him or giving thanks (Romans 1:19–21). The very next verse is about to make the same point in kinder language. God had been sending Lystra rain the whole time. Nobody in that town had been left with nothing.

Third, the Judge is good. Abraham’s question, Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25), is one of those questions that is answered in the asking, and it is the answer Scripture actually gives to the anxious. You are not being asked to certify the eternal state of people you have never met. You are being asked whether the God who did not spare his own Son can be trusted with them.

Refuse the false comfort in both directions. This verse gives no ground for supposing the nations are safe in their ignorance: Paul’s whole point is that the era of overlooking has ended and a summons has now arrived, which is exactly what he tells Athens in almost these words (17:30). Nor does it allow us to speak as though God owed the nations more than he gave, or as though we could pronounce on each individual. Scripture does teach that there is salvation in no one else (4:12), that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, and that the ordinary means is someone sent to preach him (Romans 10:14). Those who die in infancy are a separate case, and we rest the elect among them in the mercy of the God who saves them in Christ. For the rest, God has told us plainly how he deals with sinners, and has put a job in our hands: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14).

The waiting is over. Which is the real force of the verse where it stands. Paul does not raise the past generations to settle a puzzle. He raises them to tell a crowd in a small Anatolian town that the waiting is over, and that the summons has arrived in the street they are standing in.

Then can someone be saved by following his conscience and the light he has? No. Conscience and creation show enough of God to condemn, never enough to save, because no one lives up to the light he has; all have sinned (Romans 3:23). Salvation comes only through Christ, received by faith, and faith comes by hearing his word. That is precisely why Paul walked into Lystra, and why the church sends missionaries still. The right response to the question of those who have not heard is not speculation but sending, giving and going.

In a sentence. In past generations God allowed all nations to go their own way.

On a Tuesday. God’s patience has a purpose: to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4). Don’t presume on it. And if the question of those who never heard troubles you, turn the trouble into action: choose a people group or a missionary to pray for regularly, and give toward taking the gospel where it has not been heard.

For worship. For long ages the nations walked in their own ways, and God did not walk away from them. He was patient, holding back the judgment they deserved, until the fullness of time, when he sent his Son, and through his Son the summons to every nation under heaven. The Judge of all the earth is just, and the Saviour of the world is kind, and they are one and the same God.

parallels.desc: the times of ignorance God overlooked

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.

Yet he did not leave himself without witness. Even without Scripture, God left evidence of himself in creation and providence (Romans 1:19–20; Psalm 19:1). Look at what Paul chooses. He is speaking to farmers on the Anatolian uplands, and he does not reach for the stars, or the intricacy of the body, or the moral law within. He reaches for rain, harvest, dinner, and being glad.

For he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons. Lystra was a farming region. The rain and harvests they credited to Zeus came from the living God (Matthew 5:45). And notice who had been fed. The rain fell on the fields of a town that had built a temple to Zeus at its gate and paid a priest to keep him satisfied, and God sent the rain anyway, season after season, for as long as anyone could remember. The people now leading oxen up to the wrong god had eaten every day of their lives at the table of the right one.

Satisfying your hearts with food and gladness. That is a remarkable list, and the last item is the most remarkable of all. Every meal, every joy, is a witness to God’s kindness. God’s witness to himself in a pagan town included gladness: the pleasure of a good meal, the ease that settles on people when there has been enough and the year has gone well. Paul stands in front of idolaters and tells them that their happiness was evidence.

Common grace. This verse is one of Scripture’s clearest windows onto common grace. Common means not cheap but given to all in common: the goodness God shows every creature, believer and unbeliever alike: the rains and fruitful seasons, the food and gladness here; and beyond, life and breath (Acts 17:25), the restraint of evil, the skill and kindness and beauty found even among those who do not know God, and the patience that delays judgment to leave room for repentance. Jesus grounds it in the same gifts: God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45; compare Psalm 145:9; James 1:17). The astonishing thing Paul presses on these idolaters is that God had been feeding them, gladdening them, and watering their fields all along, lavishing kindness on people building altars to other gods.

Two things must be kept clear. First, common grace is not saving grace: genuinely grace, undeserved kindness, but it blesses this life without, by itself, reconciling anyone to God; the redeeming grace given in Christ is a greater thing, granted to those who believe. (To confuse them is to imagine everyone is saved because everyone enjoys God’s sunshine.) Second, see what it is for: it is a witness (v. 17), daily goodness testifying that God is real and kind, leaving people without excuse (Romans 1:20) and meant to lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4). The tragedy is to take the gifts and ignore the Giver (Romans 1:21). And the lesson is warm and practical: every good thing you enjoy, the rain on your garden, the harvest, the meal on the table, the laughter of friends, the sun on your back, is a gift from the open hand of a good God, a daily knock pointing past the gift to the Giver. It teaches you to give thanks for everything, see God’s hand everywhere, and love even your enemies as God does, doing good to all (Matthew 5:44–45).

Where Christians differ: can creation save? Some argue that those who respond to God’s witness in nature may be saved without the gospel. Verdict: God’s witness in creation is real, and leaves everyone without excuse (Romans 1:20), but it is not enough to save. It shows God’s power and kindness, not his way of salvation through Christ. That is why Paul and Barnabas came to Lystra with the gospel. General revelation points to God; special revelation, the gospel, brings us to him.

Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. Then verse 18, which is deliberately anticlimactic. Old habits die hard. Scarcely. This is one of the great short sermons in Acts, delivered by an apostle at the top of his powers in an emergency, and Luke’s verdict on it is that it only just worked. They got the sacrifice stopped by the skin of their teeth. Luke does not even say the crowd was persuaded; only that it was restrained.

When the best answer barely holds. There is an honesty in that which the church needs. The best answer, given at the right moment by the right man, may only just hold, and this crowd, a few days later, picked up stones. If you have said the true thing as well as you knew how and watched it barely land, you are in good company. Luke thought the barely was worth writing down.

Is it right for Christians to enjoy food, harvests and ordinary pleasures? Yes, and to enjoy them as from God. Paul tells Timothy that God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and that everything created by God is good if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). The sin is not enjoyment but ingratitude, or making the gift into a god. So eat, laugh, delight in a good harvest or a good holiday, and say thank you to the one who gave it. Gladness received from God and returned to him in praise is part of worship.

In a sentence. Yet God had not left himself without a witness, doing good by giving rain and harvests and filling their hearts with food and joy, and even saying this, they could barely stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.

On a Tuesday. At each meal today, before you eat, name to God one specific thing about the food or the company that you are glad of. And when you meet someone who does not believe, notice the good things in their life, and gently point out whose kindness lies behind them.

For worship. Every harvest and every good meal speaks of God’s kindness. Thank him for them. The rain that falls on the field of the atheist and the idolater falls from the hand of a Father who has not stopped being kind to his enemies. He fills hearts with food and gladness, and then he gives the gift beyond all gifts: his Son, the bread of life, so that those who have eaten all their lives at his table may at last sit down at it as his children.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.

But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium. Look at the distances before anything else. Iconium is some twenty miles from Lystra. Pisidian Antioch is around a hundred. Somebody organised this: messages sent, a journey of several days made deliberately over hill roads, by men whose entire purpose in travelling was to finish in this town what they had started in their own. Determined opponents. It is one of the ugliest sentences in Acts, and it is quietly instructive. Hatred will make an effort that indifference never makes. These men walked a hundred miles to break up a meeting.

And having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul. The same crowds. Luke does not soften it and does not explain it. The people who a few days earlier had to be physically restrained from worshipping this man now throw stones at him until he stops moving. From worship to stoning in a few days. Nothing had changed except who had been talking to them. Crowds are fickle, as with Jesus: Hosanna, then Crucify.

What a crowd’s approval is worth. That is worth knowing about crowds, and about what their approval is worth. A reputation handed to you by people who do not know you can be taken back by people who do not know you, and the same afternoon’s excitement supplies both. It is also worth knowing about ourselves. These were not monsters by the standards of their town. They were ordinary, frightened, easily led people who had just been told a persuasive story by men who sounded as though they knew.

And dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. Left for dead. They were not pretending. A stoning is not a beating; it is an execution, and this one was carried far enough that the men doing it stopped, looked, and concluded the job was finished. Paul himself had approved the stoning of Stephen; now he is stoned. He mentions it exactly once, in a list of things he had survived: once I was stoned (2 Corinthians 11:25). And writing to the Galatians, whose churches these are, he says he bears on his body the marks of Jesus (Galatians 6:17). Whatever those marks were, some of them were made here.

But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city. Two things, and the second one is the find. The first: Luke, who is a careful writer, does not say that Paul was raised from the dead. He says the crowd supposed he was dead, and that he got up. It may have been a miracle; it may have been a man surviving what should have killed him. Luke declines to say, and it is a mark of his honesty that he leaves the reader without the more impressive version, the more so since he is quite willing to report a raising when he believes one happened (9:40; 20:9–12). A recovery, perhaps miraculous. And he goes back into the city that stoned him.

The disciples gathered about him. The second: there were disciples in Lystra. In the middle of the disaster, Luke mentions in passing that the preaching had worked, and that a small group of brand-new believers is now standing in a ring round the body of their teacher outside the town wall, which took some nerve, with the crowd not yet dispersed.

Timothy, very likely. And it is very likely that one of them was a boy called Timothy. Lystra was his town; Paul finds him there on the next journey and takes him along (16:1–2). Years later, writing to him for the last time, Paul reminds him of the persecutions he endured and names Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, the three towns of this chapter, in this order (2 Timothy 3:10–11). He writes as though Timothy needs no explanation. The likeliest reason he needs none is that he was there. So the young man who became Paul’s closest colleague, a man frightened by temperament, who had to be told more than once not to be, may well have begun by watching his hero dragged out of town as a corpse. And signed on anyway.

And on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. Not convalesced. The next day, and about sixty miles on foot.

Why does God let his servants suffer like this? Scripture gives no single answer, but it gives several true ones. Suffering conforms us to Christ, who suffered first (Philippians 3:10). It proves that the message is believed, not merely sold, since nobody is stoned for a sales pitch. It strengthens other believers, who see that faith survives the worst (Philippians 1:12–14). And it is temporary and outweighed: this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). God does not waste a single stone thrown at his people.

What should I do if I am mistreated for my faith? Do not retaliate; bless (Romans 12:14). Do not be ashamed; rejoice that you are counted worthy to suffer for his name (5:41). Use proper protection where you can, as Paul later used his citizenship. Tell other believers and let them gather around you, as the disciples did here. And keep going, even if, like Paul, it is the next day and you are still bruised. The Lord who stood by Paul stands by you.

In a sentence. But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, won over the crowds, stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead, but when the disciples gathered round him, he got up and went back into the city, and the next day left with Barnabas for Derbe.

On a Tuesday. Popularity is fickle. Serve for God’s approval, not the crowd’s. If you notice you are lifted or crushed by what people say about you this week, ask whose opinion you are actually living for. And gather round someone who has been knocked down: visit, phone, stand in the ring.

For worship. Christ was carried into Jerusalem on hosannas and carried out of it to a cross, and he did not stop loving the crowd that changed its mind. Paul bore in his body the marks of that Lord, and every scar was a share in the sufferings of the one who was wounded for our transgressions. The stones of Lystra could not finish what Christ had begun, for the Lord raises up his servants and sets them on the road again.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch was about 100 miles from Lystra.

parallels.desc: once I was stoned

verseByVerse.quote: When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.

When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples. Read verse 21 as a route, and it stops being a travel note. They preach at Derbe and make many disciples there, and Derbe is the far end of the journey, out near the pass that leads home. From Derbe the road east through the Cilician Gates would have brought them to Tarsus in a few days and to Syrian Antioch not long after: downhill, familiar, and safe. And instead they turn round.

What is a disciple? Made many disciples is worth pausing on, because we easily lose the very idea of a disciple. It is the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19): not just converts, but disciples. The word (mathētēs) means a learner, an apprentice: not one who collects information but one who attaches his whole life to a master, learns his teaching and his way of living, and sets out to become like him: everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher (Luke 6:40). Jesus made it costly and total, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (Luke 9:23), yet also the ordinary identity of every believer: disciple was the word for a Christian before the name Christian existed (Acts 11:26).

Where the modern church stumbles. That is where the modern church stumbles. We can reduce the faith to a single decision, getting people converted, and forget that the commission is to make disciples, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you (Matthew 28:19–20). A disciple is not an optional upgrade for keen Christians; it is simply what a Christian is: a lifelong apprentice of Jesus. Paul and Barnabas did exactly this: not counting converts and moving on, but returning to strengthen the disciples and appointing elders to watch over them (vv. 22–23). The reminder is bracing and freeing: you were not saved to make one decision and drift, but to follow, to walk after Jesus as a learner, for the rest of your life.

They returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch. Name them in order. Back through the very cities that had persecuted them. Lystra is where Paul had been stoned and left for dead a few weeks earlier. Iconium is where both communities and their rulers had agreed to stone him. Antioch is where the leading families of the colony had had the two of them expelled from the district. He goes back to all three, in reverse order, deliberately. From Derbe, Paul could have gone home a shorter way through Tarsus. He went back to care for the new believers.

Strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith. Ask what for, because it is not to preach; the preaching has been done. Luke gives three participles: strengthening, encouraging, and saying. Follow-up. New believers need strengthening. They are going back to make sure that what they started can stand without them. And that is a judgment about what the work actually is. It would have been perfectly defensible to write to those churches, or to send somebody, or to reckon that a man recently stoned has earned the road home. Paul walks back into the town where it happened, and the reason is in the third participle.

And saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. Because think what those young churches had just watched. Their teachers had been talked out of one town, chased out of another, and very nearly killed in a third. Every convert in those cities was facing the obvious question: is this what following Jesus is going to be like? And Paul’s answer, delivered in person, on legs that had recently been stoned, was yes. Must (dei) means it is necessary: not optional, not a sign of failure. The kingdom is entered through trouble (John 16:33; 2 Timothy 3:12; 1 Peter 4:12–13). Paul did not promise an easy life; he had the scars to prove it.

We, not you. Notice that he says we, not you. He is not issuing a warning from a safe distance; he is describing a road he is standing on, to people who had seen him on it. That is the strengthening. He does not tell them it will get easier. He tells them that the difficulty is the road and not a diversion from it, which is the only kind of comfort that survives contact with real trouble, and the reason it works is that it removes the second wound. Suffering hurts. Suffering plus the suspicion that it means God has gone is unbearable, and it is the second half Paul is taking away. He says the same to Rome, that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope (Romans 5:3–4), and to Timothy without any softening at all: all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12).

Did we not already enter the kingdom? You may be puzzled. Paul says God has transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13, past tense), yet here entering is still future. Both are true; this is the already and not yet. God’s saving reign in King Jesus comes in two stages. It already arrived at his first coming (the kingdom of God has come upon you, Matthew 12:28), and every believer is already under its reign, enjoying its blessings (forgiveness, the Spirit, sonship). And it is not yet consummated: its full glory waits for his return, when he reigns openly and makes all things new, and in that sense we will yet enter or inherit it (Matthew 25:34; 1 Corinthians 15:50; 2 Timothy 4:18). The kingdom here is the future kingdom, entered fully at Christ’s return. Same kingdom, two stages: the already real but partial, the not yet full and final. (See on Colossians 1:13; 4:11.)

Two ways of speaking. So Paul speaks both ways as his point requires: to assure us of what is already ours by grace, he says we have been placed in the kingdom; to press us on in hope, as here, he points to the kingdom we have yet to enter. Picture a decisive battle already won, the outcome settled, while the victory parade still lies ahead; or dawn, the sun truly risen, the full blaze of noon still to come. And notice why he raises the future entrance here: to frame the many tribulations as the appointed road home. The trials are not a sign we have lost the kingdom; they are the path into its fullness, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17).

Does this mean every Christian will be persecuted? Every Christian will face tribulations, though not all in the same form. For some it is prison or violence; for others it is mockery, lost opportunities, family pressure, illness, grief, or the long fight against sin. The word covers the whole pressure of living for Christ in a fallen world. So do not seek suffering, and do not be ashamed if yours seems small compared with others’. But when it comes, do not be surprised, as though something strange were happening (1 Peter 4:12). It is the road, and the King has walked it.

In a sentence. After preaching in Derbe and making many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples and urging them to remain in the faith, saying that we must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. If you are going through a hard season, say this sentence out loud: this is the road, not a detour from it. Then think of a newer Christian you know and strengthen them this week: a message, a coffee, a prayer, an honest word that following Jesus is hard and worth it.

For worship. The road to the kingdom runs through tribulation. Don’t be shaken; the King walked it first. He entered his glory by way of the cross, and he leads his people home by the same road, walking beside them every step. The kingdom we enter at the end is the kingdom already given us at the beginning, and the One who has brought us into it will bring us through to the noon of its glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

And when they had appointed elders for them in every church. The verb deserves a note before anything else, because it has been fought over. Cheirotoneō originally meant to stretch out the hand, that is, to vote by a show of hands in an assembly, and by the first century it had worn down to mean simply to appoint or designate. It may suggest the congregation took part. Congregationalists have leaned on the older sense and episcopalians on the later one, and the honest answer is that a single verb will not settle a system of church government. What the sentence plainly says is that Paul and Barnabas did the appointing, that they did it in every church without exception, and that no congregation was left without it. Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogue. Plural: a group of elders in every church, not a single pastor (20:17; Philippians 1:1; Titus 1:5). Elders are also called overseers (20:28; Titus 1:5–7) and shepherds (1 Peter 5:1–2).

The timing. And consider the timing, which is the astonishing part. These churches were a few months old at most. Some had been founded, opposed and abandoned inside a fortnight. Every member was a convert of that same year: men and women who had been idolaters or synagogue attenders in the spring and were now being set apart to lead a congregation. There was no training college, no probationary decade, no New Testament to study, and in Lystra the whole church had recently watched its founder stoned. Paul did not conclude from any of this that it was too soon. He concluded that a church without elders was a church he could not leave, and so he raised leaders out of the material actually in front of him. The alternative, keeping the churches dependent on himself until somebody sufficiently impressive turned up, would have felt far safer and would have been fatal.

Was this simply what these two men happened to do, or a mandate? That they appointed elders in every church shows it was fixed practice, and the rest of the New Testament confirms it: Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5), a church without them being not yet in order. Every church we meet has them: Ephesus (Acts 20:17), Peter’s readers (1 Peter 5:1), James’s (James 5:14), Philippi’s overseers and deacons (Philippians 1:1). Two things. First, three words name the same office from different angles: elder (presbyteros, maturity), overseer or bishop (episkopos, oversight), and pastor or shepherd (poimēn, care), all used of the same men (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Peter 5:1–2). Second, it is always elders, plural: a team, not a lone ruler. Shared leadership is the apostolic norm.

Where Christians differ: church government. Episcopal churches have bishops over many churches; Presbyterians, elders gathered in courts; Congregationalists and Baptists, congregations governed by their own members and elders. Verdict: the New Testament pattern is a plurality of qualified elders in each local church, recognised with the congregation’s involvement, with deacons serving alongside (1 Timothy 3). Elder and bishop (overseer) are the same office in the New Testament. Christ alone is head of the church.

What authority does that give them, and what does it not? Elders have real, God-given authority: to lead or rule (1 Timothy 5:17), to teach and guard sound doctrine (Titus 1:9), to shepherd and watch over souls (Acts 20:28); and the flock is to obey your leaders and submit to them (Hebrews 13:17). But it is strictly bounded. It is derived: they are under-shepherds serving the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4), tending the church of God, not their own (Acts 20:28). It is Word-bound: they minister Scripture’s authority, so they may not bind consciences with rules God has not given (the error of Colossians 2); they declare God’s Word, they do not legislate. And it is not the right to dominate: not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3); they lead as servants, not lords (Mark 10:42–45), and will give an account to God (Hebrews 13:17). Real authority, but servant-authority: Christ-derived, Scripture-limited, accountable, never tyrannical. The elders are no little popes.

So how should churches choose elders today? Here the apostles appointed elders as they founded churches, with prayer and fasting; in Acts 6 the congregation chose and the apostles appointed. The more likely pattern for churches now is that the congregation recognises men who meet the qualifications Paul lays down (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9), and that existing elders confirm and set them apart. And notice that every church had elders, plural.

And what qualifies a man for it? The two lists (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) stress character, not talent. The umbrella is above reproach: a life giving no just handle for accusation. Under it: faithful in marriage (a one-woman man), self-controlled, sober-minded, gentle and not violent, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, hospitable, upright, holy, not a recent convert (mature, lest he be puffed up). He must manage his own household well, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? (1 Timothy 3:5), and be well thought of by outsiders. Only one item is an ability, not a trait: he must be able to teach, holding firm to sound doctrine to give instruction and also to rebuke those who contradict it (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:9), the chief thing distinguishing an elder from a deacon. The lesson humbles: an elder is not the most gifted or successful man in the room, but a man of proven Christlike character who knows and can teach the truth; nearly everything on the list is simply the mature Christian life, on display in one fit to model it.

Then why does Paul say an elder must not be a recent convert, when these men were all new? Because circumstances differed. In a brand-new church there was no one else, and the apostles, with apostolic discernment, chose the most mature men available and kept up close contact through return visits and letters. Some may have been Jews or God-fearers who had known the Scriptures for years. Later, in established churches like Ephesus, where mature men were available, Paul could and did insist on it (1 Timothy 3:6). The principle is the same in both: appoint the most mature, tested men God has given, and do not leave a church without shepherds.

With prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. The word behind committed is the one used of depositing something valuable with somebody else for safekeeping. It is the word Jesus used from the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Paul and Barnabas are handing over something that was never theirs to keep, to the only one who can keep it, and they do it fasting, going without food while they pray, which is what serious men did before a step that could not be taken back. They left them in the Lord’s hands. Missionaries must trust Christ with the churches they plant. The Lord, not Paul, would keep them.

And then they walked away. That is the part worth sitting with. They left congregations of new believers, in hostile towns, under brand-new elders, with no means of finding out for months how any of it was going. What made that bearable is in the last clause: the Lord in whom they had believed. Not the elders they had appointed, good men though those may have been. The churches were left with the Lord, because the churches had always been his.

Resignation or entrusting. Anyone who has had to hand something over, a work, a congregation, a child, a parent, knows the difference between resignation and entrusting. Resignation lets go because it has run out of options. Entrusting lets go into hands it can name. The test is simple enough to run: when you think about the thing you cannot control, are you bracing for the worst, or have you actually put it somewhere?

In a sentence. They appointed elders for them in every church, and with prayer and fasting entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders. And commit those you care for to the Lord; he will keep them better than you can. Name the person or thing you are most anxious about, and in prayer today hand it over, in words, into the hands of the Lord in whom you believe. If you are a man in the church, read the lists in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 as a description of the man God wants you to become, whether or not you ever serve as an elder.

For worship. The Chief Shepherd does not leave his flock unattended. He gives under-shepherds to feed them, and above every under-shepherd he keeps watch himself, for he bought the church with his own blood. What Paul could not hold, Christ holds; what Paul could not guard, Christ guards; and he who committed his own spirit into his Father’s hands receives every church and every soul committed into his.
verseByVerse.note: Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,

And when they had spoken the word in Perga. Two sentences of itinerary, and one of them is a quiet piece of repair. Perga is where the journey went wrong. It is the town they landed at on the way out, and it is where John Mark left them and went home (13:13). Luke records at the time that they simply went on from Perga: no preaching mentioned, nothing planted there. They had passed straight through it and up into the mountains, a man short. Now, coming back the other way, they stop and preach. The place that had been nothing but the scene of a disappointment gets the gospel on the return leg.

The second pass. Luke makes no comment, and it would be easy to make too much of it. But it is worth noticing how much of God’s work is done on the second pass. The road travelled in discouragement is travelled again, and this time something is planted in it. Very little in the Christian life is gone through only once, and the place where you failed, or were failed, is very often the place you are brought back to with something to give.

They went down to Attalia. Attalia was the port on the south coast, modern Antalya, the working harbour a few miles west of Perga, where they wait for a ship going east. The rest is unglamorous, and it is the actual substance of the mission. Pisidia and Pamphylia are the mountain country and the coastal plain: the same Taurus crossing as before, in reverse, and the same fever-ridden lowland at the bottom of it.

Most of a life given to God. Reckon up what Luke has covered in two chapters: well over a thousand miles of walking and sailing, the best part of two years, a string of cities evangelised, one man stoned. Almost none of it is scenes. Most of a life given to God looks like verses 24 and 25: getting to the next place, speaking there, and going on. If you have ever felt that your own discipleship is short of moments and long on plodding, this is what the plodding looks like in Scripture when it is written down by somebody who was there.

My Christian life feels ordinary and repetitive. Is that a problem? Not in itself. Most faithfulness is ordinary: daily prayer, steady work, the same church on Sundays, the same family needs, kindness repeated. God values it and writes it down, as he did these two verses. The danger is not routine but drift, going through motions with a cold heart. So keep the routine and warm it: ask God each morning for one person to serve and one word to speak. Plodding with Christ is still walking with Christ.

In a sentence. They went through Pisidia to Pamphylia, preached the word in Perga, and went down to Attalia.

On a Tuesday. Think of a place or relationship associated in your mind with failure or disappointment. Ask whether God may be bringing you back to it with something to give. And treat today’s ordinary stops, the office, the shop, the school gate, as places to speak a word when the door opens.

For worship. Every stop is an opportunity for the word. Don’t waste yours. The Lord of the second pass brings his people back over old ground and makes it fruitful. Nothing is wasted with him: not the plodding miles, not the place of failure, not the long unrecorded days. The Good Shepherd walked dusty roads too, and he knows the way of every servant who walks them now.
verseByVerse.note: Attalia was the port on the south coast.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.

And from there they sailed to Antioch. Home to Syrian Antioch, about two years after setting out. And Luke identifies home not by its geography but by what had happened there at the start: this is the place where they had been commended to the grace of God.

Where they had been commended to the grace of God. Turn back to that scene for a moment. A congregation fasted and prayed and laid hands on its two best men and let them go (13:1–3), and having done that, there was nothing else it could do. They could not send messages. They had no way of knowing whether the two were alive. Every event in these two chapters, the blinded magician, the expulsion from Antioch, the crowd with the oxen, the stoning, reached the sending church for the first time in the next verse, long after it was all over. So what had that church actually done when it commended these men to the grace of God? It had put two people somewhere it could not follow them, and left them there, and gone on praying. That is what the phrase means when it is not a formula. It is what a parent does at a door. It is what a congregation does at an airport. It is what any of us does with somebody we love and cannot help, and this verse is here to say that it is not a gesture. The ship came in, and both men were on it.

For the work that they had fulfilled. Then the last phrase, which is a small masterpiece of accounting. Not attempted. Not begun. Not made a good start on. They went out committed to God’s grace, and came back having fulfilled the work. The commission of 13:2, the work to which I have called them, is closed out here with the same word, completed. Between those two sentences lie a hundred miles of mountain road, a stoning, and churches in city after city. Grace sent them, kept them, and finished the work through them.

Work defined by the one who gave it. Very few of us ever get a sentence like that written about anything we have done. But notice what made it possible, because it is available. The work was defined by the one who gave it, not by the men doing it. They had not set out to evangelise the world, or to reach a figure, or to keep going until they felt it was enough, which is a race with no finishing line and is how a great many earnest Christians exhaust themselves. They had been sent for a work. When it was done, they came home.

How do I know when a piece of work for God is finished? Ask what you were actually given to do, rather than everything that could be done. A teacher for a term, a carer for a season, a role in a church for a few years: when the task God assigned is done, it is right to lay it down with thanks, even if needs remain. Seek counsel from others who know you, pray, and look at whether the door is closing. Finishing well is not doing everything; it is doing the given thing, and then handing over without guilt.

In a sentence. From there they sailed back to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to God’s grace for the work they had now completed.

On a Tuesday. If someone you love is out of your reach, a child abroad, a friend in hospital, a missionary, commend them to the grace of God by name today, and believe that it is not a gesture. And look at your own commitments: is there a work you are carrying that God gave you, or only one you took on? Ask him which.

For worship. What God’s grace begins, it completes (Philippians 1:6). Grace sent them out and grace brought them home, and in between grace did the work. The Son stood before his Father at the end of his course and said, I have accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4); and because his work was finished, every work of grace in his people will be finished too.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.

And when they arrived and gathered the church together. They reported to the sending church. Missionaries are accountable to the church that sends them.

They declared all that God had done with them. The report is given standing in front of the congregation that sent them, and its grammar is the whole point. Not what they had done for God. Not even what they had achieved with his help. God is the subject of the sentence and the two of them are the instrument he used. Luke has bracketed the entire journey with the same claim: commended to the grace of God at one end, all that God had done at the other. That is not modesty, and it is not a pious way of talking. It is accuracy, and it is also the only kind of report a sending church can safely be given. A congregation that hears what its missionaries have accomplished will begin, quietly, to assess them, and the next report will have to be better than this one. A congregation that hears what God has done will begin to pray. It is the right way to give a missionary report.

And how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. The image stayed with Paul for the rest of his life: a wide door for effective work at Ephesus, with many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9); a door opened for him at Troas (2 Corinthians 2:12); a request from prison that God would open to us a door for the word (Colossians 4:3). Notice who opens it. Not the missionaries. They had walked through a door; they had not made one, and they are careful to say so in the same breath as the report of their own two years’ work. And notice what kind of door it is: not a door of opportunity or of success, but a door of faith. What God had made possible was that Gentiles could come in on the same terms as anyone else, by believing, through faith alone, without first becoming something they were not.

A door that would soon be challenged. Which is precisely the sentence about to cause the worst crisis in the church’s history. Every word of that report was true and welcome in Antioch, and within a short time men would come down from Judea to say that the door had been opened too wide, and that these Gentiles must be circumcised (15:1). Luke sets the two chapters side by side without a joint. The report of an opened door is followed immediately by an attempt to narrow it, and that is a pattern worth expecting rather than being wounded by: the clearest work of God tends to be followed, quite soon, by an argument about it inside the church.

And they remained no little time with the disciples. Luke’s understatement: a good long while. Rest and fellowship. After two years on the road, four mainland churches and a stoning, the record of the greatest missionary journey yet undertaken ends with two tired men staying put for months with their own congregation. There is a permission in that for anyone who has come to believe that faithfulness means never stopping. The Spirit who said set apart for me Barnabas and Saul is the same Spirit under whose hand they now sit still in Antioch and do nothing remarkable. Rest, in this book, is not a lapse in obedience. It is part of the shape of it.

How can my church support missionaries when they come home? Do what Antioch did: gather to hear them, and listen for what God has done, not only for statistics. Give them time and real rest, not just a slot in a service. Ask about their struggles as well as their successes, and pray with them. Help with practical needs: housing, transport, medical care, the children’s schooling. Returning missionaries are often exhausted and out of step with home. A church that welcomes them well is sharing in the work as truly as when it sent them.

In a sentence. When they arrived, they gathered the church and reported all that God had done through them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles, and they stayed there a long time with the disciples.

On a Tuesday. When you tell of God’s work, give him the credit: what God has done. The next time you speak of something good in your life or your church, make God the subject of the sentence. And if you are weary, take the rest he gives without guilt: Antioch is as much a part of the journey as Lystra.

For worship. The door of faith was opened by God, and no one can shut it. Through it have come Gentiles from every nation, the people of Lystra and Iconium and, at length, us. Christ himself is the door; by him if anyone enters he will be saved. He opened it with his own pierced hands, and he holds it open still, until the last of his sheep has come in.

parallels.desc: a wide door for effective work

14.theology: Suffering as the Path of the Kingdom. Acts 14:22 is the New Testament’s clearest statement that suffering is the appointed means by which the people of God enter the kingdom. This is not peripheral; it is structural. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way. And the church that follows a crucified Lord is called to the same road. Paul writes later that he fills up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24) — not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, but that the suffering of Christ is reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes forth into the world. The church that suffers for the name is the church that looks most like its Lord. And it is the church that the watching world cannot ultimately explain away.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra, rising and walking back into the city, going on to Derbe the next morning. Returning through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch — the cities that had tried to kill him — to strengthen the believers he left behind. Appointing elders, committing them to God with prayer and fasting, and sailing home to report everything God had done. This is what faithful looks like.

Now: The Western church has largely lost the theology of suffering. We expect the Christian life to be comfortable, and when it is not, we assume something has gone wrong. Acts 14 says the opposite: tribulation is the appointed road, and the God who walked it first walks it with his people. The suffering church is not the failing church; it is often the most faithful church — and, in God’s strange economy, the most fruitful.

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>3</sup>So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. <sup>4</sup>When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? <sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>21</sup>For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, <sup>23</sup>with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. <sup>24</sup>Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, <sup>25</sup>it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <sup>26</sup>men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>27</sup>We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: <sup>29</sup>that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well.
