Farewell.” <sup>30</sup>So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. <sup>31</sup>And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. <sup>32</sup>And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. <sup>33</sup>And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. <sup>35</sup>But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
The success of the Gentile mission raises the most important question the early church faced. Some Jewish believers from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile converts cannot be saved unless they are circumcised and keep the law of Moses: in effect, Gentiles must become Jews to become Christians. This was not an odd idea. Circumcision was the covenant sign God gave Abraham, and for centuries any Gentile who wanted to join God’s people had done exactly that. Paul and Barnabas dispute it fiercely, and the church sends them to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders.

At the council, believers from the Pharisee party insist on circumcision. Peter reminds everyone how God gave the Spirit to Cornelius’s household, cleansing their hearts by faith, and asks why they would put on Gentiles a yoke that neither they nor their ancestors could bear, since Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. Paul and Barnabas tell of the signs God did among the Gentiles. Then James, the Lord’s brother and leader of the Jerusalem church, shows from the prophet Amos that God always planned to gather Gentiles to rebuild David’s fallen house, and proposes that Gentile believers should not be burdened with the law, but asked to avoid food offered to idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals and blood, practices especially offensive to Jews, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share fellowship. A letter is sent with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices. The chapter ends with a painful disagreement: Paul and Barnabas part company over whether to take John Mark on a second journey, so Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus and Paul sets out with Silas.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teachers from Judea tell the Gentile believers in Antioch that they cannot be saved without circumcision and the law of Moses. Paul and Barnabas oppose them, and the church sends them to Jerusalem. There believers from the Pharisee party press the same demand. After long debate Peter reminds the council that God gave the Spirit to Gentiles who believed, making no distinction and cleansing their hearts by faith, and that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by a yoke no one could carry. Paul and Barnabas describe God’s signs among the Gentiles. James then shows from Amos that God planned to gather Gentiles into the restored house of David, and proposes that they be asked only to avoid idol food, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. The apostles, elders and whole church agree, and send a letter with Judas and Silas declaring that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay no greater burden on the Gentiles. The church in Antioch rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith Alone — the Council's Theological Verdict

Peter's speech in vv. 8–11 is the clearest statement of justification by faith alone in the book of Acts: 'God made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith... we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.' The Gentiles are saved the same way the Jews are — by grace through faith, not by law observance. This is the verdict that Paul will develop in Galatians and Romans. The Jerusalem Council is the communal confirmation of what the Spirit had demonstrated in Cornelius's house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem Council produced a letter of pastoral decision rather than a theological treatise — practical guidance that allowed Jew and Gentile to live together in one community. Now: The church continues to face questions about what is required for full membership in the people of God. The council's method — testimony, Scripture, deliberation, pastoral wisdom — remains the model for ecclesial discernment on divisive questions.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.

Meaning first. Acts 15 is the centre of the book, and one of the most important chapters in the history of the church. The question is: must Gentiles become Jews to be saved? Must they be circumcised and keep the law of Moses? The Jerusalem council answers: no. We are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, Jew and Gentile alike, by faith. Gentile believers are asked only to avoid certain practices that would offend Jewish believers and make fellowship impossible. The gospel of grace is preserved, and the church stays one. Paul’s letter to the Galatians fights the same battle. Over the whole chapter stands the God who knows the heart, who cleanses it by faith, who planned from of old to take a people for his name from every nation, and who will not let anyone add a single step to the work of his Son.

But some men came down from Judea. Probably those mentioned in Galatians 2:12, claiming to come from James, though they had no instructions from him (v. 24).

Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved. Weigh that sentence, because almost everything in it is right. It assumes Jesus is the Messiah. It assumes he died and rose. It assumes these Gentiles must be saved and wants them saved. It is not the sentence of an unbeliever, and the men saying it were not pretending. What it does is add one condition, and that is all it takes. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17); the question was whether Gentile believers must receive it, and with it keep the whole law (Galatians 5:3). Notice what is at stake: you cannot be saved. Not a matter of custom, but of salvation. Christ plus circumcision. Paul called it a different gospel (Galatians 1:6–9).

The most dangerous sentence. This is worth grasping, because Christians tend to picture false teaching as a denial. It very rarely is. Heresy that matters is almost always an addition, made by sincere people, to a set of true statements. The most dangerous sentence in the New Testament is not one that contradicts the gospel. It is one that agrees with it and then says and.

Why does one word matter so much? Because of what it does to the whole. Suppose salvation is ninety-nine parts God’s grace and one part your compliance. That one part is now the part everything hangs on, the joint that can fail, and your standing before God rests, in the end, on you. Paul saw this instantly and wrote to these very churches in the most violent language he ever used: if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you; you are severed from Christ (Galatians 5:2–4). Not damaged. Severed. A gift with a condition attached is not a gift, and a rescue you have to help with is not a rescue.

No small dissension and debate. Luke is being dry; he means a furious row. Understatement. Paul would not give in for a moment (Galatians 2:5). And notice that Paul had it. There is an instinct in Christians, and it is usually a good one, that peace is the higher value and a man who argues has failed. This verse says otherwise. On the gospel itself, refusing to fight is not gentleness; it is desertion.

Aimed precisely. But watch how precisely Paul aims. In the very next chapter he will take a young man with a Greek father and circumcise him himself (16:3), and to the Galatians he says he would not let Titus be circumcised, nor yield for a moment (Galatians 2:3–5). Same rite, same apostle, opposite decisions, because in one case it was a free choice made for the sake of the mission, and in the other it was being demanded as a condition of salvation. That distinction is the whole of Christian wisdom about secondary things: what you may cheerfully do for love, you must refuse absolutely the moment somebody makes it necessary.

Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. The verb is passive; the church did the appointing. The church seeks unity through consultation, not separation. And there is something striking in Paul submitting to it. This is the man who insists his gospel came to him from no human being (Galatians 1:11–12), and he does not need Jerusalem’s permission to preach. He goes anyway, because being right on your own is not the same as the church being settled, and the unity of the whole was worth a journey of some three hundred miles on foot.

What does Jesus plus look like today? Rarely circumcision. It is any requirement added to faith in Christ as the ground of acceptance with God: you must be baptised in our church, speak in tongues, keep the Saturday Sabbath, perform certain rituals, reach a certain level of holiness, or belong to the right group, before God will really accept you. Many of these things may be good, or debatable, in their place. But the moment they are made conditions of salvation, the gospel is changed. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ’s finished work sufficient, received by faith alone, or does it add a step?

In a sentence. Some men came from Judea teaching that unless Gentiles were circumcised according to Moses’ custom they could not be saved, and after fierce debate with them, Paul, Barnabas and others were appointed to go to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.

On a Tuesday. Watch for Jesus plus teaching: Jesus plus rules, rituals, or works. It is another gospel. And here is the question to put to yourself before reading on. Almost every Christian has an unspoken and. Something added, privately, to faith in Christ, a habit, a level of feeling, an achievement, a version of the past put right, without which you do not quite believe God has accepted you. Name it. That is your circumcision, and this chapter was written about it.

For worship. Christ did not do ninety-nine parts of our salvation and leave the last to us. He cried, It is finished, and it was. The Father accepted his sacrifice, raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand, and nothing can be added to a work that God himself has declared complete. Blessed be the Lord who saves sinners entirely, and lets no one, Pharisee or apostle or our own anxious hearts, add a condition to his grace.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the question was whether Gentiles must become Jews to be saved. This meeting in Jerusalem, about AD 49, is often called the Jerusalem Council.

parallels.desc: Paul’s account of a Jerusalem meeting

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them.

Being sent on their way by the church. The New Testament’s phrase for helping travellers on with what they need (compare 3 John 6). With the church’s support. They are not slipping off to defend themselves; they are going as the congregation’s representatives, with the congregation behind them.

They passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles. And look at what they did on the road. They are travelling to a hearing about whether the Gentiles they have converted are really saved, and they spend the journey describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles. Not marshalling arguments. Telling the story, at length, in every church they passed. Men on the way to a tribunal turned the trip into a preaching tour.

And brought great joy to all the brothers. And it landed. Notice who those brothers were. Churches founded by the scattered believers (8:4; 11:19). Samaria is where Philip preached and where Peter and John had to come down and see for themselves (8:14). Phoenicia is where the refugees of the persecution had fled (11:19), on the road to Antioch, where Greeks first heard the gospel (11:20). These were the congregations who had themselves been outside the circle most recently, and they are the ones who receive the news with unmixed gladness. The Samaritans, once outsiders themselves, rejoice at Gentiles coming in. People who have just been let in are rarely the ones who want the door narrowed.

When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed. Warmly. And Luke is careful: they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders. The mother church received them warmly. Whatever the men of verse 1 were, they were not Jerusalem’s voice, and the letter will say so in writing (v. 24). The problem is a faction, not an institution, which is worth remembering before writing off a whole church because of who turned up from it.

And they declared all that God had done with them. The same sentence Luke used of the report at Antioch (14:27), and it means the same thing there and here: God is the subject; they are the instrument.

Is this the visit of Galatians 2? One question hovers over this visit and is worth settling honestly, because a reader with a study Bible will meet it. Is this the visit Paul describes in Galatians 2, where he went up to Jerusalem, laid his gospel before the pillars, and they added nothing to it? Many think so: the cast is much the same (Paul, Barnabas, Peter, James), the issue is identical, and so is the outcome. Others place Galatians 2 at the earlier famine visit (11:30), chiefly because Paul is listing his Jerusalem visits precisely in order to prove his independence, and it would be odd for him to skip one, which would also mean Galatians was written before this council rather than after it. The honest position is that it is not certain, and that very little rests on it. On either reading the two accounts say the same decisive thing: Paul submitted his gospel to the Jerusalem leadership, and they added nothing to it. (The one place the two men later clashed in person, Peter withdrawing from the Gentile table at Antioch, Galatians 2:11–14, is dealt with at 11:2–3 and does not need going over again.)

Why should news of conversions bring such joy? Because heaven rejoices over it first. Jesus said there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10). A conversion is a dead person brought to life, an enemy made a child, a captive set free. If we hear such news coolly, it may be a sign that we have forgotten what it meant for us. The churches of Phoenicia and Samaria rejoiced because they remembered. Joy at others’ salvation is one of the surest marks of a heart that has tasted grace.

In a sentence. Sent on their way by the church, they travelled through Phoenicia and Samaria telling about the conversion of the Gentiles, bringing great joy to all the believers, and in Jerusalem they were welcomed by the church, apostles and elders, and reported everything God had done through them.

On a Tuesday. When you are heading into a difficult meeting or conversation about church matters, spend the journey remembering and telling what God has done, not rehearsing your arguments. And the next time you hear of someone coming to faith, stop and thank God aloud, then tell someone else.

For worship. News of conversions should bring joy. Share it. The God who saves is the God who delights in saving. The Shepherd carries the lost sheep home on his shoulders rejoicing, and calls his friends together to rejoice with him. Every report of grace on the road from Antioch to Jerusalem was a small echo of the gladness of heaven over sinners brought home.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.”

But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up. Read that description twice, because Luke has put two words together that most of us keep well apart. Believers. And Pharisees. Genuine Christians, who still held a Pharisee’s view of the law. These are not opponents of the church who have infiltrated it. They are converted men, inside it, who love the God of Israel and have now come to trust his Messiah, and they are the crisis.

Feel the case from where they stood. Try to feel the case from where they were standing, because contempt for them will stop you learning anything. These were men raised to believe that the boundary of God’s people was marked in the flesh, by God’s own command to Abraham, four hundred years before Moses and never once withdrawn. They had kept the law at genuine cost. Some of them had probably been beaten for it. And they are now being asked to receive as full members of the covenant people men who were sacrificing to idols eighteen months ago and who still, as far as anyone can tell, eat whatever is put in front of them. Their objection is not malice. It is a lifetime of conviction meeting a new fact.

The man who had been one of them. And the man who will argue hardest against them had been one of them. Paul was a Pharisee, son of a Pharisee, and said so years later (23:6; Philippians 3:5). He is not refuting a position he finds strange. He is refuting the one he used to hold, which is why he does it so exactly and with so little patience. He had learned better.

It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses. Necessary (dei) is the word Luke uses through his Gospel and this book for divine obligation, the must that stood over the cross. They are not saying it would be wiser or safer or more consistent. They are saying God requires it. Their view: Gentiles must become Jews to belong to God’s people. The whole law, not only circumcision. Nothing smaller would have needed a council.

Where it lives now. So where does this live now? Not in circumcision; nobody is arguing about that. It lives wherever the church quietly attaches to salvation a mark that Christ did not attach. A particular translation. A conversion story of the right shape, with a date. A style of worship, a position on secondary doctrine, a political allegiance, a manner of speaking, a family arrangement. None of these need be stated as a condition; they only have to function as one.

A test, and a guard. Here is a test you can run this week, and it is uncomfortable. Think of the marker you privately treat as necessary. Now picture meeting, in heaven, somebody who trusted Christ and got that thing wrong all his life. If you find in yourself a hesitation, a small unwillingness, a sense that surely there would have to be some qualification, you have found your circumcision, and this chapter is about you and not about first-century Judea. And a guard, because the opposite error is just as available: this does not mean nothing matters. The council itself is about to lay down four things (v. 29) and Paul will spend his letters on how Christians ought to live. The entire chapter turns on keeping two questions apart: what is required in order to be saved, and what is required in order to live together. Collapse them in either direction and you get a false gospel or a lawless church.

Can a real Christian hold a seriously wrong view? Yes, as these men show. Being born again does not make anyone instantly correct on everything, and believers can hold errors, sometimes serious ones, out of old habits of thought. That is why the church needs teaching, patience and correction. But an error about the way of salvation is not a small matter: if it hardens into a settled rejection of grace, it becomes another gospel. So treat brothers in error as brothers, reason with them from Scripture, and do not give way on the gospel itself.

In a sentence. But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and said that Gentiles must be circumcised and ordered to keep the law of Moses.

On a Tuesday. True believers can hold wrong views. Correct them with Scripture, patiently. And before you correct anyone, run the test above on yourself.

For worship. The Lord is patient with his people’s errors. He bore with Pharisees who believed, as he had borne with disciples who argued about who was greatest, and he led them into the truth. Christ alone marks out his people, not by a knife but by his Spirit, and he will finish teaching every one of his own until they see that grace is all.

parallels.desc: as to the law, a Pharisee

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe.

The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. The first church council. The whole church was involved (vv. 12, 22).

And after there had been much debate. Open, honest discussion. Not a decree from above. Sit with that for a moment, because it is not how most Christians imagine the early church working. The first council in the history of the faith, on the most important question it would ever face, with apostles in the room, and it was a long argument. No voice from heaven. No prophecy settling it at the outset. Men talked, and disagreed, and went on talking.

Guidance through debate. And this same meeting produced the sentence it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us (v. 28). So the Spirit’s verdict came at the end of a hard debate rather than instead of one. That is worth having if you have been taught to expect God’s guidance to arrive as a feeling, or to treat the need for argument as evidence that something has gone wrong. Here is the apostolic pattern, in order: evidence of what God has actually done, tested against Scripture, argued out in the open, decided together, and then owned. Nobody in this room had a dream.

Peter stood up. And this is the last we hear from him. His last appearance in Acts. The man who preached at Pentecost, who opened the door to Cornelius, who has carried the first half of this book, speaks once more and then leaves the narrative altogether; his exit was noted at 12:17. He goes out not with a miracle but with an argument for somebody else’s freedom.

God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. In the early days: Peter is putting a date on it. Cornelius was perhaps ten years earlier (chapter 10), and the whole Jerusalem church had heard the report and given its verdict at the time: then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life (11:18). They had already settled this. And here they are, a decade on, arguing about it again. God himself chose to bring Gentiles in through Peter. Hearing and believing: that is how Gentiles came in. Nothing was said about circumcision.

Agreement that never reached the heart. Which is not a first-century failing. A church can formally agree something, mean it, and then discover ten years later that the agreement never reached the place where convictions actually live. What is being resisted at this council is not new information. It is the cost of what they already believed.

By my mouth. And notice the grammar of Peter’s claim, made in a room where his own authority is one of the pressures. God chose; Peter’s mouth was the instrument. He has the strongest personal precedent in the room and he takes no personal credit for it, which is precisely why the precedent carries.

Is it wrong for Christians to argue? Not if it is the right kind of argument about the right kind of thing. The apostles debated at length, openly, and the church was the better for it. What Scripture forbids is quarrelsomeness, harshness, pride, and fighting over trivia (2 Timothy 2:23–25; Titus 3:9). Healthy debate keeps to the question, listens to the evidence, goes to Scripture, assumes good faith, and aims at agreement in the truth rather than victory. If you find you enjoy winning more than finding the truth, step back.

In a sentence. The apostles and elders met to consider the matter, and after much debate Peter stood up and reminded them that early on God chose him so that the Gentiles would hear the gospel from him and believe.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you agreed with in principle years ago, about grace, about forgiving someone, about welcoming people unlike you, that has never yet reached your actual behaviour? Name it, and take one step toward living what you already believe.

For worship. The gospel is heard and believed. That is how anyone enters God’s family. The God who chose Peter’s mouth to carry the word to Cornelius chose some mouth to carry it to you, and behind every human messenger is the sovereign choice of the Father to call his people by the gospel of his Son. Hearing and believing are his gifts, and the glory is his alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith.

And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them. The word is kardiognōstēs, heart-knower, and it is rare enough to be worth tracing. It occurs twice in the whole New Testament, and both times in Acts. Here, and at 1:24, when the eleven had to choose between two men and prayed: you, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen. Both times the church has to make a decision about who is in. Both times it reaches for the same name for God, and the reason is the same: men can see the outside of a person and God can see the rest. In a debate about whether a mark in the flesh is required, Peter names God by the attribute that makes the flesh irrelevant.

By giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us. And then the evidence, which is not an argument but a fact. He saw their faith and gave them the Spirit, the proof that he had accepted them, before any circumcision. Not a lesser measure, not a provisional instalment pending regularisation. The same. Peter is saying, in effect: you may debate whether these people qualify, but God has already moved in, and he did it without waiting for our decision.

And he made no distinction between us and them. No first and second class. The verb is the one the Spirit used to Peter on the roof and the one the circumcision party turned against him afterwards; the wordplay is set out at 11:2 and needs no repeating. What matters here is the tense. God made no distinction. It is done. The question before the council is not whether to admit the Gentiles but whether to reimpose a distinction God has already removed.

Having cleansed their hearts by faith. Then the clause that wins the argument. Peter chooses that verb deliberately. It is the word from the sheet let down from heaven: what God has made clean, do not call common (10:15). He is quoting his own vision back to the council without saying so. Not by circumcision, not by washings, not by the law, but by faith. The heart is the place that needs cleansing, and faith is the means (Hebrews 9:14). Outward rituals cannot cleanse the heart.

The heart was always the problem. But look where the cleansing happened. Not the body: the heart. And that is exactly the organ the Old Testament always said was the problem. Moses told Israel: circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart (Deuteronomy 10:16). He promised that one day God himself would do it: the LORD your God will circumcise your heart, so that you will love the LORD your God (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah said the whole nation was uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:26). Ezekiel had God promising: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). So here is what Peter has actually said. The party of the Pharisees is asking for the sign. God has already given the thing the sign pointed at. They want the knife on the body of men whose hearts have been cut by God himself.

By faith. And the last words carry it. Not by ritual, not by descent, not by effort, not by a probationary period of good behaviour. The instrument by which a heart is made clean is empty-handed trust, which is why it is available to a Roman centurion, and why it is available to you tonight, and why no committee anywhere has ever been able to add a step to it.

How does faith cleanse the heart? Not by its own power, as if believing were a kind of moral detergent. Faith cleanses because it joins us to Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and because through faith we receive the Spirit, who makes the heart new. Faith is the empty hand; Christ is what fills it. So the cleansing is both a once-for-all washing of guilt, when we first believe, and a continuing purification, as the Spirit works holiness in a heart that keeps trusting. If you feel your heart is still far from clean, keep looking to Christ. The cleansing is his work, and he does not leave it half done.

In a sentence. Peter said God, who knows the heart, showed he accepted the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Spirit as he did the apostles, making no distinction between them, for he cleansed their hearts by faith.

On a Tuesday. Your heart is cleansed by faith in Christ, not by religious performance. When you are tempted to measure your standing with God by your recent religious activity, stop, and take your eyes back to Christ. And look at the Christian you find hardest to accept: if God has given him the Spirit, what right have you to make a distinction?

For worship. God knows the heart, and he does not stop at knowing it. He cuts it, cleanses it and makes it new, as he promised through Moses and the prophets. The Holy Spirit who fell on Cornelius is the Spirit who comes to every believer, the same gift in the same measure, because the same Christ has died for all his people. No one is a second-class member of a family where the Father has made no distinction.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.

Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test? That is a serious charge and Peter aims it at the most orthodox men in the room. The phrase belongs to the wilderness: it is what Israel did at Massah, and what God’s own summary of those forty years accuses them of (the wilderness generation is treated at 13:18). Peter tells the party of the Pharisees that they are repeating it. How? Because to put God to the test is to demand that he do it your way after he has shown you his. To demand more than God has demanded is to challenge him, to question his decision. God has already acted: he gave the Spirit, he cleansed the hearts, he made no distinction. To require circumcision now is to inform God that his method was insufficient, and to do it while calling yourself a defender of his law.

By placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? Then the image. A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the law as a yoke to be taken up. Consider who is speaking and where. Peter is an observant Jew, standing in Jerusalem, in front of Pharisees, and he says: none of us has ever managed it. Not our fathers. Not us. Not me. He does not say the law is bad; he says it is a weight no one in the history of his nation has carried, and that the honest record of Israel is a thousand years of proving it. No one kept the law perfectly (Galatians 3:10; James 2:10). The generation that received it broke it before Moses got down the mountain; the nation that was given the land was deported out of it for the same reason.

The inside. And every serious person knows the feeling from the inside, whatever his religion. You can manage the outside. You cannot manage the inside, and the law asked for the inside, which is what makes it unbearable. A rule about murder can be kept. A rule about what you want cannot. So Peter’s argument runs: you are proposing to lay on these Gentiles a burden that has crushed every one of us who has ever tried to carry it, and to do it in the name of kindness. To require the law for salvation is to put a crushing weight on believers. Jesus offers an easy yoke (Matthew 11:29–30).

But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will. And then the sentence that turns the whole council over, and it is easy to read past. The great conclusion. Read the order of it. Peter does not say that the Gentiles will be saved the way we are, by becoming Jews. He says that we Jews will be saved the way they are, by grace. The Gentiles have become the standard, and the Jewish believer is measured against them. Grace alone, through the Lord Jesus alone. The same way for everyone.

Nothing in the chapter is more startling. The people with the covenant, the patriarchs, the temple, the prophets, the law and the pedigree are told by the apostle to the circumcision that their salvation is the same bare grace as that of an uncircumcised Roman officer. Every advantage still exists (Paul will list them all in Romans 9 and call them real), and not one of them contributes anything at the point of being saved.

One low door. Which cuts in both directions, and the second is the comfort. If everything you have that makes you a better candidate counts for nothing here, then everything you have that makes you a worse candidate counts for nothing here either. The Christian of forty years and the convert of last Tuesday are saved by the identical mechanism, and neither has the smallest advantage over the other in it. There is one door, it is very low, and everybody goes through it on the same terms.

Then is God’s law useless for Christians? No. The law is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12). It cannot save, because no sinner can keep it, but it does three things still: it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ; it restrains evil in the world; and for the believer, its moral commands, summed up in love for God and neighbour, show the shape of the life the Spirit is producing in us (Westminster 19.6). What is gone is the law as a yoke to earn acceptance, and the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ. The Christian obeys not to be saved but because he has been.

Will I be saved through grace, or am I already saved? Both. Peter speaks here of the future, we will be saved, because salvation reaches its completion at the last day. But Scripture also says believers have already been saved (Ephesians 2:8) and are being saved (1 Corinthians 1:18). The point is that from first to last it is the same grace: the grace that forgave you when you first believed is the grace that will keep you and bring you safe to glory. You will never graduate from grace to something else.

In a sentence. Peter asked why they were testing God by putting on the disciples a yoke neither they nor their fathers could carry, for they believed they were saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as the Gentiles were.

On a Tuesday. If you are tired from carrying a yoke of trying to earn God’s favour, lay it down today. Say to God, in words: I will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, and nothing else. And look for one person whose background makes them feel like a worse candidate, and tell them about the low door.

For worship. We are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. All of us, the same way. Rest in grace. The yoke no one could bear was borne by one: the Son of God lived under the law, kept it perfectly from the inside out, and then bore its curse on the cross. Now he offers his own yoke, easy and light, to all who are weary. Jew and Gentile, the respectable and the ruined, stoop through the same low door into the same wide house, and the grace that brings them in is the grace that brings them home.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me.

And all the assembly fell silent. Five verses earlier there had been much debate. Now nobody speaks. Luke puts the two states of that room side by side and lets the silence do the work: the argument has run out of road, and the men who were shouting are listening. Peter’s words settled the debate.

They listened to Barnabas and Paul. And notice the order of the names. Since the proconsul’s house it has usually been Paul first. In Jerusalem the old order comes back, because in Jerusalem Barnabas is the trusted man: the Levite who sold his field for the church (4:36–37), the one man willing to vouch for Saul when everybody else was frightened of him (9:27), Jerusalem’s own emissary to Antioch (11:22). Luke’s word order is tracking the room, and it is the sort of detail a man makes up only if he was there.

As they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. What the two of them do is also worth noticing. They do not argue theology; Peter has done that. They report: facts, laid before the assembly as evidence. God had confirmed the Gentile mission with signs.

The council’s method. And that gives the council’s method, which is a model worth keeping. Testimony first: what has God actually done? Then Scripture: James is about to say the prophets agree with it (v. 15). Then judgment (v. 19). Experience is admitted as evidence and is never made the authority; Scripture decides, and had Amos not agreed, no quantity of signs would have settled the question. That order guards a church in both directions: against deciding doctrine from stories, and against being so afraid of stories that it cannot see what God is plainly doing in front of it.

James replied. Which James? Not the apostle; that James was executed with a sword at 12:2. Not the son of Alphaeus, of whom we know almost nothing. This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (12:17). A man known for strict law-keeping, respected by conservative Jewish believers. His judgment would carry weight with them.

The brother who did not believe. And the fact deserves a moment. He grew up in the same house. He watched his older brother at the carpenter’s bench and at family meals for the best part of thirty years, and he did not believe a word of it: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). When the family came to take Jesus away because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), James was presumably among them. Then Jesus was crucified, and then, Paul tells us in a bare line, he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). We are told nothing about that meeting. We only see the result: the brother who thought he was mad is now the leading man of the Jerusalem church, presiding over the decision that his brother is the Saviour of the world.

For the family you pray for. If you are praying for somebody in your own family who has heard it all and believes none of it, who knows the Christian at close quarters and is unimpressed, James is your verse. It took a resurrection. But it happened, and he was in the house the whole time.

Peter speaks, James rules. One more thing, stated plainly and without heat, because readers ask. Peter speaks here, and James rules. Whatever weight one gives Peter’s leadership elsewhere, in this room the summing-up belongs to the head of the local church, and the decision is taken by the apostles and elders with the whole church (v. 22). That is what the text shows. It is worth noticing, and it is not worth quarrelling over.

How should a church weigh experience in a disagreement? Listen to it carefully, and then test it by Scripture. Stories of what God is doing matter: they may show you that your theory was too small. But experiences can be misread, exaggerated or counterfeited, and feelings are not revelation. So ask: does Scripture teach this? Does it honour Christ and the gospel of grace? Do the fruit and the doctrine agree? The council heard the reports with respect, and then let the prophets decide.

In a sentence. The whole assembly fell silent and listened as Barnabas and Paul described the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them, and when they finished, James spoke up.

On a Tuesday. In disputes, listen to the evidence of what God is doing. Then let Scripture decide. And if there is a relative who knows you too well to be impressed by your faith, keep praying, keep living it, and remember James.

For worship. The risen Lord appeared to his unbelieving brother, and the scoffer at the family table became a pillar of the church. There is no one too close, too familiar or too sceptical for Christ to reach. He has his ways into every house, and when he has finished with a man, that man stands up in the assembly and speaks for the freedom of the gospel he once mocked.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.

Simeon has related. Three things in one sentence, and each is doing careful work. First, the name. Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter). James uses the old Jewish name (2 Peter 1:1), not Peter, not even the usual Greek Simon. In a room debating whether Gentiles must become Jews, James refers to the man who argued for Gentile freedom by his most Jewish name. He is not conceding an inch of the argument. He is signalling to the party he is about to rule against that the case did not come from an outsider. That is how a wise man wins a disagreement inside a family: he takes away every reason to dismiss the messenger before he takes away the argument.

How God first visited the Gentiles. Second, the verb. In Scripture that word is not neutral; it is what God does when he comes to rescue. He visited Sarah and she conceived (Genesis 21:1). He visited his people in their slavery and Israel bowed and worshipped (Exodus 4:31). Zechariah, holding his newborn son, sang: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68). It is the homecoming word, the word for God turning up on behalf of his own. James takes it and puts it on the nations.

To take from them a people for his name. Third, and most provocative of all. A people for his name is a phrase used of Israel (Deuteronomy 14:2). The Greek Old Testament keeps two words carefully apart: laos, the people, meaning Israel, and ethnē, the nations, meaning everybody else. James has just taken the word reserved for Israel and applied it to men taken out of the nations. In a single sentence he has called Gentiles a visited people who bear God’s name. It would have been difficult to say anything more inflammatory to the men of verse 5, and he says it gently, in their own vocabulary, from their own Scriptures.

From them. And note the small word that keeps it honest. Not all of them. God is taking a people out of the nations, which is remnant language, and it guards two errors at once: the idea that everyone is swept in regardless, and the idea that the church has simply replaced Israel. What is happening is what was always promised: out of every nation, a people, called by his name. The church is not a Gentile replacement for Israel, but God’s one people, from Jews and Gentiles, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16).

So are Gentile Christians now part of Israel? In this sense, yes: they are grafted into the one olive tree of God’s people (Romans 11:17–24), heirs of Abraham through faith (Galatians 3:7, 29), fellow citizens with the saints (Ephesians 2:19). There is one people of God, not two, gathered around one Messiah. That does not erase the difference between Jew and Gentile as peoples, or settle every question about Israel’s future; Christians read Romans 11 in more than one way. But no believer is a guest in someone else’s family. Every one who trusts Christ is a full member of God’s people.

In a sentence. James said Simeon had told how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name.

On a Tuesday. Before you correct someone in a disagreement, look for a way, like James, to honour the person you are about to disagree with. And remember that you bear God’s name: ask what in your conduct this week would honour it, and what would not.

For worship. God has taken a people for his name from every nation. You are one of them. Bear his name well. The God who visited Sarah in her barrenness and Israel in its slavery visited the nations in their darkness, and took from them a people of his own. He came down in Christ to redeem us, and he has written his name on us, and he will not lose one of those he has taken.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter).

verseByVerse.quote: "And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, ‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,

And with this the words of the prophets agree. Notice which way round that is. James does not say the prophets predicted this and therefore we must accept it. He says the testimony and the prophets agree: the Scriptures are the fixed point, and what Peter, Barnabas and Paul have reported is being measured against them. Experience is confirmed by Scripture. James does not rely only on the stories; he goes to the Bible. Scripture has the final word. Had Amos not agreed, no number of signs and wonders would have settled the matter. The council’s whole doctrine of authority is in that one verb.

After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen. Then the quotation, and the picture in it is better than most of us notice. James quotes Amos in its Greek form. The tent of David is David’s dynasty and kingdom, fallen into ruin (Amos 9:11). And Amos himself does not say the house of David or the throne of David. He says the booth of David: a temporary shelter, the kind of thing thrown up out of branches in a vineyard at harvest and taken down again afterwards. The dynasty that was promised an everlasting throne is described by the prophet as a garden hut, and a collapsed one.

I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it. And God’s answer is not to replace it with something grander. He goes back to the fallen shelter and puts that up again. James says this is being fulfilled now: in the resurrection and enthronement of Jesus, David’s son (2:30–36; 13:34), and in the gathering of the Gentiles into his kingdom.

The Hebrew and the Greek. Now the difficulty, which the honest reader will meet the moment he turns to Amos, and which is worth facing squarely rather than stepping over. James is quoting the Greek Old Testament, and at the crucial point it does not read like the Hebrew. Amos 9:12 in our English Bibles, translated from the Hebrew, says the purpose is that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name. James quotes it as that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. Edom has become mankind, and possessing has become seeking.

Three things settle it. First, the differences are exactly the kind that arise between two ancient copies rather than the kind a translator invents: in Hebrew written without vowels, Edom and mankind differ by at most one easily missed letter, and possess and seek differ by a single letter. The Greek translators were working from a Hebrew manuscript and read the consonants one way; the text behind our Old Testament read them another. Second, James is speaking to a Greek-speaking church from the Bible they actually used, which is what Paul did in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (13:41) and what any preacher does. Third, and decisively: his argument survives on either text. Even in the Hebrew, the restored kingdom of David includes all the nations who are called by my name: Gentiles bearing God’s name inside David’s rebuilt house, which is precisely the point in dispute. The council did not smuggle the Gentiles in through a variant. Both texts have them there; the Greek simply says it more warmly.

The rebuilding is under way. So James can settle a question about the present from a prophet of the eighth century BC. The tent of David is being rebuilt now, in the risen Son of David, and the proof that the rebuilding is under way is standing in the room: Gentiles seeking the Lord, exactly as Amos said they would when it happened.

Where Christians differ: when is David’s tent rebuilt? Dispensationalists see the rebuilding of David’s tent as a future millennial kingdom for Israel, after the church age. Verdict: James says the conversion of the Gentiles agrees with Amos now. David’s fallen tent is rebuilt in the risen Christ reigning on David’s throne, and in his church of Jews and Gentiles. The promise is fulfilled in the gospel age. This is the amillennial reading, which follows the apostles’ own use of the prophets.

How our dispensational brothers read it. Here too brothers read the prophecy differently, and it is worth noting kindly. On the amillennial and Reformed reading taken above, the rebuilding of David’s fallen tent is being fulfilled now in the risen Son of David and the ingathering of the Gentiles into his church, which is exactly why James cites it to settle the question. Our dispensational friends, by contrast, generally take Amos’s rebuilt tent of David to await a future, literal restoration of national Israel and the Davidic throne in the millennial kingdom; on their reading James is not declaring the prophecy fulfilled today but showing that the present Gentile ingathering is in harmony with the prophets (after this I will return and rebuild), the church age being a foretaste of what Christ will yet establish at his return. Both honour the prophets and rejoice that Gentiles are saved by grace, apart from becoming Jews, the very point of the council; the difference belongs to the larger, family conversation between amillennial and dispensational readings of God’s future for Israel, and should be carried with charity.

Is it legitimate for the New Testament to use the Greek Old Testament? Yes. The apostles quoted Scripture in the form their hearers knew, as we quote a familiar translation. Where the Greek differs from the Hebrew, the apostles never build a doctrine on a mistake; they use wording that faithfully carries the meaning, often drawing out what the Hebrew implies. And because the apostles wrote under the Spirit’s inspiration, their use of the Old Testament is itself the authoritative guide to its meaning. When James says Amos is being fulfilled, that is how we should read Amos.

In a sentence. James said the prophets agree, as Amos wrote that afterwards God would return and rebuild the fallen tent of David, rebuilding its ruins and restoring it.

On a Tuesday. Test every claim by Scripture. Experience must agree with the word. The next time you hear an exciting report or teaching, Christian or otherwise, ask the council’s question before you pass it on: do the words of the prophets agree?

For worship. God does not abandon the ruins of his promises. David’s house fell to a garden hut, and then to nothing, and God went back to it and raised it up again in a Son who will never fall. Jesus sits on David’s throne now, and the shelter of his kingdom is wide enough for the nations. Every Gentile who seeks the Lord is a stone in the rebuilding, and the One who promised it is the One doing it.
verseByVerse.note: James quotes Amos in its Greek form. “The tent of David” is David’s fallen royal house.

parallels.desc: I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things

That the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. This is the purpose clause, and it answers a question most readers never think to ask: why is the tent of David rebuilt at all? Not so that Israel may have a king again for its own sake. The prophet gives the reason, and the reason is other people: that the rest of humanity might seek the Lord. The throne is restored so that those who were never under it can come in. That single line is the answer to the whole council. If the King was raised up for the sake of the nations, then requiring the nations to become Israelites first has the prophecy backwards. (The Hebrew of Amos reads that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and the Greek translation, which James uses, read the Hebrew letters slightly differently as mankind; either way, the nations are brought under the rule of David’s son.)

And all the Gentiles who are called by my name. Gentiles called by God’s name: belonging to him, as Gentiles, without first becoming Jews. This is the decisive point. Amos does not say the Gentiles will become Jews; he says Gentiles will bear God’s name. The Hebrew idiom underneath is more concrete than the English: it is literally that God’s name has been called over them. It is what is said of the temple, this house that I have built is called by your name (1 Kings 8:43), and of Jerusalem, and of Israel itself. To be called by God’s name is to be publicly marked as his property, the way a man’s name over a door tells you whose house it is.

The strongest mark there is. Now put that against what the party of the Pharisees was asking for. They wanted a mark. They wanted something visible on the Gentiles’ bodies to show they belonged. And Amos says God has already put his own name on them, which is the strongest mark there is, and there is no room on a man for a better one.

Says the Lord, who makes these things. God does it. James does not finish on his own authority, and he is about to hand down a ruling. The last voice in his quotation is God’s.

What if I do not feel that I belong? There is a word here for the Christian who does not feel that he belongs: who sits in church suspecting he is tolerated rather than wanted, or who came in late, or from the wrong background, or with a history he would rather nobody knew. Belonging, in this verse, is not established by how you feel about the family. It is established by whose name has been called over you. That was done to you; you did not do it, and you cannot undo it by feeling unworthy of it. The Gentiles in Amos are not told to earn the name. They are told it is already on them.

Does seek the Lord mean people find God by their own searching? No. Scripture says plainly that no one seeks God on his own (Romans 3:11). When people truly seek the Lord, it is because he has first sought them and drawn them. Here the seeking is the result of God’s rebuilding: the Lord does these things, and the nations seek him as a consequence. So if you find yourself seeking God, take it as a sign that he is already at work in you, and keep seeking, for he is found by those who seek him with all their heart.

In a sentence. Amos says this was so that the rest of humanity, all the Gentiles called by God’s name, would seek the Lord, says the Lord who does these things.

On a Tuesday. God’s name is on Gentiles who believe. Wear it with gratitude. And look around your church on Sunday for the person who looks least as if they belong. Make sure they leave knowing that the name is on them too.

For worship. The Lord who makes these things has called his name over sinners from every nation, and he has done it in his Son, who bears the name above every name. We did not write it there and we cannot rub it out. He has marked us as his own house, and he will dwell in it for ever.

parallels.desc: all the nations who are called by my name

verseByVerse.quote: "'known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
known from of old.

Known from of old. If you are reading this with a Bible open you may be looking at a very short verse and wondering whether something has gone missing, particularly if you grew up with the King James, where verse 18 is a whole sentence: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world. Many people have that line by heart. The ESV gives you a few words, and attaches them to the end of Amos’s quotation: God is the one who makes these things known from of old. This is worth explaining rather than passing over, because a reader who notices a gap and is given no account of it will quietly conclude that somebody is hiding something.

A textual note. The longer sentence stands in the mass of later Greek manuscripts, which is the text the King James translators worked from. The shorter reading is in the oldest and best copies we have. On the shorter reading, the words are still part of what God says through the prophet; on the longer, they become a separate remark of James’s own about God’s omniscience in general. Now notice something that ought to be reassuring. The shorter reading, the one the modern versions print, is actually the stronger one for James’s argument. A general statement that God knows everything he does would be true but loose. What the better text says is sharper: God makes these things known from of old. This particular thing. The ingathering of the nations was published centuries in advance, and the council is not deciding a new policy but catching up with an old announcement.

Nothing is at stake. And take the general point away with you, because it will meet you again in the footnotes of any modern Bible. Nothing in the Christian faith is at stake here. God’s eternal knowledge of all his works is taught plainly elsewhere: in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me (Psalm 139:16); declaring the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10); he chose us in him before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Whichever reading is in your Bible, the doctrine stands; only the address of the proof text moves. That is what the great majority of textual variants are like, and the footnotes exist because translators are being honest with you rather than because the ground is shifting.

Not plan B. So to the verse itself. From of old. This was not a change of plan. God has always planned this, from eternity (Isaiah 45:21; Ephesians 3:9–11). The inclusion of the Gentiles was not plan B, but God’s purpose all along, made known to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). God did not revise his policy on the Gentiles somewhere in the middle of the first century in response to how the mission was going. The men in that room are discovering something that had been written down centuries earlier, in a book they had heard read aloud every Sabbath of their lives: the very tragedy Paul laid at Jerusalem’s door at 13:27, except that this time they see it.

If God planned everything from of old, do my choices matter? Yes. God’s eternal plan includes our real choices and actions, and works through them, not around them. The council still had to debate, decide and write; the missionaries still had to walk. God’s purpose is the reason our obedience is not wasted, not a reason to sit still. We act responsibly, praying and choosing as wisely as we can, and rest in the knowledge that a wise and good God has woven even our mistakes into a plan that will not fail (Romans 8:28).

In a sentence. These things were known from long ago.

On a Tuesday. The parts of your life that look like improvisation, the detour, the years that came to nothing, the door that shut, are being handled by someone who does not improvise. Name one of them to God today and thank him that he knew it from of old.

For worship. God planned your salvation from of old. Nothing about it is an afterthought. Before the mountains were brought forth, before Abraham was called out of Ur, the Father had purposed to gather a people from every nation into his Son. Known from of old is a sentence about a plan that was already old when you were born, and it will still be standing when the last of the nations has come in.

parallels.desc: who told this long ago?

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.

Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God. The word is judicial: James is not offering a view, he is handing down a decision. So it matters enormously what the decision actually is, and the first thing it does is take something away. No circumcision, no burden of the law. Gentiles are saved as Gentiles. Before one requirement is named, the ruling is: stop making it hard for them. And the verb (parenochlein) is stronger than trouble suggests in modern English: it means to harass, to pile on difficulties, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. James’s formal judgment is that the Gentile converts were being harassed by the church, and that it must stop.

Harassing people toward Jesus. Turn that on ourselves for a moment, because it is not a first-century problem. It is entirely possible to harass people toward Jesus. To attach to the gospel a cloud of expectations, about dress, vocabulary, background, politics, family shape, how quickly the drinking stops, how soon the story can be told tidily, none of them stated as conditions, all of them functioning as conditions; and then to wonder why people who genuinely turned to God do not stay. The first ruling the church ever issued about how to treat new believers begins with the words we should not trouble, and it is not a soft sentiment. It is a verdict against a church that had been doing it.

Those who turn to God. And notice what James calls them while he is at it. That is the conversion word, and he uses it as settled fact. In the act of ruling on the question, he grants the disputed point: they have turned to God. And he says it before he says anything at all about their behaviour. The order is the whole gospel in miniature: they are in, and then we talk about how to live.

But should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. Having lifted the burden, James does lay down four things, and a reader who has followed the argument this far is entitled to ask what they are doing there at all. The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living among Israel (Leviticus 17–18). Food offered to idols; sexual immorality (perhaps including marriages within forbidden degrees, Leviticus 18); meat from animals strangled rather than drained of blood; and eating blood (Genesis 9:4). These would deeply offend Jewish believers and make table fellowship impossible.

If the food laws are abolished, why forbid blood and strangled meat? First, hold on to what the council had just decided: Gentiles are saved by grace, not by keeping the law (15:11), so these are not kosher rules smuggled back in, nor conditions of salvation. Why ask them, then? For love and unity. Jewish believers were revolted by these things: meat offered to idols, and the eating of blood (which strangled meat retains). Scripture had forbidden blood since Noah, long before Moses (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17), out of reverence for the life in it. For Jew and Gentile to sit at one table and be one church, the Gentiles, free in conscience, were asked to surrender a few things that would deeply wound their brothers: liberty limited by love (Romans 14). And all four cluster around the pagan temple (idol-meat, blood, strangled animals, ritual immorality were the stuff of idol-feasts), so the decree also keeps new converts clear of their old idolatry. It is not back to the law; it is: love your brother, and stay clear of idols.

But does not Paul later allow food offered to idols? No contradiction (1 Corinthians 8–10), once two questions are distinguished. (1) Eating as an act of worship, at a temple feast: Paul forbids it as flatly as the council: flee from idolatry; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:14, 21). On idolatry, Paul and James are identical. (2) Eating meat that merely happened through a temple and is now sold in the market or served at a private meal: this Paul treats as neutral (an idol has no real existence, 8:4; eat whatever is sold in the meat market, 10:25), permitted, governed only by love: do not eat if it would wound a weaker brother (8:9–13). So Paul is not overturning the decree but applying its same two principles, flee idolatry, let love limit liberty, with more nuance. The ruling was a wise unity measure for a raw Jewish and Gentile church; its permanent heart, no idolatry, no sexual immorality, freedoms surrendered for love, never changes, even as the specific abstentions from blood and strangled meat are generally understood to belong to that moment (most Christians today do not observe them, seeing the reverence for blood fulfilled in the blood of Christ once shed). The thread from James to Paul is one: keep clear of idols, and love your brother more than your dinner.

Where Christians differ: are these rules binding today? Some groups hold that Christians must still avoid blood, for example in black pudding, or even (Jehovah’s Witnesses) blood transfusions. Verdict: these were not conditions of salvation (that was settled in v. 11), but practical rules for fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers at that time. Paul later teaches that food is a matter of conscience and love (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8–10). The rule against sexual immorality is permanent moral law; the food rules applied the principle of not offending a brother. Blood transfusions have nothing to do with eating blood.

Why is sexual immorality in a list about food? Because in the pagan world it was bound up with idol worship and temple feasts, and because Gentile culture treated it as ordinary, much as many do today. Jewish believers were horrified by it, and rightly, for it is not a matter of custom but of God’s moral law, forbidden again and again in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:18; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5). Its place on the list warned new Gentile converts that turning to God meant a break with the sexual habits of their old life. That part of the decree has never expired.

In a sentence. James gave his judgment that they should not burden the Gentiles who turn to God, but write telling them to avoid things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals, and blood.

On a Tuesday. Don’t add burdens to the gospel. But be willing to give up freedoms for the sake of fellowship. Think of a newer Christian you know: is there an unspoken expectation you have been placing on them that God has not placed? Lift it. And is there a freedom of yours that is making their walk harder? Lay it down.

For worship. The Lord does not harass those who turn to him. He receives them as they are, with their old habits and new faith, and then, with infinite patience, teaches them to walk. The blood the decree honoured pointed to the blood that was shed for us, the life poured out once for all on the cross, by which Jew and Gentile alike are brought near to God and seated at one table.
verseByVerse.note: The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living in Israel (Lev 17–18), and would let Jewish and Gentile believers eat together.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.

For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues. This is the reason James gives for the four abstentions, and it is honestly one of the more puzzling sentences in Acts. Careful readers have taken it three ways, and it is better to say so than to pretend the verse is obvious.

Three readings. Some read it as being about the Jewish believers: Moses is preached in every city, so in every city there are Christians of Jewish background who hold these scruples deeply, which makes the four abstentions the minimum floor on which a mixed congregation can actually eat together. Jews lived in every city and heard the law every week; Gentile believers should be sensitive to them, so as not to put stumbling blocks in their way to Christ, and so that Jewish and Gentile believers could eat together. The Jewish community would be watching how Gentile Christians lived. Some read it as being about the Gentiles: anyone who wants the law of Moses can hear it any Sabbath he likes, so the church has no need to impose it; the synagogue is already doing that job. And some read it as a reassurance to the party of the Pharisees that this ruling does no dishonour to Moses, who goes on being read every week regardless.

For the sake of brothers. The first reading fits the ruling’s stated purpose best and is the one most take, though the second is attractive and not to be dismissed. But notice that on any of the three, the shape of James’s reasoning is the same, and it is the point worth carrying. He does not ground the four abstentions in the Gentiles’ own holiness. He does not say these things will defile you, or damage you, or displease God in themselves. He grounds them in other people: in the existence of believers, in towns these Gentiles will never visit, who hear Moses read every Sabbath and would be unable to sit at a table where blood was served. So the Gentile Christians of Antioch are being asked to give something up for the sake of men they have not met and will not meet. Not because those men are right; the council has just declared they are not right about circumcision. Because they are brothers.

The hardest form of love. That is the hardest form of Christian love and much the commonest: surrendering a liberty you are entitled to, for somebody whose scruple you do not share and privately think mistaken. It is the principle the previous verses work out from Romans 14, and it costs more than the grand sacrifices because nobody notices you doing it and there is no credit in it.

How do I know when to give up a freedom and when to stand on it? Give it up when using it would genuinely harm a brother’s conscience or faith, cause him to stumble into sin, or block someone from hearing the gospel (1 Corinthians 8:13; 9:19–23). Stand on it when someone demands it as a condition of being right with God, because then the gospel itself is at stake (Galatians 2:4–5). The difference is between a weaker brother who is hurt and a false teacher who is imposing. With the first, love limits liberty. With the second, liberty must be defended for the sake of the gospel.

In a sentence. For Moses has been preached in every city from ancient times and read in the synagogues every Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is a short one. Name a freedom you are genuinely entitled to (you have thought it through, you are right, and Scripture permits it) that you have actually given up, in practice, because it would have wounded a particular Christian you know. If nothing comes to mind, this verse has not yet reached you.

For worship. Live so as not to put stumbling blocks in front of others. Love limits liberty. Christ did this to the uttermost: though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor; though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself. Every small freedom surrendered for a brother is a faint reflection of the Lord who gave up heaven’s glory for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: "The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings.

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church. Agreement: leaders and congregation together. Unity, after great debate. The congregation is in the sentence. The apostles had the authority, the elders had the oversight, and the whole church is named alongside them in the sending. Luke does not explain the mechanics and it is not worth manufacturing a system out of a clause; but he tells us the decision was not simply handed down from a room upstairs.

To choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. And then a piece of pastoral wisdom that is easy to walk past. They had a letter. They could have sent the letter. Instead they chose men and sent them with it. Messengers from Jerusalem would confirm the letter was genuine, so that no one could say Paul made it up. Think about the difference. A ruling that arrives as a document is a verdict; you read it, and then you are alone with your questions and with whatever tone you imagined in it. A ruling that arrives in the hands of two respected men who will stay for weeks and answer anything you ask is a pastoral act. Antioch had been unsettled by men who came with words. Jerusalem answers with men who came with words, and the entire difference is that these were sent.

They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas. Look, too, at who was chosen: leading men among the brothers. Both Jerusalem men. Both, so far as we can tell, Jewish. The delegation carrying a verdict in favour of Gentile freedom is drawn entirely from the side that had most to lose by it, which meant that nobody in Antioch could say the Gentiles had voted themselves a privilege, and nobody in Jerusalem could say the decision had been carried by outsiders. It is the sort of care that costs nothing and prevents years of trouble.

Remember the second name. Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion (v. 40; 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1) and helped Peter write his first letter (1 Peter 5:12). A Roman citizen (16:37). Silas has come to Antioch to deliver a letter and go home. Within twenty verses he will be Paul’s partner on the second missionary journey, and before long he will be singing in a Philippian cell at midnight and producing his Roman citizenship the morning after (16:25, 37). Men are forever setting out on errands that turn into their life’s work.

The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles. Then the letter itself, and its first word settles the question it was written to answer.
