Brothers to brothers: Jewish and Gentile believers are one family. Brothers, on both ends of the address. Not converts, not adherents, not Gentile believers pending regularisation. Before a single clause of argument, the salutation has conceded everything the Judaizers were contesting.

Does the Council set a pattern for church government? Apostles, elders and the whole church took part (vv. 22–23), and the decision was reached by appeal to Scripture (vv. 15–18) and to what God had done. It bound the churches beyond Jerusalem because the apostles were present and the decision agreed with Scripture. Churches today may meet together to settle questions, as Presbyterian synods do, and congregations take part in decisions; but no later council carries apostolic authority, and none can bind the conscience beyond what Scripture says.

A fingerprint. And one small fingerprint for the interested reader. The Greek word for greetings here is the ordinary opening of a Greek letter, and in the whole New Testament it appears in exactly three places as a letter’s greeting: in this letter, in a Roman officer’s despatch at 23:26, and in the opening line of the letter of James. The man who drafted this one seems to have written another.

Why does it matter that we call other believers brothers and sisters? Because it is true, and because truth spoken shapes how we treat one another. In Christ we have one Father and one elder Brother, and so we are family, not members of a club or customers of a service. Families eat together, bear with one another, tell the truth, share burdens, and stay together through quarrels. The word brother in this letter was a healing word to Gentiles who had been told they were outsiders. It can still be one: say it, and mean it, to the believer who feels least at home.

In a sentence. The apostles, elders and whole church decided to send chosen men, Judas Barsabbas and Silas, leaders among the brothers, to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas, carrying a letter from the apostles and elders to the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia.

On a Tuesday. Call every believer brother or sister. In Christ, we are family. And if something has gone wrong at a distance, do not rely on a message alone: if you can, send a person, or go yourself.

For worship. The Father has made one family out of Jews and Gentiles, and his Son is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The Lord of glory, who has every right to address us as servants, writes to us as family. The first word of the gospel to the outsider is the same as the first word of this letter: brother.
verseByVerse.note: Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,

Some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds. That is the most powerful church in the world putting it in writing that men who had used its name had no authority to do so. And notice the honesty of the wording. They do not deny that the men came from them. From us is conceded in the same breath as the disowning.

Although we gave them no instructions. The apostles disown the false teachers. They had no authority from Jerusalem. What they deny is the commission. That is exactly the right shape for an institution that has been misrepresented, and it is rarer than it ought to be, the standing temptations being either to defend your own because they are your own, or to pretend they were never anything to do with you.

Unsettling. Then the description of the damage, and Luke’s vocabulary is not gentle. The word (anaskeuazontes) is one used of dismantling a building or stripping a town, turning it upside down as in plundering a house: they took your minds apart. False teaching wreaks havoc. Sit with what the injury actually was. Not immorality. Not a split. Unsettled minds. People who had been sure they belonged to God were no longer sure, and that is the characteristic wound of adding anything to the gospel. It does not usually make people worse; it makes them uncertain. And an uncertain Christian cannot love freely, or give freely, or speak of Christ freely, because a part of him is permanently occupied with checking whether he is in. Everything else runs at half power. Anyone who has lived a season without assurance knows precisely how much of life it eats.

Having come to one accord. Unity of mind. The phrase is Luke’s word for the church’s Spirit-given unity, the same word used of the upper room and of the prayer meeting after the first arrests (1:14; 4:24). And here is the thing worth noticing about where he puts it: eighteen verses after much debate (v. 7), and twenty-three after no small dissension (v. 2). They did not reach one accord by leaving the subject alone. The unity is on the far side of the argument, not instead of it, which is the only kind that holds.

With our beloved Barnabas and Paul. A public endorsement of Paul and Barnabas, against those who questioned them. The two men whose ministry the Judaizers had been quietly undermining are named in an official document with an adjective of affection. And Barnabas first again: in a Jerusalem letter, the Jerusalem order.

How can I have assurance if my mind has been unsettled? Go back to the gospel itself, not to your feelings or your record. God promises that whoever believes in the Son has eternal life (John 3:36), and he cannot lie. Your assurance rests first on that promise, then on the Spirit’s inner witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16), and then on the fruit of a changed life, which will be imperfect but real (Westminster 18.2). If someone has told you that you need something more than Christ, test it by Scripture as Antioch did. And talk to a mature pastor or friend; unsettled minds are often settled in conversation.

In a sentence. The letter said that since some men from Jerusalem had troubled them and unsettled their minds without any authority, the apostles and elders had agreed to choose men and send them with their dear friends Barnabas and Paul.

On a Tuesday. Is there a question about your standing with God that has been quietly eating at you? Write it down, then write beside it the promise of God that answers it. And if you know someone whose mind has been unsettled by teaching that adds to Christ, go to them, as Judas and Silas did, and stay long enough to help.

For worship. False teaching unsettles minds. The truth of grace brings peace. The Good Shepherd does not leave his sheep to be scattered by hirelings and strangers who were never sent. He sends true shepherds with true words, and he himself speaks peace to his people: my sheep hear my voice, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

parallels.desc: some who trouble you

verseByVerse.quote: "'men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.

Men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Greek (paradedōkosi) is stronger than risked: they have handed over their lives, given themselves up. The stoning at Lystra (14:19). And when this letter was read aloud in Antioch, that sentence was not a compliment about people far away. The two men were standing in the room. Every person listening could see them, and some of them knew what Paul had looked like when he got back from Lystra. That is what makes the commendation weigh anything. Jerusalem is not saying these are sound men whose theology we have checked. It is saying: these are the men who have already paid for this gospel with their bodies, and the people telling you they are wrong have paid nothing. Their suffering proved their sincerity, unlike the troublemakers.

For the name. And note what they risked their lives for: not for a doctrine of Gentile inclusion, not for a mission strategy, but for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The name is the thread running through this whole chapter. God is taking a people for his name (v. 14). The Gentiles are called by his name (v. 17). These men have handed over their lives for the name. And the question the council exists to answer is simply whether that name is enough by itself, which is answered, in a way, by noticing what men will die for.

Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. Two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). The written word and the living voice, sent together and deliberately. They anticipated that a letter can be read with a hostile tone supplied by the reader, or quoted in parts, or explained away by whoever gets to it first. So they sent two men who would say the same things out loud, in the room, and could be asked follow-up questions.

Send a person. It is a small thing and it is worth copying. If something has gone wrong at a distance, a misunderstanding in a family, a quarrel in a church, a message that landed badly, a letter will very often make it worse, because the reader supplies the voice. Send a person if you possibly can.

Does suffering prove that someone’s teaching is true? Not on its own. People have suffered and died for false beliefs too. But suffering does show sincerity: it is hard to believe that someone is in it for gain when he keeps being stoned for it. And in Scripture faithful suffering is one of the marks of true servants of Christ, in contrast to false teachers who look for comfort and profit (2 Corinthians 11:23–29; 2 Timothy 3:10–12). So the test of teaching is always Scripture; but a teacher’s willingness to suffer for Christ rather than profit from him is a good reason to listen carefully.

In a sentence. Paul and Barnabas had risked their lives for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and Judas and Silas would confirm the same things in person.

On a Tuesday. Honour those who have suffered for Christ. Their scars are credentials. Find out about a persecuted church or a believer imprisoned for their faith, and pray for them by name this week. And if there is a conversation you have been conducting by text that would go better face to face, arrange it.

For worship. The name of our Lord Jesus Christ is worth a life, because he gave his life for the name of his Father and for the people he loved. He was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification. Every scar his servants carry for him is a small reflection of the wounds he carries for them, and the name they suffer for is the only name under heaven by which we must be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.

For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. That is the most audacious sentence any church body has ever written about its own decision, and it has been quoted ever since to justify a great deal that it will not bear. So it is worth being exact about what makes it available here. The Spirit led the council through Scripture, through what God had done, and through the agreement of the church. The Spirit first, then us.

Three things stand under it. Remove any one and the formula collapses. The Spirit had already acted publicly and visibly, before any of them voted: he fell on Cornelius’s household, and Peter’s entire argument is that God went first (v. 8). Scripture agreed, and James said so in as many words (v. 15). And apostles were in the room, men holding a commission that is not repeatable. A committee with none of those three has no business borrowing this sentence.

The order of the words. But look at the order of the words, because that is where the guard is. To the Holy Spirit and to us. They do not write: we have decided, and we trust the Spirit approves. Nor do they write: the Spirit has spoken and we merely wrote it down, which would have sounded far more impressive and would have been a lie, because they had argued for hours and Luke says so. Both halves are in the sentence, joined by a plain and, and Christians ever since have wanted to delete one or the other: some claiming a directness God did not give them, others reducing the church’s decisions to human management with a prayer at the start.

Guidance got right. This is what it looked like when the early church got guidance right. Evidence of what God had actually done, tested against Scripture, argued out in daylight, decided together, and then owned. Nobody had a dream. And afterwards they were willing to put their name next to the Spirit’s, which is a far more sobering thing to do than to claim a private impression.

To lay on you no greater burden than these requirements. The burden of the law is lifted. Note the honesty: it is a burden, and they say so. They do not pretend the four things cost nothing. What they promise is that nothing further will be added, which was the whole anxiety of the Gentile churches, and remains the anxiety of anyone who suspects the requirements will keep coming.

Three versions of the decree. Now something worth doing with a pencil, because Luke gives this decree three times in his book and the wording moves. James speaks it (v. 20); the letter writes it (v. 29); and years later, when Paul comes back to Jerusalem for the last time, James quotes it back at him (21:25). Set the three side by side. James’s spoken ruling was: things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, what has been strangled, blood. The letter reads: what has been sacrificed to idols, blood, what has been strangled, sexual immorality. Two changes, and both are instructive. First, the letter tightens the opening phrase: James said things polluted by idols, which is broad enough to cover almost anything connected with a temple, and the letter says what has been sacrificed to idols, which is a specific and checkable thing. That is what happens when a spoken ruling is put into a document by people who know it will be read by strangers in another country. Second, the order changes: sexual immorality moves from second place to last, so that the three food matters stand together. And it is the letter’s order that sticks: it is exactly the order James himself uses when he quotes the decree at 21:25, years afterwards. Which also settles a question a thoughtful reader will have been carrying: the decree did not quietly lapse once feelings cooled. Years later the Jerusalem church still regarded it as standing.

If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Not you will be saved, but you will do well. Advice for fellowship, not a condition of salvation. And notice how it ends. No threat, no penalty, no warning about what happens otherwise. The most important letter of the first century closes by telling a nervous congregation that they will do well. Farewell.

Where Christians differ: the authority of church councils. Some see this council as the model for later councils whose decisions bind the church infallibly. Verdict: this council included apostles, and its decision became Scripture. Later councils have no such authority. They are valuable and to be respected when they agree with Scripture, as Nicaea and Chalcedon do, but they can err (Westminster Confession 31.4). Scripture alone is the final authority. This is sola Scriptura.

May a church today say it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us? Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that the great councils of the church carry the Spirit’s guarantee and bind the faithful. Reformed churches hold that councils can err, and that their decisions bind only as far as they agree with Scripture. Here the apostles were present, and their judgment became part of Scripture itself. Churches may pray for and follow the Spirit’s guidance, but they cannot claim this sentence for their own decisions.

Are these four requirements binding today? Two of them, avoiding idolatry and sexual immorality, are permanent moral commands repeated throughout the New Testament. The food rules, about blood and strangled meat, were given so that Gentile believers would not needlessly offend their Jewish brothers in that setting; Paul later treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and love (1 Corinthians 8; 10:25–29). The principle that lasts is to use our freedom with love for others.

How should I seek the Spirit’s guidance in my own decisions? Follow the council’s pattern on a small scale. Start with Scripture: what has God already said that bears on this? Look honestly at the circumstances God has arranged. Pray, and ask counsel of wise believers, especially if the decision affects others. Weigh the options in the light of love for God and neighbour. Then decide, and own the decision humbly, without claiming that God spoke to you directly. The Spirit usually guides through his word, prayer, wisdom and the church, not through private voices, and he is no less present for that.

In a sentence. The letter said it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to put no greater burden on them than to avoid food sacrificed to idols, blood, strangled meat and sexual immorality, and they would do well to keep from these.

On a Tuesday. If you are facing a decision, run the council’s method on it this week: Scripture, circumstances, prayer, counsel, decision. And if you are anxious that God’s requirements will keep piling up, read the last line of the letter again: you will do well.

For worship. The Spirit lifts the yoke of the law from your neck. Live freely, and lovingly. The Holy Spirit is not a distant voice but the Lord who leads his church into the truth, who took the Scriptures and the evidence of his own work and brought a quarrelling assembly to one mind. He has given us the whole counsel of God in his word, and he still leads his people by it, gently, without adding burdens, toward the freedom Christ has won.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement.

Having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. Read publicly to the whole church. Read to everybody, at once, out loud. Not circulated among the leadership first, not summarised from the front by somebody who had already seen it. The people whose minds had been unsettled heard the answer with their own ears at the same moment as everyone else.

Stand in that room. Now stand in that room, because the whole chapter has been building to this and it is the point at which a doctrine becomes a person’s own relief. You are a Gentile in Antioch. A year or two ago you were sacrificing to gods you had grown up with, and then you heard about Jesus and you believed it, and something in you came alive that you had no words for. Then men arrived from Jerusalem, from the place it all came from, from the church of the apostles, and they said that you were not, in fact, saved. That there was a further thing, and until it was done you were outside. Your own teachers could not settle it and went away to ask, and you have spent the intervening months not knowing whether you belong to God. And now a letter is read aloud, from the apostles and the elders, and its first word is brothers, and it says the men who unsettled you were never sent, and that nothing further is required of you.

And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. The Gentile believers were relieved and joyful. They were saved by grace, as they were. The gospel of grace brings joy; legalism brings fear. The word is the same one the synagogue rulers used when they invited Paul to give a word of encouragement (13:15). It is what a letter can be when it says the right thing.

Joy by subtraction. And notice what produced the joy. Nothing was added to these people. They received no new experience, no gift, no vision, no fresh instruction. Something was taken away, a doubt, and the result was a congregation overjoyed with relief. Most of the deepest joys of the Christian life are like that: not additions, but the removal of something that had been standing between you and what you already had.

Why does legalism produce fear? Because if acceptance with God depends even partly on your performance, you can never be sure you have done enough. Every failure becomes a threat, every rule a test you might fail, and every other Christian a rival or a judge. That is why legalistic churches are often anxious, harsh and joyless, even when they are very busy. Grace produces a different kind of obedience: glad, grateful and secure, because it flows from acceptance rather than toward it. Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

In a sentence. The messengers went to Antioch, gathered the church and delivered the letter, and when they read it, they rejoiced at its encouragement.

On a Tuesday. So it is worth asking whether you are carrying an unsettled mind of your own: some question about whether God has really accepted you that you have never put into words and never had answered. The Christians at Antioch got theirs settled in writing, from the apostles, and rejoiced. You are holding rather more of it in writing than they were. Open the New Testament today at Romans 8 and read it aloud, as Antioch heard its letter.

For worship. Rejoice: you are saved by grace, without the yoke of the law. The God who wrote to Antioch through his apostles has written to us in the whole of Scripture, and the burden of the letter is the same: there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. The joy of Antioch is the joy of every sinner who hears that nothing more is required, because Christ has done it all.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.

And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets. Jerusalem did not send two couriers. It sent two prophets, and they did not hand over the letter and catch the next ship. They stayed.

Encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And what Luke tells us they did is the plainest description in the New Testament of what a prophet in the early church actually did with his time. Prophets here encourage and strengthen, as Paul describes (1 Corinthians 14:3). That deserves attention, because the word prophet now conjures something quite different: prediction, private revelation, a man announcing what is about to happen. There is some of that in Acts; Agabus forecasts a famine and later a binding (11:28; 21:11). But here, in the one place where Luke tells us at length what two named prophets did in a local church, the answer is: they talked to people for a long time and left them stronger. Paul’s own definition matches it exactly: the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation (1 Corinthians 14:3). Three notes, and not one of them is prediction.

With many words. Luke’s cheerful admission that it took a while. This was not a striking sentence delivered over somebody at the end of a meeting. It was hours of talking to frightened people, probably repeating themselves, in a church that had been badly shaken and needed to hear the same thing several times before it went in. Which is a comfort to anybody who suspects his own ministry is unremarkable. The treatment that healed the first church to be wounded by a false gospel was two men staying on for a few weeks and talking to people at length.

They were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. Peace restored. Hold that against the opening of the chapter. It began with no small dissension and debate (v. 2) and ran through much debate (v. 7), and now men are sent home in peace. Luke has framed the whole council between those two words, and the peace at the end is not the peace of a subject nobody raised. It is what was left when the thing was fought out properly and settled.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: that it seemed good to Silas to remain there. It is probably a later addition to explain why Silas is in Antioch in v. 40. Silas may have gone back to Jerusalem and later returned, or stayed.

Are there prophets like Judas and Silas today? In the sense of men receiving new revelation from God to stand alongside Scripture, no: that foundational gift belonged to the apostolic age, when the New Testament was not yet complete (Ephesians 2:20), and the canon is now closed. But the work Judas and Silas are described as doing here, strengthening and encouraging believers with many words drawn from the truth God has given, goes on in every faithful pastor, teacher and friend who opens the word to a troubled soul. Many Christians hold the gift of prophecy continues in some form, and they are brothers; but none should claim for any word today the authority of Scripture.

In a sentence. Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, encouraged and strengthened the believers with many words, and after some time were sent back in peace to those who had sent them.

On a Tuesday. Use your words to encourage and strengthen others today. Think of one shaken believer you know, and give them not a single sentence but an hour: listen, then speak the truths of the gospel to them, even the ones they have heard before.

For worship. The God of all comfort comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may comfort others. He did not leave a wounded church with a document; he sent it people who loved it and talked with it until it was whole. And he does the same for us, for the Spirit is the Comforter, who takes the words of Christ and speaks them to our hearts until we are at peace.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.

Teaching and preaching the word of the Lord. Back to the main work. Before the verse itself, an oddity most readers will have noticed: your Bible goes straight from verse 33 to verse 35. There is a footnote at the bottom of the page, and it is worth reading, because the missing verse is a small and unusually clear window on how we came to have the New Testament we have.

The missing verse. Verse 34 exists in the King James (Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still) and in the manuscripts behind it. The modern versions put it in the margin, noting that some manuscripts insert: but it seemed good to Silas to remain there, because it is absent from the oldest and best copies we have. Now ask why anybody would add such a sentence, because the answer is disarming. Look at verse 33: Judas and Silas were sent off, back to the men who had sent them. Then look at verse 40: Paul chooses Silas and departs. A copyist reading those in sequence sees a snag (how can Paul take a man who has gone home to Jerusalem?) and supplies a line to keep Silas in Antioch.

How variants usually arise. That is the shape of the great majority of textual variants, and it should steady rather than alarm you. The scribe was not inventing doctrine, or protecting a party, or smoothing away something inconvenient. He was tidying a narrative wrinkle, in good faith. And we can see him doing it, because the copies without his tidy-up have survived; the evidence is all still on the table, which is precisely why the footnote is there. Nothing whatever is at stake in verse 34: Luke was quite capable of leaving a gap between a departure and a return, and Silas may simply have gone and come back, or delayed his going. (The other footnoted verse in Acts that draws real attention is 8:37, and it is handled there.)

Councils are rare; teaching is daily. So to verse 35. Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord. The greatest theological crisis in the history of the church has just been resolved, and this is the next sentence: two men stayed put in their own congregation and taught.

With many others also. And then the clause that ought to be famous and is not. The ministry of the word was shared by many. A healthy church has many teachers. Luke names none of them. There were, in Antioch, a large number of people teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, and not one of their names has come down to us. They were doing the same work as the two men whose names fill this book, in the same city, in the same weeks. The record of them is a few words. If you have ever measured your own service against the people whose names are known and concluded that yours does not count, notice that Luke’s sentence puts the many others in the same clause as Paul and Barnabas, with the same verbs, and simply does not distinguish. The distinction is ours, not his, and not God’s.

The last time together. One more thing, and Luke does not draw attention to it. This is the last time Paul and Barnabas appear together as partners. The next paragraph is the quarrel.

Does every Christian have a part in the ministry of the word? Yes, though not all in the same way. Some are called and gifted to preach and teach publicly, and the church should test and recognise them. But every believer is to let the word of Christ dwell richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16): parents with children, friends over coffee, older women with younger, a word of Scripture in a hospital ward. The many others of Antioch were probably a mixture of all these. Ask where God has given you people to share his word with.

In a sentence. Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord with many others.

On a Tuesday. Share one verse of Scripture with someone today, in a message or a conversation, with a sentence about why it has helped you. You are one of the many others.

For worship. The word of the Lord is the heart of church life. Give yourself to it. Christ is the living Word, and every faithful word about him, from the apostle to the unnamed teacher in Antioch, is a channel of his life. He knows the names Luke did not record, and on the last day he will read them out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — The Parting of Paul and Barnabas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some time later Paul suggested to Barnabas that they go back and visit the believers in every town where they had preached, to see how they were doing. Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark, but Paul thought it unwise to take someone who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not continued in the work. They had such a sharp disagreement that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord. He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
verseByVerse.theology:
God's Sovereignty Over Human Conflict

Reformed theology sees in the Paul-Barnabas conflict the characteristic pattern of God's providence: working through human failure and disagreement to accomplish more than perfect human unity might have achieved. The separation produces two missionary teams instead of one. John Mark, the subject of the dispute, will prove his worth — Paul himself will later commend him (2 Timothy 4:11; Colossians 4:10). God does not waste the failures of his servants; he works through them, around them, and despite them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus — his home, the place that knows him — to restore the man he believes in. Paul took Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Both were faithful; both bore fruit. Now: The church's disagreements, when they do not touch the gospel itself, can produce multiplication rather than division if those who disagree remain committed to the mission rather than to winning the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.' Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark.

Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are. The last clause is the whole man. Paul is not proposing new territory, and he is not proposing a preaching tour. He wants to know how they are. Pastoral concern. Paul cared for the churches he planted (2 Corinthians 11:28). Planting is not enough; we must nurture. This is somebody who has been driven out of most of those towns, and what is on his mind a year later is whether the people he left behind are all right. Keep that in view through everything that follows, because the quarrel is about to make both men look small, and the sentence that starts it is one of the kindest in Acts.

Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. His cousin, who had turned back (13:13). Barnabas, the encourager, wanted to give him a second chance. Luke drops it in without comment, and any reader who has been paying attention knows at once what is coming.

The whole life of Barnabas. But before the argument, look at Barnabas: not this decision, but his whole recorded life, because it is all one thing. He first appears selling a field and laying the money at the apostles’ feet, and Luke pauses to say the apostles had nicknamed him son of encouragement (4:36–37). He appears next at the moment when a recently converted persecutor arrived in Jerusalem and the whole church was afraid of him and would not have him near: but Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles (9:27). Years later, when the work at Antioch needed a teacher, it was Barnabas who went to Tarsus to find the man everyone else had forgotten (11:25–26). And when he arrived at an unauthorised congregation of Gentiles that no apostle had planted, he looked at it, and when he saw the grace of God, he was glad (11:23). Every one of those is the same act. Barnabas’s entire biography is taking a chance on somebody other people had written off.

The irony. And now the irony, which Luke does not point out and does not need to. The man refusing to take a chance on Mark is a man whose entire ministry exists because Barnabas took a chance on him. Strike 9:27 out of the record and there is no Paul in this story at all; he is a suspect ex-persecutor whom nobody would vouch for. He is now declining to do for a young man exactly what was once done for him. That is not said in order to convict Paul, whose case is serious and comes in the next verse. It is said because it is one of the most human things in the New Testament. It is very possible to have been rescued by a kindness, to be genuinely grateful for it all your life, and to be entirely unable to see the same situation when it turns up in front of you with somebody else’s name on it.

An honest complication. And one honest complication, which Luke leaves for us to find elsewhere: Mark was Barnabas’s cousin (Colossians 4:10). Paul knew that. It does not make Barnabas wrong (a man may be right about somebody and partial to him at the same time, and most of us are both at once), but it is part of the picture, and pretending otherwise would make the scene tidier than it is.

How do I care for people I helped bring to faith? Keep in touch, as Paul wanted to: ask how they are, not only spiritually but in life. Pray for them by name. Read the Bible with them, or put them in touch with someone who will. Help them find a church and settle there. Be honest about your own struggles, so they do not think the Christian life should be easy. And do not take it personally if they need others more than you; your aim is their growth in Christ, not their attachment to you.

In a sentence. Some time later Paul suggested to Barnabas that they go back and visit the believers in every city where they had preached, to see how they were doing, and Barnabas wanted to take John Mark.

On a Tuesday. Who did you help come to faith? Check on them. See how they are. And look for the person in your church whom others have quietly written off, and take a chance on them, as Barnabas did for Saul.

For worship. The Lord himself is the great visitor of his people. He goes back over the roads where he sowed, to see how his flock is doing, and he knows each sheep by name. And he is the one who took a chance on all of us, vouching for us before the Father when no one else could, bringing us in when the whole household of heaven had reason to be afraid of what we were.

parallels.desc: Mark the cousin of Barnabas

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.

But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia. Now Paul’s case, and it is stronger than it is usually given credit for. Start with the verb Luke chooses for what Mark did. It is not left, which is how the account at 13:13 puts it. It is a heavier word (apostanta): to stand off from, to desert, to fall away, and it is the verb from which the noun apostasy comes. Whether that is Luke’s assessment or Paul’s own word reported, it is the strongest term available, and it tells you how Paul had been carrying this for two years. Paul saw it as abandoning the work. He needed reliable companions for dangerous journeys.

And had not gone with them to the work. Then look at how precisely he states the charge, because he does not say what we might expect. He does not say Mark was unreliable, or young, or homesick, or frightened. He says he had not gone with them to the work. That word, the work, is the point, and it reaches back. It is the word the Holy Spirit used in the sentence that started all of this: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them (13:2). It is the word used again when the two of them came home, of the work that they had fulfilled (14:26). Paul’s objection is not that a young man let him down personally. It is that a man walked out on a commission the Holy Spirit had named, and that the same commission is now being proposed again.

Two men looking at two things. So the two of them are not looking at the same thing at all. Barnabas is looking at a person, and asking what will become of him. Paul is looking at a commission, and asking what will become of it. Both men had a point: Barnabas saw a person to restore; Paul saw a mission to protect. Both objects are real, both men are right about the object they are looking at, and neither can see why the other will not be reasonable.

Luke declines to judge. Anyone who has sat on a church committee, or in a family, where two people of unquestioned goodwill could not be reconciled, has watched this exact thing. It is worth saying plainly that Scripture does not tell you which of them was right. The pressure you feel to award the decision is a pressure Luke deliberately declined, and it is probably the most useful thing this passage does to us, because our instinct in every such conflict is that one party must be the problem, and Luke will not let us have it.

Each right about something. What we do get, later, is that each of them turned out to be right about something. Barnabas was right about Mark, and Paul himself eventually says so in as many words; the whole of that is set out at 13:13 and does not need repeating. And Paul was right that the second journey would need men who would not go home: within a chapter Silas is in the inner cell of a Philippian prison with his feet in the stocks.

When two good Christians disagree, must one of them be sinning? Not necessarily. Two believers can look at the same situation, both seeking God’s glory, and weigh different goods differently, as Paul and Barnabas did. There may be sin in how they disagree, in harsh words, pride or refusal to listen, and there often is. But the disagreement itself may simply reflect the limits of our wisdom. So when you are in one, examine your heart before your opponent’s, assume the other person may see something you do not, and ask God to show you what each of you is rightly guarding.

In a sentence. But Paul did not think it wise to take one who had deserted them in Pamphylia and not continued in the work.

On a Tuesday. Think of a disagreement you are in. Write down, as fairly as you can, what the other person is rightly trying to protect. Then tell them you can see it.

For worship. Faithfulness matters in God’s work. But so does mercy for those who failed. In Christ the two meet perfectly: he guards his work with a holy jealousy, and he restores deserters with a tender patience. He did not drop Peter after the denials, and he did not let the work of the gospel fail either. Only he holds the commission and the person in one hand without losing either.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.

And there arose a sharp disagreement. Luke’s word is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm: irritation, provocation, a violent flaring, a fit. He does not soften it, and he does not apologise for it. Luke does not hide the conflict between two godly men. Christians, even apostles, can disagree strongly. Scripture does not say who was right.

The other place the word appears. There is one other place in the New Testament where that noun appears, and it is worth knowing: let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works (Hebrews 10:24). The word behind stir up is this one. The same heat that tears two missionaries apart in Antioch is the thing Christians are commanded to provoke in each other. Passion is not the problem in either verse; what it is aimed at is.

So that they separated from each other. A sad parting after years together. But God used it: two missionary teams instead of one. Now, what to do with this passage, because it is usually handled badly in both directions. The common comfort is that God used the quarrel to double the mission: one team became two, and twice the ground was covered. There is something in that, and Luke does let us see both men going on to fruitful work. But it must not be allowed to become approval. Luke reports a rupture between two men who had been mobbed and stoned together, and the plain fact is that they never appear working side by side again in this book. Something real was lost. A reader who is estranged from a Christian brother is not helped by being told that these things generally work out for the best; he is helped by seeing that the Bible records one that hurt, and does not tidy it.

Not permanent. And then the genuine hope, which is better than the tidy version because it rests on evidence rather than on optimism. It did not become permanent. Years afterwards, writing to Corinth about the rights of an apostle, Paul asks: Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? (1 Corinthians 9:6). It is a throwaway line, and that is exactly what makes it valuable. Long after the split, Paul assumes the Corinthians know Barnabas, puts their two names in one clause, and treats him as a fellow worker in good standing, without a shadow on it. And when he mentions Mark to the Colossians he identifies him, warmly, as the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), which means he was still close enough to the family to be using the family relations as shorthand. So: a real break, and not a permanent one. That is a more useful pattern to carry than either the sentimental version or the despairing one.

Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus. Look where he takes him. Cyprus is Barnabas’s own home (4:36), and it is the first leg of the very journey Mark abandoned: the island they worked before they crossed to the mainland where he turned back. Barnabas does not take him somewhere new and easy. He takes him back over the ground where it went wrong and walks it again with him. That is what restoring somebody actually looks like when a person does it rather than talks about it. Not a conversation and a fresh start elsewhere, but going back to the place of the failure and doing it properly, in company, at cost to yourself. Barnabas gave up the greatest partnership of his life for it, and it worked. His investment in Mark paid off: Mark became useful to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11) and wrote a Gospel. Paul and Mark were later reconciled (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). Paul spoke well of Barnabas later (1 Corinthians 9:6).

But Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. Two things. The church at Antioch commended Paul: they did not treat the quarrel as disqualifying, and they did not take sides publicly. The church sent Paul with its blessing. And they used the same words over him as when he first went out (14:26), which is where that phrase is worked through.

The camera angle. One guard as Barnabas leaves the book here. This is Barnabas’s last appearance in Acts. Luke follows Paul from now on, and we hear of Barnabas no more. That is the shape of Luke’s narrative, which is travelling toward Rome; it is not a verdict on the man. Do not mistake the camera angle for the assessment of God: a great deal of the best work in the church is done by people the story stops following.

What should I do if I have fallen out with a fellow Christian? First, own your part honestly before God, without waiting for the other person to own theirs. Then do what you can to seek peace (Romans 12:18): a humble message, an apology for what you got wrong, an offer to meet. If agreement on the issue is impossible, you may still be able to part without bitterness and speak well of each other, as Paul later spoke of Barnabas. Do not gossip about the quarrel. Pray for the other person’s blessing. And leave room for God to heal over years what cannot be healed in a week.

In a sentence. Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If you have had a sharp disagreement with a fellow believer, seek reconciliation, as Paul and Mark did in the end. Pray for that person by name today, and ask God whether this is the week to send the message.

For worship. God rules even over his servants’ quarrels. He did not approve the sharpness, but he turned one team into two, restored Mark, and in the end brought Paul and Barnabas back into warm regard. The Lord Jesus is the great Reconciler, who made peace between God and sinners by his blood and who will one day bring every estranged believer to one table, where there will be no more quarrels and every tear will be wiped away.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Mark were later reconciled.

parallels.desc: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: "And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Cilicia is Tarsus. It is Paul’s home province, and this is one of only two places we are told there were churches in it (compare 15:23). Syria and Cilicia, Paul’s home region, where he had worked during his hidden years (Galatians 1:21). The letter of the council was addressed to them (v. 23).

The hidden years. Stop on that, because Acts never records their founding. Nobody planted them in any scene Luke has given us. The likeliest explanation is sitting in the gap between two earlier verses: when the Jerusalem believers put Saul on a boat to get him out of danger, they sent him off to Tarsus (9:30), and he disappears from the narrative until Barnabas goes and fetches him (11:25). That is somewhere around a decade, and Luke tells us nothing whatever about it. This verse is the trace. Congregations existed in Cilicia, and the man walking round them now is the man who spent his obscure years there. Nobody wrote up those years. There is no account of the preaching, no list of converts, no story of a riot or a healing. There is a participle in a travel note, ten years later, and churches on the ground. That is worth having if the most obscure stretch of your own life is the one you cannot see any fruit from. Paul’s decade in Tarsus produced churches that Scripture mentions once, in passing, without crediting anyone. It was not a holding pattern before the real ministry started.

Strengthening. Luke has now used that word three times in quick succession: of Paul and Barnabas going back through the towns that had expelled them (14:22), of Judas and Silas staying on in Antioch (15:32), and now of Paul walking home through his own province. It is plainly a thing he thinks the church needs more of than it gets. Strengthening churches: the work of a pastor and apostle. And in the very next chapter we learn what part of it consisted in: he was carrying the council’s letter and delivering it as he went (16:4). The theology of chapter 15 arrives in the churches on foot.

How the second journey begins. And consider how the second missionary journey begins: the journey that will reach Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth and Ephesus, and produce most of the letters in your New Testament. Not with a vision. Not with a commissioning service. It begins with a man who has just lost his closest friend over an argument he could not win, walking through his home province, propping up small churches nobody has heard of. Luke never resolves the quarrel. He simply goes on with the story, which is what the two men did.

What does it mean to strengthen a church? It means helping believers stand firmer in Christ: teaching them the truth so they are not tossed about by every new idea (Ephesians 4:14), encouraging them in trials, reminding them of the gospel of grace, correcting error gently, and building up love among them. Every member can do some of it. A word of Scripture to a struggling friend, faithful attendance that encourages others, prayer for the leaders, a meal for a family under strain, patience with a difficult member: all of these strengthen a church.

In a sentence. Paul travelled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

On a Tuesday. Strengthen your church today with a word of encouragement, a prayer, a helping hand. And if you are in a hidden season, do the work in front of you faithfully, unseen: God keeps the records Luke did not.

For worship. The Lord builds his church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. He builds it in obscure years and small provinces, through quarrelling servants and unrecorded labour, and he strengthens what he builds. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, and he will present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle, every one of those small churches in Cilicia among her number.

15.theology: Justification by Grace Alone through Faith Alone. Acts 15 is the original council on justification. Peter’s summary — “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” — is the thesis of the Reformation stated by an apostle. The Judaizers were not wicked men; they were sincere believers who thought obedience to the law was necessary for salvation. But sincerity does not make a false gospel true. The council’s verdict is decisive and irreversible: the Gentiles are saved through grace, and so are the Jews. The law cannot save. It never could. The law was given to demonstrate the need for grace, not to provide an alternative to it. The cross of Christ is sufficient, complete, and alone — and any addition to it, however well-intentioned, is a subtraction from it.
15.examples:
Then: A church divided over the most fundamental question imaginable: what must a person do to be saved? The answer came not from compromise but from clarity, grounded in Scripture (James’s citation of Amos) and confirmed by experience (Peter’s witness to Cornelius, Barnabas and Paul’s report from the Gentile mission). The church that settles this question rightly can face every other challenge. The church that gets it wrong has nothing left to offer.

Now: The Judaizer error never stays buried. It reappears in every generation dressed in different clothes: the idea that grace plus something — baptism, church membership, moral effort, liturgical compliance — constitutes salvation. The Jerusalem Council’s answer is permanent and non-negotiable: the grace of the Lord Jesus alone. The church’s task in every generation is to say it clearly, defend it stubbornly, and live it joyfully.

16.title: Into Macedonia
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. <sup>2</sup>He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. <sup>3</sup>Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. <sup>4</sup>As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. <sup>6</sup>And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. <sup>7</sup>And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. <sup>8</sup>So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. <sup>9</sup>And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” <sup>10</sup>And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <sup>11</sup>So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, <sup>12</sup>and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days. <sup>13</sup>And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. <sup>14</sup>One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. <sup>15</sup>And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us. <sup>16</sup>As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. <sup>17</sup>She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” <sup>18</sup>And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour. <sup>19</sup>But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. <sup>20</sup>And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. <sup>21</sup>They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.” <sup>22</sup>The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. <sup>23</sup>And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. <sup>24</sup>Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks. <sup>25</sup>About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, <sup>26</sup>and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. <sup>27</sup>When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. <sup>28</sup>But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” <sup>29</sup>And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. <sup>30</sup>Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” <sup>31</sup>And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” <sup>32</sup>And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. <sup>33</sup>And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. <sup>34</sup>Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. <sup>35</sup>But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” <sup>36</sup>And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.” <sup>37</sup>But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” <sup>38</sup>The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. <sup>39</sup>So they came and apologized to them. And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. <sup>40</sup>So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
16.overview:
Paul’s second journey begins by revisiting the churches of the first. At Lystra he recruits Timothy, a young believer with a Jewish mother and Greek father, and circumcises him so that his ministry among Jews will not be hindered. Then the Spirit repeatedly blocks their plans: they are kept from preaching in the province of Asia and stopped from entering Bithynia, until at Troas, on the Aegean coast, Paul sees a vision of a man of Macedonia begging, “Come over and help us.” Here Luke slips into “we”: he has joined the team. They cross into Europe and go to Philippi, a Roman colony settled with army veterans, proud of its Roman status, where there were too few Jews even for a synagogue. By the river on the Sabbath they find women praying, and the Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a businesswoman who traded in expensive purple cloth, who is baptised with her household and opens her home to them.

Then trouble. Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a slave girl whose fortune-telling made money for her owners, who drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them, as Jews, of disturbing the city with un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and put in the stocks in the inner prison. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens the doors and loosens everyone’s chains. The jailer, about to kill himself, cries out, “What must I do to be saved?” and is told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and he rejoices that he has come to believe in God. In the morning, when the magistrates order their release, Paul reveals that they are Roman citizens, beaten without trial, and insists that the officials come and escort them out, protecting the young church before he leaves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Lystra Paul found a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers there and in Iconium. Paul wanted to take him on the journey, so he circumcised him because of the Jews in the area, who all knew his father was Greek. As they travelled from town to town, they delivered the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in numbers. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. When they reached the border of Mysia and tried to enter Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them, so they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. During the night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them. After the vision, Luke writes, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. From Troas we sailed straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a Roman colony and leading city of that district of Macedonia, and stayed there several days. On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down to speak to the women who had gathered. One of them was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, a worshipper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and her household had been baptised, she invited us to stay at her house if we considered her a believer in the Lord, and she persuaded us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit's Direction of Mission

The second missionary journey is notable for the Spirit's specific prevention and redirection: 'they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia... the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them' to go to Bithynia. The door to Europe opens only because two Asian doors close. Reformed missiology sees here the sovereignty of the Spirit over missional geography: the Spirit is not merely the empowerer of human initiative but the director of the mission's course. The church's task is to be obedient to both open doors and closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia's household was the first European church — gathered in a businesswoman's home around the word of God and the Lord's Supper. Now: The church continues to be built wherever the Lord opens hearts — in homes as often as in purpose-built buildings, through business relationships as often as through formal religious programs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium.

Meaning first. Acts 16 tells how the gospel crossed into Europe. Paul gains a young helper, Timothy. The Spirit closes doors in Asia and Bithynia, and opens one in a vision: Come over to Macedonia. In Philippi three very different people are saved: Lydia, a wealthy businesswoman whose heart the Lord opened; a slave girl freed from a spirit; and a Roman jailer who asks, What must I do to be saved? Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, sing at midnight, and see God shake the prison. Every kind of person, every kind of bondage, and one answer: Believe in the Lord Jesus. It is a chapter about the risen Lord steering his own mission by his Spirit, opening hearts, breaking chains, and gathering into one house church people the world would never have put in one room.

Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. Lystra. Stop there for a moment before meeting Timothy, because Luke expects you to remember what happened in that town. It is where a crowd tried to sacrifice oxen to Paul and, a few days later, stoned him and dragged him out of the city for dead (14:19). He is walking back into it, on purpose, for the second time. And what he collects there is the best thing he ever got out of any city.

A disciple was there, named Timothy. Every clause of that is doing something. He is already a disciple, converted on the first journey, in the aftermath of the stoning, which makes it possible he was among the disciples standing round Paul’s body outside the wall (2 Timothy 3:10–11). His mother is a Jewish believer; Paul later names her and her mother, Eunice and Lois, and tells Timothy that the faith he has lived in dwelt first in them (2 Timothy 1:5), and that from childhood he had been acquainted with the sacred writings (2 Timothy 3:15). Three generations, and the men are missing from the account entirely. He became Paul’s closest co-worker, his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), and received two letters.

The son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. A mixed marriage. The father, a Gentile, perhaps dead by now, since Luke says nothing more of him, was evidently not a believer, and he had not allowed his son to be circumcised, which tells you which way the household had leaned while he was alive. So Timothy grew up in a home divided down the middle: a Jewish mother teaching him the Scriptures from infancy, a Greek father who wanted none of it, and a boy belonging fully to neither community. To the Jews of Lystra he was the son of a mixed marriage, uncircumcised, irregular. To the Greeks he was his mother’s son, and odd with it.

Between two worlds. That matters more than it looks, because it is exactly the shape of the church Paul is building. The man who will carry more of Paul’s correspondence and receive two of his letters was formed by belonging to two worlds and being fully at home in neither, until the gospel gave him a third. If you have grown up between things, a divided home, two cultures, a family where the faith came down one side only and was resisted on the other, Timothy is in Scripture partly for you. The thing that made him awkward is the thing that made him useful.

He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. Two churches, eighteen miles or so apart, and both of them volunteered the same verdict. A good reputation is a qualification for ministry (1 Timothy 3:7). Paul did not interview him; he asked around, and the answer came back from people who had watched him grow up. That is still the soundest way anybody has found to identify a man for ministry: not what he says about himself, and not how he performs, but what the people who have known him for years say when they are asked.

I am the only believer in my home. Is there hope for my children? Yes, and Timothy is one of the Bible’s answers. His father did not believe, yet a mother and grandmother quietly taught him the Scriptures, and God made him a pastor. Paul tells a believer married to an unbeliever that the children are not shut out but set in a place of blessing (1 Corinthians 7:14). Read the Bible with your children, pray with them and for them, take them to church, and live the faith gladly in front of them. You cannot convert them, but you can put the word in front of them, and God is pleased to use exactly that.

In a sentence. Paul came to Derbe and Lystra, where there was a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers in Lystra and Iconium.

On a Tuesday. Mothers and grandmothers, teach your children the Scriptures. God may make a Timothy of them. Choose one passage to read with a child or grandchild this week. And ask yourself what the people who have known you longest would say if a pastor asked about you.

For worship. The God who shepherds the generations was at work in a divided house in Lystra, in a grandmother’s faith and a mother’s teaching, long before Paul came back down the road. He wastes nothing: not the stones of Lystra, not the awkwardness of a mixed home, not the quiet years of Bible reading at a kitchen table. The Lord who called Timothy is the faithful God who keeps covenant to a thousand generations of those who love him.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois. He became Paul’s closest co-worker.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him. To replace John Mark as helper.

And he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. Read that with chapter 15 still open and it looks impossible. Paul has just won a public fight against men who said Gentiles must be circumcised. He is at this moment carrying the letter that settles it. And the first thing he does on the road is circumcise his new colleague. The apparent contradiction dissolves once you see two things, and the second is the one usually missed.

First, the principle. What may never be conceded as a condition may be freely chosen as a courtesy, and the moment somebody makes it a condition, it must be refused absolutely. Paul held both ends of that at once, and the pair of cases that proves it is set out at 15:1. The point here is that it is the letter in his bag that makes this possible. Because Jerusalem has ruled that circumcision saves nobody, Paul is free to circumcise a man without the act meaning anything about salvation at all. Settle the doctrine and you are at liberty in the practice. Leave the doctrine unsettled and every practical decision becomes a battle.

Second, Timothy was not a Gentile. And this is the part that is usually skipped. By the Jewish reckoning that came to prevail, a child’s standing followed the mother, and his mother was a Jewess. Timothy was a Jew. An uncircumcised Jew, which was not a mild irregularity but a standing scandal, and one his own town knew about: they all knew that his father was a Greek. An uncircumcised Jew would be seen as an apostate, and would close synagogue doors to Paul.

The difference with Titus. Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5). Titus was a Gentile, and the gospel was at stake. Timothy was ethnically Jewish, and circumcision was a matter of removing an obstacle. The same act can be right or wrong depending on why it is done. When circumcision is demanded as a condition of grace, refuse; when it is chosen to open a door, it can be freedom (1 Corinthians 7:19). This is not a Gentile being made to conform. It is a Jew whose Jewishness had been left incomplete by a father who wanted no part of it.

Because of the Jews. And the reason given is entirely missional. Paul’s method in every town is to start in the synagogue. An uncircumcised companion at his elbow would have ended that conversation in the first five minutes, in every city, for the rest of the journey: not over the gospel, but over a distraction. Paul became a Jew to the Jews to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

What it cost Timothy. Now consider what it cost the man himself, because we read the verse as a decision of Paul’s and it was an operation on Timothy. He was an adult. There was no anaesthetic. There would have been days of pain, some risk, and then a long walk. His first recorded act as a missionary is to submit to that, for the sake of getting a hearing among people who had looked down on him his whole life for the very thing he was now having corrected.

How do I know when to adapt for the sake of the gospel and when to refuse? Ask two questions. First, would doing this compromise the gospel or require me to sin? If someone says you must do it to be right with God, or if Scripture forbids it, refuse. Second, would it remove an unnecessary obstacle for the people I want to reach? Then you are free to do it, even at cost. So a missionary may learn a language, change his diet, dress modestly by local standards, or give up a legitimate habit. But he may not join in idolatry, hide the cross, or add conditions to grace. Freedom in practice; firmness in the gospel.

In a sentence. Paul wanted Timothy to go with him, and circumcised him because of the Jews in that area, who all knew his father was a Greek.

On a Tuesday. Which is a searching thing to put next to our own ideas of what serving Christ costs. Timothy gave up his comfort and his body before he had preached a sermon, and he did it for people who had not asked him to and would probably never know. The question it puts is not whether you would die for Christ, which is a question most Christians will never be asked. It is whether you would accept an unnecessary personal cost, unremarked, to remove a small obstacle between somebody else and the gospel. Name one such cost you could accept this week.

For worship. Never compromise the gospel. But be willing to give up your rights to win others. Christ did both perfectly. He never yielded an inch of the truth, and he laid aside every right he had, taking the form of a servant, born under the law, circumcised on the eighth day, so that he might redeem those under the law. The Lord who bore that small wound in infancy bore the great wounds at Calvary, and every cost his servants accept for the gospel is a share in his self-giving.
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.

They delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders. Here is what happened to the Jerusalem Council. It went into a bag and was carried around Galatia on foot by two men and a young apprentice, and read out in one small congregation after another. Decisions (dogmata) are the council’s decrees. The same Paul who circumcised Timothy delivered the letter that freed Gentiles from circumcision. No contradiction: grace for salvation, love for fellowship.

When doctrine is settled. That is worth pausing on, because we are inclined to think of doctrine as settled when the argument is won. It was not settled when James gave his judgment, or when the letter was drafted, or even when it was read aloud in Antioch. It was settled in Iconium when a handful of frightened Gentile believers, who had heard the rumours and had no way of checking them, watched Paul unfold a document from the apostles telling them they were already in. And notice which churches these are. Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch: the exact towns of the first journey, and the towns most likely to have been visited by the men who had gone out and unsettled everybody (15:24). The letter is being taken to precisely the addresses where the damage was done. Somebody had thought about where it needed to go.

So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. Then Luke’s summary, and it is one of his periodic progress notes (6:7; 9:31). Take the two halves in order, because the order is an argument. They were strengthened in the faith first, made solid in what they believed, and then they grew. Luke does not present these as two separate blessings that happened to arrive together. The so at the head of the sentence ties them to the delivery of the decrees. Strength and growth together. Clear teaching about grace strengthens churches.

Assurance first. A church that does not know where it stands cannot grow, because it has nothing steady to invite anybody into, and its members are too busy checking their own footing to look outward. Remove the doubt and both things follow at once. It is the same movement as in Antioch, where the letter was read and the congregation rejoiced (15:31): assurance comes first, and then a church has something to give away.

Is doctrine the enemy of evangelism?
