So if you have wondered whether doctrinal precision is the enemy of evangelistic warmth, whether time spent getting the gospel exactly right is time stolen from telling people about it, here is Luke’s answer in one sentence, and he puts the causal word in the middle of it. Churches that know clearly that they are saved by grace alone are freed to love, to welcome and to witness. Churches that are vague about it either harden into legalism or drift into having nothing to say. Good doctrine is not the opposite of warm evangelism; it is its fuel.

In a sentence. As they went through the towns, they passed on the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in number.

On a Tuesday. Churches grow strong when they understand grace. Teach it clearly. If you were asked by a new Christian how a person is made right with God, could you explain it from Scripture in a few minutes? Practise this week, until you can.

For worship. The Lord builds his church on the truth, and he adds to it daily those who are being saved. The same Christ who settled the gospel at the council carried it on foot to the frightened, and still sends his word to the places where his people have been unsettled. He strengthens and he multiplies, and the growth is his, for he alone gives the increase.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.

Having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. Two closed doors in two verses, and both of them shut by God. Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its capital. Not the continent. Feel the strangeness of it first, before drawing any comfort. These men are doing exactly what they were commissioned to do. Asia is a populous Roman province with great cities in it, Ephesus among them, and they are forbidden to preach there. There is no suggestion of sin, no rebuke, no correction of a wrong motive. Two good men with a right aim are stopped.

We are not told how. And Luke does not tell us how. Not a word about the mechanism: no vision, no prophet, no illness, no closed road. It may have been a prophecy, an inner conviction, circumstances. Every commentator has a theory and every theory is a guess. Luke’s silence here is worth as much as his information elsewhere, because it stops us turning the episode into a method. If we knew how the Spirit forbade them, we would immediately start looking for the same signal in our own lives and grading each other on our ability to detect it.

They attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. Bithynia was a rich province in the north, on the Black Sea. Then the phrase, which is unusual enough to have been noticed for centuries. Luke has called him the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Lord, and simply the Spirit; this is the only place in Acts where he is called the Spirit of Jesus. It is a unique phrase, showing that the Spirit is the Spirit of the risen Jesus. Paul will use close relatives of it: the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), the Spirit of his Son (Galatians 4:6), the Spirit of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:19). And it appears exactly where the direction of the mission is being taken out of the missionaries’ hands. That is not decoration. The one who is steering is the same Jesus who said you will be my witnesses to the end of the earth, and he is doing the steering personally. Jesus directs his mission by his Spirit. The men on the road are not executing a strategy they devised and asking God to bless it. They are being moved.

Closed doors. Paul and his team did not sit and wait. They kept moving, and the Spirit closed doors. God guides moving feet. A closed door is guidance too. The comfort is real: a closed door may be the hand of God, and the fact that a good and reasonable plan has failed is not evidence that God has stopped paying attention. Everything you can see says Asia, and the answer is no, and the no is not a punishment.

They did not know at the time. The guard is that these men did not know that at the time. We read verses 6 and 7 already knowing about verse 9, and that ruins the experience of them. Standing on that road, they had two refusals and no explanation, no destination, and no assurance whatever that anything was being led towards. They found out later. Almost everybody finds out later, and a good many never find out at all.

Was the ban on preaching in Asia permanent? No. It was for that time and that journey; within a few years Paul spent two years in Ephesus, in Asia, and all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord (19:10). God was ordering the mission, not shutting a door for good. Not that God did not care for Asia; it was not yet the time.

Not every closed door has a Macedonia behind it. So do not turn this into a rule that every setback is a redirection with a Macedonia waiting behind it. Some closed doors are simply closed, and Scripture does not promise you the explanation. What it shows you here is that the Lord of the mission is capable of steering by refusal, and that two of the best men who ever lived spent an unknown number of weeks walking in what felt like the wrong direction with no idea why.

How can I tell whether a closed door is God’s guidance or an obstacle I should push through? Often you cannot tell at once, and that is all right. Some obstacles are meant to be overcome by perseverance, as Paul kept preaching through opposition; others are God’s no. Pray, look honestly at your motives, ask counsel of mature believers, and check that you are not running from duty or toward mere comfort. If the way stays shut after reasonable effort, accept it without bitterness and look for the open path. God holds both the doors and you, and he is not offended by sincere mistakes made in obedience.

In a sentence. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, since the Holy Spirit kept them from speaking the word in Asia, and when they reached Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not let them.

On a Tuesday. When God closes a door, trust him. He is leading you somewhere else. Name a plan that has been blocked recently, and pray over it in these words: Lord, you are steering; I will keep walking.

For worship. The risen Jesus is not an absent founder. He sits at the Father’s right hand and steers his church by his Spirit, closing what he will close and opening what he will open, and no one can shut what he opens. His refusals are as loving as his permissions. The same Lord who stopped Paul at the border of Bithynia was already preparing a riverbank in Macedonia and a woman’s heart to hear.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.

So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. A few words, and they cover a long, dispiriting walk. Look at the map they were working with. Refused Asia to the south-west. Refused Bithynia to the north-east. What is left is the road running north-west, and they take it, through country Luke does not even say they preached in, until they run out of land. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy. There is nowhere further to go without a boat. That is the position: two apostles, a young colleague, several hundred miles behind them, no commission for anywhere they can reach on foot, standing on a beach.

It looked like failure. And it is worth saying plainly that at that moment nothing in their situation looked like guidance. It looked like failure. The strategy had collapsed, the obvious fields were shut, and they had been walking for weeks toward a place they had no reason to go to. Perhaps they were puzzled. Anyone who has kept obeying while everything visible was going wrong knows exactly what that road felt like, and knows too that hindsight is no help while you are on it.

What Troas actually was. Then consider what Troas actually was, because they could not see this either. It is the port beside the ruins of Troy, the crossing point between two continents, and the place from which any ship for Macedonia would sail. Every refusal had been moving them toward the one town in the world from which Europe was two days away. God had a plan.

A meeting on a beach. There is something else here that they could not possibly have known. Troas is where Luke joins them. In two verses the pronouns will change from they to we, and the man who wrote a quarter of the New Testament walks into the story at the town they arrived at because everywhere else was forbidden. So the two refusals did not merely reroute a mission. They put an apostle and a historian in the same room. Neither of them knew that when they got there, and neither of them chose it.

What should I do when I have reached the end of my road and can see nothing ahead? Do what Paul did: keep doing the next faithful thing where you are, and wait for God to show the next step. Troas was not wasted time; it was where Luke joined and the call came. Keep up the ordinary means of grace: prayer, Scripture, the company of believers. Be honest with God about your confusion, as the psalmists were. Do not force a door just to end the uncertainty. And remember that the God who brought you to the shoreline knows exactly where the boat is.

In a sentence. So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.

On a Tuesday. If you feel you are standing on a beach with nowhere left to go, write down the faithful things still in front of you today, however small, and do them. The next step often appears only when you have reached the end of the last one.

For worship. When you reach the end of your road, God has a way you haven’t seen. Which is the only honest way to take comfort from this verse. Not that your closed doors are certainly leading somewhere you will get to see; they may not be, and Scripture does not promise it. But that the God who shut Asia and Bithynia was, the whole time, arranging a meeting on a beach that neither man would have thought to ask for. He is the Lord of the shoreline, who made a way through the sea for his people once, and makes one still.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

And a vision appeared to Paul in the night. After two refusals and no explanation, a request.

A man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, Come over to Macedonia and help us. And notice that it is a request: not an order, not a rebuke for having gone the wrong way, not a strategy briefing. A man stands there and asks for help. Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece, and this is the gospel’s first entry into Europe. The cry for help: the world’s deepest need, though it does not know it, is the gospel.

Concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. Then look at what happens in the next sentence, because it is easy to miss and it is the most important thing in the paragraph for anyone who has ever wanted God to make something plain. Concluding (symbibazontes) means putting things together, reasoning to a conclusion, working it out. Even after a night vision of a man pleading with him, Paul did not simply know what to do. The vision had to be interpreted, and the team did it together (note the plural), and what they arrived at was a judgment, not a certainty handed down. The man in the dream had not said preach the gospel. He had said help us. Working out that the help meant the gospel was the missionaries’ own conclusion. The closed doors, the vision, and the team’s discernment together showed God’s will. Guidance is often confirmed by putting the pieces together, with others.

If Paul had to conclude. That should reset most of what Christians expect from guidance. Here is the clearest, most dramatic, most unambiguous piece of direction in the New Testament outside the Damascus road, and it still required sanctified reasoning by a group of people talking it over in the morning. If Paul had to conclude, you are not failing when you have to conclude.

Immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia. And notice the speed. Having reasoned it out, they moved the same day. Long deliberation and instant obedience are not enemies; here they are consecutive.

We. Now the pronoun, which is one of the quiet marvels of the New Testament. It is the first of the we passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), where Luke joins the story as an eyewitness. Up to verse 9 the narrative runs they. From verse 10 it is we sought, we made a direct voyage, we remained. The author has joined the party at Troas and has said so by changing a pronoun and nothing else. Luke may have joined Paul at Troas, perhaps as his doctor. He never explains it. He never introduces himself, never says how he met them, and never names himself anywhere in either of his two books, and between them they make up about a quarter of the New Testament. The only place Luke appears in his own history is inside the word we.

Does the Spirit still guide like this, through visions and direct prohibitions? This was part of the founding of the church, when God gave the apostles direct revelation. Today, with Scripture complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel, the needs before us and the doors he opens and closes in his providence. He may still use circumstances to close a way, as here; but we do not wait for visions to know what to do.

A pronoun. Two things follow. The first is historical: from here on, large stretches of Acts are the report of somebody who was in the boat, and the sober, unshowy way he reports himself is part of why he is believed. The second is a matter of temperament, and it is a rebuke to the way most of us tell the story of what God has done with us. A man was present at the founding of the church in Europe, sailed with Paul, survived the shipwreck, and stayed with him to the last cold months in Rome when everyone else had gone: Luke alone is with me (2 Timothy 4:11). And in his own account of all of it he is a pronoun.

Who is crying out for help today? Everyone who does not know Christ, whether or not they put it that way. The cry rarely sounds like a request for the gospel. It sounds like loneliness, anxiety, addiction, a marriage falling apart, a question about death at a funeral, a teenager’s despair, a refugee’s need for a friend. The man in the vision asked for help; the missionaries understood that the deepest help was the gospel. Meet real needs with real kindness, and do not stop there: the greatest help you can give anyone is Christ.

In a sentence. In the night Paul had a vision of a man from Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them, and after this vision they immediately set out for Macedonia, concluding that God had called them to preach the gospel there.

On a Tuesday. When you face a decision, put the pieces together with others: Scripture, circumstances, counsel, prayer. Then, having concluded, move. And next time you tell someone what God has done through you, try telling it as Luke did, with yourself as a pronoun and God as the subject.

For worship. The world is crying, Come and help us. Answer with the gospel. The Son of God heard that cry from a whole lost world, and he came over, not across a strait but from heaven to earth, to help us in the only way that could save. Every missionary crossing since is an echo of his. And the Spirit who sent Paul to Macedonia still sends his people to the places where the cry is loudest, carrying the only help that lasts.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece — the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days.

So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis. Luke the traveller shows here. A direct voyage: straight across, no tacking, with a following wind. Two days. On the return journey later, the same crossing against the wind takes five (20:6). Somebody on that boat noticed the difference and remembered it for years. It is a small thing and it is worth having, because it is the sort of detail nobody invents. And it is the sort of thing a man notices when he is glad to be going. Neapolis was Philippi’s port.

And from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. Then Philippi, and Luke gives it two credentials. Named after Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great. A colony was not simply a town with Romans in it. It was a piece of Rome transplanted, a little Rome abroad: founded to settle discharged legionaries, governed under Roman law, its citizens holding Roman citizenship, its magistrates styled like Rome’s, its people exempt from certain taxes and immensely proud of the whole arrangement. Philippi had been made one after the battle fought on that plain in which Antony and Octavian destroyed the assassins of Julius Caesar, and it had been settled twice over with veterans. It was, in its own estimation, Italy in Macedonia.

Why Luke mentions it. Hold that beside what is about to happen. The gospel’s first European address is the proudest, most self-consciously Roman town in the province, and it will be entered through a women’s prayer meeting, held outside the gate because the city could not muster a synagogue. Within a chapter the men of that colony will beat two Jews without trial, and then discover, to their horror, that the Jews were Romans and they were not entitled to. Luke puts the city’s Roman standing in the introduction because the whole story turns on it twice: once when the charge is customs that are not lawful for us as Romans (v. 21), and once when it costs the magistrates their dignity in the street (v. 39).

Citizens of heaven. Paul later wrote to the church here: our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), a phrase they would understand. A Philippian lived in Macedonia but belonged to Rome, kept Rome’s laws and took his identity from a city he might never have seen. The church at Philippi learned to see itself the same way: a colony of heaven on earth.

We remained in this city some days. A flat sentence, and it means they were looking for a way in and had not yet found one. There is no synagogue to preach in. For several days the mission to Europe consists of three or four men walking round a strange town waiting for the Sabbath.

What does it mean in practice to be a citizen of heaven? It means your deepest loyalty, identity and hope belong to Christ’s kingdom, while you live as a good resident where God has placed you. You obey the laws of the land unless they command sin, work honestly, seek the good of your town (Jeremiah 29:7), and pray for those in authority. But you do not take your values from the surrounding culture, you are not crushed when it rejects you, and you do not set your hope on its success. Like a Philippian veteran, you live by the customs of home, and you wait for your King to come from there (Philippians 3:20).

In a sentence. Sailing from Troas, they went straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a leading city of that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony, where they stayed some days.

On a Tuesday. You are a citizen of heaven living in a colony on earth. Live by its laws. Ask today: in what one decision am I living by the customs of my city rather than the customs of my King?

For worship. The Lord who rules the winds gave his messengers a fair crossing into Europe, and he rules the nations they entered. Rome’s proud colony would pass away; the colony of heaven planted there would not. Christ is the King of the city that has foundations, and every believer, in whatever town of whatever empire, is already enrolled as its citizen.
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.

And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer. Take that sentence apart, because every clause is a step down. Outside the gate: not in the city. Foreign cults were often required to keep their meetings beyond the walls of a Roman colony, and in any case there was nothing inside to go to. Where we supposed there was a place of prayer: they were not sure. They had been in the town some days and were reduced to guessing where a handful of Jews might gather on a Sabbath, and going out to see. The riverside was probably the River Gangites, west of the city.

No synagogue. And behind all of it lies a fact Luke leaves you to work out: Philippi had no synagogue. Jews met to pray in the open by the river. It took ten Jewish men to constitute a synagogue. The leading city of the district, a Roman colony of some thousands, could not produce ten Jewish men.

And we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. So this is how Christianity arrived in Europe. Not in the forum, not in a basilica, not before the magistrates. A few travellers walked out of a side gate on a Saturday morning, found a group of women praying by a river, sat down on the bank, and started talking. The first gospel preaching in Europe was to a women’s prayer meeting by a river. Paul, the former Pharisee, sat down and taught women. The gospel honours women.

The posture. Notice even the posture. In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch Paul stood up and motioned with his hand, in the manner of a public speaker addressing a hall (13:16). Here he sits down. It is the ordinary posture of a Jewish teacher, and it is also simply what you do when you join a small group on a riverbank. The same man, the same message, and an entirely different register, because the room was different, and he could tell.

No platform. There is a lesson in that which the church keeps having to relearn. The apostles had no platform in Philippi and did not wait for one. They did not hire a hall, or hold out for a hearing before somebody important, or decide that a handful of women was too small a return on a two-day sea crossing and several hundred miles of walking. They went where people were praying and sat down among them.

The women at the river. And here is the thing worth measuring. Out of that riverbank conversation came the church at Philippi: the congregation that alone supported Paul when no other church did (Philippians 4:15–16), that sent him money in prison, that he called his joy and crown. The single warmest letter in the New Testament was written to the people who started as the women at the river.

Does Paul’s practice here mean women may preach in church? Paul taught the gospel to these women, which shows how highly the gospel values women as hearers, disciples and partners in the work; women like Lydia, Euodia and Syntyche laboured beside him (Philippians 4:2–3). That is a different question from who should preach and exercise authority in the gathered church, which Paul addresses elsewhere, reserving the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the congregation to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Both truths stand: women are equal heirs of grace and indispensable in gospel work, and the church’s pastoral oversight is entrusted to men who serve with self-giving love.

In a sentence. On the Sabbath they went outside the city gate to the river, where they expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down and spoke to the women gathered there.

On a Tuesday. If your own service to God feels absurdly small in proportion to the effort it took to get there, a handful of people, a conversation nobody will hear about, an evening that produced nothing you can point to, this verse is the shape of most of what God actually does. Nobody at that riverside knew they were founding the church in Europe. Go to your small meeting this week as though it mattered, because it does.

For worship. Great things can begin in small prayer meetings. Don’t despise them. The Lord of the harvest planted his church in Europe not in a palace but by a river, among praying women, through a man sitting on the bank. He chooses what is weak and lowly to shame the strong, so that no one may boast before him. Every great work of his began, somewhere, with a few people praying and someone sitting down to speak of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us.

A woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. Luke tells us four things about the first person in Europe to believe the gospel, and together they make a portrait of somebody no strategist would have picked. She is a woman, in a world where that meant her testimony carried little weight in a court and her name would not normally appear in a history. She is from Thyatira, which is in Asia, the province the Spirit had just forbidden them to preach in. They were stopped from going to her country, and she had already come to theirs; now an Asian is converted in Europe. She is a seller of purple goods, which was the luxury trade: the finest purple came from shellfish, took vast quantities to produce, and clothed magistrates and emperors; Thyatira was famous for its dyeing trade, and a woman running that business at a distance from home was a person of means, with a house big enough for a household and, shortly, for a church (v. 40). And she is a worshiper of God: one of the God-fearers, a Gentile who had attached herself to the God of Israel without becoming a Jew.

No strategist would have picked her. So the vision showed a man of Macedonia asking for help, and the first person helped is a foreign businesswoman. Luke sets the two side by side within five verses and offers no comment at all. God answered the request in the dream with somebody outside every category in it.

The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. Then the sentence that explains everything. One of the clearest statements of God’s work in conversion. Paul spoke; the Lord opened. Paul could reach her ears; only the Lord could open her heart. This is effectual grace: God opens hearts to receive the gospel (2 Corinthians 4:6; Ephesians 1:18). Lydia did pay attention, really, freely; but she did so because the Lord opened her heart. Both human preaching and divine opening are needed.

Effectual calling. That phrase, the Lord opened her heart, is one of Scripture’s clearest pictures of what the Reformed call effectual calling: Lydia believed because God first opened her heart, grace the cause, faith the fruit. Paul preached (the means), but only the Lord could open the heart (the power); a closed heart no sermon can pry open. (Arminian brothers say grace opened her heart while leaving her free to refuse; the Reformed read the opening itself as the decisive work that brings faith to be; see 13:48.) For you it is pure comfort and humility: if you believe, it is because God opened your heart, so no boasting, all thanks.

And after she was baptized, and her household as well. What was her household? In the first century a household was far larger than our nuclear family: servants and slaves, employees, dependants, sometimes extended kin, all under one roof and authority. Lydia seems a woman of means heading her own house (no husband mentioned), so her household likely means her servants and dependants, perhaps children, though Luke gives no roster.

And did they all believe, or were they simply baptised? Honestly, the text does not say: Luke records that Lydia believed (the Lord opened her heart) and that her household was baptised, but nothing explicit about the household’s faith. That silence is why this is one of the household baptism texts in the friendly baptism disagreement (see on 2:39). Believer’s-baptist readers fill the gap from the other households said to believe and rejoice (the jailer’s, v. 34; Crispus’s, 18:8), concluding Lydia’s household believed and were baptised as believers, Luke compressing. Covenant-baptist readers note that only Lydia’s faith is mentioned, yet the whole household is baptised on the head’s faith, the old covenant pattern (Genesis 17), including dependants and any little ones. Scripture leaves the gap; each side fills it from its view of the sign. The first is the more likely, since in the two other households Luke describes, faith is explicit (v. 34; 18:8). What is beyond dispute, and a comfort, is that God loves to save not lone individuals but whole households: the conversion of one is so often the open door of grace to a home (compare v. 31). Pray, then, for your whole household.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists see household baptisms as including infants, and so supporting infant baptism. Verdict: no infants are mentioned in any household baptism in Acts. In the jailer’s case, the word was spoken to all in the house and the whole household believed and rejoiced (vv. 32, 34). In Cornelius’s, all heard and received the Spirit (10:44). The households baptised were households who heard and believed. Credobaptists hold this charitably, respecting brothers and sisters who read it differently.

Honouring our paedobaptist brothers. It should be said warmly that many of the most godly and learned Christians in history, among them the Westminster divines, Calvin and countless faithful pastors, have baptised the infants of believers out of a sincere conviction that God’s covenant embraces the children of his people, as it did in Abraham’s day. They do not think baptism saves the child, and they long for every baptised child to come to personal faith. We differ from them on who should receive the sign, and we think the New Testament pattern is clearest when baptism follows faith, as it does for Lydia herself. But we share with them the same gospel, the same Saviour, and the same hope for our children.

If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay. And then the last thing she does, which is the first recorded act of any Christian in Europe. Faith shows itself at once in hospitality. Look at how she frames it. She does not offer hospitality; she puts her new standing on the table and makes them rule on it. If you have judged me to be faithful: the sentence dares them to say that her conversion was real and then decline to eat at her table. A woman baptised that morning has understood, within hours, that being received by Christ means being received by his people, and she will not let the two come apart.

And she prevailed upon us. The word means she forced the issue, pressed until they gave way. They said no, or hesitated: Paul was careful about being kept at anybody’s expense, and it is the one thing he mentions about this very church afterwards, that Philippi alone was allowed to support him (Philippians 4:15). And she overruled him. It is one of the very few places in Acts where somebody argues Paul down and wins, and it is a new convert of a few hours. So the first church in Europe met in that house, and it began because a woman would not take no for an answer about having people to stay. Not a strategy, not a building fund, not a preaching licence. A door held open until the missionaries walked through it.

A room. Which is worth saying to anyone who has concluded that they have no ministry because they cannot teach, or lead, or speak in public. Lydia’s contribution to the New Testament is a room. The letter to the Philippians exists because of what she did with her house.

If God must open the heart, is there any point in my praying and speaking? Every point. Lydia’s heart was opened while Paul was speaking, not instead of his speaking. God uses the very means he commands: the word spoken, and prayer for those who hear. So pray before you talk to someone about Christ, asking the Lord to open their heart. Then speak as clearly and kindly as you can. If they do not respond, you have not failed, and they are not beyond hope. You did your part; leave the opening to the only one who can do it, and keep praying.

In a sentence. One of the listeners was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira who worshipped God, and the Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message, and after she and her household were baptised, she urged them to stay at her home if they judged her faithful to the Lord, and persuaded them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Lord to open hearts as you speak. You can reach ears; only he can reach hearts. And look at your home: whom could you invite to your table this week for the sake of Christ, a missionary, a new Christian, a lonely member of your church, a neighbour who has never been in a Christian home?

For worship. The Lord opened her heart. There is no sweeter sentence about conversion in the whole book. The same Lord who opened the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf opens hearts by his Spirit, gently and unfailingly, so that a sinner who could not attend begins to listen and to love. If you believe, he did this for you. He knocked, and then he opened the door from the inside, and he came in to stay.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A slave girl whose fortune-telling earned money for her owners follows the missionaries for days, shouting that they are servants of the Most High God, until Paul casts the spirit out of her in Jesus’ name. Her owners, robbed of their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them as Jews of promoting un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens every door and loosens every chain. The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul, falls before them and asks what he must do to be saved. They tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and speak the word to his whole household. He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and they rejoice together over a meal. In the morning Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the alarmed magistrates come in person to escort them out. After encouraging the believers at Lydia’s house, they leave.
verseByVerse.theology:
Midnight Praise and the Ministry of Suffering

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight — after being stripped and beaten with rods — and the other prisoners listen. The praise is not despite the suffering but in it: the same Spirit who fills the church for witness fills the suffering church for worship. Reformed theology sees in this midnight scene the confirmation of what Paul will later write: 'we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance' (Romans 5:3). The songs at midnight are the most powerful proclamation the prisoners that night will ever hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked 'What must I do to be saved?' — the question of Pentecost (2:37) repeated in a Philippian prison. The answer is the same: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.' Now: The gospel's answer to the question of salvation is always the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.”

We were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. Before anything else, notice what she is. Luke gives her no name, and he gives her three kinds of ownership: she is a slave, she is possessed, and she is an income. Exploited twice over, by a demon and by her owners. Three things have hold of her and not one of them is her own. She is the most thoroughly owned human being in the book of Acts. And she is the first person the gospel meets on the way to the place of prayer in Europe.

The python spirit. The spirit of divination translates the Greek pneuma pythōna: literally a Python spirit, as the ESV notes. In ancient Greek religion, the Python was the great serpent that guarded the sanctuary at Delphi before Apollo killed it and claimed the site; thereafter, the Delphic priestess (the Pythia) was said to speak her oracles under the inspiration of the Python’s spirit. The Pythian oracle at Delphi was the most prestigious in the ancient world: Greek cities, kings, and generals consulted it before major military campaigns and political decisions. Slave girls believed to have such a spirit were therefore Delphic-style commercial oracles of the highest value, and their owners made substantial fortunes from their prophetic services. People believed such girls spoke Apollo’s messages. She was possessed by a demon. Paul’s encounter at Philippi is thus a direct confrontation with the dominant prophetic tradition of the Greek world: Apollo’s oracle, in miniature, following the apostles through a Macedonian street.

These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation. The girl’s testimony is formally true (Paul and his companions are servants of the Most High God proclaiming salvation), but its source is demonic, as demons spoke true words about Jesus (Mark 1:24; 5:7). This is the most dangerous kind of false witness: accurate content, corrupt source. A Delphic-style oracle endorsing Paul would associate the apostolic mission with the occult establishment, potentially drawing curiosity-seekers rather than genuine converts, and tying the gospel to the very prophetic system it was displacing. Paul is not annoyed at the content but at the source and its implications.

How the crowd heard it. There is one more thing in her words, and it is the practical reason the shouting had to stop. To a Jewish ear, the Most High God is a title for the God of Israel. To a Greek ear in a Macedonian colony, it was a title people used of Zeus. And the Greek behind the way of salvation has no article: a way of salvation, exactly what every cult in a Roman town claimed to offer, and exactly how a pagan crowd would have heard her. So her testimony was not merely true from a bad source. Heard by the crowd it was actually endorsing something else: two more travelling holy men, agents of the high god under whatever name, with one more route to blessedness for sale. Every word could be agreed to by a pagan without changing a single thing he believed. Endorsement from a demon is no help to the gospel; it confuses the message, linking it with the occult.

Neutralised by agreement. That is worth carrying out of Philippi, because it is the commonest way the gospel is neutralised now: not by contradiction but by warm agreement on slightly different terms. Christ is affirmed as one of the great spiritual teachers. The message is praised as a path to meaning. Nothing is denied and nothing is left.

Is it wrong to consult horoscopes, tarot or mediums just for fun? Yes. Scripture forbids every attempt to gain hidden knowledge or guidance from sources other than God (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are always effective, but because they are a turning away from him to rival powers, and some of those powers are real and dark. Treating them as harmless fun trains the heart to look elsewhere for direction and may open doors that should stay shut. A Christian has something far better: a Father who knows the future and holds it, a Saviour who guides, and a word that is a lamp to his feet.

In a sentence. On the way to the place of prayer they met a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who made her owners a lot of money by fortune-telling, and she followed Paul and the others, shouting that these men were servants of the Most High God telling them the way of salvation.

On a Tuesday. Listen for the warm agreement that empties the gospel: Jesus as a good teacher, faith as a path to wellbeing, Christianity as one way among many. When you hear it, from a friend, a podcast, a pulpit, gently say what is missing: Jesus is the Lord, and the only way.

For worship. Christ needs no help from the occult. Keep the gospel clear and pure. He is not one way of salvation but the way, the truth and the life; not a servant of a high god but the Most High himself come in flesh. The serpent of Delphi, like the serpent of Eden, can borrow true words, but the Seed of the woman has crushed its head, and the girl it held was about to discover it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python” — linked to the oracle at Delphi, where Apollo was said to have slain a serpent called Python.

parallels.desc: no one who practises divination

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.

And this she kept doing for many days. Many days. That is the first thing to account for, and most readers pass it. Paul did not act at once. Day after day this girl trailed the missionaries through the streets shouting after them, and day after day he let it run. Paul waited before acting.

Paul, having become greatly annoyed. Greatly annoyed (diaponētheis) means troubled, distressed, worn out, exasperated, at the end of his patience: perhaps at the confusion, and for the girl. Luke could have written that Paul was moved with compassion, or grieved in his spirit, and he wrote that Paul was thoroughly fed up. This is not a serene apostle exercising cool authority at a chosen moment. It is a tired man who has finally had enough, swinging round in the street, and God used it, and Luke recorded it without tidying it. That is worth having, because we tend to imagine that God only works through us when our motives are pure and our composure is intact. Here the most famous exorcism in Acts is done by a man at the end of his temper.

I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. Note where the authority sits. Paul speaks to the spirit, not the girl. In the name of Jesus Christ: by his authority. Paul does not reason with it, bargain with it, or require anything of the girl: no faith, no consent, not even her attention. He names a name, and the thing that had held her for years leaves within the hour. Jesus’ name is stronger than Apollo’s python. Whatever else is uncertain about this territory, the New Testament is never uncertain about the outcome of that particular collision.

And it came out that very hour. At once. The girl was set free. And now the question Luke does not answer, which ought to be asked out loud rather than quietly filled in. What became of her? She is not said to have believed. So far as the text goes, she is still a slave the next morning, and now a slave who has stopped earning, owned by furious men who have just lost a fortune. In the world’s accounting, her position that evening was worse than the day before. Perhaps she joined the church that met at Lydia’s; we do not hear. She was the one person in the story who was not consulted about anything and the only one whose ending is withheld.

Resist closing the story. It is worth resisting the urge to close that. The Bible frequently rescues somebody and then declines to tell us how it turned out, and a reader who has watched a real deliverance leave someone with a harder life afterwards, the addiction broken and the debts still there, the marriage saved and the reputation gone, needs to know that Scripture is not embarrassed by that. The spirit came out. Everything else about her was still difficult. Both of those are in the verse.

Exorcism today. This raises the question of exorcism today. (On the reality of demons, real, personal, evil beings, see 5:15–16.) The Reformed position is cautious and Christ-centred, for scriptural reasons. (1) The dramatic commanding of demons clusters in the unique era of Christ’s ministry and the apostolic founding, among the authenticating signs of the kingdom (see 5:12). (2) Strikingly, the Epistles, which teach the church to fight the devil, never establish an office of exorcist, never list it among the gifts (Romans 12; 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 4), and give no ritual of deliverance; they relocate the warfare to ordinary weapons: resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7); put on the whole armour of God and stand (Ephesians 6:10–18); resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). (3) A true believer, indwelt by the Spirit, cannot be possessed (owned): he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4; John 10:28–29); harassed from without, but not inhabited. (4) And blaming sins on demons evades repentance, when Scripture lays sin at our own heart and flesh (James 1:14; Mark 7:21–23). So deliverance comes through the gospel (conversion transfers us out of the domain of darkness, Colossians 1:13), prayer, and Christ’s authority humbly invoked when genuinely needed: never a technique, a specialist, or a spectacle.

Other views, answered kindly. The Roman Catholic church keeps a formal rite of exorcism by an authorised priest; we honour its seriousness but find no such office or fixed ritual in Scripture. Much of the Pentecostal and charismatic world practises deliverance ministry, often casting demons out of Christians and naming spirits behind particular sins; we affirm the reality of the demonic and the zeal to help, but answer that a believer cannot be possessed (1 John 4:4), that the Epistles prescribe resisting and the armour, and that treating besetting sins as demons undercuts the call to repent and mortify the flesh (James 1:14). At the other extreme, liberal and naturalistic readers reduce demon-possession to ancient mental illness; this we reject, for Scripture distinguishes the sick from the demonised (Mark 1:32–34) and treats demons as real persons subject to Christ. The two ditches (as at 5:16): do not deny the demonic, and do not see a demon behind every sin and sickness.

For you, then. You need not fear demons, nor go hunting for a deliverance minister. If you are in Christ, the strongest Being in the universe lives in you, and at the cross Christ has already disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15; see 10:38). Your warfare is daily and ordinary: resist the devil in faith, put on the armour, feed on the Word, pray, walk in holiness, lean on the church, and he flees. Do not excuse your sins as someone else’s spirits; fight them as your own, by the Spirit, resting in your Lord’s finished victory. (In settings of overt occult darkness, sober missionaries do meet real demonic confrontation; even there the remedy is the same: the gospel and the name of Christ, humbly.)

In a sentence. She kept this up for many days, until Paul, greatly troubled, turned and commanded the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her, and it came out at once.

On a Tuesday. The name of Jesus is above every power of darkness. Fear no spirit. If you are anxious about spiritual attack, read Ephesians 6:10–18 slowly today and pray through each piece of the armour. And if you have helped someone out of a bondage, do not walk away when the dramatic part is over; the hard days afterwards are when they most need a friend.

For worship. The girl was owned three times over, and one Name broke the strongest of the three in an hour. Jesus Christ is Lord over every spirit, every oracle, every power in the heavenly places. He came to proclaim liberty to the captives, and he did it finally on the cross, where he made a public spectacle of the powers and triumphed over them. Every chain that has ever fallen at his word is a preview of the day when no one will be owned by anything but him.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.

But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone. There is the motive, stated in the first clause, before any charge is laid. Nobody in Philippi objected to the theology. A girl had been set free and the accounts had changed. Luke’s phrasing is exact and unlovely. Gone (exēlthen) is the same verb as the spirit came out in v. 18: their hope of gain went out of her when the spirit did. He does not say they lost a servant, or a daughter, or even a valuable slave. What left the room, as far as they were concerned, was an income stream. They cared more for money than for the girl’s freedom.

Funded, not argued. And this is the shape of a great deal of opposition to Christianity, then and since. It is not usually argued; it is funded. When the gospel changes what people do with their money, their bodies or their time, somebody’s revenue falls, and the objection that arrives afterwards will be dressed in principle and will never mention the accounts. The same thing happens on a larger scale at Ephesus, where a silversmith gathers his trade and the first thing he says to them, before he mentions the goddess, is that from this business we have our wealth (19:25–27). The gospel threatens those who profit from evil.

They seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. Then watch the charge get built, because it is a small masterpiece of misrepresentation. Note who is seized, and who is not. Paul and Silas, the leaders, and both Jews. Timothy, whose father was Greek, and Luke, who is almost certainly a Gentile, are left alone, and Luke’s we quietly drops out of the narrative until Paul comes back through Philippi years later. The mob knew who it wanted.

These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. Not a word about the girl. Not a word about money. Two accusations instead: an ethnic one and a civic one. The ethnic one was live currency in a Roman colony at that moment; it is an appeal to prejudice. Claudius had recently expelled the Jews from Rome (Luke mentions it two chapters later, when Paul meets a couple who had been thrown out, 18:2), and a Roman town full of veterans would have been in exactly the mood to hear it. The men who had been living off a possessed child reached for the nearest available prejudice, and it was to hand.

Disturbing our city. And the civic one is the charge that will be used against Christians for the next three hundred years. Not that the message is false. That it is inconvenient: that things were quieter before. It is a complaint that never has to prove anything, and it is unanswerable, because the gospel really does disturb a city where a girl can be owned and worked.

Should Christians challenge industries that profit from evil? Yes, wisely and lawfully. The gospel sets people free, and freedom often costs someone their profit: traffickers, pornographers, exploitative lenders, gambling and drug trades. Christians should refuse to profit from such things themselves, help their victims, speak for them, and support just laws. Expect resistance, often disguised as concern for jobs, tradition or freedom. But remember Paul’s order: he did not set out to reform Philippi’s economy; he preached Christ and set one girl free. The deepest change in any city begins with the gospel changing people.

In a sentence. When her owners saw their hope of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace, telling the magistrates these Jews were throwing their city into confusion.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether any part of your income or comfort depends on something you would not want the gospel to touch. And when someone opposes the faith with an appeal to prejudice or quiet, look for the money or the comfort underneath.

For worship. When the gospel threatens profit, expect resistance. Stand firm. The Lord Jesus was sold for silver and accused of disturbing the nation, and he went on setting captives free. He values one slave girl above every fortune made from her, and he paid for his people not with silver or gold but with his own precious blood.

parallels.desc: profits threatened again at Ephesus

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.

They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice. Count the words doing the work: for us as Romans. That is the whole accusation, and in Philippi it was the one sentence guaranteed to land. A legal charge. Rome tolerated Judaism. It was an ancient national religion with its own customs, legally recognised, and Jews were excused the emperor’s rites on that ground. What Rome did not tolerate was a foreign cult recruiting Roman citizens out of their own religion. Romans were not supposed to adopt foreign religions without permission, especially by converting from the state gods. You could be a Jew; you could not make a Roman into one.

Technically shrewd. So the charge is technically shrewd. It concedes that these men are Jews and their religion is legal, and then says they are exporting it to people who are not entitled to receive it. It is aimed at magistrates in a colony whose entire identity was that they were Romans a long way from Rome, in a town settled with veterans who had been given land here for their loyalty. Tell those men that two foreigners are undermining Roman custom in their own market square and you will not need evidence. The real reason (money) is hidden behind a respectable one (religion and patriotism).

A bitter irony. And there is a bitter irony sitting inside it that nobody in the square could see. The two men in the dock are Roman citizens themselves. The accusers are appealing to Roman privilege against men who hold more of it than they do, and the magistrates are about to break Roman law comprehensively in the act of defending it. That will be discovered in the morning, and the fear in verse 38 is the sound of it landing.

The charge was, in its way, accurate. Then the deeper thing, which outlives the legal detail. Christianity did advocate customs a Roman could not simply add to his existing life. A man who confessed Jesus is Lord in a colony where the loyal formula was Caesar is lord had not adopted a new interest; he had changed allegiance, and everything from his household gods to his trade guild dinners to the civic festivals would eventually feel it. Which is why the complaint has never really gone away. The gospel is welcome as long as it is one more thing a person has. It becomes intolerable at the point where it starts reorganising what he already had.

Does following Christ make me a bad citizen? No; it makes you a better one, but never a worshipper of the state. Christians are to pray for rulers, pay taxes, obey the law and seek the good of their nation (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). But when any authority demands what belongs to God alone, worship, ultimate loyalty, or disobedience to his commands, we must obey God rather than men (5:29), respectfully and without violence. Many of the best citizens in history have been Christians precisely because their conscience was bound to a higher King.

In a sentence. They said these men promoted customs that Romans were not allowed to accept or practise.

On a Tuesday. When people oppose the gospel, the stated reason is often not the real one. And turn the question on yourself: if your faith has never inconvenienced any arrangement in your life, it is worth asking honestly whether anybody could bring this charge against you at all.

For worship. Jesus is Lord, and that confession reorders everything. Caesar’s colonies rise and fall, but the kingdom of Christ cannot be shaken. He does not ask to be added to our lives as one more interest; he claims the whole, and the claim is our freedom, for his yoke is easy and his rule is love. Blessed are those whose allegiance has been changed, for their King will never be overthrown.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely.

The crowd joined in attacking them. Mob justice. Notice how fast this is. There is no hearing. Nobody calls the girl, or the owners, or any witness. The prisoners are not asked to answer, and Luke records not one word from either of them. Between the accusation in verse 21 and the flogging in verse 22 there is nothing at all.

And the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. The clothes are ripped away in public, in the market square, in front of the crowd that has just been shouting. Then the rods. Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors, who carried bundles of rods as a sign of authority: the bundle of birch carried in front of a colony’s magistrates as the visible sign of their power to punish. A Roman flogging with rods was not a formality; it opened the back, and men died of it. No trial, no hearing.

And when they had inflicted many blows upon them. Many. Luke does not give a number and does not spare us the word. Paul refers to this day twice in his letters, and both references are worth having because they tell you what it actually cost. To Corinth, listing what he had survived: three times I was beaten with rods (2 Corinthians 11:25); this was one of the three. And to the Thessalonians, about what happened next: though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict (1 Thessalonians 2:2). He walked from this to Thessalonica and preached there with the marks still on him.

Shamefully treated. The word he uses to the Thessalonians is not injured. It is shamefully treated: outraged, insulted. What stayed with him was not only the pain but the public stripping of two men who had done nothing, in front of a town, by officials who never asked them a question.

This was injustice. And it is important to say plainly that this was injustice, and that Scripture calls it that. There is a way of reading these stories which turns every wrong into a divine arrangement so quickly that the wrong disappears. God did use this night, magnificently. He also did not need the magistrates to break their own law to do it, and Luke does not pretend otherwise. The earthquake does not make the flogging right.

They threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. Bloodied, bruised, and locked up. No charge recorded, no sentence, no term. Two bleeding men are put away with an instruction about security, on pain of the jailer’s own life, and no instruction about anything else.

If God brings good out of injustice, does that make the injustice less wrong? No. God’s sovereignty over evil never turns evil into good. Joseph’s brothers meant it for evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20): both are true, and the brothers were still guilty. So when you have been wronged, you may grieve it, name it, and seek lawful justice, while trusting that God will not waste it. Do not let anyone hurry you past the wrong in the name of his providence. Scripture never does.

In a sentence. The crowd joined the attack, and the magistrates had their clothes torn off and ordered them beaten with rods, and after a severe beating threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to guard them carefully.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for Christians who are beaten, imprisoned or shamed for their faith. Find one specific name or country, and pray for them as you would want to be prayed for in the inner prison.

For worship. The servants of Christ were beaten for setting a slave free. Remember the persecuted church. Their Lord went before them: stripped, scourged, condemned without a just charge, his back laid open for our sakes. By his stripes we are healed. And the marks his servants bear for him are written in his book, where no magistrate can erase them.
verseByVerse.note: Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors.

parallels.desc: three times I was beaten with rods
shamefully treated at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

He put them into the inner prison. Having received this order, the jailer is introduced doing his job and slightly exceeding it. He was told to keep them safely. He puts them in the innermost cell and puts their feet in the stocks as well. Both details are worth knowing exactly, because the scene at midnight depends on them. The inner prison is the windowless interior room, the most secure cell: no light, no air moving, damp and dark, the floor of it filthy, and the smell of it the thing ancient writers mention first. It is where you put a man you have been told to keep, and it is as far from the street as the building goes.

And fastened their feet in the stocks. And the stocks were not simply a lock for the ankles. The Roman device was a heavy timber with a row of holes, and the point of the row was that the legs could be forced wide apart and fixed there. It was used as a punishment in its own right, not merely a restraint: hours in it produced cramp that became agony, and there was no way to shift position, and no way to lie down properly, and no way to reach your own back. With their backs torn open, they could not lie down comfortably.

Hold the whole picture. So hold the whole picture, because Luke has built it deliberately and we are about to be told what these two men were doing in it. Backs laid open by rods and untreated. Legs forced apart and clamped. Locked in the dark in the innermost room of a Roman jail in a foreign city, with no charge, no trial, no sentence, and no reason to think the morning would be any better. That is the setting of verse 25, and every word of this verse exists to make verse 25 almost unbelievable.

The man turning the key. One more thing about the man turning the key. He does not know who he is guarding. He has been handed two prisoners at the end of a long day and given an order, and he carries it out with a little extra thoroughness, the way a careful official does. Before the night is out he will be on the floor in front of them asking how to be saved, and by daylight he will have washed the wounds that his own thoroughness left untended tonight.

What if I am in my own inner prison right now? Then you are in a place God knows well. Joseph was in the pit and the prison; Jeremiah in the cistern; Paul and Silas in the stocks; and the Lord Jesus in the darkness of Gethsemane and the cross. Your inner prison may be illness, depression, grief, a trapped situation at home or work. Do not pretend it is not dark. Tell God plainly how it is, as the psalmists did. Ask a friend to come and sit with you. And hold on to this: no cell is so deep that Christ is not there, and none is so locked that he cannot open it in his time.

In a sentence. With these orders, he put them in the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

On a Tuesday. Some of God’s greatest works begin in the darkest places. Think of someone you know who is in an inner prison of their own, and go to them this week: a visit, a meal, a message, a prayer.

For worship. There is no inner prison beyond the reach of the God who descended into the depths for us. Christ was bound so that we might be loosed; he went into the outer darkness of God’s judgment so that his people would never be left there. The Lord who knows the way into every dark cell also holds the keys of death and Hades, and he has never yet lost a prisoner who belongs to him.
verseByVerse.note: Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened.

About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God. Put that sentence on top of the last one and refuse to hurry past the join. Backs opened by rods and never cleaned. Feet clamped apart in a timber. The inner cell, in the dark, at midnight, with no charge and no prospect. And they are singing. Not groaning or complaining, but praying and singing. In pain, in chains, in the dark, at midnight. Joy in suffering (5:41; Philippians 4:4, written later to this church).

Going on singing. Both verbs are continuous: they were praying and going on praying, singing and going on singing. This was not one defiant snatch of a psalm. It went on long enough to be noticed down the corridor. And what they sang was almost certainly the psalms, which is worth knowing, because the psalms are full of exactly this. Men in the dark asking how long, and telling God the truth about it, and then turning to praise before anything has changed. Paul and Silas did not have to manufacture a mood. They had a hymnbook written for nights like this one.

And the prisoners were listening to them. Then the detail Luke keeps, and it is the one that changes the scene from private piety into something else. Listening (epēkroōnto) means listening intently, close, deliberate attention: leaning in, straining to catch it. Luke uses it nowhere else in the New Testament. Their singing was a witness. Consider what those men were used to hearing at midnight in that room, and then consider hearing this. Prisoners had never heard anything like it.

A guard. Now a guard, because this verse is regularly used as a stick. It is not a command to feel like singing, and it is not a measurement you have failed. Paul himself writes elsewhere that he was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8), which is the same apostle describing the opposite experience without any embarrassment. Scripture gives you Philippi at midnight and it also gives you Gethsemane, and the psalm that ends with darkness as the only companion (Psalm 88:18). If tonight you can only manage the praying half of verse 25, you are still inside the verse.

Where the joy was anchored. What the singing does show is where the joy was anchored. Nothing whatever in their circumstances had improved, and nothing was going to before the earthquake, which they did not know was coming. So the gladness was not a response to their situation. It came from somewhere the magistrates could not reach.

And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. God’s answer (4:31).

And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. Read the last clause again. Everyone’s. Not Paul’s and Silas’s. Every door in the building and every chain on every prisoner in it. A picture of the gospel: Christ frees the prisoners (Luke 4:18). They had been praying for themselves, presumably, and singing where others could hear. What arrived was an answer that took in every man in the prison, including men who had never asked for anything. God’s reply to the two who prayed was wider than the two who prayed, which is a thing worth remembering about the prayers you make for your own situation, in a house where other people can hear you.

Does God always deliver his people from prison like this? No. Sometimes he does, as here and with Peter (12:6–11). Sometimes he does not: James was killed (12:2), Paul spent years in custody and was eventually executed, and many believers today remain in prison for Christ. The earthquake at Philippi shows that God can deliver; it does not promise that he always will in this life. What he always does is stand by his people (2 Timothy 4:17), give them grace to endure, and bring them through death itself into his presence. Final deliverance is certain even when earthly release is not.

In a sentence. About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God while the prisoners listened, and suddenly a great earthquake shook the prison’s foundations, and at once all the doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose.

On a Tuesday. Sing in your midnight. Others are listening. Learn one psalm of lament and trust by heart this week, Psalm 42, 46 or 130, so that you have something to sing when the night comes. Your colleagues, your children and your neighbours notice how you handle trouble far more than how you handle success.

For worship. The God who inhabits the praises of his people came down into a Philippian jail at midnight and shook its foundations. He is the Lord who looses prisoners and opens blind eyes, who shook Sinai and shook the tomb on Easter morning and will one day shake heaven and earth. Praise in the dark is not wasted; it rises to a throne that is never dark, and the One who sits on it hears.

parallels.desc: at night his song is with me

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.”

When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. He wakes to an earthquake and an open building, and he reaches for his own sword before he reaches for a light. That reflex needs explaining, because it looks like panic and it was arithmetic. Under Roman practice a guard who lost his prisoners could face their penalty himself. This book has already shown it happening: when Peter got out of prison in Jerusalem, Herod examined the sentries and ordered them put to death (12:19), and Luke recorded the cost without softening it. This man knows how that goes. What is waiting for him in the morning is an execution, preceded by disgrace. Falling on his own sword was the respectable Roman way out of exactly that; suicide was considered more honourable than execution in Roman culture, and by the standards he had been raised in it was the honourable thing to do.

Not a monster. So the man about to die is not a monster and not a coward. He is a middle-ranking official who has done his job well, been overtaken by something outside anybody’s control, and worked out in about four seconds that his life is over.

But Paul cried with a loud voice, Do not harm yourself, for we are all here. Take the two halves separately, because both are astonishing. First, Paul saw him. In a pitch-dark cell, from the innermost room, a man with his feet in the stocks somehow knew what was happening in the doorway and what it meant, and shouted before the sword went in. He was paying attention to somebody else at the one moment when nobody would have blamed him for thinking about himself. Paul cares for the man who chained him. Love for an enemy.

We are all here. Second, and far harder. Every door was open. Every chain was off. They had been beaten without trial by the authorities of that town, they had every legal grievance a man could have, and the building had just been opened by an act of God which any reasonable person would have read as a summons to walk out. Nobody moved. Not Paul, not Silas, and not one of the other prisoners: men with no faith at all and every reason to run. Luke does not explain that, and it is the quietest miracle in the chapter. Perhaps Paul’s and Silas’s example held them. Something had been going on in that prison for the previous few hours, and the men who had been listening in verse 25 stayed where they were in verse 28.

The first thing the gospel did. And notice what the gospel does for this man first. Before a word is said about God, before he asks anything, before he knows who these people are, his life is saved, in the plainest physical sense, by a prisoner who did not use his freedom. The first thing Christianity did for the jailer at Philippi was stop him killing himself.

What should I do if I, or someone I love, is thinking of suicide? Treat it as urgent, as Paul did: speak up at once, and do not leave the person alone. Tell them plainly that their life matters to God and to you. Get help immediately: call emergency services or a crisis line, involve a doctor, tell a trusted pastor or friend. If it is you, tell someone today. Despair lies; it says there is no way out, but the jailer’s worst night became the night of his salvation. Christ came to give life, and there is no shame, sin or loss so great that he cannot meet you in it.

In a sentence. When the jailer woke and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped, but Paul shouted for him not to harm himself, for they were all there.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever wondered what use your obedience is when it is invisible and costs you an obvious advantage, here is the answer in one verse. Paul stayed in a cell he could have walked out of, and a man he had never spoken to was alive in the morning because of it. Look for one person today who is close to despair, and say the plain, kind word they need.

For worship. Love your enemies. Paul did, in a prison cell, with a bleeding back. He learned it from his Lord, who prayed for those who crucified him, and who, when he could have called legions of angels and walked free, stayed on the cross so that his enemies might live. We are all here, said Paul in the dark; and because Christ stayed where he was, we are all saved.
verseByVerse.note: A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Watch the reversal in the room. A few hours ago this man locked two prisoners in the dark and clamped their feet.
