Now he is calling for torches so he can see them, running into his own inner cell, and going down on the floor in front of the men he put there. And he is trembling. Not with relief that his prisoners are safe, though they are. Luke has already told us he was ready to die a moment earlier and did not tremble then. Something else has got hold of him between the sword and the torches: shaken by the earthquake, by his near death, and by the presence of God.

Then he brought them out and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? It is the best question in the New Testament, the greatest question anyone can ask, and it is worth asking honestly what he meant by it, because the answer he gets is bigger than the question he asked. On the face of it he may have meant something quite immediate. Saved was an ordinary word: saved from drowning, from illness, from a sentence. He is a man whose prison has just fallen down around him, who was seconds from suicide, and who may simply have been asking how he gets out of this alive.

More in it than that. But there is more in it than that, and the evidence is in the room. His prisoners are all present, so his immediate danger has already passed; Paul told him so in the previous verse. He is not asking how to escape execution; that is settled. And these are the men the whole city had been hearing about for days, because a slave girl had been following them through the streets announcing that they proclaimed the way of salvation (v. 17). He has almost certainly heard her. He has certainly heard them singing at midnight with their backs in ribbons. So the question is probably both, and that is exactly how such questions arrive. The earthquake had shaken more than the prison; it shook his soul. He knew he needed saving, from more than Roman punishment, and a man who had never asked anything of the sort found the words in his mouth in the middle of the night.

What must I do? Now notice the form of it. That is the instinct of every religious person who has ever lived, and it is the instinct of every irreligious one too the moment he is frightened. Tell me the task. Give me the requirement and I will meet it. It is the same question the crowd asked at Pentecost (2:37) and the rich young ruler asked Jesus, and it is the question the whole of chapter 15 has just been fought over. He is a practical man in a uniform, and he wants the procedure. What he is about to be handed has no procedure in it at all.

Saved from what? From the wrath of God against sin, which is the deepest danger any person faces, deeper than any prison or sentence. Scripture says that all have sinned and that the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; 6:23), and that those who die without Christ face a just and conscious judgment that does not end (Matthew 25:46). To be saved is to be rescued from that, forgiven, reconciled to God, given his Spirit, and brought at last into his presence. The jailer may not have grasped all of that at midnight. He grasped enough to know that he needed it.

In a sentence. The jailer called for lights, rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas, then brought them out and asked what he must do to be saved.

On a Tuesday. Has this question gripped you? It is the most important question you will ever ask. If it has never troubled you, ask God to show you your need. And if a friend ever asks it, in whatever words, do not change the subject: tell them.

For worship. The God who shook the prison is the God who shakes the soul awake. He brought a hardened official to his knees in a single night, and put on his lips the question that every heart was made to ask. And he had already answered it, before the jailer was born, on a hill outside Jerusalem, where his Son did everything that must be done for sinners to be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. He asked what he must do. The answer contains no doing in it at all. That is the first thing to see, and it is the whole gospel in the grammar. The simplest, clearest statement of the gospel in Acts. Not do, but believe. There is one verb: believe. Not believe and be circumcised, which is what men had been arguing for in Jerusalem a few months earlier. Not believe and make restitution to the two men you had flogged, which he would very reasonably have expected. Not believe and reform your life first, which is what most people privately assume is meant. Not penance, not good works. One verb, and its object is a person. Salvation is by faith alone, in Christ alone.

Believe in a person. And notice that the object is a person and not a proposition. Believe in the Lord Jesus, not believe that something is the case. The difference is the difference between knowing a bridge will hold and standing on it. A man can be entirely persuaded of every article of the faith and have trusted nobody.

The Lord Jesus. Then both words are chosen. Jesus is the name of the man from Nazareth who was executed some twenty years before: a fact, a date, a person you could have met. Lord is the word this jailer used every day of his working life about Caesar, and it is the confession that will eventually cost Christians in this colony their standing and sometimes their lives. Jesus as Lord, not merely as teacher. He is being told to transfer his allegiance, and the man saying it has the marks of the local magistrates’ rods on his back to show what that can cost.

And you will be saved. Now the promise. Future, and certain. Not you may be, not you can hope to be. The answer to a terrified man in the middle of the night is a plain statement of outcome.

You and your household. And then the clause that has been argued over ever since. Before the argument, take the pastoral force of it, because it is the reason the words are there. This man’s first coherent thought after his own rescue was his house. Paul does not tell him to sort himself out and worry about them later. The offer arrives at the door of the whole household in the same sentence in which it arrives at him, and the next verse has the missionaries doing exactly that, speaking the word to every person under that roof in the middle of the night rather than waiting for a more convenient hour. Not that his faith would save his family automatically, but that the same offer was open to them on the same terms. They too must believe, and did (v. 34). The word was spoken to all of them (v. 32).

Does you and your household promise that if I believe, my family will be saved? No. Salvation is not passed from one person to another; the next verses show that Paul spoke the word to all who were in his house (v. 32), and that they rejoiced, having believed (v. 34). The promise is that the same way of salvation is open to all of them. A parent whose grown child does not believe has not been failed by this verse. He may pray for his child, speak and live the gospel, and trust the God who saves.

The household texts. You and your household, and the household’s baptism in v. 33, is one of several household texts that feature in the friendly baptism discussion noted at 2:39: believer’s-baptist readers stress that the household rejoiced, having believed (v. 34), each coming to personal faith; covenant-baptist readers hear the familiar Scriptural pattern of God dealing with believers together with their households. The promise, all agree, reaches as wide as faith reaches.

What does it actually mean to believe in the Lord Jesus? It means to trust him: to rely on him alone for forgiveness and acceptance with God, and to receive him as your Lord. It includes knowing who he is and what he has done (he is the Son of God who died for sinners and rose again), agreeing that it is true, and then resting your whole weight on him, the way you rest on a chair. It is not a feeling, though feelings may come with it, and it is not a work that earns anything; it is the empty hand that receives a gift. If you are unsure whether you have ever believed, you can do it now: tell him that you have no hope but him, and that you trust him to save you.

In a sentence. They answered that he should believe in the Lord Jesus and he would be saved, he and his household.

On a Tuesday. Write this verse where you will see it every day this week. When you are tempted to measure your standing with God by what you have done, read it again: believe, and you will be saved. And pray by name for each member of your household who does not yet believe.

For worship. Believe in the Lord Jesus. That is the whole answer, then and now. Not do, but believe, because everything that had to be done has been done by him. He lived the obedience we owed, died the death we deserved, and rose to give the life we could never earn. The answer to the oldest and most desperate question of the human heart is a Person, and he receives everyone who comes.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family.

And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. Note the hour. It is the middle of the night, in a house attached to a prison, with an earthquake’s damage still on the floor and two men who ought to be lying down. And everybody under that roof is woken and gathered so that the whole household hears the same thing at the same time. They explained the gospel more fully, to everyone. Nobody is told they can hear about it in the morning.

What is the word of the Lord? The word of the Lord is the gospel message: the good news about the Lord Jesus (who he is, his death and resurrection, the call to believe, v. 31), and from the Lord, carrying his own authority. When Paul and Silas spoke it, the jailer was not hearing two men’s opinions but the Lord’s word delivered through his messengers (as Paul says elsewhere: when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, 1 Thessalonians 2:13).

But how can an ordinary reader be confident of what it means? Three things give solid confidence. First, God made the saving word clear (what theologians call the perspicuity of Scripture): the central message is plain enough that a rough jailer and his household grasped it and believed at midnight (v. 34). The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple (Psalm 119:130); God speaks to be understood, not to be decoded by experts. Second, he does not leave you to puzzle it out alone: the same Spirit who gave the word opens the heart and mind to receive it (the Lord opened Lydia’s heart, 16:14; the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth, John 16:13; 1 Corinthians 2:12). Third, the word proves itself: it does what no mere human word can, converting and transforming (a jailer is a new man by dawn), and we test it against the rest of Scripture, as even the apostle Paul was tested by the Bereans (17:11).

One honest limit. Not every passage is equally easy (even Peter said some of Paul’s writing is hard to understand, 2 Peter 3:16); the clarity is chiefly of the things needful for salvation and life. So you may hold the heart of it, how to be saved, how to live, with real confidence, while reading the harder edges humbly, in the church, under faithful teaching. Your assurance rests not on your own cleverness but on God’s clarity and the Spirit’s witness.

And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds. Then the sentence that follows, and it is one of the most beautiful in Acts because of the order Luke puts it in. He washed their wounds. Consider whose wounds those were. This man had received the two of them from the magistrates with their backs already opened, and had put them in the inner cell and fixed their feet in the stocks without a thought about it, because that was the job and they were only prisoners. The blood had been drying on them for hours while he slept. Now he is kneeling on the floor with water, cleaning the injuries he had been content to ignore. The change is immediate. The man who fastened them in the stocks now washes their wounds.

That is repentance. And notice that nobody asked him for it. Paul does not tell him to make amends; there is no instruction anywhere in the passage about putting anything right. The man simply cannot leave those backs untended now, because he has stopped being able to see the two of them as prisoners. That is what conversion does before it does anything else: it changes who a person is able to walk past. Repentance shows itself in deeds.

And he was baptized at once, he and all his family. In the middle of the night. No delay. And then Luke’s word order, which cannot be an accident: washed their wounds; and he was baptised at once. He washed their stripes; they washed him in baptism. Two cleansings in one sentence, the same hour of the night, and the man doing the first one is the man receiving the second. Luke never remarks on it. He simply puts them next to each other. It is worth asking which way round that runs, because we would probably have written it the other way: cleansed by God first, and then made kind. Luke has him washing the wounds before he goes down into the water. The faith was already working before the sign was given to it.

Does this household baptism support infant baptism? Christians who baptise infants see in it a pattern of whole families brought into the covenant. But Luke says the word was spoken to all who were in his house (v. 32) and that the household believed (v. 34). The more likely reading is that those baptised were those who heard and believed. That is the credobaptist conviction this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession: baptism is for those who profess repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus. Our paedobaptist brothers, who love the same Lord and the same gospel, read the household pattern through the covenant promise to believers and their children; we honour their conviction, while believing the text points to a household that heard, believed and was baptised together.

Should new converts be baptised as quickly as this? In Acts baptism normally followed conversion closely, often the same day (2:41; 8:38; 9:18; 10:48), because it was the public confession of faith in Christ and the sign of entry into his people. There was no long waiting period. Many churches today rightly take a little time to make sure that a profession is credible and that the person understands what baptism means. That is wise, especially where people have little Christian background. But the aim should be to baptise believers without needless delay, not to make baptism a reward for maturity.

In a sentence. They spoke the word of the Lord to him and all in his household, and at that hour of the night he washed their wounds, and he and all his family were baptised at once.

On a Tuesday. True faith changes behaviour at once. What has Christ changed in you? Is there someone whose wounds you once walked past, perhaps wounds you caused, whom you could now go and help? Do it this week.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was wounded for our transgressions, and by his wounds we are healed. In that night at Philippi a man who had caused wounds knelt to wash them, and then was washed himself in the name of the One whose wounds had washed him first. Grace reaches down to the hardest hands, and makes them gentle.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God.

Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. Follow the movement of these two men through one night, because Luke has been careful with it and the whole chapter is in the geography. Stripped in the market square. Beaten in public. Carried or dragged to the prison. Locked in the innermost room, in the dark. Then, some hours later, brought up: up out of the cell, up the steps, into the jailer’s own living quarters, and seated at his table. And set food before them. It is the first thing they have eaten since before the flogging, and the man serving it is the man who locked them up. Hospitality, like Lydia’s. Fellowship at table between a Roman jailer and two Jewish prisoners.

The first meal. That table is one of the first Christian meals recorded in Europe. Not in a hall, not on a Sunday, not among people who had planned it. Some time in the small hours, in a prison official’s kitchen, with the plaster down off the walls.

And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. The word for rejoiced is a strong one: exulted, was overjoyed. Joy, again. The whole household rejoiced, because all had believed. Set it against what this man was doing a few hours earlier with a sword in his hand. His despair at midnight became joy before dawn. Between those two moments nothing whatever has improved in his circumstances. He still has to explain a wrecked prison to the magistrates in the morning. His job is no more secure than it was. The earthquake damage is still on the floor around the table. Nothing in his situation changed. Everything in him did.

What he was glad about. And it is worth noticing what he is glad about, because Luke tells us exactly: that he had believed in God. Not that the prisoners stayed. Not that he was going to survive the night. His joy is fastened to the one thing that happened to him rather than to any of the things that happened around him, which is why it could survive a morning that was still going to be difficult.

Three conversions. In Philippi, God saved a wealthy Asian businesswoman, a poor Greek slave girl, and a Roman jailer. Different nations, classes, sexes, and needs. One gospel, one church. Paul later wrote: there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28).

Can I really be joyful when my circumstances are still hard? Yes, though it will not be a joy that ignores the hardship. Christian joy is gladness in God himself, in what he has done for you in Christ and promised you, and none of that is touched by your circumstances. It sits alongside sorrow rather than replacing it (2 Corinthians 6:10). It grows as you dwell on the gospel, pray, sing, and spend time with God’s people. Do not wait for your situation to change before you rejoice; the jailer did not. Begin by thanking God for one thing that is true of you in Christ today.

In a sentence. He brought them into his house and gave them food, and he and his whole household rejoiced that he had come to believe in God.

On a Tuesday. There is a test in that, and it is a fair one to run on yourself. If every circumstance in your life stayed exactly as it is tonight, the diagnosis, the arrears, the person who is not speaking to you, is there anything left that you would still be glad about? The jailer’s answer to that question was yes, and he had known the reason for a few hours.

For worship. The gospel turns midnight despair into morning joy. Rejoice in your salvation. The Lord who brought two prisoners up out of the pit and seated them at a jailer’s table will bring all his people up out of the grave and seat them at the marriage supper of the Lamb. There, people of every nation and rank will sit together, and the joy that began in a prison kitchen will be full for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.”

But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, Let those men go. Luke does not tell us why, and the silence is worth respecting rather than filling. Perhaps the magistrates had slept on it and the flogging of two men without a hearing looked worse in daylight. Perhaps the earthquake had unsettled a superstitious town. Perhaps a night’s reflection had turned up the awkward fact that nobody had actually produced a charge, or they thought a night in prison was enough. What is certain is the shape of what they do: no summons, no hearing, no finding, no record. Just a message, early, by a subordinate: let them go.

An institution that knows it has done wrong. It is the standard behaviour of an institution that knows it has done wrong and would prefer the matter to end quietly. Nothing is admitted. Nothing is written down. The problem is simply removed from the premises before anybody important asks about it. And notice who is sent. Police (rhabdouchous) means rod-bearers, the lictors, the same officers whose rods had been used on them the day before. The men who carried out the beating are sent round in the morning to say the matter is closed.

Come out now and go in peace. And the jailer reported these words to Paul. Here is the moving part, and it is easy to read past. The man delivering this message is a Christian of a few hours’ standing, and he is delighted. Go in peace is a warm, believing send-off, now spoken as a brother; he thinks it is good news, and for him it is. He has just come to trust Christ, his friends are being released, and the trouble is over. He has no idea that Paul is about to refuse.

A kind person who wants it to stop. And it is worth sitting with that for a moment, because it is a very ordinary Christian situation. A new believer, out of sheer goodwill and relief, urges a course that would leave an injustice standing and a young church unprotected. He is not wrong to want peace. He simply cannot yet see what the older man can see, which is that a quiet exit this morning will cost the Christians of Philippi something for years. Nobody in this scene is behaving badly. That is what makes it useful. Sometimes the pressure to let a thing drop comes not from your enemies but from a kind person who wants the unpleasantness to stop, and who will not understand at all why you are still standing there.

How do I know when to let something drop and when to pursue it? Ask who is affected and what is at stake. If only your own comfort or pride is involved, letting it go is usually the way of Christ (1 Corinthians 6:7; 1 Peter 2:23). If others, especially the vulnerable, will be harmed by silence, or if the honour of the gospel is at stake, love may require you to pursue it, lawfully and without vindictiveness. Seek wise counsel, especially if you are hurt or angry. And remember that wanting peace is good; the question is whether the peace offered is real or only quiet.

In a sentence. At daybreak the magistrates sent their officers to release them, and the jailer told Paul they could leave and go in peace.

On a Tuesday. If you are a newer Christian, be slow to urge an older one to let something go until you understand why they are standing firm. And if you are older, be patient with the kind people who want you to stop: explain, gently, what you are protecting.

For worship. God turned the hearts of the rulers overnight. He rules over rulers. The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. The same Lord who sent the earthquake at midnight sent the magistrates’ messengers at dawn, and both served his purposes for his church. Nothing in Philippi, from the stocks to the city hall, was outside his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.”

They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens. The first question is the obvious one, and it is the right one: why did he not say this yesterday? Because he could have. Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial; the Porcian and Valerian laws protected citizens from such punishment. To flog a Roman citizen who had not been tried was a serious crime, forbidden by long-standing law, and the claim alone would have stopped the rods. The magistrates had committed a serious crime. Paul knew that. He uses the same protection later in Jerusalem, and there he speaks up before the whipping rather than after (22:25).

Why not earlier? Luke does not tell us, and honest answers are limited. It may be that in the uproar of verse 22 (a shouting crowd, clothes being torn off) nobody was listening; perhaps he did say so, and was not heard. Luke is careful to record that the magistrates never asked them anything. It may be that he chose to suffer for Christ first. What we can say is that he did not use his rights to protect his own back, and he did use them the next morning. The difference between those two moments is the key to the whole verse.

And do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out. Because look at what he actually demands, which is not compensation and not an apology for himself. He demands that the thing be undone publicly. The offence was committed in the market square in front of the town, and a private release leaves the town’s last memory of these two men as the morning they were flogged as criminals. And Paul is not going to be in Philippi to correct that impression. Lydia is. Her household is. The jailer is, and he has to go on working for these same magistrates. There is a church of a few weeks’ standing in that colony, and it will live or die partly on whether the authorities believe they can treat its founders as vermin without consequence.

Not pride or revenge. So this is not a man standing on his dignity. It is a man securing, on his way out of town, the only legal protection his converts are ever going to have. A public acknowledgment that they had been wronged would protect the believers in Philippi from similar treatment. Christians may use their legal rights for the sake of the gospel and the church (22:25; 25:11).

When should a believer insist on his rights? Which answers a question Christians genuinely struggle with: when should a believer insist on his rights, and when should he absorb the wrong? Paul does both in this chapter, and the line between them is not comfort but other people. He took the beating without invoking the law when the only person who would have benefited was himself. He invoked it the moment the beneficiaries were the church he was leaving behind. It is the same principle he presses on the Corinthians, who were suing each other and to whom he says: why not rather suffer wrong? (1 Corinthians 6:7), because there the only thing at stake was their own advantage. So the test is not whether you are entitled. You may well be. It is whether the person protected by your insisting is you.

Is it unspiritual for a Christian to go to the police or the courts? No. The governing authorities are God’s servants for our good, to restrain wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and Paul used Roman law repeatedly. Crimes such as assault, fraud or abuse should be reported to the authorities; abuse in particular must never be hidden or tolerated, in the church or anywhere else, and victims should be protected first. What Paul discourages is believers suing one another over private disputes before unbelievers, when the church could help them settle it (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Using the law to protect others and to see justice done is a proper Christian act.

In a sentence. But Paul said they had been beaten publicly without trial, though they were Roman citizens, and thrown into prison, and now the magistrates wanted to get rid of them secretly; no, let the magistrates come and escort them out themselves.

On a Tuesday. Christians may use their legal rights, not for revenge, but to protect others and the gospel. Think of a right you are tempted to insist on this week. Ask the question: is the person protected by my insisting only me?

For worship. The Lord Jesus had every right, and laid them all down for us. He did not call on his legions or his innocence to save himself; he was condemned uncondemned, so that we who were truly condemned might go free. And the same Lord cares for his little flock, raising up servants to stand between it and those who would harm it. He is the Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and also guards them from the wolf.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city.

The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. Afraid. These are the two most powerful men in the colony, and Luke’s word for their state of mind in the morning is the same kind of word he used for the jailer trembling on the floor at midnight. Their fear was entirely rational. A magistrate who ordered a Roman citizen flogged without trial had not made an administrative error; he had committed an offence that could end his career, and a colony that allowed it could lose privileges it valued more than almost anything. They could lose their positions, or worse. All Paul had to do was write a letter to the right person in Rome.

The irony completed. And note the irony that has been building since verse 21. The charge that got these two men beaten was that they advocated customs that are not lawful for us as Romans. The only people in the story who broke Roman law were the Romans, and they broke it in the act of defending it, against two men who turned out to hold the citizenship the accusers had been so proud of.

So they came and apologized to them. They came. That is what Paul had required, and it is the sentence the whole demand was for. A public apology. The church in Philippi was protected. The men who had ordered the public stripping walked down to the prison in daylight, in a town where everyone would see them go, and appealed to the two men they had flogged.

And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. And then, having apologised, they asked them to leave. Asked, not ordered: they were in no position to order anything. They requested it, which is the exact measure of how the balance had shifted overnight.

Two things, pulling opposite ways. Two things are worth taking from this, and they pull in opposite directions, which is why both need saying. The first is that God vindicated his servants publicly, and it is right to be glad about it. Luke evidently was. The second is what the apology was worth. Luke chooses his words: they were afraid. Nothing suggests these men were sorry about the injustice, and nothing suggests they thought any better of the gospel at the end of it than at the beginning. They wanted the problem gone, and now they wanted it gone politely. An apology extracted by fear of consequences is not repentance, and the New Testament is quite clear-eyed about the difference. So the vindication was real, and it changed nobody’s heart. Those are two different things, and a Christian who has finally been proved right about something will need both halves of that sentence.

What if I am never vindicated in this life? Many faithful believers are not. Stephen was not vindicated before the Sanhedrin; countless martyrs died with their names blackened. Scripture promises that God will vindicate his people, but often on the last day rather than this one (Romans 12:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). Commit your cause to him who judges justly, as Jesus did (1 Peter 2:23). Do what is right, speak the truth where it helps, and then leave your reputation in his hands. The verdict that matters most has already been given: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

In a sentence. When the officers reported this, the magistrates were alarmed to hear they were Roman citizens, came and apologised, escorted them out and asked them to leave the city.

On a Tuesday. If you have been proved right about something recently, guard your heart against gloating; vindication is not the same as changed hearts, and it is the hearts that matter. If you are still waiting to be vindicated, hand the case over to God again today, in words.

For worship. God can vindicate his servants publicly. Leave your vindication to him. The rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, and on the third day God reversed their verdict before heaven and earth. One day every magistrate and emperor will stand before him, and every knee will bow. The Judge of all the earth will do right, and his people will be shown to be his.

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.

So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. They have been publicly vindicated and formally asked to leave. They could have gone straight to the gate. Instead the last thing they do in Philippi is walk across town to a house, to the church in her house, and sit with a handful of people.

And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed. And notice who does the encouraging. Two men whose backs were opened by rods the day before, who have not slept, encourage the church rather than the other way round. The beaten men encourage the others, not the other way round. The people who had watched their teachers dragged through the market square needed steadying, and the men with the wounds are the ones who steady them.

The strangest founding membership. Then count the church they leave behind, because it is the strangest founding membership imaginable. A foreign businesswoman in the luxury trade, with her household. A jailer, with his. A slave girl, if she came, and Luke will not tell us. And the brothers: a word that appears here without introduction, which means there were others already, whom Luke never got round to mentioning. Set those people beside each other. At the top of the town, a woman of means. At the bottom, a girl who had been owned and worked. In between, a man employed to hold people down. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank, the one place in Philippi where those three could sit in the same room was a house church.

The church Paul loved most. And that is the congregation Paul loved most. The church at Philippi became one of Paul’s most loving and generous churches (Philippians 1:3–5; 4:15–16). A dozen years later, writing from another prison, he tells them they are his joy and crown (Philippians 4:1); he thanks them for being the only church that supported him when he left Macedonia, sending money more than once; he writes the warmest letter in the New Testament to them, and the word joy runs through it from beginning to end. He wrote that letter in chains, to the church that had been born in a jail. Luke seems to have stayed behind: the we stops here and resumes at Philippi in 20:5.

What it cost. Look back over the chapter and add up what it cost to plant it. Two provinces closed. Weeks of walking toward nothing. A vision that had to be interpreted. A sea crossing. Days in a strange city with no way in. A public flogging, a night in the stocks, and an expulsion. And what was gained was a room in a woman’s house, a jailer’s household, and a letter we still read.

How can I encourage others when I am the one who is hurting? Often your hurt is exactly what makes your encouragement believable. People listen to someone who has suffered and still trusts God. You do not need to pretend you are fine; Paul’s backs were visibly torn. Tell honestly what God has been to you in the trouble, point others to the same Lord, and keep it simple. Comfort received from God becomes comfort you can give (2 Corinthians 1:4). And let others encourage you too: a church is a place where the wounded take turns.

In a sentence. They left the prison and went to Lydia’s house, and after seeing and encouraging the believers, they departed.

On a Tuesday. Those who suffer for Christ can encourage others. Let your trials become someone else’s strength. And look around your church for the people who would never meet anywhere else, the wealthy and the poor, the respectable and the rescued, and make sure they are sitting at the same table.

For worship. The church of Jesus Christ is the one room in the world where a businesswoman, a freed slave girl and a jailer sit together as brothers and sisters. It cost a flogging and a night in the stocks to plant it in Philippi; it cost the blood of the Son of God to plant it at all. He breaks down every dividing wall in his own flesh, and he gathers his people from every rank and nation into one household, where the wounded encourage one another and the joy cannot be taken away.

parallels.desc: your partnership in the gospel from the first day

16.theology: Effectual Calling and the Opened Heart. Acts 16:14 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of what the Reformed tradition calls effectual calling: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.” The Word is preached by Paul; the heart is opened by the Lord. Both acts are real and necessary. Without Paul’s preaching, Lydia has no content to respond to. Without the Lord’s opening of her heart, Paul’s words remain external noise. The Spirit works through the Word, but the Spirit’s work is the decisive one — the inward illumination that turns external proclamation into saving faith. This is why prayer for the lost must accompany every act of evangelism: we can preach; only God can open hearts.
16.examples:
Then: A purple-goods merchant, a slave girl, a Roman jailer — three people who could not have been more different in status, ethnicity, or circumstance — all met by one gospel in one city. The Philippian church is born from this unlikely trio, and Paul will write his most joyful letter to it from a prison cell a dozen years later.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts today. The Spirit who directed Paul away from Asia and toward Macedonia still directs his church. The closed doors are guidance; the midnight songs are witness; the simplest answer is still the truest: believe in the Lord Jesus. The gospel has not grown more complicated. We have.

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>5</sup>But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, <sup>7</sup>and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” <sup>8</sup>And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. <sup>9</sup>And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. <sup>13</sup>But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. <sup>14</sup>Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there. <sup>15</sup>Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>21</sup>Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. <sup>22</sup>So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went out from their midst. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview:
Leaving Philippi, Paul and Silas travel west along the Via Egnatia, the great Roman highway, to Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia and a busy port. For three Sabbaths Paul reasons in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and a number of leading women believe. Jealous opponents gather a mob, and when they cannot find Paul they drag his host Jason before the city officials, accusing the believers of turning the world upside down and defying Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Paul and Silas slip away by night to Berea, where the Jews receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to check what Paul says. Opponents from Thessalonica follow, and Paul is sent on to Athens.

Athens was no longer politically powerful, but it was still the intellectual capital of the Greek world, the city of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, crowded with temples and statues. Paul is distressed at so many idols. He reasons in the synagogue and in the marketplace, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers dismiss him as a babbler, and is brought before the Areopagus, the ancient council that met on the Hill of Ares. His speech is a model of preaching to people without the Bible. He begins from an altar inscribed “to an unknown god”: the God they do not know is the Creator of everything, who does not live in temples or need anything from us, who made all nations from one man and set their times and places so that they would seek him, and who is not far from any of us; even their own poets said we are his offspring. So God cannot be like an image of gold or stone. He overlooked their ignorance in the past, but now commands everyone everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed, and has proved it by raising him from the dead. At the mention of resurrection some laugh, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including a member of the council, Dionysius, and a woman named Damaris.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Thessalonica Paul spends three Sabbaths in the synagogue showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and leading women believe, but jealous opponents start a riot, drag Paul’s host Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Released on bond, the believers send Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where the Jews are more open-minded, receiving the message eagerly and checking it daily against the Scriptures, and many believe. When opponents arrive from Thessalonica, Paul is sent on to Athens, while Silas and Timothy stay behind for a time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean Standard for Scripture Engagement

The Bereans 'received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.' Reformed theology has always prized this as the model of how the gospel should be received: not credulity (accepting whatever the preacher says without examination) and not skepticism (dismissing the gospel without engagement), but eager reception combined with rigorous scriptural testing. The Berean standard is the Protestant hermeneutical ideal: sola Scriptura applied in the actual practice of hearing and evaluating proclamation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'These men who have turned the world upside down' — the Thessalonian accusation is the most accurate description of the gospel's social effect in Acts. Now: The gospel still turns every human order that opposes the kingdom upside down. The question for the church is not whether the gospel is socially disruptive but whether it is disrupting the right things — the powers of sin, death, and injustice — rather than merely producing comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,

Meaning first. Acts 17 shows Paul preaching in three very different cities. In Thessalonica he reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise; a church is born and a riot follows. In Berea the Jews examine the Scriptures daily to test his message. In Athens, the intellectual capital of the world, he speaks to philosophers about the Creator God who does not live in temples, who calls all people to repent, and who will judge the world by the man he raised from the dead. One gospel, adapted wisely to Jews, God-fearers and pagan philosophers. And under all three scenes runs one thread: the risen Jesus is Lord of synagogue, marketplace and council alike, and none of them can keep him out.

Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica. Two towns named and passed through in half a verse. They lie a day’s journey apart on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia, which ran from the Adriatic across to Byzantium, and the distance from Philippi to Thessalonica is about a hundred miles. Paul walked it with a back that had been opened by rods a few days earlier. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on that road, a strategic city from which a message could travel in every direction. Paul later wrote two letters to the church there, and within months he could tell them that the word of the Lord had sounded forth from them everywhere (1 Thessalonians 1:8).

Where there was a synagogue of the Jews. Luke does not say they preached in Amphipolis or Apollonia, and the reason is probably in this clause. Thessalonica had a synagogue and the smaller towns evidently did not. Paul is not wandering; he is going to the next place with a congregation of people who already have the Scriptures.

And Paul went in, as was his custom. Read that against what had just happened to him. The last time he entered a public place in this province he came out of the city stripped and flogged. His custom did not change. It was his settled practice to go to the synagogue first in each new city, taking the gospel to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16): beginning with those who already held the Scriptures and awaited Israel’s God, and showing them that the Christ they hoped for is Jesus. (On what a synagogue was, see 6:9; on how its service of reading and teaching ran, the very platform Paul uses here, see 13:15.)

And on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures. This detail has caused more argument than any other in the chapter. It is usually read as meaning Paul was in Thessalonica for three weeks, and that cannot be right, because his own letters to that church will not allow it. He tells them he worked night and day with his hands so as not to burden anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:9), which takes longer than a fortnight to be worth mentioning. He reminds the Philippians that they sent him help in Thessalonica more than once (Philippians 4:16), and Philippi is a hundred miles away, so that is at least two round trips by messenger. And he describes the congregation as people who turned to God from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9), which is not a description of synagogue Jews.

Which three weeks Luke is counting. The answer is in what Luke actually wrote. He says three Sabbaths in the synagogue. That is the length of the synagogue phase, not the length of the mission. When the synagogue closed to him, as it did in city after city, Paul went on working in the town among Gentiles for a good while longer, and it is those Gentiles who make up most of the church he writes to. It is a small harmonisation and it is worth doing carefully, because this is exactly the sort of place where a reader is told there is a contradiction in the Bible. There is not one here. There is a summary and a letter, and they fit, once you notice which three weeks Luke is counting.

He reasoned with them. The word is dialegomai, from which we get dialogue: he discussed, argued, back and forth, taking questions. This was not a monologue delivered at people. For three Sabbaths a room full of men who knew the Scriptures put their objections to him and he answered them, out of the same book they were holding. And “from the Scriptures” tells you where the common ground lay: the Old Testament, which both sides owned. Christian preaching is reasonable. It appeals to the mind as well as to the heart, and it is not afraid of a question.

Is it right to argue about the faith? Yes, if by arguing you mean what Paul did: giving reasons, from Scripture, with patience, and listening to the objection before answering it. Peter tells every believer to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). What Scripture forbids is quarrelling: the point-scoring, the raised voice, the need to win (2 Timothy 2:24–25). The test is simple. If you are still listening, still gentle, and still praying for the person, you are reasoning. If you are enjoying his defeat, you have stopped.

In a sentence. After passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue, and Paul went in as usual and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures.

On a Tuesday. Faith is reasonable. Be ready to reason with people from Scripture. That means knowing where the great promises are, so that when a friend asks why you believe, you can open a Bible and show him, not merely tell him how you feel. And notice the man with the healing back walking into the next synagogue. Whatever went wrong last time you spoke of Christ, the custom does not need to change.

For worship. The Lord of the church sent a bruised man a hundred miles down a Roman road to open his Book in a room of strangers, and he has been doing the same thing ever since. The Word that was read in that synagogue every Sabbath for generations was about him all along, and he was patient enough to let it be read for centuries before he came to explain it. He does not hide from questions. He is the answer the Scriptures were asking.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops along that road.

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”

Explaining and proving. Two verbs, and both are pictures. Explaining is dianoigō: to open up, to prise apart. Luke likes this word and keeps it for remarkable company. It is what Jesus did on the Emmaus road, when he opened to them the Scriptures and their hearts burned (Luke 24:32); it is what he did that evening when he opened their minds to understand them (Luke 24:45); and it is what the Lord did to Lydia in the last chapter, when he opened her heart to pay attention (16:14). Opening a book, opening a mind, opening a heart, and in three of the four cases the one doing the opening is the Lord himself. Paul opens the Scriptures; only God opens the person.

Setting it on the table. Proving is paratithemenos, the word for setting food in front of somebody. It is what the jailer did at Philippi when he set food before them (16:34). So the picture of Paul in that synagogue is a man taking the text apart and laying the evidence out where people can reach it. He is not performing over their heads. He is serving.

That it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead. Now the content, and it is the whole quarrel between the church and the synagogue in one sentence. Nothing in popular first-century Jewish expectation prepared anyone for a suffering Messiah. Most Jews expected a conquering Messiah, the son of David who would come in power, break the oppressor and reign; a crucified Messiah was not a disappointing version of the hope, it was a contradiction of it. Paul knew precisely how that sounded, and wrote it down: Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Where did he prove it from? He does not tell us here, but the trail is not hard to follow, because the risen Christ had already walked two disciples through the same argument, and asked the same question in almost the same words: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26)? The texts are the ones the apostles use everywhere: the servant who was pierced for our transgressions and numbered with the transgressors, and who afterwards shall see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53); the sufferer of Psalm 22, whose hands and feet are pierced and his garments divided, and whose psalm ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD; the Holy One whose body will not see corruption (Psalm 16); the Anointed One who is cut off (Daniel 9:26); the pierced one they will look upon and mourn (Zechariah 12:10). The suffering was never an accident that theology had to be rearranged around. It was in the book the whole time, and had been read aloud in that synagogue for generations.

This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ. Notice the shape of the argument, because it is two steps and most people collapse them. First, from the Scriptures: this is what the Christ must be like, one who suffers and rises. Second, from history: and here is the man who matches. He suffered and rose; therefore he is the Messiah. Paul does not begin with Jesus and search for texts to fit him. He establishes the pattern first and then produces the person. It is a model of preaching for every age: from Scripture to Christ.

How can I read the Old Testament and see Christ without forcing it? Read a passage first for what it meant to its first hearers. Then ask where it is heading: which promise it carries forward, which pattern it sets up (the lamb, the priest, the king, the temple), which longing it leaves open that only Christ answers. You are not hunting for secret codes in every tent peg. You are following roads that the New Testament itself has already walked, and Acts gives you the map: the apostles return again and again to the same psalms and prophets. Start with Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Psalm 16, read them slowly beside the Gospel accounts of the cross and the empty tomb, and you will be doing in your own chair what the Bereans did in theirs.

In a sentence. He explained and showed that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and said that this Jesus he was proclaiming is the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Take one of those texts this week and set it beside the passion narrative of a Gospel. Read Psalm 22 and then Matthew 27. Read Isaiah 53 and then Luke 23. You will not need anyone to tell you what it means. And if you teach anyone, children at home or a class at church, try Paul’s order: show them what the Scriptures promised before you show them the one who kept it.

For worship. The cross was not God’s rescue of a plan gone wrong. It was necessary, written into the Scriptures long before a nail was forged, because the Father had determined to save sinners through the suffering of his Son, and the Son had agreed to it gladly. Every lamb on every altar pointed to him, every psalm of the righteous sufferer was rehearsing his lines, and the empty tomb was promised before Bethlehem was a village. He who opened the Scriptures to Cleopas still opens them, and still makes hearts burn.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.

And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas. Persuasion: God uses argument. The Spirit does not bypass the mind; he opens it, and then the reasons do their work.

As did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. Count the three groups, because the proportions are the story. Of the Jews, some. Of the God-fearing Greeks, a great many. Of the leading women, not a few. The synagogue produced a handful; the Gentiles attached to the synagogue came in crowds. Paul’s letters show that many more were Gentiles converted straight from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

But the Jews were jealous. That imbalance is what lights the fuse. These God-fearers were the synagogue’s own fruit, Gentiles it had taught at cost over years, and they are walking out of it behind two visitors after three weeks. The same word, and the same mechanism, as at Pisidian Antioch, where it is worked out at 13:45. What is new here is the method.

Taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob. Luke’s word is agoraioi, literally marketplace men: the idlers who hung about the public square with nothing to do, loafers and thugs for hire. Every ancient city had them, and they could be had cheaply by anyone who wanted a crowd assembled in a hurry. This is not a spontaneous outbreak of civic feeling. It is a demonstration that somebody put together, out of men who neither knew nor cared what the argument was about.

Manufactured opposition. It is worth naming plainly, because it recurs in every century. The opposition to the gospel here did not come from the town. It was manufactured, by respectable people who would not have thrown a stone themselves, using men whose only interest was the day’s pay. The noise in the street was real. The movement behind it was a handful of people with a grievance. When a Christian today faces what looks like a tide of public hostility, it is worth remembering that a crowd is not always what it seems.

They set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. Here is the sentence to sit with. They wanted Paul and Silas, and Paul and Silas were not there. So the mob went through the house of the man who had taken them in. Jason was probably Paul’s host. He has done nothing except offer a spare room. He is a local. When the missionaries move on, and they will move on tonight, he stays, with his door broken, his name on a charge sheet, and his money posted as a bond. Luke tells us nothing else about him, unless he is the Jason Paul later greets as a kinsman in Romans 16:21, which would mean he came through it and was still standing years later.

The cost nobody writes down. This is the part of the cost of the gospel that gets least attention, because the people who bear it do not write the letters. The visiting preacher is beaten and moves on. The local believer who housed him has to go on living in the town afterwards, among the neighbours who watched. If you have ever quietly paid for somebody else’s ministry, in your family, your workplace or your street, Jason is in Scripture for you, and Luke thought his name was worth keeping.

Why would religious people be so jealous of the gospel? Because the gospel takes away the one thing religious pride lives on: being the ones who are in, by the right birth, the right effort, the right observance. When outsiders come in freely by grace, without going through the long apprenticeship, those who trusted in their apprenticeship feel robbed. It is the elder brother’s complaint in the parable (Luke 15:28–30). The cure is not to have less religion but to remember that we too came in by grace alone. A Christian who catches himself resenting how easily someone else was welcomed has found the same jealousy in his own heart, and should take it to the cross.

In a sentence. Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did many God-fearing Greeks and a number of prominent women, but the jealous Jews gathered some bad characters from the marketplace, formed a mob, started a riot and attacked Jason’s house, looking for Paul and Silas.

On a Tuesday. When the gospel bears fruit, expect opposition. And thank God for the Jasons who open their homes. Think of one person whose quiet hospitality, generosity or risk made someone else’s ministry possible, and tell them this week that you noticed. And if you are a Jason, housing a work whose credit goes elsewhere, know that the Lord keeps the names Luke kept.

For worship. Christ sees the broken door in Jason’s house. He who said that whoever receives one of his servants receives him (Matthew 10:40) counts every spare room opened for his sake as a room opened to himself. The world remembers the preachers; the Lord of the harvest remembers the hosts, and on the last day not a cup of cold water given in his name will go unrewarded.
verseByVerse.note: Jason was probably Paul’s host.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”

They dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities. The city authorities were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica and elsewhere in Macedonia but almost unknown in the surviving literature. Critics once said Luke made it up. The inscriptions proved him exactly right, and more than a dozen of them have since been found in Thessalonica alone. It is a small thing, and it is the kind of small thing that shows a historian who was there or who asked people who were.

These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also. It is the most famous compliment ever paid to the church by its enemies, and it is usually quoted more cheerfully than Luke meant it. The verb is anastatoō, and it is not a gentle word: to unsettle, to throw into disorder, to drive out of house and home. Luke uses it once more in this book, of an Egyptian who stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins into the wilderness (21:38). The charge is not that these men are exciting. It is that they are insurgents. And yet the charge is also a compliment, for the gospel turns the world the right way up.

Have come here also. Notice the geography inside the sentence. News of Philippi and Pisidia has arrived ahead of them. Whatever this is, it is not local. Within a few years of the resurrection, the message had spread so widely that its enemies spoke of the whole world.

And they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus. This is the accusation that could actually kill: treason. You have to know what Thessalonica was to feel the weight of it. It was a free city, self-governing, exempt from a Roman garrison, allowed to keep its own assembly and its own magistrates. That freedom was a gift from Rome and could be taken back. A city that harboured men who proclaimed a rival king would not stay free for long. So the charge is aimed with real skill. It is also, in the sense intended, false. Paul was not organising a revolt; he had spent three weeks in a synagogue arguing about Isaiah, and his settled instruction to Christians was to pay their taxes and honour the authorities (Romans 13:1–7).

Not simply untrue either. And yet, and this is the thing the accusers grasped better than many modern Christians do, it was not simply untrue. Jesus is King, the King of kings. Not a political rival to Caesar in the world’s way (John 18:36), but Lord over Caesar too. Paul really was going round the empire announcing that a man had been raised from the dead and made Lord, that every knee would bow to him, and that a day of judgment had been fixed with him as judge. He wrote to this very church, within a few months, about waiting for God’s Son from heaven and about the Lord descending with a cry of command (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 4:16), and the words he used for the Lord’s coming were the words used when an emperor visited a city. If Caesar’s men had read that letter they would have recognised their own vocabulary being used about somebody else. The early Christians would not say Caesar is Lord; they said Jesus is Lord. The mob was wrong about the method and right about the collision. There is a rival king, and his claim is total, and no political arrangement in the world is finally neutral about him.

Does “another king” make Christians political revolutionaries? No. Christ’s kingdom does not advance by the sword or the ballot box but by the word and the Spirit, and his subjects are commanded to pray for rulers, pay their taxes and do good (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But it does mean no ruler is ultimate. When a government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, a Christian must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully and accepting the cost. A Christian can be the best citizen in the town precisely because Caesar is not his god: he serves him honestly, and he will not worship him.

In a sentence. Not finding them, they dragged Jason and some believers before the city officials, shouting that these men who had turned the world upside down had come here, that Jason had welcomed them, and that they were defying Caesar’s decrees by saying there is another king, Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The charge here is that the gospel had visibly rearranged something, households, loyalties, a marketplace, a synagogue, enough for the authorities to notice. It is worth asking what, in your life, the gospel has actually turned over. If the honest answer is that it has fitted in tidily beside everything else and disturbed nothing, that is not evidence that you are peaceable. It may be evidence that nothing much has arrived. Name one loyalty this week, to career, comfort, party or reputation, that has to bow to King Jesus, and let him rearrange it.

For worship. Jesus is King, and Caesar is not. The emperors who were worshipped as lords are names in a textbook, and the carpenter they crucified sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, with every authority in heaven and on earth given to him. He rules not by fear but by love, his throne was reached by a cross, and his subjects are not conscripts but sinners he died to free. Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica. Claiming another king could be treated as treason against Caesar.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things.

And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. Notice who is disturbed, and in what order. The crowd first, then the magistrates, agitated and thrown into confusion. Nobody in this verse is calm. Treason was serious. The emperor Claudius was suspicious of disturbances among Jews (18:2), and the city could lose its privileges as a free city.

Two kinds of fear. The two groups are frightened of different things, and it is worth separating them. The crowd has just been told there is another king. Most of them had no idea who Jesus was an hour ago; what they have now is a rumour of sedition in their own town, shouted by men who sound as if they know. The politarchs are frightened of Rome. Thessalonica held its freedom at Rome’s pleasure, and a city that could not keep order was a city that would have order imposed on it. A few years later, the town clerk at Ephesus says the quiet part out loud when a riot has broken out there: we really are in danger of being charged with rioting (19:40). These men are not weighing a theological claim. They are calculating what a report to the provincial governor would cost them.

The pattern of the authorities. That explains what they do next, and it is worth having the pattern, because it repeats through the whole book and through most of history. The authorities never actually rule on the truth of the matter. Gallio will refuse to hear it (18:15). Felix will keep Paul two years and decide nothing (24:27). Festus will find no charge and send him to Rome anyway. Here the magistrates take a payment and make the problem go away. There is a lesson in it for anyone who expects public vindication of the faith from the people in charge. Institutions are not usually in the business of deciding whether something is true. They are in the business of keeping things quiet, and a church that pins its hopes on being officially found innocent will wait a long time.

Should we not want the gospel to have a fair hearing in public? Yes, and Paul used every legal right he had, as later chapters show (16:37; 25:11). It is good to seek justice and freedom of worship and to pray for them (1 Timothy 2:2). But the church does not depend on them. The gospel spread fastest in this book in cities where the authorities were indifferent or hostile. So work for fairness, and do not be crushed when it does not come. The verdict that matters has already been given, in the resurrection, and no magistrate can overturn it.

In a sentence. The crowd and the city officials were thrown into turmoil by these accusations.

On a Tuesday. The claim that Jesus is King still disturbs. It should. When the news, the office or the family group chat is agitated about Christians, notice who is actually frightened and of what, and answer the fear rather than the noise. Most people who oppose the faith have never heard it. Your calm, honest explanation may be the first time they do.

For worship. The rulers took counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens was not disturbed (Psalm 2:2–4). Cities rage, magistrates calculate, crowds are bought and sold, and the Son reigns on, unthreatened, setting his own times. Our peace is not that the world is quiet; it is that the throne is occupied.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue.

When they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. This is one of the most consequential sentences in Acts and it reads like an administrative footnote. A security is a bond. Jason and the others put up money, and they forfeit it if the condition is broken, a guarantee of good behaviour. And the condition, in a case brought on a charge of proclaiming another king, can only have been something like this: that the trouble would not recur, which in practice meant that the men who caused it would leave and not come back. So Jason has bought Paul’s freedom to leave with his own money, and the price is that Paul cannot return. Every visit would put Jason’s property, and probably Jason, at risk.

Satan hindered us. Now read what Paul writes to this church a few months later, from Corinth, and see whether it does not fit. He says he wanted to come to them again and again, but Satan hindered him (1 Thessalonians 2:18). Earlier in the same paragraph he says they were torn away from them for a short time, in person not in heart, and longed with great desire to see them face to face (2:17). We are not told what the hindrance was and should not pretend to certainty. But a bond lodged with the magistrates of a free city, which would cost a friend everything if Paul walked back through the gate, is the most natural candidate anyone has proposed. And if that is right, then the thing Paul calls Satan’s work is a piece of ordinary municipal paperwork, and he was kept from a church he loved by a legal instrument nobody could appeal.

Ordinary obstacles. It is worth holding on to. Not every obstacle to God’s work is dramatic. Some of it is a form, a rule, a signature, a condition attached in an office by men who were only trying to get home. Paul does not treat that as a lesser kind of opposition, and he does not pretend it did not hurt. Yet he did not sit still either. He wrote letters, he sent Timothy (1 Thessalonians 3:1–2), and the church he could not visit became one of the great joys of his life.

The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. By night, as at Damascus, when Paul was let down the wall in a basket (9:25). Then about fifty miles west, off the main highway, into a quieter town of no great importance.

And when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. Straight in. Not a period of recovery, not a change of tactics after two cities in a row had ended in violence. The same building, the same book, the same argument. They changed the address and nothing else. Persecution did not stop Paul; it only moved him.

Is it cowardly for a Christian to run from persecution? No. Jesus told his disciples that when they were persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul did so repeatedly, though never by denying Christ. Fleeing is wrong when it means abandoning the faith or deserting people who depend on you; it is wise when staying would only waste a life the Lord can still use elsewhere.
