Here the local believers made the decision, and Paul accepted it. Notice that he did not run from the work. He ran to the next synagogue.

In a sentence. After taking a bond from Jason and the others, the officials released them, and the believers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where they went into the synagogue.

On a Tuesday. Think of the paperwork kind of obstacle in your own life: the rule that blocks a ministry, the schedule that keeps you from a friend, the closed door you cannot argue with. Pray about it as Paul did, honestly, and then ask what letter you can write or what Timothy you can send instead. Then go into the next open door as if the last one had not slammed.

For worship. No bond lodged in Thessalonica could bind the word of God. The Lord who let his apostle be kept away kept his church instead, so well that within months Paul was boasting of them in every congregation. Satan hinders; Christ overrules, and the very door that was shut on Paul became the door through which the faith of the Thessalonians went out into the whole world.
verseByVerse.note: Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men.

Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica. The word is eugenesteroi: better born, of finer stock. It is a class word, and Luke uses it about a synagogue in a country town fifty miles off the main road, by comparison with the synagogue of the provincial capital. He is redefining the term under everybody’s nose. Nobility here has nothing to do with birth or address. It is open-mindedness, nobility of character, measured by what a man does when he is handed something new that he did not ask for.

They received the word with all eagerness. Luke tells us exactly what they did, in two halves that have to be kept together. This is the first half, and it is not the cautious half. They were not braced against it. They wanted it, and received it gladly, before they had checked it.

Examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. That is the second half, and the verb, anakrinontes, is a legal one: to sift evidence, to conduct a judicial examination, as in a court. And daily, not once but persistently, which means this went on well past the Sabbath. Men who had a living to earn went home from a synagogue meeting, opened the scrolls, and worked through Isaiah and the Psalms to see whether a visitor had told them the truth. Even Paul, an apostle, was tested by Scripture, and they were praised for it.

Neither credulous nor cynical. Take either half on its own and you get something the Bible does not commend. Eagerness without examination is how people are swept into every enthusiasm that has ever damaged a church; a congregation that receives everything gladly will receive the next thing gladly too. Examination without eagerness is the other disease, and it is the more respectable one: the hearer who arrives armed, whose Bible is open to catch the preacher out, and who has not been moved by anything in twenty years. Luke praises the men who did both at once, which is much harder than either.

Where Christians differ: the final authority. Some say the church or tradition must interpret Scripture for the believer, and that individuals should not test teachers. Verdict: the Bereans tested an apostle by Scripture, and Luke calls it noble. Scripture is the final authority by which every teaching is tested (Isaiah 8:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1). This is sola Scriptura: not that teachers and tradition are useless, but that Scripture judges them all.

Note well what to take from this. The Bereans tested even the apostle Paul against Scripture, and were called noble for it. No teacher, however gifted, learned or authoritative, stands above the Bible; the Word is the final court, and every sermon and every book must be checked against it. This is not suspicion but discernment: test everything, and hold fast what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1). The Berean way is to receive the Word eagerly and to search the Scriptures daily to see whether these things are so, never one without the other.

Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. The result is worth stating because it settles an argument people still have. “Therefore”: Luke puts a causal word in the sentence. The daily examination did not produce a congregation of sceptics who could never be satisfied; it produced faith, and more of it than the city up the road had managed. Rigour was not the enemy of belief here. It was the road to it. Honest study of Scripture leads to Christ, for these are the Scriptures that bear witness about him (John 5:39). And notice the same groups as in Thessalonica, Jews and Greek women of standing and men with them. The gospel is doing in Berea what it did there, without the riot.

Does sola Scriptura make every Christian his own pope? No. The Bereans examined Scripture together, in a synagogue, under teaching, not alone against everybody. Sola Scriptura means Scripture is the only infallible rule, not the only help. God gives the church pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11–12), the wisdom of the centuries, and confessions that summarise what Scripture teaches; all of these are valuable and all are under the Bible, to be corrected by it. A believer who thinks he has found something no Christian has ever seen should be humble and slow. A believer who hears something from the pulpit that the text plainly does not say should open his Bible, and then go and talk to his pastor.

How do I actually examine the Scriptures when I hear a sermon? Keep it simple. Open the passage the preacher is using and read the verses around it: does the point come from the text, or is the text just a launching pad? Look up the cross-references he gives. Ask whether what was said fits the rest of the Bible’s teaching on the subject. If something puzzles you, write it down and ask, kindly. And make the daily part real: a regular, unhurried reading of the Bible for yourself is what gives you the ear to notice when something is off, and the joy to notice when something is gloriously right.

In a sentence. These Jews were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica, receiving the message eagerly and examining the Scriptures every day to see whether what Paul said was true, and so many of them believed, along with a number of prominent Greek women and men.

On a Tuesday. Be a Berean. Receive the word eagerly, and test everything you hear, including this, by Scripture. When you last understood something new from a sermon, did you open the Bible afterwards to check it, and then do something about it? Try it with Sunday’s sermon: read the passage again on Monday evening, and see whether you leave the page more eager or more examined. The aim is both.

For worship. God has given his church a Word that can be checked. He did not ask the Bereans to take an apostle on trust; he put the scrolls in their hands and let the evidence speak, because his truth has nothing to fear from examination. Every promise held up under their daily search, and pointed them to the Son. Blessed be the God whose Word is pure, tried like silver in a furnace seven times (Psalm 12:6), and who rewards the honest seeker with Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there.

But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Fifty miles. On foot or by mule, over two or three days, for no purpose except to break up a meeting in a town they did not live in. Acts has shown this once before, men who followed Paul from Antioch and Iconium to Lystra and got him stoned (14:19), and the observation made there holds here: hatred will spend an effort that indifference never will.

The target. What is worth adding is what they actually did on arrival. They did not preach against him. Luke’s two verbs are agitating and stirring up, the same trade as at Thessalonica, working on people who had no stake in the question until somebody gave them one. And notice the target. Not the synagogue, where the argument would have to be conducted from the Scriptures and where the Bereans had been examining them daily and were not going to be hurried. The crowds. When a case cannot be won in the room where the evidence is, it gets taken outside to the people who have not seen any.

Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea. Paul was the main target, so Paul goes. And immediately: the Berean Christians, converts of a few weeks, read the situation and moved Paul out before it developed. These are the people who had been carefully examining the Scriptures every day, and when the moment came they acted at once. Deliberate people are not necessarily slow people.

But Silas and Timothy remained there. This is easy to miss and is the more important detail. Silas and Timothy stay, in a town that has just been stirred up against them, to hold and strengthen a young church. That is the arrangement Paul used everywhere, and it says something about how he understood his own importance. The work at Berea did not require him. It required somebody, and two somebodies stayed. A man who believed the mission stood or fell on his own presence could not have left, and would have been wrong.

How do I know when to stay and when to step back? Ask whose presence is the problem and whose is needed. Paul’s presence was drawing fire onto the believers; Silas’s and Timothy’s was building them up. Sometimes love means staying when it would be easier to leave; sometimes it means stepping out of the way so that others can do the work without you. Take counsel from mature believers, as Paul accepted the brothers’ decision. And be willing to be the one who is not the centre of the story.

In a sentence. When the Jews of Thessalonica learned Paul was preaching God’s word in Berea, they came and stirred up the crowds, so the believers sent Paul away to the coast at once, while Silas and Timothy stayed.

On a Tuesday. The gospel’s enemies are persistent. Be more persistent in the good. And ask, of anything you are responsible for, whether it could survive your absence, and whether you have arranged it so that it could. Who are you training? Who could stay behind in Berea if you were sent to the sea? Paul had arranged it. Begin arranging it this week.

For worship. The church in Berea did not depend on Paul, because it did not belong to Paul. It belonged to Christ, who builds his church and against whom the gates of hell will not prevail (Matthew 16:18). Opponents may walk fifty miles to stop his word, but the word of God is not bound, and the Good Shepherd who sends one servant away leaves two behind to feed his sheep.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed.

Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens. The escort goes home, and Paul is left standing in Athens on his own. Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, home of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. By Paul’s day it was past its political glory, but still a famous university city, full of philosophers and temples.

Alone in Athens. That is unusual enough to be worth stopping on. Paul almost never worked alone. He had Barnabas, then Silas, then Timothy and Luke; he sent people ahead and kept people with him; his letters are full of names. This is the one extended stretch in Acts where he is by himself, and Luke marks it twice, here, and again at the start of the next paragraph, while Paul was waiting for them at Athens. And we know how he felt about it, because he tells the Thessalonians. Writing a few months later, he says that when he could bear it no longer, he was willing to be left behind at Athens alone (1 Thessalonians 3:1). It is his own word, alone, and he uses it about the most celebrated city in the world.

After receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. Put the position together. He has been run out of Philippi with his back opened, run out of Thessalonica by night, and run out of Berea within weeks. He is in a city where he knows nobody. He has no synagogue standing yet, no lodging that Luke mentions, and no colleague. He has sent a message asking for company as fast as it can be managed, as soon as possible, which is a phrase with feeling in it. Paul did not like to be alone.

Not a machine. This is worth having, because there is a picture of Paul that makes him a kind of machine: indestructible, self-sufficient, always three steps ahead. Scripture will not support it. The same man who sang at midnight in a Philippian cell sends an urgent message from Athens asking his friends to hurry. And the loneliness was not a failure of faith or a gap in his usefulness; the Areopagus address was preached out of it.

Is it wrong for a Christian to feel lonely? No. Being alone and finding it hard is not a sign that something has gone wrong in your Christian life. It is a thing that happened to the apostle Paul, in writing, and he did not apologise for minding. God himself said it was not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18), and our Lord in Gethsemane asked his friends to watch with him. Loneliness is not sin; it is a need. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmists did, and do what Paul did: ask for company. Send the message. Tell a friend or your pastor you are struggling. The body of Christ exists partly so that no member has to carry that alone.

The unnamed escort. One more detail. Luke says the escort brought him as far as Athens. These unnamed Bereans, converts of a few weeks, travelled several hundred miles to see him safely there and then went home. Nobody records their names. They are in the New Testament as those who conducted Paul, and without them the next scene does not happen.

In a sentence. Those escorting Paul brought him to Athens, and left with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.

On a Tuesday. Even Paul needed companions. Do not try to serve alone. Think of someone in your church who is in their Athens at the moment, new to the area, recently bereaved, or carrying a ministry by themselves, and be the answer to their message before they have to send it. And if you are the one in Athens, send the message.

For worship. The Lord who sent Paul into Athens alone was not absent from him there. He is the friend who sticks closer than a brother, the Shepherd who was himself forsaken by all his friends so that none of his people would ever be finally forsaken. He knows what it is to be alone in a city that does not want you, and he sent Timothy back to Paul in time. He has never once left one of his own without a companion; he is that companion.
verseByVerse.note: Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though no longer politically powerful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed by the city’s idols and reasons daily in the synagogue and the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers mock him as a babbler of foreign gods, because he speaks of Jesus and the resurrection, and they bring him before the Areopagus to explain himself. Paul starts from an altar dedicated “to an unknown god”. The God they do not know made everything, lives in no temple, needs nothing, and gives life and breath to all. He made every nation from one man and arranged their times and places so that people would seek him, though he is near to each of us, as their own poets said. So he cannot be represented by images of gold or stone. He has overlooked past ignorance, but now commands everyone to repent, because he has fixed a day of judgement by the man he appointed and raised from the dead. Some mock at the mention of resurrection, others want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius of the council and a woman named Damaris.
verseByVerse.theology:
Natural Theology and Its Limits

Paul's Areopagus address is the New Testament's most extended engagement with natural theology — the knowledge of God available through creation. He acknowledges that God has not left himself without witness (14:17), that all nations are made from one blood and live in God-given boundaries (17:26), that the divine nature is reflected in creation sufficiently to leave humanity without excuse (Romans 1:20). But natural theology has limits: it can establish God's existence and general character; it cannot reveal the gospel of Jesus Christ. The movement from 'the God who made everything' to 'the man he has appointed' requires the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection; some said 'we will hear you again'; some believed. The three responses to the Areopagus address are the three responses to every gospel proclamation: dismissal, deferral, and faith. Now: The gospel continues to divide its hearers along these same three lines. The church's task is not to ensure the first response never comes but to preach in such a way that the third response is genuinely available to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.

Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him. The word for provoked is parōxyneto: stirred, distressed, angered. It is worth noticing where we last met that root. It is the noun paroxysmos that Luke used two chapters ago for the sharp disagreement that broke up Paul and Barnabas (15:39). The same capacity for strong, sharp feeling that ended a partnership is what the idols of Athens now provoke in him. Luke does not comment on that, and it would be a mistake to make him either excuse the quarrel or condemn the zeal. But it is honest to see that this is one man’s temperament, a man who felt things fiercely, and whose fierceness cost him something at Antioch and drove him into the marketplace at Athens. Our strongest characteristics do not come in two versions, one for use in church and one for private life.

As he saw that the city was full of idols. Luke’s word appears nowhere earlier in Greek literature and may be his own coinage: something like idol-infested, the way you would describe a house overrun. Ancient visitors remarked on how crowded the city was with statues and shrines, and a Roman satirist joked of one region that it was easier to meet a god there than a man; Athens would have qualified at least as well.

Every one a masterpiece. And here is the thing to feel. Every one of those idols was a work of art. This was one of the greatest concentrations of sculpture in the history of the world, on the Acropolis and in the streets below it, and any educated visitor came to admire it. Paul was an educated visitor. He walked through the finest art the human race had yet produced, and what he felt was grief and anger, because he was not looking at the workmanship. He was looking at what it was for. Paul felt for God’s honour, and for the people. The thing that moved him was not first the immorality of Athens or its arrogance. It was that the glory belonging to God was being handed to objects, beautifully (Romans 1:23).

So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons. Now watch what he did with the feeling, because this is the part that instructs. Not despair, and not denunciation. He did not withdraw from the city and he did not stand in the street shouting at it. He went and talked to people, and first, as usual, to the people who had the Scriptures.

And in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with stalls, temples, colonnades and people debating. Socrates had taught there. Paul went where the people were: shoppers, loafers, philosophers, slaves sent on errands. The word is the same in both places: he reasoned, argued, took questions. He did not have one message for the religious and another for the street. He had one message and two doorways, and he used whichever was open on the day.

Provocation turned into conversation. That is what to do with the thing that grieves you about the place you live: not a post, not a private lament, not a decision to keep away from it. Go and talk to somebody who is in it.

How can I be grieved by idolatry without becoming self-righteous? Remember that the idols of Athens are in your own heart too. Calvin called the human heart a factory of idols, and every Christian was rescued from some version of that city. Paul’s grief was for God’s glory and for the people, not against them; that is why it sent him into the marketplace to reason, not out of it to sneer. Today’s idols are rarely statues: money, success, the body, a romance, a political cause, comfort. When you see them ruling the people around you, let it move you to pray and to speak, gently and with reasons, as one beggar telling another where the bread is.

In a sentence. While waiting for them in Athens, Paul was deeply distressed to see the city full of idols, so he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearers, and every day in the marketplace with whoever was there.

On a Tuesday. Let idolatry grieve you, and move you to speak. Go where people are. Walk down your own high street with Paul’s eyes, and ask what the people around you are really worshipping, what they hope will save them. Then, instead of lamenting it, find one person in your week to talk with about the God who made them.

For worship. Paul’s spirit was provoked because God is jealous for his glory, and rightly so, for there is no one like him. He will not give his glory to another, nor his praise to carved idols (Isaiah 42:8). Yet the same jealous God did not burn Athens; he sent an apostle to reason with it. His zeal for his own name and his love for idolaters meet in the gospel, where the Son bore the wrath that idolatry deserves, so that those who had bowed to stone could bow to him and live.
verseByVerse.note: The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with statues and shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities” — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. These were the two live schools in Athens, and it is worth knowing what each believed, because Paul’s address is built to walk between them. The Epicureans held that the gods exist but are entirely uninterested in us: serene, remote, and not to be feared. The world is atoms falling; there is no providence, no design, and death is simply the end, which is the good news of the system, because it means there is no afterlife and no judgment waiting. The aim of life is pleasure, understood as tranquillity, the absence of pain and fear.

The Stoics. The Stoics held nearly the opposite. The divine is the reason, the rational principle running through all things, and everything is therefore ordered; the aim of life is to live in harmony with nature, align yourself with that order and accept fate calmly, cultivating virtue, rising above emotion and enduring what comes without complaint. God is not remote; God is diffused, and in some sense is the universe.

Walking between them. Keep both in mind and you will see Paul’s sermon doing very precise work. Against the Epicureans he will say that God made the world, fixed the times and the boundaries, is near, and has appointed a day of judgment. Against the Stoics he will say that God is personal, distinct from what he has made, and not to be identified with it. He agrees with each of them about something and disagrees with both about God.

What does this babbler wish to say? Luke preserves two reactions. The first word is spermologos, a seed-picker. It began as a name for a bird hopping about pecking up scraps, passed into slang for the men who scavenged the market floor for what fell off the carts, and ended as an insult for someone who picks up bits of ideas and passes them off as learning. It is the sneer of the professional at the amateur, and it is worth noticing that this is the first thing the finest minds in the world said about the apostle to the Gentiles.

He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities. That sentence has a shadow over it that any educated Athenian would have felt at once. Introducing new divinities was the charge on which Athens had tried and executed Socrates, four and a half centuries earlier, in this city. Luke’s readers know it, and he does not need to say so.

Because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. Luke explains why they said it. It is quite possible they misheard him. Jesus and Anastasis, the Greek word for resurrection, which is a feminine noun, sound to a pagan ear like a pair of names, a god and his consort, a new divine couple, which would explain the plural divinities exactly. If so, the cleverest men in Athens listened to the gospel and concluded that Paul was recommending two new gods, one of them called Resurrection.

And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus. And what was the Areopagus? It is the Mars Hill of the older English Bibles, the Hill of Ares. It was both a literal rocky outcrop north-west of the Acropolis and, more importantly here, the name of the venerable council that had long met there: Athens’s most respected body of elders, its supreme authority in matters of religion, morals and education. By Paul’s day the council may often have convened down in the marketplace rather than on the hill itself, but it kept the old name. So to be brought to the Areopagus was to be summoned before the cultural and intellectual gatekeepers of the most sophisticated city in the world, to give account of this new teaching: not a formal trial so much as an examination by those who oversaw what ideas and gods Athens would entertain. It is the gospel getting its hearing before the philosophers, at the very summit of human wisdom, and Paul, far from being intimidated, will preach Christ and the resurrection straight into it (vv. 22–31).

Do I need to understand philosophy to share the gospel? No, but it helps to understand the person in front of you. Paul knew what Epicureans and Stoics believed because he had listened in the marketplace. Your neighbours are rarely trained philosophers, but they all have working beliefs: that this life is all there is, that God is distant, that everything happens for a reason, that you should just be true to yourself. Learning to hear those beliefs, and kindly showing where they fall short and where Christ answers what they were reaching for, is what Paul is doing here. It takes curiosity and love more than a degree.

In a sentence. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him, some calling him a babbler, others saying he seemed to preach foreign gods, because he preached Jesus and the resurrection, and they brought him to the Areopagus asking to know this new teaching.

On a Tuesday. You may be mocked for preaching Jesus and the resurrection. Keep preaching them; they are the heart of the gospel. And if you are called a seed-picker, an amateur, by someone cleverer than you, remember who else was. The finest minds of Athens got the gospel wrong on first hearing. That is not a reason to stop telling it; it is a reason to tell it clearly enough that they cannot mishear it twice.

For worship. The wisdom of the world sat in judgment on the risen Christ and called his herald a babbler, and God was not embarrassed. He has made foolish the wisdom of the world, and chosen to save those who believe through the folly of what we preach (1 Corinthians 1:20–21). Jesus and the resurrection are not two new gods; he is the one true God made flesh, and the resurrection is not his consort but his triumph. The philosophers asked what the babbler meant. The answer was life from the dead.
verseByVerse.note: Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was a calm, untroubled pleasure; Stoics taught living by reason and duty. “Babbler” is literally “seed-picker” — like a bird pecking up scraps of learning. The Areopagus was the city’s ancient council, named after the Hill of Ares.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.

For you bring some strange things to our ears. It is a courteous sentence and it is also a summons, and both things are true at once. Strange (xenizonta) is the word for foreign, alien, surprising, belonging somewhere else. They are not saying the message is offensive; they are saying it does not fit any of the shelves they own. That is an honest report. A crucified Jewish workman raised bodily from the dead and appointed judge of the world does not correspond to anything in Greek philosophy or Greek religion, and the philosophers were quite right to find it foreign.

We wish to know therefore what these things mean. Curiosity, at least. An open door. Taken at face value that is exactly what a preacher wants to hear. And Paul takes it at face value: he does not complain about their motives, or demand a better attitude before he will speak. He gets the request and he preaches.

Interest is not yet obedience. But hold it against the sentence Luke puts immediately after it, because he has arranged these two verses deliberately. They say we wish to know; and Luke’s very next remark is that the Athenians spent their time on nothing except telling or hearing something new. He lets their request stand, and then quietly tells you what it was usually worth. That is not cynicism, and it does not mean nobody in the room was serious: two of them are named, and others counted with them, as converts by the end of the chapter. It means Luke knows the difference between an appetite for the interesting and a willingness to be changed, and he expects his reader to know it too.

A distinction to turn on ourselves. We live in the most information-rich moment in history and it has made the confusion easier, not harder. It is entirely possible to consume a great deal about God, sermons, books, podcasts, commentary, with genuine interest, and for the interest itself to be the thing that stands in for obedience. We wish to know what these things mean can be the beginning of faith, or it can be a way of keeping a subject permanently under discussion so that it never has to be settled.

What should I do when a friend is curious about Christianity? Treat the curiosity as an open door, and walk through it gladly, as Paul did. Answer the question actually asked, simply and honestly, and if you do not know the answer, say so and find out. Offer to read a Gospel together; Mark can be read in an evening. But do not confuse interest with faith, theirs or yours. Gently, at the right moment, make it personal: what would it mean for you if this were true? Curiosity can lead to Christ, but only if the conversation eventually reaches him.

In a sentence. They said he was bringing strange ideas to their ears and they wanted to know what they meant.

On a Tuesday. Curiosity can be a doorway. Be ready to explain. And run the test on yourself tonight: when you last understood something from Scripture that you had not understood before, what did you do about it?

For worship. The gospel is strange to every human ear because it did not come from any human heart. No philosopher would have invented a God who becomes a man, dies for his enemies and rises to judge the world in mercy. It is foreign because it is from heaven. And the God of that gospel delights to open doors with the smallest keys, a polite question, a passing curiosity, and to bring those who only wanted to know into the joy of knowing him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new.

Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. Luke steps out of the narrative to tell us about a city, and it is the only aside of its kind in the book. It is a wry comment, and he makes it because everything that happens in the next fifteen verses depends on it. Athens loved novelty: ideas as entertainment.

Something newer. The Greek is sharper than the English. It is not something new but something newer, a comparative. Newer than what? Than the last new thing. The appetite is not for novelty as such but for the next one, which means it can never be satisfied, only fed. And note the verb: they spent their time in nothing else. It was a way of passing a life. Athens had been a great city and was no longer one; the politics had gone to Rome and the trade to Corinth, and what remained was its reputation and its conversation. A place with a magnificent past can become very good at discussing things.

And the foreigners who lived there. Luke includes the visitors. They caught it. The habit belonged to the city rather than to the citizens, and people picked it up by moving in, which is how these things generally work. A culture forms its residents more quietly than they realise.

Investigation or entertainment. This is a description and not a denunciation, and it is worth being careful. Curiosity is not a sin; a few verses earlier Luke praised a synagogue for examining the Scriptures daily, and the Bereans were certainly interested people. The difference between Berea and Athens is not how much they liked ideas. It is what they thought ideas were for. Berea tested a claim to find out whether it was true, because if it was true something would have to happen. Athens sampled a claim to see whether it was interesting. The first is investigation. The second is entertainment with a serious face on. It is a danger for every generation: always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth, gathering teachers to suit itching ears (2 Timothy 3:7; 4:3).

The one thing that cannot be sampled. The reason Luke bothers to tell us is coming in verse 32. When Paul reaches the resurrection, the city that would listen to anything discovers it has a limit after all. An audience that prides itself on being open to everything is usually open to everything that does not require anything, and Athens is about to be handed the one item on the menu that cannot be tasted and put down. The gospel is not a novelty; it is the truth.

Is it wrong to enjoy new ideas and learning? Not at all. Every true discovery is a glimpse of God’s world and God’s wisdom, and Christians have been among the most curious people in history. The problem is curiosity that never commits, that treats God as a topic rather than as the Lord. So enjoy learning, and let it end in worship. When you meet something new about God, ask not only whether it is interesting but whether it is true, and if it is, what it requires of you. Old truths, rightly heard, are often the newest thing a person can learn.

In a sentence. All the Athenians and foreigners living there spent their time doing nothing but talking about or listening to the latest ideas.

On a Tuesday. Do not treat the gospel as just another interesting idea. It calls for a response. Notice how much of your week is spent on the newest thing: the next headline, the next video, the next opinion. Then give the same attention to an old truth this week, and do not move on from it until it has changed something.

For worship. God does not need to be new to be glorious. He is the Ancient of Days, and his mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:23) without his ever changing. The gospel is not the latest idea; it is the eternal purpose of God, hidden for ages and now revealed in Christ. The Athenians chased the newer thing and never caught it. Those who find Christ find the one who makes all things new, and never tire of him.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.

Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. The opening word is chosen with great care and it is deliberately double-edged. Deisidaimonesterous can mean religious, reverent, careful about the gods, or it can mean superstitious. Ancient writers used it both ways, and Paul’s hearers, who were connoisseurs of language, would have heard both possibilities hanging in the air. It is a compliment they could accept and an accurate diagnosis at the same time. That is not a trick. It is the honest position. Paul starts respectfully, without mocking them, but without approving either; he does not resolve the ambiguity because the ambiguity is the truth about them. These people genuinely are reaching for God. They are also getting it comprehensively wrong.

For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship. He had walked round and looked. The sermon that follows was not brought in his luggage; it was written in the streets over some days by a man paying attention to what the people in front of him actually did.

An altar to the unknown god. I found also an altar with this inscription, To the unknown god. Ancient writers mention altars to unknown gods in Athens, set up to be sure no god was offended or left out. The traditional explanation is a good story that may well be true. Diogenes Laertius tells how, centuries earlier, during a plague which no sacrifice would lift, the Athenians sent for Epimenides of Crete, the very poet Paul will quote in a moment, and on his advice turned sheep loose on the Areopagus and built an altar wherever one lay down, dedicated to whatever god was responsible and had not yet been named. It is a monument to a particular kind of anxiety: the fear that somewhere in the pantheon there is a power you have not identified and have therefore offended. So the altar was not humility. It was insurance. And it was an admission that, for all their gods, they did not know the true one.

What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. Now weigh that sentence very exactly, because a great deal is built on it that it will not carry. It is sometimes read as though Paul were saying that the Athenians were worshipping the true God all along under another name, and that all sincere religion arrives at the same place. He does not say that. He says they worship in ignorance, and within seven verses he tells them that the times of that ignorance are over and God now commands them to repent. You do not summon people to repentance for worshipping the right God correctly.

A confession filled. What he does say is subtler and better. This is Paul’s point of contact. Their altar is an admission, carved in stone in the middle of their own city, that their religion is incomplete and has not reached the end of the matter. There is a God they have not named. Paul does not baptise their worship; he takes their confession of ignorance and offers to fill it. He will make the unknown God known.

What could the Athenians know of God? Paul says elsewhere that God’s eternal power and divine nature have been clearly perceived in creation (Romans 1:20), and that the work of the law is written on every heart (Romans 2:14–15). The altar to an unknown god shows a people who knew there was more than their idols. But that knowledge left them without excuse, not without need; it could not tell them who God is or how a sinner may be reconciled to him. That is why Paul proclaims what they did not know.

Do people of other religions worship the true God without knowing it? No. This verse is often used to say so, but Paul says the opposite: the Athenians worshipped in ignorance and needed to repent. Every person knows something of God from creation and conscience, and many religions contain true and beautiful insights. But no one is reconciled to God by sincere worship of a god they do not know. Salvation comes through conscious faith in Jesus Christ, the one mediator between God and men (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). That is not narrowness; it is why Paul crossed the sea to tell them. If they could be saved without hearing, the Areopagus sermon was unnecessary.

Every person’s unknown altar. And that is the model, for anyone who has ever wondered how to begin with somebody who is not a Christian and does not want a lecture. Paul does not open with their sin, though he will reach it. He opens with the thing in their own life that does not add up, and which they have already half-admitted. Every person has an altar to an unknown god somewhere: a longing they cannot account for, a standard they hold others to and cannot meet, a fear of death they do not discuss. The question is not whether they have one. It is whether you have been paying attention as you passed along.

In a sentence. Paul stood in the Areopagus and said he could see the Athenians were very religious, for he had found an altar inscribed To an unknown god, and what they worshipped in ignorance he would now proclaim to them.

On a Tuesday. Pay attention as you pass along. Listen this week for the unknown altar in one conversation: the friend who says there must be something more, the colleague who is afraid of dying, the neighbour who cannot forgive himself. Do not rush in with a lecture. Ask a question, and then, when the door opens, tell them the name of the God they are looking for.

For worship. God is not unknown. He has made himself known in Christ, and told others to tell. The God the Athenians could only grope for has come looking for us: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). No altar to him needs to stand blank any longer. He has a name, and a face, and the scars to prove his love, and he has written his name on every one of his people.
verseByVerse.note: “Very religious” could be a compliment or mean “very superstitious.” Ancient writers mention altars at Athens dedicated to unknown gods.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything.

The God who made the world and everything in it. He begins at the beginning, and he has to, because this audience has no Bible. Paul starts with creation, not with Scripture, which they did not know. There is no point saying as it is written to men who do not accept the writing. So Paul starts with the one thing every human being has in front of him: the world exists, and it did not make itself.

Being Lord of heaven and earth. Sovereign over all. And in one clause he has already parted company with both schools in the room. God made the world, so he is not the indifferent absentee of the Epicureans. And he is Lord of it, over it, distinct from it, so he is not the Stoics’ divine reason diffused through everything. Personal, and other than what he has made. Against pantheism, which says everything is God, and against materialism, which says there is nothing but matter.

Does not live in temples made by man. Now remember where the man is standing. Within sight of the Parthenon. The Areopagus is a rocky outcrop beneath the Acropolis, and if the council met near it Paul had the Parthenon in view over his shoulder: one of the most beautiful buildings in the world, holding a statue of Athena some forty feet high, plated in gold and ivory, the pride and the treasury of the city. Around him were the temples of a dozen other gods. And he says, to the men responsible for all of it, that the God who matters does not live in any of them. It is the sentence Stephen was killed for, when he said it about the temple in Jerusalem (7:48), and Paul is saying it in Athens about theirs. The argument cuts both ways and always has: a God who can be housed is a God who can be managed.

Nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything. This goes at the whole economy of the city. Athens ran on the assumption that the gods required feeding: sacrifices, offerings, festivals, a priesthood, a supply of animals, and the meat trade that went with it. Religion was a transaction in which the gods got what they needed and the city got protection. Paul says God is self-sufficient. He does not need our sacrifices, our worship, or anything (Psalm 50:9–12), and therefore the entire arrangement is upside down. The Epicureans would agree that the gods need nothing, but Paul goes on.

Since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. Then he turns it round with a clause of enormous kindness. We need him; he does not need us. Everything is his gift. The traffic runs the other way. They have been carrying things up the hill to a God who has been supplying them the whole time, and not only them: all mankind, including the men on the council listening to him, including the ones about to laugh.

A comfort for the useless. There is a comfort here for a Christian, and it is not a small one. If God needed nothing from Athens, he needs nothing from you either. Nothing you bring him, your service, your giving, your usefulness, is a contribution to a God who was running short. He asks for those things for your sake and not for his supply. Which means the day you can do none of them, through illness, age or exhaustion, you have not become a worse investment. You were never an investment. You were always a child being given things.

If God needs nothing, why should I worship, pray or serve? Because he is worthy, and because it is good for us. A father does not need his child’s drawing, yet he delights in it and puts it on the wall. God does not need our worship, but he is glorified in it and delights in it, and we were made for it: our hearts are restless until they rest in him. Prayer does not inform God or supply him; it is how he has chosen to give us what he has promised, and how we learn to depend on him. Service does not add to his wealth; it shares in his work, as a privilege. Nothing we do makes him more. Everything we do for him makes us more fully what we were made to be.

In a sentence. Paul said the God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in man-made temples or need human service, since he gives everyone life, breath and everything else.

On a Tuesday. God does not need you. He gives you everything, including your next breath. Worship him for it. Try counting the gifts of one ordinary day, from breath on waking to sleep at night, and thank him for each by name. And if you have been serving God as though he were a demanding employer who might run short, rest: he is a Father who gives.

For worship. He made the world and everything in it, and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him. He needs nothing, lacks nothing, and has been happy from all eternity in the love of Father, Son and Spirit. And this self-sufficient God gives: breath to the men who mock him, rain on the fields of idolaters, and at last his own Son to those who had nothing to give him back. Every breath you have drawn reading this was his gift. Every breath you draw in heaven will be spent praising him for it.

parallels.desc: who gives breath to the people

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,

And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth. You have to know what the Athenians believed about themselves to feel what that sentence does. They held that they were autochthonous: sprung from the soil of Attica itself, not migrants like everybody else, born of the very ground they lived on. It was the proudest thing they said about themselves; the orators repeated it at public funerals, and it was the ground of their conviction that they were not merely different from the rest of the world but better than it. Greeks were superior to barbarians, and Athenians were the truest of the Greeks because they alone had grown where they stood. And Paul, standing in front of the council of that city, says every nation on earth came out of one man.

Every race of one blood. All humanity comes from one man, Adam (Genesis 1–2; Romans 5:12). It is one of the most quietly explosive sentences in Acts. If it is true, the Athenian in the front row and the slave carrying his shopping and the Scythian on the edge of the world are relatives. There is no superior stock. The distinction the city rested on does not exist. And the same sentence has kept doing that work ever since. Every scheme that has ever ranked human beings by descent has been in contradiction not merely of Christian sentiment but of this verse, and Paul preached it, at the summit of the ancient world’s self-regard, to the people most invested in the opposite. This is the foundation of human equality and the end of racism.

Where Christians differ: one man. Some today regard Adam as a symbol rather than a historical person. Verdict: Paul here, and in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, treats Adam as a real man from whom all nations descend, and whose sin and death spread to all. The unity of the human race, and the gospel of the second Adam, rest on it.

Having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place. Linger on this. Paul is saying that God has sovereignly fixed two things for every nation: the times they exist, the appointed seasons, the rise and the fall, the duration of every people and empire; and the places they live, the borders of their lands. Determined (horisas) means marked out, appointed, decreed. So when and where every nation, and every person, lives is no accident of blind chance, which was the Epicurean’s view, nor of impersonal Fate, which was the Stoic’s, but the appointment of the living, personal God who writes the timeline of history and draws the map of the world. He fixed the borders of the peoples (Deuteronomy 32:8); he changes times and seasons, removes kings and sets up kings (Daniel 2:21). Empires rise and fall on his schedule, not their own: a humbling word to proud Athens, and a steadying one for us when the headlines look out of control. History is not adrift; God reigns over it.

That they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Mark why he does it. God arranges the times and places of the nations with a gracious aim: so that people might seek and find him. Feel their way (psēlaphēseian) means to grope, as a blind man in the dark. This lands very personally. Your own century, your country, your town, the family you were born into: none of it is random. The God who sets the seasons of empires set your time and place on purpose, that you would seek him and find him (Esther 4:14; Psalm 139:16). Where and when you live is not an accident; it is an appointment, a kindness designed to bring you home to the God who is near.

Does this mean that unbelievers really seek God? Paul says no one seeks for God (Romans 3:11). Here he states God’s purpose in arranging the nations, that people should seek him, and his phrase feel their way toward him pictures the groping of the blind, who may not find. Fallen humanity gropes for God but cannot find him by its own search. Left to themselves, people turn away from the God they half know. Those who truly find him do so because he first seeks them (18:10; Luke 19:10).

Yet he is actually not far from each one of us. God is near. The problem is not his distance, but our blindness. This is what is meant by God’s omnipresence: not that he is spread thinly through everything, but that there is no place where he is absent and no one he is far from (Psalm 139:7–10; Jeremiah 23:23–24). Paul is preaching it to a city full of shrines built on the opposite assumption.

Does one human race mean ethnic and cultural differences do not matter? No. They matter, and they are God’s good gift: he made the nations and set their places, and in the end people from every tribe and language will stand before the throne, recognisably themselves (Revelation 7:9). What this verse forbids is ranking them. No nation is nearer to God by birth, and no race is lesser. In a church that means the stranger is welcomed as family, prejudice is repented of rather than excused, and the fellowship around the Lord’s Table is the clearest picture on earth of the one blood and the one Saviour.

In a sentence. From one man God made every nation to live on the whole earth, setting their times and boundaries, so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out and find him, though he is not far from any of us.

On a Tuesday. Every person on earth is your relative. Treat them as such. Think of the person of another background you find it hardest to love, and remember you share a grandfather. And when the news makes the world feel out of control, read this verse again: the times and boundaries are in his hand, and so is the place where you live, put there so that you, and your neighbours, might find him.

For worship. The God who drew the map of the world is not far from any of us. He set the boundaries of the nations, and then sent his Son across every boundary to gather a people out of all of them. The first Adam scattered his children in sin and death; the last Adam gathers them back in righteousness and life. One man brought us all into ruin, and one Man brings a countless multitude home. He was near all along, and in Christ he has come nearer still.

parallels.desc: he fixed the borders of the peoples

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’

For in him we live and move and have our being. Paul quotes two pagan poets to a pagan audience, and both quotations were written about Zeus. The first is traditionally credited to Epimenides, the Cretan sage of about 600 BC, from a poem addressed to Zeus. Paul uses their own literature.

As even some of your own poets have said, For we are indeed his offspring. The second is from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a Stoic poet of about 270 BC, in a poem about the stars, and Aratus came from Cilicia, which is Paul’s own home region. He is quoting a poet from home to men in another country. Paul knew Greek literature, and used it as common ground. So what is he doing, and how far does it license us to go?

A true sentence in a false frame. Notice first what he does not do. He does not say the poets were right about Zeus. He does not treat their religion as another road to the same place; he is two verses from telling them to repent. He takes a true sentence out of a false frame and puts it in the true one. Pagans said something accurate about the dependence of every living thing on God, and got the name of the God wrong, and Paul keeps the accurate part and corrects the address. He does it elsewhere too. Writing to Titus about Crete, he quotes Epimenides again, and this time the line is an insult about Cretans, and Paul says flatly that this testimony is true (Titus 1:12–13). He is quite willing to say that an unbeliever has told the truth.

What it does not mean. Paul is not endorsing Zeus or the poets’ theology. He takes true insights they had glimpsed, that we depend on God and are made in his image, and gives them their true meaning in the Creator God. All truth is God’s truth, wherever it is found. We are God’s offspring by creation, not by redemption; the latter comes only through Christ (John 1:12).

Two errors avoided. That gives Christians a settled way of handling the culture they live in, and it avoids two errors. One is the instinct to treat everything outside the church as poison, which Paul plainly did not think and could not have preached this sermon if he had. The other is the habit of quoting whatever is popular in order to seem approachable, which is not what is happening here either: Paul uses two lines and then turns them against the whole religious system the poets belonged to. He is not borrowing credibility. He is taking territory.

Total dependence. Now the content, because it is not decoration. In him we live and move and have our being is not pantheism; Paul has just spent two verses insisting God is distinct from what he made. It is total creaturely dependence: the life you are living at this moment is on loan, moment by moment, and so is the breath you are taking while you read the sentence. The Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3); in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:17).

The hinge into the next verse. And we are indeed his offspring is the hinge into the next verse. Paul lets it stand, in the sense that every human being is God’s creature and bears his image, and then he is about to turn it round on them with considerable force. If we are his offspring, then whatever God is like, he is at least as alive as we are. And that is exactly what a statue is not.

If we are all God’s offspring, are we all God’s children? In one sense yes, in another no, and the difference matters. Every human being is God’s offspring by creation: made by him, in his image, dependent on him, and loved by him as his creature. But Scripture keeps the name children of God, in the saving sense, for those who receive Christ and are born of God (John 1:12–13; Galatians 3:26). So we can say to anyone, you were made by God and for God; and we must also say, you need to be adopted into his family through his Son. Both are true, and the gospel needs both.

Can I use films, songs and books in sharing the gospel? Yes, as Paul did, with care. Look for the true thing a story or song has glimpsed: a longing for home, a hunger for justice, a sense of guilt, a hope that death is not the end. Name it honestly, and then show where it is fulfilled in Christ. Two cautions from this passage. Do not endorse the frame along with the line; Paul quoted a hymn to Zeus without praising Zeus. And do not stop at the common ground. Paul spent two lines on the poets and then went straight to repentance, judgment and the resurrection.

In a sentence. In God we live, move and exist, as some of their own poets had said, for we are his offspring.

On a Tuesday. Use common ground with unbelievers. But always lead from it to Christ. And take the first line personally: tomorrow morning, before you look at your phone, notice that you are breathing, and that he is giving you the breath. Live the day as a creature on loan, and the anxieties that come from imagining you hold yourself up will loosen.

For worship. In him we live and move and have our being. The heart that beats in your chest beats because he wills it, and the universe that he holds together has never once slipped from his hands. The poets of Zeus saw a sliver of this and did not know whose glory they were describing. We know his name. He is the Father from whom every family is named, and in his Son, by whom all things were made, the offspring of creation may become the sons and daughters of grace.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes Greek poets. “For we are indeed his offspring” comes from Aratus; the first line is often attributed to Epimenides.

parallels.desc: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,

Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone. Here is the argument, and it is devastating precisely because it is so simple. If we are God’s offspring, living, thinking, choosing, then God is at least that. And a thing made of metal or rock is not. If we are made by God, God cannot be made by us. The child cannot make the parent. In the city of statues, Paul says: your gods are made by your hands. The image is supposed to represent the greater and is made by the lesser. A living creature manufactures a dead object and then bows to it. Whatever is true of God, he cannot be less alive than the man holding the chisel.

An image formed by the art and imagination of man. Idols are human inventions. And note the two words Paul puts at the end: art and imagination. The idol is not merely stone; it is stone plus a human idea. Somebody decided what the god should look like, and then made it look like that. Which means the worshipper is, in the end, kneeling to his own conception, and the god will never require anything of him that he did not first think of himself.

The modern version. That is why idolatry is so durable, and why the modern version is not statues. Nobody reading this keeps a figure of Athena. But the manufacture of a god out of the art and imagination of man is a live industry, and it is generally done in the first person: a God assembled out of the attributes we approve of, who is offended by the sins we do not commit and relaxed about the ones we do. It is a much more comfortable arrangement than the one Paul is preaching, and it has exactly the defect he names here. It cannot say anything to you that you did not put in it. The test is uncomfortable and it is short. When did the God you believe in last contradict you?

The times of ignorance God overlooked. Overlooked does not mean excused, and it does not mean God did not care. The word means passed over, let go by without pressing the matter, holding back judgment in patience: the same patience Paul described to the farmers at Lystra, where God sent rain and harvests to people who did not know him, and where the whole question of those who never heard is set out (14:16; Romans 3:25). This is the other end of that patience. It has an expiry date, and the date has passed.

Were those who lived before the gospel saved by their ignorance? No. Their ignorance was not innocence; they had the light of creation and suppressed it (Romans 1:18–21). Overlooked means that God held back the full judgment their sins deserved, as Paul says God passed over former sins in his forbearance (Romans 3:25). Now that Christ has come and the message is going to the nations, God commands all people everywhere to repent. The reason is the coming judgment by the risen man (v. 31).

But now he commands all people everywhere to repent. But now: since Christ has come, the time of ignorance is over. Something has happened in history that changes the standing of every person alive, whether or not they have heard of it, and Paul is about to say what it was. Then the words that would have struck this audience hardest. Commands: not an invitation only, not a recommendation to those who find it congenial, but an order. Repentance is not a religious option for the temperamentally devout but a command issued to everyone. And all people everywhere, universal, said to a council that divided the human race into Greeks and barbarians and was rather sure which half mattered. Philosophers too. The universality Paul established in verse 26, one man and every nation, comes back here as a universal summons. If we all came from one, we are all answerable to one.

What repentance is. Repentance is a change of mind about God that turns the whole person round: turning from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). It is not merely feeling sorry, and it is not first giving up a list of bad habits. It is a new verdict on God, that he is real, holy and good, and a new verdict on ourselves, that we have been worshipping what is not God, followed by a turn of the whole life towards him, trusting his mercy in Christ. And notice that this is the first word of demand in the entire sermon. Paul has talked about creation, providence, nearness and poetry for eight verses, and only now, having taken the ground from under the idols, does he tell them to turn round.

If repentance is commanded, is it something I do or something God gives? Both, and Scripture says both without embarrassment. God commands everyone to repent, so no one may excuse himself by waiting for a feeling. Yet repentance is also God’s gift: he granted repentance that leads to life even to the Gentiles (11:18), and he opens hearts as he opened Lydia’s (16:14). The two do not compete. When you hear the command and turn to Christ, you are doing what you were told, and you will discover afterwards that it was God working in you to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). So do not wait. Obey the command, and thank him for the gift.

In a sentence. Since we are God’s offspring, we should not think God is like an image of gold, silver or stone made by human skill and imagination, and though God overlooked the times of ignorance, he now commands all people everywhere to repent.

On a Tuesday. God commands you to repent. Obey him today. Ask the short question honestly: when did the God I believe in last contradict me? Then open your Bible at a passage you have tended to avoid, and let God say something you would not have said yourself. Where he contradicts you, that is where repentance begins.

For worship. The living God cannot be carved, and he will not be imagined into our shape. He is not the work of our hands; we are the work of his. And yet the God who will not be made into an image has given us his own Image: the Son, who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), not formed by human art but born of a virgin by the Holy Spirit. He commands repentance because he is holy, and he grants it because he is merciful, and the times of ignorance end not with a thunderbolt but with an invitation to come home.

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.

Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness. Every clause here is calculated, and to an Athenian every clause is an impossibility. He has fixed a day. Not a cycle, not an endless recurrence of ages, which is how many Greeks thought about time. Against the Stoics, history is not an endless cycle; it has an end, a fixed day. A date, already set, in a diary that is not ours. Nothing about it is contingent on whether the Areopagus finds the idea plausible.

He will judge the world in righteousness. The Epicureans in the audience believed that death ends the matter and there is nothing to fear; that is the comfort their whole system was built to give. Against the Epicureans, there is a judgment. Paul removes their comfort in a single clause. God will judge the whole world, justly.

Judgment as hope. And it is worth saying that judgment is not only a threat. To a room of philosophers it lands as one. But a fixed day when the world is finally assessed in righteousness is, for anyone who has been genuinely wronged, the only hope there is. Every human court is partial, late, or bought. This one will not be. Nothing done in the dark to a person nobody defended will go unaddressed, which is why Scripture speaks of the coming judgment as something the whole creation waits for with longing, and the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth (Psalm 96:12–13).

By a man whom he has appointed. This is the point at which the sermon stops being philosophy. God will judge the world through a human being. Not through fate, not by a principle, not by weighing souls on a cosmic scale, but by a man, with a name, who lived at a particular address and can be identified. It is Jesus, though Paul does not name him yet. And there is mercy in that arrangement which is easy to miss. The one who will assess a human life has lived one. He knows from the inside what it is to be tired, poor, betrayed and afraid. The judge is not an outsider to the conditions he is judging; the Father has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27).

And of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead. The word for assurance is pistis, which usually means faith, but in the courts and the market it meant a guarantee, a proof, the security you offer to make a claim credible. God has posted a bond. The resurrection is not offered here as a comforting doctrine but as the evidence for the appointment: the public demonstration that the man in question is the one. It shows Jesus is the appointed judge, and that judgment is coming. The resurrection is not just good news; it is a warning. The risen man will judge you.

To all. Not to insiders, not to the initiated, not to those with the right temperament. It is a fact placed in the open, and Paul is telling the most sceptical audience in the world that they already have everything they need to check it. So the sermon that began with an altar to a god nobody could name ends with a man everybody can. That is the whole distance the gospel travels: from the unknown god to the named, dated, risen one.

Will Christians be judged too? Yes, but not to decide whether we belong to God. That was settled at the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Believers will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), where their lives are opened and what was done for him is acknowledged, but the verdict on their persons has already been given, and the Judge is the Saviour who died for them. That is why a Christian can say the last day is a hope: the man appointed to judge is the man who bore our judgment.

Why did Paul not mention the cross in this sermon? He almost certainly did, or meant to. Luke gives us a summary, and the speech was interrupted before Paul had finished (v. 32). The resurrection presupposes a death, and Paul everywhere preached Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). With hearers who had no Bible, he had to lay the foundation first: who God is, who we are, and why we need a Saviour, judgment being the reason. That is a wise order for anyone speaking to people with no Christian background. Do not begin with the answer before they know the question; but do not stop before you reach the cross.

In a sentence. For God has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed, and he has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.

On a Tuesday. The day of judgment is fixed on God’s calendar. Are you ready? The only way to be ready is to be found in the Judge himself, trusting him now as Saviour. And if you have been wronged and see no justice coming, hand the case to the one who will judge in righteousness. You do not have to settle every account yourself; a day has been fixed.

For worship. The man who stood silent before Pilate will sit on the throne of the world. The judge of all the earth has hands that were pierced, and the bond God posted to prove his appointment was the empty tomb. To his enemies that is the most terrible news in history; to those who have fled to him, it is the most glorious, because the one who will judge them is the one who loved them and gave himself for them. Come, Lord Jesus.

parallels.desc: he will judge the world in righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” So Paul went out from their midst.

Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. The room had been perfectly civil until this word. Creation, providence, the unity of the human race, even the summons to repent: all of it was strange but discussable. The resurrection is where an audience that would listen to anything stopped listening.

Why the Greeks laughed. It was not stupidity. Most educated Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd, and did not want the body back. The body was the problem: the weight, the appetites, the decay; many believed the body was a prison for the soul, and death, on the best Greek view, was the soul’s release from it. To announce that a man had been raised bodily was not to offer them a hope. It was to propose returning a prisoner to his cell. The resurrection was the stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23; 15:12).

On their own hill. There is a line that makes the moment sharper still. In the Eumenides of Aeschylus, a play set at the founding of this very council and known to every educated Athenian, Apollo declares that when the dust has drunk up a man’s blood, once he is dead there is no resurrection. The word he uses is anastasis, Paul’s word. That is the Athenian creed on the subject, spoken on the Areopagus in their own literature. Paul stands on the same ground and contradicts it.

But others said, We will hear you again about this. The second response, interested or postponing, and it is the most common one in any century. Not refutation. Postponement. It may have been sincere; some of them may have meant it, and at least one member of that council believed before the day was out. But a subject can be kept permanently open, and Felix will do the same thing to Paul at greater length a few chapters later, sending for him often and deciding nothing (24:25–27).

So Paul went out from their midst. The speech was interrupted, as speeches often are in Acts. He did not stay to soften it. He had reached the resurrection, which was the thing he came to say, and when it was refused he left. He had said enough.

Was Athens a failure that Paul learned from? It is often suggested that he over-reached with philosophy and poetry, got a poor return, and afterwards resolved to do it differently, deciding to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2), a resolve he made at Corinth, the very next city. It is a tidy theory and there are reasons to doubt it. Paul did preach Christ risen at Athens; that is precisely what they mocked, and he was not withholding the offensive part. Luke, who chose what to include, gives this speech more space than almost any other and presents it as a model of preaching to people with no Bible. And the contrast Paul draws in 1 Corinthians is not with wise engagement but with polished oratory and human cleverness as a means of persuasion, a warning about method written to a church that was addicted to celebrity speakers. What is fair to say is that Athens was hard ground and Luke does not pretend otherwise. Some places take a long time. That is not the same as having done it wrong.

What should I do when people laugh at what I believe? Expect it, and do not take it as the last word. The resurrection was laughed at on the day it was first preached to the clever, and it has outlived every one of the men who laughed.
