Do not answer mockery with mockery, and do not water down the claim to stop the laughing; Paul did neither. Say the true thing clearly and kindly, and leave it. Then notice the others in the room: the ones who want to hear again, and the quiet one who believes. Mockery is loud, but it is rarely the only response.

In a sentence. When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some sneered, while others said they wanted to hear him again on this, and Paul left the council.

On a Tuesday. Do not remove the resurrection to avoid mockery. It is the heart of the gospel. And examine your own postponements: is there something God has made plain to you that you keep saying you will hear about again? Today is a better day to settle it than tomorrow.

For worship. Aeschylus said there is no resurrection, on that very hill, and the tomb outside Jerusalem said otherwise. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the body the Greeks despised he wore out of the grave, glorified, and carried into heaven. He did not abandon our flesh; he redeemed it. The prisoner is not returned to his cell; the cell is made a palace, and death is swallowed up in victory.
verseByVerse.note: Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.

But some men joined him and believed. That but is doing a great deal of work. The mockery was real, the deferral was real, and Luke records both without softening them, and then he tells you what else happened in the same room. Not many, but some. Some think Athens was a failure, and that Paul then decided to know nothing but Christ crucified in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:2). But Luke presents it as a model speech with real fruit. Wise engagement with culture, and some believed.

Among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite. He names two people. Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council itself, a man of high standing: one of the men who had summoned Paul to explain himself, sitting in judgment on whether this teaching should be allowed a hearing in Athens. The court examined the gospel and one of the judges came over. Tradition, recorded by Eusebius, says he became the first bishop of Athens.

And a woman named Damaris and others with them. We know nothing more of her, and we should not invent her. What is worth noticing is that Luke keeps her name at all. This is one of the most male settings in the book, an ancient council of elders in a city where respectable women did not generally appear in such gatherings, and the two converts Luke chooses to name are a member of the aristocracy and a woman. She is named by Luke for ever. And others with them: unnumbered and unnamed, and that is the whole recorded harvest of the most celebrated sermon in Acts.

The honest figure. Set it against the ledger. At Thessalonica, a great many. At Berea, many. At Corinth, where he goes next, so many that the Lord tells him in a vision to go on speaking because he has many in that city who are his people (18:10). At Athens, two names and some others. And Luke writes it down. He does not pad it, does not explain it away, and does not promise that the seed sown will surely spring up later. He gives the honest figure.

The apostolic standard. That honesty is worth more to a discouraged Christian than any amount of encouragement. The best-prepared, most carefully aimed sermon in the New Testament, preached by an apostle in the intellectual capital of the world, produced a handful of people. If your own work has produced a handful of people, you are not below the apostolic standard. You are on it. And consider what a handful turned out to be. A councillor of the Areopagus is in the New Testament by name, nineteen centuries after the men who laughed at him have disappeared without one. Nobody remembers who mocked. We know who believed.

Why do some believe and others mock at the same sermon? Because faith is God’s gift, not the preacher’s achievement. The same words fell on the whole council; the difference was not in Paul but in what God did in the hearts of Dionysius and Damaris. As Luke said at Pisidian Antioch, as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (13:48). This is not a reason for careless preaching, for God uses means, and Paul prepared carefully. But it is a great comfort. You are responsible for faithfulness, not for results, and you never know which quiet listener the Lord has already chosen to open.

In a sentence. But some men joined him and believed, including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and others.

On a Tuesday. Measure faithfulness, not results. Some believed; that is enough. If you are discouraged by how little has come of your witness, your teaching or your prayers, write down the names you do know of, however few. Then thank God for them by name, as Luke did, and go on sowing.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is never defeated, even on the hardest ground. He had his own people in the council that mocked his resurrection, and he called them out by name, a judge and a woman nobody else would have mentioned. He knows his sheep, every one, and not one whom the Father has given him will be lost. The names of the scoffers have perished. Dionysius and Damaris are written in the Lamb’s book of life, and their names, like ours, are kept there by the one who rose.
verseByVerse.note: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council.

17.theology: General Revelation and the Necessity of the Gospel. Acts 17 contains the New Testament’s most developed account of what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God available to all humanity through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20). Paul acknowledges the Athenians’ religious instinct as genuine — they are groping toward God. But groping is not finding. General revelation creates the question; the gospel alone provides the answer. The God who made all nations from one man, who determined their times and boundaries, who is not far from any of us — this God has now spoken definitively in a man he raised from the dead. The times of ignorance are over. The command is universal: all people everywhere must repent. General revelation without the gospel leaves no one saved; it only leaves everyone without excuse.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, spirit provoked, standing before the intellectual elite of the ancient world with nothing but the story of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mock. Some believe. He moves on. The church in Athens is small, but Dionysius and Damaris are there — and the gospel is in Europe to stay.

Now: The contemporary West is increasingly like Athens: intellectually sophisticated, spiritually restless, full of altars to unnamed gods, suspicious of exclusive truth claims. The Areopagus sermon is the model for engagement: begin where people are, affirm what is true in their searching, and then announce the resurrection without apology. The resurrection is still the scandal. It is also still the only answer to the altar inscribed “To the unknown god.”

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>17</sup>And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. <sup>19</sup>And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. <sup>20</sup>When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. <sup>21</sup>But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. <sup>22</sup>When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
From Athens Paul goes to Corinth, the wealthy, proud commercial city on the isthmus, capital of the province of Achaia (see the introduction to 1 Corinthians). He finds Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple recently expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius, and works with them making tents. The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews because of riots “at the instigation of Chrestus”, probably disputes about Christ in the Jewish community, around AD 49. When Silas and Timothy arrive with support from Macedonia, Paul devotes himself fully to preaching. Opposed in the synagogue, he moves next door to the house of a God-fearer, Titius Justus; the synagogue ruler Crispus believes with his household, and many Corinthians are baptised. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul not to be afraid, because he has many people in this city, and Paul stays eighteen months.

When Jewish opponents bring Paul before the new proconsul, Gallio, he dismisses the case as a quarrel about Jewish words and names, not a Roman crime, a ruling that gave the church breathing space. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s year in office to about AD 51–52, one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. Paul then sails with Priscilla and Aquila to Ephesus, leaves them there, and returns via Caesarea and Jerusalem to Antioch, completing his second journey. The third journey begins with a tour of the Galatian churches. Meanwhile an eloquent, learned Jew from Alexandria, Apollos, arrives in Ephesus, preaching accurately about Jesus but knowing only John’s baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and he goes on to Corinth, where he powerfully refutes the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, where he lodges and works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews recently expelled from Rome. He reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath, and when Silas and Timothy arrive he gives himself fully to preaching that Jesus is the Messiah. When the Jews oppose and abuse him, he shakes out his clothes and declares their blood is on their own heads; from now on he will go to the Gentiles. He moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, a God-fearer. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his household believe, and many Corinthians believe and are baptised. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul to keep speaking without fear, for no one will harm him, and he has many people in this city. Paul stays a year and a half, teaching God’s word. Under the proconsul Gallio, the Jews bring Paul to court, accusing him of persuading people to worship God against the law, but Gallio refuses to judge questions of words, names and Jewish law and throws them out. The crowd beats Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, in front of the court, and Gallio does not care. After many days Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having had his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow. At Ephesus he reasons in the synagogue, but declines to stay longer, promising to return if God wills. He lands at Caesarea, greets the church in Jerusalem and goes down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tent-Making Ministry and the Support of Proclamation

Paul's tent-making partnership with Aquila and Priscilla is the first explicit mention of Paul's manual labor as a means of supporting his missionary work. Reformed theology has often discussed whether 'tentmaker ministry' (self-supported missionary work) is a normative apostolic pattern or a situational adaptation. Paul's own letters suggest the latter: he worked with his hands to avoid being a burden on new churches and to model the dignity of labor, but he accepted support from established communities (Philippians 4:15–16). The Corinthian mission itself was eventually supported by the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gallio decision — the Roman proconsul's dismissal of the Jewish charge against Paul — protected Paul's preaching at Corinth by treating it as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God continues to use civil authorities and legal processes to protect the gospel's proclamation, even when those authorities have no understanding of or sympathy with the gospel. Providence works through the decisions of those who know nothing of its purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,

Meaning first. Acts 18 tells of Paul’s eighteen months in Corinth, a wealthy, immoral city, where he works with his hands, preaches in the synagogue and then next door to it, and is told by the Lord in a vision: I have many in this city who are my people. A Roman proconsul refuses to try him, setting a precedent of tolerance. Then the second journey ends, the third begins, and a gifted preacher named Apollos is taught the way of God more accurately by a married couple, Priscilla and Aquila. God’s work goes on through ordinary believers. And over the whole chapter stands the Lord Jesus himself, who comes to a frightened apostle at night, who already owns people in the most notorious city in Greece, and who turns emperors, proconsuls and tentmakers alike to the service of his gospel.

After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. Fifty miles west, and a complete change of world. Athens was a university town living on its past; Corinth was money. Rome had destroyed the old city and left it in ruins for a century, then refounded it as a colony for freedmen and veterans, and by Paul’s day it was the capital of the province of Achaia and one of the richest ports in the empire, standing on the narrow isthmus between two seas, with a harbour on each and the traffic of both passing through it. It was about a hundred years old and behaved like it.

To Corinthianise. Its reputation was appalling and had been for centuries; the Greeks had a verb, to Corinthianise, which meant to live immorally. The temple of Aphrodite stood above it on the heights. Whatever you have heard about the immorality of Corinth is roughly what a first-century reader would have assumed. Paul later wrote two letters to the church there, and they show what kind of people the gospel found in it. So Paul walks out of the most cultured city in the world, where he got a handful of converts, into the most notorious, alone and with no contacts. It is worth remembering how this looked at the time, because he tells us: he came to them in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3).

And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla. A married couple who became Paul’s close friends and co-workers (Romans 16:3–5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19). Priscilla (Prisca) is often named first, perhaps because she was more prominent or of higher social standing. Luke never records their conversion, and never calls them converts of Paul’s; they simply appear as believers, which suggests they may already have been Christians from the church in Rome, years before Paul wrote to it.

Because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. That expulsion is datable, and it is one of the places where the New Testament and Roman history touch. The Roman biographer Suetonius, writing some seventy years later, records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, probably a garbled form of Christ, around AD 49. Chrestus was a common slave name and was also, in ordinary speech, almost indistinguishable from Christus. What a Roman official at a distance would have seen, if the gospel had reached the Jewish quarter of Rome, is exactly what Acts has shown us in city after city: disputes about Christ in the synagogues, and the synagogue in an uproar over a man called Christ.

A forced removal. If that is right, and it is the most natural reading, then the edict that threw Aquila and Priscilla out of their home was a piece of imperial policy made in ignorance about a quarrel the emperor did not understand, concerning the very gospel that was about to be preached in Corinth. And notice what it produced. Claudius emptied the Jewish quarter of Rome, and in doing so delivered to a lonely and frightened apostle in Corinth the two most useful colleagues he would ever have. They will house him, work beside him, cross the sea with him, teach Apollos, risk their necks for him (Romans 16:4), and host churches in more than one city. They did not choose to come. They were deported. And it is worth saying to anybody whose life has been rearranged by a decision taken somewhere else, by people who never considered them: the most fruitful partnership in the New Testament began with a forced removal.

What if my move, job loss or upheaval was forced on me? Then you are in good company, and in good hands. Aquila and Priscilla lost their home, their business and their city by an emperor’s signature, and the Lord used it to put them exactly where his apostle needed them. That does not make the loss painless, and you need not pretend it was. But it means the decision taken over your head was not the last word on your life. The God who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28) is not waiting for better rulers before he can use you. Ask him, in the new place, whom he has set beside you, and whom he has set you beside.

In a sentence. After this Paul left Athens for Corinth, where he met a Jew named Aquila from Pontus, recently arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome, and he went to see them.

On a Tuesday. God brings his people together through even the decrees of emperors. Your moves are in his hands. Look around the place where circumstances have put you and ask who is there because of it: a colleague, a neighbour, a lonely believer in a new church. You may be someone’s Aquila, sent by a decision you resented.

For worship. The Lord reigns over the palace in Rome and the workshop in Corinth. Claudius thought he was clearing troublemakers out of his capital; in fact he was posting two of Christ’s servants to their next assignment. The King of kings writes his purposes through the decrees of men who do not know his name, and not one edict has ever been issued that he could not turn to the good of his church and the glory of his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth, the capital of the province of Achaia, was a busy, wealthy trading city with a reputation for immorality. The Roman historian Suetonius mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome over disturbances, around AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.

And because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. Tentmakers worked with leather and with the coarse cloth woven from goats’ hair, making tents, awnings and perhaps sails: a trade of the awl and the knife, hard on the hands, and unglamorous. Cilicia, Paul’s home province, was known for that cloth. He had it because his family were observant Jews, and Jewish teachers commonly learned a trade, so as not to make money from teaching the law; the teachers of Israel were not a salaried class. So Paul the Pharisee, trained under Gamaliel, had also been trained to cut leather, and in Corinth it kept him alive.

Six days at the bench. Now consider what that means for the shape of these months, because it is easy to read Acts and imagine a full-time evangelist. In the ancient city the working day began at first light and ran until the light went. Paul was at the bench for it. He tells this very church that they labour, working with their own hands (1 Corinthians 4:12), and reminds the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden to any of them (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). Years later, saying goodbye to the Ephesian elders, he holds up his hands and says they ministered to his necessities and to those who were with him (20:34). Paul supported himself, so as not to be a burden and to remove any suspicion that he preached for money.

A workshop open to the street. So the church at Corinth was planted by a man who preached on the Sabbath and made tents the other six days, and who may well have done the two things in the same room. A workshop in that world was open to the street; customers came, apprentices worked, neighbours stopped. A great deal of the conversation that founded this church probably happened over the bench, with both men’s hands busy.

Your work is not time off from God. The first thing that follows is for anyone who has ever felt that his working life is what he does when he is not serving God. Paul’s trade was not an interruption of his ministry, and it was not merely a way of funding it. It put him among ordinary working people on their own terms, gave him a reason to be in the city, and made him impossible to accuse of being in it for the money, a charge he had to answer more than once at Corinth.

Where Christians differ: should ministers be paid? Some say ministers should always work a trade like Paul; others that the church must always support them. Verdict: Paul teaches that those who preach the gospel have a right to live by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18), and he accepted gifts (Philippians 4:15–16; 2 Corinthians 11:8–9). But he sometimes gave up that right for the gospel’s sake. Both patterns are biblical. Churches should support their ministers generously; ministers may work when the work requires it.

A right waived, not a rule. This is a guard, because this passage gets used to argue that paid ministry is a compromise. Paul did not think so. He argued at length that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel, and then said he had not made use of that right (1 Corinthians 9:14–15). It was a right he waived, in a particular city, for particular reasons, which is the opposite of a rule that nobody should be supported.

Provision that looked like a job. And it is worth noticing where the friendship came from. Not a shared theology, not a shared background, for he was from Tarsus and they were from Pontus by way of Rome, but a shared trade. God’s provision for Paul’s loneliness in Corinth arrived looking like a job.

How can my ordinary job serve the gospel? In at least three ways, all visible here. First, the work itself is service to God when it is done honestly and well, as for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23); making a good tent is not spiritually neutral. Second, it puts you among people a pastor may never meet, on their ground and on equal terms, and conversations happen naturally there. Third, it gives you a life that commends the gospel: paying your way, keeping your word, not being a burden. You do not need to preach at the photocopier. Be the kind of colleague whose faith people ask about, and be ready when they do.

In a sentence. Because he had the same trade, he stayed and worked with them, for they were tentmakers.

On a Tuesday. Ordinary work can serve the gospel. Do yours as for the Lord. Tomorrow at work, think of yourself as Paul at the bench: the task in front of you is God’s work, and the people beside you are God’s appointment. And if you are in a church, ask whether your minister is supported generously enough to give himself to the word, and whether you are part of that.

For worship. The Son of God himself worked with his hands. For most of his earthly life the Lord of glory was a carpenter in Nazareth, and he did not think it beneath him. He has hallowed the workshop and the workbench; he provided for his lonely apostle through a trade and a friendship; and he provides for us still, often in the plainest clothes. Every honest day’s work done for him is accepted by him, and no labour in the Lord is in vain.
verseByVerse.note: Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth. Jewish teachers commonly had a trade; Paul supported himself so as not to burden the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.

And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. Work during the week, preaching on the Sabbath. He reasoned, and tried to persuade, Sabbath after Sabbath, for as long as they would have him. This was not a campaign. It was a routine, worked at week after week by a man who spent the other six days cutting leather. And notice the honesty of the second verb. He tried to persuade. Luke does not say he persuaded them. Some weeks nothing happened, and Luke admits it.

When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word. Something changes when the two men arrive. Occupied (syneicheto) means wholly absorbed, pressed, held fast. From this point he is not fitting the gospel round the working day.

What changed? Luke does not say here, but Paul does. Writing to Corinth about this very period, he says that when he was with them and in need, he did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied his need (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15). Silas and Timothy came from Philippi and Thessalonica, and they came with gifts from the Macedonian churches, and with good news from Thessalonica too (1 Thessalonians 3:6). So the sequence is plain. Money arrived from two poor churches several hundred miles away, and an apostle put down his tools and preached full time in the biggest city in Greece.

What a gift buys. That is worth holding on to, because giving to Christian work is one of the more abstract things a believer does. Here it is not abstract at all. The Macedonians were not wealthy; Paul says elsewhere that they gave out of extreme poverty, according to their means and beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:2–3). What their gift bought was hours: the hours Paul would otherwise have spent at a bench, converted directly into hours in front of people. The church at Corinth exists partly because Christians in Philippi went without something.

Testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. His constant theme, and note the content he was so gripped by, because Luke states it in one clause. Not that Jesus was a Christ, or a good man, or a way. That the Christ, the one they had been waiting for, argued about, and prayed for every Sabbath in that building, was this particular man. Everything else Paul preached hangs off that identification.

How much should I give, and to what? Scripture does not set a fixed percentage for Christians, but it gives clear principles: give regularly, in proportion to what you have, cheerfully and not under compulsion, and generously, as those who have received everything in Christ (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:9; 9:7). Your first responsibility is to your own church, so that those who teach you can give themselves to the word (Galatians 6:6). Beyond that, the Macedonians show the joy of supporting gospel work far away. Many Christians find a tenth a good starting point and grow from there. The question is not how little is required but what the grace of Christ moves you to give.

In a sentence. Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks, and when Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.

On a Tuesday. Support those who preach, so they can give themselves to the word. Think of one missionary or gospel worker you know by name, and turn your gift into their hours this month. And if you teach, children, a home group, a Sunday school, notice that Paul tried to persuade week after week when nothing seemed to happen. Keep turning up.

For worship. The Christ the synagogue awaited was Jesus, and Jesus was worth a man’s whole absorption. He is the one for whom Paul put down his tools, for whom poor churches emptied their purses, for whom the gospel was carried across seas. He became poor so that we, through his poverty, might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and every gift given for his name is only grace flowing back toward its source.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue.

And when they opposed and reviled him. Reviled (blasphēmountōn) means they blasphemed, insulting Christ. The argument has stopped being an argument.

He shook out his garments. The gesture first. He shakes out his cloak, a gesture of breaking off responsibility, the same kind of prophetic sign as shaking the dust from the feet, which is set out at 13:51 (Nehemiah 5:13). It says: I have nothing of yours on me, and I carry nothing away.

Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. But the words are not from that scene at all, and they repay knowing, because they are the key to a question that troubles a great many Christians. That is the language of Ezekiel 33, and it belongs to one image: the watchman on the wall. God sets a man to watch, and an army is coming. If the watchman sees the sword and does not blow the trumpet, and somebody is taken, God will require his blood at the watchman’s hand. But if he blows the trumpet and the people do not take warning, their blood is on their own heads, and the watchman has delivered his soul (Ezekiel 33:1–9). Paul had warned them; their blood was on them, not on him. He used the same words again in Ephesus (20:26).

The trumpet and the walls. Look carefully at what the watchman is and is not responsible for. He is responsible for blowing the trumpet. He is not responsible for whether anybody comes inside the walls. Those are two different things, and Ezekiel keeps them rigorously apart. Paul has been in that synagogue every Sabbath for weeks. He has reasoned, argued, answered, and been reviled for it. And what he says, in effect, is: the trumpet has been blown. His conscience is clear, not because he succeeded, but because he spoke. It is a sobering view of the preacher’s responsibility: to warn.

For the one who grieves. That distinction is worth more than almost anything else in this chapter to the reader who carries a private grief about somebody unconverted: a father, a brother, a child who has heard it all and wants none of it. There is a burden that belongs to you and a burden that does not, and the two get mixed together until a person is worn out praying under the weight of an outcome he was never given charge of. You are answerable for the trumpet. You are not answerable for the walls.

Not a licence to give up. And note the guard on the other side. Paul says this to a synagogue that had turned hostile after months, not to someone who had said no once. And read what he does next.

From now on I will go to the Gentiles. In Corinth, at least. He will go to the synagogue first again in the very next city (v. 19).

And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. Next door! A bold, perhaps provocative, choice. He walks out of the building and sets up the Christian meeting immediately on the other side of the wall, in the house of a God-fearer who had presumably been sitting in that synagogue listening to him. Some identify him with Gaius, Paul’s host in Corinth, whose full Roman name may have been Gaius Titius Justus (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14).

Standing where they cannot miss him. There is a certain steel in that, and it is not spite. From now on, the congregation that threw him out will have the believers meeting next door, and some of their own number in it, including, in the very next verse, their own ruler. Paul has said that he is going to the Gentiles. He has not gone anywhere. He is standing where they cannot miss him, which is exactly what a watchman does.

When is it right to stop speaking to someone about Christ? Rarely, and never in the heart. Paul stopped arguing in this synagogue after months of open blasphemy, but he did not stop loving its people, praying for them or living in plain view of them; he wrote later that he would wish himself cut off for their sake (Romans 9:1–3). For most of us, with a family member or friend, the lesson is not to walk away but to change the mode: when words are only provoking scorn, keep praying, keep loving, keep living next door, and be ready when the door opens again. Jesus himself told his disciples not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), but that was about wisdom in speaking, not permission to stop caring.

In a sentence. When they opposed and insulted him, Paul shook out his clothes and told them their blood was on their own heads, he was innocent, and from then on he would go to the Gentiles, and he moved to the house of Titius Justus, a God-fearer, next door to the synagogue.

On a Tuesday. Warn people faithfully. Then leave the result with God. If you have been carrying the conversion of someone you love as if it were your job to achieve, lay that weight down tonight in prayer. Keep blowing the trumpet: speak when you can, love always, pray daily. The walls belong to the Lord.

For worship. The Lord who appoints watchmen does not leave them to carry the walls. Salvation belongs to the LORD; he alone opens hearts, and he alone bears the weight of the outcome. The same Christ who wept over Jerusalem because it would not come to him did not stop loving it, and in his mercy the very next convert from that synagogue was its ruler. He shuts no door that he cannot open again.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off responsibility.

parallels.desc: his blood shall be on his own head

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized.

Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. Read that immediately after verse 6, because Luke has put it there on purpose. Paul has just shaken out his garments at that synagogue and declared himself clear of it. And the first convert Luke names afterwards is the man who ran it. The leader of the synagogue that rejected Paul came over. It was a great blow to the opposition, and a great joy.

Who the ruler was. The ruler of a synagogue was not a rabbi but the official responsible for the building and the services: who read, who spoke, what happened on the Sabbath. He was, in other words, the man who had been giving Paul the platform for those weeks, and quite possibly the man who had to withdraw it. He is a person of standing in the Jewish community of the province’s capital, with everything to lose, and he believes. Paul remembered it. Writing back to this church a few years later, when they were quarrelling about whose party they belonged to, he says he is thankful he baptised almost none of them, except Crispus and Gaius (1 Corinthians 1:14). Crispus was one of the few Paul baptised himself.

Two rulers in a row. There is a thread here that runs to the end of the chapter, which is worth following, because Luke does not point it out. Crispus is the ruler of the synagogue in verse 8. By verse 17 the ruler of the synagogue is a man called Sosthenes, so they replaced him, as they would have to. And when Paul writes to Corinth, the letter opens with Paul and our brother Sosthenes (1 Corinthians 1:1). If that is the same man, and it is a fair guess, then that synagogue lost two rulers in a row to Jesus Christ, and the second one is standing beside Paul when he writes the letter.

Does this household baptism support infant baptism? Luke says the household believed, so this describes believers, as with Cornelius (10:44–48) and the jailer (16:34). It gives no warrant for baptising those who cannot yet believe, though Christians who baptise infants read household baptisms as a covenant pattern. Those brothers hold their view from a sincere reading of God’s covenant promises, and we honour them; but the pattern in this verse is the one Luke gives everywhere: hearing, believing, then baptism.

And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. Hearing, believing, baptism: the order again. Many. In the town whose name was a byword for vice. Paul lists later what some of them had been: idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards, swindlers, a catalogue of the sins that city was famous for. And then he writes the sentence that has carried more people out of their past than almost any other in Scripture: and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

Were. If you have a history that you assume disqualifies you, that verb was written to the church founded in this verse. Not are; were. The past is real, and it is past. The washing is complete, the justification is final, and the new name is permanent.

If I was baptised as an infant, should I be baptised now? This is a question to take seriously and kindly. On the view this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, baptism is for those who have repented and believed, so a believer baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, not as a rejection of his parents’ love or his upbringing but as obedience to Christ’s pattern. Talk it through with your pastor. If your church baptises infants, be honest with its elders about your conscience, and seek peace. Many godly Christians differ here; none of them is saved by water, and all who trust Christ are washed by his blood.

In a sentence. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord, and many Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptised.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond the gospel: synagogue rulers, or the worst sinners of Corinth. Think of the person you have quietly decided will never come to Christ, and pray for him by name this week. And if your own past still whispers that you are disqualified, answer it with one word from 1 Corinthians 6:11: were.

For worship. The grace of God reached into the synagogue and took its ruler, and reached into the gutters of Corinth and took its drunkards and adulterers, and washed them all in the same blood. No one is too respectable to need it and no one is too ruined to receive it. Such were some of us. But we were washed, we were sanctified, we were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God, and the Lamb who did it is worthy of all praise.

parallels.desc: I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.”

And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, Do not be afraid. You do not tell a man not to be afraid unless he is. That is the first thing in this verse and it should not be hurried past. Somewhere in those early months at Corinth, the apostle Paul was frightened enough that the Lord Jesus came to him at night to say so. And he had reason. He had been beaten in Philippi, chased out of Thessalonica by night and out of Berea, mocked in Athens, and he was now in a city where the synagogue had just turned on him. He came to Corinth, he tells them, in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3). The man who wrote more of the New Testament’s letters than anyone knew what it was to want to stop. Even the great apostle needed encouragement.

But go on speaking and do not be silent. Then notice what the Lord actually commands, because it is not what we would expect. Not rest. Not go somewhere safer. Go on speaking and do not be silent: the same instruction twice, once positively and once negatively, which is how you speak to somebody who is on the edge of stopping. The cure for the fear is to keep doing the thing that caused it, with the Lord beside you. And then three reasons, and each one is precise.

For I am with you. Not I will protect your reputation, or your comfort. Presence. It is the promise of God to his servants throughout Scripture: to Joshua, to Jeremiah, to the apostles at the end of Matthew (Joshua 1:9; Jeremiah 1:8; Matthew 28:20).

And no one will attack you to harm you. Protection for this time. Now read that clause very carefully, because it is easy to misquote and the difference matters enormously. It does not say nobody will attack him. People do attack him: in two verses’ time there is a united assault and he is dragged before the tribunal. What is promised is that no attack will land as harm. That is not a lesser promise; it is a truer one, and it is the shape of every promise of this kind in Scripture. Paul was not given a quiet eighteen months. He was given eighteen months in which what happened to him could not stop what God was doing through him. And in due course, elsewhere, he was arrested and eventually executed, which is not a failure of the word given here, because this word was given about Corinth and about now.

When a promise seems to fail. That is worth saying to anyone who has claimed a verse like this and then been hurt by something. God’s particular assurances of protection in Scripture are almost always attached to a work and a season, and they promise that the work will not be defeated. They do not promise that you will not be touched. The promises that cover every believer at every hour are deeper still: that nothing will separate us from the love of God in Christ (Romans 8:35–39), and that not a hair of our head will finally perish (Luke 21:18).

For I have many in this city who are my people. Then the third reason, and it is the strangest and best of them. Before they believed, they were already the Lord’s people. Corinth, wicked as it was, held many whom God had chosen. Not yet converted, but already his. This is election, and it is the greatest encouragement to evangelism. Paul preached not knowing who they were; God knew. The gospel would find them.

Does this verse teach election? Arminian Christians read it as God’s foreknowledge of those who would believe. But the Lord calls them his people before they have believed, and the reason Paul should stay and preach is that they are his. The more likely reading is that God has chosen his people, and calls them through the preaching of the gospel (13:48). Election is the reason mission cannot fail, not a reason to stop.

Where Christians differ: does election discourage evangelism? Some think that if God has chosen his people, there is no need to preach. Verdict: here election is the reason to keep preaching. God has his people; the gospel is the means by which they are called (Romans 10:14–17; 2 Timothy 2:10). Election guarantees that preaching will not be in vain.

The discouraged evangelist’s comfort. Notice how God’s election here does not cool evangelism but fires it: because God has a chosen people in Corinth who will come to faith through the preaching, Paul can keep speaking, unafraid, certain his labour will not be wasted. Election does not make sowing pointless; it makes the harvest sure, for the Lord gathers his own through the gospel preached. Paul says he endures everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory (2 Timothy 2:10). It is the discouraged evangelist’s deepest comfort: somewhere in your city are people God means to save, and your faithful witness is the means he will use.

How do I know if the person I am speaking to is one of the elect? You do not, and you do not need to. Paul did not know which Corinthians were the Lord’s; he only knew there were many. Election is God’s secret until it shows itself in faith (Deuteronomy 29:29). Our instruction is to offer Christ freely and sincerely to everyone, and to plead with them to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). Treat every person as someone the Lord may be about to call, and you will speak to them with hope. And if you are worried whether you yourself are chosen, the answer is not to search the hidden decree but to come to Christ: all who come to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. One night the Lord told Paul in a vision not to be afraid but to keep speaking and not be silent, for the Lord was with him, no one would harm him, and he had many people in this city.

On a Tuesday. God has many people in your city who are his. Keep speaking; he will gather them. Name the fear that has made you quiet: of being mocked, of losing a friendship, of saying it badly. Then hear the three reasons as spoken to you: I am with you; nothing will defeat my work; I have people here. Have one conversation this week you would otherwise have avoided.

For worship. The risen Lord came to his frightened servant in the night. He did not scold him; he stood by him, and told him a secret: that the most notorious city in Greece was full of people who already belonged to him. Before the foundation of the world he had chosen them, at the cross he had bought them, and through a trembling tentmaker he would call them. No city is too dark for the Good Shepherd who says, I have other sheep, and I must bring them also (John 10:16).

parallels.desc: do not be afraid, for I am with you

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. Eighteen months, his longest stay so far. Set that against the rest of the book and the number is extraordinary. A few weeks, perhaps months, at Thessalonica. A few weeks at Berea. Days at Athens. Everywhere in the first two journeys, Paul plants and is moved on, usually by force. Here he stops.

Permission to put down roots. And Luke puts the verse immediately after the vision, which is the explanation. The promise in verses 9 and 10 was not only an emotional comfort; it was permission to put down roots. A man being hunted from town to town does not build. A man who has been told that nothing will land as harm and that there are many in this city who belong to God can unpack.

Teaching. He was teaching, which is grounding the church: sustained instruction rather than proclamation alone. Not eighteen months of evangelistic addresses only; eighteen months of taking a mixed congregation of Jews, God-fearers and converted pagans through the Scriptures. Whatever the Corinthians later got wrong, and they got a remarkable amount wrong, they had been thoroughly taught.

Letters written from Corinth. He also wrote from here. Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this time (1 Thessalonians 3:6), among the earliest of Paul’s letters we possess, and among the earliest documents in the New Testament. They were written by a tentmaker in Corinth to a church he had been driven away from and could not get back to, and they are in every Bible on earth.

Slow work. And there is a lesson in the sheer length of it for anybody impatient with slow work. A year and a half in one city, mostly teaching the same people, is not what a reader of Acts expects of Paul, and it is what produced the church that generated more New Testament correspondence than any other. The dramatic chapters get the attention. This verse is where the depth came from.

Why does solid teaching matter so much if the gospel is simple? Because the gospel is simple enough for a child to receive and deep enough to occupy us for eternity, and Christians who are not taught are easily confused, discouraged or led astray (Ephesians 4:14). The Corinthians had eighteen months of Paul and still went wrong on factions, sex, lawsuits, worship and the resurrection; imagine them without it. Good teaching does not replace faith; it feeds it. So sit under the preaching of the Bible gladly and regularly, join a group that studies it, and be patient. Growth in grace is slow, like a tree, and most of it happens out of sight.

In a sentence. He stayed a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.

On a Tuesday. Churches need patient teaching of God’s word. Sit under it gladly. If you are tempted to move on from a church because it is not exciting, ask first whether it is feeding you on Scripture week by week. If it is, stay, and put down roots. And thank God for the pastors and teachers who give years, not weeks, to the same people.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is a patient builder. He does not raise his church in a weekend; he lays it stone by stone, sermon by sermon, over months and years and centuries, and he never tires of the work. The word he caused to be taught in Corinth is still feeding his people, and the letters written from that workshop still comfort the dying. He who began a good work in his people will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.”

But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia. Luke drops a Roman official’s name into the narrative, and in doing so hands historians the single most useful sentence in the New Testament for fixing chronology. An inscription at Delphi carries a letter from the emperor Claudius which mentions Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, and it dates his term to about AD 51–52. Proconsuls served, as a rule, for one year. So Paul was in Corinth in the early fifties, and every other date in his life, the conversion, the councils, the letters, is measured outward from this verse. This gives one of the firmest dates in Paul’s life, anchoring the chronology of his journeys and letters. The whole timeline of the apostolic age hangs on Luke having got one provincial governor’s term right. The wider case for his care as a historian is set out at 5:37–38.

The man on the bench. Gallio is not a stranger to Roman literature either. He was the elder brother of Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and tutor to the young Nero, who dedicated books to him and spoke of his charm as something nobody could resist. That is the temperament on the bench in this scene: cultivated, easy-going, and entirely uninterested in the matter in front of him.

What a proconsul was. A quick word on proconsul (Greek anthypatos). Rome’s provinces came in two kinds: the settled, peaceful ones governed on behalf of the Senate by a proconsul, and the frontier ones governed by the emperor’s own appointees. Achaia (southern Greece, capital Corinth) was a senatorial province at this time, so its governor was a proconsul: usually a senior senator sent out for about a year, holding supreme civil and judicial authority, which is why Paul is hauled before his tribunal for a ruling. In modern terms he was something like a centrally appointed regional governor who was also the province’s chief judge, combining in one man the executive and judicial powers our democracies usually keep apart, answerable not to local voters but to Rome. Luke’s precise title here is also a quiet mark of his accuracy: Achaia’s status shifted over the years, and he names it correctly for this moment.

The Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal. United: after many months in which the synagogue had lost its ruler and a good many of its members, the opposition finally coordinates. And they choose their moment: a new governor, freshly arrived, who might be expected to want a quiet province and to defer to established religious authority. Perhaps they hoped a new governor would favour them. The tribunal (bēma) was the judgment platform, and its remains still stand in the Corinth forum.

This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law. That sentence is carefully built, and the ambiguity is the whole strategy. Contrary to which law? Roman law, which permitted Judaism as a legal religion; or Jewish law? If Gallio hears Roman law, then Paul is promoting an unlicensed religion and can be shut down across the province by a single ruling. They wanted Rome to rule that Christianity was not Judaism and so illegal. If he hears Jewish law, it is a synagogue quarrel and none of his business. They are hoping he will not notice which. Everything depends on a busy proconsul hearing the word law and reaching for the wrong one.

Why does it matter that the Bible gets names and dates right? Because Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas but a report of things that happened: a man was crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised on the third day. If Luke were careless about proconsuls, we might wonder whether he was careless about the resurrection. Instead, again and again, inscriptions and histories confirm his titles, places and dates. That does not prove the gospel by itself, but it means the witness is trustworthy, and Luke wrote, as he told Theophilus, so that we may have certainty concerning the things we have been taught (Luke 1:4).

In a sentence. When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews united against Paul and brought him to the judgment seat, accusing him of persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.

On a Tuesday. The Bible is rooted in real history, with real names and dates. Your faith rests on facts. When doubts come, and they come to most believers, go back to the facts: the empty tomb, the eyewitnesses, the historian who got the proconsul right. Faith is not believing what you know is not true; it is trusting the God who acted in history.

For worship. The Word became flesh in a datable year, under named rulers, in real places, and the God of the gospel is not shy of the record. He entered our history so that we could be saved within it, and he has left his fingerprints in stone at Delphi as surely as in Scripture. Gallio’s name is remembered because it was written beside Paul’s; the Lord who governs all the governors keeps his own record, and our names are in it.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s term as proconsul to about AD 51–52 — one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. The tribunal (bema) still stands in the Corinthian marketplace.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.”

But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews. Paul never gets to speak. He draws breath to make his defence and the governor cuts across him and decides the case. Paul did not even need to defend himself. It is the only trial in Acts where Paul is not permitted to say a word, and it is the one that goes best for him.

If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. Gallio has seen straight through the ambiguity. He separates crime from religious opinion: the two categories a Roman court existed for, an actual crime or a serious fraud, and observes that this is neither.

But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. Read the phrase words and names, because it is a small window into how the gospel looked from outside. Gallio has listened to the charge and concluded that the whole business is a dispute over terminology within a foreign religion: an argument about whether a particular Jewish title belongs to a particular dead Jew. He is not entirely wrong about the subject matter and he is completely wrong about its weight.

Classification. And that is worth sitting with, because it is the commonest reaction the gospel meets in a comfortable society. Not persecution, and not conversion. Classification. The thing is filed as a matter of words and names, a private religious preference, a vocabulary that some people find meaningful, and set aside without hostility by somebody who has other things to do. Athens laughed; Gallio simply did not think it was about anything.

A crucial ruling. Now the consequence, which is enormous and entirely unintended. Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a crime under Roman law. That meant Christianity was treated, for now, as a form of Judaism, a permitted religion, under the legal shelter Judaism enjoyed as an ancient and licensed faith. A proconsul’s ruling may well have been remembered by other magistrates, though Luke does not say so. A senior Roman judge’s decision protected the gospel for years, until Nero. Luke records it partly to show Theophilus that Christianity was not a threat to Rome.

I refuse to be a judge of these things. Indifference, but useful indifference. God used it. God gave his church years of legal cover through a man who could not have been less interested in it. Gallio was not being kind, or fair-minded about religion, or secretly sympathetic. He was declining to waste an afternoon. And the protection was real. That is a useful thing to know when you look at the people who currently hold power over the circumstances of your life. God’s providence does not require their goodwill, or their understanding, or even their attention.

How should I respond when people treat my faith as just words and names? Without anger, and without accepting the label. Most people in comfortable societies are not hostile to Christianity; they simply file it as a private preference. The answer is not to shout but to show that it is about something: a real man who really rose, a real God to whom every person must give account, a real forgiveness that changes real lives. Your life is often the best argument. Gallio could dismiss a vocabulary; it is much harder to dismiss a neighbour whose marriage, honesty and hope have been visibly changed by Christ.

In a sentence. Before Paul could speak, Gallio told the Jews that if it were a crime he would hear them, but since it was a dispute about words, names and their own law, they must settle it themselves, for he would not judge such matters.

On a Tuesday. Think of the authority over your circumstances who seems most indifferent: the employer, the council, the court, the government. Pray for them, as you are told to (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and then rest. Your safety does not depend on their goodwill. The Lord who used Gallio’s boredom can use their busyness.

For worship. God can use even a pagan judge’s indifference to protect his church. He rules over courts. Gallio thought the whole matter beneath him, and he was the instrument of Christ’s promise that no one would harm his servant. The Lord does not need the attention of the powerful to carry out his purposes; he turns the heart of the king like streams of water wherever he will (Proverbs 21:1), and the words and names that Gallio waved away are the Name above every name.
verseByVerse.note: Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a Roman crime.

verseByVerse.quote: And he drove them from the tribunal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he drove them from the tribunal.

And he drove them from the tribunal. One short sentence, and the verb is not a polite one. He had them driven off, perhaps by his lictors: the court cleared, the case not merely dismissed but swept out.

The reversal. Picture it. These men had come with a coordinated complaint, timed for a new governor, framed in language designed to make a Roman act. They had brought their opponent with them. And within about a minute they are being pushed away from the bench in the middle of the marketplace, in front of the whole city, having been told that their religion is not worth a magistrate’s time. The humiliation is public and it is total, and the next verse shows what a crowd does with a public humiliation.

Protection by contempt. It is worth pausing on what has actually happened here, because it is not what the opponents intended or what Paul could have arranged. The most effective protection the early church received in Greece came from contempt. Gallio did not defend Christianity; he refused to distinguish it from Judaism, and threw the whole quarrel out of court as beneath his notice. The Lord promised no one would harm Paul. He kept his word, and he kept it by means of a man who did not believe in him.

God uses indifference. God is quite willing to use a man’s indifference. He used Pharaoh’s hardness and Cyrus’s ambition and Pilate’s cowardice, and here he uses a cultivated Roman’s boredom. None of these men was serving him knowingly, and all of them were doing exactly what he intended. There is comfort in that and there is also a warning, and both should be taken. The comfort is that the advance of the gospel has never depended on the sympathy of the people in charge. The warning is Gallio himself: he is on the right side of history in this chapter and there is no suggestion whatever that it did him any good. A man can render enormous service to the purposes of God and remain entirely outside them.

The bema. One last thing about the place itself. The tribunal Gallio cleared was the bēma, the raised platform in the Corinthian marketplace from which a magistrate gave judgment. Its foundations are still there, and it is one of the very few spots on earth where a visitor can stand on the actual stones of a scene in the New Testament. And Paul did not forget the platform. Writing to Christians who knew it well, he says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10); and writing from this same city to Rome, he says we will all stand before the judgment seat of God (Romans 14:10). The word is the same. The Corinthians knew exactly what a bema looked like, because there was one in their market square and their apostle had been dragged in front of it.

Two judgment seats. Set the two side by side, which is surely what Paul intended. At the first, the judge would not hear the case, the accused was never allowed to speak, and the verdict came from a man who thought the whole matter beneath him. At the second, every case is heard, nothing is dismissed as a quarrel about words and names, and the Judge has taken the trouble to become one of the accused.

Can God really use people who do not know him? Yes, all the time, and Scripture is full of them: Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, Caesar Augustus, whose census brought Mary to Bethlehem. God’s providence governs all his creatures and all their actions (Westminster 5.1), without making him the author of their sin or excusing them for it. That is why a Christian can pray for unbelieving rulers, employers and relatives with real hope: God can use them for good whether they intend it or not. But do not mistake being used for being saved. The only safe place is not on the right side of history, but in Christ.

In a sentence. He had them ejected from the court.

On a Tuesday. The Lord promised no one would harm Paul. He kept his word. Think of one promise of God you are holding on to for the work he has given you, and notice how he kept a promise to Paul by an unlikely means. Then, when you next pass a courtroom, a council office or a parliament, remember the other bema, and live today as one who will stand before it, held by grace.

For worship. There is a judgment seat in heaven where the Judge listens to every case and dismisses none, and on it sits the one who stood silent before Pilate’s bema for our sake. He was condemned in a court that would not hear the truth, so that those who trust him will be acquitted in the court where truth is all. Gallio drove the accusers away in contempt; Christ silences every accuser of his people in love, for who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.

And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. A crowd has just watched a group of Jews thrown out of court by the governor, and it does what crowds do with people who have been publicly stripped of protection. They take the leader of the delegation and beat him where the proconsul can see. Sosthenes was probably Crispus’s successor, and leader of the failed case. Who beat him? Perhaps Greeks, venting anti-Jewish feeling, which ran strong in a Roman colony; or Jews, angry at his failure. Either way, this has nothing to do with Paul. Nobody here is defending him. The mob is not on the side of the gospel; it simply turns on whoever has just lost.

But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. Indifference. That is the same indifference that had just protected the church, now watching a man beaten in front of the bench and declining to intervene. Luke sets the two effects of one man’s temperament side by side without a word of comment, and the reader who was warming to Gallio in verse 15 is meant to feel the chill in verse 17. Detachment is not a virtue. It served the gospel in one verse and left a man bleeding in the next.

Who was Sosthenes? The ruler of the synagogue, which means the successor of Crispus, who had believed in verse 8. Then look at the first line of the letter Paul later wrote back to this city: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes (1 Corinthians 1:1). It is not certain that they are the same man, and it should not be asserted. But it is a striking coincidence, and if it is the same man, then the beating in this verse is the last thing the New Testament records about him before he turns up as a Christian standing beside the apostle he had prosecuted. If so, the beating led him to Christ.

After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. Heading home to Antioch. He does not leave in a hurry, which is itself a mark of how completely Gallio’s ruling had changed the situation. And when he goes, the couple who took him in go with him, leaving the city and the business they had built after being deported from Rome. Luke names Priscilla first, as he does more often than not.

At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port, and a church grew there too: Paul later commends to the Romans our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), who very probably carried that letter to Rome. And there, on his way to the boat, the apostle of justification by faith had his head shaved because of a vow. Luke tells us nothing else: not what the vow was for, not when he took it, not what he had asked. It has the shape of the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, in which a man separated himself to the LORD for a period, drank no wine, let his hair grow, and cut it off at the end (Numbers 6:1–21). The vow was probably a Nazirite-type vow of thanksgiving, during which the hair was not cut, though why he took it we are not told, and guesses about gratitude for Corinth or for safety are only guesses. What cannot be avoided is the question it raises.

Whose vow was it, and why cut his hair at Cenchreae? The grammar could refer to Aquila, but Paul is the natural subject. It was probably a vow of thanksgiving, perhaps of the Nazirite kind, ended by cutting his hair as he left Corinth, with the hair perhaps offered later in Jerusalem. Luke does not explain, but it shows Paul free to keep Jewish customs where they did not touch the gospel (21:23–26).

May a believer still keep the law? Paul’s vow raises a real question: now that Christ has come, may a believer still keep the law, or parts of it? The Reformed answer distinguishes three strands in the law of Moses. The moral law (the Ten Commandments, summed up as loving God and neighbour) reflects God’s unchanging character and abides always; we are not saved by it, but the believer gladly obeys it as the Spirit-enabled pattern of a thankful life. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, feasts, clean and unclean foods, circumcision as rite) was the shadow that pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (see on Colossians 2:16–17); no Christian is bound to keep it. The civil law that governed Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though its underlying justice still instructs (Westminster 19.3–5). So: the moral law stands; the ceremonial and civil are not binding as obligations.

The careful line Paul walks. But notice the careful line Paul walks: here a Jewish vow, later a temple purification (21:23–26), and Timothy’s circumcision (16:3), yet a flat refusal to circumcise Titus (Galatians 2:3–5) and thunder against anyone who made law-keeping a condition of salvation (Galatians 5:2–4). The difference is always why. Made a means of being right with God, or imposed on others as necessary, a practice denies the gospel and is forbidden. Kept freely, as heritage, devotion, conscience, or love that wins a hearing (to the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews, 1 Corinthians 9:20), it is Christian liberty. Paul kept his vow not to earn anything but as free devotion; that is the model. Freedom in Christ is freedom to keep customs too, when not for salvation.

The two cases. So, a Jewish believer may in liberty keep ancestral customs, feasts, food traditions, even a vow, as heritage, devotion and witness among his people, as Paul did, provided he never makes them the ground of his standing nor binds them on others. A Gentile believer is under no obligation to the ceremonial law at all (the whole verdict of Acts 15); he may find devotional value in some Old Testament root, for one person esteems one day as better than another, and each one should be fully convinced in his own mind (Romans 14:5), but he must heed Galatians’ warning never to put himself under the law as a system, which is to fall from grace (Galatians 4:10–11; 5:1). The test in every case: am I doing this to be saved or accepted, or imposing it as necessary? Then stop. Is it a free, loving, Christ-honouring practice that binds no one? Then you are free. Christ alone for salvation; liberty in the rest, governed by love. Where the Lord’s Day and the Sabbath fit is one place believers differ: many, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that the fourth commandment continues as the Christian Sabbath, now kept on the Lord’s Day; others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and that no day binds the conscience. The second is the view taken here: Christ is our rest, and the Lord’s Day is a gift gladly kept, not a law (see on Matthew 12:11–12 and on 20:7).

Should Christians today make vows to God? Scripture permits them but does not require them, and warns against making them rashly: it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). Jesus forbade the kind of oath-making that treats some promises as binding and others as not, and told us to let our yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37). A lawful vow is a voluntary promise to God of something good and within your power, made thoughtfully, never as a bargain to get something from him or to earn his favour (Westminster 22.6–7). Marriage vows and church membership vows are the most common today, and they should be kept with the seriousness of a promise made before God.

In a sentence. Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the court, but Gallio took no notice, and Paul stayed on some time, then said goodbye to the believers and sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having cut his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow.

On a Tuesday. Freedom in Christ means you may keep good customs, as long as you do not trust them for salvation. Look at the religious habits in your own life, the traditions, disciplines and observances, and ask Paul’s question of each: am I doing this to be accepted, or because I am accepted? And watch for Gallio’s chill in yourself: is there someone being hurt in front of you whom you have decided is not your business?

For worship. The Lord who turned the persecutor Saul into an apostle may well have turned the beaten Sosthenes into a brother. Christ is not ashamed to take the man who led the prosecution and stand him beside the man he prosecuted. And the freedom he gives is real: we owe nothing to the shadows, because the substance has come. Every vow and feast and sacrifice pointed to him, and in him every promise of God finds its yes (2 Corinthians 1:20).
verseByVerse.note: A Sosthenes later appears with Paul as a believer. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port. Cutting the hair marked the end of a vow of special devotion.

parallels.desc: the Nazirite vow
Phoebe of Cenchreae
