verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.

And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there. That is a larger sentence than it looks. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, the greatest city in Asia, the place Paul would eventually spend three years, and the province where the Spirit had earlier forbidden Paul to preach at the start of this journey (16:6). Now the door opens. He passes through it for a few days, and what he leaves behind is a married couple with a trade.

A seed in Ephesus. Priscilla and Aquila stayed, preparing the ground for Paul’s return. They are put down in Ephesus like a seed. Within a few verses they will take the most gifted preacher in the eastern Mediterranean aside and finish his education; by the time Paul writes to Corinth from this city, there is a church meeting in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19). Paul’s strategy for the greatest city in Asia was to leave two tentmakers in it.

But he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. As always. Days off the boat, in a city he is only passing through, and he is in the synagogue arguing. There is no version of Paul that takes a week to look round a town.

When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. Now this is the remarkable thing, and it is almost never remarked on. A synagogue asks Paul to stay longer, and he says no. Think of what he has been through to get a hearing like this. Thrown out of Pisidian Antioch, stoned at Lystra, run out of Thessalonica and Berea, mocked at Athens, hauled before a tribunal at Corinth. Here, at last, is a receptive synagogue in the most strategic city in the province, asking for more. And he leaves. An open door, but not yet. Paul wanted to reach Jerusalem, perhaps for a feast, and there was a sending church to report to.

An open door is not a summons. Luke does not fully explain it, but what the passage plainly shows is that an open door is not the same thing as a summons. Paul had learned that in reverse at Troas, when every door was shut and it turned out to be direction; here every door is open and it is still not the instruction. That is worth having, because we are generally taught to read opportunity as guidance: if it is possible, and it is good, and people want it, then surely. Paul had before him a genuine opportunity, in a strategic place, urged on him by people who wanted the gospel. He said no, and went home to report to his church. Not every good thing you could do is a thing you are being asked to do. Some of them belong to somebody else, or to a later year. And Ephesus, in fact, was waiting for him. He would come back and give it three years, which is longer than he gave any other city in his life.

How do I know whether an opportunity is from God? Ask more than whether it is open and good. Ask whether it fits what God has already given you to do: your existing responsibilities, your church, your family, the work in hand. Ask those who know you well and whose wisdom you trust, as Paul reported to his sending church. Ask whether you can say yes to it without saying no to something God has clearly called you to. Pray, and be willing to wait. Scripture gives no promise of private signals for every choice, but it gives wisdom (James 1:5), and wisdom often sounds like not yet.

In a sentence. When they reached Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there and went into the synagogue to reason with the Jews, and when they asked him to stay longer, he declined.

On a Tuesday. Not every open door is for now. Wait for God’s timing. Look at the requests on your calendar this month, and before agreeing to the next good thing, ask whether it is yours to do. Saying no to a good thing so that you can do the right thing is not a lack of zeal. It is obedience.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest knows the times of every field. He held Ephesus back when Paul wanted it, opened it when Paul was passing through, and kept it waiting until the season for three full years had come. His timing is never late and never early, and the cities he plans to reach he reaches. He plants his tentmakers like seed, and waits, and brings the harvest in.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: But on taking leave of them he said, "I will return to you if God wills," and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.

But on taking leave of them he said, I will return to you if God wills. Three words that Paul evidently meant literally. Paul’s plans were always submitted to God. He uses the same qualification writing to Corinth, that he will come to them soon, if the Lord wills (1 Corinthians 4:19), and James turns it into a settled Christian habit: instead of boasting about tomorrow, you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:13–15). It is not a superstitious formula, but a humble acknowledgment.

A phrase with teeth. It is easy to hear as a pious formula, and in our mouths it often is. In Paul’s it had teeth, and this whole journey is the evidence. He had been forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia, forbidden to enter Bithynia, sent to Macedonia by a vision, and driven out of three cities in succession. A man whose plans had been overruled that often had stopped saying he would do things without adding whose permission they needed. And God did will it (19:1). He returned, for three years, the longest stay of his ministry. The qualification was not pessimism. It was accuracy about who was arranging the itinerary.

When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church. Luke’s compression here is severe, and the two little direction words carry the meaning. You always go up to Jerusalem and down from it, whatever the map says, because it is the holy city set among the hills. So went up and greeted the church, with no city named, means Jerusalem, the mother church, several days’ travel inland from the port, for a visit Luke covers in a handful of words.

And then went down to Antioch. Home to the sending church, which is where the whole thing started. The church that fasted and prayed and laid hands on Barnabas and Saul in 13:2 gets its man back for the second time. He has now been round the Aegean, planted churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth, left Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, and written the first of his letters, and he comes home and reports to the congregation that sent him. This is the end of the second missionary journey, about three years and some 2,800 miles.

Accountable to a local church. That is worth noticing about a man with as much authority as any Christian has ever had. He had seen the risen Christ, he had been given the gospel by revelation, and he still travelled hundreds of miles at the end of a journey to stand in front of an ordinary local church and tell them what had happened. The second missionary journey began with a quarrel about John Mark and it ends in the same city, with the mission enormously enlarged.

Does saying if God wills mean I should not make plans? No. Paul made detailed plans, and Scripture commends the forethought of the ant and the builder who counts the cost (Proverbs 6:6–8; Luke 14:28). What James forbids is planning as if we owned tomorrow, the boast that assumes our lives and diaries are in our own hands. So plan carefully and work hard, and hold every plan with an open hand. Say if the Lord wills and mean it: when a plan is overturned, you will be disappointed, but not shaken, because you never thought the itinerary was yours.

In a sentence. As he left them, he promised to return if God willed, and sailed from Ephesus to Caesarea, went up to greet the church in Jerusalem, and then went down to Antioch.

On a Tuesday. Make your plans, and add, if God wills. Mean it. Look at next week’s diary and pray over it item by item, handing each one back to the Lord. And if you serve in any way beyond your local church, report back to it: tell them what God has done, and let them pray and rejoice with you.

For worship. Our times are in his hand (Psalm 31:15). The God who forbade Asia and opened Macedonia, who closed Ephesus and then reopened it, writes the itinerary of every one of his servants, and he has never lost one on the road. He brought Paul home to Antioch with the gospel planted across Greece, and he will bring all his people home at last, every plan of his fulfilled and every journey ended in his presence.

parallels.desc: if the Lord wills

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After some time in Antioch, Paul set out on his third journey and travelled from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a learned man with a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and spoke with great fervour, teaching accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they invited him to their home and explained to him the way of God more adequately. When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the believers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On arriving, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed, for he vigorously refuted his Jewish opponents in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping short of the full apostolic message — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

After spending some time there, he departed. Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey, around AD 53. It will centre on Ephesus. That is the whole of its beginning. One verse. No commissioning service, no vision, no laying on of hands: before the first journey Luke gave us a whole scene in the church at Antioch, and here Paul simply leaves and starts walking.

And went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia. And where does he go? Back over the same ground. Galatia and Phrygia take in the towns of the first journey, Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch, the places where he was stoned and expelled, and which he had already revisited. He is visiting the churches founded on the first journey yet again. Notice too the phrase from one place to the next, suggesting an unhurried, methodical circuit rather than a dash through.

Strengthening all the disciples. Nothing about that is new territory or new converts. It is maintenance, and the verb Luke chooses says so: strengthening, making firm what is already standing. It is the pastoral heart of an apostle. He used the same word when Paul went back through those towns the first time (14:22) and when he set out on the second journey (15:41). Three journeys, and every one of them involves an apostle propping up small congregations he has already planted. And notice the word all. Not the promising ones, not the strategic ones. All the disciples.

Going back. There is a temptation, in Christian work as in anything else, to believe that the real thing is the founding and everything afterwards is administration. Luke does not present it that way. Paul spent an enormous proportion of his life going back, and the letters, which are the reason we know anything about him, are simply this same activity conducted by post when he could not go in person. If your own service to God consists largely of turning up again for the same people, who are not obviously further on than they were last year, you are doing the thing this verse describes, and it is what the apostle to the Gentiles did with his time.

What does strengthening other Christians actually look like? It is mostly ordinary. Turning up. Remembering what someone told you last week and asking how it went. Opening the Bible with them and pointing to a promise that fits their trouble. Praying with them, not only for them. Warning them gently when they are drifting, and reminding them that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (14:22). Sending a message on the anniversary of a bereavement. None of it is dramatic, and almost all of it matters. Paul’s word for it is the same whether he was walking to Lystra or writing a letter.

In a sentence. After some time in Antioch, Paul set out and travelled from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

On a Tuesday. Strengthen those who follow Christ. Visit, encourage, teach. Pick one believer this week who is not obviously flourishing, and go back to them: a call, a visit, a verse. The ministry of returning is the ministry of the apostle.

For worship. The Good Shepherd does not found his flock and forget it. He goes back for the one that strays, he carries the lambs in his arms, and he never wearies of tending the same sheep year after year. Paul’s long walks through Galatia were only a shadow of Christ’s patience with his church: he intercedes for us still, strengthens the weak hands, and will present every one of his people blameless before the Father.
verseByVerse.note: Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.

Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. Alexandria is worth pausing on, because it explains the man. Alexandria in Egypt was the second city of the empire, the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of the great library, and it held the largest and most cultured Jewish community outside Judea. The Old Testament had been translated into Greek there. Philo, the most celebrated Jewish thinker of the age, was writing there in Apollos’s own lifetime. A Jew educated in Alexandria was educated as well as anyone then living.

He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. Luke piles up the commendations, five of them, before he raises any difficulty. Eloquent (logios): learned, articulate. Competent (dynatos): powerful, mighty in the Scriptures. Not merely well-informed: strong in them, able to use them. A gifted preacher. Some in Corinth later preferred him to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6). Some, from Luther on, have suggested he wrote Hebrews, though that is only a guess.

He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. He knew the basics, and more than the basics.

And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus. Fervent (zeōn): literally boiling, burning with zeal, perhaps by the Spirit. Paul uses the identical phrase when telling the Romans how a Christian ought to be (Romans 12:11). And accurately. Luke is not damning him with faint praise and then correcting him; what Apollos said about Jesus was true, as far as it went.

Though he knew only the baptism of John. So here is a man who is learned, powerful in the Bible, on fire, and doctrinally accurate, and Luke’s next clause is this. Hold those two things together, because the combination is the point of the whole paragraph and it is unusual in Scripture. There is nothing wrong with Apollos. He is not a false teacher, not a self-promoter, not lukewarm, not careless. He is excellent, and he is incomplete, and the two are not in tension. His problem is not his character, or his zeal, or his handling of the text. It is simply that the news had not all reached him yet. That is a category we are not very good at. We tend to sort teachers into sound and unsound, and Apollos will not go in either box.

What does he knew only the baptism of John mean? John the Baptist’s baptism was a preparatory one, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Luke 3:3), in which people confessed their sins, turned to God, and got ready for the Messiah who was coming. John pointed beyond himself: he baptised with water, but the one coming after him would baptise with the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11). So it looked forward to Jesus; it was the getting-ready baptism, not yet the full Christian one. To say Apollos knew only John’s baptism, then, is to say his grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that preparatory point. He knew of John’s baptism of repentance and of Jesus as the coming one, perhaps even of his life and death, and proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah truly, as far as it went, but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message that followed: Pentecost, the outpouring and gift of the Holy Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus. His knowledge was real but incomplete, the fault of his teaching, not his heart: he taught what he had been taught, probably away from the centre, before the fuller news reached him.

Apollos and the twelve at Ephesus. He is the cousin of the Ephesian disciples of 19:1–7, who also knew only John’s baptism, though note the difference. Apollos, already fervent in spirit and teaching accurately, is simply taught more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila (v. 26) and is never said to be rebaptised, whereas those men, who had not even heard that the Spirit was given, are baptised into Jesus and receive the Spirit (see on 19:1–2). And the lovely lessons here: even a brilliant, eloquent, fervent Bible teacher still had more to learn, and humbly received it from a tentmaking couple, Priscilla named first. None of us has arrived; we keep growing. And the way to help someone whose understanding is incomplete is Priscilla and Aquila’s way: not to attack him publicly, but to take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately, gently, privately, helpfully.

How should I think of a Christian whose understanding is incomplete? As most of us are, in one area or another. Sorting people only into sound and unsound misses the large company of real believers who love Christ and teach truly but have not yet seen everything clearly, because no one has taught them. Such people need help, not suspicion. Be quick to recognise what is right in them, as Luke did with five commendations, and slow to assume bad motives. And turn it on yourself: there are things you have not yet understood, and the Lord may send a Priscilla to you. Be ready to be taught.

In a sentence. A Jew named Apollos from Alexandria came to Ephesus, an eloquent man with a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, who spoke with burning zeal and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only John’s baptism.

On a Tuesday. Zeal and gifts are wonderful, but must be joined to full truth. Keep learning. Choose one area of Christian teaching you know you are hazy on, the Holy Spirit, baptism, the last things, and read one good, clear book or chapter of Scripture on it this month. Boil, by all means. But boil with light.

For worship. The ascended Christ gives gifts to men: eloquent Alexandrians and humble tentmakers alike are his gifts to his church (Ephesians 4:8–12). He sets the boiling zeal in one heart and the patient understanding in another, and then brings them to the same table so that each may supply what the other lacks. He is never in a hurry with his servants, and never careless with them; he finishes what he begins in every one.
verseByVerse.note: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Bold, gifted, and incomplete. Everything about this sentence repays slow reading.

But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside. Not up. Not out. Aside: privately, away from the congregation he had been addressing, perhaps in their home. They heard a brilliant man preaching something short of the full truth in a public meeting, and they did not stand up. Not publicly correcting or embarrassing him, but wise, gentle, humble correction. Tentmakers taught a scholar.

The alternatives they declined. They could have corrected him from the floor, which would have been humiliating and would probably have hardened him. They could have warned people about him afterwards, which is the modern method and requires no courage at all. They could have said nothing, on the grounds that he was clearly gifted and it was not their place: two tentmakers against an Alexandrian scholar. Instead they took him aside.

And explained to him the way of God more accurately. Luke’s word for what they did is not rebuked or refuted but explained: set it out for him. And the comparative is careful too. Not accurately, as though he had been wrong. More accurately, because he had been right as far as he went: building on what he had, filling the gaps. That is the whole art of helping somebody whose understanding is incomplete, and there are two errors it avoids. One is the refusal to say anything, which leaves a man preaching half a gospel out of a misplaced deference. The other is public correction, which is far more satisfying and almost always makes the person defend the position he was about to abandon. If you have ever needed to say something difficult to a Christian you respect, this verse is the method: privately, personally, over a meal, beginning with what is right.

Priscilla named first. And notice who is doing it. A husband and wife, in partnership, teaching a man in their own home, and Luke names Priscilla first, as the New Testament does in most of the places the couple appear. In the ancient world that order is unusual enough to be deliberate, and a natural explanation is that she took a leading part in this, or was the more prominent of the two.

Where Christians differ: Priscilla and women teaching. Some use this verse to argue that women may serve as pastors or preachers in the church. Verdict: Priscilla, with her husband, instructed Apollos privately in their home; this was not preaching in the gathered church or exercising authority as an elder. Scripture reserves the office of elder and authoritative teaching in the church’s gathering to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women like Priscilla rightly teach, explain, and serve in many ways. This is the complementarian view, held with deep respect for women’s gifts and ministry.

Held gladly, not grudgingly. It is fair to say plainly that Christians disagree about what follows from this verse for the question of women teaching, and that the disagreement is between people who take the whole Bible seriously. Egalitarian Christians point to Priscilla, named first, together with Phoebe, Junia and the prophesying daughters of Philip (21:9), as evidence that women taught men in the early church. The more likely reading is that this was private instruction by a couple, who took him aside, not the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). But any position on the wider question has to be able to hold this verse comfortably and gladly, because Luke plainly regarded what Priscilla did as one of the most useful things anybody did in this chapter. Women may and should explain the faith in many settings, and Priscilla is honoured for it.

And Apollos was taught. Consider, finally, what it cost Apollos. He was the most gifted speaker in the room, and he sat down with two tentmakers and let them teach him. Apollos, though learned and eloquent, was humble enough to learn from them. Everything he became afterwards, the power in Corinth, the letter Paul wrote urging him to go back there, runs through that evening. The gifted man’s greatest asset here is not his eloquence. It is that he could be taught.

So what may a woman do, on this view? A great deal, and churches holding the complementarian view should be quick to say so and to make room for it. Like Priscilla, a woman may explain the faith to others, privately and in many settings, including to men, as she did here with her husband. She may teach children and other women (Titus 2:3–5), lead Bible studies among women, share the gospel with anyone, pray and serve visibly in the church’s life, counsel, write, and use every gift God has given her. What this view reserves to qualified men is the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church. The aim is never to silence women’s gifts but to honour God’s order while putting those gifts to full and joyful use.

How do I receive correction well? Like Apollos: by assuming the person might be right, and listening before defending yourself. It helps to remember that correction given privately and gently, as Priscilla and Aquila gave it, is a gift of love; faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6). Thank the person, even if you are not yet sure they are right. Then take what they said to Scripture, as the Bereans did. If they were right, change, and do it openly if your error was public. A teachable spirit is not weakness. It is the mark of a man whom God can go on using.

In a sentence. He began speaking boldly in the synagogue, and when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they invited him home and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

On a Tuesday. Correct privately and gently. And when corrected, receive it humbly, like Apollos. If there is something you have been meaning to say to a fellow believer, do not say it about them to someone else. Invite them for a meal, begin with what is right, and say the rest kindly. And if someone has corrected you recently and you bristled, go back and thank them.

For worship. The Lord who taught by a lakeside and over a supper table still teaches his church around ordinary tables. He used the kitchen of a tentmaking couple to finish the training of one of his finest preachers, and he did it gently, as he does all things. He is the Teacher who never humiliates, who breaks no bruised reed (Matthew 12:20), and who leads his people from accurate to more accurate, from glory to glory, until we know as we are known.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.

And when he wished to cross to Achaia. Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

The brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. A letter of recommendation, the ordinary machinery by which the early church moved people around a hostile world where nobody could check anybody’s credentials. A stranger arriving in a city with a letter from believers who knew him could be received at once. Paul refers to the practice repeatedly, and once, to this very church, with some feeling, asking whether he needs, as some do, letters of recommendation to them (2 Corinthians 3:1). So the Ephesian church put its name behind a man who, weeks earlier, had been preaching an incomplete gospel in their synagogue. They did not send a warning ahead of him. They sent an endorsement.

He greatly helped those who through grace had believed. Note where the grace sits in that sentence. Not he greatly helped, by grace, but those who through grace had believed. Luke has slipped in, in a passing clause about somebody’s travel arrangements, the whole doctrine of how anybody comes to faith. Faith itself is the gift of grace (Ephesians 2:8–9; Philippians 1:29). They believed because of grace. It is the same thing said of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened (16:14), and of the Gentiles at Pisidian Antioch (13:48). And Apollos helped believers: his gift watered what Paul planted (1 Corinthians 3:6).

If faith is a gift, why am I commanded to believe? Because God gives faith through the very command and promise of the gospel. When Christ is offered, you are truly called to trust him, and you truly do the believing; God does not believe for you. Yet when you do, you discover that he opened your heart to do it, so that you cannot boast (Ephesians 2:8–9). The doctrine is not a reason to wait passively but a reason for humility and assurance. If you have believed, thank God; your faith is his work in you, and what he has begun he will finish. If you have not, do not wait to feel chosen. Come to Christ now, and you will find that grace brought you.

For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Apologetics from Scripture. He answered objections publicly and powerfully. The same work Paul had done in Corinth (v. 5), now done by somebody else, and done powerfully. Apollos was better at it than Paul, at least as a speaker; the Corinthians certainly thought so, and some of them said so in terms that were less than kind about Paul’s own delivery (2 Corinthians 10:10).

A test almost nobody passes. And here is the thing worth ending on. Apollos went to Corinth, Paul’s own church, planted at the cost of eighteen months and a trial, and was such a success that a faction formed round his name. Paul had to write about it, because each of them was saying, I follow Paul, or, I follow Apollos (1 Corinthians 1:12). Watch how Paul handles a younger, more eloquent man who has become a rival name in the church he founded. He refuses the rivalry entirely: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). And later, writing about the same city, he says he strongly urged Apollos to go back there (1 Corinthians 16:12). He was pushing him toward the congregation that preferred him.

No jealous link. The chain in these five verses is worth tracing: Priscilla and Aquila, who had worked beside Paul, taught Apollos; Apollos strengthened the Corinthians; Paul urged him back to them. Not one link in it was jealous of the next.

What if someone else is more gifted than me in the same ministry? Then thank God for him, and pray for his success, as Paul did for Apollos. Jealousy in ministry is common and deadly, because it makes the work about us. The cure is to remember whose field it is: one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth. If a more gifted person waters what you planted, the harvest is the Lord’s, and you will share the joy (John 4:36–37). Ask yourself whether you would be glad if the church you love grew faster under someone else. If not, take that to Christ, who washed feet and was content to be overlooked.

In a sentence. When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the believers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him, and when he arrived he was a great help to those who had believed by grace, for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.

On a Tuesday. Your faith is a gift of grace. Thank God for it, and for those who help you grow in it. Write a short letter of commendation this week: a note to someone telling them how God has used them, or an encouraging word to a church about a believer moving their way. And pray by name for the most gifted Christian you know whose ministry overlaps with yours.

For worship. Faith is a gift of grace, and every believer in Corinth and Ephesus, and every believer reading this, believed because God first gave. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift (2 Corinthians 9:15). He plants by one servant and waters by another, and the growth is his alone, so the glory is his alone. Paul is nothing, Apollos is nothing, and Christ is all and in all; and the church that learns this sings not of its preachers but of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

parallels.desc: I planted, Apollos watered

18.theology: Election as the Ground of Courage in Mission. “I have many in this city who are my people” (v. 10) is the doctrine of election functioning as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul is afraid — he says so later. And God’s answer to his fear is not “it will go well” or “people will respond positively” — it is “I have my people here.” The ground of missionary perseverance is not optimism about human receptivity; it is confidence in divine election. God has sheep in every city, in every culture, in every hostile context — sheep who will hear the shepherd’s voice when it is proclaimed through his servants. This is not a reason for laziness; it is a reason for courage. Preach. His people will come.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, sustained by a vision and a promise, staying eighteen months because God told him to stay. The church that emerged from that eighteen months will cause him more trouble than any other — and will receive his most profound letters about the cross, the resurrection, and love.

Now: Every city has people who are God’s — people the Spirit is already preparing, already drawing, already making ready to hear. The task of the church is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay when the Lord says stay, and to trust that the harvest belongs to him. The missionary who preaches in the hardest city is not alone. God is already there, and his people are waiting.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>22</sup>And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>29</sup>So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. <sup>30</sup>But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. <sup>31</sup>And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. <sup>32</sup>Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. <sup>33</sup>Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>35</sup>And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? <sup>36</sup>Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. <sup>37</sup>For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. <sup>38</sup>If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another. <sup>39</sup>But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. <sup>40</sup>For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is the climax of Paul’s free ministry. It was the capital of the province of Asia, a port of perhaps a quarter of a million people, home of the vast temple of Artemis and famous across the empire for magic. Paul stays nearly three years (20:31), longer than anywhere else. He first meets a dozen men who know only John’s baptism; taught about Jesus, they are baptised in his name and receive the Spirit. Three months in the synagogue are followed by two years of daily teaching in a hired hall, and the word spreads through the whole province: the churches of the Lycus valley and the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 probably date from these years.

The gospel then collides with the city’s religion. God works unusual miracles through Paul; seven Jewish exorcists who use Jesus’ name as a spell are overpowered; and new believers burn their magic books, worth a fortune. Paul plans to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then to Rome, the plan the rest of Acts follows. Finally the silversmith Demetrius, whose trade depends on the goddess, stirs up a riot that fills the great theatre for two hours, until the town clerk calms the crowd: the Christians have committed no crime, and the courts are open. Luke’s summary is the key: the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reaches Ephesus and finds about twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. He explains that John pointed to Jesus; they are baptised in Jesus’ name, Paul lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes, with tongues and prophecy. Paul teaches in the synagogue for three months; when some harden and slander the Way, he moves the disciples to the lecture hall of Tyrannus and teaches daily for two years, so that the whole province hears the word. God does unusual miracles through him. Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest, Sceva, try to drive out a spirit in the name of “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims”, and the possessed man overpowers them. Fear falls on the city, believers confess their practices, and magicians burn books worth fifty thousand silver coins. Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then to Rome. Demetrius the silversmith rallies the craftsmen whose shrines of Artemis are losing trade, and the city rushes into the theatre, dragging two of Paul’s companions. Paul is kept from going in. For two hours the crowd chants “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians”, until the town clerk quiets them, points out that these men have committed no crime, sends complaints to the courts or a lawful assembly, warns of Roman displeasure, and dismisses the crowd.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word of the Lord Prevailing Over Magic and Idolatry

The burning of the magical books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — is one of the most dramatic acts of new-believer repentance in Acts. The magicians do not gradually reduce their practice; they make a clean, costly, public break. Reformed theology sees in this the pattern of genuine repentance: the thoroughgoing abandonment of what the gospel has displaced, at whatever cost. The summary in v. 20 ('So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily') is the theological verdict on the entire Ephesian episode: the word wins, over magic, over economics, over riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius the silversmith's complaint — 'there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing' — is the most honest statement of why people oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel continues to threaten economic arrangements built on idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often economic before it is theological.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”

Meaning first. Acts 19 tells of Paul’s longest mission, nearly three years in Ephesus, the great city of Asia. Twelve disciples of John receive the Spirit; Paul teaches daily for two years, and the word spreads through the whole province; God works extraordinary miracles; magicians burn their books; and the silversmiths, whose trade depends on the goddess Artemis, start a riot. The chapter shows the power of the gospel against every rival power: incomplete religion, demons, magic, and the money-making idolatry of a whole city. Over all of it Luke writes one sentence that is the real subject of the chapter: the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily (v. 20). The risen Christ, by his word and Spirit, takes on the most religious, most superstitious, most commercial city in Asia, and wins.

Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis, with perhaps 250,000 people. Paul had promised to return if God willed (18:21), and he has. And note the road he took: the inland country, the high road across the Anatolian plateau rather than the easy valley route, a journey of several hundred miles on foot.

There he found some disciples. What he finds when he arrives is a small puzzle, and Luke sets it up carefully. Disciples is Luke’s ordinary word for Christians; he uses it dozens of times in this book. So the first impression is that Paul has walked into a group of the Ephesian church. But disciples here turns out to mean disciples of John the Baptist, as verse 3 shows. Like Apollos, they knew only John’s baptism.

Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? Something prompted that question. Luke does not say what, but it is worth noticing that Paul was watching. He had been in the city a matter of days and had already registered that something was missing. And the question itself assumes a great deal. It takes for granted that receiving the Spirit is what happens to a person who believes, and that it is the sort of thing you would know about. The Spirit is received when one believes, not later. Paul is not asking whether they have had a further experience; he is asking whether the ordinary thing has happened.

No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit. Not we have not received him; they had not heard. They cannot mean that they had never heard of the Spirit at all, since John spoke of him plainly (Luke 3:16), but that they had not heard the Spirit had been given, that Pentecost had happened. That answer settles what these men are. Whatever they were, they were not people who had been converted and were waiting for something more; they were men whose information had run out before the story reached its end. Somebody had told them about repentance and a coming Messiah, and nobody had come back to tell them what happened at Pentecost.

One question. It is a sobering thing to find in a city with believers in it. These twelve had been in Ephesus, sincere and out of date, and the gap was found because one man asked one question. It is worth asking, of the people in your own congregation whom everybody assumes are fine, whether anybody has ever asked them anything.

The cousin of Acts 8. This passage is the cousin of Acts 8, and is read the same several ways (see there). These men knew only the baptism of John and had not even heard the Spirit was given (v. 2), so the Reformed reading sees them not as ordinary Christians awaiting a second blessing, but as disciples still standing at the old, pre-Pentecost stage of John the Baptist, who on hearing of Jesus believe fully, are baptised into him, and receive the Spirit: their deficiency was in the gospel they had yet to hear, not a missing stage two for already-complete believers. Pentecostal brothers read it, with Acts 8, as evidence of a Spirit-baptism subsequent to conversion. Note that Paul’s question naturally ties the receiving of the Spirit to believing, not to a later experience, which is how the letters speak of it (Ephesians 1:13; Romans 8:9). Said, as ever, with respect for those who differ.

How do I know whether I have received the Holy Spirit? Not first by a feeling or a particular gift, but by the fruit of his presence. The Spirit is the one who makes you confess that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), who makes you cry Abba, Father (Romans 8:15–16), who makes you hate the sin you once loved and fight it (Romans 8:13), and who grows love, joy and peace in you, slowly (Galatians 5:22–23). If you have truly trusted Christ, the Spirit is in you, for anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). The question for most believers is not whether to receive him, but whether to keep in step with him.

In a sentence. While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul travelled through the interior and came to Ephesus, where he found some disciples and asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit when they believed, and they said they had not even heard that the Holy Spirit had come.

On a Tuesday. Every believer receives the Spirit at faith. If you believe in Christ, he is in you. Thank God for that today, and live like it: you are not alone in the fight with sin, or in the prayer you cannot find words for. And think of one person in your church about whom you have simply assumed everything is well. Ask them, kindly, how they are really doing with God.

For worship. The Father promised the Spirit, the Son poured him out, and the Spirit comes to dwell in every sinner who believes. He is not a reward for advanced Christians but the gift of the gospel itself, the seal of our adoption and the guarantee of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:13–14). The Lord who sent Paul across a plateau to find twelve men who had not heard the end of the story does not leave his people half-told. He finishes what he begins.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis. These “disciples” knew only John’s baptism.

parallels.desc: Apollos, who knew only the baptism of John

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.”

Into what then were you baptized? Notice what Paul does with a wrong answer. He does not correct them, and he does not dismiss them. He asks a second question, and the second question is the diagnostic one: what were you baptised into? Paul connects the Spirit with baptism in Jesus’ name. And that is worth having as a method. He is not trying to establish whether they are in or out. He is trying to find out where the gap is, and he does it by tracing the thing back to its source: what were you told, and by whom, and how far did it go? A great deal of unhelpful conversation between Christians would be avoided if the second question came before the verdict.

Into John’s baptism. A baptism of preparation. So now the shape of their situation is clear, and it is a strange one. These men are not pagans. They are not half-hearted. They had submitted to a baptism of repentance, turned from their sins, and were waiting for the one John had promised. By the standards of the Old Testament they were exemplary. Their problem was that they were living some twenty years behind the news.

John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus. Look at how compact that is. Paul explains John’s baptism by explaining what John said while he administered it: that it was never a destination. John’s baptism pointed forward. The whole point of the rite was to point past itself to a person who had not yet arrived. John was the forerunner; Jesus is the fulfilment. These men had stopped at the signpost and never reached the destination. A man who stopped at John’s baptism had not misunderstood John; he had simply never been told the sequel.

That is, Jesus. The last words carry everything. Paul closes a twenty-year gap in a clause. The one you were told to wait for has come, and here is his name.

Real and unfinished. There is a particular kindness in this scene that is worth naming. Paul does not tell these men that their repentance was worthless or that their years of waiting were wasted. He tells them that what they had was real and unfinished. That is a rare and difficult combination to hold about anybody’s spiritual history, including your own, if you look back on years of sincere religion before you understood the gospel. Those years were not a mistake. They were John’s baptism, and this verse is where somebody tells you the rest.

What if I was religious for years before I really understood the gospel? Then this passage is for you. Those years may have taught you real things: that God is holy, that sin matters, that you needed someone to come. Many believers look back on a churchgoing childhood or a sincere but confused search and can see God preparing them, like John preparing the way. But preparation is not arrival. If you now trust Christ crucified and risen, you have reached the destination the signposts were pointing to. Do not despise the road, and do not mistake it for home. Thank God for both.

In a sentence. Paul asked what baptism they had received, and they said John’s, and Paul explained that John’s was a baptism of repentance, telling people to believe in the one coming after him, Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Do not stop at the signpost. Every preparation points to Jesus. When you talk with someone whose understanding of the faith seems patchy, try Paul’s method: ask a second question before you reach a verdict. What were you taught? Where did it stop? Then tell them the rest, kindly, and with his name.

For worship. Every signpost in the Bible points to one name. John’s water, the prophets’ promises, the lambs and the altars and the long years of waiting all ended in this: that is, Jesus. He is the one who was to come, and he has come, and there is no one else to wait for. Blessed be the God who did not leave the story unfinished, but sent his Son, and then sent his servants to the ends of the earth to tell the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Twelve men who had already been baptised are baptised again. It is the only case in the New Testament of people being baptised twice, and it needs stating plainly what it is and what it is not. It is not a second Christian baptism. These men had never received one. What they had undergone was John’s rite, which belonged to the era before the cross, and Paul has just explained that it was preparatory by John’s own account of it. So this is not a rebaptism at all in the Christian sense; it is their first. It was not because John’s baptism was invalid in its time, but because they had not yet believed in Jesus as the one who had come. Their first baptism was a preparation; this was Christian baptism, into Christ. Interestingly, there is no record that the apostles, who had John’s baptism, were rebaptised. They had received the Spirit at Pentecost.

On hearing this. And notice how fast it is. No interval, no long course of instruction, no probation. Luke’s pattern all through the book is that baptism follows promptly upon believing: three thousand on the day of Pentecost, the eunuch at the roadside, Lydia the same day, the jailer in the middle of the night. There is no example in Acts of a believer being made to wait for years. And the order is always the same: hearing, believing, then baptism.

In the name of the Lord Jesus. That phrase is the whole difference between the two baptisms. John’s was into a hope. This one is into a person, and into everything that belongs to him. To be baptised into someone’s name in that world was to be transferred into his ownership and his protection, which is why the same men who had been standing on the far side of the Jordan waiting are now, in one act, publicly attached to a named Lord.

Where Christians differ: rebaptism. Some use this to justify rebaptising those baptised as infants or in other churches. Verdict: this case was unique, as John’s baptism was not Christian baptism. Where someone was baptised before they truly believed, credobaptists rightly see believer’s baptism as the first true baptism, not a repetition. But those who were baptised as believers in the name of the Trinity should not be baptised again; there is one baptism (Ephesians 4:5).

Does this license rebaptism today? These twelve had received only John’s baptism, before Christ’s death and resurrection and the coming of the Spirit; this was not a repeat of Christian baptism but their first. Those who hold, as this commentary does with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to believers will baptise someone who was baptised only as an infant, since they regard that as not yet believer’s baptism. Our paedobaptist brothers regard any baptism with water in the triune name as valid and not to be repeated, and they hold that view from a sincere reading of God’s covenant promises; we honour them for it, while differing. But all agree that someone baptised as a believer is not to be baptised again.

Does in the name of the Lord Jesus conflict with Matthew 28:19? No. Jesus commanded baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Luke here describes whose name and authority the person comes under, not the exact words spoken at the water. The Oneness teaching that only Jesus’ name may be used reads a formula into a description. Christian baptism is into the one name of the triune God, revealed in Jesus Christ.

Why does Luke record such a small episode? Twelve obscure men in a large city, whose names we do not have and who are never mentioned again. He records it because the gospel had reached Ephesus in an incomplete form and God did not leave it there. Somebody had preached a half-message and moved on. Apollos had done the same. And in both cases the correction came, privately, patiently, and without anybody being humiliated.

What if I was baptised before I truly believed? Talk to your pastor, and be honest. If you were baptised as a believer, however young and however little you understood, and you have trusted Christ ever since, your baptism stands; faith grows, and baptism does not need repeating every time it does. If, looking back, you are clear that you had no faith in Christ at all at the time, and were baptised for other reasons, then many credobaptist churches would see a baptism now as your first true baptism, as with these twelve. The aim is not to chase a perfect experience but to obey Christ with a clear conscience.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you learn more truth, act on it at once, as these men did. Is there something you have come to understand from Scripture, about baptism, about church membership, about a sin or a duty, that you have not yet acted on? These men did not wait. Neither should you.

For worship. To be baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus is to be marked as his: buried with him, raised with him, owned by him and kept by him. He is not ashamed to put his name on twelve forgotten men in Ephesus, or on us. And the water is only the sign; the reality is that he has washed us in his own blood and joined us to himself for ever, and there is no name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved but his.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all.

And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them. As with the Samaritans (8:17), through an apostle’s hands. Why? Perhaps to bring this group of John’s followers fully into the one church, and to show that Paul’s apostleship equalled Peter’s.

And they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. Visible signs, as at Pentecost (chapter 2) and Caesarea (chapter 10), at a key point in the spread of the gospel. This is the fourth and last time in Acts that the Spirit comes with this kind of public sign, and the four occasions repay being seen together, because the pattern in them is not what people usually take from this verse. Jerusalem at Pentecost: Jews (chapter 2). Samaria, the half-Jews of the old northern kingdom, through Peter and John (chapter 8). Caesarea: Gentiles, in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10). And now Ephesus: men left over from the old order. Luke records tongues only at these turning points (at Samaria they are implied). Each time the Spirit falls visibly at a frontier, the first time the gospel crosses into a new group of people, and each time there is an apostle present to see it happen. They marked the gospel’s advance into new groups. After this chapter it does not occur again in Acts, and the letters never instruct any church to expect it.

The shape of the evidence. That is the reason careful readers have been slow to build a doctrine of a standard second experience out of these verses. What Luke is documenting is not the normal Christian life but the joining up of a divided world: Jew, Samaritan, Gentile and John’s leftover disciples, all publicly given the same Spirit, with apostolic witnesses to certify it.

Where Christians differ: a pattern for today? Pentecostals see a second-blessing pattern here. Verdict: these men were not yet Christians in the full sense; they had not believed in Jesus as having come. When they believed and were baptised, they received the Spirit at once. This is not a two-stage experience for Christians, but conversion. The tongues were a sign for a transitional moment in salvation history.

A family disagreement. It should be said, and gladly, that many godly Christians read these passages differently and expect the same experience today. The disagreement is a family one, and it is not about whether the Spirit is given: every side agrees he is, and agrees that a Christian without the Spirit is a contradiction (Romans 8:9).

What were these tongues and prophecy, and are they for today? They marked these disciples, who had stood at the edge of the new covenant, as fully part of the church. Many Christians, among them people of deep godliness, believe such gifts continue, and we should honour their love for Christ and their desire for his power. The more likely reading is that tongues and prophecy, as revelatory sign gifts, belonged to the foundational age of the apostles as signs of the Spirit’s coming, and ceased with it, the church being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with the canon of Scripture now complete (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). This is the cessationist view, held charitably. Nothing here makes tongues the evidence of the Spirit for every believer, and God remains free to answer prayer in wonderful ways.

There were about twelve men in all. Now the number, which Luke gives almost as an afterthought. Perhaps a hint: the full number of a renewed Israel. But Luke says about twelve, which is the sort of thing a man writes when he is reporting rather than constructing. He did not need the number to be twelve. It simply was, roughly. And consider what it means. In a city of perhaps a quarter of a million people, the work at Ephesus begins with a dozen men who had been following an out-of-date sermon. Within three years all Asia will have heard the word of the Lord, and within a decade this church will receive the letter to the Ephesians and, later still, the first of the letters to the seven churches in Revelation.

If I have never spoken in tongues, am I missing something? No. Paul asks, expecting the answer no, whether all speak with tongues (1 Corinthians 12:30). The gifts were distributed as the Spirit willed, never to everyone, and on the view held here the sign gifts have ceased in any case. What no believer lacks is the Spirit himself, with everything that matters most: union with Christ, adoption, assurance, the power to pray, and the slow growth of love. The greatest gift, Paul says, is love (1 Corinthians 13:13). If you love Christ and are learning to love his people, you are not a second-class Christian. You are filled with the same Spirit who came at Ephesus.

In a sentence. When Paul laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied; there were about twelve men.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit unites all who believe into one church. Treat the believer from a different tradition, charismatic or not, as one who has the same Spirit you have. And seek the fruit of the Spirit before any gift: ask him today for love, patience and self-control in the place where you most lack them.

For worship. The Spirit unites all who believe into one church. Praise him for his work in you. He came on Jews in Jerusalem, on Samaritans, on Gentiles in Caesarea and on twelve stragglers in Ephesus, and made them all one body under one Head. There is one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4:4–6). From the first Pentecost to this day he has never been divided, and he is gathering the whole family home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus.

And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. Three months, a longer time than usual in a synagogue. Set that beside the rest of the book, three Sabbaths at Thessalonica, two Sabbaths at Pisidian Antioch before the trouble started, and it is the longest run he ever had in a synagogue anywhere. Ephesus gave him a hearing for a quarter of a year. The kingdom of God is God’s reign in Christ (28:23, 31).

What is Paul doing when he persuades them about the kingdom of God? In plain terms, he is making the case for King Jesus. The kingdom of God is God’s kingly rule, and the great news is that the King has come: Jesus, crucified and risen, now reigns and will one day return to reign in full. So to persuade about the kingdom is to show people from the Scriptures who Jesus is and to urge them to bow to him as Lord, and so enter his kingdom, which a person does the moment he repents and trusts the King. (For what the kingdom of God means, and why the phrase fills the Gospels but is rarer in the letters, see on 8:12; for the already-but-not-yet of it, that we are brought into it now yet await its full coming, see on 14:22.)

Reasoning and persuading. And notice how he does it. He did not merely announce; he argued (the word means to discuss, to dialogue) and sought to convince, patiently, from the Scriptures, for three whole months. The faith is reasonable and invites the mind; commending Christ can mean kindly, patiently making the case and answering objections over time, not just a single quick pitch. You need not be a clever debater, but you can take heart that to persuade about the kingdom is, at bottom, simply to help people see and trust the King.

But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation. Then it ends, and Luke describes the ending precisely, in three stages that are worth separating, because they are how this generally goes. First they became stubborn (esklērynonto): hardened, set, the word used of Pharaoh’s heart and of Israel in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8). Then they continued in unbelief, which is the settled state that hardening produces. And then they began speaking evil of the Way before the congregation: not private disagreement but public disparagement, aimed at the people who were still listening. The Way was an early name for the Christian faith (9:2). It is the third stage that moves him. Paul had put up with the first two for three months. What he will not do is go on providing a platform where the thing is being poisoned for everybody else in the room.

He withdrew from them and took the disciples with him. A separate congregation. Notice that he does not leave Ephesus. In Pisidian Antioch he was expelled from the district; in Thessalonica he was smuggled out at night. Here he simply moves down the street and carries on, and he takes the converts with him, which is the clearest picture so far in Acts of a congregation separating from a synagogue and setting up elsewhere. The Christian assembly in Ephesus gets its own meeting-place on the day Paul moves into the hall of Tyrannus.

Reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. The room is worth a word. The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall, a scholē, a public room where a teacher held discourses, with no religious associations at all. Shut out of the sacred space, Paul took the gospel into the ancient equivalent of a rented conference room, open to anyone who wandered in off the street, and stayed there for two years. One early manuscript adds that he taught from the fifth to the tenth hour, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the hot hours of rest when the hall was free and workers could attend. Paul worked his trade in the mornings (20:34) and taught through the afternoon heat. Daily, for two years.

When should a Christian leave a church? Not lightly, and not because of preferences, personalities or a dull season; Paul stayed three months in a synagogue that was arguing with him. But there are times when leaving is right: when the gospel itself is denied or ridiculed, when Christ is publicly spoken against and the leaders will not be corrected, when you are prevented from obeying Scripture. Even then, go as Paul went: without bitterness, after patient effort, taking care for others who need help, and joining yourself promptly to a faithful church. Never leave the Way because you left a building.

In a sentence. Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading about the kingdom of God, but when some hardened their hearts and slandered the Way publicly, he left them, took the disciples with him, and reasoned daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.

On a Tuesday. Use the time you have. Paul taught in the midday heat while others rested. Look at your week for the leftover hours, the lunch break, the commute, the evening after the children are in bed, and give one of them to God’s word, either learning it or sharing it. Persuading people about the King does not need a pulpit. It needs a room and a willing heart.

For worship. The kingdom Paul preached is the kingdom of a King who reigns now. Jesus, crucified and risen, holds all authority in heaven and on earth, and his rule advances not by armies but by persuasion, by his word opened patiently in synagogues and lecture halls and kitchens. He bears long with hardened hearts, and when one door is shut he opens another down the street. His kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28), and of its increase there will be no end.
verseByVerse.note: The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.

This continued for two years. Plus the three months, nearly three years in Ephesus (20:31).

So that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. Take the second half of that sentence seriously, because it is an extraordinary claim and Luke makes it flatly. Asia was a Roman province of many hundreds of cities and towns, running down the western seaboard of what is now Turkey and inland for a hundred miles and more. And Luke says that in two years all its residents heard the word of the Lord.

Paul did not travel to them. That is the thing to grasp. So far as Acts records, he stayed in Ephesus the whole time, in one room, teaching daily. He never went to Colossae; he tells the Colossians that many have not seen his face (Colossians 2:1). He probably never went to Laodicea or Hierapolis. Of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, he is only recorded as visiting one.

The funnel. So how did the province hear? Because Ephesus was the funnel. It was the greatest port on that coast and the terminus of the road system from the interior; everybody in western Asia came through it: traders, pilgrims to the temple, officials, students, people selling goods. They came, some of them wandered into a lecture hall in the dead of the afternoon, and they went home. Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis were probably founded in these years, through Paul’s co-workers like Epaphras (Colossians 1:7; 4:13). Paul tells the Colossians that they learned the gospel from Epaphras, his beloved fellow servant: a man of Colossae who evidently heard it in Ephesus and carried it a hundred miles inland to his own town, where a church was founded that Paul never saw. The seven churches of Revelation 2–3 were all in Asia. Paul trained others, who went out. Ephesus became a hub. Strategic ministry multiplies.

The strategy of staying still. That is worth naming because it is not the one we would expect from Paul. The most travelled man in the New Testament reached an entire province by staying still and teaching every day for two years to whoever happened to be in the room. And it is a considerable comfort for anybody whose service to God is fixed in one place. You do not know who is in the room, or where they are going afterwards. The letters to Colossae and Laodicea, and several of the churches Christ addresses by name in Revelation, trace back to a rented hall and a man who did not travel.

A little more on the hall of Tyrannus. The word is scholē, our school: a lecture hall where a teacher or rhetorician would hold his discourses and discussions. Tyrannus (the name means ruler or tyrant) was either the owner of the building or the lecturer who normally taught there; we know nothing more of him, save that his hall outlived his name by housing the gospel. As some early manuscripts add, Paul used it from the fifth hour to the tenth, roughly 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the heat of the day, the afternoon rest when the hall stood empty and most people rested. Picture it: Paul at his tentmaking bench in the cool early hours (20:34), then teaching through the sweltering midday while the city slept, and his hearers giving up their own rest to come and learn, labour and sacrifice on both sides. And note the move: shut out of the synagogue, sacred space, Paul carried the gospel straight into a public lecture hall, secular space, the open marketplace of ideas, where any Jew or Greek could wander in. The encouragement is plain: the gospel needs no grand temple. A rented room, used in the leftover hours of the day, by a man who also worked a trade, became the hub from which all Asia, Colossae, Laodicea, the cities of Revelation, heard the word of the Lord. Ordinary, borrowed, off-peak means, and a whole province reached.

Is my work wasted if I serve in one small place where nothing seems to spread? No. You cannot see where the people you teach will go, any more than Paul could see Epaphras walking home to Colossae. The Sunday school class, the youth group, the Bible study in your home, the conversation with a colleague: any of them may contain someone who carries the gospel to a place you will never visit. Your task is to teach faithfully what you have been given, and to entrust it to faithful people who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). The spreading is the Lord’s work, and he has never been short of roads.

In a sentence. This went on for two years, so that everyone living in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Teach others who will teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). That is how the word spreads. Is there one younger believer you could meet with regularly to read the Bible and pray? Start this month. You may be teaching your Epaphras.
