For worship. The word of the Lord ran through a whole province from one rented room, because it is his word and it runs where he sends it. As the rain comes down from heaven and does not return without watering the earth, so his word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:10–11). He gathered churches in towns Paul never saw, and he is gathering them still in places none of us will ever see. Glory to the Lord of the harvest, who makes one man’s afternoons the seed of a province.
verseByVerse.note: Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period through Paul’s co-workers.

parallels.desc: three years

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.

And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul. God was doing, not Paul. Luke’s phrase is odd enough to be deliberate: ou tas tychousas, literally miracles not of the ordinary kind, unusual even by apostolic standards. Coming from the man who has already recorded the lame walking, the dead raised and prison doors opened, that is quite a qualification. He is telling us that even by the standards of this book, what happened at Ephesus was unusual. In a city famous for magic, God showed his superior power.

So that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick. The two items are very probably workman’s cloths: the sweatband a labourer tied round his head, and the apron a craftsman wore at the bench. These are not priestly vestments or relics. They are the working clothes of a man who made tents in that city for two years, taken away from his bench while he was using them. It is like Peter’s shadow (5:15).

And their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. God honoured their faith, even mixed with superstition. Now, this passage has been put to a great deal of use it will not bear, and it is worth being exact about what Luke does and does not say. He does not say Paul distributed the cloths, or blessed them, or charged for them, or recommended the practice. He does not say a word about how it worked. The grammar puts God as the subject, God was doing these things, and the cloths in a purely passive role. Somebody in Ephesus took Paul’s sweatband to a sick relative, and God, who was not obliged to do anything of the kind, healed them.

Why God stooped to it. The setting explains it. Ephesus was the centre of the magical arts in the empire; written charms from the city were known across the Mediterranean as Ephesian letters. This was a population that believed absolutely in power conveyed through objects: amulets, scraps of parchment, knotted cords, things you carried. God met that city where its convictions were, and then spent the next eight verses demonstrating the difference between his power and magic: the sons of Sceva try to work the name of Jesus as a formula and are thrown out of a house naked, and the magicians burn their books.

Where Christians differ: prayer cloths. Some ministries today sell or send anointed cloths, promising healing or prosperity. Verdict: Luke calls these miracles extraordinary, done by God through an apostle at a unique time, to confirm the gospel in a city of magic. Nothing in Scripture tells believers to use objects for healing. Paul never sold anything. Seeking power through objects is close to the magic Ephesus was about to renounce (v. 19).

Should we expect miracles like these today? Luke calls them extraordinary, and they confirmed Paul as an apostle: the signs of a true apostle were performed among them, he told the Corinthians, with signs and wonders and mighty works (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). God is still free to heal in answer to prayer, and he often does, but Scripture gives no promise that such miracles will accompany ministry today, and nothing here supports selling healing cloths. So the cloths are not a technique, and it should be said plainly that selling prayer cloths, anointed handkerchiefs and the rest to sick and desperate people is precisely the trade this chapter destroys. The Ephesians who understood this passage correctly did not start a business in it. They lit a bonfire.

So should I pray for healing when I am ill? Yes, without hesitation. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15), and the Lord often answers by healing, through medicine or without it. Pray to God directly, and ask others to pray. What this passage warns against is not prayer but technique: the idea that healing comes through objects, formulas or special people with a gift for sale. God is not a power to be accessed but a Father to be trusted. If he heals, thank him. If he does not yet, his grace is sufficient for you, and the final healing is certain (2 Corinthians 12:9; Revelation 21:4).

In a sentence. God did extraordinary miracles through Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and their illnesses were cured and evil spirits left them.

On a Tuesday. God’s power is not in objects but in himself. Pray to him directly. If you know someone who is sick, pray for them by name today, and ask whether they would like you to pray with them. And if anyone offers you a blessed object, an anointed cloth or a guaranteed cure for a gift, say no, kindly, and point them to the God who heals for nothing.

For worship. The Lord who healed the sick in Ephesus is the same Lord who touched lepers in Galilee and raised a widow’s son at Nain. His power was never in cloth or shadow but in himself, and he gives it freely, as he gave his life freely. He took our infirmities and bore our diseases (Matthew 8:17), and on the cross he purchased a resurrection body for every one of his people. One day there will be no more sickness at all, and the Healer will wipe away every tear.
verseByVerse.note: The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used while working at his trade.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.

Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists. Travelling exorcists, common in the ancient world.

Undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits. Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. Magical papyri from this period mix Jewish, Greek and Egyptian names. They added Jesus to their list, as a magic word.

A word on these Jewish exorcists. Exorcists were people who tried to drive evil spirits out of the afflicted, and in the ancient world it was a common, and often paid, trade: a kind of spiritual technician or magician for hire. They worked by technique: incantations and spells, secret formulas, herbs and charms, and above all the reciting of powerful names believed to compel the spirits to obey. Jewish exorcists were especially sought after, precisely because they could invoke the name of the one true God and the sacred names of Scripture, which were thought to carry unusual power over the dark world (Josephus describes them, and legend traced their arts back to Solomon). The point to grasp is that it was all about harnessing power by the right words, not about knowing God. They treated a holy name as a magic word.

Saying, I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims. Listen to the formula, because the whole disaster is contained in it. Not by Jesus. By the Jesus whom Paul proclaims. Second-hand faith: not my Lord Jesus, but the Jesus Paul preaches. They did not know him. They cannot name him on their own account. They have to route the name through somebody else’s relationship with him, the way you might quote an authority you have never met: the Jesus that man talks about, the one who seems to work for him. It is second-hand, and they say so in the act of trying it.

The most honest confession. That is the exact position of a great many religious people, then and now. They have watched Christianity function in somebody’s life, a parent, a spouse, a friend whose faith is obviously real, and they would like the results. What they are reaching for is not Christ but the effect he evidently has on other people. The formula in this verse is the most honest confession of that ever recorded, and these men did not know they were making it.

Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. Two details, and both are strange. No Sceva appears in the lists of high priests that we have, and the name is Latin. He may have been from a high-priestly family, or claimed the title to impress, because a high-priestly pedigree was the best possible credential in the exorcism trade: the family that had access to the divine name. If so, then the fraud runs all the way down: a bogus priest’s sons using a borrowed name they had no share in. And there were seven of them. This was a family firm.

The fatal mistake. That is exactly their fatal mistake here. Seeing Paul cast out demons in Jesus’ name, the sons of Sceva simply added the Jesus whom Paul proclaims to their list of power-words, as one more spell to try, and it ended in disaster (vv. 15–16). The lesson is sharp and freeing: the name of Jesus is not a magic formula anyone can wield. It carries authority only on the lips of those who truly belong to him by faith. Real power over the powers of darkness is not a technique to be mastered but a gift that flows from being united to Christ. You cannot borrow Jesus’ authority while keeping Jesus himself at arm’s length.

Is it wrong to end a prayer in Jesus’ name? Not at all; it is right, and Jesus told us to ask in his name (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24). But praying in his name is not attaching a password to the end of a request. It means coming to the Father on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, trusting him as your mediator, and asking what fits his character and purposes. The words matter because the person matters. A child who says please father is not using a formula; he is speaking to someone he knows. Pray in Jesus’ name as one who belongs to him, and you will never be using it as Sceva’s sons did.

In a sentence. Some Jews who went around driving out evil spirits tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over the possessed, saying, I command you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches, including seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest.

On a Tuesday. The name of Jesus is not a magic word. It belongs to a person you must know. Ask yourself honestly whether your faith is first-hand or second-hand: is Jesus your Lord, or the Lord your parents or your spouse or your pastor talk about? If it is second-hand, do not despair; ask him today to make himself known to you, and read one of the Gospels to meet him for yourself.

For worship. The name of Jesus is above every name, and it cannot be borrowed or bought. At that name every knee will bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Philippians 2:10), and the demons already tremble at it. But it is also the sweetest name there is to those who are his, because it means the LORD saves. He does not lend his name to strangers. He gives it, with himself, to all who come to him, and writes it on them for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. No high priest named Sceva is known; he may have been from a high-priestly family, or used the title for show.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

But the evil spirit answered them, Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you? It is one of the most chilling sentences in the New Testament, and in Greek it uses two different verbs. The first, ginōskō, is the word for knowing a person: Jesus I know. The second, epistamai, is the word for recognising, being acquainted with, having someone on file: Paul I recognise. And then the third clause has no verb of knowing at all: but who are you? Demons know Jesus and tremble (James 2:19). They know his true servants. They do not fear people who use his name without knowing him.

Three tiers. So there are three tiers in the demon’s answer. There is the Lord, whom hell knows exactly. There is his servant, who is known in that world because he has been doing damage in it for two years: Paul had a reputation on the other side. And there are these seven men, who are nobody. Sit with the middle tier for a moment, because it is a startling thing to be told. Paul was known to the powers of darkness. His name had come up. Whatever we make of that, it puts a question to anyone who has ever wondered whether a quiet Christian life registers anywhere: this passage assumes that the powers of darkness take note of people who are actually doing something.

And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them. Luke piles up the verbs, leaped, mastered, overpowered, and the detail is almost comic in its humiliation. Seven against one, and the one won. Seven men, professional exorcists, and one possessed man puts the lot of them into the street.

So that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. A humiliating, almost comic scene. Spiritual power is not a technique. And this is the only exorcism in Acts that fails, which is why Luke records it. He has shown the name of Jesus casting out spirits repeatedly. Here he shows what happens when the same words are used by men who do not belong to the person they name.

Not a technology. The lesson is not only that the demonic is dangerous to meddle with, true though that is. It is that Christianity is not a technology. There is no formula, no words that work, no transferable method, and this is a mercy, because a faith that worked by technique would be available to the manipulative and the cruel. The authority of Jesus is inseparable from Jesus, and cannot be detached and used by somebody who has not submitted to him.

But did Jesus not say not to stop a man casting out demons in his name? He did (Mark 9:38–40), and he also warned of some who would cast out demons in his name and yet whom he never knew (Matthew 7:22–23). The man in Mark was apparently a genuine follower outside the circle of the twelve, and Jesus would not have him forbidden. The sons of Sceva were different: they used Jesus’ name as a borrowed spell, by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims, with no faith of their own, and the demon knew it.

Should a Christian be afraid of demons? No. A believer belongs to Christ, who disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Do not be curious about the occult, do not dabble, and do not give the devil a foothold through unconfessed sin (Ephesians 4:27). Resist him, firm in the faith, and he will flee (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9). The armour God gives is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18), not rituals. If someone seems to be in serious spiritual trouble, go to your pastor and pray together. The name of Jesus on the lips of his own is enough.

The question that lands. Which means the question in this verse is one worth letting land: if the powers of darkness were asked about you, would the answer be I recognise him, or who are you?

In a sentence. The evil spirit answered that it knew Jesus and recognised Paul, but who were they? and the possessed man jumped on them, overpowered them all, and they fled from the house naked and bleeding.

On a Tuesday. Do not borrow someone else’s faith. Know Jesus for yourself. And take comfort: if you belong to Christ, you are not one of the nobodies in this verse. You are known in heaven, written in the book of life, and the powers that overpowered seven exorcists cannot pluck you from his hand.

For worship. Jesus I know, said the demon, and hell has known him since the day he cast it down. He is the stronger man who bound the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27); he went into the darkness and came out with the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The powers that trampled the sons of Sceva fled before him in Galilee and were made a public spectacle at Calvary. And the Lord whom the demons know with terror, his people know with love.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices.

And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. Consider what actually got the city’s attention. Not the extraordinary miracles of verse 11: Ephesus was full of wonder-workers and one more would have been absorbed. What went round the city was a story about the name of Jesus refusing to work for people who had no right to it. That is the opposite of what we would have arranged. A humiliating public failure involving the name of Christ turned out to be the most effective evangelism in the chapter, because it told a city of magicians something they could not have learned from a success: this name is not a commodity.

And fear fell upon them all. Note the two things that followed, in Luke’s order. Fear: not admiration. The recognition that they were dealing with something real and not manageable. Ephesus had spent centuries trying to handle the invisible world by technique, and had just discovered a power that could not be handled at all.

And the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Made great. The name they tried to use as magic was honoured as holy. The name that had just been misused was, by the misuse, magnified. God turned even the humiliation of false exorcists to his glory.

Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. Now the sting, and it is aimed at the church rather than the city. These are believers, people already converted, already baptised, sitting in Paul’s lecture hall, who had kept up their magic secretly. Divulging (anangellontes) means disclosing what was hidden. In the magical trade the spells were secret by definition, and their power was thought to depend on the secrecy; so perhaps they were revealing their spells, which were thought to lose power when made public. Real repentance brings sins into the light (1 John 1:9; James 5:16).

Keeping one door open. So there were Christians in Ephesus who had been holding on to their charms. Not out of rebellion, most likely, but out of the ordinary human instinct to keep one door open: to trust Christ and also to keep the amulet, in case. It took a violent incident in somebody else’s house to bring it out.

The modern version. Which is worth taking personally, because the modern version is rarely amulets. It is the habit you have never mentioned to anybody, the arrangement you have not brought into the light, the thing you would not want read out. These people had been genuinely converted and were genuinely holding something back, and the two states coexisted for a while without anyone noticing. Luke’s word for the cure is not only repented. It is divulged: they said it out loud, to somebody.

Do I need to confess my sins to another person, or only to God? To God always, and to others sometimes. Every sin is against God, and he forgives all who confess it to him through Christ (1 John 1:9); no priest is needed to stand between you and him. But James tells us also to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be healed (James 5:16). Secret sins grow in the dark, and naming one to a trusted, mature believer often breaks its hold. If you have wronged someone, confess to them. If a hidden sin has its grip on you, tell one wise Christian friend or your pastor. You are not seeking absolution from them; you are bringing it into the light where Christ’s forgiveness already shines.

In a sentence. This became known to all the Jews and Greeks in Ephesus, fear came over them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honour, and many believers came openly confessing what they had done.

On a Tuesday. Bring hidden sins into the light. Confession breaks their power. Ask yourself what you are keeping as a back door, just in case: a habit, a relationship, a secret source of comfort or control. Then name it, first to God and then, if it has a grip on you, to one trusted believer this week.

For worship. The Lord Jesus brings hidden things into the light not to shame his people but to free them. He already knows every secret charm and every kept door, and he loved us and gave himself for us anyway. Fear fell on Ephesus, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified, because he is holy and will not be used; and the same holy name is the refuge of every sinner who confesses, for if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.

And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. Every word of that is costly. Their books: these were not printed volumes but scrolls of incantations, charms and spells, laboriously copied by hand, the working capital of the trade and, in Ephesus, among the most valuable religious property in the empire. Ephesus was famous for magic spells, known as Ephesian letters. A magician’s scrolls were his livelihood, his reputation, and his protection.

Brought them together. They fetched them. Nobody raided the houses; the owners went home and came back carrying them.

And burned them in the sight of all. Publicly, where the city could watch, which is the one method that leaves no way back. A man who quietly disposes of something can quietly replace it. A man who burns it in the square in front of his neighbours has ended a career. Repentance cost them.

And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. Somebody added it up. That is a very human detail, and it is Luke at his most reportorial: while the fire was burning, people were working out what it was worth. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, roughly a day’s wage for a labourer, so fifty thousand of them is fifty thousand days’ wages, well over a century of a working man’s income, going up in smoke in an afternoon. A fortune. True repentance is costly.

Why not sell them? Now the thing worth noticing, because it is the point. They could have sold them. There was a ready market: every one of those scrolls had a buyer somewhere in Asia, and the proceeds could have gone to the poor, or to the church, or to Paul’s support. It would have looked like the responsible course, and somebody in the crowd probably said so. They burned them instead, because selling them would have meant putting back into circulation the exact thing they had been delivered from, which would pass the evil on. Repentance that is careful to recoup its losses has not quite finished. There is a kind of obedience that costs you nothing because you found a way to make the disposal profitable, and there is the kind in this verse.

Should Christians do the same today? Items that are themselves tools of the occult, divination or idolatry should be destroyed, not sold or passed on, since that would put them into other hands. The point is a clean break, at cost, with what once ruled us. The same principle reaches further: whatever feeds your particular sin, the subscription, the app, the bottle, the contact in your phone, should be cut off decisively rather than kept within reach. Jesus spoke of tearing out an eye rather than keeping it to sin with (Matthew 5:29–30). Not every possession is evil, and Christian freedom is real. But what has become a snare should go in the fire, not in the attic.

So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. Then Luke’s verdict, laid immediately alongside the bonfire. Another progress report (6:7; 12:24). Prevail (ischyen) means grew strong, overpowered. The word of the Lord overpowered the magic of Ephesus. And the so is doing real work. The word prevailed in Ephesus at the point where Christians destroyed their own property in public.

Two small phrases. The word of the Lord is Luke’s regular name for the gospel message: the Christian message about and from the Lord Jesus, his own word carrying his own authority (much like the word of Christ, explained at Colossians 3:16). It is, in short, the gospel as God’s living, authoritative word. Increased does not mean the gospel grew larger in content, but that it spread, multiplied, and triumphed: more and more people heard and believed, and the message gained ground and overcame opposition, prevailing mightily here over the magic arts whose books had just gone up in smoke.

Why make the word itself the thing that grows? Why does Luke put it so oddly, rather than simply saying more people believed? On purpose; it is one of his favourite ways of speaking (6:7; 12:24; 13:49). Two reasons. First, he is deliberately picturing the gospel as a living seed: the very word for increase (auxanō, grow) is the language of living, fruitful things, the word of Jesus’ parables where the kingdom-seed sprouts and grows of its own God-given life (Mark 4:8, 26–29); the seed is the word (Luke 8:11). The gospel is planted in the world and grows like wheat, and believers are its fruit. Second, and more pointedly, by making the word the actor Luke takes the credit off the preachers and puts it on God: it is not Paul’s cleverness or the church’s strategy that conquers Ephesus, but the word itself, alive with God’s own power (Romans 1:16; Isaiah 55:11). So the strange phrasing is really a confession of faith: watch the word, not the men, and take heart, for that same living word is still growing and prevailing in the world today.

In a sentence. Many who had practised sorcery brought their scrolls together and burned them publicly, and when the value was counted it came to fifty thousand silver coins, and so the word of the Lord spread widely and grew in power.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to burn? Get rid of whatever ties you to sin, whatever it costs. Do it this week, and do it so that there is no way back. And if you are tempted to find a clever way to recover the cost, remember fifty thousand drachmas, and the joy of the people who did not.

For worship. The word of the Lord prevailed mightily, because the Lord of the word is mighty. No spell, no scroll, no power of darkness in the most magical city of the empire could stand before the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ. He did not need to burn the books himself; he changed hearts until their owners carried them to the fire. That is the kind of victory Christ wins: not by force but by love, until his enemies become his worshippers and count their losses as gain.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was famous for magic spells. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, about a day’s wage: fifty thousand was a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.

Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem. This is the hinge of the second half of the book, and everything from here to the last verse of Acts is the working out of the sentence. He was collecting money from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26; 2 Corinthians 8–9), and he meant to deliver it himself.

In the Spirit. Resolved in the Spirit is slightly ambiguous: in his own spirit, he made up his mind, or in the Holy Spirit, under the Spirit’s leading. Probably both: a Spirit-led decision. Given how the Spirit steers Paul throughout, and that the Lord later confirms this very plan (23:11), the Spirit-guided sense fits well.

Saying, After I have been there, I must also see Rome. Look at the route: Macedonia, Achaia, Jerusalem, Rome. Now look at what actually happens. He goes through Macedonia and Achaia (chapter 20). He reaches Jerusalem and is arrested in the temple (chapter 21). And he gets to Rome, years later, after hearings before governors and a king, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a snakebite, in chains at the empire’s expense (chapter 28). Every stage of that plan is fulfilled and not one of them in the manner he intended. He meant to visit Rome; he arrived as a prisoner. It is worth holding those two facts together whenever this verse is read as a model of Spirit-led planning, because the plan was right, and God kept it, and the keeping of it cost Paul his liberty. The rest of Acts follows this sentence: Jerusalem, then Rome.

Must. And the little word must (dei) is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the same one that stood over the cross. It is not ambition. Paul had wanted to see Rome for years and says so to the Romans themselves (Romans 1:11–13; 15:23–24), but what he expresses here is obligation, not preference. And the Lord confirms it four chapters later, standing beside him the night after the riot in Jerusalem, and telling him that as he has testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify also in Rome (23:11).

And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus. Two things in that. The first is the method, which by now is settled: he sends people ahead. Timothy has been doing this for years. Erastus appears here for the only time in Acts, and may be the city official of Corinth, the city treasurer whom Paul mentions in Romans 16:23, whose name appears in an inscription found there: a paving stone records an Erastus who laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his office. If so, a senior municipal official is being used as a messenger.

He himself stayed in Asia for a while. The second thing is this last clause. Having decided to go, he did not go. He stayed on and finished. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus during this time (1 Corinthians 16:8). The riot in the next paragraph happens to a man who had already made up his mind to leave and had not yet left, which is exactly the moment at which most of us are least useful and most inclined to coast.

How may a believer know his decisions are Spirit-guided today? First, let the anxiety down. The apostles received extraordinary, direct steering because of their unique founding role (see on 8:26); God’s ordinary way is quieter, and he has not promised you a voice in your head for every choice. So how does the Spirit lead? Chiefly through the Word. Spirit and Scripture always go together: he guides by lighting up the Bible he inspired, which is a lamp to our feet and equips us for every good work (Psalm 119:105; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Most of God’s will is already plainly revealed: be holy, love, forgive, flee sin, serve. So the Spirit-led life is, nine times in ten, simply the obedient life.

A renewed mind. Then through a renewed mind and sanctified wisdom. For what Scripture does not directly settle, which job, where to live, the Spirit leads not by bypassing your thinking but by maturing it: be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God (Romans 12:2); and if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously (James 1:5). Add prayer (Proverbs 3:5–6), godly counsel (Proverbs 15:22), and the providence of opened and closed doors. Inner promptings and a sense of peace may play a part (Philippians 2:13), but they are never to be trusted alone; they must be tested by Scripture and wisdom, for the heart can deceive (Jeremiah 17:9; 1 John 4:1).

The shape of a life. And the most freeing thing of all: the clearest mark of being led by the Spirit is not a feeling about one decision but the shape of a life. All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Romans 8:14): led, in context, to put sin to death and live as God’s children; and the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). So a choice made in love, humility, holiness and faith, by a person walking closely with God, is a Spirit-led choice, even if no special feeling attends it; while one driven by pride, lust, greed or self-will is not, however peaceful it feels. So your checklist is simple. Does it square with Scripture? Have I prayed for wisdom and sought counsel? Is my heart surrendered, ready to do even the hard thing? Does it flow from love and holiness, or from the flesh? Then decide, and trust him with the outcome. He is sovereign over your steps: the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Proverbs 16:9). He is big enough to guide a surrendered, Word-shaped heart, and kind enough to redeem even our wrong turns (Romans 8:28). A Christian walking with God need not fear missing God’s will; the pressure is off, for the Guide is faithful.

What if I made a decision in good faith and it went badly? Then you are in Paul’s company. His plan to see Rome was right, and it took him through arrest, storm and shipwreck. A hard outcome does not prove a wrong decision; obedience often leads through suffering, as it led our Lord. If, looking back, you see that you acted in pride or haste, confess it, and receive his forgiveness. If you acted in faith and it still went hard, do not torment yourself with what might have been. The Lord who establishes our steps also works through the steps we wish we had not taken, and nothing in your path is outside his care.

In a sentence. After this Paul decided in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, saying he must then also see Rome, and sent Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia while he stayed a while in Asia.

On a Tuesday. Make your plans in the Spirit, and hold them open to God’s way of fulfilling them. If you face a decision this week, run the checklist: Scripture, prayer, counsel, a surrendered heart, love. Then decide, and stop second-guessing. And if you have already decided to move on from something, a job, a ministry, a town, finish well where you are. Do not coast in Ephesus.

For worship. The Lord who said must over Paul’s journey said must over his own: the Son of Man must suffer, and be raised. Every step of our Saviour’s road was planned in eternity and walked in love, and he walked it to Jerusalem with his face set like flint. Because his must was fulfilled at the cross, every must he lays on his people will be fulfilled too, through chains and storms if need be. He brought Paul to Rome, and he will bring all his people home.
verseByVerse.note: Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears on an inscription there.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.

About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. Understatement. Luke’s phrasing is dry and deliberate: no little disturbance means a riot that filled a theatre seating about twenty-five thousand people. He uses the same trick about the silversmith’s income a line later: Demetrius brought no little business to the craftsmen. Putting the same phrase on both is not an accident. The size of the disturbance and the size of the profits are being measured against each other, and Luke expects you to notice which caused which.

The Way. Here is one of the earliest names the Christian movement went by, and Luke uses it repeatedly (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Why the Way? Three roots run together. First and deepest, Jesus said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6), so to follow the Way is to follow him, the one road home to God. Second, it echoes the Old Testament, where the life of faith is pictured as a road one walks: the way of the LORD, the Way of Holiness (Isaiah 35:8; 40:3). Third, it captures that Christianity is not merely a creed to hold but a way of life to walk, a whole road travelled after Jesus: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6). It is a humble, vivid name: the faith is a path you travel with the Lord who is himself the Way, not just a box you tick.

For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis. Here is the mechanism. Ephesus lived on its temple. The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, said to be four times the size of the Parthenon, with 127 columns. Pilgrims came from across the empire to see it, and, exactly as at any shrine since, they bought something to take home. Miniature silver shrines of the goddess were the premium souvenir and charm, and Demetrius made them.

Artemis of the Ephesians. Artemis (the Romans’ Diana) was the great goddess of Ephesus, but not quite the classical Greek huntress: she was a distinctive local mother goddess of fertility, shown with many breasts or eggs, patroness and protectress of the city. Her temple, the Artemision, was vast and magnificent and the heart of a huge pilgrimage and tourist economy. So the gospel here collides with a formidable triple alliance: a famous false god, fierce civic pride (Ephesus called itself the goddess’s temple keeper, v. 35), and big money. When people turned from idols to Christ, the idol-souvenir business suffered, and that, not theology, is what lit the riot (v. 27). The gospel had already burned the magic books (v. 19); now it threatens the idol trade. Wherever Christ truly advances, the kingdoms of money and idolatry feel the tremor.

Brought no little business to the craftsmen. Religion was big business. So the man who starts the riot is not a priest, not a philosopher, not a theologian. He is a manufacturer with a workshop, and the thing that has gone wrong is his order book. And notice how honest Luke is willing to let him be. In the next verse Demetrius will say the quiet part aloud to his own guild, that from this business they have their wealth, and only afterwards reach for the goddess. Luke could have written this as a clash of religions. He writes it as a trade dispute with a religious vocabulary, which is what it was.

What if my own job is connected to something I now see is wrong? Then you face the choice the Ephesian craftsmen faced, and Scripture will not let you dodge it. Some work is plainly incompatible with following Christ: making idols, selling occult services, producing pornography, defrauding people. If your livelihood depends on such things, you must leave it, trusting God to provide, as the magicians did with their scrolls. Much work is a mixture: an honest job in a company that also does wrong things. There, seek wisdom, refuse to do wrong yourself, and pray about whether to stay. Talk it through with your pastor. Christ asks for costly obedience, and he has never let anyone who gave up something for his sake be a loser in the end (Mark 10:29–30).

In a sentence. About that time a great disturbance arose about the Way, for a silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought a great deal of business to the craftsmen.

On a Tuesday. Where idolatry makes money, the gospel will be opposed. Notice the places in your own society where profit and false worship are tied together, and do not be surprised when the gospel is resented there. And ask what you yourself might lose if Christ had his way in your finances. That is where the next disturbance is likely to begin.

For worship. Jesus is the Way, and there is no other road to the Father. The silversmiths made little shrines for a goddess who could not walk with anyone; the living God came down to walk with us, and then laid down his life to open the road home. Artemis needed craftsmen to keep her in business. Christ needs no one, and gives everything, and the road he opened through his own body will still be open when every silver shrine has melted.
verseByVerse.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Artemis of Ephesus was a mother-goddess of fertility, not the huntress of Greek myth.

parallels.desc: a wide door, and many adversaries

verseByVerse.quote: These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth.

These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades. A trade union meeting. He called a meeting: not of priests, not of the temple authorities, but of the guild: his own silversmiths plus the workmen in similar trades, which is a wider net, the men who supplied the silver, the ones who made the cases, the shops that sold them. Demetrius has understood that his grievance is an industry’s grievance and has organised accordingly.

Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. Then he opens with the sentence that makes this the most candid speech about opposition to the gospel anywhere in Scripture. Honest, at least. No preamble about the goddess. No theology. The very first thing out of his mouth, to a room of men he can be honest with, is the money, and the reason he can say it is that he is talking to fellow tradesmen rather than to the public. He will produce Artemis in a moment, when he needs a crowd. The first argument is money. Religion was cover for profit. As in Philippi (16:19): the gospel threatens those who profit from falsehood.

The engine and the paintwork. Watch the order carefully, because it is the anatomy of a great deal of resistance to Christ. First, in private, the interest: our wealth. Then, in public, the principle: the honour of the goddess and the dignity of our city. The interest is the engine and the principle is the paintwork, and Luke has arranged the speech so that we hear the private version first.

Not only in Ephesus. It would be comfortable to leave that with first-century idol manufacturers. It should not be left there. The mechanism is entirely ordinary and it operates in people who are not conscious of it: when the gospel threatens something we are getting, an income, a position, a habit, a relationship on terms we like, the objection that forms in us almost never presents itself as this would cost me. It presents itself as a reasonable difficulty with the Christian faith. So there is a question worth putting to your own objections, and to those of people you are talking to, gently and mostly in silence: what would this person have to give up if it were true? It is not a way of dismissing anybody’s argument, because an argument has to be answered on its merits whoever makes it. But Demetrius is in Scripture to tell us that the stated reason and the real reason are often two different things, and that the man himself may not have noticed.

Choosing which true thing to say. Notice too that he is not lying about anything. Everything Demetrius says in this speech is factually true, including the parts about Paul. He is simply choosing which true thing to say to which audience.

Is it wrong for a Christian to want to be wealthy? Wealth itself is not sin; Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and honest work that prospers is a gift of God. But the desire to be rich is dangerous: those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and many senseless and harmful desires, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:9–10). The test is Demetrius’s: when money and truth collide, which gives way? A Christian holds wealth with an open hand, gives generously, refuses to gain it dishonestly, and is content with what God provides (Philippians 4:11–13; Hebrews 13:5). If truth is bending to protect your income, money has become your master.

In a sentence. He gathered them with other workers in related trades and said they all knew their wealth came from this business.

On a Tuesday. Do not let money shape your beliefs. Let truth shape your use of money. Next time you find yourself resisting something in Scripture, ask the Demetrius question quietly: what would I have to give up if this were true? Then let the answer be heard.

For worship. You cannot serve God and money, said the Lord who owned nothing and gave everything. He who was rich became poor for our sake, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Demetrius defended his wealth with a goddess; Christ gave up his glory to purchase a people. The riches of Christ are unsearchable, and those who have them can let every silver shrine go.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.

And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people. This is a hostile witness, which makes it among the best evidence in the chapter: a testimony from an enemy to the gospel’s success (v. 10). Demetrius has no interest in flattering the mission and every interest in exaggerating the threat, but he is speaking to men who can check him, about a market they all trade in, and what he reports is that the effect is measurable across the province. Set it beside Luke’s own claim in verse 10, that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord. That could be read as an evangelist’s enthusiasm. Here is the same claim from the accounts department of the idol trade, and it agrees.

Saying that gods made with hands are not gods. That is Paul’s preaching summarised by an opponent, and it is accurate (17:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4). So many had turned from idols that sales were falling. It is also the argument of the Hebrew prophets: Isaiah’s magnificent mockery of the man who cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half (Isaiah 44:14–20), and Jeremiah’s idols like scarecrows in a cucumber field, which cannot speak and have to be carried (Jeremiah 10:5). And the irony is that Demetrius is the one man in Ephesus who cannot honestly disagree, because he makes them. He knows exactly what a silver shrine of Artemis is, having watched one being hammered out that morning.

There is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing. Now the escalation, and it is a masterpiece of its kind. Then he adds religious patriotism to the money argument. City pride, religion and profit were bound together. He begins with the trade, which is what he actually cares about, and lets it occupy one clause. Then he moves to the temple, then to the goddess herself, then to her standing before Asia and the world, and by the end of the sentence a fall in souvenir sales has become a threat to the cosmic order. It is how such speeches are always built. The personal loss goes first and briefly, so that it can be said honestly and then left behind, and everything after it is about something nobody could be accused of self-interest for defending.

Counted as nothing. But notice what he has accidentally said about the gospel, because it is truer than he knows. His fear is that Artemis will be counted as nothing. That is precisely what the gospel does to an idol: not attack it, not vandalise it, but reduce it to what it always was. Paul’s own letter to this city reminds the Ephesians that they had once been without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12).

She whom all Asia and the world worship. Within a few centuries, the temple lay in ruins and the goddess was forgotten. It was burned, rebuilt, plundered and finally lost so completely that its site had to be dug out of a marsh in the nineteenth century. Today, a single reconstructed column stands. She was counted as nothing. It took rather longer than a riot. The word of the Lord endures.

What are the idols made with hands today? Most of ours are not carved, but they are still made by us: money, status, a career, a body shaped and photographed, a home, a political cause, a relationship, a reputation, even a ministry. Anything we look to for the security, meaning or approval that only God can give has become an idol, and it is made with hands because we built it. The test is simple: what would devastate you to lose, what do you daydream about, where does your money and time go when no one is watching? Idols are not removed only by smashing them, but by finding something better. Show your heart the beauty of Christ, and the shrines lose their shine.

In a sentence. Demetrius said they could see and hear how Paul had persuaded many people in Ephesus and almost all of Asia that man-made gods are not gods, and so their trade was in danger of losing its good name, and the temple of the great goddess Artemis of being discredited, and she herself, worshipped by all Asia and the world, of being robbed of her majesty.

On a Tuesday. Every idol falls in the end. Only the living God remains. Trust him. Name one thing in your life that you have been treating as if it could hold you up if everything else failed. Then say aloud to God that it is not god, and that he is.

For worship. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands; they have mouths but do not speak, and those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:4–8). But our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases. Artemis whom all Asia worshipped is a heap of stones in a marsh, and Jesus whom Demetrius despised is worshipped in every nation under heaven. The grass withers, the flower fades, the shrine melts and the temple sinks, but the word of our God will stand for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel.

When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! A cry of civic and religious pride, used in Ephesian worship. Inscriptions confirm the title. A guild meeting about profits ends with religious chanting, and the transition takes no time at all. Demetrius has done his work: the men who came in worried about their order books go out shouting for their goddess, and the two things have fused so completely that nobody in the room could now separate them.

Sincere passion for an interest. That fusion is the most dangerous thing in the chapter, and it is not confined to Ephesus. It is entirely possible to defend an interest with real religious passion and be quite sincere in the passion. The feeling is not manufactured; these men were genuinely enraged. But it had been aroused by a threat to something else, and it is the sincerity that makes it so hard to see.

So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater. The noise, the running, the rumour outrunning the fact. It has spread beyond the guild in minutes. The theatre at Ephesus is still there, cut into the side of Mount Pion and looking down the marble street to the old harbour, and it seated about twenty-five thousand people. Its ruins still stand, and you can sit where the crowd sat. That is where a mob went when it wanted to be a public meeting.

Dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. They could not find Paul, so they took two of his colleagues instead. Gaius and Aristarchus are named, and it is worth stopping on them, because they are the men in this story who paid. Aristarchus, from Thessalonica, turns up again and again afterwards: he is with Paul on the journey to Jerusalem (20:4), he is on the ship to Rome (27:2), and he is in prison with Paul at the end, called his fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). He was dragged into a theatre by a mob and stayed with the apostle to the chains.

Seized because they were near. Nobody in Ephesus was shouting about Gaius and Aristarchus. They were seized because they were near Paul, which is the ordinary experience of everyone who works closely with a person in the front line: the family, the colleagues, the host who lent the house. Jason had it in Thessalonica. These two have it here.

How do I tell whether my zeal is for God or for something of mine? Ask what makes you angry, and why. Righteous zeal is grieved most by what dishonours God and harms others; self-interested zeal flares when our comfort, status, group or pride is threatened, and then borrows God’s name. Notice whether your passion makes you more like Christ, patient, truthful, willing to suffer, or more like the theatre, loud, vague and ready to drag someone off. And invite a wise friend to tell you honestly. Zeal is good when it is according to knowledge (Romans 10:2), and when it would be just as fierce if nothing of yours were at stake.

In a sentence. Hearing this, they were furious and shouted, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!, and the city was thrown into confusion as the people rushed into the theatre, dragging Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s Macedonian travel companions.

On a Tuesday. The crowd shouted for Artemis. We shout for the Lord Jesus, who is truly great. When the next public outrage sweeps through your feed or your workplace, wait before you join it, and ask what interest is really being defended. And think of the Aristarchuses in your church, those who suffer because they stand near the front line: the pastor’s family, the missionary’s children. Pray for them by name.

For worship. Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised (Psalm 145:3). The Ephesians shouted greatness over a goddess who needed their shouting; our God is great whether anyone shouts or not, and he is the one who made the mouths that cry. His greatness is unsearchable, his love is from everlasting, and the faithful companions who were dragged into the theatre for his name are crowned with him now. Great is the Lord Jesus, and his greatness has no end.
verseByVerse.note: The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.

But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. Of course he wished to. Twenty-five thousand people in one place, most of them listening to nothing in particular, and his two friends on the floor of the theatre: it is the largest audience he would ever have had, and he wanted to stand with his friends and go and speak. And the Ephesian Christians stopped him. Luke’s verb is plain: they would not let him. Somebody stood in a doorway and refused to move. Brave Paul; wise disciples.

Courage restrained. That is worth having, because Paul is the apostle, and these are converts of two or three years. They overruled him, and Luke records it without a hint that they were wrong. There is a kind of courage that needs restraining, and a man who cannot be restrained by the people around him is not brave but unaccountable. Paul submitted.

And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his. Now this is one of the more surprising sentences in Acts, and Luke drops it in as though it needed no explanation. The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province, associated with the provincial council, the imperial cult and the public games, appointed annually. They were, in other words, part of the official religious establishment of the province. And Luke says they were Paul’s friends. He does not say they were converted; there is no suggestion of that. But some of the most powerful men in Asia, men whose public duties included the promotion of a religion Paul preached against, had come to know a Jewish tentmaker well enough to send urgent private messages when they judged his life to be in danger. The gospel had reached the highest circles, or at least won their respect. Another sign for Theophilus: respectable men of the province did not see Paul as a criminal.

Sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. Good advice. Courage needs wisdom. Two years of daily teaching in a public lecture hall had done that. He had not been shouting at the city from a distance; he had been in a lecture hall, daily, available to anyone who walked in, and some of the men who walked in were the men who ran the province.

Both at once. It is worth noticing what that means about the way he had conducted himself. He had preached that gods made with hands are not gods, in the city of Artemis, for two years, hard enough to dent an industry. And the officers of the rival religion liked him enough to try to save his life. Those two things are meant to be held together, and most of us manage only one of them.

Can I be friends with people whose beliefs I think are false? Yes, and you should be. Jesus was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul’s friendship with the Asiarchs did not soften his message. Friendship is not endorsement. It is the ordinary love of neighbour, and it is often the road along which the gospel travels. Be honest about what you believe, never mock what they hold dear, and let them see that your convictions make you kinder, not harder. The danger is not in having unbelieving friends but in letting them shape your loves more than Christ does (1 Corinthians 15:33). Keep your heart anchored in him, and open your door.

In a sentence. Paul wanted to go into the crowd, but the disciples would not let him, and some of the officials of the province, who were his friends, sent word begging him not to go into the theatre.

On a Tuesday. Courage needs wise friends. Listen to them. Who in your life has permission to tell you no? If no one does, give it to someone this week. And think of one person of influence or of a different faith whom you could befriend as Paul befriended the Asiarchs, not as a project, but as a neighbour.

For worship. The Lord who held back his apostle from the theatre is the Shepherd who guards his sheep with other sheep. He surrounds his servants with friends they did not choose, believers who block the door and pagans who send warnings, and through them all he keeps his word that none of his will be snatched from his hand. He who laid down his life when his hour had come never lets his servants throw theirs away before theirs.
verseByVerse.note: The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the provincial cult of the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.

Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Luke’s wry humour. A mob does not think. Most did not know why they were there. Luke was apparently not in that theatre, so somebody told him this afterwards, and what they remembered was the noise and the bewilderment. It is the observation of someone who had been in the crowd and had turned round and asked his neighbour what was going on.

Ekklesia. Notice the word Luke uses for the gathering: ekklēsia. It is the ordinary Greek term for a citizens’ assembly, and the town clerk uses it in its technical sense in verse 39: the regular assembly, the lawful one. It is also the word the New Testament uses everywhere for the church. So Luke has an ekklesia in this chapter which is a mob: gathered by a grievance, chanting a slogan, most of its members unable to say why they are present. He does not comment. He has spent the book describing another kind of assembly in the same city, a dozen men, then a lecture hall, then a province, and here is what the word means when the world uses it.

What a senseless god makes. It is indeed a touch of sad comedy, and Luke surely means us to feel the irony: a whole city roaring itself hoarse for two hours (v. 34) over a god, and most of the rioters cannot even say why they are there. But Scripture has a sober teaching that this little scene puts on display. The Bible takes a dim and realistic view of the mob: you shall not fall in with the many to do evil (Exodus 23:2); crowds are fickle and passion-driven, the same Jerusalem voices crying Hosanna one week and Crucify him the next (Matthew 21:9; 27:22). And deeper still, this is what idolatry does to a mind. When men exchange the true God for idols, Paul says, they become futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts are darkened; claiming to be wise, they become fools (Romans 1:21–22; Ephesians 4:17–18). The psalmist is even more pointed: those who make idols become like them (Psalm 115:8), as deaf, blind and senseless as the mute images they worship. A senseless god makes for senseless worshippers; the confused babble of the Ephesian theatre is simply idolatry’s darkened mind made audible.

A little Babel. Set against it is the gospel, for God is not a God of confusion but of peace (1 Corinthians 14:33). The riot is a little Babel, the proud city’s voices dissolving into noise, as at the tower where God confused the tongues of the self-exalting (Genesis 11:7–9), while the gospel is the Babel-reversing word that brings light, sanity and order (think of Pentecost, undoing the confusion of tongues). It is the Word that gives a man back his right mind, as the delivered demoniac sat clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). For you it is a mirror held up to the world: so much of its frenzy, the crowds roaring for causes, fashions and outrages, is people swept along without truly knowing why, defending empty things. The Scripture’s counsel is plain: do not be carried by the herd, but let the truth of God steady and clear your mind (Romans 12:2). The gospel does not merely save the soul; it brings the muddled head home to sanity and peace.

Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. The Jewish community pushes a spokesman to the front, and the reason is not hard to guess. Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had nothing to do with Paul, since Jews also refused to worship idols. Ephesus was rioting against people who said that gods made with hands are not gods, and that had been the Jewish position in that city for generations. They were in real danger of suffering for somebody else’s preaching, and Alexander was sent out to say so. There is something bleak in it. The synagogue that had seen Paul leave two years earlier now finds that the city cannot tell the difference between them, and has to stand up in front of the whole theatre to explain that it is not with him.

And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. To distance the Jews from the Christians. He got as far as the gesture. Luke gives him the orator’s raised hand, the same movement he records of Paul at Pisidian Antioch and on the barracks steps, and then the next verse says what happened to the speech.

How do I avoid being swept along by the crowd? Know what you believe and why, before the noise starts. Read Scripture daily, so that your mind is shaped by God’s word rather than by the latest outrage. Be slow to share, quick to check, and wary of anything that makes you feel certain without giving you reasons. Keep company with wise people, not only loud ones. Pray for a calm mind (Philippians 4:6–7). And remember that the majority has often been wrong: the crowd once chose Barabbas. A Christian is free to stand alone, because he does not stand alone; he stands with Christ.

In a sentence. The assembly was in confusion, some shouting one thing and some another, and most did not even know why they were there, and the Jews pushed Alexander forward, and he motioned for silence to make a defence.

On a Tuesday. Do not follow the crowd. Know why you believe what you believe. Before you join the next wave of public feeling, ask the question this crowd could not answer: why am I here? And give thanks that the assembly you belong to on the Lord’s Day gathers for a reason it can name: Christ crucified and risen.

For worship. God is not a God of confusion but of peace. He spoke light into darkness at creation, scattered the proud at Babel, and gathered the nations again at Pentecost, so that every tongue might confess one Lord. His church is the true assembly, called out of the world’s noise by his voice, and it knows exactly why it has come together: to worship the Lamb who was slain. In a world that roars without knowing why, his people sing because they know.
verseByVerse.note: Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had no part in the Christians’ activity.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

But when they recognized that he was a Jew. Anti-Jewish feeling. To the crowd, Jews and Christians were the same: both rejected Artemis. He never said a word. The crowd worked out what he was and shouted him down before he could begin, and then went on shouting.

For about two hours they all cried out with one voice, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! Two hours of chanting. Luke, or whoever told him, was keeping track of the time, which is exactly what you do when you are stuck somewhere and nothing is happening. Thousands of people chanting five words for two hours, in the open air, in a stone bowl built to carry sound. Like the prophets of Baal crying from morning until noon, with no voice and no one answering (1 Kings 18:26). Repetition is not truth. Their goddess could not hear them.

With one voice. The one thing in the day that was unanimous. Verse 32 said most of them did not know why they had come. They did not need to know. A slogan does not require you to have a reason; it requires you to have a side, and it will supply the feeling of certainty at no cost. That is what a chant is for, and it is worth recognising because the modern forms are everywhere and they are not confined to the irreligious. Two hours of Great is Artemis settles nothing, proves nothing, and answers nobody: Demetrius’s complaint is not addressed, Paul’s argument is not refuted, Alexander is not heard. But for two hours the theatre was full of people who felt entirely sure.

Of the Ephesians. And notice what the slogan actually asserts: not that Artemis is true, but that she is ours. Great is Artemis of the Ephesians: the possessive is the whole force of it. This is civic pride wearing a goddess. Take away the temple and Ephesus is just another port; the greatness being defended in that theatre is the city’s, and the goddess is the flag it is carried under.

The noise proves the opposite. Which is why the noise proves the opposite of what it intends. Nobody chants for two hours about something that is not in doubt. The volume in that theatre is the sound of a religion that has begun to feel the ground move, and it had. Within a few centuries the temple was a ruin, and the letter written to the Christians of this city is still read every week somewhere in the world.

Is repetition in Christian worship wrong too? Not in itself. The psalms repeat, his steadfast love endures for ever, twenty-six times in Psalm 136, and heaven repeats holy, holy, holy (Revelation 4:8). What Jesus forbade was heaping up empty phrases, as if God would hear us for our many words (Matthew 6:7). The difference is whether the words are true, understood and meant. A chorus sung with the mind engaged and the heart lifted to a God who hears is worship. Five words shouted for two hours to a goddess who cannot hear is noise. So sing gladly, and sing with understanding (1 Corinthians 14:15).

In a sentence. When they realised he was a Jew, they all shouted with one voice for about two hours, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!

On a Tuesday. Loud chanting does not make something true. Truth is truth, however many shout against it. When you are outnumbered and outshouted, do not measure the truth by the volume. And when you sing in church this Sunday, mean every word, to the God who hears.

For worship. The prophets of Baal cried from morning till noon, and there was no voice. The crowd at Ephesus cried for two hours, and Artemis did not answer. But the LORD hears the whisper of the humble, and answers before they call. He is not great because we say so; he is great, and so we say so. And one day every tongue, in that theatre and in every place, will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.

And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd. One man walks out in front of thousands of people who have been chanting for two hours, and quiets them. The town clerk was not a minor official. He was the chief civic official, in a Greek city of that period the senior executive officer: the man who drafted the decrees, ran the assembly, and above all was answerable to Rome for order in the city. If Ephesus got into trouble with Rome, he was the one who would have to explain it. Which is why he is the one person in the theatre with a strong personal reason to end this, and it shows in every line of what he says.

Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis? He begins by agreeing with them, and this is the shrewdest thing in the speech. He does not tell an inflamed crowd that it is wrong. He tells them that they are so obviously right that the shouting is unnecessary. Temple keeper (neōkoros) was an official title of honour Ephesus held, confirmed by inscriptions and put on its coins, and he uses it deliberately: your status is not in question.

And of the sacred stone that fell from the sky. One Greek word, diopetēs, fallen from Zeus, or from heaven. It was probably a meteorite, worshipped as an image of Artemis. In the ancient world, before anyone understood such things, a stone that fell flaming out of the sky seemed an obvious gift from the gods: heaven-sent, holy, undeniable proof of the deity, and several pagan cults treasured such stones. The Ephesians believed their goddess, or her very image, was bound up with one, and the town clerk waves it as his clinching argument: everyone knows Artemis is real and we are her guardians, so settle down. The quiet irony is sharp: they revered the falling rock and the goddess, while missing the true God who actually made the heavens and flung the stone, worshipping the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25). A meteorite is a wonder, but it points to its Maker, not to a goddess; every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).

Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. And there is the turn. His argument: Artemis is secure; why riot? If your position is unassailable, then this behaviour is beneath it. Panic is an admission; a city that is certain of its goddess does not need to roar for two hours in a theatre. The irony: what he thought could not be denied was denied, and his goddess is gone.

A competent bureaucrat. It is worth noticing that Luke, a Christian writing for Christians, reports this speech at length and with evident approval, although its argument is entirely pagan: Artemis is great, her stone fell from heaven, calm down. He is not endorsing the theology. He is showing his readers that the riot was ended by an ordinary civic official doing his job properly, and that the church in Ephesus was preserved that afternoon by nothing more spiritual than a competent official who did not want trouble.

Why does Luke include a pagan speech in Scripture without correcting it? Because Scripture faithfully records what people said, without endorsing all of it. The Bible accurately reports the words of Satan, of Job’s comforters and of this town clerk; inspiration guarantees that the record is true, not that every speaker was right. Luke expects his readers to see the irony for themselves: a man defending what cannot be denied, in a city whose temple is now a marsh. And he wants us to see God’s hand in ordinary order. The clerk was wrong about Artemis and right about the riot, and God used the second for his people’s good.

In a sentence. The town clerk quieted the crowd and said everyone knew Ephesus was the guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image that fell from heaven, and since this was undeniable, they should calm down and do nothing rash.

On a Tuesday. What the world thinks undeniable often crumbles. God’s truth stands. Think of something your culture treats as beyond question that contradicts the word of God, and do not be cowed by its confidence. Then thank God for the ordinary officials in your town who keep the peace, and pray for them this week.

For worship. The Father of lights flung the stars into their courses and tells every stone where to fall. The Ephesians worshipped a rock that fell from the sky; we worship the Son who came down from heaven of his own will, not by accident but by love, and who returned there in glory. What the town clerk thought undeniable has been denied by history. What God has spoken in his Son will never be denied, for heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.note: The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for public order. The “sacred stone” was probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
