For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.

For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. This is a formal finding, delivered in public by the senior officer of the city, and it is worth weighing as evidence. A civic official declares Paul’s companions innocent. Two charges are named and both are dismissed. Sacrilegious (hierosylous) means temple robbers: the charge covered the plundering of shrines, a serious crime everywhere in the ancient world. Blasphemers of our goddess means public abuse of Artemis.

Without vandalism and without mockery. So the town clerk of Ephesus, who has no interest in defending Christianity, states in front of the whole city that in two years of preaching that gods made with hands are not gods, Paul and his companions had not once robbed a shrine or insulted the goddess. Think about how difficult that is. Paul had emptied the magic trade, damaged the souvenir industry across the province, and persuaded a great many people to abandon the city’s religion, and he had done it without vandalism and without mockery. He argued that the idols were nothing. He did not throw anything at them. Paul did not attack temples or mock the goddess; he simply preached the truth.

A standard often failed. That is a standard the church has frequently failed since, and the failure is usually defended as boldness. There is a way of opposing what is false that gives the opposition a grievance to point at, and it is generally the lazy way, because insulting a thing is much quicker than dismantling it. Paul’s two years produced a bonfire lit by the magicians themselves, and not one prosecutable act. A model: Christians should not insult other religions, but proclaim Christ. The truth undermines idols without our ridicule.

If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Go through proper channels. And now the clerk turns the whole thing back on the man who started it. Demetrius called this meeting. If he has a case, there is a court sitting and a governor to hear it, so bring it. Of course he does not, because he had no case at law and knew it, which is precisely why he had gone to the guild and the theatre instead. A grievance that will not go to the proper place for a hearing is usually a grievance that would not survive one.

Lawful channels. Proconsul is explained at 18:12: the Senate-appointed governor of a province like Asia, who held supreme civil and judicial authority, in modern terms roughly a regional governor who is also the province’s chief judge. The clerk’s point is simply that lawful channels exist: let Demetrius take any real grievance to the proper authorities rather than whipping up a riot. There is a quiet wisdom here too: the gospel does not fear due process, and the Christian’s way is to seek justice through lawful order, not mob passion.

But are Christians not supposed to call false religion false? Yes, and Paul did, plainly: gods made with hands are not gods. The question is how. You can say that something is untrue without sneering at the people who believe it or ridiculing what they hold sacred. Paul reasoned, explained, and pointed to the living God; he did not deface statues or mock worshippers. Speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15) means being clear about what is false and gentle with those who are deceived, remembering that we were once deceived too (Titus 3:3). Mockery hardens people; patient truth, by God’s grace, sets them free.

In a sentence. He said they had brought these men, though they had neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess, and if Demetrius and the craftsmen had a complaint, the courts were open and there were proconsuls; let them press charges.

On a Tuesday. Proclaim Christ without insulting others. Let the truth do its work. Read back over the last thing you posted or said about another religion or worldview, and ask whether a thoughtful adherent would find it fair. If not, put it right. And if you have a grievance, take it to the proper place, not to the crowd.

For worship. The Lord Jesus, when he was reviled, did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and his apostles learned it from him. His truth needs no vandalism to win; it is stronger than every idol simply by being true, and gentler than every enemy because it was purchased by love. He has disarmed the false gods not by mockery but by a cross, and he wins their worshippers one by one, until the shrines are empty and the hearts are his.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.

But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. The lawful city assembly, which met on fixed days. The word is ekklēsia again, and this time it carries its precise civic meaning: the constitutional assembly that met on fixed days with an agenda and a procedure. The clerk is drawing the line between that and what is in front of him, which is a crowd. It is a small point of vocabulary and it does a lot of work in this chapter. The same word covers a legitimate gathering that decides things properly and a mob that has been shouting a slogan for two hours, and the difference is not the number of people or the strength of their feeling. It is whether there is a process by which anybody could be shown to be wrong.

For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion. Here is the real argument, and he has kept it until last. Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting, removing its privileges as a free city. Ephesus had privileges granted by Rome, and Rome was famously unsentimental about civil disorder in the provinces. An unexplained mass assembly was exactly the sort of thing that got privileges reviewed and troops stationed. The clerk was worried about Rome, not Artemis. He is telling his fellow citizens that they have spent the afternoon handing the proconsul a reason to take their liberties away.

No cause that we can give. Note the phrase. He does not say the cause is weak. He says there is nothing they could put in writing. Somebody would have to draft the report, and that somebody is him, and there is no sentence he could compose that would not read as an admission. So the riot that was called to defend the greatness of Artemis ends with the city’s chief officer explaining that it cannot be explained.

The shape of what has happened. What none of them can see is the shape of what has just happened. A silversmith raised a mob to protect an industry; a crowd that mostly did not know why it was there shouted for two hours; and the outcome was a public declaration, from the highest civic authority in the city, that the Christians had broken no law and that any complaint against them must go to a proper court. Demetrius set out to stop the gospel and obtained for it the nearest thing to a clean record that Ephesus could issue.

Why should Christians value law and order? Because God ordained governing authorities for our good, to restrain evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), and because the gospel spreads more freely where there is peace. Paul urged prayer for rulers precisely so that believers might lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way, and so that all may hear the truth (1 Timothy 2:1–4). That does not make the state our saviour, and it does not mean every law is just. But a Christian should be a good citizen, thankful for courts that are open and officials who do their jobs, and should pray for them, as God used this clerk.

In a sentence. Anything further should be settled in a legal assembly, for they were in danger of being charged with rioting, with no reason they could give for this commotion.

On a Tuesday. God uses even worried officials to protect his people. Thank him for good order and law. Name the officials in your town or country this week in prayer: the mayor, the police, the judges. You may never know how many quiet afternoons of peace you owe to their ordinary diligence, and to the God who governs them.

For worship. God uses even worried officials to protect his people. He is the God of order, who set the bounds of the sea and appointed rulers to restrain the violence of men. He watched over his church in the theatre at Ephesus without a single miracle, through a nervous clerk and a fear of Rome, and he governs the nations still for the sake of his people. The rulers think they keep the peace; the Prince of Peace keeps them.
verseByVerse.note: Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly. That is how the greatest riot in the book of Acts ends. Not with an earthquake, not with a sermon, not with anyone being converted. A municipal officer finishes his remarks and sends everybody home, and the crowd goes.

Two assemblies. Assembly (ekklēsia) is the same word as church. Luke may be drawing the contrast: the confused, idolatrous assembly of Ephesus is dismissed; the church of Christ, God’s true assembly, remains. Once again, a Roman official protects the gospel by keeping the peace. The word of the Lord continues to prevail.

The restraint of the story. Luke could have written this chapter very differently. He had material for it: extraordinary miracles, a violent deliverance, a bonfire of fifty thousand pieces of silver. And he ends the whole Ephesian ministry with a man closing a meeting. That restraint is worth noticing, because it is how God most often works and it is not how we most often tell the story. Paul was not in the theatre. No apostle spoke. Nothing happened that anybody would call supernatural. The church at Ephesus was preserved that afternoon by the professional instincts of an official who wanted to keep his city out of trouble with Rome, and by the friendship of some provincial aristocrats, and by a few disciples who stood in a doorway and would not let Paul out.

Ordinary means. Ordinary means, all of them. And every one of them was the hand of God, and not one of the people involved knew it. There is a habit of mind that only counts God as present when something inexplicable happens, and it leaves most of a life looking empty. This verse is the corrective. The same God who threw open the prison at Philippi with an earthquake protected his people at Ephesus with a competent civil servant, and Luke gives both episodes the same weight.

How can I see God’s hand in ordinary things? By remembering that providence is God’s most holy, wise and powerful preserving and governing of all his creatures and all their actions (Westminster 5.1), and that he works through means far more often than without them. The doctor’s skill, the friend’s warning, the delayed train, the job that fell through: these are not God’s absence but his usual way of working. Practise looking back at the end of a day and asking where he kept you, fed you, warned you or guided you. You will find him everywhere. And that will make you more thankful, and less anxious, for the God of the ordinary is the God of every hour.

The three years close. And so the three years at Ephesus close. Twelve men who had never heard of the Holy Spirit; three months in a synagogue and two years in a rented hall; a province evangelised by people whose names we do not know, going home; the magic trade bankrupted by its own practitioners; a riot that ended in a legal finding of innocence. Paul will say goodbye to the elders of this church in the next chapter and tell them he will not see their faces again, and to this congregation will be written the letter that begins with God choosing his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Luke’s own summary of all of it was given at verse 20, and he does not improve on it: so the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.

In a sentence. After saying this, he dismissed the assembly.

On a Tuesday. The world’s assemblies come and go. Christ’s church remains. Belong to it. If you are not a committed member of a local church, make this the week you take a step toward it. And tonight, before you sleep, look back over the day and name three ordinary means by which God kept you. That is the God of Acts 19, and he is yours.

For worship. The assemblies of Ephesus have all been dismissed, and the temple of Artemis is a marsh, and the church of Jesus Christ is still gathering. He loved the church and gave himself up for her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27), and he has never once dismissed her. Every other assembly in history will end. His will gather at last around the throne, from every tribe and tongue, and it will never be dismissed, because its Lord lives for ever.

19.theology: The Word of God as the Power of Mission. Ephesus is Luke’s great exhibit of what the Word of God, given time and sustained proclamation, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all of Asia hears. The mechanism is not apostolic travel or institutional strategy — it is daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it wherever they go. The Reformation insight that the Word creates the church (“verbum Dei creat ecclesiam”) is visible in Ephesus: the Word goes out, conversions happen, the old life is burned, fear of God falls on the city, new communities form. The Word is not one tool among many; it is the engine of the whole enterprise. This is why Paul will later write to Timothy: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). There is no substitute.
19.examples:
Then: All of Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus. A bonfire worth more than a century’s wages lights the night. A silversmith’s trade is threatened by a theological truth. The word of the Lord prevails mightily — not with weapons, not with political power, not with cultural cachet, but with the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to replace sustained Word-ministry with more immediately impressive alternatives — spectacle, experience, technique, programme. Ephesus was not won by any of these. It was won by a man who reasoned daily from the Scriptures for two years. The Word still has this power. It has not diminished. The question is whether we are willing to give it the time and the centrality it requires.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. <sup>2</sup>When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. <sup>3</sup>There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. <sup>4</sup>Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. <sup>5</sup>These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas, <sup>6</sup>but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days. <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>13</sup>But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. <sup>14</sup>And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. <sup>15</sup>And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. <sup>16</sup>For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>33</sup>I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. <sup>34</sup>You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. <sup>35</sup>In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
After the riot Paul leaves Ephesus, strengthens the churches of Macedonia and spends three winter months in Corinth, where he almost certainly wrote Romans. A plot against him at sea makes him go back overland. He travels with representatives of the Gentile churches, who are carrying the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and Luke rejoins him at Philippi (“we”). At Troas, at an evening gathering on the first day of the week, Paul teaches until midnight; a young man named Eutychus falls asleep, drops from a third-storey window and is picked up dead, and Paul restores him. The church breaks bread and talks until dawn.

Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul sails past Ephesus and summons its elders to Miletus. His farewell is the only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders, and the nearest thing in Acts to one of his letters. He reviews his ministry: humble, tearful, open, teaching the whole counsel of God, supporting himself. He tells them he goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit and expecting chains, counting his life worth nothing beside finishing his course. He charges them to guard themselves and the flock that God bought with his own blood, warns of wolves from outside and false teachers from within, and commends them to God and the word of his grace. They kneel, pray, weep and see him to the ship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the uproar is over, Paul encourages the disciples and leaves for Macedonia, then spends three months in Greece. A plot by his opponents as he is about to sail for Syria makes him return through Macedonia. Seven companions from the churches go ahead to Troas, and after the Feast of Unleavened Bread Paul and Luke sail from Philippi to join them. On the first day of the week the church meets to break bread, and Paul, leaving the next day, talks until midnight in a lamp-lit upper room. Eutychus, sitting in a window, sinks into sleep and falls three storeys, and is picked up dead. Paul goes down, embraces him and says his life is in him. Back upstairs they break bread and talk till dawn, and the young man is taken home alive, to their great comfort. The party sails down the coast while Paul walks to Assos and joins them there; they pass Ephesus because Paul is hurrying to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — perhaps choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece.

Meaning first. Acts 20 is a chapter of farewells. Paul revisits the churches of Macedonia and Greece, raises a young man who fell from a window during a long Sunday service, and then, at Miletus, gives his only recorded speech to Christian leaders: his farewell to the elders of Ephesus. It is the New Testament’s great charge to pastors. Paul reviews his own ministry, warns of wolves, and commits them to God and to the word of his grace. Then they kneel, weep and part. And at the centre of it all stands one astonishing phrase: the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (v. 28). Every farewell, every warning and every tear in this chapter is measured by what the flock cost the Shepherd.

After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell. Two things worth getting straight before anything else. First, the riot did not drive him out. He had resolved to leave for Macedonia before Demetrius ever called his guild together (19:21). So this is not a man fleeing; it is a man who had already packed and who stayed on to see the trouble through before going. He did not leave in a hurry, or in fear. Second, look at the order of the verbs: he sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell. He did not slip away. The city had just spent an afternoon shouting about a goddess whose trade he had damaged, and the Christians of Ephesus were the ones who would still be living there after his ship sailed. So he gathered them and put heart into them, and then left.

Encouragement on the way out. That word encouraging, and its noun in the next verse, much encouragement, is one of the most characteristic things about Paul, and it is worth noticing how often it turns up on the way out of somewhere. Strengthening people you are leaving behind is a very different discipline from inspiring people you are about to lead, and it has almost no reward in it.

And departed for Macedonia. To Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea. Now read the next sentence knowing what it covers, because Luke has compressed some of the most turbulent months of Paul’s life into it. Somewhere in this journey Paul went to Troas expecting to meet Titus with news from Corinth, and Titus was not there, and he tells us what that did to him: his spirit was not at rest, so he took leave of them and went on to Macedonia (2 Corinthians 2:12–13). He had an open door for the gospel and could not use it, because he was too anxious. And when he did reach Macedonia it did not immediately improve: he was afflicted at every turn, with fighting without and fear within (2 Corinthians 7:5). Then Titus arrived with good news, and out of that relief Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia at this time: the most personal and least guarded of all his letters, in which he defends his ministry, admits his despair, and tells of the thorn in the flesh.

When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth. Luke says simply: he came to Greece. That gap between the two accounts is worth keeping. Luke is writing history and gives us the route; Paul, in his letters, gives us what the route cost. And it is a fair warning against reading anybody’s outward record, including the tidy ones in Scripture, as though it told you what was going on inside the person walking it.

What if I feel anxious even while serving God? Then you are not alone, and you are not disqualified. The apostle who wrote do not be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6) once could not use an open door because his spirit was not at rest. Anxiety is not the same as unbelief; it is a burden to be carried to God, and Paul carried his, and God comforted him by the coming of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6). So tell God plainly what you fear, ask others to pray, and look for the Titus he sends. And do not judge other Christians by their outward record. The calmest-looking believer in your church may be fighting fears within.

In a sentence. When the uproar ended, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, said goodbye and left for Macedonia, and after travelling through that area encouraging the believers, he came to Greece.

On a Tuesday. Encourage before you leave. Paul never left a church without strengthening it. When you next move on from something, a job, a house, a home group, a church, do not slip away. Gather those you are leaving and put heart into them. And ask one believer this week how they are really doing inside, behind the route they show.

For worship. The God of all comfort comforts us in all our affliction (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). He saw his apostle restless at Troas and afflicted in Macedonia, and he sent Titus down the road at the right hour. He encourages his people through one another, and he never leaves one of his churches without a word to stand on. The Father who comforts the downcast is the same yesterday and today, and our fears within are as well known to him as the fightings without.
verseByVerse.note: Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.

There he spent three months. Greece here means Corinth, and the three months are probably the winter, when the sea lanes closed and few ships sailed. Paul is staying in one city, with time on his hands.

The letter written in the wait. And this is very probably when he wrote the letter to the Romans, around AD 57, the greatest statement of the gospel ever written. Luke does not mention it, but the evidence inside the letter is as clear as such things get. Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), Corinth’s eastern port. He sends greetings from Gaius, who is host to him and to the whole church (Romans 16:23), and Gaius was one of the two men Paul baptised at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). He mentions Erastus, the city treasurer, and a paving stone at Corinth still records an Erastus who laid it at his own expense. And he says he is on his way to Jerusalem with the collection from Macedonia and Achaia (Romans 15:25–26), which is exactly where the next verse of Acts finds him.

Enforced inactivity. So the greatest letter ever written, the one that converted Augustine, set Luther free, and has shaped Christian thought for twenty centuries, was composed during a three-month wait, by a man who could not travel. Luke gives it five words: there he spent three months. It is worth sitting with that. The most productive quarter of Paul’s life, measured by what survived it, was a period when he was not doing what he wanted to be doing. The season looks, from the outside and probably from the inside, like a delay.

When a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria. Luke gives no details of the plot, but it is not hard to imagine. Perhaps they meant to kill him on a pilgrim ship bound for Passover, crowded with Jews going up to the feast, where it would be easy to throw him overboard; and Paul was carrying a very large sum of money. Somebody found out about the booking.

He decided to return through Macedonia. A longer route by land, to avoid the plot. Prudence is not lack of faith. So he goes the long way round, back up through Macedonia, many extra miles and weeks of delay. And notice what the detour produced, since Luke lets us watch: it is on this altered route that he spends the week at Troas, raises Eutychus, and gives the farewell at Miletus that is the theological centre of this half of the book. None of it happens if the ship sails.

Is it lack of faith to take precautions against danger? No. Faith trusts God; it does not ignore what God lets us see. Jesus withdrew when his enemies sought to kill him before his hour (John 8:59; 10:39), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket and changed his route here. To refuse sensible precautions in the name of faith is not trust but testing God, which Jesus refused to do (Matthew 4:7). So lock your door, take your medicine, avoid the dangerous road, and pray. Then, when danger cannot be avoided in the path of obedience, as it could not at Jerusalem, go forward without fear. Wisdom and courage are friends.

In a sentence. He spent three months there, and when the Jews plotted against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia.

On a Tuesday. Wisdom avoids needless danger. Trust God and use your head. And if you are in a season of enforced waiting, illness, unemployment, a delay you did not choose, ask what letter to the Romans God might want written in it. The season that looks like a delay may be the one that lasts.

For worship. The Lord rules the winters and the plots and the changed itineraries of his servants. While Paul waited for the sea to open, God was giving his church the letter of Romans; while enemies planned a murder, God was planning a resurrection at Troas and a farewell at Miletus. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10), and no detour in the life of his people is wasted, for he is working all things together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,

Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. Luke rarely gives a list like this, and when he does it is because the list itself is the point. Seven men, named with their home towns, from three Roman provinces: Macedonia, Galatia and Asia, much of the mission field of all three journeys, walking together in one party. And they are almost certainly there because of money.

The collection. For years Paul had been gathering a relief fund from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He gives instructions about it to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), devotes two whole chapters to it (2 Corinthians 8–9), and tells the Romans he is on his way to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints (Romans 15:25–26). These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:3–4; 2 Corinthians 8:19–21): Gentile believers carrying their gift, and a living picture of the Gentile church’s love for the Jewish church.

An audit committee of seven. Now read what Paul says about why they are coming, because it is one of the most practical sentences he ever wrote: he aims at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Corinthians 8:21). He would not carry other people’s money alone. Not because he might steal it, but because somebody might one day say he had, and the gospel would wear the accusation. It is a plain standard, and the church has suffered enormously wherever it has been ignored: never let one person handle the money, never let the arrangement depend on trusting a good man, and set it up so that the accusation cannot be made in the first place. Accountability in handling money. Paul, an apostle who had seen the risen Christ, submitted himself to an audit committee of seven.

Two names to keep. Keep two of the names, because they matter later. Tychicus will carry the letters to Ephesus and Colossae for Paul from prison (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). And Trophimus, an Ephesian, is the man some Jews will claim to have seen with Paul in the temple: the accusation, entirely false, that sparks Paul’s arrest and eventually sends him to Rome in chains (21:29). He is standing here in a list of travelling companions, and he is the occasion of much that happens in the last eight chapters of the book.

Is this Gaius the same as the others? Is this Gaius of Derbe the same as the Macedonian Gaius of 19:29, or the Gaius of Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14? Gaius was a very common name, and Luke gives these two different homelands. They were probably different men.

These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas. Us: Luke is back.

Why should a church care about financial accountability if its leaders are godly? Because godly leaders are still sinners, and because the reputation of Christ is at stake, not only theirs. Paul was as trustworthy as any man who ever lived, and he still insisted on witnesses. Good practice protects the innocent from suspicion as much as it guards against the guilty. In practice that means more than one person counting the offering, clear records, independent checking, open reporting to the members, and no leader having sole control of funds. If you serve as a treasurer or deacon, welcome scrutiny gladly. If you are a member, ask kindly how it is done. It honours the Lord.

In a sentence. Paul was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia, who went ahead and waited for the rest at Troas.

On a Tuesday. Handle money for God’s work with transparency and accountability. Paul did. If you handle money for a church, a charity or a family, ask whether anyone else could see exactly what you have done with it. And thank God for the quiet companions in your church, the Secunduses no one remembers, who travel with the gift and make sure it arrives.

For worship. The love of Christ crossed every border in this little party: a Berean, two Thessalonians, a man of Derbe, two Asians and Timothy, Gentiles from three provinces carrying a gift to Jewish believers they had never met. Only the gospel makes such a company. He has broken down the dividing wall of hostility and made of two one new man (Ephesians 2:14–15), and the money carried to Jerusalem was a token of a deeper gift: the riches of Christ, given freely to Jew and Gentile alike.
verseByVerse.note: These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days.

But we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread. The pronoun has changed again, and this time it has been a long wait. Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi, where he had stayed since chapter 16. Luke’s we last appeared at Philippi in chapter 16, when Paul and Silas were dragged before the magistrates, and then the narrative went back to they and stayed there for four chapters and some years. Now, at Philippi, it becomes we again.

Luke in Philippi. The natural conclusion is that Luke had stayed there the whole time. He had been left in the city where Lydia was converted and the jailer’s household baptised, and while Paul was in Thessalonica and Athens and Corinth and Ephesus, Luke was in Philippi. Nobody wrote about it. There is no chapter on what he did. And it is worth noticing that the church at Philippi is the one Paul singles out as the only congregation that supported him when he left Macedonia, sending help more than once (Philippians 4:15–16), and the one he writes to with more warmth than any other. Somebody had been there, quietly, for years. If your own service has consisted of staying somewhere while other people went and did things, this is the verse where the man who wrote more than a quarter of the New Testament comes back into the story after years of exactly that.

After the days of Unleavened Bread. Passover week, spring of AD 57. They waited for the feast to finish before sailing. Paul kept the Jewish calendar as a time marker, and Luke notes it without comment; the question of how a Christian relates to those observances is worked out at 18:18.

And in five days we came to them at Troas. The crossing had taken two days the other way (16:11). Contrary winds.

Where we stayed for seven days. Including a Sunday. And that is a long stop for a man in a hurry to reach Jerusalem. He is very probably waiting for the first day of the week. And that is worth stopping on, because the Sunday gathering is the only thing Luke mentions to account for a week’s delay in a journey he was racing to finish. Paul would refuse to enter Ephesus because he could not spare the days (v. 16), and he sat in Troas for seven of them. What he was waiting for was the church’s gathering. He would not pass through a town where there were believers without meeting them, and he would not ask them to reschedule: he waited for the day they already met. The apostle worked round the congregation’s diary rather than the other way about.

Is it so important to gather with the church every week? Yes. It is not the only place we meet God, but it is the place he has promised to meet his people together, in the word, the Supper and prayer, and we are told not to neglect meeting together, as is the habit of some (Hebrews 10:24–25). Paul, with every reason to hurry, waited a week rather than miss it. Illness, necessary work, caring for others or travel may sometimes keep us away, and there is no guilt in that. But a Christian who regularly lets lesser things crowd out the Lord’s Day gathering is starving himself and depriving others of his gifts. Plan your week around it.

In a sentence. They sailed from Philippi after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, joined the others at Troas five days later, and stayed there seven days.

On a Tuesday. Paul waited seven days, perhaps to worship with the church on the Lord’s Day. Make time for it. Look at your diary for next Sunday now, and protect it. And if you are a Luke, staying faithfully in one place while others travel, take heart: the Lord writes the hidden years into his story too.

For worship. The risen Lord meets with his people on the day of his resurrection, and his apostle would rather wait a week than miss it. He has promised that where two or three are gathered in his name, he is there among them (Matthew 18:20). Every Lord’s Day is an appointment with him, kept by him across every century, and the church that gathers in his name on the first day of the week is meeting the one who rose on the first day of the week, and lives for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.

On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread. This is the plainest narrative description we have of a Christian church meeting, and almost everything about our own Sundays is in it. The first day of the week is Sunday. Not the Sabbath. These are people among whom Jews and Gentiles worshipped together, in a world where the seventh day was the recognised Jewish holy day and the first day was an ordinary working day; Sunday was not a public holiday in the empire for another two and a half centuries. So they met either very early or, as here, in the evening, after work, because they had jobs. And they did it on the first day because that was the day the tomb was found empty. One of the clearest New Testament glimpses of Christian worship: on Sunday, gathered, to break bread, the Lord’s Supper, with teaching. Sunday was the day of resurrection (Luke 24:1), and became the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10; 1 Corinthians 16:2).

Already happened. Nobody in the New Testament argues for this or explains it at length. It has simply already happened, in a church a long way from Jerusalem, within about twenty-five years of the resurrection.

To break bread. Luke’s phrase covers both a shared meal and the Lord’s Supper, and in the early church the two were not separated. The gathering was around a table.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and Sunday. Seventh-day Adventists and others hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath; some Christians see no special day at all. Between these, two views are held by many Reformed and evangelical Christians. One, the historic position of the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds that the fourth commandment is moral and abiding, and that from the resurrection the Sabbath was changed to the first day, the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy in worship and rest (Westminster 21.7–8). The other holds that the Sabbath, as a sign of the old covenant, is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is the church’s day of gathering without Sabbath law. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The church from the beginning gathered on the first day, the day of resurrection. The Lord’s Day is not a burdensome law but a privilege: a day to gather, worship, break bread, hear the word, rest and do good.

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Confession, hold that it is: the creation pattern of one day in seven is for all people, the commandment stands among the Ten, and the day has moved to the resurrection, so that we rest from ordinary work and give the whole day to worship and mercy. Others read Colossians 2:16–17 and Romans 14:5 as showing that no day now binds the conscience as a law. This commentary takes the second view (see the verdict above), setting the first day apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment moved to Sunday. Both sides agree on a great deal: Christians from the beginning gathered on the first day, it is a wise and apostolic custom, the gathering should not be neglected, and Christ is our true rest. Hold your own view with conviction, keep the day gladly, and do not despise the brother who keeps it differently.

Was this the Lord’s Supper? Most likely yes, eaten within a shared meal (2:42, 46; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26). The New Testament does not fix how often the Supper should be observed; this passage suggests it was a reason for the weekly gathering, and many churches celebrate it weekly for that reason, while others hold it monthly or less often. And if Luke counts the day from sunset, as Jews did, the gathering may have been on Saturday evening; if from midnight, as Romans did, Sunday evening. Paul planned to leave on the next day, which fits either.

Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. The verb here is worth having, because it is not the ordinary word for preaching. It is dielegeto, from dialegomai: to discuss, to reason back and forth, the same word used of him in the synagogue and in the hall of Tyrannus. This was not only a monologue delivered at a congregation. There were questions. A long session, and his last chance with them. He was leaving in the morning and knew he might not be back, and so he kept going. Anyone who has sat up too late with somebody they will not see again understands exactly what is happening in that clause. It is not indiscipline. It is a man trying to get everything said.

There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. Why mention the lamps? Luke is not decorating. It is an eyewitness detail explaining what follows. Consider what many oil lamps do to a crowded upper room on a spring night: they burn the oxygen, they throw out heat, and they fill the air with smoke and fumes. Hot, smoky air, and a sleepy young man. It is the reason a young man was sitting in an open window at midnight, and the reason he could not keep his eyes open. Luke has told us the cause of the accident one verse before it happens, and he has done it so quietly that most readers take it for scene-setting.

So what does a faithful Lord’s Day look like? At its heart, what Troas shows: gathering with God’s people, hearing the word explained, sharing the Lord’s Supper, prayer and fellowship. Around that, rest from the ordinary grind of the week, time with family, works of mercy and necessity, visiting the sick and lonely, reading and conversation that feed the soul. Whatever your view of the Sabbath, avoid two errors: treating the day as just another day for shopping and chores, and turning it into a grim list of prohibitions. It is the day of resurrection. Let it feel like one.

In a sentence. On the first day of the week, when they gathered to break bread, Paul talked with them until midnight, since he planned to leave the next day, in an upstairs room lit by many lamps.

On a Tuesday. Make the Lord’s Day a delight. Gather with God’s people, break bread, hear the word. Think now about how you will spend next Sunday afternoon and evening, and plan something that will refresh your soul and someone else’s, a meal with a lonely member, a walk with your family, an hour with a good book.

For worship. On the first day of the week the stone was rolled away, and the Lord of glory walked out of the tomb. Ever since, his people have gathered on that day to break bread in his name, to remember his death and to celebrate his life. He is our Sabbath rest, the one in whom the weary find rest for their souls (Matthew 11:28–29), and every Lord’s Day is a foretaste of the eternal day when the whole church will be gathered at his table and the lamps will never need lighting, for the Lamb is its light.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, probably after the working day.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead.

And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window. Eutychus means fortunate, a common name for a slave, and given what is about to happen to him it is either the best or the worst joke in Acts. Luke keeps it either way. Perhaps a slave who had worked all day. He is a young man, Luke calls him the youth in verse 12, very possibly still a boy, and he is in the window because the room is hot and airless and full of lamp smoke, and because a boy sits where there is room, which at a crowded meeting is the ledge. He sat at the window for fresh air.

Sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And then Luke’s two stages, medically observed: he sank into a deep sleep, and then was overcome by sleep. He went under gradually and then completely. Anybody who has fought sleep in a warm room knows both stages, and knows that the second one is not a decision.

Told against nobody. Which is worth saying plainly, because this story is regularly told as a joke against the boy or against long sermons, and Luke tells it against nobody. There is no rebuke here. Paul does not scold him when he revives, and Luke does not moralise. A tired young man at midnight in a hot room fell asleep, and it is entirely understandable, and it nearly ended his life. It is a comfort to preachers whose hearers doze, and a gentle warning to long-winded ones. Even Paul put someone to sleep.

He fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. Not as though dead, not for dead. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14), who was in that room, says he was picked up dead, not just apparently dead. It is worth pausing on how the writer of this book handles that. He had every opportunity to soften it, to say the boy was stunned, or gravely hurt, and the softening would have made the story less exposed to challenge. He says the young man was dead, in a house full of witnesses, in a document addressed to a named reader who could have asked them.

Where it happened. And notice where it happened. Not at a healing meeting. Not while Paul was preaching about the resurrection to unbelievers. In the middle of an ordinary church gathering, the worst thing that can happen to a family happened, and the church was in the room when it did.

What if I struggle to stay awake or concentrate in church? Most Christians do sometimes, and God knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). Tiredness after a hard week is not a sin. But there are practical helps: get enough sleep on Saturday, sit where you can see and hear, follow the passage in your Bible, take notes, and pray before the service that God will open your ears. If you are a preacher, love your hearers by being clear and not needlessly long. And if you see someone nodding, be gentle. The Lord did not scold Eutychus; he gave him back his life.

In a sentence. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on, and overcome by sleep he fell from the third floor and was picked up dead.

On a Tuesday. Notice the young people at the edges of your church, the ones who sit in the windows. Who are they, and has anyone asked how they are? Find one this week and speak to them by name. And if you are carrying exhaustion into Sunday, ask God for grace to hear; he is patient with tired listeners.

For worship. God knows our weaknesses, even our sleepiness. He is gracious. The Lord who slept in the boat through a storm knows what it is to be tired; the Shepherd who carries the lambs in his arms does not despise weak sheep. He sees the youth at the window as surely as the apostle in the centre of the room, and when the worst falls on his people, he is already on the stairs.
verseByVerse.note: Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room would have made the air close.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.

But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms. The first thing he does is go down the stairs. The second is get on the ground. The third is pick the boy up and hold him. That posture is not an accident, and any Jew in the courtyard would have recognised it. Elijah stretched himself upon the widow’s dead son three times and cried to the LORD, and the child revived (1 Kings 17:21–22). Elisha lay upon the Shunammite’s dead boy, mouth to mouth and hands to hands, and the child’s flesh grew warm (2 Kings 4:34). Paul is doing what the prophets did, and Luke describes it in their language.

Said, Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him. He speaks to the crowd, not to the boy: the sentence is for the people standing round in the dark with a dead young man on the ground. And he says it in the present tense, as an assurance about what is now the case. Not that he was never dead, but that his life had returned. A resurrection, like Tabitha (9:40).

And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten. The Lord’s Supper, at last, after midnight. Now read that with the previous sentence still in your hand, because the ordinariness of it is astonishing. A young man has just been raised from the dead in the courtyard. And they go back upstairs and have the Lord’s Supper, and then Paul carries on talking until the sun comes up.

He conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. All night. Not boring after all. No meeting is called about the miracle. Nobody suggests that this changes the plan. The miracle does not become the subject of the rest of the night; the bread is broken and the conversation resumes, and Luke gives the raising of the dead one verse and the talking until daybreak much the same.

The extraordinary and the important. That proportion is the point, and it runs against every instinct we have about how such an evening ought to be reported. The extraordinary thing was not treated as the important thing. The church at Troas had one night with the apostle, and what they did with it, after the interruption, was eat together at the Lord’s Table and keep asking him questions until it was light.

Why does God raise some and not others? We do not know, and Scripture does not pretend to tell us. He raised Eutychus and Tabitha, and he let James be killed by the sword and Stephen be stoned. These raisings were signs, pointing to the resurrection of Jesus and to the final resurrection of all his people, not promises that every death will be reversed now. What Scripture does promise is better: that for those who are in Christ, death is not the end, and on the last day every believer will be raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:52). If you have buried someone you love who trusted Christ, their life is in them still, hidden with Christ in God.

In a sentence. Paul went down, threw himself on him and took him in his arms, telling them not to be alarmed, for he was alive, and then went back upstairs, broke bread and ate, and talked with them until daybreak before leaving.

On a Tuesday. In the middle of worship, death came, and Christ’s power answered. He is Lord of life. And notice the order of that night: the miracle, and then the bread and the word. Do not hunt for the extraordinary at the expense of the ordinary means of grace. The Table and the teaching are where Christ feeds you week by week.

For worship. He who called Lazarus out of the tomb raised Eutychus in a courtyard at Troas, and he will raise all his people on the last day. I am the resurrection and the life, he said; whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live (John 11:25). The Lord of life was himself laid in a tomb, so that death might lose its sting for everyone who is his. Every broken loaf at his Table proclaims his death until he comes, and his coming will empty every grave of his saints.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted.

And they took the youth away alive. They took him away, presumably home, to whoever had been waiting up, and Luke does not tell us anything about that scene, and it is the one most of us would want. Somebody had to be told what had happened and then told how it ended. Alive. They carried out of that house a living young man.

And were not a little comforted. Understatement: greatly comforted. Luke’s understatement is one of his settled habits, and it is worth noticing what it does. He could have written that they rejoiced greatly. Instead he uses a form that makes the reader supply the feeling, which is generally how the deepest relief is actually described by people who have been through it.

The same word. And the word he chooses for what they received is paraklēsis: comfort, encouragement, the thing that comes alongside and holds a person up. It is the same root as the word used twice in verses 1 and 2 of this chapter, of what Paul had been doing to the churches all the way through Macedonia. He had been going from town to town encouraging people. On this night, in this house, God did it, and Luke uses the same word for both. A Lord’s Day service that included teaching, the Supper, a death and a resurrection. The church went home with joy.

Not a rule about outcomes. One more thing, because the church has been carrying its own dead ever since. This is not a promise that the young man in your house will be given back; Luke has already recorded James executed in a single sentence with no rescue (12:2), and he expects you to hold both. What this night shows is not a rule about outcomes. It is what the apostle did when the worst had happened: he went down the stairs and got on the floor and put his arms round the young man.

How can I comfort someone whose loved one has died? Do what Paul did first: go down the stairs. Be there. You do not need the right words; your presence, your arms, your tears and your practical help say more than explanations. Do not offer quick answers or promise what God has not promised. Listen. Pray with them if they want it. Bring meals, remember the anniversaries, keep calling after the funeral when everyone else has stopped. And when the time is right, gently hold out the hope of the resurrection to those who are in Christ, for we do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

In a sentence. They took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church who is grieving, recently or for a long time. Go down the stairs to them this week: a visit, a call, a card. And remember that the comfort of the church is not an idea but a person, raised from the dead.

For worship. The resurrection is the comfort of the church. Every Lord’s Day remembers it. The God of all comfort sent his Son into the place of death, and on the third day brought him out alive, so that every believing household that carries its dead may carry them in hope. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Peter 1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.

But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. Luke is careful to tell us this was arranged in advance and was Paul’s own decision, and then he does not tell us the reason. It is one of the more tantalising silences in the book. Here are the facts. The ship had to round Cape Lectum, a long sail; the road across the neck of land was about twenty miles on foot. Paul had been awake all night. He sent his companions, including Luke, round by sea and walked it alone.

Why walk alone? We are not told, and the honest thing is to say so. It is often suggested that he wanted the day for solitude and prayer before the journey to Jerusalem, and that is entirely plausible for a man heading toward imprisonment who has just told a church he will not see them again. It is also possible he wanted to visit believers on the way, or simply could not face company after the night at Troas. Luke knew and did not write it down.

Hours alone, the harder way. What the verse does establish is that Paul deliberately arranged several hours by himself, at the cost of a twenty-mile walk on no sleep, at a point when time was short and he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem. That is worth registering about a man whose life we mostly see as relentless public activity. He was almost never alone; the letters are full of names, and this whole chapter is a crowd. And when he wanted some hours to himself he did not find them by cancelling anything. He found them by taking the harder route to the same place.

And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. He was there when they arrived. Whatever the walk was for, it did not delay the ship. Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor; Mitylene was on the island of Lesbos. And then the names begin: Assos, Mitylene, and in the next verse Chios, Samos, Miletus. Luke is writing down the ports of call in order, day by day, which is what a man does when he is keeping a log. This is not a summary written years later from vague memory. Somebody on that ship was making notes.

How do I find time alone with God in a busy life? Paul’s answer here was to take the harder road: he walked twenty miles rather than lose the hours. Most of us need something less dramatic but just as deliberate. Choose a regular time, often early before the house wakes, and guard it. Use the walk to the station, the drive, the lunch break, the evening walk round the block. Take a Bible and a simple plan: read a passage, think about it, pray it back to God. Our Lord himself rose very early and went out to a desolate place to pray (Mark 1:35). If he needed it, so do you.

In a sentence. The others went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, planning to take Paul aboard there, since he had arranged to walk, and when he met them at Assos they took him aboard and went to Mitylene.

On a Tuesday. Even busy servants of God need time alone with him. Find yours. Look at tomorrow and find one stretch, fifteen minutes or a walk, that you can give to God alone. Do not wait for a quiet week; take the harder road if you must.

For worship. The Son of God, who had all of heaven’s company, withdrew to lonely places to pray, and his Father was there. He knows the weight of the road to Jerusalem; he walked it himself, with his face set toward the cross. And whoever goes apart to meet with God never walks alone, for the one who said, I am with you always, walks every mile of the road with his people.
verseByVerse.note: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

verseByVerse.quote: And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.

And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. Three days, three anchorages, each recorded. Coastal ships in that world often sailed by daylight and put in at night, and Luke gives us the itinerary the way a passenger keeping a diary would. Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus.

For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia. Now that is a striking sentence when you know what Ephesus was to him. Nearly three years of his life. The church he had worked hardest for and the one whose elders he is about to weep over. His ship goes past and does not turn in. And the reason Luke gives is not danger; nobody suggests he was afraid of the silversmiths. It is that he could not afford the time. If he went to Ephesus, he would be delayed by many friends. He knew perfectly well what would happen if he set foot in that city: the whole congregation would come, and there would be meals and questions and people needing to be seen, and a day would become a fortnight. Love has a way of detaining people, and he had a deadline.

A deliberate arrangement. So he sends thirty miles up the coast for the elders instead, and meets them in a port where nobody can keep him. It is a deliberate arrangement by a man who knew that if he went home he would not get away.

For he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover. Two reasons stand behind the hurry, and both are worth having. He was carrying the collection, and Pentecost was one of the three pilgrim feasts, so the city would be full of Jews from every province: the largest possible gathering to receive a gift from Gentile churches to Jewish believers, which was much of the point of the collection. Perhaps fitting: the Gentile firstfruits bringing their offering to Jerusalem at the feast of firstfruits (Romans 15:16). And there is the plain fact that Pentecost was the day the Spirit fell.

If possible. Note also these words. He is doing everything he can and he does not claim to know whether it will come off. That is a small and healthy thing to see in a man who is elsewhere so certain about his direction: absolute clarity about the destination, and no pretence of certainty about the timetable.

Is this a proof that Paul still kept the Jewish festivals? In part, yes, but read it carefully. It does show that Paul, himself a Jewish believer, still moved within the rhythms of the Jewish calendar and valued the feast. Yet his haste was very likely as much missional as ceremonial: Pentecost packed Jerusalem with pilgrims from the dispersion, a prime moment to bear witness, as at the first Pentecost, and Paul was carrying the relief collection from the Gentile churches, which he wanted to deliver to the saints (24:17; Romans 15:25–26). So the verse shows him honouring the festival and the Jerusalem gathering, not keeping it as a binding law required for righteousness. Luke does not spell out his full motive, so we should not over-press it either way.

How does that square with dying to the law? How does it square with Romans 7, where Paul says we have died to the law (7:4–6)? It squares perfectly, once we see what died to the law means. Paul is not saying the believer is now lawless, or that God’s righteous will has been abolished; in the very same chapter he calls the law holy and righteous and good (7:12). He means we have died to the law as a condemning covenant and master, the regime that could only accuse and curse us, so that we now belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit by the Spirit, not by the old written code. A believing Jew keeping Pentecost, then, is no contradiction at all. He is not under the law as a way of being justified, for his justification is in Christ alone, so he is free to keep the feast, not to earn standing, but as heritage, devotion and a bridge to his people. The fuller framework, the threefold division of the law and the careful line between keeping a custom freely and keeping it as a requirement, is laid out at 18:18 (Paul’s vow). The test there governs here too: a practice done to be saved or accepted, or imposed on others as necessary, denies grace and must go; the same practice done freely, in love, binding no one, is Christian liberty. Paul hurried to Pentecost as a free man in Christ, not as a slave under law, and that is the whole difference.

How do I say no to people I love without being unloving? By remembering that love has a direction, not only a warmth. Paul loved the Ephesians as much as any church, and he still sailed past, because the work God had given him lay in Jerusalem. Saying no to a good thing in order to do the thing God has given you is not coldness; it is faithfulness. Explain honestly, as Paul did by sending for the elders. Make what time you can, in a way that does not derail the calling. And trust God with the people you cannot stay with. They are his before they are yours.

In a sentence. Sailing on, they passed Chios, reached Samos, and the next day Miletus, for Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus to avoid spending time in Asia, hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost if possible.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes love means saying no to good things in order to do the best thing. Look at the commitments pulling at you this month and ask which ones are your Ephesus: good, loved, and not where God is sending you now. Then make your plans for the best thing, and add, if possible.

For worship. The Lord Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him aside, not the love of his friends nor the warnings of his enemies, because he was going there to die for us. His servant hastening to the same city with a gift for the poor is a faint picture of the Saviour hastening to the cross with the gift of himself. And the Spirit poured out at Pentecost was the firstfruits of a harvest from every nation, the harvest Christ bought with his blood.
verseByVerse.note: Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Miletus Paul calls the Ephesian elders. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord humbly, with tears and trials, holding back nothing helpful, teaching publicly and house to house, calling Jews and Greeks to repent and trust the Lord Jesus. Now the Spirit compels him to Jerusalem, and the Spirit warns him in every city of prison and hardship, but his life matters to him only so that he may finish the race and the task Jesus gave him, to testify to the gospel of God’s grace. They will not see him again, and he is clear of everyone’s blood, for he has declared the whole purpose of God. They must keep watch over themselves and the flock the Spirit has entrusted to them, shepherding God’s church, bought with his own blood. Savage wolves will come, and some of their own number will distort the truth to win followers, so they must stay alert, remembering his three years of tearful warning. He commits them to God and to the word of his grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance. He has wanted nobody’s money, but worked with his own hands to support himself and others, to show that the weak must be helped, remembering Jesus’ words that giving is more blessed than receiving. Then he kneels and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him and kiss him, grieving most that they will not see him again, and they go with him to the ship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Elder as Shepherd and Overseer

Paul's address to the Ephesian 'elders' (v. 17) whom he calls 'overseers' (episkopous, v. 28) and instructs to 'shepherd' (poimainein) the flock establishes the threefold nature of the pastoral office: elder (dignity of character), overseer (responsibility of governance), shepherd (work of care). The Reformed tradition has consistently seen in this passage the defining description of the ordained ministry: those who guard, feed, and care for the people whom the Holy Spirit has placed under their oversight.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'fierce wolves' would come from outside and that 'men speaking twisted things' would arise from within the community itself. Both dangers materialized: the letter to Ephesus in Revelation (2:1–7) shows a community that had resisted external pressure but had lost its first love. Now: The threats Paul named are the threats every congregation faces in every generation: external persecution and internal doctrinal corruption. The antidote is the same: the word of God's grace, committed to Spirit-filled leadership whose lives embody what they preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him.

Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. Work out what that message cost, because Luke does not. Miletus is about thirty miles from Ephesus. A messenger has to be found and sent; he travels a day or more; the elders have to be gathered from wherever they are, drop whatever they are doing, and travel back. It would take a few days for them to come. So Paul’s ship sat at Miletus for the best part of several days waiting for them, which is a considerable sacrifice from a man who has just refused to enter Ephesus because he had no time. He would not spare a fortnight for the city. He spent days on the elders.

Priority, not inconsistency. That is not inconsistency; it is priority. The congregation would have detained him indefinitely, and he could not have said the things he is about to say to a crowded room. What he needed was the leadership, alone, for one afternoon, because everything he is about to tell them is about what happens after he is gone, and it is for the men who will have to do it.

The elders of the church. Elders (presbyterous): plural, a group of leaders in one church (14:23). There were by now believers all over that city and probably several house congregations, and Luke calls them the church in the singular and their leaders elders in the plural. The pattern of a team of elders over one city church is set out at 14:23.

The only speech to Christians. What follows is the only speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians. Every other address of his in this book is evangelistic or a legal defence: synagogues, philosophers, governors, mobs. This one is to the church, and it is the closest thing we have in Acts to Paul talking the way he talks in his letters, recorded by a man who was sitting there. What follows is Paul’s charge to them, a model for every pastor.

Three words for one group. One more thing about the summons itself. He sent for the elders, and then, in verse 28, he tells those same men that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, and instructs them to shepherd the flock. Three words for one group of men in one afternoon. So whatever distinctions later centuries drew between elder, bishop and pastor, Paul calls the same men by all three names inside eleven verses, and Luke records it without a flicker of awkwardness.

Does this settle how a church should be governed? It settles less than some think and more than others admit. Christians differ here: episcopal churches hold that bishops as a distinct order developed rightly from the apostles’ own oversight; Presbyterians see the elders of local churches joined in wider courts; Congregationalists and most Baptists see each local church, under its elders, as self-governing. What this passage plainly shows is that in Ephesus a plurality of elders shepherded one church, and that elder, overseer and shepherd named the same men. Whatever your church’s structure, these are the marks to look for: more than one leader, men qualified by character (1 Timothy 3:1–7), feeding and guarding the flock, and accountable to Christ.

In a sentence. From Miletus Paul sent for the elders of the church in Ephesus.
