On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders. They carry a heavy charge. Pray for each by name this week, for his soul, his family, his preaching and his care. And if you are an elder, notice what Paul thought worth days of delay: time with the leaders alone. Make room for it.

For worship. Christ the Chief Shepherd does not leave his flock without shepherds. He gives elders to his churches as gifts from the ascended Lord, and he takes the trouble to charge them himself through his apostle. He is never too hurried for his church. He spent his whole life and death on her, and he waits for her still, at the harbour of glory, until every one of his sheep has come home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews;

You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia. He opens by putting himself on trial and calling them as witnesses. Paul appeals to his life, not just his words. You yourselves know: he will use that kind of appeal several times in this short speech (vv. 18, 34). He is not telling them what his ministry was like. He is asking them to confirm it, and they were there for all three years, and some of them had watched him at the bench and in the lecture hall and in their own houses. Ministry is first a life lived openly before people (1 Thessalonians 2:10; 2 Corinthians 1:12). Character before charisma.

The opposite of a testimonial. A man can only speak like this if the record will bear it. It is the opposite of a testimonial, which is what you produce when the people who actually know you are not in the room.

Serving the Lord with all humility. Four things in a life’s work, and not one of them is what a man would choose for himself. Serving (douleuōn) is serving as a slave, the word for a slave’s work, not a leader’s. Paul begins the summary of his apostolic career by describing himself as somebody else’s property. With all humility: humility, the first mark. In the Greek world lowliness was not generally a virtue; it was the disposition of the servile, and Greek moralists commonly counted it a fault. Christianity took a quality the world despised and made it the first thing an apostle says about his ministry.

And with tears. Paul wept (v. 31; 2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18). Not a hard, professional minister, but a man who felt deeply. He will mention tears again before he finishes (v. 31), and the elders will shed their own (v. 37). This is a man who wept over people, repeatedly, over years, and who thought it worth recording as one of the defining features of his work.

How he would summarise it. That is worth weighing against how we would summarise a successful ministry. Paul had planted churches across a continent, written letters that would outlast the empire, raised the dead and been befriended by some of the rulers of Asia. Asked to characterise the three years, he says: I was a servant, I was lowly, and I wept a great deal.

And with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews. Suffering was part of it. The last of these is the only one that came from outside, and he names it without heat: no adjectives, no complaint, just the fact that there had been plots and they had cost him something. The man who wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Romans 9:3) is describing what some of those same people had done to him, and there is not a word of bitterness in it.

What does humility look like in a church leader, or in me? Not thinking little of yourself so much as thinking of yourself less. It looks like doing jobs no one sees, admitting mistakes quickly, listening more than speaking, being glad when others are praised, accepting correction, and refusing titles and privileges that set you above the flock. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and said, I have given you an example (John 13:15). Humility is not a technique for leadership; it is what grows in someone who has seen the cross and knows what he has been forgiven. Ask God for it, and ask the people closest to you where you most lack it.

In a sentence. When they arrived, Paul reminded them how he had lived among them from the first day he came to Asia, serving the Lord humbly, with tears and through the trials caused by Jewish plots.

On a Tuesday. Pastors: serve humbly, with tears, through trials. Everyone: pray for them. And ask the hard question of yourself: could the people who know you best stand up and confirm the way you have lived among them? If not, the remedy is not a better testimonial but a changed life, beginning today.

For worship. The Lord of glory took the form of a servant. He served with all humility, washing feet and touching lepers; he served with tears, weeping over Jerusalem and at the tomb of his friend; he served through trials, plotted against by his own people, until the plotting ended in a cross. Paul’s ministry was only an echo of his. And because the Servant became obedient to the point of death, God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name.

verseByVerse.quote: how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

How I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable. The verb (hypesteilamēn) is a vivid one: to hold back, to draw back, as a sail is lowered or furled, to shrink away from something out of fear. It is what a man does when he sees where a conversation is going and decides not to go there. And Paul chooses the negative form deliberately, both here and again at verse 27. He does not say I told you everything easily. He says I did not shrink, which admits, in passing, that there was something to shrink from. He felt the pull. He knew which subjects would cost him a hearing, or a friendship, or a household’s welcome, and he is telling these men that he went ahead anyway. Paul did not hold back anything they needed, even unpopular truths. A pastor must not keep back the hard parts.

The honest shape of it. That is a good deal more useful than a claim to have found it easy. Every person who has ever had to say a hard thing to somebody they love knows the exact moment described by that verb.

And teaching you in public and from house to house. Public preaching, and private, personal ministry in homes. Both matter, and the second is the expensive one. Public teaching is efficient: one preparation, many hearers, and you can be tired afterwards without anybody noticing. House to house means the same truth delivered again and again to small groups of people in their own rooms, where they can interrupt, and where you have to know their names. Paul taught daily in the lecture hall for two years, and he also went round the houses. Whatever else the Ephesian ministry was, it was not conducted only from a platform.

Testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Here is the content of three years, compressed into two nouns, and they are not interchangeable. The gospel in two words: repentance and faith. Turning from sin to God, and trusting Christ. They go together (Mark 1:15; Hebrews 6:1). Repentance toward God: a turning round, and note the direction, toward God, not merely toward better behaviour. Repentance in Scripture is not primarily regret about actions but a change of allegiance, and it is aimed at a person. Faith in our Lord Jesus Christ: the trusting, and it too is aimed at a person rather than merely a doctrine.

Neither survives alone. The two belong together and neither survives alone. Repentance without faith is remorse, which has destroyed people. Faith without repentance is mere agreement, which has comforted a great many people who never changed direction. Paul preached both to everybody, both to Jews and to Greeks, the religious and the pagan, the man who thought he was already right with God and the man who had never considered the question. The same message to everyone. Neither group needed less than the other.

Which comes first, repentance or faith? They are two sides of one turning, and in real life they arrive together. You cannot truly turn from sin to God without trusting his mercy in Christ, and you cannot truly trust Christ as Saviour while clinging to the sin he came to save you from. Sometimes Scripture names one first (Mark 1:15), sometimes the other (Acts 11:21). Do not wait to feel sorry enough before you trust Christ, and do not imagine you can trust him while refusing to turn. Both are gifts of grace, and both go on for the whole Christian life: we keep repenting and keep believing until we see him.

In a sentence. Paul reminded them that he had not held back from telling them anything helpful, teaching them publicly and from house to house, and testifying to Jews and Greeks about repentance towards God and faith in the Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Is there a hard truth you have been shrinking from saying to someone you love, or hearing from God yourself? Name it, pray, and do not furl the sail. And if you have stopped repenting, or stopped believing, as a daily habit, start again today: turn to God from one specific sin, and trust Christ afresh for his mercy.

For worship. Repentance towards God and faith in Christ: the whole Christian life in two words. And both are the gifts of a gracious God. He grants repentance that leads to life (11:18), and he gives faith as the gift that cannot boast (Ephesians 2:8). The Saviour who calls us to turn and trust is the Saviour who turned the wrath of God away from us by his cross, and who is himself the faithful one we trust. Every turning of a sinner to God is a cause of joy before the angels in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.

And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit. Constrained (dedemenos) means bound: under compulsion. Bound by the Spirit before being bound by chains (21:33). Compelled.

Not knowing what will happen to me there. He walks by faith, not sight. Notice what he is not told. He has the direction and the general shape of the outcome, and no details at all. That is almost always the arrangement in Scripture, and it is worth registering, because we tend to imagine that guidance means being shown the plan. Abraham was told to go to a land that God would show him, which is not the same as being shown it.

Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. Through prophets (21:4, 11). He goes knowing it will cost him. Read those two clauses together, because the combination is unusual and it settles a question that troubles readers a chapter later. He is constrained by the Spirit to go. And the same Spirit has been telling him, in city after city, what is waiting at the other end. So the Spirit is not sparing him the information. He is being sent, and he is being told what it will cost, and both of those are the work of the same Person.

Was Paul disobeying the Spirit by going on? The question arrives shortly. In the next chapter, disciples at Tyre tell Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem (21:4), and Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and prophesies his arrest, and everyone present begs him not to go (21:11–12). This verse is the answer, and it is the reason Luke put it here. What the Spirit revealed, consistently and in every city, was the suffering. What the disciples added was the conclusion, therefore do not go, and that was love talking. They had the message right and drew from it the inference any of us would draw about somebody we loved. Agabus, notably, does not tell him not to go; he says what will happen, and it is the bystanders who beg.

A warning is not always an instruction. A true word from God about coming trouble is not automatically an instruction to avoid it. That distinction is worth keeping, because it is the difference between godly counsel and a warning wrongly applied, and the people who got it wrong at Tyre were sincere, Spirit-filled Christians who cared about him.

Not tricked into it. And there is comfort in the arrangement itself. Paul walked toward Jerusalem knowing there was a cell at the end of the road, and he knew because God had told him repeatedly. He was not tricked into it. Whatever else obedience cost him, it did not cost him the truth about what he was walking into.

If God is leading me, should I expect things to go smoothly? No. Following the Spirit led Paul into chains, led the apostles into prison, and led our Lord to the cross. Hardship is not proof that you have missed God’s will, and ease is not proof that you are in it. Jesus told his disciples that in the world they would have tribulation, and to take heart, because he has overcome the world (John 16:33). So do not measure guidance by comfort. Measure it by Scripture, by wisdom, and by whether you are walking in faith and love. Sometimes the right road runs straight through the hard place, and the Lord walks it with you.

In a sentence. Paul said he was going to Jerusalem compelled by the Spirit, not knowing what would happen there, except that in every city the Holy Spirit warned him that prison and hardships awaited him.

On a Tuesday. Following the Spirit does not mean avoiding hardship. It may mean walking into it. Is there an obedience you have been avoiding because you can see what it will cost? Ask God for courage, and take the next step. And when you counsel a friend facing a costly obedience, be careful not to turn your love for them into a prophecy against it.

For worship. The Spirit who bound Paul to Jerusalem had first led the Son of God there, knowing everything that awaited him: the betrayal, the scourging, the cross. Jesus was not tricked into his suffering; he went willingly, for the joy set before him. Because he walked the road to Jerusalem with his eyes open, every one of his people can walk their own road without fear, held by the Spirit who binds them not to chains but to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.

But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course. This is the sentence the whole speech turns on, and it should not be read as bravado. Paul’s life was not his own (Philippians 1:21; 2 Corinthians 5:15). He is not saying his life is worthless, or that he is indifferent to it; he says it is not precious to himself: he has stopped treating his own survival as the thing to be protected. Finishing his task mattered more than his safety. And notice that it is a comparison, not a denial: if only I may finish. There is something he values more, and the whole force of the sentence is in the ranking.

My course. The word is dromon, a race, a runner’s track, the distance a man is set to cover: the same word used of John the Baptist finishing his course at 13:25. Here Paul uses it of himself, and he will use the picture once more, at the very end, from a Roman prison with his execution close: I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). So the same image appears early in Acts, applied to somebody else, and at the end of Paul’s life, applied to himself, and here in the middle where the outcome is still open. A course is a fixed distance. The question is never how far you have got compared with anybody else; it is whether the ground assigned to you has been covered.

And the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus. Received: it was handed to him. His ministry was given, not chosen (9:15; Galatians 1:1). He did not devise it, apply for it, or grow into it; it was given on a road to Damascus by a voice, to a man who had been travelling in the opposite direction. That is why he can hold his life so lightly. A man who chose his own work has to defend it, and himself with it. A man who was handed his work has only to finish it, and the outcome belongs to the one who gave it.

To testify to the gospel of the grace of God. And there is the whole of it, in a single phrase. The gospel is the good news of God’s grace: undeserved favour. Paul’s whole message in four words: the gospel of grace. Not to build a movement, not to win arguments, not even to plant churches, though he did all three. To bear witness to one thing: that God gives what nobody has earned.

Your own version of the sentence. It is worth asking what your own version of that sentence would be: what it is you would have to finish for the rest to be worth spending. Most of us have never written it down, which is why so much of our lives is spent protecting things we would not, on reflection, have chosen to protect.

Does this mean I should not care about my health or safety? No. Your life is a gift from God and your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and the sixth commandment requires us to preserve our own life as well as others’ (Westminster Larger Catechism 135). Paul took precautions, as we saw at verse 3. What he refused was to make safety his highest value. The question is one of ranking: when staying safe and staying faithful collide, faithfulness wins. Most of us will never face that choice in its starkest form. But we face smaller versions daily, comfort against obedience, and this verse tells us which to choose.

What is my course, if I am not an apostle? Every believer has one: the life, callings and relationships God has assigned you, and the good works he prepared beforehand for you to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). For most of us that means faithfulness in ordinary things: loving a husband or wife, raising children in the Lord, working honestly, serving in a local church, bearing witness to neighbours, enduring illness or loss with faith. It is not measured against anyone else’s race. You finish your course by keeping the faith in the place God put you, until he calls you home.

In a sentence. Paul said he did not consider his life worth anything to himself, if only he could finish his race and the task the Lord Jesus gave him, of testifying to the good news of God’s grace.

On a Tuesday. Write down, in one sentence, what you would most want to have finished when your life ends. Then look at this week and ask whether it is serving that sentence. And let the gospel of grace be the centre of it, for nothing else is worth spending a life on.

For worship. The gospel of the grace of God: that God gives what nobody has earned. The Son of God did not count his life precious to himself, but laid it down for us, finishing the work the Father gave him to do, and crying on the cross, It is finished. His race was run perfectly, and the crown he won he shares with all who love his appearing. Because he finished his course, every one of his people will finish theirs, for he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion.

parallels.desc: I have finished the race

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,

And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. A sad farewell. That is the sentence the elders will still be weeping over at the end of the chapter (v. 38), and Luke tells us so explicitly: it was this word, more than anything else, that broke them.

Did it turn out to be true? It should be said honestly that we do not know. Paul expected to go from Jerusalem to Rome and then on to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28), and the letters written after his first Roman imprisonment appear to have him back in this part of the world: he tells Timothy he had urged him to remain at Ephesus while he went into Macedonia (1 Timothy 1:3), which is difficult to fit anywhere except a later journey. Paul may later have revisited the area after his first Roman imprisonment, but he did not expect to. If that is right, then Paul’s expectation here was not fulfilled in the way he thought, and there is no reason to be uncomfortable about saying so: he says I know, and what he knew was that imprisonment awaited him (v. 23), and he drew the natural conclusion. An apostle writing Scripture is protected from error in what he teaches. He is not thereby given a timetable of his own future, and Luke faithfully records what Paul expected. This passage is one of the places where the difference shows.

Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all. This is legal language, and it is Ezekiel’s. The watchman’s words again (18:6; Ezekiel 33:1–9). The watchman who sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet has delivered his soul; the one who stays silent has the blood of the fallen required at his hand. Paul used the same formula against the synagogue at Corinth, and the responsibility it defines, the trumpet and not the walls, is set out at 18:6. Paul had warned everyone. If they perished, their blood was not on his hands. A solemn picture of a pastor’s accountability.

A handover. What is different here is who he is saying it to. At Corinth he said it to people who had rejected him. Here he says it to the men who have believed him, and it is his discharge: I have done my part; from this afternoon it is yours. And notice this day. He is fixing a date on it, the way you do with a legal handover. Everything up to this afternoon was on my account. Everything after it is on yours.

Proclaiming the kingdom. Notice that Paul sums up his whole three-year Ephesian ministry, to a Gentile city, in this church age, as proclaiming the kingdom. Acts is framed front to back by it: the risen Jesus spent forty days speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3); Philip preached the kingdom to Samaritans (8:12); Paul reasoned and persuaded about the kingdom at Ephesus (19:8); and the book closes with him in Rome proclaiming the kingdom of God (28:31). The church-age mission is summarised, again and again, as kingdom preaching. (For what the kingdom of God means and its already and not yet, see on 8:12, 14:22, Colossians 1:13.)

Where Christians differ on the kingdom. This touches a real difference among Bible-loving Christians. Many of our dispensational brothers hesitate to link the kingdom with the church at all, reserving it, especially the Davidic kingdom of the Old Testament promises, for a future, literal reign of Christ over restored national Israel in the millennium; on the classic scheme the kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected and postponed, and the present age is a kind of parenthesis. Their concern is worthy and should be honoured: they want God’s promises to Israel taken seriously and literally, not quietly absorbed into the church, and many read Romans 11 as keeping a future for ethnic Israel. And the view has developed: progressive dispensationalists (Darrell Bock, Craig Blaising) now grant that the kingdom was genuinely inaugurated at Christ’s exaltation (Acts 2:30–36), already as well as not yet, while still holding a future literal fulfilment for Israel.

The kingdom now. From the Reformed side, the simplest point is that Scripture’s own language, nowhere more than in Acts, treats the kingdom as a present reality now preached and entered, not held wholly in reserve. Believers have already been transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13) and made a kingdom, priests to his God (Revelation 1:6); the kingdom of God has come upon you, said Jesus (Matthew 12:28). The church is not simply identical with the kingdom, for God’s reign is wider, but it is the kingdom’s present people and outpost: those over whom King Jesus already reigns, awaiting the day it is consummated over all the earth. So you need not be shy of the word: if you belong to Christ, you already live in the kingdom, under the reign of the King, even as you pray your kingdom come for its full arrival. Reformed and dispensational believers keep weighing Israel and the millennium differently; but that the King reigns now, and that his kingdom was Paul’s message to the church, the text makes plain.

Am I responsible for the blood of people I never warned? The watchman’s words are first for those with a public charge, like Paul and these elders, and they are solemn. But every Christian has neighbours who will one day face God, and love will not leave them unwarned. The point is not to load you with guilt for everyone you have not evangelised; Christ’s blood covers that failure too, for those who confess it. The point is to make you faithful from today. Pray for the people around you, live so that your faith is visible, and when the door opens, speak of Christ plainly and kindly. Blow the trumpet you have been given. The walls belong to God.

In a sentence. Paul said he knew none of them would see him again, and so he declared that he was innocent of the blood of everyone.

On a Tuesday. Have you warned those around you? Do not let their blood be on your hands. Think of one person you love who does not know Christ, and pray this week for an opportunity to speak. And if you lead others in any way, ask whether you could say to them, as Paul did, that you have done your part.

For worship. The King whose kingdom Paul proclaimed reigns now at the right hand of God, and his kingdom has no end. He shed his own blood so that the blood of sinners need not be on their own heads; he took the guilt of his people and gave them his righteousness. Every herald of his kingdom is only a voice; the King himself is the gospel. One day the kingdom of the world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever (Revelation 11:15).

parallels.desc: the watchman

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.

For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. There is the ground of the innocence he has just claimed, and it rests entirely on one word. The whole. Not the true counsel of God, though it was. Not the important parts, not the parts he was good at, not the parts that went down well in a city like Ephesus. All of it. The whole counsel (pasan tēn boulēn) is God’s whole purpose, plan, will. Not selected favourite topics, not only the comfortable parts, but everything God has revealed: sin and grace, judgment and mercy, election and evangelism, doctrine and duty.

The shrinking verb again. This is the second time in seven verses that he has used that shrinking verb (v. 20), which tells you he knew exactly where the pressure lies. Nobody omits doctrine by deciding to be unfaithful. It happens by a series of small, reasonable decisions: this congregation is not ready for that; this is not the moment; I will come back to it; until a preacher has a working repertoire that leaves out whatever is most likely to cost him.

What tends to go missing. It is worth being concrete about what tends to go missing, in any generation. In a comfortable one it is judgment, hell, and the wrath of God. In an anxious one it is assurance, election, and the sheer freeness of grace. In a moralistic church it is justification; in a lax one it is holiness. Every era edits, and every era edits in the direction of what its own people find congenial, which means the omission is almost never visible from inside. The test Paul implies is not only whether your preaching is true but whether it is whole. A ministry can say nothing false for thirty years and still leave a congregation with a God who is smaller than the one in Scripture. This is why preaching through whole books of the Bible matters. A pastor who preaches only what people want to hear has blood on his hands.

A clean leaving. And notice the pastoral logic, which is the point of putting this verse where it is. Paul is not boasting about thoroughness. He is explaining why he can walk away from these people with a clear conscience. He can leave because he did not hold anything back, and a man who has been editing cannot leave cleanly, because he knows what he never said.

Counsel. Counsel here means God’s own purpose and plan, the determination behind everything he does. So what Paul declared was not a syllabus of topics. It was the whole of what God is doing, from before the foundation of the world to the day he judges it, and he gave three years to it in one city and then said he had finished.

How can I make sure I am getting the whole counsel of God? Read the whole Bible, not just your favourite parts; a plan that takes you through every book over a year or two is a great help. Sit under preaching that works through books of the Bible, so that the text sets the agenda rather than the preacher’s preferences. Notice the subjects you instinctively avoid, the passages on judgment, or suffering, or giving, or sexual holiness, or election, and go and read them. Use a good confession or catechism, which summarises the whole of Scripture’s teaching. And let every part lead you back to the centre: Christ crucified and risen.

In a sentence. For he had not held back from declaring to them the whole purpose of God.

On a Tuesday. Want the whole counsel of God, not just the parts you like. Choose one book of the Bible you have never read through, and start it this week. And if you teach, children, a class, a home group, ask what you have been quietly leaving out.

For worship. The counsel of the LORD stands for ever, the plans of his heart to all generations (Psalm 33:11). Before the foundation of the world he purposed to save a people in Christ, and in the fullness of time he sent his Son to accomplish it, and at the end he will sum up all things in him. Every doctrine of Scripture is a facet of that one purpose, and every facet shines with his glory. The whole counsel of God is not a burden to be endured but a treasure to be explored, and it will take eternity to see it all.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;

Pay careful attention to yourselves. Yourselves first. That order is not politeness and it is not accidental. Paul puts the elders’ own souls in front of the congregation’s, and every word that follows depends on it. A pastor who neglects his own soul cannot care for others (1 Timothy 4:16). The reason is plain enough once said. A man who neglects his own walk with God does not stop working; he goes on preaching, visiting and organising, and the machinery runs for years on nothing. And what he is then feeding people is his own emptiness, competently disguised. Paul has just spent three years in this city and he knows exactly how possible that is.

And to all the flock. All of it. Not just favourites: not the promising members, not the ones who contribute, not the ones who are easy to be with.

In which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Notice who did the appointing. Not Paul, though he had appointed elders in other churches (14:23), and not the congregation alone. He tells these men that the Holy Spirit put them there. Church leadership is the Spirit’s gift. That is at once the most steadying and the most frightening thing that could be said to them. Steadying, because a man who has been placed by the Spirit does not have to keep earning the position or wonder whether he is wanted. Frightening, because he cannot lay it down lightly either, and the accounting will be with the one who appointed him.

Elders and overseers. Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers: two names for one office. Overseers (episkopous) gives us bishops. In the New Testament, elder, overseer and shepherd describe the same leaders (Titus 1:5–7; 1 Peter 5:1–2): elders for their maturity, overseers for their watching over, shepherds for their care.

To care for the church of God. Care for (poimainein) means to shepherd: feed, lead, protect.

Which he obtained with his own blood. Everything about the responsibility is measured by this last clause, and it is the reason Paul reaches for it here rather than anywhere else in the speech. Before he tells them what to do, he tells them what the flock is worth. The word for obtained is a purchase word: acquired, bought for oneself. The church belongs to God, bought with a price. And the price is named.

How can God bleed? Pause on those astonishing words. God is spirit and has no blood, so how can God bleed? Only because the One who shed it, Jesus, is God. It is one of Scripture’s most powerful affirmations of Christ’s deity: the blood of the cross can be called God’s own blood because the man who hung there is the eternal Son in our flesh (so too they crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:8). Theologians call this the communication of attributes: what is true of either nature may be said of the one person. Two things shine: the deity of your Saviour, for the cross measures how high the One who died for you truly is; and the worth of the church, a flock so precious that God bought it with his own blood. Some manuscripts read the church of the Lord, and some translate with the blood of his own, meaning his own Son; but the plain, well-attested reading stands, and it expresses what the church has always confessed: the one who died is God the Son. Pastors care for people Christ died for. That is why they matter so much.

Does this mean Christ died only for the church? The verse says Christ purchased the church, which fits the Reformed teaching that he died to secure the salvation of his people (John 10:11; Ephesians 5:25). It does not by itself say only, but it shows that Christ’s death had a definite object: his church. He did not die to make salvation merely possible for everyone and certain for no one. He died to buy a people, and he will have every one of them.

What overseers should oversee. Made you overseers: and the church has always struggled to find the line of what overseers should actually oversee. The words set the scope. The same men are elders (v. 17, their maturity), overseers (episkopoi, their watching over), and shepherds of the flock (v. 28). The shepherd picture says what the oversight is: pastoral and spiritual, to feed the flock with sound teaching, guard it from wolves and error (vv. 29–30), lead it, and care for souls (Hebrews 13:17). It is the care of souls by the Word, not the managing of people’s private lives. (On elders’ mandate, qualifications and authority, see on 14:23.)

Two ditches. Now the two ditches. Overreach: Peter forbids it. Elders are not to domineer over those in their charge, but to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3); it shall not be so among you, said Jesus of those who lord it over others (Matthew 20:25–26). An elder’s authority is ministerial, not legislative: he applies God’s Word; he does not make new laws. He is not lord of the conscience, for God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2), and he may not bind believers with man-made rules where Scripture is silent (the Colossian error, do not handle, do not taste, do not touch, Colossians 2:20–23); to police what God has left to Christian liberty (Romans 14) is to meddle. Negligence is the opposite ditch and just as grave: Ezekiel’s woe falls on shepherds who fed themselves and did not strengthen the weak or seek the straying (Ezekiel 34). An elder who will not teach hard truth, stay alert to the wolves (vv. 29–31), or address serious, unrepentant sin (1 Corinthians 5) has abandoned his post, and abdication dressed as tolerance is no virtue.

Where is the line? The Word of God. Elders are firm where God is firm: on the gospel, sound doctrine, clear moral commands, the church’s worship and order, grave unrepentant sin. They are free where God leaves free, protecting liberty in disputable matters rather than policing it (Romans 14:1–4). Two reminders keep the balance. The flock is not theirs but God’s: they are under-shepherds of the Chief Shepherd, accountable to him (1 Peter 5:2–4), not owners. And Paul’s first word is pay careful attention to yourselves: the elder who watches his own soul shepherds with the right blend of courage and gentleness. The aim throughout is the flock’s good, served gladly, never for power, money or ego (1 Peter 5:2–3). And abuse of that trust, spiritual, emotional or any other kind, is never to be tolerated or covered: it is the wolf in the shepherd’s coat, and the flock must be protected from it.

I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock. False teachers from outside. Jesus warned of false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). Paul expects the attack as soon as the apostle is gone.

What should I do if I think my church leaders are overstepping, or neglecting the flock? Pray first, and examine your own heart; it is easy to mistake a leader’s faithful firmness for overreach, or his patience for neglect. Then go to him privately and humbly, as Matthew 18:15 directs, with specifics rather than complaints. Leaders are to be respected and obeyed in the Lord (Hebrews 13:17), but they are not above Scripture, and an accusation against an elder, properly attested, is to be taken seriously (1 Timothy 5:19). If there is abuse of any kind, do not stay silent: protect the vulnerable first, go to other elders or outside authorities, and report crimes to the police. Christ owns his flock, and he hates the shepherd who harms it.

In a sentence. Paul told them to watch over themselves and the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he bought with his own blood, for he knew savage wolves would come in after he left and not spare the flock.

On a Tuesday. The church was bought with God’s blood. Treat it, and its people, as precious. Think of the member of your church you find hardest to love, and remember the price paid for them. Then do one thing this week that treats them as Christ does. And if you are an elder, begin with yourself: how is your own soul?

For worship. The church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. There is no higher price ever paid for anything. The eternal Son took flesh so that he could bleed, and he bled so that he could buy a people for himself, and he will never let one of them go. He is the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, the Chief Shepherd who will appear with an unfading crown for his under-shepherds, and the Lamb who was slain and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers — two names for one office. “With his own blood” — the blood of God’s own Son. Some manuscripts read “church of the Lord”; “his own blood” may also be rendered “the blood of his Own” (ESV notes).

parallels.desc: shepherds who feed themselves

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears.

And from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things. The wolves of the previous verse were coming in from outside. This is worse, and Paul puts it second because it is worse. Not only wolves from outside, but false teachers from inside, even among the elders. From among your own selves: he is speaking to the elders of the church at Ephesus, and he is telling them that some of the men in that room, or men very like them, will do this. Not infiltrators; the leadership, people currently sound and currently trusted. That is a hard thing to say to a group of friends on the last afternoon you will spend together, and it is a measure of how seriously he meant it that he said it anyway. And it happened: Paul later wrote to Timothy in Ephesus about false teachers there (1 Timothy 1:3–7, 19–20; 2 Timothy 2:17–18). And Jesus commended Ephesus for testing false apostles (Revelation 2:2).

To draw away the disciples after them. And there is the object of the exercise, stated with brutal clarity. Not after a doctrine. Not even, primarily, into error. After them: a personal following, gathered around a man. The mark of false teachers: drawing people to themselves rather than to Christ. Which tells you where to look. The doctrinal deviation is the method; the following is the aim. A teacher whose distinctive is that he has seen something others have missed, and whose adherents are identifiable by their attachment to him, has already shown you the thing Paul is warning about, whatever the content turns out to be.

Speaking twisted things. Diestrammena: bent out of shape, perverted, distorted truth. The typical twists are worth seeing, because the pattern never changes. Heresy is rarely a flat denial; it is truth bent just enough to mislead, plausible and half-right (Colossians 2:4). Almost every distortion does one of three things: it adds to Christ, subtracts from him, or perverts his grace. Back then: the Judaizers’ legalism, adding law-keeping to Christ for salvation (Galatians; Acts 15); the Colossian error, secret knowledge, angel-worship, asceticism, intermediaries crowding the Saviour (Colossians 2), also adding; the denials that subtracted, of Christ’s true humanity (1 John 4:2–3) or deity, and of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15; 2 Timothy 2:17–18); and antinomianism, perverting grace into sensuality (Jude 4; Romans 6:1). And much was money-driven, teaching for shameful gain (Titus 1:11; 1 Timothy 6:5).

The same three twists today. Today the same three twists wear new clothes. Adding: the prosperity gospel, promising health and wealth to enough faith or giving, the old money-driven error in a fresh suit; and the perennial legalism that makes rules the measure of acceptance (Colossians 2:16). Subtracting: the liberal emptying of the faith, denying Christ’s deity, the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, the atonement, Scripture’s authority; a tame God who exists to make you comfortable, with sin and the cross quietly removed; and the universalism that twists God is love into all paths lead home. Perverting grace: a cheap grace that drops repentance and holiness. And mark the tell-tale motive Paul names: teachers who arise to draw away the disciples after them, the cult of personality, a following gathered around a man, not the Lord. So your test, the Berean way (17:11): does this teaching exalt Christ and humble me, or exalt the teacher and serve his crowd and his wallet? Does it add to Christ, subtract from him, or turn grace into licence? Hold fast to the Head (Colossians 2:19) and let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Colossians 3:16); a heart full of the real Christ is not easily sold a counterfeit.

Therefore be alert. One imperative, and it is not be learned or be organised. Grēgoreite: stay awake, watch. The word is the one used of a watchman on a night shift; shepherds keep watch at night. The danger it assumes is not that the elders will be defeated in argument but that they will not notice in time.

Remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. Paul’s example. Three years. Night and day. Every one, individually. With tears. Four measurements of the same thing, and he offers them not only as a record but as a standard: this is what it took to build what you are now responsible for, and it is what it will take to keep it.

Three years? Chapter 19 gives three months and two years (19:8, 10), and a further while (19:22). Ancient reckoning often counted any part of a year as a year, and the total comes close to three.

What was Paul admonishing them about? The word (noutheteō) means to warn and earnestly counsel, and chiefly he was guarding them from exactly these twisted teachers (vv. 29–30), pleading with each to hold fast to Christ. But it was wider: he had not shrunk from declaring the whole counsel of God (v. 27): sin and judgment, repentance and holiness, the cross, the suffering on the road into the kingdom (14:22). Why the tears? Because souls and eternity were at stake, and Paul loved these people. Real pastoral love is never bland; it warns, and warns weeping, as he told the Philippians even with tears (Philippians 3:18). Notice how the tears answer both ditches of verse 28: no negligent shepherd, for he warned relentlessly; yet no domineering one, for he warned with tears, not contempt. It is the model for every parent, friend and elder who must one day say a hard word: warn, yes, but with a breaking heart for the one you love.

How can an ordinary Christian tell a true teacher from a false one? Look at three things. His message: does it agree with the plain teaching of Scripture, and does it put Christ crucified and risen at the centre, or does it add to him, take from him, or make grace an excuse for sin? His life: is he humble, honest with money, faithful in marriage, accountable to others (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? His fruit in his followers: do they become more like Christ and more attached to the whole church, or more attached to him and suspicious of everyone else (Matthew 7:15–20)? You do not need to be a scholar. Read your Bible, belong to a faithful church, and ask whether the teacher is pointing you to Jesus or to himself.

In a sentence. Even from among them men would arise distorting the truth to draw disciples after them, so they must be on guard, remembering that for three years Paul never stopped warning each of them night and day with tears.

On a Tuesday. Watch for teachers who draw people to themselves. Follow those who point you to Christ. Think about the voices you listen to most, preachers, podcasts, authors, and ask the Berean question of each: does this exalt Christ and humble me? And if you must warn someone you love, warn them with tears, not contempt.

For worship. The Good Shepherd never stops watching. He sees the wolves before the shepherds do, and he has promised that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). He gave his church apostles who wept and warned, and he gives her still a Word that cannot be twisted beyond his power to set it straight. False teachers draw disciples after themselves; Christ draws all his people to himself, by the cross, and holds them fast.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel.

And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace. He has warned them about wolves outside and traitors inside and told them to stay awake. And now, having sobered them thoroughly, he tells them what they actually have. Two things, and he is leaving them nothing else. Not a structure, not a strategy, not a successor, and not himself. God, and the word of his grace. Paul’s last provision for them: not a successor, not a system, but God and his word. The word of grace is the gospel, now preserved in Scripture. That is the protection against wolves.

What is missing. It is worth noticing what is missing from that list. Paul does not appoint a replacement, does not set up a chain of command running back to Jerusalem or Antioch, and does not tell them who to consult. The most influential Christian who ever lived walked away from the church he had worked hardest for and left it with God and a message. That is either reckless or it is the most confident thing in the chapter, and the next clause tells you which.

Commend. Commend (paratithēmi) means to entrust, to hand over for safekeeping, like leaving a treasure in trusted hands. Paul is going and does not expect to return, so he deposits the elders with two keepers who never leave: God himself, and the word of his grace, the gospel, the message of God’s grace (v. 24). The flock is not left orphaned. The under-shepherd departs, but the Chief Shepherd remains, and his word abides. The church’s security never rested on Paul; it rests on God and his Word.

Which is able to build you up. Able: the word carries the whole weight. He is not expressing a hope that they will manage; he is stating a capacity that belongs to the word itself. Build up (oikodomeō) is the construction word: to strengthen, mature and establish. The word builds up the church (Ephesians 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). It is enough. Notice the power lies in the word: the gospel is not lifeless information but a living means by which God grows his people strong (1 Peter 2:2; 19:20). So how does a church grow after even a great leader is gone? By the word of grace, fed on and held fast.

And to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. The future hope, for all God’s holy people (26:18; Ephesians 1:14, 18). The same word that builds them up now also secures their future: a share in the eternal inheritance, the full glory of salvation, the kingdom, eternal life (Colossians 1:12; 1 Peter 1:4). And it is an inheritance, not a wage: given to children by grace, received by being in Christ, not earned.

Those who are sanctified. Sanctified (hagiazō, to make holy, set apart for God) here is a perfect passive, those who have been sanctified, so it describes a settled standing, not an achievement. It means simply all true believers, everyone whom God has set apart for himself in Christ, the saints (1 Corinthians 6:11; Hebrews 10:10). The inheritance is not for an elite who have made themselves holy enough, but for all whom God has made holy, and the believer receives his portion together with the whole company of the saved. The comfort is rich: when every human helper is gone, God and his gospel remain, strong enough to grow you now, and faithful enough to bring you home to the inheritance at the last, in the company of all the saints.

I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. And with that the tone changes completely, and a modern reader is likely to find the transition odd: from the inheritance of the saints to a disclaimer about other people’s clothes. It is not odd at all in the ancient world. Wandering teachers were a recognised trade and a recognised nuisance; the philosophers themselves complained about men who went from town to town living off admirers. Apparel belongs in the list because good clothing was portable wealth, the sort of gift a grateful household gave a visiting teacher; in the ancient world, wealth was often stored as clothing. Paul’s integrity with money: unlike false teachers, he was not in it for gain (1 Thessalonians 2:5; 1 Timothy 6:5). So Paul, having just handed the church over, immediately establishes that he is not leaving with anything. There will be no suggestion, after the ship sails, that the apostle did well out of Ephesus.

If the word is enough, why do we need pastors and teachers? Because the word is God’s chosen instrument, and pastors are his chosen servants of the word. Paul did not commend them to God and the word instead of elders; he commended the elders themselves to God and the word. Teachers do not add to Scripture’s power; they open it, apply it, and guard it, as Paul did for three years. The danger is when people trust the teacher more than the text, or think a church cannot survive without a particular man. It can. Every faithful pastor’s goal is to point his people so firmly to God and his word that they would stand if he were gone.

In a sentence. Paul committed them to God and to the message of his grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance among all who are made holy, and said he had never wanted anyone’s silver, gold or clothing.

On a Tuesday. You have been commended to God and the word of his grace. They are enough. Open your Bible. If you have been leaning on a particular preacher, author or friend for your spiritual life, thank God for them, and then go to the word yourself this week, expecting it to build you up.

For worship. God and the word of his grace: the two keepers who never leave. The Father who chose us, the Son who bought us and the Spirit who sealed us are not going anywhere, and the word that reveals them abides for ever. Preachers depart, churches change, friends sail away, but the inheritance kept in heaven for us is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, and we are being guarded by God’s power through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed (1 Peter 1:4–5).

parallels.desc: whose ox have I taken?

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’

You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. He held them up. There is no other natural way to read the demonstrative, these hands, than as a gesture, and everyone in that group knew what was on them: the calloused marks of a man who had cut leather and cloth for a living, for years, in their city. And not only for himself. And to those who were with me: Paul’s trade had supported the team. He supported himself and his team. The apostle was the one paying for others.

In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak. Now the logic of it, which is the surprising part. We would expect the argument to be that he worked so as not to be a burden, and he says that elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Here the reason is different and better: he worked so that there would be something to give away. Work, not only to support oneself, but to have something to give (Ephesians 4:28). Paul made tents in order to help the weak of Ephesus. Not to fund himself, or not only; we must help the weak, and the strength for it came out of the bench. That reframes an ordinary job entirely. The work is not the thing that prevents ministry, nor merely the thing that permits it; it is the source of the surplus that makes generosity possible.

And remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive. Stop on that, because it is unique in the New Testament. Jesus never says this sentence in Matthew, Mark, Luke or John. This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was passed down by those who heard him. It is the only saying of Jesus quoted by Paul in Acts. It sums up his life: he gave himself. Giving brings deeper joy than getting.

One line of the enormous remainder. So here is a saying of Christ that survived because the churches remembered it and repeated it, and it reached us because Paul quoted it in a farewell speech that Luke was present for and wrote down. John ends his Gospel by saying that the world itself could not contain the books that might have been written (John 21:25). This is one line of the enormous remainder, preserved by the providence of God. And notice how Paul introduces it: remember the words of the Lord Jesus. Not as it is written. These men may never have read a Gospel. What they had was what Paul had told them Jesus said, held in memory, and he expects them to have it by heart.

Does this mean pastors should work and not be paid? No. Paul insists that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17–18). Paul gave up that right for the sake of the gospel in some places. Both are honourable: a paid minister, and one who works to support himself.

A testable claim. The saying itself is a claim about where blessedness is located, and it is testable. Nearly everyone alive believes, in practice, that receiving is the better arrangement; it is why we work, save and hope. Jesus says the arrangement is the other way round, and the man quoting it had built a life on the assumption and is standing there with the calluses to prove it.

Is it wrong to receive help when I need it? No. The saying does not make receiving shameful; it makes giving blessed. Paul himself gladly received the Philippians’ gifts and called them a fragrant offering (Philippians 4:18). There are seasons, illness, poverty, old age, grief, when God calls us to receive, and pride that refuses help can rob others of the blessing of giving. Receive with gratitude and without embarrassment. And when the season turns, give with the same joy. The whole church is a circle of grace, in which every member both gives and receives, and Christ is the first giver of all.

In a sentence. They knew Paul had worked with his own hands to supply his needs and his companions’, and showed them that by hard work we must help the weak, remembering the Lord Jesus’ words: it is more blessed to give than to receive.

On a Tuesday. It is more blessed to give than to receive. Give something today: money, time, a meal, an hour of help to someone weak. And look at your own work with new eyes. Whatever you earn this week is not only for your needs; it is the bench from which you can help the weak.

For worship. It is more blessed to give than to receive, said the Lord who gave more than anyone. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor; he gave his time to the crowds, his touch to the lepers, his body to the cross and his Spirit to his church. God so loved the world that he gave. And the blessedness of giving is his own blessedness, the joy of the Father who gave the Son, the Son who gave himself, and the Spirit who is given. He shares that joy with every one of his people who gives in his name.
verseByVerse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was remembered and passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,

And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. He ended with prayer, on his knees, with them. On a beach, in front of a ship’s crew and whoever else was on the shore at Miletus, a group of grown men got down on the ground. Standing was the ordinary Jewish posture for prayer. People knelt when something weighed too much for standing: Solomon at the dedication of the temple, Daniel three times a day facing Jerusalem, Stephen as the stones came down, Peter before he raised Tabitha, and Jesus in Gethsemane. It is the posture of urgency, humility and grief. Not standing, but kneeling, in humility. Paul’s ministry began, continued and ended in prayer.

With them all. With, not over. He does not pronounce a blessing on them from a standing position; he gets down among them and they pray together.

And there was much weeping on the part of all. Grown men, church leaders, weeping. Deep love. Luke does not tidy this up, and it is worth being glad that he did not. There is a strain of Christian teaching in which composure is next to godliness and open grief looks like a shortfall of faith. Here is the apostle who wrote that we do not grieve as those who have no hope, on the ground, in tears, in public, with his arms round men he loved and did not expect to see again. Much weeping on the part of all. All of them. Nobody in that group was holding it together for the sake of the others.

They embraced Paul and kissed him. Embraced: literally, they fell on his neck. It is the very phrase used of the father running to the prodigal (Luke 15:20), and before that of Joseph falling on his brother Benjamin’s neck. Luke reaches for the language of family reunion to describe a parting, which is exactly right, because that is what these men are and what they are losing. The kiss was the holy kiss of greeting and farewell (Romans 16:16).

What the gospel does to strangers. It is worth measuring what produced this. A few years earlier most of these men had not heard of Jesus Christ, and several of them had probably bought silver shrines of Artemis like everybody else in Asia. And now they are on a beach weeping over a Jewish tentmaker who taught them in a lecture hall. That is what the gospel does to a group of strangers, and it took three years and a great many tears on his side first.

Is it unspiritual to cry? No. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, knowing he was about to raise him (John 11:35), and wept over Jerusalem. Paul wept, these elders wept, and the psalms are full of tears. Tears are not a failure of faith but often an expression of love, for those we lose, for sin, for the suffering of others. What Christian hope changes is not whether we weep but how: we grieve, but not as those who have no hope. So do not be ashamed of tears, your own or anyone else’s. God keeps count of them, and one day he will wipe every one away (Psalm 56:8; Revelation 21:4).

In a sentence. When he had said this, he knelt and prayed with them all, and they all wept as they embraced and kissed him.

On a Tuesday. Christian love is not cold. It weeps, embraces, and prays together. When did you last pray aloud with another believer, not just for them? Do it this week, with a friend, your spouse, or a member of your church. And if there is someone you need to say goodbye to, do not let reserve keep you from saying how much they mean to you.

For worship. The Lord Jesus knelt in Gethsemane and prayed with loud cries and tears, and because he did, his people may kneel anywhere and be heard. He is the Saviour who weeps with those who weep, who fell on the neck of the prodigal in his own parable because that is what his Father is like, and who has made strangers into a family that weeps at parting. And he has promised a day when there will be no more partings at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.

Being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. Luke tells us which sentence did it, and it is worth noticing that it was not the one about chains. Paul had told them he was going to prison. He had told them that wolves were coming and that some of their own number would go wrong. He had told them his life was not precious to him. And what these men could not bear, out of all of it, was that they would not see his face. Not his letters, not his teaching, not his protection. His face. The deepest grief: parting.

A human sorrow, uncorrected. That is a thoroughly human sorrow and Scripture does not correct it. Paul himself writes the same way: he longs to see the Romans (Romans 1:11), he tells the Thessalonians he endeavoured with great desire to see them face to face (1 Thessalonians 2:17), he asks Timothy to come before winter (2 Timothy 4:21). The New Testament, which is largely a collection of letters, is oddly insistent that letters are not enough. Which is worth saying in a century that has more ways than ever of keeping in contact and fewer occasions of being in the same room. These men had three years of Paul’s teaching, which we would call the substance, and what they wept over was the loss of his presence. They were not being sentimental. They were being accurate about what a relationship is. But not for ever: Christians who part on earth will meet again (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

And they accompanied him to the ship. To the very end. A touching picture of love between a pastor and his people. The last thing they do is walk him down to the water, very likely as a formal escort, the whole group going with him to the shore and standing there until he was aboard. So the great Ephesian ministry ends on a beach with a knot of men watching a ship pull out, and the next verse of the book has Luke writing that they had to tear themselves away from them (21:1): it was plainly a parting that had to be forced.

Enough. And what Paul had left them with was the two things named in verse 32: God, and the word of his grace. He would not have said it was too little. On the evidence of the following decades, the letter to the Ephesians, and the church still standing when Christ himself addresses it by name in Revelation, it was not.

Will we really know one another in heaven? Yes. The hope of Scripture is not that we dissolve into a crowd but that we are raised as ourselves and gathered together with the Lord. Paul comforts the Thessalonians with the promise that they will be caught up together with those who have died, and that is meant to be a comfort precisely because it is a reunion (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah were recognisable. And the face we will see above all others is his: they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads (Revelation 22:4). Every other face will be dearer for that.

In a sentence. What grieved them most was his statement that they would never see him again, and they went with him to the ship.

On a Tuesday. Presence matters. If there is someone you love whom you have only been messaging, go and see their face this month. And if you are grieving a Christian friend or relative who has died, let this be your comfort: you will see their face again, and his.

For worship. Christians never say goodbye for the last time. We will see each other’s faces again in glory. The parting on the shore at Miletus was real, and the reunion will be more real still, when the Lord himself descends from heaven and the dead in Christ rise and we are gathered to him. And there, at last, we shall see his face, the face that was marred more than any man’s for our sake, and is now shining like the sun, and we shall be with the Lord for ever.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God and Pastoral Faithfulness. Acts 20:27 gives the church its standard for preaching: the whole counsel of God, without shrinking. This phrase has defined the Reformed tradition’s commitment to expository, systematic, comprehensive proclamation of Scripture — preaching through whole books, teaching the full range of doctrine, refusing to select only the comfortable and suppress the challenging. The shepherd who preaches the whole counsel will declare both the tenderness of the Father and the terror of the Judge, both the free grace of justification and the necessary fruit of sanctification, both the comfort of election and the urgency of repentance. Paul could stand before his people at Miletus and say “I am innocent of your blood” because he had given them everything. That is the standard every preacher must aspire to.
20.examples:
Then: A beach at Miletus, a group of weeping elders on their knees, a man who knew he was going to chains and possibly death — and who spent his last hours with these people not arranging his escape but commending them to God and declaring his conscience clear. The tears on the beach are the overflow of three years of tears in the houses of Ephesus. Ministry that produces this kind of grief at parting has been ministry that produced this kind of love in the doing.

Now: Paul’s farewell is the standard against which every pastoral ministry will be measured. Did we shrink? Did we select? Did we give them the comfortable Christ without the demanding Lord, the free grace without the costly discipleship, the promise without the warning? The whole counsel of God. Nothing less. The flock that has been given the whole counsel will be able to stand when the wolves come — because they will recognise the deviation when they hear it.

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed <sup>6</sup>and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>9</sup>He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>16</sup>And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law, <sup>21</sup>And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. <sup>22</sup>What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. <sup>23</sup>Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; <sup>24</sup>take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law. <sup>25</sup>But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.” <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>29</sup>For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>34</sup>Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. <sup>35</sup>And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd, <sup>36</sup>for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!” <sup>37</sup>As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? <sup>38</sup>Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” <sup>39</sup>Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” <sup>40</sup>And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
21.overview:
Paul’s road to Jerusalem deliberately echoes Jesus’ own (Luke 9:51). At Tyre, disciples moved by the Spirit urge him not to go; at Caesarea, in the house of Philip the evangelist, the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and foretells that the Jews will hand Paul over to the Gentiles. The church weeps and pleads; Paul answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they say, “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul and praise God for the Gentile mission, but warn him that thousands of zealous Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses. To show the rumour is false, he joins four men completing a vow and pays their temple costs. Near the end of the week, Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing a Gentile inside, and the city erupts. The Roman tribune rescues Paul from a beating, chains him, and mistakes him for an Egyptian rebel; Paul replies in polished Greek that he is a citizen of Tarsus, and asks to address the crowd. The prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: bound, and in Gentile hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tearing themselves away from the Ephesian elders, Paul’s party sails by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, then crosses on a larger ship to Tyre. There they find the disciples and stay a week; prompted by the Spirit, these believers urge Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. When the week is over the whole church, wives and children too, walks them to the shore, where they kneel and pray before parting. From Ptolemais they reach Caesarea and stay with Philip the evangelist, whose four unmarried daughters prophesy. The prophet Agabus arrives from Judea, ties his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt, and announces that the Spirit says the Jews in Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him to the Gentiles. Everyone begs Paul not to go. He asks why they are weeping and breaking his heart; he is ready to be bound and even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. When he cannot be persuaded, they give up, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.” They go up to Jerusalem with some Caesarean disciples, who take them to lodge with Mnason of Cyprus, a believer from the early days.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guidance, and the Difference Between a Revelation and an Inference

This passage is the clearest case in Scripture of sincere, Spirit-filled Christians getting guidance wrong, and it is wonderfully instructive because nobody in it is a villain.
