The despised man from Nazareth, whom Jerusalem had crucified, is the Lord of glory speaking from heaven. He did not shed his humanity at the ascension, and he is not embarrassed by the village. The man on the throne is the man from Nazareth, and he says so.

In a sentence. He fell to the ground and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him, and when he asked who it was, the voice said, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.

On a Tuesday. Treat every believer you meet this week as Christ treats them: as part of himself. Be slow to criticise, quick to defend, and careful with what you say about Christians who are not in the room. And if you are being mistreated for following him, say it to him in prayer: Lord, they are doing this to you. He already knows.

For worship. Consider him on that road. He had every reason to announce himself by the titles now indisputably his: the Lord, the Son of God, the one seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high, before whom every knee will bow. And out of that light he said: Jesus of Nazareth. The village name. The name that had been a joke. He kept it. He carries the marks of the nails still, and he answers to the name of the town they sneered at, and he will answer to it for ever. Heaven’s glory has a carpenter’s address, and the Lamb who was slain is not ashamed of a single scar.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’

Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. This is the verse people bring as a contradiction, and it deserves a straight answer. Luke, narrating in chapter 9, says the men stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (9:7). Paul, testifying here, says they saw the light but did not understand the voice. Read carelessly, it looks like a collision. Read carefully, it is two halves of one experience. Take the seeing first: they saw no one, and they saw the light. There was a blaze of light that everyone saw, and inside it a Person whom only Saul saw. Then the hearing. The Greek verb akouō can mean to hear a sound or to understand speech, and with a slight difference of construction Luke uses it both ways. They heard, but did not understand. You do not need Greek to know the difference. Stand next to someone on a phone call: you hear a voice perfectly well, and not a word of what it says. Everyone on the Damascus road heard something. One man heard words.

Inside the light and hearing only weather. Now stay with the picture, because the resolution is not the point. There were several men in that light. They all saw the brightness and heard the sound. They were close enough to catch Saul as he went down and to lead him by the hand into Damascus. And nothing whatever happened to them. Not one is named. Not one is heard of again. Nearness to revelation is not revelation. You can sit in the same pew, under the same preaching, singing the same words, close enough to touch someone whom God is at that moment laying hold of, and hear only a noise. He who has ears to hear, let him hear, and the reason that is a warning rather than a truism is standing on the Damascus road, holding Saul’s arm.

What shall I do, Lord? Then Saul speaks a sentence he had never spoken before. The question of a new disciple: total surrender. Lord: he has a new master. Here was a man who had known exactly what to do for years. He had a programme, a mandate, letters in his bag, a route, a list of names, and the backing of the highest religious authority in the world. In one question all of it is handed over. He does not ask what has happened, or whether the letters are still valid. He asks for orders.

There you will be told all that is appointed for you to do. Look at the answer, because it is deliberately not enough. Rise, go into Damascus, the city he had come to raid, and wait to be told. Appointed: his task was already set by God. But he is not given the plan: not the journeys, not the letters, not Rome. That is very nearly always the arrangement. God gives the next step and withholds the itinerary, and the withholding is not stinginess. Had Saul been handed his whole assignment on that road, shipwrecks and beatings and cells included, he would have received it as information. Instead he received it as obedience, one instruction at a time, from a Lord he was learning to trust.

Was Paul born again at this moment? We are not told, and we should not pretend to know what Scripture does not say. Luke tells Paul’s conversion as a connected whole: the encounter on the road, three days of blindness and prayer (9:9, 11), then Ananias, the filling with the Spirit, and baptism (9:17–18; 22:16). Regeneration is the Spirit’s secret work, known with certainty only to God; we see its fruits, not its moment. What we can see is that by verse 10 Paul calls Jesus Lord, surrenders his whole programme, asks for orders and obeys, and soon is found praying, all marks of a heart already being turned by grace. Since the new birth produces faith and repentance, it is reasonable to think the Spirit was already at work beneath that submission. What Scripture leaves unclear, the when, it more than makes up for in what it makes blazingly clear, the who. Christ sought the persecutor, struck him down, named him, and summoned him. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus seized Paul.

In a sentence. His companions saw the light but did not understand the voice speaking to him, and he asked what he should do, and the Lord told him to get up and go into Damascus, where he would be told all that had been appointed for him.

On a Tuesday. Ask each day: what shall I do, Lord? Then do the next thing he has plainly shown you in his word, without waiting for the whole map. And if you have spent years near the light, in Christian homes and churches, ask honestly whether you have heard words or only weather. Pray that he would speak to you, not only near you.

For worship. Only the Lord could do what happened on that road. He took a man whose whole life was a programme against him and, in a single question, turned him into a servant asking for orders. That is the sovereign mercy of Christ, who has mercy on whom he has mercy (Romans 9:15), and who does not wait to be found. He had appointed Saul’s work before Saul existed, and he would see every part of it done. The Lord who gives his servants the next step has already walked every step of the road ahead of them.
verseByVerse.note: His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not make out the words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,

I could not see because of the brightness of that light. Blinded by glory. Then Luke’s word: led by the hand (cheiragōgoumenos), the verb for guiding a small child or a blind beggar through a crowd. Read that against what Paul has just told us he was doing. He was on his way to Damascus to bring believers back in bonds. He arrives in Damascus led by the hand, helpless, unable to find a door. He had come to make people dependent, and he entered the city more dependent than any of them. Chapter 9 fills in what these verses pass over: three days without sight, without food or drink, in a stranger’s house, praying (9:9, 11). Everything Saul had relied on, his learning, his warrants, his standing, his certainty, was taken off him in an afternoon, and what was left sat in the dark and prayed.

And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. Watch how Paul introduces him to this audience. When Luke introduced the same man in chapter 9 he called him simply a disciple at Damascus (9:10). Paul, standing before a Jerusalem crowd that believes he abandoned Moses, stresses Ananias’s Jewish piety rather than his Christian discipleship: devout, law-observant, and well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. Not by the church. By the synagogue, by neighbours who did not share his faith. A law-keeping Jew, respected by Jews, brought God’s message to him.

Same story, different rooms. Paul is shaping his testimony for the room he is in. The story is the same each time, but before a king in chapter 26 he leaves Ananias out altogether, because a provincial holy man means nothing to Agrippa; here he makes him the hinge, because to this crowd he means everything. Truthful preaching is not the same as identical preaching. Wise testimony stresses what connects with its hearers, without changing a single fact.

Is it dishonest to tell my story differently to different people? No, as long as everything you say is true. Paul never changed the facts. He chose, from among true things, the ones that would help a particular audience understand. We all do this: you explain your work one way to a child and another to a colleague. What would be dishonest is inventing details, hiding what you believe in order to be accepted, or telling one group what you would deny to another. Paul became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22), but he never became a liar. Ask of every version of your testimony: is it true, and does it point to Christ?

A good name outside the church. Notice the standard Paul reaches for. The qualification he cites is not Ananias’s gifts or his courage or his visions, all of which he had. It is his reputation among people outside the church. Paul would later write that an overseer must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and perhaps here is where he learned it: the first Christian ever to lay hands on him was a man whose unbelieving neighbours had nothing bad to say about him.

In a sentence. Blinded by the brilliance of the light, he was led by the hand into Damascus, where a man named Ananias, devout in keeping the law and highly respected by all the Jews there, came to him.

On a Tuesday. Be thoughtful in how you tell your story, and stress what helps your hearers. And ask what your unbelieving neighbours would say about you if someone asked. Ananias’s good name opened a door for the gospel; so can yours, in the small honesties of paying bills, keeping promises and treating people kindly.

For worship. The Lord humbles before he lifts up. He led the proud persecutor into Damascus by the hand like a child, and in that darkness Saul began to see. That is the gracious way of our God, who brings the blind by a way they do not know and turns the darkness before them into light (Isaiah 42:16). And he chose an ordinary, devout, frightened man to be the instrument. The Lord delights to use quiet servants with good names, so that the glory goes to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.

Brother Saul, receive your sight. The tender greeting (9:17). They are the first words the church of Jesus Christ ever addressed to the apostle Paul, and they are worth standing still for. Consider what it took to say them. Chapter 9 records what Ananias said when the Lord first gave him the address: that he had heard from many how much evil this man had done to the saints in Jerusalem, and that he had authority to bind all who call on the Lord’s name (9:13–14). Ananias knew who was sitting in that house. He knew about the letters, and that his own name was very likely on them. To knock on that door was to walk into the one place in Damascus where a Christian could be arrested on the spot.

Brother. He came anyway. And the first thing out of his mouth was not a caution, not a condition, not an interview, not a probation. Brother. Think about the Christian voices Saul had silenced, beginning with Stephen’s, outside Jerusalem, praying for the men who were killing him. That was the church’s last word to Saul: a dying man asking God not to hold this sin against them. And the next word the church says to him, three days into his blindness, is brother. Between those two words there is no negotiation, no restitution, no proving period. Ananias calls him brother because the risen Christ has claimed him, and that settles it. The church does not decide who its family is; it recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

How quickly should a church trust a notorious sinner who professes faith? Welcome and trust are not the same, and Scripture gives us both. Ananias welcomed Saul at once as a brother, because the Lord had told him plainly that Saul was his chosen instrument (9:15). The Jerusalem church, without that word, was afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him (9:26–27). Today we have no vision to tell us, so the church receives a professing believer warmly, as a brother, while positions of trust, leadership or access to the vulnerable wait for the fruit of a changed life (1 Timothy 3:6, 10). Where someone has abused others, wise safeguards are an act of love for everyone, including him. But the greeting should not wait. Say brother, and mean it.

And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. Instant. And the first thing Saul’s restored eyes rest on is the face of a man he had come to Damascus to put in chains. He is looking at his intended victim, and his intended victim is calling him family. He had been blind for three days. He had been blind a good deal longer than that: a man of formidable learning who could not see the one at the centre of his own Scriptures. Both blindnesses ended in the same room, and an ordinary, obedient disciple was the instrument of it.

In a sentence. Ananias stood beside him and said, Brother Saul, receive your sight, and at that moment he could see him.

On a Tuesday. A kind word can open blind eyes; speak one today. Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb: not a stranger, but someone with a history, and a history with you. Now imagine the Lord has laid hold of them. Ananias said brother in three days, to the man who had come to arrest him. Pray that you would be ready to do the same.

For worship. Brother. It is the word Christ himself is not ashamed to say to us. He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source, and that is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He said it first, to people who had betrayed him, on the morning of his resurrection: go to my brothers (Matthew 28:10). Every welcome the church gives a forgiven enemy is an echo of the welcome the Son of God gave us, when we were the ones with warrants against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard.

The God of our fathers appointed you. Ananias’s first phrase, and Paul repeats it to this crowd because it is the hinge of his whole defence. Not a new God, but Israel’s God: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the phrase Peter used at Solomon’s Portico (3:13) and before the council (5:30), and Stephen at the bush (7:32). The charge against Paul is apostasy. His answer is that the God who commissioned him is the God his accusers were named after. Appointed (procheirizomai): chose beforehand, selected. Sovereign choice. Paul never forgot it; he wrote that God had set him apart before he was born and called him by his grace (Galatians 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed, which is worth knowing if your own conversion looked, from the inside, like an accident.

To know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth. The Righteous One is a title for the Messiah, and Paul had heard it before. Peter used it in the temple: you denied the Holy and Righteous One (3:14). And Stephen used it in the last speech of his life, in the sentence that got him killed: they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered (7:52). Saul heard him say it. That title went into his ears from a dying man he was helping to execute, and the next time he heard it, it was being given to the one who had just spoken to him from heaven. Grace is not tidy about how it gets a word into a man.

Seeing and hearing. Those two verbs are the foundation of Paul’s apostleship. Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? he would ask (1 Corinthians 9:1), and last of all, as to one untimely born, Christ appeared also to him (1 Corinthians 15:8). His authority does not rest on his intellect, his zeal or his results. It rests on the fact that he saw the risen Christ with his own eyes and heard him speak, which is what an apostle is.

For you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. A witness, martys, the word that came to mean martyr, partly because of the man Paul watched die. A witness in court is not asked what he thinks or what he finds meaningful. He is asked what he saw and heard. That is the whole job, and it is why the least articulate Christian can do it. And listen to one word, because Paul is being deliberate and the crowd has not noticed yet. To everyone: not just Jews. Not a syllable about Gentiles, not yet. The scope is already total, said in the widest and softest form available, and they let it go by. He will say it again, six verses from now, in the word they cannot bear. He is telling them the same thing twice: once so that they can hear it, and once so that they cannot.

Are there apostles today? Not in the sense Paul was one. An apostle in this full sense had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and Paul calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church once, and we build on it through their writings in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). Missionaries and church planters are sometimes loosely called apostles, meaning sent ones, but no one today carries the authority of Peter or Paul. That is not a loss. It means the voice of the apostles still speaks, unchanged, every time we open the Bible.

In a sentence. Ananias said the God of their fathers had chosen him to know his will, see the Righteous One and hear him speak, for he would be his witness to everyone of what he had seen and heard.

On a Tuesday. You too are a witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard of Christ: in Scripture, in answered prayer, in his patience with you. Nobody will cross-examine you on systematic theology, and if they do, you may say you do not know. What you have seen and heard is yours to give. Give one piece of it to someone this week.

For worship. The Righteous One. Stephen died saying the name, and the persecutor who heard it was brought to see the one it named. He is the only righteous man who ever lived, righteous in every thought and deed, and he was betrayed and murdered by the unrighteous, and then rose to make the unrighteous righteous. For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The God of our fathers appointed Saul to see that face. One day all his people will see it, and his name will be on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.note: “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance

And now why do you wait? Urgency. You have sat in this dark room for three days, Ananias is saying. That is long enough. Stop being a secret.

Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name. In Greek: having risen, be baptised, and wash away your sins, calling on his name. This is one of the sentences people are given when someone wants to persuade them that the water itself does the saving, so it needs answering carefully. Start with what the sentence does not say. It does not say the water washes. It holds four things together, and the last clause is not decoration: calling on his name is what the whole sentence hangs on. The washing of sins is linked with calling on his name. It is faith, calling on Christ, that receives forgiveness (2:21; Romans 10:13); baptism is its outward sign and seal.

Where Christians differ: does baptism wash away sins? Some take this verse to teach that the water of baptism itself removes sin. Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it this way, pointing also to Peter’s words at Pentecost (2:38) and to the statement that baptism now saves you (1 Peter 3:21). Verdict: Saul had already met the risen Lord, called him Lord, and been addressed as brother before his baptism. Sins are washed away by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7; Revelation 1:5), received by faith; baptism is the God-given picture and seal of that washing (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal to God for a good conscience). Baptism should not be delayed, but it is not the cause of forgiveness.

Let Paul interpret Paul. Our best interpreter here is the man who obeyed this very command. If anybody had reason to believe his sins went down a Damascus drain, it was Saul of Tarsus. What did he write afterwards? That Abraham received circumcision as a sign and seal of the righteousness he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised (Romans 4:11): the sign certifies a righteousness already given; it does not manufacture it. That Christ did not send him to baptise but to preach the gospel (1 Corinthians 1:17), an impossible sentence for a man who thought baptism washed sins away. And that he could barely remember whom he had baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14–16), which is not how anyone speaks about the thing that saves. Luke’s own book agrees. In Cornelius’s house the Holy Spirit fell on Gentiles while Peter was still speaking, and only afterwards did anyone bring water (10:44–48). And the dying thief, who could never be baptised, was promised paradise that day (Luke 23:43).

The sign and the thing signified. So what is Ananias saying? Scripture often speaks of the sign in the language of the thing signified, because God does not mean the two to be pulled apart. Baptism is the God-appointed sign of a washing that only the blood of Christ performs, and to be baptised is to be publicly and visibly joined to the one who did the washing. Ananias is not telling Saul how to get clean. He is telling a man who has been made clean to go and say so, in water, before witnesses. And notice the order: Saul believed, and then was baptised. That is the pattern throughout Acts, and it is why we baptise those who profess faith in Christ, while gladly honouring paedobaptist brothers who read the covenant signs differently and love the same Saviour.

I believe in Christ but have never been baptised, so does it matter? Yes, it matters, though not because your salvation hangs on the water. Christ commanded his disciples to be baptised (Matthew 28:19), and every believer in Acts was baptised promptly after believing, often the same day. Baptism is the Lord’s appointed way for you to confess him publicly, to be marked as belonging to his people, and to receive the strengthening of faith he gives through it. Staying unbaptised is like keeping a wedding ring in the drawer: the marriage is real, but you are hiding it. Speak to your pastor or elders this week. For a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, baptism was the point of no return. It is meant to be that for us, too.

When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance. Then Paul moves the story to a place his accusers will not expect. Read that before this crowd. He is on trial for defiling the temple. And he tells them that his commission, the one they are about to riot over, was given to him inside that building, while he was praying. Not in Damascus, not among Gentiles. In the temple, in the middle of Jewish devotion, doing exactly what a devout Jew does. He had not abandoned it; he honoured it. A vision, given to a man at prayer. It is the most disarming thing he could have said, and it is simply true. The God they think he has abandoned met him in their own house.

In a sentence. Ananias asked what he was waiting for, and told him to get up, be baptised and wash his sins away, calling on the Lord’s name; and when Paul returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, he fell into a trance.

On a Tuesday. If you believe and have not been baptised, why wait? And if you have been, ask whether there is anything else in your following of Christ that you have kept unofficial: not unbelieved, but unannounced. A faith your colleagues have never had to notice, a repentance nobody has been told about, an obedience still pending because going public would cost something. Ananias’s question is the whole application.

For worship. Saul’s sins were not vague. He had faces in his memory, people whose doors he had broken, and Stephen’s blood, and he was told that the whole account could be washed. Not managed, not offset by a life of service, but washed, until the stain could not be found. That is what the blood of Jesus Christ does. It does not negotiate with sin or file it somewhere out of sight. It removes it. The man who guarded the coats at a murder was made as clean as if he had never touched them, by the blood of the Righteous One whose people he had been hunting. There is nothing in the universe like that blood. It has never met a stain it could not lift, and it never will.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you.

Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me. The Lord’s instruction is blunt, and it is negative: they will not have it, so go. Jesus himself told Paul to leave Jerusalem. This is a new detail; Acts 9 tells us that the believers sent him away because of a plot against his life (9:29–30). Both are true. Luke gives the human side there; Paul gives the divine side here.

Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. And Paul argues. That is worth noticing, because it is not what we expect from a man in a trance in the temple. He does not fall on his face and say yes. He puts a case, and it is a good one. His argument is that his testimony is uniquely credible in this city, because here they know what he was. Anywhere else, a preacher claiming that Jesus rose is a man making a claim. In Jerusalem, the man saying it is the man they hired to stop it. They have the paperwork. If a change of that size, in that man, before the people who commissioned him, will not persuade them, what could? He thought his conversion would convince them. The Lord says no.

A good plan refused. Hold on to that, because this is one of the great uncomfortable passages about guidance. Paul’s reasoning is not selfish. Jerusalem is the most dangerous city on earth for him, and he knows it. He is offering the Lord the most strategically intelligent use of his own conversion, and the answer is: get out, quickly. So the no is not a verdict on the quality of the plan. Sometimes God’s refusal has nothing to do with whether your reasoning was sound. He has a different map, a larger one, and you are not being shown it. And watch where the refusal took him: to Tarsus, Antioch, Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia, Asia, and in the end, in chains, to Rome. The whole Gentile mission flows from a no that Paul argued against.

Is it wrong to argue with God in prayer? Not if it is the honest pleading of a child who will still obey. Abraham pleaded for Sodom (Genesis 18:22–33), Moses argued for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14), and the psalms are full of complaint and reasoning. God invites us to bring him our reasons and our longings. What makes Paul’s prayer godly is what he does next: when the Lord answers, he goes. Arguing becomes sin when it turns into refusal, or into the sulking assumption that God owes us an explanation. Pour out your case; then say, as Paul effectively did, your will be done, and pack your bags.

The experiment, run at last. One more thing makes this speech remarkable. What Paul is doing right now, on the barracks steps, is making that same argument. He has told this crowd about Gamaliel, about the letters, about the imprisoning and the beating. His whole case is the one he put to the Lord in the trance, being tried at last before the very audience the Lord said would not accept it. Twenty years later the experiment is finally being run. Three verses from now we find out who was right.

In a sentence. In the vision, the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem quickly, because they would not accept his testimony, and Paul answered that they knew he had gone from synagogue to synagogue imprisoning and beating believers.

On a Tuesday. There is an ache most Christians know and few say aloud: the good thing you were not permitted to do. The ministry you were suited for and were not given. The person you were sure you could reach, from whom God moved you away. Name it before the Lord. Then look at where his no has taken you instead, and thank him for the larger map you cannot yet see.

For worship. Our hopes for how God will use us are not always his plans, and his plans are always better. The Lord who said no to Paul in the temple was sending him to the nations, to us. Every Gentile believer in every century owes something to that refusal. And behind it stands the Father who once said no to his own Son’s prayer that the cup might pass, because a greater salvation was coming through the cross. Our God does not refuse us because he is careless with our desires. He refuses us because he is bringing many sons to glory, and he knows the way.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’

And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed. He is still arguing his case to the Lord, and this is the evidence he offers. Not his training. Not his zeal. The worst thing he ever did. Witness (martys): the ordinary courtroom word, the same one used of Paul’s own calling five verses ago (v. 15). Only later did the church use it to mean someone killed for his testimony, and it came to mean that because of days like this one. Stephen was the first.

I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him. Luke gives three verbs and Paul does not soften one of them. Standing by: present, close enough to see it. Approving: not swept along, not silently appalled, but agreeing. Watching over the garments: he held the coats. It is the smallest job at the scene, the one that needs no strength and takes no aim, and it is the one he names. A man managing his own guilt reaches for the version of the story in which his part was marginal. Paul does the opposite. He understands that the man who holds the coats is not on the edge of the stoning. He is in it, making it easier, wanting the outcome. Paul never forgot it (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:13). Grace does not erase memory, but it removes guilt.

If God has forgiven me, why do I still remember what I did? Because forgiveness is not amnesia. God promises to remember our sins no more (Hebrews 8:12), meaning he will never hold them against us; he does not promise that we will forget. Paul remembered Stephen for the rest of his life, and the memory did not crush him. It humbled him and made him grateful: he called himself the least of the apostles, and in the same breath said, by the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). When the memory comes back, do not argue with it and do not wallow in it. Take it straight to the cross, and let it become a reason for praise rather than despair.

Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles. Then the Lord answers the argument with one sentence. The word that would set off the crowd. Far away (makran) is a word with a history in this book. At Pentecost, in this same city, Peter had told a Jewish crowd that the promise was for them and their children and for all who are far off (2:39), and nobody rioted, because a Jerusalem crowd hears far off and thinks of Jews in Babylon and Alexandria. Paul fills the same distance with the word they cannot hold. And I will send you is exapostellō, from the root that gives us apostle. Paul’s mission to the Gentiles was not his own idea, nor a committee’s, nor Antioch’s. It was Christ’s command, given in the temple, to a man on his knees in the middle of an argument he was losing.

The mountain top. Stand back and look at what has just happened. Here is a man confessing that he stood over the body of the first Christian to die for Jesus, and agreed with it, and held the coats. And the answer from heaven is not a rebuke, not a period of discipline, not a lesser assignment suited to a man with that record. It is a commission: go, and I will send you to the ends of the earth with the very message you tried to strangle. Stephen died praying, Lord, do not hold this sin against them (7:60), and the Lord did not hold it against them, and the first and greatest answer to that dying prayer was standing at the edge of the crowd with his arms full of coats.

In a sentence. Paul told the Lord that when the blood of his witness Stephen was shed, he stood by approving and guarding the clothes of those who killed him, but the Lord said, Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. If there is something in your past that you think disqualifies you from serving Christ, bring it to him honestly, as Paul did, without softening it. Then hear what he says to forgiven sinners: go. And pray for the persecutors of the church in our own day by name, as Stephen did. You may be praying for the next Paul.

For worship. God turns persecutors into preachers; no past is too dark for his grace. It does not merely pardon the persecutor; it hands him the gospel and sends him further with it than anyone had carried it. The blood Saul helped to spill is answered by the blood of Christ, which speaks a better word than any martyr’s (Hebrews 12:24), and which had covered him before he was told. Grace like that is not a doctrine to be admired at a distance. It is a scandal, it is the truest thing there is, and every soul ever saved has been saved by exactly this and nothing else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — The Roman Custody and Paul's Citizenship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the word “Gentiles” the crowd erupts, shouting that such a man should be wiped off the earth, tearing off their cloaks and throwing dust into the air. The commander orders Paul into the barracks to be flogged and questioned, to discover why they are shouting against him. As they stretch him out for the lash, Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog a Roman citizen who has not been condemned. The centurion warns the commander, who comes and asks Paul directly whether he is a citizen. Paul says yes. The commander says that his own citizenship cost him a great deal; Paul answers that he was born a citizen. Those about to interrogate him withdraw at once, and the commander is alarmed at having put a citizen in chains. Next day, wanting to know exactly what the Jews accuse him of, he releases Paul and orders the chief priests and the whole council to assemble, and brings Paul before them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Rights as Tools, Not Shields

Paul's Roman citizenship is one of the clearest case studies in Scripture of how a Christian may handle a legitimate privilege. He does not renounce it, and he does not hide behind it. At Philippi he took the beating with the card in his pocket and produced it only the next morning (16:37), because that beating served the gospel and produced a jailer's household. On the barracks steps one chapter ago he deliberately withheld it, because he wanted a pulpit and not a rescue (21:39). Here he plays it, seconds before the whip falls, because a scourging would have ended a man who has been told he must testify at Rome.

The deciding question is never what will hurt least. It is what will serve most. That is a harder rule than either renouncing rights or clinging to them, because it has to be asked fresh every time and it cannot be settled in advance by policy.

Underneath it lies the Reformed conviction about the civil magistrate. God gave the sword to the state (Rom. 13:4), and he uses it — often through officials with no interest in him at all. A centurion protecting his own career, a commander doing the arithmetic on his pension, an empire enforcing its own statutes: none of them knows he is keeping the apostle to the Gentiles alive and moving him toward Rome. God's providence does not require the cooperation of the people it employs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Four officials in turn — Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa — examined the case against Paul, and not one of them could name a crime. The tribune could not learn the facts in the uproar, and wrote that he found nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29). Festus said the accusers brought no charge of the sort he had expected (25:18) and finally admitted it was unreasonable to send on a prisoner without indicating the charges (25:27). Luke records all four without a word of editorial.

Now: Where the church is opposed, it is worth being clear about which thing is happening. Sometimes Christians are disciplined for genuine wrongdoing, and the right response is repentance, not a persecution narrative. But when the file keeps coming back empty — when the offence turns out to be the message itself, and no one can state a charge — that is the pattern of this chapter, and the answer is not outrage. It is to keep doing exactly what the empty file says you were doing, and to go on asking, as Paul did with his back to a whipping post, for permission to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: "Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.' And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.” And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,

Up to this word they listened to him. Luke’s precision is merciless. Up to this word. They gave him a real hearing: twenty verses of silence, the light, the voice, the blindness, Ananias, the trance in the temple. They took all of it. Then one word came out of his mouth and the crowd went off like a match in a gas leak. The word was Gentiles. They could accept a vision, even a converted persecutor, but not that God would send a Jew to save Gentiles without first making them Jews. National pride was their stumbling block, as at Nazareth, when Jesus spoke of God’s grace to a widow of Sidon and a Syrian leper and the synagogue tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:25–29).

Grace as a possession. Be exact about the diagnosis. The crowd is not rioting over the resurrection, or a claim to visions, or the name of Jesus, or even Paul’s conversion, all of which they had just sat through. They are rioting because God intends to save the nations and bring them in on the same terms. And it is not simply racial hatred, which would be easier to dismiss. It is a theological conviction, sincerely held, that God’s grace is a possession rather than a gift. Once you believe you hold something by right, everyone who receives it freely looks like a thief. The bitter thing is that their own Scriptures had said it. God promised to make his servant a light for the nations, that his salvation might reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6), and Paul had already quoted that verse in a synagogue as the warrant for his ministry (13:47). This crowd is not defending the Bible against Paul. It is shouting down the book it holds.

Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live. The cry is the one they raised at the bottom of these same steps minutes earlier (21:36), and the one Luke recorded when a Jerusalem crowd stood before Pilate and shouted, Away with this man (Luke 23:18). The servant is getting his master’s reception, in his master’s city, in his master’s words.

Throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air. Luke films the crowd. Dust in the air is an old gesture of grief, rage and rejection: Job’s friends threw it on their heads (Job 2:12), Shimei flung it at David (2 Samuel 16:13). Tearing off cloaks was a gesture of horror, as at blasphemy, or a preparation for stoning (7:58). These people are past speech. And the cloaks: read verse 23 straight after verse 20 and feel the floor move. Paul has just told them that at Stephen’s execution he was the man minding the garments. Now, before him, a mob that wants him dead is throwing off its garments. Luke sets the two sentences three verses apart and says nothing about it. He does not need to.

Could I be like this crowd? Yes, and it is the most useful question in the chapter. It is easy to read them as monsters and move on. But every one of us has a sentence about God that we would find hard to say amen to: a truth about whom he saves, or what he has a right to do, or whom he loves, that we would rather were not so. It may be that God could save the person who wronged you, or that he loves people of a nation or party you despise, or that your own good record earns you nothing. Find yours. The sentence that makes something in you go quiet and resistant marks the place where you have decided that God belongs to you, rather than you to him. Bring it to him and ask him to change your heart.

In a sentence. The crowd listened until he said this, then shouted, Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live! throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air.

On a Tuesday. Pride in our group can blind us to God’s grace for others; watch for it. Ask what kind of person you would be least glad to see converted and welcomed into your church as an equal. Then pray for that kind of person by name this week, and ask God to give you joy when he saves them.

For worship. The word that set the crowd raging is the word that brought us home. God promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, and he kept the promise in Christ, who came to gather a people from every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 5:9). Salvation was never a possession to be guarded but a gift to be given. The grace that offended Jerusalem is the grace that reached us, far off, strangers to the covenants, and made us fellow heirs. Glory to the God of the Gentiles, who is the God of Israel, who is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing dust in the air and tearing off cloaks were gestures of outrage.

verseByVerse.quote: "the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, 'Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?”

The tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging. The tribune has understood nothing. He does not understand Aramaic; he has stood through a speech in a language he cannot follow, watched a city erupt over a word he did not catch, and still has no idea what the man has done. So he reaches for the standard tool and seeks the truth by torture. Be clear what that tool was. This is not the synagogue’s thirty-nine lashes, which Paul had already taken five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge (mastix, the Latin flagellum): leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, the punishment that went before crucifixion. It laid the back open, and it could cripple or kill. Jesus was scourged (John 19:1). And here it is not even a sentence, only a way of getting information: beat him until he explains himself.

There is no malice in it. That is what makes it chilling. The tribune is not angry with Paul; he has just saved his life twice. This is simply what one did with a provincial nobody when information was needed quickly, and the officer would have thought no more of ordering it than of posting a sentry. Great cruelty is often committed this way, by ordinary people following procedure.

But when they had stretched him out for the whips. Tied, bent forward, back bared, ready. Notice how late it is. Luke lets us get right to the edge.

Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned? A calm question at the last moment, and a legal one. Two words carry it: Roman, and uncondemned (akatakritos), untried, with no verdict entered. Two crimes, then: flogging a citizen, and doing it without trial. Under the old Roman laws a citizen could not be scourged without trial, and the principle was so deeply felt that Cicero built a famous prosecution on it, declaring that to bind a Roman citizen is a crime and to flog him an outrage. Paul is not asking a favour. He is telling a Roman officer that he is about to break Roman law. Christians may use legal rights to protect themselves and the gospel (16:37).

Why did he not say this at Philippi? Because at Philippi he did not say it until afterwards. He and Silas were beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison, and only the next morning, when the magistrates wanted them quietly gone, did Paul mention that they had beaten uncondemned Roman citizens publicly (16:37). He took that beating with the card in his pocket, and out of it came a midnight hymn, an earthquake, and a jailer and his household saved. So the difference is not that Paul had learned his lesson. It is what the suffering would accomplish. At Philippi a beating served the gospel, so he took it. Here a scourging might well have killed him, and he was meant to testify in Rome. A chapter ago he held this same card on these same steps and did not play it, because what he wanted then was a pulpit, not a rescue (21:39).

So when should a Christian stand on his rights, and when should he suffer wrong? Paul’s rule seems to be: what will serve the gospel and the good of others? Jesus taught us to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39), and Paul told the Corinthians it was better to be wronged than to drag a brother to court (1 Corinthians 6:7). Yet he also appealed to Caesar and claimed his citizenship. The difference is not between strong and weak faith. Personal insults and losses we are usually called to bear quietly. But where injustice threatens our life, our ability to serve Christ, or other people who depend on us, using lawful protection is not unspiritual. Victims of abuse, for example, should never be told that Christian meekness means staying silent; the law is God’s gift for their protection. Ask God for wisdom, and ask what will honour Christ most.

In a sentence. The commander ordered Paul taken into the barracks and interrogated under the whip to find out why they were shouting against him, but as they stretched him out for the lashes, Paul asked the centurion standing there whether it was legal to flog a Roman citizen who had not been found guilty.

On a Tuesday. There is a time to suffer silently and a time to claim your rights; ask God for wisdom to know which. Paul treats his rights neither as a shield to hide behind nor as a badge to renounce, but as a tool, picked up when the work needs it and put down when it does not. The deciding question is never what will hurt least, but what will serve Christ most.

For worship. The scourge that Paul escaped, his Lord did not. Jesus was handed over to the same Roman whips, and he did not claim the protection that was his. He could have spoken one word and ended it, and he was silent, because by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Paul’s back was spared because his Master’s back had already been laid open for him. Every rescue of a believer from suffering, and every grace to endure it, is bought by the stripes of the Lamb of God.
verseByVerse.note: Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge; flogging an uncondemned Roman citizen was illegal.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, 'What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.' So the tribune came and said to him, 'Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?' And he said, 'Yes.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.”

What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen. The centurion knew the law. He does not argue with Paul or check his story. He runs. The junior officer at the whipping post knows something his commander has forgotten on a bad afternoon: that a career, and possibly a neck, is about ten seconds from ending. To flog a citizen could cost the tribune everything.

Tell me, are you a Roman citizen? And the tribune comes himself. He does not send a clerk. Falsely claiming citizenship was punishable by death, so the claim was usually believed. There were no papers to produce on a staircase; a citizen’s status was registered in the archives of his home city, and checking would take months. The empire’s law had teeth pointing both ways, and everybody knew it. A man in Paul’s position either was a citizen or was signing his own death warrant, and the tribune could see he was no fool.

And he said, Yes. A one-word answer, and that word stops the Roman army. Soldiers a moment from opening a man’s back step away from him, and the officer who gave the order starts to sweat. Now count what Paul had already absorbed while holding that word in his mouth. A mob had beaten him. He had been dragged out through the gates, chained between two soldiers, carried up a flight of stairs like freight, and tied to a post. At any point one word would have changed his circumstances, and he did not say it, because until now saying it would have bought him comfort and cost him a hearing.

The working definition of self-denial. Self-denial is not pretending you have no rights, nor the noisy renouncing of them. It is holding what is truly yours loosely enough that the question is never what may I claim but what will serve. Paul had the word all along. He spent it at the one moment it would keep him alive to preach, and not a moment sooner.

God’s quiet instruments. There is a quieter thing here too. The centurion’s alarm, the tribune’s haste, the soldiers’ retreat: none of these men has the slightest interest in the gospel. They are protecting themselves. God is perfectly able to use a frightened officer’s instinct for self-preservation to keep his servant alive, and the officer will never know he did it.

In a sentence. When the centurion heard this, he went and told the commander that this man was a Roman citizen, so the commander came and asked Paul if he was a citizen, and he said yes.

On a Tuesday. God had prepared Paul’s protection before he was born, by his citizenship; his providence reaches far ahead. Think of what God has placed in your hands, by birth or education or position, that you did not choose. Ask how it might one day serve Christ, and hold it ready, without boasting in it or being ashamed of it.

For worship. Long before Saul was born in Tarsus, God had arranged that his family should hold the citizenship of Rome, so that one afternoon on a whipping post a single word would preserve his apostle for the nations. Nothing in our lives is accidental to the Lord. He knit us together in our mother’s womb, and every one of our days was written in his book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:13–16). The God who prepared Paul’s yes is preparing, in hidden ways, every provision his children will need, all the way home.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune answered, 'I bought this citizenship for a large sum.' Paul said, 'But I am a citizen by birth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.”

I bought this citizenship for a large sum. There is a needle in that sentence. The tribune is not making conversation; he is expressing disbelief, and some wounded pride. He had paid a fortune for his status. He is looking at a battered, chained, sleepless provincial who has just been untied from a post, and being asked to accept that this man outranks him by birth. Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. The historian Dio Cassius says it was sold by officials and the emperor’s household, and that it became cheap as the market grew crowded. His own name records the transaction: Luke later tells us he is Claudius Lysias (23:26). Lysias is the Greek name his parents gave him; Claudius is the emperor’s, taken with his citizenship.

But I am a citizen by birth. Literally, but I was even born one. Paul was born a citizen, higher in status than the tribune. His father or grandfather had received it, perhaps as a grant for some service to Rome; we are not told. God’s providence had prepared it long before. Paul does not gloat or elaborate. He simply states the fact that ends the conversation, and the reversal is total. The prisoner has the older claim. The commander bought his way in. And it is the commander, not the prisoner, who is now in legal danger.

How did people become Roman citizens? It was a prized and fairly rare status, carrying real protection: no flogging without trial, the right to a proper hearing, and the right of appeal to Caesar, which Paul will later use (25:11). It could come by birth from citizen parents, as with Paul; by purchase, often through bribery, as with the tribune; by being freed from slavery by a Roman master; or by grant of the emperor, for service to Rome, for long service in the auxiliary army, or to a family or a whole city. A man could hold it as a Jew and a citizen of Tarsus at the same time, as Paul did.

The freest man in the room. What Luke is building here runs through the rest of Acts: Paul in chains keeps turning out to be the freest man in every room he is dragged into. He is calmer than the tribune, better informed than the mob, more secure in law than the officer holding him. The circumstances say prisoner. Everything else in the scene says otherwise.

In a sentence. The commander said he had bought his citizenship for a lot of money, and Paul said he was born a citizen.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you hold a citizenship higher than any passport, and you did not buy it. Let that steady you when you are made to feel small, and humble you when you are tempted to feel important. Live this week as a citizen of heaven living temporarily on earth: honest in business, gracious under pressure, unafraid of officials.

For worship. Useful as Paul’s Roman citizenship was, he prized far more one neither bought nor inherited: our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20). The tribune paid a large sum for his. Ours was not bought by us, but for us, with Christ’s blood. We were born into it by the Spirit, from above, and the price was paid in full by the one who became a stranger and an outcast so that strangers and outcasts could be fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19).
verseByVerse.note: Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. Paul was born a citizen, probably because his father or grandfather had been granted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.

Those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately. Fear of the consequences.

And the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. Read what frightens him. Not only that he nearly flogged a citizen, but that he had already bound one. Even chaining a citizen without trial was illegal. This is a professional soldier doing the arithmetic on his own career and not liking the answer. But notice the honesty of the next words: on the next day. The tribune is afraid, and still leaves Paul in custody overnight. Fear of consequences is not the same as repentance, and it does not produce prompt justice; it produces a sleepless night and a decision in the morning. Luke does not tidy this man up.

Desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews. A Roman wanting justice. He could not get it from the mob. That clause is a thread Luke has been pulling for two chapters and will not let go. At the riot, the tribune could not learn the facts (21:34). Here he still wants the real reason. Later, in his official letter, he will write that Paul was accused about questions of their law but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29). Then Festus, two years on, will find no charge of the evils he expected (25:18), and finally will say that it seems unreasonable to send a prisoner without indicating the charges against him (25:27). Official after official examines this case, and not one can find a crime in it. That is Luke’s quiet, patient defence of the faith, laid down without a word of comment. Christianity is not being convicted; it is being disliked, and everyone with authority to write down a charge keeps failing to find one.

He unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet. The council is the Sanhedrin, the same council that condemned Jesus and Stephen. Now Paul stands before it. A pagan officer summons the highest court of Israel. He has no authority over their religious business, and he issues the order anyway, and they come. The rulers of Israel are convened at the convenience of a Roman soldier trying to fill in a form correctly.

The whole way round the room. Look where the chapter has brought Paul. It opened with him telling the crowd that the high priest and the whole council could bear witness to what he used to be: that he had gone to them, received letters, and walked out of that chamber with authority to arrest Christians in a foreign city (v. 5). It closes with him standing before that same body, in Roman custody, as one of the people those letters were written against. The young man who left the council with warrants returns to it as the accused, and would not trade places with his younger self for anything in the world.

What does Luke want me to learn from all these trials? That the faith you hold is innocent of the charges brought against it. Again and again in Acts, Roman officials find that Christians have broken no law; they are opposed because of the gospel itself. That should give you courage. When Christianity is mocked as harmful or hateful, you need not be ashamed; examine the charge, admit any real faults in Christians, and then stand calmly, as Paul did, knowing that the truth will bear examination. And it should give you patience. God often vindicates his people slowly, through ordinary courts and slow procedures, rather than by lightning.

In a sentence. Those about to interrogate him backed away at once, and the commander was alarmed to realise he had put a Roman citizen in chains, and the next day, wanting to learn the real charges, he released him, ordered the chief priests and the whole council to meet, and brought Paul to stand before them.

On a Tuesday. God was moving Paul step by step toward Rome, through courts and councils, and he orders your steps too. If you are caught in a slow process, a legal case, an investigation, a long wait for a decision, commit it to him each morning and do the next right thing. The Lord who used a nervous tribune’s paperwork to move his apostle is not hindered by your bureaucracy.

For worship. The Lord sits above every council and every court. He summoned the Sanhedrin by the hand of a Roman officer, and he had already summoned Paul by the voice of his Son. Not one charge against his servant would stand, because the charge against him had already been answered at the cross. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). The one who was condemned by this council in the night stands now at the right hand of God interceding for us, and no court on earth can reverse his verdict.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

22.title: Paul's Defence Before the Crowd
22.text: <sup>1</sup>“Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.” <sup>2</sup>And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said: <sup>3</sup>“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. <sup>4</sup>I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, <sup>5</sup>as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. <sup>6</sup>“As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. <sup>7</sup>And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ <sup>8</sup>And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’ <sup>9</sup>Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. <sup>10</sup>And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’ <sup>11</sup>And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. <sup>12</sup>“And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, <sup>13</sup>came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. <sup>14</sup>And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; <sup>15</sup>for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. <sup>16</sup>And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ <sup>17</sup>“When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance <sup>18</sup>and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ <sup>19</sup>And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. <sup>20</sup>And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ <sup>21</sup>And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’” <sup>22</sup>Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.” <sup>23</sup>And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air, <sup>24</sup>the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. <sup>25</sup>But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” <sup>26</sup>When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” <sup>27</sup>So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.” <sup>28</sup>The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.” <sup>29</sup>So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. <sup>30</sup>But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.
22.overview:
From the steps of the Antonia Fortress Paul speaks to the crowd that has just tried to kill him. This is the second of three accounts of his conversion in Acts (9:1–19; 26:9–18), each shaped for its audience. Here, before a Jewish crowd and in their own language, he stresses how Jewish he is: trained under Gamaliel, zealous for the law, a persecutor of the Way; Ananias is a devout law-keeper; the God who called him is “the God of our fathers”; and his commission came in a vision in the temple itself.

The crowd listens until he says that the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. Then they explode. The tribune orders him to be examined under the lash, but as they stretch him out Paul asks whether it is legal to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen. The tribune, who bought his own citizenship, learns that Paul was born a citizen, and is alarmed. To find out the real charge, he summons the Sanhedrin the next day. Luke shows again that the real offence of Paul’s gospel is grace to the Gentiles, and that Roman law protects the messenger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Before the Sanhedrin and the Plot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul looks steadily at the council and says he has lived before God with a wholly clear conscience. The high priest Ananias orders those near him to hit him on the mouth. Paul retorts that God will strike him, the whitewashed wall: he sits to judge by the law, yet breaks the law by ordering him struck. When bystanders protest that he is insulting God’s high priest, Paul says he did not realise it was the high priest, for Scripture forbids speaking evil of a ruler of the people. Knowing that the council includes Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul calls out that he is a Pharisee, son of Pharisees, on trial over the hope of the resurrection. This splits the assembly, since Sadducees deny resurrection, angels and spirits, while Pharisees accept them. In the uproar some Pharisee scribes declare him innocent: perhaps a spirit or angel has spoken to him. The dispute turns so violent that the commander, fearing Paul will be torn apart, has soldiers snatch him back into the barracks. The following night the Lord stands beside Paul and tells him to take heart: as he has testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify in Rome. In the morning over forty men vow not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul. They ask the chief priests to request another hearing so they can ambush him on the way. Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and tells Paul, who has a centurion take the young man to the commander. Taken aside, the nephew explains the plan, and the commander sends him away with orders to tell no one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise That Does Not Remove the Danger

Acts 23:11 is the hinge of the second half of the book, and what makes it pastorally useful is as much what it withholds as what it gives. The Lord does not tell Paul he will be released, or comfortable, or vindicated. He does not mention the two years in Caesarea, the storm, or the shipwreck — all of which are still coming, and none of which is cancelled. He gives an assignment and guarantees its completion: you must testify also in Rome. The word is dei, Luke's word for divine necessity, the same word he uses for the sufferings of the Son of Man. Paul's arrival in Rome is now as fixed as the cross.

That is the Reformed doctrine of providence at work, and this chapter shows both halves of it. God ordains the end, and he ordains the means — and the means are startlingly ordinary: a boy who overhears something, an officer protecting his career, a duty roster. Paul believes the promise absolutely and immediately calls a centurion, exactly as he will later believe an angel's word that all aboard will live and then warn that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31). Certainty about the outcome does not make action unnecessary; it makes action possible without panic.

And the instruments need not be godly, or even willing. Claudius Lysias is a self-serving man who falsifies his own report. The Lord uses him unimproved, and he goes off shift with no idea what he has just done.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conspiracy of more than forty men, sworn under a self-curse, endorsed by the chief priests and elders, with the machinery of the Sanhedrin ready to supply the pretext — defeated by an unnamed young man who happened to hear something and had the nerve to walk across a city and say it out loud. He is never named, never mentioned again, and there is no tradition about him at all. Every consequence of Paul's Roman years runs through his afternoon.

Now: Very few Christians are given a Paul-sized life, and almost every Christian is at some point given the nephew's. You know something. You noticed something. You are standing near enough to do something, and you have about a minute to decide whether it is really your business. The thing that makes this hard is not courage in the heroic sense; it is that the action looks far too small to matter and you will almost certainly never be told how it turned out. He was ordered to keep quiet and sent home. Do it anyway. The size of the outcome has never been the measure of the obedience, and it is not usually visible from where you are standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And looking intently at the council, Paul said, 'Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.' And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth.

Meaning first. Acts 23 shows Paul before the Sanhedrin, the council that condemned Jesus. The trial collapses into a quarrel between Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection. That night the risen Lord stands by Paul and promises he will testify in Rome. Next morning, forty men vow to kill him; his nephew overhears; and the Roman tribune sends him under a guard of 470 soldiers to the governor at Caesarea. The chapter shows God’s promise kept through ordinary means: a boy’s ears, a soldier’s caution, a Roman letter. And at its centre stands the Lord Jesus himself, beside a bruised prisoner in the dark, saying the words that hold the rest of the book together: take courage.

And looking intently at the council. Luke chooses his verb carefully, and it is one he has used before in this very room. Atenizō means to fix the eyes on something and not look away. It is what the council did to Stephen when they saw his face like the face of an angel (6:15), and what Stephen did when he gazed into heaven and saw the Son of Man standing (7:55). Now the man who held the coats that day stands where Stephen stood, before the same body, and it is Paul who does the gazing. Steady, unafraid. He has stood in this chamber before, on the other side. He walked out of it once with letters authorising him to arrest Christians in Damascus (9:1–2; 22:5). Some of the older men in front of him will remember signing.

Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day. The verb is politeuomai: I have conducted myself as a citizen, lived as a member of God’s people. It is a public word, not a private one, and its root is the one Paul uses when he tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). He is not claiming a warm inner feeling. He is saying that his public conduct as a member of this people will stand inspection. A clear conscience before God (24:16; 2 Timothy 1:3). And he addresses them as equals: brothers, not rulers.

Is Paul claiming to be sinless? No, and he said so himself. He wrote that he was not aware of anything against himself, but that this did not acquit him, for it is the Lord who judges (1 Corinthians 4:4). That is the whole doctrine of conscience in two sentences: a clear conscience is a witness, and a witness is not a verdict. Paul knew he had persecuted the church, and called himself the foremost of sinners for it (1 Timothy 1:15), while also saying he had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13). Not sinless, then, but sincere then, and forgiven now. His claim is that he has not been playing a double game. Before his conversion he opposed Jesus because he thought it was obedience; after it he served Jesus for the same reason. There is no stretch of his life he is hiding.

And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. One sentence in, and he has not finished a second. No charge, no evidence, no witness, no verdict, and the presiding judge orders the defendant hit in the face. Striking an accused man before trial was illegal, as it was when Jesus was struck before the same office (John 18:22). Luke’s readers knew who gave the order. Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest from about AD 47 to 58. Josephus, no friend of Christians, records that he sent his servants to the threshing floors to seize the tithes that belonged to the ordinary priests, so that some of the poorer priests starved. He was violent, grasping, pro-Roman, and widely hated. When the revolt against Rome began in AD 66, Jewish rebels found him hiding in an aqueduct and killed him.

How do I know whether my conscience is really clear? A clear conscience is easy to counterfeit. It is not the same as feeling fine about yourself; anyone can feel fine with a low enough standard or a short enough memory. A conscience is only as good as what has taught it, so it must be trained by Scripture, not by your feelings or your culture (Hebrews 5:14). The practical test is Paul’s: is there anything in your life you would need to edit before it could be read aloud to the people you live and work with? Where there is, confess it to God, put right what you can, and receive his cleansing (1 John 1:9). And where your conscience still accuses you of what Christ has forgiven, remember that his blood purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).

In a sentence. Paul looked straight at the council and said he had lived before God with a perfectly clear conscience to this day, and the high priest Ananias ordered those near him to strike him on the mouth.

On a Tuesday. Live so that you can say: I have a good conscience before God. Take five minutes tonight and ask the Lord to show you anything running in your life that you would hide from the people in the next room. Then deal with it before you sleep.

For worship. The man struck on the mouth before this court was following his Lord. Jesus stood before the high priest of his day and was struck in the face for telling the truth, and he answered without sin. Every blow that fell on him fell for us, for all the guilty consciences we could never clear.
