verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him.

When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. Paul would be held here for two years (24:27), and from here he would sail for Rome. The order is correct and bureaucratic: paperwork first, then the man. Roman custody is a chain of documented handovers, and Luke records this one too. Paul has been in Caesarea before. He stayed on the way up in the house of Philip the evangelist, and it was there that Agabus took his belt and bound his own hands and feet (21:8–11). Everything Agabus said would happen has happened. Paul has been bound by the Jews in Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles, and he is back in the same city, in chains, as foretold.

They presented Paul also before him. One step closer to Rome. Paul is now, formally and finally, out of the council’s jurisdiction. From this verse to the end of the book he will be tried, guarded, transported and shipwrecked with Romans. The men who wanted him dead will have to travel to Caesarea and argue in a Gentile court, and they will lose. The high priest who had him struck in the mouth will next appear as a plaintiff, coming down in person with a hired advocate (24:1), and the advocate will lose too.

The men still waiting. Meanwhile, sixty miles away, forty men are still waiting on a Jerusalem street for a prisoner who has been gone since the previous night: hungry, under an oath they cannot keep, watching a road nobody is coming down. Luke never tells us what became of them. He simply left them a dozen verses back, waiting for a consent that never came.

A real loss and a door. About twelve days earlier (24:11) Paul had walked into Jerusalem hoping to be welcomed by the church and heard by his own people. He leaves under armed guard at night, rejected by his nation. It is a real loss, and Luke does not dress it up. But the door that shut behind him in the temple (21:30) turned out to be a door he was meant to be on the other side of.

In a sentence. When they reached Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.

On a Tuesday. Each step, even into custody, brought Paul closer to God’s purpose, and so with you. If a door has shut behind you, a job, a church, a relationship, a city, grieve it honestly. Then look at where you are standing now, and ask what God has brought you there to do.

For worship. The word of the Lord through Agabus came true to the letter, because the Lord’s word always does. Not one of his good promises has ever failed (Joshua 21:45). The servant who was handed over to the Gentiles walked the road of his Master, who was also handed over, and whose handing over became the salvation of Jew and Gentile alike. Paul came back to Caesarea in chains, and the chains were carrying the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.

He asked what province he was from. Felix’s first question is not about God, or the resurrection, or even the riot. It is a check on jurisdiction: is this case legally mine? Cilicia was then under the governor of Syria, Felix’s superior, so Felix could hear the case rather than pass it on; and since the accusers were from Judea, he kept it. A small procedural moment, and it decided where Paul would spend the next two years of his life.

I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive. Roman law required the accused to face his accusers (25:16). A reasonable ruling from an unreasonable man. He will hold the hearing, find nothing, and then leave Paul in custody anyway, partly to please the Jewish leaders, partly in hope of a bribe (24:26–27).

And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium. Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, by the sea, now the governor’s residence. Paul was a prisoner in a palace: not in a common cell, but held under guard in the governor’s headquarters, and later Felix would order that he have some liberty and that his friends be allowed to care for him (24:23).

The chapter from end to end. Look where the chapter has arrived. It opened with a man struck on the mouth by order of the high priest, in the supreme court of his own nation, before he had finished a sentence. It ends with him under guard in a Herodian palace by the sea, alive, formally recorded as charged with nothing, his accusers summoned to a Roman court, and the whole machinery of the empire slowly turning toward the place the Lord named in a barracks two nights before. And yet nothing is resolved. He is still a prisoner, well over a thousand miles from Rome, and two years are about to disappear in this palace: two years of a mission-driven man’s life with no journeys, no new churches, no visible fruit.

What do I do with long seasons of waiting? Hold both halves together, because this is where most Christian lives are actually lived. The promise is certain and the waiting is long. Paul did not waste his two years: he spoke with Felix and Drusilla about faith in Christ, received his friends, and was being prepared for Rome. Use your waiting the same way. Keep the means of grace, serve whoever is in front of you, pray for the work you cannot yet do, and refuse to call the time wasted. Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31). Waiting is not God’s absence from your life. It is often where he does his deepest work in you.

In a sentence. Felix read the letter, asked what province Paul came from, and learning he was from Cilicia, said he would hear his case when his accusers arrived, and ordered him kept under guard in Herod’s palace.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season of waiting, write down the one sentence from God’s word that you are standing on, and put it where you will see it each morning. Then do one useful, faithful thing today in the place where you are being made to wait.

For worship. Whether in a palace or a prison, Paul was in God’s hands, and so are you. Paul did not know that Luke would be with him, or that the voyage was coming, or that he would preach without hindrance in the capital of the world at the end of it. He knew one sentence, spoken in the dark by someone who stood beside him: take courage. On some days that is the whole visible foundation of a Christian life, and it holds, because of who said it. The Lord Jesus is faithful, and the one who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.note: Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, used as the governor’s residence.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.
23.overview:
Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, the council he once served. The hearing is a disaster as a trial and a triumph of providence. The high priest Ananias, a notoriously greedy and violent man, has Paul struck for claiming a clear conscience; Paul flares up, then apologises when told who gave the order, citing the law. Seeing the council split between Sadducees and Pharisees, he declares that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council dissolves into a shouting match, some Pharisees even defending him. The tribune has to rescue him a second time.

That night the Lord stands by Paul: he must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. Next morning more than forty men swear not to eat or drink until they have killed him, but Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and warns him, and the tribune sends Paul by night under an escort of 470 soldiers to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that states Paul has done nothing deserving death or chains. God’s promise is kept through a boy’s ears, a centurion’s errand and a Roman army. Paul is now in Roman custody, which will last more than four years and bring him, as promised, to Rome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five days later the high priest comes down with elders and a lawyer, Tertullus. After flattering Felix, Tertullus charges Paul with being a troublemaker who stirs up Jews everywhere, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and one who tried to desecrate the temple. The Jews back him up. Paul replies calmly: he went up to worship only twelve days ago and started no disturbance anywhere, and they cannot prove their claims. He admits that he worships the God of their fathers as a follower of the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and sharing their hope that God will raise both righteous and wicked; so he strives for a clear conscience. He came bringing gifts for the poor and was found in the temple ritually pure; the Asian Jews who caused the trouble are not even here, and the council found nothing except his cry about the resurrection. Felix, who knows about the Way, adjourns the case and keeps Paul under guard with some freedom. Later he and his wife Drusilla hear Paul on faith in Christ; when Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment, Felix grows afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. Hoping for a bribe, he often sends for him. After two years Festus succeeds Felix, who leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is the most quietly terrifying figure in Acts, because nothing about him is dramatic. He does not oppose the gospel. He is interested in it. He understands it accurately (v. 22), he sends for the preacher repeatedly (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him badly enough to end the meeting. He is the nearest thing in this book to a man under conviction — and he dies outside of Christ, so far as Scripture records, with nothing standing between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb. 3:15); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2). The reason is visible in this very chapter: Felix felt more at the first conversation than at any of the many that followed. Repeated exposure without submission does not keep the heart tender; it callouses it. The second hearing of a truth is always easier to survive than the first.

This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that conviction is not conversion. Felix's fear was real and it was the Spirit's work on his conscience — and a frightened conscience saves nobody. What God requires is not to be moved but to be surrendered. Grace is sovereign and grace is free, and the same doctrine that says no one comes unless the Father draws him says also that whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44). The only sane response to a conviction you can feel is to act on it while you can still feel it.

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast is the chapter's argument. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and settled to the point of cheerfulness (v. 10). One postpones; the other has already been told he must testify at Rome and simply waits. Circumstance is a poor guide to who in a room is actually at liberty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul was asked, by the man who could have freed him with a sentence, to speak about faith in Christ Jesus. He was a prisoner, entirely in that man's power, and the governor's known weaknesses were a court that could be bought and a wife he had taken from another man. Paul chose righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment. He did not trim one of the three, and he stayed in prison for two more years.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and nearly all of us will at some point have something true to say to somebody who holds an advantage over us — an employer, a relative whose goodwill we need, a friend whose reaction we fear. The pressure is not usually to lie. It is to select: to say the two things that will land well and leave out the third, and to call the omission tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and then ask why it is always the same one. Paul's three subjects took ten seconds to choose and cost him two years, and Luke thought them worth recording precisely because he did not shorten the list to two.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,

Meaning first. Acts 24 is Paul’s trial before the Roman governor Felix. A professional lawyer accuses him of being a plague and a ringleader of the Nazarenes. Paul answers calmly with facts: he caused no riot, he worships the God of his fathers, believes the Law and the Prophets, and hopes in the resurrection of the just and the unjust. Felix delays the verdict. Later, Paul speaks to Felix and his wife about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and Felix trembles, but sends him away to wait for a convenient time, which never comes. Paul stays in prison for two years. It is a chapter about two kinds of delay: a corrupt man putting off God, and God, who is never late, keeping his promise to bring his servant to Rome in his own time.

And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. Read that sentence as a measure of how badly they want this. Ananias is the high priest of Israel. Caesarea is sixty miles from Jerusalem, and it is a Gentile city, Herod’s showpiece, with a temple to Augustus on the hill. He goes anyway, with a delegation of elders, and he hires a professional. This is the man who a week ago ordered Paul struck on the mouth before he had finished a sentence (23:2). Now he has come down from the chamber where he was the law, to stand in a Roman hall as a plaintiff and pay an advocate to speak for him, because here his office counts for nothing. Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case in Roman legal style, perhaps a Greek-speaking Jew, or a Roman.

Since through you we enjoy much peace. Tertullus begins where every trained speaker began, with an opening designed to win the judge’s goodwill before a single fact is mentioned (the captatio benevolentiae). Flattery, the customary opening of a speech to a governor, and mostly false. Felix had governed Judea for about five years, and the province had rarely been less peaceful. He had crushed the revolt of the Egyptian prophet, the man the tribune took Paul for (21:38), and crucified rebels in numbers, but his rule provoked more unrest than it ended. Josephus records that he arranged the murder of the former high priest Jonathan, who had been urging him to govern better, by hiring assassins to mingle with a festival crowd. Under Felix the dagger-men became a fixture of Jerusalem life. Tacitus and Josephus describe him as cruel and corrupt, and the Jews later complained of him to Rome. So the high priest of Israel sits and listens while his paid advocate thanks a murderer for the peace. Luke writes the flattery out in full and adds no comment. Seven verses later he lets us hear Paul begin, and the difference between the two men is audible in their first sentences.

Why is flattery so dangerous? Because it is not a compliment but a transaction. It is offered because the flatterer wants something and judges that you will pay for it in goodwill. Felix took the payment. He let a delegation from a nation he had bled thank him for their tranquillity, and did not correct them. Scripture warns that a flattering mouth works ruin (Proverbs 26:28) and that a man who flatters his neighbour spreads a net for his feet (Proverbs 29:5). The deeper danger is to the one who swallows it. Every time we accept praise we know is false, we lose a little of our ability to hear the truth from anybody, including God. So give honest encouragement freely, but be suspicious of praise that is useful to the giver, and be most suspicious of the praise you most enjoy.

In a sentence. Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented their case against Paul to the governor, beginning with flattery about the peace and reforms Felix had brought.

On a Tuesday. Beware flattery, in giving and receiving it. Honest words are better than smooth ones: whoever rebukes a man will in the end find more favour than he who flatters with his tongue (Proverbs 28:23). This week, when you want something from someone, notice whether you reach for praise you do not mean. Say something true instead, or say nothing.

For worship. God cannot be flattered. He searches the heart and tries the mind (Jeremiah 17:10), and no smooth word has ever bought his favour. That is terrifying to the flatterer, and it is the best news in the world to the sinner, because the God who cannot be bought has given freely what no one could pay for. We do not win him with fine speeches. We come with nothing, and he receives us for the sake of his Son, whose mouth had no deceit in it and who never spoke a word he did not mean.
verseByVerse.note: Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case. Opening with flattery of the judge was standard courtroom style; Roman historians remember Felix’s rule as harsh and corrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.

In every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. More flattery, the last note of the opening.

But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. A formula so standard it was almost furniture: the promise of brevity, the appeal to the great man’s patience. Kindness (epieikeia) is gentleness, clemency, the quality of a judge who does not press the law to its harshest edge. Ironic, of Felix. Two sentences of praise, and then Tertullus turns and asks the court to destroy a man.

Respectable persecution. What is worth noticing is how ordinary it all is. There is nothing lurid about this machinery. No conspiracy in a cellar, no forty men under an oath; that failed. This is the second attempt, and it is entirely respectable: a lawful summons, a professional advocate, a formal hearing, correct procedure, courteous language. The forty assassins could not lay a finger on him. The lawyers very nearly did. Persecution rarely arrives dressed as persecution. It comes as a properly constituted committee, a correctly worded complaint, a hearing in the right tone by people who are unfailingly polite. Everyone in the room is behaving well. That is what makes it work. And Luke lets the other side’s best speaker go first, uninterrupted. A book nervous about its case does not do that.

We and I. One more thing before the charges land. Tertullus says we throughout: we accept this, we beg you, we have found this man. He is a hired speaker from outside the community, in the case a matter of days, and the we is a professional’s fiction. Paul, when his turn comes, will say I: I went up to worship, I take pains, this I confess. He has no delegation behind him and no advocate beside him. That is very often the shape of it. Opposition arrives as a body, with a spokesman and the comfort of numbers. Faithfulness usually has to be done in the first person singular, by someone standing up alone.

What should I do when I have to stand alone for Christ? Remember that you are not as alone as it feels. Paul had no advocate in that hall, but he had the Lord’s word from the barracks (23:11), and later he would write that at his first defence no one came to stand by him, all deserted him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). When you are the only one at work, in your family or in your class who will speak for Christ or refuse to join in wrong, speak calmly, speak for yourself, and do not pretend to a crowd you do not have. Then find fellowship afterwards: tell your church, ask for prayer, and let others stand with you next time.

In a sentence. Tertullus said they gratefully welcomed this in every way and everywhere, and asked Felix kindly to hear them briefly so as not to weary him.

On a Tuesday. Truth needs no flattery; speak plainly and honestly. And watch for wrong that comes dressed in good manners: the polite email, the well-run meeting, the reasonable policy that quietly sets someone up to be harmed. Courtesy is a virtue. It is not a proof of innocence.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was tried this way too: by respectable men, in proper session, with witnesses and procedure, and condemned. He stood alone, with no advocate, while his friends fled. And because he stood alone for us, we never stand alone again. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), who pleads for his people in the highest court of all, and whose case has never once been lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.

For we have found this man a plague. The flattery is over and the indictment lands. There are four charges, and the construction is expert. First, the man himself. Plague (loimos): pest, pestilence. A personal attack. Not this man is troublesome, but this man is a disease. It is the language you use of something to be stamped out rather than answered, and it is always the first move: before you can do something terrible to a man, you have to stop describing him as one.

One who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world. Second, sedition, the political charge: the most serious accusation before a Roman governor, under an emperor nervous of Jewish unrest. The word for riots is stasis, insurrection, civil disorder. Rome did not much mind what you believed; it minded a province that would not stay quiet. And notice the reach: throughout the world. And here is what makes the charge so hard to answer: it is built on a true fact with a false cause attached. Riots really did follow Paul: at Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Ephesus, and the temple days ago. Tertullus takes that pattern and reverses the arrow: trouble happens where Paul goes, so Paul makes the trouble. Whether the preacher is the arsonist or the man who turned the lights on is exactly the question the charge is built to skip.

And is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. Third, the sect. Ringleader (prōtostatēs) is the man in the front rank of the line. Sect (hairesis) means a party or school, like the Pharisees or Sadducees (5:17; 15:5); it does not yet mean heresy in the later sense, but here it suggests an unlicensed splinter group. Nazarenes: followers of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish name for Christians, still used for them in Hebrew and Arabic. It is the only time in the New Testament that Christians are called this, and it is meant as a sneer: the followers of a nobody from nowhere, from a village that prompted the question whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46).

The name heaven answers to. Which is the truth, and it is glorious, and no one in that hall had the faintest idea. The carpenter’s town is the address heaven answers to. The risen Lord named himself by it from the middle of a light that outshone the noon sun: I am Jesus of Nazareth (22:8). Men still use it as an insult. He wears it as a name.

He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. Fourth, the temple: the religious charge, and false (21:28–29). It is the one charge with teeth in both legal systems, since Rome allowed the Jews to execute even a citizen for going beyond the barrier. It is also the charge that has quietly shrunk. In the temple it was a flat assertion that he had brought Greeks in and defiled the place (21:28). Here it is that he tried. They have had days to find a witness, and the charge has already begun to soften. And we seized him is a polite description: they were trying to kill him.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verses 7–8 that they would have judged him by their own law, but Lysias took him away with violence. It is probably a later addition, shifting the blame onto Lysias. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts lack it, and it looks like a scribe’s attempt to explain how Paul came to be in Roman custody. Notice the irony in what it says: it has Tertullus complain that Lysias snatched Paul out of their hands with great violence, when their hands were at that moment beating him to death (21:31–32). A scribe’s tidying accidentally records the prosecution’s view of a rescue: how dare the Romans stop us.

What should I do when Christians are called a danger to society? First, check whether there is any truth in it, and repent of it where there is: Christians have sometimes deserved criticism. Then answer calmly, with facts, as Paul is about to do. Peter told believers to keep their conduct among unbelievers honourable, so that when they speak against them as evildoers, they may see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). Notice that the gospel does disturb things: a quiet town gets loud when the light is turned on, because sin does not like to be seen. That is not the same as causing a riot. Do not be ashamed of disturbing darkness; be ashamed only of disturbing it unlovingly.

In a sentence. Tertullus said they had found Paul a troublemaker who stirred up riots among the Jews all over the world, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, who even tried to desecrate the temple, so they seized him.

On a Tuesday. Followers of Jesus may be called a plague; let your life prove the charge false. Be the kind of neighbour, worker and citizen about whom slander will not stick: honest, kind, peaceable, generous. And be careful of the language you use about people you oppose. If you would not say it about them to their face, or to God, do not say it at all.

For worship. They called his people Nazarenes as an insult, and he made it a crown. The Lord of glory chose the despised village, the despised manger, the despised cross, so that no one could ever boast before him (1 Corinthians 1:28–29). Every insult thrown at his name has only shown how low he stooped to save us. And one day the same name they sneered at will be the name before which every knee bows: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, Lord of all.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7 a complaint that Lysias had taken Paul away by force. “Nazarenes” was a name for Jesus’ followers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.

A verse with no number. Open an ESV at this page and you will notice that the text runs from verse 6 to verse 8. That is not a printing error. The verse numbers in our Bibles are not part of Scripture; they were added in 1551 by a Paris printer, Robert Estienne, working from the Greek text then available, which was based on late manuscripts. Far older copies have been found since, and they lack the words that once made up verse 7. Translators follow the older evidence but keep the old numbering, so that four centuries of commentaries and cross-references still work. The result is a number with nothing under it. You meet the same thing at 8:37 and 15:34, and will again at 28:29.

Does this mean the Bible is unreliable? No, it shows the opposite. We can see where a line entered the text precisely because we have so many manuscripts, thousands of them, from many centuries and countries, more than for any other ancient book. Scholars can lay them side by side and see exactly where a copyist’s explanation crept in. Nothing in the Christian faith depends on any of these few disputed lines. And notice what the translators do with them: they print them in a footnote in your own Bible, where you can read them. A book with something to hide does not publish its own variants for the ordinary reader to check. God has preserved his word, and he has also given his church the means to see where human hands added to it.

By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him. That is the genuine verse 8, and it is the shrewdest sentence in the speech. Confident, but empty. Tertullus has charges and no witnesses. They offered none, and Roman law required evidence. So he does what an advocate does when the evidence is thin: he hands the work to the judge. Examine him yourself, you will find it all out. It sounds like confidence. It is the opposite. And Luke leaves an irony lying in the open. Tertullus’s advice was taken. Felix did examine Paul, often, over two years (v. 26). What he found out was not sedition. He got a sermon on righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, and it frightened him out of the room.

In a sentence. Tertullus said that by examining Paul himself, Felix could learn the truth of all their charges.

On a Tuesday. Accusations without evidence are cheap; do not believe everything you hear. When someone tells you about another person’s wrongdoing and says you can see for yourself, ask what they actually saw. And when you are tempted to accuse, ask whether you could produce a witness, or only a feeling.

For worship. The Lord has kept his word through every century of copying, and he has let us see the care with which it was handed down. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand for ever (Isaiah 40:8). Scribes have come and gone, and printers, and translators, and the word of the Lord remains, unbroken, in our hands. And the one who examines all hearts is not like Felix. When he examines his people, he finds them clothed in the righteousness of his Son, and nothing is left on the charge sheet.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so.

The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. The delegation backed Tertullus. Everyone agrees, and that is the whole of their contribution: agreement. Luke’s word is a legal one, joining in the attack, piling on. It has the flavour of a crowd rather than a witness list.

Consensus is not evidence. A courtroom is one of the few places that insists on the difference, and ordinary life almost never does. Not one of the men affirming this was in the temple court when Paul was seized. The people who were there, the Jews from Asia who started the riot, are not in the room, and Paul is about to say so (v. 19). So Felix is offered a chorus: respectable men, including the high priest, all saying yes, it is so, and no one who saw anything. Many voices do not make a lie true. Almost everything we believe about people we have never met reached us this way: not from someone who saw it, but from several people who say the same thing. And the agreement feels like confirmation, when very often it only means they all heard it from the same place.

Sincerity is not innocence. There is one more layer, the saddest in the verse. These men are probably not lying the way a criminal lies. Most of them likely believe every word. They have been told by people they trust that Paul is an apostate who defiles the temple, and they have arrived at their conclusion the way most of us arrive at most of ours: by inheriting it from a source they never checked. A man can be entirely honest and entirely wrong, and do great damage while behaving well throughout. Paul knew that better than anyone in the room. He had once held these exact convictions, with a clear conscience, on the road to Damascus with warrants in his bag.

How do I avoid joining in when everyone around me agrees about someone? Ask the courtroom question: who actually saw it, and where are they? If the answer is nobody, or someone who is not here, then you do not know it, however many people are nodding. Refuse to add your voice to a charge you cannot verify. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), and it also refuses to multiply rumours. Where there is a real concern, the right course is to go to the person, or to those with proper responsibility, not to the crowd (Matthew 18:15–17). And if you discover you have joined in unfairly in the past, put it right with the person you wronged.

In a sentence. The Jews joined in, affirming that all this was true.

On a Tuesday. The next time a group conversation turns to someone who is absent, say something true and kind about them, or ask gently whether anyone has heard their side. One sentence can stop a chorus.

For worship. Jesus was accused by many voices too; he knows how it feels. False witnesses rose against him, and their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56), and still the council affirmed that all these things were so. He stood silent before the chorus, and was condemned, so that the true accuser of our souls, whose charges against us were not false, would have nothing left to say. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,

And when the governor had nodded to him to speak. No advocate stands up for Paul. He has no Tertullus. A nod from the bench, and a prisoner in chains begins to speak for himself.

Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. Set that beside the speech that has just finished, because the contrast is the point. Felix had been in office for several years, about five or six. Paul’s opening is respectful and true, without flattery. There is not a word about peace or foresight or reforms. What he offers is a single sentence of real courtesy that happens to be entirely true, and relevant: he is glad to answer to someone who knows Jewish affairs and can actually weigh a Jewish religious dispute. So Paul shows that respect and honesty are not in competition. There is a way to address a powerful and corrupt man that neither grovels nor postures, and it consists mostly of refusing to say anything untrue.

Cheerfully. The word is euthymōs: in good spirits, confidently, with a settled heart. Consider who is saying it. This is his third hearing in under a fortnight. He has been beaten by a mob, chained, nearly flogged, targeted by a murder plot, moved sixty miles under armed guard at night, and he is standing in a Gentile hall listening to the high priest of Israel pay a man to call him a plague. And he is in good spirits. That is not temperament. A week before, the Lord stood by him in the dark and said take courage, and told him he would testify in Rome (23:11). A man who knows the assignment holds can afford to be cheerful in a courtroom, because the courtroom is not what decides.

You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem. Facts that can be checked: Paul starts with arithmetic, because arithmetic can be verified. Count the days on the record: the arrival and welcome, the meeting with James the next day, the purification, the arrest toward the end of the seven days, the council, the night march, the arrival at Caesarea. Interpreters count the twelve days slightly differently, but either way the point is the same. Set that number against the charge of stirring up riots among all the Jews throughout the world: he has been in the country a week and a half, and the governor’s own staff can confirm every day of it. Not much time to start a worldwide riot. And notice the last words: to worship. Not to organise or agitate, but to keep a feast and bring gifts to the poor.

How should I answer someone who attacks my faith? Like Paul: calmly, respectfully and factually, with gentleness and respect, as Peter says, keeping a good conscience (1 Peter 3:15–16). Do not flatter your opponent and do not sneer at him. Begin, where you can, with something true you can honestly acknowledge. Then answer the actual charge, not a different one, with facts that can be checked. Do not be rattled if you cannot answer everything; it is fine to say you will think about it. And remember that the outcome does not rest on your performance. Your Lord has his own purposes for the conversation, and you are free to be cheerful in it.

In a sentence. When Felix nodded for him to speak, Paul said that knowing Felix had been judge over this nation for many years, he gladly made his defence, and Felix could check that it was no more than twelve days since he went up to Jerusalem to worship.

On a Tuesday. When defending your faith, be calm, respectful and factual. Before your next hard conversation, ask what you can honestly say that is respectful to the other person, and say it first. Then say what is true, plainly.

For worship. Paul could be cheerful in the dock because the Lord had spoken to him, and the Lord had spoken because he is the Lord of every courtroom. The judges of the earth sit by his permission and rise at his word. He does not need his servants to win their cases; he needs them only to be faithful, and he will see to the rest. That is why a prisoner can face a governor in good spirits. The one who said take courage has never yet failed to keep what he promised.
verseByVerse.note: Felix had been in office for several years.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.

They did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Point by point, Paul denies the sedition charge, and he does it with a list of places. Not in the temple. Not in the synagogues. Not anywhere in the city. He names every place where an agitator would have had to be seen agitating, and invites them to produce one person who saw it.

Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. No evidence. This is the hinge of the whole defence. Under Roman law, the burden of proof was on the accusers, and an accuser who brought a charge he could not sustain might himself be liable. Paul is not asking for mercy or the benefit of the doubt. He is pointing at an empty table and asking the court to notice that nothing has been put on it.

A faith that asks to be examined. There is something bracing in the plainness of it. Paul does not begin with theology. He begins with: bring the evidence. Christianity has never asked to be exempted from that question, and it should never want to be. The faith is a set of claims about things that happened in public: a man executed under a named governor, a tomb found empty, witnesses who could be questioned and were. Paul’s own summary of the resurrection appearances says that most of the five hundred were still alive and could be asked (1 Corinthians 15:6). That is not the language of a religion that wants to be taken on trust.

Can a Christian always demand proof when accused? Only if he is innocent. The honest edge of this verse cuts both ways. Paul can say prove it because there is nothing to find. A Christian accused of something he has actually done may not hide behind procedure, and a church may not hide wrongdoing, especially abuse, behind lawyers, silence or a concern for reputation. The church has sometimes done exactly that and brought the name of Christ into disgrace. The right to say prove it belongs only to the one who could survive the investigation. If you are guilty, the Christian path is confession, repentance and making things right (Proverbs 28:13), not a clever defence.

In a sentence. No one had found him arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd in the temple, the synagogues or the city, and they could not prove their charges.

On a Tuesday. Live so that no charge against you can be proved. Paul’s defence in this court rests on a life lived so that an investigation would be boring. Ask what an honest auditor would find in your finances, your messages, your browsing history and your dealings this year, and begin putting right anything you would not want found.

For worship. There was once a prisoner of whom it could be said with perfect truth that no charge against him could be proved, because there was nothing to find. Pilate said it three times: I find no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). And yet he was condemned, because he had come to bear charges that were true, ours, and to answer for them in full. Paul could stand innocent before Felix only because he was already standing righteous before God in the innocence of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.

But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers. Here the defence stops being legal and becomes testimony, and Paul marks the change with one word. Confess (homologeō) is the verb for openly acknowledging what you believe, the word the New Testament uses for confessing Christ before men. He has spent four verses saying you cannot prove that. Now he says: but here is what I gladly admit, and I will say it louder than you did. Paul admits one thing: he follows the Way. He will not accept their word for it, a faction, a splinter group. Nor will he deny the reality behind it. Yes, this is the Way, and yes, he belongs to it, and no, it is not a breakaway. Not a new religion, but the fulfilment of the old. The same God: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not an import from Greece. Paul is telling a Roman court, in front of the high priest of Israel, that the man in chains is the one worshipping Israel’s God rightly.

Believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets. Everything, not the parts that suit him. This answers the rumour that started all the trouble in chapter 21, that he taught Jews to forsake Moses. He believes more of the book than his accusers, not less, and the difference is not that he has subtracted anything but that he has seen it arrive. Paul held to the whole Old Testament: we uphold the law (Romans 3:31). The Christian faith is the true reading of the Old Testament, which points to Christ. That is the sentence to hold on to whenever someone suggests Christianity is a departure from the Old Testament. Paul’s position is not that the Law and the Prophets have been discarded. It is that they have been kept.

Having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept. The Pharisees did, at least. Note the generosity: he grants his accusers their orthodoxy on this point. On the resurrection hope they are together, and he says so in open court instead of scoring a point.

That there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. Then he adds the phrase nobody asked for. This is the only place in Acts where Paul spells out that the resurrection is not only for the righteous. A clear statement of the general resurrection. It is Daniel’s vision: many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (Daniel 12:2). And it is the Lord’s own teaching: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29). Everyone will be raised: the righteous to life, the wicked to judgment. Why say it here, to a governor who has asked nothing about the last things? Because Felix is listening. A few verses later, in private, Paul will reason with him about the coming judgment, and Felix will be afraid. The charge was laid in open court, dressed as a point of Jewish doctrine. It goes off later, in a private room, in the governor’s conscience.

Where Christians differ: the resurrection of the unjust. Some teach that the wicked will simply cease to exist (annihilationism), or never be raised. Verdict: Paul says both the just and the unjust will rise. Jesus says some to eternal life, and some to eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 5:29). The wicked are raised to stand before God and face conscious, eternal judgment. This is the historic Christian teaching, sobering and true.

What will the resurrection body be like? For believers, Scripture says it will be our own body, raised and transformed: the same person, but imperishable, glorious, powerful, and fitted for the life of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The risen Jesus could be touched, ate fish, and still bore his wounds, so our future is not a ghostly existence but real, bodily life in a renewed creation. Until then, believers who die are with the Lord, conscious and at rest (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The unjust will also be raised bodily, to stand before God. That is why the question is never whether you will rise, but what you will rise to.

In a sentence. Paul confessed that he worshipped the God of their fathers as a follower of the Way, which they called a sect, believing everything in the Law and the Prophets, and hoping in God, as they did, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

On a Tuesday. Everyone will rise. Are you ready to rise to life? Most people asked about life after death say something warm. Very few have taken in the second half of Paul’s sentence. Take it in today, for yourself, and then for one person you love who does not yet know Christ. Pray for them by name, and look for a way to tell them.

For worship. Consider the God whose hope this is. He had been the God of the fathers for nearly two thousand years when Paul spoke in that hall, and he had not changed his mind, lost the thread, or grown tired of the promise. He spoke to Abraham about a family and to Daniel about the dust waking, and he kept every word, and the keeping of it was a grave outside Jerusalem that could not hold what was put in it. The God of the fathers is the God of the empty tomb. The hope of Israel and the risen Christ are not two things, and no court in the world has jurisdiction over either.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, and some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,

So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. So: because of the coming resurrection and judgment. The hope of judgment shapes how we live. Take pains (askeō) is the athlete’s word: to train, exercise, work hard at something by discipline and repetition, the root of our word ascetic. Paul is not describing a placid temperament. He is describing a practice. A clear conscience is usually imagined as something you either have or do not, like a good night’s sleep. Paul treats it as something you build, daily, the way a runner builds a season: by keeping the accounts short. When something goes wrong with God he deals with it; when something goes wrong with a person he deals with that too. He says toward both God and man because he knows that people try to settle the first while leaving the second standing. A clear conscience toward God and people (23:1). He has not retreated from the claim that got him struck on the mouth. And it is the quiet foundation of his whole defence: Paul can invite investigation because he has spent more than twenty years making sure there would be nothing to find.

How do I keep short accounts with God and others? Each day, at its end, ask the Lord to show you where you have sinned, and confess it specifically, not vaguely (1 John 1:9). Then ask whether anyone needs an apology or a repair from you, and do it soon, before it hardens. Jesus said that if you remember at the altar that your brother has something against you, you should go first and be reconciled, then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:23–24). Pay what you owe. Return what you borrowed. Correct what you said that was untrue. None of this earns God’s forgiveness, which is free in Christ. It is how a forgiven person lives, and it keeps the conscience tender instead of calloused.

Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28). Paul came with gifts, not trouble. It dominates his letters: he organises it in 1 Corinthians 16, gives it two chapters in 2 Corinthians 8–9, and tells the Romans it is why he is going to Jerusalem at all. It was the great project of his later ministry, money carried across the empire by Gentile Christians to show that the church was one body and not two. And this is the only time Acts mentions it, in a single clause, in a courtroom.

Half a line. Luke’s silence is its own lesson. For Paul the collection was years of letters, careful negotiation and personal risk. For Luke it is a subordinate clause. Much of the work that costs a Christian most is recorded nowhere, summarised by someone else in half a line, and known in full only to God. And there is a bitter irony in it. He came to bring money to the poor, and it is why he stands in the dock. The mention of alms in open court may well have been the moment a thought entered Felix’s head, because two verses from the end of the chapter we learn what the governor really hoped for: that money would be given him by Paul (v. 26).

In a sentence. Because of this hope, Paul said, he always tried to keep a clear conscience before God and people, and after several years away he had come to bring gifts for the poor of his nation and to offer sacrifices.

On a Tuesday. The coming judgment should make you careful with your conscience; keep short accounts with God. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing to God that needs confessing, and one person who needs a word from you. Then deal with both before the week is out.

For worship. Every hidden labour of love is seen by the Lord. Paul’s years of work on the collection got half a line in Acts, and every coin of it was counted in heaven, where the Lord keeps the record of cups of cold water and widows’ mites. He is not unjust so as to overlook our work and the love we have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10). And he gave more than alms: he gave himself. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Paul wrote that sentence to raise this very collection.
verseByVerse.note: The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.

They found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. Ritually pure, not profaning the temple. Every word of that dismantles a charge. They accused him of profaning the temple: he was purified, in the middle of the very rites that prove it. They accused him of stirring up riots: there was no crowd and no tumult until his accusers created one. The prosecution’s picture of the scene has been quietly reversed. Paul was standing in a holy place, having completed a purification he paid for himself, when men from Asia pointed at him and started shouting.

But some Jews from Asia, they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. The sentence breaks off: Paul changes direction mid-flow, and what he says next is the sharpest legal point of the speech. The men who actually saw the alleged offence, the Jews from Asia who recognised him, assumed he had brought Trophimus past the barrier, seized him and raised the shout (21:27–29), are not in the room. Absent. Roman law expected accusers to appear in person, and abandoning a charge you had raised was itself an offence. A legal weakness in the prosecution. Paul is saying, in effect: the people who made this accusation have dropped it, and the men standing in their place saw nothing. And notice the fairness of his phrasing: should they have anything against me. He does not call them liars. He says: if they have a case, let them come and make it. That is the confidence of a man who would rather be examined than excused.

What if someone has a complaint about me but will not say it to my face? You cannot force them, and you are not bound to answer charges that no one will own. But you can make it easy to be honest with you. Let it be known that you welcome direct correction, and when you hear second-hand that someone is unhappy, go to them gently and ask whether you have wronged them (Matthew 5:23–24). If they will not speak, commit the matter to God and keep your conscience clear. And refuse to treat anonymous accusations against others as established, especially in church. Scripture requires charges to be brought openly, on the evidence of witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19), and a church that acts on whispers will soon be ruled by them.

In a sentence. They found him ritually purified in the temple, with no crowd or disturbance, but the Jews from Asia, who should be present to accuse him if they had anything against him, were not there.

On a Tuesday. Those who accuse should be willing to face the accused; follow Matthew 18 in your disputes. Almost every damaged reputation has been damaged by an accusation whose source never appeared. Ask the only question that matters, and the one almost nobody asks: where is the person who actually saw it, and why are they not here?

For worship. The Lord is the God who brings everything into the light. Nothing whispered in the dark will stay hidden, and every accuser will one day face the Judge in person (Luke 12:2–3). For his people this is comfort, not terror. The accuser of the brothers, who accuses them day and night before our God, has been thrown down (Revelation 12:10), and when he brings his case, there is an advocate in the room who has already answered every charge with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law expected accusers to appear in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’

Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council. Having disposed of the absent witnesses, Paul turns to the men who are present. You were at the council a week ago; you have first-hand knowledge of that hearing; tell the governor what crime you established. Ask the council: they found nothing. It is a dare, and a safe one, because he knows exactly what happened there: it collapsed into a brawl between Pharisees and Sadducees and never reached a finding.

Other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them, It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day. The one real issue: the resurrection. Paul keeps bringing it back to the centre (23:6; 26:8). And this settles a question the reader may be carrying from the last chapter. When he shouted that line in the council, it looked to some like a manoeuvre, a clever man splitting his enemies. Here is the answer. A week later, before a governor who cannot be split and a delegation who cannot be provoked, with nothing to gain by repeating it, he repeats it, and offers it to the court as the one accurate summary of the whole case. A trick is something you use once and quietly drop. Paul will say it again before Festus and Agrippa (26:6–8), and to the Jewish leaders of Rome at the end of the book: it is because of the hope of Israel that he wears this chain (28:20). It was never a tactic. It was the truth, and it happened to be a truth that broke the room.

The charge sheet reduced to one sentence. Tertullus brought sedition, sect-leading and temple desecration. Paul has answered each and reduced the case to one question: are the dead raised? He has, in effect, told a Roman governor that the whole proceeding is a religious dispute about the resurrection, and that he has no jurisdiction over that. If Jesus rose, everything changes. That is a theological question, not a crime. Paul is right, and Felix knows it, which is exactly why the next thing that happens is not a verdict.

Why is the resurrection, and not something else, the heart of the matter? Because it is God’s verdict on Jesus. The cross by itself might have been the death of one more good man. The resurrection declares that the man who died was the Son of God (Romans 1:4), that the sacrifice was accepted and our justification secured (Romans 4:25), and that he now reigns as Lord and Judge, for God has given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead (17:31). Every other Christian truth rests on it. That is why apologetics in Acts keeps coming back to the empty tomb, and why your faith can too. When you are unsure what to say, say this: Jesus rose from the dead.

In a sentence. Otherwise, let these men say what crime they found when he stood before the council, apart from his one statement that he was on trial over the resurrection of the dead.

On a Tuesday. Keep the resurrection at the centre; it is what Christianity stands or falls on. This week, in your prayers and your conversations, come back to it: Christ is risen. Let it shape how you think about your work, your losses, your body and your death.

For worship. The only crime Paul could be charged with was believing that God raises the dead, and of that he was gloriously guilty. So are we. The tomb outside Jerusalem is empty, and the Lord of life holds the keys of Death and Hades. He was dead, and behold, he is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). No court can try that fact, and no power can reverse it. Every believer who has ever died is waiting on it, and on the last day every grave will hear his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs.

Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way. Luke’s aside is easy to skim, and it is the key to the man. The phrase is a comparative (akribesteron), more accurately, and it means Felix understood the Christian movement better than the people arguing before him. He knew more than they thought: perhaps from his Jewish wife, or from Christians in Caesarea, where Philip lived (21:8) and where Cornelius had believed years before. This governor knew who the Nazarenes were, knew they were not insurrectionists, and could see that the prosecution had produced no evidence. He knew Paul was innocent. And he did nothing.

Put them off, saying, When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case. A delaying tactic. He does not convict Paul, because he cannot. He does not release him, because that would cost him with the Jewish leaders. Felix did not want to offend the Jews by releasing Paul, nor break Roman law by condemning him. So he finds a third option, one of the most recognisable moves in human affairs: he asks for more information. It sounds like diligence. It is a formula. Lysias never came, as far as we know, and there is no sign that anyone sent for him. The adjournment was not a step toward a verdict but a substitute for one.

The sin that does not look like sin. This is the sin of the chapter, and it does not look like a sin at all. Felix is not cruel to Paul. He is scrupulously reasonable. He simply declines to act on what he already knows, and dresses the refusal in procedure, and because the procedure is real, nobody can accuse him of anything. Most of us are far more likely to fail this way than any other. Not by deciding against the truth, but by finding a legitimate reason to postpone deciding for it. There is always one more person to consult, one more thing to consider, one more sensible reason why now is not the moment. Felix invented nothing. He just never got round to it, on purpose, for two years.

He should be kept in custody but have some liberty. Light custody. The word for liberty (anesis) means a loosening, a relaxing of the conditions. Paul is not in a dungeon. He is held under guard in the governor’s headquarters.

And that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. Prisoners relied on friends for food and care. Luke and others probably visited. And consider what the arrangement made possible. For two years Paul is in one place, in a provincial capital, with time and free access to his companions. Luke had a Gospel to research, in a country full of people who had been there: Philip in the same city, the believers of Caesarea, anyone who could reach the coast. Some think Luke gathered material for his Gospel during these two years. Scripture does not say so, and we should not state it as fact. But the two years were not blank, and the God who gave a discouraged prisoner an open door and a doctor for company was doing something, even while the governor was doing nothing.

Is it wrong to want more information before making a big decision? No; wisdom often requires it, and Scripture commends the one who hears before he answers (Proverbs 18:13). The question is whether you are gathering information in order to decide, or in order not to. Felix already knew enough. When you notice that the facts are clear and you are still asking for more, that the right course is plain and you are still consulting, ask honestly what you are afraid it will cost you. Then name the cost before God, and decide. This applies above all to the call of Christ himself. You do not need one more argument to believe him. You need to stop postponing.

In a sentence. Felix, who knew the Way well, adjourned the case, saying he would decide when Lysias came, and ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard but give him some freedom and let his friends take care of his needs.

On a Tuesday. Knowing the truth and delaying a decision is a dangerous place to be; do not be a Felix. Name one thing God has made plain to you that you have been putting off: an apology, a confession, a step of obedience, a conversation. Set a day this week, and keep it.

For worship. Felix knew the Way accurately and did not walk in it. Our God is never like that. He does not know the right thing and delay it. He spoke, and it came to be; he promised, and he performed. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4), not a day early and not a day late. And the Lord who stood by Paul in the barracks was already using the governor’s cowardice to give his servant rest, friends and time. Even our delays are in the hands of a God who is never slow.

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.”

Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. Luke names her, and the name carries a history that makes the next verses almost unbearable. Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the king who killed James with the sword and was struck down in this very city for accepting the shout that he was a god (12:1–23). She was about six years old when it happened. Her brother was Agrippa II and her sister Bernice, and both will walk into this same palace in the next chapter to hear this same prisoner. Her great-grandfather was Herod the Great, who ordered the children of Bethlehem killed. She was about twenty. She had been married to Azizus, king of Emesa, and Josephus records that Felix, wanting her, used a Cypriot magician to persuade her to leave her husband and marry the governor instead. The Roman writer Suetonius calls Felix the husband of three queens. A marriage built on adultery, in a court where justice was for sale.

And heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. Curiosity, perhaps. They sent for the prisoner because they would like to hear him on the subject. It was a request for an interesting evening. What they got was the next sentence.

And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment. Three subjects. Look at who is in the room, because this is the most precisely aimed sermon in Acts. Paul did not soften his message for the powerful. Righteousness (dikaiosynē), which is both the character God requires and the justice a judge is meant to give: preached to a corrupt, unjust governor who was at that moment hoping the defendant would offer him a bribe (v. 26). Self-control (enkrateia), mastery of one’s appetites: preached to a couple in an adulterous marriage, with the woman he had taken from another man sitting at his side. The coming judgment: preached to a man who judged others and had never seriously considered being judged. Paul is a prisoner. Felix can hold him without charge, and does. And Paul looks at the man who owns his freedom, and at the marriage everyone at court had agreed not to mention, and preaches. The gospel addresses the conscience, and calls for repentance. Paul preached to Felix’s life, not just his mind.

Why did Paul begin with judgment, not with good news? He was asked to explain faith in Christ Jesus, and this is how he did it. It is not how most of us would begin with a governor. But it is how the New Testament habitually begins with the comfortable and the powerful: with God’s standard, our failure to meet it, and the day it will be assessed. There is no good news in a pardon until there is bad news in a verdict. A man who does not know he is condemned will not value a Saviour. That does not mean every conversation must start with hell; Paul began differently in Athens (17:22–31). It means that the gospel always includes the truth about sin and judgment, and that loving people means telling them, gently and plainly, before it is too late.

Felix was alarmed. Alarmed (emphobos): filled with fear, terrified. This is not irritation or intellectual disagreement. The governor of Judea, in his own palace, with his own soldiers outside the door, listening to a man in chains, became frightened. Nothing in the room had changed. No sign was given, no miracle done. A prisoner talked, and the word of God found the conscience of a man who had buried it, and he could not sit still under it. The Spirit was convicting him, as Jesus said he would convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8).

Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you. The most dangerous words a person can say to the gospel. A convenient time, as older translations put it. He was genuinely under conviction, and he postponed, and as far as Scripture records, the convenient time never came. There is no record that he ever repented. The opportunity was then. Conviction delayed is conviction deadened, and the convenient season for repentance almost never arrives by itself. The Bible’s word is always now: today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Hebrews 3:15); now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

What should I do if I feel convicted but not ready? Do not wait to feel ready; you never will. Conviction is God’s mercy, the Spirit showing you your need of Christ, and it is meant to drive you to him now, not to be managed until it fades. You do not have to understand everything or fix your life first. Come to Christ as you are: confess your sin to him, ask him to forgive you for his death’s sake, and trust him to receive you, for he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Then take the next step he shows you: talk to a pastor or a Christian friend, open the Bible, begin to obey. The only wrong response is Felix’s: later.

In a sentence. Some days later Felix came with his Jewish wife Drusilla, sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus, but as Paul talked about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, That is enough for now; when I find it convenient I will send for you.

On a Tuesday. If God is speaking to your conscience, do not say later. Respond today. And if you are the one speaking to others, ask whether you have been softening the truth for the powerful or the people you want to please. Love tells the truth about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and then tells of the Saviour.

For worship. Paul could preach judgment to a governor without fear, because the judgment to come holds no terror for those in Christ. The Judge has already borne the sentence for his people. He who knew no sin was made sin for us, and the wrath Felix trembled at fell on the Son of God, so that all who trust him will stand on that day without condemnation. That is why the coming judgment is, for the believer, the coming of the one who loved us and gave himself for us. Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
