At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. Luke gives the real reason, and it is squalid. A bribe. Taking bribes for releasing prisoners was illegal but common, and Felix had reason to think it possible: he had heard Paul mention in court that he had come bringing alms for his nation (v. 17), and perhaps thought Paul had wealthy friends. A man who can carry a relief fund across the empire can presumably find a purse for a governor. Paul never paid. That silence is worth a moment. A payment would have been the easy and obvious thing, arguably even reasonable, since the imprisonment was unjust and everyone knew it. Two years of his life were on the other side of the scale. He did not do it. There are things a servant of Christ cannot buy his way out of without ceasing to be one.

So he sent for him often and conversed with him. Many conversations, no conversion. Felix heard the gospel repeatedly, not once, over two years, from the best explainer of it who ever lived, in private, free to ask whatever he wanted. Very few people in the New Testament had that, and it did him no good, because he was never listening for the answer; he was listening for an opening. Felix heard the gospel many times and was hardened, not softened. Hearing without heeding hardens. That is the anatomy of a hardening heart, and it is not what people expect. Felix did not reject the gospel once and walk away. He kept coming back, interested, curious, even entertained, and each conversation left him a little less able to feel the fear he had felt the first time. Familiarity with holy things is not the same as being changed by them, and it insulates far more people than open hostility ever has. It is possible to attend church for forty years the way Felix attended these conversations.

Can I have heard the gospel too many times? You can have heard it many times without obeying it, and that is a dangerous place to be, because the heart grows used to what it resists (Hebrews 3:13). But as long as you still care about the question, the door is open. The cure for familiarity is not to stop listening but to start obeying: to stop treating sermons as interesting and to ask, each time, what God is telling you to do, and then do it. If you have grown up hearing the gospel and it has never moved you, pray honestly for a new heart, which God alone can give (Ezekiel 36:26). He delights to answer that prayer.

When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in office about two years later. Felix was recalled to Rome after violent clashes in Caesarea between Jews and Gentiles, which he had put down brutally. Two years, and Luke gives it a clause. Measure it against what the Lord had said. In the barracks at Jerusalem, at the lowest point of Paul’s life, the risen Christ stood over him and said take courage, you must testify also in Rome (23:11). Days later Paul was in Caesarea. And then nothing happened for some seven hundred and thirty days. No trial, no verdict, no release, no visible movement toward Rome. The most fruitful missionary in history, in the prime of his working life, with churches round the Aegean needing him and a promise from the Lord in his pocket, sat in a provincial palace while a corrupt official waited for an envelope that never came.

And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison. Political convenience over justice. Two years in prison, unjustly. Felix’s last recorded act is his most characteristic. On his way out of office, with nothing to gain and no case to answer, he chose one last time to keep an innocent man in custody as a parting gift to people he had spent years mistreating. It did not work. Josephus records that the Jewish leaders of Caesarea went to Rome to accuse him anyway, and that he escaped punishment only through his brother Pallas’s influence at court. He sold his integrity, and did not even get the price.

Why does God let his people wait so long? These two years are in the Bible for everyone who has been given a word from God and then handed a long stretch of nothing. The honest question is not whether God keeps his promises but what they feel like from inside the waiting. Paul did not know he had two years. He only knew he had today, and then another one. And the promise had not weakened by a syllable. Delay is not decay. God is not slower than his word (2 Peter 3:9), and a promise sitting apparently idle is not going stale. It is being carried by someone who does not need to hurry and never forgets. What looked from the cell like silence was the Lord of history arranging a governor’s recall, a successor’s ambition, an appeal to Caesar, and a ship. These years were not wasted: perhaps Luke wrote his Gospel; certainly Paul prayed; and God was keeping him safe for Rome.

In a sentence. Felix also hoped Paul would offer him a bribe, so he sent for him often and talked with him, and when two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, but wanting to please the Jews, he left Paul in prison.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a long wait, a job that will not come, a prayer not yet answered, an injustice not yet put right, do not buy your way out by compromise. Keep your integrity, keep praying, and do the faithful thing in front of you today. Write down the promise of God you are standing on, and read it each morning until he moves.

For worship. God can use years of unjust waiting; we can trust him in ours. He let Joseph sit in an Egyptian prison for years, forgotten by the cupbearer, until the day he was raised to save his family. He let his own people wait centuries for the Messiah, and then sent him in the fullness of time. And he let his Son lie in the tomb until the third day, not a moment longer. The Lord is not slow as some count slowness. Every hour of Paul’s two years was in his hand, and so is every hour of ours, and at the end of the waiting there is always a ship, and Rome, and the face of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in 62. Paul had been in custody at Caesarea for two years.

24.title: Paul Before Felix
24.text: <sup>1</sup>And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. <sup>2</sup>And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation, <sup>3</sup>in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. <sup>4</sup>But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. <sup>5</sup>For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. <sup>6</sup>He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. <sup>8</sup>By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.” <sup>9</sup>The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. <sup>10</sup>And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. <sup>11</sup>You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem, <sup>12</sup>and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. <sup>13</sup>Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. <sup>14</sup>But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, <sup>15</sup>having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. <sup>16</sup>So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. <sup>17</sup>Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. <sup>18</sup>While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia— <sup>19</sup>they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. <sup>20</sup>Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, <sup>21</sup>other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’” <sup>22</sup>But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” <sup>23</sup>Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. <sup>24</sup>After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>25</sup>And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” <sup>26</sup>At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. <sup>27</sup>When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
24.overview:
Five days after Paul reaches Caesarea, the high priest arrives with elders and a hired advocate, Tertullus, who opens with lavish flattery of Felix and then brings three charges: Paul is a public menace who stirs up Jews across the empire, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a would-be desecrator of the temple. Paul answers calmly, point by point. He went to Jerusalem to worship only twelve days ago and caused no disturbance anywhere; the accusers cannot prove their claims. He admits only that he worships the God of the fathers according to the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and hoping, as they do, for the resurrection of both righteous and wicked. He came bringing alms, was found ritually pure in the temple, and the Asian Jews who started the trouble are not even present.

Felix, who knows a good deal about the Way, adjourns the case. Over the following two years he and his Jewish wife Drusilla summon Paul repeatedly. When Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment to come, the governor, notorious for cruelty and for taking another man’s wife, becomes afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. He also hopes for a bribe. When he is recalled, he leaves Paul in prison to please the Jewish leaders. The chapter is a portrait of a man who heard the gospel often and put it off.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days after arriving in his province, Festus goes up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. The chief priests and Jewish leaders present their charges against Paul and press him, as a favour, to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, planning to kill him on the way. Festus answers that Paul is held at Caesarea and he himself will soon return there; their leaders can come and accuse him if he has done wrong. After about ten days he goes back, takes his seat in court the next day and has Paul brought in. The Jews from Jerusalem surround him with many serious charges they cannot prove. Paul declares he has done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar. Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks Paul whether he will go to Jerusalem for trial. Paul answers that he is standing before Caesar’s court, where he should be tried, and he has done the Jews no wrong, as Festus well knows. If he deserves death he will not refuse to die, but if the charges are empty, no one may hand him over to them: he appeals to Caesar. After consulting his advisers, Festus replies that to Caesar he shall go. Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrive to welcome Festus, who tells the king about the prisoner Felix left behind. The Jewish leaders wanted him condemned, but Roman custom requires that the accused face his accusers and defend himself. When they came, their charges were not the crimes he expected, but disputes about their religion and about a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claims is alive. Unsure how to investigate, Festus offered a trial in Jerusalem, but Paul appealed to the emperor. Agrippa says he would like to hear the man, and Festus promises he shall, tomorrow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Lawful Means and the God Who Uses Them

Paul's appeal to Caesar settles a question Christians still raise: may a believer use the legal protections available to him, or is that a failure of faith? Acts answers plainly. Paul had a promise from the risen Christ that he would testify at Rome (23:11), and he used a statutory right to get there. Faith in the promise did not make the appeal unnecessary; it made the appeal obvious. The same man who was told every soul aboard the ship would survive still warned that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31).

Providence does not bypass means. It employs them, and it is content to employ thoroughly unspiritual ones — a citizenship registry, a governor's ambition, an emperor's court, and a bureaucrat's need to fill in a form correctly. God ordains the end and he ordains the road, and the road here runs through Roman administrative procedure.

Two guards. First, the lawfulness of the means does not sanctify the motives of those who supply them: Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, is doing what Felix did, and Luke uses the identical phrase so the reader will not miss it. Second, God's certain purpose does not cancel real injustice. Four officials find no crime and Paul stays in chains. Scripture never asks anyone to pretend that the second fact is softened by the first. They are simply both true, and the Christian lives in the overlap.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Festus described the Christian faith to a king with complete accuracy and total detachment — a dispute about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. He had identified the hinge of the entire religion. He could have passed an examination on it. And it never crossed his mind that if it were true it might concern him personally; it was a fact about somebody else's people.

Now: This is the particular danger of a life spent near the things of God. Anyone raised in a believing home, or twenty years in a pew, or halfway through a theology course, can state the resurrection more accurately than Festus did. The question the governor puts to such a reader is not whether the doctrine is held correctly. It is whether it has ever once been allowed to be about him. Say the sentence out loud — a certain Jesus, who was dead, and who is alive — and notice honestly whether anything in you moves. Festus said it in passing and moved on.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,

Meaning first. Acts 25 brings a new governor, Festus, and the same old plot. The Jewish leaders want Paul brought to Jerusalem so that they can ambush him on the road. Festus refuses, holds a hearing in Caesarea, and then, wanting to please the Jews, suggests a trial in Jerusalem. Paul, knowing what that means, uses his right as a Roman citizen: I appeal to Caesar. And so the Lord’s promise begins to be fulfilled: he will testify in Rome. Then King Agrippa arrives, and Festus, who finds Paul’s case to be about “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive,” asks the king to hear him. The chapter is full of powerful men making decisions for their own reasons, and through every one of them the risen Christ is moving his servant exactly where he said he would.

The setting. Paul has now been in custody at Caesarea for two years (24:27). Caesarea was the Roman capital of Judea, a harbour city on the coast built by Herod the Great, about sixty miles north-west of Jerusalem. Felix, the governor who kept Paul waiting in hope of a bribe, has been recalled to Rome, and Porcius Festus has arrived to replace him, around AD 59. Festus would die in office about two years later, and within six years of this chapter the province would be in open revolt against Rome. He was taking over a difficult posting, and he knew it.

Three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem. Three days. The new governor lands, and inside seventy-two hours he is on the road to Jerusalem. That tells you what he had been told about the posting. He was taking over from a man who had been recalled to answer for his conduct, in a province that was already smouldering. He does not spend a fortnight settling in. He goes straight to the city that matters and introduces himself to the people who can make his term ungovernable. A new governor visiting the religious centre to meet its leaders: wise politics. And they are ready for him.

And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul. Stop and measure that against the calendar, because it is the most striking thing in the verse. Two years have passed. Two full years since the riot in the temple, since the forty men swore their oath, since Felix first heard the case and did nothing. Governments have changed. The high priest who ordered Paul struck has himself been replaced. Everyone involved has had seven hundred days of other business. And Paul is still the first item on the agenda: not one of several matters raised with the incoming governor, but the thing they came to say.

Two years from two sides. Set the two facts side by side, because Luke has. For Paul, two years of nothing whatever happening. For his enemies, two years of unbroken attention. The same stretch of time in which the prisoner saw no progress at all was, on the other side of the wall, a period of sustained and patient diligence. That is worth knowing about opposition, and it is not comfortable. Hatred keeps long accounts. It does not need fresh provocation to stay warm, it survives changes of personnel, and it will still be there when the new man arrives. Most of us cannot sustain a good intention for a fortnight; a grudge will run for years on nothing at all. The verb Luke uses for what they do to Festus means to press, to urge with insistence. They are not filing a complaint. They are lobbying, on day three, before the man has unpacked.

Is chief priest the same as high priest? Not quite. The high priest (singular) was the one supreme religious officer of Israel, the single man who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement (such as Caiaphas, or Ananias at Paul’s hearing before Felix). The chief priests (plural) were the wider circle of leading priests, the priestly aristocracy who ran the temple: the serving high priest, former high priests (who kept the title and influence even after Rome deposed them, which is why Annas is still called high priest in Luke 3:2), the heads of the few wealthy high-priestly families from whom high priests were chosen, and senior temple officers like the captain of the temple and the treasurers. So the high priest sits at the very top, and the chief priests are the powerful establishment gathered around and beneath him (mostly Sadducees; see 5:17). It is this priestly ruling class that appears again and again in the Gospels and Acts as the ringleaders against Jesus and his apostles.

Why was Paul left in prison for two years if he was innocent? Because Felix wanted money from him and favour from the Jewish leaders (24:26–27), and an untried prisoner cost him nothing. It was a real injustice, and Luke does not pretend otherwise. But the two years were not empty. Paul’s friends were allowed to visit and care for him (24:23), and it is very likely that Luke, who was with him, used this time to gather the eyewitness accounts behind his Gospel (Luke 1:1–4). God’s delays are never wasted time, even when they are someone else’s sin.

In a sentence. Three days after arriving in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem, where the chief priests and the Jewish leaders presented their case against Paul and pressed him with their request.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether there is anyone you have been carrying a grievance against for months or years, not acting on it, simply keeping it current and refreshing it whenever the subject comes up. Hatred does not forget; it is one of the most faithful things in a fallen heart. Bring it to God by name, and begin to pray for the person’s good. And if you are the one who has been waiting a long time with nothing seeming to move, remember the other side of this verse: your enemies are not the only ones who have not forgotten you.

For worship. Hatred keeps long accounts, but the Lord keeps longer ones, and his are accounts of love. For two years the men in Jerusalem never lost sight of Paul, and for two years the Lord never lost sight of him either. He who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. The prisoner whom the chief priests remembered with malice was remembered by the risen Christ with a purpose, and the purpose was Rome. Blessed be the God whose memory of his servants is older, deeper and more patient than every grudge against them.

verseByVerse.quote: "asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.

Asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem. The word is charis, a favour, a kindness. It is the same word the New Testament uses for the grace of God, and here it is used in its everyday sense, the ordinary currency of Roman public life: you do this for me now, and I am in your debt, and one day you will find that useful. They are not making a legal argument. They are opening an account with the new governor, a favour to start his term well.

Because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. Luke, who has been letting the scene play out straight, cuts in with the truth in a subordinate clause. Notice what he has done to us as readers. Festus does not know this. He is a competent official listening to a reasonable-sounding request from the religious leadership of the province, and there is nothing on the face of it to refuse. We know it is a murder plot. We watch him weigh a request whose real content is hidden from him and visible to us.

The same trap twice. This is the second time this trap has been laid. Two years ago more than forty men bound themselves under a curse to eat nothing until Paul was dead, and asked the council to request exactly this: a transfer to Jerusalem, with an ambush on the road (23:12–15). It failed because a boy overheard it. Whether these are the same men, Luke does not say. What he does say is that the plan is unchanged. Two years of failure has not produced a rethink, only a fresh attempt on a fresh governor. The oath-takers presumably ate long ago; the intention outlived the oath.

Respectable men. There is something worth facing in that. It is easy to picture the people who wanted Paul dead as monsters, and they were not. They were religious men, respected men, who over two years quietly kept a murder on the agenda and learned to think of it as the defence of God’s honour. Religious leaders, still planning murder. Nobody arrives there in one step. You arrive by a series of small permissions, each one granted to yourself on the grounds that the cause is good. The Lord warned his disciples of exactly this: the hour would come when whoever killed them would think he was offering service to God (John 16:2).

Does this mean the Jews as a people were against Paul? No. Luke is describing a particular group of leaders, the priestly establishment and those around them, not the Jewish people as a whole. Paul himself was a Jew, as were Jesus, all the apostles and thousands of believers in Jerusalem (21:20). Paul loved his people so much that he could wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake (Romans 9:1–3). Christians have sometimes read passages like this as permission for contempt toward Jews, and that is a grievous sin. The lesson of this verse is not about one nation’s wickedness but about what religious people of any nation can become when they decide that their cause justifies anything.

In a sentence. They asked him, as a favour, to have Paul transferred to Jerusalem, for they were planning to ambush and kill him on the way.

On a Tuesday. Watch the moment when you begin to say that the cause is good enough to excuse the method. It may be a small thing: a half-truth told to protect the church’s reputation, a piece of gossip passed on because the person really is a problem, a rule bent because the outcome matters. These men would have said they were defending the temple. It is remarkable what a settled hatred will agree to call itself. Name the thing honestly before God, by its real name.

For worship. Men plot, but God overrules, and the ambush on the Jerusalem road never happened. The Lord sits in the heavens and laughs at the counsels of those who set themselves against his anointed, and he guards those who belong to his anointed with the same unhurried power. Forty men could not do it two years ago, and the whole priestly establishment cannot do it now, because the life of Christ’s servant is in Christ’s hands and his work is not yet finished. No weapon formed against him shall prosper until the Lord himself says it is time to come home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. 'So,' said he, 'let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. “So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.”

Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea. He says no. And he says it for entirely the wrong reason, which is the point. Festus is not protecting Paul. He has never met Paul. What he is protecting is his own jurisdiction: the prisoner is in Roman custody in the provincial capital, the governor’s court sits there, and a new administrator does not begin his term by handing a prisoner over to a local council that has asked for him as a personal favour. That is not mercy. It is a man declining to be managed in his first week. Perhaps it was simple Roman procedure; but behind it stands the protection of God.

Let the men of authority among you go down with me. The offer is fair, and it is also inconvenient. If they want this case heard, they must travel: sixty miles, down from the holy city to the Gentile administrative capital, to argue in a Roman hall on Roman terms. He will hear them. He will not come to them.

And if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him. A fair procedure, and with it the ambush is dead. Not discovered, not defeated, simply bypassed, because the road Paul was to be killed on is now a road he will not travel.

Providence through procedure. Count how often this has happened. A tribune’s fear after binding a Roman citizen (22:29). A boy who happened to overhear something (23:16). A Roman rule about where a case must be heard. Three times now Paul’s life has been saved by ordinary institutional machinery operated by men with no interest in him at all, and not once has anyone in the story known they were doing it. This is the doctrine of providence at its least romantic and most reassuring. God is not confined to working through people who are willing. He works through procedure, through self-interest, through a bureaucrat defending his own patch. The men of authority will make the journey because a governor stood on protocol, and the killers on the Jerusalem road will wait for a prisoner who is not coming.

Does providence mean I will always be kept safe? No, and Scripture is honest about it. The providence protecting Paul here is the same providence that did not protect Stephen, or James, whom Herod killed with the sword while Peter walked out of prison past the guards (12:1–11). God’s care is real, and it is not a guarantee of safety. What it guarantees is that nothing will cut short the work he has assigned you, and that whatever does come will be made to work for your good (Romans 8:28). Paul had been told, in a barracks in Jerusalem, that his work included Rome, so the road to Jerusalem could not be the end of it. Your own times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15), whether they are long or short, and you are immortal until your work is done.

Should I pray for officials who are not Christians? Yes, and this passage shows why. Paul tells Timothy to pray for kings and all who are in high positions, so that believers may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and he wrote that when the emperor was Nero. God uses ordinary, unbelieving officials to restrain evil and protect his people, often without their knowing. Pray by name for your local councillors, your judges, your police and your national leaders: that they will be fair, honest and wise, and that they will come to know Christ.

In a sentence. Festus answered that Paul was being held at Caesarea and that he himself was going there soon, so their leaders should come down with him and bring charges if the man had done anything wrong.

On a Tuesday. Think of an ordinary rule or process in your life this week that protected you without your noticing: a safety regulation, a fair procedure at work, a law that kept someone from taking advantage of you. Thank God for it specifically. And if you hold any office, however small, in which you apply rules to other people, apply them fairly and without favour. You may be the instrument by which God keeps someone from harm, and you may never know it.

For worship. The Lord reigns over the paperwork of empires. He is the God who can save by many or by few, by an angel opening a prison or by a governor who prefers his own courtroom, and he is as fully at work in the second as in the first. Not a sparrow falls without the Father, and not a prisoner is transferred without him. How safe are those who are hidden in the hand that holds the whole machinery of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: "After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove.

After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days. Pause on that odd little phrase, because it is a small mark of a truthful book. Eight or ten days: Luke does not know exactly, and he says so. A writer inventing a narrative rounds the number and moves on; a writer working from testimony writes down what he was told, including the vagueness. The New Testament is full of these unhelpful details, and they are one of the quiet reasons to trust it.

The next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. The tribunal is the bēma, the raised judgment seat. There is no delay, unlike Felix. Festus is prompt, and he is formal. Everything is being done properly.

The Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him. Luke’s verb means they stood around him, encircling him. It is a physical detail and a deliberate one. This is a courtroom, and the accusers have arranged themselves round the defendant the way the mob did in the temple court, surrounding and intimidating. The setting has changed; the posture has not.

Bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. This phrase has become the refrain of these chapters: many, serious, unproven, the same as before (24:13). Two years, and still no evidence. Look at the strategy in those words, because it is one of the oldest there is and it has never stopped working. They cannot establish a single count. So they bring many, and they make each one grave. The hope is not that any particular charge will survive examination. The hope is that the sheer accumulation will do what no individual accusation can: that twenty unproven things will feel, to a listening judge, heavier than one unproven thing.

No smoke without fire. And it very often does, because that is how the mind naturally works. We are built to treat volume as evidence. Twenty complaints about a man sound like a pattern even when not one of them can be substantiated, and the reasonable-sounding conclusion, there is no smoke without fire, is precisely the error the courtroom exists to prevent. This is worth taking personally, because it is how nearly every damaged reputation is actually built. Rarely by one provable offence. Almost always by an accumulation of unprovable ones, each too small to challenge, none ever tested, all of them together forming an impression that no one can source and no one can refute. Roman law had an answer to it, and the answer is the whole of Paul’s defence: they could not prove it. Say what you can establish, or say nothing.

What should I do when someone tells me several bad things about another person? Ask the question Roman law asked: what can actually be shown? Do not let the number of stories stand in for evidence. Ask the speaker whether he has gone to the person himself (Matthew 18:15). Refuse to pass the stories on. And if you have a responsibility in the matter, insist on hearing the person accused, face to face, before you form a view; Scripture requires two or three witnesses before a charge is accepted (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19). Many charges cannot make a lie true.

What if I am the one being accused of many things I cannot disprove? Do what Paul did. Answer what can be answered, plainly and without bitterness, and leave the rest with God. You cannot chase down every rumour, and trying to will consume you. Keep doing what is right, so that those who speak against you are put to shame by your conduct (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Tell a trusted elder or friend what is happening so that you are not alone with it. And remember that the Lord Jesus was surrounded by false witnesses whose testimony did not even agree (Mark 14:56), and he entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

In a sentence. After eight or ten days with them, Festus went down to Caesarea, and the next day convened the court and had Paul brought in, and the Jews from Jerusalem stood around him bringing many serious charges they could not prove.

On a Tuesday. Before you repeat anything negative about anyone this week, ask yourself one question: could I prove it? Not, have I heard it, or does it sound like him, but could I establish it before a fair judge? If not, let it stop with you. And if you have been believing something about someone because many people have said it, ask whether anyone has ever actually shown it.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth does not count accusations; he weighs truth. Before his throne the accuser of our brothers stands day and night with charges that are many and serious, and some of them are true, and still he cannot make them stand, because Christ Jesus is the one who died and was raised, and who is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34). Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Rest there, in an innocence that is not your own and cannot be taken from you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul argued in his defense, 'Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.”

Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense. One sentence. It is the shortest defence Paul makes in the whole book, and after two years and four hearings the brevity is itself an argument: there is nothing new to answer, so he will not pretend there is. But it is not casual. Look at the three headings, because they are exhaustive: three charges, three denials, religious and political.

The law, the temple and Caesar. The law of the Jews: the charge that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses, which started the riot in chapter 21 and was never true. The temple: the charge that he brought a Gentile past the barrier, which has been shrinking steadily since it was first shouted, from he did it, to he tried, to nothing anyone will testify to. Caesar: and this one nobody in the room had formally raised today. That third heading is the interesting one, and Paul puts it there deliberately. Tertullus had called him a plague who stirred up riots throughout the world (24:5), which is sedition in all but name, and Paul knows that the charge which matters in a Roman court is the political one. So he does not wait to be accused of it. He names it himself and denies it flatly, in front of the man whose entire job is to keep this province quiet.

His Master before him. The same three kinds of charges were brought against Jesus, who was said to be misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be a king (Luke 23:2), and against Stephen, who was accused of speaking against the holy place and the law (6:13). The servant is not greater than his master. Paul is walking a road that was walked first by the Lord he serves, and the false charges against him are an echo of the false charges against Christ.

The shape of a clean answer. There is a lesson in the shape of the answer. Paul does not argue that the charges are unkind, or that his accusers are hypocrites, or that he has been badly treated, all of which were true and none of which is relevant. He addresses the actual counts, in the actual categories the court recognises, and he stops. A man with a clear conscience can afford to be brief. He is not managing an impression; he is answering a question.

Did Paul still keep the law of Moses as a Christian? He kept it among Jews, freely, for the gospel’s sake, but not as the ground of his acceptance with God. He circumcised Timothy (16:3), took part in a temple vow (21:26), and kept the feasts, because he chose to become as a Jew to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). He never taught Jews to abandon their customs. What he denied was that keeping the law could justify anyone (Galatians 2:16), and that Gentile believers had to become Jews to be saved (15:1–11). So his denial here is entirely honest: he had broken neither the law nor the temple’s rules, and he had never been disloyal to Rome.

In a sentence. Paul defended himself, saying he had done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar.

On a Tuesday. Christians should be good citizens, honouring God and the authorities he has set over them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Live so that if someone did draw up three charges against you, at work, at home and before the law, you could answer each in one honest sentence. Give no one a just charge against you. And when you are criticised, answer the actual point, briefly and truthfully, without turning it into a speech about how badly you have been treated.

For worship. There was once a prisoner who could have said, with perfect truth and in every possible court, that he had committed no offence of any kind: not against the law, not against the temple, not against Caesar, not against God. He said almost nothing, and they condemned him anyway, and he went to the cross bearing the offences of others. Paul could stand clear before Festus because Christ had stood condemned before Pilate. Glory to the spotless Lamb, whose innocence is now the robe of every guilty sinner who trusts him.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, 'Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?' But Paul said, 'I am standing before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor. Luke has used that phrase before, almost word for word. The last governor left office desiring to do the Jews a favour, and left Paul in prison to do it (24:27). Pilate before him, wishing to satisfy the crowd, handed Jesus over to be crucified (Mark 15:15). Now the new man. Festus is everything Felix was not: energetic, prompt, procedurally clean, on the road within three days, on the tribunal the morning after his return. He is, by any ordinary measure, a better official. And within two weeks Luke files him under the same sentence: politics over justice, a new governor wanting a good start with the people he must govern.

The problem with power. That is a bleak and accurate observation, and it is worth stating plainly. The problem was never Felix’s laziness. The problem is that a man whose position depends on the goodwill of people who want an innocent man dead will find a way to give them something, and he will not experience it as corruption. He will experience it as being reasonable.

Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me? Notice how mild the form of it is. Festus does not order Paul to Jerusalem; that would be indefensible. He asks. Before me, he says: it will still be my court, my authority, my verdict. What he is proposing is a change of venue that sounds like a courtesy and would in fact put Paul on a road where men are waiting to kill him, and into a city where the Sanhedrin would effectively decide the case. Festus does not know about the ambush. But he does know he is offering to move a prisoner into the reach of people who have been demanding him for two years, and he is doing it because it would be convenient. Paul knew what awaited.

I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. Paul’s answer is legally exact, and it closes the door. A provincial governor’s court was not an alternative to Caesar’s authority; it was Caesar’s authority, delegated. Festus represented Caesar. Paul is saying: I am a Roman citizen and I am already in the correct court. There is no higher Jewish jurisdiction over a Roman citizen charged with offences against Rome, and moving me to Jerusalem would not be a procedural adjustment; it would be an abandonment of the very jurisdiction you are exercising.

To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. And then he says it to the governor’s face. The phrase is stronger in Greek than it looks in English: you know perfectly well, you know better than that. Paul is not appealing to Festus’s sense of justice. He is telling a Roman governor, in open court, in front of the men who want him dead, that the governor is aware of the truth and is manoeuvring anyway. Bold, and respectful, and plain.

Knowledge without consequence. Paul could have said the same of Felix, and Luke told us Felix had a rather accurate knowledge of the Way (24:22). Two governors in two years, both of whom knew, and neither of whom did anything with the knowing. That is the danger this whole section quietly circles. Not ignorance. Knowledge held without consequence: the settled human capacity to see clearly what is right and to route around it, politely, for reasons that will sound perfectly sensible when you explain them later.

Is it wrong to want to please people? Not in itself. Paul tried to please everyone in everything for the sake of their salvation (1 Corinthians 10:33), and we are told to please our neighbour for his good (Romans 15:2). The sin is pleasing people at the cost of truth or justice, when their approval matters more to us than God’s. Paul’s own test was sharp: if I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). The question is never whether others are pleased, but whether, to please them, you are doing what you know to be wrong.

How do I speak truth to someone in authority over me? As Paul did here: respectfully, plainly and briefly. He did not insult Festus, raise his voice or accuse him of corruption. He simply stated the facts and named what Festus already knew. Address the person with the honour due to his office (1 Peter 2:17), speak to the specific issue, avoid exaggeration, and do not threaten. Then leave the outcome with God. Courage and courtesy are not opposites; in the mouth of a Christian they belong together.

In a sentence. Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asked Paul if he would go up to Jerusalem to be tried before him there, but Paul said he was standing before Caesar’s court, where he ought to be tried, and that he had done the Jews no wrong, as Festus knew very well.

On a Tuesday. Think of a decision in front of you this week where you already know what is right, and where doing it will disappoint someone whose goodwill you need. Notice the reasonable-sounding arguments forming for the other course. Ask yourself the Festus question: am I doing this because it is right, or because it will please the people I have to work with? Then do the right thing, and say it kindly.

For worship. Every earthly judge is under pressure to please someone, and the Lord Jesus is under pressure from no one. He judges not by what his eyes see or his ears hear, but with righteousness and equity (Isaiah 11:3–4). He cannot be lobbied, flattered or bought; no favour moves him, and no crowd sways him. The governor knew the truth and routed around it. Christ is the truth, and he never once turned aside from it, not even when it led to a cross. How good it is to stand at last before a Judge who is also the Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: "'If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.' Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, 'To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”

If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. Before the appeal, the offer, and the order of the two matters enormously. Paul does not begin by claiming his rights. He begins by submitting his neck. If I have done something capital, execute me; I am not asking for a way out. Paul accepts the state’s right to punish real crime, even with death. Only then, having conceded that the court has the right to kill him if the charge stands, does he point out that no charge stands. That is not a debating tactic. It is the difference between a man defending himself and a man defending the truth. He is not trying to escape justice; he is trying to stop an injustice, and he says so by putting his life on the table before he says anything else.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong. Verdict: Paul here accepts that some crimes deserve death and that the state may impose it, as he teaches in Romans 13:4 (the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain), grounded in Genesis 9:6. The state has the God-given right to punish grave crimes, including with death, though it must do so justly, with due process and certain guilt. Christians may disagree on when it is wise to use it.

But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. Not even the governor, as a favour. The verb for give up is the verb for granting a favour: no one can make me a present to these men.

I appeal to Caesar. The Latin was provocatio ad Caesarem, and it was one of the oldest and most jealously guarded rights a Roman citizen had: the right to have his case lifted out of a provincial court and heard by the emperor himself. Understand what it did, because it explains the rest of the book. Once the appeal was made it could not easily be refused, and from that moment the governor had lost the case. He could no longer convict, and in practice he could no longer acquit or release. His remaining duty was to forward the prisoner to Rome with a written statement of the charges. This is why Agrippa will remark, at the end of the next chapter, that this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (26:32).

Did Paul make a mistake? No. And the reason is not legal but theological. It was settled two years earlier in a dark barracks in Jerusalem, when the Lord stood by him and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Paul is not gambling. He is holding a promise, and he has just been handed the only legal mechanism in the Roman world that guarantees delivery: to Rome, at the state’s expense, under guard. Paul used his rights wisely, and God used them to send him where Jesus promised.

Which Caesar. Note also who the Caesar is. This is around AD 59, and the emperor is Nero, at that point still in the early years that Roman writers themselves regarded as good government, before the fire, before the persecution in which Paul would die. Paul appeals to an emperor who has not yet become the monster he became. He goes to Rome under the protection of the man who will eventually kill him.

To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go. Festus, when he had conferred with his council, gives the formula. The Greek fronts the name both times, and so does the ESV. It is final, and Festus means nothing by it beyond the discharge of a legal duty after a short consultation with his advisers. He may even have been relieved. And it is the promise of the risen Christ, ratified by a pagan magistrate who has no idea what he is saying. Two years earlier the Lord Jesus told a beaten and discouraged man that he would testify at Rome. Nothing had moved since. And now the word comes back to him out of the mouth of a Roman governor, in a legal formula, with the full weight of the empire behind it: to Caesar you shall go. Heaven’s purpose and Rome’s procedure say the identical sentence, and only one of the two speakers knows what is happening.

How the Lord governs the world. Not usually by suspending it, but by running it. He does not need to overrule the courts; he holds the whole apparatus, the statutes and the precedents and the consultations of the council, and it delivers his servant to the city he named. The kings of the earth take counsel together, and their counsel is his instrument (Psalm 2:2–4; Acts 4:27–28). He who sits in the heavens is not anxious about a provincial docket, and every decree signed against his people has, so far, only ever moved the gospel further down the road.

Using lawful rights. Worth pointing out: it is entirely right for a Christian to use his lawful legal rights. Paul, an apostle, does so without a flicker of guilt. Here he appeals to Caesar; earlier he invoked his Roman citizenship to stop an illegal flogging (22:25–29) and refused a quiet, hushed-up release (16:37). Being a believer does not mean being a doormat who refuses all legal recourse and lets injustice simply roll over him.

And this is no contradiction of turn the other cheek. That command forbids personal revenge (Matthew 5:39; Romans 12:19, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord”), not the lawful appeal to the civil authority God himself has ordained to do justice (“the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer,” Romans 13:4). Paul forgave his persecutors personally and used the courts; the two sit together.

But does this fit with Paul’s warning against going to court? In 1 Corinthians 6:1–8 Paul forbids believers to sue one another before unbelievers. Here Paul is a believer accused by unbelievers, appealing to a Roman court for justice. Christians may use the courts and civil rights to defend themselves and others; they should not take a brother to court.

Free to use them, free to give them up. So a Christian may rightly defend himself, appeal, invoke his protections, and seek justice through proper channels. These are good gifts of God’s ordering of society, and using them can even serve the gospel (Paul’s appeal carried him to Rome to preach, 23:11; 28:31). Two cautions keep it Christ-shaped: do it without bitterness or vengeance, for justice and not for getting even; and remember it is a freedom, not always a duty. Sometimes love will gladly lay down a right for a higher good (1 Corinthians 9:12, 15; 6:7, “Why not rather suffer wrong?”). Free to use them; free, for love’s sake, to give them up.

How do I know when to use a right and when to give it up? Ask what will serve the gospel and the good of others, not merely what will protect me. Paul insisted on his rights when silence would have let injustice stand, harmed others, or hindered his mission (16:37; 22:25). He laid them down when insisting would have put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12). If you are being wronged, and using a lawful protection would stop the wrong without revenge, use it. If insisting would damage a brother or a witness for a small personal gain, let it go. When unsure, seek counsel from wise believers.

In a sentence. Paul said that if he had done anything deserving death, he would not refuse to die, but if the charges were empty, no one could hand him over to them, and he appealed to Caesar; and Festus, after conferring with his advisers, said, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”

On a Tuesday. If you are facing an unjust situation at work, with a landlord, or in the courts, it is not unspiritual to use the lawful protections you have: a grievance procedure, a tribunal, a solicitor, the police. Use them honestly and without a spirit of revenge, and keep praying for the people on the other side. And before you insist on any right, ask the question Paul asked first: if I am actually in the wrong, am I willing to accept the consequences?

For worship. Two years of silence, and then a pagan governor speaks the very promise of Christ in the formal language of Roman law. The Lord’s word does not return to him empty. He said Rome, and the whole empire rose up to carry his servant there, with soldiers for an escort and Caesar paying the fare. Our God does what he pleases in heaven and on earth, and he is never more sovereign than when the world thinks it is simply following procedure. Blessed be the Lord Jesus, whose promises are kept even through the mouths of those who do not know his name.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself — at this time Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, 'There is a man left prisoner by Felix,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix,

Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. A king walks into the story, and for Luke’s first readers the name alone would have carried a chill. This is the last Herod in the Bible, and it is worth laying the family out, because nobody should have to keep four Herods straight from memory. They came, as client rulers did, to welcome the new governor.

Four generations of Herods. Herod the Great tried to kill Jesus in the cradle and murdered the infants of Bethlehem to do it (Matthew 2:16). Herod Antipas, his son, beheaded John the Baptist to save face at a birthday party (Mark 6:26–27), and when Jesus was finally sent to him on the morning of the crucifixion he treated him with contempt, dressed him in splendid clothing as a joke, and sent him back (Luke 23:11). Herod Agrippa I, the grandson, killed James the brother of John with the sword, arrested Peter intending the same, accepted the shout that his voice was the voice of a god, and was struck down and eaten by worms (Acts 12:2, 23). And now Herod Agrippa II, the great-grandson of Herod the Great and the son of Agrippa I: the last of the line, and the last member of this family the New Testament will ever mention.

Near the gospel and far from it. Four generations. The family has had the gospel brought to its door in every one of them, and in four generations not one Herod has ever done anything with it but destroy it, mock it, exploit it, or find it interesting. That is a sober thing to sit with. Nearness to the gospel is not the same as receiving it, and it does not accumulate down a bloodline. There are families in every church where the third generation is further from Christ than the first, and the reason is almost never that the truth was unavailable. It was thoroughly available to every Herod who ever lived. Access is not the scarce commodity. Willingness is, and willingness is the gift of God.

The right man to consult. Agrippa II is, however, exactly the right man for Festus to consult, and not merely because he is a king. He ruled territories to the north and east of Galilee, and Rome had given him a peculiar portfolio: custody of the temple treasury, the keeping of the high priest’s vestments, and the right to appoint and depose the high priest himself. He was the Roman-appointed manager of Jewish religion, an expert in Jewish customs and questions (26:3). If anyone in the province could tell a baffled governor what the dispute about Paul actually was, it was this man.

Bernice. Bernice is his sister. She had been married to her uncle, was widowed young, and thereafter lived in her brother’s household, an arrangement that produced a persistent rumour of incest, reported by Josephus and openly mocked in Rome by the satirist Juvenal. She would later become the mistress of Titus, the general who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70 and later became emperor. Luke names her without comment and lets the reader supply what he knows.

Festus laid Paul’s case before the king. There is a man left prisoner by Felix. Festus wanted help, and look at how he opens. Two years of a man’s life, two years of a Roman citizen held without charge by a governor angling for a bribe, compressed into one dismissive clause: Felix’s unfinished business. And note the verb: left. Not held, not detained, not committed for trial. Left, the way you leave a coat behind in a house you have moved out of.

The forgotten file. That is how the machinery of the world tends to describe the people it has forgotten. It is not usually malice. It is that nobody’s file is anybody’s priority. Which is worth remembering the next time your own situation feels like an oversight rather than a plan: Paul was a line item in a handover briefing, and he was exactly where the Lord had told him he would be. At his conversion the Lord had said that Paul would carry his name before Gentiles and kings (9:15). The forgotten prisoner was about to stand before a king.

If my family has no Christian history, am I at a disadvantage? No. Grace does not run in bloodlines, either for blessing or for doom. The Herods show that a family can be near the gospel for generations and never receive it; the rest of Scripture shows that God delights to call people from families with no faith at all, as he called Abraham out of a home of idol worshippers (Joshua 24:2). And if you are the first believer in your family, you may be the beginning of a new line. Pray for your relatives by name; God saves whom he wills, and no family is too far from him.

In a sentence. Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus, and as they stayed many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying that Felix had left a man there as a prisoner.

On a Tuesday. If you grew up near the gospel, in a Christian home or a churchgoing family, do not mistake nearness for possession. Ask whether you have yourself come to Christ, not your parents for you. And if your situation feels like a forgotten file, a matter nobody in authority is attending to, bring it to the Lord who has not forgotten it, and keep doing faithfully the work in front of you.

For worship. God was fulfilling his promise that Paul would carry his name before kings, and he is never late. Four generations of Herods tried to crush, mock or ignore the King of the Jews, and the Lord answered each one by sending the message again. The child Herod the Great tried to kill now sends his apostle in chains to preach to Herod’s great-grandson. Kings come and go, and dynasties end in a sentence; the Son of David reigns for ever, and his patience with the proud is as astonishing as his power over them.
verseByVerse.note: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I and ruled territories to the north-east. Bernice was his sister.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.

Asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. Without a trial. Festus is telling Agrippa the story of his own week, and he tells it well. He is not lying. Every clause is true.

It was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense. Roman justice at its best: the right to face your accusers and answer them. But notice what Festus leaves out. He does not mention that the priests had asked for a transfer to Jerusalem as a favour (v. 3), and when he mentions his own offer of a Jerusalem trial (v. 20) he recasts it as bewilderment, though it is the very thing that would have handed Paul over to his accusers and gutted the principle he is now quoting so proudly. He states the rule; he omits the moment he was ready to bend it. Festus presents himself well.

The flattering arrangement. This is the second time in three chapters that Luke has printed a Roman official’s own account of events the reader has just watched. Claudius Lysias did the same in his letter, rearranging one clause so that his rescue of Paul looked principled rather than accidental (23:27). Neither man invents a fact. Both arrange the true facts into a flattering shape, and Luke sets the arrangement down beside the events without a syllable of comment, because he is writing for a reader who has the transcript.

A magnificent principle. But do not miss what Festus is actually citing, because it is genuinely magnificent and it is the reason Paul is still breathing. Roman practice held that a man could not be condemned unheard, and that accuser and accused must stand face to face. Festus’s own word for give up is again the verb for granting a favour: no one was to be handed over as a present. Scripture had said it long before: a single witness was not enough, false witnesses were to be punished (Deuteronomy 19:15–19), and even Nicodemus had to remind the Pharisees that the law does not judge a man without first hearing him (John 7:51). Christian legal traditions drew on both, and the right to face your accuser is still one of the foundations of a just court.

Rome’s custom and Israel’s law. Now hold the two halves of this chapter together, because the contrast is the point and it is uncomfortable. The chief priests and elders of Israel, the men entrusted with the law of God, who had the Scriptures, who knew that a matter is established by two or three witnesses and that a judge must not take a bribe or show partiality, asked for a sentence of condemnation on a man they had not allowed to speak, asked for it as a favour, and were planning an ambush on the road. The pagan governor said no, because it was not the custom. Rome’s custom behaved better than Israel’s law, and it was not because Rome was righteous. It was because the men holding the law had stopped letting it govern them. That is always how it happens. The law does not fail; the men who hold it quietly decide that this once, in this case, for this outcome, the procedure can be set aside, and they discover afterwards that they have become the sort of people a pagan has to restrain.

Can unbelievers sometimes act more justly than believers? Yes, and Scripture is not embarrassed to say so. God has written the work of his law on every human heart (Romans 2:14–15), and by his common grace unbelievers often see and do what is fair. Abimelech rebuked Abraham for a lie (Genesis 20:9), and here Festus restrains the priests. That should humble the church, not unsettle it. It does not mean unbelievers are saved by their fairness, but it does mean Christians have no excuse for being less honest, less just or less fair than the world around them.

In a sentence. In Jerusalem the chief priests and elders had laid out their case and asked for his condemnation, but Festus told them it was not Roman custom to hand anyone over before he had faced his accusers and had the chance to defend himself.

On a Tuesday. Give everyone a fair hearing before you judge. It is justice, and it is love. When someone brings you a complaint about another person, at home, at work or in church, do not reach a verdict until you have heard the other side, if possible face to face. And when you tell the story of your own conduct, tell it whole, including the moment you were ready to bend the rule.

For worship. The God who commanded that no one be condemned unheard has himself provided that his people will never be condemned at all. At his bar every accusation is heard, every charge is faced, and still the verdict is acquittal, because the Accused has an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), who answers every count with his own blood. Justice and mercy have met in him; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.

I made no delay. Festus wants the king to notice his efficiency, and he has earned the right to mention it. On any reading he is a better administrator than the man he replaced.

But on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. True (v. 6). Set the two governors side by side. Felix heard Paul’s case, was genuinely frightened by what he heard, sent for him repeatedly hoping money would change hands, and then, in Luke’s most devastating sentence about him, desiring to do the Jews a favour, left Paul in prison for two years (24:25–27). Festus arrived and had the case on the tribunal within a fortnight. So the improvement is real, and it is worth saying that competence in office is a good thing and not a small one. A prompt hearing is a mercy to the man waiting for it. Two years of a governor’s indecision cost Paul two years. Justice delayed is justice denied.

And yet. Everything Festus claims here is true, and it did not stop him doing the one thing that would have killed Paul. He was prompt, procedurally correct, personally uncorrupt as far as we know, and eight verses earlier he asked whether the prisoner would care to be tried in the city where men were waiting to kill him, because it would please the people he had to work with.

Speed is not integrity. That is the thing to take away, and it applies well beyond Roman provincial administration. Competence is not righteousness. It is entirely possible to be efficient, punctual, organised, blameless in every procedure that can be audited, and to make the one decision that matters on the basis of who you need to keep happy. The failure never shows up in the part of the record that gets inspected. Festus’s account of himself is accurate. It is his instincts under pressure that are the problem, and no honest man can read that without wondering about his own.

How do I know whether my decisions are driven by fear of people? Ask three questions. Would I decide differently if no one important would ever find out? Am I avoiding the right course because of one person’s reaction rather than because it is wrong? Am I describing my choice to myself in words like sensible, realistic or not worth the trouble, when the honest word would be afraid? The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is safe (Proverbs 29:25). Bring the decision to God in prayer, ask what he requires, and do that, however competent the alternative looks.

In a sentence. When they came, he did not delay, but the next day took his seat on the tribunal and had the man brought in.

On a Tuesday. Be prompt in doing right. If someone is waiting for a decision from you, a reply, a payment, a reference, an apology, do not leave them in uncertainty longer than you must. Delay is a hidden burden on the person waiting. But do not let your efficiency persuade you that you are righteous. Ask where, in the part of your life nobody audits, you are making choices to keep people happy.

For worship. The Lord is not slow as some count slowness, and he is never careless. His delays are full of purpose and his speed is never hasty. He does not need to prove his efficiency to anyone, because nothing in all his ways has ever been done to win a king’s approval. His every decision is righteous, and his every timing is love. How different he is from the best of earthly rulers, and how safe it is to wait on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.

When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Stop here. This is one of the great sentences in the book, and it is great because of who says it and what he thinks he is saying. Festus had come into the hearing expecting sedition, fraud, violence, the ordinary business of a troublesome province. He got none of it: no real crimes. He is telling Agrippa, in effect, that the prosecution had nothing. That is one more official finding of no crime.

Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion. The word is deisidaimonia. It can mean religion, and it can mean superstition, fear of the gods. Festus is speaking to a Jewish king, so he chooses a word that sounds neutral; but a Roman of his class would have heard the hint of contempt in it. These were, to him, the private quarrels of a peculiar people.

And about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. A Roman governor, briefing a client king, summarises the entire Christian faith in a subordinate clause, and files it under local religious trivia. Take it phrase by phrase, because every one of them is doing something.

A certain Jesus. The Greek is tinos Iēsou: some Jesus, a Jesus, one Jesus or other. It is the phrasing you use for a name you have no reason to remember. The governor of Judea, sitting a few days’ journey from the hill where it happened, roughly thirty years after it happened, cannot be troubled to establish who the man was. The name at which every knee will one day bow is, to Festus, a detail in a religious quarrel he is trying to get out of.

Who was dead. Notice that this is not in dispute. Nobody in the room, on either side, questions that Jesus of Nazareth was executed and buried. The death of Christ is common ground between the apostle and the men trying to kill him.

But whom Paul asserted to be alive. The verb is ephasken, and the tense matters: Paul kept on asserting it. Not a statement made once under examination, but a claim he would not stop making, the thing he had said in Damascus and Antioch and Philippi and Athens and Corinth and Ephesus, and would say in Rome until they cut off his head.

Festus has got it exactly right. Here is what should stop the reader cold. He has not misunderstood the case. He has stated it more precisely than most sermons manage. A pagan’s summary of the gospel, said dismissively, and it is exactly right. Christianity is, at bottom, a dispute about whether a particular dead man is alive. Paul said as much himself, in writing, to people who were trying to spiritualise it: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Take that one clause out and there is nothing left worth arguing about. If it is true, everything changes; if not, nothing in the Christian faith matters (1 Corinthians 15:14–19). Festus, who believed none of it, put his finger on the hinge of history.

Accurate and untouched. Which means it is entirely possible to state the gospel accurately and remain completely untouched by it. Festus could have passed an examination on the content. He could summarise the claim, identify the parties, and explain what was at stake, and it never once occurred to him that if the claim were true, it would concern him personally. It was a fact about somebody else’s religion. That is the test, and it is sharper than it looks, because the people most at risk from it are the ones who have been in church longest. Could you state what Christians believe about the resurrection more accurately than Festus did? Almost certainly. And when you last said it out loud, did it cost you anything, or change anything, or move anything in you at all?

How can we be sure Jesus really rose? The evidence is strong, and it begins with the very fact this verse records: nobody disputed the death. Jesus was publicly executed by professionals and buried in a known tomb. Within weeks his followers were proclaiming in the same city that the tomb was empty, and his enemies never produced the body, though that would have ended the matter. More than five hundred people saw him alive, many of them still living when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Frightened disciples became fearless, and men like Paul, an enemy, and James, a sceptical brother, were transformed. Men do not die for what they know to be a lie. And alongside the evidence, the Spirit himself bears witness through the Word that it is true.

In a sentence. When the accusers stood up, they did not charge him with the crimes Festus had expected, but had certain disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died, but whom Paul claimed was alive.

On a Tuesday. A certain Jesus, who was dead, is alive. Believe it, and tell it. Take one ordinary decision this week, how you spend an evening, how you respond to a loss, what you fear, and ask what difference it makes that Jesus is actually alive and reigning. And when you next have a chance to speak of your faith, say this plainly, as Paul did: he died, and he is alive. It is the whole case.

For worship. Consider the one they were discussing. A certain Jesus, who was dead. He was dead: the centurion certified it, the spear settled it, the tomb received him, and the world went back to work. And he is alive. Not remembered, not revered, not living on in the hearts of his followers, but alive, in a body, at the right hand of the Majesty on high, holding the keys of Death and Hades, and reigning until every enemy is under his feet. The empire that crucified him has long since crumbled into ruin. Festus is dust. Agrippa is dust. Bernice is dust. Nero is dust. And the certain Jesus whose name the governor could not be bothered to learn is on the throne of the universe tonight, and every one of those men has since met him and knows his name now. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, and who lives for ever and ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.

Being at a loss how to investigate these questions. The word is aporoumenos, from a root meaning no way through, no passage, no road. Festus is not being falsely modest.
