He is a competent Roman lawyer standing in front of a question his training does not equip him to open: whether a crucified Galilean is alive. And the honesty is almost attractive. He does not bluster or invent a category. He says plainly that he was out of his depth in Jewish religious disputes.

I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem. He omits that it was to please the Jews. But watch what a man at a loss actually does, because this is the part worth learning. Being at a loss, he did not adjourn, or take advice, or send to Rome for a ruling. He turned to the prisoner and proposed the one course that would have ended his life: a trial in Jerusalem, in the city where the ambush was still waiting, before the men who had already asked him to hand the case over as a favour.

Confusion is not neutral. That is the lesson, and it is a hard one. When a man genuinely does not know what to do, he does not stop; he falls back on whatever pressure is strongest in the room. Festus’s honest bewilderment did not produce caution. It produced a proposal that happened to please the people he needed on his side. He would have called that pragmatism. Luke has already told us what it was: wishing to do the Jews a favour (v. 9). So the test is not whether you know what to do. Often you will not. The test is what you reach for when you do not know, and for most of us the honest answer is that we reach for whatever will cause the least friction with the people whose opinion we most need. That is exactly what Festus did, and it nearly killed the apostle to the Gentiles.

For the decision of the emperor. The word for the emperor is Sebastos, the Greek form of Augustus: the revered one, the august one, a title with a hint of worship in it. It meant Nero. Festus reports the appeal as an inconvenience he has had to accommodate. He does not know he is describing the mechanism of a promise. Two years earlier, in a barracks in Jerusalem, the Lord had stood by Paul in the dark and told him he must testify at Rome (23:11). This sentence, in a governor’s briefing, is that promise moving one more stage down the road, and the man saying it thinks he is explaining a procedural difficulty.

What should I do when I genuinely do not know what to do? Stop and pray before you act, and ask God for wisdom; he gives it generously to those who ask (James 1:5). Search the Scriptures for any principle that bears on the decision. Seek counsel from wise and godly people, not merely from the people who will be pleased by one outcome (Proverbs 15:22). Do the right things you already know, even if the larger picture is unclear. And notice which way the pressure in the room is pushing you; if your uncertainty keeps landing on the option that pleases the powerful, be suspicious of it. It is often wiser to wait than to reach for the easiest course.

In a sentence. At a loss how to investigate such questions, Festus asked whether Paul would go to Jerusalem to be tried there, but Paul appealed to be kept in custody for the emperor’s decision, so he ordered him held until he could send him to Caesar.

On a Tuesday. The next time you are unsure what to do, notice what you instinctively reach for. Is it the opinion of the person you most want to please? The course with the least friction? Write the decision down, pray over it, and ask a mature Christian friend what they think before you act.

For worship. Even confused rulers serve God’s plans, and nothing is outside his control. The Lord is never at a loss. There is no question too deep for him, no dispute too tangled, no situation in which he does not see the way through; he is the God who makes a way in the sea and a path in the mighty waters. Festus called Nero the revered one, but there is only one who is truly august, the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only God, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. His counsel stands, and he accomplishes all his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Agrippa said to Festus, 'I would like to hear the man myself.' 'Tomorrow,' said he, 'you will hear him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.”

I would like to hear the man myself. The Greek is an imperfect, and it can carry a history: I have been wanting to. This is not a passing whim. Agrippa had probably heard of Paul for years, and he has been meaning to hear him for some time. And a reader of Luke’s first volume will feel the floor shift, because a Herod has said this before.

The Herod who wanted to see Jesus. Of Herod Antipas, when reports of Jesus reached the palace, Luke wrote that he sought to see him (Luke 9:9). He kept seeking, for months. And on the morning of the crucifixion he finally got his wish: Pilate sent Jesus across to him, and Luke says he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but Jesus made no answer (Luke 23:8–9). It is the most terrible silence in the Gospels. A Herod finally gets his audience with the Son of God, asks his questions, and receives nothing at all. Curiosity had had its years to become something else and had refused, and when the moment came there was nothing left to say to him.

Tomorrow you will hear him. Now the last Herod says the same sentence about the same message, and the outcome is different. Agrippa will get his hearing, and Paul will not be silent. He will preach the gospel to a king, giving the longest and most personal defence in the book, tailored precisely to this man (King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe, 26:27), and it will bring him closer than any other ruler in Acts comes, close enough to ask whether Paul thinks he can make him a Christian in so short a time (26:28). That is mercy. Antipas mocked, and got silence. Agrippa is merely curious, and God sends him the finest preacher of the age with a message shaped for his exact history and knowledge.

Curiosity is not conversion. But be careful with the comfort in that, because the next chapter records what Agrippa did with it, and the answer is nothing. He heard the whole thing, agreed it was harmless, remarked to Festus that the man could have been released, and went home a king. Curiosity about Christ is a real gift and it can be a door, but it is not conversion. There are people who enjoy the subject, follow the arguments, would happily sit through the sermon and discuss it intelligently afterwards, and have never once been to Christ for mercy. Agrippa wanted to hear the man. He got exactly what he asked for, and it was not what he needed, because he never asked for what he needed.

How do I talk to a friend who is curious about Christianity? Welcome the curiosity and take it seriously. Answer honest questions honestly, and admit when you do not know. But do what Paul will do with Agrippa: move gently from the interesting to the personal. Ask what they make of Jesus himself, not only of the arguments. Tell them what Christ has done for you. Invite them to read one of the Gospels with you. And pray for them, because curiosity becomes faith only when God opens the heart (16:14). Do not be content to keep a curious friend interested for years; lovingly ask where they stand.

In a sentence. Agrippa told Festus he would like to hear the man himself, and Festus said, “Tomorrow you will hear him.”

On a Tuesday. If you are the curious one, the person who enjoys Christian ideas, reads the books and comes to the talks, ask yourself what you are hoping to get from it. Information, or mercy? And if you know curious people, pray for them by name this week, that God would turn their interest into faith.

For worship. How patient is our God with the curious and the proud. To a family that had tried to kill his Son, mocked him and murdered his apostle, he sends his servant once more, with the gospel in his mouth. He is not willing that any should perish, and he stretches out his hands all day long to a people who only want to watch. And to everyone who will ask, he gives not a sign but himself. Blessed be the Saviour who did not open his mouth before Herod, so that he could open his arms to sinners.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next day Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great ceremony and enter the audience hall with the senior officers and leading citizens, and Paul is brought in. Festus introduces him: the whole Jewish community, in Jerusalem and here, has petitioned against this man, crying that he must not live. But Festus has found that he has done nothing deserving death, and since Paul has appealed to the emperor, he has decided to send him. The trouble is that he has nothing definite to write to his lord. So he has brought Paul before them, and above all before King Agrippa, so that after this hearing he may have something to write; it seems absurd to send a prisoner without stating the charges.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Platform the World Cannot Help Providing

Jesus told his disciples that they would be dragged before kings and governors for his name's sake, and then said something startling about it: this will be your opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). Not your ordeal — your opportunity. Acts 25 is that promise arriving in a form nobody would have designed. The hostility of the Sanhedrin, the ambition of two governors, the curiosity of a king, and an administrative problem with a covering letter combine to assemble the entire ruling class of a Roman province in one room and sit them down in front of a preacher.

Note who did the assembling. Not the church, which had no power to convene such a gathering and no money to hire the hall. The opposition built the platform, paid for it, filled it with the most important people available, and then handed the prisoner the floor.

The Reformed instinct here is neither triumphalism nor passivity. God is not obliged to use worldly power, and he frequently works through nobodies in obscurity. But when he does use the machinery of the age, he does not ask its permission and he does not need its cooperation to be willing. Festus wanted a charge sheet. What he arranged was an evangelistic meeting for the aristocracy of Judea.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything visible in that hall belonged to the other side. The king had the title, Bernice had the jewels, the tribunes had the swords, the leading men had the money, and Festus had the authority to decide what happened next. Paul had a chain and the floor. Within a day the man with the chain had spoken so directly to the king that Agrippa had to deflect him with a joke.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and the principle does not require it. It shows up in smaller rooms — the meeting where you are plainly the least senior person present, the family table where your faith is the eccentric position, the conversation where everyone else has the confidence and the vocabulary and the standing. The instinct is to wait for a better platform, one where you are taken more seriously. Paul never got a better platform than the one his enemies built for him, and he did not ask for one. He used the floor he was given, in the clothes he was wearing, with the chain on.

verseByVerse.quote: "So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, 'King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.

Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp. Luke’s word for the pomp is phantasia. It is the root behind our word fantasy, and it means a showing, a display, an appearance put on to be looked at. He could have chosen any word for grandeur. He picked the one that means it is all surface: robes, attendants, ceremony.

They entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Fill in the room, because Luke expects the reader to see it. A king and his sister in full Herodian state. The military tribunes of the Caesarean garrison in dress uniform; there were five cohorts at Caesarea, each tribune commanding a thousand men. The prominent men of the city: the magistrates, the money, the people who mattered in the provincial capital. The governor of Judea presiding. This is the entire visible power structure of the province assembled in one hall, the most distinguished audience Paul had ever addressed.

Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. One passive verb. He does not enter; he is brought. And he is in chains: he says so himself the next day, in the most gracious sentence in Acts, when he tells this room he wishes every one of them were as he is, except for these chains (26:29). So: all the display on one side of the room, and a worn, shackled man on the other. Which was truly great? Within twenty-four hours the prisoner will be the only person present who can say why he is there. Festus has just admitted he cannot. Agrippa has come to find out. The tribunes and the leading citizens are spectators at a hearing whose subject nobody in authority understands. The one man in the room who knows exactly what is going on is the one in irons.

You see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me. Festus is overstating. The whole Jewish people is the language of a man dramatising his own difficulty, and thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem would have said otherwise. But look at what he has just entered into the record in front of the province’s assembled nobility: they were shouting that he ought not to live any longer. The demand was for a man’s death. And the governor is about to say, in the next breath, that he found no ground for it whatever.

Is it wrong for Christians to enjoy ceremony, wealth or fine things? Not in itself. God made a world of beauty, and Scripture describes the splendour of Solomon’s temple and the glory of the new Jerusalem without embarrassment. The danger is in what Luke’s word exposes: display for its own sake, splendour used to make ourselves look great, trust placed in what will fade. Enjoy good things with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4; 6:17), use them generously, and never confuse them with true greatness. The question is whether the things you have are pointing others to God or to yourself.

In a sentence. The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the leading men of the city, and at Festus’s command Paul was brought in; and Festus said this was the man about whom the whole Jewish community had petitioned him in Jerusalem and Caesarea, shouting that he should not live any longer.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week what you are tempted to admire: the impressive car, the polished platform, the confident voice, the big name. Then think of Paul in chains in that hall, and ask what true greatness looks like. Go and honour someone this week whom the world overlooks: the faithful old saint, the carer, the believer who suffers quietly for Christ.

For worship. Earthly pomp fades; the glory of Christ’s servants is in their message, and the glory of Christ himself is in his cross. The kings of this world come with display that is gone by morning. The King of kings came in a stable, rode a donkey, wore a crown of thorns, and was lifted up in shame, and he is clothed now in a majesty that will never be taken from him. Every robe in that hall has rotted. The word spoken by the man in chains is still being preached in every nation under heaven.

parallels.desc: I will speak of your testimonies before kings

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.

But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. Take the absurdity plainly first, because Luke means it to be felt. A Roman governor is putting a prisoner on a ship to the imperial court, and he cannot say what the man is accused of. He has held hearings. He has heard the prosecution. He has consulted the local expert. And the file is empty, because there is nothing to put in it.

The verdicts filed. Every authority that has examined Paul has found no crime: Gallio at Corinth on an earlier charge (18:14–15), Lysias in his letter (23:29), Festus at the hearing (25:18), and Festus again now. Agrippa will add his voice tomorrow: this man could have been set free (26:31–32). Luke never once tells the reader what to conclude. He simply files the verdicts. And they echo another set of verdicts in his first volume, when Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and sent him to the cross anyway.

But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Festus had a problem. Sending a prisoner to the emperor with no charge would make him look foolish, so he hopes that after the king has examined Paul, he may have something to write. Agrippa could help him frame a charge. Then there is the phrase that a Christian reader should not walk past: my lord. The Greek is kyrios. Festus uses it of Nero as naturally as breathing; it was becoming the ordinary courtesy for the emperor, and within a generation Domitian would want to be addressed as lord and god. In this room, on this afternoon, kyrios means the man on the throne in Rome. It was a title Christians would give in its full sense only to Jesus.

Two lordships in one sentence. Standing in front of Festus in chains is a man for whom that word means somebody else entirely. Paul had written to Corinth that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6), and he would write to Philippi that God has given Jesus the name that is above every name, so that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:9–11). He is being shipped to Caesar’s court for the specific purpose of saying so. Two lordships are named in a single sentence, and the governor can see only one of them.

Is it wrong for a Christian to call anyone lord or to honour rulers? No. Scripture tells us to honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17) and to give respect and honour to whom they are owed (Romans 13:7). Paul himself addresses Festus as most excellent (26:25). Courtesy to those in authority is right. What a Christian cannot do is give any ruler the worship, absolute allegiance or final obedience that belongs to Christ alone. That is why believers in the early centuries would honour Caesar but would not say Caesar is lord in the sense of Caesar is god, and many died for it. When a ruler’s command contradicts God’s, we must obey God rather than men (5:29).

In a sentence. Festus said he had found that Paul had done nothing deserving death, but since Paul had appealed to the emperor, he had decided to send him, though he had nothing definite to write to his lord about him; so he had brought him before them all, and especially before King Agrippa, so that after examining him he would have something to write.

On a Tuesday. Even Paul’s enemies could not find a crime. Let your life be like that: so honest at work, so faithful at home, so clean in your dealings, that anyone who looked for something to accuse you of would come away with an empty file. And look at your own life for any rival lord, a career, a person, a fear, that is quietly receiving the allegiance that belongs to Jesus.

For worship. Consider the other Lord. Nero was lord of the world, and he held it for fourteen years, and he died by his own hand at thirty, with the senate declaring him a public enemy. Jesus Christ was lord of nothing anyone could see: no throne, no legion, no province, a borrowed tomb. And he is Lord tonight, and will be Lord when the last empire has gone the way of that one. The title Festus gives Nero in passing is a courtesy. The title Paul gives to Jesus in a set of chains is a fact, and the whole creation is running down toward the day when every tongue in it, including the governor’s and the king’s and the emperor’s, says so out loud, to the glory of God the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.

For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him. The chapter ends on a bureaucrat’s complaint about paperwork, and Luke could not have chosen a better last line. Festus means it narrowly: the covering letter needs a charge, and he has not got one. But say the sentence again and hear what it actually concedes. It is unreasonable to send a prisoner without indicating the charges, and he is sending him. He knows the thing is unreasonable. He says so, out loud, in front of the king and the tribunes and the leading men of Caesarea, and then he does it anyway.

A system that worked as designed. Every authority that has touched this case has now said the same thing in its own words, and not one of them has released him. That is the honest shape of it, and it is worth refusing the tidy version: Paul is innocent, everyone with the power to judge knows he is innocent, and none of them sets him free. The system did not malfunction. It worked exactly as designed, and it still could not do the right thing, because at every stage there was somebody who needed a favour. Festus’s honesty shows something else, too: Christianity was being opposed not for crimes, but for its message. Paul was in chains for preaching that Jesus is alive.

And yet. Two years earlier the Lord had stood beside him in the dark and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Here is what that promise looks like from ground level, at the end of chapter 25: a governor who cannot fill in a form. Not an angel, not an earthquake, not an acquittal. A procedural embarrassment in a provincial capital, which will put Paul on a ship at imperial expense and carry him to the one city he had been promised. Both things are true at the same time, and the Christian life is mostly lived in the overlap. This is a real injustice, and it is not being pretended away; and it is also the exact mechanism of a promise, and that promise is not being frustrated for a moment.

Why does God allow innocent believers to remain in chains? Scripture does not give us every reason, but it gives us enough to trust him. Paul’s chains carried the gospel to places no free preacher could reach: the praetorian guard and Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:12–13; 4:22). Suffering for righteousness joins believers to Christ, who suffered unjustly first (1 Peter 2:19–23), and it bears witness to the world that he is worth more than freedom. God will one day judge every injustice openly (2 Thessalonians 1:6–8). Until then, he does not waste a single day of his people’s suffering. Many Christians today are imprisoned for no crime but their faith, and they need our prayers, our letters and our advocacy.

In a sentence. He said it seemed to him unreasonable to send a prisoner without stating the charges against him.

On a Tuesday. Find out about one believer, or one church, imprisoned or persecuted for faith in Christ today, through a ministry that serves the persecuted church, and pray for them by name this week. And if you are in a situation of real injustice that no one in authority seems willing to fix, name it honestly as injustice, and at the same time hold on to what God has promised. Both are true together.

For worship. Festus wanted something to write. Tomorrow he will get chapter 26, the fullest account of the risen Christ that any Roman official ever heard, because a man needed to fill in a form correctly. That is our God. He turns a governor’s embarrassment into a pulpit, an unjust chain into a passage to Rome, and a cross that every court agreed was unreasonable into the salvation of the world. His ways are higher than our ways, his purposes cannot be frustrated, and not one of his promises has ever failed. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations, for ever and ever.

25.title: Paul Before Festus
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <sup>2</sup>And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him, <sup>3</sup>asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. <sup>4</sup>Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. <sup>5</sup>“So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.” <sup>6</sup>After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. <sup>7</sup>When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. <sup>8</sup>Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.” <sup>9</sup>But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” <sup>10</sup>But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. <sup>11</sup>If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” <sup>12</sup>Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” <sup>13</sup>Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. <sup>14</sup>And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix, <sup>15</sup>and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. <sup>16</sup>I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him. <sup>17</sup>So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. <sup>18</sup>When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. <sup>19</sup>Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. <sup>20</sup>Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. <sup>21</sup>But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.” <sup>22</sup>Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.” <sup>23</sup>So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <sup>24</sup>And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <sup>25</sup>But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. <sup>26</sup>But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. <sup>27</sup>For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.”
25.overview:
A new governor, Porcius Festus, arrives about AD 59. Within days the Jerusalem leaders ask him to bring Paul to Jerusalem, intending to ambush him on the road, as their predecessors had tried two years earlier. Festus insists they come to Caesarea instead. They bring many serious charges they cannot prove, and Paul denies any offence against the law, the temple or Caesar. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul sees the danger and uses his right as a citizen: “I appeal to Caesar.” Festus has no choice but to send him to Nero.

The appeal leaves Festus with a problem: he must send a report to the emperor, and he can find no crime. When King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice pay a courtesy visit, Festus explains the case: the dispute concerned the Jews’ religion and “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.” Agrippa wants to hear Paul, and the next day, in a hall full of pomp, Festus presents the prisoner. Jesus had promised that his followers would stand before kings and governors for his name’s sake (Luke 21:12); this chapter sets the scene for the greatest of Paul’s defences.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Given leave to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa he is glad to defend himself before one who knows Jewish customs so well. All his people know he lived as a strict Pharisee; now he is on trial for hoping in God’s promise to the fathers, the hope that God raises the dead. Once he was sure he must oppose Jesus’ name: he jailed believers, voted for their deaths and hunted them abroad. On the way to Damascus at noon a light brighter than the sun struck him and his companions down, and a voice in Aramaic asked why he persecuted him: it was hard to kick against the goads. It was Jesus, who appointed him servant and witness, to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles and turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, to receive forgiveness and a place among the sanctified by faith. Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and its fruits everywhere; for this he was seized and nearly killed, but God has helped him. He says only what Moses and the prophets foretold: the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead and bring light to Israel and the nations. Festus shouts that Paul’s learning has made him mad. Paul answers that he speaks sober truth: the king knows, for this was not done in a corner. Does Agrippa believe the prophets? Agrippa asks if Paul thinks he can make him a Christian so quickly. Paul replies that he prays all his hearers may become as he is, apart from the chains. Leaving, the officials agree he has done nothing deserving death or prison; he could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as Israel's Hope, Not Israel's Rival

The theological spine of this speech is that Christianity is not a new religion. Paul stakes everything on continuity: he is on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers (v. 6), he says nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass (v. 22), and he asks the king the one question that would settle it — do you believe the prophets? The charge is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room and his accusers have stopped believing their own Scriptures.

That claim rests on three things the Old Testament had promised and Paul insists are now fulfilled: a Messiah who must suffer (Isa. 53; Luke 24:26), a resurrection that opens the age to come (Dan. 12:2), and light reaching the nations (Isa. 42:6; 49:6). Take away the third and the first two become a private Jewish settlement; that is precisely what his opponents wanted, and precisely what he would not give them.

Underneath it lies the doctrine this whole chapter is a case study in: grace that is entirely from God's side. Nothing in Paul's account belongs to Paul. He was not seeking, dissatisfied, or badly taught; he was convinced, exactingly trained, and in a raging fury, riding hard in the opposite direction — and he was stopped, blinded, named, and commissioned. He did not find Christ. Christ appeared to him. Every clause of the commission in vv. 17–18 is something done to people, not by them: eyes opened, a realm changed, a dominion broken, sins forgiven, a place given.

And the chapter guards that against cheapness in the same breath. Repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (v. 20). The works are never the root; they are the fruit, exactly as Paul argued at length elsewhere (Eph. 2:8–10). A sovereign work of grace produces a visibly different life, and a life with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Agrippa heard the finest presentation of the gospel any ruler in the New Testament ever received, delivered by the ablest preacher of the age, in his own theological vocabulary, by a man who prayed for him out loud in open court. He did not argue with it. He did not refute a single point. He made a joke, stood up, walked out, and remarked in the corridor that the prisoner had done nothing wrong.

Now: Notice how the refusal was actually shaped, because almost nobody declines Christ the way we imagine. There was no debate, no crisis, no considered rejection. There was wit, and then there was standing up, and the standing up was the answer. That is how it usually goes — a subject changed with a light remark, an evening that ran late, a genuine intention to come back to it. If you have been near this for years, the question is not whether you have objections; Agrippa had none worth stating. It is whether the conversation has quietly been allowed to end the same way five or six times, and whether anything is actually going to be different about the sixth. Paul's one request at the start of the speech was that the king would not become impatient before he had finished. It is still the only thing being asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.' Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: 'I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: “I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,

Meaning first. Acts 26 is Paul’s greatest defence, before King Agrippa, Bernice, Festus and the leading men of Caesarea. This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts. Paul tells how he, a strict Pharisee who hoped in the resurrection, persecuted Jesus’ followers until Jesus met him and sent him to open the eyes of the Gentiles, to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God. He insists that he says nothing but what Moses and the prophets foretold: that the Messiah would suffer and rise. Festus calls him mad; Agrippa deflects; Paul wishes they were all like him, except for the chains. And the rulers agree: this man has done nothing wrong. It is a speech in which a prisoner holds up the risen Christ before the whole power of a province, and the only free man in the room is the one in irons.

You have permission to speak for yourself. Paul has been waiting more than two years for this sentence. Count what he has been given up to now. A mob on a staircase that heard him out until one word and then tried to tear him apart. A council that dissolved into a brawl before evidence was called. A governor who understood the case well enough to be frightened by it and sent for him repeatedly hoping for a bribe. A second governor who admitted he was out of his depth and proposed the one venue that would have killed him. Four hearings, and not one of them was a hearing. Now a king with a working knowledge of the Hebrew Scriptures says: speak.

Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense. It is the orator’s gesture, the formal opening of a set speech, and Luke expects us to see it. But remember what is on that hand. Paul will mention it himself before the afternoon is out: except for these chains (v. 29). A prisoner in irons makes the gesture of a free orator in front of the assembled nobility of the province, and nobody stops him.

I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa. The word is makarios, the word of the Beatitudes: blessed, happy, well off. It is not ordinary courtroom flattery, and it is worth pausing on, because Paul is on trial for his life and has just called himself a fortunate man. Why? Not because Agrippa is powerful; Paul has stood in front of more powerful men without saying this. Because Agrippa can follow the argument. Here at last is a judge who understands Jewish matters, who knows what a prophet is, who knows what Israel has been waiting for, who will not hear the word resurrection as a piece of provincial nonsense. Paul is not counting his chances of acquittal. He is counting his chances of being understood about Jesus Christ. And Jesus’ promise is being fulfilled: Paul would carry his name before kings (9:15).

A fortunate man in chains. That is worth holding up against our own instinctive arithmetic. Most of us measure a day by what it cost us and what it returned. Paul has been in custody for two years, is being tried on a charge nobody can name, and is going to be shipped to Nero, and his verdict on the afternoon is that he is a fortunate man, because someone competent is finally going to hear about Christ. If that reordering seems extreme, it is only because it is complete.

Who were Agrippa and Bernice? Herod Agrippa II, great-grandson of Herod the Great, ruled territories north and east of Galilee and had the Roman right to appoint the high priest, so Festus wanted his advice on a Jewish matter. Bernice was his sister. Festus had recently replaced Felix as governor.

The accusations of the Jews. One note for the reader, since the phrase recurs: the accusations of the Jews. Luke’s shorthand throughout Acts means the Jerusalem leadership who brought the case, not the Jewish people as such, and certainly not Jews as a race. The man speaking is himself a Jew, defending himself as a Pharisee, arguing from the Hebrew prophets, and about to say that his one grief is that his own nation has not seen it. This book has been misread down the centuries to justify appalling things. It does not say them.

Why does Luke tell Paul’s conversion three times? Because it matters enormously to the story and to the gospel. Luke tells it first as narrator (9:1–19), then in Paul’s words to a Jewish crowd (22:3–21), and now to a king. Ancient writers repeated what they most wanted remembered. The conversion of the church’s fiercest enemy proves that the gospel is God’s work and not man’s, it explains why Paul went to the Gentiles, and it shows that Christ can save anyone. Each telling is shaped for its hearers, but the heart is the same: the risen Jesus met Saul and sent him.

In a sentence. Agrippa gave Paul permission to speak, and Paul stretched out his hand and began his defence, saying he considered himself fortunate to make his defence against the accusations of the Jews before King Agrippa.

On a Tuesday. Every opportunity to speak of Christ, even under pressure, is a good fortune. Think of the setting you will be in this week where you are least free: the hospital bed, the difficult office, the family table where faith is mocked. Ask God to let you see it as Paul saw his chains, as a place where someone may hear about Jesus. And measure the day by that, not only by what it cost you.

For worship. The Lord who chose Paul to carry his name before kings kept every word of that promise, even when the road ran through two years of prison. He opens doors no man can shut, and he opens them most often in the places that look most closed. Blessed is the Saviour who makes a chained man fortunate, because to know him and to speak of him is a greater wealth than every throne in the hall.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "'especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.

Especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Paul names the qualification precisely: customs and controversies. Agrippa knew Judaism well. He oversaw the temple and appointed high priests. He knows the practices and, more useful still, he knows the arguments. He knows that Pharisees and Sadducees have been at odds over the resurrection for generations. He knows what messianic expectation is and why it matters. He is, in the exact sense, competent to hear this case.

Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. The request tells you what kind of speech is coming. The word is makrothumōs, long-temperedly. Its family is the one the New Testament normally uses for patience or longsuffering, and it is used most often of God himself, who is slow to anger and bears with people for a very long time. Paul asks the king for a small share of that quality: do not become irritated with me before I have finished. A long speech was coming.

Not a soundbite. It is an honest request, because what follows is not a legal defence, and Paul knows it. He will barely address the charges. He will instead tell a king the story of how the risen Jesus stopped him on a road, and then argue from Moses and the prophets that this is precisely what Israel’s Scriptures had promised. That takes time. It cannot be done in a soundbite, and it cannot be done at all if the hearer has already decided how long he is prepared to give it.

The least examined reason. Which is a quietly searching thing, because impatience is the most common and least examined reason people never deal with Christ. Not hostility; hostility at least engages. Impatience. The subject is granted about ninety seconds, and ninety seconds is not enough for anything that matters, and so the verdict is reached on a case that was never actually heard. Paul is not asking Agrippa to agree. He is asking him to stay in the room long enough for the argument to be made. It is the only thing he asks of him, and it is the thing most people will not give.

What if I am the impatient one? Then give Christ a fair hearing, deliberately. Many Christians as well as unbelievers grant the Bible a few distracted minutes and then decide what they think. Read one whole Gospel, Mark or Luke, in two or three sittings, as you would read any serious book, and ask what kind of person Jesus is. Sit through a sermon without checking your phone. When a hard passage troubles you, stay with it long enough to understand it before you set it aside. God promises that those who seek him with all their heart will find him (Jeremiah 29:13).

In a sentence. Agrippa knew all the Jewish customs and disputes, so Paul asked him to listen patiently.

On a Tuesday. When you speak about Christ with someone, it is fair to ask, gently, for a patient hearing: not agreement, just time. The story of Christ is worth their time. Offer to read a Gospel with them, or to meet for a longer conversation rather than trading quick lines. And be patient yourself with those who are slow to understand; God has been patient with you.

For worship. Paul asked a king for a little patience, and the God he served has shown a patience beyond all measure. He bore with Israel for a thousand years of rebellion, he bore with the persecutor Saul until the day he stopped him, and he bears with us still, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. The Lord’s patience means salvation (2 Peter 3:15). Every day a sinner is given to hear the gospel is a day of his longsuffering kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: "'My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.

My manner of life from my youth is known by all the Jews. Paul opens his case with the public record, and the phrasing is deliberately awkward for his accusers. His past was public. He was raised in Jerusalem, trained under the most famous rabbi of the age, and made his reputation in front of witnesses who are still alive. Anyone in the Sanhedrin could confirm every word of it. That is the force of the conditional that follows: they could testify, if they are willing. The prosecution has the evidence and will not produce it, because the evidence helps the defendant. They cannot say Paul left Judaism because he never understood it. He understood it better than they did.

According to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. The word is akribestatēn, the superlative of akribēs, meaning exact, precise, no margin of error. The Pharisees were the most precise in keeping the law. It is the same root Paul used on the barracks steps when he said he was educated according to the strict manner of the law of the fathers (22:3). He is not claiming to have been religious in a general way. He is claiming to have belonged to the most exacting school available, and to have belonged to it thoroughly. Paul was no lax, half-hearted Jew.

He does not disown it. He said the same to the council: I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees (23:6). And years after his conversion he still wrote it down in a letter as a plain fact about himself (Philippians 3:5). Paul never regarded following Jesus as leaving Israel. He regarded it as Israel’s hope arriving. His conversion was not from irreligion to religion, but from the best religion without Christ to Christ.

Closing the exits. Here is why the biography matters more than it looks. There is a comfortable explanation for conversion that every generation reaches for: he did not really know what he was giving up. He was badly taught. He was unhappy. He was young. Something was missing. None of it is available here, and Paul is closing the exits one by one. He had the best training in the nation. He had status, momentum and the approval of the men who mattered. He was not drifting and he was not searching. He was riding a career, hard, in the opposite direction, and he was winning. Whatever happened to him on that road, it was not the collapse of a man who had run out of alternatives. It was the interruption of a man who had none of the usual reasons to be interrupted.

Does a strict religious upbringing count for anything with God? It can be a great mercy, because it fills the mind with Scripture and the habits of worship, as Paul’s did. But it cannot save. Paul later listed every one of his religious advantages and then said he counted them all as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:4–9). What God requires is not a good record but a righteousness that comes through faith in Christ. If you were raised in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you are trusting Christ himself and not your background.

In a sentence. All the Jews knew how he had lived from his youth among his own people and in Jerusalem, and could testify, if they were willing, that he had lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest party of their religion.

On a Tuesday. Even the strictest religion cannot save without Christ; Paul learned that. Write down, honestly, the things you might be tempted to rely on before God: your upbringing, your church attendance, your knowledge, your morality. Then thank him that none of them is your hope, because Christ is.

For worship. Glory to the God who interrupts careers that are running hard in the wrong direction. He took the most exact Pharisee of his generation, at the height of his zeal and his success, and turned him around with a word. No one is too religious for his grace to humble, and no one too far gone for his grace to reach. The best of human religion is a dim lamp beside the rising sun of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!

And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers. Paul puts the whole absurdity of his position into one sentence, and it is worth letting it land. He is standing in chains, prosecuted by the leadership of his own nation, on a charge that comes down to this: he believes what Israel has been praying for. Not a rival hope. Not an import. The promise made by God to the fathers, the Messiah and the resurrection, the thing Israel has been reaching toward, in synagogue after synagogue, morning and evening, for centuries. Paul is on trial for being a faithful Jew who believes God’s promise has been kept.

To which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. Twelve tribes: all Israel, as one people. Note the detail he chooses: as they earnestly worship night and day. Their worship was hope, waiting for God to act. He is not scoring points off his accusers’ piety. He grants it, warmly and completely. These are devout people. The prayers are real. The waiting has been real for a very long time.

And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! That is exactly what makes the charge so strange, and so sad: Jews accuse a Jew for believing the Jewish hope. The accusation, laid out plainly, is that Paul has found what Israel has been asking for, and is being tried by Israel for finding it. It is the oldest and most human of failures, and it is not confined to first-century Jerusalem. A thing can be prayed for so long that the praying becomes the settled shape of life, and the arrival of the answer feels less like fulfilment than like disruption. Paul is not accusing them of wanting the wrong thing. He is telling a king that they got it, and did not recognise it, because it came in a form that cost them something.

The threads of the hope. This hope, the promise made to the fathers, gathers up the great threads of Israel’s expectation that run all through Acts, each of which Paul insists is fulfilled in Jesus. For the reader who wants to follow them: the resurrection hope is the heart of it, and Paul says again and again that this is what he is really on trial for (23:6; 24:15, 21; 26:8; and see how it split Athens, 17:32); the coming of the promised Messiah, what God promised to the fathers now fulfilled in Jesus (13:23, 32–33; the Abrahamic promise, 3:25–26); and the redemption of Israel, the hope of Israel for which Paul wears his very chain (28:20; the disciples’ own question about restoring the kingdom, 1:6–7, and the present-and-future kingdom discussed at 20:25). All three are finally one hope, and Paul’s whole defence is that Israel’s centuries-long longing has found its Yes in the risen Christ.

Rooted in the Old Testament. And the hope itself is rooted in the Old Testament of the twelve tribes who earnestly worship night and day (v. 7). The resurrection was promised there: “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2; compare Job 19:25–27; Isaiah 26:19). By Paul’s day it was woven into daily Jewish prayer: the second blessing of the Amidah still praises God as the One who revives the dead, and the Mishnah counted denying the resurrection a grave error (Sanhedrin 10:1). The Messiah’s coming is the promise to the fathers itself: Abraham’s offspring in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18) and David’s everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16), sung by the prophets (Isaiah 9:6–7; Jeremiah 23:5; Micah 5:2). And the redemption of Israel is the prophets’ great restoration hope (Isaiah 40–66; Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 36–37), prayed for to this day in the petitions for the ingathering of the exiles, the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and the Branch of David. Paul’s claim is simply that this whole age-old, daily-prayed hope has its Yes in the risen Jesus.

Can I pray for something for years and miss it when it comes? Yes, and this verse is a warning. God often answers in a form we did not expect, and if we have fixed in our minds exactly how the answer must look, we may resist it when it arrives. Israel expected a Messiah who would conquer Rome; God sent one who conquered sin and death by dying. Pray humbly, holding your requests open to God’s wisdom. And search the Scriptures to learn what he has actually promised, so that you recognise his answer, which is always, in the end, more of Christ.

In a sentence. Paul said he was on trial because of his hope in what God had promised their fathers, the promise the twelve tribes hoped to see fulfilled as they earnestly worshipped God night and day, and it was for this hope that he was being accused by Jews.

On a Tuesday. Your hope rests on God’s oldest promises. When you feel that your faith is a small, private thing, remember that you are standing in a line of hope that runs back through David and Abraham to the first promise in Eden (Genesis 3:15). Read one of the great promises this week, Isaiah 9:6–7 or 2 Samuel 7:12–16, and thank God that in Christ it has been kept.

For worship. The hope of Israel is fulfilled in Jesus. For two thousand years the fathers waited, and the prophets sang, and the twelve tribes prayed night and day, and God kept every word. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). The faithful God does not forget what he has sworn, and in the risen Christ he has given more than Israel ever dared to ask: not only a king, but a King who has conquered death for his people.

parallels.desc: because of the hope of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "'Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? Paul turns, mid-speech, and asks a question, and the Greek is plural. Any of you. He is no longer speaking only to the king. He has turned to the whole hall: the tribunes, the leading men of Caesarea, the governor, Jews and Gentiles alike. He puts one question to a room full of pagans and a Jewish monarch, and then goes straight back to his story without waiting for a reply. The question is not a debating trick. It is asking people to state their actual objection.

Not the hard part. Think about what is being claimed and where the difficulty really sits. If there is a God at all, the Creator who gives life and breath to all (17:25), who made the heavens and the earth out of nothing, who spoke light into existence, who formed every living thing from dust, then raising one dead man is not the hard part. It is nowhere near the hard part. A God who can start life from nothing can certainly restart it. So the question is not whether resurrection is possible, but whether God is God. The resurrection is not, in fact, rejected on the grounds of power. Nobody in that room believed in a God who could create the universe and would then find one grave beyond him. The resistance is somewhere else entirely.

What would follow if it were true. Here is the test, and it is worth running slowly, because it applies as much in a modern sitting room as in a Caesarean audience hall. When someone says the resurrection is impossible, ask what would follow if it were true. Not whether it is likely; what would follow. Because if a dead man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then he is who he said he is, and the universe has an owner, and everyone in it has an appointment. Much of the case against the resurrection is not an argument about evidence. It is a preference about consequences, wearing an argument’s clothes. Paul knew that from the inside, which is why the very next sentence is about himself.

I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Paul admits he once thought it incredible too, at least of Jesus. He does not say he was indifferent, or uninformed, or had never looked into it. He says he was convinced, and that he believed opposing Jesus was a duty. Ought: he thought it his duty. He was not sinning against his conscience; his conscience was fully engaged, and it was pointing the wrong way. That is a sobering thing to sit with. A man can be sincere, disciplined, devout, thoroughly persuaded, entirely at peace with himself, and be at war with God. Sincerity is not a defence. Paul’s was total, and it made him more dangerous rather than less. Sincere, and wrong.

How do I know my own convictions are not wrong, as Paul’s were? By testing them against Scripture, not against the strength of your feelings. The Bereans checked even Paul’s preaching against the Scriptures daily (17:11). Ask whether your conviction exalts Christ or opposes him, whether it agrees with the plain teaching of God’s Word, and whether it produces love, humility and holiness or pride and harshness. Be willing to hear correction from mature believers. And pray, as the psalmist did, that God would search you and see if there is any grievous way in you (Psalm 139:23–24). A conscience must be taught by God’s Word to be a safe guide.

In a sentence. Paul asked why any of them should think it incredible that God raises the dead, and said that he himself had once been convinced that he ought to do many things in opposition to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

On a Tuesday. If God made the universe, raising the dead is not too hard for him. Believe it. When you stand at a graveside, or face your own death, say it to yourself: it is not incredible that God raises the dead. And if you talk with someone who thinks it impossible, gently ask the honest question: what would follow if it were true?

For worship. Nothing is too hard for the Lord. He spoke, and the worlds came to be; he breathed, and dust became a living man; he called, and Lazarus came out of the tomb with the grave clothes still on him. And on the third day he raised his own Son from the dead, never to die again. The God who did that will not lose one of his people to the grave. He calls into existence the things that do not exist, and he gives life to the dead (Romans 4:17). Praise him, the God of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.

I not only locked up many of the saints in prison. He is speaking to a king, and he tells him this. Nothing compelled it. He is on trial; the charge is stirring up riots; his own past as a persecutor is not in evidence, and no prosecutor has raised it. Paul volunteers the worst thing about himself to the most important man who will ever hear him speak, and he does it in detail. Take the detail, because each phrase costs him something. Many of the saints: he calls his victims saints, God’s holy people. Then he called them heretics. The people he hunted are, he now knows, the holy ones of God, and he uses their proper title in the middle of his confession.

But when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. The Greek is a voting idiom, literally I cast down a pebble, the stone dropped into an urn to register a verdict, a dark pebble for condemnation. Whether Paul was formally a member of a council or whether this is simply the language of registered approval, commentators differ, and the text does not settle it. What the text does settle is the plural. When they were put to death. Stephen was not the only one. Paul has more than one execution on his conscience, and Luke has told us about exactly one of them.

And tried to make them blaspheme. The verb is imperfect: he kept trying, repeatedly, as a method. This is pressure, punishment and pain applied to force Christians to curse the name of Christ, the worst kind of persecution, attacking the soul. It became the standard imperial test: some eighty years later a Roman governor in Bithynia, Pliny, wrote to the emperor explaining that he released anyone who would curse Christ, since none of the real Christians could be made to do it. Paul used that technique against the church long before the empire adopted it.

And in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. Here Luke plants something the English cannot easily show. The phrase is perissōs emmainomenos, exceedingly mad, and the verb is from mainomai, to rave, to be out of one’s mind. Hold on to it, because in thirteen verses Festus is going to shout, Paul, you are out of your mind, using that same root (v. 24). Paul has already answered him. The madness in this story was not the preaching of a risen Christ. It was a brilliant, devout, exactingly trained man in a raging fury, dragging women out of their houses in the name of God (8:3). Paul is honest about the depth of his sin. He would call himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), and he is the greatest trophy of grace.

Why say it to a king? Because Paul is not building a character reference; he is building an argument, and his own biography is the evidence. Something turned that man into this one. No education did it, no disappointment did it, no gradual softening did it. Three verses from now he will name what did.

The freedom of the forgiven. There is a pastoral turn here that a reader should not miss. A man who has genuinely received mercy loses the need to manage his own reputation. Paul can say the worst about himself calmly, in public, to power, without flinching or excusing, not because the sin was small, but because the pardon is settled. People who are still uncertain of their forgiveness cannot do this. They edit. The freedom to tell the truth about your own past is one of the quieter proofs that grace has actually landed.

Can God forgive someone who has done something truly terrible? Yes. Paul had helped to kill Christians, and Christ forgave him completely and made him an apostle. He says that he received mercy precisely so that Christ might display his perfect patience in him as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:16). There is no sin so great that the blood of Christ cannot cleanse it, for those who repent and believe. Forgiveness does not erase earthly consequences, and where it is possible, the forgiven person should make things right. But the guilt before God is gone, and no past can cancel the welcome of Christ.

Should I tell other people about my past sins? Not everything to everyone. Paul told his story where it served the gospel and glorified Christ, not to dwell on the sin or to shock. Confess your sins fully to God; confess to those you have wronged, and seek their forgiveness. Share your past more widely only when it will help others see the grace of Christ, and with wisdom about who is listening and what details are fitting. The aim is always to make much of the Saviour, never of the sin.

In a sentence. In Jerusalem, with authority from the chief priests, he had locked up many of the saints in prison, cast his vote against them when they were put to death, punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in his raging fury pursued them even to foreign cities.

On a Tuesday. If there is something in your past you have never been able to speak of without shame, bring it once more to the cross, by name, and hear what God says: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). And if you know someone who thinks they are beyond forgiveness, tell them about Paul.

For worship. If grace could save Paul, it can save anyone. The persecutor who voted for the deaths of Christ’s people became the apostle who would die for Christ’s name. That is not a story of human improvement; it is the triumph of sovereign mercy over the worst a sinner can do. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20). Praise the Lord whose love is stronger than our fury, and whose pardon is so complete that his people can tell the truth about themselves without fear.
verseByVerse.note: “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply that he approved of the executions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.

With the authority and commission of the chief priests. The word for commission is epitropē, a delegated authority, a warrant. Paul is establishing that this was not a private vendetta. He was on official business, carrying the paperwork of the Jerusalem establishment, doing exactly what the men now prosecuting him had authorised him to do. That is a barbed thing to say in front of a Roman governor: the prosecution’s own institution issued the warrants. Official authority. Then he met a higher authority.

At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun. Two details in this telling, and both are chosen for the man in the chair. The first he had given the crowd too (22:6); the second is new. At midday: not dusk, not a bad night’s sleep, not a lonely vigil. Noon, on a public road, in Syria, where the sun at that hour is punishing. This is the least atmospheric moment of the day, the hour when nothing looks mysterious and everything is flatly, mercilessly visible. Brighter than the sun: Paul was standing under the fiercest natural light his world knew, and something outshone it. It is a small phrase and it makes a large claim: what stopped him was not a trick of heat or exhaustion, and it was not of this order of things at all. It was the glory of the risen Christ, the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

That shone around me and those who journeyed with me. Witnesses. He is arguing like a witness rather than a mystic. Ask the men who were with me; they saw the light too. Whatever else is in dispute, something objective happened on that road at noon in front of company.

The third telling. This is the third time Luke has told this story: first as narrator (9:1–19), then in Paul’s own words to a Jerusalem mob (22:3–21), and now to a king. The differences between the three tellings are real, and they have been worked through where they arise, at chapter 9 and chapter 22; there is no need to re-argue them here. What is worth noticing is why this version is shaped as it is. To a Jewish crowd Paul made Ananias the hinge, because a devout man of good reputation in Damascus was everything to that audience. To a king, Ananias disappears entirely, and the commission comes straight from the mouth of the risen Christ on the road. Not because Ananias has been edited out of history, but because Paul is doing what every honest preacher does: telling the same true story to the person actually in front of him, and giving that person the part of it he most needs to hear. A king needs to know who gave the orders.

Does Jesus still appear to people like this today? Not in the way he appeared to Paul. Paul’s vision of the risen Christ was part of his unique calling as an apostle, and he calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared in that way (1 Corinthians 15:8). God now speaks to us through his completed Word, and he brings people to faith through the preaching of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). We hear stories, sometimes from places with little access to the Bible, of people dreaming of Jesus, and Christians assess such claims charitably and differently. But any experience must be tested by Scripture and must lead a person to the Scriptures and to the church. You do not need a light from heaven: in the gospel you have the same Christ who met Paul.

In a sentence. On one such journey to Damascus, with the authority and commission of the chief priests, at midday he saw on the road a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around him and those travelling with him.

On a Tuesday. The glory of Christ outshines the sun. When the brightest things in your life, success, pleasure, a relationship, a plan, begin to fill your whole vision, remember that there is a light beside which they are shadows. Spend a few minutes today thinking about the glory of Christ as Revelation 1:12–18 describes it, and let it reorder what dazzles you.

For worship. At noon, under a burning sky, the Lord of glory let a sliver of his brightness through, and it outshone the sun. One day the city of God will have no need of sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts. Praise the Christ whose face is the light of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language. Three things in this verse are unique to this telling, and every one of them is worth its weight. We had all fallen. The relationship between this and the account at 9:7, where Paul’s companions are standing, is a genuine question, and it has been dealt with at chapter 9. The short of it is that a party knocked flat by a light at noon does not stay flat, and Luke is not writing a police report. It is settled there; it does not need re-arguing here.

In the Hebrew language. This is the detail Paul saved for a Jewish king, and it is astonishing if you slow down over it. The Hebrew language here most likely means Aramaic, the everyday tongue of the Jews of Palestine. The risen and glorified Christ, enthroned at the right hand of God, blazing brighter than the Syrian noon, speaks the language of Galilean villages and Jerusalem streets. He did not shed his humanity at the resurrection or exchange his mother tongue for the language of heaven. The man who is Lord of all still speaks like a man from Nazareth.

It is hard for you to kick against the goads. A goad was a long pole tipped with iron, used to drive oxen. If the animal resented it and lashed backwards, its own kick drove the point deeper. Kicking against it only hurt the ox. The proverb was well known in the Greek world for resisting the gods; it appears in Euripides and in Aeschylus, so the tribunes and the leading men of Caesarea, listening in, would have caught it instantly. The Lord speaks Aramaic to Saul and uses a Greek proverb in the same breath, and both halves of the room can follow him.

A goad you have felt. Sit with what the proverb actually says about Saul, because it is the most personally revealing sentence in the chapter. You cannot kick against a goad you have never felt. The image only works if something had already been prodding him, persistently, for some time, and he had been driving himself into it. The risen Christ tells Saul, in front of witnesses, that the persecution had been hurting the persecutor.

What the goads were. Scripture does not say what the goads were, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise. But Luke has been laying things in front of us for seven chapters, and it is hard not to notice them: a face like an angel’s in a courtroom (6:15); a dying man praying for his killers, out loud, while Saul held the coats (7:58–60); people who would not curse the name however hard they were pressed; and behind it all the uncomfortable possibility, for a man trained to read Moses and the prophets exactly, that these people might be right. He would have called all of that noise. It was a goad.

The kicking does the damage. And here is where it lands on the reader, because this is not only Saul’s experience. There are people who have been arguing with something for years: a verse that will not leave, a memory of a Christian who was inexplicably kind, a suspicion at three in the morning that the case for meaninglessness is weaker than they say in daylight. It is very easy to treat that as an irritation to be managed and kicked at harder. The Lord’s word to Saul is that the kicking is what is doing the damage. The goad was never the injury. It was the mercy. Resisting God only hurts yourself, and God’s goad would win.

Effectual grace. The picture is of a resistance that God overcomes. Paul kicked, and Christ conquered him. God’s grace is not forceful against our will, but it is effectual: it changes the will, and brings us willingly (Philippians 2:13).

If grace is effectual, why does God plead with people at all? Because God’s pleading is one of the means by which his grace works. He does not save people like stones, but as persons, through his Word: he speaks, warns, invites and goads, and by his Spirit he makes the heart willing to hear (John 6:44–45; 2 Timothy 2:25). The invitations of the gospel are sincere, and everyone who comes will be received (John 6:37). And when someone does come, it is because God first drew him. That is why we pray for unbelievers and keep speaking to them: the goads are God’s, and he uses them.

In a sentence. When they had all fallen to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him in Aramaic, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.”

On a Tuesday. Is there anything God has been pressing on you for a long time, a sin to give up, a person to forgive, a step of obedience, a truth you keep arguing with? Stop kicking. Name it before him today and yield. Surrender is freedom. And if someone you love seems to be resisting God, pray that the goads will keep pressing, and that the Lord will win.

For worship. How patient, how persistent, how kind is the Lord who goads his enemies until they come home. He let Saul see Stephen’s face, hear Stephen’s prayer and watch his people suffer without cursing their Lord, and every goad was mercy. Then he spoke his name, twice, in his own language, and the war was over. No sinner was ever conquered more gently or more completely. Praise the Shepherd who does not leave his sheep to kick themselves to ruin, but calls them by name and brings them in.
verseByVerse.note: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. It was a Greek proverb for resisting fate — or here, God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,

Who are you, Lord? I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. Saul asks the shortest and most important question a human being can ask, and he gets a name in reply, as before (9:5). Not a title. Not a description of divine glory. A name belonging to a man from a village in Galilee whom Saul knew perfectly well to be dead, and whose followers he was at that moment travelling to arrest.

Whom you are persecuting. Present tense, and note the object. Not whose people. The Lord of glory says that to lay hands on a believer in Damascus is to lay hands on him. It is the seed of everything Paul would later write about the church as the body of Christ, and since it belongs to the road rather than to this hearing, it is worked out where Paul first told it (22:7). The point for Agrippa is simpler and harder: the man you all agree was executed is speaking, and he is taking the arrests personally.
