But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose. The words are Ezekiel’s. Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you (Ezekiel 2:1), spoken to a man flat on his face before the glory of God, who is then sent to a rebellious people. Paul is being commissioned in the language of the prophets, and a king who knows his Scriptures would hear it. This is the commission of a prophet.

To appoint you as a servant and witness. Then the two words that define the rest of his life. The first is hypēretēs, an assistant, a subordinate officer, a man under orders; the word was once used of an under-rower in a ship. He does not choose the course; he does what he is told. The second is martys, a witness, one who testifies. A witness has no authority of his own and no freedom to improve the account. He reports what he saw. Both words are humble and solemn. It is the plainest possible description of a preacher, and it is the reason Paul could say later that he decided to know nothing among the Corinthians except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). He was not at liberty to be original. In this account, Paul compresses Ananias’s words into Jesus’ own, since they came from Jesus.

To the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you. There is a phrase at the end that is easy to miss. The Damascus road was not the last of it. There would be more revelations to come: the night vision at Corinth (18:9), the Lord in the temple (22:17), the Lord standing by him in the barracks (23:11), and whatever it was he could not put into words (2 Corinthians 12:1–4). Christ was not commissioning him from a distance and leaving him to it.

When was Paul born again? On the much-debated question of when in this Damascus-road encounter Paul was actually born again, whether he is already regenerate as he answers Who are you, Lord?, see the honest discussion at 22:10. The short of it is that Scripture does not pin the moment, the marks of a heart already being turned are plainly present, and the certain thing is not the when but the who: sovereign grace seized the persecutor.

Am I a servant and witness too, if I am not an apostle? Yes, in your own measure. Paul’s commission was unique: he was an eyewitness of the risen Christ, sent with apostolic authority. But every Christian is called to serve Christ under orders and to bear witness to what he has done (1 Peter 2:9; 3:15). You are not asked to be original or impressive. You are asked to tell the truth about Jesus as Scripture reveals him and as you have known him: what he has done, who he is, and what he has done for you. A witness only reports. That frees you from the pressure to persuade by your own cleverness.

In a sentence. He asked who it was, and the Lord said, “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you.”

On a Tuesday. Christ appoints his people as servants and witnesses. That is your calling too. Ask yourself this week where you are under orders and where you are choosing your own course. And think of one person to whom you could simply report what Christ has done for you, without trying to be clever.

For worship. The risen Lord takes every blow against his people as a blow against himself. He is not a distant Master who leaves his servants to suffer alone; he is the Head who feels every wound in his body. And he takes the man who struck him and makes him his servant and witness. What a Lord, who answers persecution with a commission, and turns an enemy into a friend who will carry his name to the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: "'delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.

Delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles. Read the promise carefully, because it is not the promise we would have written. The word is exairoumenos: rescuing, plucking out. Not protecting you from. Not keeping you clear of. Rescuing you out of, which presupposes being in. It is protection of the kind Jeremiah was promised (Jeremiah 1:8). And that is exactly how it went. He was stoned at Lystra and left for dead, flogged five times by his own people, beaten with rods three times, shipwrecked, imprisoned, and eventually executed. The Lord promised him rescue, and every single rescue happened, and not one of them was an exemption. Paul was delivered out of things, never spared them.

To whom I am sending you to open their eyes. Then the commission itself, and it is the fullest statement of it anywhere in Scripture: five clauses, and every one of them deserves plain words. To open their eyes: not to inform people, but to make blind people see. The assumption underneath is that the human problem is not primarily a shortage of information. Paul had all the information and was blind. And Paul, struck blind, was sent to open eyes.

So that they may turn from darkness to light. A change of realm, not of opinion. Darkness to light: from ignorance and sin to truth and holiness.

And from the power of Satan to God. This is the clause modern readers skip, and it should not be skipped. The New Testament says people are not neutral: they are held. Not usually in anything dramatic, but mostly in the ordinary machinery of self-interest, appetite, fear of what people think, and the settled conviction that one’s life is one’s own. It is a real dominion with a real ruler, and getting out of it is not a matter of trying harder. Conversion is a change of kingdom: God has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). It is a transfer of allegiance.

That they may receive forgiveness of sins. Receive: the posture of someone with open hands, not someone settling an account. This is the first gift.

And a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me. A place: the word is klēros, a lot, an inheritance, a share, a seat at the table with the holy ones. Sanctified: set apart as God’s holy people. And the ground of it is faith in Christ, stated at the end so nobody can mistake what the whole chain hangs on. Not by works or law, but by faith in me. It is a summary of the gospel from the lips of Jesus himself.

The Servant’s commission. Notice where this language comes from. A light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon: that is Isaiah, describing the task of the Servant of the LORD (Isaiah 42:6–7, 16). Christ takes the Servant’s own commission and hands it to Saul of Tarsus. What the Messiah was sent to do, he now sends this man to do in his name.

Does being under Satan’s power excuse unbelievers? No. Scripture holds together two truths: people are held captive by the devil (2 Timothy 2:26), and they love the darkness and choose it (John 3:19). Satan’s rule is not something done to unwilling victims; it is a rule people prefer, because it lets them keep their lives as their own. That is why no one is excused, and also why no one can free himself. Only Christ, the stronger man, can bind the strong man and set his captives free (Luke 11:21–22). This should make us humble about our own conversion and full of hope for others.

What does sanctified by faith mean here? It means set apart as God’s own, made holy in status, at the moment of faith. In the New Testament sanctification has two sides. There is the once-for-all setting apart of the believer, so that every Christian is a saint (1 Corinthians 6:11). And there is the lifelong work of the Spirit making us actually more holy (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Here Jesus speaks of the first: by faith in him, a person is given a place among God’s holy people. The second follows, and the first is its foundation.

In a sentence. Jesus said he would rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles, to whom he was sending him to open their eyes, so that they would turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, and receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those sanctified by faith in him.

On a Tuesday. You have been turned from darkness to light, forgiven and set apart by faith in Christ. Live as a child of light (Ephesians 5:8). Ask this week where in your life you still behave as though the old kingdom has a claim on you, and say no to it in Christ’s name. And when you pray for unbelieving friends, pray specifically that God would open their eyes.

For worship. Consider what the risen Christ says he is in the business of doing. He opens eyes that have been shut since birth. He fetches people out of the dark, not by improving them, but by moving them, out of one dominion and into another, against the will of the power that held them. He forgives, freely and finally, the sort of man who had been dragging his followers out of their homes. And then he gives that man a share in the inheritance of the saints, as though he had never done any of it. Not one clause of that is achievable from below. The whole chain, from the opened eye to the place at the table, is the work of the Lord Jesus Christ upon people who were doing nothing but resisting him, and there is no other explanation for a single Christian who has ever lived.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant.

parallels.desc: to open the eyes that are blind

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.

Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. It is one of the great understatements in Scripture, and the understatement is the point. Set the sentence against what it is summarising. Roughly twenty-five years. Three missionary journeys across Cyprus, Asia, Macedonia and Greece. Churches planted in a dozen cities. Five floggings of thirty-nine lashes from his own people, three beatings with Roman rods, one stoning that left him for dead, three shipwrecks, a night and a day adrift, constant danger from rivers, robbers, his own countrymen, Gentiles and false brothers; hunger, thirst, cold, sleeplessness; and daily anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). I was not disobedient. That is his own summary of it, offered to a king who asked what he had been doing. There is no sense of achievement in it, and no self-pity either. Just a man reporting that he did as he was told. A vision without obedience is useless, and grace makes obedience possible.

But declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles. Trace the geography and you are looking at the outline of the book: Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and the end of the earth (1:8). Paul’s career is the programme of Acts 1:8 walked out by one pair of feet.

That they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. Here is the message, and it is worth noticing how ordinary it sounds and how carefully it is built. Repent: change your mind. Turn to God: change your direction. And then do things that match, as John the Baptist preached (Luke 3:8). Deeds do not save; they show that repentance is real. This needs a guard, because it is the apostle of justification by faith saying that repentance must produce deeds, and someone will hear a contradiction. There is none. Paul is not saying the deeds earn the turning; he spent whole letters demolishing that. He is saying the deeds demonstrate it. By grace you have been saved through faith, not a result of works, and then, in the very next breath, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:8–10). The works are not the root. They are the fruit, and a tree with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.

Where Christians differ: faith and works. Some think Paul and James contradict each other on faith and works. Verdict: Paul teaches that we are justified by faith alone (Romans 3:28), and here, that true repentance produces fitting deeds. Works are not the root but the fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:18). Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

Name one. This turns into a plain test, and it is more searching than a general resolution to do better. Repentance in the New Testament is specific. It has an object. So: name one. Not a category; a thing. A conversation you have been avoiding because you were in the wrong. Money that is not yours. A habit conducted privately. A person you have written off. What is the deed that would be in keeping with the repentance you would say you have? If nothing comes to mind at all, that is worth sitting with rather than hurrying past.

What if I have repented but keep falling into the same sin? Then keep repenting, and do not despair. Repentance is not a single act at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life. A believer may struggle with the same sin for years, as Paul himself describes (Romans 7:15–25). The question is not whether you ever fall, but whether you hate the sin, confess it, and fight it, using the means God gives: prayer, Scripture, accountability and removing what feeds it (1 John 1:8–9). Fitting deeds include getting up again. And remember that your standing with God rests on Christ’s obedience, not on your record of victory.

In a sentence. So Paul had not been disobedient to the heavenly vision, but had declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God and perform deeds in keeping with their repentance.

On a Tuesday. Has your repentance shown up in your deeds? Ask God to make it visible. Choose one specific deed this week that fits the repentance you profess: the apology, the repayment, the conversation, the habit broken. Do it, quietly, and thank God for the grace that makes it possible.

For worship. The Lord who gave Paul the vision also gave him the obedience. Twenty-five years of floggings, shipwrecks and sleepless nights were not the strength of a hero but the faithfulness of Christ in his servant, who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). Christ himself was obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross, and his obedience is the righteousness of every believer. Praise him, the faithful Son, whose perfect obedience covers our failures and whose grace produces our fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:

For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. Paul puts the cause plainly: this, the Gentile mission, the opened eyes, the place among the sanctified given to outsiders by faith, is why they tried to kill him. Not the resurrection in the abstract. The resurrection with the door left open. He was attacked because he preached to Gentiles.

To this day I have had the help that comes from God. The word is epikouria, and it is rare; it appears only here in the New Testament. In ordinary Greek it carried a military flavour: the aid an ally brings, reinforcements arriving for a position under pressure. Paul does not say he has been resilient, or that he has coped, or that he has a strong constitution. He says help arrived from outside. This is the secret of Paul’s survival.

To this day. That phrase gathers up an extraordinary list. The basket over the Damascus wall. The plot at Jerusalem. The stoning at Lystra. The prison at Philippi. The riot at Ephesus. The plot at Corinth. The mob in the temple court. The flogging that was stopped. The forty men and their oath. Every one of those should have ended the story, and Paul’s account of why it did not is one word: help came. That is a truer picture of the Christian life than the one we usually carry. Perseverance does not feel like strength of character from the inside. It feels like being kept, like arriving at the end of another week still believing, and being unable to identify a single heroic decision that accounts for it.

And so I stand here testifying both to small and great. He is standing in front of a king, a governor, the tribunes and the aristocracy of a Roman capital, and he mentions the small first. Slaves and kings alike; today, the great. That order is not accidental in a man who had said the same things to a jailer at midnight, to a slave girl in the street, and to a group of women at a riverside. The gospel Paul preached to Agrippa is the gospel he preached to the man who guarded him. There was no upgraded version for the room with the tribunes in it.

Saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass. And this is the hinge of his whole defence. Paul’s claim is not that he has founded something. It is that he has not added a syllable. Everything he preaches, he insists, was already in the books Agrippa’s own priests read out every Sabbath. The charge against him is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room, and his accusers are the ones who have stopped believing their own Scriptures. Paul’s gospel was not new, but the fulfilment of the Old Testament. Christianity is not a break from Moses, but his goal.

How do I experience God’s help today? Usually not in dramatic rescues, though God can give them, but in being kept: given strength for the day, grace to endure, wisdom at the moment you need it, the encouragement of a friend, a promise from Scripture that comes alive, a door that opens or closes. God has promised never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5–6), and his grace is sufficient in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Ask for his help specifically in prayer, and then look back regularly and notice where it came. Most believers, when they look back honestly, can say what Paul said: to this day, I have had help from God.

In a sentence. That was why the Jews had seized him in the temple and tried to kill him, but to that day he had had the help that comes from God, and so he stood testifying to small and great alike, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses had said would come to pass.

On a Tuesday. Look back over the past year and list three times when God helped you, whether you saw it then or only now. Thank him for each one. Then think of someone who is small in the world’s eyes, a child, an elderly neighbour, a cleaner, a refugee, and give them the same gospel and the same respect you would give anyone important.

For worship. Consider what it means that they were all speaking of him. Moses at the burning bush and the passover lamb; the prophet like Moses yet to be raised up; the seed of Abraham in whom the nations would be blessed; David’s son on a throne that would not end; the child born in Bethlehem, too small a town to matter; the Servant with no beauty that we should desire him, despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions not his own, silent before his shearers, numbered with the transgressors, and afterwards seeing the light of life and being satisfied. Some thousand years of writing, by men who mostly never met each other, in Hebrew and Aramaic, and all of it converging on one week in Jerusalem and one man walking out of a tomb. The whole library was about him. Every promise God ever made has its Yes in Jesus Christ, and the God who kept all those promises is the help of his people to this day and every day.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.' And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.”

That the Christ must suffer. This is the summit of the speech, and Paul has built the whole thing to land here. Three claims, tightly packed, every one of them contested. That the Christ must suffer: the must is doing enormous work. For most first-century Jewish expectation, a suffering Messiah was not merely unexpected; it came close to being a contradiction in terms. The Messiah was the one who ended suffering, not the one who absorbed it. Paul says the suffering was never an accident or a setback; it was the appointment. The Scriptures foretold a suffering Messiah (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22). The Lord himself made the same point on the Emmaus road: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26; see 24:46).

And that, by being the first to rise from the dead. This needs a careful word, because it is easy to trip over. Others had been raised before: the widow’s son, Jairus’s daughter, Lazarus. But every one of them died again; they were returned to the life they had, and each of those graves was eventually reopened. Christ is the first to rise and stay risen, out the far side of death permanently, in a body that cannot die. That is why Paul elsewhere calls him the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20, 23) and the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18): not the only sheaf, but the first of a harvest, and the guarantee that the rest is coming.

He would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles. And here Paul says the thing that has been getting him beaten for twenty years, and says it to a king, in a room full of Romans, without softening it. The risen Christ proclaims light, through his messengers (Isaiah 49:6).

What did Paul mean by proclaim light? Not a vague glow of enlightenment, but something concrete: God’s saving rescue dawning on a world sunk in darkness. Paul is not coining an image; he is quoting Isaiah. The very phrase, light to our people and to the Gentiles, is the Servant Songs’ language: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6); a light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners (Isaiah 42:6–7). In Isaiah, light stands with three things: salvation, the opening of blind eyes, the freeing of prisoners. That is what the light is: God’s saving deliverance, sight for the blind, rescue for those in the dark.

We are not guessing. The lines converge. Paul had already applied that exact text to his mission: “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth” (Acts 13:47, quoting Isaiah 49:6), so light means salvation reaching the nations. The immediate context defines it too: a few sentences earlier (26:18) his commission was to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness. And the engine of the verse is that it is by being the first to rise from the dead that Christ proclaims light: the resurrection itself is the sunrise, new-creation life breaking over the grave (Isaiah 9:2; 60:1–3).

Where did Moses and the prophets say this? Paul does not list the texts, but the apostles preached from them: the suffering servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and the sufferer of Psalm 22 for the death; Psalm 16:8–11 (compare 2:25–31; 13:35) and Isaiah 53:10–12 for the resurrection; and the promise to bless the nations through Abraham and to make the servant a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6; compare 13:47).

Simeon’s song. One more confirmation, and it is beautiful. Luke opened his Gospel with old Simeon lifting the infant Jesus and calling him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” (Luke 2:32), again Isaiah 49, again light for Gentiles and Israel. What Simeon sang at the cradle, Paul declares at the climax of the mission: the same Isaianic light, for the same two peoples. So the meaning is sure: Christ crucified and risen is God’s promised light, salvation, sight and life, now streaming to Jew and Gentile alike. (The image of sons of light and sons of darkness was current in Paul’s Jewish world, and the Dead Sea community used it freely, but the source he cites is Isaiah.) For everyone who has ever sat in a long inward darkness, this is the gospel: the Light has come, and his name is Jesus.

Why must the Christ suffer? Because there was no other way to save sinners. God’s justice required that sin be punished, and his love purposed to save. At the cross both met: Christ bore in our place the penalty our sins deserved. He was pierced for our transgressions, and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:5–6). God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The must is not fate; it is the necessity of holy love. And because he suffered, he could rise as the first of a great harvest.

Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind. And as he was saying these things in his defence, Festus shouts. The governor of Judea, presiding, loses his composure in public and interrupts a prisoner mid-sentence, and note precisely where. Not at the light for the Gentiles, which no Roman would object to. At the resurrection. Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd (17:32). His diagnosis is almost affectionate: your great learning, literally your many letters, is driving you mad. A compliment and an insult: you are too clever for your own good. Festus has decided that Paul is a scholar who has read himself into a delusion. It is the oldest way of not answering an argument: locate a cause for the belief and you need not examine the reasons for it. He is not saying Paul is wrong. He is saying Paul is unwell, which is easier. Jesus too was called mad (Mark 3:21; John 10:20).

In a sentence. Paul said the prophets had foretold that the Christ must suffer and, as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light both to the Jewish people and to the Gentiles; and as he was saying these things, Festus shouted that Paul was out of his mind, his great learning driving him mad.

On a Tuesday. If you are called foolish for believing the resurrection, you are in good company. Do not answer contempt with contempt. Answer as Paul is about to: calmly, courteously, with the facts. And if you yourself have ever been tempted to explain away someone’s faith rather than listen to their reasons, notice that this is what Festus did.

For worship. The light of the world was put out on a Friday afternoon, when darkness covered the land from the sixth hour to the ninth. And on the third day, before dawn, the Sun of righteousness rose with healing in his wings. He suffered because he must, for our sake; he rose because death could not hold him; and now he proclaims light to every nation under heaven. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Glory to the risen Christ, the firstfruits of them that sleep, whose rising is the morning of the new creation.
verseByVerse.note: Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said, 'I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.

I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus. Paul has been interrupted, publicly, by the most powerful man present, and told he is insane in front of the entire provincial establishment. Watch what he does with that. He does not lose his temper, and he does not grovel. He addresses Festus by his correct title, most excellent, the formal style of address for a governor, and then flatly denies the charge. Calm and courteous, not offended. Courtesy and contradiction in the same breath. He gives the office its honour and gives the accusation nothing at all.

But I am speaking true and rational words. Then he picks his words with precision. True (alētheias): factually true, words of truth. Rational (sōphrosynēs): soundness of mind, sober judgment, the settled self-possession the Greek moralists prized above almost everything. It is the exact opposite of mania, the word Festus has just thrown at him. Paul is not merely denying the charge; he is claiming the opposite virtue, in the vocabulary the room respects. Christianity is not madness but sober truth. Faith is reasonable.

The madness already located. And the reader who has been paying attention already knows how this argument comes out, because Paul settled it fourteen verses earlier without anyone noticing. When he described himself hunting Christians in raging fury (v. 11), the word he used was built on that same root, mainomai. The madness in this story has already been located, and it was not on the Damascus road. It was the exactingly trained Pharisee dragging people out of their houses in the name of God.

For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. Agrippa knew the facts. He is not being asked to accept a private experience he has no way of assessing. He is being asked about recent, public, checkable history in his own territory.

For this has not been done in a corner. A proverb, and a claim, and it has been the backbone of Christian apologetics ever since. The mystery religions of the ancient world did their business in corners: secret rites, private initiations, truths for insiders that could never be checked. Paul says his message is the opposite kind of thing. The life, death and resurrection of Jesus concern events that happened in public, in a known province, in a named city, under a Roman governor whose name is on record, in front of hostile witnesses who are still alive and could be called. Which is still the shape of the thing. Christianity does not ask anyone to accept a feeling that occurred to somebody in private. It stakes everything on a claim about a particular execution and a particular tomb, in a particular week, in a city you can still walk around. Paul was content to have that investigated. He was, in fact, asking for it.

Is faith opposed to reason? No. Biblical faith is not believing without evidence or against it; it is trusting God on the basis of what he has shown and said. Paul reasons here from history and from Scripture, and the New Testament everywhere appeals to witnesses and facts (Luke 1:1–4; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8; 1 John 1:1–3). Faith goes beyond what reason alone can reach, because it is personal trust in Christ worked by the Spirit, but it is never unreasonable. Christians are to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in them, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

In a sentence. Paul answered that he was not out of his mind, most excellent Festus, but was speaking true and rational words, for the king knew about these things and he could speak to him boldly, being persuaded that none of this had escaped his notice, since it had not been done in a corner.

On a Tuesday. When your faith is mocked, take Paul as your model: honour the person, deny the charge, and point to the facts. Be ready to explain, in a sentence or two, why you believe Jesus rose: the empty tomb, the witnesses, the changed lives. Your faith rests on facts, not feelings, and you need not be afraid to say so.

For worship. The gospel happened in public history. The eternal Son did not whisper salvation in a corner; he took flesh in a known town, walked real roads, was crucified under a named governor, and rose from a tomb that anyone could visit. God has done his greatest work in the open, before the eyes of the world, so that his people might know the certainty of the things they have been taught. Blessed be the God of truth, whose word is sober, true and wholly to be trusted.

verseByVerse.quote: "'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' And Agrippa said to Paul, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?”

King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe. Paul turns from the governor, who has just called him mad, and puts a direct question to the king, and then does not wait for the answer. He supplies it himself. Paul turns from defence to evangelism: a direct, personal question to a king. It is the boldest moment in the speech, and it is also a beautifully laid trap, though not a cruel one. Consider Agrippa’s position. If he says yes, I believe the prophets, he has conceded the entire argument, because Paul has just spent twenty verses demonstrating that the prophets promised a suffering and rising Messiah who would bring light to the Gentiles. If he says no, he has publicly renounced the Scriptures in front of the Jewish subjects whose high priest he appoints, with Roman officers listening. He can neither affirm nor deny. He is in a corner. So he does the third thing.

In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian? The Greek here, en oligō, is genuinely ambiguous, and honesty requires saying so. It can mean in a little time, and it can mean with little effort, by a little argument. The ESV notes that the question can also be read: in a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian? The King James took it as degree and gave us the famous rendering, almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian; most modern translations take it as time. The tone is not recoverable from the page. Read one way it is a courtroom deflection with a smile in it, probably ironic or evasive: do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly? Read another, it is the nearest a Herod ever came. The old rendering became a famous hymn and sermon, but probably misreads him.

Christian. What is not ambiguous is the word he reaches for. It appears only three times in the New Testament: coined as a nickname at Antioch (11:26), used by Peter of those who suffer under it (1 Peter 4:16), and here, on the lips of a king, almost certainly with an edge on it, probably said with a sneer. Agrippa will not name the man; he names the party. And whichever way the irony ran, the effect was the same. He changed the subject, and a few sentences later he stood up and left.

Almost persuaded. Whatever Agrippa’s exact tone, the old rendering, almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian, has fixed on a tragic spiritual place, and it is worth naming. To be almost persuaded, interested, impressed, moved, near the kingdom, is still to be on the wrong side of the line; almost saved is wholly lost. Many perish not as scoffers but as the almost: those who came close, admired the gospel, felt its pull, hesitated, and never crossed over. Mark Paul’s reply (v. 29): he longs that Agrippa and all who hear would become such as I am, not almost, but altogether, except for these chains. Do not stop at almost.

How should I respond when someone deflects the gospel with a joke? Gently, and without letting it close the door, as Paul does in the next verse. Smile, take the humour in good part, and then return kindly to the real question: but what do you actually think of Jesus? Humour is often a shield people raise when a subject gets too close. Do not attack the shield or force your way past it. Show that you care more about the person than about winning the exchange, and leave the door open for another time. Then pray, because only God can turn a deflection into a question.

In a sentence. Paul asked King Agrippa if he believed the prophets, saying he knew that he did, and Agrippa replied to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?”

On a Tuesday. Do not deflect the gospel’s personal questions. Answer them honestly. If you have been near the kingdom for a long time, interested, moved, attending, admiring, but have never actually come to Christ for mercy, do not stop at almost. Come today. He receives all who come.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is never almost anything. He was not almost obedient, or almost crucified, or almost raised; he finished the work the Father gave him to do, and cried, It is finished. He does not almost save; he saves to the uttermost all who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The kings of this world may hover at the edge of his kingdom and walk away, but he who began a good work in his people will bring it to completion. Praise the Saviour who saves altogether.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the question can also be read “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” “Christian” was still a nickname used by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.' Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.” Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them.

Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am. Agrippa has just deflected him with a piece of wit, and everyone in the hall would have understood that as the end of the exchange. A king makes a joke; the room smiles; the awkward moment passes. Paul does not let it pass. Whether short or long: he picks up the king’s phrase and refuses the exit. Little or much, quickly or slowly, it does not matter to me; what I want is the thing itself. A heart for the lost. Paul does not care how long it takes; he wants them all saved.

He prays out loud. And then he does something that should stop us. In a Roman audience hall, on trial, in front of a governor, a king, the tribunes and the leading men of the city, Paul prays out loud. I would to God is not a figure of speech; it is a wish addressed to God in the hearing of everyone present. He stops arguing and starts interceding, in public, for the man judging him. Love for his judges.

Such as I am. Consider what he is offering, and from what position. He owns nothing. He has been in custody for over two years. He is going to be put on a ship to Nero. Everyone in that room outranks him, and every one of them will sleep tonight somewhere better than he will. And he looks around it, the king in his state, Bernice in her jewels, the officers, the money, the governor, and what he feels is not envy. It is pity. He wishes every one of them had what he has. A prisoner wishing a king were like him. He was richer than all of them: forgiven, free in soul, a child of God. That is either delusion or it is the most serious claim in the book. There is no third option. A man in irons pitying a king is either out of his mind, as Festus has just said, or he possesses something that makes a Herodian court look impoverished.

Except for these chains. The kindest clause Paul ever spoke, with a touch of grace and wit; he may well have lifted his chained hands. It does two things at once. It tells you what he was actually asking for. Not sympathy. Not release. Not agreement in a debate. He wanted them to have Christ, and he was careful to specify that he was not wishing his suffering on them, only his Lord. He wishes them his faith, not his chains. And it tells you the chains were on his mind. He is not posturing as a man above his circumstances. He knows exactly what he is wearing and mentions it lightly, without complaint, as the one part of his life he would not pass on.

Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. Nobody answers. The king had heard enough, and he ended the hearing. The most direct appeal in the New Testament, made by the finest preacher of the age, to a man who knew the Scriptures, and the response is that everyone stands up and the meeting ends. Not a refutation. Not an argument. An adjournment. That is how most people decline Christ, then and now. Not with an objection, which at least takes the thing seriously, but by finding that the hour is late and there are other matters and the conversation has reached a natural close. Agrippa did not say no. He simply stood up, and the standing was the answer. We know of no response of faith. He heard the gospel from the greatest apostle, and walked away.

Is it proud to wish that others would become like me? It would be, if Paul meant his personality, achievements or opinions. He means his faith in Christ, his forgiveness, his standing as a child of God: things he received as a gift and did not earn. Paul could say, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), because what he wanted others to copy was his Saviour. A Christian should long for others to have what he has in Christ, and this is not pride but love. The test is whether you would gladly see them surpass you, as long as they have Christ.

In a sentence. Paul replied that, whether in a short time or long, he prayed to God that not only the king but all who heard him that day would become such as he was, except for these chains; then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those sitting with them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for everyone you know to become a Christian, whether in a short time or long. Make a list of five people, and pray for them by name this week. And ask yourself honestly whether, when you look at those richer or more powerful than you, you feel envy or pity. If you have Christ, you have more than all of them.

For worship. A man in chains pitied a king, because he possessed the unsearchable riches of Christ. That is what the gospel does: it makes a prisoner wealthy and a beggar a prince. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). In him we have forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, and an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading. Every throne in that hall was poorer than Paul’s cell. Praise the Lord who gives himself to his people, and with himself, everything.

parallels.desc: an ambassador in chains

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, 'This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.' And Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment. The verdict is delivered in the corridor, after the doors have closed, where it costs nothing and changes nothing. That is the fifth time. Gallio at Corinth threw the case out (18:14–15). Claudius Lysias put it in writing that he found nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29). Festus told Agrippa the prosecution had brought no charge of the kind he expected (25:18), and then admitted to the assembled province that he had nothing to write (25:25–27). And now a Jewish king, a Roman governor and the senior officers of the garrison agree among themselves that the prisoner has done nothing at all. Luke has been laying these down for eight chapters without a word of comment. He does not need one. It is just as it was with Jesus before Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:14–15). Christianity was investigated repeatedly by the authorities best placed to convict it, and the file kept coming back empty. Christianity is no threat to lawful government.

This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar. The last line of the chapter, and it is layered. Legally, Agrippa is right, and it is worth understanding why. Once a citizen’s appeal to the emperor had been formally registered, the provincial court’s jurisdiction was gone. Festus could not now release Paul even if he wanted to; the case belonged to Rome. Paul’s own act had closed the door behind him. So the natural reading is that Paul made a mistake: that he was a few weeks too quick, and talked himself out of an acquittal.

The appeal was the road. Except that the reader knows something Agrippa does not. Two years earlier the Lord had stood beside him in a barracks cell in the dark and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). The appeal was not a miscalculation. It was the road. And notice what the alternative would actually have been. Released in Caesarea, Paul walks out into a province where a standing conspiracy has already sworn to kill him and where the leadership has twice tried to have him moved somewhere they could reach. Freedom in Judea was not a long-term prospect. What looked like the closing of a door was, in fact, the only route to the city he had been promised, and he would travel it at imperial expense, under armed guard, as a protected prisoner of the state. Paul’s chains would carry the gospel to the capital of the world and into the emperor’s own guard (Philippians 1:12–13).

Both things standing. That leaves both things standing at the end of the chapter, and the Christian life is usually lived with both. Paul is innocent, and everyone who matters knows it, and he will not be released. That is a real injustice, and Luke does not soften it. And it is also, at the same moment, the exact mechanism by which a promise made in the dark is being kept.

The saddest line in Acts. There is one more thing here. Agrippa has just delivered the correct verdict on Paul, and walked out of the room without dealing with a word Paul said. He got the legal question right and the only question that mattered wrong. He pronounced the prisoner free, and left as the one still bound.

What if a decision I made seems to have closed a good door? Bring it to God honestly, and remember Paul. A choice that looks like a mistake may be the very road God intends. If you acted in good faith and with prayer, trust that the Lord, who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11), has not been taken by surprise. If you acted wrongly, confess it, and know that God weaves even our failures into his purposes for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Either way, do not live in endless second-guessing. Ask what faithfulness looks like now, on the road you are actually on.

In a sentence. As they withdrew, they said to one another that this man was doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment, and Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

On a Tuesday. What seems a mistake may be God’s way. Paul’s appeal took him exactly where God wanted. Think of a door in your life that closed, a job lost, a plan that failed, a choice you regret, and ask God to show you how he may be using it. And if you have heard the gospel many times and agreed that it is harmless and true, do not be like Agrippa. Do not leave the room still bound.

For worship. Every court found Paul innocent, and none set him free, and through it all the Lord was keeping his word. So it was with his Master: Pilate found no guilt in him, Herod found nothing deserving death, and still they crucified him, and by that injustice God accomplished the salvation of the world. The Lord turns closed doors into open roads and unjust chains into the means of his promise. He is never thwarted, never late, never mistaken. And he still sets free the ones who were bound, if they will only come to him. Glory to the Christ who was condemned so that we, the guilty, might go free.
verseByVerse.note: Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Paul innocent.

26.title: Paul Before Agrippa
26.text: <sup>1</sup>So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: <sup>2</sup>“I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews, <sup>3</sup>especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. <sup>4</sup>My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. <sup>5</sup>They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. <sup>6</sup>And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, <sup>7</sup>to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! <sup>8</sup>Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? <sup>9</sup>I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. <sup>10</sup>And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. <sup>11</sup>And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. <sup>12</sup>In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. <sup>13</sup>At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me. <sup>14</sup>And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ <sup>15</sup>And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. <sup>16</sup>But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you, <sup>17</sup>delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles—to whom I am sending you <sup>18</sup>to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, <sup>20</sup>but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. <sup>21</sup>For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. <sup>22</sup>To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: <sup>23</sup>that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” <sup>24</sup>And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” <sup>25</sup>But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. <sup>26</sup>For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner. <sup>27</sup>King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” <sup>28</sup>And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” <sup>29</sup>And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains.” <sup>30</sup>Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. <sup>31</sup>And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” <sup>32</sup>And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
26.overview:
This is Paul’s fullest and most polished defence, given before King Agrippa II, Bernice, the governor Festus and the leading men of Caesarea. It is the third account of his conversion in Acts, now shaped for an audience that includes a Jewish king expert in the Scriptures. Paul presents his whole life as one story of Israel’s hope. He was a strict Pharisee; he is on trial for believing God’s promise to the fathers, the hope of resurrection. He once thought he must oppose Jesus’ name with all his strength, imprisoning and voting against believers. Then on the Damascus road, at noon, a light brighter than the sun stopped him, and the risen Jesus commissioned him as servant and witness, to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles, to turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, that they might receive forgiveness and a place among the sanctified by faith in him.

Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and its fruits everywhere, and he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets foretold: that the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead and bring light to Israel and the nations. Festus interrupts, shouting that Paul’s learning has driven him mad. Paul replies that his words are true and sober, and appeals directly to the king: do you believe the prophets? Agrippa deflects with a wry question; Paul answers that he wishes everyone listening would become what he is, except for the chains. The officials agree that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. In Luke’s design, the gospel has now been heard before a king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Setting Sail and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and other prisoners are handed to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort, and sail with Luke and Aristarchus on a coastal ship. At Sidon Julius kindly lets Paul see friends. Contrary winds take them past Cyprus to Myra, where they board an Alexandrian grain ship for Italy. Progress is slow, and they reach Fair Havens on Crete. It is now after the autumn Fast, and sailing is dangerous; Paul warns of disaster. But the centurion follows the pilot and the owner, and the majority vote to try for a better winter harbour at Phoenix. A gentle south wind tempts them out, then a violent northeaster rushes down from the island and drives them helplessly before it. Behind the island of Cauda they haul in the boat, brace the hull with cables, and, fearing the Syrtis sandbanks, lower the sea anchor. They throw cargo and tackle overboard. For many days there is no sun or stars, and all hope is lost. Then Paul stands up: they should have listened, but now they must take heart. An angel of the God he belongs to and serves has told him that he must stand before Caesar, and that God has given him the lives of all on board. They will lose only the ship and must run aground on an island.
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Actually Promised

The theology of this section turns on a distinction most Christians need more than they need another verse about victory: the difference between what God promises and what we assume he promises.

The angel's word was precise, and it had two halves. There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22), and then we must run aground on some island (v. 26). God guaranteed every person. He explicitly did not guarantee the vessel, the cargo, the owner's fortune, the crew's wages, or a safe arrival at a chosen port — and he said so in advance. Every one of those was lost, and the promise was kept in full.

That is the pattern of the promises Scripture actually makes. Nothing will separate his people from his love (Rom. 8:38–39); he works all things together for their good (Rom. 8:28); he will never leave them (Heb. 13:5). Read the list and notice what is not on it. Comfort is not on it. Property is not on it. The preservation of your circumstances is not on it. A believer standing in the surf watching his ship break up is not watching God fail; he may well be watching God keep his word exactly as given.

Alongside that runs the chapter's second theme: providence works through means, and never around them. God decreed that all 276 would live, and he decreed the whole chain that delivered it — the frapping cables, the four stern anchors, the sailors kept aboard, the meal at dawn, the swimmers going first. Paul's absolute confidence in the angel's word and his urgent practical interventions are not in tension; they are the same faith, and the sharpest expression of it is his own sentence at v. 31: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.

And note the instruments God employs. Not one of them is a believer. A centurion's professional kindness, a crew's seamanship, an officer's fear for his own career — the Lord uses them all, unimproved and unconsulted, and they go off duty with no idea what they have been part of.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The disaster began with a harbour that was perfectly safe and thoroughly boring. Fair Havens would have kept 276 people alive all winter. It was small, it sat beside an unremarkable village, it had no facilities, and staying there meant four idle months with a valuable cargo earning nothing. So the professionals took a vote and ran for somewhere better, forty miles down the coast, on one day's easy sail — and a gentle south wind came up that morning and seemed to confirm it.

Now: Most people can spot the obviously ruinous choice and avoid it. Far fewer notice the other moment — when something safe and unglamorous was working, and the only real argument against it was that it was dull. The job that was steady. The church that was ordinary. The routine that was quietly keeping you upright. The stretch of life that felt like stagnation and was actually shelter. And when you moved, the circumstances seemed to agree with you, because a following wind on the morning of a decision feels overwhelmingly like a green light and is very often just the weather. Before the northeaster, every soul on that ship would have told you they had made a sensible call. Afterwards, every one of them would have given everything they owned to be back in the boring harbour.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica.

Meaning first. Acts 27 is one of the most detailed accounts of a sea voyage from the ancient world, and an eyewitness story of shipwreck. Paul, a prisoner, sails for Rome. He warns against sailing late in the season and is ignored; a hurricane drives the ship for two weeks; all hope is lost. Then Paul stands up and says: an angel of the God I belong to has promised that not one life will be lost. He encourages them, gives thanks for bread, and every one of the 276 reaches land. The prisoner becomes the leader. God’s promise is kept, through storm, sailors and planks. It is a chapter about the sovereignty of God over wind and water and the decisions of men, and about the faithfulness of a God who never mislays a single soul entrusted to him.

And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy. The we is back, and it has been gone a long time. Luke last used it as the company arrived in Jerusalem (21:18), and everything since, the riot, the barracks, the council, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, has been told from outside. Now, as the ship casts off for Italy, the narrator is aboard again. That matters for how you read the next forty-four verses. What follows is the most detailed account of a sea voyage to survive from the ancient world, and it is detailed because a man who was there wrote it down: the ports, the winds, the depths in fathoms, the sailors’ slang for a particular gale, the exact sequence of emergency measures. Luke is not reconstructing. He is remembering. His seamanship details are remarkably accurate, as studies by experienced sailors have shown.

A centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. An imperial regiment, and a name worth remembering. Julius treats Paul well throughout, and before the chapter is over he will save Paul’s life.

Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. The ship was a coastal trader heading home, and it would hug the coast, calling at ports where they could find a ship for Italy.

Accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. Do not walk past that name. Aristarchus first appears when a mob in Ephesus seized him and dragged him into the theatre because he was known to travel with Paul (19:29). He was one of the companions who carried the collection to Jerusalem (20:4). And years later, writing from prison in Rome, Paul calls him my fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10). Paul is being shipped to Caesar under guard. Prisoners do not travel with friends; a Roman transport is not a passenger service. The most likely explanation, and the one most commentators reach, is that Luke and Aristarchus were permitted aboard as Paul’s personal attendants, which prisoners of status were allowed. That is to say, they accepted the status of a prisoner’s servants in order to be allowed to go.

Who would get on the boat with you? Two men, at the end of Paul’s usefulness to anyone, arranged their lives so as to be on that ship. Neither of them had to. Aristarchus had already been mobbed once for the association, and Luke had a profession he could have practised anywhere. That is worth turning on yourself before the storm starts, because it is a plainer question than it looks. Paul spent twenty-five years pouring himself into people, and at the end of it there were two who would get on the boat. Not two hundred. Two, and that was riches. Who would get on the boat with you? And whose boat are you on?

Who was Luke, and how do we know he was there? Luke was a doctor (Colossians 4:14), a Gentile companion of Paul, and the author of both the Gospel of Luke and Acts (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1). In several passages of Acts he slips from they to we (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), quietly telling us that he was present. He was with Paul on this voyage and later in Rome, and he stayed with him to the end (2 Timothy 4:11). That is why this chapter reads like a log: it is the testimony of a careful eyewitness.

In a sentence. When it was decided that they should sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius, and they embarked in a ship of Adramyttium bound for the ports along the coast of Asia, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica.

On a Tuesday. Friends who stay with you in hard times are a gift from God. Be one. Think of a believer you know who is going through a long trial, illness, imprisonment, a hard marriage, a slow grief, and who has fewer friends now than when life was easy. Get on the boat: visit, write, sit with them, stay.

For worship. The Lord who sent his servant to Rome did not send him alone. He gave him Luke and Aristarchus for the voyage, as he gave Elijah a widow and Jesus the women who stood by the cross. He is the God who sets the lonely in families, and who himself has promised, I will never leave you nor forsake you. And above every friend stands the Friend who laid down his life for his friends, who got into the boat of our humanity and went with us all the way down into death. Blessed be the Lord who never abandons his own.
verseByVerse.note: “We” returns: Luke sails with Paul. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. Aristarchus later shared Paul’s imprisonment.

parallels.desc: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner

verseByVerse.quote: "The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.

The next day we put in at Sidon. Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre, about seventy miles up the coast from Caesarea. It was the first day of the voyage.

And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. The phrase for being cared for means to receive attention, to be looked after. It is the word you would use of medical care or convalescence, and Luke the physician chose it. Paul has spent two years in custody and has just endured a season of hearings; the man is worn out, and the centurion lets him go ashore at Sidon to be tended by his friends, the believers there, probably under guard. The church cared for Paul. Julius did not have to do that. A prisoner appealing to Caesar was a serious charge to be responsible for, and letting him out of sight in a friendly port was a professional risk. He took it on the first day.

Keep an eye on this centurion. He will side against Paul at Fair Havens and be wrong; he will act on Paul’s word at the anchors and be right; and at the very end, when the soldiers propose killing every prisoner aboard, he will overrule them because he wants Paul alive (v. 43). Luke is not sentimental about him. He is a Roman officer doing a job. But he is one of a long line of decent pagans in this book whose ordinary kindnesses God uses without their knowledge.

Letting himself be cared for. It is also worth noticing what Paul receives here. He is the apostle; he has spent his life being the one who gives. And on this occasion he is simply a tired man being looked after by friends, and he lets them do it. There is a kind of Christian who cannot accept help and mistakes that for strength. Paul, on the first afternoon of the last voyage of his life, went ashore and let the church at Sidon take care of him.

We sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. Under the lee means on the sheltered side, out of the wind. They hug the eastern and northern coast of Cyprus to get some protection, because the prevailing westerly winds of late summer are already dead against them. Three verses in, and the wind is contrary. It will stay contrary for the entire chapter. Luke will use some form of with difficulty or slowly four times before the storm even arrives. This is not a voyage that goes well and then goes wrong. It is a hard voyage from the first hour, and the hardness is itself part of what Paul will read at Fair Havens.

How can I care for Christians who are in prison or hardship? Do what the believers at Sidon did: when the opportunity comes, receive them, feed them, rest them and encourage them. Scripture says to remember those in prison as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3). In practice that may mean writing to persecuted believers through organisations that serve them, supporting the families of those imprisoned for their faith, visiting Christians in local prisons through a chaplaincy, or simply caring practically for a worn-out pastor or missionary home on leave. Small kindnesses, offered at the right moment, can strengthen someone for the storm ahead.

In a sentence. The next day they put in at Sidon, where Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for, and from there they sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against them.

On a Tuesday. If you are worn out, let yourself be helped. Accept the meal, the offer of a lift, the day off, the prayer. And if you have any authority over others, at work or at home, use it as Julius did: notice who is exhausted, and give them leave to rest.

For worship. God gives his servants favour with unexpected people. He turned the heart of a Roman centurion toward his prisoner, as he gave Joseph favour with the keeper of the prison and Daniel with the chief of the eunuchs. The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD, and so is a centurion’s. And when his servant was weary, he provided a harbour full of brothers and sisters to care for him. How tender is the Lord with his tired children: he knows our frame, he remembers that we are dust.
verseByVerse.note: Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre. “Under the lee” means sheltered from the wind by the island.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia.

Along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia. A geographical note that Luke leaves entirely alone, and it is the kind of thing a careful reader is meant to notice for himself. Cilicia is Paul’s home province. Somewhere off that coastline, over the northern horizon, is Tarsus: the city he was born in, the city he named to the tribune on the barracks steps with a flash of pride, a citizen of no obscure city (21:39), the city he was sent back to for years of obscurity after Jerusalem became too dangerous (9:30). He sails past it in chains, on his way to Rome, and there is no record that he ever sets foot there again.

Places that slide past. Luke does not remark on it. There is no wistful sentence, no backward look. The ship is making slow progress against a headwind and the narrative moves on to Myra. But the man at the rail knew exactly what was behind that coastline, and it is one of the quiet costs of a life spent going where you are sent: the places that formed you slide past on the horizon, and you do not get to stop.

We came to Myra in Lycia. Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was one of the great transhipment ports of the eastern Mediterranean, a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt. It was later the home of Bishop Nicholas, the original Saint Nicholas. And it is here for a practical reason. The Alexandrian grain fleet, sailing from Egypt to Rome, could rarely make the direct westward run against the prevailing winds. The standard route was north to the Asian coast, then west along it. Myra is where you changed from a coastal vessel to an ocean-going one.

How ordinary the mechanism is. That is exactly what happens next, and it is worth registering how ordinary it is. The Lord had said Paul must testify also in Rome (23:11). The way that promise advances, on this particular afternoon, is that a centurion goes down to the harbour at Myra looking for a westbound ship, and finds one.

The safe part is over. And there is a second reason Myra matters. Up to this point the voyage has been coastal: hopping from port to port along a shoreline, always within sight of land, on a small vessel whose master knew these waters. From Myra onward Paul is on an ocean-going freighter making for Italy across open water. The safe part of the journey is over, and nobody notices it happening. There is no warning at Myra, no sense of a threshold crossed. A centurion books passage on a bigger ship because it is going the right way, and everyone steps aboard. Luke is a careful enough writer that the reader is meant to feel this only in retrospect, which is, of course, how it usually works.

What about the costs of going where God sends? They are real, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. Following Christ may mean leaving home, family, familiar places and plans, and sometimes never returning (Luke 9:57–62). Jesus promised that no one who leaves such things for his sake will fail to receive many times more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life (Luke 18:29–30). It is not unspiritual to feel the loss; Paul surely did. But it is never wasted. The places that slide past on your horizon are in God’s keeping, and the city he is taking you to is better.

In a sentence. When they had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, they came to Myra in Lycia.

On a Tuesday. Every port on the way was in God’s plan, and so is every stage of your journey. If you are in an ordinary in-between place this week, a waiting room, a commute, a temporary job, a season of transition, thank God that he is moving his purposes forward through it, even when nothing seems to be happening.

For worship. The God who numbered the stars has charted every port of his people’s voyages. He led Abraham out not knowing where he was going, he led Israel through the wilderness by a pillar of cloud, and he led his apostle past his birthplace and on toward Rome. Not one stage of the journey is outside his map. We are strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a homeland, and he is not ashamed to be called our God, for he has prepared for us a city.
verseByVerse.note: Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone.

There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy. An Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy means one thing: a grain freighter, and it is worth knowing what that was, because it explains most of what goes wrong in this chapter. Rome could not feed itself. The city’s bread depended on Egyptian wheat, shipped every year in enormous merchantmen, vessels far larger than most others afloat, some well over a hundred feet long, perhaps up to 180, carrying a thousand tons or more. The emperors treated the grain supply as a matter of state security, offered the shippers guarantees and inducements under imperial contract, and expected the fleet to keep running. That is why there are 276 people aboard this one, and it is also why she is at sea this late in the year with a cargo she cannot afford to hold over till spring. The commercial pressure behind the whole voyage is standing in the background of every decision that follows.

We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus. Read the verbs. Slowly. With difficulty. The wind did not allow. Luke has now used this vocabulary three times in seven verses, and he will use it again in the next. Cnidus is on the south-west tip of Asia Minor. The intended route was west past Cnidus and then across to Greece and Italy. The wind will not permit it.

As the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. So they turn south-west, round the eastern cape of Crete at Salmone, and creep along the island’s sheltered southern shore: a substantial detour that puts them where they must not be at the time of year they must not be there.

How disasters are assembled. Nothing dramatic has happened yet. There has been no storm, no crisis, no decision anyone would call a mistake. Just weeks of a wind that will not cooperate, and a schedule quietly falling apart, and a ship being pushed by ordinary weather toward a place nobody chose. That is how most disasters are assembled. Not by one bad decision, but by a long accumulation of small pressures, none of which seemed worth stopping for.

Do contrary winds mean God is against my plan? Not necessarily. Paul was exactly where God wanted him, on the way to the city God had named, and the wind was against him from the first day. Difficulty is not proof of disobedience, and ease is not proof of blessing. Sometimes God closes a road to redirect us (16:6–7); sometimes he lets us struggle on the right road to teach patience. The question is not how hard the journey is but whether you are going where his Word and wise counsel point. If you are, keep going, slowly if need be. And watch for the small pressures that push you toward decisions you would never have chosen at the start.

In a sentence. There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put them on board, and they sailed slowly for many days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow them to go farther, they sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week the small pressures in your life that are quietly pushing you somewhere you did not choose: the schedule that keeps slipping, the commercial pressure at work, the habit that creeps.
