Name one, and ask whether it is worth stopping for now, before it delivers you somewhere dangerous.

For worship. Slow progress and contrary winds are not outside God’s control. He brings out the wind from his storehouses, and he gives it its commission; every breeze that delayed that ship blew at his word. And he is never slow in his purposes, though he is patient in their unfolding. The God who took forty years to bring Israel through a wilderness that could be crossed in weeks knew exactly what he was doing, and so he does with us. His timing is perfect, and his ways are past finding out.
verseByVerse.note: Ships from Alexandria carried Egypt’s grain to feed Rome. Cnidus lay at the south-western tip of Asia Minor; they turned south to shelter behind Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.

Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens. Fourth time: with difficulty again. And then the name, which Luke surely enjoyed writing: Kaloi Limenes, Fair Havens. It is a small bay on the southern coast of Crete, and it still bears the name today. The one genuinely safe place in the chapter is called Fair Havens, and they will leave it.

Near which was the city of Lasea. Ruins have been found nearby. There is nothing wrong with the harbour. What is wrong is that it is small, not well protected for winter, exposed to part of the weather, and dull: a roadstead beside a minor town, with no facilities, no society and nothing to do for four months. It would have kept them alive. It simply would not have been comfortable, and it was not where anyone wanted to spend the winter.

A safe place that was inconvenient. Sit with that, because the whole disaster turns on it. The ship is not lost through recklessness or wickedness. It is lost because a safe place was inconvenient. That is worth a test, and a fairly searching one. Most people can identify the obviously ruinous choices in their lives and avoid them. Far fewer notice the moment when something safe and unglamorous was available, a job that was not exciting, a church that was ordinary, a routine that was working, a period of quiet that felt like stagnation, and the whole reason for leaving it was that it was dull. The northeaster is six verses away, and every soul aboard would give everything they own to be back in the boring harbour.

What safety looked like from inside. There is one more thing about Fair Havens worth registering. Wintering there would have cost them roughly four months: a small anchorage beside an unremarkable town, with a valuable cargo sitting idle, an owner losing money daily, a crew with nothing to do, and 276 people confined to a village that could barely feed them. It would have been tedious, expensive and completely uneventful. That is what the safe option looked like from the inside on the morning of the decision: not obviously safe at all, merely obviously irritating. Hindsight makes Fair Havens shine. Nobody standing on that beach in October could see the harbour the way we see it, and it is worth being honest about that before drawing any lesson from their choice. The right decision very rarely announces itself as the right decision. Usually it just looks like the dull one.

How do I know whether to stay or move? Begin with Scripture and prayer, and ask whether either option would require you to disobey God. Then ask honest questions. Why do I want to leave: because something is wrong, or because it is dull? Is the new thing necessary, or only better? What would I lose if it went badly, and could I bear it? Seek the counsel of mature believers who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Weigh your responsibilities to family and church. If staying is faithful and safe, boredom alone is a poor reason to go. And if you do move, go humbly, knowing that God can redirect you.

In a sentence. Coasting along it with difficulty, they came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.

On a Tuesday. A place can be called fair and still not be a safe place to stay, and a place can be dull and be exactly where you should be. Look at the ordinary, unexciting good things in your life this week, a faithful church, a steady job, a quiet marriage, a routine of prayer, and thank God for them instead of restlessly looking past them.

For worship. The Lord is our true fair haven, the refuge to which his people run in every season. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble; therefore we will not fear though the waters roar and foam. He never grows dull to those who know him, and he never fails those who shelter in him. He is the harbour that does not need to be left, and whoever dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.
verseByVerse.note: Fair Havens was a small bay on the south coast of Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, 'Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”

Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous. Sailing in the Mediterranean was considered dangerous from mid-September, and stopped altogether from mid-November to March. They are somewhere in the dangerous window, with the door closing.

Because even the Fast was already over. The Fast is the Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or October; in AD 59 it fell on 5 October. A Jewish writer dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar, a small sign of the world he and Paul actually lived in. And for the Christian reader there is a quiet irony in it: the great day of the old covenant, when the high priest sprinkled blood for the sins of the people, has passed, and the apostle of the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ is on his way to proclaim it at the heart of the world.

Paul advised them. A prisoner giving advice. Paul was an experienced traveller: writing to Corinth some years before this voyage, he had already listed three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea (2 Corinthians 11:25). Three. Before this one. The man warning them had been in the water more often than most of the crew.

I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives. Here is something that needs saying carefully, because it is easy to get wrong in the direction of piety. Paul is not prophesying. Look at his verb: I perceive, I observe, I can see. It is the language of assessment, not revelation. He does not say thus says the Lord, and Luke does not present it as a word from God. This is common sense from experience: the season is gone, the ship has fought a headwind for weeks, and the passage ahead is open water.

Right about the storm, wrong about the deaths. But notice the honest thing, and do not let it slide past. Paul read the danger rightly, but not its outcome. He said there would be loss of life. There was not: not one person died, as the angel would tell him later (v. 22) and as the last verse of the chapter records. Luke leaves the discrepancy standing without a word of explanation, and that is a great mercy to the reader. It means Scripture is not claiming that a godly man’s seasoned judgment is the same thing as divine revelation. Paul, giving his best assessment, was right about the storm and wrong about the deaths. Paul, delivering a message from an angel thirteen verses later, was exactly right about everything.

Two kinds of speech. Those are two different kinds of speech, and mature Christians distinguish between them. A wise believer’s strong sense about a decision is worth hearing and may well be right; Paul’s was right about the danger. It is not a word from God, it is not infallible, and it should never be presented as one. The damage done in churches by sincere people who could not tell the difference is considerable.

How do I tell a godly person’s opinion from a word from God? Ask where it comes from. A word from God for us today is what Scripture says, rightly understood, and it binds the conscience. Anything else, however wise or sincerely felt, is counsel: to be weighed, tested against Scripture and received with gratitude or set aside. Be wary when anyone, including yourself, says God told me about a decision that Scripture does not address. Better to say what Paul said here: I perceive, I think, this is my judgment. That is honest, humble, and often very helpful.

In a sentence. Since much time had passed and sailing was now dangerous, because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying that he perceived the voyage would bring injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of their lives.

On a Tuesday. Christians can give wise, practical advice in ordinary matters. Speak up when you see danger, at work, in your family, in your community, and speak with the right kind of confidence: I perceive, not God has told me. And when you are given such advice by a sensible believer, listen.

For worship. The Lord gives wisdom to his people for ordinary things as well as eternal ones: for the timing of a voyage, the running of a household, the work of their hands. Every good gift of sense and skill comes down from the Father of lights. And above all human perceiving stands his perfect knowledge, which is never mistaken and never partial. He sees the end from the beginning, and his word, unlike ours, is always exactly right. How precious are his thoughts, and how vast the sum of them.
verseByVerse.note: “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, in late September or October. Sailing became dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether in winter.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there.

But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And who would not have? It is important to be fair here, because there is a lazy reading of this verse in which the worldly men ignore the man of God and get what they deserve. That is not the situation, and pretending it is will teach the reader something false. Consider the room. On one side, the kybernētēs, the sailing master, the professional who handles this ship for a living, and the nauklēros, the owner or charterer whose money is aboard. On the other, a prisoner in chains with a religious reputation, no nautical qualification and no standing to be speaking at all. Understandable: the experts against a prisoner.

Because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in. The question is where to spend the winter. Fair Havens is a poor harbour, exposed and next to a village. Phoenix, some forty miles farther west along the same coast, is a proper wintering port, a harbour of Crete facing both south-west and north-west. The distance is a single day’s easy sail.

The majority decided to put out to sea from there. It was not the centurion’s decision alone. Luke records something like a vote, and the professionals, the owner, the officers and most of the company all landed the same way. Every part of that is reasonable. On any ordinary reckoning, they were right and Paul was wrong. But the majority was wrong. Truth is not decided by vote.

The competent men got it wrong. So resist the moral that expertise is not to be trusted; Luke is not saying that, and the crew’s expertise is about to keep everyone alive for two weeks. The point is narrower and stranger. The competent men, deciding competently, with good information and sound reasons, on a matter squarely inside their professional field, got it wrong. Expertise and profit can blind. And the one man who had no business having an opinion got it right, and he got it right by ordinary observation, not by revelation.

How do you know in advance? That leaves a genuinely uncomfortable question rather than a tidy lesson: how do you know, in advance, which kind of situation you are in? Most days the pilot and the owner are right. Luke does not offer a method for telling. He simply records that on this occasion the majority of qualified people, voting sensibly, sailed a ship into the worst storm of their lives. The one protection Luke does show is small and available to anyone: the harbour was safe, and the alternative was better rather than necessary. Nobody on that ship had to move. They moved because forty miles of improvement seemed worth a day’s risk at the wrong time of year.

Should Christians defer to experts? Generally, yes, in their fields. God gives real skill to doctors, engineers, pilots and lawyers, and it is wise and humble to listen to them. But experts are fallible, they can be influenced by money or pressure (the owner had a cargo to sell), and they cannot speak with authority on moral questions or on what God has said. So listen carefully, ask questions, seek a second opinion when much is at stake, and notice when someone with less standing but real experience is raising a concern. And never let a majority, however expert, persuade you to do what Scripture forbids.

In a sentence. But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and the owner of the ship than to what Paul said, and because the harbour was not suitable for wintering, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, hoping somehow to reach Phoenix, a harbour of Crete facing both south-west and north-west, and to spend the winter there.

On a Tuesday. The experts and the majority can be wrong. Listen to wise voices, even unexpected ones. In the next decision you face with others, ask the quiet person in the room what they think. And before you choose the better option over the safe one, ask whether you actually need to move at all.

For worship. The wisdom of the world is often folly with God, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men. He chose a prisoner in chains to be the wisest voice on that ship, as he chose fishermen to confound scholars and a crucified carpenter to save the world. He is never outvoted. Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. Blessed be the only wise God, whose counsel is perfect even when every expert on deck agrees against it.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenix was a better harbour farther west along Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land.

Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose. This is the most dangerous sentence in the chapter, and it describes perfect weather. A gentle southerly is exactly the wind you want to run west along the southern coast of Crete. It arrives as if on cue, immediately after the decision, and it confirms everything the majority concluded. Luke’s word for their state of mind is precise: supposing. They supposed that they had got what they wanted, the thing was settled, the plan was working. A gentle breeze, and false confidence.

Weather is not confirmation. That is worth stopping on, because a favourable circumstance following a decision feels overwhelmingly like confirmation, and it is nothing of the kind. Every soul on that ship read the soft south wind as a green light. It was simply the weather. Christians are especially prone to this. A door opens easily, a house sells, a job comes through, the money arrives just in time, and it is taken as evidence that the decision was right and God has blessed it. Sometimes it is. But the gentle south wind blew for the ship that was about to be destroyed, and it blew at precisely the moment that made the destruction possible. If they had met a headwind that morning they would have stayed in the harbour and lived through the winter in perfect safety and considerable boredom. Pleasant conditions can lure us into danger.

But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. Luke gives the sailors’ own name for it: Eurakylōn, a rough dockside hybrid of the Greek word for the east wind and the Latin for the north, the sort of word professionals use and outsiders do not know. It appears nowhere else in Greek literature. This is a landsman writing down the term he heard shouted on deck. And the word for tempestuous is typhōnikos, typhoon-like, a hurricane-force wind. Struck down from the land is exact too. Crete’s mountains rise to some eight thousand feet, and the killing winds there do not come across the water; they fall off the high ground without warning, hitting a ship from the shore she was hugging for safety. The very coastline they were sailing close to for shelter is where the wind came from. It usually is.

How do I tell whether an open door is God’s guidance? An open door alone tells you very little; it may be God’s provision, or simply the weather. Guidance comes first from Scripture: is the choice in line with what God has commanded and with his priorities for your life? Then pray, seek the counsel of wise believers, and consider your gifts, responsibilities and motives honestly. Circumstances can confirm a decision made on those grounds, but they cannot replace them. Be especially cautious when the circumstance happens to give you exactly what you already wanted. And whatever you decide, hold it humbly, ready for God to redirect you.

In a sentence. When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had obtained their purpose, so they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore, but soon a hurricane-force wind called the Northeaster struck down from the land.

On a Tuesday. Life’s storms come suddenly. Build on the rock before they come (Matthew 7:24–25). Do not wait for the northeaster to start praying, reading Scripture, or putting your house in order. And if something has gone smoothly for you this week, thank God for it, but do not read it as his signature on every choice you have made.

For worship. The winds belong to the Lord. He makes the clouds his chariot and rides on the wings of the wind; the gentle south wind and the howling northeaster both run at his command. And the Lord who sends the storm is the Lord who stands in it with his people. When the winds of Galilee fell on the disciples’ boat, he was there, and with a word he rebuked them. The storm that struck down from the mountains of Crete did not catch him by surprise; it was already folded into his promise to bring his servant to Rome. Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
verseByVerse.note: The northeaster (Euraquilo) was a violent wind sweeping down from the mountains of Crete.

parallels.desc: he raised the stormy wind

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.

And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind. Three phrases, and each one is a stage of surrender. The ship was caught: Luke’s word is the one used of a person seized or arrested, the same idea as a man taken into custody. The ship is not struggling any more; she has been taken. Could not face the wind: the word is antophthalmein, literally to look in the eye. Ancient ships often had eyes painted on the bow, and the ship could not look the wind in the eye. A vessel that cannot keep her head into a gale has lost the one thing that keeps her safe, because a ship survives heavy weather by facing it. Turned broadside, she rolls; turned tail, she runs wherever the wind sends her.

We gave way to it and were driven along. They stop trying. Luke puts it in the passive: we were driven along. Helpless; no longer sailing, but cargo. They let the storm carry them.

There is a time to stop fighting. It is worth being honest about what that means, because there is a kind of Christian teaching that cannot allow it. There are situations in which the correct, competent, faithful thing to do is to stop trying to make headway. Not every storm is to be fought through. Sometimes seamanship consists entirely in keeping the hull together while you go where you are being taken. Anyone who has sat with a serious diagnosis, or a bereavement, or a stretch of depression, knows the difference between the phase where effort still moves you and the phase where it does not. The instinct is to treat the second phase as failure, to interpret being carried as a lapse of faith or nerve. Luke does not treat it that way. He records it as what the professionals did, and it was right. They gave way, and were driven, for fourteen days, and the promise held the whole time, and the ship came apart at the end, and every single person walked out of the surf alive. Being carried is not the same as being lost. The question in a storm is never whether you are making progress. It is whose hands the wind is in.

Why does God not calm every storm, as Jesus did on Galilee? Because he has more than one way of saving his people. Sometimes he stills the storm (Mark 4:39); sometimes he brings us through it, as he did here; and sometimes he takes us home through it. In every case he is equally sovereign and equally present. A calmed storm shows his power over creation; a storm endured shows his power to keep his people and to fulfil his word in the worst conditions. If he has not calmed yours, it is not because he cannot, or does not care. It is because he is doing something through it that a calm would not do (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

In a sentence. When the ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind, they gave way to it and were driven along.

On a Tuesday. When you cannot steer, remember who rules the wind (Mark 4:41). If you are in a season where effort no longer moves anything, a long illness, a grief, a dark stretch, do not condemn yourself for being carried. Keep the hull together: the simple means of grace, rest, prayer however feeble, the company of believers. And leave the direction to him.

For worship. When we cannot face the wind, the Lord faces it for us. He is the God who rides upon the storm, who sat enthroned over the flood and sits enthroned as king for ever. His people may be driven, but they are never out of his hand; no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. The sea is his, for he made it, and every gale that drives his children along is carrying them, by his good pleasure, exactly where he has promised they will go.

verseByVerse.quote: "Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship's boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along.

Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda. Cauda is a scrap of land about twenty-three miles south of Crete, and running past it buys them a few minutes of slightly calmer water. Luke gives us what the crew did with those minutes, in order, and every item is exactly what a competent crew would do.

We managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. The dinghy had been towing astern, normal practice in fair weather. By now it was swamped and battering the hull, and if it broke loose they would lose their only means of getting ashore. Hauling a waterlogged boat aboard in a gale is brutal work, and Luke says we managed it with difficulty. The doctor and the prisoner’s companions were on the ropes.

They used supports to undergird the ship. Cables were passed under the hull and winched tight over the deck, like a belt around a barrel, to stop the timbers working apart, as the strain could split the ship open. It was a last-resort measure, and everyone aboard knew what it meant: the ship was already beginning to come apart.

Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis. Here is the fear that shaped the next fortnight, and a reader should feel it. The Syrtis were vast shifting sandbanks off the coast of Libya, south-west of them and directly downwind, notorious for wrecking ships. Ancient sailors spoke of them as later sailors spoke of the Goodwin Sands: shallow, unmarked, constantly moving, a place where a ship went aground miles from anywhere and was slowly broken up while the crew watched. Roman writers used the name as a byword for hopeless destruction. So the crew were not merely being blown about. They were being blown toward the one place they most feared, and they knew it.

They lowered the gear. The phrase is vague in Greek and probably means they set some kind of drag, a sea anchor, or lowered the mainsail, to slow the drift and keep the bow steady. Slow the drift: that is the whole strategy. Not escape, not progress, not rescue: buy time, and hope the wind changes before the sandbanks arrive. And it worked, in the sense that matters. They drifted for two weeks and never reached the Syrtis. Nobody aboard could have told you why.

Is it faithless to take precautions when God has promised to keep us? No. The crew did everything a competent crew should, and Paul never rebuked them for it; later he would insist that they stay and use their skills (v. 31). Faith does not mean neglecting means. Nehemiah prayed and set a guard (Nehemiah 4:9). Take your medicine, buckle your seat belt, save for the future, lock your door, and trust God. Precautions become faithless only when we trust them instead of him, or when fear drives us to grasp for control he has not given us.

In a sentence. Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, they managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat, hoisted it up, used supports to undergird the ship, and fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, lowered the gear and so were driven along.

On a Tuesday. Do what you can in the storm, and trust God for what you cannot. Make a short list of what is actually in your hands this week in a hard situation, and do those things faithfully. Then hand the rest, the things you cannot control, to God in prayer by name.

For worship. The Lord sets the bounds of the sea and says, Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed. The Syrtis lay downwind for fourteen days, and the ship never reached it, because the God who marks out the sands with his finger had marked out a different shore. He holds the drift of every ship and the course of every life. We do not see his hand on the tiller, but it is there, and it is steady.
verseByVerse.note: The ship’s boat was a dinghy towed behind. Cables were passed under the hull to hold it together. The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

They began the next day to jettison the cargo. Two days, two decisions, and together they measure how bad it had become. Day two: the cargo. This is an Egyptian grain freighter, and the wheat in her hold is the entire purpose of the voyage: the owner’s investment, the crew’s wages, the reason they were at sea in October at all. Rome was waiting for it. They begin heaving cargo over the side, as Jonah’s sailors did (Jonah 1:5), and the last of the wheat will follow on the final night (v. 38).

And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. Day three: the tackle. Spare spars, rigging, gear, perhaps the main yard: the equipment you need to sail the ship even if you survive. Throwing it away is an admission that there may be no sailing left to do. Luke adds a phrase that is easy to skim: with their own hands. He means it literally. There is no orderly unloading; the sailors are hauling their own livelihood to the rail and pitching it into the sea, personally, one armful at a time. Desperate. Everything that could go, went. There is no record of an argument about it.

Profit, tools, hope. Watch the sequence, because it is the sequence of every serious trouble. First you give up the profit. Then you give up the tools. Then, in the very next verse, you give up hope.

Valuable, and correctly thrown away. There is something worth noticing about what went overboard: every single item was valuable, and every single item was correctly thrown away. The wheat was worth a fortune. The tackle was worth having. In a storm the question stops being what is this worth? and becomes will this keep me afloat? Those are completely different questions, which most of us only ever learn to distinguish under duress. People discover in a hospital corridor, in a matter of hours, what took the crew three days: that almost everything they had been carrying was cargo. It was genuinely valuable. It was also, at the critical moment, weight. The ship that reached Malta arrived with nothing in the hold and every soul aboard alive.

How do I let go of things I have valued? Begin by naming them before God honestly: possessions, plans, reputation, comfort, a dream. Thank him for them, because they were gifts. Then ask which of them you are holding so tightly that they are weighing you down, keeping you from obedience or peace. Jesus said a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15), and Paul counted everything loss compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). Letting go is often painful, and grief over what is lost is not unbelief. But what you lose for Christ, or in the storms he sends, is never the thing that keeps you afloat. He is.

In a sentence. Since they were violently storm-tossed, the next day they began to jettison the cargo, and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

On a Tuesday. In storms, we learn what really matters. Possessions can go; people and souls matter. Walk through your home or your diary this week and ask of one thing: is this cargo or is it life? Do not wait for the storm to teach you the difference.

For worship. When everything else goes over the side, the Lord remains. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion for ever. Wheat sinks, tackle drifts, fortunes vanish in a night, but the inheritance kept in heaven for his people is imperishable, undefiled and unfading. Blessed be the God who is himself the treasure that no storm can throw overboard.

parallels.desc: the mariners hurled the cargo into the sea

verseByVerse.quote: "When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, 'Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.

When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days. Understand what that sentence meant to a first-century sailor, because it is not scene-setting. There was no compass. Position and heading were worked out from the sun by day and the stars by night, corrected by known landmarks. Take away sun and stars for many days and a ship does not merely feel gloomy. It is genuinely, absolutely lost. Nobody aboard knows where they are, how far they have run, or which way they are pointing. They are somewhere in the middle of the sea, in the dark, going fast, in an unknown direction.

All hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Luke’s no small tempest is deliberate understatement, and the phrase after it is not. Note three things about it carefully. First, the verb is in a form that suggests it happened gradually: hope was being stripped away, day after day, not lost in a single moment. Nobody gave up on day four. They gave up by degrees, and the ESV catches it exactly: at last. Second, the word for saved, sōzesthai, is the word for salvation; here it means rescue from the sea, and Luke will sound it again and again until the last verse. Third, and this is the sentence to sit with: Luke includes himself. All hope of our being saved. The man writing this is a Christian, a companion of Paul, an eyewitness of the early church, and he says plainly that he stopped believing they would live.

Despair is not the same as unbelief. Scripture does not tidy that up. It does not report that the believers aboard maintained a serene confidence while the pagans panicked. An apostle and two of his friends were on that ship, and Luke’s account of their inner state is that hope ran out. If you have been taught that despair is the same thing as unbelief, that verse is worth writing down. The man who wrote a Gospel gave up hope in a storm, and God did not hold it against him, and the promise did not depend on his morale. Paul himself once wrote that he despaired of life itself, so that he would rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Hopelessness, before God acts.

Since they had been without food for a long time. Fourteen days of this. No cooking fires in a pitching hull, stores soaked with seawater, and men too frightened and too sick to eat what there was. They are starving as well as terrified.

Paul stood up among them. And into that, one man stands up. The prisoner takes charge. His opening line is not what a modern reader expects: Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete. It sounds like an old man’s grievance, and it is not. It is not I told you so for its own sake. Paul is doing something specific and necessary. He is about to tell 275 exhausted, hopeless people an extraordinary thing, that an angel spoke to him and nobody will die, and there is no earthly reason for a single one of them to believe him. So he establishes the one credential he has. I told you before, and I was right. Now listen to what I am telling you. He is not scoring a point. He is buying a hearing, and he needs one badly.

What should I do when I have lost all hope? Tell God, honestly; the psalms are full of people doing exactly that (Psalm 88). Do not make big decisions alone in the dark. Eat, sleep and let others help you, as Paul is about to insist. Hold on to God’s promises even when you cannot feel them; your feelings do not change his faithfulness (Lamentations 3:21–24). Speak to your pastor or a trusted believer, and if despair has become persistent or you are thinking of harming yourself, seek medical help at once; that is not a lack of faith but a good use of God’s gifts. And remember: the promise did not depend on Luke’s morale. It does not depend on yours.

In a sentence. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and no small tempest lay on them, all hope of their being saved was at last abandoned; and since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.”

On a Tuesday. If you know someone who has lost hope, do not lecture them. Sit with them, make sure they have eaten, and when the time is right, tell them gently what God has promised. If you are the one without hope, read Psalm 88 and then Psalm 42 aloud, and let someone know.

For worship. When neither sun nor stars appear, the Lord still knows exactly where his people are. Even the darkness is not dark to him; the night is bright as the day. He kept that ship through fourteen days of blackness without showing his hand, and he keeps his children through every night of the soul. Hope may run out in us; it never runs out in him. He is the God of hope, and in the darkest hour he speaks.
verseByVerse.note: Without sun or stars, ancient sailors had no way to navigate.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,

Yet now I urge you to take heart. Yet now: two words turning the whole chapter. Everything before them has been loss: the cargo, the tackle, the sun and stars, and finally hope itself. Everything after them is promise. The word Paul uses for take heart is euthymein: be of good cheer, keep your spirits up, take courage. It is worth being exact about it, because it is a different word from the one the Lord spoke over Paul in the Jerusalem barracks, where it was tharsei, take courage (23:11). The Lord’s word to Paul in the dark was courage; Paul’s word to a shipful of starving pagans is cheer. He is not asking them to be brave. He is telling them, on a sinking ship, that things are actually going to be all right, and that there are grounds for something close to good spirits. A prisoner encouraging the crew.

For there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. A promise of God, now revealed, and astonishingly precise. Both halves matter, and both will come true to the letter: not one person will die, and the vessel will be smashed to pieces. Notice that Paul does not soften the second half to make the first more welcome. He tells them the ship is gone in the same sentence in which he tells them they are safe. A lesser comfort would have promised everything and delivered part; this promises exactly what will happen.

For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship. He names his God before he passes on the message, and the two phrases he chooses are the shortest complete description of a Christian in Acts. To whom I belong: a possession, not a client. Paul is owned. And whom I worship: the word is used of religious service; he serves and bows to this God. Belonging and serving, in that order, because the second follows from the first. Not a god among many, but the God who owns him. He says it to a deck full of men who worship Isis and Serapis and the emperor, and he says it without apology or embarrassment, at the one moment they are all guaranteed to be listening. In a ship full of pagans, Paul bears witness.

At the blackest hour. Picture it: a prisoner on a doomed ship, a two-week storm, sun and stars blotted out, everyone given up for dead (v. 20), and at the blackest hour an angel stands by Paul in the night. Notice what it brings: not a weather-charm, but a word against fear (do not be afraid), a reaffirming of God’s sovereign purpose (you must stand before Caesar; no storm can sink his plan), and a stunning gift of grace (God has granted you all those who sail with you, v. 24): 275 pagans spared for the sake of the one man God is carrying to Rome. And mark Paul’s confession before the heathen crew: the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, owned by God, and bowing to him.

Should believers expect an angel like this today? The fuller answer is at 8:26. In short, angelic appearances were never everyday even in the Bible; they cluster at the great hinge-moments, and Acts is exactly such a moment, God steering his apostle on a once-for-all mission. Today God ordinarily guides and comforts by surer, settled means: his completed Word, indwelling Spirit, prayer and unseen providence; “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). Angels are not idle. They are still ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), often unseen, so God remains free to use them; what we must not do is expect or chase visible appearances (Colossians 2:18).

Everything the angel gave Paul, you already have. But here is the comfort that should settle your heart. Everything the angel gave Paul, you already have, by a surer voice. Paul got one whispered do not be afraid; you hold a whole Bible of God’s fear not, and the promise “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Paul was told the storm would not wreck God’s purpose; you have the pledge that nothing will be able to separate us from the love of God, and that he works all things, every storm included, for your good (Romans 8:28, 38–39). Paul had an angel beside him for a night; you have the Spirit of Christ within you for life, and the Son himself, greater than all angels (Hebrews 1:4). An angel is only a servant; you have the Master. So in your storm, do not pine for a vision. You have the God of the vision, his Word, his Spirit and his unbreakable promise. The same God who would not let the sea swallow Paul reigns over every wave of yours.

What does it mean to belong to God? It means you are his by creation, and if you are a Christian, his by redemption: bought with a price, the precious blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 6:19–20; 1 Peter 1:18–19). You are not your own. That is a claim on your whole life, your body, money, time and choices; and it is also the deepest security there is, because God does not lose what belongs to him (John 10:28–29). The Heidelberg Catechism begins here: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ.

In a sentence. Yet now Paul urged them to take heart, for there would be no loss of life among them, but only of the ship, for that very night there had stood before him an angel of the God to whom he belonged and whom he worshipped.

On a Tuesday. You belong to God; that is your security in every storm. Say Paul’s phrase to yourself this week whenever fear rises: the God to whom I belong and whom I worship. And look for a moment, as Paul did, when the people around you are listening, to name your God plainly and without embarrassment.

For worship. How faithful is the God who sends his word into the blackest hour. When sun and stars had vanished and hope was gone, he stood by his servant in the night, as he had stood by him in the barracks, and as the Son of Man walked in the furnace with the three young men. He owns his people, and he does not abandon his property to the sea. To belong to him is to be safer in a sinking ship than any king on his throne. Blessed be the God to whom we belong, and whom we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and he said, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you." So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.

Do not be afraid, Paul. Paul was afraid too. The angel does not begin with information but with comfort for the apostle himself. The man who would stand up and encourage 275 people had first to be encouraged.

You must stand before Caesar. The angel’s message has two halves, and the second is more surprising than the first. The word for must is dei, Luke’s word for the fixed purposes of God, the same one used of the Son of Man who must suffer, and the same one the Lord used in the Jerusalem barracks: you must testify also in Rome (23:11). Two years and a fortnight of storm later, the promise has not moved. The storm has changed the route and not the destination. Paul could not die at sea, because God had promised Rome. Notice how the reassurance is framed. The angel does not say you will survive. He says you must stand before Caesar, which means the guarantee of Paul’s life is not a promise about Paul’s safety at all. It is a promise about God’s purpose, and Paul’s survival is simply what that purpose requires between here and Rome. That is a sturdier thing to stand on than a promise of protection, and it is also more sobering. God’s plan for him guaranteed his survival.

And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you. The verb is kecharistai, from charis, grace. It means to give freely, as a favour, with no obligation on the giver. God has graciously given Paul the 275 other people on the ship. Perhaps Paul had been praying for them. Stop and take in what is being said, because it is startling. A cargo of pagan sailors, Roman soldiers and prisoners, men with no interest in the God of Israel, several of whom would cheerfully have killed Paul and one group of whom will propose exactly that in eighteen verses, are spared, as a gift, because of one man’s presence among them.

The pattern of the righteous one. Scripture does this repeatedly, and it is worth seeing the pattern. Potiphar’s whole household was blessed for Joseph’s sake (Genesis 39:5). Abraham pleaded with God down to ten righteous men who would have saved a city (Genesis 18:32). Here the ratio is one to two hundred and seventy-five. The presence of a righteous man can bless those around him. The ordinary Christian reading this has no idea what his presence is worth to the people around him, and will not find out in this life. Paul did not know either until an angel told him. The office where you are the only believer, the family that finds you difficult, the ship you happen to be on: you are not able to see the accounts, and it is a mercy that you cannot.

So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. The whole of Christian confidence is in that last clause, and in what it rests on. Paul’s assurance is not about the weather, the ship, the crew or his own resilience. He does not say I have a good feeling, or I am sure it will work out. He says: I believe God, and therefore it will be exactly as I was told. The certainty is borrowed entirely from the character of the one who spoke. He is standing on a disintegrating ship in a fortnight-old gale, having eaten little for two weeks, unable to see the sky, with no evidence whatsoever, and the sole ground of his composure is that God is not a liar. Faith is believing God will do what he said. Not wishful thinking, but trust in a promise.

Were the 275 saved eternally because of Paul? No. They were spared from drowning because of Paul; that is the gift God gave him. Eternal salvation is never inherited from someone else’s faith or presence. Each person must personally repent and believe in Christ (16:31; Romans 10:9–13). A believer’s presence can bring real blessing to unbelievers around him, protection, kindness, the restraint of evil, and above all the hearing of the gospel. But only Christ’s righteousness saves, and it is received by each one through faith. Pray that those around you, blessed by God’s kindness for your sake, will come to know him for themselves.

In a sentence. The angel had said, “Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you”; so Paul told them to take heart, for he had faith in God that it would be exactly as he had been told.

On a Tuesday. Faith is trusting that God will do exactly what he said. Choose one promise of God this week, Romans 8:28, Hebrews 13:5 or John 10:28, and when the storm rises, say Paul’s words over it: I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. And pray by name for the unbelievers around you; you may be on their ship for a reason.

For worship. Consider the generosity of the God who said it. He owed that ship nothing. Not one man aboard her had asked him for anything, or knew his name, or would have thanked him for it: a crew that would shortly try to desert, soldiers who would shortly propose murder, and prisoners being shipped to Rome to face judgment. He was under no obligation to any of them, and the promise he had made concerned one prisoner only. And into that promise he swept every last soul on the vessel, freely, as a gift, because it pleased him to give them to his servant. That is the character of the God of heaven. He is never merely sufficient. He gives more than was asked, to people who did not ask, and he does it so quietly that 275 men walked up a beach on Malta that morning without the faintest idea that they had been handed to somebody as a present.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we must run aground on some island.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we must run aground on some island.

But we must run aground on some island. Do not hurry past this verse. It is one of the most useful sentences in the chapter, and it is easy to read as an afterthought. Paul has just delivered magnificent news: nobody dies. And in the same breath, from the same angel, comes the rest of it: the ship is going to be destroyed, and everyone aboard is going to be wrecked on an island somewhere in the dark. Must again: God’s plan included the shipwreck. Not rescue from the storm, but rescue through it. Safety, not comfort. The ship would be lost; the lives saved.

The wreck is inside the promise. The shipwreck is not a failure of the promise, not an exception to it, not something that happened despite it. God told them in advance that the disaster was part of the plan. Sit with how differently that reads from how we normally think. Almost every instinct we have treats catastrophe as evidence that a promise has failed. The ship breaking up on the rocks looks, to anyone in the water, exactly like God not keeping his word. And it was the word. Notice too what the promise did not include. It did not include calm seas, or a change of wind, or an escort into a safe harbour, or the salvage of a fortune in wheat, or the ship. It included precisely one thing: every person would live. The owner lost everything he had. Every sailor lost his tools and his wages. And the promise was kept in full.

What exactly did God promise? Here is a test worth running slowly, because most Christians need it more than they need another verse about victory. Think of the thing in your life you have been treating as proof that God did not come through. The illness that was not healed. The marriage that ended anyway. The job that went. The prayer that got the answer you were not asking for. Now ask a harder question than why did this happen? Ask: what exactly did God promise? He has never promised the ship. He has promised, to those who are his, that nothing will separate them from his love (Romans 8:38–39), that he works all things together for their good (Romans 8:28), that he will never leave them (Hebrews 13:5), and that he will bring them home. Read the list again and notice what is not on it. Comfort is not on it. Property is not on it. The preservation of your circumstances is not on it. The wreck may well be inside the promise.

Told in advance. There is one more thing here, quietly enormous. God tells them the bad part in advance. He does not spare them the shipwreck, and he does not hide it from them either. For the rest of the storm those men live with the knowledge that the ship is doomed, and also with the knowledge that they are not. That is very often exactly how God deals with his people. Not by removing the wreck, but by telling the truth about it early enough that when the timbers finally go, it is not the end of the world. It is the thing he said would happen, on the way to the thing he promised. Jesus did the same for his disciples: in the world you will have tribulation, he told them, but take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

Does God promise that Christians will be spared suffering? No. He promises to be with his people in it, to use it for their good, and to bring them safely home. Jesus warned that his followers would suffer (John 15:20), the apostles taught that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (14:22), and Paul himself would die in Rome. Teaching that faithful Christians will always be healthy, prosperous and safe is not the gospel. But neither is despair. What God promises, he keeps entirely, and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed (Romans 8:18).

In a sentence. But they would have to run aground on some island.

On a Tuesday. God does not always spare us the wreck, but he brings us through it. Write down, honestly, one disappointment you have been holding against God. Then write next to it what he has actually promised you in Scripture. Ask whether the disappointment touches any of those promises, or only the ship.

For worship. The Lord tells his people the truth. He does not flatter us with promises he will not keep or hide from us the trials he means to send. He told Paul of the wreck before the wreck, as he told his disciples of the cross before the cross, and in both cases the disaster was the road to the promise. Jesus went down into the shipwreck of death itself, and came up on the far shore on the third day, the firstfruits of all who will be brought safely through. He is faithful who promised, and he will surely do it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adriatic, the sailors sense land near. Soundings show the water growing shallower, so they drop four anchors from the stern and pray for daylight. When the sailors try to escape in the boat, pretending to lay anchors from the bow, Paul tells the centurion that unless they stay, the rest cannot be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. Before dawn Paul urges everyone to eat after two weeks of fasting: they need strength, and not a hair of their heads will be lost. He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it and eats, and they are all encouraged and eat. There are 276 on board. After eating they lighten the ship by throwing the grain into the sea. At daybreak they see an unfamiliar coast with a beach and decide to run the ship ashore. They cut the anchors, loosen the steering oars, raise the foresail and head for the beach, but strike a sandbar. The bow sticks fast and the stern is broken up by the waves. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners to prevent escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. He orders those who can swim to jump first and the rest to follow on planks and wreckage. And so everyone reaches land safely.
verseByVerse.theology:
Certainty and Effort Are the Same Faith

Verse 31 is the hinge, and it is one of the clearest answers in Scripture to the oldest bad question about providence: if God has already decided, why bother?

Nine verses after announcing an unconditional promise — not one life will be lost — Paul says something that sounds like its opposite: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Both are true, because God does not merely decree ends; he decrees the means that bring them about. The sailors staying aboard was not an alternative to the promise. It was the promise arriving. The same logic governs the meal at dawn: eat, because God has guaranteed you will live and you will need the strength.

So Paul's serenity and Paul's urgency are not in tension. A man who thinks everything hangs on his own vigilance is too frightened to act well; a man who thinks nothing depends on him does not act at all. Paul is neither, and the doctrine he lived by he also wrote down: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil. 2:12–13). The for in that sentence carries the whole argument.

The section also shows how God's promises are typically fulfilled — not by suspending the ordinary world but by working through the wreckage of it. There is no calmed sea here, no parting of the waters, no angel carrying anyone ashore. There are exhausted people swimming, and non-swimmers clinging to splintered planks off the ship that has just been destroyed beneath them. The debris of the disaster is the means of the rescue, and the promise is kept down to the last person on the roll.

And one thing more, quietly at the centre: the prisoners live because the centurion wanted Paul. Condemned men, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. Luke does not press the point. He does not have to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An hour before the ship broke apart, with an unknown shore ahead and no boat left, Paul took a piece of bread and thanked God for it out loud where everyone could hear. He had nothing. He had not eaten in two weeks, he was in chains, the vessel was doomed, and he was about to swim for his life. And a shipful of frightened people watched a man be visibly grateful to God, and something in them changed — Luke says they were encouraged, and they ate.

Now: Notice what actually moved that ship's company. Not Paul's argument; he had made his case at Fair Havens and been outvoted. Not his warning; they had ignored it. What reached them was watching one man's confidence in God hold steady when there was no visible reason for it, and do something ordinary and cheerful in front of them. People around you are far better at reading that than at following reasoning. They will discount what you say about God when things are going well, and they will not forget what you did with a piece of bread on the worst morning of your life. Courage is contagious in a way that argument is not — and the place it becomes contagious is almost always the small, practical, unembarrassed act done in front of witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms.

When the fourteenth night had come. Fourteen nights. Two full weeks of being carried through a gale with no sight of sun or stars, little food to speak of, and no idea where they are.

As we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea. One clarification for the reader, because the geography misleads. The Adriatic in ancient usage was not the narrow sea between Italy and the Balkans that bears the name today. Sailors used it for the whole central Mediterranean, the open water between Greece, Italy, Sicily and North Africa. Luke is not saying they were blown up past Italy; he is saying they were somewhere in the middle of a very large sea.

About midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. Suspected: not saw. It is the middle of the night in a storm, and there is nothing to see. So how did they know? Almost certainly they heard it. Surf breaking on a shore carries a long way across water, and it makes a sound no experienced sailor mistakes for anything else. After a fortnight of hearing nothing but wind and open sea, somebody on that deck caught a different note in the darkness and knew what it meant.

The most dangerous sound. Here is the sharpest thing about this moment: the sound of land is the most dangerous sound they could possibly hear. Out in deep water a ship can be driven for weeks and survive. Land is where ships die. A lee shore in a gale, in the dark, with no chart and no way of knowing what lies under the surface, is the single worst place a vessel can be. The thing they have been longing for is the thing that is about to destroy them.

They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little farther on, fifteen fathoms. A weighted line dropped over the side, the standard method. A fathom was about six feet: a hundred and twenty feet, then ninety. The bottom is coming up fast. Two soundings, and now they have a rate as well as a depth, and the arithmetic is terrifying. At that rate of shoaling they will be in the rocks within the hour.

Details only a witness could supply. A small note that has interested historians: the depths Luke records, taken in that order and at that spacing, correspond closely to the approach to St Paul’s Bay on Malta as it has been surveyed. And modern sailors who have calculated the drift of a large ship from Cauda in such a wind reckon that it would reach Malta in about fourteen days. Luke’s account fits exactly. It is the kind of detail no one inventing a story would think to include, and no one but a man who was standing there could have supplied.

Do these accurate details really matter for faith? Yes, in their place. Faith does not rest on nautical measurements, but on Christ and his Word. Yet the accuracy of Luke’s details, the winds, the ports, the depths, the titles of officials, has been confirmed again and again, and it shows that he was a careful historian who wrote what happened (Luke 1:1–4). If he is trustworthy about the soundings off Malta, there is every reason to take him seriously about the empty tomb in Jerusalem. The Bible’s history is not a decorative frame around spiritual truths; it is the place where God has acted.

In a sentence. When the fourteenth night had come, as they were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected they were nearing land, so they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms, and a little farther on they took another and found fifteen fathoms.

On a Tuesday. When you have no idea where you are in life, keep doing the simple, faithful things: the soundings. Read, pray, worship, work, listen. God is bringing you somewhere, even in the dark. And if you are tempted to think of the Bible as a book of nice stories, read this chapter again slowly, and notice that it was written by a man who was there.

For worship. God knew exactly where the ship was, even when no one else did. He knows where you are. For fourteen nights, while sailors guessed and soundings fell, the Lord who counts the drops of the sea and the grains of sand knew the latitude of that hull to the inch. If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. Blessed is the Shepherd who never loses track of a single one of his sheep.
verseByVerse.note: In ancient usage the Adriatic Sea included the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily. The ESV notes that twenty fathoms is about 120 feet and fifteen about 90 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship's boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,

They let down four anchors from the stern. Four anchors off the stern is unusual, since a ship normally anchors by the bow, and it is precisely right here. Anchoring by the stern holds the vessel with her bow pointed at the shore, so that at first light they can cut the cables, hoist a sail and run her straight up the beach without having to turn in the surf. It is a considered manoeuvre by men who know exactly what they intend to do at dawn. Admiral Nelson was said to have read this chapter before the Battle of Copenhagen, where his ships anchored by the stern.

And prayed for day to come. Then Luke writes a phrase he could easily have left out. The verb can mean to wish or to pray, and these are the sailors praying. Not Paul, not Luke, not Aristarchus. Pagan seamen who worship whatever gods sailors worshipped, hanging on four cables in the dark with rocks somewhere ahead, praying for morning. The longest night. Luke reports it without comment and without scorn. He does not call it superstition and he does not pretend it was conversion. It is simply what men do when there is nothing left to do, and the God who was actually holding that ship let them pray to whatever they prayed to, and gave them the morning anyway.

The sailors were seeking to escape from the ship. Then, in the same breath, the ugliest thing in the chapter. The crew decide to save themselves, abandoning the passengers. They swing out the dinghy, the one they nearly killed themselves recovering days earlier.

Under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow. A lie, and a good one: bow anchors would be a genuinely sensible addition, and running them out by boat is how it is done. Nobody watching would question it. What they are actually doing is abandoning more than two hundred and fifty people on an anchored ship they believe is about to break up, taking with them the only boat and all the seamanship aboard. And they had heard Paul’s promise. They were on deck for it. They knew an angel had said that not one life would be lost, and their considered response was to leave in the dark while everyone else was praying.

Assenting and resting. That is worth being honest about rather than merely condemning, because the instinct is not exotic. Under real pressure, people who have genuinely heard a promise of God still make private arrangements. The promise is believed in the way one believes a weather forecast: taken seriously, hedged against. There is a difference between assenting to a promise and actually resting your weight on it, and the difference does not show up until it is dark and the boat is in the water.

Does God hear the prayers of unbelievers? God hears everything, and in his kindness he often gives good things to people who do not know him: sun and rain, food and gladness, and a morning after a terrible night (14:17; Matthew 5:45). But the promise that God will hear and answer as a Father is for those who come to him through Christ, the one mediator (John 14:6, 13–14; 1 Timothy 2:5). An unbeliever’s cry for help can be the first stirring of seeking God, and he invites all to call on him in truth. If you pray for morning, pray to the God who made it, through the Saviour he has sent.

In a sentence. Fearing that they might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come; and the sailors tried to escape from the ship, lowering the ship’s boat into the sea under pretence of laying out anchors from the bow.

On a Tuesday. In a crisis, some look after themselves. Be the one who stays and helps. And ask yourself where you are quietly making private arrangements against God’s promises: the secret savings you trust more than God, the escape route you keep open in case obedience costs too much. Close one this week, and rest your weight on what he has said.

For worship. The God who was holding that ship gave the morning to men who did not know his name. He makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and his patience with the faithless is as wide as the sea. And while men lie and scheme and hedge, he does not. He is not a man, that he should lie; has he said, and will he not do it? In a world of lowered lifeboats and false pretences, his word is the one anchor that holds.
verseByVerse.note: Anchors from the stern kept the bow pointing toward land, ready for beaching.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, 'Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.' Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go.

Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Here is one of the most important sentences in the Bible on the relationship between God’s promises and human action, and it is spoken by a man in chains in the middle of the night. Set it against what Paul said nine verses earlier. There, on the authority of an angel: there will be no loss of life among you, an absolute, unconditional promise, no exceptions, no fine print. Here, on his own authority: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Read flatly, those two statements contradict each other. Either everyone is certainly saved, or their salvation depends on whether some sailors stay aboard. Both are true, and seeing why is worth the trouble.

The decree includes the means. God does not merely decree ends; he decrees the means by which the ends arrive. When he determined that every soul on that ship would live, he determined the whole chain that would bring it about, including a boat cut loose at midnight, the seamanship needed to beach a ship at dawn, and a prisoner noticing what the crew were doing and saying something. The sailors were needed to beach the ship. The promise did not float free above the events. It was fulfilled through them. So Paul’s absolute confidence in the promise and his urgent intervention to secure it are not in tension at all. They are the same faith. He believed the outcome was certain, which is exactly why he was not paralysed. A man who thinks everything depends on his own vigilance is too frightened to act well, and a man who thinks nothing depends on him does not act at all. Paul is neither.

Divine sovereignty and human means. Some say that if God has determined something, our actions don’t matter. Verdict: this verse refutes it. God had decreed the end (all saved) and the means (sailors staying, eating, swimming, planks). God’s sovereignty doesn’t make human action pointless; it makes it meaningful. As with salvation: God has chosen his people, and calls them through preaching (Romans 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:10). The decree includes the means.

If God has already decided, why bother? This is the answer to the oldest bad question about providence. Because the bothering is part of what God decided. The sailors staying aboard was not an alternative to the promise; it was the promise arriving. And it lands on ordinary life immediately. If God has promised to keep you, then read your Bible, go to church, confess your sin, and stay away from what will ruin you, not although he has promised, but because the keeping happens through exactly those things. Paul writes it out plainly elsewhere: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). The for in that sentence is the whole doctrine.

Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. The soldiers act instantly, and perhaps slightly too enthusiastically: cutting the boat adrift removes it as an escape route and as a piece of equipment. There will be no ferrying anyone ashore now. Everybody swims. But notice who is giving orders. A chained prisoner speaks, and a Roman centurion’s men reach for their swords and do it, at once, without checking. Now the centurion listened to Paul. At Fair Havens nobody listened to Paul at all. Thirteen days of storm later, he is the only voice on the ship that carries. Authority in a crisis has a way of migrating to whoever turns out to know what is actually happening.

Does this mean salvation is conditional and can be lost? No. Saved here means rescued from the sea, as in v. 20 and v. 44. But there is a parallel: God had promised that all would be saved (v. 24), and the promise was kept through means, including the sailors staying aboard. In the same way, God keeps his people to the end, and the warnings and commands of Scripture are among the means he uses.

Should I still evangelise if God has chosen his people? Yes, all the more. God’s choice is the reason evangelism will not be in vain. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10), and in Corinth the Lord told him to keep speaking because he had many people in that city (18:9–10). We do not know who the elect are; we are told to preach to everyone. God brings his chosen ones to faith through ordinary means: the gospel spoken, a book given, a friend’s invitation, a prayer. You may be the means he has decreed.

In a sentence. Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go.

On a Tuesday. God’s promises do not make your obedience unnecessary; they make it certain to succeed. Pick one means of grace you have been neglecting because you assumed God would keep you anyway, Bible reading, prayer, gathered worship, accountability, and take it up again this week, gladly, as the way he keeps his promise.

For worship. The Lord is sovereign over the end and over every step that leads to it. He decreed the rescue of that ship and every rope and plank and swimmer’s stroke that would bring it about. He has chosen a people for himself before the foundation of the world, and he has ordained the preaching, the praying and the believing by which he brings them home. Nothing is left to chance, and nothing we do in obedience is wasted. Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God; for from him and through him and to him are all things.

verseByVerse.quote: "As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, 'Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.”

Paul urged them all to take some food. As day was about to dawn, the most spiritual man aboard spends the last hour before the wreck telling everyone to have breakfast. That is worth noticing before anything else. He has an angelic promise, an audience that is finally listening, and one hour left. He could preach. Instead he does triage, and the triage is physical. Practical care: the apostle was also a sensible man, and they would need strength for the swim. Spiritual and physical care together.

Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food. The phrase for in suspense means watching, waiting, keyed up: fourteen days of continuous vigilance with no relief. And without food does not mean a total fast. On a pitching ship with no galley fire and stores fouled by seawater, it means nobody has eaten a proper meal in a fortnight. Too anxious or sick to eat properly, they have been living on scraps. So they are about to attempt the most physically demanding thing any of them will ever do, beach a disintegrating ship and swim through surf to an unknown shore, in a state of near-collapse.

For it will give you strength. The word is sōtēria, literally salvation, safety, deliverance. Eating is part of their rescue. Look at the logic of the sentence, because it is the same logic as the boat and the sailors, applied to a man’s body. The reason to eat is that God has promised nobody will die. Not despite the promise, but because of it. God has guaranteed the outcome, therefore get some bread inside you, because you are going to need the strength for the swim. Faith in the promise produces practical preparation for the thing promised. There is a kind of piety that would have prayed instead of eating. Paul does both, and he is not confused about which one supplies calories.

Ordinary pastoral care. And do not miss how ordinary the pastoral care is here. Fourteen days of terror have left 276 people exhausted, frightened and unfed, and the apostle’s response is to make them eat something. Elijah under the broom tree wanted to die, and God’s first provision was a meal and a sleep, twice, before a single word of correction (1 Kings 19:5–8). A great deal of what looks like spiritual crisis is a body that has not eaten or slept, and Scripture is far more willing to say so than we usually are.

For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you. The phrase is an old Hebrew proverb of complete safety: it is how the people swore that Jonathan would not be touched (1 Samuel 14:45), and how David reassured a widow about her son (2 Samuel 14:11). It is also almost exactly what the Lord Jesus promised his disciples about the persecutions coming on them, not a hair of your head will perish (Luke 21:18), said, remarkably, in the same breath as some of you they will put to death (Luke 21:16). Which tells you what the promise actually guarantees. Not that nothing will touch you. That nothing will be lost.

Is it unspiritual to care about food, sleep and medicine when I am struggling? No. God made us bodies as well as souls, and he cares for both. Jesus fed the hungry crowds, and told his tired disciples to come away and rest (Mark 6:31). Eating properly, sleeping, exercising, and seeing a doctor when you need one are ways of receiving God’s good gifts, not signs of weak faith.
