Low mood and spiritual dryness are often made worse by exhaustion and hunger. Look after your body, and then bring your soul to God as well. Paul did both, and so should we.

In a sentence. As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying that for fourteen days they had continued in suspense and without food, taking nothing, and he urged them to eat, for it would give them strength, since not a hair was to perish from the head of any of them.

On a Tuesday. Care for people’s bodies as well as their souls; Paul fed a hungry crew. If someone you know is in crisis, take them a meal before you take them advice. And if you are the one in crisis, eat something, sleep, and then pray.

For worship. The Lord who numbers the hairs of our heads promises that not one will be lost. He feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies, and he knows that his children need food and rest. The Bread of Life who multiplied loaves for the hungry and cooked breakfast on the shore for his tired disciples is the same Lord who stood behind Paul’s plain words: take some food. He is not too lofty to care for our bodies, and not too small to keep our souls. Blessed be the God of complete safety.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves.

He took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Four verbs: took, gave thanks, broke, began to eat. Luke has written most of that sequence before. He wrote it in an upper room: he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them (Luke 22:19). He wrote it at a table in Emmaus, where two disciples recognised the risen Christ in exactly that gesture (Luke 24:30). And he is writing it again now, on the deck of a doomed grain ship, in front of soldiers and sailors and prisoners.

Is this the Lord’s Supper? Almost certainly not, and it is worth being careful rather than romantic about it. There is no cup, no words of institution and no gathered church; this is a shipload of pagans, and the Lord’s Supper is not given to unbelievers. What Paul is doing is what any devout Jew did as head of a household before a meal: taking bread, blessing God for it and breaking it. But Luke chose those verbs, and Luke does not use that sequence carelessly. He wants his reader to hear the echo, and the echo says something true: the same Lord who broke bread with his disciples on the night he was betrayed is present with his servant on this ship, and the ordinary act of thanking God for food is the sign of it.

In the presence of all. That is the phrase to stop on. He does not mutter it. He does not wait until he is alone or make it discreet out of tact. In front of a shipful of frightened pagans, a chained prisoner audibly thanks the God of Israel for a piece of bread, an hour before the ship breaks apart. A public witness on a sinking ship. He has nothing. He is a prisoner, the ship is lost, he has eaten little in two weeks and is about to swim for his life on an unknown coast, and his posture toward God is gratitude, out loud, where everyone can hear it. It is the habit of a man who gave thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. And there it is. A shipful of people who had abandoned hope watch one man give thanks, and something changes in them. Luke’s word is the same one Paul used at v. 22: they became of good cheer. Not because the danger had lessened; the rocks were still there and the ship was still doomed. Because one man’s confidence in God was visible, and courage is contagious in a way that argument is not. One man’s faith lifted 275 people.

Should I give thanks for meals in public, in a restaurant or at work? It is a good and natural habit, and it can be a quiet witness, as Paul’s was. There is no rule about how long or how loud it must be; a brief, sincere thanks is enough. Avoid display, which Jesus warned against (Matthew 6:5), but do not hide your gratitude out of embarrassment either. If you are with unbelievers, you might simply say, I am just going to thank God for this, and do it. Thanksgiving for daily bread is one of the simplest ways to show that you live before God.

In a sentence. When he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat, and they were all encouraged and ate some food themselves.

On a Tuesday. Give thanks before meals, even in public, even in storms. It is a witness. And in the hardest moment of your week, try saying aloud one thing you are thankful to God for. Watch what it does to you, and sometimes to the people around you.

For worship. Consider the Lord who was worth that much confidence. He had not calmed this sea. For fourteen days he sent no light, no let-up, no sign: nothing but wind and black water and a ship coming apart at the seams. And he was as fully in command of every one of those days as he was on the evening he stood up in a fishing boat on Galilee and told a storm to be still, and it was. The One who gathers the wind in his fists is not less sovereign when he does not use them, and he is not absent when the sky is shut. He kept every soul on that vessel through a fortnight of darkness without once showing his hand, and then brought them all out of the surf onto a beach, exactly as he had said. That is who is worth thanking for a crust of bread on a sinking ship.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives thanks as the head of a Jewish household did before a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: "(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.

We were in all 276 persons in the ship. Luke drops the number in parentheses, in the middle of the action, like a man checking a ledger. And that is more or less what it is. He has recorded a promise, there will be no loss of life among you, and he is establishing the figure that promise has to be measured against. Everything now depends on how many people walk out of the water, so he tells you exactly how many went in. Two hundred and seventy-six. Not about three hundred, not a great many. Luke counted, or heard the count, perhaps for the food rations, and wrote it down.

Some manuscripts read seventy-six. The ESV notes the variant. The number 276 is far better attested, and the shorter reading probably arose from a copyist’s confusion of Greek numerals. A large grain ship could easily carry that many; Josephus tells of sailing in one with six hundred aboard.

Every one counted. The number is also a reminder of the scale of these grain freighters. A vessel carrying nearly three hundred people plus a great cargo of wheat was among the largest things afloat in the ancient world, and Rome ran a fleet of them because the city’s bread depended on it. But there is something else in the number, and it is worth saying plainly. God did not promise to save a shipload. He promised not to lose a person, and Luke gives us the arithmetic because the arithmetic is the point. Two hundred and seventy-six individuals, soldiers, sailors, prisoners, the owner, a doctor, a Macedonian, an apostle, and every single one of them is counted, and every single one arrives.

When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. The last of the cargo goes over the side. They need the hull riding as high as possible so she will run as far up the beach as possible before grounding; every foot of shallower draught is a few yards less surf to swim through. So the wheat goes, and with it goes the entire purpose of the voyage. This ship left Alexandria to carry Egyptian grain to Rome. That is what she was built for, that is what the owner invested in, that is why she was at sea in the wrong month, and that is the reason 276 people were aboard her at all. Every ounce of it is now at the bottom of a bay off Malta.

Failed and succeeded. The voyage failed completely, by every measure it was undertaken for. And it succeeded entirely, because the one cargo God cared about on that ship was a prisoner he had promised to get to Rome, and 275 people he had thrown in as a gift.

Does God care about me as an individual, or only about his people as a whole? Both, and the one does not swallow the other. God loves his church as a whole, the bride of Christ, and he also knows each of his people by name (John 10:3). Jesus told of a shepherd who left ninety-nine to find the one, and said there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:4–7). He counts the hairs of your head. Luke counted 276, and God counted each one. You are never lost in the crowd to him.

In a sentence. There were 276 people on board in all, and when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.

On a Tuesday. God counts every person; none is forgotten. Look around your church this Sunday and notice someone you have never spoken to. God has counted them. Learn their name. And if you feel lost in the crowd, remember the number Luke wrote down: every one.

For worship. The Lord is a God of exact accounts. He determines the number of the stars and gives to all of them their names; he wrote the names of his people in the book of life before the foundation of the world. The Good Shepherd said of those the Father had given him that he would lose nothing of all that had been given, but raise it up on the last day. Not one of his sheep will be missing when the roll is called. How safe is the sheep whose name the Shepherd knows.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach.

Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land. Daylight at last, after fourteen nights, and they still do not know where they are. Not one man aboard, including a crew that had worked these waters for years, recognises the coastline in front of them. It is Malta, at the place traditionally called St Paul’s Bay, off the main shipping route, and they will not learn its name until they are ashore (28:1).

But they noticed a bay with a beach. A place to run aground. Note Luke’s caution: on which they planned, if possible, to run the ship ashore. Nobody is confident. They can see one feature that offers any hope at all, a bay with a beach rather than cliffs, and the plan is to drive the ship straight at it and hope.

So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea. Three actions, and any sailor reading this will recognise every one. They cast off the anchors: not weighed but cut. Four anchors and their cables abandoned on the bottom, because hauling them up would take time they do not have and weight they cannot carry. This is a one-way manoeuvre. The instant those cables part, there is no stopping and no second attempt.

Loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Ancient ships were steered by two great oars, or rudders, one each side of the stern. They had been lashed up out of the way for a fortnight so the storm would not smash them. Now they are freed, because for the first time in two weeks the ship is going to be steered somewhere on purpose.

Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. A small headsail, enough to give steerage way and drive her forward. They need speed to reach the beach and control to hold the line. It is a good plan, executed correctly by professionals who have been awake for two weeks: skilled seamanship, and Luke records each step. Everything they can control, they control. And in the next verse it goes wrong, through something no seamanship on earth could have prevented.

Is it right to admire unbelievers’ skill? Yes. Every good skill comes from God, the giver of every good and perfect gift (James 1:17), and he gives them to believers and unbelievers alike by his common grace. Bezalel’s craftsmanship was the gift of God’s Spirit (Exodus 31:1–5); the pagan sailors’ seamanship here was his gift too. Thank God for the surgeon, the pilot, the engineer and the electrician, whether or not they know him. Honour their work, and pray that they will come to know the Giver.

In a sentence. When it was day, they did not recognise the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach on which they planned, if possible, to run the ship ashore, so they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, loosened the ropes that tied the rudders, hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach.

On a Tuesday. God gives skill to sailors and doctors and workers. Thank him by name this week for one person whose skill has served you: the mechanic, the nurse, the teacher. Tell them you are grateful. And do your own work with the same care, as for the Lord.

For worship. The Lord is the teacher of every craftsman. He instructs the farmer rightly and teaches him, the prophet says, and the same God taught those sailors how to cut the cables, free the rudders and hoist the sail. All skill is borrowed from his wisdom, which laid the foundations of the earth and set the bounds of the sea. When the morning came on that unknown coast, it was his morning, and the beach was his beach, prepared from the creation of the world for that one ship.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf.

But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. Luke’s phrase is a curious one: literally, they fell into a place between two seas, as the ESV notes. It describes a shoal or a spit with open water on both sides, the sort of hidden bar that produces a cross-current where two bodies of water meet. There is such a formation in St Paul’s Bay, between the mainland and a small island. The point is that it was invisible. From a ship’s deck at dawn, in surf, with the coastline unrecognised, there was no way to see it. Nothing in the crew’s handling of the vessel was wrong. They simply hit something they could not have known was there.

Not how we prefer disasters to work. That is worth pausing on, because it is not how we prefer disasters to work. The wreck of this ship is not caused by the bad decision at Fair Havens; that produced the storm, and they survived the storm. The wreck is caused by an underwater ridge that nobody could see, a short distance from safety, at the end of a manoeuvre performed correctly.

The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. The two halves of the sentence are the two halves of their situation. Forward, the ship is jammed solid in the bar, going nowhere. Aft, she is being systematically demolished by the sea, plank by plank, with 276 people standing on her. This is the worst moment of the entire voyage, worse than the northeaster, worse than the fourteen nights. The storm was survivable because the hull held. Now the hull is coming apart underneath them, in surf, off an unknown shore, and there is no boat, because they cut it away in the dark.

Half the promise kept. Notice that the angel’s promise is at this moment exactly half fulfilled. There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22). The ship is being destroyed in front of them, precisely as God said it would be. The ship broke apart, as Paul said. The destruction of the vessel is not the promise failing; it is the promise coming true, and the half they are watching is the half they were told to expect. That leaves them standing on a breaking wreck with only God’s word for it that the other half will hold too. That is very often the exact position of faith: the painful part of the promise arriving on schedule, and nothing yet to show for the good part but the character of the one who said it.

Why do bad things happen when I have done everything right? Because we live in a fallen world where hidden reefs exist, and not every hardship is a punishment or the result of a mistake. Jesus said the man born blind was not suffering because of his sin or his parents’ (John 9:1–3), and that those killed when a tower fell were no worse than anyone else (Luke 13:4–5). God is sovereign over such things, and he has purposes in them, often hidden from us. Do not torment yourself searching for what you did wrong when Scripture gives you no reason to. Bring the pain to God, and hold on to what he has promised.

In a sentence. But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground; the bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf.

On a Tuesday. God’s word came true: the ship was lost, but not one life. Trust his word in every detail. If you are in the half of the promise that hurts this week, write down the other half, the part God has said he will do, and read it every morning until it comes.

For worship. The God who keeps his word does not keep it halfway. He told them the ship would be lost, and it was lost; he told them every life would be saved, and he was about to save every life. He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? The cross looked like a ship breaking up in the surf, the bow stuck fast and the stern smashed, and it was the very moment God’s promise was being kept. Blessed be the faithful God, whose word stands when every timber gives way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas” — perhaps a sandbar where currents met.

verseByVerse.quote: "The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,

The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. A brutal verse, and it needs its context or it simply looks like cruelty. Under Roman military discipline, a guard who let a prisoner escape could be made to suffer the penalty the prisoner would have suffered. Luke has already shown us this twice: Herod executed the sentries when Peter got out (12:19), and the Philippian jailer drew his sword on himself rather than face what was coming (16:27). These soldiers are not simply sadists. They are men doing brutal arithmetic about their own necks, at the one moment when several prisoners are about to be in open water in the confusion of a wreck. It is also a reminder of who Paul’s fellow passengers were. Some of those prisoners may well have been bound for the arena. They have just survived fourteen days of storm on the promise of a God they do not know, and their reward at the water’s edge is nearly a drawn sword.

But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. Julius intervenes, and Luke tells us exactly why: he wanted Paul alive. Julius had come to respect him. Not the prisoners: Paul. And because he wanted this one man to live, he vetoed the killing of every man in the group, so a shipload of anonymous convicts, whose names nobody recorded and whose crimes we will never know, walked out of the surf alive because of who they happened to be chained near. Because of Paul, all the prisoners were spared. God’s promise was kept, through a centurion’s will.

The third time. That is the third time in this chapter that Paul’s presence has saved people who had no idea it was doing so. The angel gave him the lives of all 275 others (v. 24). His warning about the sailors kept the crew aboard (v. 31). And now his value to a Roman officer turns aside the swords.

The shape of the gospel. It is impossible to read that pattern and not see the shape of the gospel in it, not because Luke says so, but because the shape is unmistakable once you have seen it elsewhere. People with nothing to commend them, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. Abraham found it in Sodom: ten righteous men would have saved a whole city (Genesis 18:32). And at the centre of everything stands One who did not merely happen to be standing nearby, but who deliberately took the place of the condemned and let the sentence fall on himself instead. The prisoners on that beach owed their lives to a man they had probably never spoken to. Every Christian alive owes rather more than that, to a Man who sought him out.

He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land. And having saved their lives, the centurion organises the evacuation, swimmers first, so that the strongest are ashore and able to help the rest. Orderly evacuation: sensible, decent, competent leadership from a pagan officer, and it is the last thing he does in the book.

Should I stay in a workplace or family where I am the only believer? Usually, yes, unless you are being drawn into sin or are in danger. Paul taught that each believer should remain in the situation in which God called him, as far as it is right to do so (1 Corinthians 7:17–24), and that a believing husband or wife can be a blessing to an unbelieving household (1 Corinthians 7:12–16). Your presence may be doing more good than you know: restraining evil, showing kindness, earning trust, and keeping the gospel within reach. If you are in danger, abused, or being pressured to deny Christ, seek help and safety; God does not ask you to stay in harm’s way.

In a sentence. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim away and escape, but the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan, and ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land.

On a Tuesday. One faithful Christian’s presence can save others. Your faithfulness matters to those around you. Be the kind of colleague, neighbour or relative whose integrity earns respect, so that when a crisis comes, your word carries weight. And thank God this week, by name, for the Saviour who took the sentence that was yours.

For worship. Consider the One whose worth spares the guilty. The prisoners on that beach lived because a centurion valued one man. We live because the Father values his Son, and has accepted us in the Beloved. Christ did not merely stand near the condemned; he took our place under the sword of justice, bore our sentence and gave us his life. For the sake of one Man, a multitude no one can number walks out of the surf of judgment alive. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation.
verseByVerse.note: Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.

And the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. Look at how the promise of God is kept. Not by a calmed sea. Not by an angel carrying them ashore, not by the waters parting, not by a single thing that anyone would call a miracle. Two hundred and seventy-six starving, exhausted, half-drowned people go over the side into cold surf at dawn and thrash their way to a beach, and the ones who cannot swim cling to broken bits of the ship that has just been destroyed under them. The wreckage is the lifeboat. The very timbers of the disaster are what carry them in. That is worth holding on to, because most Christians spend a good deal of energy waiting for God to keep his promises in a manner they would find impressive. He rarely does. He is far more likely to keep them by way of a plank: something splintered off the thing that fell apart, floating within reach at the moment you go into the water.

And so it was that all were brought safely to land. Luke’s last word on the voyage is the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is perfect. Two hundred and seventy-six went aboard. Two hundred and seventy-six came ashore. The angel had said there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship, and the ship is matchwood in the bay behind them and not one human being is missing. Paul’s own earlier assessment had feared the loss of lives; the word of God went further.

Brought safely. Notice the verb Luke chooses at the very end. Brought safely, diasōthēnai: saved through, rescued completely. It is built on the ordinary Greek root for save, and he has been sounding that note through the whole chapter: all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned (v. 20); unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved (v. 31); and now, at last, all were saved through to land. A reader who knows what that word carries in the rest of Acts is meant to feel the resonance, and Luke does not press it.

Is the shipwreck a picture of salvation? Luke does not present it as an allegory, and we should not turn every plank into a symbol. The story is history, about real people rescued from a real sea. But some have rightly seen in it a picture of how God saves: the ship of this world breaks apart, but all whom the Father has given to Christ are brought safely home, some swimming, some clinging to planks, but all safe (John 6:39). The parallel is in the faithfulness of God. He promised, and he lost no one. That is exactly what Jesus says of those the Father has given him.

Every word, in order. Everything the God of Israel said would happen has happened, in order, exactly. The storm came, as Paul warned. The ship was lost, as the angel said. Every soul survived, as the angel said. And the man God had promised to bring to Rome is sitting on a beach on Malta, soaked and shivering and still hundreds of miles short of it, with the promise entirely intact.

In a sentence. The rest followed, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship, and so it was that all were brought safely to land.

On a Tuesday. God keeps every promise to the last soul. All whom he has promised to save will be brought safely home. If you are clinging to a plank this week, a small mercy, a single verse, a friend’s phone call, a thin thread of hope, hold on. It may be exactly how God is bringing you to shore.

For worship. He said not one of them would perish, and not one of them perished. That is simply what his word is like. It does not arrive tidily, or on the schedule anyone would have chosen, or in a form that would look well in a painting, but it arrives, in full, down to the last person on the roll, because the One who gave it does not deal in approximations and has never yet mislaid a single thing entrusted to him. Two hundred and seventy-six people stood dripping on a foreign shore that morning as living proof of it, and most of them had no idea whose word they had been carried in on. Glory to the God who keeps his promises to the last soul, and to the Saviour who will lose none of those the Father has given him.

parallels.desc: three times I was shipwrecked

27.title: Storm, Shipwreck, and Sovereignty
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. <sup>2</sup>And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. <sup>3</sup>The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. <sup>4</sup>And putting out to sea from there we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. <sup>5</sup>And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <sup>6</sup>There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. <sup>7</sup>We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <sup>8</sup>Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea. <sup>9</sup>Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, <sup>10</sup>saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” <sup>11</sup>But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <sup>12</sup>And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there. <sup>13</sup>Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. <sup>14</sup>But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. <sup>15</sup>And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <sup>16</sup>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. <sup>17</sup>After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along. <sup>18</sup>Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. <sup>19</sup>And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. <sup>20</sup>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. <sup>21</sup>Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss. <sup>22</sup>Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <sup>23</sup>For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, <sup>24</sup>and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ <sup>25</sup>So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. <sup>26</sup>But we must run aground on some island.” <sup>27</sup>When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. <sup>28</sup>So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms. <sup>29</sup>And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. <sup>30</sup>And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, <sup>31</sup>Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” <sup>32</sup>Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. <sup>33</sup>As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. <sup>34</sup>Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.” <sup>35</sup>And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. <sup>36</sup>Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. <sup>37</sup>(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) <sup>38</sup>And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. <sup>39</sup>Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. <sup>40</sup>So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. <sup>41</sup>But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. <sup>42</sup>The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <sup>43</sup>But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land, <sup>44</sup>and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.
27.overview:
Luke’s account of the voyage to Rome is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring that survives. In 1848 James Smith, a Scottish yachtsman who sailed these waters, showed that its winds, depths, distances and manoeuvres fit the conditions exactly: this is the log of an eyewitness. Paul, a prisoner under the centurion Julius, sails with Luke and Aristarchus up the coast to Myra, then on an Alexandrian grain ship towards Italy. Late in the season, against Paul’s warning, the ship leaves Fair Havens on Crete for a better harbour, and is caught by a violent north-easterly gale. For two weeks it is driven helplessly west, without sun or stars, cargo and tackle thrown overboard, until all hope is gone.

Then the prisoner takes charge. An angel has told Paul that he must stand before Caesar and that God has given him the lives of everyone aboard; they will lose the ship but not one life. When land is near, Paul stops the sailors abandoning ship, urges everyone to eat, gives thanks and breaks bread. At dawn they run the ship onto a sandbar off Malta; the stern breaks up, the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them, and all 276 reach land. The chapter is a parable of providence: God’s promise is certain, and he keeps it through ordinary means, sailors, anchors, food, a centurion’s decision, and planks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Malta and the Journey to Rome
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Safe ashore, the travellers learn the island is Malta. The islanders show unusual kindness, lighting a fire and welcoming everyone, for it is raining and cold. As Paul puts a bundle of sticks on the fire, a viper driven out by the heat fastens on his hand. The islanders conclude he must be a murderer whom Justice will not let live, even though he escaped the sea. But Paul shakes the snake into the fire and is unharmed. They wait for him to swell up or drop dead, and when nothing happens, they change their minds and say he is a god. Publius, the island’s chief official, has an estate nearby and welcomes them generously for three days. His father is ill with fever and dysentery; Paul visits him, prays, lays hands on him and heals him. Then the rest of the sick on the island come and are cured. The islanders honour them in many ways and, when they sail, supply what they need. After three months they leave on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered there, with the twin gods as its emblem. They stop at Syracuse for three days, then Rhegium, and with a south wind reach Puteoli, where they find believers and stay a week. And so they come to Rome. Believers there hear of them and travel out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet them; seeing them, Paul thanks God and is encouraged. In Rome Paul is allowed to live on his own, with a soldier guarding him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Through People Who Never Know

Everything Paul needs in this section is supplied, and hardly any of it comes from a believer. A fire lit by islanders who worship other gods. Three days' hospitality from a Roman official. A winter's provisions loaded aboard by people who thought Paul was a deity. A ship dedicated to Castor and Pollux. A favourable wind. God furnishes the last stage of his apostle's journey almost entirely out of pagan hands, and not one of those hands knows what it is doing.

That is the same doctrine the storm chapter taught, arriving now in a gentler key. There God used a centurion's fear and a crew's seamanship; here he uses simple human decency. The Reformed conviction that God governs all things through secondary causes is not an abstraction in Acts — it is a bonfire on a wet beach.

The viper episode adds the other half. The Maltese read Paul's circumstances and drew a confident conclusion about his standing with God, and they were as wrong as it is possible to be — twice, in opposite directions, within one evening. Scripture is consistent about this: you cannot read a person's standing before God off the surface of their life. Job's friends could not, the disciples could not at the blind man (John 9:2–3), and neither can we, in a sickroom or anywhere else.

And the section's tenderest theology is in v. 15. Paul took courage, which means he needed to. God's provision for a discouraged apostle was not an angel — he had used angels earlier and would again — but a handful of ordinary Christians who walked two days out along a road to be standing there when he passed. The means God most often uses to keep his servants going is other believers turning up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Believers in Rome heard that a prisoner they had never met was on the road. They had one letter from him, written three years earlier. So they walked — thirty-three miles to Three Taverns, forty-three to the Forum of Appius — stood at the side of the Appian Way, and waited. They did not free him, feed him, or improve his legal position by a single clause. They just turned up. And the apostle to the Gentiles looked at them, thanked God, and found he could go on.

Now: Two things follow, and both cut. The first is that the strong Christian you know is more likely to need this than to say so. Paul had faced down a mob, survived a shipwreck and shaken off a snake, and he still arrived on that road with his courage low. The assumption that mature believers are past needing encouragement is one of the loneliest lies in the church. The second is that showing up almost never feels worth the trip. It accomplishes nothing you can point to, it costs a day you did not have, and you will usually never learn whether it mattered. Luke thought it mattered enough to record, in a book with no room to spare, in the sentence immediately before Paul walks into Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold.

Meaning first. Acts 28 brings Paul to Rome at last. On Malta he survives a viper’s bite and heals the sick. In spring he sails for Italy, is met by believers on the road, and enters Rome as a prisoner. He meets the Jewish leaders, explains the hope of Israel from Moses and the Prophets, and when many reject it, quotes Isaiah and declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. The book ends with Paul under house arrest for two years, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. The gospel has reached the capital of the world. The story of Acts ends, but the story of the word goes on, because the risen Christ who began this work is still building his church.

We then learned that the island was called Malta. They did not know where they were until somebody told them. Two hundred and seventy-six people stand dripping on a beach at dawn, and the first piece of information anyone acquires is the name of the place. Malta is a small island about sixty miles south of Sicily, well off the route to Italy. They have been blown something like five hundred miles in a fortnight.

The native people. Luke’s word is barbaroi, which came into English as barbarians and has picked up a sneer it does not carry here. To a Greek speaker it simply meant people who did not speak Greek; the word imitates the sound of unintelligible speech, bar-bar. The Maltese spoke a Punic dialect descended from Phoenician. Luke is not insulting them, or calling them savage; he is telling you that nobody on that beach could understand the locals and the locals could not understand them.

Showed us unusual kindness. The word is philanthrōpia, literally love of human beings, the root of our philanthropy: humanity, kindness to people. And Luke marks it as unusual, out of the ordinary, more than anyone had a right to expect. Now put the scene together, because it is easy to read past it. Nearly three hundred strangers come out of the sea at dawn in a storm: soldiers, prisoners, sailors, a shipwrecked crew with nothing left, speaking a language nobody understands, on a small island at the start of winter. They are a burden of the first order. Every one of them will need feeding.

For they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. And what the islanders do is build a fire for wet, cold, exhausted survivors in late October or November. There is no sermon here, no miracle, no revelation. There is wet wood, and rain coming on, and people who did not have to bother going to the trouble of getting a blaze going for a crowd of foreigners who could not thank them in any language they knew.

How God provisions the journey. Keep an eye on how God has been provisioning this journey, because it is nearly all like this. A centurion’s professional courtesy at Sidon. A crew’s seamanship in the gale. And now a bonfire on a beach, lit by people who had never heard the name of the God who sent them the guests. God’s common grace in unbelievers. He does not appear to feel any need to use religious instruments. He simply uses what is there, and the people he uses generally never find out.

Should Christians accept help from people who do not share their faith? Yes, gratefully. Paul accepted the islanders’ fire, Publius’s hospitality and the provisions they loaded on board. All good things come from God, and he often gives them to his people through unbelievers. Receive such kindness with thanks, honour the givers, and let your gratitude be a witness. And remember the obligation that runs the other way: Christians are to do good to everyone, not only to fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). The islanders’ kindness is a standard the church should never fall below.

In a sentence. Once they had been brought safely through, they learned that the island was called Malta, and the native people showed them unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed them all, because it had begun to rain and was cold.

On a Tuesday. Show kindness to strangers in need. It reflects God’s kindness to us. Think of the newcomers in your street or church this month: a refugee family, an international student, a lonely new neighbour. Light a fire for someone: an invitation, a meal, a lift, a warm welcome. You do not need to share their language to share your kindness.

For worship. The God who brought 276 people out of the sea had already prepared a fire for them on the shore. He is the Lord who goes before his people, who sets a table in the presence of their enemies and lights fires on strange beaches. And once, on another shore, after a long night on the water, the risen Christ himself stood by a charcoal fire with fish laid on it and bread, and said to his weary disciples, Come and have breakfast. How kind is the God who meets the shipwrecked with warmth.
verseByVerse.note: Malta lies south of Sicily. The islanders spoke a Phoenician dialect, not Greek — hence “native people.”

verseByVerse.quote: "When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, 'No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”

When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire. Stop on that before the snake. Paul is the senior figure in this company by any spiritual measure: an apostle of Jesus Christ, the man whose God has just brought 276 people through a fortnight of storm, the one person aboard whose word turned out to be worth anything. He is also, by now, an ageing man who has been beaten more times than he can count and has just struggled ashore from a wreck. And what he is doing is collecting firewood. Not directing the collection of firewood. Not resting by the blaze while others fetch it. Luke says he gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, and Luke says it so plainly that it is possible to read the whole chapter without noticing. No task is beneath him. A servant to the end. That is the same man who wrote that Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He had learned it from someone.

A viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. Exactly what happens when you throw a bundle of sticks on a fire: something cold-blooded that was sleeping in it, sluggish from the cold, wakes up in the heat.

No snakes on Malta today? A word on an old objection, since a thoughtful reader may meet it. There are no venomous snakes on Malta today, and sceptics have made something of that. It is not much of an argument. Two thousand years of dense settlement on a small island, which was more wooded then, can easily wipe out snake populations, and the more telling detail is in the text itself: the islanders recognised the creature on sight and knew precisely what to expect from it. They were not guessing. They stood there waiting for a specific and familiar death.

No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live. They saw his chains. They have a theology, and it is worth taking seriously because it is a good deal more common than its pagan dress suggests. Justice is Dikē, a Greek goddess, retribution personified, the power believed to pursue the guilty and make sure they do not get away with it. Their reasoning is tight: this man survived a shipwreck, which looked like a reprieve; now a viper has him; therefore the reprieve was an illusion and the debt has been collected. The universe is morally accountable, and it has caught up with him.

Half right. Half of that is right, and it is the half we are least comfortable with. There is a moral order. Guilt is real, and it is not finally evaded. What is wrong is the arithmetic: the assumption that you can read a person’s standing with God off the surface of their circumstances. Popular religion assumes that suffering proves guilt. It is exactly the mistake Job’s friends made across forty chapters. It is what the disciples assumed when they saw the blind man and asked whose sin had caused it (John 9:2–3), and what Jesus rejected when he spoke of the Galileans killed by Pilate and the eighteen crushed by the tower in Siloam (Luke 13:1–5). And it is alive in every sickroom where somebody wonders aloud what they did to deserve this. The islanders’ logic is coherent. Their conclusion is the precise opposite of the truth. The man with the snake on his hand is the one person on that beach whom God had personally promised to bring safely to Rome.

Does my suffering mean God is punishing me? Not necessarily, and for a Christian, never in the sense of paying for your sins. Christ has borne the punishment for all the sins of his people (Isaiah 53:5; Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, out of love, to train them (Hebrews 12:5–11), and sometimes suffering is the natural consequence of a particular sin, which should be confessed and forsaken. But much suffering has no direct link to any sin of ours; it comes from living in a fallen world, and God uses it for our good and his glory (John 9:3; Romans 8:28). If you are unsure, ask God to show you anything you need to repent of, and then rest in his love.

In a sentence. When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand, and when the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”

On a Tuesday. Suffering does not prove guilt. Do not judge others by their misfortunes. When you hear of someone’s illness, accident or loss, guard your tongue and your thoughts against the islanders’ conclusion. And look for the firewood job this week: the small, unglamorous task in your home, church or workplace that nobody wants, and do it.

For worship. The Lord of glory gathered sticks too. He who made the trees of the forest worked with wood in a carpenter’s shop in Nazareth, and took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet. He did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. And the justice that the islanders feared, the real justice of the holy God, did catch up with sin, not on a beach in Malta, but on a hill outside Jerusalem, where it fell on the Innocent One in the place of the guilty. Praise the Servant King, who bore our sentence.
verseByVerse.note: “Justice” was a goddess who was believed to pursue the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. The understatement is magnificent, and it is Luke’s, not Paul’s. No drama, no speech, no gesture toward heaven. He shakes his hand over the flames and goes on with the evening. This is God’s protection. Paul must stand before Caesar (27:24), and no snake could stop that. Jesus had promised his messengers authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and that nothing would hurt them (Luke 10:19).

They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. Luke, who was a doctor, gives the two things the islanders were watching for, and uses medical terms for them: local swelling and inflammation, or sudden collapse. They knew the symptoms. Everyone on that beach is now staring at one man’s hand.

They changed their minds and said that he was a god. And there is the whole fickleness of human judgment in a single sentence. Within the space of one evening, on exactly the same evidence, Paul goes from murderer to deity. Nothing about him has altered. He has not spoken. He has not argued his case or defended his character. The crowd simply ran their theology forward, found the result unacceptable, and reversed it entirely, and their second verdict is as wrong as their first, and considerably more dangerous. Popular opinion swings wildly. Paul was neither.

Lystra in reverse. He had been through this before, at Lystra, but in the opposite order: there a healing brought out the priest of Zeus with oxen and garlands, and Paul tore his clothes and ran into the crowd shouting that he was a man like them (14:11–15), and soon afterwards the same crowd stoned him. Luke does not record a protest here, but there is no shrine on Malta and no cult of Paul in the record; only, in the next verse, a sick old man being visited and prayed for. He answered the compliment by behaving like a servant.

Judged by the crowd. That is worth turning on the reader, because most of us are governed by verdicts of this quality far more than we would like to admit. The people who decide you are wonderful and the people who decide you are worthless are frequently the same people, working from the same evidence, a fortnight apart. A man who needs the first verdict will be destroyed by the second. Paul appears to have taken no notice of either.

Where Christians differ: snake-handling. Some groups handle venomous snakes in worship, citing this and Mark 16:18. Verdict: Paul didn’t pick up the snake on purpose; it bit him by accident, and God protected him. Mark 16:9–20 is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and is not a command. Deliberately testing God this way is forbidden (Matthew 4:7). God protects his servants in their work; he doesn’t ask us to court danger.

A promise on the road, not a stunt. It is worth saying plainly what is wrong with snake-handling, since this passage has been put to a use it will not bear. Paul did not seek the snake; he was collecting firewood, and it bit him. Every genuine instance of divine protection in Scripture comes upon a servant in the course of duty, never as a stunt performed to prove something. To pick up a viper on purpose is not faith; it is precisely what the Lord Jesus refused to do when he was invited to throw himself off the temple, and he answered it with a verse: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7). Protection is a promise to be received on the road, not a mechanism to be triggered.

How should I respond to praise and to blame? With the same steadiness, because neither is the final verdict. Paul wrote that it was a very small thing to him to be judged by any human court; it is the Lord who judges him (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Receive praise graciously and pass the glory to God; receive criticism humbly, asking whether there is truth in it, and change if there is. But do not build your sense of worth on either. Your standing rests on God’s verdict in Christ, and that does not swing with the crowd.

In a sentence. But he shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm, and they waited for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead; but when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

On a Tuesday. Do not test God by courting danger, but trust him in the dangers you meet. And notice this week how much the opinions of others move you, up or down. Write down one thing God says about you in Christ, Ephesians 1:3–7 is a good place to start, and come back to it whenever the crowd changes its mind.

For worship. The Lord is the shield of his servants. The serpent struck, and the hand that held it was the hand God was keeping for Rome. And far greater than the shaking off of a viper is the victory foretold in Eden, when the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head, though his own heel would be bruised. On the cross the old serpent struck the Son of God, and the Son of God crushed him. All glory to the Christ who has disarmed the powers and triumphed over them, and in whom his people need fear no serpent at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him.

The chief man of the island, named Publius. Luke’s title for him is prōtos, literally the first man, and it is one of those small details that quietly vouches for him. Inscriptions found on Malta, in Greek and in Latin, show that first man of the island was the actual formal title of the leading official there. Luke did not guess it and did not generalise it. He used the local title correctly, in the right place, long before anyone could have checked him from a reference book. Another precise detail.

Who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. Do the arithmetic on that hospitality. This is not a dinner party. Publius takes on the feeding and sheltering of the shipwreck company for three days, and even if it is only the officers and their charges rather than all 276, it is a serious act of generosity at the beginning of winter. Kindness from the top. Once again the provision comes from someone with no interest in the God who is arranging it.

The father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. Here Luke the physician shows his training. The Greek reads, literally, fevers and dysentery, the plural for fever being the standard medical idiom of the period for a condition that comes in recurring bouts. A recurrent fever of exactly this kind was so well known on the island that when nineteenth-century physicians identified it, a bacterial infection often carried in goat’s milk, they named it Malta fever. It was common there until the twentieth century. Luke describes, in correct medical language, a disease characteristic of the place he says he was in.

And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. Three verbs, and the order is the whole of it. He visited: the apostle goes to the sickroom. Whatever else the miracle involves, it begins with a man walking down a corridor to sit with someone who is ill. He prayed: before he touched him. Prayer first, because the power was God’s. Paul does not treat the gift as something he carries in his pocket; he asks. He laid his hands on him and healed him. Luke, who elsewhere is careful to say that it is the name of Jesus that heals (3:16; 4:10), here writes it plainly and briefly. Paul repays kindness with kindness.

Does this mean healing ministries continue today? These healings confirmed Paul as an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), as the gospel came to a new people. Yet Paul himself left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Believers still pray for the sick, as James teaches (James 5:14–15), and God heals as he wills; but no one today holds the apostle’s gift.

Healing as correction. There is something worth noticing about the order of this chapter. Paul has just been declared a god by the people of the island, and the next thing he does is go and sit with one sick old man and pray for him. The healing does not follow the acclaim as a demonstration. It follows the acclaim as a correction of it.

How should I pray for someone who is sick? Pray boldly and humbly together. Ask God plainly to heal, because he is able and he invites us to ask (James 5:14–16; Philippians 4:6). Ask also for what he has certainly promised: his presence, strength to endure, wisdom for the doctors, and the person’s spiritual good. Use medical help gratefully, as one of God’s means. Visit, as Paul did; sometimes the visit is the greatest comfort. And leave the outcome to God without guilt. If healing does not come, it is not because your faith was too small; God’s will is wiser than ours, and for his people the final healing is certain at the resurrection.

In a sentence. In the neighbourhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, Publius, who received them and entertained them hospitably for three days; and the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery, and Paul visited him, prayed, put his hands on him and healed him.

On a Tuesday. Repay kindness with kindness, and with prayer. Think of someone who has been good to you recently, perhaps someone who does not share your faith. Do something kind in return, and pray for them by name, including for their health and their salvation. And visit someone who is ill this week.

For worship. The Lord who healed the father of Publius is the same Lord who went about all the towns and villages healing every disease and every affliction. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows. Every healing in this world, by prayer or by medicine, is a small foretaste of the day when he will wipe away every tear, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain. Blessed be the Great Physician, who heals the body for a time and the soul for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Chief man” (literally “first man”) was the title of the Roman official on Malta, found in inscriptions there. Luke, a doctor, names the illness precisely.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured.

The rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. The word spreads, and Malta comes to the door. Luke’s verb for what happens to them, etherapeuonto, is the one that gives us therapy; it is the ordinary word for being treated and made well, and Luke uses it throughout his Gospel for what Jesus did. It is in a tense that suggests this went on: not one occasion, but a stream of people over the weeks. A healing ministry for three months. Some suggest that Luke the doctor also treated them medically. Either way, God’s kindness came to Malta.

No sermon in the text. Here is a question the passage raises and does not answer, which is worth being honest about. Luke records no preaching on Malta. Three months on that island, and not one sermon in the text. Two things should be said, and the second matters more than the first. First, Luke plainly is not telling us everything. He is compressing three months into a few verses, and it is inconceivable that Paul spent a winter among people who had just watched God heal their sick and said nothing whatever about him. The silence is Luke’s, not Paul’s, and a church has existed on Malta from early times. Second, and more usefully: what Luke does record is a season in which the gospel travelled almost entirely by kindness received and kindness returned. A fire lit by strangers. A house opened for three days. A sick man prayed for. A queue of islanders healed. Provisions loaded aboard at the end.

Mercy and the message. Now, mercy shown to a body is not a substitute for telling people about Christ, and it must never be offered as one; a man can be cured of dysentery and still be lost for ever. Paul knew that better than anyone and spent his life saying so. But mercy is not less than a sermon either, and it is very often the thing that gets a sermon listened to.

The Maltese test. Here is the test, and it is a plain one. Most Christians will not preach a sermon this year. Every Christian will have a winter’s worth of small chances of exactly the Maltese kind: the practical thing done for someone who cannot repay it, the visit made, the meal taken round, the help given to people whose language you do not really speak. Paul gathered sticks and sat with an old man with a fever. There is no record that he thought either activity was beneath his calling.

How do I hold together good deeds and gospel words? Do both, and do not let either crowd out the other. Jesus healed and preached; the early church fed widows and proclaimed Christ. Good deeds show the love of God and give credibility to the message (Matthew 5:16; 1 Peter 2:12). Words explain whose love it is and how a person can be saved, because faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). In practice: serve people generously, and when the door opens, as it often will, gently tell them why you do it and about the Saviour who has done so much more for you.

In a sentence. And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured.

On a Tuesday. God’s goodness spreads through his servants wherever they are washed up. Bloom where you are planted. Wherever you find yourself this season, a new job, a hospital ward, a place you never planned to be, look for the sick, the lonely and the needy around you, and serve them in Christ’s name.

For worship. The kindness of God came to Malta in the wake of a shipwreck. He took a disaster and made it the door of mercy for a whole island. That is his way: he makes the valley of trouble a door of hope. The God who scattered the church from Jerusalem so that the word went everywhere, who sent his apostle to Rome by way of a wreck, is the God who works all things together for good. His goodness is not stopped by storms; it rides in on them.

verseByVerse.quote: "They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead.

They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. The company arrived on Malta having thrown literally everything they owned into the sea: cargo, tackle, gear, the last of the wheat. They had lost everything in the wreck. They leave three months later with a fully provisioned ship. The honours may well have included gifts, though Luke does not say; what he does say is that the islanders supplied their needs. God provided through the islanders. Every scrap of that provision came from people who worshipped other gods and had no notion that they were outfitting the apostle to the Gentiles for the last leg of his journey to Caesar.

After three months we set sail. Early in the spring, around February, when sailing resumed. They set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island: another Alexandrian grain freighter, the same class of vessel that was smashed to matchwood in the bay three months earlier. They get on board anyway, which is its own quiet comment on how the promise of God is meant to be held: not by avoiding the kind of thing that went wrong last time.

A ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. And Luke names the figurehead, which he did not have to do. As the ESV notes, the twin gods are the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus in the old stories, and the patron deities of sailors. Their images rode on the bow, and Mediterranean seamen prayed to them for safe passage. Ships were often known by their figureheads, so this vessel was, in effect, called the Heavenly Twins. So the apostle of the living God completes his journey to Rome aboard a ship dedicated to two pagan gods, under their painted faces, having been fed all winter by islanders who had thought he was a god himself. A touch of irony: the true God had protected them, not the twin gods. Luke notes it, perhaps with a smile.

Composure under the figurehead. Luke reports it with a completely straight face, and there is no anxiety in it anywhere: no suggestion that Paul should have sought a more suitable vessel, no hint that the figurehead compromised anything. The gods on the bow were nothing, and the God who governs the wind had already said where this ship was going. That composure is worth learning from. There is a kind of Christian nervousness that needs the world to be scrubbed of every pagan trace before it can be used or enjoyed, and it is not the confidence of the New Testament. Paul, who wrote that an idol has no real existence (1 Corinthians 8:4), sat under the twin gods all the way to Puteoli and thought nothing of it.

Should Christians avoid everything linked with other religions? Not everything. Paul taught that an idol is nothing, and that the earth is the Lord’s, so a Christian may eat food bought in the market, travel on a ship with a pagan figurehead, use the days of the week named after Norse gods, or live in a city full of temples (1 Corinthians 10:25–26). What we must never do is take part in the worship of other gods, or act in a way that leads a weaker believer to violate his conscience (1 Corinthians 8:9–13; 10:20–21). Ask: am I worshipping, or merely living in a world where others worship? Am I harming anyone’s faith? Then act with freedom and love.

In a sentence. They also honoured them greatly, and when they were about to sail, they put on board whatever they needed; and after three months they set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead.

On a Tuesday. The true God protects, not the gods of the sailors. Trust him. Notice this week the things people around you trust for safety and success: luck, horoscopes, money, health routines, charms. Do not mock them, but quietly put your own trust in the living God, and be ready to explain why.

For worship. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see. Castor and Pollux rode on the bow and could save no one; the Lord of heaven and earth rode with his servant and brought him safely to Italy. All the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Blessed be the only true God, who needs no figurehead and shares his glory with no other.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the figurehead was the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus and protectors of sailors.

verseByVerse.quote: "Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.

Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. Read the geography and feel the pace change. Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily, and they stopped there three days.

And arrived at Rhegium. Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy, at the Straits of Messina, and Luke’s phrase we made a circuit probably describes tacking, working the ship up the coast against an unhelpful wind.

And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. A south wind. After everything, a following breeze. The distance from Rhegium to Puteoli is around two hundred miles, and they cover it in two days, a fast passage by any standard, the sort of run a master would remember. A good wind at last. The contrast with the previous voyage is total, and Luke does not point it out. Weeks of fighting a headwind, then a fortnight driven blind through a gale, then a wreck; and now, in the last stretch, the wind simply gets behind them and they fly.

Puteoli. Puteoli, on the Bay of Naples, was the main port for the Alexandrian grain ships, about 170 miles from Rome. Ships of this class were famous there; the philosopher Seneca describes the crowds of Puteoli turning out to watch the Alexandrian grain ships come over the horizon, because the whole city knew what they carried. So the voyage ends the way it should have ended months ago: an Alexandrian grain ship making a fast run into Puteoli with a south wind behind her. Whatever is in her hold, what she is actually delivering is one prisoner, and neither the master nor the centurion nor the port has any idea that this is the only cargo the voyage was ever really for.

God was in charge of the northeaster too. There is one more thing worth noticing about this leg of the journey, now that the danger is past. Nobody on that ship prayed for this wind, so far as Luke records. Nobody fasted for it or held a meeting about it. After months in which every single thing had gone wrong, the weather simply turned helpful, and a company of exhausted men made good time up the Italian coast in early spring. God had been just as much in charge of the northeaster.

Should I be suspicious of easy times, after what happened with the south wind in chapter 27? No; be thankful, and humble. The lesson of the gentle south wind at Crete was not that good weather is dangerous, but that good weather is not proof that every decision was right. Here the south wind is simply God’s kindness after the storm, and Luke records it without suspicion. Receive easy seasons as gifts, enjoy them, give thanks for them, and keep walking carefully. God is as much in the fair wind as in the gale, and both serve his purpose.

In a sentence. Putting in at Syracuse, they stayed there for three days, then made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium, and after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day they came to Puteoli.

On a Tuesday. After the storm, God sends good winds. Wait for them, and when they come, thank him for them. If this is an easy season for you, write down what God has given you in it, so that you remember when the next storm comes. If it is a hard one, remember that the south wind came for Paul in the end.

For worship. The God of the northeaster is the God of the south wind. He sends the storm and he stills it; he brings low and he lifts up. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning. He who drove the ship through fourteen dark nights now carries it lightly up the coast of Italy in the spring. All his ways are faithfulness, in the gale and in the following breeze alike.
verseByVerse.note: Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily; Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy; Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for the grain ships.

verseByVerse.quote: "There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.

There we found brothers. Few words, but worth their weight. Nobody sent them. There is no record in Acts of a mission to Puteoli, no apostle assigned to the Bay of Naples, no church-planting strategy that took in the port towns of Campania. Paul arrives in Italy for the first time in his life and discovers that Christians are already there, before Paul ever came. The gospel had spread without him. The church is bigger than any apostle. That is how the gospel had actually been moving all along, underneath the narrative Luke has been telling: along the trade routes, in the luggage of merchants and sailors and slaves whose names nobody wrote down. Someone carried the message to this port, and Luke does not know who, and neither do we.

And were invited to stay with them for seven days. They take the company in for a week, which means the centurion Julius agreed to it, one last courtesy from a man who has been quietly decent to Paul since Sidon, and a sign of his respect for him. A week would have included a Lord’s Day together, worshipping with brothers they had never met.

And so we came to Rome. There it is. A few words, dropped in without ceremony, and the entire book has been travelling toward them. Luke does not build to it. There is no flourish, no paragraph of reflection: just a plain sentence of arrival tucked between a week’s hospitality at Puteoli and the details of the final road. From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, along the Appian Way.

What stands behind the words. Consider what stands behind them. Paul’s great desire to see Rome (19:21; Romans 1:10–15). A promise made in the dark of a Jerusalem barracks by the Lord himself: you must testify also in Rome (23:11). A conspiracy of forty men sworn to prevent it. Two years wasted in a cell at Caesarea under a governor angling for a bribe. A hearing before Festus, an appeal to Caesar, a hearing before Agrippa. A fortnight in a storm with the sun and stars blotted out. A shipwreck. A viper. A winter on Malta. And Luke’s whole account of the fulfilment is: and so we came to Rome. Not as Paul had planned, but as God had promised.

Who founded the church in Rome? Not Paul, who wrote to it before he had visited (Romans 1:13; 15:22–24), and nothing in Scripture says Peter did. It most likely began with Jews and converts from Rome who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (2:10), and with believers who moved there. Here the Roman Christians come out to meet Paul.

The right way to record it. That restraint is not coldness. It is a man who knows that the promise never needed decorating. God said Rome, and here is Rome, and the correct way to record it is flatly, because that is what happens to the things God has said.

Does a church need a famous founder to be real? No. The churches at Puteoli and Rome were real churches long before an apostle arrived, planted by ordinary believers whose names are lost. What makes a church is not a famous founder or an unbroken line of bishops, but the presence of Christ among believers gathered under his Word, with the preaching of the gospel and the ordinances he gave (Matthew 18:20; 28:19–20).
