The foundation of every true church is the teaching of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). An ordinary congregation of faithful believers is as truly the church as the church at Rome.

In a sentence. There they found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days, and so they came to Rome.

On a Tuesday. God’s promises are fulfilled, in his time and in his way. Think of a promise of God you have been waiting on for a long time. Write it down, and next to it, the words: and so we came to Rome. And thank God for the unknown believers who first brought the gospel to your town, your family or your church.

For worship. And so we came to Rome. Every word of God arrives like that: plainly, at last, exactly as he said. Not one of his good promises has ever failed. The Lord who said Rome brought his servant to Rome through plots and prisons, storms and serpents, and he will bring all his people to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God. One day the whole redeemed church will say it together, standing in the new Jerusalem: and so we came home. Faithful is he who calls you; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.note: From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, the Appian Way.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. These are Roman Christians who have heard that Paul’s party is on the road, and they walk out to meet him, like citizens going out to meet a dignitary. The distances are worth having. The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, about forty-three and thirty-three miles from Rome. On foot, that is a long day or two out and as long again back for the first group. They may have gone in two waves, or the nearer group may have set out later. Either way, ordinary believers with jobs and households took days to go and stand at the roadside on the chance of meeting a prisoner.

They had never met him. Paul had written to this church perhaps three years earlier: the letter we call Romans, his greatest letter, the most closely argued document in the New Testament, sent to a congregation he had never visited and had wanted to visit for years (Romans 1:11–13; 15:23–24). The last chapter of that letter greets some twenty-six people by name. Some of them, in all likelihood, were standing on that road. Now they met face to face.

On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. This is the tenderest sentence in the last quarter of Acts, and it should not be hurried. Notice first what it admits. Took courage means he needed some. Even Paul needed courage. Paul, who faced down a mob from the barracks steps, who told a shipful of despairing men that not one of them would die, who has just walked away from a snakebite without comment, is, on the road into Rome, a man whose courage is running low. That is entirely understandable, and almost never how we picture him. He is going to the capital as a prisoner to be tried before Nero, uncertain of his trial. He is ageing, he has been at sea for months, he has lost everything he owned in the wreck, and the outcome is a matter of life and death.

Not an angel, but brothers. And what God sends him is not an angel. He had an angel earlier in the story, and it was exactly what was needed then. Here, on the Appian Way, the provision is a small crowd of Christians standing by the road because they wanted to see him. Notice too what Paul does with them: he thanked God. He does not merely feel better. He looks straight past the people to the one who sent them and gives him the credit, and then his courage comes back. Christian fellowship is God’s gift for weary souls.

The strong need it too. There is a test in this, and it cuts two ways. If Paul needed this, the strong Christians around you need it, and they will not tell you so; the assumption that a mature believer is beyond encouragement is one of the loneliest lies in the church. And on the other side: the walk to the Forum of Appius accomplished nothing practical. Those men did not free him, feed him or improve his legal position by a single clause. They simply showed up on a road, and the effect on the apostle to the Gentiles was that he thanked God and found he could go on. Almost nobody thinks turning up is worth the trip. Luke thought it was worth a verse.

And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. House arrest, chained to a soldier, probably in a rented apartment. A mild form of custody, perhaps on the strength of Festus’s letter and Julius’s report.

Was Paul in prison? He was in military custody, chained to a single soldier, but allowed to live in his own rented quarters and to receive visitors freely (vv. 23, 30). He was a prisoner awaiting trial before Caesar, and the gospel still went out unhindered.

How can I encourage a mature Christian, such as my pastor? Simply, and specifically. Turn up: be there, at the hospital, the hard meeting, the anniversary of a loss. Tell them, in a sentence or a short note, one particular way God has used them in your life. Pray for them and let them know you do. Offer practical help without waiting to be asked. Do not assume they have plenty of encouragement; often the people who give the most receive the least. Paul’s courage was renewed by people who did nothing but walk out to meet him.

In a sentence. The brothers in Rome, when they heard about them, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet them, and on seeing them Paul thanked God and took courage; and when they came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

On a Tuesday. Go and meet those who are weary. Your presence can give them courage. Think of one believer this week who is carrying a heavy load, and go and stand at their roadside: a visit, a call, a card, a meal. You do not need to fix anything. Just turn up, and let them thank God for you.

For worship. The God of all comfort comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may comfort others with the comfort we have received. He sent a crowd of brothers to the Appian Way as surely as he sent an angel to the ship. And the Lord himself is the one who comes out to meet his weary people: the father who saw his son a long way off and ran. One day he will gather his whole church to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Thanks be to God, who gives us courage through one another, and gives us himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, roughly 40 and 30 miles from Rome. Paul was kept under house arrest, chained to a soldier.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later Paul calls together the Jewish leaders in Rome. He tells them that although he has done nothing against their people or ancestral customs, he was arrested in Jerusalem and handed to the Romans. They examined him and wanted to release him, finding nothing deserving death, but when the Jews objected he had to appeal to Caesar, not to accuse his own nation. He has asked to see them because it is for the hope of Israel that he wears this chain. They reply that they have received no letters about him from Judea and no visitor has reported anything bad, but they want to hear his views, since people everywhere speak against this sect. On an agreed day many more come to his lodging. From morning till evening he explains and testifies about the kingdom of God, seeking to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded, others refuse to believe. As they leave, disagreeing among themselves, Paul makes one last statement: the Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah to their fathers about a people who listen without understanding and look without seeing, whose hearts have grown dull, who have closed their eyes and ears so as not to turn and be healed. So they should know that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen. For two whole years Paul stays in his own rented house and welcomes everyone who comes to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without hindrance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Book Has No Ending

The abrupt close of Acts is a decision, not an accident. Luke had written the death of Stephen and the death of James; he could have written the death of Paul. Instead he stops with his hero alive, chained, and preaching.

The reason is that Luke's subject was announced in his first chapter and it was never Paul: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). That programme is now complete. The word has travelled from an upper room in Jerusalem to rented lodgings in Rome, and it is being preached in the capital of the world without restriction. There is nothing left to report.

Hence the final word, akolytos — unhindered — the last word of the Greek text and Luke's verdict on everything that came before it. The Sanhedrin ordered the message silenced; it spread. Stephen was stoned; it spread. Herod killed James and jailed Peter; the door opened. It was flogged out of Philippi, mocked in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, tried in four courts, sworn against by forty men, driven into a fortnight's storm, wrecked on Malta, and bitten by a snake. At the end, the emperor's soldiers have the preacher chained by the wrist — and the word walks in and out of that room for two years and nobody can touch it.

Two guards keep this from becoming triumphalism. First, unhindered does not mean unopposed; every hindrance in the list was real and several were lethal, and Paul himself would die under Nero within a few years. Second, the man is still in chains as the book closes. Luke's claim is not that the church wins its comfort, but that the word of God cannot be stopped — which is a very different and much sturdier promise, and the only one he offers.

As for Paul himself: early tradition outside Scripture, and therefore to be held loosely, says he was released, travelled again — perhaps to Spain as he had hoped (Rom. 15:24) — was re-arrested and executed at Rome. The Pastoral Epistles read like letters from that later period. Luke declines to tell us, and his silence is the point.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The last thing Luke shows us is a prisoner in a rented room, chained by the wrist to a soldier who changed shift every few hours, unable to leave the building. He could not travel to a single one of the churches he had planted. And out of that room, on the traditional reckoning, came Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon — letters that have reached further than all his journeys put together — while the guard rotation carried the gospel through the imperial barracks until there were believers in Caesar's own household.

Now: The circumstance that looks like the end of a person's usefulness is very often the beginning of the part that outlasts them. Illness that stops a working life. A redundancy. A move to somewhere with no ministry to speak of. Children, or care of a parent, that shrinks the world to a few rooms for a decade. Every one of those feels like being taken off the field, and every one of them puts you in a room with a small number of people who cannot easily get away from you. Paul's chain did not interrupt his ministry; it relocated it, narrowed it, and made it permanent. He did not know that at the time either. He simply welcomed whoever came through the door, every day, for two years — and that is the last thing the book of Acts records anybody doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, 'Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.

After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews. Three days. He has just arrived in the capital of the world after a journey of months that nearly killed him, he is under house arrest chained to a soldier, and he waits only three days before convening a meeting. And notice who he sends for first. Not the Roman church, though they had walked forty miles to meet him and he plainly loved them. The synagogue. Paul could not go to the synagogue, so he invited the synagogue to come to him. Jews had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion (18:2), and there were many synagogues in the city.

To the Jew first. This is the pattern of his entire ministry, held to the very last scene of the book: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16), the principle he had written to these very people. In Pisidian Antioch, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus he went to the synagogue first and was thrown out of it, city after city, year after year. It never once altered the order in which he knocked on doors. There is a kind of faithfulness in that which is easy to miss. Paul had every reason to have given up on the synagogue as a matter of policy. He kept going, and he kept going because he loved them, and he had written to this city that he could wish himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers (Romans 9:3).

Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers. Every word of that opening is chosen with care, and the care is pastoral rather than legal. He calls them brothers, still. He speaks of our people and the customs of our fathers. Before he defends himself at all, he plants himself inside the family. Whatever these men have heard about the sect that is spoken against everywhere, the person in front of them is not an outsider making a case against them. Paul never stopped loving his people (Romans 9:1–5).

Yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. Then the summary, which is scrupulous. He does not say the Jews of Jerusalem tried to murder him, though some did. He does not mention the forty men and their oath. He uses a passive, I was delivered, and moves on. And the phrase carries an echo: the Son of Man too was delivered into the hands of sinful men (Luke 24:7). The servant walks his Master’s road.

When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty. The Romans found him innocent: there was no reason for the death penalty in his case. The book has now recorded one official finding of no crime after another. Gallio threw the case out at Corinth. Claudius Lysias wrote it in a letter. Felix heard it and did nothing. Festus admitted he had nothing to write. Agrippa said the man could have been freed. And now Paul states the cumulative verdict to the Jewish leadership of Rome as simple fact, because by this point it is.

Should Christians share the gospel with Jewish people today? Yes, with love, respect and humility. The gospel is for the Jew first and also for the Greek (Romans 1:16), and Jesus is the only way to the Father for all people (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Paul’s example shows how: as a brother, honouring the Scriptures and customs Jewish people cherish, showing that Jesus is the fulfilment of Israel’s own hope, and never with contempt. The history of Christian mistreatment of Jews means that many Jewish people hear the name of Jesus with pain, so earn trust, listen well, and let your life show the love of the Messiah.

In a sentence. After three days Paul called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,” who, when they had examined him, wished to set him at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in his case.

On a Tuesday. Love your people, even when they have wronged you. Paul still called them brothers. Think of the family, community or church from which you have received the deepest hurt. Ask God for grace to speak of them, and to them, as Paul did: as one who still belongs, still loves, and still longs for their good.

For worship. The love of Christ never gives up on his people. He wept over Jerusalem, the city that would crucify him, and longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood. His apostle, who bore the marks of Jerusalem’s hatred on his body, went to the synagogue first in Rome, because he had learned that love from his Lord. God has not cast off the people he foreknew. Blessed be the faithful God, whose love is stronger than every rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.

But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar. Two things are being said, and the second is the one that matters. First, the appeal was forced. Compelled is the word: he was left with no other route. Festus had proposed sending him back to Jerusalem for trial, which would very likely have been a death sentence, and the appeal was the only door left open.

Though I had no charge to bring against my nation. And second, this. Read it slowly, because it is one of the most gracious sentences Paul ever spoke, and it costs him something to say it. An appeal to Caesar was not a passive act. It put a case before the emperor’s court, and it would have been open to Paul to raise counter-charges: attempted murder, false witness, conspiracy, malicious prosecution by the leadership of his own people. He had ample evidence and he had suffered enormously. Any competent advocate might have advised it. He declines. He tells the Jewish leaders of Rome, on his first day of business with them, that he has come to their city with no accusation against his nation. Paul was not in Rome to accuse the Jews before Caesar. No bitterness, no revenge. He had come to defend himself, not to attack them.

What he declined to prosecute. Consider what he was declining to prosecute. A mob in the temple court that beat him and would have torn him apart. A high priest who ordered him struck on the mouth without a charge. Forty men under an oath to assassinate him. Two years of his life spent in a cell at Caesarea. A campaign of hostility spanning a quarter of a century and half the empire. And when he finally reaches the court with the power to do something about all of it, he says: no charge.

He had written the reason. The man had written the reason to this city already. He had told them of his great sorrow and unceasing anguish of heart, so that he could wish that he himself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers, his kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:1–3). That is not diplomacy. A man who could wish himself cut off for their sake is not going to sue them.

The test of the justified. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in proportion to how justified you are. Paul had a genuine case. The wrongs were real, documented and serious, and nobody would have blamed him for pressing them. He let it go: not by pretending it had not happened, not by minimising it, but by declining to use the leverage he actually had, because the people who had wronged him were the people he most wanted saved. Most of us do not release grievances because we are still waiting to be told we were right. Paul was right, and everyone in the story knew he was right, and he came into Rome with nothing to file.

How do I forgive without pretending that nothing happened? Forgiveness is not saying the wrong was small or did not matter; Paul named exactly what had been done to him. It is releasing the debt: giving up the right to make the other person pay, and leaving judgment to God, who will judge justly (Romans 12:19). It does not always mean restoring full trust at once, especially where there has been abuse; trust is rebuilt over time, if repentance is real, and safety matters. But it does mean refusing revenge, praying for the person’s good, and, where you can, doing them good. Ask God for help; this is the work of grace, not willpower.

In a sentence. But because the Jews objected, he had been compelled to appeal to Caesar, though he had no charge to bring against his own nation.

On a Tuesday. Do not seek revenge on those who wronged you. Leave it to God (Romans 12:19). Is there a case you are still keeping ready to file, in your heart if not in court? Name it before God today, and ask him for the grace to come into the room with nothing to file.

For worship. The Lord Jesus had every charge to bring against us, and he did not bring it. He stood before the Father with the full evidence of our rebellion, and instead of accusing us he interceded for us: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. He did not count our trespasses against us, but bore them himself. Paul’s mercy to his nation was a small reflection of that great mercy. Blessed be the Saviour who, being right, did not press his case, but laid down his life for his enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.' And they said to him, 'We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.

It is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain. He says it with the chain on his wrist. There is a soldier attached to the other end of it, standing in the room while Paul talks. The hope of Israel: he has used the idea before, at every stage of this long legal ordeal, to the council (23:6), to Felix (24:15), to Agrippa (26:6–8), and it has meant the same thing every time: the resurrection of the dead, and the coming of the Messiah in whom the promise to the fathers is kept. Paul’s whole defence, from first to last, has been that he is not on trial for abandoning Israel’s hope but for believing it has arrived. Christianity is the fulfilment of Israel’s hope, not its rejection.

Because of it. And notice the logic of the sentence. He does not say despite the hope of Israel I am in chains, as though the two were in tension. He says because of it. The chain is not the price of a mistake or the interruption of his ministry. It is what holding Israel’s own hope has cost him, and he may well have lifted his wrist to make the point: I wear this for Israel’s hope.

We have received no letters from Judea about you. Their answer is unexpected, and honestly a little surprising. Nothing has arrived from Jerusalem: no formal notification, no warning, no character assassination in advance. Why not? Luke does not say, and the honest commentators do not pretend to know. The most likely explanation is simply the sailing season: Paul left Caesarea in the autumn and the sea closed behind him, so no ship could have carried a dispatch ahead of him through the winter. It is also possible that the Jerusalem leadership, having twice failed to get a conviction and once failed to get him killed, had concluded the case was not worth pursuing to Rome, where they could not win.

None of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. What it means practically is that for the first time in years Paul is speaking to a Jewish audience that has not been prepared against him. No prejudice; an open door. There is no riot waiting to happen in this room. Nobody here has been told what to think of him. It is a small mercy and a real one, and it is the kind of thing that never looks like providence at the time: a winter storm closing the shipping lanes, and an old man in Rome getting a fair hearing because of it.

Should a Christian be ashamed of suffering for the faith? No. Peter writes that if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name (1 Peter 4:16). There is a difference between suffering for doing wrong, which brings no credit, and suffering for Christ, which is an honour (Acts 5:41; 1 Peter 2:19–20). Paul wore his chain without embarrassment because it was the badge of the hope he held. If you are mocked, passed over or opposed because you follow Jesus, you are in the company of the apostles and of Christ himself.

In a sentence. For this reason Paul had asked to see them and speak with them, since it was because of the hope of Israel that he was wearing this chain; and they said they had received no letters from Judea about him, and none of the brothers coming there had reported or spoken any evil about him.

On a Tuesday. The hope of Israel is your hope too: the risen Messiah. Hold it up without shame. If your faith has cost you something, a friendship, an opportunity, a reputation, thank God that you have been counted worthy to bear a small chain for so great a hope.

For worship. The hope of Israel is not a doctrine but a Person: the Messiah promised to the fathers, crucified for sinners and risen from the dead. For him Paul wore the chain, and for him the prophets longed, and in him every promise of God is Yes. And he himself was bound for us: arrested in a garden, led bound to Annas and Caiaphas, bound and handed over to Pilate, so that we might be set free. Glory to the Christ who wore chains for his people, and who is the hope of Israel and of the nations.
verseByVerse.note: “The hope of Israel” is the promised Messiah and the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.

But we desire to hear from you what your views are. An honest and rather appealing reply. They know nothing about Paul; they know something about the movement; and what they know is that it has a bad reputation in every city. Openness.

For with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against. That was true. Luke’s own book is the evidence: riots at Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth, Ephesus and Jerusalem. Wherever the message went, trouble followed it. These men are not slandering the Way; they are reporting the state of its public reputation accurately. And it was exactly what Simeon foretold over the infant Jesus: this child is appointed for a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34). Christianity was already notorious, about thirty years after the cross. Within five years Nero would blame the Christians for the great fire of Rome, and the Roman historian Tacitus would call the faith a deadly superstition.

A party within Judaism. The word they use is hairesis, a party or school of thought. It is the word from which we get heresy, but without that weight yet; it is the same word used of the Pharisees and Sadducees as parties within Judaism (5:17; 15:5). At this stage the Christians are, to a Roman synagogue, one more faction inside the Jewish world, and a disreputable one.

History in the room. There is also history in this room that Luke does not spell out. Around AD 49, the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome, and the Roman historian Suetonius, writing decades later, says the expulsion followed disturbances stirred up over one Chrestus, which is very probably a garbled reference to disputes about Christ. Luke has already told us the consequence in passing: Aquila and Priscilla turning up in Corinth because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (18:2). So when these leaders say the sect is spoken against everywhere, some of them may be remembering being put out of their homes over it. Their caution is earned.

Only fairness. And yet: we desire to hear from you what your views are. They have every reason to shut the conversation down, and instead they ask him to explain himself, and they set a date. That is more than Paul got in most cities, and it is worth naming for what it is: a group of people with a bad impression, real grievances and genuine reasons for suspicion, who nevertheless decide to hear the man out before deciding. It is not faith. It is only fairness. But Christianity has rarely asked for more than that as a starting point, and it does not often get it.

Should we try to make Christianity more acceptable, so that it is not spoken against? We should remove every unnecessary offence: harshness, hypocrisy, foolishness, unkindness, a bad reputation that we have earned (1 Peter 2:12; 3:15–16). But we must never remove the offence of the gospel itself. A crucified Messiah was a stumbling block and folly from the start (1 Corinthians 1:23), and Jesus warned his followers that they would be hated for his name (Matthew 10:22). The aim is not to be spoken well of by everyone (Luke 6:26), but to be spoken against, if at all, only for Christ.

In a sentence. But they said they wished to hear from him what his views were, for with regard to this sect they knew that everywhere it was spoken against.

On a Tuesday. If the faith is spoken against, do not be surprised. It always has been. Speak for it, gently and clearly. And when you meet someone with a bad impression of Christianity, do what these men did for Paul: ask honestly what they have heard, and listen before you answer.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the stone that the builders rejected, and he has become the cornerstone. He was spoken against in his life, despised and rejected by men, and he has been spoken against in every generation since; and still his name is above every name, and his church spreads to the ends of the earth. The rage of the nations is a vain thing. He who sits in the heavens laughs, and has set his King on Zion, his holy hill. Blessed is everyone who takes refuge in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved.

They came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. They set a date, and when the day comes there are more of them than before. Word has gone round the synagogues of Rome, and the room is full. A house meeting.

From morning till evening he expounded to them. Let that stand as it is written. Sunrise to sunset. A full day, perhaps ten or twelve hours, of one man teaching the Scriptures to a room of people who had come to make up their minds about him. A whole day of Bible teaching. Luke stacks up three verbs for what Paul did, and each says something different. He expounded: the word, exetitheto, means to set out, to lay open, the patient work of taking a text apart and showing what is inside it. This is exposition, not oratory.

Testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus. Testifying: bearing witness, the courtroom word. He is not offering an opinion; he is reporting what he has seen. Trying to convince them: the verb means to persuade, and it is in a tense that means he kept at it. He is not content to state the case and leave the outcome to atmosphere. He argues, all day, because he wants these particular men to believe. And the two subjects are the two great themes of Acts together: the kingdom of God, and Jesus (v. 31; 1:3).

Kingdom-proclamation from first to last. Notice how the book ends: Paul testifying to the kingdom of God, and the last verse says the same (v. 31). Acts opens with the risen Jesus speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3) and closes with Paul preaching it in Rome: the whole church-age mission framed, start to finish, as kingdom-proclamation. (On what that means now, and the gracious difference between the Reformed already-in-the-kingdom reading and the dispensational instinct to reserve the kingdom for a future Israel, see 20:25 and 8:12.) The point here is simply that the kingdom was Paul’s message to Jew and Roman alike, in this age, now.

Both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. As Jesus did on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27, 44): the whole Old Testament points to Jesus, and Paul’s method to the end is Scripture. But does the Law of Moses and the Prophets leave out the Psalms, the wisdom books, the histories? It is standard shorthand for the whole Old Testament. The Jews divided their Scriptures in three: the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi’im) and the Writings (Ketuvim), together the Tanakh. Two things. First, the Prophets is broader than we might guess: it includes not only Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest, but the great narrative books, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings (the Former Prophets), so much of the story already falls under that word. Second, the Law and the Prophets was simply the everyday twofold name for the entire Bible (Matthew 5:17; 22:40; Romans 3:21).

The whole Old Testament testifies to Jesus. The threefold shape was known in Paul’s day too: the prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC) speaks three times of the Law and the Prophets and the other books that followed; and Luke elsewhere gives the fuller form on Jesus’ own lips: “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44), where the Psalms stands for that third division. So the Law and the Prophets here means the whole Old Testament; and in practice Paul ranged across all of it. His sermon in Acts 13 reasons from the Psalms (Psalms 2 and 16) as freely as from the Prophets (Isaiah, Habakkuk). The deeper wonder is Luke’s constant point: all of it testifies to Jesus. Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, the risen Lord interpreted to the Emmaus disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). Paul spent a whole day doing just that: showing the kingdom and the King hidden in plain sight on every page Israel already revered.

And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. After all of that, the full day, the whole Old Testament, the finest mind in the early church working at the top of his powers on an audience that was genuinely willing to listen, the outcome is split. The same result as always: the gospel divides. That is worth sitting with, because it is the last word Acts has to say about how people respond to the gospel, and it declines to be tidy. Paul did everything right. The hearers came in good faith. And some believed and some did not. Luke has been reporting this same division since Pentecost, and he reports it here without embarrassment and without explanation. The next thing Paul says will offer an explanation, and it will come from Isaiah.

What if I share the gospel faithfully and people still reject it? Then you are in the company of Paul, of the prophets, and of Jesus himself. Your responsibility is to be faithful, clear and loving; the results belong to God, who alone gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Do not conclude that you did it wrong, or that the message needs changing. Keep praying for those who said no; some who reject the gospel today will receive it later. And remember that in this very room some were convinced. God always has his people, and his word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

In a sentence. When they had appointed a day for him, they came to his lodging in greater numbers, and from morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets; and some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved.

On a Tuesday. Open the Scriptures and show people Jesus. Some will believe. Choose one Old Testament passage this week, Genesis 22, Psalm 22 or Isaiah 53, and read it slowly, asking where it points to Christ. Then share what you see with one person.

For worship. The whole Bible is about him. From the first promise in Eden to the last prophet’s cry, every page bears witness to the Son. He is the true Passover Lamb, the greater Moses, the Son of David, the suffering Servant, the Lord our righteousness. Paul could spend a whole day in Rome and not exhaust him; we could spend eternity and not exhaust him. Blessed be the Word made flesh, the King of the kingdom, of whom Moses and all the prophets wrote.

verseByVerse.quote: "And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: 'The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: "Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: ‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.’

And disagreeing among themselves, they departed. The day ends without resolution. Divided, they are still arguing as they go out of the door, and Paul lets them go with a single parting statement: a quotation.

The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet. Before the quotation itself, look at how Paul introduces it, because that clause is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament about what Scripture actually is. The Holy Spirit was right in saying: the speaker is God. Not Isaiah wrote, not it says in the prophets: the Holy Spirit said this. Through Isaiah the prophet: and yet it came through a man, in his own idiom, in the eighth century BC, out of his own vision in the temple. Both at once, in one sentence, with no sense of strain. That is the doctrine of inspiration in the form Scripture usually gives it: God speaking, and a real human being genuinely writing. Peter puts it the same way: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Scripture has a divine author.

To your fathers. There is a third thing in the clause, easily passed over. The Spirit said it to Isaiah’s generation eight hundred years earlier, and Paul applies it, without apology, to the men walking out of his lodging that evening. Your fathers: Paul identifies them with their unbelieving ancestors. Scripture is not a record of what God once said to other people. It is God’s address to whoever is in the room.

You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. The quotation is Isaiah 6:9–10: the words given to Isaiah at his commissioning, in the year King Uzziah died, when he saw the Lord high and lifted up and the seraphim covering their faces. It is worth knowing what a heavy thing Paul has just picked up. This is the hardening passage, the Old Testament text the New Testament quotes most often on the subject of unbelief. Jesus quoted it to explain why he taught in parables (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10). John quoted it to explain why the miracles had not produced faith (John 12:40). Paul reaches for the same theme in Romans 11:8. Every writer who has to account for the fact that Israel heard the Messiah and did not receive him goes to the same place: the words God gave a prophet on the day he called him. The New Testament’s explanation of Israel’s unbelief is that it was foretold, and that it is God’s judgment on hardened hearts. Acts ends with it, as the Gospels do. Notice also that Paul does not soften it, and does not aim it at them personally as an accusation. He states it and leaves. The text does the work.

If God hardens hearts, is that unfair? No, though it is deeply sobering. God never hardens an innocent heart; he gives over to hardness those who have already closed their eyes to the light they have (Romans 1:21–24). Pharaoh hardened his own heart before God confirmed it (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:12). Hardening is judgment, and judgment is just. At the same time, no one who longs to see and hear and turn will ever be turned away; the desire itself is a sign of grace (John 6:37). If you are worried that you are hardened, the worry is good evidence that you are not. Come to Christ now.

In a sentence. Disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: ‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.’”

On a Tuesday. Hearing without understanding is a judgment. Ask God for an open heart when you read his Word. Before you open your Bible this week, pray the psalmist’s prayer: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law. And treat each passage as God’s address to you, today, in the room where you are.

For worship. The Holy Spirit speaks. Through prophets and apostles, across eight centuries and two testaments, the one voice of God has been heard, and it is never wrong. The Spirit was right in saying it to Isaiah, and he is right still. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand for ever. How precious is the Book that is the very breath of God, and how gracious the Spirit who opens blind eyes to read it.

parallels.desc: keep on hearing, but do not understand

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.

For this people’s heart has grown dull. The word is epachynthē: grown fat, thickened, insensitive, like thick skin. The heart hardens over time. And look at the order of the verse, because Isaiah built it deliberately, and it is a small piece of architecture. Going in, the sequence runs heart, ears, eyes: the heart dulls first, then the hearing goes, then the eyes shut. Coming out, in the healing clause that follows, it runs the other way: eyes, ears, heart. Lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn. The way out is the way in, run backwards. Sight, then hearing, then a heart that understands, and then the turning. It is a description of how a person actually comes to faith, written in reverse as a description of how they avoid it.

And their eyes they have closed. Now the hard part, and it should not be dodged. Their eyes they have closed: they closed them. That is active. Nobody did it to them. In the Greek Paul is quoting, the shutting of the eyes is something the people do to themselves: the deliberate refusal to look at something they suspect they will have to act on. This is responsibility. And yet in Isaiah 6 the prophet is commissioned to produce this effect: make the heart of this people dull, lest they see with their eyes. God sends the message knowing, and in some sense intending, that it will harden. Hardening is both their choice and God’s judgment (Romans 1:24; 11:7–8).

Both sides held together. Both are in the text, and Scripture never flattens them into one. Paul himself wrestled with it for three whole chapters in the letter he had already sent to this city (Romans 9–11), and his conclusion was not a formula but worship: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). What he refuses to do, and what we must refuse, is to let either side cancel the other. The hardened are genuinely responsible; they closed their own eyes. And God is genuinely sovereign over the outcome. A reader who has to flatten one of those to keep the other has stopped reading the Bible and started tidying it.

Never a weapon. What must not happen is that this verse becomes a weapon. Paul quotes it in sorrow, about his own people, having just spent a full day trying to persuade them, having said he could wish himself cut off for them if it were possible.

Lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them. And then the last clause, which changes the colour of everything before it. The sentence does not end with judgment. It ends with a physician. The whole terrible mechanism of dulled hearts and stopped ears and shut eyes exists in the text as an explanation of what is being kept out, and what is being kept out is healing. The tragedy is that healing was available, if they would turn. God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). But hardened hearts refuse.

Israel’s future. This is not the end of Israel. Paul, writing to Rome a few years earlier, said the hardening is partial and temporary: until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). There is hope.

How would I know if my own heart is growing dull? Watch for the signs Isaiah describes, in their order. Does God’s Word still move you, or do you hear it without being affected? Do you avoid passages or sermons that might require you to change? Has a known sin stopped troubling you? Do you find yourself more interested in arguing than in obeying? A dull heart rarely notices its own dullness, so ask a trusted friend too. The remedy is the healing clause run forward: look honestly, listen to God’s Word, ask him to give you understanding, and turn. He still says, I would heal them.

In a sentence. For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and God would heal them.

On a Tuesday. Do not let your heart grow dull. Keep it soft before God by daily repentance and his Word. Name one area of your life where you know you have been closing your eyes, and open them this week: read the passage, have the conversation, make the confession.

For worship. That is the God being refused. Not a God looking for a reason to condemn, casting about for an excuse, but a God standing at the door of a nation with medicine in his hands, saying that if they would only look, and listen, and understand, and turn, he would heal them, and grieving that they have shut their eyes rather than let him. The tragedy of Israel in this verse is not that God was unwilling. He was never unwilling. He says so in the same breath in which he describes their refusal, and he has been saying it since Isaiah stood in the temple, and he is saying it still. Blessed be the Physician of souls, who heals all who turn to him.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.

Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles. Paul’s last recorded words to a Jewish audience in Acts, and they need to be handled with care, because they have been badly misused. First, what the sentence says. This salvation of God: the same salvation, not a substitute or a second-best. It has been sent: a passive; God sent it, and this is not Paul’s decision or Paul’s reprisal. This is the third and final turning to the Gentiles in Acts (13:46; 18:6): in Asia, in Greece, and now in Rome. The pattern is complete: to the Jew first, then to the Gentile.

They will listen. A plain future, and a confident one. It is a prophecy, fulfilled through the centuries: Gentiles in their millions have listened and believed. Most Christians reading this are Gentiles who listened.

What it does not say. It does not say God has finished with Israel. It cannot, because the man speaking had already written, to this very city, the definitive answer to that question: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite” (Romans 11:1). Paul is himself the counter-example, and he says so. He goes on in that letter to speak of a remnant now, a hardening that is partial and temporary, and a future in which mercy comes round to Israel again (Romans 11:5, 25–26). And note what happened in the room that very day: some were convinced (v. 24). Even in this final scene the response is divided, not uniform. Some Jews in Rome believed Paul that afternoon.

Where readers differ on Israel. This is also the point in Acts where readers in our own congregations will differ, and the difference should be handled with respect rather than scored. Many dear brothers and sisters hold that God’s promises to national Israel await a literal future fulfilment, and they hold it because they take the promises seriously and refuse to spiritualise them away, and that instinct deserves respect. Teachers who have shaped many of us have taught it warmly and carefully. The Reformed reading emphasises rather that all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ and that Jew and Gentile are made one new man in him (2 Corinthians 1:20; Ephesians 2:14–16), and that is the more likely reading, because the New Testament itself declares the promises fulfilled in Christ and his one people. What both readings hold, and this is far more than what separates them, is that God has not finished with the Jewish people, that his covenant faithfulness does not fail, and that Romans 11 forbids any Gentile Christian from the smallest trace of superiority: do not be arrogant toward the branches (Romans 11:18).

A note on the missing verse 29. Readers following in an older Bible will find a verse 29 here: that when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves. They will not find it in the ESV, which prints it only as a footnote, noting that some manuscripts add it. This is not something being removed from Scripture. It is the opposite: the earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have the sentence, and it appears to have been added later by a copyist, most likely drawn from v. 25 to smooth the transition into v. 30. Modern translations set it in a footnote so the reader can see exactly what the evidence is. Nothing whatever hangs on it; the substance is already in v. 25, where they departed disagreeing among themselves. It is worth knowing that this openness is a strength rather than a weakness: the manuscript record of the New Testament is so rich that we can see precisely where a later hand has smoothed a seam, and say so out loud in a footnote.

Does this mean Gentile Christians have replaced the Jews? No, not in the sense of Gentiles taking Israel’s place while Jews are shut out. Paul’s picture is of one olive tree: unbelieving branches broken off, Gentile branches grafted in by faith, and natural branches able to be grafted back in if they do not continue in unbelief (Romans 11:17–24). There is one people of God, made up of believing Jews and believing Gentiles, saved the same way, by grace through faith in the same Messiah. Gentile believers stand only by faith, and must never boast. If anything, this verse should make every Gentile Christian humble and grateful, and eager to see Jewish people come to their Messiah.

In a sentence. Paul declared, “Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.”

On a Tuesday. If you are a Gentile believer, you are the fulfilment of this verse. You listened. Praise God. Then pray this week for Jewish friends, neighbours or people you know of, that God would graft them back into their own olive tree. And examine your heart for any trace of pride toward them.

For worship. The salvation of God has been sent to the nations, and they have listened: from Rome to Africa, from the islands of the sea to the ends of the earth, in a thousand languages. The Lord promised Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed, and he has kept his word. And he has not forgotten Israel; the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 29: “And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves.”

parallels.desc: your saving power among all nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

He lived there two whole years at his own expense. Two years, around AD 60 to 62. Luke gives no verdict, no trial, no execution, no release: just two years, and then he stops writing. Take the picture first, because it is a strange one. Paul is under military custody, chained by the wrist to a rotating guard, in rented lodgings he is paying for himself, perhaps with gifts from the churches (Philippians 4:10–18). He cannot go out. So everyone comes in.

And welcomed all who came to him. All. Jews and Gentiles, the curious and the convinced, householders and slaves like Onesimus (Philemon 10), and, since the guard changed shift by shift, a steady procession of soldiers who had no choice but to stand there and listen. Paul mentions the result in a letter very likely written from this house: the gospel had become known throughout the whole imperial guard, and there were saints in Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:13; 4:22).

The prison letters. On the traditional view this is where the prison letters come from. Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon: written in these two years, in this room, by a man chained to a soldier. The chain that stopped him travelling produced the documents that reached further than his travelling ever did. Chained, he wrote words that have fed the church ever since.

Proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ. Luke’s last sentence, and every word of it is chosen. Proclaiming the kingdom of God: the book opened with the risen Christ spending forty days speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3). It closes with his prisoner doing the same in Rome. The two ends of the book are tied. The kingdom of God, which has come in Jesus; and Jesus himself, Lord and Christ.

With all boldness and without hindrance. With all boldness: parrēsia, the frank, unguarded speech of a free man. It is the word the church prayed for when the authorities first told them to be quiet (4:29), and God gave it then and has not withdrawn it now. Without hindrance: akōlytōs. This is the very last word of the Greek text of Acts. Luke ends his two-volume history on an adverb, and the adverb is unhindered. Paul was in chains; the word of God was not (2 Timothy 2:9).

Why does it stop there? The question every reader asks is what happened to Paul. The honest answer is that Luke does not tell us, and the reasons offered are worth weighing. Some think he wrote before the case was decided, which would explain the abruptness. Others suggest a third volume may have been intended. But the strongest reason is simply that Luke has finished the story he set out to tell. His subject was never Paul’s biography; it was announced in the first chapter: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). The gospel has reached the capital of the world and is being preached there without restriction. That is the end of the story.

What happened to Paul. As for the man: early tradition, outside Scripture and therefore held loosely, says he was released, travelled again, possibly to Spain as he had hoped (Romans 15:24), was re-arrested, and was beheaded at Rome under Nero, around AD 67. The Pastoral Letters read as though they come from that later period, and 2 Timothy sounds very much like a man writing his last letter. But Luke will not end there, and it is important to see that this is a decision rather than an accident. He could have written the death of Paul; he had written the death of Stephen and the death of James. He ends instead on an adverb about the word of God. Luke’s story is not about Paul; it is about the word of God, which runs on, unhindered, from Jerusalem to Rome and to the ends of the earth. The book is unfinished because the story is unfinished. We are in it.

What the word came through. Consider what that word has come through to earn the adverb. It was ordered silenced by the Sanhedrin, and it spread. Its first martyr was stoned outside the city, and it spread. Herod put James to the sword and Peter in prison, and the angel opened the door, and the word spread. It was flogged out of Philippi, shouted down in Thessalonica, laughed at in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, and dragged through four courts. Forty men swore an oath to stop it and failed. The sea rose against it for fourteen days and put it on a beach, alive. A snake fastened on it, and it shook the snake into the fire. And here at the end, the emperor of the world has the preacher chained by the wrist in a rented room in his own capital, and the word of God walks in and out of that room, all day, every day, for two years, and no one on earth can lay a finger on it. That is why the book has no ending. It is not a story that has finished; it is a story that is still running, and the last word Luke wrote is the reason. Unhindered.

If the story of Acts continues, are there still apostles and apostolic miracles today? The mission continues; the apostolic office does not. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, sent by him personally, and they laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Corinthians 15:8). Their teaching, now written in the New Testament, is complete and sufficient. What continues is the work they began: the word preached, the gospel spreading, the Spirit giving new birth, Christ building his church through ordinary believers and faithful pastors. You are not an apostle, but you are part of the story they started, and the same Lord is with you to the end of the age.

In a sentence. For two whole years Paul lived there at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

On a Tuesday. The story of Acts continues, and you are in it. Wherever your own limits are this year, illness, age, a small life, a hard place, ask how the word can go out through you without hindrance: to the people who come to your door, the letters you write, the friend you pray for, the child you teach. Proclaim the kingdom and speak of the Lord Jesus Christ, boldly. The word is not bound.

For worship. The last thing to say about the book of Acts is not about Luke, and not about Paul. Thirty years before that rented room, a handful of frightened people stood on a hillside outside Jerusalem watching a man go up out of their sight. They had nothing: no standing, no money, no protection, no plan anyone would have funded. What they had was his word that they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth, and the promise of his Spirit, and the memory of an empty tomb. And he did it. Not they; he. He poured out the Spirit at Pentecost, and three thousand came in. He struck down his own worst enemy on the Damascus road and made him the apostle to the nations. He opened a businesswoman’s heart at a riverside in Philippi and, some days later, shook the prison doors open. He stood beside his servant in a barracks cell in the dark and told him he would see Rome, and then he held a ship’s company together for fourteen days to keep the appointment. Every mile of it was his doing, and every soul brought in was his. The Lord Jesus Christ is building his church, exactly as he said he would, and the gates of hell have not prevailed and will not. He is doing it still, in places no apostle ever heard of, in languages Luke could not have pronounced, through people whose names will never be written down, and he will not stop until the last of them is home. The chain was on the apostle’s wrist. It was never anywhere near the word of God.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment. Luke ends with the gospel preached “without hindrance” at the heart of the empire.

parallels.desc: the word of God is not bound

28.title: Rome at Last
28.text: <sup>1</sup>After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. <sup>2</sup>The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. <sup>3</sup>When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. <sup>4</sup>When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” <sup>5</sup>He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. <sup>6</sup>They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. <sup>7</sup>Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. <sup>8</sup>It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. <sup>9</sup>And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. <sup>10</sup>They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. <sup>11</sup>After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. <sup>12</sup>Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. <sup>13</sup>And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. <sup>14</sup>There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome. <sup>15</sup>And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. <sup>16</sup>And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. <sup>17</sup>After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. <sup>18</sup>When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case. <sup>19</sup>But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—though I had no charge to bring against my nation. <sup>20</sup>For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” <sup>21</sup>And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. <sup>22</sup>But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.” <sup>23</sup>When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. <sup>24</sup>And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. <sup>25</sup>And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: <sup>26</sup>‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. <sup>27</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>28</sup>Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.” <sup>30</sup>He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, <sup>31</sup>proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
28.overview:
The book ends where Jesus’ commission pointed: the word has reached the capital of the world (1:8). On Malta the shipwrecked party is welcomed by the islanders. A viper fastens on Paul’s hand; the locals assume divine justice has caught a murderer, then, when he is unharmed, decide he is a god. Paul heals the father of Publius, the island’s chief official, and many others. After three months they sail on a ship with the twin gods as its figurehead, land at Puteoli, and walk the Appian Way to Rome, where believers come out to meet them and Paul takes courage.

Under house arrest, chained to a soldier, Paul calls the leaders of Rome’s Jewish community. He explains that he is innocent and bound “because of the hope of Israel.” They have heard nothing against him but know the sect is everywhere opposed. On an appointed day he explains the kingdom of God and argues from Moses and the Prophets about Jesus from morning until evening. Some are persuaded; others refuse. Paul quotes Isaiah 6 on hearing without understanding and announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles: they will listen. Luke closes with Paul spending two years in his rented house, welcoming all, preaching the kingdom and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. The prisoner is chained; the word is not (2 Timothy 2:9).
